Ethical Birding – The Only Way K Sudhir Moorti I am happy that birding has become an increasingly popular hobby amongst the urban population in India of late. I would like to shed some light on the proper and ethical way of birding, for the benefit of people who are new to this wonderful hobby – especially the younger lot, in whose hands the future of birding rests. • Do not litter! Anything that is not organic is potentially harmful to the habitat. Plastic is a major threat. So don’t throw any such things carelessly. • Do not hack your way into the woods to create a new path. Try to stay on existing paths and trails most of the time. What is birding? I feel birding is more than just sighting birds – it involves observing, studying and recording all about birds – their physical attributes, habitat, behaviour, breeding and, in some cases, migration. Unlike popular misconception Birding is not just sighting birds and identifying them with the help of field guides, the Internet, and senior birders. That is just a part of it. The Welfare of our Avian Friends As birders, I am sure everyone would agree that we are their friends and well-wishers. We all love birds, hence the passion towards this great hobby. So here are a few tips to ensure their welfare: In the first place what makes you a birder? I have many times asked other birders what is their favourite species; it’s usually a species that is not sighted frequently. It is quite natural to attach more value to things less available. Therefore we have ‘common’ and ‘rare’ birds. I would be lying if I said that sighting a rare bird does not excite me. Of course it does! But while in search of these ‘rare’ species, the more common ones also do bring a smile to my face. The antics of a Drongo, the restlessness of an Ashy Prinia or the noisy hopping around of a bunch of gregarious Babblers – that for me is the pure joy of birding. Sighting a rare bird, or a bird not usually found in the region, makes one ‘famous’ and surely there is great satisfaction attached to such a feat. However, a word of caution here – do not seek such glory; bird in an ethical way and glory shall definitely come to you. I have personally gone through all these phases and I am sure I made a lot of the mistakes which I am cautioning you against. Over the years, I have learnt that the key is to just enjoy watching birds – the emotions are very important. I once chanced upon a group of birders, who went about adding species to their list in a flurry of activity, some of them hardly looking at the bird! While the group leader shouted out the common names of the birds, the rest blindly accepted and moved on. In such activity, the checklist becomes a scorecard and birding becomes a race. Some may feel that there is nothing wrong with that – but there are a few do’s and don’ts, which we tend to ignore in our overzealous effort to be the top scorer. I shall endeavour to enlist a few hazards here. Avoid disturbing birds or other species present; do not make loud noises or shout. Remember we are guests in their land. • Try not to get too close to them in your effort to get a better shot. • Definitely do not throw stones at them to make them fly (don’t be horrified – I’ve seen some photographers do it in their quest for “action shots”!) • Do not try to flush the birds. E.g. don’t send a partner to the other side to draw the bird out of the bush. • Do not crowd the area; try to be as subtle as possible. E.g. one member of the group shouts out a sighting, and the others start running at breakneck speed for a shot. • Do not drive deep into the habitat with your vehicle. • Do not use flash/artificial light while photographing in low light. • Form small groups of not more than 4 or 5 people while going birding. • Do not play the call/song to attract the bird – it is highly hazardous. E.g. a female may abandon a potential partner, on listening to the fake breeding call. This is interference and totally unethical Identification A very interesting topic, and sometimes also the most controversial. Identifying and recording a bird on a field trip is the essence of birding. It is also a very important part of the data recorded globally to ascertain various aspects of the existence of a particular species. Therefore, it is advisable to be prudent and slightly conservative when identifying birds. Birders follow the good old ‘honour system’, i.e. your word is taken at face value – so the only person you are answerable to when identifying and recording birds is yourself. Hence, it is all the more important to be careful about what one reports. The Habitat: As you may already be aware, different kinds of habitats are home to different species of birds. While on a field trip, please remember the following: • • The habitat is home to many species of flora and fauna. Every single species is important to the eco-system of that place. So try not to disturb the status quo. 9

• Understand the different parts of a bird’s anatomy before you get on the field, so that you are able to put down in words what you have seen. counts, the authenticity of their sighting and reporting is put at risk. Use your own judgement in deciding what to record or what not to. • Carry a reliable local field guide. • Before your field trip, try to do some research on the birds found in the area, and their habits. • If you get a photograph of the bird, well and good; if not, try to remember distinct features of the bird and note them down so you can refer and identify it later. Birds in Breeding Birds breed seasonally, and many have interesting breeding rituals, plumages, calls etc. It is great to see and photograph the same, but keep in mind that it is a very important activity for the birds, and the propagation of the entire species may depend on this. Hence, I advise extra caution at such times. • Earlier, birders used to sketch the bird and mark the features observed by them; I, however, am not averse to using technology. A photograph is a good way to record, probably the best in today’s conditions; either way, be sure of what you have seen. • If you could not get a photograph, be extremely cautious in recording. Consult experts. If still not sure, just let it go. You can always go back to that place, or see the same bird elsewhere; after all luck is also vital in birding. • Do not record a species on speculation or conjecture. Only record what has been positively identified. Many times we may go looking for a particular species in that area, which would be a ‘lifer’ for us – this can make us fall prey to wishful thinking, with every bird looking like the target ‘lifer’. • Check for all factors before confirming the sighting – visible distinctive features; habitat; whether it’s a ground bird, bush bird or arboreal; and so on. • Calls can be very useful in identification, but they are tricky. Lots of birds have similar calls; some have several different calls; some even imitate the calls of other birds. So tread carefully. According to a report by Joanna Burger and Michael Gochfeld titled “Human Distance and Birds: Tolerance and Response Distances of Resident and Migrant Species in India”, the distance at which a bird could feel disturbed depends on a lot of factors, including the bird's migratory status, the number of people approaching, the time of day, and the bird's total bodylength (including tail). This distance is called the flushing distance, and varies among different species of birds. So the safest approach would be to stay as far away as possible, or get as close as possible without disturbing the bird. The number of people approaching is also an important factor. Bird in smaller groups and maintain a decent distance. Look for signs when the birds become alert; stop right there and don’t go any closer. Nesting Many times while birding, we come across nests of birds. Nesting is a very interesting and complicated process in birds, and absolutely critical to their survival. Nesting habits differ from species to species. While the male Baya Weaver tries to impress the female with an intricately woven nest, a Hornbill seals off its nest to protect the female and chicks. There is a lot we can learn from nesting habits of birds. Disturbing a nest or birds during nesting is criminal – the bird may move the nest to a less safe and predator-prone area due to your interference; it may also lead to loss of eggs, chicks or even abandonment of the nest. I strongly advise to exercise extreme caution while observing nesting birds. Maintain a safe distance and do not disturb them. When you are new to birding, you usually depend on seniors in the group for identification help. Here’s what you can do: Reporting It is we birders who provide data to scientists across the world on a daily basis. The wealth of information we provide is invaluable to their research and studies. It also goes a long way in the conservation of birds. Wrong data, therefore, could also lead to ill-planned or wrongly-directed conservation efforts, and a waste of precious resources. Gently question the basis for identification; this will help you learn to identify on your own, and also understand the strength of your senior’s conviction. Understand how your senior or group leader regards identification. Is he a dedicated and passionate birder, who can say “I am sorry, I don’t know” when at a loss? Or does he treat it casually, and just toss out names of species even when he is unsure? Go back and do some research. This is an important part of the learning. Some group leaders take it upon themselves to make their group the ‘best’ in the region. In the quest to increase their species • Reach out to eminent birders and seniors and take their opinion. • Report all rare sightings to proper authorities with adequate evidence and confirmation of the sighting. Here’s to sensible and ethical birding! *** 10

Bird of the Month Text: Umesh Mani; Photo: Bhamidipati Srikanth Jungle Myna (Acridotheres fuscus) Jungle Myna (Ooty, 03-09-2016) Order: Passeriformes Family: Sturnidae Genus: Acridotheres Species: A. fuscus Size: 20-23 cm birds of the species. Sexes are similar, but juvenile birds are browner. Description & distribution: The Jungle Myna, a fierce-looking member of the Starling family, is a resident breeder across its range covering Pakistan, Nepal, India, Bangladesh and Myanmar, east to Indonesia. It is a typical myna, but has dark grey plumage (as against the browner plumage of the Common Myna) and darker on the head and wings. The prominent forehead tuft and bright yellow bill and legs are distinctive. It has a white tail tip and large white wing patches which are very clear in flight. There is no bare patch around the eye. The irises are blue in the southern Indian race, whereas they are yellow in other Habitat & behaviour: The Jungle Myna is usually seen in forests or near cultivation (like paddy fields), close to water. It is omnivorous and an opportunistic feeder, and its diet includes grains, fruits, insects and flower nectar. Nesting: The Jungle Myna nests in holes, usually in trees, but has been known to nest inside pipes, and in vents or crevices in buildings. The usual clutch consists of 3 to 6 eggs. Local name: The Jungle Myna is known as ‘pahari myna’ or ‘jungli myna’ in Hindi, ‘adavigorina’ in Telugu, and ‘kaattu myna’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. * ** Trip Report – Tadoba WLS Text and Photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati Bengal Tiger My love for the wild was triggered when, as a kid, I saw my first tiger, walking majestically and then vanishing into the woods. Many years passed with frequent visits to different forests in the country with the sole purpose of spotting this majestic mammal and in the bargain learning about other beings. In recent times, this craze for people wanting to spot a big cat in the wild has increased so much that they don’t respect the basic fact – “live and let live - IN PEACE”. 2

We (Lawrence, Amritha, Hemant, Nupur, Ravi, Jayati and I) had planned a visit to Tadoba Andheri Tiger Reserve (TATR) in June 2016. TATR, once a national park converted into a tiger reserve, gave a massive boost to the tourism in that region. The terrain varies from old teak trees to open Savannah-like grasslands and gives scope for many other species as well. The weather during our travel was a little unpredictable. We had planned for a 4-day trip and initial logistics arrangements were underway. The sightings during that time period looked very promising and we hoped for some lovely sights of birds and mammals. Upon reaching Chandrapur railway station, we hopped onto our pre-booked taxi to the resort where we had booked our accommodation. Excitement levels were high considering the activities we were undertaking in the next few days. On our way towards TATR we crossed small villages and also a huge quarry a few kilometers away from the forest entrance. This put me off as I thought that might affect the sanctity and peace of the forest, but considering the distance to the forest entrance, I was relieved. Tawny-bellied Babbler We walked into the clearance area of the buffer zone and while we all were busily trying to locate a species, our master photographer Hemant captured the image of a bird which was hiding in the bushes – Indian Thick-knee (Burhinus indicus). After the small stroll, we headed back to the resort for lunch and then geared up for our first drive into the core area. The drive into the core area was in a modified Gypsy and we were happy with the open vehicle, for we were sure we wouldn’t miss anything. As we were entered the core area there was a sea of vehicles in front of us and they were excited at seeing the Panderpauni tigress. We were amongst the last few to enter the forest. Our aim was spotting birds and this was clearly explained to our guide and the driver. Asian Paradise-flycatcher On our way towards the forest we spotted quite a few birds which are commonly found everywhere, including an Asian Paradise-flycatcher (Terpsiphone paradisi). Upon reaching the forest entry gate, our driver had to make an entry and during this time we got our gear ready, hoping for some sightings along the way. Driving through the forest area listening to the calls of the Banded Bay Cuckoo was an amazing feeling. On reaching the resort we checked into our tents and immediately got into action as we planned for a busy day ahead. After getting ready and having a good breakfast, we decided to go for a walk into the surrounding areas of the resort. Indian Pitta From the main road we drove onto a smaller road where calls of the Spotted Owlet (Athene brama) and Indian Pitta (Pitta brachyura) caught our attention. The sightings were a bit difficult and we saw some Flowerpeckers and Sunbirds flying on top of the tall tree line. Just as the open forest welcomed us, we had our first important sighting of the day - Sirkeer Malkoha (Taccocua leschenaultii). Our guide was hell-bent on tracking a tiger for us, but with no luck that day. While walking into the area we first encountered the Asian Paradise-flycatcher which was flying in the bushes, trying to dodge the shutter bugs. We also saw the Tawny-bellied Babbler (Dumetia hyperythra), Common Hoopoe (Upupa epops) and a few Minivets. 3

The Indian Pitta, which is a rather shy bird and not seen often even during its season, was the highlight of the trip for us – we saw nothing less than 17 during this trip! As we finished our day, we returned to our resort with some good sightings – about 89 species of birds, Sambar, a few Langur, Gaur and Spotted Deer. One interesting observation was the large proportion of Greater Racket-tailed Drongos (Dicrurus paradiseus) with single elongated tail-streamers – nearly 6-7 out of the 10-odd birds that we saw. were pretty hard to spot. We also spotted a frightened hare that was trying to save itself from being run over by the vehicles. As all this was happening, I realized that family never forgets you!! There was a family of Gaur who were looking in the direction of the tigress. The previous evening a calf had been attacked by the tigress and she had hidden it in the bush. The way the Gaurs were looking at that spot was heartbreaking and this is when I understood the circle of life. Oriental Honey-buzzard Next morning we went early to the core area and hoped for some good sightings, but there were the same species we had seen on the first day. During our drive, one thing which grabbed my attention were the camera traps set to observe the animals. It was disappointing that technology was being used only to track the movement of these wonderful beings and not for the love and protection of animals. I will explain this a little later. We continued our journey and added about 30 more birds which included an Indian Nightjar (Caprimulgus asiaticus) sitting astride its baby. We then headed back to our resort where a nice lunch awaited us. Brahminy Starling Next morning we had the chance to visit the buffer zone again. The sightings weren’t too many – it was quite a quiet morning – but the forest was amazing with fresh air coming in from all directions. While driving around aimlessly, we spotted a few raptors, a Black Bittern (Dupetor flavicollis) and 2 Mottled Wood Owls (Strix ocellata) which were being harassed by a Brahminy Starling (Sturnia pagodarum). We returned to our guest house with not much of luck in the morning session. Indian Nightjar Lesser Adjutant We had booked for another visit to the forest and this time we visited the buffer zone of the forest. We spotted the Woollynecked Stork (Ciconia episcopus), a few Quails, Owls, Bitterns and other ducks. In the meantime our driver got to know of a tigress sitting in the bushes nearby. When we reached that place there were about 6 more jeeps eagerly waiting for it to come out into the open. After a long wait the Tigress, Madhuri, stood up and glanced at the hungry souls trying to capture the moment in their cameras. She then went back to resting with her 2 cubs that In the evening we drove into the forest hoping for some good sightings. We drove to a water hole, our eyes fixed on one particular bird that turned out to be the most important sighting of the trip – the Lesser Adjutant (Leptoptilos javanicus). Just as we headed to another location, our driver got information of a tiger sitting in a water hole in the open. The soul of Michael Schumacher seemed to have possessed him, as he drove very fast to get to that location. 4

The crowd of vehicles Crested Hawk Eagle The male tiger, Pandu, was having a good time resting by the water hole and he was least bothered about the people around. Scores of people had gathered there. We decided to leave the location and move forward as most of the people seemed to have no regard for nature, and it’s saddening that a responsible department is not doing anything about it as its primary motto seems to be to increase tourism. With these thoughts, we returned to the guest house hoping that the next day would be better. On the way, we spotted the highly trained and organized hunters – the wild dogs or Dhole. There were about 5 of them and seemed to be in search of food. Barking Deer As we were headed back towards the gate, we spotted a Crested Serpent Eagle (Spilornis cheela) sitting at eye level, and to our surprise a Paradise-flycatcher was attacking it! We later realized that there was a nest with its chick and parents always are protective. Dhole Next morning we again headed back into the core area. En route, we saw Spotted Owlets and a Mottled Wood Owl right above our heads in the open. There wasn’t enough sunlight to capture a good image but the mere sighting was sufficient. As soon as we entered, the Indian Pitta, Asian Paradise-flycatcher and a female Indian Golden Oriole (Oriolus kundoo) gave us a warm welcome and some good poses. A few meters away there was a Crested Hawk Eagle (Nisaetus cirrhatus) which was sitting on the road and taking a dip. It gave us a good 20 minutes of time during which we all clicked some 300-400 images each. Then we proceeded into the forest to a water hole and found Barking Deer and some Munias. Crested Serpent Eagle That was practically the last sighting of the trip, and we had gathered some awesome memories to carry back. Some more photos taken during the trip: 5

Bird of the Month Text and photo: Umesh Mani Himalayan Bulbul (Pycnonotus leucogenys) Himalayan Bulbul (Chopta, 09-10-2016) Order: Passeriformes Family: Pycnonotidae Genus: Pycnonotus Species: P. leucogenys Size: 18-20 cm Description & distribution: The Himalayan Bulbul, a very attractive-looking member of the Pycnonotidae family, is a resident breeder across its range from Iraq and southern Iran east across the Arabian Peninsula to Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan, north-western India, Nepal and Bhutan. It has the distinction of being the national bird of Bahrain. Clear white cheeks, with a black crescent at the rear, and a prominent forward-pointing crest differentiate it from the somewhat similarlooking White-eared Bulbul; the crest may not be as prominent in the birds found on the plains within its range. The head, face and throat are black, and the long brownish-grey tail has a terminal whitish patch. The upperparts are also brownish-grey, and underparts are pale grey-buff to grey-white, with a rich yellow vent. The irises are reddish-brown, with a narrow yellow eye ring, and the bill and legs are black. Sexes are similar; juvenile birds show a duller brown head. Habitat & behaviour: The Himalayan Bulbul is usually seen in pairs or small flocks, in dry alpine forests and shrub, wooded valleys and bushy hillsides, as well as sub-Himalayan plains, including bushes around towns and villages. A bird of open country, it prefers bushes rather than trees. It is generally seen up to an elevation of around 2400 metres, although it may venture higher if fruiting trees are present. It also frequents cities, parks and gardens near human habitat, especially where food scraps are left, since that attracts the flies and other insects that form part of its diet. It tends to hunt from a perch, hawking insects in the air or on the ground. Besides, it also feeds on fruits, berries, seeds, buds and nectar. Nesting: The Himalayan Bulbul nests in low bushes or branches of low trees, generally between 0.5-3m above the ground. The nest is a cup made of grass, twigs, stems, leaves and roots, and lined with finer rootlets, lichen and grass. The nest is built by the female. The usual clutch consists of 2 to 5 eggs, incubated mainly by the female, but the young are fed by both parents. Local name: The Himalayan Bulbul is known as ‘safed kaan bulbul’ in Hindi, ‘shwet-karna bulbul’ in Sanskrit, and ‘pahari bulbul’ in Punjabi and Bengali. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report – Ananthagiri Hills, Sep 2016 Text: Dr Jayati Mitra; Photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati Golden Orb-web Spider When our birding trip to the Ananthagiri Hills was announced, it was almost the end of September. The retreating monsoon, overactive with its torrential rains, had left many city streets inundated. The drab grey dawn kept many people indoors but for a few of us this seemed to be the best opportunity to observe nature. As we drove along, the trees along our path, with their dense canopy of lush green leaves, looked strikingly beautiful against the backdrop of an overcast sky interspersed with bluegrey clouds. A light drizzle continued, restricting our en route sightings to a few Spotted Doves (Stigmatopelia chinensis) and White-throated Kingfishers (Halcyon smyrnensis). 1

A piping hot breakfast with tea energized us, but it was disappointing not to find birds near the Hanuman temple owing to the non-stop drizzle, and the dense undergrowth which blocked our way on familiar trails leading into the forest. branches, a dark object could be noticed. It took quite some time before Anita could convince everyone that it was an Indian Nightjar (Caprimulgus asiaticus). The sighting gave a lot of pleasure to all of us, especially the photographers. A few Yellowbilled Babblers (Turdoides affinis) were foraging on the ground. The weather, however, gradually improved by the time we reached the Padmanava temple gate. This is not the season to expect migrants but the tiny Asian Brown Flycatcher (Muscicapa dauurica) was sighted immediately. More birds were seen as we proceeded down towards the banyan tree. An Indian Grey Hornbill (Ocyceros birostris) flew across our path. The partiallyhidden Coppersmith Barbet (Megalaima haemacephala) was feeding on the topmost branch of a tree. Tawny-bellied Babblers (Dumetia hyperythra) hopped around on the bushes and, when two of them flew up and perched on the overhead cable, we could observe their bright orange-brown underbellies. White-throated Fantail After panning for a while, the colourful Lesser Goldenback (Dinopium benghalense) was spotted holding on to the main trunk and circling it while pecking for insects. Myriad calls pervaded the atmosphere but one whistle seemed to be a clear and distinct sound like peew-peew-piu. T he approaching birds were a pair of Jacobin Cuckoos (Clamator jacobinus), said to be the harbinger of the monsoon season. The slim black-and-white birds with crests and long tails were looking very graceful in flight. They sat for a while in the tree and moved about quietly on the branches. The restless Great Tit (Parus major) was preening all the time and it soon disappeared into the dense foliage. Nothing could distract the Bay-backed Shrike (Lanius vittatus) from its would-be prey. We moved on cautiously over the wet soil and ended up at a deep gorge full of uneven boulders .The swirling waters gushed over the boulders, making it difficult for most of us to go across. However, a few of the more adventurous birders managed to cross over to the other side. We were walking along slowly when, suddenly, a group of Jungle Babblers (Turdoides striata) started calling and hurriedly flew into hiding. We sensed the presence of some predator and, sure enough, there was a Shikra (Accipiter badius) which glided down and perched on the top of a nearby tree. All of a sudden there was silence; a typical sign of imminent danger in the wild. Great Tit Small winding streams resulting from the abundant rainfall flowed downwards, some merging to form small rivulets along our muddy path. The sight of the age-old trees, some of them parasitic, growing together, with their gnarled branches spreading far in many shapes and sizes, always leaves one awestruck; numerous species of birds are being sheltered and protected on these branches. We observed the White-bellied Drongo (Dicrurus caerulescens) and Plain Prinia (Prinia inornata) among them. Hanging cobwebs of giant spiders were swinging in the breeze. Suddenly a sharp piercing call was heard above. The Crested Serpent Eagle (Spilornis cheela) was flying, slowly rising higher and higher in the sky. Large-billed Crow As we moved along, we also saw the Common Hawk Cuckoo (Hierococcyx varius), Indian Golden Oriole (Oriolus oriolus kundoo) and the Common Iora (Aegithina tiphia). The latter was confusing us with different calls, some of which were mimicking other birds. It was enjoyable to hear the sweet music till we caught the culprit red-handed! By this time the sun had come up and quite a few tiny birds were moving around. One of them was a Greenish Warbler (Phylloscopus trochiloides). It took quite some time and great patience before Srikanth could photograph its greenish yellow underbelly to confirm its identity in the presence of other similarlooking birds. Rose-ringed Parakeets (Psittacula krameri) in flight made the atmosphere cheerful with their calls and bright green plumage. We climbed onto the small mounds of earth and crossed over into the open space towards the front. Several trees spread their branches, intertwining with the leaves like a huge umbrella. With great effort a Grey-breasted Prinia (Prinia hodgsonii) was seen. Still further away, at a fork-like juncture between two shooting 2

Rose-ringed Parakeet Indian Silverbill Near the gate a mixed flock of Brahminy Starlings (Sturnia pagodarum), Asian Pied Starlings (Gracupica contra) and Common Mynas (Acridotheres tristis) were calling excitedly. Red-rumped Swallows (Cecropis daurica) were circling overhead, trying to feed on the swarms of insects in the air. We then gathered together and, as always, checked the final list of birds sighted and shared our experiences with each other. The number of species seen was less than expected, but it was definitely worthwhile to visit the beautiful hills and bird in the rain. A Day Trip To Rollapadu, Oct 2016 Ambika Pradhan Eurasian Collared Dove (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Winter is always a merry time for birders, with so many migrant species arriving at different parts of the country. We just could not afford to miss such an opportunity and hence five of us (Srikanth, Humayun, Umesh, Lawrence uncle and I) decided to visit Rollapadu WLS. Considering the amount of time it would take to reach the sanctuary, we started from Hyderabad at 4:00AM. Large Grey Babbler (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) But there was one bird that kept us on our toes – the Lesser Florican! We were optimistic that the male Florican would jump out in its mating display at any moment. But having no luck with it, just as we decided to go back to the town for lunch, we spotted a raptor swooping down into the grassland, scanning the area for prey. Although it initially looked like a Short-toed Snake Eagle, we later realized from the photos that it was a Montagu’s Harrier (female). Grey Francolin (Photo: Umesh Mani) Proceeding to Rollapadu after a brief stop at Kurnool to pick up Umesh, and also to recharge ourselves with steaming hot breakfast, we arrived at the sanctuary by 8:00AM; this gave us ample time to explore the place and look for the beautiful resident as well as migratory birds. As soon as we entered the sanctuary, we were welcomed by a lone Blackbuck peeking curiously through the tall, lush green grass. A few moments later we spotted a small flock of Grey Francolin wandering around on the track, undisturbed by our presence. Large Grey Babbler, Laughing Dove and Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark were some of the other common species we spotted there. As the Harrier disappeared in the grasslands, we spotted a Shikra perched on a tree, not more than 5 feet away from us. It was an amazing sight, and we clicked its photos to our hearts’ content before heading back for lunch. 4

Blue-capped Rock Thrush (female) (Photo: Umesh Mani) We went back to the sanctuary, still optimistic of spotting a Lesser Florican. Later in the evening, moments after we decided to start back for Hyderabad, a Hen Harrier (female) hovered in front of us and gave good views. As we headed back to Hyderabad, I prayed that at least the next time I visited this place, I should get to spot the Lesser Florican and watch its mating display. But the heavy rains that had lashed the region over the last couple of months had flooded the waterbody, which was overflowing and was blocking our access. We returned to the Forest Department Guest House, where bird activity was at full swing, with Rose-ringed Parakeets chattering continuously, a Black Drongo restlessly chasing a Spotted Owlet around, and a Blue-capped Rock Thrush silently moving from tree to tree, undisturbed by the constant chattering around it. Bird of the Month Text and photo: Umesh Mani Blue Whistling Thrush (Myophonus caeruleus) Blue Whistling Thrush (Sattal, Uttarakhand, 18-04-2015) Order: Passeriformes Family: Muscicapidae Genus: Myophonus Species: M. caeruleus Size: 31-35 cm Description & distribution: The Blue Whistling Thrush is a resident breeder across its range from Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Pakistan east across the Himalayas in Nepal, Tibet, Bhutan and India, to Arunachal Pradesh, and extending into south-east Asia, including Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. The widely-dispersed populations show significant differences in size and plumage, and several of the populations are considered as sub-species. The adult Blue Whistling Thrush is dark purple-blue, and it shows glistening silvery-blue spangling on the head and the tips of its body feathers (except for the lores, abdomen and undertail). The forehead, shoulders and fringes of wings and tail are brighter blue. It has a strong yellow bill, and the inner webs of its flight and tail feathers are black. Sexes are similar, but juvenile birds are browner, lack the spangling, and the wings and tail are not as bright blue as the adult. Habitat & behaviour: The Blue Whistling Thrush is usually seen singly or in pairs, near rivers in heavy forest and well-wooded areas, and quite conspicuous near fast-flowing mountain streams and rivulets; it can, however, often be seen at fair distances from water. It is active well after dusk. It hops about on rocks or grass, and moves about in quick spurts. While foraging, it turns over leaves and small stones to look for its prey. Its diet consists primarily of fruits, snails, crabs, earthworms and insects, but it has been known to prey upon mice and small birds. The alarm call is a shrill kree, and it spreads and droops its tail when alarmed. Its usual call, however, is a strident tzeet-tze-tze-tzeet, and the song is a very human-like whistle that follows a definite pattern. Nesting: The Blue Whistling Thrush breeds from April to August, and sings even during the darkness of dawn and dusk, when most other birds are silent. The nest is a cup made of moss, grass and roots, placed on a ledge or inside a hollow near a stream. The usual clutch consists of 3 to 4 eggs, and it is known to sometimes raise a second brood in the same season. Local name: The Blue Whistling Thrush is known as ‘pahari neeli kasturi’ in Punjab, ‘kuljel’ or ‘kaljit’ in Uttar Pradesh, and ‘kastura’ in Himachal Pradesh and Kashmir, where it also goes by the very evocative name of ‘hazar dastaan’. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. The Art of Observation Text & photos: Humayun Taher About a month ago, I was going through my old field notebooks. What I found interesting, apart from some of the exotics that were commonly seen in those days, was the multiple uses to which we put our notebooks. I found the last page of one of these notebooks full of telephone numbers of people! Another had a page full of names (the old BSAP tradition of taking a membership roll call on every field trip – a tradition that is now extinct – as are a lot of other things!). 1

After a while, it became a bit of a pain to write out the names laboriously. Obviously, if we saw something we didn’t recognize, the notebook still came out; but the need of the hour was an easier way of recording what we saw on the trips. Also part of the old BSAP tradition was a reading out of the day list at the end of the trip, while we were enjoying the post-birding chai and other comestibles. Enter the famous “Tick-list”… 2

Still later, we found even this a bit of a fag. More importantly, people decided that all they really wanted to do was to tramp out into the field, peer through their camera viewfinders – and occasionally through binoculars…) – make appropriate admiring noises and then return home. The joys of birding were limited to the time in the field. Post-field activities (which are such an integral part of birding fun and learning) became either critically endangered or presumed extinct. In all this, it was far easier to have a standard checklist on our computers, which could quickly be modified for the day list. So, the electronic lists came into being… A very basic electronic list A slightly more “advanced” electronic list Sherlock Holmes is said to have believed in the adage that “There is nothing new under the sun, my dear Watson. It has all been done before”. How true this adage is, is now shown by the below photos. Taken during a recent birding trip… 3

All of which just goes to show that “What goes around, comes around”! *** Migration Watch Srikanth Bhamidipati “Migration” – this one word brings a lot excitement for birdwatchers all over the world. It’s that time of the year again, when people gear up to welcome the migratory birds to our country and region. the course of the migration. Body toning, bulking up the body, and molting of feathers are important aspects of a successful migration; molting especially is very important as it produces new light feathers that enable birds to fly efficiently and handle the ensuing wear and tear. Migration is the seasonal movement of animals from one part of the world to another. Many creatures migrate, including butterflies, fishes and mammals, but the most famous migrants are birds. During the migration the birds generally rely on the following: Sight: They look for locations where they have access to a coastline, river beds, mountain ranges and lakes. Bird migration is an amazing seasonal phenomenon as many species of birds migrate in search of food, which is abundant in warm, sunny places and scarce in dark, snowy locations. Ample food is found in places with longer daytime and this gives enough time for the birds to look for food. Smell: Every bird has a keen sense of smell, but how far they use this as a sensor/navigation tool needs to be further investigated. For some birds, scents are a confirmed sign of food source, and they may even navigate through the skies following the scents. Sun: The sun is their guiding force for directions. They get a sense of time and direction by using the position of the sun to identify South. They fly left of the sun in the morning and right of the sun in the afternoon to fly South. Change in the daylight hours is the first trigger for birds to migrate. Weather, which can vary sometimes, can be unpredictable compared to the daylight hours which are more constant every year. The changes in the biological clocks of the birds act on the hormonal system and cause a few physiological changes like molting and plumage differences, and hence they grow restless and tend to start their migration. Stars: Some scientific theories postulate that birds fly at night based on the position of the stars. Community Flocking: The birds generally migrate in large flocks and help each other reach their destinations. Unlike other fauna, birds need to make a lot of pre-migration preparations, one of the most important of which is to prepare the body for the arduous journey. The birds aim to build up the fat content of the body, as the generally cannot feed properly during 4

Sudden changes in climate, food and other aspects of the migration location may also impact migration – for instance, sudden storms may blow birds off course leading to exhaustion and enforced halts at unfamiliar or unfavourable locations. The Risks Migration is a very risky process for birds. The risk factors are predators, bad weather and human conflicts – which includes wetlands being drained or shrinking, forests being cut down, and other developmental activities which are carried out at the migration sites. Migration is a critical part of a bird’s lifecycle, and a great challenge. Let us do our part to help these migrants in having a safe and pleasant stay. *** Sighting of the Oriental Turtle Dove at Ananthagiri Hills, Sept 2016 Text and photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati Size Weight IUCN Status Length: 33-35 cm; Wingspan: 55 cm 165-274 g Least Concern from the ground. Each nest usually holds 2 eggs which are incubated for 15 to 16 days. The chicks leave the nest after 15 to 17 days. The Oriental Turtle Dove usually breeds in open broad-leaved forests, mixed pine and forest edges and groves, wintering in more open and disturbed habitats, including cultivation. (Source: ARKive, 2016) The Oriental Turtle Dove (Streptopelia orientalis), also known as the Rufous Turtle Dove, is identified by the unique black and white stripes on either side of its neck. Reddish-brown underparts, black centers on the wings, reddish edges, red feet, grey bill and scaly appearance are some of the other physical characteristics of the bird. Sexes are similar, but juveniles lack the neck stripes and are much paler in color. In winter, Oriental Turtle Dove populations from north Asia migrate to areas further south, and large flocks may form as they undertake this considerable journey. The majority of the South Asian population, however, does not migrate. The Oriental Turtle Dove occupies a variety of habitats and has been found as high as 4,000 metres in Nepal. The Oriental Turtle Dove forages on the ground for pine seeds, herbs and plant shoots, but it has also been observed raiding paddy fields. Like other pigeons and doves, the Oriental Turtle Dove drinks frequently, consuming up to 15 percent of its body weight in water every day. Oriental Turtle Doves are monogamous breeders, and both sexes are known to share in the domestic chores. A breeding pair usually moves together, except when a male or female partner is incubating eggs or nestlings. Sightings in Telangana There are some unconfirmed records of this bird in Hyderabad, but the first known photographic record for this bird was on May 12, 2013, by Anand Madabhushi at Sanjeevaiah Park (17.4358° N, 78.4758° E) (vide Email dated 12/05/2013). On September 28, 2016, we visited the Ananthagiri Hills (17.3120° N, 77.8636° E) and found 2 individuals of this species sitting in the top canopy of a tree at a distance. The breeding season depends on the location; in the north of the range, breeding takes place between May and August, while in south India the breeding season is between November and February (Ali & Ripley, 1989). During the breeding season, the male performs an elaborate display to attract a mate, flying up in the air and then gliding down with the wings and tail stretched outwards. After mating, a nest is constructed from twigs in a bush or tree at a height of no greater than five metres Initially we mistook it for a Spotted Dove (Spilopelia chinensis) but looking closely at the images we had captured (Fig-1) we realized that these were Oriental Turtle Doves. This makes our sighting only the second documented sighting of this species from the Hyderabad region. 5

Although the species is reasonably common in its preferred habitat, records from the southern states are scarce. As such, there is a need to undertake regular surveys to investigate the possibility of this species being found in higher numbers in the southern part of the peninsula, or even the possibility that the Hyderabad Plateau lies on its migration route. 2. Bird of the Month Text and photo: Umesh Mani Emerald Dove (Chalcophaps indica) Emerald Dove (Sattal, Uttarakhand, 19-04-2015) Order: Columbiformes Family: Columbidae Genus: Chalcophaps Species: C. indica Size: 23-28 cm extending as broad lines down the sides of the neck. The other recognized sub-species are the nominate C. i. indica of south-east Asia, C. i. maxima and C. i. augusta of Andaman and Nicobar Islands respectively, C. i. natalis of Christmas Island, Australia, and C. i. minima of the Numfor, Biak and Mios Num Islands of Indonesia. Description & distribution: The Emerald Dove, also known as Asian Emerald Dove, Grey-capped Emerald Dove, Green Dove or Green-winged Pigeon, is a resident breeder in most parts of its range, comprising the tropical and sub-tropical parts of the Indian sub-continent, and extending east across Myanmar, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines, Taiwan and parts of Japan. The Emerald Dove is a medium-sized, stocky, broad-winged, pigeon having very distinctive emerald-green upperparts. The male has a prominent white supercilium and forehead, and a grey crown and white shoulder-patch which are missing in the female. The underparts and sides of the head are deep vinaceous pink, fading to greyish on the lower belly. Tail and flight feathers are blackish. In flight, the latter show chestnut undersides; also visible are buff underparts and black-and-white barring on the lower back. It has a bright red bill, rufous feet and legs, and darkbrown eyes. The female has a generally browner complexion, with a warm brown crown, neck and underparts, and a grey shoulder-patch. The juvenile is similar to the female, but has dark-grey barring on a buffy-white forehead, narrow buff borders on neck and underparts, a brownish bill, rufous rump, and brown primaries and tertials with chestnut tips. The Sri Lankan subspecies, C. i. robinsoni, shows the grey colour of its crown Habitat & behaviour: The Emerald Dove, which is usually seen singly, or in pairs or small groups, frequents dry deciduous forests, rainforests and broad-leaved forests in wet regions like mangroves, farms, gardens, coastal green patches and woodlands. It is mainly terrestrial, foraging for fallen fruits, and is fairly approachable, tending to walk away rather than fly when disturbed. Its flight is fast and direct, with typical pigeon-like rapid wingbeats and the occasional sharp flick of its wings. It is quite agile while flying through forests. Its diet consists mainly of fruits, berries and seeds of a wide variety of plants. Its soft cooing call consists of a series of six to seven coos, progressively increasing in volume; they also sometimes utter a nasal hoo hoo hoon. Nesting: The Emerald Dove nests mainly between January and May, with some local variations. The nest is a bare, flimsy twig platform, built on trees or bamboo clumps up to 5 metres above ground. The usual clutch consists of 2 creamy yellow eggs. Local name: The Emerald Dove is known as ‘raj ghughu’ in Bengali, ‘andi bellaguvva’ in Telugu, and ‘padaki pura’, ‘maragada pura’ or ‘thamil pura’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 7 PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Mangalajodi – A Paradise of Wetland Birds Text & photos: Sudipta Bhattacharya Northern Pintail (male) There are many interesting places in Orissa that attract millions of tourists across the world. Mangalajodi is one such jewel of Orissa, popularly known for Eco-Tourism. This is a paradise for wetland birds. There are more than 200 species of birds as claimed by Orissa Govt. It is located in the north-eastern part of the famous Chilika Lake. The place has a shallow and marshy water body, which is an ideal residence for waterfowl. The half-drenched grassland is a huge source of natural food for different bird species. It is learned from the locals that this is a permanent residence for around 150000 birds; in peak season the number doubles. The migratory birds are visible in winter which starts from midOctober. 1

Large-scale poaching was a common threat to the avian population. Alternate means of livelihood for the families was started in 1996-1997 by Mr. Nanda Kishor Bhujabal and the members of Wild Orissa, an organization working on wildlife conservation issues. Poachers became protectors and were made members of this Samiti (committee). The members of the committee carry out daily surveillance and patrolling in the whole area. The Orissa Wildlife Department also chipped in by providing seasonal employment to some Samiti members. The Samiti provides small wooden boats for patrolling, monitoring and carrying tourists and birdwatchers deep into the wetland. Chilika Development Authority funds this conservation initiative. frustrated due to the late start, but after reaching Mangalajodi, it was like a miracle. Grey-headed Lapwing It was an amazing sight as the wetlands began to fill up with lakhs of Ruffs, Godwits, Plovers, Sandpipers and migratory ducks; the Peregrine Falcon (Falco peregrinus) perched exactly at the same point on the mud bund as it had done the previous year; while the Bluethroat (Luscinia svecica) could have perched on your brown shoe if you sat motionless long enough. Thousands of the rarer Grey-headed Lapwings (Vanellus cinereus) took off while hundreds of Gulls sat motionless three metres from the boat, nonchalant, as if they were roadside spectators watching a parade. The famous take-offs by the Northern Pintails (Anas acuta) and the colourful Ruddy Shelducks (Tadorna ferruginea) were a birder’s delight. The Whiskered Terns (Chlidonias hybrida) readily obliged the photographers with their gracious poses while the River Terns (Sterna aurantia) allowed us to observe them closely and at a flight speed that allowed the photographer to focus without trouble. Black-tailed Godwit From January onwards the Ruddy-breasted Crakes (Porzana fusca), the Baillon’s Crakes (Porzana pusilla), the Slaty-breasted Rails (Gallirallus striatus) and the Greater Painted-snipes (Rostratula benghalensis) start showing up; Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa), Oriental Pratincoles (Glareola maldivarum) and Pacific Golden Plovers (Pluvialis fulva) with their breeding plumages appear by April, and in May one can see the largest congregations of Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus) and Fulvous Whistling-ducks (Dendrocygna bicolor). Mangalajodi has been my learning ground. I learned that there are several people from Kolkata travelling to Mangalajodi, and experiencing something new each time. They travel in different seasons to experience and study different birds. In January 2016, we started our journey from Barkul at around 7:30 am. Barkul is a famous tourist spot located at the western fringe of Chilika Lake just 44 km from Mangalajodi. We were informed that food and water was not available at Mangalajodi, so, we had to start after breakfast. On a family trip, the hardcore birders and photographers have to compromise on their desire to bird. As I too was with my family, initially, I was a little Ruddy Shelduck 2

Purple Swamphen A Warbler was frisking between the large grasses, not allowing me to identify it; this was later identified as the Clamorous Reed Warbler. River Tern On the way to the eco-tourism spot from Mangalajodi village we spotted Asian Openbills (Anastomus oscitans) and Grey-headed Lapwings at a distance of barely ten feet from the car. Asian Openbill Clamorous Reed Warbler The spot where the Orissa Forest Department staff took charge of us was a small marshy jetty. We entered into a covered boat arranged for bird watchers and photographers separately. I occupied the photographers’ seat leaving my family to become birdwatchers. Soon, the boat started moving steadily through the narrow water channels. We noticed Greater Painted-snipes fighting in the bush, marking their territory. The Indian Moorhens (Gallinula chloropus) were floating around our boat. Purple Swamphens (Porphyrio porphyrio) and Black-Tailed Godwits were aplenty just like our crows and pigeons in Hyderabad. My large lens could barely cover the whole body of the birds. Indian Moorhen 3

My family was enjoying the sight of the Black-winged Stilt (Himantopus himantopus) resting on a single leg. Suddenly a Pied Starling (Gracupica contra) was visible close to our boat. The competition among the Terns for fish was a great moment, and capturing the flight shots at ground level was really enjoyable. Black-winged Stilt The first duck sighted was a Northern Pintail. There were hundreds of Northern Pintails, Ruddy Shelducks, Northern Shovelers (Anas clypeata) and Garganey (Anas querquedula). Terns fighting for fish Travelling from Hyderabad to Mangalajodi is very convenient. All the trains bound to Howrah or Bhubaneswar stop at Balugaon. Mangalajodi is just 50 km from Balugaon. There are cottages in Barkul as well as Mangalajodi. The Barkul cottages are well maintained by Orissa Tourism. The Mangalajodi cottages are a bit challenging as they are maintained by local cooperatives. Other birds sighted in significant numbers are listed below: 1. Marsh Sandpiper 2. Common Sandpiper 3. Little Stint 4. Common Redshank 5. Wood Sandpiper 6. Common Sandpiper 7. Great Egret 8. Grey Heron 9. Purple Heron 10. Pheasant-tailed Jacana 11. Black-headed Ibis 12. Glossy Ibis 13. The list is somewhat limited as my primary focus was on photographing the birds and their actions. The total program was ideal for bird photography as the camera was set at the water level. Pheasant-tailed Jacana Barn Swallow *** Trip Report: BSAP Field Trip to Cherlapally Lake, 18th December 2016 Humayun Taher Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya It had been some little time since I had been out with the BSAP on a field trip so I wasn’t going to let this opportunity slip. Cherlapally has been a rather interesting destination in the past and, now that the winter migrants were in, it could be expected to give us a decent bag of species. So I thought and I made haste to sign up for the trip. There was also a promise of something more on this trip, as one of our members was bringing in some school students for a morning field session. One convert, of course, is worth more than a dozen saints, so this was definitely something that could be fruitful. led to the lake by the very pleasant feminine voice which slowly and carefully spells out the directions on this most excellent app. What a boon this has been to the directionless birding community! The school students had arrived before us and, as we parked the cars and started to unpack our binoculars and spotting scope, our most energetic Shafaatsaab started proceedings by addressing the students about birds and birding in general. Professor Moorty then took over the class and soon all the students were peering through binoculars and cameras at the birds around. I was most interested to see a solitary Brown Shrike (Lanius cristatus) sitting composedly on a scrubby little tree on the shores of the lake. This is one of the early migrants and I have regular records from this location, so it is possible that this is the same bird that I had seen in the previous years too. How I wish there was some way to colour tag the birds we see; it would add so much interest to the sightings of the migrants. Picking up Shafaatsaab in the morning, I reached our Punjagutta rendezvous in good time. The early morning nip was a little in abeyance on this day, but still it was very pleasant. A few more members joined up and we started out for the location. Taking a couple of incorrect turnings, we had to stop and ask for directions… a proceeding which completely stumped us when our informant asked us which Cherlapally we were looking for. We eventually took refuge in Google maps and were successfully 6

I was further dismayed to note that the lake now has become a sort of fish pond for the local folk. Nets are stretched across the lake in all directions and there are also a couple of fisherfolk out on boats and taking up the catch. A thriving market is to be seen on the shores where the fresh-caught fish are being sold. I am not unduly critical of such a proceeding as I have ample proof that this sort of activity actually helps the lake to survive. When the lake is a source of livelihood, the local people will take care of it. They may chase away the birds, and the nets definitely will take a toll of a few cormorants and coots, but in the long run, the survival of the lake will be assured. Cattle Egret (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) This is the sort of thing that conservationists these days need to keep in mind. It is all very well to say that the place is a haven for birds so let’s protect it, but people seem not to realise that the reason the place is a haven is because of the large supply of fish in the lake. This is the reason why I was against the old Ameenpur Lake being turned into a biodiversity preserve. What was needed there was sturdy common sense and the setting up of a community reserve that would benefit the fishermen, not the birds. By protecting the activities of the fishermen, better results would have been obtained in the matter of preserving the habitat, which would have also helped the bird populations. Habitat and food are the prime factors affecting bird populations and protection of the one assures the other. Indian Pond Heron (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Scanning the lake, we were in for a disappointment. There seemed to be very little on the waters. Pollution had taken hold here and the ubiquitous water hyacinth was flourishing in the shallows. Fish seemed to be in good supply, and the Large Cormorants were doing themselves rather well. The presence of numerous Cattle Egrets (Bubulcus ibis), Indian Pond (Ardeola grayii), Grey (Ardea cinerea) and Purple Herons (Ardea purpurea) and a few Little Cormorants (Phalacrocorax niger) also showed this to be so. The water, though somewhat inky in colour, did show a fair number of small fry coming up to the surface and creating scaly patterns on the surface. I was reminded of my last trip to this lake, when I had occasion to remark on this singular phenomenon of the fish coming out of the water to breathe; it seemed that conditions had either not improved here, or else the fish in question were a species that are used to taking their air from the open and not through the water. Indian Roller (Photo: Humayun Taher) The students continued to exclaim at the activities and variety of species to be seen around. Under the able guidance of the good professor we all set off along the shores and on to the bund. A pair of White-browed Wagtails (Motacilla maderaspatensis) stared at us in horror and made haste to be elsewhere. Purple (L) and Grey Heron (R) (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) 7

Ashwin caught a fleeting glimpse of a Yellow Bittern (Ixobrychus sinensis), which was just as retiring as the Wagtails and wanted nothing to do with us. The Pond Herons and Cattle Egrets, on the other hand, were busy victualling up in the shallows and the hyacinth beds, and could not be bothered with the group on the shore. They believed in getting theirs and to hell with what it does to their figures! Black Drongo (Photo: Humayun Taher) Yellow Bittern (Photo: Humayun Taher) The large schools of fish that could be seen frequently popping their heads out of the waters had a lot to contend with. Not only the herons and egrets, they also needed to keep an eye on the splendid and graceful River Terns (Sterna aurantia) floating around. One enterprising Tern decided to try wading, but was quite unsuccessful: Methinks it should stick to angling! Grey Herons were also to be seen making a decent catch of piscatorial delicacies, and no doubt there was enough there for all. Green Bee-eater (Photo: Humayun Taher) Black Drongos (Dicrurus macrocercus) were also on the wing, and Green Bee-eaters (Merops orientalis) were to be seen cheerfully hawking insects. One was using the telegraph wires from which to make its forays, and these wires are low enough for all of us to get a brilliant view of the bird as it sailed out, snapped up a passing bee and glided back to the wire to dispose of its catch. Occasionally, we could hear it twittering away triumphantly, the sound somewhat muffled by the large insect it held in its beak! About midway along the bund was a temple, the flat terrace of which made a capital place to set up the spotting scope and peer all around to see whether there were any sights we had missed out. I did a sweep of the lake and regretfully noted that there are no waders and no ducks in residence at the moment. The students then took over the instrument and were soon peering through it at distant spots on the far shore where a few more egrets and herons were to be seen. Clamorous Reed Warbler (Photo: Humayun Taher) Walking along the bund, we saw both species of Reed Warbler (Clamorous and Blyth’s – Acrocephalus stentoreus and Acrocephalus dumetorum) and also the little Ashy Prinias (Prinia socialis). The rich yellow-orange colour of the underparts of these little birds showed that the breeding season was nigh upon them and they were hard at work. A pair of Red-vented Bulbuls (Pycnonotus cafer) also seemed to be thinking of setting up house together. I saw one carrying a twig in its mouth and diving into a peculiarly dense shrubbery. No doubt there was a nest in the making here. Lawrence led a particularly energetic group of students down towards the fields on the far side of the bund, where they put up a Common Snipe (Gallinago gallinago) and disturbed a Whitebreasted Waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus), which took to its heels, voicing its harsh booming call in disapproval of this unwarranted intrusion. 8

The keen eyes of the students spotted a small pod of Coots floating about in the water; but apart from these, there was a singular lack of bird-life in the area. I reflected that one reason could have been the size of the group, but it is also to be expected that with the unseasonal heavy rains that lashed the state a couple of months ago, it is all too probable that the small lakes and ponds that were dry last year, were now full, and the migrants may well have scattered to these small refuges. Still, a list of about 45 species was quite good going and so, well content, we repaired to the cars for breakfast. Shafaatsaab opened up shop with some of the students who were all eagerness to enroll in the Society, which was an encouraging way to end the trip; we don’t often get as many as 6 memberships in a single day. Rounding off the snacks with a well-earned cup of the vital bohea, it was time to head back, well-content with the sightings of the early winter morning. Sl. Bird of the Month Text and photos: Umesh Mani Grey Bushchat (Saxicola ferreus) Grey Bushchat male (L) and female (R) (Chopta, Uttarakhand, 12-10-2016) on the head and mantle, and less pronounced on the neck and breast. Order: Passeriformes Family: Muscicapidae Genus: Saxicola Species: S. ferreus Size: 15 cm Description & distribution: The Grey Bushchat, also known as the Dark Grey or Iron Grey Bushchat, is a resident breeder in the Himalayas and North-eastern Indian hills, and winters south in the North Indian plains. It is distributed from North-western Pakistan east across North India to South-central and Southeastern China, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Myanmar and West Malaysia. The male has dark grey to almost black upperparts (depending on the extent of wear) with streaked black wing coverts, whitish underparts with a dull grey breast and flanks, a solid white supercilium, white outer tail feathers and a white throat. The female also shows a muted white or buff supercilium and white throat, but the upperparts are rufousbrown with a rusty rump and outer tail feathers, and the underparts are yellowish-brown. Ear coverts are dark brown. The juvenile is similar to the female, but with spotting that is marked Habitat & behaviour: The Grey Bushchat is usually seen alone or in pairs, and tends to keep to open country and scrub, forest edges, cultivation etc. Its preferred habitat is tropical or subtropical, moist montane or lowland forest. It favours a perch on top of bushes or poles, flying to the ground on spotting an insect; while sitting, it flicks its tail often. Its diet consists mainly of insects like beetles, grasshoppers, and spiders; it also takes small molluscs and, sometimes, seeds. The usual calls are a sharp tak tak and a softer zee chunk. Nesting: The Grey Bushchat breeds mainly between March and July; its nest is a shallow cup made of grass, moss and fine roots, and lined with fibrous material, hair, leaves, fur, feathers etc. The usual clutch consists of 4 to 5 pale to deeper blue, slightly glossy eggs. Local name: The Grey Bushchat is known as ‘sarrak chak pho’ in Lepcha. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Jamnagar – A Birding Wonder Text & photos: Sita Susarla View from the Khijadia watch-tower Pelicans, Cranes, Avocets, Eurasian Curlews (Numenius arquata), Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa), various Gulls and Terns, Knob-billed Ducks (Sarkidiornis melanotos), Northern Pintails (Anas acuta) and Northern Shovelers (Anas clypeata) to name a few. Located on the coast of the Gulf of Kutch in Gujarat, Jamnagar houses a number of unspoilt islands, beaches and hills and is home to both sea birds and shore birds. We visited the Khijadia Bird Sanctuary in the first week of December 2016 and were thrilled to see flocks of Flamingos, 1

feed on cereals and vegetables. Demoiselle Cranes often gather in large flocks and use cultivated areas in India and roost in the nearby wetlands. Knob-billed Duck Common Crane We stopped by at the freshwater tanks to see Ferruginous Ducks (Aythya nyroca), Common Pochards (Aythya ferina), Little Grebes (Tachybaptus ruficollis), Gadwalls (Anas strepera), Cormorants, Coots, Shovelers and Pintails. Eurasian Curlew We camped at Hotel President, whose owner Mr. Mushtaq is an avid birdwatcher. His guidance was of great help in locating many endemic birds. Our birding itinerary included visits to Khijadia Bird Sanctuary, Saltpans of Sachana, INS ValsuraRoad, Dhinchda, Bedi Port and Rosy Port. Gadwall Male (L) and Female (R) Demoiselle Crane The Khijadia Bird sanctuary is spread over an area of 6.05 km2 and provides an ideal habitat for sea and shore birds. There are 3 watch towers for birdwatchers, as well as inspection paths leading deep into the foliage. Our first sighting on the early winter morning was a flock of Demoiselle Cranes (Grus virgo) flying above us and, a little later, some Common Cranes (Grus grus) in the fields adjacent to the sanctuary. The guide told us that the cranes visit local cultivations early in the morning and Great White Pelican 2

A little further in the sea water we spotted Eurasian Curlews in huge flocks and Great White Pelicans (Pelecanus onocrotalus) almost everywhere. There were a few Dalmatian Pelicans (Pelecanus crispus) also. Pied Avocet As we moved deeper into the sanctuary we had to hold our breath at the sight of Lesser Flamingos (Phoenicopterus minor) and Pied Avocets (Recurvirostra avosetta) in hundreds. Along with them there were also hundreds of Gull-billed Terns (Gelochelidon nilotica) and a few Heuglin’s Gulls (Larus heuglini). Dalmatian Pelican White-tailed Lapwing Eurasian Oystercatcher Moving further on the guide showed us a few Eurasian Oystercatchers (Haematopus ostralegus) in non-breeding plumage and Great Thick-knees (Esacus recurvirostris). Desert Wheatear On Day 2 we went to the Phase-II of the sanctuary and were lucky to spot a White-tailed Lapwing (Vanellus leucurus), a rare winter visitor to the sanctuary. The Desert Wheatear (Oenanthe pleschanka), a winter visitor to NW India, was very active as we could sight it at many places in the sanctuary. We, however, could not get to see the Great Crested Grebe despite our best efforts. Great Thick-knee 3

Crab-plover On day 3 we set out in search of Crab-plovers (Dromas ardeola) and found them in the water creek between Sachana and Balachadi beaches. It was a great sight. The plovers tend to move closer to the land during high tide and away from land as the tide recedes. This bird resembles a plover, but has very long grey legs and a strong heavy black bill similar to a tern. It has black-andwhite plumage, a long neck and an upright posture. Its bill is unique among waders, and specialised for eating crabs. Among the other birds we saw were Terek Sandpiper (Xenus cinereus), Curlew Sandpiper (Calidris ferruginea), Little Stint (Calidris minuta) and Temminck’s Stint (Calidris temminckii). Temminck’s and Little Stints Slender-billed Gull Crested Lark We also went scouting for the Indian Skimmer in Bedi and Rosy Port areas but could not locate any. However, we sighted many Western Reef Egrets (Egretta gularis), Black-eared Kites (Milvus migrans lineatus) and Crested Larks (Galerida cristata). Curlew Sandpiper We wound up our visit watching the spectacular display of murmurations of Rosy Starlings (Pastor roseus) at the Lakhota lake in Jamnagar city. Terek Sandpiper We also drove along INS Valsura road and, amidst the saltpans, saw a large number of Slender-billed Gulls (Chroicocephalus genei), Little Stints and Temminck’s Stints. Photos: Dr G Samuel Sukumar The group We had a most thrilling birding trip to the Hyderabad Golf Club. We were invited by our life member Santaram, not only for birding, but also for breakfast. Santaram is a keen golfer and is based in USA but is a regular ‘winter migrant’ to Hyderabad. Since the club is busy with golfers on week-ends, we had to settle for a week day. We were altogether 17 members who attended, not bad for a working day. 6

The golf course, with Golkonda Fort in the background The golf course is situated in and around the Golconda Fort and near Qutub Shahi Tombs. It occupies an area of approximately 80 acres, 20% outside the fort and the rest right inside the fort. It is a full-fledged 18-hole course as per international norms. The manicured lush green lawns are known as ‘fairways’ which average a length of about 300 to 400 meters each. Since it is an 18-hole course, there are eighteen such fairways. When a player completes all the holes, he would have walked about 8 kms. The peripheries of the fairways are lined by wild growth, grasses, thorny bushes, trees and various old structures and ruins of the fort. The golf course is a fascinating place and according to Santaram, one of the most unique golf courses in the world! Common Myna We cut across to the left of the lake to approach a thick forested area. Here we spotted both the Purple (Cinnyris asiaticus) and the Purple-rumped Sunbirds (Leptocoma zeylonica), Plain Prinia (Prinia inornata) and Scaly-breasted Munias (Lonchura punctulata). Rose-ringed Parakeet We all gathered at the club house at seven in the morning and started our walk from the first hole, walking along the side paths, avoiding the grass. The first to confront us was a noisy flock of Rose-ringed Parakeets (Psittacula krameri), nesting in the holes and crevices of a tall and old wall-like structure, and at the bushes at its base, a pair of Indian Robins (Saxicoloides fulicatus). This was followed by the sighting of the Common Mynas (Acridotheres tristis), monopolizing some other old structure. Further up we came to a small but beautiful lake, where a solitary Little Cormorant (Phalacrocorax niger) was enjoying a swim. Black Kite 7

Plum-headed Parakeet Male (L) and Female (R) Proceeding further, we entered the main fort through a tunnel under the impregnable ramparts. Inside the main fort, were lush green fairways, wedged in between old structures and ruins. Here we encountered Plum-headed Parakeets (Psittacula cyanocephala), Green Bee-eaters (Merops orientalis), Black Drongos (Dicrurus macrocercus) and plenty of Barn Swallows (Hirundo rustica). There is one more beautiful water body here, where Indian Pond Herons (Ardeola grayii), Little Egrets and a couple of Large Cormorants were busy finding their breakfast. Hathiyaan Ka Jhaad One cannot miss to mention a tree which we passed by. It was the iconic “hathiyan ka jhaad” (elephantine tree), a baobab tree, approximately 400 years old, presented to one of the Qutub Shahi kings by a traveler from Madagascar. It is healthy and still flowering and its trunk is so huge that it can accommodate about 50 people in its hollow! After having taken a full round of the course within the fort, we came to the 16th hole where there is a small canteen, which serves as a rest area for the golfers. In its vicinity is a fairly good forested area where we spotted the Indian Grey Hornbill (Ocyceros birostris), Indian Peafowl (Pavo cristatus), Spotted Owlet (Athene brama) and a White-throated Kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis). Soon, it was almost nine o’clock and time to head back. The management provided us with battery-operated golf carts which ferried us back to the club house, saving us considerable walking. We chalked up a list of about 50 species but the migrant Wagtails were conspicuous by their absence. Spotted Owlet 8

A sumptuous breakfast awaited us at the club house. We were seated at the verandah, overlooking the lush green lawns as far as the eye could see, with automatic water sprinklers creating mini rainbows. After having done full justice to the hot puris and masala dosas we took leave of Santaram, after thanking him profusely. I would also like to take this opportunity to thank our Life Member and President of the Club, Mr Vikram Deo Rao, Gr Capt Raksha, GM, and Lt Col Reginald, Manager, for their hospitality. Bird of the Month Text: Umesh Mani; Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica) Bar-tailed Godwit (Coringa, 04-12-2016) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Limosa Species: L. lapponica Size: 37-41cm largest sub-species, breeds in the far north-eastern parts of Asia, east of the Kolyma River delta and in western Alaska, and winters in Australia and New Zealand. Description & distribution: The Bar-tailed Godwit, also known as Barred-rumped or Small Godwit, is a short-legged Godwit, and males are, on average, smaller than females (although there may be regional variations in size). The adult bird has blue-grey legs, while its head, neck, breast and belly are off-white in the non-breeding season and brick-red in breeding season. Upperparts are mottled grey. The sexes are alike, and the juvenile is similar to the non-breeding adult, but with a buff wash to the underparts, and buff edges to the mantle and scapulars. The bill is very long and slightly upturned, and is pink at the base and black towards the tip. An inverted ‘V’ on the rump and lack of white wing-bars (both seen more easily in flight), and a barred tail, help distinguish it from the other Godwit seen in India, the Black-tailed Godwit. Three sub-species are recognised. L. l. lapponica, the smallest sub-species, breeds from northern Scandinavia east to the Taymyr Peninsula, and winters in the western coasts of Europe (British Isles, Netherlands), South Africa and the Persian Gulf. L. l. menzbieri, intermediate in size, breeds in north-eastern Asia, from the Taymyr Peninsula east to the Kolyma River delta, and winters in Australia and south-eastern Asia. L. l. baueri, the Habitat & behaviour: The Bar-tailed Godwit is usually seen in small-to-large mixed flocks, along with Black-tailed Godwits, Dunlins and other waders. It is mainly a saltwater species, tending to keep to seashores, mudflats and edges of marshes, although it is occasionally seen in nearby grasslands also. It uses its long bill for foraging by probing the mud for marine invertebrates, crustaceans and insects, which constitute its main diet, and it may also locate insects by sight in short vegetation. Besides, it is also known to eat some parts of aquatic plants. Its call, usually heard in flight, is a sharp a-wik, a-wik, a-wik, while the alarm call is a two-syllabled te-ten, te-ten or chitiu-chitiuchitiu. Nesting: The Bar-tailed Godwit breeds only from its fourth year, mainly between April and August. Its nest is a shallow cup in the ground, lined with moss, fine grass, lichen or other soft vegetation. The usual clutch consists of 4 eggs which are beige with scattered brown patches. Incubation and care of the young are handled by both sexes. Local name: The Bar-tailed Godwit is known as ‘gudera’, ‘gairiya’, ‘fangral’ or ‘khag’ in Hindi and ‘tondu ulanka’ in Telugu. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034.
