Newsletter of the Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh New Series Volume 14 Number 3 March 2017 FIELD OUTING: Sunday, 26th March 2017: Mrugavani Deer Park, Chilkur, 6.30AM. Chilkur is located around 25km from the city and is home to a lot of woodland birds. Keep a lookout for the Asian Paradise-flycatcher and other scrub forest birds. The Blue-faced Malkoha and the Pied Crested Cuckoo are also usually seen here. This will be a half-day trip. For further details and to co-ordinate, please contact Ms Surekha Aitabathula (99490-38532). Trip report: Papikonda, Dec 2016 Dr Jayati Mitra View at Papikonda (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) It was a cool morning in the month of December 2016 at Rajamundry. After an overnight journey by train from Hyderabad we reached the makeshift jetty on the bank of river Godavari, where a bright yellow boat with a blue baseline was waiting to pick us up. After walking down the uneven slope, we carefully crossed over the shaky wooden plank to reach our boat and seated ourselves comfortably. The boat sailed to our destination, Papikonda. The surrounding atmosphere was very calm and quiet. The vast expanse of water on all sides led to the distant shoreline which appeared mostly sandy but at times gave way to beautiful rock formations, gradually blending with dense vegetation uphill. At this point we were served piping hot breakfast, and informed that the journey to our camping site would take more than six hours. Naturally we tried to look for birds amidst this pristine setting but they were few and far between. There was an occasional sighting of a Little Cormorant (Phalacrocorax niger) sitting quietly and a White-throated Kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis) trying to fish in the quiet waters. Flocks of egrets flew across trying to reach the river bank on the other side. At one point the boat came closer to the bank and moved parallel to it, when we sighted a huge flock of Little Stints (Calidris minuta) flying right over the water’s surface. When they abruptly turned, their pointed wings glistened in the sunlight. On the boat (Photo courtesy: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) 1

House Crow (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) River Lapwing (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) House Sparrow (female) (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) By this time it was noon and our boat was anchored for a short while at a local village. There was a small temple where we saw birds like House Crows (Corvus splendens), House Sparrows (Passer domesticus) and Cattle Egrets (Bubulcus ibis). Great Thick-knee (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Green Sandpiper (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Amidst some huge boulders we saw a River Lapwing (Vanellus duvaucelii) perfectly camouflaged against the natural settings. A small island in the middle of the river had a mixed flock of sandpipers, Small Pratincole (Glareola lacteal) and other waders. A Kentish Plover (Charadrius alexandrinus) was running around and feeding on the bank. Cattle Egret (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) 2

Sirivaka Resort (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) The boat sailed again. It was about 3:00PM when our camping site, Sirivaka Resort came into view. There were rows of brightly coloured bamboo huts, red blue and yellow, set amidst the surrounding hills covered with deep vegetation. We finally disembarked at the jetty of the resort at Koruturu village. After settling down we set out for an evening walk along the winding path that led to the right side of the forest area. than sitting around a bonfire on that cold moonlit night near the river bank. We finally retired after having a delicious dinner. Black Eagle (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Next morning we started on a long trek along a path parallel to the river bank. Bird calls were very few, quite unusual for such a densely forested area. A Common Hoopoe (Upupa epops) was seen flying across. The most heard call was that of the Whitebrowed Bulbul (Pycnonotus luteolus) which we could also see quite often. The small shrubs lined along the path had colonies of Ashy Prinias (Prinia socialis). At sunrise flocks of Pale-billed Flowerpeckers (Dicaeum erythrorhynchos) flew from tree to tree. There were Common Ioras (Aegithina tiphia) singing different tunes which confused us at times. A flowering tree was full of Oriental White-eyes (Zosterops palpebrosus). Chestnut-headed Bee-eaters were also present in good numbers. Chestnut-headed Bee-eater (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Initially we sighted only a Laughing Dove (Stigmatopelia senegalensis), but as we went further we could hear a lot of chirping around us. About half a dozen Chestnut-headed Beeeaters (Merops leschenaultia) were lined up on the electric cable, facing the warm glow of the setting sun. We stood there for a while to look at these pretty, colourful birds. The commonly-seen Green Bee-eater was not present among them. Barbets, both Coppersmith (Megalaima haemacephala) and Brown-headed (Megalaima zeylanica), called in unison. The forest trail led to a place covered with teak, bamboo and fig trees. We could spot a Pied Bushchat (Saxicola caprata) sitting on the fence dividing the adjacent cultivated fields. Dusk was setting in as we started back and were greeted by a flock of Indian Silverbills (Euodice malabarica). Barn Swallows (Hirundo rustica) and Wire-tailed Swallows (Hirundo smithii) started circling the field full of pulses. As night approached nothing seemed more appropriate Red-naped Ibis (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) 3

We spotted a White-bellied Drongo (Dicrurus caerulescens) and Black Drongos (Dicrurus macrocercus) but after a while our attention was focused on a Crested Serpent Eagle (Spilornis cheela) that was sitting still for quite a while on a bare branch of a distant tree. It flew up into the sky spreading its wide wings, slowly gliding up and finally disappearing from our sight. As we were returning, a warbler was restlessly flying among the branches but the dense green foliage made it difficult for us to observe it properly. Indian Golden Oriole (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) At this point we noticed something dark creeping up the main trunk when we could make out the bright red crown and white spotted black plumage. It was the Fulvous-breasted Woodpecker (Dendrocopos macei) pecking on the trunk but it soon disappeared on to the other side and we lost the sight of this beautiful bird. Crested Serpent Eagle (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Fulvous-breasted Woodpecker (Photo: Dr Jayati Mitra) By this time it was late morning. We saw a Tawny-bellied Babbler (Dumetia hyperythra) flying, its bright rufous underbelly visible in the bright sunshine. A shy Blue-faced Malkoha (Rhopodytes viridirostris) quickly hid out of view. The Purple Sunbirds (Cinnyris asiaticus), however, remained very active, calling from the flowering trees lined all along our path. Red-whiskered Bulbul (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) We crossed the village and walked to the end of the path where female Indian Golden Orioles (Oriolus kundoo) and a juvenile posed for us. Both Red-whiskered (Pycnonotus jocosus) and Red-vented Bulbuls (Pycnonotus cafer) were visible throughout the trek. As we reached our camp another notable sighting was that of a small brown bird perched on a dead stump on the outskirts of our resort. After observing the scaly pattern on its wings we identified it as a female Blue Rock Thrush (Monticola solitarius). 4

Blue Rock Thrush (female) (Photo: Dr Jayati Mitra) Green Bee-eater (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) A little later a few of the more enthusiastic birders made another quick trek on the right side of the resort. After reaching a huge tree with a dense canopy we could hear numerous birdsongs. All were a little tired and decided to rest beneath the tree. It was here that a bird was seen very high up on the tree moving like a black shadow. We patiently sat and enjoyed the sweet music till the Golden-fronted Leafbird (Chloropsis aurifrons) flew and showed up in front of us on another tree. As we walked along we could hear the chattering as a flock of Plum-headed Parakeets (Psittacula cyanocephala) greeted us. The path ultimately led to a small stream flowing merrily and meandering through the boulders where a Yellow Wagtail (Motacilla flava) was running around rapidly and calling sweetly. It was a very scenic spot with this small stream in the centre surrounded by distant verdant hills on all sides. Golden-fronted Leafbird (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Brown Shrike (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) After lunch we crossed the river and reached Tadivada village .The river bank was very steep and we had to tread through the deep slippery sand which held back some of the members. Anyway, the Ashy Woodswallow (Artamus fuscus) was clearly visible from the bank. The path was very scenic with broadleaved trees lined on both sides. Here there was a Green Beeeater for a change. A Brown Shrike (Lanius cristatus) was hunting among the shrubs towards the edge of the forest. In the meantime our friends Sheetal and Shweta had left our small group to explore an alternative path near the river bank. When we returned we were in for a surprise. They narrated the sighting of a flying pair of Great Hornbills (Buceros bicornis) which made our day. 5

Now it was time to return. We walked through the cashew plantations and also observed the smouldering vegetation in the surrounding areas; it seemed to be an indication that the forest is being further cleared for future farming. After a hurried lunch we again boarded the boat to return to Rajamundry and back home to Hyderabad. A point to ponder over was that bird density was very low despite the rich vegetation and abundance of water in the area but nevertheless it had been a very memorable journey. Pied Kingfisher (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) It was the final morning of our trip. We left for Papikonda National Park which is known for the presence of leopards. The Peramtalapalli village came en route. The villagers here were pretty skilled in crafts and they displayed beautiful objects made out of bamboo for daily use as well as for decorative purposes. The terrain was hilly with a stream cutting across through the forest. A parallel path followed the stream at a higher altitude. We walked along this trail listening to mixed calls of barbets, orioles and ultimately stepped into the stream to sooth our tired feet. Rufous Treepies (Dendrocitta vagabunda) flew from treetops. Ruddy Shelducks (Tadorna ferruginea) were also seen by some members. Report: Spangled Drongo in Secunderabad Cantonment, February 2017 Text and photos: Yella Prakash Rao Spangled Drongo Its spring time once again and here they come. Yes, the Spangled Drongos (Dicrurus hottentottus) have arrived and can be seen on the same trees as of last year. This species surely stands out as it has wrinkled tail feathers and shiny feathers around its neck resembling a diamond studded necklace. The field guide distribution map indicates isolated records, one or more in the same area, where they have been tracked for the past four years foraging on the same trees. They were absent in the area between April to December. It is heartening to know that they are visiting the same trees year after year and I pray that this ecosystem survives this way. These birds have been visiting Secunderabad Cantonment between January and March every year and are seen feeding on the flowers of the Flame of the Forest and Indian Silk Cotton trees. A ringing effort with GPS trackers may reveal their journey details. *** A Visit to Kawal Wildlife Sanctuary, January 2017 Sita Susarla A view of Kawal WLS (Photo: Sita Susarla) The Kawal Wildlife Sanctuary is located in Mancherial district (erstwhile Adilabad district) and is spread over an area of 893 km2. The sanctuary houses Dry Deciduous Teak Forests mixed with Bamboo, Terminalia, Pterocarpus, Anogeisus and Cassias. River Kadem flows through this area. 8

Kadem Dam (Photo: Sita Susarla) We, a team of five people, set out on a birding trip to Kawal on a winter morning in January. Our first halt was at Kadem Dam. As we stepped into the Haritha Resort, we sighted an immature Barred Buttonquail (Turnix suscitator). It was not as shy as quails generally are. We managed to get some pictures before it disappeared into the nearby bushes. Very close to them were a Green Sandpiper (Tringa ochropus), an Asian Openbill (Anastomus oscitans), some Ruddy Shelducks (Tadorna ferruginea), a Pied Kingfisher (Ceryle rudis) and a Common Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis). There were many Bluetailed Bee-eaters (Merops philippinus), Large Grey Babblers (Turdoides malcolmi) and Black-headed Ibis (Threskiornis melanocephalus). Barred Buttonquail (Photo: Sita Susarla) After a quick breakfast we walked along the dam and nearby areas. There was a Blue Rock Thrush (Monticola solitarius) perched on an electric pole. We spotted a pair of River Lapwings (Vanellus duvaucelii) at the rocky edge of the dam. Painted Sandgrouse (Photo: Sita Susarla) From Kadem we drove up to the Kawal Wildlife Sanctuary, some 30km away. At 3:30PM, we went for a safari inside the sanctuary. Though the guides were used to showing animals they took special care to assist us in spotting birds also. But for them we would not have seen Painted Sandgrouse (Pterocles indicus), 5 of them, that were completely camouflaged by layers of dry leaves. It was a great sighting! The forests around the pristine water bodies were home to flycatchers, Plum-headed Parakeets (Psittacula cyanocephala), Black Redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros) and Chestnut-shouldered Petronias (Gymnoris xanthocollis). River Lapwing (Photo: Sita Susarla) 9

Openbills, Common Teals (Anas crecca), Yellow-footed Green Pigeons (Treron phoenicopterus), Ashy Woodswallows (Artamus fuscus) and White-naped Woodpeckers (Chrysocolaptus festivus), to name a few. One of the teammates sighted a Whiterumped Munia (Lonchura striata). Mottled Wood Owl (Photo: Ashis Pradhan) Spotted Redshank (Photo: Ashis Pradhan) We waited till dusk to hear and feel the life in the forest. A Mottled Wood Owl (Strix ocellata) with its distinct call echoing across the forest was another interesting species. We halted for the night at the Forest Department guesthouse in Jannaram, at the end of the sanctuary. That is when the forest officer gave us information of a birding hotspot about 20km from Kawal. Yellow-footed Green Pigeon (Photo: Sita Susarla) Woolly-necked Stork (Photo: Gopalakrishna Iyer) Black Stork (Photo: Ashis Pradhan) This place, Kalpakunta by name, was a real find. It was a breathtaking location – a small water body with an open area that was surrounded by the forest. We reached there by 7:30AM and sighted Woolly-necked Stork (Ciconia episcopus), Black Stork (Ciconia nigra), Spotted Redshank (Tringa erythropus), Asian White-naped Woodpecker (pair) (Photo: Ashis Pradhan) 10

White-browed Fantail (Photo: Ashis Pradhan) Within the Forest Department guesthouse compound, we saw a White-browed Fantail (Rhipidura aureola) and a Red-breasted Flycatcher (Ficedula parva). The drive back was full of excited conversations of the fantastic sights of the forest and our winged friends that live in its environs. White-eyed Buzzard (Photo: Sita Susarla) By 10:30AM we were back in the sanctuary for another safari to see the remaining part. Here we sighted a White-eyed Buzzard (Butastur teesa) perched on a tree branch right in front of us. We could take some quick pictures of the raptor. Moving forward we sighted Common Woodshrike (Tephrodornis pondicerianus), Small Minivets (Pericrocotus cinnamomeus), and Alexandrine Parakeets (Psittacula eupatria). Some Olive-backed Pipits (Anthus hodgsoni) were seen bathing in the pond waters. Bird of the Month Text & photos: Umesh Mani Northern Shoveler (Anas clypeata) Northern Shoveler Male (L) and Female (R) (Chennai, 19-03-2017) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Anas Species: A. clypeata Size: 44-52cm Description & distribution: The Northern Shoveler is a duck that is found commonly across large parts of the world. It is most easily identified by its large, spatulate bill. The breeding male has an iridescent, dark green head, white breast, and chestnut belly and flanks, and orange legs. A flying bird shows pale blue forewing feathers, separated from the metallic green speculum by a white patch or border. By early fall, the male also has a white crescent on the sides of the face. In non-breeding plumage, the male is similar to the female, which is drab mottled brown, much like the females of most other dabbling ducks, and has grey forewings. The broad bill which, on the cutting edge and the lower mandible, is grey tinged with orange, helps distinguish it from other similar birds. The Northern Shoveler breeds in northern areas of Europe, Asia, and North America. It is strongly migratory and winters south of its breeding range, in southern Europe, Africa, the Indian Subcontinent, South-east Asia, and Central & northern South America. It is also a rare vagrant to Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. No living subspecies are accepted today. Habitat & behaviour: The Northern Shoveler is not as gregarious as other dabbling ducks, and is generally seen in small-to-large mixed flocks, usually including Northern Pintails, Pochards, Grebes and various Egrets. Its flat, wide bill is equipped with numerous lamellae – small, comb-like structures that act like sieves and allow it to skim crustaceans, plankton and aquatic invertebrates from the water surface. It feeds by dabbling along the water, swinging its bill from side to side, straining the water while retaining any food material. Wet grasslands with some vegetation, and mud-bottomed marshes that are rich in invertebrate life, are therefore its preferred habitat. It is a relatively quiet species. The call of the male is a clunking call, whereas the female usually utters a quack. Nesting: The Northern Shoveler breeds mainly between April and June. Its nest, a shallow depression in the ground lined with down, grass or other plant material, is usually built in grassy areas away from open water. The usual clutch consists of 7-16 plain, off-white or buff eggs, sometimes with a greenish tinge. Local name: The Northern Shoveler is known as ‘tidari’, ‘punana’, ‘tokarwala’ or ‘ghirah’ in Hindi and ‘mattimikh cherevi’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Report: Bird Race, 19th February 2016 Srikanth Bhamidipati Brown Fish Owl (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) On February 19th 2017, birders and photographers from the City of Pearls gathered to race and search for birds across the city, as part of the event which is popularly known as the HSBC Bird Race. All the participants gathered early in the morning at Tourism Plaza, Begumpet and made strategies for winning the race. Registrations done and breakfast hampers collected, all the participants were now eager to leave the starting point and record some birds. After a few photographs and flag off by the chief guest, Dr Christina Z. Chongthu IAS, Managing Director, Telangana State Tourism Development Corporation, 18 teams left in different directions in search of birds. 1

As the day progressed, the teams had a lovely time documenting their findings while also keeping an eye on the time, as they had to get back to the venue by 6:00PM. Even on returning after a long day, the enthusiasm was still the same, as all the teams discussed their sightings, but none willing to let out their total tally – it reminded me of my school days! The Judges JVD Moorty, Gubbala Ramakrishna Rao and Humayun Taher vetted all the sightings submitted by the teams, and occasionally called the team members to provide proof for certain sightings. Finally, the judges completed the screening and came to a decision. All present were served refreshments and geared up for the evening event and the results. The panel (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) The chief guest for the evening event was Mr. Mahesh Iyer, Head of Oncology Biometrics for Novartis, and the Guest of Honour was Mr. Sam Alex, Vice President and Branch Head, HSBC Hyderabad. Along with Mr. Mahesh and Sam on the dais there were also our very own JVD Moorty, Hon. Vice President of BSAP, Shafaat Ulla, Hon. Secretary of BSAP and Diyanat Ali, Founder of GHAC, along with Sagarika Melkote, who was compering. Many participants shared their experiences, but there were 2 things which people were eagerly waiting for – the Results, and the FOODDDDDD!!!!!! Chestnut-tailed Starling (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Wood Sandpiper (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) *** Trip Report: Urulanthanni and Edamalayar Forests of Kerala Text and photos: Sita Susarla A view of Urulanthanni Forest On a visit to Kerala we took a day off to visit the Urulanthanni rainforest and the tropical evergreen forest of Edamalayar which are situated close to Thattekad. Though our plan was to visit Thattekad, the guide suggested these forests as they reported very high birding activity. We too did not mind as our aim was to have a nice birding experience. Grey Junglefowl 5

We started off early in the morning from Kothamangalam and by 7:00AM the guide took us to Urulanthanni Forest. It being the first week of February, peak birding time, we were able to see many bird species. The forest was, in fact, teeming with birds. The Malabar Grey Hornbills (Ocyceros griseus) and Greater Racket-tailed Drongos (Dicrurus paradiseus) were everywhere and we watched them to our heart’s content. There was a Velvetfronted Nuthatch (Citta frontalis) climbing down the bark of a tree, which is typical of nuthatches. The forest vegetation included Cheeni trees, Bhadraksha trees, Vellapine or White Pine, Teak trees and Bamboo bushes. Most of these trees were 40-60ft tall and the birds were perched on them. Malabar Barbet Velvet-fronted Nuthatch White-bellied Blue Flycatcher We saw Malabar Barbets (Megalaima malabarica), Flamethroated Bulbuls (Pycnonotus (melanicterus) gularis), an Asian Fairy Bluebird (Irena puella) and some Grey-fronted Green Pigeons (Treron (pompadora) affinis). The photos had to be shot with the head held tilted back on the neck most of the time. Some relief was provided by a White-bellied Flycatcher (Cyornis pallipes), Blue-capped Rock Thrush (Monticola cinclorhynchus) and an Orange-headed Thrush (Zoothera citrina), all perched closer to the ground. Little Spiderhunter Soon the guide recognized the characteristic tzeck tzeck call of the Little Spiderhunter (Arachnothera longirostra). We followed the call and came upon two of them. Generally found in Montane (mountain) ecosystems, the Spiderhunter feeds on nectar of flowers. It builds nests out of spider cobwebs and, therefore, probably the name. Our next sighting was the Crested Goshawk (Accipiter trivirgatus) which is very rare to find. It was seen resting under the canopy of broad leaves and we could take many pictures. However we were not as lucky with the Malabar Trogon (Harpactes fasciatus) and only had a fleeting glance of the bird before it disappeared into the thick foliage. Malabar Grey Hornbill 6

Crested Goshawk Lesser Yellownape After a quick lunch and some rest we set out to Edamalayar Forests at 3:00PM. These evergreen forests are located at a distance of 20km from Thattekkad Sanctuary. We decided to cover a stretch by foot. Very soon we knew we were doing the right thing. The Heart-spotted Woodpecker (Hemicircus canente), Lesser Yellownape (Picus chlorolopus) and Whitebellied Treepies (Dendrocitta leucogastra) were the highlight here. Sitting on the topmost part of a teak tree, the Yellownape was calling for nearly 15 minutes with very short breaks while the Heart-spotted Woodpeckers, four of them, were busy feeding on the bark of a 60ft tree. Here I have to acknowledge my Nikon P600 Camera – but for its 2000mm zoom, I would not have got clear pictures of these woodpeckers. We also got to see the Legge’s Hawk Eagle, though not for long. Sri Lanka Frogmouth The guide then took us on a 10-minute trail to see the Sri Lanka Frogmouth (Batrachostomus moniliger). Undisturbed by our presence, the bird remained very calm and composed, allowing us to take some very good pictures. Another interesting point was that, while trekking through the forest, at several places we saw evidence of the presence of elephants, through their droppings and footmarks. White-bellied Treepie On our way back to Kothamangalam the guide took us to Chelad to show us Pin-tailed Snipes (Gallinago stenura). We saw five of them resting in a field about 10ft below us. They didn’t fly away as most snipes do and so we could watch them till sunset. There were also many White-cheeked Barbets perched on cable lines. Heart-spotted Woodpecker 7

Malabar Parakeet Though it was only a one day birding trip, we were thoroughly satisfied as we could see some of the beautiful birds of Kerala. We decided to visit again for a longer duration to see more of them soon. BUS BIRDING Trip Report: ICRISAT, February 2017 Text and photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati A scene at one of the lakes in ICRISAT BSAP had organized a trip to ICRISAT campus in February. It has always been a great place for birding, owing to the great vegetation cover and the undisturbed habitat. Expectations were high for the day. Walking around the lake, we saw a few waders, warblers and other species which were flying around. After clicking a few images and birding for a while we proceeded towards the next lake – Surisehgal Lake. This lake was filled with the regulars – Eurasian Coots (Fulica atra), Indian Spot-billed Ducks, Cotton Pygmy-goose (Nettapus coromandelianus), Darters (Anhinga melanogaster), Herons and other common species. Here we also sighted a few River Terns (Sterna aurantia). It was interesting to see that every bird that flew past had a fish in its mouth. It looked like they were having a barbecue party where every guest was asked to bring their own fish! Eurasian Marsh Harrier As we boarded the bus, we spotted a couple of Eurasian Marsh Harriers (Circus aeruginosus) and Eurasian Spoonbills (Platalea leucorodia). This seemed like a good start and we proceeded to the first lake. Here we spotted a few Lesser Whistling-ducks (Dendrocygna javanica) and Indian Spot-billed Ducks (Anas poecilorhyncha) which seemed restless due to our unexpected arrival…looks like ICRISAT forgot to give them a memo warning of our arrival! Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark Later we proceeded towards another lake where the first thing we did was to open up our breakfast boxes. It was more like a pot luck scene, so everyone picked up what they like and filled their tummies. Common Greenshank and Common Redshank 9

Ruddy Shelduck Indian Courser Now it was time to again get back to some serious birding, so we set up our scopes and started counting and checking all the birds across the lake and on the small islands. There were about 5 Barheaded Geese (Anser indicus) and a number of Ruddy Shelducks (Tadorna ferruginea). Along with these there were other common woodland species, but the best sighting for me that day was the Indian Courser (Cursorius coromandelicus) which was spotted just close to the gate on our exit. There was a pair, and their behavior was interesting. It looked like they were protecting something important – probably a nest. After watching them for a while, we all left after a wonderful day of birding. Another group went to the other side of the bund and they discovered more birds there. We immediately went and found a flock of 40 Bar-headed Geese, about 70 Terns and many waders and ducks. This place was like heaven for birdwatchers! Finally after taking some good pictures and compiling a long list we proceeded to the final lake. There were a lot of Herons, Ibis, Egrets and Cormorants. After carefully identifying them and taking some photographs, I turned to the opposite side to see a few waders sitting at a distance. One of them was a Pacific Golden Plover (Pluvialis fulva) which was an interesting record for that location. A fellow birder spotted 24 Yellow Wagtails (Motacilla flava). Ruff *** Bird Humour Contributed by: Bharadwaj Korni 10

Bird of the Month Text & photo: Umesh Mani Rusty-tailed Flycatcher (Ficedula ruficauda) Rusty-tailed Flycatcher (Sattal, Uttarakhand, 19-04-2015) Order: Passeriformes Family: Muscicapidae Genus: Ficedula Species: F. ruficauda Size: 14 cm 3600m, and winters in evergreen broadleaved forests mostly in South-western India from the North Kanara region to Kerala. However, there have been occasional records from Rajasthan, Kutch as well as the Eastern Ghats, where presumably it is a passage migrant. Description & distribution: The Rusty-tailed Flycatcher is a small, seasonally migratory passerine in the family Muscicapidae (Old World chats and flycatchers) that breeds in central Asia and the western Himalayas. It is drab brown, and its rufous uppertail coverts and tail give it a female Redstart-like appearance. Structurally, it can be confused with the Asian Brown Flycatcher, and the differentiating features are a larger size, flatter forehead, and sometimes, slightly raised crown feathers, that may give an impression of a crest. It has (sometimes) a faint supercilium, a noticeable pale eye-ring (though less distinct than the Asian Brown), a grey-brown throat and breast, and a white belly. The lower mandible is entirely orange (unlike the Asian Brown, where it is only partly orange). The sexes are alike, but the juvenile has buff spotting on upperparts and dark scaling on underparts. Habitat & behaviour: The Rusty-tailed Flycatcher is a solitary bird, and frequents the edge of forests, generally keeping to the canopy of large trees, though it may venture lower while hunting for flies and other insects, which are its main prey. Its call consists of three or four rapidly-repeated loud, clear notes; a bullfinch-like peu peu; or a short, deep churr. The song is a drawn-out, rising and falling mournful whistle, followed by some rapid warbling. The Rusty-tailed Flycatcher breeds in mixed coniferousbroadleaved forests in the Western Himalayas, from Pakistan across to central Nepal, between the altitudes of 2100m and Nesting: The Rusty-tailed Flycatcher breeds mainly between May and July. Its nest is a solid cup made of moss, coated with lichen and cobwebs, located on bushes or horizontal forks in trees. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 pale sea-green eggs with reddish freckles. Local name: The Rusty-tailed Flycatcher is known as ‘lalpunchh makhimar’ or ‘badamipunchh makhimar’ in Hindi and ‘chempuvalanpakshi’ in Malayalam. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 11 PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. BIRDING DIARIES Trip Report: Nehru Zoological Park, 21st May 2017 Anwesha Chaudhuri Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar At the crack of dawn, my parents and I set off to Nehru Zoological Park. BSAP had provided us with a rare opportunity – a chance to experience the zoo in the wee hours of the morning, avoiding the Sunday crowds and the afternoon heat of Hyderabad. It was indeed a special day, for we were going to encounter a familiar environment at a time when it remained untouched by human presence. Turns out the zoo transforms into a bird hub before the cacophony of people encroaches onto the peaceful haven! Oriental Magpie Robin (Photo: Anwesha Chaudhuri) 1

We were welcomed into the zoo by an Oriental Magpie Robin, singing into the morning. THE BANYAN TREE Report: Ananthagiri Hills, May 2017 Text and Photos: Sita Susarla The Banyan Tree Standing majestically in front of the Anantha Padmanabhaswami temple in Ananthagiri (Vikarabad District) is a Banyan Tree. It is situated on the other side of the road and is easily distinguishable from the trees around because of its size. Though we had visited Ananthagiri many times, and parked our vehicle close to this tree, it had not attracted our attention earlier. So what was different this time? Well, it was the chorus of bird calls. As we turned around we saw a lot of activity around this tree. For a second we did not know where to look. Within half an hour of observation we spotted nearly 25 bird species! Black Redstart & Olive-backed Pipit Feeding on the fallen berries, also, were the Jungle Babblers (Turdoides striata), and a few feet from them was a lone Grey Wagtail (Motacilla cinerea). Orange-headed Thrush There was an Orange-headed Thrush (Geokichla citrina) moving secretively and feeding on the berries. The Black Redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros), on the other hand, was bolder and moved about the base of the Banyan tree along with the Olivebacked Pipit (Anthus hodgsoni). Jungle Babbler 7

were feasting on them. Interestingly the Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher was also seen feeding on the insects closer to the ground while the Drongos were at the top of the tree. Grey Wagtail Sitting on the prop roots was a pair of Tickell’s Blue Flycatchers (Cyornis tickelliae) and one Asian Paradise-flycatcher (Terpsiphone paradisi). A couple of Yellow-footed Green Pigeons (Treron phoenicopterus) were resting on the topmost branches, enjoying the warmth of the morning sun. Yellow-footed Green Pigeon The Oriental White-eyes (Zosterops palpebrosus), which are mainly arboreal, were also very active. February end, being the beginning of their breeding period, may have been the reason for this. As we moved around the tree we saw a Greenish Warbler (Phylloscopus trochiloides), a few Common Tailorbirds (Orthotomus sutorius), White-browed Bulbuls (Pycnonotus luteolus) and Small Minivets (Pericrocotus cinnamomeus). A Large Cuckooshrike (Coracina macei) flew by. Never before did we see such a spectacular sight! The impact was so great that on our subsequent birding trips we kept looking at Banyan trees in the hope of spotting an equally large numbers of birds. All this brought back memories of Chandamama and the pictures of Banyan trees full of birds pecking at the red berries, monkeys playing on its prop roots, and people resting under its shade. A perfect and blissful co-existence of flora and fauna! The Banyan, known as Ficus benghalensis, is native to India and is the National Tree of India. It is a perennial that spreads through prop roots and is considered to be the world’s largest tree in terms of canopy coverage. The fruit are food to many birds and animals. Bird of the Month Text: Umesh Mani; Photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati Russet Sparrow (Passer rutilans) Russet Sparrow Male (L) and Female (R) (Gushaini, Himachal Pradesh, 07-05-2017) Order: Passeriformes Family: Passeridae Genus: Passer Species: P. rutilans Size: 14-15cm Description & distribution: A medium-sized member of its family, the Russet Sparrow is a seed-eating bird that is found commonly in the Himalayas, from Himachal Pradesh to Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Nepal, south-eastern Tibet and Bhutan, and across large parts of eastern Asia, including some parts of mainland Russia and northern China, and across southern China, Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Myanmar, Laos, northern Thailand and Vietnam. It is also known as the Cinnamon Sparrow or the Ruddy Sparrow The Russet Sparrow is sexually dimorphic, with the general patterns being similar to those in the corresponding sex of the House Sparrow. The breeding male has bright russet or cinnamon brown upperparts, from the crown down to the rump, with some black streaking on the mantle. A thin white supercilium, running from the bill to the rear of the head, separates the russet crown from the black around the eye. It has an off-white neck and cheeks, a small black bib, and pale grey or yellowish underparts. The wings are light brown tinged with black, while the shoulders are chestnut. The tail is blackish-brown. The non-breeding male is not very different, being somewhat paler, and the upperparts being more orange than russet. The female has pale brown upperparts and pale grey underparts, and has a bold dark brown stripe through the eye, and a marked cream supercilium that goes from above the eye nearly all the way around the head. The wings are greyish brown, and the back is streaked with black and buff. Juvenile birds are similar to the female, though more pale and sandy in colour. The bill is thick, suited for eating seeds of herbs and grains that form its main diet, and is black on the breeding male, horncoloured on the non-breeding male, and yellowish with a dark tip on the female. The irises are chestnut, and the legs are pale pinkish-brown. Thirteen subspecies have been described, but only three are widely recognised – the nominate subspecies, Passer rutilans rutilans, which breeds in Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and southeastern and central parts of China; P. r. intensior, which breeds in southwest China and parts of India, Myanmar, Laos and Vietnam; and P. r. cinnamomeus, which breeds in the range between northern Arunachal Pradesh west to parts of Afghanistan. Habitat & behaviour: The Russet Sparrow is found to be quite widespread in different habitats and altitudes across its range. It seems to prefer areas close to terraced cultivation, but is quite common in gardens, open spaces, light woodland, agricultural areas, riverine grasslands and riparian forests. Breeding generally takes place at higher altitudes. In some behavioural aspects, it resembles its ‘cousins’, the House Sparrow and the Eurasian Tree Sparrow – e.g. it feeds on the ground. In non-breeding season, it is quite gregarious and forms big flocks, and also roosts in large communal roosts. Flocking Russet Sparrows feed close to the ground, and show ‘roller feeding’, where the forward movement of the flock is through birds at the rear of the flock moving to the front, turn by turn. 12

In the breeding season, though, it is not gregarious, and nests tend to be dispersed. Though the Russet Sparrow eats insects during breeding season, and berries when available, it is mainly a seed-eater, favouring seeds of herbs, weeds, rice, barley and other grains. Nestlings, however, are mainly fed insects like caterpillars and larval beetles. display consisting of a raised head, drooping wings, a chest pushed forward and a lowered tail; this is followed by bowing up and down in front of the female. It nests in tree cavities, holes in stone walls, embankments and under thatched roofs, in electric junction boxes, as well as free-standing nests in bushes. It is also known to use disused nests of Black Kites, Red-rumped Swallows, woodpeckers and, occasionally, Spot-winged Tits. The basic call of the Russet Sparrow is a soft, monosyllabic cheep or chilp, usually uttered in flight or during display, or a trilled cheeeep. The male may also string together some of these notes in a sequence, though the actual song is a thin swee-swee, similar to that of a robin, interspersed with some sibilant chuswik notes, and is often described as the most melodious of any of the sparrows. The nest is usually a loose bunch of dry grass that fills the nest cavity, lined with feathers and fur. The usual clutch consists of 46slightly glossy elongated ovals with a fine texture, whitish with a grey tinge and brown spots, streaks or blotches; there are usually two clutches laid in a year. Local name: The Russet Sparrow is known as ‘lal gouriya’ in Hindi,‘chakli’ in Gujarati, ‘angnadi kuruvi’ in Malayalam and ‘adaikala kuruvi’ in Tamil. Nesting: The Himalayan subspecies of the Russet Sparrow, P. r. cinnamomeus, breeds between April and August. THE PEN & THE BINOCULAR (part-1) Humayun Taher It was still dark when I was woken up by the pressure of my father’s hand on my shoulder, with a whispered warning to make haste and not make noise. I still don’t know how to balance these two, but what I did that day was apparently acceptable as I didn’t have to listen to any lectures on the subject. A quick biscuit washed down with some water, and then bus number 127 carried us to the Koti bus stand. Kamat Hotel Koti was the habitual BSAP rendezvous in the 1980’s and having reached the place, we looked eagerly for the others. Small boys in those days were not allowed to drink tea until they had passed their tenth birthday (“It will make your teeth rot and fall out…”!). Happily it seems that this chemical reaction is restricted to teeth that are less than 10 years old. Having crossed this almost mythical age some little time ago, my young heart was gladdened by being allowed to partake of a steaming cup. I’ve kept at it ever since! While quaffing the refreshing beverage, other members were seen coming in and soon the café was half-full of BSAPians. Someone then announced that the jeeps had arrived and, a few minutes later, a white government Ambassador drove up with our society President, Mr. Pushp Kumar and Maj. A. A. Aziz inside. Having exchanged pleasantries, we climbed into the jeeps, and started off for our field trip for that day, the Vanasthalipuram Deer Park (now called the Mahavir Harina Vanasthali). The date was the 20th of February, 1983! The Forest Department jeeps had not yet arrived, but Aasheesh’s Ambassador was drawn up by the kerb and so we knew that he, at least, was there. Crossing the road, we purposefully made our way to the “Light of Asia” café, where, sure enough, a few members were refreshing themselves with the iconic “Irani chai”. Alas, this wonderful institution, a more popular rendezvous than the even then defunct Kamat Hotel, has also fallen prey to the ravages of time, and the “Light of Asia” has been extinguished. I can’t pass the place these days without feeling more than a twinge of nostalgia. Below is the field list of this trip… 1

The highlight of the trip was the huge flocks of Rosy Pastors (now the Rosy Starling Pastor roseus). The flowering Flame of the Forest trees in this Deer Park were favourite feeding grounds for the beautiful birds and flocks of several hundreds were a common sight. Also interesting are the sightings of the two species of Gyps, the King or Black (Sarcogyps) and the Egyptian (Neophron) Vulture. These were also very common in those days and at that place particularly, because of the municipal garbage dump just outside the boundary wall of the Park. The trip ended with hot chai and biscuits served by the Forest Department staff at the park. There used to be a lovely open-air sitting area just outside the park gates and we always forgathered there after our trips to this location. While refreshing ourselves with the soothing oolong and the contents of our snack boxes, the field trip list was read out by Kulkarni. Others pitched in with their sightings, the combined total coming to some 40 species. 2

After discussions of the species sighted, and after deciding the site for the next field trip, we called it a day and, climbing back into the jeeps, we returned to the Kamat Hotel, where the faithful bus (route No. 127) brought us back home in time for a late lunch, or an early high-tea. But the tea was, unhappily, not for me. It seems that the circumstances of the rotting teeth are different when one is out for birding and when one is back at home. Still, two cups of tea for a day is not bad going, at my age (I was pushing 13)! Note: Several names may be unfamiliar to the younger set of birders. Dillon Ripley *** Report: Sighting of Great Knot, Kakinada, 7th January 2017 Text & Photo: Gurukumar KR Great Knot flock The annual wetland census has been an exciting time for me ever since I joined BSAP. The variety and sheer numbers of the migratory birds can amaze any birding enthusiast. This year was no different and when presented with a chance to participate in AWC in Kakinada area, I just could not let the opportunity pass. Though I had been told about the huge flocks of migratory birds that one could see in such a habitat, I was definitely not prepared for such a visual treat! contrasting with the white of the belly. The larger size of the bird and its bill, along with the strong streaking on the throat and breast, helps in distinguishing it from its more common cousin, the Red Knot (Calidris cantus). These species forage on the mudflats and beaches looking for insects and molluscs, picking them up by sight. They are usually seen roosting with other waders. The flock seen at the port area was a huge mix of Grey Plovers (Pluvialis squatarola), Whimbrels (Numenius phaeopus) and Eurasian Curlews (Numenius arquata). The Great Knots are listed as endangered by the IUCN and the diminishing of their feeding areas like these mudflats, does not seem to help in their conservation. The East Godavari River and Estuarine Ecosystem is rich in floral and faunal diversity and forms an important feeding and breeding ground and a nursery for a wide variety of animals and birds. The census was on for three days and during this time one of the areas visited was the Kumbabhishekam fish landing area near Kakinada port. In this area the mudflats were being developed into a port, and a lot of boats and fishing activity was seen. On what remained untouched or less disturbed, there was lot of bird activity and among them was a huge flock of Great Knots (Calidris tenuirostris). Other birds that were seen in the same area were Ruddy Turnstone (Arenaria interpres), Lesser Sand Plover (Charadrius mongolus), Kentish Plover (Charadrius alexandrinus), Blacktailed Godwit (Limosa limosa), Brown-headed Gull (Chroicocephalus brunnicephalus), Little Egret (Egretta garzetta), House Crow (Corvus splendens), Pacific Golden Plover (Pluvialis fulva), Little Stint (Calidris minuta), Curlew Sandpiper (Calidris ferruginea), Terek Sandpiper (Xenus cinereus), and Brahminy Kite (Haliastur indus). The Great Knot is a small wader and the largest of the Calidris species. These birds migrate in huge flocks to southern Asia during winters from their breeding habitats of north-eastern Siberia. They have short dark legs and a medium-length thin, dark bill. The face, throat and breast are heavily spotted, *** 3

Report: Sighting of Watercock, Fox Sagar, Hyderabad, 23rd July 2017 Text & Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya Watercock (female) The scientific name of the Watercock is Gallicrex cinerea. It belongs to the Rallidae family of crakes and rails. The Watercock is a widespread resident but basically a summer visitor to the Indian subcontinent. It is the only member of genus Gallicrex. The male is significantly different from the female. Female birds have buff underparts with fine barring, and buff fringes to dark brown upperparts, and are usually around 35 cm in length. The males are 42 cm, and have grey-black plumage with an extended red frontal shield and a red ‘horn’. Food Habits: The Watercock feeds on small fish, invertebrates, aquatic insects, terrestrial insects, worms and mollusks. It searches for food with its bill in shallow water. Breeding: The breeding season of the Watercock in the Indian subcontinent is mainly during June to September, and nesting starts just after the rainy season. In one clutch, the female Watercock lays 3 to 6 eggs. The BSAP monthly outing to Fox Sagar Lake, Hyderabad on July 23, 2017, was an eventful day as a Watercock (female) was seen after a long spell of time. It was interesting to watch how the Watercock was chasing the local inhabitants – the Purple Swamphens. Movement: Watercocks are mostly resident. However they move locally for foraging and breeding. Northern Watercocks in China and Japan usually move south during winter. Concerns: The global population of Watercocks has never been quantified; however, the overall population is decreasing due to habitat loss. Still it is not considered as a Vulnerable species due to fairly widespread presence. The clearing of reeds around wetlands and ever-expanding agricultural activities are the main threats for the survival of the Watercock. Habitat: The Watercock inhabits reedbeds, wetlands, marshes, swamps, flooded pasture, flooded meadows, irrigated lands and flooded agricultural field. The picture below of the female Watercock was taken in marshes of Fox Sagar Lake. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani HAGAR THE HORRIBLE (From Deccan Herald, 11-03-2015) *** 4

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Green Sandpiper (Tringa ochropus) Green Sandpiper (Ankola, Karnataka, 15-01-2012) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Tringa Species: T. ochropus Size: 21-24cm behind the eye. The juvenile has browner upperparts with buff spotting. Description & distribution: A somewhat plump member of the Tringa genus, the Green Sandpiper is a small migratory wader that breeds in sub-Arctic Europe, and winters in southern Europe, the Indian subcontinent, south-east Asia and tropical Africa. The genus Tringa was named by Aldrovandus in 1599 based on the Ancient Greek trungas, which was a white-rumped, tailbobbing wader earlier mentioned by Aristotle. The Green Sandpiper, and its only other close relative, the Solitary Sandpiper (T. solitaria) of North America, are, interestingly, the only members of the large Scolopacidae family of waders that nest in trees. The Green Sandpiper is dark greenish-brown on the back and wings, with variable light or whitish spots that are most abundant in the breeding adult, and less so in non-breeding and younger birds. It has a greyish head and breast, with a delicate contrasting neck and chest pattern, white underparts, and dark green legs and bill. The crown and breast are heavily streaked in the breeding adult. In flight, besides the easily-seen dark upper- and underwings, contrasting with the white belly and vent, it has a brilliant white rump that is conspicuous and a diagnostic feature that distinguishes it from the otherwise similar Solitary Sandpiper. It is darker and less heavily-spotted than the Wood Sandpiper (T. glareola), and the white supercilium is indistinct or absent Habitat & behaviour: The Green Sandpiper is primarily a freshwater bird, and often frequents smaller waterbodies like village ponds that other waders may avoid due to their preference for a clear all-round view. It is also seen along rivers, freshwater estuarine channels, and irrigation pools. It is not a very sociable species, usually seen singly, though small numbers may occasionally congregate if they come across a suitable feeding ground. Its diet mainly consists of small invertebrates, though it has been known to take insect and mosquito larvae, worms, molluscs, crustaceans, dragonfly nymphs, beetles, etc. The bill is thin and not very long, and enables it to probe the mud and pick small invertebrates as it steadily covers ground along the edges of ponds or lakes. Foraging methods have been found to vary depending on the specific habitat. The basic call of the Green Sandpiper is a three-note tuee-weetweet call, uttered usually in flight; it also utters a ringing tlueetueet call. Nesting: The Green Sandpiper usually nests in old nests of other birds in trees. The usual clutch consists of 2 pointed oval eggs, off-white or cream, spotted with dark brown. Local name: The Green Sandpiper is known as ‘nalla ulanka’ in Telugu,‘aathuchuzhi ullan’ in Tamil, ‘shwetapoonch thuthvari’ in Gujarati and ‘hara retal chaha’ in Punjabi. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, 5 PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. INDOOR MEETING: Talk by Anuradha Vinodh: THE INCREDIBLE INSECT WORLD Thursday, 17th August 2017, 6.00PM: Hamburg Hall, Goethe-zentrum Hyderabad, 20 Journalist’s Colony, Road No. 3, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500 034. (For directions, please contact 94905-09251 or 04065526443/23350040) Anuradha Vinodh, nature and wildlife enthusiast, has been working in the field of wildlife and environmental education since 1997. She was nominated for the Indira Gandhi Paryavaran Puraskar in 2014. She has worked in organisations such as Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), C.P.R. Environmental Education Centre and Telangana Forest Department (previously A.P. Forest Department) till March 2016. Presently she is working as a freelance consultant with WWF India-Telangana State office, Telangana Forest Department, CEE, APFA, etc. What is the difference between butterflies and moths? Why do fireflies glow? How do cicadas make noise? Is Cricket an insect? Did you know that ants build nests too? Why aren’t spiders called insects? These and many more questions will be answered by Ms Anuradha Vinodh. Insects are the most intriguing creatures on this earth. Go to any corner of the earth, the first creatures to mark their presence are the insects. They comprise almost two-thirds of the world’s animal population! This talk will take a peep into the incredible world of insects which play a very important role in our ecosystem. Ants, bees, butterflies and wasps aid in pollination. They also play a major role in maintaining a balance in nature. They are the chief source of food for birds, amphibians, reptiles, mammals and even other insects! Unfortunately, these benefactors of nature are often looked down upon with disgust. To clear out all the false beliefs about these magnificent creatures, a presentation on the ‘Incredible Insect World’ is a necessity. Please join us in this beautiful journey and explore the incredible world of insects! THE PEN & THE BINOCULAR (part-2) Humayun Taher This was a field list with a difference! Our equipment was somewhat contradictory… two air-guns of, even then, ancient vintage, three binoculars, one well-equipped lunch-cum-tea basket and one well-preserved Honorary Wildlife Warden! Eccentric, did you say… You have no idea! informed of an area along the banks of the Musi River, where these birds were nesting in large numbers. That was enough for us! Back home, we laid plans to go out to this place on a combined bird-watching and collecting trip. No doubt this sounds almost sacrilegious in this day and age, but it must be remembered that in those days, cameras were almost unheard of – at least in this part of the country – and the only way to get a particular species identified was through a specimen. Talks with the BNHS high-command further encouraged us as they also told us to obtain a specimen and send it to them. Ever since we got into this fascinating world of birds and birding, hardly a week went by without either myself or my father, usually both, making a short trip to a nearby bird-shop. This particular one was just opposite the GPO building in Abid Road. We had, a few weeks back, noted the presence here of Baya Weavers, Streaked Weavers and another species of weaver that was new to us, the Black-breasted Weaver. Questioning the birdseller, we were told these birds had been caught around Hyderabad, and when we went deeper into the matter, we were But why this fuss? Simply because, at that time, the Blackbreasted Weaver was unknown in this region. Apparently, the range did not extend this far south. The question remained how they got here, whether these were caged birds that had escaped 1

and established a breeding population, or whether they had always been there and had not been recorded. All such pleasant questions were rather above my young mind, but since my prowess with my old BSA air-rifle was well-known, I was recruited to play the part of collector-in-chief in this trip. Rajeev was collector number two (armed with his “modern” Diana airrifle); Siraj saab and Aasheesh donned the garb of the “scientific ornithologists”, and Maj. AA Aziz represented the awful majesty of the law (he was Honorary Wildlife Warden for the state!). Thus equipped, the expedition started off on a Sunday afternoon, for a place called Kothapet, near Dilsukhnagar, on the banks of the Musi River. The date was the 5th of June, 1983! Below are the pages of our field notes from this trip… 2

By the time the trip came to an end, both riflemen had been blooded: a male and a female in breeding plumage had been collected and stored on ice for their trip to Mumbai. More importantly, we had firmly established that there was a considerable breeding population of these birds in this area. Now, more than 35 years later, of course, the species is wellknown in the Hyderabad regions. The next time you see one however, spend a few moments thinking of the trials and tribulations we had to go through to get them on the Hyderabad list! The defunct birds were housed overnight in the freezer box of the refrigerator (to the scandalised horror of my mother), and the following day, (a taxidermist having been called in), a stout carton was soon on its way to Mumbai. What happened later? Well, the Black-breasted Weaver found a place on the list of birds of Hyderabad! Remember this, the next time you see one! Dillon Ripley *** HUNT UNDER THE CLOUDS Report: Rollapadu, 26th August 2017 Text & Photos: YSRK Prasad Bonelli’s Eagle The Nimbostratus clouds welcomed our team of four birdwatchers, early on the morning of August 26th, with the smoky greyish cloud spreading like a perfectly woven carpet, and preventing the sun rays from kissing the green pastures of the Rollapadu Wildlife Sanctuary, the unique dry grassland of the Andhra Pradesh. Formed in 1988 to protect the endangered bird, the Great Indian Bustard, the sanctuary has 77 species of grasses, as mentioned in the one of the research papers authored by C Sudhakar Reddy and K Thulsi Rao. raining the previous night. Spread across 6.4 sq kms, the sanctuary is known for the Lesser Florican display. This sanctuary also attracts a good variety of raptors, such as Blackshouldered Kite, Oriental Honey-buzzard, Short-toed Snake Eagle, Indian Spotted Eagle, Greater Spotted Eagle, Booted Eagle, Tawny Eagle, Bonelli’s Eagle, White-eyed Buzzard, Eurasian Marsh Harrier, Hen Harrier, Pallid Harrier etc. Unperturbed by the danger posed by the cauliflower-shaped clouds, our birding commenced with an interesting sighting of a raptor. We could see a silhouette, which was a long distance away and quite unidentifiable. We approached a bit closer and found it was the ferocious Bonelli’s, perching with its natural instincts of a killer, dominating the scene. Our curiosity pushed us closer to the tree. The weather was calm, and the scene was dull and uninteresting except for the raptor on the high tree. I was sanguine of grabbing a decent photograph or at least a record shot. A detailed photograph, at the time, was beyond imagination due to the bad weather. Having settled like the Egyptian Pharaoh on a throne, the majestic raptor had a good chance of making use of the low vegetation cover that provides access to prey. A herd of Blackbuck, with beautiful spiral horns, grazed on the droplet-covered blades of grass. The clouds blotted out the sun and didn’t provide very positive signs of happy birding. A threat to a birder’s plans results in utter pandemonium. While we were hesitating slightly to explore the unique open grasslands of Rollapadu, due to the unsupportive climate, the members of the Corvid family greeted us by crowing at the top of their lungs. There was nothing more consistent than rain on the day, which transformed the brownish-orange summer grass to a green cover, and exposed the sprawling greenish blades of grass to the birds of prey to hunt with ease. I had missed the petrichor, as it was 3

The haughty eagle’s hungry eyes combed every corner of the green carpet, investigating every quarter for a prey, just like the General Atomics MQ-9 Reaper, the hunter-killer surveillance drone. While I was watching the eagle with a sense of joy, a small-sized animal ran across my sight, disturbing my observation of the eagle. My focus immediately shifted from sky to the land. Yes, it was a fox. The black tip on the tail could be clearly seen. The fox ran few feet away from us, unaware of the veiled danger called eagle. And the very next moment, I witnessed the silence being overtaken by violence. The areas surrounding Rollapadu are filled with cotton and paddy crops. Farmers use pesticides to kill the insects and worms. The whole region is converted into a chemical zone, which is no longer an attractive destination for birds. Many birds such as Harriers have stopped or reduced their visits to the sanctuary due to non-availability of grasshoppers, owing to the change in the landscape forced by the Telugu Ganga project. The excessive use of insecticides seems to have killed the beneficial insects along with the harmful ones. Less number of birds might have forced the raptors to hunt prey – whatever helps them survive! My internet research revealed several instances of eagles killing foxes. If there had been a hit on the skull or nape of the fox, wouldn’t the eagle feast on the meat? It definitely would, in my opinion. The event that would happen in the next few seconds would be remembered forever. The Bonelli’s tried to attack the fox! Did the eagle chase away the scavenger fox to protect its food, hidden in the tall grass? There is no clear evidence to postulate that the eagle was chasing away the fox from the scene to protect a kill. We had observed the perching eagle for almost 20 minutes from a distance. If there had been a kill, wouldn’t the eagle have stayed next to the kill, instead of perching on the tree? I believe the eagle would not have allowed the fox to come closer. But the point of perch was far from where the fox appeared. The grass not being tall enough to conceal a kill, I feel the eagle would have remained on the same patch to eat the kill, after chasing away the fox. But we saw the Bonelli’s flying to another part of the sanctuary. The fox managed to escape in the first attempt, after being flogged by the implacable raptor. The next attack was more ferocious than the first. The eagle, with no delay and hesitation, tried to hit the fox. The fox looked utterly clueless. After sensing the danger to its life, the fox immediately made a quick dive and jump to escape into the den and disappeared from the scene. The surprise attack on the fox intensified my curiosity, as a wildlife enthusiast. Undoubtedly, the openness of the habitat determined the eagle’s hunt. Now, did the eagle try to kill or chase the fox? Second impression Based on the observations made by Humayun and Phani Raavi, I cross-checked the photographs once again and noticed the following aspects, which differ from my first impression: 1. The eagle swooped down to the ground and almost hit the fox. The fox escaped and stood at a distance from the eagle. The eagle, after missing a chance, didn’t display eagerness to attack immediately. Did the eagle intend to just chase away the fox? 2. The fox stared at the eagle and did not try to run away, which indicates the animal was not expecting an attack. The fox, at this stage, would have started to think about its next move. The eagle was also waiting to launch the next powerful attack. Large wings, powered by the merciless instinct of the eagle, tried to knock down the fox. In the scene, where a battle was fought for survival, the fox relied on its strength of dominance over the area. If the fox had panicked, it could have easily fallen prey to the hunting eagle. First impression Some experts, like the veteran birder from BSAP, Humayun Taher, opined that the eagle was not trying to kill the fox, but was chasing the fox away, either to save a fallen prey, or its nest. I cannot rule out Humayun’s observation. A doubt arose as to whether Bonelli’s eagles kill foxes for food. A quick research on the internet revealed that Bonelli’s eagles do indeed kill foxes. Sabyasachi Patra, a well-known wildlife filmmaker (www.indiawilds.com) has mentioned one incident that involved Eastern Imperial Eagle killing a desert fox. The eagles are different, but the instincts remain the same. Foxes and wolves also form the diet of the Bonelli’s eagles (refer http://www.oiseaux-birds.com/card-bonelli-eagle.html). 4

If the eagle’s intention was to kill the fox, then it would have directly pounced on the animal with all might and killer intention. Why would the eagle wait and launch the attack a bit later? Is this kind of ‘wait and attack’ part of the wild? The moment the Bonelli’s chased the fox, my instincts conveyed it as a hunt. A few photographs also convey that the eagle chased the fox. The team left the spot immediately and further probe into the event didn’t occur, which is much needed for a birdwatcher, and which possibly may have provided more relevant information. 3. The eagle decided to hit, or maybe chase away, the fox, and the fox escaped. The eagle then landed again after clearly communicating its intention. 4. In the last stage, the final attack looked wild and dangerous, as the eagle almost knocked the fox, though the fox escaped. Anyway, whether it was a chase or a hunt, the Bonelli’s showed its strength, supremacy and uncompromising character, whereas the fox displayed its clever thinking. Smartness eventually prevailed over the brutality. *** Trip Report: Fox Sagar, Hyderabad, 23rd July 2017 Vinit Nair Painted Stork, Lesser Whistling-duck, Glossy Ibis and Spot-billed Duck (Photo: Vinit Nair) It was a wonderful morning and I was looking forward to join the BSAP group for an exciting day of birding. I reached Panjagutta Circle at 6:00AM, where I met Aasheesh and Surekha. After the introductions, we headed out to Suchitra Circle, where we met the rest of the group. Since we intended to cover two lakes – Fox Sagar and Shamirpet Lake backwaters, we started without much delay. Fox Sagar is locally known as Kolla Cheruvu. The interesting thing about such trips is that you learn so many amazing facts about places that you never knew existed. I was intrigued by the name ‘Fox Sagar’, and after some enquiring, I learnt that the Nizam had constructed a dam on the lake naming it Fox Sagar. In 1897, a pump house was built on the bund, in characteristic Nizam architecture. Red-wattled Lapwing (Photo: Vinit Nair) We saw a brown streaked bird chasing away the moorhens in the hyacinth-covered lake. The photographers stormed into action to take shots of the bird, which was difficult, considering it was hidden in the hyacinth. However, after some initial attempts, we managed to capture good record shots of the bird. Excitedly, we reviewed the shots and exchanged thoughts and theories on what the bird was; some suggested it could be a juvenile moorhen, others a juvenile lapwing, but none of us were sure. Further investigation revealed it to be the Watercock (Gallicrex cinerea).We had had a rare sighting. A lucky start indeed! As soon as we got there, we were greeted by the traditional calls of the Red-wattled Lapwing (Vanellus indicus); they were warning other birds that birders were around. The lake was covered in water hyacinth which had taken over a considerable portion of the lake, and thus provided a good cover for a pair of Common Moorhens (Gallinula chloropus). 5

Watercock (female) (Photo: Vinit Nair) Indian Grey Hornbill (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Plain Prinia (Photo: Vinit Nair) We then saw many birds like Grey Heron (Ardea cinerea), Plain Prinia (Prinia inornata), Ashy Prinia (Prinia socialis), Rosy Starling (Pastor roseus) and several others. Our tally ended with a total sighting of 30+ birds which was a great start for the day. While returning to our vehicles, Aasheesh identified a pair of Jacobin Cuckoos (Clamator jacobinus) sitting on the topmost branch of a nearby tree. We were then joined by Srikanth and Gokul, who escorted us to Shamirpet Lake. River Tern (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Needless to say, the zoom lenses and binoculars came out of the bags once again, and we got to work. We also spotted some raptors like Black Kite (Milvus migrans) and Short-toed Snake Eagle (Circaetus gallicus) flying high above us. Shortly after this, people started to move around the lake individually or in small groups. Ashy Prinia (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Recharging ourselves with some snacks and tea, and a much needed break, we proceeded towards our next destination, Shamirpet Lake. Srikanth and Gokul took a different route which led to a better section at the back of the lake. As soon as we reached the location, we could see that the lake housed many water birds like Painted Storks (Mycteria leucocephala), Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus), Lesser Whistling-ducks (Dendrocygna javanica), River Terns (Sterna aurantia), Ruddy Shelduck (Tadorna ferruginea) and Little Grebes (Tachybaptus ruficollis). Red-necked Falcon (Photo: Vinit Nair) As I walked towards a mound, I saw a bird perched on a thorny bush that looked like a raptor. I was lucky enough to get some decent shots of the bird. Unsure of the identity of the beautiful bird, I took the pictures to Srikanth. He immediately identified the bird as a Red-necked Falcon (Falco chicquera). I was thrilled that I could get a shot of this elusive raptor. 6

heavy heart that we returned to the concrete jungle, only to look forward to another weekend with birds. Sykes’s Lark (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) The bevy of larks in the nearby fields, including the Ashycrowned Sparrow Lark (Eremopterix griseus) and the Sykes’s Lark (Galerida deva), was a delightful sight and they played cheerful hosts to our cameras. Asian Pied Starling (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Purple Swamphen (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) As the day went by, the group decided to head back to the city. Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Plain Prinia (Prinia inornata) Plain Prinia adult (L, Inkriyal, Hyderabad, 15-11-2009) and juvenile (R, Inkriyal, Hyderabad, 31-10-2010) Order: Passeriformes Family: Cisticolidae Genus: Prinia Species: P. inornata Size: 13-14 cm tail than in summer. Both sexes are identical. The Sri Lankan race retains its summer plumage, including the shorter tail, all year around. Description & distribution: A small warbler of the Cisticolidae family, the Plain Prinia is a resident breeder in most parts of its range, that extends from Pakistan and India across to south China and south-east Asia. The Plain Prinia is a typical Prinia, with a slender body, longish tail, short, rounded wings with rufous fringes, and strong legs, orange in colour. The face is off-white, with a whitish ear panel and a marked white supercilium. The upperparts in the breeding male are greyish brown, deepening in colour towards the rump. Underparts are whitish buff. The bill is black in breeding birds, and shows a dark upper mandible and pale base to the lower mandible in non-breeding birds. Juvenile birds may have an entirely pale lower mandible. Winter birds show warmer brown upperparts and more buff underparts, and generally have a longer Habitat & behaviour: The Plain Prinia is shy and skulks more often than it ventures out into the open. It is usually found singly or in pairs, in wet lowland grassland, open woodland, scrub forests and occasionally gardens near human habitation. Its diet mainly consists of insects, though it does occasionally take butterflies, dragonflies, beetles etc. The basic call of the Plain Prinia is a monotonous chee chee, while the song is a repetitive tiee-tiet-tiet call. Nesting: The Plain Prinia usually builds its nest on a shrub or in tall grass. The usual clutch consists of 3-6 oval eggs, off-white or cream, with variable brown veins, spots or blotches. Local name: The Plain Prinia is known as ‘phutki’ in Hindi, ‘lota-kun-jitta’ in Telugu, ‘piddi’ in Punjabi and ‘pan fadakfutki’ in Gujarati. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. TRIP REPORT: OSMAN SAGAR, September 1, 2017 Text: Shubha Murti Greater Flamingo (Photo: Krishna Murti) We set out in a convoy of cars and motorbikes from Punjagutta Crossroads to Osman Sagar in the early morning hours of September 17th. It was wonderful to see such a large turnout (close to 30 people), including several first time birders. was noticeably cleaner, being far removed from the hustle and bustle of Hyderabad city. Driving down a small dirt road en route to the lake we saw several Blue-tailed Bee-eaters (Merops philippinus), Green Beeeaters (Merops orientalis), Ashy Prinias (Prinia socialis), House Crows (Corvus splendens), Red-wattled Lapwings (Vanellus indicus), Greater Coucals (Centropus sinensis), etc. It was just an early preview to what lay ahead. After a short break for tea and a second brief stop at a prearranged meeting point near the Outer Ring Road, we reached Osman Sagar. The overcast sky and cool temperature made for a comfortable morning, though the lighting was less than ideal for the photographers in the group. It was pleasantly quiet and the air 1

As we stepped out of our cars and walked up to the lake, someone in the group spotted a lone Greater Flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) at the north end of the lake. We newbies got excited and strained to get a good sighting through our binoculars. Our excitement increased ten-fold when we later came upon a large group of them feeding in the lake at the south end. I presumed they were migratory birds but would later learn during the debriefing that the Greater Flamingos have been residents in Osman Sagar since summer and have maintained an extended presence in this area over the past 3 or 4 years. Kentish Plover (Photo: Krishna Murti) Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Plain Prinia (Photo: Krishna Murti) Looking out into the water, we spotted many shorebirds including Eurasian Coots (Fulica atra), a Grey Heron (Ardea cinerea) and Little Cormorants (Phalacrocorax niger). Flying overhead from time to time were Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus), Indian Spot-billed Ducks (Anas poecilorhyncha), and several other birds, including a Pied Kingfisher (Ceryle rudis). Oriental Skylark (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Given the large entourage, we naturally separated into smaller, manageable groups and set about exploring the area around the lake. Some of the experienced birders like Anita were happy to guide the newbies and point out various birds – Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark (Eremopterix griseus), Oriental Skylark (Alauda gulgula), Plain Prinia (Prinia inornata), Kentish Plover (Charadrius alexandrinus), etc. nestled among the brush and marshy grass around the lake. Some of the expert birders ventured out in separate groups and spotted many other species that we missed. Pied Kingfisher (Photo: Krishna Murti) 2

Purple Heron (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Wood Sandpiper (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) A few Whiskered Terns (Chlidonias hybrida) and Common Terns (Sterna hirundo) were resting or preening alongside the River Terns. Numerous Kentish Plovers, with the distinct black bars on either side of the breast, were spotted feeding along the bank near the Terns. Black-winged Stilt (Photo: Krishna Murti) As we headed south to get a better view of the Black-winged Stilts (Himantopus himantopus), Little Stints (Calidris minuta) and Wood Sandpipers (Tringa glareola) feeding frantically in the marshy area, we saw a large flock of River Terns (Sterna aurantia) nesting along the muddy banks of the lake. Sykes’s Lark (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) As the morning grew late, we all gathered for a debriefing and feedback session. Humayun Taher thanked everyone for their participation and noted the number of new birders present. He then solicited input from the group on birds spotted. Fortunately, Sreenivas Nalla had tabulated a fairly complete list which he agreed to update with any omissions and to forward to the team. Humayun then briefly discussed the mystery of the extended presence of the Greater Flamingo in the Hyderabad area. Over the past 3 to 4 years, this migrant has been staying in the area much longer than expected and the presence of juveniles suggest that they may even be breeding nearby (though no direct evidence of local nesting has been observed). Lastly, Humayun asked the group for any feedback. Feedback was generally very positive with a suggestion that, going forward, the group try to get an earlier start to ensure optimal birding. Indian Peafowl (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Baya Weaver (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Following the feedback session, most of the group sat down to enjoy their packed breakfast, and a few of us left early.
