With overall drab plumage, Bulbuls make up for the expected avian aesthetics by strikingly coloured vent feathers, cheek and throat feathers or a pointed crest. With over 140 species found across the vast span of Africa and Asia, India is home to 22 species of Bulbuls with several species found nowhere outside the country. together to forage, this timid and shy bird avoids mixed foraging with other Bulbuls. Can being passive and submissive have evolutionary benefits? That can be a good research problem to address, but for me, I was more interested in the bird’s DNA which holds the window to its millions of years of evolution. I wished to know how this bird evolved. When did this bird evolve and come to occupy its present habitat? Also, how are the different populations connected – do the birds move across regions to breed or are they landlocked within tiny suitable habitats? One such endemic bird is the Yellow-throated Bulbul. This bird is largely found in scrub forests along the slopes of Eastern Ghats and inland hillocks. However, this shy and rare bird is threatened with extinction (IUCN category ‘Vulnerable’) due to habitat destruction. The region where the bird is found is quarried for granite and the habitat is also under the pressure of grazing and lopping. To address these questions, I collected blood/feather samples from the birds and processed the samples and isolated DNA at LaCONES. Birds were caught using mistnets under the vigilance of the Forest Department and the birds were tagged with leg rings which makes the individual identification easier. Several characteristics of this species caught my attention that made it an ideal model for my PhD research. In the past 170 years since its description, only 7 nests have been identified and breeding details published so far. This bird clearly has discrete small populations spread across Peninsular India which makes it more vulnerable to stochastic extinctions. Unlike other congeneric Bulbuls – Red-vented Bulbul, White-browed Bulbul and Red-whiskered Bulbul – which do not hesitate to flock So far, the results show that the Yellow-throated Bulbul does not have a closely related sister species and has a unique evolutionary history. I am working towards delineating the historical time when this species evolved and understanding the geology of Peninsular India back then, which may answer the question why this bird is restricted to Peninsular India. *** 5

Bird of the Month Umesh Mani Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) Northern Pintail Male (L) and Female (R), Chennai, 20 Dec 2014 Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Anas Species: A. acuta Size: 56-74 cm Description & distribution: The Northern Pintail is a fairly large duck of the Anatidae family, with the female being up to 10 cm smaller than the male. It has a wide distribution, breeding across northern parts of Europe and Asia (south till about Poland and Mongolia) and North America (including Canada, Alaska and mid-western United States), and wintering south of its breeding range almost all the way to the Equator, including Panama, northern parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and tropical South Asia. Unusually for a bird with such a large range, there are no recognized sub-species, with the exception of Eaton’s Pintail (A. eatoni), which is often said to be a separate species with its own sub-species, A. e. eatoni of the Kerguelen Islands and A. e. drygalskyi of the Crozet Islands. The Northern Pintail male, in breeding plumage, is unmistakable, with a chocolate-brown head, bluish bill and bright white breast, with the white extending up the sides of the neck. It has attractively-patterned grey-brown-and-black upperparts and sides, with elongated grey feathers with black central stripes laid across the back from the shoulders. The legs are blue-grey. The underside of the tail is black, contrasting with a yellow vent. However, the easiest diagnostic feature is the set of long, pointed central tail feathers, extending up to 10 cm beyond the tail tips. The female is mainly mottled in light brown and buff, with the same characteristic elongated body and tapering tail, though without the pins. The non-breeding male resembles the female, but retains the upperwing pattern and the long grey shoulder feathers. The juvenile is similar to the female, but have less marked mottling and duller brown speculum. Habitat & behaviour: The Northern Pintail is usually found in pairs or flocks, in unwooded wetlands like wet grasslands, the sides of lakes, or tundra, but prefers reed-fringed, vegetationcovered lakes and jheels. While wintering, it also uses other water habitats like sheltered estuaries, brackish marshes and coastal lagoons. In non-breeding season, it is highly gregarious, forming very large mixed flocks along with other species of ducks. It walks well on land, and is also a good swimmer. The flight is very fast, with the wings slightly swept back (unlike other ducks whose wings stick straight out of the body). It shows a speculum in flight, which is black in males and dark brown in females, bordered at the rear with a white so prominent that it is visible even at a distance of around 1,600m. The call of the male Northern Pintail is a soft proop-proop whistle, while the female utters a descending quack, and a low croak when flushed. Its diet is mainly plant material that it picks up by dabbling or upending in shallow water. Its long neck enables it to take food from the bottom of water bodies up to 30 cm deep, which is beyond the reach of other dabbling ducks. The wintering diet is mainly seeds and rhizomes of aquatic plants, occasionally including roots, grain and other seeds in fields; during breeding, it mainly eats invertebrate animals, including aquatic insects, molluscs and crustaceans. Nesting: The breeding season of the Northern Pintail is mainly between May to July. The nest is a shallow depression in open marshy grassland, but often at some distance from water. It is lined with down feathers, rushes and other plant material. The usual clutch consists of 7-12 eggs, cream or pale sea-green with buffish tinge. Birds have also been known to produce a replacement clutch as late as July, in cases where the first clutch is destroyed by predators. Local name: The Northern Pintail is known as ‘Sand’ or ‘Seenkhpar’ in Hindi, ‘Markalian’ in Tamil, ‘Dig hans’ in Bengali and ‘Nejal hans’ or ‘Dighal negi’ in Assamese. *** 6

BAR-TAILED vs BLACK-TAILED GODWIT Srinivas Nalla The two cousins, Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica) and Black-tailed Godwit (Limosa limosa) belong to the family Scolopacidae and genus Limosa. The Black-tailed Godwit has a long bill, neck and legs. During the breeding season, the bill has a yellowish or orange-pink base and dark tip. The legs are dark grey, brown or black. In winter, adult Black-tailed Godwits have a uniform brown-grey breast and upperparts in contrast to the Bar-tailed Godwit's streaked back. The Bar-tailed Godwit breeds in Arctic coasts and tundra, and winters in temperate and tropic regions. Its migration is the longest-known non-stop flight of any bird. For the Black-tailed Godwit, on the other hand, the breeding range extends from Iceland through Europe and areas of central Asia and its wintering region ranges from the Indian Sub-continent to Australia, Western Europe and West Africa. The adult Bar-tailed Godwit has blue-grey legs and a slightly upturned bi-coloured bill, pink at the base and black towards the tip. The neck, breast and belly are unbroken brick-red in breeding plumage, and off-white in winter. The back is mottled grey. Bar-tailed Godwit (Breeding) (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) The Bar-tailed Godwit is distinguished from the Black-tailed Godwit by its barred, rather than wholly black tail and a lack of white wing bars. When they are on the ground, it is not so easy to notice the tail pattern and it would be difficult to identify them by referring to the tail pattern; however, the Black-tailed Godwit’s longer bill, legs and neck and its slender body can serve as the diagnostic features. Black-tailed Godwit (Breeding) (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) It can also be noticed that, in flight, only for the Bar-tailed Godwit, the legs project beyond its tail, whereas for the Blacktailed Godwit, the toes and a portion of the legs are also projected beyond the tail. The Black-tailed Godwit’s upper parts are relatively plainer, whereas for a Bar-tailed Godwit, they are heavily patterned. Both the birds have been classified as Near Threatened in the IUCN Red List. Their population, in recent times, is found rapidly decreasing owing to changes in agriculture practices. Black-tailed Godwit (Non-breeding) (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) *** THE PEN & THE BINOCULAR (part-3) Humayun Taher Ananthagiri Hills in Vikarabad was about the farthest destination for the members of the BSAP in the early days. The drive was long (more than 80 km) and the area was so interesting that we seldom spent less than five to six hours in birding. Then a hot lunch at the old PWD guest house on the hill and back home. Consequently, it was always a full day trip and we hardly ever returned before sundown. This trip was special for me; because I had recently been presented with a new “modern” pair of binoculars and I was proudly flaunting it: a brand new “Crown” 7x35! It certainly helped to get a better look at the elusive little critters that we encountered during the trip. 7

In those days, Ananthagiri was very different from what it is today. To begin with, the massive edifice of the Anantha Padmanabha Swamy Temple had not even been conceived. The deity was represented by a small stone, painted red, with a small alcove built over it, and presided over by a venerable ancient, dressed in raiment that had once been ochre coloured. He sat there, telling his beads and occasionally smiling at the gambols of the Bonnet Macaques as they played around beside him. An occasional patient from the nearby TB Sanatorium sometimes stopped to make obeisance and deposit his token offering of a flower or two to the deity, and the old man would nod complacently and mutter a prayer for the devout offeror. There were no other habitations here except for the largely deserted old PWD bungalow, which was a most quaint building and, though old, was well-maintained. I always used to love this elegant structure; it was positioned in the best possible place and caught the breeze from different directions. The large and sprawling veranda running around the house was always delightfully cool and refreshing, even during the summer months. Our current trip however, was in the cooler month of November; the date being the 20th of November, 1983! having been once recorded at a place called Gundala, which is close to a small village called Chevalla on the Vikarabad road. Since we had to pass this way on our return, we decided to make a short detour to the Gundala Village and perhaps interview some of the local inhabitants about the presence (or otherwise) of this interesting bird. Rollapadu, in those days, had not yet reached its present height of popularity, so the possible presence of the GIB so close to Hyderabad would indeed be a fine report to make to the scientific savants of Indian Ornithology. So to Gundala Village we went, and found it somewhat bereft of people. It was late afternoon and probably most of the village folk were out tilling the fields. Passing through the village, we at length espied a species of tea stall where sat several greybeards engaged in desultory conversation. We stopped the jeeps and got down and instantly caused a small sensation! Picture to yourself a very serviceable looking jeep, crammed to bursting point with about 8 young fellows, clad mostly in jungle-camouflage raiment, and led by a hefty gentleman, similarly clothed: add that to the fact that of late there had been considerable Naxalite activity in this area, and it is not to be wondered that all the ancients present would have been prepared to take their oath that the much-feared ultras had finally discovered their little village. To this day, I do not know if they ever learned of their error. But the upshot of this unfortunate meeting was that we got precious little co-operation from these old gentlemen. However, (please turn your eyes away Recording Angel), over the genial influence of a pot of palm-wine, tongues were loosened and we got the information we wanted. Bustards had been present in significant numbers in this area many years ago, but it had been long since any had been seen in recent times. The best estimate we got was a possible record from some 8 years back, and that too was a somewhat hazy timeline because none of our informants could keep track of years. Still, it was something gained, and this particular piece of information had a most interesting sequel. But of that, anon! Our birding trips always started along a small track leading down from the PWD bungalow towards heavy forest in a direction diametrically opposite from the valley which we now frequent. This little path led to an area behind the TB Sanatorium and had good forest and tree cover. We had a good trek through the forest, starting about 8.30 in the morning and, by the time we returned to the guest house, it was past lunch-time. The Forest Department staff, in honour of the occasion (the Chief Conservator of Forests Mr. Pushp Kumar was, after all, the president of the BSAP) had organised a gastronomic orgy in the guise of a full three-course luncheon. Our own lunch-boxes augmented this Falstaffian spread, and it was a very jolly bunch of birders who, whilst enjoying the post-prandial chai, paan and cheroots (for those who were so inclined), wrote up the day-list and planned the next trip. Meantime, our society president, Mr. Pushp Kumar, regaled us with stories of Great Indian Bustards Below are the pages of our field notes from this trip… 8

The sequel to this trip and the information about the GIB was that two of us made it our business in later years, to make several trips to this place (on a sturdy Rajdoot 175cc motor-cycle). Although we never saw any Bustard, we learnt a few things. Bustards were called Peddedu Pitta in this area (this name was very localised and not known from other bustard areas. In Rollapadu, for example, the bird was called Batta Meka Pakshi). One farmer that we spoke to also identified Lesser Florican, which were also apparently seen in early days. Notwithstanding the lack of either Bustard or Florican, we did see some very interesting sights. A flock of more than 60 Indian Coursers in one field, a breeding pair of Red-headed Merlins, nests of Ashycrowned Finch Larks and Sykes’s Crested Larks, several roosting Harriers in the long grass-covered fallow fields. Oh yes, there were plenty of sights to make up for the lack of Bustards. Alas, many of these youthful memories have been rudely splintered. None of those ancient institutions now survive. The old PWD bungalow at Ananthagiri has been replaced by the Haritha Tourism Resort, Gundala Village is now almost a part of Chevalla town, and the fallow field where we saw 60 Indian Coursers is now the site of a five-storied apartment complex! All in all, the first trip with the new Crown binoculars, was certainly the beau-ideal of an exciting inauguration! What think, others!? BIRDS AT EDULABAD THROUGH THREE SEASONS Text & Photos: Sita Susarla The Lakshminarayana Lake or the Edulabad Lake is situated in Rangareddy district, Ghatkesar Mandal. We have been visiting this lake regularly since November 2016, and our birding experiences through winter, summer and rainy seasons have been quite interesting. We visited the lake about half a dozen times between November 2016 and August 2017, hoping to see the birdlife during different seasons. We could not do any birding during the visit in November 2016, as the lake was full and reaching almost all the way up to the road. In February 2017, the waters had receded and we were able to access the lake shore. The Little Stints (Calidris minuta), Wood Sandpipers (Tringa glareola), Painted Storks (Mycteria leucocephala), Black-winged Stilts (Himantopus himantopus), Red-naped Ibis (Pseudibis papillosa), and Little Egrets (Egretta garzetta) were seen in moderate numbers. There were two Spotted Redshanks (Tringa erythropus), two Blacktailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) and four Spot-billed Pelicans (Pelecanus philippensis). Spot-billed Pelican The Black-tailed Godwit had begun to develop breeding plumage. On referring to the Grimmett & Inskipp book ‘Birds of the Indian Subcontinent’, we felt that this Godwit was an Eastern Black-tailed Godwit (Limosa limosa melanuroides) with horizontal bars across the belly. 1

By May 2017, the lake had receded a lot. The highlight of this visit was the sighting of Pacific Golden Plovers (Pluvialis fulva) on the lake shore. There were four of them that we observed for a full half hour before they flew away to the other side of the lake. One of them was in complete breeding plumage while the other was still developing it. This Plover was very distinctly different from the other plovers, with a jet-black head and breast, and a golden-yellow back. It also had a continuous white flank line that separated the upperparts and underparts, running from above the eye to the tail. The Grey Plover (Pluvialis squatarola), which we had earlier sighted in Narara Marine National Park, is the one that bears the closest resemblance to this Plover. Eastern Black-tailed Godwit One of the Spotted Redshanks also had breeding plumage, with darkening of the head and neck regions. Two Black-eared Kites (Milvus migrans lineatus) were seen hovering very close to the ground. After some time one of them landed on a rock and sprawled its wings in a bid to bathe them in the morning rays of the sun, while the other perched on a nearby pole. Pacific Golden Plover The other highlight of the day was the sighting of about twenty to twenty-five Eastern Black-tailed Godwits, with a few of them in complete breeding plumage. There were around 47 Red-naped Ibis. A lone Eurasian Spoonbill (Platalea leucorodia) was also spotted. Black-eared Kite A couple of months later, in April 2017, we visited the lake once again to have a glimpse of the winter birds probably in their breeding plumage. There were more than a hundred Little Egrets and a similar number of Black-winged Stilts and a few Great Egrets (Casmerodius albus). There were many Black-tailed Godwits that had developed deeper colors than when we had seen them in February, and it was an amazing sight. There were also about five juvenile Wood Sandpipers. Red-naped Ibis In August 2017, the calls of the Rain Quails (Coturnix coromandelica) welcomed us. However, the froth in the inflowing waters of a stream, and the smell at that location, suggested that it had some pollutants in it. It was a reminder of the deteriorating condition of lakes in Hyderabad. As the stream made its way into the lake, the waters were teeming with Cormorants and Little Egrets. Little Egrets 2

Indian Silverbill Red Avadavat As we continued with birding on a small plateau-like area near the lake, flocks of Indian Silverbills (Euodice malabarica) and Red Avadavats (Amandava amandava) were sighted resting on dried twigs. Just then a loud call of the Rain Quail was heard and a few feet ahead we saw it flying away. They had been calling all day; there must have been at least four of them calling from different areas around us. All in all, Edulabad has been a very productive location for us, and we plan to keep visiting as often as we can. *** Editor’s Note: We bring you two different write-ups on the field trip to Himayat Sagar, written by two of our young members. Bird of the Month Umesh Mani Garganey (Anas querquedula) Garganey Male (L) and Female (R) (Chennai, March 19, 2017) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Anas Species: A. querquedula Size: 37-41 cm Description & distribution: The Garganey is a small dabbling duck with a fairly wide distribution, breeding across large parts of Europe and western Asia; in winter, though, the entire population moves to South Africa, Australia, or the Indian subcontinent, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. The Garganey male is unmistakable, with a pinkish-brown whitespeckled head having pronounced white broad eyebrows extending down the sides of the neck. The brown breast stands out in contrast with bluish-grey flanks, wings and shoulders. The female is similar to, and can be confused with, the female of the Common Teal (Anas crecca) but is paler, has a more patterned head, with a more prominent pale supercilium, whitish loral spot, a pale line separating the dark eye-stripe from a dark cheek-bar, and a whiter throat (rather than brown-speckled, as in the female Common Teal). It also tends to shake its head more frequently while dabbling. In flight, the Garganey shows a distinct white belly, blue-grey forewing, and a broad white trailing edge to the wings; the speculum is also very indistinct in comparison to that of the Common Teal. The eclipse male is similar to the female, but with the upperwing pattern of the breeding male. Habitat & behaviour: The Garganey is usually found in large mixed flocks along with Northern Pintails, Northern Shovelers, Common Teals, and other ducks, in freshwater wetlands, coastal lagoons, grassy jheels, marshes, reservoirs and lakes. It is usually shy and keeps to emergent vegetation, and does not venture out much on open water. One of the earliest migrants, along with the Common Teal, it starts arriving by August. The Garganey is very fast on the wing, and can also take off very quickly from the water with a fast, twisting wader-like flight. Its diet is mainly vegetarian, including grain, seeds, tender rice shoots, marsh plants and other aquatic vegetation. During the breeding season, however, it shifts to aquatic invertebrates like crustaceans and molluscs, insects and their larvae or pupae, worms, leeches, tadpoles, small fish and small amphibians. Unlike other dabbling ducks, it does not ‘up-end’ much, generally preferring to feed by skimming, or by foraging on the edges of the water. The male utters a distinctive cracking mating call, while the female usually restricts herself to a feeble quack. Nesting: The breeding season of the Garganey is mainly between May to June in the Palearctic region (northern Europe to eastern Siberia). The nest is a depression in the grass in wet meadows, lined with down feathers and sometimes with fine grass or other plant material. The usual clutch consists of 6-12 eggs, buffy white with a glossy texture. Local name: The Garganey is known as ‘Chaita’,‘Kheera’ or ‘Patari’ in Hindi,‘Ghila hans’ in Assamese, ‘Kardio’ in Gujarati and ‘Surit angouba’ (i.e. ‘white teal’) in Manipuri. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. RENDEZVOUS WITH THE AMUR FALCONS Doyang Reservoir & Pangti Village, Nagaland, October 2017 Yella Prakash Rao Amur Falcons This visit had been on my mind ever since I watched the video titled ‘The Race to Save the Amur Falcon’ by Conservation India. A recent news paper report confirming the arrival of Amur Falcons at Doyang Reservoir on October 13, 2017 was the trigger point and had me working out the finer details for this important event. We set out from Dimapur post lunch on October 28, 2017 and drove through Kohima and Wokha to reach Pangti village located on the edge of the Doyang Reservoir. We retired for the night at the residence of Mr Mhonjan, one of the homestays earmarked for visitors. A boatman-cum-guide Mr Lipithung met us at 3.30AM on the D-Day to drive us to the roosting point. On reaching the roosting site at around 4.30AM, we saw silhouettes of the falcons milling around the trees. As the sun got brighter, it was truly enchanting to see thousands of Amur Falcons taking to the skies and flying all around us. We spent the next four hours or so admiring this spectacle and enjoying their presence all around us. The birds were first sighted in 2001 and, thereafter, kept growing in numbers, probably attracted by the abundant food reserves created as the dam filled up towards completion of the project in 2010. Owing to lack of awareness of conservation of wild life, the villagers, who are hunters by tradition, began to hunt the birds as a delicacy. By 2006, this had gone commercial and these birds were trapped in large numbers and traded in nearby towns. As news of this massacre spread to rest of India and the world, urgent measures were put in place to preserve these birds and the efforts of all agencies involved bore fruit. I was glad to see the same hunters become protectors of these migrants. A local body called the Amur Falcon Roosting Area Union (AFRAU) was formed to protect these birds every season. This is by far one of the greatest success stories in conservation of wild life in India!

In 2013 a scientific team satellite tagged three birds and named them Pangti, Wokha and Naga to collect data to understand these birds and their journey to Southern Africa. The bird named Pangti returned the following year to roost again at the Duyong Reservoir. A total of 8 birds have been tagged so far of which one female falcon named Longleng is still active. This bird, after having roosted in Manipur, set out on November 13, 2017 and reached Somalia on November 17, 2017, covering almost 5000km in 5 days. As on December 4, 2017 it was found in Central Tanzania. A complete trip profile and migration routes taken by these birds can be found on www.satellitetracking.eu As per the reports of the President of the Amur Falcon Roosting Area Union, Mr N Thungbemo Shitri, the birds have been seen roosting at Longleng, Hakhizhe and Phom areas in Nagaland in addition to Duyong Reservoir. They have been found in large numbers in Manipur and Meghalaya too. The last batch left Duyong reservoir on November 26, 2017. Having changed dollars to the Tanzanian Shilling, we boarded our bus and drove to Meserani Snake Park beside Maasai Cultural Museum at Arusha. The Maasai are a NiloHamatic ethnic group. The Museum guide told us about the Shuka, a colourful blanket-like garment, where red represents blood and blue represents the sky. Maasai women wear large flat-beaded necklaces and very long elaborate ear ornaments. Speckled Mousebirds, Collared Dove and Guineafowl were seen in the open. We had the experience of wearing a live snake as a necklace. Finally, we moved to the Arusha Backpackers Hotel to end the day. We were all very excited in anticipation of see the Big Five of Tanzania: Lion, Leopard, Rhino, Elephant and Cape Buffalo. The term ‘Big Five’ was coined by big-game hunters not due to the size of the animals, but because they are the five most difficult animals to hunt on foot in Africa. During our trip, we were lucky enough to see all except the Leopard; however, we saw the Cheetah with its antelope prey. We learned that in the Maasai culture, both boys and girls go through circumcision to mark the transition from childhood to adulthood. There is also a practice of drawing cow blood from the neck while the cow is alive; the Maasai believe that drinking of cow blood makes the body stronger and warmer. The next day, October 11, while having breakfast at the rooftop of the hotel, we spotted the Speckled Pigeon on the opposite roof. Then we headed to Tarangire National Park; en route we saw several birds with spectacular colours. Reaching around noon, we sat under the Baobab tree for lunch. The Baobab tree looks dry from outside, but actually, just beneath the bark of the tree is a vital resource of survival in Africa. We were very much excited to see the wild in front of our eyes. We passed several Maasai villages en route to Serengeti during the later part of the tour. At one model village, we got the opportunity to dance the Hop dance with the Maasai. We observed that they keep their cattle in the middle of the village with a barricade made of Acacia sticks, to protect them from the wild animals, but their houses do not have any barricade from the wild. The Maasai masks are very interesting, with carved of big animals like elephant, giraffe, zebra, buffalo, lion, leopard etc. On the whole, it is a very interesting culture. We noticed a flag in the middle of the forest, which our guide Mike told us was meant to capture the tsetse fly. We had expected encounters with mosquitos and bugs, and were prepared with mosquito repellent, but had never imagined that flies could bite! We too got bitten by the tsetse fly, and the itching effect of the bite continued even after 10 days. Reaching the Meserani Snake Park, we saw Black and Green Mambas, Red Spitting Cobra, Spotted Eagle Owl, Barn Owl, White-backed Vulture etc in the enclosures. Crocodiles, 2

The next day, October 13, we enjoyed the sunrise from the view point of the hotel, where we also had our breakfast. Here we saw several weavers along with their nests in the yellow-barked acacia. I was astonished to see the Pied Crow flying very high. Then it was time to bid good-bye to Panorama Igloo. We were now ready to move to the most exciting part of the tour: Serengeti camping. Mike pointed out a Cheetah with its cub, resting after having hunted an antelope. Moving towards Tarangire River viewpoint, we saw two lionesses resting under the shade of a tree. On the bank of the river, we saw several Wildebeest, as well as a few Blacksmith Lapwings, and a family of baboons. In the park, we saw elephants, a water buck and black-backed jackals. We also saw many birds: Grey-headed (Chestnut-bellied) Kingfisher, Von der Decken's Hornbill, Hadada Ibis, Go-awaybird, Widow Bird, White-headed Buffalo Weaver, Tanzanian Red-billed Hornbill, Laughing Dove, Crowned Plover, Southern Ground Hornbill, White-bellied Bustard, Fischer's Lovebird, Little Bee-eater etc. Before entering the Serengeti National Park, we needed to ensure that our vehicles were reliable; hence all our vehicles were thoroughly checked in the garage and repaired. Soon, we were in front of the gate of Ngorongoro Conservation Area. We were very excited. Mosses hanging from the trees; white, violet and yellow wild flowers all around; rich greenery provided by Nature soothed our eyes. We were welcomed by the Giraffes, and we also saw mating ostriches. We reached the Ngorogoro view point: Vast crater, the natural wonder was in front of us. That night, we stayed at the Hotel Panorama Igloo, where we had to use torches for moving around. During dinner we enjoyed some African music with dancers and acrobats. They made music using the Hakuna Matata, which was made of bamboo and sounded like a piano, some big drums, and even simple tin sheets. Reaching Serengeti, I felt that I was standing on a big disk, and understood that the name Serengeti ('endless plains') was perfectly matched with the landscape. The next day, at the Lake Manyara National Park, we saw the wild mango tree with white flowers, which are favoured by the Blue Monkey. One elephant was eating the dry bush. We saw some red-barked and yellow-barked acacia trees. The Germans earlier called the yellow-barked acacia trees as Yellow Fever trees, because they thought that these trees were the cause of yellow fever. Later on, it was proven otherwise, but the name remained. We saw an Eastern (pale) Chanting Goshawk sitting on a stone. Several Tawny Eagles with their nests were seen on the acacia trees. Helmeted Guineafowl were wandering around. An Elephants’ family, with a baby elephant, was spectacular. One Giraffe was standing alone, and a Cheetah was peeping out from the grass. Bird of the Month Umesh Mani Ferruginous Duck (Aythya nyroca) Ferruginous Duck (Kaddam, January 24, 2016) (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Aythya Species: A. nyroca Size: 38-42cm Description & distribution: The Ferruginous Duck, also known as Ferruginous Pochard, Common White-eye or White-eyed Pochard, is a medium-sized diving duck from Eurasia. The breeding male is unmistakable, showing a rich chestnut head, neck and breast, with contrasting pure white undertail coverts, and a white iris. The females are duller and browner than the males, but have a dark iris. The white belly, almost completely white underwings and a conspicuous white wing-bar are visible in flight. The eclipse male is similar to the female, but has brighter chestnut on head and breast, and has a white iris. It breeds from Iberia (south-west corner of Europe) and the Maghreb (northern parts of Africa) south to Arabia and east to western Mongolia, Kashmir and Ladakh. It winters in the Mediterranean Basin, the Black Sea and parts of sub-Saharan Africa; eastern birds winter in south and south-east Asia, including Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Maldives. Habitat & behaviour: The Ferruginous Duck, although less gregarious than other Aythya species, is usually found in large mixed flocks along with other diving ducks like Tufted Ducks and Common Pochards, in coastal lagoons, and in shallow freshwater (and occasionally saline or brackish) pools and irrigation tanks that are rich in submerged or floating aquatic vegetation, with dense stands of emergent vegetation on the fringes. In coastal areas, it prefers to stay out of reach of the surf. It is usually shy; it spends the day resting in the middle of water bodies, away from human interference, and approaches shore or moves to inundated inland paddy fields to feed mainly after dusk or at night. Its diet consists mainly of aquatic plants and some molluscs, aquatic insects and small fish. Feeding is usually by diving though it may occasionally upend for food. Its flight is swift. The call is a harsh koor-ker-ker. Nesting: The Ferruginous Duck generally breeds between May to June; the nest is a pad of reeds or rushes lined with finer grasses and a thick layer of down feathers, built among reeds close to water. The usual clutch consists of 6-10 pale buff eggs. Local name: The Ferruginous Duck is known as ‘Kurchiya’ or ‘Burar mada’ in Hindi, ‘Tamni’ in Gujarati, ‘Lal bigri’ or ‘Bhutihans’ in Bengali and ‘Kali muri’ in Assamese. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. MANGA: PLANTS IN THE LIFE OF BIRDS Dr. (Mrs.) V.A. Manga, Life Member of BSAP, is a retired Associate Professor, Bhavan's New Science College, Hyderabad. After retirement, she took to her hobby of bird-watching and bird photography as a full-time occupation. As we know, birds depend on plants for food, shelter and their very survival. Trip Report – Narsapur, January 21, 2018 Text and Photos: Shilka Chaudhari White-breasted Kingfisher The new year started on a cheerful note with a birding trip to Narsapur Forest. We (my father and I) met the other birders (around 12 of them) at Dundigal Air Force Academy gate for a cup of hot tea on the cold morning before heading to our destination. We planned to cover both the forest and the lake in our trip. Located 45km north of Hyderabad in the Medak district, the forest spreads between Gummadidala and Narsapur towns. It spans over 30 sq.km. and is blessed with diverse flora and fauna. On our way, I was quite surprised by the barrel of monkeys on the roadside, which seemed to be used to offerings by passersby. As we were driving, we suddenly noticed an Indian Grey Hornbill (Ocyceros birostris) in flight. On reaching the forest and parking our vehicles, we were greeted by the call of the White-browed Bulbul (Pycnonotus luteolus), as informed by our birding expert Shafaat Ulla saab. Heading inside, a few birders spotted the Plum-headed Parakeet (Psittacula cyanocephala) and a Long-tailed Shrike (Lanius schach).

Rosy Starling Brahminy Starling Some of the birders had already reached the lake and made a note of lots of water birds, especially three different kinds of ducks – Northern Pintails (Anas acuta), Spot-billed Ducks (Anas poecilorhyncha) and Lesser Whistling-ducks (Dendrocygna javanica). The Cotton Pygmy-goose (Nettapus coromandelianus) deserves a special mention. Indian Moorhens (Gallinula chloropus), Common Snipes (Gallinago gallinago), Great Egrets (Casmerodius albus) and Bronze-winged Jacana (Metopidius indicus) were also seen around in the lake. On our way towards the marshy land, we came across some common species like Brahminy Starlings (Sturnia pagodarum), Red Avadavat (Amandava amandava), Oriental Magpie Robin (Copsychus saularis) and some Drongos. We spotted a flock of Oriental White-eyes (Zosterops palpebrosus) chirping in the reed, and Green Bee-eaters (Merops orientalis) flying around. On our first stop, the marsh land covered in reeds and grass, we spotted a Common Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis). It was a pretty sight! The other notable sightings around the water body were the White-breasted Kingfisher (Halcyon smirnensis) and Baya Weaver (Ploceus philippinus). Our final sighting was of a Eurasian Marsh Harrier (Circus aeruginosus) hovering around the water for a good catch. The trip was concluded with a hearty breakfast, and drafting a list of our findings. We had seen close to 38 species. The highlight of the trip was the Clamorous Reed Warbler with the sharp call saying, ‘Look at me, I’m here’! Moving further down the path, a distinct call caught the attention of some of the birders. The sighting of the bird in the reeds, which was almost the size of a Babbler, led Shafaat Ulla saab to refer his book and identify it as a Clamorous Reed Warbler (Acrocephalus stentoreus). Reconnecting with nature in a pollution-free environment was indeed a good way to start a brand new year. It was a good edition of Sunday Times! The call of this warbler was quite sharp. On the other side, a few birders were trying to identify the bird on the ground close to a tree as to whether it was a Pipit or a Lark. After taking a few snaps, referring to books and the following lengthy discussion, it was concluded that the little bird was a Singing Bushlark (Mirafra cantillans) and not a Paddyfield Pipit as thought earlier. Again, I was lucky enough to spot the Common Hoopoe (Upupa epops) close by. They happen to be one of my favourites. As we are heading towards the lake, we noticed a flock of Rosy Starlings (Pastor roseus) on one side, and a lone Painted Stork (Mycteria leucocephala) perched on top of a tree on the other side of the path. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Tufted Duck (Aythya fuligula) Tufted Duck Male (L) and Female (R) (Pulicat, December 24, 2017) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Aythya Species: A. fuligula Size: 40-47 cm Description & distribution: The Tufted Duck, also known as Tufted Pochard, is a small diving duck that breeds across temperate and northern Eurasia, and is a winter visitor to southern and western Europe, southern Asia – including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, though rare in Sri Lanka – and even, occasionally, coastal United States and Canada. It is also seen almost around the year in most parts of the United Kingdom. It gets its name due to a visible tuft on the rear of the head. The breeding male is completely glossy black except for white flanks, blue-grey bill, and golden-yellow eyes; nonbreeding males are duller, have greyish flanks and a less prominent crest. The adult female is dusky brown with paler brown flanks, and can be confused with the females of other diving ducks, especially the Greater Scaup, due to the similar, though less extensive, white patches around the base of the bill occasionally seen in the Tufted Duck. However, the iris is yellow in the Tufted Duck, unlike the dark iris in the Baer’s and Common Pochards and the Ferruginous Ducks, with whom it can be confused. In flight, both sexes show a broad white band on the trailing edge of the wings is visible. Habitat & behaviour: The Tufted Duck is a fairly gregarious species, and is usually found in mixed flocks along with other diving ducks like Common Pochards, in open waters like coastal lagoons, sheltered ponds, estuaries and tidal bays. Breeding habitat is close to marshes or other waterbodies that have plenty of vegetation that allows the Tufted Duck to build wellconcealed nests. Its diet consists mainly of molluscs, crustaceans, aquatic insects, seeds, roots and some aquatic plants and weeds. It can remain under water for considerable periods of time. Feeding is usually by diving in deep water, though it may occasionally upend for food. Like many other ducks, it may feed at night. Females utter a harsh karr, usually in flight, whereas the males are usually silent, although they give out a soft whistling wit-oo during courtship. Nesting: The Tufted Duck generally breeds between May to early August. The usual clutch consists of 9-10 greenish eggs, laid on the sides of lakes or other small water bodies, in small nests built of available leaves, grasses, reeds and feathers and concealed deep in vegetation. Local name: The Tufted Duck is known as ‘Dubaru’, ‘Ablak’ or ‘Rahwara’ in Hindi, ‘Nalla chiluwa’ in Telugu and ‘Kurungalian’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. KARTHIKEYAN VASUDEVAN: TROPICAL HERPETOFAUNA OF THE MOUNTAINS AND ISLANDS IN INDIA Dr. Karthikeyan Vasudevan, Ph.D., Senior Principal Scientist, CSIR is the head of the Laboratory for the Conservation of Endangered Species (LaCONES), located at Attapur, Hyderabad. Trip Report – Pulicat & Nelapattu, December 2017 Ambika Pradhan Spot-billed Pelican (Photo: Umesh Mani) Day 1: Sullurpet As the sleepy town of Sullurpet was gearing up for the annual ‘Flamingo Festival’, we went there for our Annual Waterfowl Census (AWC). A team of four – Lawrence uncle, Guru, Jayati and I – started from Hyderabad on December 23, 2017, and reached Sullurpet early next day. After a quick couple of hours of sleep, and a hearty breakfast with Umesh and Shivaji who joined us from Chennai, and Naveena who came from Tirupati, we geared up for the day ahead. Starting the count with water bodies around Sullurpet, we first headed to Chinnanna Cheruvu, one of the water bodies we cover every year. Having spotted only few waterbirds like Grey Heron (Ardea cinereal), Little Grebe (Tachybaptus ruficollis) and Eurasian Coot (Fulica atra), we headed to our next location, Peddanna Cheruvu. Although the lake looked empty in the beginning, birds slowly started showing up one after the other.

Fulvous Whistling-duck (Photo: Umesh Mani) We spotted many ducks like Fulvous Whistling-duck (Dendrocygna bicolor), Tufted Duck (Aythya fuligula), Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) and Northern Shoveler (Anas clypeata), in good numbers. The Tufted Ducks, especially, seemed to be more than 150 in number! Brown Shrike (Photo: Umesh Mani) Satisfied with the good numbers, we moved ahead to Minjur Lake. En route, the roads were lined with lush green paddy fields, dotted with Black-headed Ibis (Threskiornis melanocephalus), Little (Egretta garzetta) and Cattle Egrets (Bubulcus ibis) and Asian Openbills (Anastomus oscitans). Tufted Duck (Photo: Umesh Mani) We spotted several other species too, like Little Cormorants (Phalacrocorax niger), Caspian Terns (Hydroprogne caspia) and Brown Shrikes (Lanius cristalus). Asian Openbill (Photo: Umesh Mani) We also spotted many Wood Sandpipers (Tringa glareola) bobbing about occasionally, accompanied by smaller waders like Little Ringed Plover (Charadrius dubius) and Lesser Sand Plover (Charadrius mongolus) probing the shallow waters in the fields. As we reached Minjur, we spotted a few Spot-billed Pelicans (Pelecanus philippensis) and Painted Storks (Mycteria leucocephala). While counting the number of Storks and Pelicans, a big flock of Whiskered (Chlidonias hybrida) and Caspian Terns arrived near the tank. Much to my delight, these terns were hunting very close to where we stood, letting us have a close look at these skilful hunters. Caspian Tern (Photo: Umesh Mani) 2

On the way back from Minjur Lake, as we stopped for another quick scan, we spotted some Whiskered Terns and a few Eurasian Spoonbills (Platalea leucorodia) flying overhead. The day ended on a good note with a sighting of a Spotted Owlet (Athene brama) late in the evening. Day 2: SHAR Road The first day’s count proved to be very fruitful and our ecstatic bunch visited SHAR road in the hope of waders, small and big. Moments after entering the road, a flock of Black-headed Munias (Lonchura malacca) greeted us, as also the mixed flock of Plovers foraging on the either side of the road. The entire stretch was full of waders and ducks, much higher in population compared to the previous year. Setting up the scope along the road for the counts sparked curiosity among many. One young boy, Shreyas was curious enough to make his father accompany us the entire day, and also helped us count Asian Dowitchers (Limnodromus semipalmatus) in the lake! The energetic young boy even persuaded his father to take a PDF copy of a bird field guide from me, so that it would help him in his future birding endeavours. Painted Stork (Photo: Umesh Mani) A little way ahead from Minjur, we encountered a water body having a mixed flock of Northern Shovelers, Eurasian Wigeons (Anas penelope) and Northern Pintails. Further ahead of this flock, was another mixed flock of waders, consisting mainly of Plovers and Sandpipers. Mixed flock of waders (Photo: Gurukumar KR) As all these birds peacefully foraged in the water, a Harrier swooped into action, quickly scanning the lake for its prey. Having seen the raptor, all the ducks took off at once, resulting in a huge cloud of birds! We couldn’t get a good look at the Harrier, but based on what we could see, it seemed to be the Pallid Harrier (Circus macrourus). Asian Dowitcher (Photo: Umesh Mani) As we moved further, we saw an increasing number of mixed flocks of waders consisting of Godwits, Stints, Plovers and Sandpipers. Looking through the scope, I could see Northern Pintails and Flamingos as far as the eye could see! At one point, we came across a big flock of Egrets, including two dark-morph Western Reef Egrets (Egretta gularis). Mixed flock of Egrets (Photo: Umesh Mani) Mixed flock of birds in flight (Photo: Umesh Mani) 3

Red-crested Pochard (Photo: Umesh Mani) Day 3: Irakam Island The day started early with a visit to Irakam Island bordering Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. While travelling by boat to reach the island, a flock of Caspian Terns kept following the boat in the hope of some catch. After a hearty breakfast while soaking in the mild winter sun, we started birding on the island. On reaching the water body, we were greeted by a Eurasian Curlew, walking freely on the shore, not in the least bothered by our presence. Further ahead were a huge flock of Painted Storks and Asian Openbills, along with other waders like Common Redshank, Common Greenshank and Marsh Sandpiper (Tringa stagnatilis). Peregrine Falcon (Photo: Umesh Mani) Another great sighting was a Peregrine Falcon (Falco peregrinus), perched on an electric pylon close to the road. Also present was a lone Eurasian Curlew, which gave us very good views. Eurasian Curlew (Photo: Umesh Mani) Marsh Sandpiper (Photo: Umesh Mani) By the end of the day, we had spotted ducks like Northern Pintail, Northern Shoveler and Eurasian Wigeon (Anas penelope), and many mixed flocks of waders, including Common Redshanks (Tringa totanus), Common Greenshanks (Tringa nebularia), etc, and I just couldn’t wait for the following day to explore more! Garganey (Anas querquedula), Northern Pintail and Common Teal (Anas crecca) too were in good numbers. Of course, we also had the Grey-headed Lapwing (Vanellus cinereus), which we have always had good sightings of on Irakam Island. On finishing Irakam sooner than expected, we decided to go back to SHAR road, to try and identify waders that were previously unidentified. Grey-headed Lapwing (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Indian Roller (Photo: Umesh Mani) 4

Reaching SHAR road before noon proved fruitful as we had the rest of the day to identify waders from the huge mixed flock. Spotting waders from Lawrence uncle’s spotting scope was really advantageous since we could see all the features of the birds up close, which helped in differentiating one wader from the other. That’s how we spotted all the waders we missed out on the second day like Ruff (Philomachus pugnax), Dunlin (Calidris alpina) and Temminck’s Stint (Calidris temminckii). One of the best sightings for me was seeing Eurasian Spoonbills nesting. What an amazing sight it was! Seeing Nelapattu brimming with life after a year of emptiness made me realise how vital wetlands are for these amazing creatures to survive. Day 4: Nelapattu Like the saying, “save the best for the last”, we saved Nelapattu for the last day. On the way to the bund, I could hear herons and pelicans' calls ringing in the air. On reaching the bund, seeing herons, pelicans and egrets nesting in such huge numbers took my breath away! The place which was virtually empty last year, was brimming with life this time around. As we set the scope to count the birds, we couldn’t comprehend where to start from! For as far as I could see, there were flocks of Pelicans, Herons, Openbills, Cormorants and Egrets nesting. Almost every species we spotted, except the Knob-billed Duck (Sarkidiornis melanotos), was either nesting or in the process of building a nest. Eurasian Spoonbill (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Having finished the counts in Nelapattu, we returned to the urban jungle of Hyderabad the next day. Although, we spotted less raptors compared to the previous year, Pulicat threw up many surprises with regard to the water birds and their numbers. Asian Brown Flycatcher vs Brown-breasted Flycatcher Mona Have you ever been in a difficult situation on field while identifying birds which look almost similar? I realized some birds can be REALLY difficult to distinguish from one another, for instance, the Asian Brown Flycatcher and Brown-breasted Flycatcher. Both belong to the Muscicapidae family. Here I have tried to provide some handy pointers that you can make use of while in the field. Brown-Breasted Flycatcher (Muscicapa muttui): Unlike its cousin, this bird is found mostly in the lower levels of trees, usually in open broad-leaved forests. A little larger in size, it is around 14 cm long. The upperparts are olive brown, underparts have a more pronounced brown or grey-brown breast band, and its legs and feet are pale or flesh-coloured. The lower mandible is entirely pale. Like the Asian Brown Flycatcher, it has a conspicuous white eye ring. Order: Passeriformes Family: Muscicapidae Genus: Muscicapa Asian Brown Flycatcher (Muscicapa dauurica): This bird is usually found in open woodland and cultivated areas, and is more of a canopy bird. It is 13 cm long. The upperparts are a little paler, mostly grey with a tinge of brown, and the underparts are pale, with a light grey-brown wash on its breast and flanks. Its bill is mainly black, with a little yellow on the lower mandible. Its legs are grey, and it has a conspicuous white eye ring. Brown-breasted Flycatcher (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Fun Facts:   Muscicapa has a Latin origin, musca meaning ‘to fly’ and capere meaning ‘to catch’. The Brown-breasted Flycatcher is also known as ‘Layard’s Flycatcher’ (named after Layard, the famous ornithologist). Its scientific name Muscicapa muttui is a homage to Layard’s loyal servant, Muttuswamy. Happy identifying! Asian Brown Flycatcher (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) *** 6

Bird of the Month Umesh Mani Eurasian Wigeon (Mareca penelope) Eurasian Wigeon Female (L) and Male (R) (Pulicat, December 24, 2017) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Mareca Species: M. penelope Size: 42-52 cm Description & distribution: The Eurasian Wigeon is a small dabbling duck that breeds in the northernmost reaches of Europe and Asia, and is a winter visitor to southern Asia (including Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka) and Africa and, occasionally, to some parts of the United States, like the southern Appalachians and the Four Corners region in the Southwest. It is also a common winter visitor in Great Britain and Ireland, though not so often in Scotland. The breeding male has a chestnut head with a creamy crown, small, narrow blue-grey bill, brownish pink breast, finely-speckled grey flanks and back, a bright white patch on the closed wings, dark green speculum, grey legs and feet, and black tail-coverts. In flight, broad white shoulder-patches near the leading edge of the wings are conspicuous. The female is generally lighter brown, with a brownish head, breast and flanks, and darker brown upperwings. Both show a white belly and rather pointed tail in flight. The eclipse male is similar to the female, but more rufous on head and breast. Habitat & behaviour: The Eurasian Wigeon is a highly gregarious species outside the breeding season, and is seen in large flocks, often along with other species like Tufted Ducks, Common and Red-crested Pochards, Northern Pintails and others. It prefers open wetlands like open lakes, reservoirs, rivers, shallow grassy jheels, marshes with some vegetation, wet grasslands, tidal creeks and salt-marshes. It is a mixed surface feeder, feeding mainly by grazing on grass shoots, aquatic weeds, and a wide variety of leaves, stems, roots and seeds, on the waterside grasslands and wet paddy-fields; it may also sometimes up-end in shallow water while feeding. It is a strong and swift flier, often among the first to take off and reach heights when a threat is perceived. The call of the male is a shrill, piped whistle wheeooo, uttered in flight as well as when on the ground or in the water. The female, on the other hand, utters a growled rawr. Nesting: The Eurasian Wigeon breeds during the summer months. Several males may compete with each other in courting one female, jostling for position. The breeding display of the male includes lifting the tips of folded wings to expose the white wing patch, raising the head while giving a whistled call and lowering the head to display the buffy crown patch. The nest is a shallow depression in the ground, lined with grass, down or vegetation, under cover of scrub or vegetation near the water. The usual clutch consists of 6-12 off-white or pale buff eggs. Local name: The Eurasian Wigeon is known as ‘Patari’, ‘Peasan’, ‘Pharia’ or ‘Chhota lalsir’ in Hindi, ‘Namam batu’ in Telugu, ‘Mahudi thara’ in Tamil and ‘Wijan’ in Punjabi. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. MANGA: PLANTS IN THE LIFE OF BIRDS Dr. (Mrs.) V.A. Manga, Life Member of BSAP, is a retired Associate Professor, Bhavan's New Science College, Hyderabad. After retirement, she took to her hobby of bird-watching and bird photography as a full-time occupation. As we know, birds depend on plants for food, shelter and their very survival. Their dependence on grains, nectar and fruits is obvious. Similarly, the tree-hole nesters' requirements of wooded areas is apparent. Bird of the Month Umesh Mani Red-crested Pochard (Netta rufina) Red-crested Pochard Female (L) and Male (R) (Pulicat, December 24, 2017) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Netta Species: N. rufina Size: 53-57 cm Description & distribution: The Red-crested Pochard is a large diving duck that breeds in the southern Europe and central Asia, and is a winter visitor to parts of Africa and the Indian subcontinent, where it is seen abundantly in Pakistan and North India, and decreasing east till Assam and south till Chennai – it is not seen further south, or in Sri Lanka – and in smaller numbers in Myanmar. The adult male is distinctive, with a rich chestnut and golden orange head and mop-like crest, bright crimson or pinkish-red bill, black breast and tail, white flanks and light brown upperparts with white wing-mirrors. The female is primarily light brown, with a darker sooty brown back, nape and crown clearly demarcated from white face and neck, yellowishtipped black or dark grey bill, and a whitish speculum. Nonbreeding males are similar to the females, but with pinkish-red bills. Habitat & behaviour: The Red-crested Pochard is a highly gregarious species, and is seen in large flocks, often along with other species like Tufted Ducks, Common Pochards, Northern Pintails and others. It prefers open wetlands like open lakes, shallow jheels, marshes with some vegetation and wet grasslands. Though a diving duck, it is often seen feeding on the surface, dabbling and upending. It feeds mainly on shoots and roots of aquatic plants, molluscs, insects and crustaceans. It is a skittish bird, and keeps silent more often than not. The call of the male is a wheezy veht, while the female utters a series of raspy vrah vrah vrah calls. Nesting: The Red-crested Pochard usually breeds between midApril and early June. The nest is built among vegetation by the lakeside, and the usual clutch consists of 8-12 pale green eggs. Local name: The Red-crested Pochard is known as ‘Lal chonch’ or ‘Lal sir’ in Hindi, ‘Deo hans’ in Assamese, ‘Hero hans’ (for male) or ‘Chobra hans’ (for female) in Bengali, ‘Lal siri pochad’ in Punjabi and ‘Yerra tala chiluva’ in Telugu. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. THE KASHMIR OF ANDHRA PRADESH Trip Report – Lambasingi, October 2017 Text and Photos: Sita Susarla Lambasingi On a pleasant October morning we set out on a visit to Lambasingi, a village in the Eastern Ghats located at a distance of 100km from the coastal city of Visakhapatnam and 3000 feet above sea level. A picturesque location surrounded by hills and green pastures, the hamlet had witnessed snowfall in January 2012 – hence the nickname ‘Kashmir of Andhra Pradesh’. We started off quite early from Visakhapatnam and stopped for breakfast at Narsipatnam, a town that is located at a distance of 30km from Lambasingi and 70km from Visakhapatnam. In the nearby rice fields, we spotted a Tawny Pipit (Anthus campestris), a Paddyfield Pipit (Anthus rufulus), two Blackwinged Kites (Elanus caeruleus), some Cattle (Bubulcus ibis) and Little Egrets (Egretta garzetta) and a couple of Black Drongos (Dicrurus macrocerus).

Narsipatnam After a quick breakfast we began the climb to Lambasingi. Gecko After about an hour of climbing we reached the Lambasingi village. The calls of Common Ioras (Aegithina tiphia) reverberated across the meadows. As we moved through the meadows and hills that were partly hidden by descending clouds, we spotted Green Bee-eaters (Merops orientalis), Oriental White-eyes (Zosterops palpebrosus) and Drongos. Malabar Giant Squirrel We stopped at some very beautiful viewpoints during our climb. At one of these points we sighted a Malabar Giant Squirrel very actively feeding on the forest fruit and seed. As we moved further up a juvenile Crested Serpent Eagle (Spilornis cheela) crossed our path and perched on the branches of a nearby tree. It looked very majestic with the thick foliage spread all around. It is known to feed mainly on snakes and lizards and, therefore, the name. Tricolor Shrike The Tricolor or Black-headed Shrike (Lanius schach tricolor), a subspecies of the Long-tailed Shrike (Lanius schach), was sighted at many places in the village. Crested Serpent Eagle (juvenile) Black-winged Kite While scanning the trees for birds we chanced upon a woodcoloured Gecko. The camouflage was amazing. 2

There were also many Black-winged Kites hovering and flickering the tail without any sidewise movement. A Grey Wagtail (Motacilla cinerea) and a few White-browed Wagtails (Motacilla maderaspatensis) were seen by the side of a nearby stream of water. After a quick lunch under the shade of a tree we resumed birding. A Paddyfield Pipit was seen hopping around and the metallic tuk tuk sound of the Coppersmith Barbet (Megalaima haemacephala) with occasional song of the Asian Koel (Eudynamys scolopaceus) filled the air. As we prepared for the climb down we sighted many Spotted Doves (Stigmatopelia chinensis) along with small Green Bee-eaters sitting on cable lines. We had planned to visit Paderu also, but the darkening skies and imminent rain forced us to wind up for the day. As we climbed down the thundershowers increased, but this did not deter us from stopping to buy a few smoked corn bhuttas. At Narsipatnam the sky cleared and we stopped by a paddy field once again. Here we saw some Common Sandpipers (Actitis hypoleucos), Cormorants and Scaly-breasted Munias (Lonchura punctulata). All in all, it was a great trip. Trip Report – Khichan Bird Sanctuary Text and Photos: Ajit Kumar Mahendra Demoiselle Cranes While planning a trip to Jodhpur recently, I looked up Lonely Planet to see if there were any good birding sites in and around Jodhpur. I came across a paragraph describing the famous Demoiselle Crane wintering spot 140 kms NW of Jodhpur near Khichan, a small village, and decided to include it in our itinerary. The birds were quite comfortable with human company, including a group of noisy kids who joined us out of curiosity. I was so thrilled by the sight of these pretty birds in such large numbers that I captured a few pictures on my mobile and sent them to Shafaatbhai instantly. I wondered how such a large flock could feed in a barren desert. The kids informed me that they fed these birds millets first thing in the morning. Reaching there, we drove down the well-maintained state highway and reached our destination in about 3 hours. On the way we passed Osium, a town located at the edge of the Thar desert that serves as a hub for desert safaris. The drive through the semi-arid terrain was pleasant. One could just experience the desert landscape. En route, we saw a stray Spotted Deer grazing on the sparse vegetation. As per Lonely Planet, 2007, these birds are fed 600 kg of millets per day twice a day. The secret of such a large flock of birds making Khichan their winter home is the human factor – a rare case of human-animal co-existence. On scanning the Internet, more details came to light. The villagers have integrated these avian species into their lives. Some of the songs and legends of the village are about kuraj, the local name for these cranes. Ratanlal, a villager, said that some families even named their children kuraj. He recalls feeding these birds as a young boy before migrating to Mumbai in search of a livelihood. Fate brought him back after 20 years. Now, he organises the daily feeding activity. Because of an assured source of food, the number of birds is increasing every year and so is the expenditure. The villagers depend on donations, so during the off season, Ratanlal travels to Mumbai to collect funds to feed these birds. The taxi drove right to the pond where the cranes gather in large numbers to quench their thirst and just relax or bask in the sun. The villagers have built a platform which reaches into the pond. We could see and photograph the cranes at close quarters. This small village has become quite an attraction. When Shalini and I were driving in, we saw a bus load of tourists coming out after watching the birds. Later two satellite TV broadcasting vans were spotted, probably to shoot a video on this wonderful example of symbiosis. It was a wonderful experience. *** 4

Bird of the Month Umesh Mani Eurasian Curlew (Numenius arquata) Eurasian Curlew (Pulicat, December 24, 2017) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Numenius Species: N. arquata Size: 50-60 cm Description & distribution: Also known as the European, Common or Western Curlew, or as the Whaup (in Scots), the Eurasian Curlew is a large wader of the family Scolopacidae. It breeds across temperate regions of Europe and Asia, like the United Kingdom, Scandinavia, Russia, Kazakhstan, northern Mongolia and north-eastern China, and is the most widespread of the curlews. It is a winter visitor to the coastal regions in Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, the Indian subcontinent, south-east Asia, south-eastern China, Taiwan Japan and South Korea. It is, however, seen throughout the year in milder parts of the United Kingdom. Vagrant birds have been observed far from its normal range, like the USA, Canada, Norway, Denmark, New Zealand and the Bahamas. The only other bird with a similar bill is the Whimbrel, which is smaller, and the bill is shorter and straighter with a kink, unlike the smooth curve of the Curlew. The non-breeding bird is greyer, lacking the buff on the head. The sexes are similar, with the female being bigger and having a slightly longer bill. In flight, its toes extend beyond the tail. The juvenile is more buff on the breast, and the upperparts have some buff streaking and fringes. Habitat & behaviour: Outside the breeding season, the Eurasian Curlew is a highly gregarious species. It is usually seen on the edges of water-bodies like lakes and jheels, flooded agricultural lands, and around cultivated areas, and feeds by probing the wet mud with its long bill while walking along slowly. Due to the differing bill lengths, the males and females forage in different areas. It feeds mainly on small invertebrates, crabs, earthworms, molluscs, spiders, grasshoppers, crickets, lizards, amphibians, and small rodents and fish. It is a skittish bird and moves away on human approach. The call is a loud, rising curloo-oo, while the song consists of a series of long, trilled, bubbling phrases, which is also heard in winter and on passage. The overall plumage of the bird is greyish-brown. Trip Report – ICRISAT, February 25, 2018 Ajit Kumar Mahendra Red-naped Ibis (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) Birding at the International Crop Research Institute for the SemiArid Tropics (ICRISAT) has always been a pleasurable experience for several reasons. It is located in the outskirts of the city and can be reached comfortably, more so on a Sunday morning. There is greenery everywhere with no pollution – air or sound – and it is immaculately clean and boasts of an abundance of avian species, both terrestrial and aquatic. While we see birds everywhere on the campus, there are 3 or 4 lakes that are the best sites to park oneself to feast on nature’s bounty. As usual, we all assembled at the entrance of the campus. After finishing the security formalities and saying hello to all, members and guests, we boarded the ICRISAT bus with our backpacks. All age groups were represented from ‘single digiters’ to yours faithfully at 70+, and all were excited at the prospect of birding in salubrious surroundings. Aasheesh perched himself on the navigator’s seat in the front and looked prim and young in his shorts and shirt.

Little Egrets (Egretta garzetta), the ubiquitous Indian Pond Herons (Ardeola grayii) and Eurasian Coots (Fulica atra) were spotted in the pond or in the vegetation on the banks. A lonely Grey Heron (Ardea cinerea) was seen in the tall grass on the water’s edge. Barn Swallows (Hirundo rustica) and Whitethroated Kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis) on Tacoma Stans branches with their purple flowers were a photographer’s delight. Baya Weaver (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) Being spring time, several trees were in full bloom, the most attractive being Tabebuia Argentea with its spectacular yellow blooms. Our first stop on this pleasant morning was a pond with lots of reeds, an ideal setting for Baya Weavers (Ploceus philippinus), and we were richly rewarded. Several of them were fluttering around. Barn Swallow (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) Black-rumped Flameback (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) On the trees around, we could spot a pair of Black-rumped Flamebacks (Dinopium benghalense), Indian Golden Oriole (Oriolus oriolus), Spotted Owlet (Athene brama) and Rosy Starlings (Pastor roseus). Indian Peafowl (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) Indian Peafowls (Pavo cristatus) were making shrill calls and our deft shutterbugs captured some breathtaking shots of them. Grey Francolins (Francolinus pondicerianus) marked their presence through their distinct call but eluded our sight. Indian Golden Oriole (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) Bar-headed Goose and Darter (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) 2

The largest tank was our second pit stop. A tree on the island in the middle of the lake had a nest with chicks in it. We spotted 4-5 Bar-headed Geese (Anser indicus), a few Pelicans, Cormorants and a pair of Darters (Anhinga melanogaster) perched on some the branches jutting from the water. They made a pretty site as they craned their elegant necks. Being close to the shore they could be seen sans binoculars. A fenced pond was our penultimate stop. Peeping through the fencing, we could see Little Egrets, Eurasian Coots, Purple Swamphen (Porphyrio porphyrio) and Indian Spot-billed Ducks (Anas poecilorhyncha). Spot-billed Duck (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) A pair of juvenile Bronze-winged Jacanas (Metopidius indicus) were foraging in the vegetation on the water’s edge. A Eurasian Marsh Harrier (Circus aeruginosus) landed on a boulder very close to the fence and we could hear the camera shutters whirring incessantly till it took to the wings. Spot-billed Pelican (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) Darter (Photo: Ajit Kumar Mahendra) Marsh Harrier (Photo: Ajit Kumar Mahendra) A pergola provided excellent shade for us to relax and do birding at the same time. Most birders retired to the shade of the trees to do justice to the breakfast they had carried. Sharing made the culinary experience richer. The richest spot in terms of the number of avian species is the lake with 2 islands, which is always the last halt in our birding itinerary at ICRISAT. Spot-billed Pelicans (Pelecanus philippensis) perched on tree tops as Cormorants, drying their wings, perched on the water’s edge. Purple Swamphen (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) Ruddy Shelduck (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) 3

Ruddy Shelducks (Tadorna ferruginea), Indian Spot-billed Ducks, Northern Shovellers (Anas clypeata), Garganey (Anas querquedula), Black-headed Ibis (Threskiornis melanocephalus), etc were spotted in large numbers. Members who had participated in the peafowl census reported many more species during their visit a month earlier. Purple Heron (Photo: Ajit Kumar Mahendra) Garganey (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) We had a continuous flow of snacks in the bus. No wonder I love to limp around in spite of my arthritis – for the sheer pleasure of birding and the wonderful company of fellow birders. Black-headed Ibis with Cormorants (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) While driving back towards the entrance, we suddenly heard shouts of ‘stop, stop’. Some of our birders had spotted an Oriental Honey Buzzard (Pernis ptilorhynchus) perched on a tree. We had a ringside view of this not-so-common raptor before it flew away. Little Cormorant (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) All parted quickly on reaching the gate, having spent the best part of Sunday in the lap of nature. These weekend trips are memorable not just for the excellent birding they offer but also for the excellent company that cuts across all age groups and diverse professions. Long-tailed Shrike (Photo: Barnali Chaudhuri) *** 4

Trip Report – Rollapadu, September 2017 Text and Photos: Sita Susarla Lesser Florican The Great Indian Bustard (Ardeotis nigriceps) and the Lesser Florican (Sypheotides indicus) are the main attractions of Rollapadu Wildlife Sanctuary. Established in the year 1988 for the conservation of these two species, the park is the only habitat in Andhra Pradesh for these birds. Birders visit the sanctuary to see these two species and also the Montagu’s Harrier (Circus pygargus) that visits the park in winters. Having heard about the recent sightings of a Bustard and a Florican in the park, we set out from Hyderabad to see them and the other birds too. It being the month of September, the whole sanctuary was echoing with the calls of the Rain Quails (Coturnix coromandelica). Lesser Florican As we moved around the park, a guide offered to show us the Florican. We agreed instantly and were lucky to find it in the designated location. The Lesser Florican belongs to the bustard family and is endemic to the Indian subcontinent. Come monsoon, the males leap into the air in an elaborate courtship display. We watched these spectacular leaping displays for a long time. Black Buck As we walked across the dry grassland we came across hundreds of Black Buck nibbling at the tall grass. The increase in the Black Buck population was supposed to be one of the reasons for the disappearance of the Bustard and Lesser Florican in the park, the other being cattle grazing. Together they reduced the grass cover which in turn led to reduction in the locusts and grasshoppers that serve as food for the Florican and the Bustard. The Montagu’s Harrier too feeds on grasshoppers. With half the mission accomplished quite early, we began to look around for the Bustard. The guide however did not know of its presence in the park. Slightly disappointed we continued to bird by ourselves. The chirpy Indian Silverbills (Euodice malabarica) were everywhere and so were the Laughing Doves (Stigmatopelia senegalensis). 5

Red Collared Dove At one place we saw the Red Collared Dove (Streptopelia tranquebarica) and Eurasian Collared Dove (Streptopelia decaocto) foraging together on the ground – a beautiful sight. The Grey Francolins (Francolinus pondicerianus) were also present in large numbers. We climbed the watch tower to have a complete view of the park. It was a great sight. Sirkeer Malkoha From the park we now drove to the Alaganur Reservoir behind the sanctuary. Here we saw Streak-throated Swallows (Petrochelidon fluvicola) in plenty, a few River Terns (Sterna aurantia), one Asian Openbill (Anastomus oscitans), and a few Egrets and Herons. Though we could not see the Bustard and the Montagu’s Harrier, we were more than happy to have seen the Florican. It was a dawn to dusk birding and we enjoyed every bit of it. The sanctuary is worth visiting any number of times given its bird activity. Eurasian Collared Dove After having lunch at a nearby hotel we rested at the forest guesthouse till about 3:30PM. Now it was cooler and we could see some activity around us. We sighted a Sirkeer Malkoha (Taccocua leschenaultia) preening its feathers. This was a lifer for us. Brown and rufous in color, it had a cherry red and yellow beak that was slightly hooked. Though a shy bird, we could watch it for quite some time and also take good pictures. A little later we stopped to look at the display of a Red-vented Bulbul (Pycnonotus cafer). As we looked around a brood of Bush Quails emerged from a nearby bush. We just had a glance at them before they disappeared. Streak-throated Swallow The complete list of birds is given below: 6
