Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Whimbrel (Numenius phaeopus) Whimbrel (Pulicat, December 24, 2017) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Numenius Species: N. phaeopus Size: 37-47 cm known as Hudsonian Curlew (Hudson Bay to north-eastern Canada). Habitat & behaviour: Outside the breeding season, the Whimbrel is a highly gregarious species. It is usually seen on the edges of water-bodies like tidal flats, mangrove-lined creeks, lakes and jheels, flooded agricultural lands, and around cultivated areas, and feeds by probing the wet mud with its long bill for small invertebrates, crabs (especially fiddler crabs), molluscs and other similar prey off the surface. It also takes insects, especially butterflies like the Blue Tiger, and berries are an important part of their diet before migration. A skittish bird, it usually moves away on human approach. The call is a 7-9 syllabled rippling whistle tetti-tetti-tetti-tet, which is elongated into a trilling song, and may be heard clearly even during nocturnal migratory flights. Description & distribution: The Whimbrel is a large wader of the family Scolopacidae. It breeds across subarctic North America, Europe (as far south as Scotland) and Asia, and is among the most widespread of the curlews. It is a winter visitor to the coastal regions in Africa, South America, southern parts of North America, and south Asia up to Australasia. The bird is overall greyish-brown, with a back and rump that are white (in N. p. phaeopus and N. p. alboaxillaris) or quite heavily streaked (in the other sub-species). Superficially similar to the Eurasian Curlew, it is, however, smaller in size, and the bill is long (though shorter and straighter than the Curlew’s) and has a kink rather than a smooth curve. It has a central crown stripe and a strongly marked supercilium. The sexes are similar, with the adult female being bigger and having a slightly longer bill. Nesting: The Whimbrel is highly territorial while nesting, and may even attack humans if approached too closely. It usually breeds between April and July. The nest is a shallow scrape on tundra or open moorland. The usual clutch consists of 3-5 buffcoloured eggs speckled with brown. Seven sub-species are recognized: N. p. islandicus (found in Iceland, Ireland and Britain), the nominate N. p. phaeopus (Norway to south-central Siberia), N. p. alboaxillaris (western Kazakhstan to south-western Siberia), N. p. rogachevae (central Siberia), N. p. variegatus (north-eastern Siberia), N. p. rufiventris (Alaska and north-western Canada) and N. p. hudsonicus, also Local name: The Whimbrel is known as ‘Chhota Gounch’ or ‘Chhota gulinda’ in Hindi, ‘Nani khalili’ in Gujarati, ‘Kuthirai malai kottan’ (a name it shares with the Eurasian Curlew) in Tamil and ‘Tetti kokku’ in Malayalam. *** 8

Brief report : Red-vented Bulbul raiding nest of Common Tailorbird Hyderabad, May 2018 Text and Photos: Azam Common Tailorbird nest A few months back at my residence in Banjara Hills, I observed a Common Tailorbird (Orthotomus sutorius) building a nest by binding a fig leaf with soft cotton threads. The soft material that comprised the nest included cotton from our mattresses that had been kept out for sunning! Within a few days they had laid eggs and started incubating. A couple of days later we observed a pair of resident Red-vented Bulbuls (Pycnonotus cafer) start to build their nest. The initial structure was ready in a day or two and made out of neem twigs and coconut fibres from dry coconuts. What I found interesting was that the Bulbuls did not even try to drive away the Tailorbirds but ignored them completely and single-mindedly went for their nest. The Bulbuls went on to raise two chicks – their 3rd successful family from the same spot – and moved on. I am not sure whether the Bulbuls were trying to eliminate competition. They kept ignoring the material that was readily available and chose what was in the Tailorbird’s nest instead. Since then, they have had one more nesting in the same place but I have not seen any soft lining to their nest. They used husk and twigs. One day there was a lot of commotion in the garden. The Tailorbirds were in an agitated state, constantly giving out alarm calls. A few seconds later I saw a Bulbul emerge from the Tailorbird’s nest with some material which it used to line its own nest. The Tailorbirds tried to drive away the Bulbuls who were not deterred and kept making trips to and fro. I tried placing some soft material in the path of the Bulbuls but they did not relent, and in the end the Tailorbird’s nest was completely destroyed and the eggs lay on the ground. I think the attacks had started early in the morning and the damage had been done by the time we noticed what was happening. I have also observed Tailorbird chicks in our garden subsequently – a positive sign that they are still nesting in the area. Note: The above photo was taken from a safe distance and the birds were not disturbed. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Below: Throat dark blue; breast rufous: belly and under tail coverts white washed with buff. ID features – Female: Above: Olive brown tinged with rufous on rump; pale lore’s and eye ring. Below: Throat buff; breast brownish yellow, rest underparts white. Field Identification: Several other flycatchers, particularly females, have a rufous breast and are very similar. They may be eliminated as follows: Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (Cyornis tickelliae) has blueish tail. Snowy-browed Flycatcher (Ficedula hyperythra), Brooks’s Flycatcher (Cyornis poliogenys) and Sapphire Flycatcher (Ficedula sapphira) may have more or less yellowish-brown belly but not white. ECOLOGY OF THE GREY PELICAN AT TELINEELAPURAM Report – Indoor Meeting, July 12, 2018 Surekha Aitabathula Photo: Amardeep Singh Research Associate at the Prof Jayashankar Telangana State Agricultural University and a Master’s Degree holder in Environmental Biotechnology from JNTUH, Sravan is an erudite scholar as well as an avid birder. He is in the final stages of submission of his thesis on "Resources utilised by the Grey Pelican and the conservation measures which could be implemented for the species sustainability." His thesis is geographically specific to Telineelapuram village in Tekkali Mandal of Srikakulam District in Andhra Pradesh. Sravan spoke to our members on July 12, 2018 about the location of his research being selected for its importance as a nesting site of the near threatened Grey Pelican (Pelecanus philippensis). Speaking about the Grey Pelicans, Sravan explained that Pelicans nest on low trees near wetlands and sometimes near human habitation. Sharing more details, Sravan said that Tamarind trees are a favourite for nesting, as these strong trees can withstand the weight of very closely built nests of the Pelicans. Grey Pelicans are colonial breeders and often breed in the company of other water birds like Painted Storks. The nest, built by the male, is a thick platform of twigs. The clutch size is three to four chalky white eggs that turn a dirty off-white as they age. Eggs hatch in 30 to 33 days. Interestingly the Pelican does not hatch the eggs under its body – it hatches by tucking them under its webbed feet. The young stay near the nest for three to five months after which they take one straight flight out. When heading to their roosts they fly in formation in small groups with steady flapping. During the hot part of the day they are known to soar on thermals and they cool themselves using gular fluttering and panting. The tip of the bill is yellowish orange, hence the other name Spot-billed Pelican. It catches fish in its huge pouched bill while swimming at the surface. Sometimes Pelicans indulge in group hunting by lining up together and driving the fish towards the shallows. The wingspan is a massive 1.8 to 3.5 metres; the adult bird is four feet tall, tipping the scales at 6 kg. A near threatened species, Grey Pelican is protected by law in India, Sri Lanka, China, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos. *** 3

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Cotton Pygmy-goose (Nettapus coromandelianus) Cotton Pygmy-goose (Chennai, January 27, 2018) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Nettapus Species: N. coromandelianus Size: 26-37 cm Description & distribution: The Cotton Pygmy-goose, also known as the Cotton Teal, is the smallest of the wild ducks seen in India, and individuals on the lower end of the size range are among the smallest waterfowl in the world. In the male, the plumage is predominantly white, with the head glossy black on top. The neck and underparts are also white, and it has a prominent black collar and breast-band, and broad white wingbar, which is clearly visible in flight, markedly contrasting with the metallic greenish wings. The goose-like bill is short and deep at the base. The female is paler and more brownish, has a dark eye-stripe, and lacks the collar and wing-bar, though its wings have a white trailing edge; the non-breeding male also resembles the female, except for the white wing-bar. It is resident, and sometimes locally migratory, across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Maldives. Habitat & behaviour: The Cotton Pygmy-goose is usually seen in small to mid-sized flocks, on all kinds of inland water bodies – village tanks, jheels, lakes, ponds, channels, shallow lagoons, inundated paddy fields, etc. It can become very tame when it is undisturbed and gets used to human presence – for instance, in village tanks. It has a fast flight and utters a clucking call while flying. It feeds mainly by foraging in wet grasslands or marshes, and its diet consists mainly of vegetable matter like aquatic plants and leaves, though it may also occasionally take insects, crustaceans etc. It is often seen perching on trees. Nesting: The Cotton Pygmy-goose breeds mainly between July and September. The nest is a natural hollow in a tree-trunk, in or near water, and is usually lined with grass, reeds, feathers or other soft material. The usual clutch consists of 6-12 ivory-white eggs. Local name: The Cotton Pygmy-goose is known as ‘Girri’, ‘Girria’ or ‘Girja’ in Hindi, ‘Dudu chuluva’ in Telugu, ‘Kaanuk hans’ in Sanskrit and ‘Kannadi cheravi’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. The lap in question belongs to the Bannerghatta National Park (BNP) which is a beautiful lung space right in the middle of an urban labyrinth. Declared a National Park in 1974, Bannerghatta encompasses 13 Reserve Forests, covering an area of 260 sq km. Tucked into the northernmost tip of Eastern Ghats in Karnataka, BNP is contiguous in the Southeast with the North Cauvery Wildlife Sanctuary. BNP is the last large surviving scrub forest, that supports an annual population of 100 to 150 Asian Elephants, apart from photographic records of a Tiger, Dholes, Sloth Bears, Leopards and Honey Badger which were reported in 2015. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Alexandrine Parakeet (Psittacula eupatria) Alexandrine Parakeet (Bairluti, Andhra Pradesh, October 22, 2016) (Photo: Sudhir Moorti) Order: Psittaciformes Family: Psittaculidae Genus: Psittacula Species: P. eupatria Size: 56-72 cm Description & distribution: The Alexandrine Parakeet is one of the larger members of the Psittacidae family. It is named after Alexander the Great, who is said to have carried many birds from Punjab to various parts of Europe and the Mediterranean. It was first described in 1760 by French zoologist Mathurin Jacques Brisson as Psittaca gingi after the south-eastern Indian town of Gingee. Later, in 1766, Carl Linnaeus re-described it as Psittacus eupatria. Predominantly green, the male Alexandrine Parakeet has a light blue-grey sheen on its cheeks and nape, a very heavy red bill with yellow tips, bright red shoulder-patches and yellow-green underparts. The tail is yellow on the underside, while the upperside is green at the top, melding into blue and then to yellow at the tips. Additionally, the adult male has a black stripe across the lower cheek, and a pink band on the nape, both of which are missing in the adult female. Young birds resemble the female, except that the tails are shorter. The nominate sub-species P. e. eupatria is seen in Western and Southern India, and in Sri Lanka. P. e. nipalensis, also known as the Large Indian Parakeet, is seen in Afghanistan, Pakistan, North, Central and Eastern India, Nepal and Bhutan. P. e. avensis, or the Large Burmese Parakeet, is seen in north-east India, Bangladesh and Myanmar. The Large Andaman Parakeet P. e. magnirostris is seen in the Andamans and the Coco Islands. Both P. e. avensis and P. e. magnirostris have a blue band on the nape. P. e. siamensis, although known as the Thai Rose-ringed Parakeet, is considered a sub-species of the Alexandrine Parakeet and is seen in Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia and Thailand, and has a blue wash on the back of the head and neck. Habitat & behaviour: The Alexandrine Parakeet is generally seen in small flocks in forests, woodlands, mangrove forests and agricultural lands, although the groups may be larger where there is adequate food or in communal roosts. The calls are deeper and harsher than those of the Rose-ringed Parakeet, and vary from a ringing trrrieuw to a loud kree-aar or keeak, a deep klak-klakklak-klak and a resonant gr-aak. It calls loudly and harshly when alarmed or while mobbing predators. Large flocks also may sometimes call excitedly together. As with the Rose-ringed Parakeet, the Alexandrine Parakeet also is known to mimic human speech in captivity. Nesting: The Alexandrine Parakeet breeds mainly between November and April. Nesting is usually in natural tree hollows, although it may occasionally use cracks in buildings, or holes excavated by itself in trees. The usual clutch consists of 2-4 blunt oval-shaped white eggs. Local name: The Alexandrine Parakeet is known as ‘Rai tota’ or ‘Hiraman tota’ in Hindi, ‘Pedda chiluka’ or ‘Mandi rama chiluka’ in Telugu and ‘Periya kili’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. BIRDING IS FOR CUCKOOS Sudhir Moorti “So, let me get this straight – you work 14-15 hours a day and, to relieve your stress, you go on a ‘Birding’ trip, where you fly long distances, travel for hours on bumpy roads, go to remote hardly-known places, get barely 3-4 hours sleep every night, walk for kilometres in dense jungles carrying that monstrosity you call a camera, get your blood sucked by leeches, bitten by ticks and God knows what other horrors – and this is what you do willingly?” Repeated requests to my closest non-birder friends to join me on a birding trip always elicit an unconstitutional response and some anatomically impossible suggestions as to what I can do with my proposal. I calmly listened to my non-birder friend’s tirade, impressed by his breathless rendition, and said, “Yes, this is what we do.” The other day, I was on the phone with a couple of my closest birding friends. So what exactly is a birding trip? It’s a ritual, it’s a pilgrimage, it’s a... it’s a... It’s a birding trip, nothing else compares. Here’s an example of how it goes. “Let’s do Mishmi this time,” says my brother-in-arms. This set off some thoughts in my mind. Aren’t we birders crazy – or, better still, Cuckoo? “Mishmi is great, but a tad expensive,” I chip in. “How about...” Why would anyone in a sane state of mind decide to bring upon themselves such hardships? All this to get a fleeting glimpse or maybe a decent shot of a bird? And this goes on for an hour or so. My wife later asks me, “You guys planning a trip again?” So why watch birds? I have no straight answer to this one. It’s like asking, why climb mountains? I say, “No, no, that’s for March.” I had once suggested to my wife that she accompany me on one such trip; she gave me a look as if I had lost all my marbles in one fluid motion, and told me to go hang myself from a tree or jump off a cliff. I couldn’t help but think, “If it’s a fruiting tree, then there could be a lot of frugivores; a cliff could mean some raptor sightings...” “But… This is July!” she splutters. “Yes, we need to plan in advance,” I smugly reply. “You guys are nuts!” she hisses in exasperation. “Cuckoo,” I say, “Cuckoo.” She saw the faraway look in my eyes and naturally walked away in a huff. “What???” 1

“I said we birders are Cuckoo.” With that she storms out of the room. Sometimes I pack and unpack several times before I am completely satisfied. Anyway, the process begins – we finally zero in on a location, the itinerary is built, tickets are booked, birding guides fixed up, rooms booked. Phew!! Then D-Day arrives, and we are off. A typical birding day involves walking/driving around for 12-14 hours. The birding day starts around 5:00AM, and goes on till about 6:007:00PM. And now – we wait! Some great sightings and some not so great ones are a part of the game. There are some species of birds which really get our goat – for example, the Blue Whistling Thrush in the Himalayas, the Red-vented Bulbul and Oriental Magpie Robin closer home. While we would be searching for some particular bird, these species have a habit of turning up every time and irking the bejabbers out of us. Expletives are muttered, names called. We even have our own names for them, which I cannot divulge here for obvious reasons. Daily telephone sessions begin when we dreamily discuss what are the possible lifers that we can get. Then we shop. A visit to the nearest Decathlon is mandatory. Several other frivolous online purchases are made. Some of which may never be put to use. Once a friend asked me, looking at a small gadget, “What’s this?” Back in the room after a gruelling day’s birding, one would think it’s over. Not really. The days’ Photographs are copied, backed up etc. There’s one particular gentleman who takes forever, copying them into at least 2-3 locations/devices before feeling secure… and to top it off, he doesn’t budge from in front of the laptop the whole time – I wonder if he can actually see the files getting copied in binary like Neo (from the Matrix movie)! But then we are, to put it mildly, a little paranoid about storing the photographs. “That’s a USB Battery Charger. We use it to charge camera batteries, connecting it to a power bank when we travel to areas where power supply is not available.” “Why are there two of them?” he asked. “Back-up,” I replied. “OK, what’s this?” Everyone takes a quick bath and then we settle down to write down the day’s bird list, buoyed by some much-needed restoratives. The ‘discussion’ then begins. Two or more people start writing down the list as one person runs through the field guide. “That’s a battery grip which fits into the camera, and enables us to use rechargeable AA batteries.” My friend sat in silence for a few minutes, then said, “So you have 4 camera batteries, 1 AC charger, 2 USB chargers, 16 rechargeable AA batteries, 2 AA chargers and 4 power banks. Back-ups for back-ups for back-ups. You guys are mad.” Sometimes there are disagreements over the ID or some other thing. Lips are pouted, brows are furrowed, but the mention of a rare (for the lack of a better word) species changes the mood. Smiles are back. Glasses are clinked. Cheers!! And then off to sleep, for the morrow brings yet another day of birding, and our hopes of spectacular sightings rise with the morning sun. Cuckoo, the word is Cuckoo. Packing for the trip is yet another sacred ceremony. I usually withdraw unostentatiously into my spare room (where I stash all my birding stuff) and mull for hours. Unfortunately, the trip itself whirrs by and is over in a flash (pun intended). We return home with photographs in the digital memories and unforgettable moments etched in the human ones. Sipper – check, field guide – check, batteries – check, binocs – check... And then, the next day, my friend calls me… “Bro, what about Sikkim in November?” We have many idiosyncrasies, we birders do. We have lucky charms to which many great sightings are attributed. It can be a ring, a toy, a lucky bag or even a pair of shoes. So obviously we better not forget to pack these, no Sirree. And so it starts all over again. Cuckoo, the word is Cuckoo. *** 2

IN PURSUIT OF THE BUSTARD IN ALIEN LANDS… Trip Report – Portugal, July 2018 Text and Photos: Krishna Nukala A view of Iberia Time and again my efforts to spot the Great Indian Bustard (GIB) had failed. The search for it in Rollapadu and the tristate confluence of Telangana, Karnataka and Maharashtra (at Nannaj, Sholapur) over the last three years ended up in vain. GIB is a critically endangered species (only about 150+ remain) and is sighted mostly in the arid regions of Rajasthan and the rest being scattered in other three states. It is one of the heaviest flying birds in the world and experts say that its mass has become its own nemesis, having been hunted for its meat. There are, of course, other reasons too like loss of habitat which has brought it to the brink of extinction in India. According to me, I have to say that its name has become its nemesis – as the story goes, when the birdman of India, Dr Salim Ali proposed the GIB as India’s national bird, the government officials mistook its spelling and opposed the scientist’s proposal, replacing it with the Peacock as the national bird of India! You never know when and how the opportunity to fulfil your dream knocks at your door. So, when my sister from the US suggested that we meet in the Iberia for a holiday, I grabbed the opportunity with both hands. I knew that the southern part of Iberia has some great sighting locations for the Great Bustard. But there is a difference. The GIB and the Great Bustard do look very similar, but scientifically they are not one and the same. Nevertheless, a Bustard is a Bustard, and I embarked upon my quest for TGB! More of it later... Great Indian Bustard (Ardeotis nigriceps) Great Bustard (Otis tarda) Found in the Indian sub-continent. Migratory in nature and flies long distances both for breeding and in search of food. Critically endangered, their numbers are estimated to be below 150 in entire sub-continent. Unless sustained conservation efforts are undertaken, GIB may totally disappear from Indian sub-continent in next 3-5 years. Found mostly in southern Europe chiefly in grass land areas of Portugal and Spain. Also found in some parts of Mongolia and central Asia. They are chiefly resident birds, and the male sometimes reaches up to 18 kgs. Sustained conservation efforts in Europe have increased their numbers to around 48,000 with about 30,000 in Spain alone. Bernardo Barreto, a local contact in Portugal who belongs to www.birds.pt agreed to help me sight not only TGB but also, if possible, the Iberian Imperial Eagle (also known as the Spanish Imperial Eagle) – but before that he suggested that there is a lot of birding to be explored in the environs of Lisbon. He suggested that we bird in the Tagus estuary on July 12, followed by birding in the Southern region of Alentejo around Castro Verde and Mertola regions on July 14. On July 12 morning, we started early. River Tagus is the largest river in Iberian Peninsula and drains into the Atlantic Ocean at Lisbon. The striking part of the estuary is its width, forming into a mammoth lake and blessing Lisbon with a natural harbour. Our destination lay on the other side of Lisbon, for which we had to cross the gigantic 17 km long Vasco da Gama Bridge. Little Ringed Plover The birding started immediately after we hit the bridge and one could see the salt pans with the Black-headed Gulls, Black-winged Stilts, Black-tailed Godwits etc in plenty. 3

I was excited but Bernardo wouldn’t allow me to take pictures because one cannot halt on the bridge and driving slow on it would be too risky. “There is plenty of opportunity to shoot when we cross the bridge”, Bernardo said. Taking a left turn after the bridge, we reached Antalaya, a private farm which Bernardo said was the prime place to watch all kinds of birds. Alighting from the car, I looked around and the first things that struck me are the trees. Cork Trees! I have never seen a cork tree earlier in nature and already the bonuses were piling up! Cork (quercus suber) belongs to the oak-wood family. Its bark is harvested every 9 years and used for making mostly wine bottle stoppers. Besides, the cork tree also houses many kinds of birds, the most common being Eurasian Nuthatch. Squacco Heron (Photo: Faisca) Cork trees at Tagus Estuary Common Hoopoe After spending some time at the ponds we ventured into the cork tree groves. Bernardo heard a short, bursting crickety song of a Reed Warbler in the distance, but try as we might, it was not visible. Greater Flamingo Leaving the bird to itself we went on for other birds. Suddenly I came across a brightly colored black-and-yellow gregarious bird and I uttered “Goldfinch”. Bernardo corrected me and said that it was the Yellow-crowned Bishop. The place was teeming with all kinds of birds. Far away on the salty marshes we could see hundreds of birds like Flamingoes, Black-winged Stilts, Green & Common Sandpipers, Common Redshanks, Whimbrels and many more. We reached a small pond and I saw a heron not quite like the ones I knew of. This one had a creamy brownish colour and, through the telescope of Bernardo, it looked magnificent with its shining brown body feathers and pale violet, sharp beak with a black tip. Bernardo said that it was a Squacco Heron. There were Mallards, Little Grebes, Great Cormorants, Little Bitterns, Night Herons, Great Egrets, Great Herons, Eurasian Coots, Common Moorhens and Spoonbills all around. Yellow-crowned Bishop 4

We came across the finches later – both Eurasian Goldfinch and Greenfinch. European Bee-eater (Photo: Faisca) Eurasian Goldfinch Overall, we covered various birding points on the Tagus estuary at Barroca rice fields, some central gardens at Freeport and old salt pans on the river bank at Ribeira das Enguias. There were more birds as we headed back and I couldn’t stop murmuring in my mind, “Birding is so easy here, one has to be just in the place and they are everywhere around you!” Then I spotted a magnificent black-headed, blue-winged bird similar to the Eurasian Magpie and Bernardo confirmed it as the Iberian Magpie. July 14, 2018 Bernardo arrived right on time at 6:00AM. We had to start early as the drive was about 260 km south of Lisbon and en route there were plenty of birding sites to cover. First we halted for petrol at a place called Cepsa-Grandola, and there were hundreds of Swallows and Swifts flying all around. Under the petrol pump roof, there were dozens of muddy nests all around. This petrol pump was owned by Cepsa Oil & Gas Company; they have taken it as a social responsibility to protect the birds and proudly displayed a poster (in Portuguese) reading: “The swallows chose us – We ask our clients for the best understanding for any inconvenience.” Little Owl Birding continued with sightings of Little Owls hiding in the burrows of the cork trees, Crested Larks, Sand Martins, Barn Swallows, Red-rumped Swallows, Yellow Wagtails, Great Tits, Blue Tits, Eurasian Jays, Common Waxbills and so on. I expected to see the local variant of our Green Bee-eater but couldn’t find any. I asked Bernardo about it; he said the Beeeater spot was not far away and we went in search of it. Ultimately, we found them perched on the electric lines, voraciously feeding on the insects – what a beautiful bird it was! Just replace brilliant hues of blue in place of green in our Green Bee-eater – that’s what a European Bee-eater is. The CEPSA poster 5

Bernardo, the guide Reluctantly we left the area as we had so much to catch up with. We headed towards Castro Verde and Mertola and Bernardo stopped at a place with a big board which roughly translated into – “Bio Diversity Area – Protected zone” with a picture of the Great Bustard. At last we had arrived. This zone has been taken up and protected by “League for Nature Protection” (LPN), an EU body to protect air, water, nature, and the environment. The Portuguese government has allocated 1,700 hectares of land to protect the Great Bustard here. We started looking for the bird and for more than half an hour nothing happened. I was losing hope and beginning to think that my visit was wasted and that I was not destined to see a Bustard in my life. Suddenly Bernardo pointed out to the horizon and with naked eyes I could see the unmistakable heads of two Bustards. They were very far off and even the telescope view was not satisfactory. I was, however, happy that a bird from my bucket list had been ticked off. After a few minutes, the Bustards vanished and they were not to be seen more. By now it was getting late for lunch and Bernardo suggested that we go for lunch at Mertola and look out for other birds. White Stork The drive towards Alentejo continued, with cork and olive trees all along on either side of the road. Shortly we entered another private farm at Aparica where a small lake was teeming with White Storks, Mallards, Coots, Red-crested Pochards, Great Crested Grebes and several others. A couple of Lesser Kestrels were to be seen in the distance on the electric lines. Suddenly Bernardo pointed to a bird about 400 meters away perched on top of an electric pole. It looked like an eagle to me and Bernardo as usual corrected me – “Shorttoed Snake Eagle”. He readied his tripod within seconds, focused the telescope right into its eye and said, “Look”. Short-toed Snake Eagle “OMG, what a magnificent bird!” I exclaimed. It stood there, not in any hurry to take off. It was a male bird and Bernardo said that it had probably sighted some prey and was waiting for the right moment to strike. So we waited, keeping an eye on the Snake Eagle and looking out for other birds. After about 20 minutes, it took off and dived into the dried grass field below. The next thing we saw was a two-foot snake hanging from its beak as it flew off with its meal. Suddenly the memories of the Bonelli’s Eagle hunting the Blackbuck fawn at Rollapadu came to me (Pitta – October 2014 issue). Eurasian Griffon (Photo: Faisca) 6

We arrived at a place called Alcaria Ruiva where, on the faroff cliffs, were a big group of Griffon Vultures. There must have been at least 20, and Bernardo informed that this was their usual habitat. Just at that moment, there arrived a huge black vulture, which sat itself at some distance from the Griffons with wings spreading like Dracula’s black cloak – it was the Cinereous Vulture. After some time we spotted a Golden Eagle perched on a far off oak tree. Bernardo was driving the other side of the Bustard National Park and was trying his best for a better view of the Bustards. Dusk was approaching but there was sufficient light. A gentle breeze was blowing from west to east and on the horizon, one could see flocks of White Storks and other birds returning to their nests. Suddenly there appeared a Bustard in full sight, followed by another two. They were much nearer than the two we spotted in the afternoon and I stood still there. All the three were full grown females and remained there for quite some time. I took some pictures and left the place with a humbling feeling. A view of Mertola Mertola, the Moorish municipality town on top of the hill, lies near Guadiana River which, in ancient times, served as a useful port. Mertola is full of ancient history with records going back to 8th Century BC with intermittent occupations by the ancient Greeks, Romans, Muslims and Christians. On top of the town where the ruins are still being dug out, one can find several Common and Lesser Kestrels in the crevices of the ancient walls. Mertola is famous for protecting Kestrels, and one can see specially made out boxes outside the local homes for these birds to nest. Having settled into our accommodation at Havelock, we refreshed ourselves, then my daughter introduced me to her friend Amit Adikari. This young self-made birder and naturalist was a big reason this trip was so memorable. Over the next three days, our birding windows were decided by the Rain God and the times he could take off from work. The few hours we could get were amazing as Amit knew where each of the species were found – for instance, he would take us to a small culvert, and say that the Blue-eared Kingfisher was to be found feeding there during the high tide. Havelock Island is part of Ritchie’s Archipelago, in the Andaman Islands. It is known for its dive sites and beaches, like Elephant Beach, with its coral reefs. The island has one road from the Jetty till the market area of Govind Nagar, where the road divides into two – one road turning right and ending at Radhanagar Beach, and the other continuing all the way to Kalapathar village. On either side of the road are resorts and residences, and the rest of the area is covered with forest. Crescent-shaped Radhanagar Beach is a popular spot for watching the sunset. On the island’s east side, rocky sections mark long, tree-lined Vijaynagar Beach. The island's forested interior is home to birdlife such as White-headed Mynas and many woodpeckers. With all the rain, I had given up on the night birding we had planned. However, as the rain let up, we started searching for the Owls, though Amit was doubtful of finding any as it was windy and wet. I was returning to Havelock Island after a birding trip four years ago; this time I was accompanying my daughter for collecting her Dive Master’s certificate and her equipment from the Andaman Bubbles, where she had completed her course. We decided that since we were coming to Havelock anyway, we may as well get in a couple of days of birding, if the weather permitted. Since the owls were not to be seen, he said, “Let me show you some water snakes.” I agreed and ended up at this culvert under which we found half a dozen snakes hunting fishes. The locals called it the Dog-faced Water Snake (Cerberus rynchops) (Schneider, 1799). 9

As we continued searching for owls along the road, Amit pointed out spots where the Andaman Scops Owl, Andaman Barn Owl etc would normally be found. However, it seemed like it was not my day to see them. Having checked all areas and finding none, we decided to get back as the rain was starting up. As we were driving back, Amit suddenly stopped and switched on the flash light, and I saw the Hume’s Hawk Owl! I couldn’t photograph it, with the rain coming down; however, we watched this handsome bird till he took off. The night turned out to be a Snakes’ Night. August 6, 2018 The next day we planned for an early morning trip if the rains permitted. Luckily, though it was cloudy, it was not actually raining, and we set off. The canopy was lush green, and sighting birds was difficult. The Andaman Shama could be heard singing, Parakeets of all types were rushing around trying to grab as much food as possible within the raineffected curfew. We could see glimpses of Long-tailed, Redbreasted and Alexandrine Parakeets, and the fluttering Vernal Hanging Parrots. In the lush green foliage hid the Green Imperial and the Andaman Green Pigeon, barely visible. Dog-faced Water Snake A little further, crawling very slowly on the forest floor beside the road was the Common Cat Snake (Boiga trigonata), also known as the Indian Gamma Snake. Andaman Green Pigeon Common Cat Snake Further down, where the road met the beach, we found this beautiful Yellow-lipped Sea Krait (Laticauda colubrine) also known as Banded Sea Krait. Andaman Imperial Pigeon Yellow-lipped Sea Krait 10

Violet Cuckoo On top of a very tall tree sat a Violet Cuckoo framed against the cloudy sky. Red-whiskered Bulbuls kept popping up all around, the Indian Golden Oriole and the Black-naped Oriole were peeping and the Small Minivet was playing hide and seek. Andaman Serpent Eagle As we went on towards Kalapathar village the landscape began to change – there were paddy fields, and open land on either side of the road. In one of these open spaces, on a dry stump sat the White-breasted Woodswallow. White-breasted Woodswallow Indian Golden Oriole (female) Far away on a branch sat the Dollarbird, complaining about something. Beside us, on the electrical wires, we had a Greater Racket-tailed Drongo watching us, its tail swaying in the wind. Black-naped Oriole Further down beside the road sat the Andaman Serpent eagle, waiting for the sunshine. Greater Racket-tailed Drongo 11

Oriental Dollarbird Red-whiskered Bulbul As we were moving down the road I found a Vernal Hanging Parrot sitting on a telephone pole, dipping now and then into the opening at the top of the pole. It seemed like it had found something to feed on, or was feeding, and this I would find on many of these poles beside the road. A little further we found the Asian Fairy Bluebird busily trying to pluck a large berry, not bothered that we were watching close by. Asian Fairy Bluebird Vernal Hanging Parrot As we had reached the end of the road we turned back, since Amit had to report to work. We planned to meet in the evening to continue searching for the owls, but the night and next morning plans were washed out as it rained right through. August 7, 2018 Though the morning session was washed out, there was a small pause in the rains in the afternoon. However, with a cloudy sky and the rain threatening to come down any time, we birded close the resort. As soon as we started, we saw the Red-whiskered Bulbul pecking away on a ripened papaya. White-rumped Munia 12

As we moved on, we found another Andaman Serpent eagle watching us from a perch high up under the canopy, as we were walking surrounded by small patches of vegetable fields. In the shrubs we some small birds moving around; on closer scrutiny I realised they were a flock of White-rumped Munias. that maybe we were blocking its path to its nest. Quickly moving about ten meters away, we saw it fly across to where we had stood watching it, and into the thick shrubs. An Orange-headed Thrush, an Oriental Magpie Robin, some sparrows, Oriental White-eyes and House Crows were busy searching for food. Out in the open area some Red Collared Doves were feeding. Andaman Shama We moved ahead, feeling pleased with ourselves for having understood what the bird needed to do. On the base of a hybrid coconut tree we saw an Olive-backed Sunbird. Red Collared Dove Having reached the foot of a hill where the vegetable fields ended, we decided to walk around the farms towards the road. A flock of White-headed Starlings could be seen on the tree top along with the Hill and Common Mynas, Emerald Dove, Large-billed Crow and Small Minivets. Olive-backed Sunbird As the light was good with the clouds clearing, Amit suggested that we could try looking for the Kingfishers, and we set out to the area where the Blue-eared Kingfisher was usually seen. Spot-breasted Woodpecker As soon as we reached, we saw a Collared Kingfisher streaking across the water, picking up fish from more than one place in a single pass, then sit on a branch munching away in quick time before launching himself once more. On a dry tree sat a Spot-breasted Woodpecker preening itself. Suddenly, without any call, the Andaman Shama, holding some insects, landed on a twig near the strings tied above the vegetable plants. As we kept watching it, we realised that the bird had not moved away, even after five to six minutes, and continued to hold the insects in its mouth – then it struck me 13

Blue-eared Kingfisher Hume’s Hawk Owl He kept looking up to the sky as if telling us, “Take your pictures quickly so that I can go and take care of my own stuff too”. As soon as we lowered our camera after a few clicks, he took off silently into the shrubs around. As the drizzle started up we called it a day. As we parted it was decided that we will bird on the Radhanagar Beach side of the island on the last day of our trip. August 8, 2018 Having boarded the ferry back to Port Blair at 3:30PM, we set off towards Radhanagar Beach. Starting off with a clear sky, far off we saw a juvenile White-bellied Sea Eagle sitting on a tall tree, waiting to be fed. The Orioles, Minivets and Whiteeyes were busily feeding all around. We left the road and took a trail which led us to an open space surrounded by shrubs and trees. On one of those trees far away sat the bird I had missed on our last trip four years ago – the Andaman Woodpecker. Collared Kingfisher It was again getting dark as the clouds had arrived, so we took a break, refreshed ourselves and started for our night birding. The evening session started with hopes of being granted a darshan of at least one of the owl species. Though the weather kept threatening us, we continued and almost at the point of giving up and returning, one of them showed up on his regular watch tower and gave us the pleasure of being in his majestic presence. It turned out to be the Hume’s Hawk Owl. Andaman Woodpecker 14

Andaman Coucal White-headed Starling As we went further on the trail, we were welcomed by an Andaman Coucal and a Yellow Wagtail. In the shrubs this little dash of blue and grey kept fluttering from one bush to another curiously trying to find who was encroaching on its territory. The little fellow turned out to be the Black-naped Monarch. The area was filled with activity. White-headed Starlings, Andaman Drongo, Red-breasted and Long-tailed Parakeets – all were present. Andaman Drongo So engrossed were we in watching the activity we hardly realised it was time to pack up and leave for our return journey home. It had been a beautiful trip – thanks to Amit Adikari, our young guide, who made this trip most enjoyable. Black-naped Monarch The complete list of birds is given below: Sl. Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Golden-fronted Leafbird (Chloropsis aurifrons) Golden-fronted Leafbird (Yelagiri, Tamil Nadu, October 21, 2018) Order: Passeriformes Family: Chloropseidae Genus: Chloropsis Species: C. aurifrons Size: 19 cm bamboo), wooded stands in coffee and tea estates, and wooded gardens, from the up level to around 1,200m (around 1,800m in Sri Lanka). It tends to stick to the canopy where it contorts itself into various acrobatic positions as it forages for spiders, insects, berries, fruits and nectar. The song of the Goldenfronted Leafbird, as with the other Leafbirds, consists of a series of undulating liquid chirps reminiscent of Bulbuls. The call consists of harsher notes, but it is also known to mimic many other birds – for instance, Common Tailorbird, Redwhiskered and Red-vented Bulbuls, Black Drongo, Common Iora, White-breasted Kingfisher, Rufous-backed Shrike and Oriental Magpie Robin – and it often mimics migratory species well after they have left, which indicates a strong ability to retain and retrieve calls. Description & distribution: The Golden-fronted Leafbird is one of the Leafbird species found in the Indian subcontinent, south-western China, and across to south-east Asia and parts of Indonesia. The adult bird is predominantly green, and has a black face and throat, with a blue throat patch and yellow borders, dark brown irises, blackish bill and feet, a yellowish orange forehead and a blue moustachial line. However, it lacks the blue flight feathers and tail sides seen in the Blue-winged Leafbird. The black colour of the face and throat is duller in female birds and absent in young birds, which also have a plain green head. Nesting: The Golden-fronted Leafbird breeds mainly between May and August over most of its range, but seems to prefer November to February in Sri Lanka. The nest is a loose shallow cup of tendrils, moss, rootlets, etc lined with soft grass or fibres. It is usually well concealed, and usually situated at the extreme end of an outhanging branch near the top of a high tree, making it difficult to access. The usual clutch consists of 2 cream or reddish-cream eggs, with profuse reddish-purple specks all over. Two sub-species are described: C. a. frontalis, seen in Southern India, has a narrower yellow border to the face, a blue sub-moustachial stripe and a duller orange forehead. C. a. insularis, seen in extreme South India and Sri Lanka, is smaller than C. a. frontalis. Habitat & behaviour: The Golden-fronted Leafbird is generally seen singly or in pairs, or sometimes in small groups, and inhabits deciduous woodlands, evergreen broadleaf forests, forest edges, secondary growth (including Local name: The Golden-fronted Leafbird is known as ‘Pachchaku pitta’ in Telugu, ‘Pachai kuruvi’ in Tamil and ‘Chhota harrial’, ‘Chhota harewa’ or ‘Sabz harewa’ in Hindi. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra 17 Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. INDOOR MEETING: Friday, 2nd November 2018, 6.30PM: SAVING FISHING CATS, SERVING LOCAL COMMUNITIES, SOLVING CLIMATE CHANGE: Talk by Ashwin Naidu A Master’s and Ph.D. in Wildlife Conservation and Management and a Carson Earth Fellow from the University of Arizona, member of the IUCN/SSC Cat Specialist Group, and a TEDx speaker, Ashwin is the President and CEO of the Fishing Cat Conservancy. Trip Report – Ameenpur, August 28, 2018 Text: Anuraag Jonnalagadda; Photos: Madhuri Mondal Ameenpur Lake As winter was approaching, my friends and I decided to go to one of the lakes to look for migratory species. As if on cue, we got a mail from BSAP informing us about the next birding trip to Ameenpur Lake. So, on the 28th of October, we set out to Ameenpur Lake at 6:30AM with a group of about fifteen people. We were also joined by three cyclists from IIT Hyderabad. They had started at 4:30 in the morning and had cycled over 40km to be with us. It was a diverse group of people; there were some who were completely new to birding and there were experienced birders like Shafaat sir and Aasheesh sir. 1

Little Cormorant From the bund we got a good view of the lake and were able to spot up to six pelicans. Other common birds around included Eurasian Coots (Fulica atra), Little (Phalacrocorax niger) and Great Cormorants (Phalacrocorax carbo), Whitebrowed Wagtails (Motacilla maderaspatensis), Black-winged Stilts (Himantopus himantopus) and River Terns (Sterna aurantia), among others. Baya Weaver nest A Black-winged Kite (Elanus caeruleus) sitting on top of a nearby tree made for good viewing. The highlight was a thick 3-feet-long snake slithering in the water towards some Blackwinged Stilts. We anticipated some action, but the snake just calmly moved along and the stilts did not even bother to move aside. While none of us was able to identify the snake since it was quite far away, the consensus was that it could have been a Checkered Keelback. There were many Dusky Crag Martins (Ptyonoprogne concolor) and Barn Swallows (Hirundo rustica) flying over us along with a few Wire-tailed Swallows (Hirundo smithii). White Wagtail, Common Kingfisher, Little Cormorant The next spot that we went to was a short distance away on the banks of the lake. From this spot, we could clearly see two beautiful Painted Storks (Mycteria leucocephala) perched on a nearby tree. With his scope, Aasheesh sir showed us some of the plovers that were feeding at the water’s edge. With his help, we were able to identify a Wood Sandpiper (Tringa glareola), a Green Sandpiper (Tringa ochropus) and a Common Greenshank (Tringa nebularia), although all of them seemed very similar to each other. Cattle Egret, Glossy Ibis Next, we moved onto a spot further ahead along the lake. Some interesting species that we saw here included a good number of River Terns, a Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus) and a Black-headed Ibis (Threskiornis melanocephalus). One of the new birders wanted to see the state bird of Telangana, the ‘Pala Pitta’, which he had heard a lot about. Barely 2 minutes later, an Indian Roller (Coracias benghalensis) landed on a pole behind him, thereby fulfilling his wish almost instantly. There were good numbers of Green Bee-eaters (Merops orientalis), Scaly-breasted Munias (Lonchura punctulata) and Indian Silverbills (Euodice malabarica) at this place. We also got to see a Blue-tailed Bee-eater (Merops philippinus) and a Red Avadavat (Amandava amandava). By this time, it had become quite hot and many birds were soaring above us riding the thermals. We were fascinated to see a Darter (Anhinga melanogaster) flying high up in the air. From down below, its thin neck was barely visible and it looked like a bird with just body and wings and no head. Other interesting finds here included two Knob-billed Ducks (Sarkidiornis melanotos) which flew over us, Asian Pied Starling (Gracupica contra) and Baya Weaver (Ploceus philippinus) nests, a few White Wagtails (Motacilla alba), a Grey Wagtail (Motacilla cinerea), a Little Ringed Plover (Charadrius dubius), and a Ruff (Philomachus pugnax) which was also feeding with the sandpipers. 2

The yellow fields and the blue waters beyond were indeed a wonderful sight and we tried our best to capture this in our group photo. Indian Silverbill After some time spent watching these flying birds, we moved further ahead along the lake to a place surrounded by beautiful yellow fields. On the way, we crossed a few birds, which we assumed were ordinary sparrows. Later, we came to know that these were actually Chestnut-shouldered Petronias (Gymnoris xanthocollis), a.k.a. Yellow-throated Sparrows. We rushed back for a look but the birds had disappeared by then. Pied Bushchat (female) It was already past 9:30AM and so we decided to wind up for the day. The cyclists set off on their long journey; they were far beyond their planned schedule but were delighted, nevertheless, at having seen so many birds on their first outing. On our way back, we were lucky to spot two Rednaped Ibises (Pseudibis papillosa) sitting on top of an electric tower. Thus, we ended the day, pleased at having seen all the Ibis species found in India. Back near the fields, a Long-tailed Shrike (Lanius schach) stayed with us for a while, moving from place to place before finally catching an insect and settling down. A bright blue White-throated Kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis), a Common Rose butterfly and a Common Jezebel butterfly were some colourful delights that we saw at this place. Ditch Jewel (Brachythemis contaminata) dragonfly *** 3

SIGHTING OF A SPECIAL MIGRANT – RED-NECKED PHALAROPE Text and Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati Red-necked Phalarope Rare sightings are always a treat for us in the birding community, and especially when we sight such a migrant in the city, we get more excited. In recent times in Hyderabad, we have had many such good encounters with these migrants, one of them being the Red-necked Phalarope (Phalaropus lobatus). It was first sighted at Fox Sagar Lake, Hyderabad in 2016 (as per the available reports) and thereafter every year – at the same location in 2017, and at Fox Sagar along with Osman Sagar and Ameenpur, this year. To our delight, two birds were spotted this time. The Red-necked Phalarope is the smallest of the 3 Phalaropes; they generally breed in the mid- to high altitudes in the northern hemisphere, and winter in the south. During the migration season, they travel long distances from their breeding grounds, migrating over land and ocean to gather in the fall at saline lakes, before returning to the breeding areas. The bird we saw this time was very friendly, and was wading at the shore, not bothered by our presence in the vicinity. It was casually wading for food on the surface of the water, giving us plenty of opportunity for some good shots. *** Bird Humour Contributed by JVD Moorty *** 4

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Verditer Flycatcher (Eumyias thalassinus) Verditer Flycatcher (Sattal, April 22, 2015) Order: Passeriformes Family: Muscicapidae Genus: Eumyias Species: E. thalassinus Size: 15-16 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Verditer Flycatcher is generally seen singly, in deciduous, evergreen or light coniferous forests, open areas, groves and gardens. It prefers exposed perches like tree tops or bare branches, from where it makes aerial sallies to hawk insects and flies. It is different from other flycatchers in that it prefers to forage above the canopy level. The song consists of a series of rapid, undulating, jingling notes; it is silent in winter. Description & distribution: The Verditer Flycatcher is an Old World flycatcher, found across almost the entire Indian subcontinent (including Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Myanmar, but excluding Sri Lanka, which has an allied species, the Dull Blue Flycatcher, Eumyias sordida), South-east Asia and east to Sumatra. The adult male bird is an intense turquoise, greenish or copper-sulphate blue all over, except for the black lores and bill base, and a grey vent. The adult female is duller and greyer, and has dusky lores. The juvenile bird has grey-brown upperparts with a turquoise cast and fine orangebuff spotting, while the underparts are brown with bold orangebuff spotting; it also has wings and tail similar to the adult but with buff tips on the coverts. Nesting: The Verditer Flycatcher breeds mainly between April and July, in the Himalayas. The nest is usually a thick-sided cup made of moss, root hair, grass etc, among exposed roots of trees, under eaves of houses, or inside holes in walls or embankments. The usual clutch consists of 4 pale pink eggs with a darker cap-like ring at the broad end. Local name: The Verditer Flycatcher is known as ‘Nili tik-tiki’ in Punjabi, ‘Harithnil makhimar’ or ‘Piroji makhimar’ in Gujarati, ‘Nil katkatia’ or ‘Puthir chitta’ in Bengali and ‘Neelameni’ in Malayalam. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 15 Number 9 November 2018 (Special Issue) Editor’s note Some of our members had been to Tanzania for a week-long trip from 9th to 15th of October, 2017. In this Special Issue of the Pitta, we are happy to bring you the experiences shared by the participants, along with a number of colourful photographs. (With inputs from Ajit Kumar Mahendra, Yella Prakash Rao, Shantisree, Gulshan Vegesna, Divya Shafeela, Ishika, JVD Moorty, Dr Geetanjali and Dr Samuel Sukumar) TRIP REPORT: TANZANIA Day Zero to Three – October 09-12, 2017 Ajit Kumar Mahendra Photo: Dr Samuel Sukumar October 9-10, 2017 Ever since Shafaat saheb announced the trip to Tanzania, volunteers started pouring in and it was oversubscribed in no time. The trip planning had begun by April and all the finer aspects, including the detailing of Safari vehicles and tipping amounts to the catering staff were taken care of. Regular mails were shot off on aspects of the tour and the participants also had a chance to meet each other a week prior to the journey. We were 29 of us in all and the ladies almost beat the men this time with a participation of 14 members! The journey began at Shamshabad on October 9, 2017, with most of the enthusiasts hailing from Hyderabad, while others joined us in Mumbai and some joined directly at Arusha in Tanzania. We had to Arrival at Addis Ababa (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) wait at Mumbai for over 8 hours to take the ‘cheap and best’ Ethiopian Airways flight at 5:00AM on October 10, 2017. We utilized this time discussing everything under the sun, including birds 1

and possible adventures that were awaiting us at the Savannah. The flight from Mumbai to Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, was ahead of schedule and it took us a little over 4 hours to reach the African Continent. It was a pleasant flight with most of us trying to determine our position in space and identify land features as we crossed over onto the Horn of Africa. The change over at Addis was quick and as per plan. We reached Kilimanjaro airport by 1:00PM local time, where we were greeted by the tour operator. We were quickly herded into a bus that took us to the Meserani Snake Park on the outskirts of the town of Arusha. The park had a large collection of reptiles including the deadly Black Mamba, the Green Mamba, the Egyptian Spitting Cobra, Puff Adders and a variety of owls, vultures, crocodiles and turtles. Some of the members had a special experience of coiling the snakes around their necks. Apart from this, the park had a large collection of birds which including Wagtails, Mousebirds, varieties of Doves, Weavers and nesting Herons. We headed towards the city for the night stay after a meal en route. Ishika handling a snake (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) October 11, 2017: Tarangire National Park It was an early morning start for all. Everyone was ready and packed for the first shift from the Backpacker’s Camp at Arusha to the Panorama Camp site which was to be our sojourn for the next 2 days. We started after a delicious continental breakfast. The highlight for us, particularly vegetarians, was the ragi porridge and hibiscus juice. The beautiful rooftop setting gave us a view of the town and the early morning workers going to work in sleek minibuses. Neatly packed vegetables, fresh from the market, were being taken in hand drawn carts. Driving through the small and beautiful town of Arusha, we soon came onto the highway. The convoy of 4 Land Rovers carrying our group of 29 was driving at a constant speed. Lot of our misconceptions Photo: Yella Prakash Rao about Africa, mostly gleaned from our exposure to television, came crumbling down. It was a pleasant feeling to drive through a town and not see much traffic. We passed through coffee plantations on the outskirts of the city. Two things struck us - there was no garbage anywhere in the town, and plastic was nowhere to be seen. Soon we passed through a cantonment. I noticed that our driver – Dickinson was his name but everyone affectionately called him Dick – was driving at a steady speed of 50-55 km, and did not overtake any vehicle ahead of him. When I commented on this, he informed that there are restrictions in the cantonment about driving and even honking. We spotted groups of young boys, dressed in black and their bodies also painted in black and their faces decorated in white. Dickinson informed us that these boys had recently undergone circumcision and that they would dress this way till their wound healed. Incidentally, circumcision is practiced by most tribes in Africa and is not restricted to Muslims alone as in India. 2 Breakfast time at Panorama Camp (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao)

The first sighting of the day was the White-bellied Go-away Bird which was spotted by Moorty and his group who were ahead of us. We missed it and never could sight this bird again. The convoy halted at a petrol pump. Everyone got down to stretch their legs and bought a few packets of snacks. Sukumar and a few others, already had their heads in the Photo: Yella Prakash Rao sky and were clicking away. We all joined them and found the source of attraction on a jacaranda tree which was in full bloom. Atop it we could spot the Scarlet-chested Sunbird and the Red-Throated Bee-eater. A third bird with dull plumage may have been a female sunbird. A Speckled Pigeon was perched on the roof of the petrol station and could be captured. White-bellied Go-away Bird (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) The subsequent drive was uneventful and we reached the gates of Tarangire Game Reserve around noon. Our guides-cum-drivers soon got busy in completing the formalities to enter the reserve. The office of the Game Reserve was in a large tent, well-furnished and with computers. The registration was manual though. We entered our names in 2 registers. The place around was shady with lots of trees. We realized that the entrance to each reserve is a well-furnished office with excellent toilet facilities and a good restaurant with snacks and drinks. Outdoor seating was available. Similar facilities were available within the reserve. Cleanliness was the hallmark of all these points. Visitors are not permitted to get down anywhere else and the way the guides were strict in imposing the rules speaks about enforcement. Each one of us had to register and entry fees was paid. Since it was noon and we had had a very early breakfast, we decided to enter the reserve after lunch which we had under the shade of a banyan tree. The leftover food and the packing were segregated and I later noticed that it was loaded, to be carried bank to the camp. A lesson for us to learn on environment and its protection. Scarlet-chested Sunbird (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) During the time we spent relaxing after lunch we could see lots of birds at close quarters. We saw Superb Starling, Whiteheaded Buffalo-weaver near the restaurant, and Meyer’s Parrots and Blue-cheeked Cordon Bleu by the dozen bathing and hovering around a pipe used for watering plants. These birds are seen close to water and human habitation. We drove into the park around 2 pm. We saw several Lions, Zebras, Wildebeest, Mongoose, Ostriches and Vultures. We returned to Panorama Camp well after dark. We were all accommodated in igloo-type rooms. They looked cute from the outside but were small Scarlet-chested Sunbird with very little ventilation. We had (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) two options, to either shut the door and feel cramped or to keep the door open in the wild and run the risk of being visited by the local inhabitants! We quickly unpacked and settled in the dining hall for an early dinner and were entertained by a local group to some local dance, music and acrobatics. 3 Banded Mongoose (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Elephant at a termite mound (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao)

October 12, 2017: Lake Manyara National Park Photo: Dr Samuel Sukumar Photo: Yella Prakash Rao The Panaroma Camp site was situated on a high ground and commands a breathtaking view of Lake Manyara. We were the biggest group of tourists at the campsite. After an early breakfast we got down the ghat road to the Lake Manyara reserve. We first drove to a marshy stretch of shallow water where we spotted a number of waders, Stilts, Pelicans, African Jacanas, Saddle-billed Stork, Sacred Ibis, Egyptian Goose etc. The reeds in the water were a good site for the Weaver bird’s nests and we did see one. A few Terns challenged our photographic skills because of their swift movements. We could see a few Hippopotamuses, though only their snouts and upper torso. A Cattle Egret was giving company to a lone Buffalo. Dick informed us that the herd abandons old members, who in turn form small herds to protect themselves. Probably this was one such. Sad that even animals sometime behave like humans and abandon their seniors. African Jacana (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Having done with the residents of this marshy stretch, reminiscent of our own Kolleru & Chilka Lakes, we drove to the main entrance of the Manyara Game Reserve. After quickly completing formalities and a quick brief, we drove into the forest and we were greeted by some monkeys who cutely posed for our shutter Egyptian Goose (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) bugs. The noisy Hornbills soon attracted our attention and were captured in our Canons and Nikons for posterity. We reached a small stream and spotted an African Paradise-flycatcher and a Grey-headed Kingfisher. The flycatcher eluded our cameras and flew off. Several Elephants, Giraffes with Red-billed Oxpeckers perched on them and some other birds kept us engaged. Around noon, we reached the first resting spot. We could get down and stretch ourselves. En route, we spotted the Red-and-yellow Barbet, a cute cousin of our own Coppersmith Barbet. Relaxing here for some time we could see the ubiquitous weaver birds at fairly close range and photograph at ease. Grey-headed Kingfisher (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Red-and-yellow Barbet (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) 4

Hamerkop (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Olive Baboon (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Southern Ground Hornbill (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) We were soon herded into vehicles and were off to our final destination of the day – Manyara Lake. As we approached the lake, we were greeted by a stretch of water dotted with hundreds of pink spots. Flamingoes in hundreds, nay thousands, were the source of pink. On the water’s edge we could spot lots of waders – Egyptian Geese and Red-billed Teal, most of whom were resting with their heads hidden in their wings. A teal similar to these except a black beak was also in the group – Grey-headed Teal. Water Thick-knee, Ringed Plovers, Whitefaced Whistling-ducks, African Spoonbills were some of the species we spotted amongst hordes of large flamingoes. Because of a walkway built over the waters, we could see the birds at very close range. It was fascinating to see the way these birds feed, particularly the flamingoes. They literally sweep their large curved Zebra (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) beaks on the water’s surface. A group of school kids joined us with their incessant banter, giving us anxious moments lest the birds take to the wings. But the animals in this part of the globe seem to take all such human interventions in their stride, confident that we mean no harm. The smell of rotten flesh assailed our vegetarian nostrils as we approached the water’s edge. The source was a dead buffalo. There were no signs of predators having made the kill. It seemed to be due to more other causes – old age or illness. This carcass attracted a Whitebacked Vulture and helped increase our tally of vultures. In between birding and photography, we finished our lunch and, having paid a visit to the hot water spring on the water’s edge, started the journey to our next destination. This was Photo: Yella Prakash Rao not a birding site but a cultural one – the Masai tribal village. Here, we were received by all the villagers who gave us a traditional welcome, dancing for us in their traditional dress. We were all dressed in their tribal attire. This was followed by a visit to the houses and exhibition of their handicrafts. Having spent an hour at the village, we drove back to camp. Reaching camp after dark, we realized that there was no power supply. We spent most of the night in darkness and woke up early next morning to be greeted by dry taps in the toilets. Water supply was restored in time for all us to have a bath before breakfast and pack to move to our next birding area and the most memorable camp of the trip. We were informed by the staff at campsite that a snake was slithering near the toilets which we were all frequenting in the night with help of our torch lights. However, he was put to rest. Some of our fellow birders paid a visit and paid their last respects to the departed soul – an Egyptian Spitting Cobra! Lilac-breasted Roller (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) 5

Day Four – October 13, 2017 Yella Prakash Rao Photo: Dr Samuel Sukumar Serengeti It was another bright and sunny Savannah morning and our photographers could not have asked for anything better. After savouring the best of pineapples and sweet potatoes for breakfast, the team was all set for one of the most happening wildlife arenas in the African continent, the Serengeti. Ngorongoro Crater (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) After a short drive we reached the Ngorongoro Conservation Area (NCA) where we had to pass through the crater wall to proceed to Serengeti. A short halt here attracted us to the coffee shop selling home grown Tanzanian coffee and also some interesting curios. Black-headed Heron (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Namaqua Dove (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) 6

Eastern Chanting Goshawk (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Pied Crow (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) The drive from the crater wall into the Serengeti was truly breathtaking with the usual Acacia trees of all heights and shapes. The terrain was truly a geologist’s lab as was briefed in the info room. En route we came across some Masai model villages and their tribesmen and women, grazing their cattle. A lion king was waiting at the entrance to welcome us, and we were really elated to see it sitting almost next to the track. This was followed by the sighting of the Eastern Chanting Goshawk with its typical black and white stockings! At the lunch spot we had the usual Superb Starlings, Lovebirds, Bulbuls, Weavers and the unperturbable Marabou Masai Model Village (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Storks giving us company. Post lunch we passed a nest of a Tawny Eagle and a Secretarybird with a fledgling exercising the wings for a takeoff. A pride of lions too passed by, comprising a lot of young ones enjoying themselves in the protection of the lionesses. The drive through these large expanses of grasslands was mesmerizing with no end in sight. The excitement continued as we sighted one new bird after another, with the same being documented meticulously by Ishika in our jeep. We met a lone giraffe and some elephants when our number one vehicle got stuck in the mud. We had some anxious moments when the same herd of elephants had to pass through our column of vehicles. The vehicle was cleverly unstuck by the guides by pushing it out of the mud using another vehicle. We had never seen a recovery of these sorts so far! It was close to sunset and a number of birds including the Egyptian Geese flew past in flocks, probably on their way to the roosting sites. The Serengeti sunset was beautifully captured by most of the members, and a lone Hyena near the Airport added to the excitement. We were desperate to spot a few more animals and birds in the fading light while the drivers/guides were finding their way to the campsite for the night stay. We were initially happy to be lost and doing night safari in the comfort of the jeep but we Giraffe (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) realised this could not continue any longer as it was getting cold. Just then we saw the silhouette of a Verreaux’s Eagle-owl perched on the Acacia nearby. We all struggled to get a shot of it but it was too quick and escaped into the darkness. The safari came to an abrupt stop when we chanced upon the campsite via radio Mr Rogate, expert bird guide instructions from the other vehicles. (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) 7

African Elephant (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Red-billed Firefinch (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Now we were at the Seronera Camp site and were pleased to see our tents pitched and Chef John and Co preparing dinner. We collected our bedrolls and occupied the nominated tents for the night. It was a scary feeling to know that we were in the open game reserve without any protection around us. But the fact that we were a large group helped us gather the minimal courage required to pass the night in the wilderness. After a hot cup of coffee some of us volunteered for the cooking and cutting jobs in the kitchen so as to expedite the dinner preparations. A bottle of Jack Daniels and Amarula wine gave us company under the starry Serengeti sky as we discussed wild and exotic destinations that were in our check lists. It was an evening every one of us will remember for years to come. The Land Cruiser stuck in the mud (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) John treated us to a hearty vegetarian meal – meat is not cooked in the camp to dissuade the carnivores from visiting the camp area. We retired to bed after having made preparations mentally and physically to deal with intruding hyenas, snakes and the lions. The hyenas did call on us at around 1:00AM, but decided to limit it to a few cries and songs. The next morning saw most of us ready before sunrise and taking selfies with the Serengeti sunrise. After a sumptuous breakfast and a forced Swachh Tanzania Abhiyan, we set out to the most awaited event of our trip, the visit to the Ngorongoro Crater. On the way to the crater we were fortunate to witness a Rufouscrowned Roller chasing away a Black-chested Snake Eagle. Typical to its flight, it flew banking violently to the left and to the right calling out as it chased the eagle away from its nesting area. All in all, every one left Camp Seronera wishing that they could spend one more night amongst the hyenas! Rufous-crowned Roller chasing Black-chested Snake Eagle (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) 8

Day Five – October 14, 2017 Gulshan Vegesna & Divya Shafeela Ngorongoro Crater (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Ngorongoro On Day 4, I thought we had passed through the most exciting part of the safari in Serengeti, the rim of the crater Ngorongoro – we had crossed this rim on the way to Serengeti and had stopped at a view point. Right after lunch on Day 5, as we reached this UNESCO World Heritage site, we felt looked barren except for a few water points. I wondered what kind of wildlife can possibly exist there. Little did I know that life exists in the most unlikely of places – that’s the beauty of this wonderful world that we live in. We saw a few black spots on the crater floor below which I thought were small shrubs, when one of our group members pointed out that they were elephants! That is when I realized we were at 610m height from the floor of the crater, and kilometres away from the elephants. The best of our binoculars could only enlarge them to the size of an ant! We still hadn’t met all the Big 5, with the Leopard and the Rhino still evading us. We started our journey from Serengeti to Ngorongoro Crater quite upbeat, though. Enter the Ngorongoro crater! The drive down the crater was beautiful. As we entered, it felt like we were in a wildlife documentary (how I wished we would go off the designated mud track!) Wildebeest, Zebras and Thompson’s Gazelles were grazing around lazily, occasionally looking at the passing tourists in Land Cruisers. As we trailed along the mud roads, we saw Schalow’s Wheatears, Egyptian Geese, a pair of Grey-crowned Cranes pecking away happily, and a Kori Bustard. We also spotted the Secretarybird. It was interesting to see it rapidly trample the prey with its feet. Its tail resembling a quill justified the name, along with its black and white feathers, the way secretaries used to dress in earlier days according to our tour guide Dickinson. Grey-crowned Crane (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) As we drove on, we saw lush green water plants in blue waters, an oasis in the midst of a dry crater – it was the beautiful Lake Magadi. Its scenic beauty was a feast to the eyes, which were till then straining to find animals and birds camouflaged in the savannah and the jungles. Far away, there were hippos lazing in the water, beating the heat of the day with their glistening backs. Right around them were Lesser Flamingos with their long legs – it was a beauty to behold. As much as we wanted to linger on and soak in God’s beautiful creation, our tour guide lured us away with the promise of taking us closer to the hippos. We had our lunch in what may have been the most scenic spot of the whole trip, with a couple of Pelicans and the hippos in the lake for company. We could also see the elephants in the farthest distance. Secretarybird (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) 9

A group of Hippos (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Lunch by the Lake Magadi (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Post lunch, we started our mission on the Big 5 but spotted 3 lions having an afternoon siesta while the peafowl were at some distance from them. And then you think… “wow what a life”. We were suddenly reminded of the fact that it was our last day and our target was the big 5. Oh boy, were we glad we listened to Dick! The next stop took our breath away – we stopped at a marsh that was filled with Hippos and Sacred Ibis. The Hippos tossing and turning around to cool themselves against the backdrop of a small hillock was a sight to behold. We observed that some Hippos had dry backs with bird droppings on them, which was a bit strange. That is when we saw a pack of hyenas around. They were attempting to reach the dead hippos. The hyenas were emerging from the lake all covered in mud, eagerly looking toward the dead hippos – their meal for the day. We saw a lone jackal too lurking around probably to get a few crumbs from the leftovers. Sadly, we couldn’t stay longer to see the action as we had to move out of the crater by 4:00PM. We embarked on the last leg of the safari, out of the crater. As if to cheer us up, a Waterbuck appeared out of the trees on the edge of the crater. Elephants too came out to bid us goodbye as they fed on the dry twigs and barks of trees. Hyena (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) Waterbuck (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) A colony of Weavers (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao) We embarked on the last leg of the safari, out of the crater. As if to cheer us up, a Waterbuck appeared out of the trees on the edge of the crater. Elephants too came out to bid us goodbye as they fed on the dry twigs and barks of trees. The climb up was smooth and uneventful giving us time to enjoy the crater in all its beauty at various heights. We once again stopped at the same view point on the rim, only this time around I knew what was down there – untouched creation of God in perfect harmony! 10 Jackal (Photo: Yella Prakash Rao)

We headed to Arusha with a heavy heart. Leaving Ngorongoro was not easy. We reached the Backpacker’s Den for the night stay. The next morning was spent visiting various places of interest around Arusha, including the Heritage Village and some Tanzanite shopping. While we could see Mount Meru while crisscrossing the city of Arusha, Kilimanjaro looked ever elusive. We tried to get a glimpse of the peak on the return flight but the clouds never gave us a chance. Maybe we will need to return to Tanzania and climb the Kilimanjaro to see the summit! The return journey to India too was pleasant and uneventful. In all, we were able to see over 200 species of birds and a number of wild animals of Africa. This trip also helped in bonding the BSAP members in bonhomie. And finally, we all learnt why monkeys and elephants savour the Amarula fruit in the African wild!
