Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 15 Number 11 December 2018 (Special Issue) Editor’s note Some of our members had been to Binsar, Pangot & Sattal for a week-long trip from April 24th to May 1st, 2018. In this Special Issue of the Pitta, we are happy to bring you two different perspectives of the trip, along with a number of colourful photographs. We hope you will find this Special Issue interesting. WILD AND IN COLOUR TRIP REPORT: BINSAR, PANGOT & SATTAL Shilka Chaudhari The group at Binsar (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) On exploring, Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary (WLS) at Almora reveals a diverse range of flora and fauna, mesmerizing views of snowcapped Himalayas and lush jungles echoing with the sounds of streams and melodious chirping. This hidden gem in the Almora district of Uttarakhand offers the best of nature, wildlife and adventure and is the best place for bird watching. The Sanctuary is located in the Himalayas atop the Jhandi Dhar Hills, about 33km north of the Almora town. We looked forward to a one-week trip with 19 birders. The journey route was Hyderabad-Delhi-Kathgodam. From Kathgodam we hired local vehicles to travel around Binsar, Pangot & Sattal. We were greeted by the sighting of two Indian Grey Hornbills (Ocyceros birostris) right outside the Kathgodam station. Calls of Barbets could be heard from a distance. We spotted a Blue-throated Barbet (Megalaima asiatica) near a local hotel where we had our breakfast. We also spotted a number of species like Rufous Treepie (Dendrocitta vagabunda), Himalayan Bulbul (Pycnonotus leucogenys), some Swifts and a Crested Serpent Eagle (Spilornis cheela). Himalayan Bulbul (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) 1

Crested Serpent Eagle (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) We reached the KMVN (Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam) Tourist Rest House located at an elevation of 2,412m above sea level. The property was constructed in 1988 and was being renovated. It was made of wood and bricks with sloping slate roofs coloured in orange. The estate overlooked a sweeping panorama of the Kumaon Himalayas that includes the perennially snowGrey-winged Blackbird (Photo: Ajit Kumar Mahendra) capped peaks of Trishul, Nanda Devi, Sunanda Devi, Panchachuli, and Nanda Kot. The forest is a protected reserve with a variety of flora, avian life, a sizeable population of deer, wild boar, and fox. We decided to take a walk in the evening on the scenic forest trail, and the dense rhododendron and oak provided much-needed fresh air and tranquility. We often spotted Grey-winged Blackbirds (Turdus boulboul). We decided to spend two-anda-half days at Binsar. The mornings were nippy and evenings quite cold. The view Coal Tit (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) of the sunrise across the snow-covered Taking in the sunrise at Binsar (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Himalayas was rejuvenating. During our stay we spotted a number of species like the Green-backed Tits (Parus monticolus), Coal Tits (Periparus ater), Eurasian Jay (Garrulus glandarius), Black-headed Jay (Garrulus lanceolatus), Lesser Racket-tailed Drongo (Dicrurus remifer), Verditer Flycatchers (Eumyias thalassinus) and Ultramarine Flycatchers (Ficedula superciliaris). Oak and pine trees presented an opportunity to sight a variety of woodpeckers like Himalayan Woodpecker (Dendrocopos himalayensis), Black-headed Jay (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) 2 Eurasian Jay (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Verditer Flycatcher (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari)

Rufous-bellied Woodpecker (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Rufous-bellied Woodpecker (Dendrocopos hyperythrus) and Brown-fronted Woodpecker (Dendrocopos auriceps). We were graced by the presence of the melodious Rufous Sibia (Malacias capistratus). White-tailed Nuthatch (Sitta himalayensis) and Bartailed Treecreepers (Certhia himalayana) were also spotted. Point Zero provided an unhindered view of the peaks of Chaukhamba, Panchachuli, Nanda Devi and Mt. Trishul. White-browed Shrike-babbler (Pteruthius flaviscapis) was sighted with nesting material in its beak. Black Eagle (Ictinaetus Brown-fronted Woodpecker (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Yellow Wagtail (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) malayensis) was seen hovering around cliff edge of hilly terrain. Oriental Turtle Doves (Streptopelia orientalis) were commonly sighted from the terrace of the hotel. While walking around in the forest we could hear the calls of Barking Deer although few had seen it upfront. A few seasoned birders had spotted the Eurasian Griffon Vulture (Gyps fulvus) in flight. Some of them spotted Whiskered Yuhina (Yuhina flavicollis) and Kalij Pheasant (Lophura leucomelanos) on their way to Point Bar-tailed Treecreeper Zero. Common Rosefinches (Carpodacus (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) erythrinus), Yellow Wagtails (Motacilla flava) and Yellow-browed Warblers (Phylloscopus inornatus) were also spotted. Spotting of the Cheer Pheasant (Catreus wallichii) deserves a worthy mention. Scaly Thrush (Zoothera dauma), Hill Partridge (Arborophila torqueola), Mistle Thrush (Turdus viscivorus) and Grey Bushchat (Saxicola ferreus) were also seen. We could hear the distant calls of Coppersmith Barbet (Megalaima haemacephala) and Black Francolin (Francolinus francolinus). Puran Singh, a local of Almora district, was a seasoned birding guide, and his insightful knowledge regarding birding locations was very helpful. White-browed Shrike-babbler (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Our stay at the Rest House was comfortable with sumptuous breakfast and meals, though one major issue was that every day the electricity was available only between 6:30PM to 9:00PM. My favourite place was the rest house terrace. A view of Sattal Lake (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) The next three days were to be spent in and around Sattal. 3 Grey Bushchat (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari)

Sattal, which translates to seven lakes, is a cluster of seven interconnected lakes in Nainital. Located at the foothills of the Himalayas, the region is nestled between fragrant forests of oak and pine. It is one of the last few unspoiled freshwater biomes in the country, and attracts birds and bird watchers alike. Slaty-headed Parakeet Female (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Slaty-headed Parakeet Male (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Plum-headed Parakeet Male (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) The drive around hilly terrains was scenic. On our way to the destination we stopped midway to see a flock of Slaty-headed Parakeets (Psittacula himalayana). We also spotted Verditer Flycatcher, Ashy Drongos (Dicrurus leucophaeus), Spot-winged Starlings (Saraglossa spiloptera) and Kalij Pheasant. After reaching our guest house, we dropped our belongings and headed for some evening birding. We spotted the Russet Sparrow (Passer rutilans) and Brown-fronted Woodpecker. Meanwhile a poster outside the guest house canteen caught our attention. The Uttarakhand Forest Department and Strabo Pixel Club were organizing a 3-day bird festival in Nainital. Sattal was one of the birding spots included for the avian festival. Early mornings we would head towards a place nicknamed ‘The Studio’. It turned out to be our favourite spot for observing birds at their best. We descended down a flight of moist and mossy stairs which was a gateway to this birding heaven. We saw a number of photographers trying to get a shot of the Long-tailed Broadbill (Psarisomus dalhousiae). I got the perfect shot when it perched on its nest for a few seconds. Walking down to the Studio (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Blue Whistling Thrush (Photo: Ajit Kumar Mahendra) Meanwhile, walking down further we spotted Scarlet Minivets (Pericrocotus (flammeus) speciosus), Bar-tailed Treecreepers, Asian Paradiseflycatcher (Terpsiphone paradisi), Oriental Whiteeye (Zosterops palpebrosus), Blue Whistling Thrush (Myophonus caeruleus), Eurasian Blackbirds, Long-tailed Broadbill Common (Acridotheres tristis) and Jungle Mynas (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) (Acridotheres fuscus), White-tailed Nuthatch, Wedge-tailed Green Pigeon (Treron sphenurus), Red-wattled Lapwing, Red-billed Blue Magpies (Urocissa erythrorhyncha), Coal Tit, Lesser Yellownape (Picus chlorolophus), Oriental Magpie Robin (Copsychus saularis), White-throated Fantail (Rhipidura albicollis), Black-lored Tit (Parus xanthogenys) and the Red-billed Leiothrix (Leiothrix lutea) (a.k.a. Pekin Robin or Chinese Nightingale). As we headed further down to get a closer view of the waterfall, we noticed a woodpecker with a huge crest. There is a possibility that we might have caught a glimpse of the Himalayan Flameback (Dinopium shorii), but unfortunately the identity remains unverified. The native Black Bulbuls (Hypsipetes leucocephalus) were also spotted on the way. 4

White-throated Laughingthrush (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Common Kingfisher (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Meanwhile, a few seasoned souls had sighted Blue-winged Siva (Siva cyanouroptera), Kalij Pheasant and Chestnuttailed Minla (a.k.a. Bar-throated Siva) (Siva strigula). Vikram, Sheetal and the others had spotted a giant owl being chased by flock of Drongos. The Ashy Drongo was a common sight. The Common Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis) was often sighted at the lake. We had spotted a flock of Whitethroated Laughingthrushes (Garrulax albogularis) taking a dip in one of the streams near the lake. So were Striated Laughingthrush (Garrulax striatus) noticed. We spotted a number of small-sized birds. But their constant hopping on trees and shrubs made it almost impossible to photograph and equally difficult to identify. We also spotted a Brown Dipper (Cinclus pallasii) in one of Brown Dipper Juvenile (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Spotted Forktail (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) the lakes. Our birding guide Suresh helped us to locate a Spotted Forktail (Enicurus maculatus) and Crested Kingfisher (Megaceryle lugubris). We also spotted a pair of Plumbeous Water Redstarts (Rhyacornis fuliginosa). In Pangot, we saw a number of Barn Swallows (Hirundo rustica) living in harmony with humans. We spotted a nest with three chicks in it on a ceiling, outside a local kirana shop. In the forests we sighted a female Kalij Pheasant flying across the road. We did not have much luck at birding in this spot except for the fact we spotted a number of beautiful butterflies. I got one good shot of the Common Mormon Butterfly. On our return journey towards Sattal, it started to rain. We decided to stop at a local restaurant for lunch. We are amazed to see a huge flock of Jungle Babblers (Turdoides striata) in the garden. We also spotted a number of Greater Yellownapes. On the last day some of the members opted to shop and go kayaking. The stay at Sattal forest guest house was splendid. Barn Swallow chicks (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) On our way back to Kathgodam station we decided to stop at a small hotel for a coffee break. We decided to birdwatch in the backyard which was lush green. It had a plantation of bananas and mangoes. We spotted some interesting species like a flock of Grey Treepies (Dendrocitta formosae) and Red-billed Blue Magpies. We saw a bright red bird perched on top of a banana tree, which was the size of a sunbird. Siddharth photographed the bird. After a few minutes of discussion over the identity, it was concluded that it was the Mrs. Gould’s Sunbird (Aethopyga gouldiae). Kudos to Sagarika in our group who spotted White-crested Laughingthrush (Garrulax leucolophus) perched on the ground. Red-billed Blue Magpie (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) 5

Our beautiful holiday amidst forests, close to Himalayas was a welcome change from the sweltering Hyderabad summer. Spotting of Mrs. Gould’s Sunbird was the highlight of my trip. Thanks to Shafaat Saab for arranging a lovely trip. Taking a break (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) *** TREKKING IN THE HIMALAYAS TRIP REPORT: BINSAR, PANGOT & SATTAL Dr Barnali Chaudhuri Bineshwar Mahadev Temple, Binsar (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 19 of our members had gone to Binsar and Sattal on a birding trip. Starting from Hyderabad on April 24, 2018, we flew to Delhi, then boarded Ranikhet Express and reached Kathgodam early the next morning. Three Tavera vehicles were waiting for us. Thus began our journey to Binsar. We stopped for breakfast on the way at Paulriya restaurant. The area was full of birds. We saw three kinds of Barbets – namely Coppersmith, Blue-throated, and Brown-headed – near the restaurant. Moving on, we stopped by the roadside to get a better view of a Crested Serpent Eagle. Driving along the Kosi river, we stopped for a Shikanji (lemon soda) near a Hanuman temple. Our driver, Prakash, informed us that the Kosi is a dangerous and turbulent river during the rainy season, despite its dried-up appearance now. We observed for the first time the golden-coloured Bottlebrush flowers. After getting our tickets at the Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary (WLS) check point, we 6 A nearby village (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri)

reached Binsar KMVN (Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam) guest house, 2310 metre above sea level. We felt happy to visit Binsar, where Swami Vivekananda stayed for two or three days at the Binsar Dak Bungalow during his second visit to Almora in 1897. The guest house is in the midst of a thick Himalayan Oak and Buran forest. Buran (Rhododendron arboreum) is the state tree of Uttarakhand. The forest was dressed with the jewellery of red Buran flowers. Local people drink the juice of its flower which helps keep the heart healthy. As there is no electricity available at Binsar Guest House, they supplied power through a generator till 9:00PM. Consumption of non-vegetarian food is prohibited under the Wildlife Act; eggs are the only non-vegetarian food allowed in Binsar. Campfires are not allowed as a precaution against forest fires. Jayati, Anjali and I were allotted room no. 202. I was surprised to note that instead of the 2nd floor up, it was 2nd floor down! All meals were provided at the guest house itself; with breakfast we also had the rhododendron flower juice, which was delicious. The warmth and generosity of the guest house staff touched our hearts. Rhododendron flowers (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) We stayed there for two days. During our stay we explored two main birding areas of Binsar: 1. Binsar Zero Point, located in the heart of Binsar WLS, Almora, is the highest view point, from where one can have a 360-degree panoramic view of the Himalayan Beauties namely Kedarnath, Chaukhamba, Trishul, Nanda Devi, Nanda Kot and Panchachuli peaks. Zero Point is a trek of around 2km from the guest house. 2. Bineshwar Mahadev Temple, which is the 13th century temple built by King Kalyan Chand of the Chand Dynasty. Langur family (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Near the guest house, we saw several Langur families on the road side. A Jungle Crow was watching the road from a high tree top. A Blackthroated Tit foraged for food among the mosses on an oak tree branch, and a Eurasian Jay was peeping out from the foliage. I noticed some small, beautiful white flowers on the road side. We enjoyed the sunrise from the roof top view point of Binsar guest house. Around 5:30AM, the reddish sky welcomed the sun, which was rising from behind a mountain. The sun suddenly appeared like a golden plate and reached the top of the mountain in no time! We could see some Himalayan peaks, which were covered with snow as if they had draped themselves in white shawls. A few birds were chirping – we saw some Greenbacked Tits moving around in the trees. The guest house staff Indian Tortoiseshell (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) served tea on the roof top view point itself, and used only steel cups, as Binsar is a plastic-free zone. I saw an Indian Tortoiseshell butterfly nearby the guest house rooftop, and some Purple Iris flowers also caught my attention. Black-throated Tit (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 7 Eurasian Jay (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Sunrise at Binsar (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri)

The peaks barely visible through the clouds (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) During our stay at Binsar we went to Zero Point twice: once during sunset and then during early morning. Unfortunately both times we could not see the faraway Himalayan ranges clearly because of the clouds, though we did get some glimpses. We all enjoyed a lot trekking through the Zero Point trailing road, with the road-side stones glowing due to the mica content. We also did see some birds. The Verditer Flycatcher, with its shining rich copper-sulphate blue colour, is a common bird in this part of the Himalayas. We saw a Grey-winged Blackbird singing its very sweet song at the same place each time, protecting its territory. We saw a Black Kite in flight, and heard the call of the Barking Deer and, in fact, saw one running away no sooner than we saw it. We spent some time after dinner on the roof top, exchanging ghost stories in the moonlight! It was freezing cold, and we had to manage the rest of the night with candles. It was really a thrilling experience. On April 26, our guides, Puran Singh and Ram Singh, showed us the birding spots near Bineshwar Mahadev Temple. We saw a Chestnut-bellied Rock Thrush, an Oriental Turtle Dove calling from a nearby oak tree, and a Grey Bushchat. There was a flock of what seemed to be Rosefinches nearby; one adult male was red-headed, as if it had played Holi with sindoor. A Black-headed Jay was moving around in the field. Orchids on the tree trunks enhanced the beauty of the forest. Trekking up to the opposite side of the temple, we saw a Himalayan Woodpecker on a Silver Oak tree, searching for food in the moss. Violet-coloured thistle-like flowers on the thorny tree attracted butterflies. GreenOriental Turtle Dove (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) backed Tits were playing around. Some wild flowers showed their beauty by the side of the trail. After breakfast Arabinda, Shafaat Sir, Jayati, Anjali and I sat for some time in the shade on the hillside, enjoying the natural beauty all around us. Some small red insects were on the tree leaves. New leaves of Silver Oak looked like flowers. At Zero Point (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Green-backed Tit (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Around 11:00AM, we started trekking again. The Rhododendron buds were attracting insects. We saw a Drongo sitting in between two tree trunks, a Rufous Sibia on a rhododendron tree trunk and an Ultramarine Flycatcher moving here Black-headed Jay (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) and there. A Nuthatch was moving from this side to that side on a tree trunk. A Sailer butterfly was sitting nearby while an unidentified yellow butterfly was enjoying the honey from a wild white flower. One halved tree trunk was full of mushrooms, and wild red berries were aplenty. A Eurasian Jay was very busily finding its food, while some yellowish-green insects were moving on the dry leaves. On the way back for lunch, we saw more Verditer Flycatchers and Greenbacked Tits near our guest A Sailer sp. butterfly house. (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 8 The group at work (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa)

After lunch we again stepped out for birding under the guidance of Puran Singh. He is truly knowledgeable about the birds and their behaviour, and also about the trees in the forest. Having a learned guide like him opened up a new world. It reminded me again that travelling is indeed a part of education. Rosefinch flock (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Blueberry tree (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Holly plant (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) An Oak tree was leaking resin, and Puran informed us that the resin is used for Ayurvedic purposes. He told us that all oak trees cannot produce resin. The root of Blueberry trees is used as a medicine for diabetes patients. Below the bark of the Holly plant used for Christmas decorations, we saw a yellow colour that can be used as a natural water colour. A pair of Turtle Doves was feeding on small pebbles which would strengthen their digestion systems. We chased the call of a Large Hawk Cuckoo and finally spotted the bird calling from high up on a tree. The guide showed us some small trees whose leaves smelled like ajwain, and told us that the leaves of the walnut tree emit odours to keep insects at bay. The lush green Chinese Bamboo trees, which Puran informed would not be as big as our bamboo trees, and the white Orchids on the oak tree, looked beautiful. We saw some perfectly round tree holes, and learnt that these types of tree holes were made for nests. One tree trunk was twisted around like a wire. There were some very small trees that were very soft to the touch; the guide said that the wool of those tree leaves would be used by Sunbirds to make their nests, along with generous use of spider webs. On the trek to the Bineshwar Mahadev temple, we saw some woody white flowering plants called anaphalis; members of this genus are commonly known by the name Pearl or Pearly Everlasting. Tree with twisted trunk (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) We were very fortunate to see a raptor show that lasted for 5 minutes. The show started with a Black Eagle. Within a moment a Himalayan Griffon was seen flying high. Then, one after another, the raptor show went on, with Red-headed and Eurasian Griffon Vultures also marking their attendance. After enjoying the raptor show, I visited the temple, and saw for the first time two temples together, one for A temple in Binsar Shiva and another with yoni only. (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Many of us went into the coffee shop opposite the temple, where we saw a bonsai rhododendron tree. Puran showed us the bichchu plant, which would give a burning sensation if touched. On the way back, we noticed another very small old temple on the hillside. A butterfly caught my eye because of its size – as big as a small bird! – it was the Orange Oakleaf. I found a Horse Chestnut fruit, which Puran informed us was toxic and inedible. Sunset (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) The bichchu plant (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Orange Oakleaf (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) The sun was about to set by the time we got back. While enjoying the sunset from the dining hall, I was astonished to see a light hanging from the rhododendron tree outside the dining hall, which later turned out to be the reflection of the dining hall lamp shade. 9

Before saying goodbye to Binsar, we picked up some rhododendron juice and miscellaneous mementos like Uttarakhand T-shirts, shawls, scarves, sweaters etc from the guest house shop. Having thoroughly enjoyed our stay at Binsar, we started for Sattal around 11:00AM on April 27. Sattal or Sat Tal means ‘seven lakes’ in Hindi. All of them are freshwater lakes filled mostly by underground springs located A scenic view (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) in the Nainital district of the Kumaon region. Most of these lakes are named after the Hindu mythological characters; they are called Ram Tal, Lakshman Tal, Sita Tal, Nal Dayamanti Tal, Panna Tal, Purana Tal and Sukha Tal. As the name suggests, Sukha Tal remains dry except during the monsoon. Just a few minutes on the road, we saw a jeep toppled over and stuck in a tree on the side of the hill. Our drivers went to check whether anybody was injured or if any help was needed, but there was nobody inside the jeep. I found the humanity in these people moving, something we often lack in urban areas. Grey-hooded Warbler (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Driving along, we saw a Himalayan Woodpecker trying to get its food from a pine fruit. Birds like the Ultramarine Flycatcher, Alpine Swift and Green-backed Tits were seen here and there. A Rufous-bellied Woodpecker was also foraging on a tree. We had lunch at Maruti Restaurant, Nainital, where I noticed a local dog, which had thick hair to combat the cold. The trees covering the mountain tops looked like hair on the mountain head. We passed by the Bhimtal Lake and reached Sattal tourist guest house around 4:15PM. There was a lake in front of the guest house; here electricity was available. There were monkeys sitting near the lake with their adorable babies, and Kayaking was under way in the lake. Ultramarine Flycatcher Male (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) After getting refreshed, Jayati asked us if we would like to go to visit Sattal Studio. I thought that it was a normal studio and did not take my binocular and camera. Just a 2-minute walk beside our rest house, we stepped inside the Sattal park, which is under the Reserve Forest, Bhowali Range, Sattal. A Blue Whistling Thrush looked like it was wearing a pearl necklace. After walking for another couple of minutes, we noticed many people with their big cameras sitting near a watery spot. I saw the live show of birds in front of my Blue Whistling Thrush (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) eyes, and realized the justification of the name ‘Studio’. All the birds, specially the small ones, were coming, sitting on a twig, having a quick bath, and taking off into the nearby trees. It really was an amazing show. After sunset, we moved to the lake for a while. We saw some Nightjars flying around, and Vikram captured a Brown Fish Owl in his camera. After some time, we returned to an enjoyable our dinner at the rest house canteen. 10 Brown Fish Owl (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa)

The next day, April 28, we moved out for birding at 5:30AM. I noticed that a person was sweeping the road, and the garbage consisted of twigs, leaves and nothing else, whereas our garbage is mainly plastics or non-biodegradable materials. It is high time we seriously rethink before using disposable plastic products like glasses, straws etc in our daily routine. We entered the Sattal park and started trekking. A Jungle Myna was moving around, and a Chestnut-bellied Rock Thrush was sitting on a tree. Along the trail, we saw a Red-billed Blue Magpie, a Red-wattled Lapwing near the pond, and some Green-backed Tits. A Green Pigeon sitting on a branch, Drongos busily protecting their territories, a Grey-winged Blackbird female on the grass near the pond, Jungle Myna (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) White-throated Laughingthrushes searching for food under the dry leaves, and some blue Nuthatches going up and down the tree trunk, added to White-throated Laughingthrush the (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) tally. Suddenly we noticed many people looking and pointing their cameras at a spot near the park entrance. A nest was hanging from a tall tree, and a Long-tailed Broadbill was sitting on the top of the nest! I saw the spectacular dance of the Red-billed Blue Magpie. There was moss growing on a broken tree trunk, and a Grey Treepie was sitting on it. A Fantail was dancing nearby, a Bartailed Treecreeper was creeping, and a Red-billed Leiothrix was moving around inside the bushes. Red-billed Leiothrix Bar-tailed Treecreeper Anjali spotted a (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Speckled Piculet while going towards the water falls in Sattal park. We heard the calling of some Green Pigeons nearby, and spotted them on the branch of a tree. We also heard the calling of the Chausingha, the four-horned antelope, from the top of a hill. A Eurasian Blackbird was bathing in the stream, and we also saw a pair of Asian Paradise-flycatchers. While returning for breakfast, I saw a Long-tailed Broadbill, probably the same one seen earlier, sitting with some nesting material in its mouth. I was mesmerised to see the vivid colour combinations in the bird from so close up, and it was easily the bird of my trip. Nature is really so beautiful. All of a sudden, we saw three men trying to fix some ropes on trees for the Flying Fox adventure activity (a.k.a. Zip Line) – probably, as the bird festival was going on in Sattal, they may have thought they could make some money out of it. Anjali immediately took a bold step: she enquired if they had permission, which they did not, so she asked them not to disturb the forest habitats, and tried to make them understand that if the forest was disturbed like this, there would not be any forest left for their children (the next generation). She also threatened them that she would bring it to the notice of the District Forest Officer. That scared them off and they dropped the idea. I really salute her for taking this bold initiative. Long-tailed Broadbill (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 11 White-throated Fantail (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri)

A competition for women bird photographers was going on, and hence we faced a problem getting proper guides. However, we somehow managed to arrange Suresh as our guide, who took us deeper into the Sattal Park after breakfast for more birding. Setting out, near the guest house we saw a Lesser Yellownape, a Black-headed Jay was moving around ignoring us, and an Oriental Magpie Robin was calling and dancing around. Entering the Sattal park, we saw a pair of Purple Sunbirds, a Greater Yellownape was peeping from inside a tree hole, and a Slaty-headed Parakeet was perching. A Blue Whistling Thrush was playing around in the pond, and a Red-billed Blue Magpie was on an oak tree, picking up insects from the moss. Green Pigeons were calling, and a Kingfisher was sitting near the pond to target fish. Some villagers were taking dudhela tree branches to feed their cows so as to get good milk. The last part of the trek towards the waterfalls was really difficult. We Lesser Yellownape could hear the waterfalls but were (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) not able to see it. Finally we reached a point, from where we could see the waterfalls, around 12:30PM. Returning, we saw a Spotted Dove near the Studio; also White-throated Laughingthrushes, Mountain Bulbul, Ultramarine, Verditer and Fantail Flycatchers, Drongo, Oriental Magpie Robin etc. I saw a Praying Mantis under a pine tree. Anjali spotted a Long-tailed Minivet with spectacular orange colour. Local women with the dudhela branches (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) After lunch we went to explore some other nearby birding spots with our guide Suresh. We reached Chanfi village around 4:00PM, hoping to see the Brown Dipper. On the bank of Kalsa river a Sandpiper welcomed us. The river bed was full of stones of all sizes, and we spent some time on the river bed, enjoying the surroundings. We saw a Red-vented Bulbul, a Dragonfly and an Oriental Praying Mantis Turtle Dove. Pink-coloured grass flowers were (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) dancing in the wind. After waiting for quite some time, the Brown Dipper finally came out and flew from side to side, showing its face to everybody who was eagerly waiting for its darshan. We saw a Woodpecker on a pine tree, but it was too far to identify. We boarded the vehicle again for the next spot, but had to get down on the road at a spot where the river was flowing across. We saw a Great Barbet, and some big mushrooms on the tree trunk caught my eyes. We saw Plumbeous Water Redstarts, both male and female; I liked their broad tails, which looked like colourful clips at the end of a braid. We trekked to a bridge, from where we saw some Red-billed Blue Magpies. As we crossed the bridge, we saw a couple of Rufous-chinned Laughingthrushes on the trail road. One of them was calling while sitting on a nearby tree. Long-tailed Minivet (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Great Barbet (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) Plumbeous Water Redstart Male (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Plumbeous Water Redstart Female (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) 12

The next day, April 29, we started at 7:35AM for Pangot. We stopped for some snacks at a general store, where we were surprised to see a nest of Barn Swallows with its adorable babies. Prakash, our driver, pointed out Naini Lake down below, shaped like a mango. We reached the Snow View Point Barn Swallow Adult (L) and Chicks (R) (Photos: Vikram Penmetsa) at 8:30AM. Due to the clouds, there was not much visibility of the Himalayan peaks. Through the telescope we observed a Hanuman temple, Army trekking point, cinema shooting spot, step farming etc. Our breakfast, paratha and potato curry, had already been packed from the guest house, and we enjoyed the same at 9:45AM, sitting on the road side. We saw an unusual Ashy Drongo with a white spot on its head, down the side of a hill. I also saw a tree full of larva. Surekha and I were enjoying photographing the butterflies. A Tortoiseshell butterfly was resting on a roadside stone. A big, colourful bee was sipping honey from a violet flower of a thorny tree. Another type of beautiful butterfly was sitting on a big stone. Ashok spotted a big Langur far away, sitting on Step farming (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) a tree down the hill. Villagers were carrying dry wood from the forest for their fuel. Ashok pointed out a tree stump that looked just like an owl. Anjali was birding by herself and enjoying the natural surroundings. We passed a small waterfall, and came across the skull of some animal. Suddenly we realized that Shafaat Sir’s vehicle had got disconnected from us; we could not reach each other as there was no mobile signal, but managed to do so after A colourful bee visiting a flower a while. Clouds were kissing at the top of the mountains and coming further down. (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Soon it started raining, and we dropped the idea of birding at Vinayak and decided to head back. There was a big traffic jam while going back to Nainital. I was overjoyed at the sight of some very colourful flowers hanging from the balcony of a house. Around 1:40PM, a hailstorm also started. Hydrangea flowers (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) We stopped at Machan Chinese restaurant for lunch, but unfortunately it was closed on Sundays, so we decided to have lunch at Maya Regency. On the way, we saw a rich violet bed of Jacaranda flowers. The restaurant was full of beautiful flowers of different types. Hydrangea flowers were everywhere. I was astonished to learn that the green flowers would become sky-blue within a short period of time. Roses of different colours attracted our eyes. I have never seen such huge orange hibiscus. There were many types of zinnia flowers. Many birds were dancing nearby – Oriental White-eyes, and both Lesser and Greater Yellownapes – on a nearby tree. The hotel surroundings were just like a dream. I regretted not carrying my camera here. Monkeys’ Tail trees were hanging in the balcony of the restaurant. After lunch, we visited the Uttarakhand Textile Development Corporation, Khutani, Bhimtal at 3:45PM. After we came back to Sattal, I could not resist going to the Sattal park again with Sagarika and Siddharth. After dinner, we attended a function arranged by YMCA Campsite Cum 13 A type of Bracket Fungus (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri)

Programme Center, Sattal. An artist was singing Hindi songs, accompanied by an orchestra; I especially enjoyed the flute. The next day, April 30, was our last day of birding on this trip. By this time we knew every nook and corner of Sattal Park. Jayati and I went to the Studio; this time there were no men with cameras around, since the bird festival had already concluded. While we were refreshing ourselves in the serene nature of Sattal park, some stunning bird activity caught our attention. An apparent display of motherly affection was spotted by Anjali in one corner of the park. Far away a Great Barbet was moving around and coming back to feed On the field (Photo: Dr Geethanjali) her baby on the branch of a tree. The baby, perhaps concerned about its mother’s whereabouts, became restless and flew to a branch of another tree right over our heads. Interestingly, on the same tree, a Spot-winged Starling pair (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Parakeet was also affectionately feeding its baby in a tree hole. Noticing the intruder nearby its nest, the Parakeet became agitated – perhaps it sensed that the safety of its baby was at stake. It immediately screeched at the baby Barbet in its shrill voice. In all probability the baby Barbet never expected such rude behaviour, and for a few seconds it was totally puzzled as to what to do, particularly in the absence of her mother. Terrified with this incident the baby Barbet flew away. The entire incident taught us that birds like to live in their own territory. Some Drongos were also making sure of their territories. They were catching their prey in flight and coming back to the same branch of the tree from where they took off. While coming back Arabinda suddenly pointed to the pond. We all rushed there, and noticed a Kingfisher diving into the pond with a laser focus; within seconds it came out with a small fish in its mouth. The most amazing part was to see the bird sharing the fish with another Kingfisher who was sitting on the same tree. Then we went to see the Kalij pheasant. Both the male (a spectacular blue colour with its crest) and the female (overall a brownish colour) came down from the hill top to feed. A Oriental Magpie Robin was hanging around nearby. I noticed some wild strawberries on the side of the road. A Treecreeper was moving on the trunk of an oak tree in search of its food, and several Nuthatches were also moving here and there, along with a Fantail. Anjali spotted its nest which was just like a small cup. A flock of Red-billed Leiothrix popped up at the side of the trail in front of us, and flew away to the nearby dry bushes immediately. After breakfast, Arabinda Kalij Pheasant (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) and I enjoyed kayaking in the lake for one hour. Around 3:00PM, we started for Kathgodam Railway Station. We stopped at the same Paulriya restaurant for some tea/coffee at 4:30PM. I simply enjoyed sitting in the lap of nature. The youngest member of our group, Siddarth, spotted the Mrs. Gould's Sunbird, and Sagarika spotted the Chestnut-bellied Nuthatch (Photo: Vikram Penmetsa) White-crested Laughingthrush down the hill, enriching our bird list. Around 5:45PM, we reached the Kathgodam station. Geetanjali, Anjali, Jayati, Siddarth and I went out of the station for a walk, and wandered through a residential area behind the railway station. The sun was setting with all its colour in the sky while a Gulmohar (Krishnachura) tree with all its red flowers was standing majestically by itself. Anjali spotted a Chestnut-shouldered Petronia, which reminded us of the story of Salim Ali, as it was the key to his introduction into ornithology. We boarded the train for Delhi again at 7:50PM, and the next day, May 1, we reached Hyderabad by flight, thus concluding our trip to the Himalayas. Kayaking in Sattal Lake (Photo courtesy: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) I would like to thank BSAP, and especially Shafaat Sir, for arranging this type of bird watching tour, and also all the fellow members of this trip for making it a grand success. I look forward to more such tours in future too. 14

MY BIRDWATCHING DEBUT Trip Report – Anna Sagar, Jogipet, November 25, 2018 Text: Samata Srinivasula; Photos: Gurukumar KR Woolly-necked Stork Birding is a concept introduced to me by my father. My experience of bird watching was always confined to spotting a few common birds during wildlife safaris. I was introduced to exclusive bird watching at Annasagar Lake, Sangareddy. The Annasagar lake is located about 100 kilometers away from the city of Hyderabad and a kilometre away from a town called Jogipet in Sangareddy district. birds, which is why it is a popular spot for exotic and unusual birds during the migration season. I was a little apprehensive about what to expect from this journey as this was my first exclusive birding trip ever. All I carried with me, apart from food and water, were binoculars, my phone and a handbook of birds. To my surprise, I was welcomed heartily by the Deccan Birders team. They introduced me to the art of birding and made me understand the beauty of it. Mr Shafaat Ulla, Mr Aasheesh, Ms Anita and the others were encouraging and helped me spot and identify many species. My debut birding trip began at 6:00AM when we started from our houses and reached the destination by 8:00AM. As soon as we stepped out of our cars at the view point, we had a panoramic view of the lake with flocks of various migrant 1

Short-toed Snake Eagle The birds that immediately caught my eye were the Greater Flamingos (Phoenicopterus roseus), about 75 of them (males, females and juveniles). There were over 100 Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus), a dozen Eurasian Spoonbills (Platalea leucorodea) and Painted Storks (Mycteria leucocephala), a couple of Avocets (Recurvirostra avocetta), Asian Openbills (Anastomus oscitans) and Grey Herons (Ardea cinerea). Each of these birds were unique in their own way and it was an immensely exciting experience to get to know the birds and identify them. Common Hawk Cuckoo At about 12:30PM, we started looking for some shade beneath the trees to have our food. As we were having tasty sandwiches, paneer, curd rice and fruits, we were also fortunate enough to spot a few arboreal birds like the Ashy Prinias (Prinia socialis), three Black Drongos (Dicrurus macrocercus), three Blue-tailed Bee-eaters (Merops philippinus) and two Indian Golden Orioles (Oriolus oriolus). Right before starting back, three Black Kites (Milvus migrans) graced us with their presence high up in the sky. The one thing that bothered me was human interference around the lake. A huge crowd consisting of the local people gathered right next to the lake for reasons best known to them. Although they did not disturb the birds intentionally, their presence definitely resulted in the birds moving to the other side of the lake away from the humans. All in all, however, it was a spectacular experience for me as a debutant birder, as I had the opportunity to experience professional birding with the elite team and also got to learn a lot from them. I look forward to the next birding trip. Ruff Among the Ducks, the Red-crested Pochard (Netta rufina) was my personal favourite. A Garganey (Anas querquedula), two Northern Pintails (Anas acuta), a Northern Shoveler (Anas clypeata) and Common Teals (Anas crecca) were among the others. We first spotted these birds from the view point of the lake and later moved closer to the water body to explore a few other species and to get a closer and clearer glimpse of these magnificent birds. The group at Anna Sagar *** 2

SIGHTING OF THE INDIAN SKIMMER AT KAKINADA Sudhir Moorti K Indian Skimmer (Photos: Umesh Mani) Come winter and all of us birders make a beeline to the wetlands to watch, record and photograph our lovely visitors from far off lands. This winter was no different for us and we set off to the coastal town of Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh. Apart from the famous Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary, there are lesser known birding hotspots in Kakinada which are quite amazing. bank. A large congregation such as this is very rare and unprecedented for this region. Other than sightings of 1 or 2 individuals reported from this region – and one instance of around 23 birds – there is no record of such a large flock. They are, however known to winter in coastal estuaries and there have been a few reports from Chennai, further down south. One such hotspot is a place known as Kumbabhishekam. With the Kakinada deep water port on one side and a Ravana Temple on the other, with a fishing jetty right next to it, it is a unique mudflat habitat. The Indian Skimmer is a part of the Genus Rynchops in the family Laridae. These birds resemble the Terns, but with a bright orange bill with a longer lower mandible, which they use to plough the water as a method of catching aquatic prey. Known breeding populations are found in the Chambal River Area and Mahanadi River. The Kumbhabhishekam mudflats comprise a small area of about 100 acres. Each year thousands of waders like Little Stints, various plovers, sandpipers etc., are sighted here; Great Knots (Calidris tenuirostris) have also been regularly reported from Kumbhabhishekam. The world population of this species is estimated at less than 10000 individuals, and declining. The IUCN has classified the species as Vulnerable (Vu) which indicates that the existence of this species is threatened due to rapidly declining population and loss of habitat. Here’s hoping that this sighting is a good omen and the numbers of this magnificent species grow by leaps and bounds! On the 7th of January, 2019, four of us – Mrutyumjaya Rao garu, Umesh Mani, Srikanth Bhamidipati and I – visited this area and were awestruck to find a flock of more than 200 Indian Skimmers (Rynchops albicollis) squatting on the far *** 3

Trip Report – Aravalli Biodiversity Park, Gurugram, August-September 2018 Text and Photos: Sita Susarla Woolly-necked Stork The Aravalli Biodiversity Park in Gurugram spreads over 153.7 hectares and is a symbol of restored ecology. Its transformation from a mining and stone-crushing hub to a biodiversity park is the result of unrelenting efforts of passionate nature-lovers. When we visited the park on two consecutive weekends in the months of August and September, it was buzzing with the calls of Black (Francolinus francolinus) and Grey Francolins (Francolinus pondicerianus), Jacobin (Clamator jacobinus) and Common Hawk Cuckoos (Hierococcyx varius), Koels, Babblers and Prinias. Our main interest was to see the Black Francolin, Savanna Nightjar (Caprimulgus affinis) and Eurasian Roller (Coracias garrulus) that are commonly seen in this season. chestnut collar and golden-scalloped black body, the Black Francolin is a complete contrast to the Grey Francolin. As we walked back on this trail amid the chirping of Indian Silverbills (Euodice malabarica) and the song of the Indian Bushlark (Mirafra erythroptera), we found ourselves at the exit gate of the park. We ventured out about a furlong from this gate to another mining pit that lay bare, probably because this is outside the park area and, therefore, not restored to its original ecology. Here we saw many Blue-tailed Bee-eaters (Merops philippinus) and Red Avadavats (Amandava amandava) amidst the sparse vegetation. Black Francolin The park had different trails to explore. Walking on one such path we heard the "kwee-kweeeee-kwee" call of a Black Francolin. We followed the call and reached the edge of an erstwhile mine pit that was now green with the native Aravalli plants. Standing majestically on the other side of the pit was the Black Francolin. It kept calling at regular intervals and there was an occasional response call from the distant hillocks, probably from its mate. With a white patch on its cheek, a Red Avadavat On the ground a bunch of Lemon Emigrant butterflies were mud-puddling. The butterflies, it is said, draw their minerals from mud as it is not available in the nectar of flowers. 4

(Turdoides caudata) and Baya Weavers (Ploceus philippinus) were all there. So were the Common Hoopoes (Upupa epops). Lemon Emigrant Common Hoopoe A White-eyed Buzzard (Butastur teesa) flew past us and landed on a distant tree top. We had to deviate to a different trail to reach the Buzzard. After half an hour of walking we found ourselves face to face with a vast stretch of denuded hillocks. Luck was on our side and we found Eurasian Rollers, about half a dozen of them, very actively flying from one tree to another. The bird was almost the same size but paler than the Indian Roller. The Eurasian Roller is a passage migrant in this region in autumn, as some populations are known to migrate to Africa through India. Savanna Nightjar As we walked through the grass bushes a Savanna Nightjar got flushed out. After a sluggish flight it landed on a rocky patch. We readied our cameras to take pictures but due to camouflage it took us a while to spot it again. In the bright sunlight it sat where it landed, unmoved by the clicks of the cameras. This was the first close look we had had of any Nightjar, and we were very excited to see it in the open, and that too for a very long time. The upper parts were brownish and vermiculated with brown speckles. The Savanna Nightjar is a resident bird and nocturnal in nature. It resides in open forests among tall grasses. Eurasian Roller Now we scanned for the Buzzard and sighted a juvenile one. All this time the Black Francolins were calling and so were the Jacobin Cuckoos. One interesting behaviour was that of a juvenile Jacobin Cuckoo amidst a few Jungle Babblers. It immediately reminded me of the brood parasitic nature of the Jacobin Cuckoo, wherein it lays its turquoise-blue eggs in the nest of the Babblers. The Babblers probably were still nurturing the juvenile cuckoo, thinking that it was a bird of its own flock! Jungle Prinia On the second weekend we were at the park half an hour earlier than our previous visit and tried two different paths that we had not covered earlier. We hoped to see the Eurasian Roller this time. The Black Francolin, Jungle Prinia (Prinia sylvatica), White-eared Bulbuls (Pycnonotus leucotis), Common Babblers Overall, it was wonderful birding in the Aravalli Biodiversity Park. *** 5

DIVING EXPERIENCES OFF THE UNEXPLORED WEST COAST Text and Photos: Amritha Lawrence The author with Bluestreak Cleaner Wrasse The Indian subcontinent is the most beautiful place in the world – it has everything to offer, from spirituality to one of the most diverse ecosystems that houses some of the most exotic species in the world, both on land and in water. The unexplored paradise of water is something that has always been a mystery to people, with a lot happening under the surface of the deep blue. Join me, as we explore these places and see the world that lives below the blue waters of this country. The island is surrounded by different dive sites and each has a uniqueness that belongs only to that particular place. From watching Cuttlefish mating, to watching a group of Surgeonfish just rubbing themselves on the boulder surface to take away the fungus, and Moray Eels just wandering about their own business - this place always has action with not a single dull day. As a dive master, currently working in the west coast of this country, every day is a joy. To wake up each day and sail along this coast for diving is always a different experience, right from boarding the boat to reaching the dive destination. Netrani is an island that gives me this experience. It is situated 20km off the coast of the small town of Murudeshwar (156km from Mangalore). This island is a diving, snorkeling and birding paradise. The sight of pelagic birds soaring in the sky, and a group of Snappers swimming right underneath, make you wish you were a four-eyed fish. Surgeonfish Snapper Honeycomb Moray Eel 6

Some surprises, like being greeted by Whales and sometimes watching Turtles just burrow under small piles of corals, make you want to wake up every day. Each and every corner of the rocks here have something to offer, like for instance the Nudibranchs, tiny colourful slugs that are just crawling about doing what they do the best. The best part about my job is that I get to find these things and explore the unexplored blues over here. This life-changing experience is something I would recommend to everyone. It gives you a sense of achievement, the chance to watch marine life in all its beauty and, most importantly, it allows you to be a part of something new and gives you a chance to explore the unexplored depths of this country. To explore a totally different world – this incredibly vibrant deep blue world – is such a pleasure. Why restrict ourselves to images of underwater life when we can just watch it come to life every day? Nudibranch *** A DANDELI ADVENTURE Trip Report – Dandeli, October 2018 Text and Photos: Barnali Chaudhari A view of Dandeli forests Bestowed with natural beauty and lush green forests, Dandeli is the ideal mix of wildlife, adventure, scenic beauty and birding. The four of us (Surekha, Kalyani, Dr Jayati and I) started our journey towards Dandeli from Hyderabad to enjoy a long weekend. Dr Sheila and Dr Vipin joined us from Mumbai. events, we had to take the scenic route to avoid a road accident on the highway. While it took us longer to get our destination, we were blessed to see the beautiful landscape in the rain. We reached Castle Rock Nature Education Camp around 4:20PM. We passed through a small hanging bridge. After crossing the bridge, the road was made of concrete with pebbles for added friction during rain: an innovative idea! We had some breathtaking views of hills, and soon I felt like a part of Mother Nature. On October 19, 2018, we reached Hubli. I was amazed at the Warli art on the subway walls of Hubli railway station. We started our journey from Hubli around noon in a hired car, escorted by a Forest Department jeep. Mr Gundappa, our forest guide, was always with us and taking care of us. In a twist of 7

(Muscicapa dauurica) was sitting on the railing of the canopy walk. Bastilla sp. Moth Sheila noticed a moth on the pathway which was camouflaged by dry leaves. Unfortunately, we could not spot any animals. In spite of taking precautions like applying Dettol on our sneakers, leeches did not leave us alone. However, overall, it was an experience we will always cherish. At Castle Rock We saw several Golden Orioles (Oriolus oriolus), Orange Minivets (Pericrocotus flammeus), and assorted Drongos. We walked around exploring nearby areas and watched the beautiful colors of the sunset. We heard the call of the Castle Rock Night Frog which was just like somebody typing on a typewriter. Hence it was nicknamed the ‘Typewriter Frog’. After dinner we rested in the tent. Next day during breakfast we saw some Flycatchers and Sunbirds. I enjoyed the panoramic view from the observatory tower. After that we said good bye to Castle Rock. River rafting on Kali River After enjoying the Canopy Walk our next target was river rafting on Kali River. We reached our destination around 11:00AM. We were equipped with a life jacket, helmet and pedal. The Dandeli river rafting trail stretches for around 12km. Kim, our guide, was the head of the instructors and had 28 years of experience. Before starting he briefed us about the techniques of pedaling and safety measures. Kim first put water on us through his pedal. Then some of us jumped inside the water and bathed in the river. We climbed the raft again and started downstream. We were 11 rafters including Kim. The first rafting stretch is the most exciting one. This path is full of huge boulders, hence, requires expert steering. Our boat went hurtling down the river towards the rapids and bumpy rocks and narrow passageways. The first and second rapids are named 'Adi's Beard' and 'The Stitch' respectively. We experienced the thrill of a lifetime. We saw a pair of Great Hornbills and a Brahminy Kite (Haliastur indus) in flight. All of us loved river rafting, even those of us who were nonswimmers. Asian Brown Flycatcher Our day unfolded with lots of adventures. First, we headed towards Canopy Walk which is India's first, just 65 km away from Dandeli, near Castle Rock of Uttara Kannada. It is made of several hanging bridges connected to each other with big tree trunks. We explored the beauty of the Western Ghats at close quarters. Installed at a height of 30ft, the 240m walkway has multiple viewing areas. It has been developed jointly by Karnataka Tourism and the Forest Department. We saw Malabar Tamarind, Cinnamon, Bamboo, Eucalyptus, Lantana, Silver Oak, Teak trees, etc. We took in the sounds of the jungle and became one with it. An Asian Brown Flycatcher 8

was sitting on a tree. Jungle Babblers (Turdoides striata) and Spotted Doves (Stigmatopelia chinensis) were moving around. Jungle Babbler Mr Gundappa with Green Vine Snake Our next destination was Supa Dam. There are many dams built across Kali River for the generation of electricity. Supa Dam is one of the important dams and is situated at Ganeshgudi. It has two electricity generators of fifty megawatt each. Around 2:00PM we started back. As we boarded our vehicle, Mr Gundappa came with a Green Vine Snake in his hand. We learnt from him that this snake is a mildly venomous tree snake found in India and is very common in the Western Ghats. Malabar Giant Squirrel Syntheri Rock Our last destination for the day was Syntheri Rock. We reached at dusk. We entered the park and tried to enjoy as much as possible in the dim light. We went down about 200+ steps to get a glimpse of a monolithic rock hidden amidst the forests. On our way down, different types of rock samples were displayed with a board explaining the type of the rock and its characteristics. One stone attracted my attention – the Banded Iron Formation (BIF): Meta sedimentary rock showing alternating bands of silica and iron. Various trees were also described. Malabar Pied Hornbill We reached Kulgi Nature Camp and had lunch. We saw a Giant Squirrel on a tree trunk. A pair of Malabar Pied Hornbills 9

Banded Iron Formation Malabar Grey Hornbill All of us have heard the proverb that the force of water flow can even cut a stone. The caves of the Syntheri Rock are an example of that. The caves were created at the base of the rock due to the constant flow of water. A huge monolithic single boulder 300 feet high and 400 feet long stood in front of us with the river Kaneri (a tributary of Kali River) flowing down. It is believed to have been formed due to volcanic eruptions several thousand years ago and one can see homogeneous rock that has different colors and textures in different parts. It was named after Ms Cinthera, an English lady, who is believed to discovered the place a century ago. We took a kaccha ramp (easier path) while coming back. By this time the sun had set and it was dark. Timber Depot, with its logs lying scattered over a vast area, is famous for the sightings of all the three hornbills – Great Hornbill (Buceros bicornis), Malabar Pied Hornbill (Anthracoceros coronatus) and Malabar Grey Hornbill (Ocyceros griseus) – found in the Western Ghats. That is why Timber Depot is also called Hornbills Trail. We were lucky to spot all the three. By around 7:30PM we came back to our tent at Kulgi Nature Camp. The tent was named Jenukallu after a village. In the video room named Nagzari, we learnt about the Kali River and wild elephant rehabilitation. Then we had dinner at the dining hall. Wooden logs with the designs formed by wood-boring beetles We sat on the logs and noticed some special designs on the logs. Dr Vipin told us about one of the wonders of nature - a type of wood-boring beetle lays eggs and the larvae which feed on wood after hatching from the egg, create characteristic tunnels in the process. After pupating and developing into adults they leave the timber. Little Spiderhunter Early the next morning we went for birding with our guide Jogi. He was a good birdwatcher with an in-depth knowledge of calls, species and habits. At one spot beside the road, we saw the Little Spiderhunter (Arachnothera longirostra). Then we visited the Timber Depot. Here we saw a live demonstration of a dog trained to track down poachers in the forest by his master Venkatesh. Jacobin Cuckoo 10

We saw a Jacobin Cuckoo (Clamator jacobinus) perched on a tree trunk. We also observed a lot of bird activity over the fully-bloomed African Tulip trees with beautiful red flowers. Several birds were busy with their morning activities. The Jerdon’s (Chloropsis jerdoni) and Golden-fronted Leafbirds (Chloropsis aurifrons) were totally camouflaged in the leaves. The Blyth’s Starling (Sturnia (malabarica) blythii) was busy getting honey from the flowers. We spotted both Whitethroated (Halcyon smyrnensis) and Stork-billed Kingfishers (Pelargopsis capensis). After breakfast at Hornbill Resort we went to Old Magazine House. Like Sattal Studio, Old Magazine House offers bird watching at a very close range. There is no concept of walking and tracking birds as they come to bathe at the camp itself. Heart-spotted Woodpecker There we saw a pair of Heart-spotted Woodpeckers (Hemicircus canente). We also saw Langurs and Bonnet Macaques on the trees. One Bonnet Macaque was spitting out the fibrous leftovers of the sticks after consuming the juice in it, just like we eat sugarcane. Jerdon’s Leafbird Cruiser Soon, it was time to say good bye to Dandeli. Thanks to Surekha for arranging such a memorable trip. INDOOR MEETING: Talk by Mr M Ram Mohan, Forest Range Officer, Bejjur Reserve Forest on “Vultures of Palarapu Cliff”. Tuesday, 19th February 2019, 6.30PM: Goethe-zentrum Hyderabad, 20 Journalist’s Colony, Road No. 3, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500 034. (For directions, please contact 94905-09251 or 040-65526443/23350040) Mr Ram Mohan brought into light the breeding colony of the Long-billed Vulture, a Critically Endangered species, at Palarapu Gutta (cliff) in the Kagaznagar Forest Division of Adilabad Circle in 2013. Trip Report – Manjeera Barrage, December 23, 2018 Madhuri Mondal Part of the group at Manjeera (Photo: Dr Samuel Sukumar) The last BSAP field trip of 2018 was at the Manjeera Reservoir. It is a man-made reservoir situated inside the Manjeera Wildlife Sanctuary (MWS). MWS covers an area of 20 sq.km, and is located in Medak district, 50 km away from Hyderabad. It was notified as a wildlife sanctuary in 1978 to protect the riverine ecosystem. The reservoir is a marshy wetland, surrounded by grassland. By December, small pools and islands had formed as the water level had come down. 1

I had been missing the opportunity to visit Manjeera for birding since the last couple of years. So, this time, when I saw the mail announcing the field trip, I made up my mind to attend it somehow and voila! it turned out to be an amazing trip. Grey-headed Swamphen (Photo: Raghu SR) Red-rumped Swallow (Photo: Dr Samuel Sukumar) As we reached the barrage, we were greeted by a mixed flock of swallows on a wire. There were Barn Swallows (Hirundo rustica), Streak-throated Swallows (Petrochelidon fluvicola) and Red-rumped Swallows (Cecropis daurica). Purple Heron (Photo: Madhuri Mondal) Cotton Pygmy-goose (Photo: Dr Samuel Sukumar) The first glance at the reservoir rewarded us with the sightings of a large group of Cotton Pygmy-goose (Nettapus coromandelianus) and a basking Marsh Crocodile or mugger. Glossy Ibis (Photo: Dr Samuel Sukumar) Marsh Crocodile (aka Mugger) (Photo: Raghu SR) As I scanned through my binoculars, other waterfowl also revealed themselves. Amongst them were the purple beauties – Grey-headed Swamphen (Porphyrio porphyrio) and the Purple Heron (Ardea purpurea). Little Grebe (Photo: Raghu SR) 2

Bronze-winged Jacana Adult (L) and Immature (R) (Photos: Dr Samuel Sukumar) Next on the radar were the Bronze-winged Jacana (Metopidius indicus) and the Pheasant-tailed Jacana (Hydrophasianus chirurgus). While I was appreciating their beauty and observing their foraging behaviour, a Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus) landed in the marshes. I watched a Little Grebe (Tachybaptus ruficollis) dive into the water and disappear, only to reappear elsewhere. A Common Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis) was perched on a wooden pole, looking for prey. While all this drama was unfolding, the surprise of the day appeared. We noticed a grey-coloured Egret foraging in the marshes. A good observation, along with a look at the field guides, led us to conclude that it was the Western Reef Egret (Egretta gularis), a rare sight for this location. Black-headed Ibis (Photo: Madhuri Mondal) Then appeared the Black-headed Ibises (Threskiornis melanocephalus), graceful in their black and white attire. At a distance towards the marshy grasslands, I saw Painted Storks (Mycteria leucocephala) and Asian Openbills (Anastomus oscitans) gliding smoothly over the grasslands. A few Black Drongos (Dicrurus macrocercus) were sitting on the bushes looking for prey. Common Kingfisher (Photo: Madhuri Mondal) River Tern (Photo: Raghu SR) Western Reef Egret (Photo: Madhuri Mondal) 3

Grey Wagtail (Photo: Dr Samuel Sukumar) Whiskered Tern (Photo: Raghu SR) We then decided to watch some forest birds and walked around the reservoir, which turned out to be a rewarding experience as well. One of my friends pointed out an Asian Paradiseflycatcher (Terpsiphone paradisi). In the process of getting a better look, we also saw a White-Breasted Waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus) and a Grey Wagtail (Motacilla cinerea) around a stream nearby. Other interesting birds on the barrage were the Terns. Along with the commonly-seen River Terns (Sterna aurantia), there was another small Tern species flying swiftly over the reservoir; it was later identified from photographs as a Whiskered Tern. Osprey (Photo: Raghu SR) One of the most interesting sightings of the day was the Osprey (Pandion haliaetus). Though I wasn’t lucky enough to see it directly, one of our friends had sighted it and took some photos of it. Blue-tailed Bee-eater (Photo: Madhuri Mondal) Green Bee-eater (Photo: Madhuri Mondal) Asian Paradise-flycatcher (Photo: Raghu SR) We got to see the elegant Blue-tailed Bee-eater (Merops philippinus) sitting on a wire. The bird gave us enough time to appreciate its beauty. A Green Bee-eater (Merops orientalis) and a few Wire-tailed Swallows (Hirundo smithii) with their beautiful hanging wire-like tails were sitting on another wire. 4

excitement, we started towards the lake, which is beside Tallapalli village. The walk towards this lake added few more species to the list. There were Eurasian Coots (Fulica atra), Egrets and other common waterfowl in a small lake on the way. In the bushes, we spotted Ashy (Prinia socialis) and Plain Prinias (Prinia inornata). Flocks of Red Avadavats (Amandava amandava) flew out from the shrubs while we walked past. We saw some Collared Pratincoles (Glareola pratincola) gliding high in the sky and a Shikra (Accipiter badius). Wire-tailed Swallow (Photo: Madhuri Mondal) One of the lifers for me that day was the Chestnut-tailed Starling (Sturnia malabarica). Blue-tailed Bee-eaters and Chestnut-tailed Starlings are winter migrants to this part of the country. The other starlings we saw that day were Brahminy Starlings (Sturnia pagodarum) and Rosy Starlings (Pastor roseus). A little ahead, we spotted a Long-tailed Shrike (Lanius schach) and the elusive White-browed Bulbul (Pycnonotus luteolus). We also spotted the Indian Golden Oriole (Oriolus oriolus), Purple-rumped Sunbird (Leptocoma zeylonica) and Common Tailorbird (Orthotomus sutorius) on that trail. Collared Pratincole (Photo: Raghu SR) On reaching the lake, we saw a flock of Flamingos through the binoculars. We counted 37 one-legged pink beauties. Some of them were resting or taking a nap, while some of them made loops with their long necks. There was also one lone Eurasian Spoonbill amidst the Greater Flamingos. Trip Report – Tadoba Andhari Tiger Reserve, December 10-14, 2018 Text and Photos: Janardhan Reddy Chhoti Tara Eight of us in 2 vehicles left Hyderabad for Tadoba early on December 10, 2018. We decided to take the longer route – NH44 to Karanji and then MHS6/7 to Chandrapur via Wani. This route is 60km longer than the one via Mancherial, but we had heard that the Mancherial-Chandrapur road was in bad condition. Our decision was wise as we got to Tadoba well in time for a quick lunch, after which we went into the forest at 2:30PM. A new rule bans the carrying of mobile phones and tablets into the forest. This is to prevent phones from being used to inform others about tiger sightings. In the waterhole One cub was visible but stayed inside the forest. Chhoti Tara Chhoti Tara’s cub We started the afternoon well with a tiger sighting of Chhoti Tara and one of her cubs. They were on a kill and the mother walked straight towards us and then entered a small water hole to quench her thirst after a heavy meal. 8

Soon after, we glimpsed a Leopard that ran across the road. Over the next couple of days, we sighted 2 more leopards, including a melanistic one (Black Leopard). It had been recently sighted and is quite a rarity in Central India. It is more common in the Western Ghats, Nilgiri Biosphere and the North-east. The 4th adult tiger that we saw was a 3-year-old progeny of Chhoti Tara. A beautiful specimen! He occupied the road and had a long nap, resulting in all of us having to find another route out of the forest. Sadly, his brother had been electrocuted in the buffer zone a couple of days earlier. The next couple of days continued with great sightings of tigers and their cubs:  Maya and her two 12-to-14-month-old cubs in a playful mood Spotted Owlet The playful cubs  Sonam and her cub Grey Junglefowl Sonam and her cub Some visitors had also witnessed Sonam earlier hunting and killing a Sambar fawn. White-eyed Buzzard Chhoti Tara’s 3-year-old blocking the road 9

Alexandrine Parakeet The bird life was equally exciting, with sightings of Blackwinged Kite (Elanus caeruleus), Spotted Owlets (Athene brama), Indian Peafowl (Pavo cristatus), Grey Junglefowl (Gallus sonneratii), White-eyed Buzzard (Butastur teesa) (possibly juvenile), Alexandrine Parakeet (Psittacula eupatria). Red-naped Ibis Great Egret We also saw the Green Bee-eater (Merops orientalis), Whitethroated Kingfishers (Halcyon smyrnensis), Red-naped Ibis (Pseudibis papillosa), Red-wattled Lapwings (Vanellus indicus), Great Egrets (Egretta alba), unidentified Ducks and Teals, and finally a Crested Hawk Eagle (Nisaetus cirrhatus) with its prey of a Hare. Green Bee-eater Crested Hawk Eagle with kill We could hear plenty of other birds – perhaps many more than on earlier visits. White-throated Kingfisher 10

Other animals sighted were Gaur, Sambar, Chital, Barking Deer (Muntjac), Wild Boar, Nilgai and Mongoose. The forest was in excellent condition and all the animals looked healthy and well-fed. Sadly, on the 14th, we had to leave this beautiful forest and return to the humdrum of the city. All in all a great trip. Bay-backed Shrike *** Trip Report – Sultanpur National Park, Gurugram, December 2018 Text and Photos: Sita Susarla Common Cranes at Sultanpur National Park With an area of 1.43 sq km, the Sultanpur National Park in the Gurugram district of Haryana is well carved out for migratory birds. Special bunds and islands, four tube wells that pump Yamuna water to the park, trees that are popular with birds like Acacia Nilotica, Acacia Tortilis, Beris and Neem have all contributed significantly to making the park a sanctuary for birds. A visit to this park and nearby mudflats, and the Najafgarh Jheel, during the winter months is a fascinating experience for any birder. We set off with a guide to see the Variable Wheatear that had just arrived in the mudflats of Sultanpur. It seems the Variable Wheatear was seen again after a gap of 2 years and our guide happened to have spotted it a couple of days before. Apart from the Variable Wheatear, there were also the Common Starling, Northern Lapwing, Long-legged Buzzard and Stolickza’s Bushchat on our target list. Isabelline Wheatear While looking for the Wheatear we came across the beautiful Isabelline Wheatear, the Desert Wheatear and a flock of Greater Short-toed Larks – all migrants. 11

A pair of Southern Grey Shrikes kept calling to each other as we walked the length of the flats scouting for the new arrival. After a few clicks of the Shrike, that perched very close to us, the guide turned our attention to the Long-legged Buzzard sunning atop an electric pole. We scrambled for the Binoculars and Cameras to take some quick pictures, but soon realized that the Buzzard was in no hurry to leave its warm perch. A little further up a Tawny Pipit, an Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark and a Long-tailed Shrike were seen in conversation on a bund. Desert Wheatear female Long-legged Buzzard Greater Short-toed Lark As the sunrays streamed through the cold winter morning on the late November day, a Marsh Harrier flew by close to the ground as if to warm up for the day. Tawny Pipit As there was no sign of the Wheatear, we decided to visit the nearby Najafgarh Jheel and come back to the flats after lunch. We drove for about ten minutes to reach the Jheel where a flock of Common Cranes happened to be regular visitors. Here we saw a flock of Common (aka Eurasian) Starlings perched on adjacent shrubs. The Starlings in dark dotted colours were glistening in the bright light. The calls were a series of different notes, distinctly different from those of other Starlings. Southern Grey Shrike 12

white-bellied and the white-crowned. What we saw in Sultanpur was black-bellied morph. Common Starling The Jheel side was a serene wetland with not a soul around and a perfect birding place. We saw a flock of Common Cranes feeding on grain. As we approached them, they fluttered into the sky only a few feet above us, circled and turned away to a distant field. This gave us an opportunity to take some pictures of the Cranes in flight. There were around ten Pied Avocets, some Black-winged Stilts, and a few Painted Storks, Wood and Common Sandpipers wading through the marshes. Variable Wheatear Our guide was already looking for Stoliczka’s Bushchat by the time we were finished with the Wheatear. With no sign of it we returned to the National Park to see some ducks. It was around 3:30PM and two Greater Spotted Eagles were actively hunting for prey, swooping over the waters. The park was brimming with Painted Storks and their chicks, and huge flocks of Great Cormorants, Greylag Geese, Shovellers, Pintails, Grebes and Coots. After scanning for an hour for any new arrivals we decided to call it a day. We thanked the guide, a keen observer of birds for the last twenty years around Sultanpur, for showing us around. With five lifers it was indeed a great field day for us. Common Stonechat After a quick bite at the eateries we set off once again to the mudflats in search of the Variable Wheatear. This time our guide spotted it exactly at the same location it was a couple of days ago. It is a common practice in Delhi to approach the bird in a car, and shoot pictures also from there. This way we get to observe the bird without disturbing it. Isabelline Shrike The polymorphic Variable Wheatear is a winter migrant to Sultanpur. Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Red Avadavat (Amandava amandava) Red Avadavat Male (Left), Female (Centre) and Juvenile (Right) (Manjeera WLS, January 10, 2019) Order: Passeriformes Family: Estrildidae Genus: Amandava Species: A. amandava Size: 10 cm flavidiventris is seen in Myanmar, and parts of China, Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam, while A. a. punicea is the Javan species, and A. a. decouxi is seen in Cambodia. Habitat & behaviour: The Red Avadavat breeds across the Indian subcontinent in the flat plains, grasslands and open fields with standing crops or tall grasses, usually near water. It is usually seen in small flocks, and tends to fly with rapid wingbeats before descending into grass clumps or reeds. Birds often ruffle their head feathers as an invitation, and in a flock, preen each other. Description & distribution: The Red Avadavat (aka Red Munia or Strawberry Finch) is a member of the Estrildidae family. It is around the same size as a Sparrow; the male has a striking deep red body with distinct white spots on the upperparts and wing feathers. It also has a black eye-stripe, darker belly, dark pinkish legs, rounded black tail, and a seasonally red bill. The non-breeding male is duller but still has a red rump. The female is duller overall, with lesser number of white spots on wings, but the reddish bill and black eye-stripe are still noticeable. Interestingly, the scientific name amandava and the common name Avadavat are both derived from the name of the city of Ahmedabad, from where it used to be exported for the pet trade in older times. Pairs stay together for the breeding season. The call is a single-note pseep, usually given out in flight; while the song is a series of low notes. The diet consists mainly of grass seeds, although it does occasionally take insects like termites. Nesting: The Red Avadavat breeds mainly between November and April. The nest is globular and made of grass blades. The usual clutch consists of 5-6 white eggs. The bill undergoes a seasonal change in colour, turning red in May, darkening towards November/December, and turning black rapidly in April before starting the cycle again in May. Local name: The Red Avadavat is known as ‘Laal munia’ in Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi and Punjabi, ‘Torra jinuwayi’ or ‘Yerra jinuwayi’ in Telugu and ‘Chevenna munia’ in Malayalam. The nominate sub-species A. amandava is seen in Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Pakistan. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 16 Number 4 April 2019 FIELD OUTING: Sunday, 28th April 2019: Nehru Zoological Park, 6.30AM. Established in October 1959 and opened to the public in October 1963, the 380-acre Zoo, located adjacent to the Mir Alam Tank, offers its denizens a variety of habitats, including patches of forest, a water body, grassland, etc. Not surprisingly, the zoo has usually yielded a good selection of bird sightings. The various enclosures hold a lot of small ground and tree birds, as well as a number of water birds. Eurasian Thick-knees have been known to breed near the Sambhar enclosure.
