AVIAN EXPEDITION IN EASTERN GHATS Trip Report – Lambasinghi, January 4-6, 2019 Shilka Chaudhari The group during the trip (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) The Eastern Ghats is known for its pristine forests and dense canopies. It is home to some amazing birdlife. Hence a twoand-a-half-day avian quest was planned and organized by Vikram for a group of 26 members early in the new year. On January 4th, we started in the evening from Hyderabad by Godavari Express and reached Vizag the next morning. An AC coach was arranged for the trip and accommodation was provided in a hotel close to Ramakrishna Beach on the first day. Season: Winter Temperature: 15°C to 26°C 1

First leg: Dali Cheruvu, Teelineelapuram and Naupada Swamps After a hearty breakfast, our journey began from Vizag to our first destination of the day, Dali Cheruvu in Srikakulam district of Andhra Pradesh, a distance of 115km which we covered in around 3 hours. Walking the last stretch to the lake along an unpaved road, the common species we came across were Indian Roller, Green Bee-eater, Blue-tailed Beeeater and Black Drongo. Bronze-winged Jacana (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Spot-billed Pelican, Cotton Pygmy-goose & Common Coot (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Blue-tailed Bee-eater (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Little Grebe with chick (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Purple Heron (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Walking further down the trail, we came across Indian Pond Herons, a Purple Heron well camouflaged in the surroundings, Cattle Egrets, Alexandrine Parakeets and a Southern Coucal. A Brahminy Kite was also seen flying at high altitude, and White-breasted Kingfishers were a common sighting. Cotton Pygmy-goose (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) We crossed a small village settlement to reach the huge Dali lake, which was covered with lilies, lily pads and lotus. The muddy trail had the lake on one side and paddy fields/cultivation, mango and banana plantations on the other. The water bird species we noticed were Common Coot, Little Grebe, Pheasant-tailed Jacana, Bronze-winged Jacana, Wigeon, Cotton Pygmy-goose and Little Cormorant. The lake had Spot-billed Pelicans as well. White-breasted Kingfisher (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) 2

On our way back to the coach, Barnali and Manjira came across birds like Chestnut-tailed Starling and Yellow-billed Babbler. Nylon nets were tied to some of the trees, which served the purpose of protecting new fledglings falling down from their nests. Surekha remarked in dismay that the number of trees and the count of birds had drastically come down compared to her earlier visit around 3 years back. The reason for this decline could be attributed to deforestation and human habitation. During a brief discussion with Shafaat uncle and Vikram regarding these birds flying down from Siberia and other European nations, I was informed that these bird species could be residents and not migratory as informed by tabloids or webpages. The last spot to be covered late that evening was Naupada Swamps. We sighted and photographed species like Common Sandpiper, Black-winged Stilts, Red-wattled Lapwings and Pond Herons. Calling it a day, we headed back to Vizag. Chestnut-tailed Starling (Photo: K Karthik Sai) We had lunch in a town named Tekkali, and then headed towards the Telineelapuram Bird Sanctuary. Telineelapuram is a village situated in Ichchapuram, a Mandal headquarters in the Srikakulam district. The place is visited by a lot of migratory birds. We were thrilled to see the colonies of Spot-billed Pelicans and Painted Storks in the village. Little Egret (Photo: K Karthik Sai) Painted Stork colony (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Black-winged Stilt (Photo: K Karthik Sai) Second Leg: Lambasinghi Painted Stork adult (above) and chicks (below) (Photos: K Karthik Sai) (Note: The photographer confirms that the photos were taken from a safe distance) Kondakarla Bird Sanctuary The group at Kondakarla Ava (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) 3 and

Early the next morning, some of the group members visited the popular Ramakrishna Beach. We (my father and I) spent around 40 minutes in a park next to the beach and got to see the glorious sunrise with the backdrop of Bay of Bengal. After breakfast we headed towards Kondakarla Ava lake, which is the second largest freshwater lake in the state. Located in the foothills of the Eastern Ghats, it is situated 50km from Vizag. The lake is home to a diverse array of flora and fauna. Purple Swamphen (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Barn Swallow (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Indian Pond Heron (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) The fishermen use palm logs converted into canoes to ferry villagers across and to take tourists on fun rides. We enjoyed our ride too. After clicking a number of interesting snaps we decided to take our lunch break. Later in the afternoon, we headed to Lankapakala. On our hilly drive, we saw a number of tourist camps around, all littered with plastic. It was a sad sight. One of the boats (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) We were greeted by the Forest Officer Mr Krishna Babu. The Forest Department had arranged lovely evening snacks and piping hot ginger tea in the cold weather. Sightings of Tricolored Munia, Common Mynas perched on top of a dry shrub, and Plain Prinia flying over the water, were noted. Late in the evening, we decided to return for an overnight stay in a hotel in Narsipatnam town. The serene lake was surrounded by coconut and palm trees and green hills all around. The lake water was full of lotus flowers and lilies. Barn Swallows were observed cruising low, flying just inches above the water for insects. We hired 4 boats (2 pairs of boats tied together with the help of sticks and ropes) to explore the fresh water lake and enjoy the beauty of water birds. The few notable species we came across, besides the Barn Swallows, were Little Cormorant, Pheasant-tailed Jacana, Purple Swamphen, Indian Moorhen, a lone Purple Heron and several Indian Pond Herons. Common Myna (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Third Leg: Chintapalle Forest At 5:30AM on the last day, we kickstarted our journey to Lambasinghi which is about 31 km from Narsipatnam. Lambasinghi is popularly known as Kashmir of South India, and is also called the second Ooty of the South, as mentioned by our coach driver. It is a popular tourist destination. Pheasant-tailed Jacana (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) 4

A coffee plant (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Indian Giant Squirrel (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) On reaching the place, the enthusiastic birding team alighted from the coach to take some group snaps and to enjoy the chilly morning weather. Mr Krishna Babu had arranged for our birding expedition in the dense forests of Kothapalli and Lankapakala in the Chintapalle plateau. The habitat consisted of moist deciduous and evergreen forests and coffee and pepper plantations. On reaching the forest we were greeted by Grey Wagtails on the street near a trail. Further down the moist trail, we were delighted to hear the calls (kutroo…kutroo) of a Brown-headed Barbet. After a long walk around the forest, a delicious South Indian breakfast arranged for the team by the Forest Department revived our energy. Small trees of wild curry leaves were seen in abundance. Tropical shrubs and small trees of bixa orellana, also known as Lipstick Trees, looked really pretty in the bright sun rays. After a while, we noticed a bird of prey soaring high over the dense canopy and making loud, sharp calls. Good photographs of the raptor were clicked by Jayati and Dr Samuel. After a brief discussion based on the photographs, which showed the bird having prominent wide black-and-white bars on the underside of broad flight feathers and tail, and the piercing calls, we concluded that the raptor was a Crested Serpent Eagle and not a Short-toed Snake Eagle as presumed earlier. Red-whiskered Bulbul (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) The commonest birds in these habitats were the Bulbul species. The Red-vented and Red-whiskered Bulbuls were seen flying over the treetops. The other species we encountered were Vernal Hanging Parrot, Oriental Whiteeye, Black-rumped Flameback and Purple Sunbird. A Coppersmith Barbet was spotted and photographed by Dr Samuel. We noticed some Giant Squirrels hopping from one branch to another and running up and down the trees. Crested Serpent Eagle (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) We continued walking up a trail and saw a huge owl land on one of the trees. Everyone aimed their cameras for a good shot, but due to the long distance and the number of trees coming in the way, most of the shots turned out to be grainy, except for one clicked by Dr Pravin. An inspection of the snaps showed the prominent ear tufts and helped identify the owl as a Brown Fish Owl. In the midst of this commotion we heard the calls of the Black-hooded Oriole. Some members of the team had seen a Scarlet Minivet and a Greater Yellownape woodpecker. Mr Moorty mentioned spotting a flock of Yellow-wattled Lapwings which I was unlucky to miss. He also added that they had earlier seen a large flock of waders in one of the lakes inside a high-security submarine zone in Vizag. Vernal Hanging Parrot (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) 5

Our forest walks came to an end, and we headed back to Narsipatnam for a quick lunch peppered with fresh strawberries offered by Mr Ajitkumar. Later in the day, we got back to Vizag to catch our Hyderabad-bound train. Besides the birds, this trip was very enriching in terms of flora and varied lush green coffee and pepper plantations which I had seen for the very first time. From my end, I believe the total bird count would be around 50+ species. Alexandrine Parakeet (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Jungle Myna (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Southern Coucal (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) The other common species that we came across there were House Crows, House Sparrows, Common Mynas, Black Kites and Blue-tailed Bee-eaters. Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Lesser Flamingo (Phoenicoparrus minor) Lesser Flamingo (Jamnagar, February 8, 2019) Order: Phoenicopteriformes Family: Phoenicopteridae Genus: Phoenicoparrus Species: P. minor Size: 90-105 cm feeds primarily on the Spirulina algae which, though itself blue-green in colour, contains the photosynthetic pigments that give the Flamingo its pink hue. Since Spirulina grows only in very alkaline lakes, the presence of Flamingos indicates the alkaline nature of the water, making it unsuitable for irrigation. Description & distribution: The Lesser Flamingo is one of the two species of Flamingos seen in India, and the smallest of all the Flamingo species. It is a tall rosy-white stork-like bird with long spindly legs, an overall pinkish-white plumage, and a heavy dark bill with a pronounced kink. While the Lesser Flamingo is smaller than the Greater, it is not a reliable diagnostic indicator in the field unless the two species are together, since the size can vary considerably between the sexes too. The bill, which has crimson feathers at the base, is the feature that most easily differentiates the Lesser Flamingo from the Greater, which has a more pink bill with a dark tip. In flight, the crimson and black underwings, and the shorter trailing legs, are diagnostic. The Flamingo feeds by swiveling its bill in the water as it walks along, and the bill is specialised for filtering tiny food items. The call is a harsh croaking call, usually uttered in flight. Nesting: Besides Africa, which is its main breeding ground, the Lesser Flamingo has been known to breed in some parts of the Rann of Kutch, and the Zinzuwadia and Purabcheria salt pans in north-western India. The breeding season, usually June to July, can extend up to January the next year; during this period, the Lesser Flamingo lays its single chalky-white egg on a mound built of mud. Soon after hatching, the chicks join communal ‘creches’ managed by a few adult birds, which lead the chicks by foot to fresh water, a journey of, sometimes, up to 30km. Post breeding, its movements are erratic; it is seen in the Little Rann of Kutch, Sambhar Salt Lake in Rajasthan, Point Calimere in Tamil Nadu, Pulicat Lake in Andhra Pradesh, Chilika Lake in Orissa, and several other inland waterbodies. Local name: The Lesser Flamingo is known as ‘Chhota rajhans’ in Hindi, ‘Nano balo’ or ‘Nano hunj’ in Gujarati, ‘Chhota rohit’ in Marathi and ‘Vankara mooti konga’ in Telugu. Habitat & behaviour: The Lesser Flamingo is generally seen in flocks in lakes or other water bodies with shallow water. BIRD RACE OR BIRD SAVIOURS? Report – Hyderabad Bird Race, February 17, 2019 Manideep The group during the trip (Photo courtesy: Manideep) I have had fond memories of participation in the Hyderabad Bird Race since 2016. Every time I participate, I learn something new and make new friends. This year was no exception. I was too excited to sleep the previous night. We did not have our own cars. Hence the organizing committee was kind enough to provide us transport. Our great group (Adnan, Mallesh, Manideep, Mahesh, Vivek, Sravani, Tejasri and Vijaya) consisted of three Deccan Birders and five students from Forest College and Research Institute (FCRI). Our first pitstop was a remote location at Langar Houz nestled amidst thick bushes along the banks of River Musi. The first bird for the day was a Grey Francolin flying right above some scrub. The place looked stunning with hundreds of Baya nests hanging from the trees with background of Golconda Fort. We identified more than 35 species in no time. As the day started to get warmer, we decided to venture to Osman Sagar. Last time I visited this place was four years ago to watch the beautiful Lesser Flamingos late in the evening. Rest of them were visiting Osman Sagar for the first time. The route was so tricky that it reminded us of a maze. 1

Our team led by experienced birders Adnan and Vivek ensured that each member had sufficient time to get to know details about the birds. After identifying 40 more species for nearly two hours, we were in for a shock. We saw a female Garganey trying hard to fly from the surface of water. As we approached closer to the bird, it started flapping the wings uncontrollably. She was stuck in a fisherman’s net right underneath her neck and was fifteen feet away from the shore. As they approached the bird, our anxiety increased watching her panic even more and trying desperately to fly away. The nylon strings were too strong around the bird to be snapped with bare hands. Garganey with nylon string entangled around its wings (Photo: Manideep) At this moment the tiny pencil knife of one of the team members came in handy. She was safely brought to the shore after carefully disentangling the strings. Garganey (Photo: Mallesh) Mallesh & Mahesh assessing the depth (Photo: Manideep) After much discussion and planning, Mahesh and Mallesh from FCRI volunteered to get into the water to rescue the bird. Braving the squishy mud, the duo entered the lake with the support of a long stick which was held by rest of us on the bank. Checking for injuries (Photo: Manideep) All of us were so relieved and happy to see her flying away into the sky that, we forgot the squishy mud and the struggle to get her free. Suddenly we realised that most of the afternoon had gone by. We made a quick dash to Ameenpur Lake and managed to get our final list to 110. We felt so strongly bonded with each other after the rescue that we decided to name Garganey as our bird of the day. It was a fantastic day with so many beautiful memories and amazing camaraderie between everyone in our team. As we walked around the habitat, it lifted our spirts, as we never knew what we were going to see next. Watching birds with their delicate wings flying from branch to branch and taking food to their young made us feel one with nature. As I watched the Garganey fly away, I felt like a bird expanding my wings, learning new things and flying high. Mallesh & Mahesh to the rescue (Photo: Manideep) *** 2

Wood Sandpiper (Photo: Ritish Kannayagari) The pink Flamingos with their long necks & long legs kept me rooted there. While I was in search of warblers my teammate spotted a Eurasian Wryneck, which was a lifer for me. I was very happy to see it. An Indian Nightjar flew right in front of us. We went in search of the Short-eared Owl but unfortunately, we couldn't find it. On our way back we spotted raptors like Steppe Eagle & Osprey. As we completed birding in Osmansagar we headed to Himayatsagar. Due to hot weather conditions there was not much activity of birds. In the whole day of birding what attracted me most was the cloud of Rosy Starlings flying above our heads. There were about 100. From the farm we walked along the banks of the lake. My love towards birds will never change. *** 3

ARE COMMON BIRDS STILL COMMON? Report – Hyderabad Bird Race, February 17, 2019 Dr Barnali Chaudhuri Asian Paradise-flycatcher (Photo: Umesh Mani) “I did not notice any house sparrows during the whole day of birding”, Sanjeevani, the youngest member of Deccan Birders, wondered after the Hyderabad Bird Race. As we proceeded further into the forest, we noticed a Jungle Nightjar sitting quietly on the branch of a big tree. We spotted another one on a tree nearby. A Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher justified its name with its beautiful blue colour. On 17th Feb 2019, we all gathered at the Tourism Plaza at Begumpet at dawn. As the sun rose in the east, lighting up the place, our bird race had already begun. Common (Blue Rock) Pigeons were stationed under the shades of the building. Black Kites soared through the sky canvassing the area for prey. We were assigned to a group. Each group had four to five members, and the groups were named after bird species like Kingfisher, Bulbul, Swan, etc. I was a part of “Hawks” along with Ambika, Ritish (our Captain), and Dhruva. After the ceremonial waving of the flag from the Plaza, we were on our way to Ananthagiri hills. En route, we saw raptors gliding in the sky. One of them was a Greater Spotted Eagle. A Black-winged Kite perched on a wire. Red-vented Bulbuls were everywhere. Ambika listed the birds as we progressed towards our first destination. The game was on. Coppersmith Barbet (Photo: Ambika Pradhan) Short-toed Snake Eagle (Photo: Umesh Mani) Sulphur-bellied Warbler (Photo: Umesh Mani) We reached Ananthagiri hills. A forest guard tried to stop us from entering the forest since it was banned for general public, but we had special permission. Upon entering the forest, we were greeted by a male Asian Paradise-flycatcher flashing its long white tail. It was so beautiful – I couldn’t take my eyes off it! It hopped from one branch to another, posing perfectly for pictures. We saw a Jerdon’s Leafbird beside the Paradise-flycatcher. We also found a Coppersmith Barbet showing off its awesome colour combinations. Mother Nature has painted it with her own brush, creating a spectacular combination of colours which seems impossible to replicate. On our way back from the forest, we observed a spotted deer that seemed to ignore our existence entirely. 4

Jungle Nightjar (Photo: Umesh Mani) Rufous-tailed Lark (Photo: Umesh Mani) Common Tailorbird (Photo: Umesh Mani) Sykes’s Lark (Photo: Umesh Mani) By 12:45PM we had decided upon our next destination Osmansagar reservoir, popularly known as Gandipet. Coincidentally, the security here wasn’t welcoming either. So we took a kuchcha road to get to the reservoir. Gandipet gave us the perfect opportunity to observe several species of wetland birds along with some forest birds. Twelve adult Greater Flamingos were a bit too far away from us, but four juveniles had stationed themselves in the shallow water, close enough for us to get a good look. I wonder why the flock was split that way in the same lake. A Common Greenshank roamed near the shore, seemingly aimlessly. Cormorants rested on a rock island inside the Osmansagar Lake. Small Pratincole (Photo: Ritish Kannayagari) Black-winged Stilts strutted around in the shallow water along with Common and Wood Sandpipers. The bigger birds – Grey Heron, Pond Heron and Purple Heron made their presence known there along with egrets. Spot-billed Ducks seemed to enjoy the cool water as the sun rose further up in the sky. Black-tailed Godwits were filling their stomachs with the help of their long beaks. Common Coots, exhibiting white tilaks on their heads were swimming happily in the water. A little Green Bee-eater posed for its own personal photoshoot. The Glossy Ibis stayed true to its name showing off its velvety texture in the sunlight. A flock of Bar-headed Geese were about to dive in the water. Indian Silverbill (Photo: Umesh Mani) A flock of Indian Silverbills were in flight. One Little Ringed Plover was nesting on the mudflat of the reservoir. The bird looked like a cap on its own nest. Pipits and Larks were feeding on the field camouflaging with the surroundings perfectly. After having dried its feathers, a Black Drongo chased its prey. A White-breasted Kingfisher was patiently waiting to get hold of its next catch of the day. 5

nature. Everybody shared their experiences during the day. They were interested, not only in birds, but also their habitats. Birding is a very good medium to inculcate love for nature. Nature has done a beautiful job of creating stunning colours through a masterstroke we call birds. We cannot afford to destroy their home. Thanks to the parents who introduce their kids to nature through something fun like a Bird Race at such a young age. Once kids start loving nature, they cannot let it be destroyed in front of their eyes. If we can inculcate a love for nature in their young minds, we can rest assured that Earth lies in safe hands. Making youngsters aware of the value of nature is probably the most crucial step towards protecting the world from humans who wilfully destroy wildlife habitats for personal profit. Once-common House Sparrows are not common anymore and the number of common bird sightings keep dwindling every day. Our team, Hawks, saw more than 150 species and was declared the winner of the Hyderabad Bird Race 2019. Little Stint (Photo: Ritish Kannayagari) I was enjoying the nature along with bird songs throughout the day. But alas, soon it was time to go back. On our way back from Osmansagar, we spotted an Indian Roller perched on a wire. Before we knew it, we were back to the venue for the evening function. Our bird race had come to an end, but not before dinner was served. Though we were happy at receiving the prize, we were also deeply saddened by accelerated urbanization that poses a direct threat to the birds we saw that day. We had to really search for birds even in habitats like Ananthagiri Hills. Counts for already established flocks have been at an all-time low. This is alarming. Nature is resilient but she can only take so much abuse. It is high time for our government to take firm steps to conserve nature effectively. The use of plastic has to be strictly regulated. We noticed plastic bottles and bags almost every step of our way. There is enough pollution in our lakes to clog natural flow, and our animals and birds are eating plastic without even realizing it. It is a sad state of affairs. A ban on single use plastic must be considered under such dire circumstances. Deforestation in the name of urban and rural development must stop. The erection of concrete jungles will never make up for the destruction of natural habitats in the long run, socially or economically. We have to become environmentally accountable for our actions. Black-rumped Flameback (Photo: Umesh Mani) Common Iora (Photo: Umesh Mani) Hyderabad Bird Race 2019 witnessed many first-time birders. Many youngsters and children had participated in the Bird Race with the ultimate goal of getting a little closer to nature while enriching their experiences with birds. The Bird Race is meant to kindle the curiosity of the general public in Rose-ringed Parakeet (Photo: Ambika Pradhan) *** 6

THE BUZZ OF THE CICADA Sudhir Moorti Cicada (Photo: Gurukumar KR) I have been birding in different kinds of forests in India for almost 15 years now, and my experience has taught me that birding in forests takes a lot of patience and can be quite frustrating. At times I have wandered for kilometres without encountering a single bird and suddenly there is a frenzy of activity, known as a ‘Hunting Party’, that descends into the trees. So, while birding in the forests, I learnt to make a few mental notes on how to locate birds. Usually I follow the calls but there are some other indicators which I find reliable, one such indicator being cicadas. phenomenon, and have found that it never fails – wherever the cicadas are calling, I couldn’t find a single bird. I alerted my fellow birders to this fact and they also seemed to agree... There were times when, the forest on one side was abuzz with cicada calls, and there was no sign of birds, while on the other side of the forest, where cicadas were not calling, there was plenty of bird activity. This certainly baffled me; the cicadas are not toxic to birds. How are they able to drive the birds away? The cicadas are a super family of large oval-shaped, winged insects with over 3000 species worldwide and about 250 species found in India. They are well known for their ‘call’ which reverberates through the forest. The buzzing sound they make is a mating call produced by a complex soundmaking mechanism. Noted ornithologist Walter Koenig, who has been studying this phenomenon for quite some time, suspects that cicadas and birds mutually influence each other’s populations, but we still don’t know how. While Koenig’s research is focussed on the periodical cicadas, I feel that this is not just applicable to the periodical cicadas, but that birds don’t venture into the areas where cicadas are present for some reason. Are the cicadas, which feed on liquid from the tree roots, able to introduce some sort of bird-repelling chemical into the tree’s system? Wild speculation? Maybe not. Cicadas live most of their life underground and emerge only for a few weeks to a few months at the most. There are two types of cicadas – the annual cicadas and periodical cicadas. The annual cicadas emerge at a particular time every year, whereas the periodical cicadas emerge once every x number of years, which is a constant and mostly a prime number, and which can be as high as 17 years in some species. The fact remains that similar observations have been made by birders globally and there is something going on between the cicadas and the birds. Meanwhile, when birding if you hit a patch with cicadas in chorus...may as well move on, you’re not likely to find a single bird. Cicadas are herbivores – they eat vegetable matter. Young cicadas or Nymphs eat/drink liquid from plant roots, while moulting cicadas eat twigs and adult cicadas do not feed at all! References 1. Koenig, W. D. and A. M. Liebhold. 2005. Effects of periodical cicada emergences on abundance and synchrony of avian populations. Ecology 86: 1873-1882. 2. Anonymous. 2019. Web Resources On Indian Cicadas. In Marathe, K., V. Sarkar, B. W. Price, P. Roy, and K. Kunte. Cicadas of India, V. 1. Indian Foundation for Butterflies. 3. Sarkar, Vivek, 2015, How to study Cicadas in the field – A manual to study Cicadas The cicadas are very mysterious; it is still not known how they keep count pf the months and years to emerge at exactly the same standard time/interval. A few years ago, I made an interesting observation while walking through the forest – if there are some pockets of woods where a group of cicadas is calling (called a ‘chorus’), astonishingly these pockets are totally devoid of birds. For years I have been checking and re-checking this *** 7

Trip Report – Pocharam, February 24, 2019 Dr Jayati Mitra The group (Photo courtesy: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Every year Deccan Birders usually arranges a field trip to ICRISAT campus in the month of February and this year also we were looking forward to it, but there was a change. A leopard was lurking around the said campus and so, for security reasons, our venue was shifted to Pocharam. It was indeed a good alternative because this place has a vast forest area with rocks and a water body as well – an ideal habitat for all types of birds. Brahminy Starling (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Red Collared Dove (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) On our way we had to pass through Narsapur forest but it was a dismal sight. Our favourite birding spot near the temple was denuded of all forest cover, and instead of sweet birdsong we could hear the thunderous noise of a ball mill set up right amidst the jungle. The small lake had also dried up and the surrounding area consisted of dry, parched land with a few burnt tree stumps standing haphazardly in between the areas marked for civic work. Common Woodshrike (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) We left the place with a heavy heart and moved forward but the development all along the way was so bewildering that we were unable to recognise the familiar landmarks and overshot by almost ten kilometres before realising our mistake. We reached Pocharam at last, pretty late around ten in the morning, but some Small Minivets and Purple Sunbirds were still active and feeding. A male Asian Paradise-flycatcher with its long white streamers, was an eyecatching sight. The only heartening sight was that of a red silk cotton tree in full bloom at the corner of the road, which provided shelter to a flock of chirping Brahminy Starlings. A few Indian Robins were still seen around the place which was once home to colourful Woodpeckers, Minivets, Kingfishers and so many other avian species. 8

Bar-headed Geese (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) A flock of about twenty-five Bar-headed Geese maintained a safe distance from us as they rested on the far end of the lake. Brown-headed Gulls were also present around them. It was difficult to cross over the marsh to see a flock of Terns clearly from this end, but we could observe the ones which were flying overhead, and amidst them a Black-bellied Tern was conspicuous. The majority were River and Whiskered Terns. Blyth’s Reed Warbler (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Some of the birders sat down under a tree to rest and have breakfast while some others continued birding around the area. There was a small puddle across the fence where quite a few birds came to quench their thirst. We saw a Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher, Red-winged Bushlark, Black Drongo, Rufous Treepie, Green Bee-eater to name a few. A Large Cuckooshrike moved surreptitiously amidst the dense foliage of the age-old trees. Black-bellied Tern (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) The swimming ducks were mostly Eurasian Wigeons and a few Garganeys and Northern Shovelers. Waders such as Common, Wood, Green and Marsh Sandpipers and a few Black-winged Stilts were feeding at the edge of the lake. It was immensely satisfying to spot the majestic pink birds - the Greater Flamingos at the far end. Large Cuckooshrike (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Thereafter, we left for a visit to the lake around noon. A group of Large Grey Babblers were chattering continuously as we walked towards the shore. The water level had receded in the recent past, thus exposing a large portion of the bed of the lake. A pair of Glossy Ibises were visible at the far bank. There were a few other species foraging in flocks on the dry bed, like Small Pratincole, Little Ringed Plover and Kentish Plover. Paddyfield Pipits, Ashy-crowned Sparrow Larks and Yellow Wagtails were also seen moving around restlessly on the ground. Marsh Sandpiper (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Little Ringed Plover (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) 9

Temminck’s Stint (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Green Sandpiper (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) We spent about half an hour here enjoying the sightings and slowly, one by one, all of us dispersed, hoping to meet again soon in future for happy birding moments. After spending some time here we went towards the other end of the lake, where stood a century old dilapidated building called ‘bhoot bangla’. It was a shady place and the air was filled with the sweet fragrance of frangipani. On the edge of a jutting rock a Common Kingfisher sat motionless for a while. It was fully focused on catching its prey and we relished the whole action till it finally dived and rose from the water proudly displaying its catch of a big fish between its beak. Greater Flamingo (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Red-rumped Swallow (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) It was past noon by now and there was another interesting sighting - a bigger group of Greater Flamingos that were moving on this side of the lake. We saw sixteen of them, feeding quietly. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From The Times of India, May 19, 2017) *** 10

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker (Dendrocopos nanus) Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker (Narsapur, February 8, 2009) Order: Piciformes Family: Picidae Genus: Dendrocopos Species: D. nanus Size: 13 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker is generally seen in singly or in pairs, in groves, deciduous and semi-evergreen forests, lightly wooded open country and secondary growth. It also often associates with mixed hunting parties of other small bird species. The call is a rapid metallic rattle, or a feeble click-r-r-r used as a contact note between the pair. It feeds on the stems of saplings close to ground, as well as higher up in the thinner branches and end-twigs of trees. It tends to run jerkily up and down and around trees, as agilely as the Nuthatches, before flying across to another nearby treetop. Its diet consists of insects, flower nectar, and soft pulp of berries and banyan and peepal figs. Description & distribution: The Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker, also known as the Indian Pygmy Woodpecker, is seen across almost all of India, Bangladesh, the Himalayan foothills of Nepal and Sikkim, and Sri Lanka. It is a small pied woodpecker with a light brown crown and mantle, darker brown and white barring on upperparts and dusky white underparts with faint brown vertical streaking. It has a distinct white stripe starting from the eye and going down the side of the neck, and a crimson streak on the sides of the hind crown, which is lacking in the female. The irises are white and rimmed with pink. The throat is streaked with brown, and the central tail feathers are white-spotted, a feature that distinguishes it from the otherwise very similar Grey-capped Pygmy Woodpecker. Nesting: The Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker breeds mainly between February and April, with some local variations in parts of its range. The nest is usually a natural hollow in a rotten branch, or in a hole excavated by the birds themselves. The usual clutch consists of 2-3 blunt ovalshaped glossy white eggs. The Sri Lankan sub-species, D. n. gymopthalmus, has a darker crown, concolorous with the upperparts, and the underparts are whiter and almost unstreaked. Some authors describe D. n. cinereigula of the South-western peninsula as an intermediate. Local name: The Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker is known as ‘Chhota kathphodwa’ in Hindi, ‘Chitta suruti pachhi’ in Telugu, ‘Siru maramkotti’ in Tamil, ‘Bharati (or bharatiya) nano lakkad-khod’ in Gujarati and ‘Chhota sutaar’ in Marathi. Some taxonomic authorities have placed the Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker in genus Yungipicus or genus Picoides. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. E-group: http://groups.google.co.in/group/bsap_online. Website: www.bsap.in. Society membership (in Rs.): Annual: 500 per annum; Student: 200 per annum; Corporate: 2000 per annum; Life: 3000. Trip Report – Ananthagiri Hills, March 17, 2019 Dr Jayati Mitra The group during the trip (Photo: Satish Grama) If we look around Hyderabad, we cannot help but notice the rapid development of concrete jungles all around us. However, there is one place nearby where one can always go to unwind and relax in the lap of nature and that is none other than Ananthagiri Hills near Vikarabad. March is the season when return migration takes place and very often the sighting of species of birds at their temporary destinations, makes it an interesting period for birding. We eagerly looked forward to this trip as Ananthagiri is a forest which, most of the time, throws up some surprises for birders. White-bellied Drongo (Photo: Dr Jayati Mitra) The main show began after we entered the forest. There was no noise initially except for the trampling of dry leaves under our feet, but suddenly the surroundings became vibrant with a riot of colours as a Golden Oriole pair moved around, calling sweetly amidst a flock of chattering Rose-ringed Parakeets. A pair of Grey Hornbills flew across piping loudly. We decided to stand quietly beneath the old intertwined ficus trees and watch the drama unfold. Common Myna (Photo: Prabhu Patruni) As we approached our destination, the distant verdant hills slowly came into our view. The sky was clear and the sun shone brightly. A few of us quickly had a glimpse around the ancient temple till all of us finally gathered at the gate to enter inside the forest. Spring was in the air. The huge mango tree at the entrance bore tiny raw mangoes which were gently swaying in the cool morning breeze. A White-bellied Drongo was the first bird to show up in front of the gate along with a flock of Small Minivets, all hopping on the nearby banyan tree. Rose-ringed Parakeet (Photo: Prabhu Patruni)

White-browed Fantail (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Ashy Prinia (Photo: Prabhu Patruni) Slowly one by one the birds appeared amidst the dense foliage. We could see a White-browed Fantail unfurling its tail feathers, the Common Iora whistling, and an Indian Treepie quietly moving around, puzzling us with multiple calls sounding like many different birds till we actually sighted it. Meanwhile another bird on the ground distracted me as it glanced furtively with its black, beady eyes. It was a Brownbreasted Flycatcher, flying and feeding restlessly on the ground. Asian Paradise-flycatcher (Photo: Prabhu Patruni) Brown-breasted Flycatcher (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) But the highlight of the moment was the beautiful blackcrested white bird we always long to see, the Asian Paradiseflycatcher. I watched intently as it fed. It glided smoothly down upon the prey with closed wings almost vertically, with its long, white streamers floating behind and pointed upwards. In no time it caught the insect and rose straight upwards and perched at the same spot again. It repeated this activity multiple times. What followed next was the most memorable observation of the day for me. A small blue bird with orange underbelly appeared momentarily behind the huge trunk of an old tree. It seemed like a Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher from behind but, just to be sure, I stood in silence, waiting for it to reappear – and was rewarded for my patience. The bird came into clear view for a short while but that was enough to observe it. Its white supercilium gave away its identity as a bird rarely seen in this area – the Indian Blue Robin! Indian Blue Robin (Photo: Dr Jayati Mitra) Ashy Drongo (Photo: Satish Grama) In my excitement I looked for other people around me but they all had moved away to some other spot. I searched for it again and during that period saw quite a few more birds, a beautiful pair of Tickell’s Blue Flycatchers, a Blue-capped Rock Thrush, and an Olive-backed Pipit quietly feeding on the ground. But I could not find the Blue Robin again.

A noisy group of Jungle Babblers were moving amidst the dried leaves on the ground. The forest was dry and most of the trees had shed their leaves but at the end of this path stood a majestic rain tree spreading its green canopy, dotted with dainty pink blossoms like an umbrella. Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Yellow-footed Green Pigeon (Photo: Satish Grama) My friend Anjali waved excitedly towards me but despite rushing down I still missed the sight of the Yellow-crowned Woodpecker feeding on the orange-red blossoms of an Indian Coral tree. I had to remain satisfied by just looking at the brilliant pictures clicked by my lucky friends. Olive-backed Pipit (Photo: Dr Jayati Mitra) I quickly increased my pace and walked forward along the winding trail to catch up with the other birders and on my way, I saw an Orange-headed Thrush hidden among the leaves of a tree. I heard the sweet whistling calls of the Oriental Magpie Robin. Yellow-crowned Woodpecker (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Oriental Magpie Robin (Photo: Prabhu Patruni) Ultramarine Flycatcher (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Chestnut-shouldered Petronia (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) But at the same time there was a rewarding sight of an Indian Nightjar which was resting higher up on a branch seemingly unaware of our presence. This bird is not commonly seen in crowded urban areas and we were indeed lucky to have sighted it.

Indian Nightjar (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Brown Fish Owl (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Purple Sunbird (Photo: Prabhu Patruni) After spending some time, we started walking towards the gate but enjoyed birding all the way back. A pair of Blue-faced Malkohas were chasing each other and a few of us were engrossed in watching them. Red-vented Bulbul (Photo: Prabhu Patruni) Our trips always end with a special breakfast and this one was no exception. We relaxed and ate to our heart’s content. And as we bade farewell to Ananthagiri, we sighted a Plum-headed Parakeet. Blue-faced Malkoha (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Soon everyone started moving towards a huge tree near the gate. The matter became very clear as I reached the place. Our friend Srikanth stood there pointing upwards. A Brown Fish Owl perched on its upper branch was dozing with its face turned in the opposite direction. Even after making a lot of effort, we could not get a view from the front. Nevertheless, we were very happy at the sight of this majestic bird of prey. Plum-headed Parakeet (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar)

The complete list of birds sighted is given below: Species name White-bellied Drongo Species name White-browed Fantail Species name Indian Nightjar Rose-ringed Parakeet Purple Sunbird Indian Golden Oriole Indian Grey Hornbill Oriental Magpie Robin Pale-billed Flowerpecker Jungle Babbler Blue-faced Malkoha Brown Fish Owl Rufous Treepie Asian Paradise-flycatcher Red-vented Bulbul Yellow-footed Green Pigeon Black Drongo Chestnut-shouldered Petronia Brown-breasted Flycatcher Olive-backed Pipit Common Myna Yellow-crowned Woodpecker Ashy Prinia Oriental White-eye Small Minivet Orange-headed Thrush Indian Blue Robin Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher Common Tailorbird Plum-headed Parakeet Common Iora Blue-capped Rock Thrush *** BIRDING THE BEAUTIFUL SNOW PEAKS Trip Report – Munsiyari et al, Uttarakhand, November 26 - December 1, 2018 Text and Photos: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri Himalayan peaks during sunset Our trip to Munsiyari and other nearby areas was a longawaited one. Jayati and I flew to Delhi, and then reached Kathgodam by train early on November 26, 2018. Our driver Mandeep came with flowers to welcome us. November 26, 2018: Kathgodam to Chakori We started for Chakori well before sunrise. Around 6:30AM, the sun peeped out from behind the hills and the sky started becoming reddish. In around 15 minutes, the sun came out and threw red colour like sindoor on the hills. It was so beautiful, and I immersed myself in the beauty of the sunrise. Getting a move on, we drove through Dharampuri, from where the rear view of Chakori could be seen. Clouds kissed the hill tops, and a river flowed between two hills. The roads were generally made by cutting the hill sides, but sometimes, the hills were connected with a bridge. I was enjoying the natural beauty as if some spectacular show of canvas paintings by nature was going on in front of my eyes. A flock of birds against the sky Around 8:30AM, a Steppe Eagle opened up our book for birding. We came out of the vehicle to take some pictures and relax for a while. After some time, dense fog covered everything between the hills, and it like an ocean of pure white waves.

Steppe Eagle Plumbeous Water Redstart and Cinereous Tit Soon, we were crossing Nainital, where houses of different colours looked like match boxes stacked together on the hill. A Blue Whistling Thrush was whistling, and a Plumbeous Water Redstart, a Cinereous Tit and a Russet Sparrow were busy with their morning activities. An Alexandrine Parakeet was nesting on a nearby tree. But I felt sad because the surroundings were full of plastic bags and sachets. The car was moving through an oak forest. As the fog cleared, the snow-clad peaks glistened in the sunshine, appearing just like molten silver. Nanda Devi, Trishul, Panchachuli – all the snow-covered peaks gave us their magnificent views. View of Nanda Devi peaks from the guest house Blue Whistling Thrush Kalij Pheasant A male Kalij Pheasant was feeding on the side of the road. A White-crested Laughingthrush was sitting on a branch, and a Himalayan Bulbul was resting on a wire. We found a Rufousbreasted Accentor perfectly camouflaged in the surroundings. Alexandrine Parakeet Himalayan Bulbul

Rufous-breasted Accentor A flock of Yuhinas The hilly road sometimes seemed to be ending in the gorge but in reality it was not. Driving the turning roads, we reached Patal Bhubaneswar Temple at 2:30pm. En route to the temple, we saw a flock of Yuhinas chirping on a tree. Mandeep informed us that the deodar cedars were used to make fibre for garments. During the walk, we came across Yellow-billed Magpie, Oriental Turtle Dove, European Goldfinch and Streaked Laughingthrush. Black-headed Jay Common Hoopoe After taking it in for a while, we started trekking nearby. A flock of Common Mynas were together on a flight. Blackheaded Jay, Common Hoopoe, Red-billed Blue Magpie, a Woodpecker and Barn Swallows were active. A monkey was cuddling her young one in her lap. Chestnut fruits looked like spherical thorny flowers. The main temple was inside a cave. The entrance of the cave was so narrow that it was very difficult for even one person to move into the cave. One had to crawl into the cave by sitting on the stairs! Around 4:00PM we started for Chakori. A Spotted Forktail was quenching its thirst at a roadside puddle, and the setting sun was beautiful. We reached Chakori (2010m above sea level) just before 6:00PM. KMVN cottage no. 002, allotted to us, was made of wooden planks, and jute curtains were hanging from the window. Barn Swallow November 27, 2018: Chakori to Munsiyari We were ready bright and early in the morning, and by around 6:30AM, were out of our cottage to see the beauty of the sunrise. The sun’s rays were falling on the snow peaks and scattering light as if calling everybody to wake up. The sun was just like a golden dish coming out on the sky. Everything was bathed in the morning sun’s rays. Monkey with young one

After breakfast around 9:30AM, we climbed the observatory to see the 360-degree views. Then it was time to say good bye to Chakori. After checking out we started our journey to Munsiyari by 11:00AM. Slaty-headed Parakeet Jungle Babbler Red-billed Blue Magpie Mayurpankh tree Mandeep stopped the car to show us the mayurpankh tree, whose leaves looked like peacock feathers. He also told us about the Ram bamboo, where the middle part was used for getting fibre to make garments. A Streaked Laughingthrush was calling. Grey-headed Woodpecker Pine flowers used for making fibre for clothing Streaked Laughingthrush Long-tailed Shrike, Slaty-headed Parakeet, Yellow-billed Blue Magpie and a Grey-headed Woodpecker were busy with their morning activities. Our car was going through the pine forest, alongside the Ramganga river. We stopped and entered the river bed of the Ramganga. The riverbed was full of rocks of different sizes, and we collected some small stones from the riverbed. Around 2:00PM, we started again for Birthi falls, and reached there by 3:00PM. It looked like a white chiffon cloth was hanging from the hill top.

Himalayan Mountain Lizard We saw many different kinds of mountain lizards there. At 3:45PM we started off again for Munsiyari. En route, we saw many mountain goats, full of fur, climbing up the hill. By 5:30PM, we reached Munsiyari guest house. Chestnut-bellied Rock Thrush Mountain goats November 28, 2018: A Grasshopper species Coming back to the KMVN guest house by 9:00AM, we had breakfast, then visited the shop in the KMVN guest house, called Mati Tana Bana Samagri, which was selling handmade garments and Himalayan spices from village Sarmoli, Munsiyari. Panchachuli peaks European Goldfinch Tharpachuli peak in Nepal seen from Uttarakhand We started off for birding around 7:00AM. We wanted to explore the nearby area for birding. We saw some Butiya dogs, which had thick fur to combat the cold. We trekked inside the Swatantrata Sangram Senani Shahid Trilok Singh Pankti, from where we could see Panchchouli snow peaks. There was also a helipad on a hill. We then started off for birding at Nanda Devi temple, and reached there by 10:00AM. A big flock of beautiful European Goldfinches were chirping. There was no crowd at the temple, which was surrounded by mountains. The chirping of birds attracted us to the front of the temple premises. Trekking out to the hill, we spotted many small birds, all busy with their morning activities – Variegated Laughingthrush, Rustycheeked Scimitar Babbler, and some warblers among them.

Spotted Forktail Variegated Laughingthrush After some time, we heard a bird call, and saw that the Forktail was calling from near the same tree. Soon it entered into the kund again; we had never thought that we could see a Forktail from so close. The beautiful Forktail, with its white and black combination of colours, made our day. On our way down, we stopped near the Nanda Devi temple again, and saw a Redstart moving beside the road. Rusty-cheeked Scimitar Babbler We got back to our guest house around 4:30PM, and saw that everybody had gathered around to get a view of the spectacular sunset on the majestic snow peaks. The sun was about to set and playing with colours in the snow peaks. I could not believe my eyes – it was the best sunset I have ever seen! Every second, the mountains were changing colours, just like sarees of different colours, and during that time, the clouds were also in party dresses. It was unbelievable, amazing and beautiful, and we were very lucky to see it. Sunset November 29, 2018: Trekking to Khuliya Top Western Crowned Warbler Trekking to Maheswar Kund: Around 11:30AM we left for our next destination – Maheswar Kund. We reached there by 1:30PM and started to trek to reach the kund. It was a muddy place, with very less water. When we reached, people who had come earlier left the site, so there was no human disturbance. We relaxed for a while and took in the fresh air near a small waterfall, when suddenly we saw a Spotted Forktail, which was moving around actively and feeding. After a while it flew to sit on a nearby tree, and disappeared from there. We enjoyed sitting in the lap of nature, listening only to the chirping of birds, the sound of the cool breeze and the waterfalls nearby. Yellow-breasted Greenfinch We started with a pair of Yellow-breasted Greenfinches outside our guest house. We got breakfast packed from the guest house, and reached Khuliya Top base at 7:50AM with our guide Gopal. Some horses were climbing up the hill with luggage. We started on the trail road - 6km up and 6km down!

It was a sunny day. I was the slowest person among the three. The Panchachuli snow peaks were glowing with the sun’s rays like pure gold. We saw several birds and kept moving in a slow but steady pace. At some places, the snow covered our trail path. Finally we reached the restaurant around 12 noon where we had our breakfast. There we observed that some crows were moving around with eggs in their mouths. After taking some rest, we started climbing again. While climbing, Gopal showed me the hues of the sun – it was so beautiful. The sun acted like a prism – all the colours were coming out from the white rays of sun. We came across lots of snow, and Gopal showed us rhododendron trees of different coloured flowers – blue, pink, purple. It was not flowering season, but I painted those trees in my mind with different coloured flowers. Gopal pointed out Bhoj patra trees also. The bark of the tree was used for writing in ancient India. The white bark was shining in the sunlight. Jackal Grey Wagtail Large-billed Crow We reached Khuliya Top at 2:15PM. There were lots of Largebilled Crows. An open area was totally covered with snow. I was looking for the Himalayan Monal but unfortunately could not find any. We spent some time playing in the snow. With the 360-degree view, we saw several ranges of mountains and snow peaks as if we were at the level of Panchachuli and other snow peaks. On the way down, we picked up the wrappers, sachets and plastic that we saw on our trail road, and educated Gopal so that he, being the guide, could educate visitors not to throw those at the Himalayas. By the time we got back around 5:10PM, the sun was setting and the snow peaks were glowing with red light. Then it became darker and darker as the time passes by. Some animal was making a sound and there was no light to see the trail road, and we were quite scared! We used our mobile torches and kept walking. I was thinking that I might fall from the hill; it was very difficult getting down. Finally I could move a little faster by holding Gopal’s hand. At last we reached the base of Khuliya Top, where Mandeep was waiting, and returned to KMVN guest house. White-capped Water Redstart We started for Kausani at 9:45AM and reached Kalamuni temple at 10:10AM. After a quick darshan of Kali Mata, we started off within ten minutes. The hairpin bends en route were beautiful. We passed through some villages where we saw step farming, and some orange trees full of oranges. We crossed Birthi falls by 11:00AM, and Mandeep pointed out a road on the hill across the valley, and informed us that we had to cross the Kosi river to reach there. We crossed the river by 2:20PM and headed towards Bageswar. November 30, 2018: Munsiyari to Kausani Kausani was not originally in our plan, but I thought we could cover Kausani for a day and then move the next day to Jageswar. We started our day with a Shrike, and also saw a Jackal crossing the road. A Grey Wagtail and a Redstart caught my eye. Step farming

As usual, we were ready for morning birding before 7:00AM. Snow peaks were getting up from sleep. We came down and went inside the Rajakiya Inter College, Kausani on the trail road. While walking on the road, I noticed a Great Barbet. Later on, inside the college trail, we saw a flock of Barbets and Woodpeckers. A beautiful Thrush attracted our eyes. Tree full of oranges View of Kosi River We stopped at a sweet shop where I wanted to taste singari, made of palkhoya (kheer) wrapped in a cone made of Molu leaf. We also purchased the famous baal mithai, with chocolate covered with sugar globules. We then started off again around 3:00PM for the Baijanath Temple, a 13th century temple located about 22km away. The Baijanath temple structure was like the Jageswar temple. After visiting the Ganesh temple, we went to visit the famous Ardhanariswar Temple. The beautifully carved statue of Ardhanariswar (God in the form of Half male and half female) was worth seeing. At the rear of the temple, there was a small water body where we saw lots of kites on a nearby tree. We returned by 4:30PM, and went to the silk handloom unit, where we observed how they prepared woollen materials on the handloom. We could see a tea garden up the hill, but as the sun was already setting, we did not climb to the tea garden. We left there by 5:00PM, stopped for a while at Anasakti Ashram, where Gandhiji spent a few days, and named the place ‘the Switzerland of India’, and then reached our destination, the Kausani guest house around 6:00PM. It was dark outside, but we were very happy to see snow peaks from our cottage. It was so cold outside that we requested them to serve our dinner in the cottage itself. The cottage did not even have a fan, indicating that it was never required. December 1, 2018: Kausani to Jageswar Scaly-bellied Woodpecker We came back to the guest house, had breakfast, checked out and started for Jageswar by 10:00AM. Along the way, the green paddy field next to the Countrywide Public School, Someswar, Almora looked like the mountain dressed in a green saree. This part of our trip was devoted to temple visits and some shopping. We reached the Jageswar temple complex by 12:45PM. There were so many temples together in the temple premises. The oldest temple was named Maha Mritunjay Mandir; after visiting that we went into the Jageswar Jyotirlinga Temple. After pooja and abhishek, we went to the Archaeological Museum which was just beside the Jageswar Temple. It was a very beautiful museum. We stopped at the Chitai Golu Devta (God for Justice) Temple at 2:30PM for darshan. The temple was full of bells of different sizes. For the first time, I saw a temple having papers with wishes written by devotees, hanging with the bells. By 3:45PM we left for our next destination. Within 5 minutes Mandeep stopped to show the ancient Panthashala (tourist rest room) beside the road. Soon we reached a place where we could pick up pahari pishai namak (‘hill crusted salt’) which we could sprinkle on salads. We visited the Uttarakhand Textile Development Corporation shopping centre, where they had several interesting items – mosquito-repellent bed sheets made of bichuya tree, shirts made of bamboo and devdar tree fibre, rajai with fur, silk saree and scarves made from banana fiber, etc. With that, our trip came to an end. We started by 6:40PM for Kathgodam, reached by 8:00PM, and boarded our train to Delhi at 8:40PM, and then took the flight back from Delhi to Hyderabad the next day. Great Barbet

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani White-rumped Shama (Copsychus malabaricus) White-rumped Shama (Maredumilli, June 1, 2019) Order: Passeriformes Family: Muscicapidae Genus: Copsychus Species: C. malabaricus Size: 23-28 cm opisthopelus, javanus, omissus, ochroptilus, abbotti, eumesus, suavis (Borneo); the other island races are C. m. nigricauda, stricklandii and barbouri. Of these, the last two are sometimes clubbed under C. stricklandii and regarded as a separate species, the White-crowned Shama. Description & distribution: The White-rumped Shama was originally classified under the Turdidae family of thrushes and was known as the White-rumped Shama Thrush or simply the Shama Thrush. It is seen in the forested tracts across India (including Andamans), Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. The male has a white rump, a long, graduated dark tail with white sides, and is glossy blue-black on the upperparts and rufous-orange on the underparts and breast, while the female is duller and has brownish-grey upperparts. The juvenile has orange-buff spotting on the upperparts and an orange-buff throat and breast with fine scaling. Habitat & behaviour: The White-rumped Shama is generally seen in singly or occasionally in pairs, in dry-deciduous or moist-deciduous secondary forest, hilly bamboo forest and forested foothills, where it shows a preference for shady ravines. It is very similar to the Oriental Magpie Robin, which it replaces in these forests, except for the fact that it is more shy and usually avoids human habitation. It is prized as a cage bird due to its mellifluous song, which is loud, clear and rich in musical quality. It feeds mainly on insects picked off the ground or from bushes or under leaves. Nesting: The White-rumped Shama breeds mainly between April and June, although breeding has been known to take place any time between January and September. The nest is usually a shallow cup in a natural hollow in a tree, or in the tangled base of a bamboo clump, and built with roots, bamboo leaves, grass, ferns and stems. Incubation is done by the female, though feeding duties are handled by both parents. The usual clutch consists of 4-5 eggs, white to light aqua in colour, with variable brown blotches. There are several races described. The race found in Western Ghats and southern India is the nominate, whereas north India has C. m. indicus. In C. m. leggei of Sri Lanka, the female is similar to the nominate male. The Andaman race, C. m. albiventris, is now considered a separate species, the Andaman Shama; the male is similar to the nominate male but with a white belly, while the female is also similar but with a shorter tail and less glossy upperparts and throat. Besides these, there is race C. m. interpositus from southwestern Asia-China to Myanmar, Thailand and the Mergui Archipelago; C. m. minor from Southern China; C. m. mallopercnus in the Malay peninsula; C. m. tricolor in the Sumatra, Java, Banka, Belitung and Karimata islands; C. m. mirabilis from the Sunda Strait, C. m. melanurus from northwestern Sumatra; C. m. Local name: The White-rumped Shama is known as ‘Shama’ in Hindi and Bengali, ‘Shyama’ in Sanskrit, Marathi and Gujarati, ‘Poda nalanchi’ or ‘Tonka nalanchi’ in Telugu, ‘Solai padi’ in Tamil and ‘Shyamakkili’ in Malayalam. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. SCIENTIFIC NAMES OF BIRDS – AN EXPLORATION INTO THE HOW AND WHY Text and Photos: Col SS Cheema (Retd) I have no formal training in ornithological studies but I was always intrigued by the scientific names of the birds I used to come across during birdwatching. So I have been on to this task of learning more about how the birds are named and what is the logic behind it all. I am sharing the findings from my studies over the past almost six months, and have tried to lay them down in as easy a language as possible. Firstly, the moot question - should we address these names as ‘scientific names’? Or ‘Latin names’? ‘Latin names’ is what we call them fairly commonly, though that may not be true any longer. Many languages have contributed to names of the birds: Latin is/was very common, but many names of birds now originate from Greek, Old English, Russian, Malay, South American native languages etc. That being said, regardless of the origin, generic names are required to have a form of a Latin noun, with defined gender, and specific names are required to decline according to rules of Latin adjectives. This was how the system was at that time when Latin was the language of international communication. However, today, calling them ‘scientific names’ may be more correct, as some names are not Latin at all. There are in all four parts of the full scientific name. The first part of the name describes the genus that distinguishes a group of isolated, distinctive species. This must be a form of a noun or a substantivised adjective treated as a noun. This has to begin with an Upper-case letter. The second part of the name begins with a lower-case letter and describes the species within the genus and may take many forms though it is commonly an adjective or a noun in the genitive case. The third and the fourth part reveal the name and the year in which that name was first validly published as a Binomen. We will tackle the first two parts of the names in this article. Now that we know that the scientific names are to be addressed as 'Scientific Names', let us look at the criteria that were used while coining the names. These categories/criteria are as below: 1. Morphonym: (Gr. morphē form; onuma name) – Based on plumage, colours and physical characteristics of the birds, and is the largest category, accounting for over half of all specific names and nearly half of all generic names. An example is the India’s endemic White-bellied Blue Flycatcher, whose scientific name is Cyornis pallidipes. Here:   Cyornis: derived from the Greek kuanos, meaning ‘dark blue’; and ornis, which stands for ‘bird’; pallidus: in Latin, stands for ‘pale’; pes stands for ‘foot’. So, the name describes the plumage and physical characteristics as ‘dark blue bird with pale feet’. 2. Eponym: (Gr. epōnumos named after) – Commemorates a real, mythical or fictional person. These mostly honour the name of the collector or the discoverer of species, but at other times may just honour another person. Grey-breasted Prinia The example of this bird is Grey-breasted Prinia, whose scientific name is Prinia hodgsonii. Here:   Prinia: a Javanese name ‘Prinya’; hodgsonii: a name given in honour of Brian Houghton Hodgson (1800-1894), an English diplomat, resident of Nepal from 1833 to 1844, who was an ethnologist and a collector. His name figures in a number of species scientific names as hodgsoni / hodgsoniae / hodgsonii / Hodgsonius etc. 3. Autochthonym: (Gr. autokhthōn indigenous or native; onuma name) – Based on the indigenous or native name. They are more often used generically rather than specifically. White-bellied Blue Flycatcher Chukar

 An example of this bird is the beautiful Chukar whose scientific name is Alectoris chukar, where:   chrysaea: meaning ‘golden’. 6. Bionym: (Gr. bios life; onuma name) – The popularity of habitat names reflects this diversity. Alectoris: a derivation of Greek word alektoris, meaning ‘farmyard fowl/chicken’; chukar: a derivative of Hindi name Chukor. 4. Toponym: (Gr. topos place; onuma name) – These have proved more popular as specific names than generic names. There are over 1,100 specific toponyms or geographical epithets. Black-tailed Godwit As an example of this category, I have picked out this bird, Black-tailed Godwit (Limosa limosa).  Black-rumped Flameback As an example of this category I have picked out Blackrumped Flameback (Dinopium benghalense), where:   Limosa: Latin derivative of limosus, which means ‘muddy’. The birds are very mobile and occur in a large variety of habitats. This bird, true to its name, is found on the muddy shores of oceans or lakes. Dinopium: derivative of Greek deinos, meaning ‘might’, and ōpos, meaning ‘appearance’; benghalense: this Toponym part depicts the geographical state of Bengal – historically a large part of India and Bangladesh. 7. Ergonym: (Gr. ergon work, occupation; onuma name) – This category refers to display, typical habits, temperament, mode of flight, parasitism or breeding behaviour. 5. Taxonym: (Gr. taxis arrangement; onuma name) This is based upon suggestive relationship or resemblance. Golden Babbler Streaked Weaver A good example is the Golden Babbler (Stachyridopsis chrysaea). Here: As explained above, the name is a derivation of the work or occupation. An example is the Streaked Weaver (Ploceus manyar):  Stachyridopsis: derivative from genus Stachyris that roughly translates stakhus as ‘ear of wheat’; rhis, referring to ‘nostrils’, points to the shape of opercula or scales almost closing the nostrils; and opsis, meaning ‘appearance’;   5 Ploceus: a derivative of Greek word plokeus, meaning ‘weaver, braider or plaiter’, (plekō being ‘to plait’ or ‘to entwine’); manyar: the Tamil name Manja for various weavers

8. Phagonym: (Gr. phagein to eat, onuma name) – The names in this category reveal the variety of food items or prey of birds, including spiders, bananas, carrion, crabs, lizards etc. the birds. Surprisingly, this category has yielded relatively few names in spite of the fact that the birds are so often associated with the songs or calls, and have been admired throughout the ages for the same. Common Chiffchaff An example here is Common Chiffchaff (Phylloscopus collybita): Little Spiderhunter  Take the example of the Little Spiderhunter (Arachnothera longirostra), where:    Arachnothera: literal translation of Greek word arakhnēs, meaning ‘spider’; and thēras, meaning ‘hunter’; longirostra: derivation of Latin longus, meaning ‘long’; and rostris, meaning ‘billed’. Phylloscopus: derived from two Greek words, phullon meaning ‘leaf’; and skopos, meaning ‘seeker’; collybita: it is the second word, collybita, that is based on Latin collybista, meaning ‘money-changer’. In Normandy, Common Chiffchaff is called ‘Compteur d'argent’ from its song that resembles the clinking of coins. This article just about scratches the surface of this fascinating subject of scientific naming of birds, and a lot of interesting study can be done. As I mentioned earlier, the above is a result of my interest and self-study, and it is possible that there may be some inconsistencies or differing interpretations/opinions. That would make for quite an interesting discussion. So, all in all, the scientific name means ‘spider hunter with a long bill’. 9. Phononym: (Gr. phōnē voice or sound, onuma name) – This category uses the names based upon the sounds/songs of *** THE MIGHTY KOEL Text and Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati May 19, 2019 was just another normal bird watching trip for Gokul and I at Osman Sagar, with some regularly irregular species. After a few clicks and sightings, we decided to head back home and, exiting the west side farms road, hit the Chevella highway. That was when we observed two birds perched in a tree on the other side of the road– a Blue-faced Malkoha and an Asian Koel. and as far as we could tell, it was not a fight for food. We feel this calls for a good discussion about the unusual behaviour of these birds. To our surprise, the Koel suddenly took off to attack the Malkoha, and they both went crashing down on the ground. We hurriedly parked the car and exited the vehicle to see what was going on – and we were stunned at seeing the Koel pin down the Malkoha on the ground for a few seconds! As we approached to click an image – which was not possible earlier since there was no view of the birds as they went down – the Koel got distracted and the Malkoha had a great escape. We looked around for any nests but there were none to be seen, Asian Koel pinning down Blue-faced Malkoha *** 6

A FIRST TIMER’S MUSINGS Trip Report – Nehru Zoological Park, April 28, 2019 Jayasurya Pathapati Yellow Bittern (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Bird watching was never on my ‘lifetime bucket list’, at least until the past 4 months. In fact, I’d never heard of such a thing until I met a friend a while ago, who had a lot to say about it. and so many other birds which I had only read about in books. It all started with a budding interest in wildlife conservation activities, thanks to a few articles published in The Hindu, and I wanted to gain deeper knowledge into the best practices. As I was searching online, I came across a Home Study Course in Ornithology, offered by Rishi Valley Institute of Bird Sciences, which promised to shed light on Wildlife Conservation apart from its main focus, i.e., Bird Studies. One of the quotes from the textbook says, “World without birds is unimaginable. If birds die, we all die”. This shows how important a role they play in the collective ecosystem. As I read more and more about birds, I really wanted to get into birdwatching. I naturally Googled to check if there are any activities in Hyderabad, and that’s how I came across the Deccan Birders. Honestly, I was quite surprised to see that the club has been established way back in 1980! I didn’t waste a moment to register as a member. Indian Peafowl (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) I was also glad to meet experienced birders, photographers, and kids of whom I was jealous! I wish all the kids learnt how to love and protect mother nature, and also that we made environmental studies a major part of their education. I realized birdwatching is one such activity where people gather together, amidst lush greenery, to spot beautiful species, and get to know each other along the way. It’s a wonderful outdoor activity at the least. Oriental Magpie Robin (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) This second Zoo trip of mine, which was very similar to the first (as a six-year-old kid!), was filled with so much awe and information, but unlike the first trip, here the species were in the wild, uncaged. I will always cherish my first sightings of the Oriental Magpie Robin, Black Drongo, Golden Oriole, Painted Stork (Photo: Satish Grama) 7

Purple Swamphen Adult (L) Chick (R) (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Black Kite (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Bronze-winged Jacana (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) I observed even the most common birds such as Parakeets, Kites, Pigeons etc, paying particular attention to their physical structure, and how it is interconnected with their feeding, nesting, and mating habits, which are all crucial for their survival. “Every bird has its own niche”, I read in my course, which tells us how diversity is important for survival of the ecosystem. Grey Heron (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) The lake was where I spotted the most variety of species – Moorhens, Jacana (the Jesus Bird), Kingfishers, Painted Storks, Herons, Cormorants etc. This is where I saw the Darter for the first time, and also got to know, thanks to Shafaat sir, why is it called the Snakebird. I was amazed at how it swims with its thin long head stuck out of the water, looking almost like a Black Mamba! Indian Grey Hornbill (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) One thing that stood out about the Zoo is its well-maintained ecosystem and the variety of flora, be it the wooded region or surroundings of the lake, all of which, in turn, must have contributed to such diverse avifauna that is hard to find in other parts of the city. This places emphasis on the saying “Take care of the habitat, and birds will take care of themselves”. Rose-ringed Parakeet (Photo: Satish Grama) 8

Common Moorhen juvenile (Photo: Satish Grama) Large Grey Babbler (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) *** Report – Sighting of a Leucistic Common Coot at Himayatsagar Lake, June 16, 2019 Text and Photos: Gokul Krishna Addanki Leucistic Common Coot (L) with a normal individual (R) This was the first time I was taking my younger son Abhinav, 5 years old, on a birding trip. I was hoping to inculcate in him a love for nature, but I was a little unsure as to how he would take it. To my surprise, as soon as he got out of the car, he ran towards the lake and started shouting, “Daddy, look at the birds there”! Leucism is caused by a genetic mutation that prevents pigments being deposited correctly on the birds’ feathers. It can be of various types, like bold white patches, paler coloration than the original, or completely white-looking birds with no coloration. Incidentally I also happened to have observed a leucistic Baya Weaver in the same area some time ago. The smile on his face said everything, and I just enjoyed looking at him run around excitedly like that. We then sat down near the lake shore and started checking out the birds. He started asking me the names of all the birds he saw and wanted to watch them closely using the binoculars. Later he started telling me features of birds and then matching the names to the features of the birds. Looks like my son’s presence brought me another reward, besides the joy of watching him enjoy himself so much! While observing the birds, one of the group members saw something that looked different in the crowd of birds there. We initially thought it was one of the Knob-billed Ducks swimming along, but a closer look revealed that it was a leucistic Common Coot. This one was the lone white individual among a bunch of regular black-coloured Coots there. We clicked a couple of photos to make sure it was a Coot and then just started observing the behaviour. Bird of the Month Text: Umesh Mani; Photo: Gurukumar KR Lesser Whistling Duck (Dendrocygna javanica) Lesser Whistling Duck (Safilguda, March 16, 2019) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Dendrocygna Species: D. javanica Size: 42 cm Duck by the chestnut forewing patch (absent in Fulvous), chestnut rump (white in Fulvous) and lack of a dark brown line down the hind neck (present in Fulvous). The sexes are alike; juvenile birds are duller in colour. Habitat & behaviour: The Lesser Whistling Duck is gregarious and is usually seen in small to large flocks in vegetation- or weed-covered tanks, ponds, flooded grasslands and paddy fields, oxbow lakes and freshwater marshes. It prefers water bodies with emergent vegetation or partly submerged trees. It is a nocturnal feeder, and spends the day resting, usually on the water, though it does quite often perch on trees. Its diet consists mainly of aquatic vegetation, grasses, tender shoots and stalks, and grain from cultivated rice, although it also eats small fish, frogs, and invertebrates such as molluscs and worms. It may dabble or dive while feeding, but also walks well on marshland, often foraging like geese. It flies with rapid wingbeats on broad, dark, rounded wings and utters a characteristically incessant shrill, wheezy seasick-seasick or tsee-tsee call in flight or during take-off, a clear whistled whiwhee at rest, and also, sometimes, a subdued quacking. Description & distribution: The Lesser Whistling Duck, also known as Lesser Whistling Teal or Indian Whistling Duck, is a member of the sub-family Dendrocygninae of Tree Ducks or Whistling Ducks, under the family Anatidae, and are not regarded as true ducks. The genus Dendrocygna consists of eight species of Whistling Ducks; additionally, another species, the White-backed Duck (Thalassornis leuconotus) is considered by some authorities (e.g. Paul Johnsgard) to be also part of the same sub-family. All the Whistling Ducks have long legs and necks, a hunched appearance, and dark underwings. Of these, two species – Lesser and Fulvous Whistling Duck – are seen in India. The Lesser Whistling Duck is resident across most of India (including the Andaman & Nicobar Islands), Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, east to south-east China and south through south-east Asia to Sumatra, Borneo, Java and Bali, although it may show some local movements depending on droughts and floods. Nesting: The Lesser Whistling Duck breeds coinciding with the start of the monsoon, i.e. between June and October, across most of its range; in Sri Lanka, it has been seen to breed also between December and January. The nest is usually a shallow natural hollow in a tree, lined with grass and twigs, though it often builds nests on the ground among reeds. Incubation is done by both parents. The usual clutch consists of 7-12 ivorywhite eggs. The Lesser Whistling Duck is a small, pale-brown and chestnut duck, and the only other duck of similar size that it can be confused with is the Fulvous Whistling Duck. The Lesser Whistling Duck has a greyish-buff head and neck, dark brown crown and nape, indistinct yellow eye-ring, warm chestnut underparts, darker brown upperparts with buff fringes to feathers, a bright chestnut patch on forewings, chestnut rump, dark grey legs and bill, and uniformly chestnut uppertail coverts. It can be differentiated from the Fulvous Whistling Local name: The Lesser Whistling Duck is known as ‘Seelhi’ or ‘Seelkahi’ in Hindi, ‘Eelavese china chiluva’ in Telugu, ‘Chilli thara’ or ‘Mahudi thara’ in Tamil and ‘Yeranda’ in Malayalam. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034.
