Trip Report: Ananthagiri Hills, June 28, 2019 Siddharth Mani There is something about Ananthagiri – lying unassumingly on a hilly tract in the midst of ‘plaintive’ chaos. When I had first found myself passing through the place in between field visits, I had resolved to be back there with more time to spare. It was apt, then, that my first trip with the Deccan Birders would be to these hills. Sunday morning, we rode in our mildly stringed convoy to Ananthagiri. And as the groups sprang out from their cars at the entrance to the Padmanabha Swamy temple, I realised how the bird-watching activity had, over the years since I first began, transitioned from old-school, stationary ‘watching’ to a transect-based photo-capturing ‘birding’ event! There were binoculars to spare as sophisticated cameras were the muchin-demand instrument now, and we the contented-to-watchthem-birds people capitalised on this luxury!

The group during the trip (Photo courtesy: Gunbir Singh) The walk began, and I immediately – and unknowingly – hit a lifer! Many had already gathered under an electricity wire and begun admiring a bird I could barely make out from afar, though I had definitely heard its sweet song many times before. All these years, I had assumed this song to be that of the Golden Oriole, but it was attributed by the group to the Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher which was nonchalantly seated on the wire, singing away like no one’s business. I looked on astounded through my binoculars (despite it being clearly visible through the naked eyes): a bird I had only heard of – and heard – many times, but today, was seeing! A short walk brought us to a flowering banyan tree: easily the most productive spot in the entire trip! Our novice sub-group itself (that’s my brother-in-law, nephew and me!) observed around 7-8 different bird species here, so of course the actual count would have been much higher. We did overhear many other oohs and aahs followed by newer names spilling out from the other sub-group tongues, which we never identified! But definitely a happening location, this, where I could have been utterly satisfied sitting through the rest of the trip, allowing the birds to reveal themselves to me. Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) White-bellied Drongo (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Post-visit Mental Note 1: The Golden Oriole offers a more rounded song, while this Flycatcher has – coincidentally – a more wiry offering, though I would like to believe that the melodic pattern is similar. Rose-ringed Parakeet (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Further downhill, we approached a tree known to be the dwelling spot of the Brown Fish Owl. Now for a person who only once in his entire life has ever seen an owl in the wild (that’s me!), this was appetising news. While the experts in the group set about searching for our wise fellow (God bless them!), I contented myself with spotting another lifer – the Jerdon’s Leafbird – flitting around in some distant foliage. At the same time, a White-throated Kingfisher gave out its perch call – the ‘laughter’ I knew so well… or did I? People around me immediately murmured about a ‘Flameback’, and I was greeted by the knowledge that this Woodpecker had a call very similar to the Kingfisher’s! As I stood there, mouth agape, the cohort moved ahead – having already spotted the Fish Owl too (which I never got to see eventually). Post-visit Mental Note 2: While both the Black-rumped Flameback and the Whitethroated Kingfisher are known for their ‘laughter’ calls, the Woodpecker has a clearly demarcated crescendo/decrescendo connotation to its song, whereas the Kingfisher appears to favour just the decrescendo mode.

Large-billed Crow (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) All this while, there were the abundance of Indian Grey Hornbills (with their alternatively flapping-gliding flights), Ashy Prinias (oh, their rolling chirps!), Oriental White-eyes (a sweet little one even perched precariously over her microscopic nest), Common Tailorbirds (busy grubbing), Coppersmith Barbets (berry-picking) and other garden/scrub birds we are wont to take for granted elsewhere – but here, in their secure universe, they remained oblivious to the intrusive eyes that we brought along. Yellow-eyed Babbler (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) But as I reflect on the magic of being in a group which understands the value of birds for their own sake, on the smallest of joys cascading onto every one of us by merely the awareness of another sighting, on the brilliance of an almostrainy weather prodding us onward to uncover the eternal enigma of a living forest – I realise I can wait. I am home; and targets do not matter here. It was a lovely hike, with kids enjoying their gadget-free time too really well. Many an evocative revelation happened through their eyes (“That bird we saw there is apparently the Oriental Black Pie Robin”… “My grandmother stays in Kanha, and I go meet her every week and will soon be moving there too”…) which triggered some futile research and sometimes misplaced admiration among the adults. Overall, the trip yielded a tally of about 63 different bird varieties – of which I witnessed less than half. I sorely regret missing the Indian Paradise-flycatcher (always wanted to know this handsome bird), and the Indian Nightjar (the last I saw this bird was as a child, travelling on highways in the night) – apart from the star attractions of the day mentioned earlier in this post! A view of the forest (Photo: Gunbir Singh) *** Snippet: Litter-picking Crows Contributed by Shafaat Ulla A historical theme park in France has enlisted some unlikely help in clearing up litter left by visitors: six rooks (Corvus frugilegus). The Puy du Fou park in the Vendee region has trained the birds to pick up litter by installing a small box that delivers a nugget of food each time one of the birds deposits a cigarette butt or piece of rubbish. Nicolas de Villiers, president of the park, which receives two million visitors a year. De Villiers says the birds are “very fast” and can fill a box in less than 45 minutes. “We want to educate people not to throw their garbage on the ground,” he says. Sometimes it’s good to make people feel a little bit guilty”. “The goal is not just to clear up, but also to show that nature itself can teach us to take care of the environment,” says (Source: Reader’s Digest, April 2019) ***

TREASURE TROVE IN MY BACKYARD Part-1 Ambika Pradhan A view of Safilguda Lake (Photo: Ambika Pradhan) Being a birder is one of the most fulfilling experiences one can ever have. There's never a dull moment, really. Rummaging through 3 years’ worth of pictures makes me realise how many moments there had been, that filled my heart with gratitude to have found peace in the woods and to have found people who share the same sentiment. But you don't need to go great distances to find these incredible moments. There's so much bird activity unfolding right around us which so many people fail to notice. Many of my memorable birding moments have happened right outside my balcony and sometimes even in my own house. Staying at the top floor of the apartment building may be a bane during summer when the heat sweeps through the house. But for most of the year, I've been blessed with great bird activity, almost like an adventure movie that takes place right there. Little Grebe (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Staying a stone’s throw away from Safilguda Lake in Secunderabad, I believe my interest in birding sparked here, by the species roosting on the island located right in the middle of the lake. The beginning months of my time as a birder are still fresh in my memory, when I would take a walk around the periphery of the lake, noting birds purely by plumage and features, and then going back home, leafing through Salim Ali’s Book of Indian Birds to identify the species. Those were the days of pure joy of solitary birding when the rest of the world thought I was crazy to spend so much time looking at birds. (They still do, though!) Black-winged Stilt (Photo: Gurukumar KR) On countless evenings I've shared silence with a Sunbird or a Bulbul that kept me company on my apartment terrace, while we eagerly awaited the flock of Glossy Ibises that would cross over and roost in the lake nearby for the night. All you need is patience and a good eye. And I’ve been blessed with the latter and also with pure luck to be there at the exact time during those crucial moments that give you a peek into the lives of these creatures of evolutionary wonder. A flock of Egrets (Photo: Ambika Pradhan)

Come summer, the island hosts huge flocks of egrets, which would paint the sky white while circling around the island before settling down for the day. Watching this action unfold from my terrace vantage point has given some of the best memories. Some days, the flock would fly so close over my head that I could actually listen to their wing beats! But as with any other wetland, the real pleasure of birdwatching takes place during winter, when various species of ducks and ibises roost together in the lake and in the island. person to ask about the phenomenon and the name of the species. After the Ibises, the Ducks arrived, although they’d only arrive once the dusk set in. Almost every evening, as the winter sky is painted pink to dark purple, one would listen to the whistle of the Lesser Whistling-ducks, as smaller flocks would come back to roost. The flocks only consisted of 6-15 ducks. But the call (read ‘whistle’) would be heard far and wide, so much so that even if I weren’t at the vantage point, I’d still know that the ducks have come back to roost through the whistle that reverberates in the neighbourhood. Ducks at the island (Photo: Ambika Pradhan) Spot-billed Duck (Photo: Gurukumar KR) The Glossy Ibises arrive first, indicating the change in season. Then come the Lesser Whistling-ducks and Northern Shovelers. Winter evenings always consisted of the flock of Ibises flying back to the lake in perfect V-shaped synchrony. On many days, the flocks were so huge that it would turn the heads of my non-birding neighbours, to whom I am the go-to These are only some of the experiences I’ve had since I started birding nearly five years ago and almost every day brings up a surprise. So next time you’re looking for some bird action, just look around. Your best birding memory might well be just around the corner! Ibises at sunset (Photo: Ambika Pradhan) *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From The Times of India, January 25, 2018) ***

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Black-tailed Godwit (Limosa limosa) Black-tailed Godwit (Jamnagar, Gujarat, February 7, 2019) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Limosa Species: L. limosa Size: Male 36-44 cm, Female 40-50 cm Andaman & Nicobar Islands), Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka; wintering populations are also known from Australia, Indonesia, Philippines and Taiwan. Habitat & behaviour: The Black-tailed Godwit is sometimes seen singly or in pairs, but more often in small to large flocks, often along with other waders, in inland water bodies like lakes, flooded grasslands, paddy fields and freshwater marshes, as well as brackish lagoons, marshes, tidal flats, estuaries and sea coasts. It feeds in deep water by probing the mud with its long bill, and feeds primarily on worms, molluscs, crabs and aquatic insects. Black-tailed Godwits are mostly monogamous, and even reunite with the same partner at the breeding grounds after spending the winter apart, but in the event of late arrival of one of the partners, an individual may mate with a new partner. The call is a strident weekaweeka-weeka or, in flight, a yapping kek-kek-kek. Description & distribution: The Black-tailed Godwit is a member of the shorebird genus Limosa. It is a large wader with long legs, neck and bill. Legs vary from dark grey to black or brown. The bill is long, slender, straight with a slight upcurve, and is dark-tipped with a pink base which turns yellowish or orange-pink while breeding. In breeding plumage, the adult bird has blackish barring on white belly and reddish underparts, and the mantle and scapulars are unevenly patterned; male birds also develop a distinctive rusty-orange head, neck and breast. The sexes are similar, but female birds are larger and duller than the males, and even have longer bills, which enable them to avoid competing for food resources. Juveniles have cinnamon underparts and cinnamon fringes to dark-centred upperparts. In non-breeding plumage, the birds are more grey-brown and more uniformly patterned on breast and upperparts. White wing-bars and rump with black tail band, visible in flight, are diagnostic and helps separate it from the similar-looking (though somewhat smaller) Bar-tailed Godwit. Nesting: Nesting is in loose colonies, and the nest is a shallow scrape on the ground, amidst low vegetation. Incubating parents may also use vegetation to hide the nest. The Blacktailed Godwit breeds generally from April to August, and the usual clutch consists of 3-6 olive green to dark brown eggs. Local name: The Black-tailed Godwit is known as ‘Gudera’, ‘Gairiya’ or ‘Jangral’ in Hindi, ‘Kalipunchh’ or ‘Moto gadera’ in Gujarati, ‘Tondu ulanka’ in Telugu, ‘Kannadi ullan’ in Tamil and ‘Pattavalan godwit’ in Malayalam. WATERING THE BIRDS IN THE GARDEN Text and Photos: Sita Susarla The scorching summers of Delhi make birds and birders alike stay in the comfort of their homes. As it is also breeding season for many of our birds, we found the birds in our garden hovering around the water taps and shady trees supplying water to their young ones. To try and help them out, we placed a few bowls of clean water under the bamboo bush and the Pilkhan (Ficus virens) tree, and also left the tap beneath slightly open so that water would trickle down and keep the mud cool. We also took care to ensure that the water levels in the bowls were maintained at one fourth of the container for small birds to bathe and at half levels for the use of bigger birds.

Indian Thick-knee Birds cooling off near the tap On some days the spotted owlet too would drop in around 4.00PM and spend a good amount of time drinking water; somehow, the crows did not bother the Owlet. After a few days when it became hotter the crows were attacked ferociously by these birds to get to the water. It was amazing to see the Thick-knee arriving well before dusk for a sip and chasing the crows. Among the smaller birds the Starlings would drive away most of the birds. The Brahminy Starlings would raise their loose crest and hold them straight up in a threatening manner. The Brown-headed Barbet, however, was oblivious to all these threats as it quenched its thirst. The sociable White-eyes seemed to be not bothered by any bullies, either, as they were very quick in their movements; also, their bowl of water was the smallest and only one-fourth full. As the mercury levels rose, the number of birds visiting the water containers increased tremendously and the Pilkhan tree and the adjacent bamboo bush became the preferred perching spot for many a bird. We had fifty species of birds sipping water and resting in this corner of the garden. Most of these birds were seen puffing and panting with their mouths open, exhaling heat from their bodies. On hotter days we had to refill the water two to three times daily as they would run dry within hours of filling up. The happiest time for the birds, however, would be when the gardener would go watering the plants. Asian Koel pair Laughing Dove Asian Koel (female) threatening Jungle Babblers Here are some observations that we made over a period of three months beginning from the month of May. At Around 11.00AM and 3.00PM, there would be a large gathering of birds either drinking or bathing in the water, or taking mud baths in the wet mud around the water taps. A pair of crows kept chasing away the White-breasted Waterhen, Greater Coucal and the Koels but not the smaller birds like Bulbuls, Oriental White-eyes and Barbets. This may be because these birds drank a lot of water spending a whole five minutes doing so. The crows would chase away the Indian Thick-knee too that would come at dusk. The Indian Thick-knee surprisingly spent fifteen to twenty minutes drinking water. Eurasian Hoopoe taking a mud bath It was a pleasure watching the White-eyes bathe in twos and threes; sometimes even six to seven birds would enjoy the cool bath. The Jungle Babblers, Eurasian Hoopoe, Laughing Doves and Collared Doves tucked themselves well into the wet mud all through afternoon. So did the Grey Francolins. The Whitethroated Kingfisher would only take a mouthful of water before it swooped back to its perch, all in two seconds. 2

There was a pair of Black Kites that would often come for water. As this disturbed the other birds, we placed a big bowl of water in the open, far away from the bamboo bush. This helped a lot, as birds like Parakeets, Doves and Pigeons preferred the open area. Red-wattled Lapwing The Red-wattled Lapwing was seen carrying water in its belly feathers to its new born chicks. Water War – Jacobin Cuckoo with Brahminy Starling In the month of July came the Jacobin Cuckoo, known to be the harbinger of the monsoon. It is a pretty bird but most ferocious at the water gate. From the comfort of home, we shot some great pictures and videos of these birds and their activities, and were as satisfied as we would have been, had we spotted some new species of birds. He suggested that we go to Tirthan Valley in Kullu district, a three-day camping at 3000 metres. Sounded interesting. The question popped up in my mind: Do I get to sight birds? And the answer? Oh yes! – since the camp is inside the Great Himalayan National Park, declared a heritage site by UNESCO in 2014, and home to about 180 bird species. snow-capped mountains, making it one of the finest adventure destinations in the Himalayan region. Tirthan Valley – Nature preserved. Situated at 1600m above sea level in the Kullu district, the place gets its name from the Tirthan river, which is considered holy among the locals, and gradually merges into the Beas river which today is the source of some of the largest hydel power projects in India. It is a place with a vast variety flora and fauna, V-shaped valleys and Rolla Camp 3

A view during the trek Blue Whistling Thrush: It is known for its whistling sounds, usually at the dawn and dusk times, and feeds on life available on marshy lands. Great Himalayan National Park Rolla camp/Shilt trek Spread over 1100+ sq km, this National Park is a rich biodiverse environment, which is home to many endangered species like Western Tragopan (the state bird of Himachal Pradesh), Snow Leopard etc. Situated at 2000m is the Rolla camp site, a base camp to further treks which go up to 6000m. Shilt was our next halt situated at 3000m, with moderate to steep ascent. Covering 1000m through a trek of 5 km through thick vegetation and not much of a trail made it an exciting and strenuous journey. Birding at GHNP: During my chat with our guide, I came to know that this park has been identified by BirdLife International as an Important Bird Area in the western Himalayan region. Birds sighted commonly are Redstarts, Wren Babblers, Laughingthrushes, Whistling Thrushes, Blue Magpies, Long-tailed Minivets, Yellow-bellied Fantails, Little Forktail, Rufous-breasted Accentor etc. I am sharing some of the bird sightings below: Blue Whistling Thrush Brown Dipper: It is found near fast moving river streams, and its behaviour is characterized by its frequent dipping in the waters. It is an aquatic songbird. Plumbeous Water Redstart: both Male and Female. It belongs to the Flycatcher family and mostly lives near streams. Brown Dipper Plumbeous Water Redstart Male Scaly-breasted Wren Babbler: It is a tiny tailless terrestrial bird, which is mostly found in damp thick growth regions near to water bodies. It feeds mainly on insects and seeds, and is mostly found in the Himalayan region. Plumbeous Water Redstart Female Scaly-breasted Wren Babbler 4

Yellow Billed Blue Magpie: It is usually found in high elevations. It has a distinctive long beautiful tail. These birds usually travel in groups and stick to a place where they continue to stay. They usually feed on insects and the eggs of other birds. They have a harsh call. Little Forktail: It is a difficult-to-spot bird due to its tiny build and fast moving actions. But the aura and the unknown energy of the place always kept me enchanted, wanting more. Once, Humayun Bhai, with whom birding is always a way to gain a deep understanding about the history of the place, reminisced on how a decade ago Tigers and Leopards would frequent the stream next to the temple in the night. Ever since, I’ve been smitten by fantasies of coming across the big cat. Every time we’d go birding in the night, I’d imagine a Tiger watching me, tracking every movement. The feeling of being watched by a creature larger than life, larger than any human purpose has a spiritual connection with me. Something I regard highly and other-worldly. White-rumped Shama So, when Deccan Birders announced a trip to a location so special to me, I couldn’t pass up the opportunity. On the second Sunday of July, when Sudhir organised the trip to Umamaheshwaram, I saw it as an opportunity to unwind from the pressures of the job (read ‘adult world’). And hence we started early, and as a bonus, I also had a little reunion with my teachers from the school and my literature professor from college who joined us for birding. 5

It was an overcast Sunday morning devoid of any activity. We drove up to the hill, where we would usually bird. I walked a little further from the temple, looking forward to seeing all the species I’d usually spot. But to my horror, there weren’t any, at all! Instead, all the birds were replaced by metal sheets of permanent shelters and benches and many other new constructions that have mushroomed around the temple. Brown-headed Barbet, whose call reverberates constantly through the forest, seemed to have fallen silent. Changeable Hawk Eagle In hopes of finding at least a few more species, we trekked up to the top of the hill. But that route too was met with disappointment as the path was full of human faeces and an unbearable stench. Somehow, we made it to the top and then, finally, I spotted the first raptor of the day! Rising up from the other side of the hill, a Crested Goshawk briefly hovered right in front of us, before disappearing into the other side of the woods. The permanent shelters act as obstructions to bird activity Over the years, I have noticed the crowd coming to Umamaheshwaram gradually increase. But this new development is only set to increase the crowd there, hence posing a grave threat to the bird and wildlife population there, especially the vulnerable Yellow-throated Bulbul. Oriental Honey Buzzard Even through all the despair about the anthropogenic disturbance, Umamaheshwaram still threw up lifer surprises for me. All I was left with was with the hope that Umamaheshwaram would be restored to its former glory someday and that the wildlife would find its way back here. Report: Waterhole Survey, May 2019 The Telangana Forest Department had carried out a Waterhole Survey during the month of May 2019, in which several of our members had also participated and made significant contributions. We give below reports from two different teams that took part in the exercise. Amrabad Tiger Reserve Text and Photos: Anuraag Jonnalagadda One of the waterholes covered during the survey The Telangana Forest Department has been organizing a waterhole survey in summer since the past two years. The idea of the waterhole survey is to get an estimate of the number and the type of animals that flock to the waterholes (which are very few in number in the summer), thereby getting an understanding of species density and diversity in different areas of the parks. This is often followed by a camera trapping exercise at select locations to get more concrete evidence of tigers, leopards and other such threatened megafauna. The Forest Department invites volunteers for this exercise mainly to ensure that there are no errors, accidental or otherwise, in the data collection process, and they get a fair assessment of the faunal presence in that area. This also enables the volunteers to understand how the Forest Department functions and the on-field difficulties that they have to face on a daily basis. The waterhole that I went to, turned out to be a very small pool, filled with rotting mangoes, courtesy of a very large mango tree overhead and the water seemed completely undrinkable. This was basically a small section of a dried up stream where there was still some water left. While I was wondering how the animals managed to survive on this water, the forest guide, who was a Chenchu himself, said that there was a Chenchu hamlet about a kilometer away and this was their primary source of water. Though I always knew how tough tribal lifestyles could be, this was something which I found very hard to digest. While many of us may blame tribals for forest degradation and decreasing animal numbers, we very rarely appreciate the kind of dangerous, vulnerable life that they are still leading in the wild, something we can never even imagine doing. This year, the waterhole census was conducted on May 11 and 12. Volunteers were asked to report at Aranya Bhavan at 6 am on May 11. Volunteers were already divided into separate batches to cover all tiger reserves in the state – Amrabad, Kawal and Eturnagaram. We, along with about 40 others, hopped onto the bus to Amrabad Tiger Reserve. The journey was hot and uneventful and soon enough, we reached the Forest Department office at Mannanur, where we were joined by others who came by their own transport. In all, it was close to 60 volunteers for Amrabad Tiger Reserve. After a briefing session by the Forest Department officials, we were divided into groups and assigned to different ranges. The area I was assigned to was Vatavarlapally beat in Dommalapenta range, about 20km ahead of Mannanur towards Srisailam. We were supposed to do the survey on two trails, one in the evening and the other the next morning. Our evening trail was supposed to start at 3:30 which we were a bit worried about, given the scorching heat. But less than 20 minutes after lunch, grey clouds came out of nowhere and it soon started pouring. And since none of us were prepared, we were completely drenched by the time we came back in the evening. Tiger scratch marks Due to the rain, animal pugmarks that might have been present near the waterhole were washed out and we got no fresh carnivore signs. We did however see Tiger and Leopard scratch marks on different trees and 2 dead Sambhar skeletons, supposedly killed by a tiger more than a month back. Along the trail, there was plenty of Sloth Bear evidence, mainly in the form of scat and occasional scratch marks. There were traces of Tiger, Leopard and Dhole scat as well, but more than 2-3 weeks old. 9

Sloth Bear scat Herbivore presence was surprisingly low, there were no direct sightings and hardly any scat on the trail. The only animals we saw were a couple of Hares and 2 Giant Squirrels near the waterhole. Thanks to the rain, bird count was also very low, with the major bird sightings being Indian Grey Hornbill, Rufous Treepie, White-bellied Drongo and Black-hooded Oriole. My trail was about 4.5km one way, and due to the breaks that we had taken to avoid the rain, by the time we came back it was already dark. Having heard a lot of stories of Sloth Bear attacks, and having seen enough evidence of their presence, I was thankful that we were able to reach the Beat Office safe and sound. Sloth Bear scratch marks Our accommodation was right on the Srisailam highway at a popular break point where there were plenty of roadside shops catering to the tourists. As a result, the forest patch upto a 100m away from the road was completely littered with plastic waste. And, as we witnessed that night, a large number of Spotted Deer come to this section every night to feast on all the food that is thrown inside those plastic wrappings. Despite all warnings, and the provision of a good number of dustbins along the highway, tourists are still managing to completely trash the forest. This negligence can be quite costly and it is a possibility that many of those Deer may be ingesting good amounts of plastic every day. Sloth Bear scratch marks Indian Star Tortoise Eturnagaram Tiger Reserve Text and Photos: Anuraag Jonnalagadda Having missed out earlier on the mail confirmation of my participation in the Waterhole Survey, to be carried out on May 11-12, 2019, it was literally at the last minute that I realized that I had a ton of things to do to get ready for the same! adequate water supply for the wild animals and thus help in wildlife conservation. Initially, I was included in the team for Amrabad Tiger Reserve, which I had already been to several times, so I requested the officials for a shift to the Eturnagaram team, so that I could explore a new place. All set, we started from Aranya Bhavan at 7.40AM and, after a break of 45 minutes at Hanamkonda Divisional Forest Office, we reached Divisional Forest Office, Tadvai at 2.30PM. We were well received by rain at the entry of Eturnagaram borders. A hectic few hours later, after 2½ hours of sleep, I reached Aranya Bhavan at 5.50AM, where the volunteers participating from different organizations were teaming up. Mr. Shankaran, OSD, addressed the participants about the survey, explaining how it helps to frame the management plan in ensuring 10

Mr Khader Mohiuddin, ACF, in the presence of Mr Akbar, CCF Warangal, Mr Ramalingam, DFO (Urban) Warangal, and Mr Pradeep Kumar Shetty, DFO Bhupalpally, gave a brief introduction about the area and program theme and flagged off the teams involved in the study. One of our teammates rued missing a chance for star trail, as the sky was full of cloud cover. The trail had led us to a waterbody where we found hoof marks of Spotted Deer and Cattle on the wet soil at the bank. A little further, a Blacknaped Hare popped into sight. Our team was led by Mr Ch. Srinivas Rao, FRO Lingala Range and Mr Padma Rao, FSO. We headed towards Lingala Range, core zone for the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary. While en route, we were charged up by the sighting of Gaur at one location; team members also had a few bird sightings - Spotted Dove, Common Myna, Brahminy Starling, Rufous Treepie, House Sparrow taking a dust bath, and Indian Robin. Indian Nightjar Observing the footprints of animals at Lingala Percolation Tank and natural stream Reaching the nursery at Lingala Range, as a token of commemoration, the team members planted a tree at the nursery. The light was already failing so, as per the work plan, we decided to do a twilight/nocturnal survey (a trail of around 3km through the forest. Beginning the trail, we heard the call of a Black Drongo and found it along with a Racket-tailed Drongo. Black-naped Hare The trail ended with a return to the road, from where we reached Lingala base camp in vehicles, where the other teammates had been reminiscing about the day, and personal stories of the past, and had a delightful dinner prepared on firewood for us. The base camp area had no power supply as the transformer had gone bust due to the rain, and a leaking roof made it difficult for us to stay at the base camp. Alternate accommodation was arranged at Lingala village; everyone was reminded of their childhood vacations where we would sleep on the rooftop under the open skies. Greater Racket-tailed Drongo All along the trail, we were accompanied by the calls of the Common Hawk Cuckoo, Indian Nightjar and Indian Cuckoo. It was hard to sight and count their numbers. Crested Treeswift Day 2: 12th May 2019 The day started at 4.00AM. The first team (Team-A) started off by 5.15AM and reached the location, Pochapur village of Lingala range, by 5.40AM. We walked a trail of almost 13km till we reached Vaddugudem by 12.20PM. The trail passed through a Sal forest in the foothills at Durgagutta; at a few places, with the saline soil in the non-perennial gullies, the new tender green foliage added by Hardwickia binate trees was delightful. Indian Nightjar 11

On the trail, the first live water source we came across was a natural spring, where the wet soft soil had footprints of Spotted Deer (Axis axis). While we walked along the length of the stream to observe any other footprints, Mr Srinivasa Rao, FRO, and his staff recorded details, cleared leaf litter and built a bund for water to accumulate at places along the stream. At one particular spot, I was fascinated with the slope of the terrain where the water would run down the slope to form a gully between rocky slabs. Observing me going off the trail, Mr Rao too joined me, and we found a big burrow under the rock, with the freshly dug out soil from the burrow covering the footprints. Mr Rao called one of his staff members and asked him to arrange a camera trap to track the animal using it. Dried-up rocky bed in the rivulet Dayyala Wagu Scat samples on the trail clearly showed the presence of Chowsingha, Spotted Deer, Gaur, Civet Cat and Sloth Bears around the area. A 500m walk from the rivulet took us to a percolation tank, the Sammaka Saralamma Percolation Tank (SSPT). At a bund across the gully, we found the hoof marks of ungulates at the inner edge of the tank which had very shallow water in it. A further walk of 1.6km from SSPT took us to the Bison Percolation Tank (BPT), which was built by raising a rock-strewn bund across the stream between the two hill slopes for a depth of 3-4m of water storage capacity. Black-hooded Oriole In the core part of the trail, the bird life recorded was Plumheaded Parakeet, Black-hooded Oriole, Red-vented Bulbul, Brown-headed Barbet, Rufous Treepie, Golden-fronted Leafbird, Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker, Yellowcrowned Woodpecker, Oriental Magpie Robin, Small Minivet, Oriental White-eye, and a pair of Crested Hawk Eagles seen perching on the tree tops. Sammaka Saralamma Percolation Tank Bison Percolation Tank By the time we reached BPT everyone was out of water in their bottles. Fortunately, a good shower started, so we took a break while waiting for the rain to stop. We had thoughts of harvesting the rainwater by spreading ponchos and thus refilling the bottles. Meanwhile a pair of Greater Racket-tailed Drongos were flying in the nearby trees and making calls at different frequencies. Crested Hawk Eagle Moving ahead we reached a rivulet, Dayyala Wagu, in which even after a walk for approx. of 400m, we found not one ditch with water to trace, but we did find a Crested Serpent Eagle perching on a tree at the banks. Stream originating from the natural spring Crested Serpent Eagle 12

Mr Yadgiri, Forest Watcher, appeared with a bottle filled with water and, on questioning, pointed us towards a natural spring nearby. Everyone in the team got rehydrated, refilled all our bottles from the spring, and started walking back to the road. Soon after crossing the tank, we came across a stream and the wet bund has a footprint identified to be that of a Sloth Bear. A 2km walk from there and we reached the road. 2. During summer it was mainly the natural springs that were serving the wildlife in quenching their thirst. Hence, explorations in identification and monitoring of natural water springs should be continued regularly. 3. The identified natural water springs, and any new ones in future, can be helpful in propagation of plant species, such that the area can become a pocket of heterogenous habitat which can favor the growth of Biodiversity. 4. All through the 13km trail, we did not come across a single saucer/waterhole facility. Efforts have been put in by the Forest Department in restoring and providing water for wildlife in the core forest areas, but still more efforts are needed. 5. The regular track we walked covered a very narrow field width; for better observations in the whole block, more manpower is needed for successful monitoring and management. 6. Although the big cats or other carnivores are not seen in this Range, the Department should try to put a check on cattle grazing in the core area of the forest, to avoid human-wildlife conflicts while sharing the available resources. 7. Not only the higher vertebrates, but other small vertebrates (mammals, birds, reptiles) and arthropods/insects should also be considered for monitoring and conservation, as they too play role in the survival and flourishing of the forest. Black-shouldered Kite Soon we arrived at Forest Department Office at Tadvai, where we shared our observations with the gathering and also documented the same on a feedback form which we submitted to the Department. OBITUARY It is with great regret that we inform of the demise of our Life Member, Major Ahmed Abdul Aziz. Major Aziz was a nephew of Nawab Din Yar Jung. He joined the Hyderabad State Army in 1947, and was stationed in Hyderabad. Later he went to work for the Sarf-e-Khas (the private security of Nizam Osman Ali Khan). Following his retirement, he took to conservation and was one of the early members of the erstwhile Birdwatchers Society of Andhra Pradesh (now Deccan Birders). Aziz sahab, as he was better known, was full of wit, humour and high spirits. An enthusiastic observer, he enjoyed being out in natural surroundings. Like many of his contemporaries, he started out in the study of natural history through the sights of a rifle and often used to recount his adventures and stories from his shikar trips. Though not in any sense of the term a big-game hunter, he had some decent records to his credit. From shikari to conservationist is a short step and he bridged that gap effortlessly and was made an Honorary Wildlife Warden for the erstwhile undivided state of Andhra Pradesh. He served on the Advisory Committee of the Nehru Zoological Park and was also elected as a Vice-President of the then-fledgling Birdwatchers Society of Andhra Pradesh. Aziz sahab was also an amateur philatelist and has exhibited his collection of stamps (with the theme being "Animals") in regional and national philatelic exhibitions. He entered into this hobby just as keenly as he did everything else. In his passing away, at the age of 94, the society has lost one of its oldest surviving members. 14

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Cotton Pygmy-goose (Nettapus coromandelianus) Cotton Pygmy-goose (Hyderabad, January 10, 2019) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Nettapus Species: N. coromandelianus Size: 26-37 cm also extends into parts of Australia, where the sub-species N. c. albipennis is seen. Populations are known to move in response to seasonal variations like rain or drought/water scarcity; they also disperse widely in winter, as far west as Jordan and other parts of the Arab region, as well as east to Maldives and the Andamans. Description & distribution: The Cotton Pygmy-goose, also known as Cotton Teal or White-quilled Pgymy-goose, is a perching duck, and among the smallest waterfowl in the world. The male has a dark brown forehead and crown on a whitish head, red irises, a goose-like short black bill deep at the base, a white neck with a broad blackish green collar at the base, and dirty white, irregularly-streaked underparts. Legs are black, but turn greenish in breeding males. The upperparts – back, wing coverts and scapulars – are dark brown with a green-andpurple gloss. In the female, the cap is duller, the neck collar is replaced by spots, neck is finely vermiculated, face is flecked and there is a brown line through the eye. In non-breeding plumage, the male is similar to the female except for the face that the white wing-band is broader. In flight, dark wings and white flight feathers with black tips are visible in the male; the female shows dark wings with a narrower white trailing edge to the secondaries (and some primaries). Chicks are downy, and have marked white superciliary stripes meeting at the back of the dark head. Face is whitish with a dark eye-stripe, and they have a dark grey-to-black tail, buff underparts, a greyish neck, grey-brown mantle and two white patches on the scapulars. Habitat & behaviour: The Cotton Pygmy-goose is usually seen in pairs or groups of pairs. They are found in small as well as large waterbodies with good aquatic vegetation, including irrigation tanks, village ponds, jheels, lakes, channels and lagoons. They are known to become tame and comfortable with human proximity in village tanks if they are left undisturbed. They forage among the emergent vegetation, and many pairs may be seen foraging near each other. They feed near the surface of the water, and the diet consists mainly of small fish, molluscs, crustaceans, insect larvae, as well as plant matter. Roosting and nesting is on trees near water. Flight is strong, with quick takeoffs without any running, before wheeling away in different directions. They can fly close to the water and are nimble enough to be able to avoid predators like falcons. Injured birds have been noted to hide by submerging themselves with only the head or bill out of the water. The call is a peculiar clucking, uttered in flight. Nesting: The Cotton Pygmy-goose breeds between June and September in most of its range, and between January and March in Australia. The nest is a natural hollow in a tree trunk in or near water, and may be lined with grass, feathers or other soft material. The nest may be as high as five metres above the surface, and chicks leap off to follow their parents into water. The usual clutch consists of 6-12 ivory-white eggs. It is widely distributed across most of Asia (including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka), east up to New Guinea, with the nominate race being seen; distribution *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 15Hyderabad – 500034. We wish all our members a very happy Deepavali A SMALL BEGINNING Report – Ameenpur Lake Clean-up, September 10, 2019 Rama Sarvani A scene at Ameenpur Lake (Photo: Rama Sarvani) An eventful and enlightening, but tiring, day finally came to an end. It had left an indelible mark on me; memories that have probably changed me in profound ways. For instance, when I stopped at the supermarket today evening to buy some ‘essentials', all I could think of were the single-use plastics and the likes that have come to be such an integral part of our daily lives. Shampoos, lotions, deodorants… Can I stop using all that? It seems impossible, right? Well, not if every time I hold one, instead of the shiny hair, flawless skin and incredible confidence these products supposedly give me, I see their empty containers littered on the shores of a pristine water body, our very own Ameenpur Lake!

We, a group of four friends with a shared interest in birdwatching – Ram, Raghu, Deepa and myself – decided to put this holiday weekday to maximum use. However, today’s trip to Ameenpur was special. Usually armed only with our binoculars and cameras, this time we also brought along a pair of gloves each and some trash bags. Spot-billed Pelicans relaxing on the rock islands (Photo: Rama Sarvani) Some portion of the total trash we managed to collect Greater Flamingos taking flight (Photo: Rama Sarvani) Bearing the pain that came with confronting the reality of the state in which we find our precious wetland ecosystems, I started posing some questions to myself. Why don’t people think twice before throwing their trash into a lake? Why don’t people come out of their comfort zone to avoid using plastic? How do we solve this problem? I have no clue what the answers are going to be, but when we next went to the Pragati Nagar dump yard, ironically located right next to another lake, I did get a perspective about the city’s waste removal system: Composting, waste segregation for recycling, incineration, the inability to dispose of certain kinds of waste (notably thermocol and flammable cans like deodorants) – and the crippling issues faced by Hyderabad’s waste management system. Several beautiful birds, including Pelicans and Flamingos, call Ameenpur Lake their home. Every trip to this incredible urban bird haven would leave us both bewildered by the biodiversity it hosts, and disappointed by what humans have done, and are doing, to the place. During our last trip we had resolved to do something about it; today, we took the plunge (quite literally) and ended up collecting six big bags of trash from a small part of the lakeshore. Sadly, the diversity of trash could easily give the birds a run for their money – we counted several polythene bags, plastic water bottles, liquor bottles, and pieces of thermocol apart from the odd pairs of footwear we managed to fish out of the water. Oh, and did I tell you we also found a discarded helmet?! An Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark uses rocks as a lookout to survey its territory (Photo: Rama Sarvani) Raghu salvaging a waste polythene bag from the boulders to be used for trash collection (Photo: Rama Sarvani) One such rock, which was covered with glass pieces from broken liquor bottles (Photo: Rama Sarvani)

us. In a moment of whimsical clarity, we decided to clean up a portion of Ameenpur. Although we faced some challenges along the way – garbage bags coming undone, municipal workers stopping us at the entrance of the dump, etc – we used them to learn and equip ourselves with the requisite information for future clean-ups. The dump yard in-charge, Mr Ratnam Raju, who was extremely friendly, gave us a tour of the dump yard and explained the nitty-gritties of waste management on location. He encouraged us and welcomed the possibility of more such clean-up drives across the city’s lakes. What we did in one day was not even a tiny portion of what we, as responsible citizens and birdwatchers, are capable of accomplishing. I am certain that this is only a small beginning. We have a long road ahead. So, the real question is: Are we going to do something about it? Or just like any other issue, do we say “that’s the most we can do” and get on with our lives? Liquor bottles collected as part of the trash (Photo: Raghu SR) Part of the dump yard, overlooking Pragati Nagar Lake (Photo: Rama Sarvani) What we did today is not something extraordinary. Many other groups have carried out such cleanliness drives before. When we go out for birding, we expect to watch birds in their element, doing ‘bird’ things in their pristine habitats. Instead, seeing them entangled in nets and watching them suffer and die, I expect, would bring out the humane side in each one of The team with Mr Ratnam Raju (second from right) (Photo: Rama Sarvani) Things to keep at hand and in mind for a hassle-free clean-up: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● Use good quality trash bags, preferably reusable ones. Each large bag can hold up to 5 kg of plastic trash. (Caution: Poor quality polythene bags can get easily torn from stray glass pieces! They may also result in leaching of garbage.) Wear a pair of sturdy, waterproof gloves. Use gumboots and poles, if you are planning to collect trash floating on water. Carry ropes or twine to tie off the bags once they are filled. Use a separate bag for intact glass bottles. Segregate waste material on the spot as much as possible. Thermocol wastes aren’t accepted at dump yards. So, segregate them and make alternative arrangements for their disposal. Do not dispose of batteries or pressurized containers like deodorants in the dump yard. Inform the in-charge of a nearby dump yard at least a day before your planned clean-up. Ideally, permission for dumping at the yard must be sought from the Corporator. Carry a hand sanitizer. It is likely that you will feel hungry in between the clean-up! ***

TREASURE TROVE IN MY BACKYARD Part-2 Text and Photos: Ambika Pradhan Shikra How people spend so much of their lives so utterly oblivious to the beauty of birds, I will never understand. If you saw the world with my eyes, you’d be dunked in love for birds. I’m beginning to lose track of the number of times flocks of birds have kept me company on days when I felt incredibly low. This may be my personal superstition, but I’d like to believe that it’s some kind of sign of the good things yet to come. And being surrounded with birds, these good signs come pretty often. Over the years, I’ve realised that once you start your pursuit for birds, or once your eyes actually open up to the world of birding, you can NEVER un-see a bird. There’s always that one bird that keeps you company, wherever you go. And now, trips without having an opportunity to watch birds don’t seem like productive trips at all! Right from my childhood, I’ve been raised in an area that is a stone’s throw away from Safilguda Lake. But it is only in my late teens that I actually started looking at the everyday beauty that birds are. And ever since, I haven’t stopped looking! The world is a better and so much more interesting place when your vision opens up to the life of birds. The Raven’s Claw One striking memory takes me back to my very first days of birding, nearly 6-7 years ago, when I had just started identifying common birds through their calls. One morning, as I was going about my routine, a persistent screeching call greeted me from the balcony. It was a call the likes of which I had never heard. As I rushed out to see what bird it was, I noticed a crow, which, to my surprise, wasn’t the source of the screech. On further inspection, looking for the source of the call, I found a tiny bat grappling for its life in the crow’s claw. Out in broad daylight, the crow perched on a thin electric wire with a bat in its claws, pecking at it occasionally, as the bat screeched for its life! Soon, the bat managed to free itself, swiftly flying into the thick canopy of a nearby tree. But the crow was close on its heels, chasing it through the canopy. The chase lasted nearly for 10 minutes, before the crow let out a groan and gave up! That day, as I lost myself in the moment, I forgot to dash inside for the point-and-shoot I had back then, at least to document whatever I could of the moment. Looking back, I really wish I had had a camera handy that day! Casual Tenants Over the years, I have made so many futile attempts to get Munias and Sparrows to nest in the balcony of my apartment. So many small wooden boxes, disguised as nests were placed strategically so that my winged tenants would feel at home. But everything failed and for a long time, no bird nested in the balcony. But my hopes were finally fulfilled when a Scalybreasted Munia couple finally started placing small twigs in the little nook between the wall and the A/C component in the balcony. Any initial attempts by my family to remove it was met with fierce hostility and warnings – from yours truly! Scaly-breasted Munia Every day, I’d be delighted to find more dried blades of grass as the nest-making process picked up speed. For nearly 2 months, I woke up to the chirping of the Munias. What an honour it was, to share the heath with these creatures and to have them feel so perfectly safe in my space. And when the chicks hatched, I just couldn’t contain my happiness!

Every day, I would watch them grow. With each day’s passing, I would worry that I wouldn’t be able to catch a glimpse of the fledglings taking their first flight (like a parent worried about missing their child’s first steps!) felt as if the fledglings had waited all along for me to witness the event! As the first fledgling took off, it flew clumsily, perching just a foot away from me, before it took off for good. Slowly, the other two flew away too. But to think that there was some kind of telepathy, as if they had heard my deepest desires to see them take flight, still warms up my heart. But one eventful afternoon, as I stepped into my balcony, I found all the 3 fledglings trying to take flight, coming out of the nest one after the other. What a feeling that was, to have the honour of witnessing the very first flight of a bird’s life! Now that the Munia pair is back to nesting in my balcony after a year, I cannot wait for more magical sightings to happen right in my treasure trove backyard! I am very certain no special sighting can ever replace the happiness I felt that day, witnessing this magical moment. I *** Who Am I? (Part-4) Srikanth Bhamidipati 1. DECCAN BIRDERS’ ANNUAL FLOCKING Report – Annual Dinner, September 28, 2019 Surekha Aitabathula Seventy happy folks were on the same page on the 28th of September, 2019 at the Deccan Birders Annual Dinner. It was a night of flocking, bonding, chirping, watching and listening together. Those of us who usually meet in birding gear in forests met each other in a festive let-your-hair-down kind of environment. The function began with the welcome address by Bharadwaj, who delineated the activities of Deccan Birders. After the welcome address the floor was thrown open for the Chief Guest Kalyan Varma's presentation on various aspects of nature. Kalyan Varma (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) A bit about the renowned Chief Guest. Kalyan Varma is a wildlife photographer, film maker, naturalist and explorer who quit his IT job in Yahoo and promised himself to work fulltime for wildlife. He freelances with many of the world's leading magazines, environmental NGOs and television channels like National Geographic and BBC. Vizag-born, Bangalore-based Kalyan has, over the last decade, worked on blue chip wildlife series for the BBC and the National Geographic Channel. His work has appeared in many publications world-wide, such as National Geographic, Nature, The Guardian, BBC Wildlife, GEO, Smithsonian and Lonely Planet. founder of Asia's largest nature photography festival Nature InFocus. He has made several films and nature documentaries like the Brahmaputra - Sky River of the Himalayas series, Wonders of the Monsoon, Secrets of Wild India: Tiger Jungles, Wildest India: Western Ghats and Million Snake Bites. His recent film Wild Karnataka has won much acclaim. His latest outing, The Swamp Tigers of Sunderbans, on which he spent 600 hours of shooting, has been nominated for the Emmys this year. The engrossed audience (Photo: Bharadwaj Korni) With such an accomplished speaker, the packed house listened in rapt attention to Kalyan's compelling narrative. The opening statement of his presentation – that he is basically a story teller – was apt: he went to share many slices of life in the wild through his stunning visuals. For instance, how the wolves follow the shepherd and his sheep; how an elephant that trampled a ten-year-old girl and devastated her family found that its own family got disturbed too. He showed powerful visuals of a hapless elephant's agony and trauma during capture. Kalyan interacting with the audience (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Kalyan addressing the gathering (Photo: Bharadwaj Korni) India Nature Watch, which he co-founded with a team of photographers, has today become the largest platform for upcoming wildlife photographers in Asia. He is also the co-Kalyan also showed us the trailer of his film Wild Karnataka, which has galloping music and tremendously rich visuals. The presentation concluded with a small clip on the making of his film The Swamp Tigers of Sunderbans.

Kalyan receiving a memento from Aasheesh Pittie (Photo: Bharadwaj Korni) The photo display (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) The photo display adorning the wall was much appreciated by one and all. Finally, after a sumptuous dinner and much camaraderie, warm good nights, handshakes and smiles were exchanged with a promise to rejoice again at the next flocktail. After his talk, everyone trooped down to the dinner gallery where four best photographs taken by about ten of our members were displayed. Kalyan was taken around the gallery and introduced to the photographers. *** Trip Report – Pashamylaram/Patancheru/Ameenpur Lakes, August 31, 2019 Dr G Samuel Sukumar A view of Patancheru Lake (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) On August 31st 2019, three of us – Mr Shafaat Ulla, Thomas Rajendra Prasad and I – decided to visit the Pashamylaram Lake, located about 47 km from Hyderabad on NH-65, and 8.9 km beyond Patancheru Lake. This lake is located in the industrial area of Pashamylaram. The main purpose of this visit was a reported sighting of a large flock of Greater Flamingos by Mr Vijay Kumar. It was raining lightly when we started at 6.30AM. Passing through the industrial area we reached the lake edge, only to be disappointed as there was no trace of any flamingos anywhere in the lake. An Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark was seen hovering above, and a pair of Spot-billed Ducks flew around at a distance. Shafaatsaab said that if the flamingos had been seen in such large numbers earlier, they must be visiting nearby lakes. The industrial area was covered with smog and a nauseating smell, so we decided to move on and have a look at a couple of other lakes – Patancheru and Ameenpur. Black-headed Ibis and Grey Heron (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) We reached Patancheru Lake, where we were welcomed by a Grey Heron and an Ibis which were attracted by fish waste in the banks. A lone rock outcrop in the water had a Darter preening its wet feathers. Photographs of the Darter showed something around its beak, possibly its own feathers.

Darter (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Asian Openbill (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Presence of some of the Flamingos indicated we were getting closer to the large flock. So we then moved to the Ameenpur Lake. As we stopped at the bund temple, we saw a pair of Flamingos very close to the shore. Baya Weaver at work (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Walking on the bank, we saw Baya Weavers busily weaving their nests, Asian Openbills, Common Coot, Little Grebes in breeding plumage, Spot-billed Pelicans and a few Flamingos. Little Grebe (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Greater Flamingo (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Spot-billed Pelican, Darter and other birds (Photo: Thomas Rajendra Prasad) Driving beside the bund to reach the lake bed, we saw Spotbilled Pelicans in the first small water body, along with Purple Swamphens and Coots. At the main lake, we saw a lone Whitebreasted Kingfisher on a granite boulder and a Pied Bushchat.

Eurasian Spoonbill (Photo: Thomas Rajendra Prasad) White-throated Kingfisher (Photo: Thomas Rajendra Prasad) At a distance we could see the large flock of about 200-plus Greater Flamingos in the lake. So what we had presumed earlier turned out to be true: these large flocks appeared to be moving around between these three lakes. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Black Bittern (Ixobrychus flavicollis) Black Bittern in its habitat Black Bittern (Krishna Delta, January 5, 2019) Order: Pelecaniformes Family: Ardeidae Genus: Ixobrychus Species: I. flavicollis Size: 54-66 cm Description & distribution: The Black Bittern is by far the largest member of its genus Ixobrychus. It is a dark grey, sooty black or dark brown Bittern having uniformly black upperparts with a bluish sheen and buff-tipped wing coverts, while the underparts are whitish heavily streaked with brown. A loose tuft of elongated feathers on the foreneck may overhang the upper breast. It has a yellow patch extending from the throat across the sides of the neck till the base, and hence is sometimes referred to as the Yellow-necked Bittern. Another alternate name is Mangrove Bittern. The feathers on the crown and nape are fairly long – almost long enough to be called plumes. The bill is relatively long and variable in colour, though generally dark – the upper mandible is dark brown to red brown, while the lower mandible is pale green or purple, sometimes suffused with a reddish tinge with a yellowish tip. It has dark grey, dark brown, black or olive green legs with yellow-green soles. The irises are yellow to red brown and the skin around the eye is variable, dusky to green or pink. The female is paler than the male, and has a yellowish wash to its underparts. The juvenile is similar, but has distinct fringes to its upperparts. It is widely distributed across most of Asia, including East Pakistan, India (except Andaman & Nicobar Islands), Southeast Asia, Indonesia and Philippines, as well as Australia, New Guinea and Solomon Islands. The nominate race, I. f. flavicollis, breeds in Pakistan, India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, central and south China, Malaysia, Indonesia and Philippines. I. f. australis breeds in Indonesia, Papua-New Guinea (including Bismarck Archipelago) and coastal Australia. I. f. woodfordi is confined to the Solomon Islands. Birds of the Moluccas are sometimes separated as race I. f. gouldi. Populations are known to move in response to seasonal variations like rain or drought/water scarcity; they also disperse widely post-breeding. Habitat & behaviour: The Black Bittern is solitary and usually seen singly, if at all – it is a highly shy and secretive skulker, and rarely seen out in the open. It inhabits both terrestrial and estuarine wetlands, especially the thick vegetation growing at the edges of densely forested freshwater streams, pools or other permanent wetlands, including grasslands, forests, woodlands, rainforests and mangroves. Foraging and feeding is mostly nocturnal and crepuscular, usually trying to grab prey from a perch on shady trees over water, though it may also occasionally stalk prey slowly, or stand at a vantage point and wait for the prey to emerge. Its diet consists mainly of frogs, reptiles, fish and invertebrates, including crabs, snails, dragonflies, shrimps and crayfish. During the day, it roosts in trees or on the ground amongst dense reeds. When disturbed, it freezes in characteristic bittern posture (stretched tall, bill pointing up, so that its shape and streaked pattern blend with upright stems of reeds), or flies to cover where it would freeze again. The territorial call is a characteristic loud drum-like booming, mainly heard during the breeding season, at day or night. It is a long drawn out, slightly descending whoo-o-o-o-o, uttered at roughly 15-second intervals. There is also a softer coo-oorh call, given when approaching the nest.

clumps, cane stands or reeds in swampy areas. The usual clutch is 3-5 blue or green-ringed white eggs. Nesting: The Black Bittern breeds generally between June and September, with some variation depending on amount of rainfall. Like other bitterns, but unlike most herons, nesting is solitary. The nest is a bed of sticks and reeds on a base of larger sticks, and is built in tree branches overhanging water, bamboo Local name: The Black Bittern is known as ‘Kala bagla’ in Hindi, ‘Karuppu kokku’ in Malayalam, and ‘Karuppu madayan’ or ‘Karuppu narai’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 16 Number 11 November 2019 INDOOR MEETING: Talk on “Rainwater Harvesting – A Solution to Three Urban Problems” by Ajit Kumar Mahendra. Friday, 1st November 2019, 6.00PM: Goethe-zentrum Hyderabad, 20 Journalist’s Colony, Road No. 3, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. (For directions, please contact 94905-09251 or 040-65526443/23350040) Ajit Kumar Mahendra, our Life Member, retired as Senior Deputy Director General of Geological Survey of India (Southern Region). He was instrumental in conducting a temporal analysis of Hyderabad city after a record rainfall of 24cm in 24 hours in a freak flood in 2000. The results revealed that the flooding had happened because the natural drainage and sewerage lines were all blocked by garbage, while the natural drainage streams, rivulets and tanks into which these emptied were blocked by illegal constructions. This prompted Ajit Kumar to actively take up Rainwater Harvesting and Solid Waste Management since then. Ajit has set up a demonstration unit at which he conducts Lecture-cum-Demonstration sessions. With Telangana state being on the brink of a water crisis, it is imperative that we learn to tap rainwater for storage/usage and for groundwater recharge. BEYOND SPARROWS, EAGLES AND CRANES Trip Report – Rollapadu, October 12-13, 2019 Nitish Nagabhairava The group in action (Photo: Nitish Nagabhairava) The recent birdwatching trip to Rollapadu Bird Sanctuary was my first real birdwatching trip. Before this I barely knew what “birdwatching “meant. My friend Surya had recently started this as a hobby, and he eventually got so interested in it that he started studying it seriously and also began doing courses on it. It was he who got me into this too. To be honest, I only went because he dragged me along to keep him company! But I got interested after seeing a variety of birds. When I went on this trip, I had no idea what to expect and my knowledge about birds was very minimal. For me, all the small birds were sparrows, all birds flying high were eagles and all water birds were cranes! I also came to know about GIBs after Kalyan Sir’s speech, and the fact that their importance at the moment is greater than our national bird, the Peacock. But after this trip I came to know a lot about different species of birds and the other members really helped me to spot birds and to differentiate them. Later, I also got the opportunity to attend an event conducted by the Deccan Birders at Hyderabad, where the keynote speaker was Kalyan Varma, a B.B.C wildlife photographer. His speech about wildlife piqued my interest and I decided to give birdwatching a real try and learn how to spot different kinds of birds. Spotted Owlet (Photo: Umesh Mani) The first bird I saw was a Spotted Owlet (Athene brama). I also learnt how to differentiate between a male and a female Rose-ringed Parakeet (Psittacula krameri). Common Hawk Cuckoo (Photo: Umesh Mani) I was fascinated at the way the other birdwatchers were able to spot very small birds and determine their species. I have to admit it was difficult for me to spot the birds amongst the bushes and trees. My favorite moment was getting to witness a Black-winged Kite (Elanus caeruleus) preying on a lizard.

Indian Eagle Owl (Photo: Umesh Mani) Bay-backed Shrike (Photo: Umesh Mani) Later I saw an Indian Eagle Owl (Bubo (bubo) bengalensis), which was the biggest Owl I have ever seen in my life. It felt like I was in a special episode of National Geographic channel spotting different species of birds. We travelled around the whole afternoon, spotting varieties of kites, shrikes and harriers. In the evening, we travelled in a safari van to watch the Blackbuck which Rollapadu is famous for. The best part of the evening was seeing a male Lesser Florican (Sypheotides indicus) jumping to attract the female. It was amazing to see what the male birds do to impress the other gender. I was very happy that I was able to watch this action. (2) (1) (3) (4) (6) (5) (7) Lesser Florican displaying (Photos: Umesh Mani)

We were really looking forward to spotting Rain Quails (Coturnix coromandelica) but they are really shy birds and difficult to spot in the grass. We only got to hear them. After a long day which started at 3.00 in the morning and ended at 6.00 in the evening, I thought we would be resting. However, after dinner the group took out their cameras and went in search of Indian Nightjars (Caprimulgus asiaticus), Owlets and Owls. They returned at 12.00 midnight! The next day we woke up early, since there is high bird activity in the morning. We had a great view of Blackbuck running as a pack, and the males fighting playfully. We also spotted a male Lesser Florican displaying for the 2nd time. While travelling back, we discussed the decline in the number of bird species and how the present-day birdwatchers are getting to see only a fraction of the bird species as compared to the senior birdwatchers. It was sad to see how human encroachment has drastically affected the habitat of the GIBs, which are now a critically endangered species. It is shocking to know that there are barely any left in Rollapadu now. On a positive note, I had a beautiful trip and I would like to thank the trip organizers from the Deccan Birders. If not for them, I wouldn’t have got an opportunity like this. It feels good to see that such clubs are providing a means to enjoy nature at its finest without altering it. I am really grateful for this opportunity and I am looking forward to my next birdwatching trip, as a member! KOMODO: BEYOND AND BELOW THE DRAGON’S REACH DIVING EXPERIENCES Part-2 Text: Amritha Lawrence; Photos: Ashley Weems, NASE AOW Diver Hawksbill Turtle There's a different kind of magic that makes people fall in love with diving - be it the first breath you take underwater, or for an adrenaline junkie like me who loves to just jump and fight a current, or for an underwater photographer who loves to show the world this spectacular underwater heaven that's beyond anything you can ever imagine.    With that thought in mind, I boarded the plane to my first international diving trip abroad and I chose to do this around the island of Komodo in Indonesia, famously known for the largest and most dangerous lizards of the world. Beyond the blue waters of Komodo, hides a spectacular life that is something right out of our dreams. Siaba Besar (Turtle paradise), Makasa (Manta point), Mauvan (Turtle point) in the middle. Batu Bolong, Tatawa Besar, Police Corner and Sebayor in the north east Cauldrons, Castle and Crystal Rock in the north (Manta point and Shotgun point for current junkies). I will try and share a detailed discussion of more dives in the coming articles; this is just a brief overview. Nurse Shark Reef Octopus The best part about all these sites is not just the abundance of marine life you find there, but also the challenges you encounter. Most of the dives in Indonesia are drift dives, meaning you will be diving in medium to strong currents; Komodo is one place where you will not just enjoy the currents, but also understand how dangerous it can be if you don't have enough experience or a good guide. What I loved about Komodo was not just the marine life I saw, but also the currents I dived in. The gigantic dive sites make you feel humble about life and also respect the ocean for all its majesty. Komodo taught me to respect and flow with the elements, and I will always carry that in my heart. Trip Report – Osman Sagar Lake, August 4, 2019 Text: Arun Kumar; Photos: Umesh Mani A distant flock of Greater Flamingos at Osman Sagar Lake I had seen Osman Sagar, aka Gandipet Lake, on Google Maps, and had read a lot about it. It was created by damming the Musi River in 1920, to provide an additional source of drinking water for Hyderabad and to protect the city after the Great Musi Flood of 1908. It was constructed during the reign of the last Nizam of Hyderabad State, Osman Ali Khan, hence the name. It was on the 4th of August 2019 that I actually got to travel right up to the lake and see the avian habitat that it supports. Spread over 46 sq km, it was truly a wondrous sight to behold – an ocean of water in all respects. Surrounding the lake was a carpet of green nourished by wet clay soaked to the brim with water from the lake. The first sight was one of white and black. Hundreds of River Terns (Sterna aurantia) and Eurasian Coots (Fulica atra) were seen dotting the banks. Among them were Plovers and Lapwings too. Little Ringed (Charadrius dubius), Kentish (Charadrius alexandrinus) and Sand were the types of Plovers we encountered that day. Egrets in majestic breeding plumage were a sight to behold. While monsoons might be a bit cumbersome in terms of convenience and logistics, I believe it is one of the best times for birding, especially water birds – they all put on their best plumage to attract their mates. Early in the morning, I met Sudhir, Umesh, Srikanth and Lawrence in Lawrence’s 4x4 – the Mahindra Thar, a perfect vehicle for the terrain of Gandipet. In fact, my car got stuck in the mud even before we entered the final trail. That being sorted somehow, we proceeded merrily in the Thar for a wholesome day of birding. There was a light drizzle and a pleasant chill, adding to the ambience of Gandipet. Purple Swamphen River Tern Next up we saw a few Purple Swamphens (Porphyrio porphyrio). A Pied Kingfisher (Ceryle rudis) posed for interesting photo opportunities. Great Egret and Eurasian Coot Pied Kingfisher

Black-winged Stilts roamed around searching for food. Among the bigger birds, we saw the Asian Openbill (Anastomus oscitans), Greater Flamingos (Phoenicopterus roseus) and Eurasian Spoonbills (Platalea leucordia). Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark (female) Eurasian Spoonbill After having feasted our eyes and senses, and a lot of photographs later, we turned our attention to the elusive Amur Falcon (Falco amurensis). We crisscrossed the muddy trails looking for the Amur Falcon among the black rocks that dotted the landscape. This falcon is a small raptor of the falcon family. It breeds in Siberia and then migrates all the way to Southern Africa! It would have been nice to catch a glimpse of these falcons, but it seemed fate had reserved it for another day. We turned our attention to Francolins now. In our hunt for the falcons, we came across Grey Francolins (Francolinus pondicerianus) and Painted Francolins (Francolinus pictus). These partridges are once again an elusive bunch – they just disappear among the reeds once they are alerted. A lot of patience and walking is needed to get a glimpse. During this Francolin chase, a very interesting bird call excited all of us – a metallic chrink-chrink. It was a Rain Quail (Coturnix coromandelica) calling for its mate. We went on a ‘wild quail chase’, driven only by the chrink-chrink that punctuated an otherwise calm drizzly morning. Like the Amur Falcon, fate reserved a glimpse of the Rain Quail for another day. Scaly-breasted Munia We came across a massive group of Rock Pigeons – 200 to 300 in number. Seeing so many pigeons in their natural habitat was very refreshing. There were interesting variations among them, with a few that looked like Albino and Melanistic. We also came across their close relatives – the Doves – notably the Eurasian Collared Dove (Streptopelia decaocto) and the Laughing Dove (Stigmatopelia senegalensis). Another aquatic species that we encountered was the Lesser Whistling-duck (Dendrocygna javanica). However, in the process, we came across a few more birds – Ashy-crowned Sparrow Larks (Erimopterix griseus), Oriental Skylarks (Alauda gulgula), Paddyfield Pipits (Anthus rufulus), Indian Silverbills (Euodice malabarica) and Scaly-breasted Munias (Lonchura punctulata). Eurasian Collared Dove Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark (male) It was a pleasant birding experience at Gandipet. The habitat supports a wide variety of birds – aquatic and otherwise – and one would never go back disappointed. The only concern is the encroachment happening all around the lake. I wish we were wise to learn from past mistakes and visionary enough to save our rich biodiversity for our future generations. Let us sensitize our friends, family and society to be more responsible towards our environment.

water were a feast for the eyes. The light drizzle, the fresh air and hundreds of birds – it was an unforgettable experience! Finally, it was time for us to return. A Black-winged Kite (Elanus caeruleus) was waiting alongside the route to bid us goodbye. Cattle Egret After a few hours on the banks of the expansive Osman Sagar, one is completely refreshed. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Bar-headed Goose (Anser indicus) Bar-headed Goose (Gujarat, February 9, 2019) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Anser Species: A. indicus Size: 71-76 cm cultivated fields while foraging, feeding mainly on rice, barley and wheat. It is skittish and difficult to get close to, slowly moving away as one approaches, and taking off when alarmed. Its call is a loud, honking and quite musical aang aang, produced in different keys. Description & distribution: The Bar-headed Goose is a stoutbodied grey, brownish and white goose, with a white face and two distinctive broad black bands across the nape or crown, which make it easy to identify. It has a white line down the grey neck, pale steel-grey plumage (paler and more uniform than the Greylag Goose), yellowish or orangeish legs and a black-tipped yellow bill. In flight, it appears greyish with a dark trailing edge to the wing. The sexes are alike, while the juvenile has a white face and dark-grey crown and hind neck. The most interesting aspect of its behavior is its ability to undertake grueling migration flights at high altitudes – the Bar-headed Goose is known to be among the highest fliers in the bird world. The challenge of extracting oxygen from the hypoxic air, coupled with the fact that it does not soar or glide, but continuously flaps its wings in flight, makes it one of the most iconic avian migration journeys. Migrating skeins have been recorded at altitudes of almost 28,000ft (approx. 8000m); in fact, George Lowe, the New Zealand-born climber who supported Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay during their ascent of Mt Everest in 1953, said he had seen Bar-headed Geese flying over the top of Mt Everest – which measures nearly 29,000ft! The Bar-headed Goose is the only true goose native to central southern Asia, including Russia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia and Tibet. It breeds in colonies of up to several thousand near mountain lakes, and winters across North and North-eastern India (with small numbers going down to Central and even South India), Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Small introduced populations are also present in parts of Europe and North America. Nesting: The Bar-headed Goose breeds generally between April and June, in Ladakh and Tibet, the breeding areas closest to us. The nest is a depression in lush green bushes, well-lined with feathers. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 ivory-white eggs. Habitat & behaviour: While the Bar-headed Goose summers in high-altitude lakes, in winter it is usually seen in small to mid-sized flocks, foraging in young gram fields or resting on the banks of lakes or on the sandbars in the middle of rivers or lakes. It is quite crepuscular and nocturnal, and frequents Local name: The Bar-headed Goose is known as ‘Hans’, ‘Kareyee hans’ or ‘Raaj hans’ in Hindi, ‘Tella pedda batu’ in Telugu, ‘Kuriththalayan’ Malayalam, and ‘Neer vathu’ or ‘Vari kazhutha thara’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034.
