Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 16 Number 12 December 2019 INDOOR MEETING: Talk on “The centipede’s sanctuary: biogeography and diversification of the Western Ghats biota” by Dr Jahnavi Joshi. Tuesday, 3rd December 2019, 6.30PM: Goethe-zentrum Hyderabad, 20 Journalist’s Colony, Road No. 3, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. (For directions, please contact 94905-09251 or 040-65526443/23350040) For the past two centuries, one of the main endeavours of evolutionary biologists has been to understand the origins of biological diversity, i.e. how plants and animals proliferated across the world. Increasingly over the past decade, researchers have used molecular tools (DNA sequences) together with morphological and climate data to characterize species, and draw on that information to elucidate the process of species' origins. Jahnavi Joshi, Project Scientist, Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, is an evolutionary biologist and studies arthropod diversity and its evolutionary origins in the tropical forests of peninsular India. She will talk about the biodiversity of the Western Ghats and its evolutionary origins, focusing on centipedes, which are ancient predatory arthropods. Do make it a point to attend this interesting talk. INDOOR MEETING: Talk on “Emerging threats to Indian Birds - Challenges of Conservation” by Dr Asad Rahmani. SOLITARY BIRDING Trip Report – Desert National Park & Khichan, October 2019 Text and Photos: Sravan Kumar R Great Indian Bustard in its habitat In the month of October, a trip to Rajasthan was planned, following the trip to Rollapadu, with Deccan Birders. I felt comfortable with the warmth of Rajasthan at 36-40 °C; an escape from the extended rains in the Deccan region. I was accompanying a friend on work to Jaisalmer. Soon we wound up our work and my friend returned to Hyderabad. I stayed back, extending my trip by three more days, to visit some wellknown IBAs nearby, the Desert National Park (DNP) and Khichan. This was my first visit to the desert landscape. (Neophron percnopterus) flying overhead across the road and a White-eared Bulbul (Pycnonotus leucotis). Common Buzzard The birds here are so habituated to human presence that they feed unconcerned at the feeders hung up on trees in the middle of congested, busy areas. They even nest in the pots provided on the trees! White-eared Bulbul and House Sparrow House Sparrow at a feeder in a busy area Egyptian Vulture Earlier, the other day en route to work at Ramghar village, 65km from Jaisalmer, we had observed Common Babbler (Turdoides caudata), White-eared Bulbul and House Sparrows (Passer domesticus) quenching their thirst at a ditch formed by an underground pipeline leakage. Now, on the way to Jaisalmer city, we were greeted by an Egyptian Vulture A walk along the canal (Indira Gandhi Irrigation canal) yielded Eurasian Collared Doves (Streptopelia decaocto) (more in number than others from the family), Common Buzzard (Buteo buteo), Common Babblers in the woods and scrub along the canal, Common Sandpiper (Actitis hypoleucos), Red-wattled Lapwings (Vanellus indicus), White Wagtail (Motacilla alba), Red-naped Ibis (Pseudibis papillosa), Grey Herons (Ardea cinerea) and Brahminy Kites (Haliastur indus).

Red-naped Ibis Southern Grey Shrike On the way to Laungewala Yudh Sthal (Indo-Pakistani war of 1971), 108km from Jaisalmer, Eurasian Rollers (Coracias garrulus) and Southern Grey Shrikes (Lanius meridionalis) were recorded perched on electric wires and feeding on a swarm of locust nymphs prevailing at that time (a serious agriculture pest issue in the region). We also observed that the locusts were cannibalizing road kills of their own kind! Grey Heron At a very shallow pond, an Egyptian Vulture and a group of 68 Pallid Harriers (Circus macrourus) were seen relaxing by perching on ground in the shades of Calotropis bushes, and Tawny Pipits (Anthus campestris) and Crested Larks (Galerida cristata) on the grass and in the bushes. Desert Locust Tawny Pipit Eurasian Roller Desert (or Red) Fox Nilgai

During the return to our station in the twilight hours, a Desert (a.k.a. Red) Fox leapt into our way from the desert sand dunes and we also came across a Nilgai on the Ramghar village periphery. A day before I started for DNP, I visited the Divisional Forest Officer (DFO), DNP office at Jaisalmer for general introduction and enquiry. During my conversation with the DFO, I was told that DNP would be closed for visitors for another two months as it was the breeding period of Great Indian Bustard (GIB( )गोडौन्(, but that a portion of DNP was open for researchers with permissions from Divisional Officer, DNP at Sudasaree. As suggested by the DFO, I went with the officer and his team at Sudasaree village near Sam. I was also told that the area under DNP was being expanded by securing and adding new locations that had been recorded for GIB nesting. The Rajasthan Forest Department had also established a conservation unit at Sam to monitor the Bustards and established artificial incubation units as a part of the GIB conservation program. Brown Rock Chat reminded of the movie, “Edge of Tomorrow”, seeing sand dunes, sparse population and distantly occurring villages. At the entrance to Desert National Park, Sudasaree Just after turning in from Sam towards Sudasaree, a small water body was quenching the thirst of a White-rumped Vultures (Gyps bengalensis) and some cattle. I came across eagles, vultures and harriers along the way. White-rumped Vulture In the evening, along with my friend, I visited Gaddisar Lake in the city, which is a tourist spot. However, being obsessed with birds, I observed that the structures at the lake were completely infested with Common Pigeons (Columba livia), a few Cattle Egrets (Bubulcus ibis) and Grey Herons perched on trees in the water. As a stray flash flickered, I also observed four Brown Rock Chats (Cercomela fusca) inhabiting a private property next to the lake. Sudasaree, DNP: Sudasaree village is located 15km from Sam village which is 45km from Jaisalmer. Public transportation was infrequent and hiring a taxi would be heavy on the pocket and I wasn’t sure of the time I would spend at the location. Hence, I extended the rental period of the bike I was using and started early with a hope of reaching within an hour. But I ended up birding on the way! Driving down, I was Cattle at a waterhole I reached Sudasaree by 11:30AM. It was a picturesque and tranquil place, with yellow grassland in the background and sparsely grown green bushes of Euphorbia species, that filled the heart with pleasure.

The camp at Desert National Park, Sudasaree An army personnel on his day off was relaxing at the gates. The team had been deployed to help the Forest Department in guarding the DNP. Accompanied by a Forest Department staff, I went inside the National Park for only a small distance (as it needs skill to drive a two-wheeler on the slippery sand) and sighted Variable Wheatear (Oenanthe picata), Desert Wheatear (Oenanthe deserti), Black-crowned Sparrow Lark (Eremopterix nigriceps), Greater Short-toed Larks (Calandrella brachydactyla), Chinkara (Indian Gazelle) and Nilgai. One time, a Black-crowned Sparrow Lark that I was observing made a quick leap to a wasp flying with a caterpillar and stole it from the claws of the wasp! The wasp swooped down, following a little behind the Lark (as if, in shock) and soon took off. The caterpillar was beaten and consumed by the Lark; unfortunately the action was too quick to capture with my camera. Black-crowned Sparrow Lark with caterpillar Variable Wheatear In the evening, accompanied by another person (an expert in driving a two-wheeler in the sand), I went outside the National Park, trying to cover as much terrain as possible. A swarm of locusts was seen flying across. Desert Wheatear Swarm of locusts Chinkara (Indian Gazelle) Great Indian Bustard

At the end of the day, I felt blessed for the delightful sight of GIBs (which I had missed at Rollapadu) – four individual females were sighted entering the protected area, flying over the fence from the adjoining agricultural fields. Great Indian Bustards flying in Laggar Falcon pair mating All of a sudden, a pair of Laggar Falcons (Falco jugger) came flying from behind us. The female positioned herself on a tree branch and the male followed her, hovering above her and gradually descended and mated with her. Indian Fox As it darkened, a pack of five Indian Foxes approached the army camp and waited for the left-over chapatis. At night, the temperature fell to accord a comfortable sleep under the clear sky with a tangential line of the Milky Way (I missed my wideangle lens for the star trail, though). Throughout the night, the wind carried sounds from the grassland that were heard whenever the sleeping bag slipped off my ears. Sunrise in the country’s west happened at 6:59AM. This same time last year, I had witnessed the sun rise in Nagaland at 5:30am (Amurs were out from the roosts)! Having got ready for another day around the park, I observed a Short-toed Snake Eagle (Circaetus gallicus) preening the flight feathers, getting ready for its first flight of the day. Short-toed Snake Eagle Isabelline Wheatear Variable Wheatear was recorded from day 1, mobbing Desert Wheatears and Isabelline Wheatears (Oenanthe isabelline). There was no sign of the GIB. Richard’s Pipit

Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse Lesser Kestrel female On the way from Sudasaree to Sam, I spotted Egyptian Vulture, Southern Grey Shrike and Richard’s Pipit (Anthus richardi). Flocks of Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse (Pterocles exustus) were performing a morning drill, shuttling between the barren land and adjoining shallow waterbody. Montagu’s Harrier Greater Spotted Eagle With extended time at DNP, I missed a train from Jaisalmer to Phalodi-Khichan and then to Jodhpur. So, I took a bus to Jodhpur, reserved my accommodation at a hostel and enquired about bike rentals to go to Khichan (170km from Jodhpur) in the early hours of next day. Unfortunately, the suppliers did not rent bikes to go outside Jodhpur city and the online portal was open only till 8:00PM. The only other option was by train, which would take me to Phalodi by 2:30AM. Another 5km and I could reach Khichan village. A co-traveler I had befriended in the train accompanied me to the bus station, but I learned that the buses would start only after sunrise. Waiting there with the mosquitoes was very hard. Pallid Harrier Montagu’s Harrier (Circus pygargus), Pallid Harrier (Circus macrourus) and Lesser Kestrel (Falco naumanni) were following and disturbing the perched flocks. On the way back to Jaisalmer I sighted a Greater Spotted Eagle (Aquila clanga) flying high above the rocky terrain. Unable to wait any longer, at 4:50AM, I started walking with the help of Google Maps. Within a few minutes, I had reached the outskirts of Phalodi, and beyond that it was completely dark. I continued walking in the cold breeze and the moonlit night on Prosopis tree-lined avenue. It reminded of the Nilgai that bounced onto the way at Ramghar, hence I was on high alert. The stray dogs were pretty cool; they obeyed orders with a single word “thaamo... thaamo”! I reached Khichan by 5:35AM. It was still too dark to enter the village and I didn’t want to risk being challenged by the villagers who may have mistaken me for a rogue. A little friend helped fill the gap till dawn – Ram Sukh, an 11-yearold boy, studying in Std 8 at the Government school, Khichan, and his grandpa who were waiting at the bus stop from 4:00AM.

Demoiselle Crane flock flying into Khichan Khichan: Around 6:30AM, Demoiselle Cranes (कुजा) flew in with their trumpeting calls, in a “V” formation. The birds flew all over the village creating such a racket that the entire village woke up. Comparatively, this was much louder than the Telineelapuram Pelicanry, where the only sounds come from Painted Stork nestlings begging for food from the parent birds and the bill-clapping of adult Grey Pelicans and Painted Storks. Anyway, I managed to make a ‘bridge’ by aligning the camera’s viewfinder to the mobile camera and managed to take some photos, which I was also able to share with friends on social media soon from the location. Supported by the village panchayat, a secure area has been set aside for the birds to feed and is fenced in all directions; they are fed with grains here. Demoiselle Cranes The Demoiselle Crane feeding area When I got ready to click a few good pictures, I found my memory card adapter was missing – I had left it with the laptop after I transferred the old images at Jodhpur! Though I had extra micro-SD cards, they were not useful without the adapter. I was reminded of Sudhir Moorti’s article in the Pitta (October 2018, “Birding is for Cuckoos”), that gave a hilarious description of the mental state of a birder in various unforeseen situations. The birds were seen flying over the village till 8:30AM after which they left for the waterbodies. “They’ll return in the afternoon when they’ll be fed,” said Mr Sevaram Malli Parihar, a resident of the village, who is a wildlife enthusiast and has received many awards for his service towards the bird life in the vicinity. “A total of ~7000 Demoiselles had arrived till date and more would arrive (~10000)”, said Mr. Sevaram. The photos might not have come out so great, but I was happy with my effort, given the circumstances. Having had my fill of lifers, I packed up my tools and returned to Jodhpur, and the next day I started for Hyderabad. Birding alone wasn’t a new experience for me – the times spent for my doctoral studies were mostly solitary until I moved to Hyderabad. But it was after a long time that I had travelled alone again, a solitary birder, accompanied by the imaginary voices of my friends. I would like to express my gratitude to my sponsors, Kosher Climate Private Limited, Bangalore, for their concern towards Ecology and Wildlife. My thanks also to Anita, Gowthama, Srikanth and Sudhir from Deccan Birders for helping me in confirmation of bird identities from a landscape that was new to me. BIRDING IN MANIPUR Text and Photos: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao Loktak Lake, Manipur Manipur is one of the seven sister states of North-east India and has a unique terrain unlike the others. The uniqueness is evident from the fact that it has a large oval-shaped valley, surrounded by blue mountains, with an average elevation of 2500 feet at the valley bottom and rising to an average of 5000 feet on the rims. Thus, the state has a diverse mix of birds owing to its terrain. I frequently visit Imphal, the capital city, and its surroundings as part of my work. This report is the result of a few weeks of birding across the state during the months of August and November. The areas covered include the city of Imphal and surrounding hills, the airport zone, Kangla Fort, Loktak Lake and Keibul Lamjao National Park. Kangla Fort, in the heart of the city, has a large repository of flora and fauna owing to it being protected from general public. Jungle Cat at Kangla Fort The Loktak Lake, known for its vast expanse and the floating biomass called ‘Phumdis’, is an important birding area in the state. This lake has been designated as a Ramsar wetland. The Phumdis at Loktak Lake

The lake has seen deterioration owing to human intervention and exploitation. The number of migratory birds visiting the lake has reduced considerably over the years, primarily due to the presence of human settlements on the lake over the Phumdis. However, large flocks of Brown-headed Gulls (Chroicocephalus brunnicephalus) and Lesser Whistlingducks (Dendrocygna javanica) have been seen in and around the lake area. to be protecting the last of the Great Hornbills (Buceros bicornis) as well. The most common birds found here are the Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica) and the Eurasian Tree Sparrow (Passer montanus). The common House Crow and House Sparrow are conspicuous by their absence. Barn Swallow Sangai Deer juvenile The Keibul Lamjao National Park is located on the South-west edge of the lake and covers an area of 40 sq km. This park is home to the endemic Sangai Deer. The entire park area is a floating bed of grass and biomass. One can actually experience the feeling of jumping over a water mattress on this biomass! A large number of native birds have taken shelter in the park and are believed to be thriving. Tamenglong, a hill district, supports the Amur Falcon (Falco amurensis) migration. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Black-capped Kingfisher (Halcyon pileata) Black-capped Kingfisher (Krishna Delta, January 5, 2019) Order: Coraciiformes Family: Alcedinidae Genus: Halcyon Species: H. pileata Size: 28 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Black-capped Kingfisher is usually seen singly in coastal and mangrove habitats, creeks and estuaries, although it is occasionally seen inland too, away from usual range, as a result of movements related to rainfall. It is usually seen perching on conspicuous, exposed perches, while it waits to dive and catch fish; its diet also includes large insects, crabs, frogs, lizards, beetles and even bees and wasps. It is easily disturbed, and tends to move away when approached. Its flight is fast and direct, and one can easily hear the whirring of the wings as it flies past. Its call is a cackling ki ki ki ki ki, similar to, but shriller than, the call of the Whitebreasted Kingfisher. Description & distribution: The Black-capped Kingfisher is a tree kingfisher with a distinctive black head and shoulders contrasting with a dirty-white collar and throat, coral-red bill, and deep cobalt-blue back and wings. Underparts are rufousorange with the patchy white of the throat extending down the breast, while the legs are bright red. In flight, it shows large white ‘mirrors’ at the base of the primaries, which are diagnostic. The sexes are alike, with the juvenile a duller version of the adult and with streaks on the throat. Nesting: The Black-capped Kingfisher breeds generally between May and July. The nest is a tunnel in the earth-bank of a river or creek, ending in a wider egg chamber. The usual clutch consists of 4-5 spherical white eggs. The Black-capped Kingfisher is found in India (including remote islands of Andaman & Nicobar), Bangladesh, Thailand, Myanmar, parts of China, Philippines, Sri Lanka, the Malay Peninsula, Borneo and Sumatra east up to Sulawesi. Pakistan has also had some reports of winter vagrants. Local name: The Black-capped Kingfisher is known as ‘Kourilla’ (a name used for all Kingfishers) or ‘Kala kilkila’ in Hindi, ‘Kappu taleya meenchulli’ in Kannada, ‘Kalya topicha khandya’ in Marathi, and ‘Krishna meelran’ in Sanskrit. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report – Narsapur, January 12, 2020 Text: Sheetal Vyas; Photos: Satish Grama Laughing Dove Trips to Narsapur Forest have always been a very pleasant and exciting birding experience. It was here, after all, that we had once seen the Grey-headed Canary Flycatcher, and where the elusive Eurasian Wryneck was spotted. So I asked long time birding pal Arjun Surendra if he’d join me on the jaunt and happily, he managed to fulfil fatherly duties to his threemonth-old son and get away for a morning in the sun. The group of nearly 25, led by Dr Krishna Nagarajan, joined up at the main gate of the Air Force Station at Dundigal. We took the forest to the south of the main road, and even as we parked, had an auspicious start with a couple of Small Minivets, a Plain Prinia and an Indian Grey Hornbill. We trooped in, and came across a pair of Chestnut-shouldered Petronias, and in a picturesque spot, framed with fronds, a Common Iora and a Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher. Already there was a menacing thrum of earth movers in the distance. We prepared to shrug it off and move into the thickets – but alas, came upon a large swathe of forest cleared and the earth being prepared for what seemed like a road! We stood around dismayed as Sathvik Reddy darted to a point where he remembered seeing a Nightjar on a previous visit. Shaking our heads, we pushed on into the jungle on the side and flushed a dark-coloured bird that may or may not have been a Nightjar. Part of the group We arrived shortly at a newly constructed two-storied machan. It was a charming place, breezy and affording a beautiful vantage to the forests around. We brought out the food and turned our binoculars all around. Our reward – apart from the Babblers, Drongos and Cisticolas – was a few gorgeous Plumheaded Parakeets. About half a dozen of these chattered and screeched companionably at each other, and we got a close, leisurely look at their plumage... the deep pink of their heads glowing in the sun, the sharp line of the collar followed by a cyan blush tapering off into an indeterminate yellow and eventually a rich green of the body.

Once again, I pondered on the joys of quality birding. New discoveries are exciting, of course, but I would rather a good look at a familiar bird over a tick against a new species, fleetingly seen. All in all, an excellent winter morning, and Narsapur was as exciting as it always promises to be. The complete list of birds seen during the trip is given below: Plum-headed Parakeet Sl. Trip Report: Osman Sagar, January 2020 Text and photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati Short-toed Snake Eagle It was a regular Monday. When I saw everyone getting ready to rush to their work and back to the usual robotic lifestyle, I decided that it was time for me to break the stereotype – I said to myself, “It’s a Monday and I am not a Robot”, and decided instead to visit my favourite birding place in Hyderabad, Osman Sagar. While everyone was in a hurry, I was laid back and reached this amazing place around 7:30AM. Driving past the entry point, I was greeted by the usual Chats, Robins and some Strawberries (Finches, I mean!). It was a quiet morning out there as I drove around the lake, looking for the magnificent raptors which have been attracting a lot of people to that location lately.

During this time, I spotted the fastest diving bird on the planet, the Peregrine, and then another winter visitor to this location, the Common Kestrel. The Peregrine gave a very short time this day unlike the previous visits, but as usual the Kestrel was ready to pose. This Kestrel, instead of sitting on a rock or on the ground, or fly away, decided to hunt a grasshopper right next to me! That’s when I was able to click a nice diving shot. Eurasian Spoonbill Another interesting sighting nearby was the Indian Courser. Common Kestrel After that, I continued driving, with an escort of Swallows following me. Indian Courser Barn Swallow After some time, I decided to get off the car and pay a visit to the water birds which have come from various locations. For the past few years I have been seeing the Sand Plovers being regular visitors to this site, accompanied by others like Stints, Sandpipers, Stilts and other Plovers. This time, there was a total wader population of around 250-300. A lot of ducks were seen this time compared to my previous visits, with Bar-headed Geese leading in numbers; along with them there were a lot of Whistling-ducks, Shelducks, Cotton Pygmy-goose, Red-crested Pochards and others. It was, as usual, a great sight to watch the Flamingos, but the presence of Spoonbills, Pelicans and other Storks made the wetland look much beautiful. Osman Sagar is a perfect habitat for bird population to survive, as it provides all the necessary elements required for their survival. However, there has been a systematic change in the habitat, wherein trees have been cut down and the natural protection for these birds has been lost. In general, the land is currently used for the below reasons:     Agriculture Livestock grazing Drinking water source Fishing Additionally, there are many threats to this lovely habitat like:       Tourist and Recreational Activities Plastic & Waste disbursal Grazing Encroachment or settlement Forest fires Agricultural activities

Paddyfield Pipit Spotted Owlet As mentioned earlier, this place is a heaven for Raptors. On this day, I sighted around 9 Raptors and 2 Owls (1 Owl and 1 Owlet). It is the abundance of food, good source of water and good places to protect themselves, that has resulted in our sighting a lot of birds of prey here over the past few years. Report: Leucistic Rosy Starling in Nizampet, January 2020 Text and photo: YSRK Prasad Leucistic Rosy Starling Birding is a delightful activity and the feeling of being a birdwatcher heightens up when we see something unusual. An unusual sighting for a birdwatcher could include sighting a rare species, sighting a bird that has not been recorded in a particular area though not rare, sighting a bird with a band, or observing an interesting behaviour you have never seen before. So the sudden appearance of a bird with unusual coloration on its body is sure to call an observer’s attention and lead to some exciting moments. I had a similar experience when I saw a leucistic Rosy Starling, which is a rare phenomenon, though relatively more common than albinism. quite different from the others and that could make it vulnerable to predators. Bird Leucism: Is a genetic mutation that results in a total or partial reduction of color in a bird’s plumage. The reduction of color in the bird’s plumage is due to an inadequate deposition or fixation of pigments only in the bird’s feathers. Other parts of the bird’s body have normal coloration. Source: www.avianreport.com Leucistic birds face several challenges in the wild. Flashy plumage reduces the bird’s protective camouflage and makes it more susceptible to predation. Plumage colour plays a key role in courtship displays, so in some species of birds where plumage colour is important in attracting mates, Leucistic birds find it difficult or even impossible to find a mate, and may lose breeding opportunities. Even though there has been a sudden spurt in the construction activity at Nizam Talab vicinity, leading to loss of habitat, the area has many Acacia trees that provide a home to many species of birds. Every year, I see a flock of not less than 150200 Rosy Starlings in the area. On January 8, 2020, I observed a flock of some 50 Rosy Starlings (Pastor roseus), while birding in the evening at Nizampet Road in Telangana. The flock of Starlings was found perching on the Acacia tree, a few feet away from the Nizam Talab. One particular individual looked different – the faint wash on its feathers confused me. Following are some interesting facts about Leucistic birds:   Initially, Albinism flashed through my mind, looking at the pale colour of the bird at first glance. Albinism refers to the complete absence of melanin. The eye colour, along with the plumage, determines if a bird is albino or leucistic: Albino birds have completely white plumage, with pink eyes and skin, whereas the eyes of leucistic birds are darker coloured, as they still have pigment in their eyes. The colour of eyes, bill, legs, and bare parts in leucistic birds are normal. Leucism is less rare than Albinism.   A careful look at the photographs and some quick research helped me understand the bird as leucistic. The feathers looked faded, but the eyes and bill were dark. The bird, in this case, was not alone, and looked lighter in comparison. There was an acceptance from the rest of the birds; however, the bird looked A bird with Leucism may pass it down to their offspring, meaning Leucism is hereditary. Leucism affects only feathers with melanin pigment, usually dark feathers. However, some Leucistic birds can lose all the pigment in their feathers. Such birds’ feathers appear completely white. Project FeederWatch, an online database of bird species observed and reported by citizen scientists, has recorded only about 1,600 Leucistic birds of any species out of 5.5 million distinct birds reported. Environmental hazards show an impact on Leucism and Albinism. The Chernobyl disaster that occurred on April 26, 1986, exposed wild birds to massive radiation. Follow-up studies with an experimental group of Barn Swallows near Chernobyl showed up to a ten-fold increase in Leucism and Albinism over control groups of Barn Swallows in places such as Italy. Reference: https://www.avianreport.com/bird-leucism ***

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Yellow-billed Babbler (Turdoides affinis) Yellow-billed Babbler (Chennai, November 2, 2019) Order: Passeriformes Family: Leiothrichidae Genus: Turdoides Species: T. affinis Size: 23 cm Babbler does sometimes go up to the lower reaches of trees, groups are usually seen foraging on the ground, while one member perches high up and acts as a look-out. Its diet primarily consists of insects and vegetable matter, including fruit, nectar and human food scrap, though it occasionally also eats other small animals like garden lizards, scorpions, grasshoppers etc. It has short rounded wings, and its flight is weak; it does not fly long distances, and gains height by climbing up a tree or tall bush before taking off. Its call is a musical trilling tri ri ri, pitched higher than the Jungle Babbler, and its presence is often announced by the loud, continual chirping, squeaking and chattering of birds in the group. They roost communally, with several birds lining up next to each other; juveniles often wedge themselves in the middle of such line-ups. Mornings are generally spent foraging, while the afternoons are usually less active hours, with birds indulging in resting, allopreening, or bathing during the afternoon. Description & distribution: The Yellow-billed Babbler is a common resident breeding bird, endemic to its range of Southern India and Sri Lanka. It has greyish-brown upperparts, a grey head and nape, and bluish-white eyes. The nominate race of Southern India has a whitish crown and nape with a darker mantle and ear coverts, while the Sri Lankan race, T. a. taprobanus, as also birds of the nominate race seen towards extreme Southern India, has a darker grey crown and back. The rump is paler and the tail has a broad, dark tip. Throat and breast are mottled grey and fairly heavily streaked, and the belly is a pale buff. Individuals of the Sri Lankan race are very similar to, and often confused with, the Jungle Babbler (T. striatus), which does not actually occur in Sri Lanka, and with the Orange-billed Babbler (T. rufescens). The Yellow-billed Babbler was earlier also known as Whiteheaded Babbler, but that name is now used for the African species, T. leucocephala. The sexes are alike. Nesting: The Yellow-billed Babbler breeds almost around the year, but breeding activity generally peaks during March-June and October-November. The nest is an open, messy cup of twigs and roots, built in dense masses of foliage and placed in a fork of a branch, generally within around 4m from the ground. The usual clutch consists of 2-5 turquoise blue eggs. Both male and female share parental duties; however, other adult birds of the flock also feed the young, and communal nest-building, feeding and rearing of young is common. Brood-parasiting has been noted by the Pied Crested Cuckoo and the Common Hawk Cuckoo. The Yellow-billed Babbler is found in Southern India (including Andhra Pradesh south of the Godavari, Telangana, Karnataka south of Belgaum, Tamil Nadu and Kerala) and Sri Lanka. Habitat & behaviour: The Yellow-billed Babbler is gregarious and usually seen in small groups of 7-10 birds – due to which tendency groups are often referred to colloquially as ‘seven sisters’ – in gardens, orchards, village greens, and especially dense scrub like Lantana. It prefers lower altitudes and drier habitats than the Jungle Babbler. Though the Yellow-billed Local name: The Yellow-billed Babbler is known as ‘Chinna sida’ or ‘Chinda sida’ in Telugu, ‘Kariyilakili’ in Malayalam, and ‘Thavittu kuruvi’, ‘Pandri kuruvi, or ‘Velaikkara kuruvi’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. OBITUARY HEINZ LAINER 09.08.1943 – 09.02.2020 Heinz was of German origin and had settled down in Goa a very long time ago. He had a passion for birding and was therefore rightly referred to as ‘Birdlainer’. He was a birder par excellence and was well known in our Indian birding community. He did intensive birding surveys in and around Goa and had authored the book, ‘Birds of Goa’, an authentic and comprehensive record of bird species in that region. It was in September 2010 that a few members of our Society decided to go to Goa for a birding trip. I therefore requested Aasheesh for an introduction to his good friend Heinz, with the intention of approaching him for help with an itinerary. Heinz replied promptly and asked me to send him my postal address. Within a week, he couriered me a detailed itinerary, including meticulously drawn hand sketches with amazing details showing places to visit, roads and routes to take, and even where to eat! Our trip was finalized, and fifteen of us went to Goa and, as advised by him, met him at Anjuna beach on the morning of 24th September 2010. He was waiting for us with a ready smile. After introductions and exchange of pleasantries, he took us to a couple of good birding spots and then, after a hearty breakfast, we bid him good bye. For the next three days we were on our own, following his instructions. Before leaving Goa I called him to express our thanks for all he had done for us. He said he would be visiting Hyderabad in the near future. But alas, he never did. We shall all miss the “Birdman of Goa” who gave so much to Indian ornithology. Let us pray that his soul rests in peace. I am sure he is now content and happy, rubbing shoulders with the Birds of Paradise. - Shafaat Ulla

‘SKUA’RING THE ARABIAN WATERS Trip Report – Goa Pelagic Trip, November 22-24, 2019 Rama Sarvani, Deepanwita Purohit & Sravan Kumar R The group during the Pelagic tour (Photo courtesy: Srikanth Bhamidipati) INTRODUCTION Rama Sarvani I am filled with gratitude towards the organizers of Deccan Birders for planning the Pelagic tour. I could not have asked for better company to travel and bird with. We greeted each other at Vasco Bus Depot and talked about the birds we saw en route, which was not very many as it was a closed sleeper bus. But I did manage to spot Brahminy Kites (Haliastur indus) circling above us. There were approximately 40-50 of them. Sravan, however, saw a few Hornbills and some Egrets on the way. After the topsy turvy ride, we finally entered Konkan. Though I’ve never been to the northern part of the Western Ghats, the surroundings looked pretty familiar to me. It brought back a lot of memories from my trip to Valparai earlier this year. The Western Ghats are supposedly older than the Himalayas, stretching approximately 1600km, positioned parallel to the west coast of the sub-continent. After freshening up at our accommodation, we got our designated hired scooters with chauffeurs! On the first day of the trip, since the morning session was already gone, we went birding along Morjim Beach. This beach, known for its tranquil and calm ambience, is also a nesting site for the Olive Ridley Sea Turtles. Also known as “Little Russia”, this is one of the most visited beaches in North Goa after the Baga Beach. More on this beach and our birding experiences during the trip follow below. DAY 1 – MORJIM BEACH Deepanwita Purohit When I first heard of ‘Pelagic Birding’, it evoked a sense of curiosity in me. The word ‘pelagic’ is derived from the Greek word for ‘open sea’. Birds that spend most of their life on open sea and venture ashore only for breeding are called pelagic birds, a rarity in terrestrial habitats. Thus, a trip to Goa to explore this unique avian group and other fauna amid the vastness of the Arabian Sea, seemed like a ‘never to miss’ opportunity. With this common goal, our team of 13 birders arrived at Goa on the morning of 22nd Nov, hoping for some unique birding experience over the next 72 hours. With the pelagic trip scheduled on 23rd, we had a day in hand to explore the other nearby habitats. Topographically Goa is a part of the Konkan region, which is an escarpment rising up to Western Ghats and is a biodiversity hotspot. One can expect a rich floral and faunal diversity here. We checked into a hotel where the rooms had balconies overlooking a small patch of vegetation - a perfect spot for some casual birding. After we settled down in our respective rooms, we got hold of our binoculars for a quick scan of the surroundings.

After a quick refreshment, we headed to Turtle Beach in Morjim, which is located in the Northern bank of Chapora river estuary. Along the mountainous terrain facing the boundless sea, we spotted White-bellied Sea Eagles (Haliaeetus leucogaster) and Brahminy Kites gliding across in pursuit of prey. There were also some small water bodies on the way, where Common Sandpipers (Actitis hypoleucos) and Cattle Egrets (Bubulcus ibis) could be seen, and some mudflats, which hosted large numbers of Gulls and Terns. Grey-headed Bulbul (Photo: Umesh Mani) What caught our attention first was the call of a Grey-headed Bulbul (Pycnonotus priocephalus) and the next moment we spotted it perched on a tree. What a start! Gulls & Terns on the mudflats (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Scaly-breasted Munia (Photo: Umesh Mani) Soon after, a small flock of Scaly-breasted Munias (Lonchura punctulata) arrived on a roof top next to our building in search of some insects from an algal bloom. The other notable sightings from the balcony were Small Minivets (Pericrocotus cinnamomeus), Greenish Warbler (Phylloscopus trochiloides), Red-whiskered Bulbul (Pycnonotus jocosus) and Chestnuttailed Starling (Sturnia malabarica) to name a few. Chestnut-tailed Starling (Photo: Umesh Mani) White-bellied Sea Eagle (Photo: Umesh Mani) Morjim beach is a nesting ground for the Olive Ridley Sea Turtle and home to many resident and migrant birds. We were welcomed by a visual delight of hundreds of migratory Lesser Sand Plovers (Charadrius mongolus) walking about in large groups on the warm sand of Morjim. Lesser Sand Plover flock (Photo: Sravan Kumar R)

Also seen were Brown-headed Gulls (Chroicocephalus brunnicephalus), Black-headed Gulls (Chroicocephalus ridibundus), River Terns (Sterna aurantia) and Gull-billed Terns (Gelochelidon nilotica) flying around and scanning the water for food. Lesser Sand Plover (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Amur Falcon (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) While a few of us busy playing splashing about in the waves, Sravan spotted an Amur Falcon (Falco amurensis) making its journey across the Arabian Sea to Southern Africa. Interestingly, the very next day on the pelagic tour we spotted the dragonflies which the Falcon primarily feeds on during its migration. Brown-headed Gull (Photo: Umesh Mani) DAY 2 – PELAGIC TOUR Rama Sarvani We started our trip with a weather update from Siri that charged me up. Sunrise was at 5.00AM. I woke up early because I was excited to venture into the sea. This is the first time in many years that a Pelagic Tour was organized by Deccan Birders and I wanted to make complete use of the time I had. We had been informed that seeing the pelagic birds was a rare sight and I wanted to be all set for a whole day trip without giving in to seasickness. Many of us took the antinausea medicine and we embarked on our journey into the sea on our modified fishing vessel. Black-headed Gull (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Gulls following a fishing boat (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) The sea was calm and as soon as our boat started, the Brown and Black-headed Gulls started following our boat. These birds have learnt over time that fishing boats have fish and they fly in close proximity to the boats. There was a flock always following us even as we went 30-40 km further into the sea.

While my eyes were searching for those species which Omkar had talked about, I somehow realized midway, that I was ignoring some other common birds and moths and also a lot of migrating Crimson Rose butterflies. There was so much activity all of a sudden, that I just couldn’t process all of it at once. Arctic Skua (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) My enthusiasm spiked as we spotted the first Arctic Skua (Stercorarius parasiticus) about 10 km into the sea. As expected, we saw a few Lesser (Thalasseus bengalensis) and Greater Crested Terns (Thalasseus bergii) which were following their usual fishing regimen. Though I had not had enough of the Arctic Skuas, I wanted to see some other pelagic species as well, like the Shearwaters, Petrels and, at least, one Booby. Flying Fish (Photo: Umesh Mani) Brown-headed Gull with Conger Eel catch (Photo: Umesh Mani) I saw the ‘Flying Fish’ also. These marine fish are members of the family Exocoetidae, and are colloquially known as ‘flying fish’ or ‘flying cod’. Though these fish glide long distances, one can never predict when they come out of the water and so it was almost impossible for me to take a single picture. However, to watch them glide over the water was such an amazing feeling. The brilliance with which they glide made me wonder, why do they glide? A little reading up on it later told me that they usually glide to escape from the predators, which, to them, at that moment, was the boat. Though they do not fly like birds, they still ‘fly’. There are around 64 species of flying fish globally and 5 of them are seen in Indian waters. Nevertheless, I saw a lot of birds and at one point, when everyone was relaxing, I went to the forward part of the boat with our guide Omkar, who was kind enough to share his knowledge about the birds he saw on some of the earlier pelagic trips and his experiences. He had seen Wilson's, Swinehoe’s and even Joaquin’s Storm Petrels, hundreds of Humpback Dolphins and also quite a number of whales during his trips. While we were still talking, I suddenly spotted a Skua flying past me. It was the Pomarine Skua (Stercorarius pomarinus), another lifer for me. Common Tern (Photo: Umesh Mani) I realized that one Pelagic birding trip is not enough and the probability of seeing a lot of lifers was very slim. However, watching the same birds, again and again, gave me a new experience each time, because I could see their behavior change when they were getting food from a fishing boat nearby or when they were just floating around on the waters along with the currents, just chilling. It was a sight to behold! Pomarine Skua (Photo: Sudhir Moorti)

Bottlenose Dolphin (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Brahminy Kite with catch (Photo: Umesh Mani) One aspect that I would like to document and bring attention to, is the large quantity of balloons, plastic containers and thermocol pieces floating around. I have heard people saying, “it’s just a balloon, release it”, but now when I saw this sight, I felt terrible. We must stop and think how balloons and other trash affect lives in the sea. Bottlenose Dolphin (Photo: Umesh Mani) While returning, we saw some Bottlenose Dolphins and clicked pictures. Their moist skin glistening in the setting sun made this experience exhilarating and a standout memory. What an end to the trip! It will always stay engraved in my memory. Western Reef Egret (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) Greater Crested Tern (Photo: Umesh Mani) A view of the mudflats (Photo: Sravan Kumar R)

DAY 3 – SOCORRO & SERULA VILLAGES Sravan Kumar R A view of Socorro Plateau (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Socorro Plateau was once a part of the communidade and the larger village of Serula. It is named after its Parish church, the ‘Nossa Senhora de Socorro’, built in 1667. Socorro is a Portuguese word, meaning ‘succour’, ‘help’ or ‘relief’. Socorro Plateau is also a known birding hotspot. also recorded. A little ahead, a Pompadour (or) Grey-fronted Green Pigeon (Treron (pompadora) affinis) was looking for the ripe fruit on the Singapore Cherry (Muntingia calabura) tree. As we walked uphill, we heard the calls of Blue-throated Blue Flycatcher (Cyornis rubeculoides) and the Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (Cyornis tickelliae) in the thick vegetation. Birding on the roadside (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) On Day-3, eight of us visited the place on for birding. En route, turning in from the highway, our team halted for a tea break and for buying some refreshments. We pre-booked our breakfast because of a busy Sunday. Moving ahead for a short distance, a group of White-rumped Munias (Lonchura striata) appeared on electric lines, and later moved down to the ground. Grey-fronted Green Pigeon (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) On reaching the plateau, we were amazed to see a grassland on the rocky terrain. It was very different from the grasslands of Desert National Park in the sandy soils of Rajasthan and Rollapadu grasslands in the red soils of Kurnool district, AP. White-rumped Munia (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) A pair of Oriental Magpie Robins (Copsychus saularis) was also perched and was making courtship calls. We observed Red-whiskered Bulbuls and White-rumped Munias feeding in the paddy fields. On the opposite side, an Indian Pond Heron (Ardeola grayii) perched on a boundary pole and a Yellow Bittern (Ixobrychus sinensis) peeped at us through the leaves. Jungle Mynas (Acridotheres fuscus) and Brahminy Kites were Purple Heron (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Part of the team on bikes went ahead for conducting recce about the surrounding habitat. Meanwhile the rest of the group continued to search for birds and butterflies in the grasslands. The streams in the gullies of grasslands form a perfect niche for amphibians and other aquatic insects. Ashy-crowned Sparrow Larks (Eremopterix griseus), White-browed Bulbul (Pycnonotus luteolus), Red-vented Bulbul (Pycnonotus cafer), Purple Sunbird (Cinnyris asiaticus), Purple-rumped Sunbird (Leptocoma zeylonica), Spotted Dove (Stigmatopelia chinensis), Asian Pied Starling (Gracupica contra), Common Myna (Acridotheres tristis), Common Hoopoe (Upupa epops), Small Minivet, Nilgiri Flowerpecker (Dicaeum concolor), Tree Pipit (Anthus trivialis), Eurasian (or) Common Cuckoo (Cuculus canorus), Asian Koel (Eudynamys scolopaceus) and Montagu’s Harrier (Circus pygargus) were recorded before we decided to ‘break the fast’. Booted Eagle (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Our birding continued till we reached the other edge of the plateau from where we could see a big water body and a spreading concrete jungle at the foothill. Eurasian (or Common) Cuckoo (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Peacock Pansy (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Small Minivet (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Towards the end of breakfast, a Booted Eagle (Hieraaetus pennatus) came soaring above us and perched on a tree nearby. From the photographs clicked, we found it was blind in one eye. Glassy Tiger (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) While walking down the inclined road, we added Verditer Flycatcher (Eumyias thalassinus) and Crimson-backed Sunbird (Leptocoma minima) to the list. The habitat seemed favourable for many butterflies; Southern Birdwing, Monkey Puzzle, etc.

Upon bringing it to a wildlife hospital, though, they found out it was the animal’s bold behaviour that had led to its bold colour: The distressed bird was a seagull that had managed to get itself covered in curry. Seagulls are inquisitive by nature and are known to put themselves in similarly spicy situations. Thankfully, a couple of baths returned it to its naturally unseasoned state. Report: Mangar Bani, New Delhi Text and photos: Sita Susarla Crested Bunting One of the birding hotspots in the Delhi NCR region that we have visited half-a-dozen times in the past few months, is the hundred-hectare Mangar forest located in the Faridabad district of Haryana. It is called Mangar Bani in the local Haryanvi dialect. The Mangar forest represents the last remains of the Aravalli forest and the vegetation is mainly comprised of Dhau (Anogeissus pendula), Palash (Butea monosperma) and Ber (Ziziphus mauritiana). The forest is also home to arid-region trees like Kareel (Capparis decidua), Kair and Roheda (Tecomella undulata). The 700-year old local Gujjar community believes in a legendary ‘Gudariya Baba’, whose spirit is believed to curse anybody who dares to harm the forest in any way. The forest is therefore well preserved, enchanting and a birder’s delight. and Marshall’s Iora (Aegithina nigrolutea) to name a few. The Indian Pitta is known to nest here every summer and so is the Crested Bunting. Known by the name Navrang, the Pitta is a beautifully coloured bird and the two-note call reverberates across the forest during the breeding season. The persistent loud calls help birders to locate the bird easily in this season. Otherwise the Pitta is a very elusive bird and prefers to perch on trees with broad leaves to conceal itself. The Dhau tree probably is its favourite. Even while foraging for food a thick undergrowth habitat is preferred. The Crested Bunting, locally called Yuvaraj, is spotted near Mohit’s farm, situated a few kilometres from the forest area. Unlike the Pitta it is not perturbed by human presence and is easy to photograph. Its preferred habitat is the steep rocky slopes and open cultivation of Mangar village. Indian Pitta Mangar Bani is the summer abode of Himalayan birds like Indian Pitta (Pitta brachyura), Crested Bunting (Emberiza lathami), Black-headed Cuckooshrike (Lalage melanoptera) Black-headed Cuckooshrike

see it, because at some places the canopy of trees was such that standing underneath it you can hardly see the tree tops. However, it was as though we were in Cuckoo-land, listening to four different Cuckoos all calling at the same time. The Indian Golden Oriole (Oriolus kundoo), the Asian Paradiseflycatcher (Terpsiphone paradisi), the Black and Whitebellied Drongos (Dicrurus macrocercus and D. caerulescens respectively) and Rufous Treepies (Dendrocitta vagabunda) seem to constitute a bird wave as they were always spotted in the vicinity of each other in this forest. Common Woodshrike The Black-headed Cuckooshrike, Grey-throated Martin (Riparia chinensis), Marshall’s Iora, Common Woodshrike (Tephrodornis pondicerianus) and the White-browed Fantail (Rhipidura aureola) are the other beautiful birds that adorn the forest. The Fantail was spotted in the open, happily bathing in a puddle of freshly collected rainwater, proudly displaying its fan-like tail while the other birds looked at it in awe. Grey-breasted Prinia One interesting feature of birds in Mangar is that each species seems to have an area earmarked for itself and when you visit the forest in the next season, you can easily locate the bird you want to see at the same location. The forest being at the edge of the village there is also plenty of food available for the resident and migrant birds. On Big Bird Day in February 2019 we sighted the majestic migrant raptor, the Steppe Eagle (Aquila nipalensis). There were two of them scouting for prey when two Egyptian Vultures joined them. The Steppe Eagle is a winter visitor to north and central India while the Egyptian Vulture is endemic to this region. Booted Eagle (Hieraatus pennatus), Black Eagle (Ictinaetus malayensis) and Bonelli’s Eagle (Aquila fasciata) are some of the other raptors that are regularly seen here. Birders from Delhi and surrounding areas often visit Mangar Bani to sight raptors. White-browed Fantail The Marshall’s Iora, also known as White-tailed Iora, kept calling from the canopy above us. The Black-headed Cuckooshrike too was perched on the higher branches of the trees and would call occasionally. The resident Chestnutshouldered Petronia (Gymnoris xanthocollis), or the Yellowthroated Sparrow, can be seen in large numbers everywhere in the forest along with House Sparrows. The Grey-throated Martin is also endemic to this region. Come the month of July the beautiful Jacobin Cuckoo, heralder of the monsoons as per our ancient culture, visits the forest along with Grey-bellied Cuckoo, and the two are welcomed by their resident cousin, the Common Hawk Cuckoo. A common resident of open habitats, farmland and human habitation, it has adapted to living in cities as well. It is often found near human habitation. The species shows great variation, including clinal variation, in size, and forms a superspecies with the very similar Little Owl. It generally roosts in a small group in the hollows of trees or in cavities in rocks or buildings. Nesting is usually in a hole in a tree or building, laying 3–5 eggs. Spotted Owlet

Spotted Owlet at the nest Late last year (2019), I was fortunate to locate and observe a family of Spotted Owlets near my farm in Aziznagar. The Owlets resided in an open well. There were four in number, probably the parents and two young (now almost adult). The young were born and nurtured in the small cavity in the wall of the open well, and I had opportunity to observe them regularly. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Slender-billed Gull (Chroicocephalus genei) Slender-billed Gull breeding (L) and non-breeding (R) (Jamnagar, Gujarat, February 8 & 9, 2019) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Laridae Genus: Chroicocephalus Species: C. genei Size: 37-40 cm artificial habitats like salt pans and aquaculture ponds. It is usually seen singly, in pairs, or in small flocks, and usually in association with the much commoner Black-headed Gull; the flock size increases during feeding and roosting. Feeding occurs mostly in marshes, grasslands and deltas, although it is also known to feed at landfills and garbage disposal sites. Like many gulls, it tends to stay on the coast and does not venture far into the sea. Its diet consists largely of fish, although it often feeds on aquatic invertebrates at the mudflats, as well as insects that it catches on the wing. It often feeds by flying a few metres above the water and diving when it spots a fish. Its call is a sharp ka ka ka or a kra kra kra. Description & distribution: The Slender-billed Gull, also sometimes referred to as the Rosy Gull, is a mid-sized gull that breeds in the Mediterranean region, and in the countries bordering the north-western part of the Indian Ocean, e.g. Pakistan. It winters further south, in north Africa, India and western parts of Europe. It has a white head, neck, breast and underparts, lower rump and tail, and pale grey upperparts, with the wings showing black-tipped primaries. The neck appears long, forehead is sloping, and the bill is elongated, tapering and red in colour. Irises are yellow, and legs are bright red or dark red. It has a faint dusky ear-spot, much like the Blackheaded Gull, but during breeding season, the head becomes clean white; the bill becomes darker red, and the breast and underparts may also develop a pinkish flush. First-year immature birds show a dark terminal tail band and darker areas on the wings. Nesting: The Slender-billed Gull breeds generally between March and May in most of its breeding range. It nests in large colonies, numbering sometimes up to several thousand pairs. The nest is a shallow scrape or natural depression in the ground, sparsely lined with feathers, grass or other vegetation. The usual clutch consists of 3 spotted, pale buff eggs. Local name: The Slender-billed Gull is known as ‘Kal-siri gangachilli’ in Hindi and ‘Gulabi dhomdo’ or ‘Vadhomadi’ in Gujarati. Report: Asian Waterfowl Census at a few waterbodies around Hyderabad, January 2020 Text and Photos: Sravan Kumar R Northern Shoveler I had the opportunity to participate in the Asian Waterfowl Census at some of the waterbodies around Hyderabad this year. Some details of the trips are given below. January 19, 2020 1. Manjeera Reservoir This reservoir earlier catered to the water requirements of people of the twin cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad. It is now in a situation where it is not just unable to fulfil these functions but also struggling to quench its own thirst. The reservoir area resembles a grassland with traces of water limited only to the canals dug deep in the catchment area and towards the dam gates. It is hard to believe that a once-thriving reservoir could be reduced to this state. Manjeera catchment area

The reservoir catchment area once attracted and hosted many resident and migratory bird species around the year, but now there are hardly any birds there. During my visit, I recorded a few Grey Herons on the bank of the canal, Cattle and Intermediate Egrets, Little Cormorant, Purple Heron and two Wood Sandpipers. Due to the paucity of water, a few Mugger Crocodiles were also seen. The Eucalyptus and Copperpod trees at the entry gate of the reservoir, which used to be the roosting place of Fruit Bats, have disappeared and no bats were seen in the location. In the bushes next to the EEC, the usual species like Small Minivet, Indian Golden Oriole, Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher, Asian Paradise Flycatcher and White-breasted Waterhen were recorded. Also seen were Red-vented Bulbul, Asian Pied Starling, Green Bee-eater, Barn Swallow, Streak-throated Swallow, Red Avadavat, Scaly-breasted Munia, Little Swift and Dusky Crag Martin. 2. Tallapalli Waterbodies Greater Spotted Eagle pale morph (A. c. fulvescens) The mud road led to the Tallapalli cheruvu (lake), with less water level but with more shallow areas, and with Ipomea bushes towards the edges of the bund and open water to the centre of the water body. This appeared to host good numbers of birds; there were ducks visible behind the Ipomea bushes and a pair of Greater Spotted Eagles perching on the ground in the lake area. A Pied Harrier female and Eurasian Marsh Harrier were on the hunt. Tallapalli In a north-east direction from the Manjeera approach road, on the mud road behind the overhead water tank is a small lake with very shallow water and good growth of waterlilies (Nymphae). This lake had one Wood Sandpiper, one Common Sandpiper, two Little Grebes, two Indian Pond Herons, a Cattle Egret and a couple of Common Coots. Further ahead, on the left side to the road the paddy fields were being harvested, and this looked like a favourite habitat for Raptors/Harriers: we saw a Pied Harrier soaring and a Blackshouldered Kite on a nearby electric pole. Pied Harrier female Eurasian Marsh Harrier Greater Spotted Eagle adult (L) and juvenile (R) The lake had a good number of large waders: 44 Eurasian Spoonbills and some Great, Intermediate and Little Egrets. There were also Common Teals, Spot-billed Ducks, Garganey, Eurasian Wigeon, Little Stints and Kentish Plovers.

January 26, 2020 Each waterbody visited on this day was special, in terms of the list and the population of avian fauna they hosted. This induced me to record the conditions prevailing at locations and the conservation measures followed at some of these locations. 4. Garganey and Common Teal mixed flock Annasagar, Jogipet, Medak Our team of 4 members started very early in the morning in view of the distance to be covered. We planned to start our birding from the far side of Annasagar Lake. Reaching the location before sunrise, we stopped and had a good breakfast while waiting for the fog to disperse and the sun to rise higher. The hotel owners seemed to be fascinated with poultry species and had a collection of fowl of many varieties from various locations – for instance, the Turkey, Kadaknath (the black variety of chicken), along with some other native species of fowl, etc. Little Stint 3. Kandi Cheruvu, Kandi Moving back towards Hyderabad from Manjeera, Google Maps showed a waterbody on the left, approachable from the highway, so we decided to check it out. While the lake is actually quite large, there was very less water, and with no weeds around. The surrounding area looked deserted, but it seemed to be a popular venue for evening parties, as the lake side was littered with empty bottles and food parcels in the open scrub area. This lake provided us with a list of ~30 species of birds including Gadwall, Eurasian Wigeon, Eurasian Spoonbill, Black-winged Stilt, Grey Heron, Little Ringed Plover, Common Sandpiper, White Wagtail, Oriental Skylark, Indian Bushlark and Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark. Bar-headed Goose and Lesser Whistling-duck The first view of Annasagar filled me with pleasure and fulfilled my desire to see a waterbody filled with ducks! This lake had ducks of different species in large numbers, and Barheaded Geese were also there in the hundreds. Roosting trees at Annasagar Common Sandpiper Humayun wanted to start the session from an earlier known heronry on the western edge of the waterbody. Unfortunately, those trees were now all gone, but another growth of trees closer to the water edge seemed to have been taken over by the birds and although we couldn’t see any signs of nesting, it seemed a fairly large roosting spot for various species. We started enumerating the species and their individual counts at different stopover points all along the length of the waterbody.

interesting to see where they might be coming from and if there are roosting areas nearby. After a short tea break, we moved on to the next waterbody, at Andole. 5. Andole Lake, Andole, Medak Incoming flock of Eurasian Spoonbills Suddenly, Gokul alerted us to a large flock of birds flying in, which turned out to be 67 Eurasian Spoonbills. We observed as they glided in and perched on the trees of the heronry. At another point, we observed a very interesting courtship behaviour among the Cotton Pygmy-geese: two males and a female were first seen together, with the two males continually flying at each other and apparently fighting. Then all three took off and made a round of the lake, returning to their original spot; once again, the two males started flying at each other, although the female now drifted off. The two males seemed to be very quarrelsome and continued to spar for a long time. Checkered Keelback We reached Andole and started walking along the length of the waterbody to carry out the count. On the way, we came across a basking Checkered Keelback snake on the bund near some bushes, and it gave us a chance to click a few pictures. Eurasian Marsh Harrier being mobbed by House Crow Cotton Pygmy-goose Initially we saw nothing much on the water, other than a few Common Coots and Cotton Pygmy-geese. As we proceeded, however, a Eurasian Marsh Harrier quartering the lake disclosed the presence of Spot-billed Ducks and Lesser Whistling-ducks on an island with a lot of reeds around it. Common Pochard Throughout the time spent around the lake, Cormorants kept flying in, adding to the waterbody counts. It would be Spot-billed Duck and Cotton Pygmy-goose

We also spotted a Greater Spotted Eagle perching on a tree on the opposite side of the waterbody. In this way, observing and counting as we went, we moved towards the other edge of the bund and reached a conduit where, behind a picturesquely located Roads & Buildings Department guest house (though in a dilapidated condition) we recorded a couple of Bluethroats hopping about in the bushes. Egrets following a tractor Bluethroat Initially the lake appeared empty and without any birds other than a few Indian Pond Herons, a Grey Heron and some Common Coots. After waiting for a while on the bund, the southern edge of the lake revealed a small white patch. Hindered by fog and with the sun being in the wrong direction, it was very difficult to see, but somehow we managed to view the Bar-headed Geese and Black-winged Stilts perched on the ground. A few Lesser Whistling-ducks in a small flock were also resting on the far side of the lake. Scoping the waterbody from this location, we could see an Osprey perching on what appeared to be a stout fishing stake. The bird was not easy to see even with the scope due to the distance and background. Zitting Cisticola Osprey landing at perch 6. Beside the main lake, a small patch had reeds and Prosopis trees in it, and hosted a few Grey-headed Swamphens, Bronzewinged Jacanas, Common Coots, Lesser Whistling-ducks, Spot-billed Ducks and a few Little Cormorants. However, we also noted that this portion of the lake is acting as a sink hole with the trash it is accumulating from the neighbouring residential areas. Mehboobsagar, Sangareddy There seems to be a lot of development on this lake for tourism activities. There is organized boating, as a result of which the lake has lost most of the reeds and grasses on the bund. The exception is on the east side, where the lake still has some Prosopis bushes outside the water line. The main bund serves as a viewpoint for the entire lake. The other side of the main bund has agricultural fields, where farmers are preparing for the next crop season. We observed that ploughing was in progress and good numbers of Egrets, Herons and Ibises had gathered in the fields and were foraging and following behind the ploughing tractors. Grey-headed Swamphen

7. Nizam Talab, Nizampet After lunch, while on our way back to the city, YSRK Prasad suggested we visit a waterbody which he frequently visits in his neighbourhood, known as Nizam Talab at Nizampet. It turned out to be well worth a visit. before returning to settle back on the waterbody. While scanning the flocks in flight, we witnessed a Black-headed Ibis which seemed to have got mixed up with the circling Shovelers. Since it could not fly in synchrony with the flocks, nor could it get out of their way, it was getting pushed about and had a hard time landing. Nizam Talab surrounded by a concrete jungle The route passed through some urban and semi-urban areas, then on to a mud road, and we finally reached the location. On this side, the waterbody was bordered by the mud road with upcoming concrete structures nearby; on all the other sides, the concrete nests for humans were already established. Black-headed Ibis amidst a flock of Northern Shovelers My personal opinion is that these birds have picked this waterbody is an alternative for the Pragatinagar lake which, at present, has very low water levels. The boulders are all exposed, and the surface is now covered with dry and decomposing layer of water hyacinth with very few birds inhabiting it. It remains to be seen how secure the birds feel at this new location and whether they would continue to use it or would return to Pragatinagar in case its condition improves later. 8. Northern Shoveler The water level in the waterbody was good and one small corner was occupied by water hyacinth. But the rest of the water surface was full of Northern Shovelers in the hundreds, and a few Lesser Whistling-ducks, Grey-headed Swamphens, Common Moorhens and Common Coots. Prasad told us that this was the first year that he has observed such numbers of ducks on this waterbody. Patancheru Lake, Patancheru, Medak Located next to the ICRISAT campus and the industrial area of Patancheru, the lake is in use by the fishermen community for fish rearing. Within a span of one week, I visited this lake twice, on January 26 & 31, 2020. On both the visits we recorded almost the same avifauna: Common Coots in the hundreds dominated the waterbody, although more open waters are still vacant. We could see only five Northern Pintails (during both the visits) on the lake but, at the other end of the waterbody, towards the ICRISAT fields on the outer edge of the waterline, approximately 60 Red-wattled Lapwings and Cattle Egrets were observed perching in the Ipomea bushes. We spent a little more time here, waiting for some action. Finally a Eurasian Marsh Harrier appeared, gliding over the water and swooping down to attack a Glossy Ibis. Ducks at Nizam Talab A sound of crackers blasting in the adjoining area suddenly disturbed the birds and several different flocks lifted into the air and were seen flying around the lake for about 20 minutes Eurasian Marsh Harrier and Glossy Ibis

The Ibis was lucky to escape from the Harrier’s grasp. I wondered if the Ibis did actually escape, or if it was because the Harrier was not that serious about that particular hunt, or whether it mistook the Ibis for some other prey and let go when it realized its error. Do Raptors make mistakes in identification? ICRISAT Main Lake Green Bee-eater Lake-1: The main ICRISAT Lake: The bamboo, Acacia nilotica, Lecaenea leucocephala, the Tamarind tree community on the walkway bund towards the water, and a few more trees on the islands in the water were occupied by Painted Storks and Grey Herons for nesting. Many Darters were perched on the trees and were seen preening. Duck populations were very low compared to earlier visits. It was very pleasant watching the Painted Storks. Even though I have worked for years on this species, something always draws my attention: their activity of collecting the nesting material from the Tamarind trees and gliding close to the water surface as they returned with the nesting material in their beaks; at nest, when the partner arrives, their behaviour of greeting each other with bill-clattering; their neck movements up and down and side by side (Alai Balai). Red-vented Bulbul After jotting down the birds in the bushes – Green Bee-eater, Red-vented Bulbul, Asian Koel, Rufous Treepie, Spotted & Eurasian Collared Dove, etc at this locality, we returned from the lake. On January 31, 2020, besides the repeats, an Indian Spotted Eagle and a Shikra were recorded. January 31, 2020 9. ICRISAT Ruddy Shelduck Other birds recorded here were Ruddy Shelducks, Spot-billed Ducks, Black-headed Ibises, Lesser Whistling-ducks, Grey Herons, Black-winged Stilts, Common Coots, Spot-billed Pelicans (only two) and Grey-headed Swamphens. With some help from Dr Chitra Shanker, we got an opportunity to bird at the ICRISAT campus and to record the status of waterbodies. Darter

Lake-2: Red Lake: This is the waterbody where we suspected that the Spot-billed Pelicans were nesting. The waterbody has many trees on the islands, which seemed suitable; there were sufficient signs in earlier months that a Pelicanry was in the process of being established here. But in the whole of the ICRISAT campus, only 13 Spot-billed Pelicans were recorded, of which two were seen on the ICRISAT Lake and the remaining here at Red Lake. Spot-billed Pelican Lake-3: Suri Sehgal Lake: Passing through the fields and among the Leucaena leucocephala trees on either side, we reached this lake with very shallow water level, and recorded a few Cattle Egrets on the bunds at the edges of the water. Other than this, there was very little other bird life on this lake. Northern Pintail This place also hosted some Northern Shovelers, Northern Pintails, Common Teals, Spot-billed Ducks and Blackcrowned Night Herons. Some Grey Herons and a few pairs of Painted Storks were recorded nesting on the trees on these islands. Suri Sehgal Lake surface covered by grass We observed that the whole waterbody was occupied by grass grown in the water, leaving no open water and we observed very few birds on the edges of the bunds, close to the shallow waters. One interesting observation at this location was some courtship behaviour between a pair of Black-shouldered Kites. Northern Pintail Black-shouldered Kite courtship behaviour Grey Herons at Red Lake Lake-4: Mary Cummins Lake or Campus Ponds: These are three small pools with clear, open and still water, providing accommodation to Common Coots, Spot-billed Ducks and 3 Cormorants perching on the nearby Ficus religiosa tree. Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Common Babbler (Argya caudata) Common Babbler (Kolleru, January 2, 2020) Order: Passeriformes Family: Leiothrichidae Genus: Argya Species: A. caudata Size: 23 cm from six to twenty individuals. Its preferred habitat is sparse and low thorny scrub in dry regions. It is a noisy bird, moving around on the ground with other members of the group keeping watch from bush tops. It forages amidst the undergrowth by hopping along, often with tail raised, or scuttling around like rodents on the ground. Its flight is weak – just a few rapid wingbeats followed by a short glide on outspread wings and tail. The diet consists mainly of flower nectar, berries, grains and insects. Its call is a trilling whichwhich-whichi-ri-ri-ri-ri, while the alarm call is a high-pitched squeak, with the whole group joining in. Description & distribution: The Common Babbler is a small babbler. Earlier placed in the genus Turdoides, it was moved to the genus Argya in 2018 after a comprehensive molecular phylogenetic study. It has warm buffish-brown or buffish-grey upperparts with profuse, marked streaking on its head, mantle and back, and unstreaked, paler buff underparts with some streaking on the sides of the breast. The eyes are dark and throat is pale – two features that separate it from the Striated Babbler – and the bill is slim and decurved. Another distinctive feature is its slim, long, graduated and finely cross-rayed olivebrown tail. Two subspecies are recognized, A. c. eclipes, seen from northern Pakistan to northwestern India, and the nominate A. caudata, seen in southern Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, and almost all across India (including the Lakshadweep Islands). It is not seen in Sri Lanka or Myanmar. The sexes are alike. Nesting: The Common Babbler breeds generally between March and July, though it may irregularly breed at other times of the year too. The nest is a compact cup of grass, rootlets and twigs, usually built in low thorny scrub less than 2m from ground. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 glossy turquoisecoloured eggs. Both parents share nesting duties. The nests are often parasitized by the Pied Crested (Jacobin’s) and the Hawk Cuckoos. Local name: The Common Babbler is known as ‘Chilchil’, ‘Sor’, ‘Genga’, ‘Chhota Genga’ or ‘Dumri’ in Hindi, ‘Chinna sida’ in Telugu, ‘Huni’ in Tamil, and ‘Chilappan’ in Malayalam. Habitat & behaviour: The Common Babbler, like most other babblers, is gregarious and usually seen in groups ranging *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034.
