Details of upcoming activities will be communicated once the situation improves. Report: Visit to Yapral Lake, Secunderabad, January 26, 2020 Text and Photos: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao Yapral Lake Yapral Lake, located in the northern parts of Secunderabad (17 30 51N 78 32 32E), is a small water body not more than 20 acres in size. The lake, however, has been able to draw large flocks of birds this season, thanks to the abundance of rains during the last monsoon. The lake is witnessing some developmental work of late, like the creation of a high bundcum-walkway to the east, a cemented drain all around, and a plantation of the Indian Date Palms to retain the bund itself. The lake retains the monsoon rainwater briefly for 4-5 months each year. In the past 10 years the lake has seen full water level only on three occasions including the current season. available holiday was January 26, 2020 (Republic Day) and what better way than to spend the morning hours in service of the Nation and Nature. So we decided on a 3-in-1 program – to carry out Bird Survey, the Asian Waterfowl Census and Swachch Bharat (clean up) of the lake and its surroundings. A message was sent around to the residents of the colonies adjoining the lake, to participate in the birdwatching, followed by cleaning of the lake. The response was positive and a lot of volunteers of all ages stepped up to participate in both the events. I live in Swarnandhra Colony, which is just a stone’s throw from this lake. A lot of over-flights by Herons, Egrets, Ducks and Ibises near my house forced me to investigate on the status of the lake. To my pleasant surprise I found the Yapral Lake filled with varieties of birds and bustling with activities – like fishing, diving, wading, preening and nest building – like never before. I decided to go there day after day and motivated a couple of more enthusiasts to join me. While the bird watching was enjoyable, the abuse of the lake and its surroundings by the locals with liquor bottles and plastic was distressing. We felt we had to do something to tidy up the place and Deccan Birders readily pitched in. The next Spot-billed Duck

Lesser Whistling-duck Grey Heron A Eurasian Marsh Harrier was also camping at the lake on the Neem tree on the western edge of the lake, where I had seen it regularly hunting its breakfast every morning. Northern Shoveler When the Deccan Birders members along with other volunteers reached the bund, they were happy to see the lake brimming with water and a large number of waterfowl. Spotbilled ducks, Lesser Whistling-ducks, Northern Shovelers, Common Coots, Glossy Ibises, Grey Herons, Black-crowned Night Herons, Common Sandpipers and various Cormorants were seen in large numbers. Eurasian Marsh Harrier The northern part of the lake has a large number of Black Acacia Trees submerged in the water and thus presents an ideal haven for the birds for nesting. This area is relatively devoid of human movement and this increases the bird numbers. This area has been chosen by the Glossy Ibis, Grey Heron, Black-crowned Night Heron, Lesser Whistling-duck, Spot-billed Duck, Common Coot and Little Grebe for nesting and breeding. Glossy Ibis Little Grebe with chick Black-crowned Night Heron

Apart from this, it is heartening to see hundreds of Egrets, Ibises and Cormorants return to roost here every night. The calls of the Indian Nightjar and the Indian Thick-knee were heard from the lake side at night. About a dozen Garganey were observed in the lake from 25 Mar onwards post the AWC count and were seen well into April. heartening to see one and all pitch their bit to get the lake in order. Change of gear happened in an instant. Cameras gave way to gloves and garbage bags. Children from Swarnandhra and Prakrutik Vihar colonies were leading the way and were quite a motivation for others to follow. By the end of the cleanup activity, we managed to fill up a GHMC truck which was requested by our Colony Administration in advance. After a quick wash up at the Katta Mysamma temple, sweets were distributed to all the participants. Blyth’s Reed Warbler The visit of the Blyth’s Reed Warbler to the lake and the surroundings is an annual feature that happens with unfailing regularity. I have recorded, for the past 5-6 years, its arrival in the first week of November and departure by the last week of March of the following year. This year the departure is probably delayed owing to pleasant weather in the area and late arrival of the summer – as of April 11, 2020, the birds were still seen foraging around. Clean-up activity in full swing Coming back to our event, after the birdwatching wound down, we started the lake clean-up activity, and it was Indian Golden Oriole The team The range of flora and fauna in and around the lake is to be appreciated, considering the rate at which other water bodies and the environment are being abused by human intervention in and around the city. This lake too like all other water bodies in any urban environment is facing encroachment from all directions and shrinking in size. The problem is accentuated by release of untreated sewage by the surrounding colonies, thus polluting the lake waters. The bund of the lake offers a safe and convenient place for impromptu parties. Empty bottles and snack wrappers can be found on any given day over here. Kite flying, though an annual affair, adds its share of casualties around the lake. The arrival of the migratory birds to Yapral Lake every winter and the significance of protecting this water body was brought to the knowledge of our local MLA Sri M Hanumantha Rao during one of the post-flood meetings at our Swarnandhra Colony. We are hopeful that this lake continues to flourish and support local and migratory birds in times to come. Some other photos taken at Yapral Lake: Thick-billed Flowerpecker

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Asian Openbill (Anastomus oscitans) Asian Openbill (Kolleru, January 2, 2020) Order: Ciconiiformes Family: Ciconiidae Genus: Anastomus Species: A. oscitans Size: 68-76 cm in Bangladesh, as far as 1500km away from Thailand, where they were ringed. They are broad-winged soaring birds and small groups can often be seen soaring on thermals and dropping rapidly into their feeding grounds. Groups often forage together in the preferred foraging spots like shallow water, marshy ground or flooded fields. Besides water snakes, frogs and large insects, its diet mainly consists of large molluscs, especially freshwater snails (Pila species) – it inserts the tip of its beak into the shell of the snail, and extracts the body with the bill still under water. In fact, Jerdon had noted that it was able to capture snails even while blindfolded. The theory that the bill gap is used as a nutcracker was originally proposed by Sir Julian Huxley, but has since been disproved. Also, while the brush-like edges of the mandibles supposedly give it a better hold on slippery shells, the fact that young birds without the gap are still able to forage on snails, is not explained. Some current schools of thought hold that the gap may give the bird the ability to strike at a better angle and apply more force on the snail shells. Smaller snails, however, are often crushed or swallowed whole. It is a noisy bird, especially while flying in flocks, with a constant hubbub being clearly audible. Its call is a mournful hoo hoo. Description & distribution: The Asian Openbill is a large stork and is found mainly in the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. The head, upperparts, neck and underparts are predominantly white (in breeding season) or smoky greyish (in non-breeding season), while the wings and tail are glossy black with a greenish or purple sheen. It has a strong horn-grey or reddish-black beak, with an arched upper mandible and a recurved lower mandible; this gap between the mandibles is what gives the bird its name. The cutting edges of the mandibles have a fine brush-like structure that is believed to give them a good grip on the outer shells of snails, although young birds, which do not yet have this gap, are also able to feed on snails. As a result, there are some authorities that question this belief regarding the exact function of the gap between the mandibles. The legs are short and pinkish or greyish, but can turn reddish prior to breeding. Young birds are usually more brownish-grey. Nesting: The Asian Openbill breeds after the rains, and therefore, generally between July and September in Northern India and Nepal, and between November and March in Southern India and Sri Lanka. In drought years it may skip breeding entirely. It is a colonial breeder, building a rough platform of sticks and twigs on half-submerged trees (e.g. Barringtonia, Acacia or Avicennia). These trees are usually shared with several other species like Painted Storks, Egrets, Cormorants, Darters, Herons, etc. Since the nests are crowded together on these trees, there are often quite aggressive and vocal interactions between neighbouring birds. Like most The Asian Openbill is found in most parts of Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, Thailand, Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia. Habitat & behaviour: The Asian Openbill is seen occasionally singly, but usually in small to large flocks, in inland wetlands, agricultural fields, lakes, irrigation canals and seasonal marshes, and is not usually seen on river banks, tidal flats or coastal areas. Flocks can move widely depending on habitat conditions – for instance, some ringed birds have been spotted 7

Storks, the birds are usually silent, except for the clacking of bills between pairs during mating, and the low honking sounds accompanied by up-and-down movements of the bill when greeting a partner arriving at the nest. The usual clutch consists of 2-4 white eggs. Both parents share incubation duties, and once the chicks emerge, they are often shaded by loosely spread wings of the parent. Local name: The Asian Openbill is known as ‘Ghungil’, ‘Gungla’ or ‘Ghonghila’ in Hindi, ‘Galu konga’ in Telugu, ‘Naththai kuththi narai’ in Tamil, and ‘Cherakokkan’ in Malayalam. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From The Times of India, September 20, 2017) *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 17 Number 4 April 2020 (Special Issue) Editor’s note Some of our members had been to Australia for a ten-day-long birding trip from November 16th to 24th, 2019. In this Special Issue of the Pitta, we are happy to bring you an account of the trip, along with a number of colourful photographs. We hope you will find this Special Issue interesting. AUSTRALIA – THE OTHER CONTINENT Dr Barnali Chaudhuri Sydney Opera House (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Travel is the only thing you can buy that makes you richer! It is this that drives me to travel as often as I can, and so, when the opportunity unfolded to visit Australia, I was very excited. Australia is the smallest of the six continents and the entire continent is one country. As a result, a very strange array of endemic flora and fauna have developed over millions of years. I was full of anticipation at what we would see on the trip. Of the 22 Deccan Birders who had signed up for the trip, 17 of us reached Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad, by 8:30PM on November 14, 2019. The rest were to join us directly at Australia. Our flight took off at 12:15AM the next day and, after a brief stop-over at Kuala Lumpur, we reached Sydney just after 9:00PM. By the time we reached Travelodge, Sydney by shuttle, it was around 12:30AM on November 16. November 16, 2019: Blue Mountains: Jenolan Caves, Three Sisters The plan for the first two days, in Sydney, was for members of the group to independently go around for sight-seeing and cover any locations that they were keen to see. Accordingly, Jayati and I decided to do some exploring, and started off to the Blue Mountains. As we left our hotel, we were welcomed by several Noisy Miners. 1 Noisy Miner (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri)

The Blue Mountains lie to the west of Sydney in New South Wales, with a lot of steep cliffs, eucalyptus forests and caves. The forests of eucalyptus, popularly known as gum trees, discharge eucalyptus oil from their leaves which combines with air and dust particles to form a mist. The mist refracts, mainly, blue light – this makes the whole area look blue from a distance, and hence the name. We walked to Mascot Station and took a train to Katoomba town, at the edge of Blue Mountains. I enjoyed the train ride and the scenic views thoroughly: the quiet, serene and rustic village life, a stark contrast to the cacophony of the high-rise buildings of Sydney. We reached Katoomba in three hours. While waiting for the bus to Jenolan Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage site near Katoomba station, we saw the beautiful Sulphur-crested Cockatoos calling with their shrill voices. Jenolan Caves are 340 million years old - the world's oldest known open caves as declared by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (CSIRO). Amongst over 300 caves that exist, only 8 caves – Lucas, Imperial, Chifley, Orient, River, Ribbon, Diamond and Jubilee – are open to the public. We opted to see Lucas Cave, one of the most popular caves. We had about one and half hours before the guided tour began, and decided to make use of the time to get in some birding. Sulphur-crested Cockatoo (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) First, we went towards the cave house. A male Superb Fairywren was dancing near the mountain lodge. After a while, three more joined, along with one female. Butterflies were also enjoying nectar from flowers. Somebody pointed out a Superb Lyrebird that was walking around nearby. Superb Lyrebird (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Pied Currawong (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Superb Fairywren (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Then the time came to explore the other side of the Grand Arch of Jenolan Caves. We started walking towards the dam wall on the River Walk, which was constructed in 1908 to create the Jenolan Lake, known locally as Blue Lake. The blue colour of the lake is an illusion caused by the reflection of light through the dissolved particles of limestone. The Blue Lake is famous for its unusual colour and for a resident Platypus. Tree-fern (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Grand Arch of Jenolan Caves (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 2

The reflection of Soft Tree-ferns on the blue water, creating a perfect inverted photographic image, was beautiful. The pine fruit looked like green-coloured eggs. Eastern Water Dragon (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Pine Fruit (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) We were not fortunate enough to see the Platypus, but I was excited at seeing an Eastern Water Dragon for the first time. New Holland and Crescent Honeyeaters were busy drinking honey from flowers. River She-oak (Casuarina cunninghamiana) and River Gum trees (Eucalyptus bicostata) were seen covering the circumference of the lake. New Holland Honeyeater (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Crescent Honeyeater (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) There were also a number of interesting trees and plants there, as well as butterflies and moths. Broad-leaved Drumstick (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Mountain Devil (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 3 Soft Tree-fern (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri)

Bunya Pine (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Japanese Dogwood (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Spidery Tea Tree (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Yellow Admiral (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Anthelidae sp Moth (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Unfortunately, due to our time constraint, we had to leave this beautiful spot and return to join the Lucas Cave tour. The guided tour started with a group of about 40 people. The guide articulated the features of this striking limestone formation of stalagmite which is an upwardgrowing mound of mineral deposits that have precipitated from water dripping onto the floor of a cave. A stalactite hangs like an icicle from the ceiling or sides of a cavern. The deposits consist of calcite (calcium carbonate). As we went through the stairs, a spacious cavern led us to the heart of the mountain. I got the opportunity to see several limestone caves. Surprisingly each one was uniquely gorgeous. Lucas Cave (Photos: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Our guide narrated the story of the sages who used these caves once upon a time. I marveled at the grandeur of a particular stalactite, which looked like a huge curtain. Stalagmites rising from the bottom and stalactites coming in from the top met with each other to form pillars. We entered the Cathedral inside the cave, an arching chamber often used for concerts, where our guide played recorded music just to give us a flavour of the experience. Lastly there was a light show, when the cave glowed in different hues, as if in a dream. On our way to Katoomba, we were excited to see a Kangaroo, with its Joey (young one) peeping out from its sack. Later, though, when we learnt the difference between Kangaroos and Wallabies, I realized that it was not a Kangaroo but a Wallaby! 4 Red-necked Wallaby (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri)

The bus driver dropped us off at Echo Point, Katoomba. We enjoyed the view of the Three Sisters from the clifftop viewing platform. The Three Sisters were formed by land erosion – the sandstone from the Blue Mountains was eroded over time by wind, rain and rivers, causing the cliffs surrounding Jamison Valley to be slowly broken up. Echo Point, Three Sisters, Blue Mountains (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) But there is an interesting Aboriginal story about three sisters named Meehni, Wimlah and Gunnedoo, who lived in Jamison Valley as members of the Katoomba tribe. They fell in love with three men from their neighboring Nepean tribe, but marriage was forbidden by tribal law. The brothers were not willing to accept this and decided to abduct the three sisters, thus causing a major tribal battle. The sisters were turned into stones by an elder to protect them, but as he himself was then killed in the fighting, there was no one to turn them back to life. I found the story very interesting. After enjoying exploring the Three Sisters, along with the surroundings, thoroughly, we came back to Katoomba by city bus, then boarded a train to Mascot and reached Travelodge by 10:30PM. Pacific Black Duck (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) November 17, 2019: Sydney Bridge, Sydney Opera & Royal Botanic Garden of Sydney Jayati and I boarded the train from Mascot and got down at Quay station. NSW Ministry for the Arts has engraved famous quotations of many legendary writers like James A Michener, Germaine Greer etc. on Writers Walk – a unique way to pay homage. Writer’s Walk (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) As we walked down Writers’ Walk, we saw many Silver Gulls also walking around freely, and several small ships were sailing near the Sydney Bridge. Just beside the Bridge, Sydney Opera House stood tall. I had earlier seen these in pictures only, and I was amazed to see both in front of me side by side. Silver Gull (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 5

We first went to explore the huge 74-acre Royal Botanic Garden of Sydney, near the Opera House. We saw many interesting and beautiful trees and plants there: Wollemia Pine (Wollemia nobilis), one of the world’s rarest plants; Narrow-leaved (aka Queensland) Bottle Tree, so unique, and aptly named for its shape; Golden Wattle (Acasia pycnantha), the national flower of Australia; Purple Flag flower (Patersonia occidentalist); Spiral Ginger (Costus barbatus) with red inflorescence and bright yellow tubular flowers, native to Costa Rica; Kangaroo Paw (Anigozanthos manglesii) flowers; a yellow flower cluster on an Aeonium arboreum succulent; Water Lily (Nymphaeaceae sp); Peace Lily (Spathiphyllum wallisii); Bromeliad, a tropical rain forest flower; Kaffir Lily (Clivia miniata); and Green Shell Ginger (Alpinia zerumbet) flowers. We then moved on to the Sydney Opera House, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a masterpiece of 20 th century architecture. The roofs of the Sydney Opera House, consisting of a series of large precast concrete ‘shells’ each composed of sections of a sphere, are set on a podium of monumental size. Jørn Utzon, the Danish architect, designed the Opera House in 1957. It won an international design competition and was opened in October 1973. The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre. Utzon designed it with inspiration from bird wings as well as the shape and form of clouds and shells. Sydney Opera House Shell (L) and Key (R) (Photos: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Inside Sydney Opera House Concert Hall (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) We took a guided tour inside the Opera House. We were lucky enough to see a concert rehearsal, which was to be presented that afternoon. I marvelled at and saluted the technology used to create the Sydney Opera House. No microphone was required. The design of the shells absorbed the sound without forming any echo. Glass rings were hanging from the roof-top of the concert hall to make sure that the feedback sound reaches to the artist only. The grand organ inside the Concert Hall was amazing. It is the largest mechanical tracker action organ in the world with over 10,000 pipes. The technology used to construct the Sydney Opera House is simply mindblowing. The Sydney Harbour Bridge is a heritage-listed steel arch bridge that carries rail, vehicle, bicycle and pedestrian traffic. The view of the Bridge, the Harbour, and the nearby Sydney Opera House is widely regarded as an iconic image of Australia. The Bridge is nicknamed ‘Coathanger’ after its arch design. It connects Sydney Central Business District and North Shore. The flag of Australia was flying high over the Bridge. We then wound up for the day, returned to Travelodge and got ready for our flight to Melbourne, scheduled for 6:00PM. We landed at Melbourne just after 8:00PM and arrived at Hotel Urban Central around 9:45PM, all charged up for the next day, when our ‘real’ birding tour was to begin. Sydney Harbour Bridge (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) November 18, 2019: Western Treatment Plant (WTP) Our expedition began with the Western Treatment Plant (WTP) located in Werribee. WTP is one of the most popular and internationally recognized wildlife and bird habitats for bird watching in Victoria. After breakfast at Hotel Urban Central, we piled into two vehicles, led by Martin and Janine (our tour guides). They had already arranged our permit and access key for bird watching in WTP. We started our journey around 8:00AM and soon, the tall buildings of Melbourne were replaced by meadows and ponds, with some mountains in the distance. Eucalyptus forest (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 9

We stopped at one point on the roadside for birding – a Nankeen Kestrel was planning its next move sitting on a wire; White-faced Cows were grazing in a nearby field; some ducks swam around in the pond; Pied Stilts were in a hunting mood, and a Nankeen Night Heron was resting on a tree trunk. White-faced Cow, Grey Teal (extreme left), Pacific Black Duck, Chestnut Teal (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Pied Stilt (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Nankeen Night Heron (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Soon, we reached our destination. I listened in amazement as Janine explained how WTP works. She told us that WTP treats half of Melbourne’s sewage using a series of large ponds, called lagoons. Sewage flows slowly through anaerobic and aerobic lagoons, gradually becoming cleaner as bacteria breaks down the organic material in the water. The leftover solids are dried and stored in large piles and reused as biosolids. The whole process uses very little energy and produces Class C water in 30 to 35 days. WTP can also produces Class A water, the highest standard of recycled water. The production of biogas (or sewage gas) enables the WTP to be energy Lake Borrie, part of WTP (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) self-sufficient. There are times when the water is too clean, hence depriving its flora and fauna of the essential nutrients required for thriving. So WTP always monitors the nutrient levels of ponds so that these birds can stay healthy. WTP is internationally important (as per Ramsar convention) for the conservation of the remaining wetlands through proper use and management. After the lesson was over around 12:30PM, we finished our lunch and got ready to start birding. We started walking towards Lake Borrie through a bird hide. En route to the bird hide (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) The hide (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Inside the hide (Photo courtesy: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) This was the first time I had ever seen a bird hide; I thought it was an excellent idea – birds would not be disturbed by human presence. A page in the world of WTP was unfolding in front of our eyes. We saw Great Egrets, Purple Swamphen, Great Crested Grebe, a flock of Straw-necked Ibises in flight, Australian Pied Oystercatchers, a flock of Grey Teals swimming, Welcome Swallows sitting around, Australian Pelicans, Yellow-billed Spoonbills, Royal Spoonbills, Whiskered Terns, etc – and a Black-fronted Dotterel! The most spectacular sight was one of innumerable Black Swans with their vibrant red beaks. WTP is really a birding paradise! 10

Janine showed us the Short-beaked Echidna, earlier called the Spiny Anteater, foraging for ants and termites. It has sharp spines like the Porcupine, a beak like a bird, a pouch like a Kangaroo and it lays eggs like a reptile. Echidnas and the Platypus are the only living egg-laying mammals. Janine explained that the female lays a single softshelled egg directly into her pouch. The young Echidna, called a Puggle, takes milk from its mother. In around 45-55 days, when the baby starts developing spines, the mother ejects the baby out of its pouch into the burrow. She comes back every five days to nurse the baby, which is weaned at around seven months. I was surprised to see Noisy Miners attacking the Echidna. We reached the traditional land of the Krowathunkoolong clan of the mother tribe Gunai (Kurni). An interesting Aboriginal mythology about the origin of water was depicted on a nearby board. The story went like this: One day, a frog named Tiddalik, who woke up with an unquenchable thirst, drank up all the fresh water, and the animals and plants began to die due to lack of water. A wise old Owl told the animals that water could be released if the frog could be made to laugh. An eel managed to make the frog laugh by tying himself up into comical shapes. Many animals drowned in the resulting flood, but the Aborigines were saved by the Pelican (who was an Aborigine once) who made a giant canoe. All these myths show the intricate and strong link with Aboriginal people and animals. Snowy River, near Orbost (Photos: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) The Snowy River Valley has sustained Aboriginal people and provided food, transport and social order for at least 40,000 years. Tree bark was used to make canoes, shields and shelter. These trees are called Scar Trees; we were happy to see one of them. In autumn, the trunk of the Black Wattle was deliberately notched. The resulting balls of gum were eaten or dissolved in water with flower nectar to make a sweet drink. The gum was also mixed with ashes of wood or mussel shells to form cement that sealed bark buckets to carry water. Hard wooden spears, clubs and digging sticks were made from the long straight stems of the Tea Tree (Melaleuca Species). The soft papery barks of larger trees were used to wrap babies. Kangaroo grass and other barks were used to make fishing nets. Tea Tree bark was used for floating and stones were used for sinking the fishing nets. The river was fished. Forest animals such as Possum, Kangaroo, Wallaby and Emu were hunted to complement their diet; the skins were also used by the people to wrap themselves in winter. Aboriginal people used everything from nature to lead a self-sufficient and peaceful life. After a very interesting day, we returned and reached Orbost just before 7:00PM. We had dinner at the Orbost Club Inc and returned to our Inn. Great and Little Pied Cormorants were sunbathing on the rocks. Pacific Gulls were happily swimming in the ocean. Australian Pied Oystercatchers were racing with each other. A large Brown Kelp (seaweed) was found on the sea shore. I was astonished to know that kelp is full of good nutrients and a natural source of vitamins, minerals and antioxidants. There was some seaweed known as Neptune’s Necklace (Homosira banksil) lying on the beach as well. 27

Australian Pied Oystercatcher (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Neptune’s Necklace (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Nature is truly amazing. I was immersed in the rough and rocky landscape of the beach with the serene blue color of the sea. While there, we took some group photographs at Salmon Rocks Beach. We came across the White-browed Woodswallow, Echidna and a Bull Ant with its prey. Common Fringe Lilies (Thysanotus tuberosus) and some Ferns were spectacular. Bull Ant with prey (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Common Fringe Lily (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Giant Fern (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) At the Grass Tree field (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Martin stopped our car to show us Grass Tree (Xanthorrhoea) flowers on a spear-like spike around 3 to 4m long. We tasted the nectar of the Grass Tree flowers. The flowers were arranged in a spiral up the spike, producing nectar and attracting various birds, insects and mammals. Martin informed us that a bush fire stimulates the flowering of the Grass Tree. The fire burns the leaves and blackens the trunk, but the tree survives as the dead leaves around the stem serve as insulation against the heat of the wildfire. 28

After a good lunch at the General Store, we went to see Cabbage Tree Creek. Cabbage Tree Palms (Livistona australis) have straight trunks with shining crowns reaching beyond the canopy and towering overhead. We saw Brown Gerygone, Black-faced Monarch, Grey and Rufous Fantails. Brown Gerygone (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Black-faced Monarch (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Rufous Fantail (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) We heard some whipping noises in the middle of the forest which, as Martin educated us, was the call of a male Eastern Whipbird. Martin dropped us around 3:45PM for some shopping near the Orbost Clock Tower, a short walking distance from our Inn. So after shopping, we returned to our rooms and freshened up for the evening tour to see some nocturnal animals. After an early dinner at Marlo Hotel, we piled into two cars and headed towards a forest area. The sun was just setting. We walked along the forest trail while looking for the Common Wombat and the Common Brushtail Possum. A Red-necked Wallaby popped up its head as we passed. Its eyes were glowing in the red light thrown by Martin. Next to it, Martin pointed out a Common Brushtail Possum on a gum tree trunk, eating its leaves. Its black and brush-like tail was hanging from the tree, justifying its name. Common Brushtail Possum (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) The Common Brushtail Possum is a tree-climbing nocturnal marsupial (a mammal that has a pouch). The baby Possum, like its cousins, the Kangaroo and the Wallaby, is called Joey. Unfortunately, we did not spot a Wombat, though we saw its burrow. Common Wombat burrow (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Long-legged Fly (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 29

November 23, 2019: Marsdenia Rainforest Walk, Krowathunkooloong Keeping Place, Mitchel River The majority of Australia’s trees are hardwoods, with a predominance of eucalyptus trees. There are more than 700 species of eucalyptus and most of them are native to Australia. They are commonly known as Gum Trees because they exude copious kino (gum) from any break in the bark. As we walked through the Marsdenia Rainforest Walk, I was astonished to see the gigantic Gum Trees kissing the sky. Marsdenia Rainforest Walk (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Gum Tree (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) I found it extremely difficult to spot the Striated Thornbill (Acanthiza lineata), endemic to Australia, because of its very small size. But at last, I succeeded, not only in spotting it, but also in capturing it in my camera. Striated Thornbill (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Crested Pigeon (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Long-billed Corella feeding (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Common Starling (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 30

Crested Pigeons and Long-billed Corellas were sitting on tree trunks while the Common Starlings, Black-headed Ibis, Australian Magpie and Magpie-larks were in the field. Australian Magpie (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Magpie-lark (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) It was easy to differentiate between Australian Magpie and Magpie-lark – the Magpie-lark is a little smaller than the Magpie and has a slender bill that is all white, whereas the Magpie’s bill is pale with black tips, heavier and triangular. The colours of the upperparts and underparts are also interchanged. Gippsland Lakes (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) After visiting the mouth of Gippsland lakes, we went to Krowathunkooloong Keeping Place. It is a heritage museum dedicated to preserving and showcasing Aboriginal culture. It is located in Bairnsdale near St. Mary’s Catholic Church. It is named after Krowathunkooloong tribe that occupied the Orbost and Snowy River area. Little Pied Cormorant (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) We entered East Gippsland Art Gallery inside Krowathunkooloong. The place was filled with beautiful Aboriginal art canvases. We went inside the museum with our guide. He explained that the Gunaikurnai people are the traditional owners of Gippsland, having five major clans: Brabralung, Brataualung, Brayakaulung, Krowathunkooloong, and Tatungalung. We learnt a little about their history, heritage and culture. Red and yellow were colors used in festivals while white was used as a sign of peace and respect to the old and deceased. Gum Tree bark was used to make canoes, shields and shelter. The shapes of hand palms were scarred on tree stems as a symbol of respect to the elderly. These trees are called Scar Trees. Some trees are carved or decorated also. The scars exposed the sapwood of the trunk or branch. There is no written script in the Aboriginal language, but they use symbols. Aboriginal people are not supposed to speak in their language outside their premises. Our guide showed us a Possum skin blanket where the other side was totally stitched with symbols. How one wore the blanket could mean different things depending on the direction of symbols. Martin told us an interesting story of the creators of Gunaikurnai. Borun the Pelican, the first Gunaikurnai, came down from the mountains in Victoria’s northwest, alone and carrying a bark canoe on his head. He crossed the river and continued his journey. During his journey he heard a constant tapping sound but could not figure out its source. Finally, he reached the deep water of the inlet and put his canoe down. To his surprise, he saw a woman sitting in it. She was Tuk, the Musk Duck. They got married and became the parents of the five clans, the creators of Gunaikurnai. Very interesting! 31

We saw some Boomerangs, which are wooden Aboriginal throwing devices. The name is said to have its origin in the word ‘wo-murrang’, which was a spear-throwing device. It served as an extension of the human arm, enabling a spear to travel at a greater speed and force than is possible with only the arm. The guide explained about the Boomerangs. They were used to hunt in many different ways. Some Boomerangs used by Aboriginal hunters could get close to birds high in the sky where it might circle multiple times before it hit the target. A returning Boomerang is designed to return to the thrower. However, if it hits something, it will affect its flight path and the boomerang will not come back to the thrower. It is a weapon used by indigenous Australians for hunting. Mitchel River (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Grey-headed Flying Fox (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) After seeing the museum, we passed through the beautiful Mitchel River side road. White clouds looked like a splash of water in the blue sky. We saw a colony of Grey-headed Flying Foxes hanging from a tree. Around 6:15PM, we returned to Hotel Urban Central. Our journey with Martin and Janine ended here. I thanked both of them for their wonderful presentation, efforts and patience. After freshening up, Geetanjali, Jayati and I walked up to Flinders St and Elizabeth Station and saw St Paul’s Cathedral. Our target was to explore Docklands and to visit the Giant Wheel by tram. We reached Docklands where all the high-rise buildings were lit, making the night scene very beautiful. The dock was shining with garlands of light. The reflections of light in the water were amazing. Bolte Bridge view from the Docklands (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Melbourne Docklands (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Bolte Bridge from the Melbourne Docklands looked beautiful. The Melbourne Star Observation Giant Wheel was illuminated with lights of different colours. Sandridge Bridge over Yarra River with symbolic art works and metal sculptures caught our eye. Roads and buildings were decorated to welcome Christmas in advance. It was all so beautiful. 32

Sandridge Bridge on Yarra River (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Buildings decorated for Christmas (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) We came back by the free tram near Southbank. The Crown was full of life. Everybody seemed to be enjoying themselves outside the Crown. Unexpectedly, we saw a fire show at the Crown which was amazing and took us by surprise. Both the towers of the Crown were spouting fire high into the sky making an otherwise cold night atmosphere hotter. Then we started moving back and got to Urban Central around 11:30PM. November 24, 2019: Royal Botanic Garden, Melbourne On our last day, we had only three hours to go around, as we were scheduled to leave Australia in the afternoon. Jayati and I decided to use those three hours by checking out the Royal Botanic Garden, Melbourne. We took a short cut and saw a little tower that resembles the Eiffel Tower. We reached Alexandra Gardens, and Queen Victoria Gardens was on the opposite side of the road where we saw the statue of Queen Victoria. The Myer Music Bowl (MMW) was all set for music. We visited the King’s Domain where the King’s Pillar stood tall. The Seeds of Friendship – the statue of Australian Turkish Friendship Memorial – was noteworthy. Angel sculpture beside Yarra River, made with hand-painted ceramic tiles (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Garden House (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Gallipoli Memorial Garden is made to commemorate the service and sacrifice of the Australian and New Zealand Army in the Gallipoli campaign. Lone Pine was the name given to a solitary tree on the Gallipoli Peninsula in Turkey, which marked the site of the Battle of Lone Pine in 1915 during World War One. It was the sole survivor of a group of trees that had been cut down by Turkish soldiers who had used the timber and branches to cover their trenches. Lone Pine seeds have been planted throughout Australia and have come to symbolize the courage and sacrifice of Australians in the Gallipoli Campaign. Australian Wood Duck family (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) 33

Tea Tree (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Restio (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Finally, we reached the Royal Botanic Garden. The lakes, lawns and garden beds there are home to thousands of different plants from around the world and provide a convenient habitat for local birds and animals. We went through the Oak Collection section, and saw many different types of oak from all around the world. Different flowers bloomed with their varied colours in the Gardens House section. By now, we didn’t have much time left and so we returned to the hotel to check out. We took a shuttle to Melbourne Airport for our flight back to India, scheduled at 03:10PM. We reached Hyderabad airport around midnight on November 25, 2019, via Malaysia Airlines through Kuala Lumpur. I learnt a lot throughout our Australian tour and enjoyed each and every moment. I must thank the Australian people for all their help during our travel, especially the day we explored the Blue Mountains. I was very sorry to hear from Janine about the bush fire that engulfed Buchan where we sat at the little stream and enjoyed birding on November 21, 2019. I would like to thank Janine and Martin for showing us and explaining everything to us so patiently. A special thanks to Shafaat Sir and Vikram for arranging the tour so smoothly, and to all the team members for making the trip such a memorable one! The group at Australia (Photo courtesy: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) *** 34

FARMERS OF THE FOREST Report: Visit to Coorg, February 2020 Jayasurya Pathapati Organic paddy fields at the resort (Photo: Jayasurya Pathapati) It was just past mid-February when my better half and I went on a trip to Coorg. We had heard great reviews of a resort, Evolve Back Coorg (Orange County), built amidst a 300-acre coffee and spice plantation, and had decided to spend a few nights there. The resort was known for its location, right by the river Kaveri, and the luxury, but what really floored me were the measures they have taken to conserve biodiversity in and around the resort. You would be aware that coffee plants are ideally grown amidst tall trees because they need good shade to grow properly. Of course, they do grow without the shade but the quality is usually sub-optimal. So, to maintain good quality, a lot of estates grow the coffee plants amidst tall trees, and most of these trees are cash crops such as Silverwood, Rosewood etc. The problem is, vast acres of forests with indigenous varieties of trees are cleared to grow coffee plants along with the cash-generating trees – which is obviously bad for the fauna, especially birds, too. A 100-year-old Mango tree (Photo: Jayasurya Pathapati)

However, some conscientious coffee estate owners have started working towards conserving the biodiversity by not cutting down these indigenous tree varieties, at least in a large part of their estates, if not the whole. Evolve Back Coorg is certainly one of those estates where a good part of the estate still has these 50 to 100-years-old trees of different varieties – the estate was started in 1908! – and the result? They are home to about 300 varieties of avifauna, different wild cats, otters, insects etc, and are also one of the pioneers of responsible tourism in India. other material for protection from predators, while leaving a small slit open – just enough for the male Hornbill to pass in some yummy fruits and wild berries! The male Hornbill collects hundreds of small berries and fruits to feed its mate and the hatchlings and, while doing so, covers a huge area of the forest, dispersing the seeds of the berries all across. This very behaviour has earned it the name, Farmer of the Forest! Our birdwatching guide was a local, trained by experienced naturalists, who got into this profession with a passion for wildlife, especially the insects. Since birdwatching is still relatively new for me, marking exactly a year spent in birdwatching around Hyderabad, we took his help to spot and identify a few birds endemic to the Malabar region. Walk through the coffee & spice plantations (Photo: Jayasurya Pathapati) Malabar Parakeet (File photo courtesy: Umesh Mani) Just five minutes into the walk, we spotted my first lifer of the day, the Malabar Parakeet. It was nicely perching on a palm tree with its back towards us. This beautiful bird had long blue feathers on its tail and wings. Pepper being sun-dried (Photo: Jayasurya Pathapati) During our three nights of stay there, we enjoyed different activities such as nature walk, plantation walk, and of course birdwatching! Just before the start of our birdwatching session early in the morning, we were shown a video on the Malabar Grey Hornbills and their feeding and nesting activities. This fascinating bird is an indicator of rich biodiversity and also plays a crucial role in sustaining the forest. Upon successful mating, the female Hornbill nests in burrows of tall trees to lay its eggs, and seals the opening of the burrow with mud and Plum-headed Parakeet (File photo courtesy: Srikanth Bhamidipati)

Rose-ringed Parakeet Male (File photo courtesy: Umesh Mani) Rose-ringed Parakeet Female (File photo courtesy: Umesh Mani) Moving on, in about 45 minutes of birding, we had spotted a number of Rose-ringed & Plum-headed Parakeets, Golden Orioles, Barn Swallows, White-Rumped Munias, Egrets of all sizes, Malabar Whistling Thrush (call heard), Chestnut-headed Bee-eaters, White-cheeked Barbet etc – all of which had made this beautiful coffee plantation their home. Chestnut-headed Bee-eater (File photo courtesy: Srikanth Bhamidipati) White-cheeked Barbet (File photo courtesy: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Just as the clock struck 8:00AM, our guide rushed us to a particular tree, which was apparently the nesting spot of a pair of Malabar Grey Hornbills! We waited there for about 10 minutes and suddenly heard a ruffle in a nearby tree. We spotted a Hornbill flying in in a rush, in its typical flap and dive style, and behind it was a Shikra chasing it away from our sight! The guide made us wait for a few more minutes, after which the Hornbill, which seemed to have tactfully escaped from the Shikra, slowly approached its nest and started regurgitating out berries from its throat. It dropped the berries into the nest with its beak through the slit. We noticed that it was all being done in a rush, so as to not risk being pursued by the Shikra again. Even the female, which typically thrusts out its beak to receive the food, did not peek out. We also noticed a berry slip out of the Hornbill’s beak, and our guide with a surprised look, told us that whenever a berry slipped out of its beak, the Hornbill would generally swoop down to catch the berry midair; however, today it seemed to be in a hurry! It was definitely a great encounter and worth every bit of the longing we had felt to sight it, ever since we heard of these fascinating birds! Barn Swallow (File photo courtesy: Srikanth Bhamidipati)

some birds. I would love to wake up to beautiful bird calls, not just in such trips, but every day of my life from right where I live. Malabar Grey Hornbill (File photo courtesy: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Malabar Giant Squirrel (Photo: Jayasurya Pathapati) Also, being a great coffee lover, I have started sourcing my coffee from estates that take biodiversity conservation seriously, and are duly certified for it. Solid Waste segregation (Photo: Jayasurya Pathapati) In this trip, apart from seeing a good variety of birds and plants, I witnessed how amazing the results of well-planned biodiversity conservation and responsible tourism could be. Right from waste management to controlling noise pollution (no loud music/DJ parties), the resort stood as a shining example for activities directed towards inclusivity of nonhuman beings. They have also started an interesting activity called ‘Shinrin Yoku’ – a Japanese activity popularly known world-wide as “Forest bathing”. During this trip, I have also developed an interest in trees, especially those that attract varieties of birds. I aspire to plant such trees around my neighbourhood, which in turn will attract Kaveri River (Photo: Jayasurya Pathapati) ***

FIGHTER MOM: The Sparrow Story Text and Photos: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao House Sparrow female with young ones The House Sparrow population in my colony is gradually showing an improving trend, thanks to some of the residents putting up wooden nest boxes and bird feeders around their houses. I remember in 2010 there were just about 5 or 6 Sparrows in the colony, struggling to locate living spaces. That year there were just about two nests made of hay in the toilet ventilator of an unoccupied house. The situation since then has changed for good. Currently there are more than a dozen pairs in the colony and we can see and hear them at any given time during the day. I had put up four wooden nest boxes around my house in 2012 and since then they have been occupied by the Sparrows, churning out fledglings season after season. These nest boxes have also served as maternity wards to Indian Robins, Oriental Magpie Robins, Scaly-breasted Munias and Indian Silverbills, on a time share basis! The current episode relates to the nest box placed on the western wall of my house behind the bedroom. We started hearing mild chirping of the chicks from this nest box in the second week of April. The parents were generally restless and were not very happy to see us in the balcony, due to the presence of the chicks in the nest. On April 14, 2020 we woke up to a commotion of distress calls of the Sparrows. When I entered the balcony, all the birds flew off and thus I could not identify the cause of the commotion. In the past a Southern Coucal and a Rufous Treepie had attempted to steal the chicks from the nest, but were unsuccessful due to the design of the nest box, and I thought there may be a similar predator around. The next day, there were similar distress calls and, on entering the balcony, I noticed a couple of feathers on the balcony floor. A few minutes later I heard the noises again while standing on the terrace and this time I noticed a male Magpie Robin attacking the tailless mother Sparrow as it was entering the nest. The Sparrow parents fought valiantly to ward off the threat. It was then that I realised that the feathers on the balcony floor were that of the Sparrow mother, probably plucked out by the Magpie Robin a few minutes earlier while she was in the process of feeding the chicks. The mother, which had a tail the previous day, was now devoid of it and thus it was easy for me to identify the mother. It was apparently a fight for occupation/control of the nest box, as a similar battle had ensued the previous season too. During the course of the day I noticed the mother Sparrow engaging the Magpie Robins in several aerial encounters around the nest. Finally the Magpie Robins had to give up the fight and choose another nest box a floor above. Sparrow fledgling after the first flight The Sparrow parents, especially the mother, put up a brave front in a tense atmosphere to ensure the chicks fledged wellnourished. On April 22, a week after the attack, the chicks successfully completed their first solo flight, to a nearby Neem tree.

The tailless mother was seen around the house, busily foraging for the young ones. And the good news is that Magpie Robins are not troubling the Sparrows any more, and the mother is growing her tail feathers back! Tailless mother Sparrow The mother Sparrow with the tail growing back *** Report: Sighting of Isabelline Wheatear, Osman Sagar, Hyderabad, November 2019 Text and Photo: Sudhir Moorti K On November 16, 2019, Srikanth, Gokul and I had visited the Osman Sagar Lake as a part of our regular birding visits to this hotspot. By then, the winter visitors had started moving in, promising us a great morning of birding. colouration; ‘Isabelline’ or ‘Isabella’ is described as a pale grey-yellow, pale fawn, pale cream-brown or parchment colour. The Isabelline Wheatear has a wide breeding range extending from Southern Russia, Central Asia and North-western Pakistan, and winters in Africa and North-western India, during the breeding season. It is seen mainly in open tracts of land and dry, arid regions. As usual we were scouting around near the lake shore, looking for waders etc. As we drove ahead, I spotted a bird perched on a rock a little ahead, which looked somewhat different from the birds usually seen there. We were not really sure, but closer examination and a few photographs confirmed our suspicions. It was an Isabelline Wheatear! Finding it this far down the subcontinent was surely a rare treat, although I had personally sighted it a few years ago elsewhere in Telangana. This is probably a first record for Osman Sagar Lake, but record or not, the sighting had definitely made our day. The Isabelline Wheatear (Oenanthe isabellina) is a small insectivorous passerine belonging to the Muscicapidae family. The common name sounds like it refers to a person’s proper name, but it does not: ‘Isabelline’ actually refers to the bird's Isabelline Wheatear ***

Report: Sighting of Smooth-coated Otter, Himayat Sagar, Hyderabad, May 10, 2020 Text: Srikanth Bhamidipati; Photos: Gokul Krishna Addanki Smooth-coated Otter On May 10, 2020, at around 8.25AM, Gokul and I were birdwatching in Himayat Sagar, one of the prime habitats near Hyderabad, when we stopped to observe a flock of Terns creating a ruckus behind some boulders at the edge of the lake. The behaviour seemed unusual, as they were away from the water and it looked like they were mobbing something. In south India generally we find the Smooth-coated Otters; previously these species had been found in Adilabad, Karimnagar, Khammam, Medak, and Warangal districts. Sighting one so close to the city of Hyderabad is a very important and key find, as this species is on the IUCN Red List, and it is also a Schedule 2 species under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972. Suddenly, we saw a mammal running towards the water and started taking photographs. To our surprise it turned out to be a Smooth-coated Otter, and we were surprised to see this mammal so close to the city. Since this is a species that usually moves in packs, we walked towards the lake, hoping to see more of them, and did spot multiple tracks; however, we were not able to conclude if it was indeed a pack, or just one individual. Hence, it is important to protect the species and the habitat supporting it as well. Creating awareness is key and there is a great need to educate the people in this region of the importance of conserving this habitat, both for themselves as well as the Otters and other key scheduled species that visit this location. While the habitat has been under a lot of strain, there is the need for a set policy with guidelines that accurately explain the measures required to be put in place to preserve and protect this prime location. This species is marked as Vulnerable in the IUCN Red List. India is home to three of the 13 species of Otters in the world: 1. 2. 3. Smooth-coated Otter Eurasian Otter Small-clawed Otter This sighting is a really important one. Also, these 2 locations – Himayat Sagar and Osman Sagar – are home to about 300 species of birds, 5 mammals, various fishes and other species of plants, including more than 5 species of birds and mammals falling under the IUCN Red List and Scheduled Species list. Therefore, necessary steps must be taken, involving all wildlife communities, for the search of potential dens and the possibility of existence of the species in nearby habitats and hotspots like Osman Sagar and other parts of the Musi River. They feed mostly on fish, crabs, lobsters, crayfish, shrimps, prawns, krill, woodlice, and barnacles. The Smooth-coated Otter, which is the largest of the three species in the country, is traditionally a freshwater species but adapted to estuarine habitats. Smooth-coated Otter ***

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Black-winged Kite (Elanus caeruleus) Black-winged Kite Adult (L) (Rollapadu, October 4, 2018) and Juvenile (R) (Ankola, February 19, 2012) Order: Accipitriformes Family: Accipitridae Genus: Elanus Species: E. caeruleus Size: 31-35 cm grasslands and are often seen perched on wires, scanning the ground for rodents. They are best known for their ability to hover in one place before making a dive to catch the identified prey. Although generally seen in the plains, there are several records at higher altitudes in the Nilgiris, Sikkim, Nagaland and some parts of the Western Ghats. Besides rodents, their diet includes grasshoppers, crickets and other large insects, and occasionally, small snakes, frogs, lizards and injured birds. They usually feed on a perch but may eat on the ground in case of large prey. The call is a high-pitched squeal or a soft whistle, uttered mainly during breeding season or at the roost, where communal groups of 15 to 35 may sometimes be seen. Description & distribution: The Black-winged Kite is a small diurnal bird of prey. It is primarily white and grey in colour, with black shoulder patches, wing tips and eye stripe. Head and underparts are white. Bill is black with a yellow cere, short, and has a hooked upper mandible. The wings are long and pointed, as in Falcons, and extend beyond the tail when perched. In flight, the short, unforked tail is clearly visible. Central tail feathers are bluish-grey while outer tail feathers are white. Inner vanes of feathers have velvety barbules; their soft feathers have sometimes been seen as instrumental in dispersing grass seeds, though it may interfere in flight. Short bare legs and feet are yellow, and the feet show zygodactyly – that is, two toes face forward and two face back. The large owl-like forward-facing eyes, placed under a bony shelf, have red irises. Sexes are similar, but juvenile birds have a scaly back, sooty-grey shoulders, fine brownish streaks on breast, and a brownish wash on head and underparts. Nesting: The Black-winged Kite breeds at different times across its range. In India, it is known to build nests around the year, while it seems to breed throughout the year except in April and May. Courtship is noisy and often involves chases; once the pair is formed, they copulate frequently. The nest is a loose platform of twigs, and the usual clutch consists of 3-4 pale creamy eggs with deep red spots. Nest-building and incubation duties are shared by both parents, but once the chicks are hatched, the male focuses more on foraging. Females also hunt, usually close to the nest, and handle the initial feeding. Once fledged, the young birds continue to depend on the male parent for food, for around 80 days. Females are also known to desert the nest before the young birds fledge, leaving the hunting and feeding to the male. Both males and females show considerable nomadism. Three sub-species are recognized: the nominate E. c. caeruleus, seen in southwest Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal), sub-Saharan Africa and southwest Arabia; E. c. vociferus, seen across the Indian sub-continent, east China, Malay Peninsula and Indochina; and E. c. hypoleucus, found in Greater and Lesser Sunda Islands (Sumatra, Java, Borneo, Sulawesi), New Guinea and the Philippines. Local name: The Black-winged Kite is known as ‘Kapassi’ or ‘Kapasi’ in Hindi, Gujarati and Bengali, ‘Adavi ramadasu’ in Telugu, ‘Chitti’ in Punjabi, and ‘Velli-eriyan’ or ‘Ukussa’ in Malayalam. BLAST FROM THE PAST Report: Lonar Crater, October 2012 & 2019 Text: N Shiva Kumar (with inputs from MS Kulkarni) Photos: N Shiva Kumar (unless specified otherwise) Lonar Lake Wildlife Sanctuary on its revival path It was October 19, 2012, and I had just finished my office tour to Bombay and landed in Aurangabad on my way back to Delhi. This was my second visit to the sleepy town of Aurangabad, famous as the tourist hub in Maharashtra state. Situated 370km from Bombay, Aurangabad is surrounded by historical monuments, including the Ajanta and Ellora Caves; both are World Heritage Sites. So is the 17th-century marble Bibi-ka-Maqbara, styled on the Taj Mahal. The medieval Daulatabad Fort and nearby Museum, dedicated to the Maratha king Shivaji are other attractions. As I had seen all of them before, my visit was focused on getting a glimpse of the unique Lonar Crater and quenching my long-pending curiosity. Off the beaten track and not on regular tourist circuit, even the tourist office in Aurangabad was not forthcoming with useful information on Lonar. I hired a cab for a full day trip, and even the driver was not aware of Lonar Crater, so we made enquires beforehand. The next day, October 20, 2012, we hit the road at 4:00AM to escape the heat of the day. The road was an unpaved mud motorway, good to go, but dimpled and dusty. The road-ride of 170km was nevertheless pleasant due to the moist morning aroma of the earth wafting through the vehicle windows. Most of the drive was bland as sun-up was many minutes away, and the horizon was still warming up with its predawn glow. Suddenly, across the road, we saw an animal lying on the road with fresh red blood oozing from its mouth. It was a Jackal, a healthy specimen with no physical body injuries, probably hit on the head, but an unfortunate victim of road kill, which seem to have happened in the wee hours. The rest of the journey was spent in muted mood. On reaching the sleepy village of Lonar after nearly four hours, I stopped to have some tea to uplift my spirits, and enquired about the crater to begin my exploration. The Lonar Lake is an exceptional ‘bowl of biodiversity’ nearly 3km across from rim to rim, ensconced inside the Lonar Wildlife Sanctuary. It is land-locked with extraordinary water qualities, has no inlets or outlets, nor does the water seep into the ground. The only escape is by evaporation, as the region experiences temperatures of up to 47℃. The Crater Lake is fed by small underground streams that are now drying up due to human folly. However, since ancient time, every summer the lake would go mostly dry and the salt cakes that were formed at the lake bottom would be harvested and sold as therapeutic soaps. History tells us that that even Emperor Akbar was fond of these soap bars, and in the mid-1990s there was a mini-factory within the crater harvesting the salt cakes.

The remarkable shape, size and samples of celestial leftovers have rendered exceptionality to this crater. The extraordinary traits have attracted steady attention of geologists, ecologists and astronomers from across the globe, though only in a trickle. It has been the subject of several sample scientific studies on various aspects of crater ecosystem, yet it is seemingly unknown to the general public. Strangely, NASA seems to have more information about our Lonar Crater than we have in India. Incredibly old at 50,000 years, the Lonar Crater is the youngest and best preserved ‘impact crater’ formed in basalt rock and is the only one of its kind on earth. Formed by a blazing ball of fire that weighed over one million tons in deadweight, it was a meteorite travelling at an awesome speed of 80,000 kilometres per hour. It is believed to have pierced our blue planet and hit the earth with such fire, force and fury that it dug a deep depression in the rock-solid Deccan plateau. It apparently crashed, exploded, erupted and spewed molten rock, creating a magnificent crest on the rim covering a 2KM diameter. Even though it was a mere chip off the moon, the hypervelocity impact of the 380,000 kilometre journey from the moon to the earth, has left a dent 200 meters deep. India’s vast territory has various remote terrains, but none as extraordinary as the Lonar Crater, which forms a lake that lies close to the world famous Ajanta and Ellora caves, yet it is in obscurity. It is evident that urbanization at the neighbouring Lonar village coupled with ever-increasing pilgrim population has led to an indiscriminate invasion of human activities. Langur trying to bite open a plastic bottle We came across a few scattered temples with intricate carvings but all in ruins. Further up the jungle path the flat lake was visible. Here we reached another set of temples on the edge of the lake where pilgrims were busy being pious. I noticed a hovering Kestrel. For the birder, there was much to see: a Redwattled Lapwing creating a ruckus, fleeting glimpses of a Golden Oriole, a Green Bee-eater flitting around. There were also some squirrels screeching, and a few Langurs lingering around the temple, hoping to be offered food by the devotees. The blaring sounds of rustic devotional songs killed the silence. After three hours of walking around the lake and inside the crater, with plenty of pictures and some bird watching, I was hot and thirsty. While the initial anticipation of going down was interesting, the exploring, and the prospect of climbing up was not enticing, as it was steep and sultry with the sun blazing down with intensity. I was cursing my friend MS Kulkarni, who was supposed to accompany me to Lonar but did not turn up on time, as he had to catch multiple buses from Hyderabad to reach Aurangabad. On my return from Lonar, after spending nearly nine hours in the open and on the move, I was dog-tired and retired early to bed. Live temple on lake shore polluted by trash When we visited in 2012, we could see that the Lonar Crater and Lake was visibly violated by human presence, and this created a constant threat to the ecosystem and its remarkable biodiversity. The lake also happens to be a captive water-body; hence the concentration of chemicals has been on the rise and has caused irreversible pollution. Accompanied by a local man who claimed to be a guide, we made our way down into the crater as there was no clear-cut path. We just followed the worn tracks made by pilgrims, the hoof prints of cattle and the trail of discarded of water bottles and paan masala sachets and other trash. The going was slow as the rudimentary path was pebble-strewn, inclined and zigzag. There are quite a few such winding paths to go down into the crater but we chose the one with lesser gradient and the crater walls less high. As we walked down the variety of shrub and bush growth gave way to tall trees and plenty of shade to walk. The hum of the insects and the birds chirping were enchanting. With the sun somewhere up there, I could feel the heat even though it was dim and damp on the forest floor. Greater Flamingo (adult & juvenile) at Jayakwadi Bird Sanctuary near Aurangabad However, the next day, October 21, 2012, I met Kulkarni at Aurangabad and went bird watching at the Jayakwadi Bird Sanctuary on the Godavari River near Aurangabad. We sighted Flamingos, Brahminy (or Ruddy) Shelducks, some Pochards, Common Teals, Northern Pintails, Eurasian Wigeons, Northern Shovelers, Glossy Ibis, etc. We promised ourselves that we would return again sometime to spend at least two/three days at Lonar for a full survey of the area.

That second journey to Lonar Lake Sanctuary finally materialized after seven years, on October 10, 2019, when we reassembled in Aurangabad and spent two days at Lonar on October 11-12, 2019. This time we were better prepared, as we had sought the help of Dr S Kurhade, Professor of Zoology from Ahmednagar, who is also one of the Wildlife Wardens of Maharashtra. He not only made arrangements to stay at the Forest Guest House right next to the rim of the crater, but also took us in his vehicle from Aurangabad to Lonar and introduced us to some wonderful people of Lonar village. On arrival, I was pleasantly surprised to note that practically a full facelift had been given to the ‘geological gem’ in Maharashtra. The maddening crowds stampeding into the Lonar Lake had disappeared, a bold step was taken to decommission the ancient temples and stop all religious activities. The entire Sanctuary was fenced, plenty of tree plantation was noticeable, educative sign boards were evident and there was a visible change in the lush vegetation allround. A very pleasant surprise! up the crater and its surrounding areas. It was a low-key costless campaign, started simply by sending out SMS and WhatsApp messages; whoever wished to, could join voluntarily. The Lonar population is about 25,000, far from the madding crowds of the nearby cities. Very few visitors come by, and those who do are mostly day tourists who take a dip in the natural spring around which an intact ancient temple survives. Farmers from far and near also visit to buy and sell their produce in the local markets. The tiny hamlet, nevertheless, ranks as one of the topmost ‘geological gems’ in the world as the Lonar Crater here is considered distinctive. Trekking routes and nature walks had been plotted out to the bottom of the crater. The idea was, ‘Walk, and pick up the trash accumulated over the years, while communing with the ecology in the crater’. World Environment Day on June 5, 2017, was a landmark one, as people voluntarily participated for an hour and, thereafter, once a week, particularly on holidays, in operation clean-up. What started with four people went on to become 40-strong in four months, swelling up to 400-strong in four years. Importantly, over the years, tons of trash was removed and it was indeed a stupendous achievement for a self-help group in a remote village. Walls of the Lonar Crater with flourishing greenery We met Arun Mapari, a web designer, who had worked for 20 years in Aurangabad. One day in 2015, he simply gave up the ordeal of city life and decided to settle in his home town Lonar and started a restaurant. Similarly, Sachin Kapure, a software consultant, quit urban life in Pune to set up a boutique hotel in Lonar. Meanwhile, Santosh and Vilas, known as the Jadhav brothers, employed with the State Government and active in social work, joined Arun and Sachin, to stimulate the location. Collectively they have inspired the inhabitants of sleepy Lonar to lead by example instead of knocking on the door of the authorities. Kulkarni, Vilas (with backpack) & Sachin during the walk Abundant wild Custard Apples in the forest ‘One great hour for Lonar’ T-shirts distributed to volunteers The four have started a movement of sorts, calling it ‘Mi Lonarkar’, beseeching the local population not to neglect the site that is known worldwide. They launched a local campaign, ‘One great hour for Lonar’, that entailed cleaning On our first day, after the know-each-other-meeting, we went on a walk along the rim of the crater until sunset and found it very fascinating. The next day we went down into the crater, exploring much of the vegetation and bird life, with Sachin and Vilas as guardians. I was particularly pleased with the vast improvement, with no pilgrims and unruly tourists having picnics inside the crater.

grouped for souvenir selfie poses, some photo shoots at the floor’s centre and, after a walk around the lake, got ready for the hike back up to the rim. Frothy spittle mass produced by Spittlebugs The jungle was luxurious and filled with the calls of birds, particularly peacocks making merry with their guttural sounds. Koels peeped from the tree tops and bright Orioles loitered amongst the leafy branches, as smaller birds moved in the bushes, and butterflies with their lazy flight alighted at sunny spots. Dead trunks had plenty of mushrooms sprouting, and the ground was littered with large beetles, colourful bugs and plenty of fat millipedes and centipedes. Millipedes curled up on the forest floor Once the most busy temple, now used only to collect mineral water from the natural spring Sprouting Fig Tree leaves seeking sunlight filtering through the canopy The temperature was still blazingly hot, and we were tired, but imbibing plenty of water kept us going. It was amazing to stand in the middle of the crater and look all around at the walls towering on all sides. I shot a couple of panoramas and wideangle pictures. With the blue sky above and the crater bottom terrain all around, you certainly got a taste of the thinking of what it would be like to be standing in the middle of a small crater on the Moon. Common Hoopoe foraging inside the crater As we were busy looking up into the canopy searching for birds, a large six-foot snake slithered across our path, and we nearly stepped on it. Recovering from the shock of finding a snake, I could only shoot some photos of the disappearing tail into the bushes, as the healthy Rat Snake slithered away. Up close at the lake waters, there were plenty of large ‘soap bubbles’ floating on the waters – maybe methane and ethane emanating from the lake bottom. The active temple I saw seven years ago was silent, locked up, now under the ASI, but the monkeys hung around relaxing near the premises. We Common Jezebel (Photo: Dr Sudhakar Kurhade)

Oriental Garden Lizard Red Pierrot (Photo: Dr Sudhakar Kurhade) Dr. Kurhade, who has visited Lonar on many earlier occasions, says, “The unique Lonar Lake with alkaline and saline waters was being polluted over the years by waste waters discharged and dumped from the nearby village. Even though the environmental area of the crater has been declared a Wildlife Sanctuary, it needs enhanced protection. Plantation by the forest department has given it a green look at least on the periphery of the water and slopes of the crater. The principal vegetation of the area is of a dry deciduous type, mainly of Acacia trees, thorny bushes and different types of grasses. Teak, Neem, Acacia species and Babul are the other trees of common occurrence. Earlier there was a patch of about 22 hectares of land under cultivation within the crater and thankfully now it has been removed. The crater forest attracts a good number of bat species due to several fruit-bearing plants in the area. Roosts of insectivorous bats are common in the abandoned temples inside the Sanctuary. More than 50 species of butterflies are found in the area: Tailed Jay, Common Mormon, Lime Butterfly, Common Rose, Grass Yellow, Common Jezebel, Common Pierrot, Zebra Blue etc, to name a few. The notable insects are Painted Grasshopper, Praying Mantis, different types of Beetles, Termites, Rock Bees, Bumblebees, various species of Wasps etc. Sometimes Lantern Flies are also seen and plenty of Dragonflies are always hovering over the lake waters as the water volume increases during the seasonal monsoons.” Lonar Crater was first noticed 190 years ago by British explorer, AJ Alexander, who went investigating the region. He found ancient temples in a dilapidated condition and strange ecology in a cavernous basin. It was vastly different from the surrounding flat landscape even though it was discovered 57 years before the Ajanta Caves. Strangely, both the Lonar Crater and the Ajanta Caves were chance discoveries by British explorers. Even more bizarre is ‘Lonar’, the name of the nearby village that is akin to the English word ‘lunar’, as if early Indians had the requisite knowledge that the crater was created by moon rock. It was initially thought to be a deepthroated volcanic formation, which was later refuted by scientists who concluded that it was moulded by a piece of flying moon rock or most probably a vagabond meteorite. Maskelynite, a kind of naturally occurring glass only formed by extremely high-velocity impact, has been found in the crater to prove that it was indeed a heavenly body that crashed here. Sudhakar Bugdane with a specimen from his collection Painted Grasshopper (Photo: Dr Sudhakar Kurhade) Sudhakar Bugdane, a retired school principal, who was the first to publish an informative booklet on the Lonar Crater, rues the degradation of the environment around the crater. “It is evident that urbanization, coupled with ever increasing population, has led to an indiscriminate invasion of human activities in the Lonar Lake area, and has created a constant threat to the ecosystem and its remarkable biodiversity,” he says.

Saving the Lonar Crater, which started as a hobby 40 years ago, has become a mission for the 74-year-old Bugdane. He regularly lectures about it and encourages the youth to research and celebrate the rare cosmic collision with earth. Kulkarni and I went to his house one evening, and he told us the entire story with fascination and enthusiasm akin to a youngster. He showed us the various special stones he had collected when he was young and also displayed its unique properties of floating on water and their curious magnetic properties with a handheld compass. Arun and Sachin explain that Bugdane was the first man to have started the battle for active conservation of the Lonar Crater many years ago. “We saw his aggressive approach for the cause of the crater, engaging doggedly with various departments. Despite many failures, he brought Lonar into the limelight. We decided to further the cause, but with a different stance and gathered similar-minded people to make it a movement. Without approaching the authorities, we started in a small way and spearheaded easy methods of implementing, like weekly trash collection etc. Steadily, various local and State departments began to understand our point of view without going to court for solutions.” Today, after five years of constant team work, the ‘One great hour for Lonar’ initiative has been able to put up a fencing around the crater rim, stop religious processions within the crater, stop cutting of trees and the drainage of municipal waste into the lake. Regular patrolling is on to protect the crater. Even the Archaeology Department is repairing the cluster of heritage temples in the vicinity, many of which are over 1,000 years old. The Forest Department has declared it as the Lonar Wildlife Sanctuary and is reaping the harvest of practical conservation methods, as native flora and fauna is thriving and, surprisingly, a family of Leopards has made it their home. A bird-watching festival was also conducted recently and recorded over 150 species of birds. “Our team has gained the confidence and involvement of not only the citizens but also politicians and bureaucrats, while scientists were always backing our effort”, says Arun.
