COVID-19: BOON OR BANE? Report: Birding from a Human Zoo, March-May 2020 Text and Photos: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri Purple Sunbird (male) It is astonishing that a microscopic non-living particle has the capability to force a lockdown on a global scale, effectively halting the world economy. Maybe, this is nature’s revenge. We destroy forests every day to erect concrete jungles, causing irreversible damage to our world. Nature’s revenge has rendered us prisoners in our own home. For decades, we have imprisoned animals in enclosures for our entertainment. Today, we are the ones imprisoned, and possibly our absence from the streets has invited different fauna to come out and watch us, much like they would have in a human zoo. Ironically, this makes for some great birding opportunities for us puny humans. Asian Koel (female) Tree full of mangoes Asian Koel (male) It has been calm and quiet outside in the absence of air and noise pollution – I can hear the birds sing louder with every passing day, and even a few dogs bark in the middle of the day. While we sit inside our homes, the animal kingdom takes a further step towards reclaiming what was originally theirs. Asian Koels seem to be competing about whose cooing will win this year’s Koel Idol – and they also allow us spectators a repeat performance around midnight for a couple of minutes. Alarms have lost all value now since I am woken up every day by the cacophony caused by the birds’ singing in the ‘bramhomuhurta’ (around 3:30 to 4:00AM). I reside on the 2rd floor of a corner house at Salt Lake, Kolkata. I am lucky that my house has three balconies, one of them being an open terrace which looks directly over a giant mango tree. It is currently blessed with enough mangoes to feed a village. The tree is so close to the balcony that I can touch and feel these mangoes. I have come to realize that much like humans, birds love mango trees as well. A Common Tailorbird calls from that tree very loudly every day – it is hard to believe that such a small bird can call that loudly.

While it has been a lonely storm for many of us during this lockdown, there have been actual heavy thunderstorms here in West Bengal. The sky rages with dark clouds, followed by the release of heavy rains. The clear skies that follow after are always reassuring – as though to say that indeed, this too shall pass. The trees always look happy to be drenched in rainwater. One such evening, as I enjoyed the aftermath of rain from my eastern balcony, I observed something rather peculiar. I noticed that a Tailorbird was bathing in the rainwater remaining collected on the mango leaves. It was a truly spectacular sight to see it enjoy its bath in nature’s bathtub. It was rolling from one leaf to another, carefully scrubbing its feathers in the available rainwater. It is a myth that birds don’t fly in stormy weather. I have observed many peculiar activities from my verandah during these pre-monsoon rains. While there are fewer birds flying in the sky during the showers, the ones that choose to do so fly at slower speeds and usually halt on treetops, using these as rest stops before embarking on their connecting flights. I have also seen a Red-vented Bulbul hop upwards from branch to branch until it reached the treetop repeatedly, only to come back and perch on the original starting point. The only explanation that I can think of, is that the Bulbul was enjoying a shower. Common Mormon Common Tailorbird bathing in water drops remaining on leaves Common Jay Purple Sunbird bathing A few days later, I saw a Purple Sunbird do the same thing. It claimed its turn to bathe in the same mango leaves. Once it realized that it was too big for the rather narrow mango leaves, it flew across the road to a Kathgolap or White Plumeria (Plumeria alba) tree, since that tree has larger leaves. It has been a delightful revelation to observe these tiny intriguing behaviours. Tailed Jay Birds haven’t been the only guests outside my windows. The Common Mormon, Common Jay and Tailed Jay butterflies, and some honeybees, have made regular appearances as well. The butterflies usually enjoy nectar from the flowers of a Curry Leaf tree. Around 4:00PM every day, right after the scorching heat of the sun subsides to reveal the beginnings of the evening, hundreds of dragonflies take to the skies to mark the end of the afternoon. Green and yellow Dragonflies seem to love certain spots on the mango tree, hopping from one twig to the other. Kathgolap (White Plumeria)

Granite Ghost Mud Dauber with prey To contrast that, a Mud Dauber actually built a nest in my husband’s backpack! The backpack has been untouched since the beginning of lockdown, and obviously the wasp thought the backpack was a stationary object that provides a perfect real estate opportunity for a nest. It put live green caterpillars inside it. Wandering Glider Krishnachura in full bloom Green Marshhawk (aka Slender Skimmer) We have also had a few intruders. The Tiger Moth, a fake wasp species of moth that mimics the real wasp, has zoomed through our house a few times. From the north side of my balcony, I can see the striking red flowers of the Krishnachura (Delonix regia) tree, also known as Royal Poinciana, Flamboyant or Flame of the Forest. A Purple Sunbird pair usually hangs out on this tree. They whistle and fly from one branch to another, often resting on a cable wire. Interestingly, one day I caught sight of the Sunbird’s tongue which was hanging from its beak. This was the first time I had noticed it from a very short distance. Tiger Moth Red-vented Bulbul

minute into the hunt – a sorry caterpillar. The Oriole picked it up by its beak and smashed it several times against the tree trunk. Before I knew it, it had swallowed it whole – amazing! This was my husband’s favourite birding moment during this lockdown. A few days ago, a White-throated Kingfisher with its two chicks landed on the same drumstick tree. The mother bird had caught a big cockroach and smashed it against the trunk. Shen then carefully divided it into equal halves and fed it to the chicks. Comparing the chicks to their mother, the juveniles have dark beaks and feet whereas the adult has a red beak and feet. Either way, though, I can feast my eyes on these spectacular and vividly coloured birds. Oriental Magpie Robin White-throated Kingfisher juvenile (L) and adult (R) Asian Pied Starling The nearby Eucalyptus tree hosts a musical chair competition everyday – bird entry only. The Red-vented Bulbul (the bengalensis sub-species, with the brown ear patch), House Crow, Oriental Magpie Robin, White-breasted Kingfisher, Asian Pied Starling etc. fight for the first place. The Eucalyptus does not discriminate – all species are welcome to roost in it, provided you get there early enough. Moreover, trees are not the only sought-after roosting spot for birds. I have found that Black Kites love to perch on the top of mobile towers after their morning sky surveillances. The Yellow Gulmohar (Peltophorum pterocarpum) tree, slightly far away east of my terrace, is currently in full bloom with beautiful yellow flowers. A few Rose-ringed Parakeets roost in that tree every day. They come there every morning, and fly off towards the west every evening. I don’t know where they come from, or where they go, but oftentimes (as in life), it is the journey that matters. Coppersmith Barbet A close second was finding the Coppersmith Barbet, a bird that was initially introduced to me during our trip to Himachal Pradesh. I recognized its call but was unable to spot the magnificent bird for quite some time. My search efforts finally paid off when I found the beauty sitting on a neem tree. Black-hooded Oriole with prey Our guest of honour, though, was a Black-hooded Oriole. It sat on the drumstick tree barely 20ft away from my east side balcony. It was on the prowl – it detected its prey within a House Sparrow

Thanks to this lockdown and reduced human activity, birds that were once a common sight on the streets of Kolkata, but had gone missing in recent years, have once again resurfaced in urban areas of this giant metropolis. I have seen Sparrows practicing their high jump capabilities at a nearby house window. I think they were trying to find and eat insects through this exercise. The Magpie Robin sings its sweet call every day. The Rufous Treepie is back with its shrill call, which probably agitates all the Jungle Babblers who constantly quarrel with each other. I’ve also heard the trilling call of the Black-rumped Flameback. I have been trying to spot it for a while now, but in vain so far. front of my eastern veranda. It was eye-opening to observe how the two birds built their nest in a span of mere three days. One of them sat in the nest, functioning as the center for the other bird to build around it, giving the nest its trademark round bowl-like shape and perfect dimensions. It refused to leave its nest even under heavy rains. For two full days, I did not see it abandon the nest even for a single second. On the third day, it left to sit on a different branch of the same tree. The other Crow was feeding it there. After eating, it returned to the nest. The next day, it flew from the jackfruit tree to the drumstick tree where they repeated the feeding ritual. When it returned to its nest a few hours later, it was startled by the presence of a betel nut bark in its nest, and began calling in exasperation. The other one came to its rescue in no time but both of them flew away together. The Crow came back to inspect the nest the following day. It tried to fit inside but could not. It started calling again, and the other one came and tried its hand at fixing it. However, it could not do so, and the Crows flew away. A few days later, a Cuckoo came to investigate the abandoned nest, only to be fiercely shooed away by the protective creators. Nevertheless, now their architectural masterpiece sits on the jackfruit tree much like a haunted nest. This lockdown has been an illuminating experience. I have travelled far and wide to look at birds through the lens of my binoculars/camera. When we venture into forests to feel closer to Mother Nature, we still experience these lovely birds from a fair distance. This experience has taught me how to be effectively birding from the comfort of my home. I have been blessed with the opportunity to experience a few of nature’s most spectacular creations from a very close distance, enjoying their vivid colours and learning about their behavioural eccentricities. This has been a much-needed silver lining to my weeks in captivity. Rufous Treepie Thus, I say – while the world grapples with the horrors of the Covid-19 bane, the animal kingdom rejoices in the boon of the absence of human presence. So, is it a boon or a bane? Pied Crested Cuckoo: The Monsoon Bird… Or Not! Text and Photo: Humayun Taher Pied Crested Cuckoo It started as a brief message on the Deccan Birders WhatsApp group. Since lockdown began most birding has been on mobile phone apps and social media. Someone mentioned that the IMD has predicted the arrival of the monsoons on the coast of Kerala on June 5 this year. The time had come to update my “Pied Crested Cuckoo calendar” for the year. And I came up with my first snag right away. Perhaps I should explain. Since 2003, I have been sedulously maintaining, what I call my “Pied Crested Cuckoo rain calculator”. It’s nothing very fancy – just a simple table of dates. Here it is… Year Date sighted First rain date Rain in (No. of days) 2003 28-May 10-Jun 13 2004 01-Jun 11-Jun 10 2005 20-May 09-Jun 20 2006 02-Jun 10-Jun 8 2007 30-May 15-Jun 16 2008 25-May 09-Jun 15 2009 29-May 12-Jun 14 2010 Was not in India from March to August. 2011 30-May 16-Jun 17 2012 2013 19-May 09-Jun 21 18-May 29-May 11 2014 01-Jun 21-Jun 20 2015 30-May 09-Jun 10 2016 01-Jun 20-Jun 19 2017 27-May 11-Jun 15 2018 04-Jun 18-Jun 14 2019 23-Jun 14-Jun -9 2020 3-May (Online record) The species is known to move across the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean to reach India in May or June; sightings from Oman, Saudi Arabia and the Seychelles have been reported during the migratory season. Some believe that the bird uses the monsoon winds to assist its flight during this migration. But why all this recording of dates? Is there a relationship here? The claim to fame here is that within 21 days of the first sighting of this species, the monsoon is supposed to break. There seems to be a strong association between this bird and rain. In part, this could be because this species migrates to large areas across northern India around the monsoon, and has often been called the ‘harbinger of rain’.

Some of the notes In the early days of the BSAP, when we learnt this important fact, I remember how eagerly we used to look forward to that first sighting. As the first week of June approached, the anticipation became almost painful: every field trip we made during those days was given over, almost exclusively, to the search for black-and-white feathers. And when we did happen to see it, there were exclamations and back-slapping and handshaking and smiles all around and summer was ‘officially’ considered to have ended! This year, not having gone birding since early March, I am not sure of the date I have inserted in the table above. The 2020 record is from a Tadoba Live Safari episode of 3rd May, where a Pied Crested Cuckoo could be heard calling in the background. I am not sure if this is an actual call in the background or added during post-production; if the latter, the record becomes valueless. But I am using it as a working hypothesis. In recent times, we have become aware that there is a small ‘resident’ population of these birds in Southern India. Given this fact, it does seem a bit far-fetched to assume that the resident population goes into hiding during the summer and only emerges a few days before the rains. There are indeed two separate Pied Crested Cuckoo populations in the subcontinent and that is one of the reasons that the scientists are not certain about the reliability of the bird as a rain indicator species. But I still think that the coincidence is a remarkable one. And while it is true that we occasionally get an odd sighting of this species during the summers, the bulk of the sightings do come in just before the monsoons – which seems to suggest that the birds we get here are mainly from the African population. Coming back to the table, the 21-day interval seems to hold remarkably well. There is only one instance of the sighting being after the rains, and that was in 2019. This in part could be because I was a little busy that year and hadn’t been birding during that critical time between May and June, when the bulk of the sightings of the species usually occur. But this one exception notwithstanding, the relationship between the sighting of the Pied Crested Cuckoo and the coming of the rains seems remarkably consistent. And until science can provide a more detailed explanation, I am going to continue to cling fondly to my own pet theory. If for no other reason than that I want the monsoon to arrive at the time the Cuckoo says it will! Pied Crested Cuckoo ***

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Sanderling (Calidris elba) Sanderling flock foraging Sanderling (Pulicat, December 30, 2018) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Calidris Species: C. elba Size: 18-20 cm large lakes. Flocks are usually seen scurrying back and forth as though ‘chasing’ the waves. Their diet primarily consists of invertebrate prey like sand crabs, which are usually buried a few centimetres beneath the sand – the only time the crabs come out is when the incoming wave brings in the plankton that they feed on, before rushing back into their burrows in the sand as the wave retreats. Since their bills can only penetrate 2-3cm into the sand, the Sanderlings try to catch the crabs just as, or immediately after, they go back into the burrows – hence the ‘chasing’ behavior. Besides crabs, they may also feed on amphipods, isopods, insects, marine worms, small mollusks and, occasionally, carrion. During breeding, they may also feed on flies and other insects, some seeds, algae and leaves. They can be territorial, with the males defending their territory. Pairs can be monogamous or polyandrous (one female and two males). Flight is free and rapid, and they readily take wing, in flocks, and usually staying low in the air. Besides a conversational chatter (like a soft, squeaky wick wick) when in flocks, the call is a sharp kip, and has been compared to frog calls or an unpleasant alarm clock. During breeding displays, consisting of alternate fluttering and gliding, males utter croaking, frog-like trills, and females signal their willingness to mate with low buzzing notes that can sound like a typewriter. Description & distribution: The Sanderling is a small, sprightly wader, with the name being derived from the Old English sand-yrðling (sand-ploughman). The scientific name is rather evocative of the overall whitish appearance of the bird: the genus name Calidris is derived from the Ancient Greek Kalidris or Skalidris, a term Aristotle used to describe grey water-side birds, and the species name alba is Latin for ‘white’. It is a small, plump wader, and has a somewhat chunkier and rounder appearance than the Sandpipers; the bill also looks stouter and the head looks larger. The wintering (non-breeding) bird seen in India is very pale – it has white underparts and greyish upperparts, with a broad white wingstripe, seen conspicuously in flight, bordered by a small dark shoulder patch – and in general, looks much paler than other similar-sized shorebirds. The bill and legs are black. During the breeding season, it develops rusty or brick red mottling on face, throat and breast; the sides, however, remain unmarked. Juveniles are more starkly coloured than the adults, and are boldly spangled black-and-white above. Nesting: The Sanderling breeds generally from late May to late July or early August, in its breeding range. The nest is a shallow scrape in open and barren ground, somewhat higher than the surroundings. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 eggs, olive green to pale brown, with sparse brown and black spotting. The Sanderling is a circumpolar breeder, breeding in the High Arctic areas of North America, Europe and Asia, and is a longdistance winter migrant, wintering in the coastal areas almost across the world – South America, Southern Europe, Africa, Asia (India and Sri Lanka) and Australia. Migration may involve a journey of anywhere from 3,000 to 10,000km. Local name: The Sanderling is known as ‘Moondru viral ullan’ or ‘Manal ullan’ in Tamil, ‘Thirakkada’ in Malayalam, ‘Dariyayi khichdiyo’ in Gujarati. BACKYARD BROUHAHA Text & Photos: Sudhir Moorti K Pied Bushchat (male) I have been travelling like a proverbial top from my childhood, unhindered. My grandma once told me that I had ‘Chakram’ on my feet and I would be roaming around all my life. God bless her soul, what more could I wish for. My mother, however, was of a very contrasting opinion. She would look at me with fire in her eyes whenever I prepared for a birding trip. It took a lockdown to tie me down to the homestead. Anyhoo! I started exploring the backyard and garden instead of the Western Ghats and the Himalayas. The summer was mostly uneventful initially but later, much to my delight, a pair of Red-vented Bulbuls, some Common Tailorbirds, Purple Sunbirds and Scaly-breasted Munias started using my improvised bird bath. The Bulbuls would turn up at odd times: I would be looking out for them in the morning or evenings, but they would come for a bath in the afternoon, the rascals. Red-vented Bulbul The eternal vocal presence of the Asian Koel was quite pleasant, with the neighbourhood kids going “Koo-oo Koo-oo” along with the noisy fellow. Some evenings a Bulbul and a Koel would have a shouting match raising quite a din. I could never figure out why. Was the Koel trying to slip an egg into the Bulbul’s nest? I wonder.

Come June and the Tailorbirds started their breeding season with the males going into a non-stop song (and dance?) and soon, we had three young fledglings hopping around on the Neem tree in front of our house. The nest building began; the female was doing most of the work while the lazy male sat around singing or disappeared from the scene. The nest was in a kind of hole/crevice in the construction debris (left uncleared by the neighbours) in the empty plot next to my house. I didn’t try to approach the nest, as I didn’t want to disturb or scare them; also the Chiku tree (Manilkara zapota) in my backyard was obstructing the view of the nest, and so I couldn’t capture the actual process of nest-building. However, a few days later, I began to notice that the female was absent most of the time. The incubation was on, I deduced, and started keeping a watch. Although the nest was not directly visible to me, I could see the male carrying food to the nest area, feeding the female while she was incubating. The male did not seem to share the incubation duty, but did hang around the nest most of the time. Grey-bellied Cuckoo The Grey-bellied Cuckoo too showed up in June, somewhat late this year. The song was an absolute treat, even though the fellow went on and on. After a few days the male was successfully able to charm the lady, I guess – I could see them playfully bouncing around the Neem tree. Soon the pair got into squabbles with Mr & Mrs Tailorbird, maybe a nest issue. I don’t know if the Cuckoos were successful in fooling the Tailorbirds. A couple of weeks later I noticed the pair got awfully busy, scurrying to and fro with ants, earthworms and other insects in their beaks. Through the foliage I could see both the parents feeding the nestlings; at this point I didn’t know how many were there. I could hear the “Chik Chik” call of the young ones throughout the day. The chicks were relentless in their demand for food. The parents alternated at intervals of 5-10 minutes in supplying regurgitated titbits to the insatiable mouths. Boy! Parenting is tough. I was glad to see that both the parents took equal responsibility in feeding the young ones. This went on for a few days. Pied Bushchat fledgling Pied Bushchat (female) The male Pied Bushchat started singing in the mornings, such a beautiful song that brought me great joy. Couple of days later I observed the Bushchat pair fluttering around – nest site inspection? In this species the male shows the female a few possible nest sites, and the female then selects one. So I thought to myself, “Wow, that was quick!” One fine morning I was out in the garden sipping my morning coffee, when I saw the first fledgling. All cute and speckled, he/she sat on a dry branch. Papa Bushchat was feeding him/her. Then I noticed two more on the lower branch of an adjacent bush. I came in beaming all over; my folks looked at me as if I was quite mad. I didn’t bother, in fact they soon got used to me grabbing my camera and running every time the chicks started calling frantically. Indication that it was feeding time. The next day I was overjoyed to see a total of four fledglings. This was too good!

The female then went and pulled out another worm from the mud like she was showing them from where the worms came. Their hunting classes had started. Of course it may be conjecture on my part but I felt that Papa took the advanced classes on how to catch flying insects etc. Day by day the juveniles started flying longer distances; they started perching on the wires. I noticed that all the juveniles were not developing equally. One guy/gal was a bit slow and was depending on the parents to bring food a little longer than the others. Pied Bushchat fledglings Every day, I started watching them being fed. How they would scream their heads off when the parent approached them with food! I don’t know how the parent decided which one to give the food to – possibly the loudest one got the first morsel. Pied Bushchat in transition to adult plumage Pied Bushchat fledgling begging to be fed Slowly they started taking small flights. I thoroughly enjoyed watching them hop clumsily on the branches; I would chuckle silently while they learned to control their landings instead of crashing face first into the bush. One day, as usual, I parked myself in my patio waiting for the show; Mama Bushchat arrived on the scene first, with a worm in its beak. She went up to the juveniles which were waiting eagerly for grub. Instead of doling out the yummy worm Mama flew to the nearby mound of rubble (the construction debris) and threw the worm on the ground. Then the day came when none of them were seen; I kept checking the whole day but nope, no signs of them. 3-4 days later I saw one of the juveniles – he had started developing male adult plumage! “Bacche bade ho gaye,” I thought while grinning from ear to ear. I heard my better half mumbling something that sounded like Paagalpan etc etc... I was so addicted to the whole activity every day; it had become a part of my routine. I will definitely miss them but was also glad they all had survived and made it to adulthood. Maybe I wouldn’t even recognize if one of them came and nested in the same place again next year. Pied Bushchat fledgling looking for the worm in the rubble Indian Silverbill with nesting material The little ones were bewildered at first but slowly understood. One of them picked up the worm and ate it.

Scaly-breasted Munia *** Notes on Observation of Barn Owl in Hyderabad, 2015-2020 Rajashekar Tummala Barn Owl (File photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) I have seen the Barn Owl (Tyto alba) several times in Gokul Nagar, Tarnaka, in Cherlallapally near the Jail area and in Lalapet marshy area, along the discarded factories in Cherlapally area over the past five years. The locality has many old workshops and railway warehouses since the 1930s which abut our colony. In our area a lot of old Neem trees are still existing along the avenue roads. Here I have heard them calling, and have observed expelled pellets containing remnants of hair and parts of skull/bones of rodents. As these birds are local migrants, I have seen adult as well as juvenile birds. I have tried to dispel the misconceptions of the local people and educate them about the ecological importance of the Barn Owl; also, I have tried to ensure that the green canopy and native trees in our colony are maintained, thus providing a conducive and safe environment for other avian visitors like Red-vented Bulbuls, Ashy Prinias, Common Tailorbirds, Purple Sunbirds, Rose-ringed Parakeets, etc. I have also been requesting house-owners not to hack the old dead trees, as they serve as owl perches. I have noted a marked decrease of the Lesser Bandicoot Rat (Bandicota bengalensis) due to the presence of Barn Owls. As a result, since more than two years, rodent control pills are not used in my apartment complex, and the water collected in the rain water pit is also pure, without any chemical traces. It is evident that the presence of Barn Owls brings many benefits. The Barn Owl is easily identified by its heart-shaped, milky white facial disc, white underparts, and spotted brown-grey upperparts. It is in the size of a crow and primarily hunts rodents at night, mostly through sound. It is hard to distinguish whether it is a male or female while in flight, but a closer look may give a clue: females often have darker brown feathers around the rim of the facial disc, as well as darker bars on the tail and small black spots on the chest and underside of the wings. Females are slightly heavier than males at around 360gm (males usually weigh around 330gm). However, during the early breeding season, females may weigh as much as 425gm before egg laying.

Breeding season of the Barn Owl is all through the year. Barn Owls swallow their prey whole – including skin, bones, etc – and expel or cough up the undigested material, instead of it passing through their digestive system. These owls are endowed with excellent low-light vision, and can pin-point the prey at night by sight, but also have the ability to locate their prey by sound. They can locate rodents (mice) in complete darkness, not just in controlled conditions of the laboratory – out in the real world too, they are adept hunters. A bird to observe for the night owls! crevices of barns and silos near agrarian settings. They are distributed across all the continents except Antarctica. In India, Barn Owls are protected and listed in the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and under Schedule-IV of the Act. In Hindu Mythology, the Barn Owl is often depicted in paintings as the ‘vahan’ or vehicle of Goddess Lakshmi. They are one of the most persecuted species in India and the Middle East owing to superstition: in dim light their white, heart-shaped face gives them a ghost-like appearance and their high-pitched shrieks are considered a bad omen. Farmers, however, generally recognize their ecological importance and role in keeping rodents in check. They are widely used in Israel’s Kibbutz farming communes, and in parts of Southern Ontario and Canada/British-Isles, for this purpose. They are found in the forest fringes, villages, open grasslands, old buildings abutting farm lands, etc. They roost in the Barn Owl (female juvenile) roosting on neem tree (Photo: Rajashekar Tummala) *** Some Garden Birds of Amberpet, Hyderabad Text and Photos: Dr G Samuel Sukumar Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (juvenile) The Lockdown from April 2020 onwards, due to Covid-19, brought the world to a complete standstill. With nowhere to go, I decided to concentrate on improving my garden. One morning near the end of May, I heard a familiar call of a Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (Cyornis tickelliae). I started to scan the undergrowth, only to see a juvenile. At first, I thought it could be an Indian Robin due its underparts being mostly greyishbrown. I quickly brought my camera to photograph this bird. The bird only came out occasionally and did not give me a clear shot. About a week later, one afternoon, it again appeared close by and tolerated me at a distance of about 20 feet. I took the opportunity to photograph it all around the garden. Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (juvenile)

When the garden was cleared of weeds and dry twigs it was on its job of collecting insects and caterpillars – a master in hunting. I, now, realised it was showing its presence more visibly because cleaning of the undergrowth made food available to it. Its plumage was still developing into the typical blue and orange. A few days back, in mid-July, it showed its presence again, albeit briefly. This time the plumage had already turned into its adult colours. Birding during the lockdown was confined to our backyards. During this period I have seen many birds around the house – Purple-rumped Sunbirds (Leptocoma zeylonica), Red-vented Bulbuls (Pycnonotus cafer), House Crows (Corvus splendens), Asian Koel (Eudynamys scolopaceus), Ashy Prinias (Prinia socialis), Tickell’s (or Pale-billed) Flowerpecker (Dicaeum erythrorhynchos), Common Mynas (Acridotheres tristis), Indian Grey Hornbills (Ocyceros birostris), Common Tailorbirds (Orthotomus sutorius), Spotted Doves (Stigmatopelia chinensis) and the Shikra (Accipiter badius). Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Striated Heron (Butorides striata) Striated Heron Striated Heron foraging in typical habitat (Chennai, January-February, 2015) Order: Pelecaniformes Family: Ardeidae Genus: Butorides Species: B. striata Size: 40-48 cm waiting patiently to ambush prey, which it usually picks up by stabbing into the water as the prey passes by. It is known to sometimes use bait, dropping a small leaf or feather on the water, and grabbing the fish that come to investigate. Younger birds sometimes give a threat display, stretching out their necks and pointing their bills to the sky. Its diet mainly consists of small fish, frogs, crabs, shrimps and aquatic insects. It is reasonably confiding, and has similar habits to, but is not seen as easily as, the Indian Pond Heron. Its flight is steady and typically heron-like, with its neck pulled in. It is a relatively silent bird, but the primary call is a sharp keeuuk, usually uttered in flight or as an alarm or advertising call. A sneezing tech-aah call and a softer hoo call are reported during courting. Description & distribution: The Striated Heron is a small heron and is also known as the Little Green Heron, Little Heron, Mangrove Heron or Green-backed Heron. It is a resident breeder in most of its range, from parts of western Africa east to Japan and Australia, and in South America. The adult has blue-grey, steel-grey or grey-buff back and wings (which can also have some patterning), ashy grey or white underparts with a buff wash, white chin and throat, black cap and short yellow legs. The bill has a darker upper mandible and a patchy blackand-yellow lower mandible, and a black stripe running from the base of the bill below the eye and some distance behind. The sexes are alike, while the juvenile is brownish and dark-spotted above and has streaked underparts. Nesting: The Striated Heron breeds generally between March and August, with some local variations, but usually in the rainy season. However, they have been known to nest three times a year, and hence the nesting season may vary. The nest is a rough stick platform, built singly – not in colonies – in trees, bushes or shrubs overhanging water, or in a mangrove swamp. The usual clutch consists of 3-5 pale greenish-blue eggs. Habitat & behaviour: The Striated Heron prefers small wetlands, stagnant water or slow-running streams, mangrove swamps or intertidal creeks. It is usually crepuscular, but can also be active in the daytime, especially on overcast days or in shady spots with bushes near the water. It is generally seen singly at the edge of the water or on overhanging branches, Local name: The Striated Heron is known as ‘Kancha bagla’ in Hindi, ‘Dosi konga’ in Telugu, ‘Chinna kokku’ in Malayalam, and ‘Doshi kokku’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 17 Number 8 July 2020 (Special Issue) SPECIAL ISSUE – SATTAL & MANDAL

Editor’s note Some of our members had been to Sattal & Mandal in Uttarakhand for a week-long birding trip from December 15 th to 21st, 2019. In this Special Issue of the Pitta, we are happy to bring you an account of the trip, along with a number of colourful photographs. We hope you will find this Special Issue interesting. A WEEK IN PARADISE Report: Sattal & Mandal, December 15-21, 2019 Smita Chatterjee & Gurukumar KR A view of snow-capped peaks at Chopta (Photo: Gurukumar KR) The foothills of the Himalayas are a haven for the most colourful birds we see in India and many are endemic to this region. The planning for a trip to this wonderland of birds started a few months earlier, thanks to the organizers from Deccan Birders. Although the initial plan was to visit Munsiyari, heavy winter snowfall in the area prevented us from going there. Due to the efficient planning of the organizers we did not have to cancel the entire trip but went instead to Sattal, Mandal and Chopta areas of Uttarakhand. As the trip was a first time visit to the Himalayan region for many of us, we were fortunate to be part of a group which included some extremely knowledgeable birders. We started counting days as soon as we confirmed our participation. The day came and we landed in Delhi. After a little confusion in finding other friends through Google Maps, ‘few’ phone calls, and last minute shopping by some of us, we all got together at the meeting point. We took a night bus from Delhi to Kathgodam. It was fun being among people like Lawrence sir, Geetanjali, Anita and others and the discussions during the journey were lively and comfortable. We reached Kathgodam in the morning and travelled by road for one and a half hours to Sattal in two vehicles. As we got down from our vehicles, we could see a lot of birds near our Hotel premises itself – Himalayan Bulbul (Pycnonotus leucogenys), Russet Sparrow (Passer rutilans), House Sparrow (Passer domesticus), Oriental White-eye (Zosterops palpebrosus) and others. Russet Sparrow (female) (Photo: Umesh Mani) Himalayan Bulbul (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Russet Sparrow (male) (Photo: Gurukumar KR)

The sight that greeted us the first morning was a magnificent sunrise right across our rooms. It was such a treat for the eyes and a reminder that the landscapes were as mesmerizing as the birds. Dheeraj got a Blue-fronted Redstart (Pheonicurus frontalis) nearby that whetted our appetites for more. Slaty-headed Parakeet (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Blue-fronted Redstart (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) At around 6:00AM we eagerly started our first bird walk. Immediately after walking for some distance, we started spotting the birds – Black (Hypsipetes leucocephalus), Ashy (Hemixos flavala) and Himalayan Bulbuls, Slaty-headed Parakeet (Psittacula himalayana), Blue Whistling Thrush (Myophonus caeruleus), Velvet-fronted Nuthatch (Sitta frontalis), Bar-tailed Treecreeper (Certhia himalayana), Greyhooded Warbler (Phylloscopus xanthoschistos), Blackthroated Tit (Aegithalos concinnus), Lemon-rumped Warbler (Phylloscopus chloronotus) and Black-lored Tit (Parus xanthogenys). Ashy Bulbul (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) Velvet-fronted Nuthatch (Photo: Umesh Mani) Black Bulbul (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Bar-tailed Treecreeper (Photo: Gurukumar KR)

Grey-hooded Warbler (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) Black-lored Tit (Photo: Umesh Mani) Yellow-bellied Fantail (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Black-throated Tit (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) We, then, visited an interesting place known as the Studio. This was a location with a small stream of water flowing in to a small pond, along which a couple of bird perches and a few stones had been arranged. A lot of birds visited the stream for a sip of water and a quick bath. We got to see the Rufousgorgeted Flycatcher (Ficedula strophiata) here but nothing much else happened here on our first visit, as it was already a little late in the morning. In the afternoon session we visited Chafi and Khasi Rivers. Here we got to see the Yellow-bellied Fantail (Chelidorhynx hypoxantha), White-capped (Chaimarrornis leucocephalus) and Plumbeous Water Redstarts (Rhyacornis fuliginosa), Slaty-backed Forktail (Enicurus schistaceus), Great Barbet (Megalaima virens), Crested Kingfisher (Megaceryle lugubris), Grey Treepie (Dendrocitta formosae), Streaked Laughingthrush (Garrulax lineatus), and the most interesting bird, the Brown Dipper (Cinclus pallasii). It was very cutely diving inside the water to look for food and coming back on to the rocks. I was seeing this unusual behaviour of a bird for the first time. Brown Dipper (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Rufous-gorgeted Flycatcher (Photo: Smita Chatterjee)

White-capped (L) & Plumbeous Water Redstart (R) (Photo: Umesh Mani) Crested Kingfisher (Photo: Gurukumar KR) The next morning, we sat in a ‘bird hide’ for a couple of hours. A hide is a small enclosed space from where birders can sit and observe birds without disturbing them. It was made of some green net-like material. For the photographers, a narrow plank was made on which they could rest their cameras and capture images of the lovely birds from a very short distance. The birds were fed at a particular time by local caretakers. At the appointed time, once the food was placed, it was a riot of birds. Never had we seen so many birds in such colourful plumage, and from this short a distance. White-crested Laughingthrush (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Grey-headed Woodpecker (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) The birds we saw here were Grey-headed Woodpecker (Picus canus), Brown-fronted Woodpecker (Dendrocopos auriceps), Greater Yellownape (Picus flavinucha), Kalij Pheasant (Lophura leucomelanos), Red Junglefowl (Gallus gallus), Common Green Magpie (Cissa chinensis), Whitethroated (Garrulax albogularis) and White-crested (Garrulax leucolophus) Laughingthrushes, a big flock of Oriental Turtle Doves (Streptopelia orientalis), Red-billed Blue Magpie (Urocissa erythrorhyncha) and Grey Treepie. Greater Yellownape (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) Common Green Magpie (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Rufous-chinned Laughingthrush (Photo: Gurukumar KR) The interesting thing to note here was that a few species came in big flocks, stayed there for some time and flew away as another species came in. We reluctantly left the place when our guide told us to wind up. The hide did help us see a lot of birds in a short time and photograph them from a very short distance. The experience was like a movie and suddenly it was all over. Red-billed Blue Magpie (Photo: Gurukumar KR) From Sattal we started to Mandal. The journey took us nearly ten hours along winding roads through huge ice-capped mountains – it was so wonderful! En route, we saw a Wallcreeper (Tichodroma muraria) literally creeping on the steep valley walls. Wallcreeper (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) Steppe Eagle (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Himalayan Griffon (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Grey Bushchat (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Eurasian Jay (Photo: Gurukumar KR)

Other birds we saw en route were Steppe Eagles (Aquila nipalensis), Himalayan Griffon (Gyps himalayensis), Common Kestrel (Falco tinnunculus), Striated Prinia (Prinia crinigera), Grey Bushchat (Saxicola ferreus), Jungle Babblers (Turdoides striata), Grey Treepie, House Sparrow, Lesser Yellownape (Picus chlorolophus), Bay-backed Shrike (Lanius vittatus), Black-headed Jay (Garrulus lanceolatus), Eurasian Jay (Garrulus glandarius), Rufous Sibia (Malacias capistratus), and others. As we started gaining altitude, the temperatures were plummeting. We reached Mandal, where we were to stay for the next four days. It is a small town and the place we stayed in was comfortable and cosy. White-throated Laughingthrush (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Black-headed Jay (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Brown-fronted Woodpecker (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) Rufous Sibia (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Next morning our birding started with a session at another hide. It was really cold and our fingers were numb. Taking pictures while wearing hand gloves was quite challenging, but that did not dampen our enthusiasm. Some of the species we saw were White-throated Laughingthrush, White-crested Laughingthrush, Brown-fronted Woodpecker, Himalayan Woodpecker (Dendrocopos himalayensis), Scaly-bellied Woodpecker (Picus squamatus), amongst others. Himalayan Woodpecker (Photo: Gurukumar KR)

Scaly-bellied Woodpecker (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Chestnut-crowned Laughingthrush (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) We came back to the hotel for brunch, after which we headed out for another session of birding on foot. We split into two groups, each covering a different location with a guide. Both the groups saw different birds which were compiled later. Some of the birds were Blue-winged Siva (Siva cyanouroptera), Rusty-cheeked Scimitar Babbler (Pomatorhinus erythrogenys), Golden Bush Robin (Tarsiger chrysaeus), Striated Laughingthrush (Garrulax striatus), etc. Grey Treepie (Photo: Umesh Mani) Blue-winged Siva (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Rusty-cheeked Scimitar Babbler (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Streaked Laughingthrush (Photo: Bala CS Dasari)

Golden Bush Robin (female) (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Golden Bush Robin (male) (Photo: Gurukumar KR) The next day started with a flock of vibrantly coloured Scarlet Finches (Haematospiza sipahi). Initially they were too far, but after some time they came closer, delighting everyone, especially the photographers. We also spotted a pair of Asian Barred Owlets (Glaucidium cuculoides) in their hollow. Scarlet Finch female (L) and male (R) (Photo: Umesh Mani) Yellow-billed Blue Magpie holding head of White-throated Laughingthrush (Photo: Gurukumar KR) We attempted a trip to Chopta but had to return halfway due to the thick snow. En route, we spotted a Yellow-billed Blue Magpie (Urocissa flavirostris) holding the head of a Whitethroated Laughingthrush in its beak – an amazing sight – and a flock of Eurasian Jays in hot pursuit. Asian Barred Owlet (Photo: Gurukumar KR)

Another great sighting – seen only by a few of us, unfortunately – was the Collared Owlet (Glaucidium brodiei). Chestnut Thrush (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Collared Owlet (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) We returned to the hotel, cold and a little disappointed at being unable to bird properly. The next day, on the way to Chopta, we saw an assorted group of Thrushes – Chestnut Thrush (Turdus rubrocanus), Whitecollared Blackbird (Turdus albocinctus), Grey-winged Blackbird (Turdus boulboul) – and a few other birds, including the beautiful Himalayan Bluetail (Tarsiger rufilatus). White-collared Blackbird (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Himalayan Bluetail (male) (Photo: Bala CS Dasari) Grey-winged Blackbird (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Himalayan Bluetail (female) (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Bar-throated Siva (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati)

Chopta is famous for one of the most colourful and beautiful birds – the Himalayan Monal (Lophophorus impejanus). We had good sightings; some were quite far but, thanks to Anita, one was seen very near. Chopta was covered in snow and watching the contrast of the colourful Monals on this snow was amazing. (Hemitragus jemlahicus), Golden Jackal (Canis aureus) and Yellow-throated Martens (Martes flavigula) along with many colourful birds during our stay at Mandal. Himalayan Tahr (Photo: Umesh Mani) Himalayan Monal (male) (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) Yellow-throated Marten (Photo: Umesh Mani) The weather now started to play spoilsport and it started snowing heavily. We were faced with the risk of getting stuck in Mandal if the weather turned worse. However, if the weather did not worsen, we could get a chance to see one of the Himalayan endemics like, possibly, the Western Tragopan or one of the other pheasants. But on balance, the risk seemed too much, and we decided to go back to Sattal and spend an extra day birding there. Himalayan Monal (female) (Photo: Umesh Mani) Dog with head of monkey (Photo: Umesh Mani) Golden Jackal (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Many of us were seeing snow for the first time, and we were so excited that we started playing in the snow like kids. During our drives, we also saw mammals like the Himalayan Tahr There were some Himalayan dogs around, and they seemed lively and extremely friendly. We thought they were very cute and playful, but one day, we were shocked when we found that one of them had managed to charge up to a monkey and kill it! It had grabbed the monkey some time after we had left for our bird walk in the morning, and when we returned all that remained was the monkey’s head and an arm firmly held between its paws – like a trophy. We realized that however calm and mild-mannered the pets could be, they still do harbour a wild, killer instinct.

Streak-breasted Scimitar Babbler (Photo: Gurukumar KR) We started our journey back to Sattal after a 4-day stay at Mandal. This was the day we all learned another lesson – never to leave behind one’s camera or birding gear for a cup of tea! We had entered a town on the confluence of Karna Prayag. As it was a crowded place with a lot of human activity, we thought there would be very less chances of spotting birds. We all got down from the bus to have breakfast. While getting down from the bus, everyone left their long lenses and cameras, and carried only their smartphones. We went to a hotel with a small terrace facing the Alaknanda and Pindar river confluence and the mountains. As we were eating breakfast, a huge raptor suddenly swept across in front of everyone and took off into the valley. It was the White-tailed Eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla)! A very rare raptor, and a lifer even for the more experienced birders in the group – and we suddenly realized that none of us had a camera to capture this moment. No one could get a good picture as it flew very far, and there wasn’t a single person in the group who did not regret leaving their cameras behind. After a little discussion with our guides, we decided to turn and drive back to try and locate it. We drove back around 2km – which, in those roads, meant a drive of a couple of hours! – and were fortunate enough to find this raptor again. Great Barbet (Photo: Umesh Mani) Green-tailed Sunbird (female) (Photo: Smita Chatterjee) Green-tailed Sunbird (male) (Photo: Umesh Mani) White-tailed Eagle (Photo: Bala CS Dasari) It was an exhilarating sighting. We were awestruck by the knowledge of the birders in this group about birds which they had not even seen earlier and yet, knew so much about them. We reached Sattal that evening. It rained all night and was still drizzling the next day. It was so nice to see everyone’s enthusiasm to go birdwatching even in such weather. We saw the White-browed Scimitar Babbler (Pomatorhinus schisticeps), Great Barbet, female of the Green-tailed Sunbird (Aethopyga nipalensis), and the Rufous-bellied Niltava (Niltava sundara), which had such attractive colours and shone beautifully.

Brown Fish Owl (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) Rufous-bellied Niltava (male) (Photo: Dheeraj Chavadi) We went back to the Studio for some time, and today, we did watch several birds having fun bathing in the cold water of the stream – we saw the Rufous-gorgeted Flycatcher, Whitethroated Laughingthrush and many others. We learned a lot about different species and their behaviour. It was an awesome experience, mainly because we were amongst such experienced birders. We would like to thank Srikanth, Sudhir and the other members of Deccan Birders for organizing this trip. The stay and other arrangements were just perfect and the birding, absolutely blissful – so much so that we would love to go to this place again and again to observe many more species. White-throated Laughingthrush (Photo: Gurukumar KR) We also saw a huge Brown Fish Owl (Ketupa zeylonensis) near the lake. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 17 Number 10 August 2020 DECCAN BIRDERS EVENTS In light of the Corona virus (COVID-19) epidemic, all Deccan Birders Field Trips and Indoor Meetings are on hold until further notice. Details of upcoming activities will be communicated once the situation improves. GOD BE WITH YE, ASHOK! JVD Moorty Deccan Birders has lost a dedicated birder, friend and member. G Ashok Kumar passed away on August 14, 2020 after a heart attack in the hours after having partaken dinner with his family. This was the only illness he suffered in his life. will be remembered by all. He was persistent about inviting our birders to Nizamabad, and a wonderful host – he always ensured that food and hospitality were the best. He last played host to a small group of birders in February 2020. Ashok was a warm, welcoming, and kind person with a positive outlook on life and a fundamental faith in humanity. He could always put you at ease with his candour and there wasn’t a person who did not feel close to him. He loved to tell stories and his one-liners never failed to raise a laugh. His passion for nature led him to the founding of an NGO in Nizamabad, the Maya Foundation, which works towards the promotion of sustainable development. His love for learning shows in his establishing and running a school as well, and all this while pursuing his career as a banker with the Syndicate Bank. While he regretted his lack of mastery over English, he was still very proud of his Telugu heritage. Ashok had a passion for bird watching, ever since he became a member in the year 2000, and he combined his other hobby – photography – with his love for nature. There wasn’t a single birding camp, either in India or abroad, that he missed. His quick wit, infectious smile, and kind and compassionate spirit He leaves behind a grieving wife, son and daughter. May his soul find eternal peace.

Source: https://kaavyaalaya.org/satpura_ke_ghane_jungle (Translated into English by Abhishek Shroti) My narration of a recent trip to Satpura Tiger Reserve could not be complete without this beautiful poem by the legendary poet, Shri Bhavani Prasad Mishra. Ever since my childhood days, the verses of this poem have enticed me into visiting these forests and, possibly, have played a role in drawing me towards nature. MADHAI Since my last visit in 1992, I have had two opportunities to visit these forests in quick succession. My first trip, in April 2019, was to the northern end of the forests near Madhai, and the next, in December of the same year, to a famous hill station named Pachmarhi, also called the “Queen of Satpura”. Both the trips were short but quite fulfilling in terms of enjoying nature and watching birds. Let me first start with the trip to Madhai. Bison Resort

Place of stay – We stayed at Bison Resort - an excellent place. However, there are several other options, including the Forest Department guest house at the edge of the forest. Nearest Airports – Jabalpur and Bhopal (a 4-hour journey by road from either place) Nearest Railway Station – Sohagpur on the Itarsi-Jabalpur line Red-wattled Lapwing Dense forests of Madhai, where the safaris take place Black-bellied Tern Sonbhadra River We went to Madhai in April 2019, not generally considered the best time to visit the place. Since this area offers a varied topography of backwaters and dense forests, a visit during January to March can be very fulfilling in terms of watching birds. When we went there, there was hardly any water in the dam, but with whatever little water it had, we saw a great variety of birds. Woolly-necked Stork A detailed list is given at the end of the article, but some of the highlights among the birds we saw near the water were:     River Lapwing    Terns – River Tern, Whiskered Tern, Little Tern and Black-bellied Tern; Lapwings – Red-wattled Lapwing and River Lapwing; Storks – Asian Openbill and Woolly-necked Stork; Ducks – Garganey, Knob-billed Duck, Indian Spot-billed Duck and Ruddy Shelduck; Stints – Little Stint & Temminck’s Stint; Egyptian Vulture; Yellow Wagtail, etc.

We could see a number of Gaur, Sambhar, Spotted Deer, Indian Giant Squirrels and a Sloth Bear. Unfortunately, we could not spot any tigers. Ruddy Shelduck Temminck’s Stint and Little Ringed Plover The river valley where tigers are often seen Sal forests of Satpuda, possibly the easternmost Sal forests in India Yellow Wagtail The trip to the forest was, essentially, a tiger safari. Hence, birding was basically done from the vehicle. These forests are truly impressive with a great variety of flora and fauna. Jungle Owlet Sloth Bear quenching its thirst Indian Scops Owl

Mottled Wood Owl But the trip was quite satisfying from the bird perspective. Some of the other birds we spotted were:      Crested Serpent Eagle Owls – Jungle Owlet, Indian Scops Owl and Mottled Wood Owl; Raptors – Crested Serpent Eagle, Oriental Honey-buzzard, White-eyed Buzzard, Changeable Hawk Eagle and Indian Vulture; Minivets – Small Minivet and Scarlet Minivet; Tits – Cinereous Tit and Indian Yellow Tit; Puff-throated Babbler; etc. Natural salt flats where animals lick the mud to obtain minerals There is a lot to explore here, including a night safari in the buffer zone and the huge expanse of agriculture fields that have their own wonders including large herds of Blackbuck. Notes on Sighting of Rufous-bellied Eagle in Telangana and its Status in Eastern Ghats Srikanth Bhamidipati, Humayun Taher, Sudhir Moorti, Gokul Krishna Addanki, Lawrence Mathappan, Rishi Reddy (7 Yrs) Rufous-bellied Eagle (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) The Rufous-bellied Eagle (Lophotriorchis kienerii) is a bird of prey in the family Accipitridae that is found in the forested regions of tropical Asia. Relatively small for eagles and contrastingly patterned like a falcon, this species was earlier placed in the genus Hieraaetus. Adult Rufous-bellied Eagles are very distinctive in the field. They have a black hood with a short crest. Chestnut underparts and wing coverts contrast with the white on the throat and breast. The sexes are similar, but females are slightly larger and have more black on the face. They perch in a very upright stance and the wingtips almost reach the end of the tail. The tarsi are fully feathered. Juveniles have very white underparts with dark markings on the sides of the body, head mask and edge of underwing coverts. They can appear similar to a lightphase Booted Eagle (Aquila pennata). In flight, the underwing lining is dark and the greater coverts are black. The flight feathers are thinly barred with a black edge, and the tail is dark and barred. The species is traditionally known from the Western Ghats. The distribution, as given in the Handbook (Ali & Ripley, 1987) is “Resident. With a curiously discontinuous Indo-Malayan distribution: Eastern Himalayas from (Nepal?), Sikkim to E. Assam, Manipur, E. Pakistan; the Western Ghats strip in South India from c. Goa and N. Mysore through Kerala (up to c. 1200 m), and Ceylon (all zones). Absent in the intervening country.” On a recent visit to Umamaheshwaram temple area in the Nallamala Hills on June 13, 2020, a single adult Rufous-bellied Eagle was sighted in flight. Photographs were taken and the sighting was very clear. This sighting prompted us to go further into the details of the distribution of this species in the Eastern Ghats, and several records started to emerge. Almost a month later, there was another sighting of a juvenile bird from Adilabad District on July 11, 2020 by a Forest Department official. GARP Predictive Models, using a computational procedure with 16 records (Shyamal, 2007) showed a strong probability of the species also occurring in the Eastern Ghats, even though the original subset of 16 records did not include any records from the Eastern Ghats as, at that time, the only published record was a sighting from the Tirumala Hills by members of the then BSAP (Taher, 1992). So even though the species was not supposedly found in the Eastern Ghats, it was likely that the stray record from the Tirumala Hills was not just a vagrant. However, over time there were very few records that came in from the Eastern Ghats strip, so the single record stood as a vagrant sighting. Records from our own sightings from the Eastern Ghats are given in the below table: Number Date of Sighting Location Region 1 August 25, 1990 Japali, Tirumala Hills Eastern Ghats 1 October 10, 2016 Maredumilli Forest Eastern Ghats 1 November 13, 2016 Japali, Tirumala Hills Eastern Ghats 1 August 13, 2017 Maredumilli Forest Eastern Ghats 1 June 13, 2020 Umamaheshwaram, Nallamala Hills Eastern Ghats The availability of eBird records has significantly helped in getting details of other sightings of this species, and we have found several records from the Eastern Ghats strip. Mapping these sightings along the Eastern Ghats, we can see that the data covers almost the entire range. However, we cannot discount the Western Ghats records; more so because this species was originally predominantly known only from the Western Ghats. There are close to 750 sightings and records in eBird, and these covers all of the calendar months. There are also confirmed breeding records from the Kerala region. Another interesting – and important – observation we made, based on the data from personal records and from eBird, was that the species may well be a resident in Eastern Ghats, with sightings during 10 months of the year (all months excepting September and December).

Additional records from the region would be extremely interesting and may help to strengthen this argument. References & Bibliography: 1) Ali, S & Ripley, S D (1987): Compact Handbook of the Birds of India and Pakistan, together with those of Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Sri Lanka. Oxford University Press, India 2) Shyamal, L. (2007): Opinion: Taking Indian ornithology into the Information Age. Indian Birds 3 (4): 122–137. 3) Taher, H. (1992): Rufousbellied Hawk-Eagle Hieraaetus kienerii (E. Geoffroy) in Andhra Pradesh. J. Bombay Nat. Hist. Soc. 19 (3): 368. Map showing sightings recorded in the Eastern Ghats Although the current data set from the Eastern Ghats is not exhaustive, it still allows us to make a reasonable assumption that the Rufous-bellied Eagle has two different populations in Southern India, and that the sightings from the eastern regions point to the probability of there being a separate and distinct population of the species in the Eastern Ghats. 4) Map courtesy: Google Earth (Version 9.3.114.1) 5) Data sets: eBird – extracted on 8-Jul-2020 *** Notes on Observation of a Melanistic Large Grey Babbler in and around Hyderabad Text and Photos: Humayun Taher Melanistic Large Grey Babbler In the second week of August, there was a discussion on the Deccan Birders WhatsApp group on colour aberrations in avian species, with particular reference to leucism and melanism in birds. I pointed out a couple of old, known photographic records of melanistic (or at least dark-coloured) birds and the discussion sparked off other members also sharing their own sightings of aberrant dark-coloured birds. Melanism is not all that well-known amongst birds, particularly dryland birds. One of the reasons for this is that frequently the colour aberration is found to be extraneous (the most common is if the birds have been foraging in a burnt area and have become partially or fully covered in soot). However, it is instructive to note that in recent times, several instances of melanistic specimens have been recorded for different species of birds. These records occasionally appear on social media, and for a few hours there is a furious discussion and several congratulatory messages, and then the furore dies down and the record gets lost. This particular record also was in similar danger, and so I felt it would better if it were documented. On Sunday, April 15, 2018, members of the erstwhile Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh (BSAP) had visited the Nehru Zoological Park in Hyderabad for a field trip. During this trip, towards the later part of the morning (at approximately 09:30AM) a flock of Large Grey Babblers (Argya malcolmi) was seen foraging on the leaf litter. This flock seemed composed of two different groups, as there were more than 11 birds around. One group of 6 was of particular interest as there were two birds in the group showing distinct melanistic properties. One of the birds was almost completely black, while the second was dark brown with a few black feathers on the flanks, quite unlike the usual dusty grey-brown plumage. In the second group of 5 birds, there was a single all-black specimen, very similar to the black one in the first group. Photographs of the birds were obtained for record.

Babbler Turdoides striata (Pande et al. 2003, Mahabal et al. 2016). Some other members came forward with their records (on the earlier mentioned WhatsApp thread) – Aasheesh Pittie recollects a flock seen near the Public Gardens; Srikanth Bhamidipati also remembers a flock from this area and mentioned that he has photos of his sighting also. Aasheesh further mentions a record from Banjara Hills, and Kishore Bakshi has seen one near Kokapet, and he says he might have a photograph too. All these are records of Large Grey Babblers. Even if some of these records are what might be termed ‘artificial colours’ (which can happen if the birds have been foraging in soot covered areas), still it seems that there is sufficient evidence here to suggest that melanism in this species might perhaps be more prevalent than is commonly supposed. Partially melanistic Large Grey Babbler I was curious to see what I could find about melanism in the Turdoides species and did some checking online to retrieve relevant literature, via the online ‘Bibliography of South Asian Ornithology’ (Pittie, 2018). To my surprise, though I found some reference to albinism, I was unable to find any reference to melanism in Babblers. Wikipedia tells me that "This longtailed and large babbler has a brown body with creamy white outer tail feathers which are easily visible as they fly with fluttery wing beats low over the ground. The lores are dark and forehead is grey with white shaft streaks on the feathers. The rump and uppertail coverts are pale grey. The mantle has dusky blotches and no shaft streaks. The three outer tail feathers are white and the fourth pair has the outer web white. The wings are dark brown. The iris is yellow and the upper mandible is dark brown, while the lower mandible is yellowish. The tail is faintly cross barred. Abnormal specimens showing albinism or leucism have been reported.” This therefore becomes an interesting record, as yet another instance of melanism in the Large Grey Babbler. I would be very keen to know if other members have any similar observations. References: 1. Ali, S. & S.D. Ripley (1989): Compact Handbook of the Birds of India and Pakistan. Oxford University Press, New Delhi. That monumental work on Indian Birds – Compact Handbook of the Birds of India and Pakistan – also has no reference of melanism in the Large Grey Babblers. I checked against other babbler species and again could not find any known reference to melanistic specimens, although it seems that albino or leucistic specimens are not unknown amongst almost all the babbler species. The only known reference to melanism that I have been able to source is a possible instance in Jungle 2. Bird of the Month Umesh Mani White-bellied Minivet (Pericrocotus erythropygius) White-bellied Minivet Male (Zaheerabad, Sangareddy Dt, July 11, 2020) (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) White-bellied Minivet Female (Zaheerabad, Sangareddy Dt, July 19, 2020) (Photo: Anand Kalinadhabhatla) Order: Passeriformes Family: Campephagidae Genus: Pericrocotus Species: P. erythropygius Size: 15 cm Habitat & behaviour: The White-bellied Minivet is usually seen in small groups of 6-8, in dry deciduous forest, open grassy forests, dry thorny scrub and grassy plains. It is less arboreal than the other Minivets, and is often seen coming down to the ground while foraging. Its diet consists mainly of spiders and other insects. Its flight is dipping and quite similar to that of the Wagtails. Its call is a whistling tseep tseep, also similar to the Wagtails. Description & distribution: The White-bellied Minivet is differentiated from the other Minivets by its mainly pied colouration. The male has a glossy black head, neck and upperparts, with a V-shaped white wing patch (when seen from behind) and white underparts, orange-red breast and rump, and a black tail. The female has dark grey head and upperparts with a white forehead, black wings showing white wing patches similar to the male, dark lores, white and orange rump and black tail. Nesting: The White-bellied Minivet breeds generally between June and October. The nest is a small fibre cup coated with down and cobwebs, usually placed in a vertical or horizontal fork of a bush. The usual clutch consists of 3 greyish-white eggs covered with grey-brown blotches. Local name: The White-bellied Minivet is known as ‘Safed rajalal’ in Hindi, ‘Kabao rajalal’ in Gujarati and ‘Chitti saheli’ in Punjabi. The White-bellied Minivet is found in India (Peninsular India south-east of a line from Ambala to Belgaum and the Deccan in the south, and east to west Bihar and south-east Bengal) and in Nepal. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034.
