BIRDING DURING PANDEMIC TIMES Report: Bodhan, Dt Nizamabad, June-July 2020 Text & Photos: Mohd Adnan Uddin A view of Bodhan It was disturbing living alone in a flat in Hyderabad and working from home, while the world, at large, was grappling with a pandemic. I was longing to be amidst nature and was waiting for the moment when I could finally go out and spend time in the wilderness. For a number of reasons, I had not been birding regularly as I used to. The lockdown had made me even more restless and I was yearning to break free. As soon as travel was permitted, I rode all the way to my hometown on May 23, 2020, and the very next morning I left for the nearby Bellal Lake for birdwatching. That was the moment I realized what I had been missing for so long! My hometown Bodhan (District Nizamabad) is located in the north-western region in Telangana. Although the town has historical significance, it achieved recognition for having one of the biggest sugar factories in Asia – Nizam Deccan Sugars Limited (NDSL). Unfortunately, the factory is closed now but it left us with some fond memories. Agriculture and allied activities form the backbone of the town’s economy. Bodhan has predominantly black soil, formed from rocks of cretaceous lava. As the region falls under the Deccan plateau, large piles of rocks are strewn all over the town, some of them really huge. The rocks are related to the Archaean and Deccan Trap formations. Several folktales are associated with the rocks found near Bellal Lake in the town. 1

When I reached my town, the summer season was coming to an end but there was no respite from the heat although it was late May. After the confinement in the city, though, it was refreshing to spend time in the open verdant surroundings amidst the chattering of birds, as they went about their business. I was able to spot several common birds near the lake. reeds nearby and a bird rose from the reeds and flew towards a tree. I immediately pointed my camera towards it and got a few pictures. Within a few days, monsoon set in and the transformation of landscape was fascinating. The Indian monsoon lays a green carpet on earth and it is enthralling to see how the everyday landscape completely transforms after the rains. It is as if the engines of nature get oiled during the monsoons. Monsoon also heralds the start of breeding season for many species. There is increased availability of food, and nesting activity and courtship rituals become commonplace. I would regularly frequent places in my town, especially around Bellal Lake. Every visit of mine resulted in the discovery of different bird species and the numbers kept adding up every week. It wasn’t just the birds but also the diversity of species like butterflies, insects and reptiles that fascinated me. It was then I realized that I needed to document them. After all, documenting species of one’s own hometown is an honour. Years of birdwatching have made me appreciate the importance of patience and silent observation. The rewards have been great. I managed to find diverse species and was able to document many of them. Cinnamon Bittern When I saw the pictures, I could not contain my excitement – it was my first sighting of the Cinnamon Bittern (Ixobrychus cinnamomeus)! It is a shy bird which is very good at concealing itself. Though not overly secretive, it flies away on seeing humans. It is usually found near reedbeds and paddy fields, and is found throughout Asia, especially Southeast Asia. The bird feeds on fish, worms and frogs. I observed that the males fed mainly in the paddy fields, and, at dusk, took refuge in reedbeds or any trees nearby and rendered their characteristic croaking calls. Many a time I observed them perched on trees and calling continuously at dusk. There was once a small skirmish between two of the males. There were four males in all. If there is one bird that enthralled me the most in this trip, it is the Cinnamon Bittern. Indian Peafowl male displaying I spotted a good number of Indian Peafowl (Pavo cristatus). The State of India’s Birds 2020 Report has highlighted the growth in numbers of Indian Peafowl. Thanks to their loud may-awe calls, it is easy to detect their presence in the vicinity. These National Birds of India are commonly found foraging near agricultural fields, and are quite active at dawn and dusk. It is such a treat to watch their courtship behavior – the peacock displaying his fan-shaped crest and brightly coloured plumage to the peahen. I was able to catch this on camera. One day in mid-June, I was walking through a small stream near the lake when, suddenly, there was some movement in the Yellow Bittern A few days later, I spotted another Bittern – the Yellow Bittern (Ixobrychus sinensis). It inhabits vegetated wetlands and reedbeds and is really difficult to spot. Its habitat and behaviour are almost similar to that of the Cinnamon Bittern. Watching the bird move through the reeds by clinging to the leaves was a sight to behold! I found a breeding pair in the reedbeds near the lake. 2

winds of the monsoon, there is another population which is believed to be resident to India. Ruddy-breasted Crake On the same day, at the same spot, I spotted two elusive water birds – Ruddy-breasted Crake (Porzana fusca) and Brown Crake (Amaurornis akool). The birds belong to the Rail and Crake family, Rallidae. Found near marshes, Ruddy-breasted Crakes are extremely shy and rarely venture out from the reeds. With their long toes and short tails, they look very cute as they run around chasing insects on the ground. Pied Crested (or Jacobin) Cuckoo Birdwatchers in India have been trying to see the correlation between the first sighting of this Cuckoo and the onset of monsoons in India. Recently Dr Suresh Kumar from Wildlife Institute of India (WII) and his team have tagged a Pied Cuckoo with a satellite transmitter to study the migration of the species. The tagged bird has been named ‘Megh’, a short for ‘Meghdoot’, meaning ‘cloud messenger’. It will be interesting to see if the study unravels the legend of the bird. Indian Nightjar One day, as I was walking near the rocks, I suddenly saw a bird rush out near my feet. I realized immediately which bird it could possibly be – I had had similar experiences in the past when I had, unfortunately, missed seeing it. It was the Indian Nightjar (Caprimulgus asiaticus). Fortunately for me, it did not fly far away and rested on a rock nearby. Completely mesmerized by its presence, I slowly sat down on a rock and took a few pictures. After all, it is not easy to spot them as they are great masters of camouflage, blending spectacularly into their environment. Even at a short distance, it is quite difficult to spot them. A nocturnal bird, it snoozes during the day and gets active at dawn and dusk, scouting for insects. The Latin name of the bird translates to “goat sucker”, referring to an ancient myth that the bird sucks on the milk of goats in the night. However, their diet mainly consists of insects. They are such masters of disguise that I could not find the pair again after the initial sighting. I hope to see them soon again. Before the monsoon set in, I spotted the Pied Crested (or Jacobin) Cuckoo. Sighting this bird is considered welcome as it is said to herald the onset of monsoon in India. Although the bird is believed to reach India through Africa by riding the Jungle Cat Once, I was also rewarded with the sighting of a solitary Jungle Cat. It is usually shy and it is difficult to get a glimpse of it. As soon as I spotted the cat, it hid in the bushes and I had to spend quite some time, standing far, to just have a look at it. Finally, after a long wait, I finally caught a glimpse of it. A beautiful feline, its coat was a mix of reddish and sandy brown. Jungle Cats are mostly found near swampy and marshy areas and near reedbeds and paddy fields. They are carnivorous and their diet includes rodents, birds and small mammals. The town has two major crops – paddy and sugarcane. After the arrival of the monsoon, there was hectic sowing activity in the fields. I could see paddy cultivation everywhere I went. It provides the ideal habitat for various species, with its bountiful supply of food. The interaction between the species makes for interesting observations. 3

The constant chattering of the birds, and their displays on their nests, coupled with the inspection of the nests by female birds, makes for a very pleasant sight. Many a time I would sit nearby and simply observe the entire process. Indian Pond Heron The Indian Pond Heron (Ardeola grayii) is ubiquitous in paddy fields – no wonder it was also called the Paddybird. These birds are seen not only at the edges of the wetlands, but also in the fields, wading through water and feasting on worms and other insects. Baya Weaver Cattle Egrets (Bubulcus ibis) are also commonly found in agricultural fields, especially when tractors are tilling the soil. The movement of the vehicle disturbs the soil, thereby flushing the invertebrates, which are gleefully eaten by the birds. The Black Drongo (Dicrurus macrocercus) is another bird which is commonly seen perched on the wires across the agricultural fields. With its graceful, deep forked tail, the bird makes short bursts of flights to catch insects. I have always admired the fearless attitude of Drongos. They are quite protective of their territory – I once saw one chattering harshly and swooping down at a Shikra (Accipiter badius) and chasing it away! Drongos not only have a vast range of calls, they can also mimic other birds. I have noticed that Black Drongos roost quite late so, during my birding trips, I would usually spend some time even after sunset. Streaked Weaver I was also fortunate to spot a colony of Streaked Weavers (Ploceus manyar) near the lake. The birds were nesting on reeds near the lake bed. Their nest looks quite different from the one that the Baya Weavers build. The nest of a Streaked Weaver is retort-shaped, woven on to the leaves of the reeds. Black Drongo anting I have also observed anting behaviour in Black Drongos. Once, there was a pair sitting on the ground in a field, and I saw them picking up ants and wiping them all over their feathers. It is believed that the formic acid of the ants helps destroy the avian parasites such as lice and mites. I have seen several colonies of Baya Weavers (Ploceus philippinus) near the paddy fields. The palm fibre, grass, and paddy crop provide good nesting material for the Weavers. Black-breasted Weaver In the same place, I also spotted a few Black-breasted Weavers (Ploceus benghalensis). They looked so different from the other weaver species, with the male having a prominent golden-yellow crown. 4

passerinus) very intriguing. Back in Golconda in Hyderabad, I would listen to the calls of this bird all night long. I also spotted a hepatic female Grey-bellied Cuckoo one day. With dark barring and reddish-brown colour, this morph of the cuckoo looks quite beautiful. There were a few Common Hawk Cuckoos (Hierococcyx varius) too. They are popularly known as the Brainfever Bird, as the call of the bird resembles the words “brain fever”. Black-headed (or Tricolored) Munia There were scores of Black-headed (or Tricolored) Munias (Lonchura malacca) and Indian Silverbills (Euodice malabarica) near the wetland. Many a time I have seen both, collectively feeding on the abundant seeds in the undergrowth. There were also many Scaly-breasted Munias (Lonchura punctulata) and a few Red Avadavats (Amandava amandava) near the paddy fields. Common Hawk Cuckoo Grey-bellied Cuckoo Grey Francolin Quails and Partridges are also quite active in monsoons. Grey Francolins (Francolinus pondicerianus) are widespread here, and I was lucky enough to spot the Painted Francolin (Francolinus pictus) too. Initially I was not familiar with its call. Members of Deccan Birders helped me identify the species. Compared to Grey Francolin, the Painted Francolins are even harder to spot. But they are very vocal during the monsoons as it is their breeding season. When one bird gave a call, I could, immediately, hear another call in response. Grey-bellied Cuckoo hepatic female Cuckoos are pretty active in the monsoon season. Their repetitive whistle-like calls are so soothing to hear. I have always found the Grey-bellied Cuckoo (Cacomantis I have always wanted to photograph Quails, but given their shy nature, it is very difficult to click their pictures – especially the Buttonquails! With thick undergrowth due to monsoons, it becomes easier for the reclusive birds to scoot into the vegetation and hide themselves. After several such encounters with the birds, I realised, no matter how keen my eyes were, theirs were sharper and could spot me before I could spot them! Every time I was sure I would find Quails nearby, they would spot me first, and disappear into the bushes. 5

Barred Buttonquail Pied Kingfisher Finally, one sunny afternoon, I was lucky to find a pair of Barred Buttonquails (Turnix suscitator) foraging in the grass. I could finally get a picture of the bird. I failed to spot the Black Bittern (Dupetor flavicollis) in the reeds, though, and could do so only when it took flight. Pheasant-tailed Jacana (Hydrophasianus chirurgus), Bronzewinged Jacana (Metopidius indicus), Black-winged Stilt (Himantopus himantopus) and Purple Swamphen (Porphyrio porphyrio) are some of the other species thriving near the lake. Bronze-winged Jacana immature White-breasted Kingfisher Common Kingfisher Large Grey Babbler There is also a healthy population of Kingfishers in the town. While the White-breasted Kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis) is commonly seen near the agricultural fields, the Common Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis) is mostly found near small streams and ponds. Large Grey Babblers (Turdoides malcolmi) and Yellow-billed Babblers (Turdoides affinis) are commonly found foraging in groups and also indulging in allopreening. I could spot Yellow-eyed Babblers (Chrysomma sinense), mostly in pairs. There were a few Tawny-bellied Babblers (Dumetia hyperythra) foraging under the shrubs and feeding on jungle berries. There are a few Pied Kingfishers (Ceryle rudis) too, usually perched on wooden poles and fishermen’s boats in the lake. I could find all the three resident Ibis species of the state – Red-naped Ibis (Pseudibis papillosa), Black-headed Ibis (Threskiornis melanocephalus), and Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus). 6

Glossy Ibis are high in number. I always enjoyed their fascinating flying formation in the sky every day. These birds move in flocks and forage in rice fields. Their curved bill helps them probe into the mud to catch aquatic invertebrates. Sadly, these birds are seen as pests by some farmers. They believe that the feeding behaviour of this bird in paddy fields destroy the rice saplings and cause huge losses to them. To avert this, they spray grains laced with poison to kill the birds. As the birds collapse, feral dogs devour the birds. I have seen other species of birds dying after consuming the poisoned grains. I wish there could be a solution for this ‘conflict’. Watercock In the last week of July, I saw a male Knob-billed Duck (Sarkidiornis melanotos) in flight. The clouds were ready to pour down and watching the bird take flight in the backdrop of dark clouds was a beautiful sight. A few moments later I was stunned to see an Asian Palm Civet (Paradoxurus hermaphroditus) coming out of the bushes. The moment it saw me, it disappeared into the thick rice fields. Indian Roller I had to wait for two months before I finally spotted the Indian Roller (Coracias benghalensis). On a day when the sky was overcast, I finally saw a pair perched on the power lines. I was surprised by the absence of Shrikes. There is not much woodland habitat in the town and I had not spotted any Woodpeckers either. I tried exploring some areas that are not easy to access. Right from day one, I had to navigate through difficult terrains to reach the agricultural fields, and with the monsoons, the woes just multiplied. With muddy roads and large puddles, it became extremely challenging to reach the lake bund. An exciting development was finding a pair of Woolly-necked Stork (Ciconia episcopus) hovering in the sky. The bird is listed in IUCN Red List as ‘Vulnerable’. The population of the birds has been declining. I have been searching for different species of Storks but so far, I could only find a few of them. House Sparrows (Passer domesticus), once so ubiquitous, are now confined only to a few pockets in the town. I found them mostly near human habitations which have still retained the old house architecture. Waking up to the sound of the chirpy and chattering calls of the Sparrows, is a lovely childhood memory I always cherish. Another bird that is a part of my childhood memory is the Vulture. More than two decades ago, I could easily spot Vultures perched on trees just as one finds Mynas and Crows today. Vultures were commonly seen in the market grounds and near slaughterhouses. I really wish both of these species regain their earlier status. As I watched birds by myself, I recollected the chapter we studied in school on Salim Ali’s experiences in birdwatching. It was titled ‘Thrills of Birdwatching’. Sometimes birders get themselves into tricky situations as they completely immerse themselves in watching birds. There have been several occasions when I found myself walking endlessly in pursuit of birds. Sometimes I walked so much that I ended up in a neighbouring village! Lesser Whistling-duck Soon after, I visited some new areas around the town and I found more species such as Lesser Whistling-duck (Dendrocygna javanica), Little Grebe (Tachybaptus ruficollis), Barn Owl (Tyto alba) etc. One day I heard the loud booming call of the Watercock (Gallicrex cinerea) in the paddy fields. The bird looked so beautiful. It was one among the several lifers I had recently seen. I was so happy that I slept with a smile on my face that night. A view of the fields at Bodhan 7

I also asked the farmers and fishermen about ideal locations, and they would guide me, while warning me of the lurking dangers. It is always advisable to ask the local people about the area one wants to visit. Although my focus was more on birds, along with the avian fauna I also spotted several species of Butterflies (Crimson Rose, Crimson Tip, Lime Butterfly etc) and reptiles like Lizards (Oriental Garden Lizard, Fan-throated Lizard) and Snakes (Rat Snake, Checkered Keelback, Striped Keelback, Red Sand Boa etc). A group of feral dogs There also has been a rise in the population of feral dogs. Some of these dogs do not hesitate to attack. These dogs have become a menace to the wildlife too, and it has become a common sight to see groups of dogs living alongside agricultural fields and lake beds, attacking livestock and birds. There is sufficient documentation of wildlife predation and extinction by feral dog populations all over the world. There is an urgent need to tackle this problem. After two months of birding, I prepared a checklist of the birds sighted in my town, and to my surprise, the number of resident bird species went up to 108. I was pleasantly surprised to see so many species thriving in and around my town. I still have some areas to cover. Also, the migrants start arriving by late August or early September. There will be many more bird species yet to be sighted! Fan-throated Lizard Checkered Keelback The presence of different types of species in a small town signifies the biodiversity potential of towns and villages in the Telugu states which is yet to be explored properly. Bodhan is just one among the 141 towns present in the state. Knowing species distribution is essential for wildlife conservation. I hope more and more people in the states take to birding or any wildlife activity that would help map the species in the region. Crimson Tip This is especially important because, during the initial phase of COVID global lockdown, social media was awash with pictures and videos depicting the healing of nature and the appearance of animals into the urban spaces, inviting discussions on human impacts on environment. To conclude that nature would heal in such a short span of time feels a stretch, given the destruction the planet has seen post Industrial Revolution. There are vital lessons to be learnt from the pandemic. There are complex interconnections between humans and animals along with the environment which they live in. Destruction of environment is something we have to, ultimately, pay for. It is important that we don’t imperil our own existence. Conservation should be encouraged. Thoughtful citizens and a responsive government can work together to protect our environment. The checklist of the bird species spotted in these two months is as follows: Lime Butterfly 8

Notes on Sighting of Indian Nightjar chicks & Pied Crested Cuckoo young Text & Photos: Azam Khan Indian Nightjar chick We have a piece of land about 4km from Chevella town. We have retained part of it in its natural state and allowed the natural vegetation to take over. At some places under the large trees of Jungle Jalebi (Pithecellobium dulce, also known as Madras Thorn or Manila Tamarind, ‘Vilayati Imli’ in Hindi and ‘Seema Chintakaya’ in Telugu), Jamun and Mahua, there is thick undergrowth of Lantana and some Bamboo. In the last week of August, at another farm in Kumera village of Chevella, we disturbed a flock of Jungle Babblers sitting on a Jungle Jalebi tree. They initially moved to a nearby Neem tree and continued making loud alarm calls. I thought there was a snake nearby and started to look out for it. Then I saw a bird stuck in the Jungle Jalebi tree, trying to free itself from the thorny branches. It had plumage similar to that of a Bulbul but was larger in size, had a different beak and had a small crest. It looked quite familiar but I was unable to identify it. In the month of July, I came across two dull-coloured eggs on the ground, apparently abandoned under a Mahua tree. They did not resemble Francolin or Lapwing eggs, which is what normally I would have expected on the ground in our area. A couple of weeks later, while crossing the same patch, from the corner of my eye I saw a slight movement. On closer inspection, I realised it was a chick covered in down feathers of almost the same colour as the mud and dried leaves around it. The camouflage was so perfect, it ensured that the chick was not spotted by any aerial or ground predators. The chick was sitting motionless with its head half raised and eyes closed. The adults did not seem to be around, but since I regularly see Indian Nightjars in the vicinity, logically it could be assumed that this was the chick of an Indian Nightjar, too. I noticed that there was a second one close by only when it moved a few inches away to hide itself under a pile of leaves. I took a couple of quick photos and moved away, as I didn't want to disturb them further. It is heartening to know we have a pair of resident Nightjars raising their chicks at our farm. Pied Crested Cuckoo young We freed it from the thorns and it immediately hopped to a nearby branch. It was flapping its wings but made no sound. All the while, the Babblers were making an incessant clamour, and the group was joined by a curious Lapwing, which also contributed its expert comments. We moved away and soon saw that the chick flew over to the Neem tree and joined the Babblers. The experts of our group identified it as a Pied Crested (or Jacobin) Cuckoo fledgling which was probably brought up by the Babblers. The one point I did not understand is why it kept quiet – whether it was out of fear or just so that it did not give away its identity. I would also like to state for the record that all due care was taken to ensure that the young birds were not disturbed or put at risk in any way. Indian Nightjar chicks *** 12

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Asian Barred Owlet (Glaucidium cuculoides) Asian Barred Owlet (Mandal, Uttarakhand, December 19, 2019) Order: Strigiformes Family: Strigidae Genus: Glaucidium Species: G. cuculoides Size: 23 cm Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam. It migrates from higher to lower elevations or plains during winter. Habitat & behaviour: The Asian Barred Owlet prefers open submontane or montane forests of pine, oak, rhododendron etc, and subtropical and tropical evergreen forests at lower elevations. It is generally diurnal and is usually seen singly during the day on exposed perches like tree stumps, bare dry branches, telephone wires etc. It is most vocal at dawn and for a couple of hours afterwards, although it may at times vocalize during the day too. The usual call is a mellow hoop, while the song of the male is a combination of musical notes – kwuhk kwuhk-ke-kwuhk kwuhk-kekekwurre kwurre kwurre-kwurre – beginning with a soft stuttering series, accelerating from one note per second to around four notes per second, and building to a harsh crescendo before ending abruptly. The diet of the Asian Barred Owlet consists mainly of beetles, grasshoppers, crickets, locusts, mantids, termites, cicadas and other large insects, and it also takes small birds (which it is known to catch in flight), frogs, lizards, mice and other rodents. Its undulating flight consists of a series of several rapid flaps followed by a pause with its wings closed. Description & distribution: The Asian Barred Owlet, also known as the Cuckoo Owl or Cuckoo Owlet, is a mediumsized, rotund owl, brown overall with brown-barred underparts. It is similar to the Collared Owlet, but it is larger, has darker brown barring on the sides, and does not have the false eye spots on the back of the head. It has fine, pale buff spotting on the head, the mantle is plain or lightly barred, and upperparts, sides of head and neck, and wing-coverts are dull brown or olive-brown with buff to fulvous barring. It has white eyebrows extending beyond the eyes, and a white moustachial streak. The bill is yellowish-green, cere is greenish-horn and irises are lemon-yellow. The facial disc is diffuse. It has a clear white throat patch and the dark-brown barring on the upper part of the breast changes to weak streaking towards the lower part of the breast. Tarsi are feathered, and the olive-yellow toes are bare and sparsely bristled, with yellow soles and hornbrown claws. The tail is blackish or brown with (usually) six white or whitish widely-spaced bars. Juveniles have buff spotting on crown, nape and mantle, and the barring on breast and flanks is diffuse. Nesting: The Asian Barred Owlet breeds generally between April and June. The nest is an unlined hole in a tree trunk; it is known to reuse an abandoned Barbet or Woodpecker nest, or even sometimes to kill these birds and take over their nestholes. The usual clutch consists of 4-7 rounded white eggs. The Asian Barred Owlet is resident across north-east Pakistan, northern, central and north-eastern parts of India, Nepal, Bhutan, north Bangladesh, south-east Tibet, south-east China, and south-east Asia, including Myanmar, Thailand, Local name: The Asian Barred Owlet is known as ‘Bada dundul’ in Hindi, ‘Ashiya dagipecha’ in Bengali, ‘Tanpum’ in Lepcha and ‘Dao ku-ra-ru-ru’ in Cachar. *** 13

OUTDOOR DURING THE LOCKDOWN Trip Report: Ameenpur Lake, July 3, 2020 Text and Photos: Sravan Kumar Railla A view at Ameenpur Lake A plan to meet a new friend had been pending for a long time, but due to the pandemic we had been unable to get together or step out for birding. Finally, we decided that this couldn’t wait any more and, on the evening of July 3, 2020, four of us – Kishan, Chinthan, Hussain and I – managed to combine this meet with a birding trip to Ameenpur Lake. An Ashy Prinia was seen carrying a Neoscana Sp. spider in its beak, hopping among the reeds on its way to the nest. A bushy Berry tree had an Indian Palm Squirrel nest with a litter of three young ones; we saw them coming out, following behind the parent. A pair of Green Bee-eaters and a Common Myna also were seen among the reeds around the fallow lands. Traffic was lean enough to enable us reach the lake by 5:00PM. Birding over the bund, we could record a few common birds like Little Cormorant, Red Avadavat, Asian Pied Starling, Barn Swallow, Pied Bushchat, and a House Crow (nest with 3 chicks). At the end of the bund, we saw a pair of Ducks flying overhead towards the water. Their bodies appeared bright orange, enhanced by the setting sun, and we identified them as Ruddy Shelducks, only to later revise the ID, after looking at the photographs, to Lesser Whistling-ducks. Down the bund towards the catchment area, we documented a fascinating, brightly coloured Rock Agama on the boulders. Along the bund are the agricultural fields, where the seasonal harvest activities had been completed, and they now remained damp but fallow lands, not currently in use. These fields yielded us a group of Grey-headed Swamphens foraging, a flock of Baya Weavers shuttling around among the reeds and the fallow fields, and two male Greater Painted-snipes foraging. Grey-headed Swamphen Ashy Prinia Moving east to the ‘Kingfisher pond’, we recorded solitary individuals of several species: a Grey-headed Swamphen feeding on grass weeds, a Grey Heron, a Little Egret, a Spotbilled Duck, and an Oriental Darter perched on substrata in the waterbody. 14

Assorted birds at the ‘fish stall point’ At the ‘fish stall point’, a mixed flock of Painted Storks, Cattle Egrets, Large Egrets and Black-crowned Night Herons were all seen foraging for fish waste dumped in the shallow water at the corner of the lake. From the scrub-covered boulders, a troop of Indian Peafowl was added to the list. Moving down to the lake side, some birds from the larger flock of Spot-billed Pelicans rowed the waters, irregularly dipping their bills and sweeping their pouches, trying to catch their fish, and shuttled from the water to the perches provided by the artificial platforms. It was an uneasy scene – the Pelicans with the background of smoking industrial vents, and the crowd playing cricket on the opposite bank (during the pandemic!). Painted Stork & Cattle Egret A Black-naped Hare, sighted in the grass patch between the boulders, was feeding on the tender grass. The chorus by the Purple and Purple-rumped Sunbirds echoed around the boulders as they collected nectar from the flowering plants. The artificial platforms at Ameenpur Lake Spot-billed Pelican In contrast to this, towards the west, we got to observe the silhouettes of the flying birds on a cloud canvas, and witnessed the dusk rolling into night above the ripples of the water body. An update on the Asian vulture crisis – Current priorities and a South India perspective Christopher GR Bowden Long-billed Vulture chicks (Photo: Chris Bowden) The dramatic declines in vulture populations across South Asia over the past twenty years were caused foremost by diclofenac being used as a veterinary painkiller in cattle and causing gout and kidney failure in vultures that have fed on the carcasses of recently treated cattle (Pain et al. 2008) 9. 24 partner organisations of the Saving Asia’s Vultures from Extinction (SAVE) consortium have been working together with regional and state governments to implement the agreed priority actions from a regional perspective, and supported by sound scientific information. A national summary and vulture policy has recently been agreed by Indian SAVE Partners and its Technical Advisory Committee ahead of updating the Government National Vulture Action Plan, last produced back in 2006. This summary highlights how, despite the landmark steps taken so far – the veterinary diclofenac ban in 2006, and the diclofenac vials size restriction in 2015 – it is these veterinary drugs (including new compounds) that caused the catastrophic declines and still pose the greatest ongoing threats across India. So the priority actions for India are bans of further veterinary drugs, and even more immediately, the vulturesafety-testing of further drugs by the Indian Veterinary Research Institute, together with Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS). The BNHS breeding and release programme is also important, as a way to secure populations of the species in captivity at least, but more immediately to release birds back to the wild, thereby raising the profile of the issues, and checking the safety of the environment. Probably the most significant recent development has been in Nepal, where there has been strong endorsement of the combined measures to remove diclofenac from veterinary use – both through legislation and through on the ground Vulture Safe Zone (VSZ) work – resulting in the first strong evidence for regional population recoveries of White-rumped and Slender-billed Vultures (Galligan et al. 2019)5. The population trend for both species switched from strongly negative to strongly positive at about the time that the national awareness-raising and education campaign about diclofenac became fully effective. The actions taken in Nepal have had major impact and are encouraging more initiatives on the ground in India, and in Bangladesh (where the VSZs are formally gazetted by the government, and ketoprofen bans imposed at this regional level). However, these initiatives still need further follow-up, especially in India, to avoid undoing all the hard work over the past twenty years. Undercover pharmacy surveys are showing mixed trends across the region, and that other vulture-toxic drugs are increasing in most areas (Cuthbert et al. 2011, Galligan et al. 2020)2,6, but in Nepal at least the use of veterinary diclofenac is almost down to zero. This has added confidence to proceed with the release programme of captive birds, with 30 White-rumped Vultures now released in three batches, all close to Chitwan National Park. A further 30 wild birds have been satellite-tagged in the area to understand their movements and allow a quick response to any mortality for diagnosing the exact cause. So far, so good, but vigilant monitoring of the fate of the tagged birds is essential. White-rumped Vultures emerging from aviary for release (Photo courtesy: Bird Conservation Nepal) 4

Recently released immature White-rumped Vultures enjoying their freedom (Photo courtesy: Bird Conservation Nepal) Recently released White-rumped Vulture in flight (Photo courtesy: Bird Conservation Nepal) Meanwhile, the very first release of eight White-rumped Vultures has taken place in India in early October 2020 in Haryana, although there are some significant lingering concerns as to whether the environment there is sufficiently cleared of diclofenac, so at this stage this is very much a test release which will be carefully monitored. Immature Himalayan Griffon with White-rumped Vultures in the background (Photo: Chris Bowden) The colony aviary in Pinjore, Haryana (Photo: Chris Bowden) At Haryana, the breeding program for the Long-billed (or Indian) Vulture is going very well, as for the Slender-billed and White-rumped Vultures at the other centres. Long-billed Vulture in flight (Photo: Mandy West) White-rumped Vulture (Photo: Chris Bowden) The increasing engagement and financial commitment of the Indian government, especially in recent years has been encouraging, and now supports the bulk of the vulture breeding and release programmes, bringing with it important profile to the issue. Pilot releases of rehabilitated Himalayan Griffons happened earlier in Haryana and, more recently, in West Bengal where satellite tags were deployed in India for the first time on released vultures. These releases add important impetus for getting the environment safer and taking the necessary steps more widely. 5

West Bengal also yields intermittent sightings of the rarest of the vultures, the Slender-billed Vulture. Globally, the stronghold of the Slender-billed Vulture is in nearby Assam, with approximately half the world population of around 1500 birds being found there. Five tagged Himalayan Griffons ready for release in West Bengal, December 2019 (Photo: Chris Bowden) First Himalayan Griffon to leave the aviary in West Bengal (Photo: Chris Bowden) Slender-billed Vulture (Photo: Chris Bowden) An updated vulture policy document for India The Indian SAVE partners recently agreed on a summary policy document highlighting the key actions needed. This includes an important summary of which NSAIDs are the key threats, and the key references: Release aviary in Buxa, West Bengal (Photo: Chris Bowden) Drug name Meloxicam Threat / Safety Safe Known effect Tested and shown to be safe for vultures (Swarup D. et al. 2007)12 Tolfenamic acid Probably safe Currently being tested and so far results are positive (to be fully confirmed shortly) Carprofen Toxic at high doses Shown to be at toxic levels for cattle tissues around the injection site (Fourie et al. 2015)3 Flunixin Toxic Shown to be toxic to Gyps vultures in Spain and Italy Nimesulide Probably toxic Banned in many countries due to safety issues in humans and banned in India for under 12s. Fast becoming popular across India. There have been several cases of dead wild vultures with gout and nimesulide but no diclofenac Aceclofenac Confirmed toxic Metabolises into diclofenac in cattle so equivalent effect to diclofenac (Galligan et al. 2016, Sharma 2012) 4, 11 Ketoprofen Confirmed toxic Trials carried out on Gyps vultures showed toxicity at concentrations found in treated cattle in India (Naidoo et al. 2009)7 Diclofenac Confirmed toxic Confirmed highly toxic in 2003 (Oaks et al. 2004)8, and banned as veterinary drug since 2006 Table 1. Veterinary drugs which threaten vultures 6

The IVRI and BNHS safety-testing urgently needs to progress, and one brighter piece of news to emerge is that an additional safe drug, tolfenamic acid (Table 1), is likely to be confirmed very shortly – but otherwise it is only meloxicam that is fully confirmed as a safe alternative for use by the veterinarians since 2005 (Swarup et al. 2007)12. This new development for tolfenamic acid will be particularly welcome positive news, as otherwise there are increasingly urgent concerns regarding the growing popularity of nimesulide, aceclofenac, ketoprofen, flunixin and others, which remain in legal use despite the growing body of evidence that shows they are also vulture killers (see Table 1 above). Encouragingly, some Indian state governments have agreed not to distribute these other toxic drugs to their veterinary services, ahead of formal bans, and we hope that others will follow this example. But meanwhile, the important IVRI safety testing needs to be extended quickly to include the full set of available drugs, and ultimately to any new drugs ahead of their licenses being approved. Unfortunately, further surveillance of which veterinary drugs are being used has shown that both Cambodia and Myanmar have recently started using veterinary diclofenac. The Cambodia consortium, Cambodia Vulture Working Group successfully lobbied for a ban, which was agreed and legally implemented less than a year after this request was made – a highly commendable step. Indeed, this and India’s readiness to ban veterinary diclofenac was commended at the recent 13th meeting of the Conference of Parties to the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS CoP13) held in Gujarat, as an important example for European countries like Spain to follow. Secondary threats, notably of poison baits (usually retaliatory and targeting dogs or large carnivores – please note, this is the most widespread threat for European and African vultures) and threats of power infrastructure (electrocution and collision with wires, pylons and wind turbines) are emerging in South Asia and need attention. Developing a database of all vulture mortalities is underway, to better clarify and update the respective importance of these, and messaging will need to incorporate these problems, along with vulture sensitivity mapping being carried out ahead of installation of power infrastructures. This is an important area where birdwatchers can contribute – both by reporting all their vulture sightings on eBird and, if any carcass of a dead vulture is found, to urgently report it and find ways to get an autopsy and take tissue samples to ascertain the cause of death. South India has never had quite the same super-abundance of vultures as the northern ‘cow-belt’ states of India, but has nevertheless still suffered catastrophic declines in vulture densities, and there is reason to believe that diclofenac was the major cause here too. There was a workshop and report reviewing the situation, held in Ooty in January 2018. The recommendations agreed were for coordinated surveys and monitoring both of vultures and of veterinary drugs, but also acknowledging that poison-baits may have played a role in earlier declines (where extensive cattle rearing meant that they were very susceptible to being preyed upon), and that there may be some useful synergies between countering this threat targeting tigers and leopards, and accidentally poisoning vultures. But this again reiterates the need for quick reporting and autopsy of any dead vultures found in future, and note here that Karnataka Veterinary College in Bangalore is offering to carry out such autopsies free of charge to support this cause. It was also agreed that Vulture Safe Zone initiatives have an important role to play and such work should be supported where these scientifically-backed messages are carefully highlighted. Despite the recent progress and lessons from Nepal, and the growing numbers of captive bred birds available for release, there are recent reports of ongoing declines from Gujarat (where NSAIDs are implicated), and also Cambodia (where other threats including poison-baits are key). The ongoing need for monitoring the vulture population and threats through documenting causes of vulture mortality is clear, and if the NSAIDs threats can be taken care of – and this is something that really can be resolved given the political will – then other issues faced by vultures can be understood and addressed. For more details on the NSAIDs and all of these updates, you can consult the NSAID Alert, Resources and News pages of www.save-vultures.org10. Also note that the SAVE Blueprint is the main resource that feeds into the Convention of Migratory Species’ Vulture Multispecies Action Plan (Botha et al. 2017)1 which is a major resource and more formally underpins the actions needed that are mentioned above. Recognizing the sovereign rights of States to use their own biological resources, the Convention expects the parties to facilitate access to genetic resources by other parties subject to national legislation and on mutually agreed upon terms (Article 3 and 15 of CBD). Article 8(j) of the Convention on Biological Diversity recognizes contributions of local and indigenous communities towards the conservation and sustainable utilization of biological resources through traditional knowledge, practices and innovations, and provides for equitable sharing of benefits with such people arising from the utilization of their knowledge, practices and innovations (Biological Diversity Act, 2002). India has only 2.4% of the world's land area, but harbours 78% of all recorded species, including over 45,000 species of plants and 91,000 species of animals. It is also amongst the few countries that have developed a biogeographic classification for conservation planning, and has mapped biodiversity-rich areas in the country. Of the 34 global biodiversity hotspots, four are present in India, represented by the Himalayas, the Western Ghats, the North-east and the Nicobar Islands. Considering the outstanding universal value and exceptionally high levels of endemism in the Western Ghats, 39 sites in the States of Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra have been inscribed on the United Nations Education Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage List in 2012 (India’s Fifth National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity, 2014). 8

Pocharam Lake & Wildlife Sanctuary Telangana State, separated from the erstwhile Andhra Pradesh on 2nd June 2014, is situated in the central stretch of the eastern seaboard of the Indian Peninsula. Telangana state has an area of 114,840 sq km. The area is divided into two main regions, the Eastern Ghats and the plains (Pullaiah, 2015). One of the interesting species recorded by C. Srinivasulu et al during in February 2011, the Jerdon’s Baza, was unfortunately not seen during our study. Several owl species are there in the area, but given the practical constraints of traveling in the night and early morning hours, we could record only a few species. Pocharam Wildlife Sanctuary, named after Pocharam village and lake, was created by construction of a dam across Allair river (a tributary of Manjeera river) during the early part of the 20th century. The sanctuary, covering an area of 130 km2, is spread across parts of Medak and Nizamabad districts. With damming of the river and consequent water outflow into the forests in the vicinity, forests here flourished well supporting rich and diverse biota. This had prompted the erstwhile Government of Hyderabad State to declare the area as a Wildlife Sanctuary in 1952. It was observed that communities living close to the alluvial area relied the most on the protected area due to their lack of permanent agricultural land. Resources from Pocharam Sanctuary play an important role in the livelihood of communities living in its vicinity; for instance, it was noted that: The Sanctuary, with its rich forest patch, and the associated lake is critical for the survival of wildlife in the area. It is located at a distance of 115 km from Hyderabad. Though the Sanctuary harbours rich floral and faunal wealth, not much documentation work has been undertaken, and there is scope for enhanced utilization of this information for conservation and scientific management.  Hence, we had carried out a one-year study at Pocharam Wildlife Sanctuary, Medak district, with the intention of generating baseline data about avifaunal diversity present in the area and assessing the need for conservation efforts for the habitats in that region. A total of 237 species of birds were recorded during the study. Methodology All observations were conducted on foot and were aided by the use of binoculars; photo documentation was also obtained with the help of cameras with zoom lenses. Avifauna was recorded by direct count method from vantage points. A total of 237 bird species, including migratory and resident birds, were recorded; these were identified using the Salim Ali and the Grimmett & Inskipp field guides. Observations & Discussion The study was carried out in the Sanctuary and fringe villages from August 2019 to July 2020. Most of the avifauna listed were observed in Pocharam lake and Sanctuary area – especially Parvatapur area, which is in the core area of the Sanctuary, and has unique forest cover and rich biodiversity. About 150 species of birds were recorded near Pocharam Lake during the summer season and monsoon. We observed that the number of bird species increased during the pre-monsoon as compared to summer season; the reptile population also increased around monsoon.   People collect wild fruits (Custard apple, chironji, amla, tamarind, jamun, etc) for their own consumption; Fringe villagers take their animals to the forest for grazing; Water from the Pocharam lake flows to various locations for agriculture and industrial purposes The high volume of vehicular traffic passing through the area, however, leads to numerous road kills every day. In the interest of wildlife, forest conservation and sustainable development, it would be good if existing roads within protected areas (PA) like Pocharam could be provided alternative alignment. Conclusions Invasive species: They are one of the major causes of biodiversity loss in forest, aquatic and agricultural ecosystems. In terms of flora and fauna, we need to take the necessary measures to eradicate these species. Household dependency on the PA: Local communities living adjacent to PAs play a vital role in biodiversity conservation. Understanding communities’ use and perceptions of a PA will increase conservation effectiveness through reducing anthropogenic pressures and improving park-people relationships. Protected area demarcation: Considering that the forest resources are limited owing to the small size of the Sanctuary, it seems prudent to increase the size by integrating the potentially rich and ecologically fragile areas, which are adjacent to the PA – for instance, the contiguous forest areas of Lingampet Reserve Forest on the northwest side, and Gangapur Reserve Forest in the southeast side of the Pocharam Wildlife Sanctuary. This is critical for augmenting and conserving the natural resource base of the Sanctuary in the long term. 9

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Indian Skimmer (Rynchops albicollis) Indian Skimmer (Kakinada, January 8, 2019) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Laridae Genus: Rynchops Species: R. albicollis Size: 40-43 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Indian Skimmer is usually seen singly or in small groups, near the larger river systems, where it is seen perched on the sandbars, or skimming along the surface of the river with the lower mandible dipped into the river at a gentle angle, ploughing the water for fish; the upper mandible is held open, ready to snap down on any fish that it finds. It may hunt actively during the day as well as during moonlit nights. Flocks sometimes display elaborate maneouvres, taking off together, then wheeling around before settling down again. The usual call is a shrill, chattering scream; sometimes it also utters a nasal kyap, kyap. The diet of the Indian Skimmer consists almost exclusively of fish, although it may occasionally take small crustaceans and insect larvae. Its undulating flight consists of a series of several rapid flaps followed by a pause with its wings closed. Description & distribution: The Indian Skimmer, earlier known as the Indian Scissors-bill, is the only one of three Skimmer species in the Rynchops genus that is seen in India. It somewhat resembles the Terns, but is easily differentiated by the longer lower mandible, which is knife-like and flexible. It has a black cap, laterally flattened bright orange bill with a yellow tip, black-brown upperparts and clean white underparts. The long, pointed wings show a white trailing edge, and the legs and feet are red. Non-breeding birds are browner and duller coloured. Juvenile birds are greyish-brown above, and show pale fringes to back and wing feathers. The head is whiter, and the bill is orange-brown and black-tipped. Interestingly, young birds have normal horn-coloured bills, with the lower mandible being of the same length as the upper; the lower mandible grows with age. The sexes are similar, though the female is smaller. Nesting: The Indian Skimmer breeds generally between February and May. It breeds in colonies of up to 40 pairs, along with River Terns and other birds. A low level of brood parasitism has been reported, with the Indian Skimmer laying its eggs in the nests of River Terns. The nest of the Indian Skimmer is an unlined depression in the sand in a dry river bed, sandy inlet or sand bar in the middle of a stream. Incubation happens mainly during the cooler hours, and it is also known to belly-soak to cool the eggs. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 pale pinkish buff or greyish white eggs, blotched and streaked with brown. The Indian Skimmer is resident near the river systems across northern and central India (like the Indus, Ganges, and Brahmaputra) south to around the Krishna river, and in the Nepalese terai. In winter, they may be seen in the coastal estuaries as far south as Karwar on the western coast, and Chennai and Pondicherry on the eastern coast. There are also vagrant records from Kutch, Rajasthan and Maharashtra, as well as from Oman, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Thailand. Local name: The Indian Skimmer is known as ‘Panchira’ in Hindi and Marathi, ‘Pancheera’ in Punjabi and ‘Jal-hal’ in Gujarati. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report: Ameenpur, October 3, 2020 Text & Photos: Abhinav Udupi Painted Stork In the first week of October I got a chance to visit one of the very popular birding destinations in Hyderabad – Ameenpur Lake. The lake is around 30 kilometers from Hyderabad. I had heard that in the month of October the lake teems with migratory birds and was hoping to spot quite a few. Indian Silverbill Spot-billed Pelican 1

During my four-hour visit I was able to spot almost 15 species of birds and tried to photograph most of them. Out of these I spotted at least 9 new species of birds. It was my first time birding at a water body and I fully enjoyed it. Red Avadavat There were lots of birds of various species and that enabled me to photograph them from a lot of different perspectives. I thoroughly enjoyed the trip and learnt a lot about birding and photographing birds. Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark Black-winged Stilt Black-headed Ibis Indian Robin *** LOOKING BACK AT ANANTHAGIRI Text & Photos: Ambika Pradhan Asian Koel male It all started with the new-born dawn, grey, dull and overcast, giving way to thick water heavy clouds that quickly turned the morning to dusk, dark and carrying a heavy silence of the impending downpour that was round the corner. I was drenched in no time, but I did not spare a moment to stop somewhere, until the deluge passed – I had to keep going. Soon, the dawn reclaimed what rightfully belonged to it. Now, the only thing on my mind was to reach the destination on time, before the birds I’d never seen flew away. Drab, dull urban structures were soon replaced by lush green pastures, roads lined with age-old trees that looked like old wise forest lords. 3

When I finally arrived at the destination, I found myself in what I’d say was a crayon drawing: pastels of blue sky, and overly saturated sun, surrounded by trees that were teeming with life that left me eager and restless. Vikarabad, or even on the way, raptors begin to greet you. Sometimes, if one has the luck, Short-toed Snake Eagle and Indian Spotted Eagle grace with their presence over the fields, hovering in all their glory. What a sight it is, as a raptor glides above stretching out its mighty wingspan! In less than 10 minutes, I spotted nearly 5 new species I’d only ever seen in bird guides and Google images. As a teenager flipping through Dr Salim Ali’s Book of Indian Birds, I had been awestruck by the sheer beauty of Asian Paradise-flycatcher and thought it was an elusive bird that I would spend years searching for. But, only a few years later, while birding in Ananthagiri, a flash of white flew right into the shafts of sunlight that fell between the two trees. That flash of white turned out to be the Paradise-flycatcher, a moment of celebration for me back then, as it still is today. “Oh, you’re what they call Yellow-footed Green Pigeon? Pleasure indeed to meet you, good sire”. “Now I see you, now I don’t. No wonder they call you Leafbird. Glad to make your acquaintance.” “Ah, the graceful Hornbill flying overhead, we meet after all!” Come Bird Race, Ananthagiri would be one of the first spots we’d plan to go, year after year. The Bird Race was a time to socialise with other birders from the city and everybody would gush about the legend of the Brown Fish Owl at Ananthagiri and how it would always be perched atop the mango tree at the entrance of the forest. And a couple of years after listening to the legend, while participating in the Bird Race, I finally did manage to spot the Brown Fish Owl! These were the dialogues running in my head, while spotting the diverse bird life. Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker Crimson Rose pair mating This is how vividly I remember the first time I visited Ananthagiri Hills for birding. Life everywhere you’d care to look. Birders had only started arriving, but a sense of conquest filled me, for I had arrived early and spotted so many lifers in a short span of time. That morning, nearly 5 years ago, is etched in my memory – a bright July morning spent watching the Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker, an Orange-headed Thrush, some Leafbirds and Yellow-footed Green Pigeons. In these COVID times, locked up inside the house, I find myself thinking of Ananthagiri more often than not. When the restriction lifts, would we still enjoy birding like we did Before Covid, sans sanitizers, masks and the constant fear of being infected? One lives in hope! Yellow-footed Green Pigeon Over the years, Ananthagiri has come to become my go-to place for a good day of woodland birding. As soon as you enter Indian Grey Hornbill *** 4

Baby Sparrow On My Stoop Louise Fairley Summoned to my screen door: an insistent vocalise punching through bird-chatter, fledgling artist thirsty for attention, untutored in vocal technique. Testing independence, yet too naïve to be chary of me looming in the doorway. Emphatic cheeping paused, you preen a riotous thistledown of baby feathers; turning, fix me with your penetrating eye. Devoted mother, patiently swaying on the daylily, awaits her turn at the feeder, gleaning soggy seeds pounded to mush by last night’s torrents. I was about to empty the mess, not knowing it was just right for baby birds. At your summons, she returns again and again. Soon you will do this for yourself; become sleek, chatty, self-assured, indistinguishable from the cohort of sparrows frequenting my yard. The thought of which leaves me vaguely bereft. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From The Times Of India, January 20, 2018) *** 5

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Black Bulbul (Hypsipetes leucocephalus) Black Bulbul (Sattal, June 7, 2018) Order: Passeriformes Family: Pycnonotidae Genus: Hypsipetes Species: H. leucocephalus Size: 24-25 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Black Bulbul prefers tall moistdeciduous and evergreen broad-leaved forests, gardens and cultivated areas. It is arboreal and is usually seen in small groups of 6 to 10, although sometimes more, either roosting in the canopies of tall forest trees, or flying around foraging for food. It is a noisy species, with flocks making a variety of sounds like cheeping, grating and mewing calls – chirp, cheechee-chee, whew-whe etc. The Himalayan subspecies, H. l. psaroides, is also known to make a call like a goat kid. Its diet consists mainly of insects and seeds, and they are especially fond of berries like Celtis, Rosa, Melia and Ehretia in the Himalayas. They also partake of nectar from flowers like Rhododendron, Salmalia, Erythrina etc. Description & distribution: The Black Bulbul, also known as the Asian Black Bulbul or Himalayan Black Bulbul, is a passerine that has ten subspecies currently recognized, and is found in southern Asia, from north-eastern Afghanistan and northern Pakistan across northern, central and north-eastern India east to Myanmar, central, southern and south-eastern China, Taiwan and Sri Lanka. The plumage varies from a glossy black to slaty grey overall, depending on the subspecies, and with the underparts being slightly lighter than the upperparts. The head is black and has a fluffy crest, while the bill, legs and feet are bright orange. The tail has a slight fork. The sexes are similar, but younger birds have whitish underparts with a grey breast-band, brownish upperparts and do not have the crest. They may also have a black streak behind the eyes and on the ear coverts. Three of the subspecies found in China – H. l. stresemanni, H. l. leucothorax and H. l. leucocephalus – have white heads. The birds of the Western Ghats belonging to the subspecies H. l. ganeesa, are also known as the Square-tailed Bulbul. Nesting: The Black Bulbul breeds generally between May and July. The nest is a neat, though flimsy, cup made of grass, dead leaves, moss and lichen, bound with cobwebs, and lined with rootlets, fine grass etc, and built in a fork of a tree, at least 10m above the ground. The usual clutch consists of 2-4 pale pink eggs, blotched all over with red-brown, purple-brown and grey. Local name: The Black Bulbul is known as ‘Kala bulbul’ in Hindi and Marathi, ‘Kaki’ in Pahari, ‘Karuppu kondai kuruvi’ in Tamil, ‘Myna-bulbul’ in Malayalam and ‘Dao-bulip gashim’ in Cachari. The Black Bulbul stays mainly in the hills but sometimes descends to the plains in winter. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Website: www.deccanbirders.in. E-group: http://groups.google.co.in/group/deccanbirders.
