Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 17 Number 13 October 2020 (Special Issue)

Editor’s note Some of our members had been to Gujarat for a week-long birding trip from February 5th to 10th, 2020. In this Special Issue of the Pitta, we are happy to bring you an account of the trip, along with a number of colourful photographs. We hope you will find this Special Issue interesting. WESTERN WANDERINGS Report: Gujarat, February 5-10, 2020 A view of Great Rann of Kutch (Photo: Prashant Yella) Day-1: Nalsarovar, February 5, 2020 Dr Jayati Mitra We were a group of five members of Deccan Birders waiting at the Ahmedabad airport on a bright and sunny morning on February 5, 2020. Our final destination was the Great Rann of Kutch, but we had a stopover for more than half a day at this city. Our trip coordinator Umesh came up with the idea of taking us for a meticulously planned birding trip to Nalsarovar, a vast wetland lying near Sanand village about 60km from Ahmedabad city. The shallow lake, about 120.8 square kilometers in area and four to five feet deep, is dotted with around 36 small islands. The presence of a rich variety of birds consistently in the past in this location has been noted by ornithologists and it has been declared as a Ramsar site since September 24, 2012. It was almost noon when we reached the periphery of the sanctuary. Our country has a great variety of landscapes and this western region is known for its dry deserts and thorny shrubs. On the way, the common bird species seen were mostly Bank Mynas, Eurasian Collared Doves, Green Bee-eaters, Black Drongos and House Sparrows. We also spotted the Whiteeared Bulbul, conspicuous with its yellow vent, as it is a common species of the western plains of our country. White-eared Bulbul (Photo: Umesh Mani) After a long drive we reached a prominent carrefour before the entrance to the sanctuary. The weather was becoming increasingly hot and dry as the day progressed, but we had ample quantities of juicy apples to quench our thirst, thanks to our friend Shalini who had thoughtfully packed them for us during the journey. Our first halt was a small pond near the roadside where we noticed some waders, the most significant of them being the near-threatened Curlew Sandpiper and the Dunlin. Some other birds present were Common Sandpiper, Painted Stork, Asian Openbill, Red-naped and Black-headed Ibis.

Dunlin (Photo: Umesh Mani) As we had limited time we decided not to visit the main water body but to bird only at selected locations on the fringes of the sanctuary. The electrical wires served as suitable perching sites for quite a few birds in the absence of tall trees. We observed the Long-tailed Shrike, Southern Grey Shrike, Indian Roller and Common Kestrel, all perched high up, waiting to catch their prey. Baillon’s Crake (Photo: Umesh Mani) Finally the highlight of the day – a beautiful Spotted Crake – appeared and scurried to the middle, moving back and forth repeatedly as it fed. It had a light coloured breast and white spots all over its light brown plumage with a buffy undertail. I couldn’t help admiring its yellow beak with the bright red spot. At about 12.30PM, our guide made a stop at a small patch of marsh surrounded by reeds, which seemed to be a favourable site for water birds. Silently all of us crouched and leaned over the stones at the edge of the patch to look for the presence of any creature amidst the thick vegetation. Occasionally a Siberian Stonechat or a Warbler diverted our attention till we heard a crackling call. Spotted Crake (Photo: Umesh Mani) All this happened within a few minutes but it was a great opportunity to record the activities of these very shy birds at such close quarters in my mind’s eye. Viewing all the three Crakes together was a great moment in my life and, while I was fully engrossed in watching these beautiful creations of nature, a pair of Collared Pratincoles appeared in the sky. They had pointed brown wings with a whitish underbelly and, while flying and circling overhead, they were feeding on insects before disappearing out of view. Ruddy-breasted Crake (Photo: Umesh Mani) A Ruddy-breasted Crake peeped out into the open area and disappeared in no time, but we didn’t lose our patience. It showed up again, wading across the water with its long toes, head bent down in a slightly stooping posture but this time it started feeding comfortably in the centre of the marsh, oblivious of our presence. We had ample time to enjoy viewing its glossy reddish-brown plumage. After it left came the Baillon’s Crake, a pretty bird with a much brighter brown colour and white streaking on its back. Collared Pratincole (Photo: Umesh Mani)

After this birding bonanza we moved out from the main road into the interior region. Among the raptors, we could sight an occasional Oriental Honey-buzzard or a Eurasian Marsh Harrier and even a Shikra in flight. Our vehicle made way to some extent through the loose dry soil of the uneven undulating path, kicking up clouds of dust, while scraping through thorny Acacia and other scrub species which obstructed our way. Finally, we got down and trekked through this very dry, vast terrain which was mostly barren other than for a few clumps of dwarf bushes growing haphazardly all over. Here it was actually possible to gaze all around in a full circle till the horizon! thousands of kilometers from Central Europe to spend the winter here. Short-eared Owl (Photo: Umesh Mani) Sociable Lapwing (Photo: Umesh Mani) In this open environment, we soon noticed a Short-eared Owl. This bird hunts during the daytime also and though we were very far away it could still feel our presence and it cleverly dodged us every time we tried to approach it. Finally we could locate it beneath a bush and got a glimpse of it from a safe distance. Another special species of this region, the Stoliczka’s Bushchat, also showed up for a while in the distance. Unfortunately, all I saw was a small brown bird with some streaks on its head and back, before it disappeared. There were quite a few Ruff feeding along with the Sociable Lapwings. These are also winter visitors to our country. After a while we watched the entire flock flying together gracefully for a short period and ultimately diving down to rest again a little further away from the previous position. This type of visual treat of a flock in flight is always cherished by a bird watcher. Some time later, we were fortunate enough to see a whole flock of another highly sought-after species – the Sociable Lapwing. This is a critically endangered bird which has got its name from gathering in large flocks. The bird is olive brown in colour, with a bold white supercilium bordered by a dark eye stripe and crown. It is known to breed in grasslands of European steppes, where cattle grazing and agriculture in the same area is ruining its habitat; at the same time, it is often hunted on its migratory route over central Europe. White-tailed Lapwing (Photo: Umesh Mani) While returning from this spot we came across another good finding in a shallow stretch of water – two White-tailed Lapwings! It was a very graceful slim grey-brown bird with long yellow legs, whitish face and a white tail. It migrates Jungle Cat (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Quite a number of Demoiselle Cranes were sighted on the way but our main interest was to look for the Sarus. As we tried to focus on the Cranes, we saw a Jungle Cat scurrying across the fields. It kept moving away, maintaining some distance and hiding itself among the crops growing in the fields. Coming back to the Sarus, this resident bird of our country pairs for life and we could observe a pair fanning their wings and swaying their bright red heads from time to time. A couple of juveniles also were present; they lacked the bright red head colour of a mature adult. They were feeding in the paddy fields and one of them was trying to gobble up a frog for its evening meal. Another vulnerable species, the Woolly-necked Stork was also present nearby, feeding in the same field. Sarus Crane adult (Photo: Umesh Mani) Woolly-necked Stork (Photo: Umesh Mani) It was evening by now and light was fast fading away. We watched the sun set below the horizon and as darkness set in, it was time to head back towards Ahmedabad city. After this excellent birding trip we went for dinner at a city hotel and ended up tasting a bizarre variety of Chopsuey with pineapple! Every journey throws up a surprise and we accepted this one also with great moments of enjoyment and learning. This trip was a great beginning and it had greatly heightened our expectations for the coming days. We were all very excited and ready for the night journey to reach Bhuj the next morning and explore other birding areas in Kutch. Sarus Crane juvenile (Photo: Umesh Mani) *** Day-1: Thol Lake Bird Sanctuary, February 5, 2020 G Ramakrishna Rao Arriving early on February 5, 2020 in Ahmedabad for our trip to Great Rann of Kutch, Vikramjit and I, instead of accompanying the rest of the group to Nalsarovar, decided to use the time and go to Thol Bird Sanctuary. We hired a taxi from Ahmedabad and spent around half a day at Thol. Our decision paid off, as we got to see a good number of water birds from fairly close. Some interesting sightings were a large flock of Demoiselle Cranes, a Darter sunning itself and an Osprey on the hunt. Demoiselle Crane (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao)

The important plant species are Gum Arabic (Acacia nilotica), Umbrella Thorn (A. planifrons), Indian Jujube (Ziziphus mauritiana), Jhar Beri (Z. nummularia), Neem (Azadirachta indica), Jungli Kikar (Prosopis juliflora), Assyrian Plum (Cordia myxa) and Tree of Heaven (Ailanthus excelsa). Submerged rooted aquatic vegetation in Thol water body are Tape Grass or Eel Grass (Vallisneria spiralis), Waterthyme (Hydrilla verticillata), Pondweed (Potamogeton sp.), Yellow Lotus (Nelumbo lutea), Water Morning Glory (Ipomoea aquatica), Narrowleaf Cattail (Typha angustata) and some floating perennial grass (Paspalum sp.). The grass species are Bermuda Grass or Dog’s Tooth Grass (Cynodon dactylon), Canegrass or Lovegrass (Eragrostis sp.), Sedge (Cyperus sp.) and Broomsedge (Saccharum sp.). Darter (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) We saw many Nilgais and Common Langurs in the Thol tank area. There were some Warblers, Prinias and Flycatchers that I could not identify on the spot, but they were identified from photos later and added to the list. Thol Sanctuary has sufficient tree growth of Prosopis along with adequate undisturbed tank foreshore, and is a good area for the breeding of migratory birds. We saw good numbers of Greylag Geese and Bar-headed Geese. Osprey (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Thol Bird Sanctuary is situated in Mehsana District of Gujarat and lies between 23.15 to 23.30’N latitude and 72.30 to 72.45’E longitude. It is a shallow water reservoir situated 25 km north-west of Ahmedabad. Thol water body occupies a total area of 6.99 sq km and its periphery is 5.62 km long. Its canals, distributaries and sub-distributaries are about 20 km long, and have a catchment of 320 sq km in surrounding villages. Greylag Goose (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Jungle Babbler (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Black-winged Stilt & Bar-headed Goose (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) ***

Day-2: Banni Grasslands, Great Rann of Kutch, February 6, 2020 Prashant Yella The Deccan Birders’ trip to Great Rann of Kutch was my first visit to the state of Gujarat. As I landed in Ahmedabad on the 5th of February, I remember being really stoked about getting a chance to capture the stunning landscapes of the region, and about witnessing some of the iconic raptors that have been on my bucket list for some time now. Cottages at the homestay (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) We reached the homestay on the morning of February 6th after an overnight journey from Ahmedabad. Located just outside Lodai village, the camp was setup in a tranquil location surrounded by hills and a lake. After we checked in to our respective cottages, I found myself trying to unpack as quickly as possible in order to get my gear ready and charge an extra set of batteries for the day. Later, over a cup of tea we were introduced to the guides and caretakers of the camp. We buckled up in the vehicles assigned to us and headed out to Banni Grasslands. Desert Wheatear (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) The first sightings of the day included Red Collared Doves, Rosy Starlings, Green Bee-eaters, Desert Wheatear and an Oriental Honey-buzzard. On entering the grassland area, we made a stop and huddled around for a wholesome Gujarati breakfast organized by our guide. We then took a quick look around on foot and got a chance to closely observe the soil and vegetation. We then resumed birding from our respective vehicles, which shielded us from the harsh midday sun. We spotted some winter visitors like Pallid Harrier, Isabelline Wheatear, Eurasian Spoonbill, and Cream-colored Courser. An arid part of Banni Grasslands (Photo: Prashant Yella) The Banni Grasslands are an arid ecosystem belt on the southern edge of the desert of the Great Rann of Kutch. The land here was formed from the sediments that were deposited by the Indus and other rivers over thousands of years. Isabelline Wheatear (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao)

Driving on, we came across a small patch of water near a culvert that had a good number of birds. Spotted Redshank (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Cream-coloured Courser (Photo: Umesh Mani) We also saw some horses in the distance. Laughing Dove (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) A herd of horses (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Another special sighting of the session was the Jack Snipe. It was so well-camouflaged that even from a distance of barely 6-7 feet, it was difficult to locate it! We headed back to the homestay for lunch but did not really take a break from birding. Many of us were kept busy by the bustling of House Sparrows, Red-vented Bulbuls and Laughing Doves around the bird feeders that were set up at the homestay. House Sparrow (Photo: Umesh Mani) Jack Snipe (Photo: Umesh Mani)

During this break, my father photographed a Grey-necked Bunting near the camp, which caused great excitement. We also saw an Orphean Warbler close to the lunch area. Bumblebee on Milkweed (aka Calotropis) (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Grey-necked Bunting (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Post lunch, we headed back into the grasslands. Most of the birding was done on our road journey towards the desert, where small water bodies yielded common water birds like Egrets, Grebes, and Herons. Sightings of the Booted Eagle and Greater Hoopoe Lark were also made during this time. Orphean Warbler (Photo: Umesh Mani) Greater Hoopoe Lark (Photo: Umesh Mani) The highlight of the day, though, was the sighting of the Merlin. Small Orange Tip (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Merlin (Photo: Umesh Mani)

On our way back we made a stop to see the Indian and Sykes’s Nightjars that were sitting around on the roads. A productive day indeed! Following a peculiar encounter with a couple of Desert Foxes, we stopped to enjoy a beautiful desert sunset with a cup of hot tea. Indian Nightjar (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Desert Fox (Photo: Umesh Mani) Sykes’s Nightjar (Photo: Umesh Mani) Sunset at Banni Grasslands (Photo: Prashant Yella) *** Day-3: Mandvi, February 7, 2020 Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao All that birdwatchers want on any trip, besides birds, is a bright and sunny morning – which all of us had rightly predicted a few hours prior to sunrise. It was a no-brainer as the waxing moon, nearing its full size, went down under our gaze in the western sky. While it was still dark, we set off to our destination, Mandvi Beach, which was around 100 km away from the homestay. The drive was pleasant and the time was well-utilized discussing ecology, geography and bird flight. A view of Mandvi Beach (Photo: Prashant Yella)

Demoiselle Crane (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Black-tailed Godwit (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) A Eurasian Marsh Harrier was seen hunting in the background. En route to the beach we were given a brief appearance by a pair of Nilgai. Yellow-wattled Lapwing (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) On reaching the port town of Mandvi, we were welcomed by a flock of Demoiselle Cranes, Yellow-wattled Lapwings and Grey and Citrine Wagtails. There was a small marshy patch across the beach and we got to see a large number of wetland birds including the Western Reef Egret, varieties of Gulls, Egrets, Cormorants, Black-tailed Godwits, and Black-winged Stilts. Nilgai (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) We reached the beach in time for a sumptuous breakfast laid out by our good friends Bharat, Dinesh and Kishore. It was a mix of local cuisine, some fruit and the evergreen bread and jam. However, an Oriental Honey-buzzard sitting on a bush distracted and delayed us for a while. Western Reef Egret (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Oriental Honey-buzzard (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao)

A mosaic of sea shells (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Greater Flamingo immature (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) We saw and recorded a number of Gulls and other waders, besides a lone Eurasian Curlew. On the return we saw a couple of camel carts used by the fishermen to lug their equipment and catch. Greater Flamingo adult (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) We quickly moved on to the shoreline where we met some birdwatchers from the Western world. We bashed on regardless and achieved our objectives. The star attractions were the Greater Flamingos, Pied Avocets, Eurasian Oystercatchers and Crab-plovers. Eurasian Curlew (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Eurasian Oystercatcher & Pied Avocet (Photo: Umesh Mani) Camel cart used for transporting man and material (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Pied Avocet & Crab-plover (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao)

We moved back to the marshy patch next to the factory once again to witness an interesting aerial combat. We saw three Great White Pelicans descend towards the marsh. This was not liked by the incumbent self-declared ruler, the Black-necked Stork. It rapidly clattered its long mandibles, as if firing a volley of shots! The Pelicans, undeterred, continued their approach ignoring the warnings. The Stork, forced to demonstrate its interceptor skills, quickly flew up a few hundred feet and gave a painful jab to one of the members in the Pelican formation! The formation had to break loose and flee the battle zone. The Stork, having warded off the invaders, descended rapidly to resume its hunt. An exciting encounter! Mallard (Photo: Umesh Mani) Black-necked Stork chasing off Great White Pelican (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) White Wagtail (Photo: Umesh Mani) Black-headed Gull (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Indian Softshell Turtle (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Indian Cormorant (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) After lunch we went to a nearby tank in the city where we saw a number of Cormorants, Ibises, Lapwings, Ducks, Painted Storks and the Indian Softshell Turtle. Grey Heron (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri)

An hour later we drove to a nearby scrub forest patch and saw the Rufous-fronted Prinia, the White-naped Tit and the Marshall’s Iora. We birders returned to our roost after a fruitful birding trip and were welcomed back with a hot dinner. Marshall’s Iora (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) White-naped Tit (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) *** Day-4: Chari Dhand, Great Rann of Kutch, February 8, 2020 Dr Barnali Chaudhuri A dozen Deccan Birders visited Bhuj and the Great Rann of Kutch, both known for their rich wildlife and biodiversity. I was excited and looking forward to my first ever experience of desert birding. Our convoy reached a vast landscape unbroken by any human construction. An Indian Peafowl sat on a tree. The dry riverbed was spectacular. After three days of excitement, we were ready to unfold Day4. Our destination was Chari Dhand, 100km from our homestay in Lodai village, where the 2001 earthquake in Bhuj had originated from. We woke up around 4:00AM to the calls of Nightjars. It was still dark and the stars were twinkling. We observed the ‘Seven Stars’ constellation – Saptarshi – along with the North Star. We enjoyed a hot cup of chai before starting off. Around 6:10AM, our convoy of three vehicles started for birding while it was still moonlight. The search lights of our vehicles illuminated the road ahead. The full moon spread its light as if guiding us towards our destination. As the time passed, the sun rose, overshadowing the moon. The land was aglow with the red light scattered by the sun. Dry riverbed with Aravali Mountains in the background (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Indian Peafowl (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Greater Spotted Eagle (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Steppe Eagle (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Yellow Wagtail (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) An Isabelline Shrike was flying from one tree to another. A Stoliczka’s Bushchat was looking for prey. The highlight sighting among the raptors, though, was the Eastern Imperial Eagle. Long-legged Buzzard (Photo: Umesh Mani) We observed a number of raptors – the Greater Spotted Eagle, Steppe Eagle, Eurasian Marsh Harrier, Long-legged Buzzard, etc. Alpine Swifts were seen in flight. Before I could take a picture, a Black-eared Kite replaced the Swifts. Several hundred Common Cranes were flying in their beautiful V formation. A pair of Yellow Wagtails was busy feeding. Eastern Imperial Eagle (Photo: Umesh Mani) Bharat, our tour guide, advised us not to linger too long as we had to reach our destination in the early hours if we wanted to see the rare Grey Hypocolius, a winter visitor from the remote areas of central Asia. Isabelline Shrike (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) The big lake at Chari Dhand (Photo: Prashant Yella)

Common Crane (Photo: Umesh Mani) Grey Hypocolius (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Following his advice, we drove up toward the big lake, Chari Dhand. Bharat, who was on the lookout for the Grey Hypocolius, was finally able to locate it. We noticed a Rosy Starling quarreling with the Grey Hypocolius in a bid to secure its territory. Bharat told us to wait patiently. After a while we saw the Hypocolius without any disturbance from the Rosy Starling. I was thrilled to watch the bird feed on the little berries of Salvadora persica. After a while I saw a Bluethroat feeding in the field under the shade of a tree. Common Kestrel (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) After spotting a Common Kestrel on a tree, we headed towards a rocky area. A Red-tailed Wheatear was perched on the rocks and looking around, patiently posing for our photographers. Bluethroat (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Far in the lake, hundreds of water birds were on display. Among them, Pelicans were distinctly visible. Soon, the second half of the raptor show began, giving us innumerable sightings. We spotted a Golden Jackal looking towards us. Hundreds of Common Cranes were roosting in the valley of a nearby mountain range. Red-tailed Wheatear (Photo: Umesh Mani) A wonderful spread of idli, bread with butter and jam, bananas and tea awaited us on the hoods of our vehicles. After a sumptuous breakfast arranged by Bharat, we visited the natural rock formations on the Layari River Bed and saw a spectacular Eurasian Eagle Owl with prominent ear-tufts. After a while it flew from one side to the other and camouflaged perfectly with the rocky surroundings.

A view en route to Moti Virani (Photo: Prashant Yella) The rocks with the Eurasian Eagle Owl nest (Photo: Prashant Yella) Driving on, we came upon two Golden Jackals. We stopped for lunch in a small village named Moti Virani around 12:45PM. The Centre for Desert and Ocean (CEDO) was totally different from other restaurants. I liked the quotations hanging on the walls – for instance, ‘Sea water is the future’, ‘Photosynthesis is the answer to world problems’, ‘Butterflies are flying flowers, flowers are tethered Butterflies’, etc. It was only when Shivam, the owner’s son, explained about their activities that I realized that CEDO was not just a restaurant and homestay, but also did a lot of work in the fields of environment, ecology and social causes. That place had a soothing effect on our eyes as it was surrounded by many big trees. Shivam also explained about the trees and their uses. Behind the restaurant were teak trees (Tecomella undulata), locally known as Rohida, blooming with orange and red flowers. Layari River (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Purple Sunbird male in eclipse plumage (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Rock formation en route to Moti Virani (Photo: Prashant Yella) I spotted a beautiful male Purple Sunbird in eclipse plumage enjoying nectar from those flowers. Rohida produces quality timber used for furniture. Shivam became emotional as he explained the medicinal power of Rohida and how the extract of the leaves had cured a dying leukemia patient. There were also Drumstick trees with beautiful flowers.

Indian Courser (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Ammonite fossil (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) After lunch Shivam was kind enough to show us their vast collection of fossils. Among them the fossilized sea shells, conches, Pela carpilius crab and the ammonites attracted my eyes. I suddenly realized that back in our village, we worshipped a fossil of ammonite in black stone as our Kuladevata (the God Narayana). Shivam also took us to the nursery near the restaurant. We saw several trees along with Rohida and Shami. He explained that an infusion of Shami leaves can be used as an astringent and a remedy for diarrhoea and dysentery, as the extract of the leaves can kill intestinal parasitic worms. Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Drumstick flowers (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) After tea, we left the Centre at 3:15PM, for the second half of our birding. After driving for a while, Kishore stopped our vehicle to show us a pair of Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse in the open ground. I wondered how they survived in the most parched environment on earth. Later I came to know that they needed water only once in 24 hours. In fact, some of the species can live longer than 24 hours without water. Moreover, male Sandgrouse carry water for their little ones in their specially-built breast feathers, which can soak water like a sponge. Meanwhile Bharat, who was in another vehicle, spotted the Indian Courser and informed us. We rushed to the spot to see the colourful bird. After enjoying the bird, we came across another pair of Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse. Grey Francolin (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) After a while, we saw a pair of Grey Francolins enjoying their food. It was very difficult to distinguish between male and female. We looked around for the Painted Sandgrouse, but sighted the third pair of the Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse instead. We also came across a Rufous-tailed Lark, a flock of Greater Short-toed Larks and some raptors.

Rufous-tailed Lark (Photo: Umesh Mani) Sunset over the water body (Photo: Prashant Yella) The setting sun looked like a golden plate disappearing in the far horizon in the Great Rann of Kutch. There was not one cloud in the sky. The entire sky became reddish. The red colour demarcated the land from the sky and it was a spectacular sight. As time passed, the moon rose. Though the sun had set, there was enough light. In that dim light, we spotted a few Northern Shovelers. Greater Short-toed Lark (Photo: Umesh Mani) Northern Shoveler (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Maldharis on their way home (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) We reached the homestay by 8:30PM and enjoyed a delicious dinner. I thank Umesh for organizing the trip and Sudhir for coordinating. Bharat’s guidance and timely, delicious food, made the trip unforgettable. I also thank all the team members for making this trip as a memorable one. As the sun went down, Common Cranes went back to their roosting area. Maldharis, a tribal community in Gujarat, were seen going back with their camels. We reached a water body where I noticed plenty of small ammonites scattered. We saw a Greater Flamingo along with six juveniles. *** Day-5: Banni Grasslands, Great Rann of Kutch, February 9, 2020 Prashant Yella Growing up in a household of birders, I received my first guidebook at the age of nine. I remember being immediately drawn to the wide variety of Raptors and Owls that I had never seen or heard of. Over the past few days, I was finally able to witness some of these majestic birds in their habitat and happily, I can now tick some off my list. The excitement of finally seeing the Eurasian Eagle Owl (Bubo bubo) is something that I will cherish for a long time. It was our last day of birding out in the Great Rann of Kutch. The energy levels in the camp were as high as Day One, even though the schedule for the day was not as jam-packed. Most visits were planned around a few local sites. At the break of dawn, all of us gathered around for some tea and a quick briefing. We headed into the grasslands in an attempt to spot the Bimaculated Lark (Melanocorypha bimaculate) amongst hundreds of Greater Short-toed Larks. However, it proved unfruitful. One of the other teams got a glimpse of the Macqueen’s Bustard, but could not get a photograph. On the brighter side, sightings of the Short-eared Owl, Steppe Eagle and Montagu’s Harrier were made before we got together for breakfast and a group photo session.

There was also an interesting bit of action when we saw a male Steppe Eagle chase a female off what seemed to be a preferred perch. Short-eared Owl (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Steppe Eagle female (L) being displaced by male (R) (Photo: Umesh Mani) After breakfast, our main sightings consisted of Variable Wheatear, Asian Desert Warbler, Streaked Weaver, Green Bee-eater and Indian Silverbill. A Stoliczka’s Bushchat gave an exhibition of its famous puff-and-roll display. Montagu’s Harrier female (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Stoliczka’s Bushchat (Photo: Umesh Mani) It was fascinating to see that our guides not only understood the ecosystems of the region really well, but also were wellversed in locating and identifying birds that were tricky to spot. The group at Banni Grasslands (Photo courtesy: Prashant Yella) Variable Wheatear (Photo: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri) Desert Whitethroat (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Some of us visited a temple of a local saint named Mekan Dada. Here we got a chance to interact with the residents of Lodai and learn a bit more about their history and culture before heading back for lunch. Brown Rock Chat (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Common Hoopoe (Photo: G Ramakrishna Rao) Later in the evening we headed out to a few more local spots for birding. Additions to our list were Common Babblers, Grey Francolins, Isabelline Wheatears and the Indian Courser. Sunset en route to Bhuj (Photo: Prashant Yella) Finally, we headed back to Bhuj for some shopping and the traditional Gujarati thali, before commencing our overnight journey to Ahmedabad. Today, as I look back at the photographs of the landscapes that I had captured, I feel immense gratitude to our guides who enthusiastically showed us a wide variety of locations with unique topographies. From canyon-like rock formations to still ponds and salt deposits in the desert, we were able to cover all the quintessential landscapes of Great Rann of Kutch. Common Babbler (Photo: Umesh Mani) The final stop for the day was a Sun temple where we saw Brown Rock Chats and Dusky Crag Martins. Sun Temple (Photo: Prashant Yella) Steppe Eagle (Photo: Umesh Mani) ***

Day-6: Thol Lake Bird Sanctuary, February 10, 2020 Sudipta Bhattacharya On the way back from Great Rann of Kutch, two photography enthusiasts accompanied two ardent birders to Thol Lake. The day started with some refreshment at a sophisticated waiting room in the Ahmedabad Railway Station. This was a transit day from Bhuj to Hyderabad, and the trip to Thol was a sudden decision as our flights were in the evening, and we had reached Ahmedabad by the early morning. It was a sunny day with clear sky. As soon as we reached Thol Lake Bird Sanctuary after a quick sip of tea, we were welcomed by a Eurasian Collared Dove and an Indian Palm Squirrel. Purple Heron (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Eurasian Collared Dove (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Long-tailed Shrike (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) A Lesser Whitethroat was spotted immediately. A Long-tailed Shrike appeared suddenly for a short while, followed by a couple of Bluethroat engaging in a territorial dispute. Indian Palm Squirrel (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) We went through a display explaining the background of the lake, and learnt that this lake was artificially established in the year 1912, with the objective of providing irrigation facilities to nearby farmers. This lake has the capacity to store about 84 million cubic meters of water, and is spread over an area of about 699 hectares of land. It is currently owned and operated by the Forests and Irrigation Departments of the Government of Gujarat. While going around the lake we observed that the place had a combination of habitats – forest, scrub and wetland. Naturally, all kinds of birds were seen flying around, including winter migratory species. Bluethroat (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) There was a small water outlet surrounded by scrub as seen in the photograph below. This area had good activity.

Ruddy Shelduck (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Booted Warbler (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Knob-billed Duck (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) As soon as we climbed up the bund surrounding the lake the vast area of the lake was visible. A large number of migratory ducks were visible in the islands in the middle of the lake. Several Ruddy Shelducks, Knob-billed (or Comb) Ducks, Northern Shovelers, Northern Pintails etc. were visible. Lesser Whitethroat (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) The female of a Purple Sunbird was showing its flying tricks in front of us. A Green Bee-eater was taking a sunbath, and a Booted Warbler was foraging on ground as it usually does. Suddenly a Lesser Whitethroat appeared in front of us. A large number of Dusky Crag Martins were flying around. Dusky Crag Martin (Photo: Umesh Mani) Purple Sunbird female (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya)

Purple Sunbird male (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) We all got to take some close shots of a Purple Sunbird in search of food. While going to the other side we saw a Blackeared Kite hovering over us. Black-eared Kite (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Red-breasted Flycatcher (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Greater Spotted Eagle (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) While returning to our car we saw a Red-breasted Flycatcher and a Greater Spotted Eagle. A Great Egret flew over our head; I was happy at the chance to take a flight shot. Pied Kingfisher hovering (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) The acrobatics in flight by the Pied Kingfisher was, as always, an interesting sight. Great Egret (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya)

Red-vented Bulbul (P. c. benghalensis subspecies) and a vocal Indian Robin. Red-naped Ibis (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) The Red-naped Ibis was also visible in the marshy lands beside the grassy areas. The Steppe Eagle was seen on the way back to the parking space. Red-vented Bulbul (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Indian Robin male (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) We had a late lunch, breaking our long exile from nonvegetarian food, then reached the Ahmedabad airport on time for a peaceful journey back home. Clamorous Reed Warbler (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Near the parking, in the area where we had previously seen the Bluethroats, we observed Clamorous Reed Warblers having an argument. We wish all our members a Merry Christmas and a Healthy and Happy New Year 2021 Report: Birds of Chincholi Wildlife Sanctuary, Karnataka Text: Srikanth Bhamidipati; Photos: Anand Kalinadhabhatla Common Woodshrike Located about 140km from the city of Hyderabad lies Chincholi WLS, an amazing dry/moist deciduous forest. This forest borders the states of Telangana and Karnataka and has one major dam - Chandrampalli - and 4 smaller check dams. The forest is home to amazing biodiversity with more than 150 species of birds, 50-plus species of butterflies, and mammals like Indian Fox, Four-horned Antelope, Leopard and many others. Outside the sanctuary, there are farmlands and eucalyptus plantations and a small tribal settlement area with a population of about 50-100 people. During our first visit to this location in 2011, we had entered from the Karnataka side and were amazed by the biodiversity of the location and the variety of sightings. It was not until late 2017, however, that we found out that there is a way in from the Telangana side as well, and that is when we started further exploring the place. In late 2019 and early 2020 this place became a hotspot for many birders with some very interesting sightings like Shaheen Falcon, Bonelli’s Eagle, Fork-tailed Drongo Cuckoo and many other species, but the star of the show was undoubtedly the White-Bellied Minivet. 1

White-bellied Minivet male (L) and female (R) During our regular visits to this site, we observed that some of these species, like the White-Bellied Minivet, Bonelli’s Eagle and Shaheen Falcon, were nesting in this place, and we also got confirmed records of the Minivet breeding here. While looking for some older records of White-bellied Minivet with help from Humayun Taher, we were able to trace the existence of this species in Telangana to as far back as 1840, in the hills of Mannanur, and also found that nesting records with flock of 4-5 birds were recorded 25km north-west of Trimulgherry in the early 1900s, as mentioned in the Hyderabad State Ornithological Survey. This species now goes by the scientific name, Pericroctotus erythropygius, but in the early 1840s, it was called Muscicapa erythropygius, as recorded and published by TC Jerdon in the Madras Journal. Similarly, Bonelli’s Eagle and Shaheen Falcon were seen carrying nesting material close to the Chincholi sanctuary, and it was indeed a treat to the eyes to watch them fly by. Earlier this year, we had also observed many other species of birds nesting in this location, like Scaly-breasted Munia, Indian Silverbill, Black-rumped Flameback, White-browed Fantail, all the Prinias mentioned in the list, Plum-headed and Roseringed Parakeets, Grey Francolin and Jungle Bush Quail. There is great potential to find more species of birds here, as the habitat here is very diverse. We have seen dense forest landscapes, grasslands, a water body, scrub and other ecosystems which support the existence of many species. Short-toed Snake Eagle This year, I have visited this place around 4-5 times and seen more than 150 bird species, including 8 raptors and 3 owl species. A larger survey of this location across various seasons would definitely help evaluate and measure the potential of the location and gather substantial data which can be used for conservation purposes. The land here is mainly forest area but around the periphery there is farming, very minimal fishing activity in the lake inside, and some recreational activities. In this context, we have observed some major threats to this location, including farming, cattle grazing, some amount of poaching, the presence of tourist population leading to uncontrolled littering and waste disposal and, above all, movie/television shootings. This is a major concern and, I feel, we must conduct organized surveys here to showcase the incredible biodiversity of the place and make sure that it is preserved and adequately protected. 2

We did a couple of walks in the forest around the resort with a well-informed naturalist from the resort. We saw plenty of birds; a list is attached later in the report. 5

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Darter (Anhinga melanogaster) Darter (Bharatpur, December 13, 2019) Order: Suliformes Family: Anhingidae Genus: Anhinga Species: A. melanogaster Size: 85-100 cm changes from yellow-pink to black, and the yellow or greenish-yellow facial skin turns turquoise. The irises, which are usually white with a yellow ring, may also change colour between yellow, red or brown, and the tarsi and toes become darker grey with yellow webbing. The Darter is monogamous. Description & distribution: The Darter, also known as the Oriental Darter, is a large waterbird and one of only four members of the Anhingidae family, which consists of a single genus, Anhinga. The name Snakebird is also used to refer to whichever member of the genus is allopatric to the region, and is popularly used because of the distinctive neck, which looks like a snake when the Darter is swimming with the rest of its body submerged in the water. This resemblance to a snake is also seen, more infrequently, during their bonding displays, when the mating pair sometimes twist their necks around each other. The Darter is seen across Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and east across Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. It inhabits tropical, sub-tropical and sometimes warm temperate regions, and prefers freshwater lakes, rivers, marshes, swamps and, less frequently, brackish estuaries, lagoons and mangroves; it is often seen perching on trees near or overlooking water. The Darter is largely black and brown in colour, with conspicuous silvery-grey streaking on its scapulars and upper wing coverts, a velvety brown neck and head with no external nostrils and a long whitish stripe extending down the side of the neck, paler creamy-white and mottled-black chin and throat, and a long, wedge-shaped tail. The bill is yellow, slender and dagger-like, with serrated edges, and the Darter frequently uses the bill to impale fish, its main prey. The legs are short, set far back on the body, and completely webbed. The sexes are alike, although the female may be a little larger and may show paler colours, especially on the neck and underparts. There is no eclipse plumage, but some of the bare parts may change colour during breeding season: the gular sac Habitat & behaviour: The Darter is mostly resident and does not migrate, except for some local movements in response to climatic conditions or food scarcity. It is usually seen singly, in pairs or in small groups, but often associates with herons, storks and ibises. It is a colonial nester, but is still highly territorial when on the nest. While walking it shows a highstepping gait, with wings spread for balance, while its flight is laboured, and so it prefers to get up high and then soar or glide on thermals. The usual call is a two-syllabled chigi chigi chigi, and it may emit a series of clicks or rattles while flying. When perched, adults communicate with croaks, grunts or rattles while young birds may emit squealing or squawking calls. Its diet consists mainly of mid-sized fish and, occasionally, aquatic vertebrates or invertebrates like molluscs, frogs, eels, water snakes, and even small turtles. It uses its sharp bill to impale its prey, then brings it out of the water and tosses it up in the air before swallowing it head-first. 8

Nesting: The Darter breeds generally between May and August in northern India, and between November and February in southern India. Egg laying seems to be related to water levels and usually happens when water levels are high, thus ensuring that abundant food resources are available. The nest is a twig platform, similar to other colonial nesters like the cormorants, storks and herons with whom the Darter associates while nesting in a mixed heronry, and generally near water. The usual clutch consists of 3-6 elongated, greenish-white or pale greenish-blue eggs. Local name: The Darter is known as ‘Panwa’, ‘Pan dubi’ or ‘Banbe’ in Hindi, ‘Bhujanga’ in Punjabi, ‘Pamubatu’ in Telugu, ‘Pambuttara’ in Tamil, ‘Sarpagreeva’ in Gujarati and ‘Sarpapakshi’ or ‘Tirandaz’ in Marathi. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From The Times Of India, January 25, 2018) *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. A PULICAT JOURNAL December 24-28, 2020 Rishi Reddy Kalliath (8 years) Painted Stork flock (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) My mother and I got a chance to go to Pulicat recently, because my grandfather Lawrence and two of his friends were going there for the Asian Waterfowl Census. Day-1: December 24, 2020 I felt very very happy that I was in Pulicat once again. We went to Shar Road at Pulicat, the road that leads to ISRO, around 4pm. We went to Flamingo Point on Shar Road where you see Flamingos. When we reached there I felt very very excited to see Flamingos again and it was a nice sunny day. But we just saw 40-50 Flamingos – we didn’t see as many as last year. We saw many Painted Storks (not sure of the number of birds). I think the water level was too high for Flamingos so they couldn’t find algae, so not many Flamingos were seen. We had only a little time before it got dark, but the sunset was very beautiful with the Painted Storks and water all around. Sunset at Shar Road (Photo: Umesh Mani) 1

Black-tailed Godwit (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Caspian Tern with catch (Photo: Umesh Mani) Day-2: December 25, 2020 It was a very sunny day and hot, but it was good because I was riding a boat to go to Irakam Island. I felt happy. I felt very thirsty and I finished my bottle of water very soon. I felt very cool when I put my hands and legs in the water and I got way more energy with all that coolness. I was very active, I didn’t sleep on the boat like last time. It was around 2 hours of boat ride to get to the island. On the way I saw Caspian Terns, Whiskered Terns and Cormorants. When the boat goes on the water, the propeller moves and disturbs the fish under water and they come out – so the Gulls and Caspian Terns kept following the boat to eat the fish that come out of the water. I also saw a Grey Heron and a Common Greenshank. Jacobin’s Cuckoo (Photo: Umesh Mani) I got off the boat and walked a little on the island, and we saw Spot-billed Ducks, Black-winged Stilts, Pied Kingfisher, a few Median Egrets and many other birds. Common Greenshank (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Grey Plover (Photo: Umesh Mani) Little Egret (Photo: Umesh Mani) Common Sandpiper (Photo: Umesh Mani) 2

After some time, I came back to the boat because I was feeling very thirsty. We boarded the boat and came back to the mainland, seeing the same birds we did while going to the island. Day-3: December 26, 2020 The area we went to was quite muddy and I got a lot muddier – it was so much fun. Pacific Golden Plover (Photo: Umesh Mani) We had lunch at a dhaba and then went to another place where we saw many Pacific Golden Plovers and Eurasian Curlews. After that, we went to another place where we took another boat to cross a small stream and get to the opposite bund. Here we saw Black-headed Ibis, a flock of Curlews and a few Pacific Golden Plovers. White-eyed Buzzard (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) We saw a White-eyed Buzzard and a Spotted Deer. I wanted to take a photo but missed the Deer. It ran away by the time I got out of the car. I was sad that I couldn’t see it again. Then we went to another place, where I ran around a sandy place for some time – I found it difficult to run on the sand. On the way back from there, we spent a lot of time taking pictures of an Indian Roller and a Green Bee-eater. The Indian Roller and Bee-eater were facing opposite directions. Black-headed Ibis (Photo: Umesh Mani) Eurasian Curlew (Photo: Umesh Mani) There were lot of natural habitats there. When we came back, some kids asked me to show my photos, but I didn’t understand much of what they were asking as they were talking in Tamil. The fisherman who took us across the water to the bund refused to take any money. Then we returned to the hotel and had dinner. Indian Roller (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) We then had lunch in a clearing. The lunch was from the home of our local auto driver friend, Chalapathi. While eating we saw a very fat Drongo chasing an Indian Roller. Red-crested Pochard (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) 3

Asian Openbill (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) Eurasian Oystercatcher (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) After lunch we went to Nelapattu. I was happy to see the Pelicans in Nelapattu again. I remember that there were way more Openbill Storks in Nelapattu than last year. But there weren’t as many Spoonbills as last time. I got a good photo of a Spoonbill – it was in perfect view – and some Pelicans. We took a video of a Snail eating a Krackjack biscuit. I saw a sandbar with the Oystercatcher and a dead Olive Ridley turtle. The dead Turtle’s eyes were gone. Right next to the sandbar with the Oystercatcher, I saw a huge flock of Caspian Terns and Greater Crested Terns. Eurasian Spoonbill (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) Sanderling (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Then we saw some more Golden Plovers and a small group of Sanderlings. We got down on one sandbar, and I played in the water – which was actually the Bay of Bengal. I played and I played, and got fully wet and had to change in front of everybody! Then, we came back to the hotel, showered and ate lunch. Spot-billed Pelican (Photo: Umesh Mani) Day-4: December 27, 2020 As a side trip, we went on another boat ride on the Tamil Nadu side of Pulicat. I had a lifer there – the Eurasian Oystercatcher! The water during the boat ride was very calm. It became very sunny by afternoon. Indian Pond Heron (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) 4

Black-winged Stilt flock (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) Grey-headed Lapwing (Photo: Umesh Mani) Pallid Harrier (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) Glossy Ibis (Photo: Umesh Mani) After lunch, we had to finish a few remaining areas for the AWC, so we went back to Shar Road to the Flamingo Point but couldn’t find any Flamingos. A Pond Heron posed nicely for us. We saw a lot of Painted Storks and Brown-headed Gulls. The Gulls were in non-breeding plumage. Then we went for a coffee break near the Sriharikota entrance. I met two calves and hugged one of them. There were also around 9-10 puppies that were chasing us around for food because we had biscuits. I felt angry at the Crows as they were taking the puppies’ food away. Pheasant-tailed Jacana (Photo: Umesh Mani) Day-5: December 28, 2020 White-bellied Sea Eagle (Photo: Rishi Reddy Kalliath) We saw a White-bellied Sea Eagle, a huge flock of Blackwinged Stilts and a beautiful Pallid Harrier. Spot-billed Pelican (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) 5

On our way back from Pulicat, we stopped for some time at Uppalapadu. There we saw many Openbill Storks, Pelicans and Painted Storks. I got way better photographs here. In Uppalapadu I saw more baby Pelicans than in Nelapattu. Then we got started back to Hyderabad and reached home around 9pm. when I touched the Bay of Bengal. I have been in three oceans in my life – Indian Ocean, Bay of Bengal, and Pacific Ocean. I feel happy when I am birding. I get to learn so much about the birds, and how they look and behave. I liked everything about the Pulicat trip – the boat rides, the birds, and the long car rides. The only thing I didn’t like about Pulicat is that people are throwing a lot of plastic junk and chips packets in the lake and birds are dying. I have become way more interested in birds because now I am asking myself what makes this bird this bird and what makes that bird that bird. I met some nice people and kids during the trip. But next time I want to start taking care of my own things – because this time Lawrence thatha was charging my batteries. I also want to see way way way way more birds! But what I enjoyed best was when I was putting my legs and hands in the water during the boat ride. I also felt very happy Here are some other photos we took during the trip: This time there were lesser birds than last year. ANDAMAN & NICOBAR ISLANDS: A FLASHBACK Text and Photographs: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao A view of an active volcano at Barren Island If there is one thing good that happened due to the Corona Virus pandemic, it was the return of ‘home time’. And what better way to spend this precious time other than going through old photo albums that had been forgotten thanks to the invasion of digital media. Another spinoff was that the Deccan Birders’ Executive Committee went ahead full steam, setting up webinar after webinar, sometimes even two a week! My sincere appreciation to the Executive Committee for organising these sessions, enabling us to gain a variety of knowledge and virtually interact with many eminent personalities about whom we had only heard of or read about. Two such speakers were Dr Shirish Manchi and Dr K Sivakumar. During their talks, they narrated their adventures in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands – and this triggered a flashback for me, enabling me to relive some of my fondest memories. Hence, I decided to pen down some reminiscences of my tenure there. number of Black Bazas (Aviceda leuphotes) into the Andaman Islands. View from Port Blair, used in the old Rs Twenty currency note Being a nature and wildlife enthusiast, I had volunteered for a posting to the islands. I served there from 2006 to 2008, post the tsunami. Apart from some desk work in the headquarters, I also flew the Air Force helicopters on Car Nicobar Island. That gave me the real freedom that I sought, and the job got very exciting with each passing week. While there, I was able to travel the length and breadth of the archipelago of 572 islands/islets/rocks by land, sea and air. I stayed in Jayant Park Colony in the Minnie Bay area of Port Blair, located in the thick, tropical rainforest with a scenic view of the Port area and Viper Island. This place had a lot of birds, including Red-whiskered Bulbuls (Pycnonotus jocosus), Brown (or Andaman) Coucal (Centropus andamanensis), Andaman Drongo (Dicrurus andamanensis) and the Greater Racket-tailed Drongo (Dicrurus paradiseus). The Drongo was notorious for making a variety of calls and confusing the residents. At night, it could be seen fetching multiple meals to the lamp posts in the colony. Andaman Green Pigeons (Treron (pompadora) chloropterus) would be seen in large fig trees and would reveal themselves only during take-off or landing. The Northern Migration was signified by the arrival of a large Andaman Day Gecko Snakes were very much a part of daily life, and also other reptiles like the Andaman Day Gecko (Phelsuma andamanensis) and the Common Water Monitor Lizard (Varanus salvator). The harbour area and the coast line remained under the surveillance of White-bellied Sea Eagles (Haliaeetus leucogaster). 9

Two more views of the active volcano at Barren Island Chidiya Tapu, the southernmost point on the South Andaman Island, and Mount Harriet are popular birding destinations. Narcondam and Barren Islands are far flung from Port Blair and pose severe logistical problems for any defence tactician. Barren Island is the only active volcano in India and we were lucky to see smoke billowing from the sulphur-coated dyke and crater. Some feral goats could be spotted on the grassy patches close to the shore. birds. One such notable patch was on the northern end of the runway where hundreds of Oriental Pratincoles (Glareola maldivarum), along with other waders, could be seen. Submerged portion of runway at Car Nicobar Island Narcondam Island This did pose a challenge to the aviation activities of the air base. White-headed Starlings (Sturnia erythropygia) and Black-naped Orioles (Oriolus chinensis) were a common sight here. Narcondam Island is 250km north-east of Port Blair and has a small armed presence in the form of a police post at the base of the hill. The island is actually a dormant volcano, rising up to 710m above sea level. This island is the only home to the Narcondam Hornbill (Rhyticeros narcondami) and these birds can be seen flying around from a Maritime Reconnaissance airplane too! An Early Warning Radar was proposed to be located on the Island by the Defence Ministry but the same was shelved later owing to widespread backing for the Hornbill by various environmental agencies. Car Nicobar Island is the northernmost island of the Nicobar group of islands with a perimeter of about 60km. It was severely affected by the tsunami, with the tidal waves destroying whatever came in their path. Thus, some of the lowlying areas were filled with saline water that attracted shore Pied Imperial Pigeon 10

Some of the notable sightings at Great Nicobar were the Nicobar Parakeet (Psittacula caniceps), Long-tailed Parakeet (Psittacula longicauda), Great Nicobar Serpent Eagle (Spilornis klossi), a rescued Nicobar Pigeon (Caloenas nicobarica), Pied Imperial Pigeon (Ducula bicolor), the iconic Nicobar Megapode (Megapodius nicobariensis) and Malayan Night Heron (Gorsachius melanolophus). Long-tailed Parakeet The Great Nicobar Island is the southernmost one and mostly covered by dense forests. During the tsunami, the island saw severe destruction and sinking of a part of it on the southeastern side. A statue of former Prime Minister Late Smt Indira Gandhi had also been swept away from Indira Point. It took an extensive search and recovery operation by a combined team of the Army, Navy and Air Force before the top half of the statue was located, retrieved and ferried back to Campbell Bay in May 2005. The lower half of the statue was located almost two years later in 2007, hidden in the web of fallen trees in the marsh, and another Herculean effort was mounted to retrieve the same. The statue was once again erected at a spot close to the original location. Rescued Nicobar Pigeon Nicobar Megapode Top half of the statue of former Prime Minister Late Smt Indira Gandhi, retrieved from the sea after the tsunami Malayan Night Heron rescued by the rescue centre A Territorial Army Battalion is stationed on this island and it has been instrumental in successfully running an animal and bird rescue centre. Unfortunately, the birds of the islands are, currently, battling on two fronts – loss of habitat to human developmental works and poaching of natural wealth by seafarers within and from the neighbouring countries. It would be good if some effective conservation measures could be put in place for these unique habitats, as soon as possible. Partially submerged Light House at Indira Point *** 11

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Ruddy Turnstone (Arenaria interpres) Ruddy Turnstone breeding (L) and non-breeding (R) (Pulicat, September 9, 2020) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Arenaria Species: A. interpres Size: 23 cm plant material at times. While breeding, it also eats a good proportion of insects. It has been observed to raid unattended nests of Gulls, Terns, Ducks and even other Turnstones, piercing the eggshells to get at the material inside. While foraging it often flips over small stones, leaves or flotsam – hence the name ‘turnstone’. But there are other ways in which it forages – routing through piles of seaweed or probing into the sand for gastropods, surface-pecking or digging small holes in the sand for concealed prey like sandhoppers, and hammer-probing by cracking open the shell of the prey with its bill. Description & distribution: The Ruddy Turnstone is one of the two species of Turnstone in the genus Arenaria, the other being the Black Turnstone of western United States. The Ruddy Turnstone is a small wader which was earlier placed in the Charadriidae family of Plovers, but was later reclassified into the Scolopacidae family of Sandpipers. A small, stocky bird, the Ruddy Turnstone has a dark, slightly upturned wedgeshaped bill, immaculate white chin and throat, black breast with white side patches, white belly and bright orange legs. The head has heavy streaking, while the upperparts are strong grey-brown with black mottling. During breeding season, the upperparts turn reddish-brown with black markings, the head is black with white streaking, and the face becomes white with an irregular black pattern. The female is similar to the male, but a little duller and the head is browner. Juvenile birds have a pale brown head and pale fringing on upperparts, giving a scaly appearance. While breeding, it prefers the Arctic tundra and rocky coastal areas, marshes and bare rocks near water, whereas during the non-breeding season, it frequents the coastlines in its wintering range. During breeding season, it can be quite territorial and aggressive. It is monogamous, often staying with the same mate for several years. The Ruddy Turnstone arrives at its breeding grounds by late May or early June, and pair bonds are formed at the breeding grounds within 7 to 10 days, and renewed through courtship displays on returning to the same breeding grounds in subsequent years. Display may be initiated by either male or female. Once the pair bond is established, the male and female stay within sight of each other until egg-laying. The Turnstone displays a lot more variation in its breeding plumage, and may use these patterns to recognize mates, or differentiate intruders from other individuals who happen to be nesting nearby. The Ruddy Turnstone breeds in the Arctic tundra from Alaska, east across Canada, Greenland, Scandinavia, the Baltic Islands, and across northern Siberia to the Bering Sea. It winters on coastlines in north America (from northern Massachusetts and northern California) to the Antilles, Central and South America, as well as coastlines across Europe, Africa, and Asia (southern China, Japan, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and India, including the Andaman & Nicobar Islands), and even as far south as New Zealand, Tasmania and some of the Pacific islands. Some birds are known to stay over during the summer in many parts of their wintering range, even assuming breeding colours at the appropriate time. Nesting: The Ruddy Turnstone breeds generally from late May till early July in its breeding range. The nest is a shallow scrape on high ground, lined with leaves and lichen, not far from water. Egg laying is influenced by availability of prey, and may be delayed if adequate animal food is not available. The usual clutch consists of 2-5 dark brown or olive eggs with a lot of mottling or splotches. Incubation duties are shared by both parents. Local name: The Ruddy Turnstone is known as ‘Patthar palta’ in Hindi, ‘Kal purratti’ or ‘Kottan’ in Tamil, ‘Tirakkata’ in Malayalam, ‘Kachabarangi’ in Gujarati and ‘Mutara’ or ‘Rangit tutari’ in Marathi. Habitat & behaviour: Outside the breeding season, the Ruddy Turnstone is usually seen in small to large flocks, scurrying around on the edge of the water while foraging. Its diet consists mainly of invertebrates like crustaceans, molluscs and worms, though it may also take small fish, carrion, eggs and *** 13

A MEDICINAL OUTING Trip Report: Moolika Vanam, Chilkur, December 19, 2020 Surekha Aitabathula A view of Moolika Vanam (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) Early on the morning of Sunday, December 19, 2020, when the reluctant winter was refusing to settle in Hyderabad, Srikanth, Rama and I hitched a ride with Gokul and off we went to the Forest Department's Moolika Vanam (medicinal plantation) in Chilkur, opposite the Mrigavani National Park. The task at hand was to carry out a survey for the birds and butterflies on the campus. Finally gaining entry, we walked into the medicinal plantation, and found one long linear pathway bisecting it. The first avian species to give us a grand stand were the Indian Silverbills. They looked well fed and did not shy away from us. Thank God for small mercies! We thought it best to fuel up with morning cuppas of tea and coffee before we began the survey, so we made a pit stop at a very brightly lit shack. Fuelled up happily with our favourite beverages, we were really raring to go. The same phenomena that happens with every birding group happened to us too – we faced a forbiddingly tall, prison-like locked iron gate that had a ‘no-entry - back-off!’ demeanour. The message hadn’t trickled down to the watchman from the higher-ups who had given us permission to enter. So the dutiful watchman with a heavy Bengali accent refused to unlock the gate. Srikanth called and woke up the higher-up at that early hour and put the gentleman onto the watchman through the ‘prison’ bars. After speaking to his boss, the watchman wiped off his previous suspicious expression and gave us a mini lecture about how he was being sincere and only following orders. Indian Silverbill (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Plain Prinia (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) There was a garden patch full of medicinal plants and we were introduced to nine different varieties of Tulsi. We thoroughly enjoyed taking in the lovely subtle and not-so-subtle aroma of crushed leaves. Striped Tiger (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) 14

By this time, the sun had come up, and this brought out the butterflies. Blue Tigers and Striped Tigers were aplenty. A funny thought surfaced in my mind – Wouldn’t I love to see the expression of our national animal when he is told that humans have named the delicate butterfly after him! There were some not-so-tall Neem (Azadirachta indica) trees too, whose medicinal properties are well known and widely in use. Neem is said to cure leprosy, eye disorders, intestinal worms, skin ulcers, diabetes and gingivitis. While we were walking through the shrubbery single file, Srikanth suddenly stopped because a really long thorn had pierced into his sole through his shoe! He took off his shoe, removed the thorn and calmly said, ' Guys, I am losing a lot of blood." Blue Pansy (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) From the manicured herbal garden we walked into a scrub-like setting where Amla (Phyllanthus emblica) trees were all around. Pre-clinicial studies have shown that the gooseberry possesses antipyretic, antibiotic, analgesic, cardioprotective, gastroprotective, nephroprotective and neuroprotective properties. Not to forget that Amla pickles are a gastronomic delight in both the Telugu states! I was right behind him and saw drops of blood falling to ground pretty quickly. Gokul immediately took charge, ran to his car, drove closer to Srikanth, pulled out First Aid Kit and bandaged Srikanth's foot. All within a span of twenty minutes. It happened so fast that it was almost like it never happened! Brave Srikanth limped a little but he was as good as new half an hour later. It is another matter that after he went home he saw a doctor who gave him a shot of tetanus. All of us birders who roam the hills, forests, lakes and riversides are used to little incidents like these. We all take it in our stride, I suppose. Anyway, after this incident, we continued looking out for birds and butterflies. A Blue-faced Malkoha, seven Blue Tiger butterflies together and a Three Spotted Grass Yellow butterfly were an absolute treat to the eye. As a bonus, we spotted some moths and a beautiful Signature Spider. Signature Spider (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) We also saw a Flax seed tree, a Samudrapala tree and a Sappan Wood tree. All possess medicinal properties. Swift spp (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) Parnara Swift spp (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) Flax seed (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) 15

Caesalpinia sappan (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) The team with Mr Rahiuddin, DRO, Moolika Vanam (Photo courtesy: Surekha Aitabathula) Medicinal plant usage is slowly coming to the fore. There is no denying that a certain level of awareness has arisen amongst the people that the side effects of allopathy can be avoided by shifting to herbal medicine. Trip Report: December 2020 Text & Photos: Shivakumar N (With inputs from Partho Ghosh, Sharad Khanna and Rajesh Bhalla) Changeable Hawk Eagle Almost every year, for the past 20 years, I have been making ‘pilgrimage’ trips to Corbett National Park. My first trip to Corbett was in 1991; before that I had only seen Eturnagaram and Pakhal Wildlife Sanctuaries. Being a resident of New Delhi has its advantages, one of them being its proximity to Corbett. I have always been in love with Corbett because of its magnificent jungles and varied landscapes. Every visit has sprung pleasant surprises for me. However, in recent years, due to its popularity and the increase in the number of curious tiger watchers and photographers, it has become difficult to get bookings for the lovely Forest Rest Houses (FRH) located deep inside the jungles of Corbett. My most recent trip to Corbett was in the third week of December, 2020. It was not easy as many trains were cancelled and taxis were not willing to go that far from Delhi because of COVID. We were asked by the authorities at Dhikala to get COVID-Negative certificates. Added to this was the severe cold at Dhikala. In spite of this, and the very basic facilities offered at Dhikala, the lure of the jungle was too overpowering and we took the plunge. The late-night train from Delhi railway station dropped us at Ramganga station at 5.00AM – in the pitch darkness, only cops were seen on the deserted platform ensuring we had COVID permits. 1

White-rumped Shama Scarlet Minivet Of the seven safari trips into the jungles, the first and the last were the most fascinating. As we soon as we entered one morning we saw the reclusive Yellow-throated Martens sauntering across the road. On the last day of the last jungle safari we were extremely lucky to see a mother tigress hunt down a male Chital deer while coordinating with her three young cubs, all in full view of the tourist gypsies. Equally surprising was the arrival of two Red-headed Vultures within 15 minutes of the kill, magically dropping out of the azure sky. Dhikala also happens to be a gateway to the interiors of the park. The place offers a panoramic view of the valley with the Kanda ridge in the backdrop. The old Forest Rest House at Dhikala range is a historic structure built over a hundred years ago, and having a unique charm of its own with elephant stables, canteens, parking space and a dormitory. Unfortunately the elephant rides have long been stopped but the tame elephants still live at Dhikala performing forest duties and/or leading a retired life. Tiger with Chital kill During the other safaris, we had a whale of a time watching many species of birds like the White-rumped Shama or the White-browed Fantail. This time, there seemed to be more Changeable Hawk Eagles and less of Crested Serpent Eagles in comparison to my earlier trips. Photographing the feathered friends in the subdued light of the forest was challenging as the digital cameras often refuse to read the light right. The FRH of Dhikala is the most sought after due its fantastic location, with open grasslands, tall tree patches and the magnificent Ramganga River. Not to mention the forest denizens – tigers, herds of elephants, deer and a variety of birds. Chestnut-bellied Nuthatch The speciality of Corbett National Park is that it is among the few National Parks of India that permits night stay inside the buffer zone. The age-old Forest Rest Houses are built right inside the core area of the Tiger Reserve, assuring a real taste of the wilderness. A fine balance is created in the safari zones enabling better tourism management without disturbing the natural habitat of the wildlife species. 2

Grey Bushchat Oriental Pied Hornbill This time around, we had an assured two-night stay in Dhikala range but also ensured a one-night stay at Malani and Gairal Forest Rest Houses. Malani is located next to a gurgling brook 12km northwest of Bijrani. Strategically located at the edge of core zone of the tiger reserve, Malani has a lot to offer, with the most picturesque surroundings and complete solitude. It has just two large high-roofed rooms with one pantry, and the raw provisions have to be brought and cooked, which make the meal even more romantic in the inky night. The jungle drive to Malani is also quite a rewarding experience, meandering through ancient forests with massive banyan trees having their aerial roots hanging like tresses and filled with bird life. The diverse wildlife and breath-taking landscapes of Corbett Tiger Reserve are indeed tempting even to a layman. The natural uniqueness of the area was recognized long ago as a result of which, in 1936, Corbett attained the distinction of becoming the first National Park to be established in mainland Asia. Initially it was named as the ‘Hailey National Park’ but was later renamed as ‘Corbett National Park’ after James Edward Corbett, the noted hunter-turned-conservationist of the area, during the British era. The area came under Project Tiger in 1971 when Government of India launched this ambitious conservation project. Geographically it is located between the Shivalik Himalayas and the Terai region. The streams, rivers and ridges crisscrossing the topography, present Corbett with a remarkable variety of landscapes. This vivid mosaic of habitats – wet and dry, plain and mountainous, gentle and rugged, forests and grasslands – supports numerous plant and animal species, representing the Himalayan ecosystem as well as that of the plains. Corbett is one of the richest bird regions of the country and has been declared as 'Important Bird Area' (IBA) by Birdlife International. Scaly-bellied Woodpecker According to the Botanical Survey of India (BSI) and the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI), Corbett has 600 species of plants and an equal number of birds. This perfect combination is possibly the highest that is encountered anywhere in the subcontinent. Trees, shrubs, ferns, grass, climbers, herbs and bamboos and equal number of avifauna are spell-binding. The forests make an ideal home for some unique mammals and reptiles too. Corbett National Park is rich in flora, with more than 75% of the total area dominated by Sal forests. Red-whiskered Bulbul After one midday brunch at Dhikala before the evening safari, we saw waves of Cormorants fly by, hugging the river waters, while we had an aerial view from the high banks. The spectacle was truly fascinating to the lazy afternoon eye. On another occasion we saw a hunting party of Otters in the Ramganga River below, while the trees above had Fish Eagles ready to soar. 3

Panoramic view of the Gypsy breakdown location During one trip into the jungle, the Gypsy broke down and we were stranded in the middle of nowhere. We were aware that tigers were no threat but elephants were known to be unpredictable! This added to the thrill of getting lost in the jungle. But the driver, being very resourceful, got the Gypsy going soon enough. Binoculars for hire Crested Kingfisher Red Junglefowl Plumbeous Water Redstart male One night we were put up at Gairal Forest House located in another part of the park that could be accessed by a short detour from the Dhangarhi-Dhikala main forest road. The prime attraction of this Rest House is that it lies on the banks of River Ramganga. It has large modern rooms but the canteen is not quite up to the mark. We spotted at least two Crested Serpent Eagles occupying different trees along the curving riverside. Situated in the lap of nature, Gairal presents ideal conditions for nature watch and wildlife viewing from the guesthouse itself. Small and big crocodiles were seen basking on the banks soaking in the winter sun. Common Hoopoe 4

Corbett attracts a large number of wildlife tourists and is divided into seven ecotourism zones with respective gated entrances for proper regulation and management. I am fortunate to have stayed in almost all the Forest Rest Houses except the one created recently. Here are some of the interesting Forest Rest Houses of the Corbett National Park located in different tourism zones – Bijrani, Sultan, Gairal, Sarapduli, Khinnanauli, Jhirna, Dhikala, Dhangari, Durgadevi, etc. Unfortunately in recent years there is an immense influx of corporate tourists from the concrete jungles of the cities who come to escape the daily drudgery. To accommodate this surge, a number of luxury motels have cropped up surrounding the National Park. My only grouse is that the unruly visitors create a lot of ruckus and din, spoiling the tranquillity of Corbett. It is very important to control this menace and preserve the pristine beauty of Corbett National Park.
