Report: Sighting of Common Shelduck in Hyderabad M S Ram One could argue that there's nothing more relaxing in the world than engaging in a familiar hobby in a familiar place with a familiar person. This was certainly my expectation when, within a couple of hours of arriving from Bangalore, I decided to go birdwatching with a close friend, Rama Sarvani, in Sanjeevaiah Park, Hyderabad, located at the edge of Hussain Sagar Lake. Hussain Sagar has been, more than once, a symbol of a new and resurgent city and has borne the brunt of an unplanned expansion as well as civilian and institutional neglect, and become the butt of insidious jokes about asphyxiation. However, Rama had been briefing me about her daily trips to the park, and how she had been seeing unusually high bird activity in the park, and especially in the waters around it. Thus tempted, we arrived at Sanjeevaiah Park, we proceeded with the routine. Rama wielded her pair of binoculars in one hand while brandishing the eBird app on her phone in the other. The Great Backyard Bird Count had just begun. We saw the Large Cuckooshrike (not ‘Cuckoo-shrike’; I always wondered why), Indian Golden Oriole, Indian Grey Hornbill, Green Sandpiper, Spot-billed Duck, Red-vented Bulbul, House Crow, Intermediate Egret, Common Myna, Common Tailorbird, Ubiquitous Prinia (just kidding) and a host of other birds that we were expecting to see. But something was not right on the rocks. “Wait, the one on that rock doesn't look like a Shoveler”, I said to myself while quietly borrowing Rama's binoculars for the thousandth time. “Hey, is that a Common Shelduck?” After a few seconds of frantic back-and-forth with the binoculars and seeing images of the bird on the Internet, we both let out a squeal of confirmation (the seeds of doubt were yet to be sown; “It could be a domestic duck”). We were elated because it was a lifer for both of us. Rama pointed out that it was recorded as a rarity in eBird. Neither of us realised that gravity of that statement at that time. Rama took a photo on her phone through her binoculars, a technique she seems to have mastered by now. Happy with the result, we went on to other pastures, had a heated argument about the identity of a Warbler, gave chase to a putative Woodpecker and called it a morning. It wasn't long before we realised that the ‘Common’ Shelduck is not that common at all in the Indian subcontinent. In fact, there seemed to be no record of it from Hyderabad or even from Telangana. This was probably a vagrant and a true owner of the widely misused hashtag, #SingleChallenge. While I was initially sceptical about Rama's claim that there were around 300 Northern Shovelers in Hussain Sagar, my scepticism was soon put to shame by the sight I witnessed that morning – hundreds of Shovelers, near and far, on water, on rocks and in the air. Common Shelduck (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Common Shelduck, Northern Shoveler female, and a freshwater turtle (Photo: Rama Sarvani) 6

But what are the chances that the first record of a bird from a large state is from a polluted lake overlooked by most birdwatchers? One could forgive people for thinking that it was a case of mistaken identity, for domestic ducks (Mallard look-alikes) have been spotted in Hussain Sagar before. One could also forgive them for not being aware of the distribution of a rare species. But can one be forgiven for giving misleading common names to birds? user, @stu_bot3000, shot into ornithological limelight by starting a tweet thread on ridiculous bird names, with such notable mentions as Sad Flycatcher, Drab Seedeater, Noisy Pitta, Satanic Nightjar and Typical Swift. While their motive may have been to instigate ‘bird stans’ (‘stan’ is a slang word that refers to obsessive fans of a celebrity) like ourselves, birders were quick to join the bandwagon and make their own contributions to that riot of a thread with Invisible Rail (can we see it?), Intermediate Egret (is there an Advanced Egret?), Crested Goatsucker (yes!) and Pearly-vented Tody-tyrant (I had to look this up). “What's in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet”, wrote William Shakespeare in his infinite wisdom, blissfully unaware of the different kinds of Thrushes, Tits and Chats that might have called his backyard their home. He might have had second thoughts if only he had experienced half the plight today's birdwatchers have to go through day-in and day-out, dealing with synonyms and name changes that reflect species splits (though this usually has merit). And then, there's the unfortunate tale of the great Indian Bustard missing out on the National Bird tag due to its name. Birds that contain ‘common’ in their names give the impression that they are common throughout their distribution when this may not be the case. There will, invariably, be regions in its distribution where it wouldn't be as abundant as in other regions. This could be due to sub-optimal environmental conditions, competition for resources from sympatric species, or stochastic processes. The Common Babbler, for example, is not the commonest Babbler species in a significant portion of its distribution. Even species such as Common Myna may be rare at the fringes of its distribution. This calls into question the practice of using the misleading prefix 'common', especially when alternative nomenclature that reflects their specific morphology, behaviour or distribution would be more apt. How about Yellow-eyed Myna instead of Common Myna, or White-necked Shelduck instead of Common Shelduck? An ‘interesting’ hypothesis about the etymology of the Greenish Warbler (Source: Twitter) Given this mess, I wonder if we should instead start using binomial nomenclature during our birding trips. So maybe the next time you see me grab someone else's binoculars to check out a domestic duck in a polluted lake, you might just be able to hear me think aloud – “Hey, is that a Tadorna tadorna?” Surely, life would be much simpler if bird nomenclature followed some logic. Well, tough luck! Recently a Twitter *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From The Times Of India, September 18, 2017) *** 7

DIMINISHING MANGROVES Report: Krishna Delta, February 5-7, 2021 Text & Photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati Eurasian Curlew The Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary, which I prefer to call the Krishna Delta Sanctuary, is about 90 km from Vijayawada, near a small town named Repalle. It has brackish water and one of the prime mangrove habitats. The area of the sanctuary is roughly about 200 sq km. There are many islands within the sanctuary forming a group of Reserve Forests – like Yelichetladibba, Kottapalem, Adavuladivi, Pittalaadavi, NagayyaLakna, Uppurevu and Lankivanidibba. An estuary of the Krishna River flows through the mangroves of the sanctuary. This region is very rich in fauna and avifauna and species like Bottlenose Dolphin, Whale Shark, Fishing Cat, Golden Jackal, Blackcapped Kingfisher and many other species are found here. There are also permanent breeding grounds and hatcheries created for the Olive Ridley Turtles. Having visited this place regularly over the past few years, I have fallen in love with the boat ride through the mangroves that ends up close to the high seas. Over the years, we have seen many improvements in terms of the effort put in by the Forest Department officials to ensure strict imposition of wildlife laws related to shell trade and bird protection. The Forest Department has also ensured the involvement of the community and educated them on the importance of wildlife and its protection. One of the important activities undertaken here is to educate fishermen on safe disposal of the nets. Kudos to the FD team for successfully driving these activities. However, in spite of the above efforts by the FD, there are still many challenges and threats to this location: 1. 2. 3. 4. Destruction of mangrove forests – a common problem we are facing nowadays in all parts of the country; Extensive fishing; Industrial waste discharge; Pesticides and Insecticides used for agriculture in areas surrounding the sanctuary Year 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 Black-capped Kingfisher Year-Wise Species & Counts AWC Species 39 58 54 71 81 Count 1,021 7,857 26,055 31,601 29,000 During this visit, we saw a total of 137 birds in the sanctuary, of which about 81 species are covered under the Waterfowl Census. A brief report on the trip, written by my 8-year-old travel partner Rishi Reddy K, is given below. Our trip to Krishna Delta, Feb 5-7, 2021 Text: Rishi Reddy Kalliath; Photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati Mudskipper We started for Krishna Delta on Feb 5 evening, and I was very excited and happy to go to another place for birding. I learned a huge lesson in the car, that you should never watch anything or read anything in the car: I watched a movie for a little while, and I ended up feeling very nauseated. Anyway, after a few hours we reached the hotel and went to sleep.  A lot of Cormorants in flight, several Marsh Harriers, a Reef Egret (another Lifer) and many Gulls and Terns. The next day, Feb 6, my mother woke me up early in the morning, and in a second I was fully awake. I quickly got dressed, then we went to the boat place and got into the boat. The boat smelled of fish and sea creatures. We went in the boat with a few Forest Department people who came from Guntur to help us. The weather was cold and I was very excited. I felt the boat was a bit rocky, but I had a life vest. There was all these mangrove plants and the boat went from between these plants. They are the only plants that survive in salt water. Eurasian Marsh Harrier Common Kingfisher In the mangroves, we saw: Western Reef Egret     Black-capped Kingfisher – a Lifer for me; Common Kingfisher – one of my favorite birds; A Curlew taking a bath; Many Collared Doves, one Purple Heron, and a Green Bee-eater; 9

Peregrine Falcon attacking Laggar Falcon Ghost Crab (Ocypode sp) I ate a whole packet of murukku in the boat. Then we approached a sandbar and saw a Peregrine Falcon attacking another raptor – we couldn’t identify the other raptor initially, but later found out that it was a Laggar Falcon! Some people said the Laggar Falcon’s catch was a Golden Oriole, but in the photos I thought it seemed to have a Duck’s head. Later the Peregrine Falcon flew away. The Laggar Falcon was guarding its food by spreading its wings to cover its food, but when the boat touched the island, it flew off with its catch. Then we started on our way back. First my Amma was sleeping, then when she woke up Lawrence Thatha went to sleep. While Thatha was asleep we saw a Golden Jackal. I saw a live turtle on the way back – it was running around in random directions. Golden Jackal Laggar Falcon with Golden Oriole kill We docked and went to explore the sandbar. We walked and walked, and we barely saw any birds. I noticed some lines on the sand – Srikanth Uncle thought they were made by a snake and Lawrence Thatha thought they were made by crabs. I learned that the crabs make holes in the sand and live in there. We saw a live crab inside a shell, which we examined before I put it back in the water. After we got back, we went for lunch to a restaurant where they served us very super spicy biryani. Once we got back to the hotel, I had a bath and a nap, before we went out for some more birding. We were looking for a beach where we could see some birds. On the way I saw an Indian Roller, a Black Drongo and a lot of Great Egrets. I collected a lot of shells on the way back – I thought they were very beautiful. Srikanth Uncle told me that collecting shells from a sanctuary is illegal, and asked me to go and ask the Forest Department Aunty about the shells. She told me that collecting shells was illegal, so I put the shells back in the water. I saw a dead turtle. Many many insects were eating it. We then went back to the boat. That’s when we saw the Ghost Crabs – they were bright red in colour! All the Ghost Crabs were running and jumping into the water. One was very scared and ran too fast and fell into the water. Great Egret We finally reached the entry to the beach but there was a huge fight going on because the watchman was saying it was already 5.00PM and people couldn’t enter, and other people were arguing with him. Anyway, we returned to our hotel, had dinner and some chocolates, and slept. 10

On Day-3, the last day of the survey, we got ready early and picked up some people on the way to the boat. Before we reached, I saw a Flameback Woodpecker. It was my Lifer. It was so beautiful – its crest was like the colour of the sunset. there was a Sandwich Tern here, but I didn’t see it. I saw a Tern with a crest but that turned out to be the Lesser Crested Tern. When we reached and I saw the boat, I was so happy – it was a boat with a roof. As soon as I got into the boat, the generator started and I lost my balance! Terek Sandpiper There were a lot of Gulls on that sandbar – to me, it seemed like there were 10,000 Gulls! The actual number was around 3,000 Gulls, though. Common Redshank Then we set off. We saw a few Redshanks, Greenshanks, a Marsh Harrier and a Purple Heron. We reached a sandbar and I got off. We got very close to the Redshanks and Plovers. I saw two Black-winged Stilts flying, and many Terns and Gulls – Caspian Tern, Whiskered Tern, Pallas’s Gull etc. I was running around and playing in the water – I felt very happy to be back in the water. Heuglin’s Gull Pallas’s Gull Striated Heron Lesser Crested Tern We then got back to the boat and we reached another sandbar and stopped the boat in the water. We saw some Pallas’s Gulls, Caspian Terns and Whiskered Terns. I heard someone saying Then the boat started moving again and, after sailing for some time, guess what we saw? We saw some Dolphins! I saw around 5 or 6 Dolphins. Then we started moving again. We ate lunch on the boat – the Forest Department people seemed to really like the lemon rice, but I wasn’t eating any of that rice – so I just ate some bondas. We all then had dessert – it was a cannonball-shaped chocolate but smaller. We didn’t see many birds on the way back. We came back to the hotel, packed and returned to Hyderabad. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Ruddy Shelduck (Tadorna ferruginea) Ruddy Shelduck male (L) and female (R) (Gajoldoba, West Bengal, January 24 & 25, 2021) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Tadorna Species: T. ferruginea Size: 61-67 cm The Ruddy Shelduck is a dabbling duck and mainly nocturnal. It is omnivorous and feeds on a variety of food sources – grasses, young shoots, grain, aquatic vegetation, as well as molluscs, crustaceans, aquatic insects, fish and reptiles. While foraging on land, it stays on grass or moist foliage; in shallow water it dabbles, and when the water is deeper, it up-ends but does not dive. The usual call is a nasal aang aang, like a quieter version of the honking of the Bar-headed Geese. Description & distribution: The Ruddy Shelduck, also known as the Brahminy Duck or Brahminy Shelduck, is a very distinctive duck, easily identified due to its largely orangebrown plumage. The head of the male is paler orange-brown than the body plumage, and is separated by a thin black collar. It has white lower and upper wing-coverts, contrasting starkly with the black rump, tail coverts, and tail and flight feathers. The inner surfaces of the wings show iridescent green speculum feathers. It has a black bill and dark grey legs. The female is generally similar, but the head and neck are almost white, and the black collar is absent. Plumage tends to fade as the birds grow older. Juvenile birds are similar to the female, but darker brown. The Ruddy Shelduck breeds mainly in south-eastern Europe, east across the Palearctic region to Lake Baikal, Mongolia and western China, although there are small resident populations in Ethiopia and north-west Africa. It has also been known to breed in the high-altitude lakes and swamps of Jammu and Kashmir. The Ruddy Shelduck winters mainly in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and occasionally Sri Lanka, arriving by October and leaving by April. While breeding, they form strong pair bonds, and many even believe they pair for life. Pairs are very territorial and aggressive towards intruders – the initial charge is usually made by the female, with head lowered and neck outstretched, and uttering loud anger calls; if unsuccessful in chasing away the intruder, she may return and run around the male, trying to incite him to attack. The courtship display involves head dipping, neck stretching, tail raising and sometimes wing flapping, and mating usually takes place on the water. Nesting: In the Asian breeding grounds – Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Nepal and Tibet – the Ruddy Shelduck breeds generally between April and June. The nest is built by the female and is a thick pad of grasses, feathers and down; it is away from the water, in a hole in a tree or abandoned building, cliff crevice, sand dune or even the burrow of another animal. The usual clutch consists of 6-10 pearly white or creamy white, mildly glossy, smooth-textured eggs. Habitat & behaviour: The preferred breeding habitat of the Ruddy Shelduck is large wetlands, rivers, mud flats and rocky beaches, lakes and reservoirs. In the non-breeding season, it prefers slow-moving streams and rivers, ponds, lakes, marshes, flooded grasslands and brackish lagoons. During breeding season it often forms large congregations, but otherwise is usually seen in pairs or small flocks in inland water bodies like rivers, jheels, lakes and reservoirs. Local name: The Ruddy Shelduck is known as ‘Chakwa’, ‘Chakwi’ or ‘Lal surkhab’ in Hindi, ‘Brahmani batak’ in Gujarati, ‘Bapana chiluwa’ in Telugu, ‘Thara’ in Tamil, ‘Thangathu thaaraavu’ in Malayalam, ‘Kesar pandia’ or ‘Panda hansa’ in Oriya, and ‘Chakrawak’ in Sanskrit. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Report: Participation in Bird Photography Workshop at Bharatpur, January 27-31, 2021 Jairamchander Pingle & Vikramdev Rao A view of Keoladev Ghana National Park, Bharatpur (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) It was sometime in October 2020 that we got to know about Ms Rathika Ramasamy's Photography Masterclass Workshop to be held at the Keoladev Ghana National Park at Bharatpur over four days i.e. January 27-31, 2021. We were still in the midst of the Covid pandemic, of course, but the situation had eased a bit, so we felt that it may not be so much of an issue by the end of January. Rathika asked us to send some of our bird photographs and give her some information about our interest in photography. She is one of India's foremost wildlife photographers, so we were happy that our request to join her workshop was accepted. We came to know later that she had apprehensions about our participation as we are both in our late 70s and the workshop had an arduous four day schedule, starting at 6:30AM and going on till 6:00PM. The cold temperatures – day temperatures in the low 20s, and night temperatures in single digits – were another factor. We would like to think that despite our age we dispelled any doubts that she had, as we were among the first ones up and ready to go every day! 1

Anyway, once we got confirmation of our participation, we booked our flights, deciding to reach Bharatpur via Jaipur rather than Delhi, the distance by road being almost the same. The flight to Jaipur was uneventful but for the mandatory Covid protocol of wearing masks and face shields, besides a full body gown for the passenger in the middle seat. We were picked up at Jaipur airport and drove straight to Bharatpur. We arrived at the Iora guest house, where we were put up, by around 3:00PM, and met up with Rathika and the others. There was an evening session covering all the intricacies of bird photography – it was quite a detailed session, with emphasis on camera settings, lighting at different times of the day and consequent changes in white balance settings, etc. We were asked to give our preference for a single occupancy or shared cycle rickshaw. Both of us chose a single rickshaw as it would not be cramped and we would be free to roam as we wished. During the coming days, the rickshaw drivers not only helped us with our gear but also turned out to be quite knowledgeable about the flora and fauna in the park. Glossy Ibis (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) Since we were independent of each other, we could stay as long as we wanted at a particular spot waiting for opportune moments to take photographs. There was also a lot of walking to do, as the rickshaws could not go into certain areas. Breakfast and lunch – simple but wholesome food – was sent by the guest house and we were given a time and a place where we were to meet. We had also been advised to carry plenty of snacks like chocolate bars, biscuits etc. in case we felt hungry in between. At the end of the day, it was back to the guest house and a wellearned rest. We assembled again around 8:00PM to go over some of the photos taken during the day; Rathika reviewed and offered suggestions on what we could do differently for a better photograph. Sunrise (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) The next day, the rickshaws arrived at the guest house at 6:00AM, and we took off in the cold weather – which felt even colder because of the open rickshaw! We realized that we should have brought gloves to keep our hands warm for the first few hours. As the day progressed, the temperature became comfortable but we still kept our warm jackets on. The early morning haze made for some interesting photographs of the sun as it broke through. Once the haze cleared we were able to get some nice shots of the different birds that frequent the park. Black-necked Stork (Photo: Jairamchander Pingle) Great White Pelican & Gadwall (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) Ferruginous Duck male (Photo: Jairamchander Pingle) 2

On the third day, we went in early to take some shots of the sun rising over the swamps and through the haze, before proceeding with the usual routine of photographing birds during the day. Every evening, we would also wait until the sun set, hoping to get some shots of birds silhouetted against the setting sun. A foggy morning (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) On the second day, the rickshaw drivers called to inform that there was heavy fog and visibility was almost zero, and suggested that we start out at 7:30AM. 7:30AM came around and the fog still hadn't fully lifted, but we ventured forth anyway. A sunset in Bharatpur (Photo: Jairamchander Pingle) The sun would set around 5:30PM, and we would get back to the guest house around 6:45PM for a short rest and a review session with the whole group. One major issue was keeping batteries charged, as apart from photographing for 12 hours every day, the batteries also tended to discharge faster because of the cold. Fortunately the power supply was stable. Rhesus Macaque (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) As we entered the park, we found that a whole troop of Rhesus Macaque monkeys had come on to the road and had parked themselves there. The whole group got down and spent at least a half hour photographing them before moving on. It was great as we were able to get up close to them without scaring them away. The rest of the day was spent very much like the first, photographing birds both stationary and in flight. Cheetal mother & fawn (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) Golden Jackal (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) Red-crested Pochard male (Photo: Jairamchander Pingle) 3

Besides the birds, we did spot quite a few animals that inhabit the park as well – amongst them were Nilgai, Cheetal, Sambhar, Jackals, Foxes, Rhesus Macaques, Rock Pythons, Monitor Lizards, Hyenas etc. we were able to get some clearer shots of this beautiful bird, which is our largest flying bird and the state bird of Uttar Pradesh. It was a fitting finale to four days of a thoroughly satisfying and truly memorable visit to the Keoladev Ghana National Park at Bharatpur. Sarus Crane pair (Photo: Jairamchander Pingle) Rock Python (Photo: Vikramdev Rao) On the fourth day, as we were due to leave by midday to catch our flight to Hyderabad, we ventured out into the park for a session in the morning, and this proved to be the highlight of our trip – suddenly, our rickshaw drivers-cum-guides heard the whooping of the Sarus Crane, which had eluded us until then! We quickly jumped into our respective rickshaws and went looking for the Cranes. We saw them initially in the haze and spent a considerable amount of time taking photographs. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Common Teal (Anas crecca) Common Teal male (L) and female (R) (Gajoldoba, West Bengal, January 25-26, 2021) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Anas Species: A. crecca Size: 34-43 cm a Garganey minus the pale loral spot and dark cheek bar. The iris is brown and bill is dark grey in all birds, but the base sometimes shows some greenish or brownish at the base for the male, and some yellow for the female. The juvenile is much like the female, but with a stronger pattern. The birds moult in summer, including flight feathers, and are flightless for up to four weeks. Description & distribution: The Common Teal, also known as the Green-winged or Eurasian Teal, is a small dabbling duck that is quite common and widespread. It breeds across a wide range including almost all of Europe and Asia north of the Himalayan foothills, and parts of North Africa. It is generally migratory in winter, moving well south of its breeding range, except for the temperate parts of Europe, for instance the United Kingdom and Ireland, where breeding and wintering ranges may overlap. Large wintering populations are seen in the Nile Valley, the Mediterranean, the near East and Persian Gulf, East and South-east Asia, Myanmar, Korea, Japan and Taiwan. In the Indian subcontinent, where the Common Teal is seen in large numbers – Salim Ali called it ‘perhaps our commonest migratory duck’ – it is seen across Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. Habitat & behaviour: The Common Teal breeds in sheltered freshwater lakes, ponds and rivers with dense fringing vegetation in forested areas. In its wintering grounds, it prefers sheltered lakes and shallow inlets, lagoons and bays along the seashore, and sheltered wetlands with some vegetation or reeds nearby. It is a dabbling duck, feeding by foraging on the water surface, upending or sometimes diving to pick up food from under the surface, or even by grazing on the edges of the water body. Its main diet consists of grain, tender shoots of rice and marsh plants, grass and grass seeds, and aquatic vegetation, but when breeding, it shifts to a diet consisting mainly of aquatic invertebrates like insects and their larvae, crustaceans, mollusks and worms. It is diurnal during breeding season and crepuscular or nocturnal feeders during nonbreeding. The male Common Teal is a beautiful duck, with an overall pencil-grey body, and a chestnut head and throat with a broad metallic green band from behind the eye to the nape, bordered above and below by thin yellowish-white lines; one such line also extends from the eye below and along the base of the dark bill. It has a marked white scapular stripe running along the flanks, a yellowish patch on undertail coverts, and a buff breast with small brown spots. The belly is white on the centre, and marked elsewhere with thin, dense dark vermiculations, giving it a greyish appearance. It has a distinctive tri-coloured speculum – black, green and buff – that is especially conspicuous in flight, and dark grey legs. The underwing is whitish, with darker spotting on inner coverts and a dark leading edge. The non-breeding (eclipse) male is more like the female, more uniform in colour and with vestigial facial markings. The female is greyish- or yellowish-brown, with slightly darker wings and back, and greyish-olive or greyishbrown legs. It has a dark greyish-brown head, hind-neck and eye-stripe; the feather pattern consists of dense short streaks on head and neck, and scaly spots on the rest of the body. The overall appearance is somewhat like a small female Mallard or Breeding pairs are formed in the wintering grounds and arrive together at the breeding grounds. During breeding season, the Common Teal can be aggressive and chase away other ducks that approach the nest, although in the non-breeding season, it is gregarious and can form large flocks. Its flight is fast and the large flocks wheeling in unison as they fly makes for a pretty sight. Nesting: The Common Teal breeds generally between March and June. The nest is a deep hollow on the ground, near water and under dense vegetation, and lined with dry leaves, down feathers, reeds, rushes, grasses etc. The usual clutch consists of 7-11 oval, cream-coloured eggs with a glossy texture. Local name: The Common Teal is known as ‘Chhoti murghabi’, ‘Chowtee’, ‘Lohiya kerra’ or ‘Patari’ in Hindi, ‘Siravi’ or ‘Kilawai’ in Tamil, ‘Parza’ in Telugu, ‘Yeranda’ in Malayalam, ‘Nani batakh’ or ‘Nani murghabi’ in Gujarati and ‘Rohinik hansak’ in Sanskrit. HOOTING FOR THE OWLS Text and Photos: Prachi Mehta, Ph.D. Forest Owlet The Guardians of the Night Owls are apex carnivorous birds who feed on live prey, just like eagles and kites. But unlike other birds, owls are highly specialized birds of prey. To avoid competition with other birds of prey, owls have adopted the night life. Most owls are nocturnal but a few like the Forest Owlet are diurnal, that is, they are active during the day. There are some every unique aspects about owls. Owls can rotate their heads up to 210 degrees so that they know what is going on behind their back. The flight feathers of owls are unique too – they are arranged in such a way that they can fly completely silently in the night and swoop down to catch the unsuspecting prey by surprise. In fact, owls are more often heard than seen. However, unlike other birds, owl songs are far from being melodious – in fact they are eerie and spooky. At night in a forest area, if you hear a medley of deep sounds reminding you of a softly uttered questioning “wut? wut? wut?”, rapacious laughter “whoohaha… whoohaha… whoohaha”, something that sounded like the scream of a strangled woman, a deep resonating “Ghughu… ghughu… ghughu…” or a high pitched screech – then you should know that you have owls for company. 1

Owls are like the proverbial Golden Goose for the Sorcery business. They are kept as pets in cages where their powerful wings and talons are severed so they can’t fly, their eyes are injected with coloured dye to make them appear formidable and finally, they are made to perform on the diktats of the owner as an evil and malicious power. Brown Fish Owl inside tree cavity Most birds build nests… here again, owls are an exception. They stay in tree cavities, hollows, ravines, cliffs and even in abandoned quarries and houses. Not exactly pleasant places to be at night, but owls prefer them. Their diet is enriched by rats, shrews, lizards, snakes, fish, frogs, smaller birds, scorpions and insects. Owls gulp down their prey intact without bothering to tease it apart. The indigestible parts such as skulls and dentitions of mammals, beaks and feet of birds, scorpion stings, and insect heads and bodies are then regurgitated out of the mouth in the form of pellets. Owl pellets are a treasure trove full of colourful prey remains. Analyzing the pellet of owls is akin to forensic science where the evidence of remains provide a clue about what was eaten by the owl. Owls are killed for their powerful eyes, talons, beaks, tails, and feathers for use in fake traditional medicines that purportedly help the consumer develop the prowess of owls. If owls really possessed such super powers, they would not get caught and killed so easily! Eggs and chicks of owls are stolen from the nests for gambling and earning a quick buck. Every year during the Deepavali festival, owls are captured in large numbers for trade and for gambling. For those who want to learn further on owl trade in India, I suggest reading “Imperiled Custodians of the Night”, an eyeopening report by WWF and TRAFFIC India. This report was published a decade ago – unfortunately, nothing has changed much since then. Owls provide an immensely important ecological service by feeding on rodents. A single owl can feed on 1000 mice in one year, which would otherwise damage 1/3rd of the grain in a crop field. In some parts of the country, enlightened farmers install a pole in their field for the owls to perch and hunt out the rodents. The owl is considered to be the vehicle of Goddess Lakshmi, and some farmers believe that worshipping owls will bring wealth in their lives. But in most other places, owls are not so lucky. Owls help to maintain the balance of ecosystem by occupying a nocturnal niche so that diurnal predators can live. Owls exploit the nocturnal prey at night which otherwise would have proliferated and could have caused a lot of damage to the ecosystem. Owls keep the populations of destructive rodents under natural control and thus provide the farmers with a prosperous harvest. Imagine, if the rodents were not controlled, how much damage would they cause to grain crops – where would we get our next meal from? A WRCS publication on identification of prey remains from owl pellets The magnificence of owls is misinterpreted in many cultures across the world, including India. There are many negative effects of this. Though owls show their wisdom by selecting a nocturnal niche to avoid competition with other birds, they are considered to be stupid and foolish (ullu) for some bizarre reasons. Owls are considered to be inauspicious and messengers of death just because they fly at night! They are considered evil because of their unconventional appearance. Indian Eagle Owl 2

There are over 230 species of owls in the world, of which 34 species are found within India. However, in India, owls still have a long way to go before they make it to the official priority list of species that need protection efforts. One may wonder why owls need any protection – it seems like they are all over and doing fine. Well, this is not entirely true. To understand further let us discuss the case of one species – the small but powerful Forest Owlet. The enigmatic Forest Owlet The Forest Owlet (Athene (Heteroglaux) blewitti) is a curious bird, both by name and nature. It has captured the imagination of many within and outside the country, and for the right reasons. The Forest Owlet has an interesting past associated with it. Let us travel back in time to the 19th century. It was in 1872 when an Irish officer, Francis Robert Blewitt (FR Blewitt) saw this different-looking owl near Phooljhar in eastern Madhya Pradesh (now in Chhattisgarh). Perplexed by its somewhat confusing appearance, he sent the specimen to AO Hume, a well-known British taxonomist and a civil service officer serving in India. Hume immediately recognized this owl as a species new to science, and named it after Blewitt. Recent literature mentions that the bird was originally collected by William Blewitt, who was FR Blewitt’s younger brother. Apparently, William Blewitt was a Customs officer in Punjab, so he decided to use the pseudonym of his elder brother – to avoid his boss’s wrath for spending time away from his office in Punjab, for collecting birds in Central India! However, for us it is still Blewitt’s Owl. The Forest Owlet is endemic to India, that is, it is not found anywhere outside India. This small-sized owlet has been placed among the top seventeen birds in the world that are in endangered category. The International Union of Conservation of Nature (IUCN) had declared it as a Critically Endangered species owing to its isolated and perhaps declining population. The Forest Owlet is placed in Schedule I of Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1974, indicating it as a species of priority conservation concern. Recently it has been downlisted to the Endangered category, as the records of its occurrence are appearing from a few more locations. A Ghost from the Past The story of the Forest Owlet’s apparent extinction and rediscovery is equally dramatic. Between 1872 and 1884, six Forest Owlet specimens were collected from the country; the first one in 1872 by Blewitt as mentioned earlier, the second one in 1877 by Valentine Ball from Orissa, and four more during 1880-1883 by James Davidson from Central Maharashtra. After 1884, there were many reports of Forest Owlet sightings all over the country, but all of them were cases of the Spotted Owlet being mistaken for the Forest Owlet. In 1961, Colonel Richard Meinertzhagen reported having collected a Forest Owlet way back in 1914 from Mandvi in Gujarat, thus extending its range further west. Once again an intensive search was carried out for the Forest Owlet all over the country, but it drew a blank. Finally, in 1972, Dr SD Ripley considered the possibility that the Forest Owlet may have become extinct. So the Blewitt’s Owl became known as a possibly extinct species in India! Given this background, one can imagine the surprise and excitement that was generated by the news of its rediscovery in 1997. Dr Pamela Rasmussen, the American ornithologist, was studying some preserved skins of Forest Owlet. She realized that the bird looked very different from those shown in the illustrations in Indian bird books, and Indian scientists were looking for it based on a wrong picture of its appearance. Her museum research also found that the record of Forest Owlet from Gujarat was a false one, as Col Meinertzhagen had stolen one specimen from Davidson’s collection and claimed it as his own! So much fuss and fraud over an owl! So Dr Rasmussen decided to carry out a survey for sightings of the bird at its historical locations In India. They started with a search in Odisha and Chhattisgarh, where the erstwhile forests had disappeared giving way to crop fields, and they could not locate any Forest Owlet there. In November 1997, they started a survey in Maharashtra near Nandurbar district and, much to everyone’s surprise, they found two Forest Owlets. Thus the Forest Owlet made its reappearance after 113 long years! The bird was not extinct – it was overlooked by so many people for so many years. The rediscovery renewed the interest of scientists and naturalists in the Forest Owlet in India. Present Status of the Forest Owlet in India After its rediscovery, several organizations carried out surveys to determine the distribution of the Forest Owlet. The Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) initiated the surveys in 1999 and reported the presence of the Forest Owlet from Northwestern Maharashtra and Melghat Tiger Reserve. Our organization, the Wildlife Research and Conservation Society (WRCS) also carried out a survey of the Forest Owlet in five central Indian states – Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat – where they were originally known to be present. Our surveys were successful in locating the Forest Owlet from Khandwa and Betul district in Madhya Pradesh, and a few more locations in Northern Maharashtra. At present the Forest Owlet is known from three states in India – Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat. It appears as though the Forest Owlet is existing in small and isolated fragments along teak dominant forests. Training of field staff 3

Indian Scops Owl Colour-banded Forest Owlet Spotted Owlet Jungle Owlet From 2012 onwards, we have been carrying out an ecological assessment of the Forest Owlet in the Central Indian landscape. Our study is trying to understand the possible reasons for localized distribution of the Forest Owlet in Central India, its small population, and why it has not been able to colonize as successfully as other similar-sized owls such as the Spotted Owlet, the Jungle Owlet and the Scops Owls, although they are often found sharing the same habitat and using the same resources for feeding and nesting. The mystique of the life of the Forest Owlet remains to be unraveled. Meanwhile, the study has provided valuable insights into strategies that owls have adapted for survival, and how thoughtlessly we humans destroy them out of personal insecurities and irrational beliefs. The genus of the Forest Owlet was another issue of recent contention. At the time of its discovery in 1872, Hume established the genus Heteroglaux for the Forest Owlet based on its distinct morphology. Although the Forest Owlet possesses superficial similarity to the much more commonly seen Spotted Owlet (Athene brama), it has several distinctive features that distinguish it from the Spotted Owlet. The Forest Owlet has an unspotted crown, a full throat collar and thickly feathered legs; its habits of lateral tail-flicking and undulating flight are some of the most visible characteristics that made the taxonomists create a unique genus, Heteroglaux, for a single species! A recent phylogeny study by SACON in collaboration with our organization WRCS has finally settled the long-standing dispute on the taxonomy of the Forest Owlet as belonging to Athene genus. A serious case of identity crisis has been averted. 4

For the last one decade we have been studying the Forest Owlet in the Central Indian landscape, and we have just seen the tip of the iceberg. Our study involves examining the factors that may be impacting its distribution, site occupancy, foraging, nesting, and ultimately its breeding success. We have been using time-tested methods of color-banding and radiotelemetry, which provide robust scientific data to gain further insights into the ecology of the species. We work in close collaboration with the Maharashtra Forest Department and Madhya Pradesh Forest Department, who have been very supportive of the research. Local communities are our main conservation partners in this project. By integrating good science, supportive Forest Departments and community conservation initiatives, the situation is beginning to look up for the owls. Some instances of community conservation initiatives involving Korku tribal folk from Melghat: Women making owl tote bags (L), Men being trained on bamboo craft work (C), Hand-painted keychain made by the tribals (R) Owls are super-evolved birds with a strong will to survive. Owls don’t hoot to spook. They are incapable of casting an evil spell or predicting lucky numbers. A wise old owl sat on an oak, The more he saw the less he spoke, The less he spoke the more he heard… Why can’t we all be like that wise old bird? If at all, owls are the true guardians of the night and the onus is on us to let them fly fearlessly in the sky. This proverbial rhyme, though meant for children, offers some much-needed wisdom to us all. Editor’s Note: Dr Prachi Mehta is Senior Scientist and Executive Director – Research with the Wildlife Research and Conservation Society (www.wrcsindia.org). Indian Golden Oriole pair (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) Nehru Zoological Park (NZP) is a dense verdant patch that is an absolute blessing to the resident and migrant birds. The proximity to the large vegetation cover of the Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel National Police Academy and the green cover of the Agriculture University in Rajendra Nagar nearby, create conducive habitats for the birds in NZP. The USP of NZP is the several types of habitats that it offers to the birds so that the various species of birds can find their own ideal surroundings. Some of the old trees in the Nehru Zoo (Photo: Bharadwaj Korni) NZP also affords the longest bird walks. In all the NZP houses 1500 species of birds, animals and reptiles. There are neat moated enclosures for wild animals, Lion Safari, Dinosaur Park, Heronry, Nocturnal Zoo and Butterfly Park. For a nature enthusiast boredom is non-existent in NZP. Some views of the surroundings (Photos: Dr Geethanjali Ramachandra) With scrub, grasslands and water bodies, the 380 acre site houses a large number of old trees that support tremendous bird life. It was declared as a Biosphere Reserve in the year 2010. The Sri Venkateswara National Park is housed in the Seshachalam Biosphere, and is a birding hotspot with nearly 175 bird species. Globally threatened Yellow-throated Bulbuls, and some Himalayan and Western Ghats birds like Grey-fronted Green Pigeons are seen here. The Mamandur Forest is situated between Chittoor and Cuddapah districts and forms the foothills of Seshachalam Hills. The area receives water from Thumbura Thirtham of Tirumala Forest. The vegetation here is mainly of dry deciduous type, and a few evergreen plants are also seen though to a lesser extent. It was a cloudy morning when we entered the forest and we could hear faint chirps from here and there. We were mainly hoping to see the White-rumped Shama, Western Crowned Warbler and Grey-fronted Green Pigeon. We had the good fortune to visit the park in the middle of February 2021. Guided by a couple of birders from Tirupati, we spent a day each at Mamandur Forest and Talakona, and also visited Kalyani Dam. 13

Brown-breasted Flycatcher and Ashy Drongo, amidst the calls of White-browed Bulbuls. Black Shaheen Just as we entered, we sighted a Black Shaheen perched on a pylon, and some Scimitar Babblers and Paradise-flycatchers were calling from the nearby bamboo bushes. Brown-breasted Flycatcher The rufous morph Paradise-flycatchers were everywhere in this forest. A little further on, a flock of Puff-throated Babblers crossed our path and right there, perched on the lower branches of a tree, was the Shama! Deeper in the forest we came across a very scenic and enchanting stream adorned with forest flowers and filled with the songs of many a bird. There were the Golden-fronted Leafbirds, Black-naped and Black-hooded Orioles, Common Kingfisher, Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker, Large Cuckooshrike, White-browed Bulbul, White-spotted Fantail, Common Iora and Jungle Babbler. White-rumped Shama It was still dark inside the forest and the Shama, being crepuscular in nature, was quite active. We waited for about quarter of an hour watching it when another pair of Shamas appeared, foraging in the open. By now the clouds had cleared out a little and as the first rays of the Sun streamed through the thick canopy of leaves, the Shamas disappeared into the thickets. Black-naped Oriole The Grey-fronted Green Pigeon and Western Crowned Warbler however could not be sighted. Instead we saw a Bamboo Bush Brown butterfly on our way back and this was a lifer for us. As we moved on, the bird activity started increasing, and we saw the Orange-headed Thrush, Common Woodshrike, 14

From Talakona we set off to Kalyani Dam, constructed on river Swarnamukhi. En route, we stopped at a few places to gaze at the beautiful hills of Seshachalam. At one of the viewpoints we saw a Black Eagle with a prey in its claws. The local birders pointed out that the Black Eagle was a common sight at Tirupati. By now it was nearly three o’clock in the afternoon and we quickly drove to the Dam site. This was a crowded place but there was a small patch of birding ground nearby. Surprisingly, it had an unbelievable number of birds besides the perfect habitat for the Brown-breasted Flycatcher. There were a couple of Blue-faced Malkohas, many Black-hooded Orioles, and some Common Woodshrikes, White-browed Bulbuls and Common Ioras. It was a real feast for the eyes. Bamboo Bush Brown On the next day we were at Talakona, in the Sri Venkateswara National Park. It was a well-wooded forest, unlike Mamandur. At the entrance of the Park we sighted many Crested Treeswifts. The highlight here, however, was the Browncheeked Fulvetta, with its calls reverberating across the forest. There were also a large number of Common Woodshrikes, Common Ioras, White-bellied Drongos, about five Green Imperial Pigeons, some White-browed and Yellow-browed Bulbuls, a couple of Yellow-throated Bulbuls and the Verditer Flycatcher. We also witnessed a large number of Common Crow and Blue Tiger butterflies, probably in migration. It was an amazing sight. The last time we had seen such a butterfly migration was that of Blue Tigers, Common Crows and Striped Tigers at Peechy Dam, in Kerala. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Gadwall (Mareca strepera) Gadwall male (L) and female (R) (Gajoldoba, West Bengal, January 25-26, 2021) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Mareca (formerly Anas) Species: M. strepera Size: 39-42 cm grassy areas, rather than open or deep marshes. In the nonbreeding (winter) season, it prefers brackish water marshes with a good amount of leafy aquatic vegetation. Populations have often been noted to demonstrate wintering site fidelity, returning to the same marshes, ponds or water treatment plants. Description & distribution: The Gadwall is a fairly common dabbling duck from the family Anatidae. Genetically it is a sister species of the Falcated Duck (Mareca falcata), and closely related to the Eurasian Wigeon (Mareca penelope), which may be the reason why it is usually found in their company. The Gadwall breeds in northern Europe and across all of the Palearctic region (i.e. across all of Eurasia north of the foothills of the Himalayas, and North Africa), as well as central North America. It is not a very long-distance migrant – it travels mainly to the areas north of the tropics, including coastal Alaska, southern Canada and central America, and parts of southern and central Europe and Asia – particularly in Pakistan and northern India, and a little less commonly in peninsular or southern India. It is a vagrant in Sri Lanka. It usually forages for plant food by picking up items from the surface or by dabbling with head submerged. It may occasionally up-end or dive for food, but would hardly ever forage on land. Its main diet consists of aquatic plants, and it tends to eat more of the stems and leaves, and less of the seeds. It may also eat small quantities of mollusks, crustaceans, aquatic insects and small fish. The usual call of the male is a short, deep, reedy burp, given in steady succession or 2-5 at a time in flight; it also gives high-pitched whistles. The female utters a quack or a gag-gag-gag. The Gadwall is generally a quiet bird, especially in its non-breeding grounds. It moults out of its breeding plumage after successful mating, during which period it is flightless and vulnerable to predation. Nesting: The Gadwall is generally monogamous – though extra-pair copulations have occasionally been reported – and even renews pair bonds in subsequent years. It breeds generally between May and late July in its breeding grounds. The male performs two elaborate courtship displays – the Head-Up-Tail-Up (where the male throws the head back and jerks the body with tail raised, mainly to display the white speculum) and the Grunt-Whistle (where the male rears out of the water and slowly sinks back while emitting a loud whistle). The nest is built on dry land near water, surrounded by dense weeds or grass. It is built by the female while the male stands guard, and is made of grasses and weeds in a shallow depression and lined with down. The usual clutch consists of 8-11 white eggs, though this number can sometimes go to 513. If the nest is predated, the Gadwall may lay another clutch in the same season. The Gadwall is a medium-sized dabbling duck with very nondescript plumage, leading to it being often misidentified in the field. The female and the non-breeding male are very similar and look like a dull version of the female Mallard. The male, though, is greyer on the upperparts than the browner female, and has less orange in the bill. The dark orange-edged bill and smaller size help differentiate the female from the female Mallard. The breeding male is mainly grey with a very delicate vermiculate pattern over the scapulars and upperparts, a whitish belly, black upper and lower coverts, light chestnut wings, and a marked white speculum (present also in females) that is more easily visible in flight. The legs are bright yellowish orange. Juvenile birds are very much like the female. Local name: The Gadwall is known as ‘Myla’, ‘Buari’ or ‘Beykhur’ in Hindi, ‘Yella repalla batu’ in Telugu, ‘Gaidwal’ in Punjabi, ‘Gadwal eranda’ in Malayalam, ‘Luhar’ in Gujarati and ‘Malin hansak’ in Sanskrit. Habitat & behaviour: The Gadwall is usually seen in pairs or small groups. In breeding season, it prefers marshes, ponds, and small lakes near grasslands in both fresh and brackish water. It generally avoids wetlands near woodlands or thick vegetation, and is more abundant in jheels and marshes near *** 17

Trip Report : Hyderabad International Airport, January 2, 2021 Text and Photos: Sudipta Bhattacharya The group birding at Hyderabad International Airport On the foggy winter morning of January 2, 2021, the Deccan Birders (DB) team visited the forest area opposite to Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad. The team had been invited by GMR Hyderabad International Airport Limited (GHIAL) officials responsible for maintenance of the airport land under the management of GHIAL, to carry out a field survey of the birds present in the forest area. I was also part of the team, as I usually try to participate in field trips unless busy with some other assignment. We reached the GMR Nursery opposite the Airport stretch at around 7.00AM that winter morning. As it was foggy, we had to drive quite slow and hence were slightly behind schedule. But it was a blessing in disguise, as the sunrise during winter is usually late and light would have been a bit of a problem if we had reached much earlier. We received a courteous welcome from the GHIAL officials, who joined us in the field survey along with their family members. After the initial introductions, we started walking through the nearly 12kilometer stretch of the road surrounding the forest. The place had two parts – one was a naturally grown tropical forest, and the other was a Eucalyptus forest. There were also some small water bodies surrounded by tropical bushes. 1

Some observations Although we reached the location around 7.00AM, the dense fog prevented us from proceeding faster. Visibility was very poor and our optical instruments were not of much help in locating birds at a distance, in spite of the chirping of birds prevailing all around the place. The walk started from the area where residential quarters are provided to the GHIAL staff. The natural forest patches surrounding the quarters seemed to have more birds because of the presence of more shrubs compared to the dense forest area. The roads were well maintained and both sides were full of tropical trees and bushes, so numerous birds were chirping all around us. As the light improved, we began to see some of the migratory warblers flying around. Common residential birds were also seen, like Bulbuls, Sunbirds and Flowerpeckers. Blyth’s Reed Warbler Booted Warbler View of playground on a foggy morning After the residential stretch, we entered the main forest area, where one side had Eucalyptus trees and the other side was tropical forest. It was clear from the field examination that birds prefer the naturally grown forests rather than the artificially-created forest having exotic trees. Most of the birds were observed on the natural forest side, except for the Prinias. At the beginning of the forest, flocks of Rosy Starlings were sitting on the branches; looking at them I presumed that there might be numerous birds inside the forest, but the number was limited as there was no visibility. Indian Golden Oriole female After about 500m of walking, we reached a playground where the sunrise under the haze made for a nice scenic view. There we saw the female Indian Golden Oriole, Black Drongo, Laughing Dove, Indian Roller, Grey-bellied Cuckoo and of course several Warblers, which have always been a personal interest for me as they are a challenging subject both for identification and photography. Eucalyptus forest 2

The visual of the Eucalyptus forest and the roads was quite nostalgic, as I used to travel in the mountains during my holidays, and I had been missing this for years. This was a nice picturesque view that I didn’t want to miss. The other side of the forest was quite dense and did not offer improved visibility to observe birds. As a result, there were plenty of calls of birds but they were not visible. For instance, we just missed a yellowish heron-like bird, which flew off just as we came upon it, and we could not identify what type of Ardeidae it was, due to the poor visibility. Kingfisher. As we were significantly trailing the other members of the team, we realized that we needed to focus on some fast walking to come out of the woods and catch up with the other members. After a significantly long walk, we came out of the dense forest and there were concrete roads surrounded by open forest area with naturally grown herbs and trees. While walking through the woods, we saw a family of Greybreasted Prinia, a small passerine. Seasoned birders and researchers would probably know it very well, but for relatively newer birders, this bird was earlier called the Franklin’s Prinia, and Prinias themselves were called Wren Warblers. I was able to take the photograph of one of the young members of the family. Green Bee-eater We observed the Green Bee-eater, Common Iora, House Crow, Ashy Prinia, White-browed Bulbul, Jungle Babbler and Yellow-billed Babbler in that area. Apart from birds, I have ardent interest all kinds of nature photography, including flowers. The roadsides had many different herbs and flowers. We were enriched by the knowledge of herbs of our member Azam Khan. The roadsides had a lot of Natal Grass, Silver Cockscomb and many other unknown wild flowers. Grey-breasted Prinia A Large-billed Crow was continuously calling on seeing this group of another species walking in their territory. The Cinereous Tit, earlier known as Great Tit, was visible in the dense part of the forest. But their hyperactivity and the poor visibility ensured that I didn’t get an opportunity to take its photo – although I waited for what seemed like hours, even though Mr Venkatesh of GHIAL, who was accompanying me, was probably feeling bored! But photo-enthusiasts are like that. Natal Grass (Melinis repens) A marshy area in the GHIAL campus After a few yards there was a waterbody on the left side. Though the water level was low, yet we could see a few species like White-breasted Waterhen, Common Sandpiper, Little Egret, White-throated Kingfisher and Common Sanguinarea (Alternanthera ficoidea) 3

There was a scenic, landscaped waterbody on the left side of the road, but we could not observe any species there, only the nice fall of sunlight on the green water and the hide-and-seek play between light and shadow. By that point of time, I could see that I had already walked around eight kilometers and hence was in dire need of rest. Coincidentally, we saw a tractor on the way, and a few of us, including me, got into it and travelled a few kilometers. But the circumference of the total forest would probably be more than twelve kilometers. As I was walking around and taking photos here and there, a car came to take me to the nursery. At the end, when we were relaxing and relishing the tea and excellent breakfast offered by Mr & Mrs Azam Khan and the GHIAL officials, we saw the Rufous Treepie on the tree above us, as also the Black Kite, Booted Eagle and Oriental Honey-buzzard flying over us. The trip ended with a nice group photo taken with my newlypurchased Sony A6600 camera. Bougainvillea spp The group during the trip We saw around 38 species during the trip. STORY OF THE IBISBILL AND AN ARROGANT BIRDER Text and Photos: Col SS Cheema (Retd) There are birds and then there are target birds – like the one mentioned in the title, the Ibisbill, a bird that I chased for a long long time. The chase happens when you plan to go to a place, and research the likely birds in that season at that place. When I planned a trip to the Corbett National Park, it was not the tigers on my mind, but two birds that had so far refused to be ticked as my lifers, the Collared Falconet and the Ibisbill. The Falconets are residents in and around Corbett and seen very regularly, though usually on the very tops of the tall trees. So I was not really concerned – I was sure that I would be able to see them. It was the Ibisbill that was my main target. With March around the corner, and the weather slowly changing, it was difficult to guess if the bird would be there. The last sighting logged was a week or so before my trip, so the odds that the bird would be around were anything but a certainty. Anyway, I tried to get hold of a bird guide but unfortunately, it being high season, none of the better guides were available. The alternative – getting a Gypsy driver with a permit for the forests – is sometimes better than hiring a bird guide; the good drivers often rival the best of the guides spending years learning on the field. I contacted and managed to convince Mr Kaleem Khan to be with me for a day and a half. Next morning, he was there dot on time, waiting for us at the gates of our hotel. There was a quick exchange of pleasantries and, as we chatted, I listed out the birds that I wanted to see, and stressed especially on the Collared Falconet and the Ibisbill. He replied almost immediately: Falconet – a sure thing – but Ibisbill… I could see the gears of his mind turning to process the information. binoculars when on top of a tall tree. After the first safari, we dropped my father and son back at the hotel, and drove off to look for the place, a few kilometres away, where the Ibisbill had last been seen. The chances of getting to see it were anybody’s guess, as the last sighting was a full week back and the weather had been getting hotter since then. The bird being an altitudinal migrant that moves to the higher reaches of Himalayas in the summer, it was always possible that it had moved to the upper reaches of the streams in the Himalayas. In any case we were not giving up yet – so here we were, on our way to the river bed where the bird had been seen regularly during the season. We reached the location, walked almost a kilometre, and I was quickly disappointed. I scanned, quite meticulously, the entire riverbed on both sides – and saw no signs of the Ibisbill. Two to three scans, and I had already started checking out the other birds in the area. All this while my guide Kaleem kept saying, “Sir, this is a difficult bird to see. It merges with the rocks and you have to be careful while scanning the area and it takes time.” I thought to myself, “Ah, after birding (as in, birding with effort and dedication) for almost 30-odd years, you are telling me that a bird the size of a chicken can hide from me? No way!” – and I disregarded his advice. All the same, Kaleem kept scanning both banks of the river, looking for clues. As he worked out his reply I was thinking of my own next steps. With my father (who was nearing 80) and my son, who had both accompanied me to Corbett, the chase of the tiger was a priority as of now as we were to do a safari. I thought I would bird on the safari if possible, then drop my father and son back to the hotel and go for some unadulterated birding, looking for the Ibisbill in particular. Little Egret Collared Falconet Though we were lucky enough to see some animals and birds, by and large the first safari was fairly uneventful. For the record, we did see some Falconets but as expected, a bird the size of a bulbul can hardly be appreciated even with the Pied Kingfisher 5

movement from the corner of my eye – and there was Kaleem in the distance, pointing to some place towards the river with great excitement. I hobbled over the big stones of the river bank and took almost 10 minutes to reach him – and in a hushed but excited voice, he said “Ibisbill – there!” Meanwhile, the disappointed me chased and clicked a flock of Little Egrets (including some flying shots), a Pied Kingfisher and some River Lapwings. River Lapwing Ibisbill Then I spotted a Crested Kingfisher in the far distance; I pointed it out to Kaleem, who seemed almost disappointed in me. He had his eyes focused on the banks, peering through the binoculars, looking for my main target bird with all his concentration. I just could not believe it – birding for so many years, I had been arrogant enough to ignore the advice of someone who was perhaps more dedicated to my desire than myself. We saw the bird and there it was – a lifer, and a bird that I did not know how I could have missed. I moved to position myself for some pictures, but the bird did not oblige. As we moved closer, it kept flying a little further. So all the shots I am sharing here are highly cropped – but I celebrate the moments spent with my lifer. Crested Kingfisher Meanwhile I started making my way to the Crested Kingfisher, confident of getting close to it. The tactic was simple – move at a tangent, not looking towards the bird, take a few steps, stop, click and pray that you will not agitate the bird enough to fly away. Take another few steps, stop, slowly raise the camera, click. Repeat it till you are satisfied, while also respecting the bird’s space. Ibisbill All this went on for almost an hour and a half. I looked back at Kaleem, and he was still doing his thing – scanning the banks of the river. I thought to myself, “Why is this guy so hell-bent on finding the bird that I was sure was not there?” This incident taught me a very important lesson of my birding life – be patient and listen to the guides – after all, they have more experience in their location and conditions. Oh, how arrogant I had been. I thank the Ibisbill and Kaleem for teaching me a lesson in humility, and getting me back to the roots of being a good birdwatcher. Another half hour passed, and by now I was chasing all the birds other than what I had targeted. Suddenly, I saw some I still sit and fondly remember the moments… Oh what a fool I had been… *** 6

Report: Rosy Starling congregations at Vijayanagar Colony Park, Hyderabad Text and Photos: Dr G Samuel Sukumar A section of the Rosy Starling congregation seen in 2019 Vijayanagar Colony, where I live, has a park with a good number of lush green trees, mostly Ashoka and Neem. The park has a walkers’ pathway, used by residents for walking in the morning and evening. In 2020, due to the lockdown, we were unfortunately unable to jot down any observations regarding the numbers of Rosy Starlings. However, Dr Ramamurthy called again this year to inform that the birds had arrived in large numbers. So, on March 24, 2021 – almost exactly two years later – Shafaatsaab, his son and I went to the park. We noted that the Rosy Starlings generally congregated on trees on the periphery of the park till around 5:30PM, as most of the trees in the park were occupied by Crows and Mynas in fairly large numbers. After 6:00PM the Starlings all flew into the park, forcing the Crows and the Mynas to leave the trees, and hid themselves in the thick foliage of the Ashoka trees, making it almost impossible to spot them. We observed that this year the Starlings were less in number as compared to 2019. One day in March 2019, Mr Shafaat Ulla received a call from Dr NV Ramamurthy, a colony resident, regarding a huge congregation of birds every evening in the park, so we decided to pay a visit and see for ourselves. Accordingly, Shafaatsaab, Aasheesh Pittie, Ajit Kumar, Chowdhary, Shilka, and I went to the park on March 25, 2019. It was 5:30PM, and we saw the Rosy Starlings slowly starting to congregate on the high mobile towers around the park. Occasionally they took off, forming huge murmurations – it was a feast for the eyes to see such huge flocks of birds. Initially, the birds could not perch on the trees in the park, as they were already occupied by House Crows, Common Mynas and a few Red-vented Bulbuls – it was only after some waiting that they were able to move to the trees. A part of the Rosy Starling flock seen this year A regular study to document the date of arrival and departures every year would help in understanding more about their migration. Rosy Starling flock *** 7

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Grey Plover (Pluvialis squatarola) Grey Plover breeding (L) and non-breeding (R) (Pulicat, September 09, 2020 & December 27, 2020) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Charadriidae Genus: Pluvialis Species: P. squatarola Size: 27-30 cm ‘armpits’, white rump and tail, and a whitish wingbar are also clear and diagnostic. The plumage also lacks the golden spangling seen in the Pacific Golden Plover. Juvenile birds have a clean salt-and-pepper look with crisp spangling above and a clearly-streaked head and breast. Description & distribution: The Grey Plover, also known as the Black-bellied Plover, Silver Plover or Grey Sandpiper, is a chunky medium-sized plover that breeds in the Arctic islands and the coastal regions of Alaska, Canada and Russia, and has an almost world-wide wintering range, generally in coastal regions, although it is sometimes seen inland as a rare passage migrant.. It has relatively long, dark legs and a short, stout black bill. In breeding plumage it has a striking black face, neck and belly, clean white rump, and bold black upperparts, profusely barred and spangled with silvery grey or pearly white, sometimes with some buff edging to the patches. The black face and neck have a clear white border. Habitat & behaviour: In winter, the Grey Plover is usually seen in the intertidal zone in its coastal wintering areas. It is gregarious, usually seen in small to medium flocks of up to 30 birds. However, it does not form large, dense flocks as seen in the case of other waders, except while roosting during high tide. While foraging, it tends to forage widely dispersed along beaches, with individuals being spaced widely apart. It is rather shy, moving away as one approaches it. Its flight is the typical fast, twisting flight shown by most waders. Its call is a shrill musical piping similar to the Pacific Golden Plover, or a mournful chee-woo-ee, and the alarm call is a double whistle. Nesting: The Grey Plover breeds generally between April and August in their breeding range. The nest is a shallow scrape on the ground, in dry open tundra with good visibility. The usual clutch consists of four elongated oval, brownish-beige eggs strongly mottled or blotched with black. In non-breeding plumage, the Grey Plover is more uniformly drab grey with a smudgy face and breast, whitish belly and brownish mottling on the upperparts. Sides of head, neck, uppertail coverts, tail and rump are white streaked or barred with brown. On the underparts, foreneck, breast and flanks are streaked and spotted with brown. It is often confused with the Pacific Golden Plover, but can be identified by its stockier appearance, and the shorter, stouter bill; in flight, the black Local name: The Grey Plover is known as ‘Bada batan’ in Hindi and Bengali, ‘Anathalai ullan’ in Tamil, ‘Chara plover’ in Malayalam and ‘Moti batan’ or ‘Batana titodi’ in Gujarati. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034.
