NATURE WATCHING IN THE CARIBBEAN Trip Report: Sint Maarten, December 2018-January 2019 Text: Dr Barnali Chaudhuri; Photos: Anwesha & Dr Barnali Chaudhuri A view of Pinal Island, Sint Maarten With an area of only 34 square miles, Sint Maarten is one of the smallest Caribbean islands, barely securing a tiny dot on the map of the north-eastern Caribbean Sea. It has been labelled a tropical paradise because of its beautiful weather and breath-taking landscape. This tiny island is jointly governed by France and Netherlands. The French sector is spelled Saint-Martin while the Dutch side is spelled Sint Maarten. This particular island is exceptional in its blend of Caribbean island culture infused with European charm. It is well-known for its 37 pristine beaches, each with its own distinctive nature. I was very excited to visit Sint Maarten as I would be able to experience two different European countries in just one vacation! I could experience the unique culture of the Caribbean set in a French/Dutch aesthetic. My husband and I had decided to visit our daughter Anwesha during Christmas 2018. She is an M.D. student at the American University of Caribbean (AUC) in Sint Maarten. We started from Kolkata. After 43 long hours of journey stretching between Dubai, Milan and JFK, we finally reached Princess Juliana Airport in Sint Maarten. After passing through immigration, we were welcomed by four Brown Pelican statues at the entrance/exit of the airport. I later found out that the Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) is the national bird of Saint Maarten. 1

Brown Pelican statue We reached our destination, Lagoon View apartments, by a local taxi. The apartment complex was aptly named: we could see a beautiful lagoon from my daughter’s apartment. Our friends Ritta and Rahul were to join us from USA a few days later. Carib Grackle male Most of the birds were lifers for me. Carib Grackles (Quiscalus lugubris) in Sint Maarten are as abundant as House Crows in India. These social birds are smaller in size than House Crows, though. The male Carib Grackle is a shiny black bird with bright yellow eyes, while the female is brown. I spotted a nest where some chicks were hiding behind their mother. Strikingly, the male, female and chicks have different song registers. View from the apartment Despite being an urbanized island whose economy depends primarily on tourism, it provides a safe haven to myriad endemic flora and fauna. The mangrove forests, rocky islets and dense wetlands harbour an incredible variety of bird species, making this volcanic landscape a birdwatcher’s paradise. My daughter’s apartment on the second floor overlooked a patch of rugged wilderness, making it a perfect perch for me to watch birds to my heart’s content. We would come across new species of birds and iguanas every day during our twenty-day stay on the island. My only regret was that I was unable to spot hummingbirds on the island. Hummingbirds had not entirely returned to the island since the Category 5 hurricane, Irma, had destroyed it and left it in shambles in September 2017. I spotted a Zenaida Dove (Zenaida aurita). It was orangishbrown in colour. A hen was teaching its chicks how to dig for food from the ground. Eurasian Collared Doves (Streptopelia decaocto), locally known as Barbie Doves, flew from one tree to another, playfully chasing each other. Carib Grackle female Eurasian Collared Dove Zenaida Dove 2

One of my most startling discoveries was finding iguanas. As I looked into the foliage for birds, all of a sudden, I saw something green fall from a tree, only to discover that a huge iguana was moving in the ground. A quick scan of the ground yielded 4 more of the kind, each a different species of iguana – ranging from bright sap green to a heavily muted ashy brown. It didn’t take me long to realize that I had come upon their regular sun-bathing/hangout spot. but it was no more. Like much of the island, it too had fallen prey to Irma. Another group of tourists also ended up at Happy Beach in search of the park. However, they chose not to stay on at the beach. My husband spotted a pair of Brown Pelicans sitting on an abandoned boat tied to a pole in the ocean. After a while one of them flew and dived into the sea to catch fish. It was an excellent view. Unlike some other seabirds, they dive directly into the water rather than hover at the surface. Owing to its excellent eyesight, it can spot fish from a height of 20 meters! We spotted two other Brown Pelicans diving into the sea to catch fish. It was a treat to watch these majestic birds at work. Iguanas basking in the sun Great Blue Heron My daughter had noticed a creek on the way to the beach, so we stopped to check it out. There, we spotted a Great Blue Heron (Ardea Herodias), a Great Egret (Ardea alba), a Grey Kingbird (Tyrannus dominicensis) and a few Brown Crabs (Cancer pagurus). Common Buckeye On our first day, we rented a car for transport, as we wanted to explore Sint Maarten’s Butterfly Park. After forty minutes of driving and a few questionable turns, we ended up at a lonely beach. It was serene, with perfectly white and sticky sand. Grey Kingbird Happy Beach The tides had brought a whole crop of red algae onto the beach and this contrasted beautifully against the white sand. I would later realize that by a happy accident, we had landed at Happy Beach. The Butterfly Park had once stood tall near this beach, St Andrew’s Cotton Stainer 3

I noticed an aggregation of St. Andrew's Cotton Stainer (Dysdercus andreae). They are red bugs that feed on the halfopened cotton balls and seeds. In addition, adults of this species produce an indelible yellow dye that stains cotton lint, hence earning its name. Plane landing over Maho Beach We all were astonished when one plane took off towards the sea. If one were to stand behind the plane while it was taking off, one would feel the intense speed of the wind, which would be very hard to control. It would create ripples in the ocean. We also saw many Navishankh, also known as Gomti Chakra, at Maho beach. The Gomti chakra is the operculum of a kind of rare sea snail in the family Turbinidae. A scene at Mullet Bay We walked to Mullet Bay one fine morning, which was only a ten-minute walk from my daughter’s apartment. We had to walk through a golf course with 18 golf holes to reach Mullet Beach. In the early morning, we enjoyed the unpolluted air while crossing the golf course, which was separated from the beach by a mid-sized sand dune. The beach was devoid of any human presence in the wee hours of the morning. However, several Ruddy Turnstones (Arenaria interpres) were feasting in the fine sand, running around like they were participating in the Avian Olympics Marathon! A view of the Caribbean Sea from Maho Beach Ruddy Turnstone The Atlantic Ocean in the Caribbean is a spectacular shade of blue. As the sun shone higher in the sky, the beach became progressively crowded with people. A young boy called to everybody’s attention a baby Hammerhead Shark which had seemingly become isolated in the sea-shore muddle. Everybody was busy taking photographs of the lost creature, while we could not because we had left our phones at home for our day out in the beach. An older gentleman guided the gentle youngling to deeper water, and after a while with a big wave, we bade it goodbye. Brown Booby Before we knew it, the sun was setting. The Brown Booby (Sulidae leucogaster), a large seabird, and a Brown Pelican were fishing out in the sea. After enjoying the sunset, we went to the adjacent Sunset Bar restaurant on Maho beach for snacks. While eating we saw the Carnival cruise ship sailing through the sea. It looked like as if the ship had donned the jewellery of lights. The ambience was beautiful – the restaurant was built on a pier, and we could hear and feel the waves crash onto ragged rocks underneath the wooden flooring. The seemingly endless darkness of the ocean was cut by a distant light that, we assumed, belonged to a lighthouse. Maho Beach is famous for planes landing just meters above the sandy beach to the Princess Juliana International Airport. Most planes land from the ocean onto the runway and take off towards the mountains on the opposite side. Undoubtedly, it makes for a brilliant photo-op, and everyone on the beach was busy clicking away, trying to get their classic Maho shot. 4

Anwesha took us to her favourite French bakery, La Sucriere Pastry, for breakfast at Philipsburg, the Dutch capital of Sint Maarten. I had never imagined we would be able to do some birding in the patio of the restaurant itself. With a fantastic view of the Simpson Bay Lagoon cutting through mountains in the background, breakfast turned into a perfect opportunity to do some birding. We sat at their rear outdoor patio. Food was good and fresh. A Zenaida Dove was in front of us, asking for food, and there were Carib Grackles everywhere. every day. We tried out many restaurants: Rendezvouz, GongFu Tea, Mama’s. House Sparrow We saw a few House Sparrows (Passer domesticus) and a Bananaquit (Coereba flaveola) in the premises. Bananaquits are also called Sucriere or Sugar Bird locally due to their love for sugar. And, true to its reputation, it was enjoying the leftover chocolate at Porto Cupecoy Marina. Magnificent Frigatebird A male Magnificent Frigatebird (Fregata magnificens) was flying high in the sky, as recognized by its red gular sac. I was amazed to know that the Frigatebird has the largest wingspan (7.5 feet) of all birds compared to the body size. It can fly effortlessly for an entire week by taking naps in the air. But it does not have waterproof feathers. It must depend on food from the water surface and by stealing food from other birds. Hence Frigatebirds are also named ‘man o’war’. Locally, this bird is called the Scissorbird because its tail looks like scissors while flying. Royal Terns (Sterna maxima) were circling the lagoon far away. The striking orange-red beak was beautiful. We even spotted two iguanas, brown and green, which came onto the patio where we were enjoying our breakfast, in search of food. Bananaquit Iguana looking for food scraps Yellow-crowned Night Heron Anwesha had discovered the preferred roosting place of a Yellow-crowned Night Heron (Nyctanassa violacea) near a water body inside the AUC campus. We attempted to look for it on multiple nights but failed each time. To our surprise, one night, Rahul spotted the Yellow-crowned Night Heron searching of food just behind our apartment. It looked elegant, with its colourful yellow-tan crown that extends behind its head and a white band below the eye. Its large red eyes were glittering in the night. We also saw a Banana Spider there. Inside Porto Cupecoy Marina Our favourite spot on the trip was Porto Cupecoy Marina. There are several restaurants inside the Marina and shops in the peripheral area. A few of the restaurants offer live music 5

Following that, we went to Porto Cupecoy Family Beach to see the sunset. It was remarkable. It justified why Sint Maarten is also known for the golden sun. The stunning beauty of Caribbean sunsets mesmerized us. Banana Spider Sunset at Family Beach, Porto Cupecoy It was a rocky beach, and we saw cotton flowers, tamarind trees and shoe flowers. Our Christmas dinner was scheduled at Mama’s, an Italian restaurant at Porto Cupecoy Marina. The restaurant was totally full, and there was a beautifully decorated Christmas tree. We relished the traditional Italian food with live music. Sunset at AUC campus A scene at Pinal Island Pinal Island is a tiny island located off the North Shore on the French side. We wanted to explore it on Christmas day. We had to take a ferry that departed from the Cul-de-Sac Port. As our speed boat zoomed through the blue waters, everybody enjoyed the ride. Pinel Island was chock full of Hermit Crabs. Each one had a different coloured shell of varying sizes. We stayed there for 45 minutes and sailed back to Sint Maarten. Statue of fisherman at Simpson Bay Marina Simpson Bay is a very popular area, buzzing with business and marinas. Tourists come here to see the fisherman’s statue right outside the main Marina. The Simpson Bay Bridge is a swing bridge which allows vessels in and out of Simpson Bay and the open sea. This is the only place on the island which has traffic lights – otherwise, traffic is normally controlled by roundabouts. Monuments depicting historical or memorable incidents were displayed on most of the roundabouts. One of the most famous roundabouts has the Salt Pickers display. It is a group of bronze sculptures depicting the lives of slaves engaged in the various aspects of salt harvesting. It is a memorial dedicated to all the people who were exploited, and acknowledges the country’s history, however painful it may have been. Caribbean Hermit Crab 6

Pelicans hovering over the Great Salt Pond. People were enjoying water sports like parasailing, paragliding, and speedboats. Coal Bay Parasailing at the beach Bell’s Lookout Point There is a flag pole at Bell’s Lookout Point on Coal Bay Hill. It houses a huge St Maarten’s flag. It was a bit of a trek to the Lookout Point, but it was worth the climb just to see the vast ocean from the cliff on which the flag is hoisted. The serene aqua blue colour of the ocean was soothing to the eyes. I was amazed to see that the national bird of Sint Maarten has a place in their flag too! Cruise terminal at Philipsburg Three cruise ships were anchored nearby at the cruise terminal. People were queuing up to get back onboard the ships. Street performers were dancing the hip hop and breakdance on the streets. There was a wonderful collection of restaurants, souvenir shops and jewellery shops along the boardwalk beach. We enjoyed the ocean view under the scorching heat of the sun while walking on the boardwalk. I secretly wondered why there was a statue of a cow that was kept alone on the beach. Ritta had planned a long drive around the entire island that would last a whole day. After breakfast we started early in the morning. The roads were very hilly taking us through crests and troughs of different mountains on the island. We were cruising through the coastal roads when Anwesha spotted an Orange Iguana in a field of thorny bushes off the road. We stopped to take a few pictures, but suddenly it began to pour. Visibility had become poor, and we had to stop for safety. We took shelter in a French restaurant named Oasis for lunch. After lunch the sky cleared up, and we were ready to embark upon the last leg of our long drive. We caught glimpses of both Dutch and French localities. The ride was memorable. Boardwalk shopping at Philipsburg Statue of cow at Great Bay Beach Philipsburg is the capital of the island state. It is particularly famous for its boardwalk – a giant, lively market on the beachside that is especially known for precious gems. We parked our car alongside the Great Salt Pond and walked to the boardwalk along Great Bay beach. We spotted a few Brown The first church of Sint Maarten stands there with the statue of St Martin of Tours, who was a fourth-century Roman soldier. He had left the army to become a monk and was later acclaimed as Bishop of Tours in France. This Caribbean island was named after St Martin by Christopher Columbus. 7

I wanted to explore the bus service on the island. Fort Louis at Marigot was our target. I was surprised that the term ‘bus’ was being used fairly loosely on the island – 10-seater vans were masquerading as buses. The number plate itself was the only indication that it was a bus (BUS92)! On the tallest surviving tower of the fort flew a French flag. The flag had been torn by strong wind. It was surprising that the flag had not been taken down and replaced. We enjoyed the 360-degree views from the top of the hill. We noticed a big tree trunk full of thorns. While returning, Anwesha spotted an American Kestrel (Falco sparverius) sitting on a tree. The American Kestrel is a small falcon, and it is probably the only raptor breeding on the island. Local people called it killy-killy. The bus stop was five minutes’ walk from our apartment. We had to take a couple of buses, stopping at the local KFC to board a bus to Marigot. A view of Marigot Port From Marigot, we trekked to Fort Louis. It was a very nice place. The weather was also on our side – it was a clear, windy and a sunny day. A huge cross welcomed us onto the fort’s grounds. Beyond that statue, a staircase began that would ultimately get us into the fort itself. Hence there was no problem climbing. Green Iguana We spotted many iguanas scattered through the thorny terrain. A pair of Black-faced Grassquit (Melanospiza bicolor) was playing in the nearby bushes. The winds were so strong that tall grasses bent to its will and touched the ground, as if they were bowing to Mother Nature. The sun was about to set, and it was the time to return. Cannon at Fort Louis, Marigot The fort was completely in ruins. There were several cannons placed on top of the fort, facing every direction. An island off Guana Bay Geneva Beach is the best beach if one wants to connect to nature in solitude and enjoy a crowd-free adventure. After hurdling through the steep hilly roads leading up to the cliff where the trail started, we finally reached Guana Bay. As expected, it was deserted. An abandoned and destroyed house stood eerily on the top of the cliff, serving as a ghostly reminder of the devastating effects of Hurricane Irma. A pair of mountain goats was grazing on the tough grass that grew haphazardly on the rocky cliffs. Their appearance was quite different from normal goats. Torn French flag 8

It was a beautiful sunny day. We started our trek on a very narrow hilly road. We took lots of pictures – the ambience was ideal for a photoshoot. A really narrow trail road opened into a mid-sized grassy field. On one end was a hill and the other end was a steep cliff opening into the ocean. Here we saw a pair of Common Ground Doves (Columbina passerina) foraging for food. They were much smaller than the other doves. Mountain Goat male Common Ground Dove We were surrounded by different species of cacti of all shapes and sizes. We also saw a lot of lizards, as they ran from one rock to another. There were many iguanas as well. A few hundred feet out into the ocean, there were giant offshore rocks and islets that are relatively inaccessible to humans, making them important nesting areas for seabirds. Mountain Goat female We listened to the roar of the waves aggressively crashing into the rocks over and over again. As I looked over the cliff, I could see about 100 feet down. The unruly yet coordinated waves of Guana Bay had eroded through the hilly structure to create a steep, sharp and vertical overhanging of rocks. The white froth against the Prussian blue sea waves seemed to be forming V-shapes as they rushed towards the cliff. “This could be a big advertisement for surf”, Anwesha felt. American Kestrel pair Anwesha spotted a pair of American Kestrel sitting on top of some giant boulders on the hilltop. The male and female were taking turns to hunt – we had chanced upon a fantastic opportunity to observe hunting behaviour in these relatively tiny predators. We saw one of them staying still in the air without seemingly moving its wings, before it dived straight towards the ground to hunt a small lizard. As we were watching this magnificent hunting technique, we spotted three Brown Pelicans flying right over our heads. The Baie Rouge Beach is also known as Red Bay Beach due to its red sand. I was excited to explore it and see the red sand, but was disappointed as the sand was the normal sandy colour and not red! However, there were red rocks on the beach. Despite the disappointment, the beach was really beautiful. On the last day of our stay at Sint Maarten, we wanted to walk to the Rouge Pond which was on the French side. After we crossed Porto Cupecoy Marina, an uphill climb began. The name Cupecoy means Lowlands. Porto Cupecoy abuts the French Saint-Martin and Dutch Sint Maarten border. Some views of Guana Bay 9

Greater Yellowlegs We continued northward on the same road and peeped through the thin layers of Mangroves, literally functioning as a bird hide. It separated the pond from the busy main road. I recognized an Orange-horned Tarantula Hawk (Pepsis ruficornis), a species of Spider Wasp, by its vivid blue colour and orange horn. Interestingly, the female Tarantula Hawk paralyzes a tarantula and drags it to its pre-dug burrow as living food, lays a single egg on the belly of the paralyzed tarantula, and leaves after covering the den's entrance. On hatching, the larva digs a hole into the abdomen and feeds on the flesh of the still-living tarantula. Border between French and Dutch regions of Sint Maarten We crossed the border where the flags of both the countries were hoisted together with no place for no man’s land. It signifies and justifies the other name of Sint Maarten as ‘The Friendly Island’. We had crossed this border several times by car. But we would have missed a lot if we had not taken this walk. The houses were different from the Dutch side. During our walk, we came across Bananaquit (Coereba flaveola), American Kestrel, Gray Kingbird (Tyrannus dominicensis), and Eurasian Bullfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula). Locally, the Grey Kingbird is also known as the chincherry. Orange-horned Tarantula Hawk Green Heron An adult Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) was seen roosting on the other side of the pond. Several Brown Pelicans were roosting on small dead trees sticking out of the middle of the pond. A few others were fishing. Adult Brown Pelicans have a white head and neck, although the top of the head may be yellowish or tan. We enjoyed watching their fishing practices. Black-necked Stilt It took us more than one hour to reach Rouge Pond, which is a protected area. We saw several water birds as was expected. The southeast part of the pond is almost a mudflat where Anwesha spotted a Green Heron (Butorides virescens). It was perfectly camouflaged in the surroundings. A few Blacknecked Stilts (Himantopus mexicanus) were busy picking food. A Greater Yellowlegs (Tringa melanoleuca) was looking for food. We also saw numerous crabs in the mudflat. Brown Pelican 10

The Brown Pelican is the only member of the pelican family that catches its prey by plunge diving, with its long broad wings partly folded. I was amazed to see the large skin pouch under its long grey bill. The pouch can hold two to three times as much food as its stomach and it serves as a net to catch fish also. It was magnificent to see that some of them were diving head first. know the successful conservation story of the once endangered Brown Pelicans. If it weren’t for the 43-hour journey to the island, I’d love to go back there at the drop of a hat! I would like to thank my daughter Anwesha – she not only made it possible to take in some great birding there, but also contributed her pictures and other inputs to this article. By the 1970s the Brown Pelicans were on the endangered species list. The populations of Brown Pelicans increased again after DDT was banned. In 2009, Brown Pelicans were removed from the endangered list, a successful conservation story. The most unique aspect of this trip was experiencing the Caribbean culture in a European backdrop. All the pristine beaches of Sint Maartin were so clean – this not only demonstrates an environmental awareness amongst the locals, but also a healthy attitude towards nature among tourists. I loved watching the planes land over our heads at Maho beach. Our trek to the Red Pond was memorable as we saw innumerable Brown Pelicans in their habitat. I was amazed to View of island from the plane Some other photos taken during the trip: Firecracker (Russelia equisetiformis) Hydrangea Lesser Antillean Bullfinch Alamanda Brown Pelican *** 11

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Ruff (Philomachus pugnax) Ruff (Kakinada, January 7, 2019) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Philomachus Species: P. pugnax Size: Male 26-32 cm, Female 20-25 cm the underparts show a strong buff tinge, and the upperparts have a neat, scale-like appearance with dark-centred feathers. Habitat & behaviour: The Ruff is gregarious and is usually seen in medium to large flocks on marshes and tidal mudflats, often along with other waders like Sandpipers, Redshanks, etc. Its behavior is generally similar to other waders, with the bird tending to stay on mudflats and marshes, or on the sides of water bodies like creeks, lakes, saltpans, lagoons and estuaries. The Ruff is known for its promiscuous breeding habits – the females are also polyandrous – and elaborate courtship displays. In breeding season, the males in varying plumages tend to gather communally at selected open grassy spots known as ‘leks’ or ‘hills’; females, however, seem to prefer larger leks taller plants nearby, which offer better nesting habitat. In the leks, individuals often occupy adjacent territories of barely a few square inches, and posture threateningly towards other males by puffing up their ruffs and ear tufts, flexing their legs, lowering their heads with bills pointed upwards, and sometimes leaping at each other. Female birds that are ready to breed visit the leks from time to time, and mate with the male of their choice. Mating may also occur with the male actively ursuing the female outside a lek, or waiting to intercept her near good feeding areas. Thereafter, the nesting duties are handled by the female, with the male taking no part. As a result, the males also leave the breeding grounds earlier – in late June or early July – and are followed later in July by the females and juveniles. Description & distribution: The Ruff is a medium-sized wader that breeds in northern Eurasia, and winters in southern and western Europe, Africa, southern Asia and Australia. In our region, the Ruff is seen across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Myanmar. It is one of the few species where the female is also known by a different name, the Reeve. It is a distinctive bird, with a small head, long neck, relatively short sandpiper-like bill and a pot-bellied body. Legs can be variable in colour but are usually yellow or orange. In flight, it shows an indistinct white wing bar and white patches on the sides of the tail base. The Ruff shows sexual dimorphism, with some clear differentiating features between male and female. The male is around 6-7cm bigger on average than the female. During breeding season, the male shows bright orange on the legs, bill and the bare facial skin, and has distinctive head tufts and a neck ruff, which can be of different colours – black, chestnut or white – and with variable colouring – solid, barred or irregular. The back is grey-brown with black or chestnut feathering and a scaly appearance, and the underparts are black with a black breast. It is believed that the extreme variations in breeding plumage have evolved to help in individual recognition in a species that demonstrates communal breeding displays. In the non-breeding season, which is the plumage we usually see in India, the male becomes plainer – the legs and bill become dull orange, the head and neck ornaments and facial colour are lost, and the upperparts become dull greybrown. The underparts are still white, but the breast and flaks show grey mottling. The female, or the Reeve, in breeding plumage, shows grey-brown upperparts with feathers having white fringes and dark centres. The breast and flanks have variable black blotches. In non-breeding season, the female is similar to the male, but can be told apart by the smaller size. Juvenile birds are similar to the non-breeding adult male, but The Ruff is usually silent, even while displaying, although it does occasionally emit a soft gue gue gue call, or a soft tu whit when flushed. During breeding, its diet consists almost exclusively of adults and larva of terrestrial and aquatic insects like beetles and flies. Outside breeding season, its diet includes insects (like caddis flies, water-beetles, grasshoppers, mayflies), crustaceans, spiders, mollucks, worms, frogs and small fish, as well as aquatic plants, sedges, grasses and the seeds of rice or other cereals. 12

Local name: The Ruff is known as ‘Gehwala’ or ‘Bagbad’ in Hindi, ‘Geowala’ in Bengali, ‘Ruffreev’ in Punjabi, ‘Galabandh panlawa’ or ‘Gherbala’ in Marathi, ‘Vara cheravi’ in Tamil, and ‘Bahuvarnan manaloothi’ in Malayalam. Nesting: The Ruff breeds generally between early March and early June in its breeding grounds, with some variations based on latitude. The nest is a shallow scrape in the ground, lined with grass leaves and stems, and hidden in between tall marsh plants close to the lek. Nesting is solitary, although there may be several nests in the same general vicinity. The usual clutch consists of 4 buff-coloured eggs with brown splotches. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (Received on Whatsapp, March 23, 2021) *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. WEEKEND BIRDING Trip Report: Bettakote Kere & Singanayakanahalli Kere, Bengaluru, July 10 & 11, 2021 Text & Photos: Arthit (age 11) A view of Bettakote Lake I woke up at 5:30AM, packed everything I needed and left for birding with my father. We live not very far from Lake Bettakote, so we arrived in just half an hour. There were a few other people there. It was drizzling when we arrived, and I took shelter under my father’s umbrella. A sudden gust of wind turned the umbrella upside down, but luckily it had stopped raining by then. We waited for a few other people. By 7:00AM everyone had arrived and we were ready. spotted a Cotton Pygmy-goose. Once my father spotted the Goose, he told me where to look. The water was camouflaging the bird well and we all had a hard time spotting it. I finally found it after a lot of effort. We went across a field of palm trees, watching the habitat for birds. We spotted a Rose-ringed Parakeet. When we arrived at a great field near the lake, we saw many Lesser Whistlingducks on the surface of the water. There was an airport just ahead. Everyone tried to click photos of the Whistling-ducks. I, being a beginner, had a beginner’s camera with less zooming power, and the birds were a little distant. We walked across the great plain, exploring the area. While doing so, I saw a Common Tiger butterfly. Suddenly someone Great Cormorant 1

After this we took some more pictures of Egrets and Whistling-ducks. There were many aeroplanes departing and arriving from time to time. Once a plane flew really close to us, so I decided to take a picture of it. Grey Heron Common Kingfisher We saw an Egret, which turned out to be an Intermediate Egret. I never knew there also was an ‘Intermediate’. By now it was time for me to go back home, as I had a class, and so I did. Plantation on lake bed We then walked into the distant hilly areas. We saw many Paddyfield Pipits, Baya Weavers, some Red-rumped and Streak-throated Swallows, etc – and kept seeing them throughout the morning. Then we arrived at a dense forest. It looked very beautiful as the trees had no spacing in between, and were very wide and short. The lower part of the trees was light pink. That night, as I went to sleep, I grew more and more impatient for the coming day. Singanayakanahalli Lake Again the next morning, I woke up at 5:30AM. This day was much more fresh, and I was glad. This time we were the first to arrive at Singanayakanahalli Lake. Just about 7 minutes later, 2 more people came, and then another. We began to walk across the huge sloped plain. Unlike the previous lake, this one was almost fully dry. There were only small ponds in certain areas, but the lake was actually humongous. We immediately saw a Brahminy Kite, perched on top of a pole. We got quite close to it, but maintained a distance. Plain Prinia We went inside the forest. On almost every tree, there were small toadstools growing. The big toadstools were growing on the ground and some people took photos of them. We also saw many spiders. In the end we saw a Common Indian Tree Frog, and everyone took photos of this too. We then walked across a part of the dry lake bed to find a small region filled with water. In the middle there was a big net, and a Grey Heron was standing right on it. We took multiple shots of it. In the net, we saw the corpse of another poor Grey Heron hanging, and we were all very sad. By now we were thinking of returning home. Before we did so, we decided to check out a nest-filled tree. We climbed up to a higher region, went a bit closer and saw many birds near that tree. Now our desire was complete and we took leave. It was quite an interesting weekend and I also learned some new bird names. They are – Paddyfield Pipit, Streak-throated Swallow and Common Indian Tree Frog. 2

BIRDS, BUTTERFLIES & AN INSTITUTE Report: National Institute of Tourism & Hospitality Management (NITHM), Hyderabad, July 3, 2021 Surekha Aitabathula Some views of NITHM (Stock photos courtesy: Yadagiri, NITHM) Corona Virus – first wave, then second wave and multiple lockdowns. All these had brought birding to a halt for Deccan Birders. In this scenario a call from Sri Chinnam Reddy, Director, National Institute of Tourism & Hospitality Management (NITHM), inviting Deccan Birders to do bird watching in their campus, was like manna from heaven. Due to the prevailing COVID conditions, and also since we wanted to initially just do a recce to assess the scope for a future Deccan Birders' regular monthly field trip, we did not take a big group. Rather, only seven of us reached NITHM on 3rd July – a fine Saturday morning. Common Coot (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) We saw Common Coots (Fulica atra) with fledglings, Indian Spot-billed Ducks (Anas poecilorhyncha), Little Grebes (Tachybaptus ruficollis) and a White-throated Kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis). The group in action (Photo: Yadagiri, NITHM) The 26-acre campus threw up 41 bird and 14 butterfly species. We spotted the first 25 species just about 100 metres into the main entrance gate. There was a small water body to the left of the entrance gate. Indian Spot-billed Duck (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Checking out a well in the campus (Photo: Yadagiri, NITHM) 5

Little Grebe (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Scaly-breasted Munia (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Also present were Green Bee-eater (Merops orientalis), Indian Silverbill (Euodice malabarica) and Purple-rumped Sunbird (Leptocoma zeylonica). A Shikra (Accipiter badius) gave a beautiful glimpse of itself when it flew out of and back into the vegetation in a sweeping arc. Green Bee-eater (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Large Grey Babbler (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) A little ahead of the water body is the Administrative Block. Here we saw Large Grey Babbler (Turdoides malcomi), Scalybreasted Munia (Lonchura punctulata), Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica) and Pale-billed Flowerpecker (Dicaeum erythrorhynchos). Purple-rumped Sunbird (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Pale-billed Flowerpecker (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Stinking Dapperling (Lepiota cristata) (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) 6

Purple Allamanda (Allamanda blanchetti) (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) Chinese Hibiscus aka China Rose (Hibiscus rosasinensis) (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) There were several interesting sites on the campus, such as the Sculpture Park and the Miyawaki Forest. The stepped pathway around the campus went up and down giving us some mild exercise of sorts. The campus was quiet and peaceful, a nice green lung in the middle of the hustle bustle of Gachibowli with lots of coconut trees lining it. We heard the harsh and grunting calls of Indian Peafowl (Pavo cristatus) and the melodious Common Iora (Aegithina tiphia) and the Asian Koel (Eudynamys scolopaceus) as though in a welcome chorus. One by one, the butterflies came out to dry their cool nightsoaked wings in the sun. These colourful and delicate creatures delighted us no end. We saw lots of Small Grass Yellows (Eurema brigitta) and Common Grass Yellows (Eurema hecabe), magnificent little bursts of bright yellow flitting from plant to plant, never seeming to rest. Common Grass Yellow (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Common Iora (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Pioneer (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Plain Tiger (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) We spotted several Pioneers (Belenois aurota) and Common Leopards (Phalanta phalantha). Psyche (Leptosia nina) was a happy sighting. So rapt was I in watching the butterflies that I fell down after catching my foot in a creeper bed. This fall offered some comic relief to my fellow birders! 7

NITHM was established in 2004. As Director Mr Chinnam Reddy and the Principal walked along with us, they informed us that NITHM offers BBA and MBA in Tourism and Hospitality and also BSc in Hospitality and Hotel Administration. A substantial number of foreign students from Africa and Southeast Asia come to study in NITHM. The Institute has hostel accommodation on campus and a cricket ground, an upcoming walking path and a five star hotel which would be up and about by December 2021. Common Leopard (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) We were taken on a tour of the Institute's training kitchens. There was a Bar & Restaurant used solely for the purpose of training. No consumption here! The posters in the restaurant were very interesting. The posters taught the students a lot of what there is to know about serving. Purple Sunbird in eclipse plumage (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Some posters at the training kitchen (Photo: Surekha Aitabathula) We do not realise when we go to a restaurant that a lot goes into the process of serving food and drinks. There is actually a method in glassware, flatware, steward's toolkit and napkin folds. I was happy to learn something new. When we sat down to the fabulous breakfast arranged for us by the Director, we laughed about how birding early in the morning, always revs up our appetite for breakfast. Mr Chinnam Reddy leading the walk (Photo: Yadagiri, NITHM) As we drove back I thought there are umpteen educational institutions in Telangana. If only each institution would strive to create some substantial green space within its campus, everyone could experience how good it feels to take in lungfuls of oxygen. 8

The team during the walk (Photos: Yadagiri, NITHM) Common Moorhen (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Laughing Dove (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) *** MY BIRDING DIARY - A glimpse of Keoladeo Ghana Bird Sanctuary Trip Report: Bharatpur, December 2016 Text & Photos: Dr Jayati Mitra Eurasian Marsh Harrier I was chugging along in a train in Rajasthan in the month of December 2016. I had just completed my work and it was time to return home but an idea held me back. I checked the route of the train and found that it passed through a station called Bharatpur. Immediately the picture of the famous wildlife sanctuary flashed through my mind and I decided to halt there for a short duration and visit this place. I pressed my cheek against the window pane to catch a glimpse of the outside scenery but could only sense the tiny droplets of condensed mist becoming more and more magnified, obscuring my view. Therefore, I remained focussed on the display board to see the name of the approaching station. Finally I stepped down from the train and looked around the small dilapidated station. Just three days were left for the New Year to arrive, and the intense cold weather had already gripped this small town. I made my way towards the exit, which was shrouded in a thick layer of fog. A few rickshaws were available outside and I boarded one to reach my temporary abode. 11

Keoladeo Ghana Bird Sanctuary was born out of a natural depression present at the confluence of rivers Gambhir and Banganga in Bharatpur. The area attracted a lot of birds and, around 1726, Suraj Mull, the Maharaja of this princely state, took advantage of the situation by creating an embankment – the Ajan Bund – in the south-west of the city, for sustenance of the area. This man- made water body lay along the West Asian flyway and attracted many migratory species of birds to the lake. Thus it became a regular, favourite spot for the hunting of ducks. Even though it had been declared a sanctuary in 1952, the shooting of wild birds continued for another twenty years till it was legally banned in 1972.The place was declared a world heritage site in 1985. Today, it encompasses an area of around 29 sq km. The park, surrounded by a two metre wide boundary wall, has faced droughts several times and, on the other hand, is also prone to seasonal flooding. In recent years, the Goverdhan drain, originating in Haryana, supplies water to the lake before it empties itself into the Yamuna. I had decided to stay in an area called Sarus Circle which was pretty close to the sanctuary. It was almost noon by now but the fog still had not lifted. I was tired and hungry after the journey and settled down for a while after enjoying a hearty meal. I waited patiently for the sun to come out and then walked down towards the main gate. It was almost 3:00PM. There were multiple options available to roam around inside the park – walking, bicycles, rickshaws and an electric vehicle. I purchased my ticket and opted to travel in a cycle rickshaw. The vehicles were labelled with conspicuous brass number plates and the owners waited patiently in a queue for their turn to arrive. We made our first halt at a very old dead tree stump where I sighted a Spotted Owlet (Athene brama) with half-closed eyes. I noticed the parched lowlands on both sides covered with dried grass, where about half a dozen Grey Francolins (Francolinus pondicerianus) were feeding. Grey Francolin Further inside was the boating area, where I watched two raptors, a Eurasian Griffon Vulture (Gyps fulvus) and a Black Kite (Milvus migrans) circling overhead. In the shrubs adjacent to the road, some sunbirds were hovering above the wildflowers in bloom. The vulture gradually rose higher in the sky and disappeared out of view. Once inside the gate we rode along a straight metalled road through the middle of the sanctuary. The road roughly divided it into two sections in the eastern and western directions. My rickshaw puller introduced himself and shared his knowledge of the birds of the park and about the training he had undergone to act as a guide. He also informed me that there was a leopard on the prowl in the sanctuary, and warning boards had been put at many places to caution visitors. Ferruginous Duck Northern Pintail Spotted Owlet 12

Common Teal We soon approached a densely wooded area with tall jamun trees lining both sides of the road, forming bowers. The dense foliage hardly allowed any light to filter through and it took a while for my eyes to get adjusted to the sudden darkness after coming from a brightly lit area. It was very damp and there were swamps on the eastern side. Here I observed a variety of water birds, namely – Indian Spot-billed Duck (Anas poecilorhyncha), Northern Pintail (Anas acuta), Common Teal (Anas crecca), Ferruginous Duck (Aythya nyroca), Common Pochard (Aythya ferina) and Knob-billed Ducks (Sarkidiornis melanotos). Common Woodshrike Bluethroat Spot-billed Duck & Knob-billed Duck On the opposite side of the road a different picture emerged. The huge trees growing side by side around a swamp had quite a few passerine species. I found a highly energetic and restless Grey-headed Canary Flycatcher (Culicicapa ceylonensis) diving frequently to the ground to catch insects, a Redbreasted Flycatcher (Ficedula parva) waiting for its turn to feed, a Bay-backed Shrike (Lanius vittatus) and several Common Woodshrikes (Tephrodornis pondicerianus). The light brown ones on the ground, moving among the rotten leaves, furtively searching for insects among the vegetation were the beautiful Bluethroats (Luscinia svecica). I saw four of them together and admired the dainty blue and orangebrown bands around their necks. Amidst all this action there was a Brown Fish Owl (Bubo zeylonensis) resting peacefully on top of a tree, face down in the canopy. It simply refused to turn around and I could only manage to observe the back plumage clearly. Suddenly my guide alerted me to a shrill call. They were the Sarus Cranes (Grus antigone) returning after feeding In the fields outside. We had to travel fast to catch a glimpse of the birds. We rushed forward in search of the cranes and reached a swamp called ‘Sapan Mori’. There was a path to the west and I had to trek along till the end and return to the rickshaw parked on the main road. The journey started again, and I saw a huge number of Purple Swamphens (Porphyrio porphyrio). There were swallows flying above the fields but no trace of the Sarus. The light started fading and I suddenly realised that there was no one else around me. I could see a faint apparition of a watch tower in the distance and was wondering what to do when a little bird came into my view. It was moving on the ground by my side and had a glossy black back and a reddish orange underbelly – a beautiful male Black Redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros). It was not shy at all and hopped along by my side. Red-breasted Flycatcher 13

A little later my guide pointed towards the distant fields on the eastern side. Through the slight haze I clearly saw the Sarus Cranes! I watched the graceful movements of these heavy birds in the golden morning light. As they unfolded the wings and raised their necks upwards and downwards by twisting them symmetrically together it looked like a scene from a ballet show. There were three of them present at the spot and it was so satisfying to get a glimpse of them together. I learnt that there were about six of them in the sanctuary and they left each day at dawn to feed in the distant fields, and returned only late in the evening. The other species of cranes, Common (Grus grus) and Demoiselle (Grus virgo) were irregular and had not yet arrived in this season at the site. The famous Siberian Crane, of course, had not come since 2002. Black Redstart Day two dawned slightly chilly and hazy. I had missed seeing the Sarus the previous evening and mentioned this to my new rickshaw puller-cum-guide. He took me straight to the densely wooded area and there was something interesting happening here. A flock of Bar-headed Geese (Anser indicus) were feeding along with some domestic animals that were allowed into the sanctuary to graze, and this seemed to be a regular affair. Golden Jackal Bar-headed Goose Yellow-footed Green Pigeon & Rose-ringed Parakeet By this time, the sun had moved higher up in the sky and lit up the surroundings. I could see a few Yellow-footed Green Pigeons (Treron phoenicoptera) and Rose-ringed Parakeets (Psittacula krameri) chattering on the topmost branches of the trees. Suddenly I spotted something different lying on a rock beside the road – a Monitor Lizard was basking in the sun, lying absolutely still while curious visitors looked on. Sarus Crane 14

Monitor Lizard I moved straight ahead and saw some Painted Storks with juveniles on the eastern side which was lined with trees. It seemed to have been their nesting area. The rows of trees slowly became fewer and far between and gave way to marshes which housed a number of cormorants and kingfishers. It was pleasant seeing them diving and catching fish at lightning speed. There were Eurasian Spoonbills (Platalea leucorodia) and egrets, as well, resting on the small hillocks interspersed amid the marshes. I moved straight towards a temple and had a surprise there. A huge flock of ducks shot up into the sky above the tree line, with heads tilted upwards and wings fully spread out like multiple arrows. It was a sight that made me gasp in wonder. The scene changed dramatically within seconds with the birds flapping their wings frantically trying to escape in different directions, finally disappearing out of sight altogether. The story became clear as I found a Greater Spotted Eagle (Clanga clanga) gliding towards them, probably out hunting. Indian Scops Owl Keoladeo Temple This was the end of the straight vehicular road and I could see a path on my left towards the east, for further trekking. I climbed up a watchtower in front and observed the surroundings. Greater Spotted Eagle White-cheeked Bulbul The narrow muddy trail leading towards this site was inaccessible to me. My guide drew my attention towards some palm trees in the distance. There was an Indian Scops Owl (Otus bakkamoena) with a young one hidden amongst the fronds. I had almost reached the Keoladeo temple which is dedicated to Lord Shiva and from which the name of the park had originated. There were Red-vented (Pycnonotus cafer) and Whitecheeked Bulbuls (Pycnonotus leucotis) flying around and a few different species of warblers. I spotted a Eurasian Hoopoe (Upupa epops) and a few more Bluethroats on my journey along the path. 15

species. I spotted a Nilgai on the way and admired its sleek body and antlers. I strolled along the path to my left beside the forest bungalow and crossed some residential houses. I could hear the screeching of Indian Grey Hornbills (Ocyceros birostris) and the rhythmic calls of Brown-headed Barbets (Megalaima zeylanica). I finally found them hidden among the foliage of the huge trees. The row of buildings finally ended and the path curved towards the right. Eurasian Hoopoe Black-necked Stork Lesser Whistling-duck Here I made another noteworthy sighting of the trip. There were two Black-necked Storks (Ephippiorhynchus asiaticus) standing still and resting. I waited patiently expecting some action but they remained motionless, like statues. I walked ahead a little and found many Red-crested Pochards (Netta rufina), Northern Shovelers (Spatula clypeata), Gadwalls (Mareca strepera) and Bar-headed Geese in the water. The surrounding area was a muddy swamp which housed more than a hundred Lesser Whistling-ducks (Dendrocygna javanica). I did spot a few sandpipers and lapwings in the shallow water, most of them being Wood Sandpipers (Tringa glareola). Gadwall, Red-crested Pochard, Northern Pintail & Eurasian Spoonbill Red-wattled Lapwing As I watched a group of Ashy Prinias (Prinia socialis), I suddenly caught sight of a Booted Eagle (Hieraaetus pennatus) in flight. It perched atop a tree but my movement was again restricted by yet another yellow warning sign board. I returned to the temple, walked a little ahead and watched the vast water body in front of me. It had a few Great White Pelicans (Pelecanus onocrotalus), but they were very far off and barely visible even through binoculars. Northern Shoveler & Common Coot I turned back along the same path and made one final attempt to explore some other areas in the hope of finding some more 16

It was late afternoon and time for me to leave. I did feel a little disappointed at not being able to move around freely in the park due to the leopard menace but overall it was still a great trip to remember for a long time. Common Kingfisher A Marsh Harrier (Circus aeruginosus) was hunting above the water surface and so was a Common Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis). Unfortunately I could not move any further because another warning sign blocked my way. A local guide present there told me that there were Greylag Geese (Anser anser) present in that area but I had to reluctantly return without seeing them. I walked back to the rickshaw. My journey was almost over but there was a little bit of excitement waiting for me towards the end. A group with huge cameras was trying to focus on something a few metres ahead. I stepped down and was delighted to find a Black Bittern surrounded by layers of thick reeds on all sides .It was there for quite a long time giving me ample time to view it closely. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Sociable Lapwing (Vanellus gregarius) Sociable Lapwing breeding (L) and non-breeding (R) (Nalsarovar, Gujarat, February 05, 2020) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Charadriidae Genus: Vanellus Species: V. gregarius Size: 27-30 cm scalloped back with prominent buff fringes and dark subterminal crescents to its scapulars and coverts. Habitat & behaviour: The Sociable Lapwing is usually seen in small to medium flocks, in scrub country, dry wastelands, temperate deserts, steppe, and in ploughed, stubble and dry fallow fields, as well as cultivated fields, rural gardens, grassland or other arable land. It forages by walking or running in short bursts, stopping abruptly and probing for prey with its body tilted forward. It also vibrates its foot rapidly on the surface, to flush out invertebrates. Its diet consists primarily of insects, caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers, cicadas, spiders, scorpions, and crickets. It may also feed on grains, seeds, leaves and flowers. Its flight is slower than the flight shown by other Lapwings, with steady but slow wing-beats. Its call is a rapid chattering sound or a harsh kretsch or kereck.. Description & distribution: The Sociable Lapwing, also known as the Sociable Plover, is a critically endangered wader from the lapwing family. It breeds in Russia and Kazakhstan, and winter in parts of Central Asia, northern Africa and northern and western India; it is also occasionally seen in parts of the Middle East (Oman, UAE, Saudi Arabia), Pakistan and Sri Lanka. They are known to show wintering site fidelity. It has relatively long, black legs and a short black bill. In breeding plumage, it shows a striking pattern on the head, with a black crown, thin blackish-brown lores and irises, pronounced white supercilia joining at the forehead and nape, olive brown upperparts, grey throat and breast, black belly and white undertail. The breeding male has a yellowish wash on the sides of the face, and a maroon-red belly patch. It is unmistakable in flight, with its long black legs, white undertail with a black terminal band, and white secondaries contrasting with black primaries and sandy-brown upperwing coverts. Non-breeding and juvenile birds show a less distinct head pattern, white belly and browner back and breast, the latter also showing streaks. Additionally, the juvenile has a Nesting: The Sociable Lapwing breeds generally between April and July in their breeding range. They are monogamous and breed in small colonies. The nest is a shallow scrape on the ground, usually near water on saline plains or on short vegetation, and may be bare or lined with twigs, grass and pebbles. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 pale buff oval eggs with dark olive-brown mottling. Incubation duties are shared by the parents. Local name: The Sociable Lapwing is known as ‘Sangachari tithari’ in Hindi, ‘Maltavdi titodi’ in Gujarati and ‘Hot-ti-ti’ in Bengali. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. MY QUEST FOR THE HONEYGUIDE Report: Chopta, Uttarakhand, April 2021 Text & Photos: Col SS Cheema (Retd) Yellow-rumped Honeyguide Honeyguides are interesting birds and there are a number of them – ten, to be precise – in the genus Indicator. Eight of them found in Africa and two in Asia, of which one species is seen in India. I had been chasing the Indian species, the Yellow-rumped Honeyguide, for quite some time. I will get on to it after telling this story to start with. So I wanted to see this bird – like all other birds of the world, I must add! – and had set my mind on it. Every time I visited the Himalayas, I was on a constant lookout – I was waiting for an encounter in Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and, of course, on my last visit to Uttarakhand. Well, to be fair, I had also been looking out for the Honeyguide during my visit to Borneo, although that was the other Honeyguide of Asia – the Malaysian Honeyguide. 1

But of course, being on a lookout and actually seeing the bird are like the sip and the lip – both close, but it will be when it will be. My visits to Sikkim, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and even Borneo were a washout, and this happened over a period of more than 5 years. As luck would have it, just about 200m ahead, there was a flutter in a tree nearby and both the guide and I let out a shout simultaneously – Honeyguide! I was shaking with excitement and moving my feet barely a few inches at a time to ensure the bird did not fly away. The bird was still not clearly visible, even though we were hearing it and catching the glimpses of it in that tree. I first got one clear shot, and then the bird decided to show more confidence in me. Then came the last birding trip to Chopta in Uttarakhand, squeezed in between the first two Covid lockdowns – and I still had this bird as a target species, along with a dozen others. Our bird guide was absolutely certain that we would see the bird, but in heart of hearts, I was not so sure. The past failures were weighing heavy on my mind, to say the least. It perched on to a branch an arm’s length away, and was not at all afraid. My heart jumping with joy, I called out to the rest of the team. The bird did not mind my shout at all; they all came rushing over, and the bird was still there, singing in front of all of us. What a day it turned out to be! Finally the day arrived, and we walked upstream from the road on the first day at Chopta, to the place where we were to see the bird for sure – like a 100% sure – or so our guide had said! Well, we waited, scanned the area for any signs at all of the birds – but excepting the huge beehives humming with bees in the far distance on a ledge, there was nothing. There were other birds, and pretty ones too – but a sighting of the Honeyguide was not to be. We waited and scanned the nearby areas for over an hour. But since our destination was still a few hours away, we had no choice but to cut short the chase and, after a small Maggi lunch, we moved on. The disappointment on my face was quite obvious. A few hours down the road, we stopped again at a place with a cliff in the distance, and the guide told us that we might be lucky here, as the Honeyguide was seen at this place also sometimes. Having missed the bird at a place where it was ‘100% sure’, now hoping to see it at a place where it was sighted ‘sometimes’ – I was really not very hopeful. Anyway, we stopped at the stream, and all the group members started looking out for some beautiful birds around the stream. Yellow-rumped Honeyguide The scientific name of the Yellow-rumped Honeyguide is Indicator xanthonotus. The first part of the name, Indicator, means exactly what it does in English – to indicate. The second part, xanthonotus, can be broken into two parts – xanthous, meaning yellow, and ~nōtos, meaning ‘backed’. This basically adds up to an indicator bird that has a yellow back – so now we can correlate with the common name, the Yellow-rumped Honeyguide. I asked our guide if we could walk along the road to the spot near the beehives, about half a kilometre away. Since the others did not respond enthusiastically, the guide and I decided to move ahead. The story of the bird is an interesting one and it goes something like this. This bird is known for leading mammals and humans to the bees’ hives, enabling the stronger mammal to break open the hive/nest and benefit from the honey, whilst the Honeyguide eats the grubs, bees and the wax. A local (African) superstition demands that some of the honey be left for the Honeyguide, otherwise next time it would lead the searcher towards a hidden snake or leopard! Well, search the Internet and you will find many such videos, but most of them are not proven or verified. All the same, the folklore lives on. And this is the reason birding is my passion – every bird has a story and every story has a bird! Yellow-rumped Honeyguide *** 2

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Greylag Goose (Anser anser) Greylag Goose (Little Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, February 03, 2019) Order: Anseriformes Family: Anatidae Genus: Anser Species: A. anser Size: 75-90 cm North America gets occasional vagrants, and Australia and New Zealand both have small, established feral populations. Habitat & behaviour: In their wintering ranges, the Greylag Goose is gregarious and is usually seen in large flocks, in jheels, rivers and lake sides, as well as cultivated fields, grassland or other arable land. It usually rests during the day and feeds at night in the agricultural fields and wet meadows. Its diet consists primarily of vegetable matter, grass, winter crops like rice, beans or cereals, aquatic weeds and tubers, but they do also consume small fish, amphibians, crustaceans, molluscs and insects. Its call is a loud, cackling ahngg ung ung, uttered on ground or in flight, and sometimes a conversational gay gay gay while feeding. Interestingly, there are subtle variations in the calls used in different situations, and individual geese seem to be able to identify other known geese by their voices. Goslings utter chirps or light whistles, while adults may also hiss if threatened or angry. Description & distribution: The Greylag Goose is the type species of the genus Anser, and the largest Goose species seen in India. It has a rotund, bulky body, with mottled grey and white underparts with some variable black spotting, barred brownish grey and white upperparts with a white line bordering its flanks, and a grey rump and white vent. The neck is long and thick, with prominent ‘concertina-ed’ folds in the neck feathers, and the grey head is unmarked. The eyes are black with a yellow eye-ring. The fleshy-pink bill is stout and has a white ‘nail’, which is distinctive. Legs and feet are pink. Wing coverts are light, contrasting with darker flight feathers, and it shows a pale grey forewing in flight. The juvenile is similar to the adult but with less prominent pale fringes to upperparts, flanks and belly. Nesting: The Greylag Goose generally breeds generally between April and June in its breeding range. It forms longterm (mostly life-long) monogamous pair bonds. The nest is built on the ground among heather, rushes, small shrubs or reeds, and is built using pieces of reeds, twigs, grass, moss and heather. The usual clutch consists of 4-6 eggs, initially creamy white but soon turning a stained buff or off-white. Incubation duties are handled by the female, with the male standing guard nearby, but both parents are involved in feeding and care after the birds are hatched. Two subspecies are recognized: A. anser anser, the western Greylag Goose, which breeds in Iceland and northern and central Europe, and A. a. rubrirostris, the eastern Greylag Goose, which breeds in Romania, Turkey and Russia east to northeastern China. Some authorities also recognize a domesticated subspecies, A. a. domesticus. The subspecies are known to intergrade in areas where their ranges overlap. Males are larger, and this sexual dimorphism is more prominent in the eastern subspecies. Local name: The Greylag Goose is known as ‘Hans’, ‘Raj hans’, ‘Sona’ or ‘Karria sona’ in Hindi, ‘Raj hans’ in Bengali and Gujarati, ‘Tella pedda batu’ in Telugu, ‘Kurith-thalayan’ in Malayalam and ‘Neer vathu’ or ‘Vari kazhutha thara’ in Tamil. The Greylag Goose breeds across the entire Palearctic region, including Europe and northern Asia. European populations winter in northern Africa and the Mediterranean region, while the Asian populations migrate to Azerbaijan, Iran, Pakistan, northern and central India, Bangladesh and east to China. *** 3

BIRDING AT THE BARRAGE Trip Report: Manjeera Wildlife Sanctuary, August 1, 2021 Dr Jairamchander Pingle Baya Weaver (Photo: Pingle Janardhan Reddy) On one of my Sunday birding trips I met Rajiv, a fellow birder, who mentioned that one of the good birding spots now is the Manjeera Barrage, and that there was a possibility of seeing the Mottled Wood Owl. So I asked my cousins Vikram Dev Rao and Janardhan Reddy to join, and we went to Manjeera on August 01, 2021. We reached a birding spot on a bund there, and coincidentally we met Rajiv also there, which made it easier for us. Pheasant-tailed Jacana (Photo: Pingle Janardhan Reddy) Grey-headed Swamphen (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) Red Avadavat (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) Tricoloured Munia (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) We were lucky to see the Tricoloured Munias and the Red Munia also. While walking on the bund, we saw several Pheasant-tailed Jacanas. In particular, one bird was sitting quite close to the bund and, when we drew near, it moved away a short distance and stayed in the water close by. We were told that it had been nesting there, and that a floating nest had been seen close to the reeds near the bank of the bund the week before. 4

To our pleasant surprise, though with great difficulty, we were able to spot the nest with three eggs through the reeds. We did not approach closer, as it would be wrong to disturb them, so I took a few photographs with a long lens and quickly moved away. We continued with the rest of the trip, looking for the Mottled Wood Owl near the disused area of the water treatment plant. Unfortunately, we could not find it, but were lucky to see a Spotted Owlet in one of the trees. Pheasant-tailed Jacana with chicks (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) When the sun came out, the mother Jacana moved into a clearer area of the lake and kept calling, and finally the chicks moved out a little in the open. I was fortunate to photograph and videograph them along with the constant calling of the mother Jacana. Spotted Owlet (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) On reading up a little, I found that interestingly, the male Jacana sometimes carries the chicks under its wings and their long toes hanging down outside may be the only part visible. And happily for me, when I went back and checked my photos, I found that I had actually got a photograph where this phenomenon could be seen! Baya Weaver & Zitting Cisticola (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) Anyway, I decided to go back the next week – on Sunday, August 8, 2021 – to see if the eggs had hatched. The mother Pheasant-tailed Jacana was still there; this time, she did the same thing, that is, flying a short distance away from the reeds, but this time she was constantly calling out. We felt that most likely she was calling out to the chicks, and I was pleasantly surprised to see two little newborn chicks moving around near the reeds. It was difficult to photograph them due to the presence of the reeds, so I kept my distance, sat on the portable stool and patiently waited. Pheasant-tailed Jacana with chicks under its wings (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) I felt very lucky that I could make a follow-up visit to see the chicks. I hope they are doing well now.
