Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 18 Number 9 September 2021 MY TRYST WITH BIRDWATCHING Lt Cdr Antriksh Duggal Bluethroat (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) My tryst with bird watching began when I got transferred to Hyderabad from Mumbai about three years ago. I obtained accommodation at the Naval Officers’ Mess in the DRDO Township in Kanchanbagh. Being already a lover of nature, I was delighted to find that the Township had an abundant cover of wooded areas with some parts tending to be untouched forests. If one were to behold before one’s eyes a swath of the Township as a sample, one would see a view of a pied parity between concrete and natural jungle. The mottled melding of manmade structures and foliage seemed as an interlocked mosaic of marble. It was in an environment such as this, also, where time seemed to sleepily pass by, that I took my first steps in the field of birding. It started off with my little avian friends, which earlier would just be little specks flying by or bobbing about on a branch, now beginning to appear conspicuously in my sight. It was as though a new awareness had descended upon me that enabled me to take better note of my feathery friends. The reasons for this new awareness could be attributed, I dare say, to the luxury of more time in hand, which I earlier did not have, and an enhancement in patience. Nonetheless, the torch was lit and the shimmery sunlight began to shine upon the emerging branches of my freshly germinated hobby. Asian Paradise-flycatcher (Photo: Lt Cdr Antriksh Duggal) As the plant of my newfound interest grew and the skill of observation burgeoned, I was able to discern colours and plumage patterns, disparate shapes and sizes, calls and cries. Each new point of observation was an enhancement akin to a brick being laid upon a new wall being built. 1

I purchased a field guide to help me identify species. My list of successful identifications of species was like a new personal collection. Every augmentation in the list made me swell with pride and afforded a sense of satisfaction, while, also, leaving a thirst for more in its wake. Each new species identified was a ‘lifer’ and made me wonder how much more there was to see and record and enjoy. With the theatre of my balcony and immediate environs of the Mess as my playing field, I had donned the cap of a ‘backyard birder.’ jungle or lakeside or montane valley, where I would have invariably gone birding (perchance with the Deccan Birders). My initial implements consisted of the aforementioned guide, a notebook and a pair of naked eyes. With straining eyes I would try edging in as close to a bird as I could in order to observe it; only, to my chagrin, to find the little thing fly away before I could get much idea of its identity. With varying degrees of success in observation based on my stealth, I dragged my way forward within the shackles of my impediment. A pall of frustration found a seat in my heart, making me feel that I was doing things in a woefully wrong way. I was trying to pierce the darkness with a candle where an omnidirectional torch light was essential. Little did I know then that, to emerge from this pall, I would be steered by fate toward the Deccan Birders. Painted Francolin (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Since that cardinal day, I have been on numerous birding trips with various members of the club, and had many varied experiences, from the soothing hum of lapping waves at Gandipet Lake and Ameenpur Lake to the rich verdure of the Ananthagiri Hills, Damagundam Forest and Manjeera Wildlife Sanctuary. Stalking the spoor of the Indian Pitta in the undergrowth, patrolling the woods for the Eurasian Wryneck, anticipating the arrival of the Bluethroat alongside fields on village roads, trying to catch some time to observe the constantly flitting Tricoloured Munias, meditating over the magnitude of the Painted Stork colonies, earnestly following its cackling call to get a sight of Painted Francolin, scanning the grasses to spot the Rain Quail, jumping excitedly on sighting a bird of prey, trying to track the elusive Forest Wagtail – these are just a few of the experiences I’ve had hitherto. I wish, with alacrity, to add to the foregoing corpus of my experiences under the able fold of this esteemed club. The members of the club are like mentors to me in the field from whom I wish to learn greatly through my future association. I had finally decided to buy a pair of binoculars. After an initial technical study and survey I had homed on to a model and a place from where to buy it. The vendor who sold me the binoculars also mentioned to me in passing about a ‘Mr Lawrence’ who was a birder and gave me his number. Tricoloured Munia (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) At this juncture I would like to bring to one’s consideration the nature of fate or destiny, if one wishes to so call it. What is it that made that gentleman mention to me what he did? What made me zero in on this particular vendor? What if I had approached another vendor who would have merely minded his own beeswax? Would I never have gotten to find out about the Deccan Birders or would I have stumbled upon them, nonetheless, but at a later date? Rain Quail (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Alas! While I write this, I am under transfer to New Delhi. My frequent interaction with the club will reduce, but certainly not wither away. For personnel in the defence, transfers become commonplace and are a part and parcel of life. I have become a member of the club and hence my future association will remain. It is a bittersweet time and I am also excited to see what avenues unfold before me at my next station in the field of birding. The skills that I’ve learnt and the knowledge that I’ve gained have become part of my quiver, which I shall put to use in future pastures of birding. What started off as a tryst has transformed into a passion that will last lifelong. I do not have answers to these questions, but I do believe that one can, to a certain extent, shape one’s destiny and alter one’s fate by grasping opportunities or taking risks/chances through informed thought and action. It does not do my article well to dwell too much upon this subject and I also do not wish to digress. However, I would like to add that I wish to muse over the nature of such things at length in the solitudes of some *** 2

BIRDING IN BOUNTIFUL BHUTAN Trip Report: Bhutan, August 2017 Text and Photos: N Shiva Kumar A view of snow-clad mountains at Bhutan Like a giant metallic bird, the Drukair airliner deftly negotiated the ring of mountains to land at a small airport, albeit with remarkable surroundings. I was at Paro in Bhutan; a tiny aerodrome nestled among the mighty Himalayas and reckoned to be one of the most hazardous in the world. Paro airfield in Bhutan is 7300 feet above sea level and surrounded by sharp peaks of up to 18,000 feet high. So challenging is the landing that only about two dozen pilots in the world are said to be qualified to navigate on to the tarmac. The manual bydaylight-only approach through a winding valley and onto a runway that is only about 7500 feet long is complicated. For the passengers, though, the views are breathtakingly beautiful from the aircraft and windows seats are at a premium. regions, and a number of Important Plant Areas and wetlands. The biodiversity and ecologically floristic zones have made Bhutan home to a wide array of wildlife; hence Bhutan is regarded as one of the world’s major biodiversity hotspots. Biodiversity is measured at different levels of biological niches together with genus, species and ecosystems along with their interactions. The Bhutan constitution demands that a minimum of 60% of the land must remain forested for all future generations; this currently stands at over 72%. It is the world’s only carbon-negative country and its forests absorb more carbon dioxide per year than pollutants emitted. The small runway is snug as a bug in a rug in the middle of a pristine forest-clad valley. Strangely it was once a football field, converted to a petite international airport in 1968 by the Indian Army, initially for helicopters and later upgraded in stages to accommodate bigger aircraft. Even before I arrived in the Land of the Thunder Dragon, there were awesome views of Himalayas with sparkling snowcovered peaks. And as I stepped out of the airplane, I was welcomed by the wonderful whiff of crisp air laden with loads of oxygen. Coming in from New Delhi, one of the most polluted cities in the world, the air of Bhutan was like a breath of fresh air. The blaze of balmy sunshine from the azure sky combined with the mountain views was indeed invigorating. Bhutan ranks in the top ten countries with the highest wildlife density on earth, and it also has the highest acreage of land under Protected Areas (PA) as well as the highest percentage of forest cover of any Asian nation. Bhutan has twenty-three Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs), eight eco-Lesser Adjutant 3

My Mission Bhutan was to take cognizance of the flora and fauna in the landlocked Himalayan country having vast swathes of forested land. The tour director, Mincha Wangdi, a qualified environmentalist, was forewarned about my specific needs and he designed the itinerary to include not only the flora and fauna but associated cultural aspects of nature. Noting my profound interest, he personally escorted me on a whirlwind seven-day tour of Bhutan searching for elusive birds and animals, and also showcased the iconic sights and sounds of Paro, Chele La, Thimphu, Pele La, Dochula and Punakha. Ibisbill Right after the delightful Dippers, we spotted a rarity, the Ibisbill, at another junction of Paro Chu. The Ibisbill is related to the waders, but adequately distinctive to merit its own family categorisation called Ibidorhynchidae. The Ibisbill looks like a combination of two different birds, sporting as it does the bill of the much more common Ibises. Hidden in the shingles of the river, well camouflaged and resembling a pebble, it was tricky to locate the bird. At sunset, the Ibisbill started to stir after a midday breather, searching for food in the mineral-rich waters, and I went trigger-happy taking pictures before the daylight dimmed. River Paro Chu Almost immediately after we started – just four kilometres from the airport – we stopped at the Paro Chu River to watch the Brown Dipper. These birds, as the name suggests, dunk their heads into the fast-flowing waters to feed. Dippers are small chunky birds, constantly on the move with a characteristic bobbing movement as they perch on boulders abutting the running waters. They were encountered many times during the seven day trip, all along the rivers flowing into Bhutan. Like a harbinger, the Dippers would always be the first to show up, and constantly put up a show and regaled us with their dip-feeding and melodious calls. The next morning at 4:30AM, we ventured into the darkness in pursuit of more elusive birds. Driving uphill in the biting cold weather to Chele La pass, the Bondey-Haa Highway was pretty steep, with numerous twists and turns. Our morning sojourn was specifically to look for pheasants, which are stocky but spectacular ground birds. From a lower altitude of 7200 feet at Paro, we travelled towards Bhutan’s highest motorable road. After a two-hour drive on winding roads covering a distance of just 50km, we reached Chele La pass at an elevation of nearly 14,000 feet by 6:30AM. At the crack of dawn, warm sunshine lit up the valley and we saw a Blood Pheasant saunter on the roadside. A little later, driving another five kilometres on curvaceous roads we espied some Himalayan Monals that swiftly disappeared into the jungles. However the beautiful Satyr Tragopan did not show up, and I was left with a bittersweet feeling. At the top of the Chele La pass, we stopped for a blissful picnic breakfast under the azure sky, devoured our refreshments and washed it down with piping hot coffee. A mob of Red-billed Choughs flew in to check us out and then disappeared behind the high hills. The short break energised me to continue the journey eastwards towards Haa Valley. Before we could reach the rim, a couple of Black Eagles appeared in the sky and wheeled in circles giving views of their flight patterns. Another raptor was sighted plonked on a tower and troubled us with its identity for a while. After sustained scrutiny it was deciphered as a White-eyed Buzzard with ruffled feathers, hence looking larger than usual. Brown Dipper 4

Black-tailed Crake White-winged Grosbeak A nearby flutter of wings indicated some White-winged Grosbeaks on the treetops that were dispersed by the grunts of feral horses grazing on the hillside. As we reached the rim of the Haa Valley, a flock of Snow Pigeons made their presence felt with loud wing beats. Bhutan is packed with mountainous landscapes which are interconnected by several passes, and many of these valleys are well-known for trekking. Between April and June, one can enjoy pleasant weather along with blooming Rhododendron sprawled across the vibrant landscape of the valleys. It is the perfect time for picnicking and camping along with friends and family. From October to March, this area experiences winters and the spectacular views of the snow-capped towering mountains can be mesmerising. A view of the forest-covered mountains I had originally planned the trip for October to encounter nature at its maximum but fortunately, though this was August, saw a fleeting glimpse of a bulky Black Bear. We returned to Paro for lunch and proceeded to the National Museum of Bhutan, which is perched on a high point and offers fabulous views of the Paro Valley. At a distance, a group of Ravens rejoiced in their mid-air pranks. We also saw several other usual species. The rest of the day was spent in relishing the relics and artefacts at the National Museum. On Day-3, an early photo-hunting session led us to another uncommon bird, the Black-tailed Crake, at a site quite close to our hotel. At the lush swamp, a single Crake peeped in and out briefly but quickly concealed itself in the marshes skirted by reed beds. This Crake, because of its skulking habits, is infrequently recorded in its range and the global population has not been properly estimated. The riverside marsh also had noisy River Lapwings, White-capped Redstart, Pied Kingfishers and more Dippers enjoying the gentle morning sun. Stray specimens of Sandpiper also drifted on the riverbank picking up morsels and, further afield, a big group of Snow Pigeons took off towards the iconic Tiger Hill, as if in salutation. The next day, leaving Paro, we travelled towards Thimphu, the capital of Bhutan, located 70km away in a valley with impressive modern and traditional buildings jostling for space. Later, getting away from the capital environs, we were on the lookout for the mysterious White-bellied Heron, a Critically Endangered species that occurs alongside rivers. Driving along the Pho Chhu River for many kilometres, we finally came to a known site of this rare bird. After four hours of waiting and watching, at the bifurcation of the river, we finally sighted the White-bellied Heron (WBH) hunting for fish. We were ecstatic and eagerly got out of our minivan to inspect the bird, but the commotion alerted the bird and it took off into dense vegetation! Recently the 19th WBH annual count was conducted for five days in March 2021, using a hi-tech digital data collection platform. The survey established twenty-two Herons, which is five less than the previous year, and their status has become more precarious. “Habitat disturbances and degradation are seen as the main causes for its population decline,” says Wangdi. On Day-5 morning, we again went searching for the Whitebellied Heron along the Pho Chhu River, but five hours of exploration did not yield any results. En route, the countryside showed up a group of Buntings, Sparrows and other passerines playing hide-and-seek among the reeds. A flock of Finches and some Drongos on the wing were joined by assorted Babblers, Doves, Sunbirds and Black Bulbuls with their melodious tweets. 5

Yellow-rumped Honeyguide Rufous-vented Yuhina Our morning disappointment turned to delight as we explored the Royal Botanical Park at Lampelri, which forms a biological corridor spread over 120 sq km between two National Parks. Here we sighted the National Animal of Bhutan, the Takin, a strange goat-antelope combination which is deeply ensconced in local mythology. The reason for selecting the Takin as the National Animal is based on a legend, which goes thus: when a prominent Lama, known as Divine Madman, visited Bhutan in the 15th century, devotees gathered to witness his magical powers and urged the monk to perform a miracle. He, in unorthodox methodology, demanded that he first be served a whole cow and a goat for lunch. He devoured these with relish, then took the goat's head and stuck it onto the skeleton of the cow. Then with a snap of his fingers he commanded the strange beast to come to life. To everybody’s astonishment the new animal did come alive and, to this day, these beasts can be seen grazing on the mountain sides of Bhutan. The day ended with us exploring a few trekking trails in the park, where we encountered an assemblage containing a Brown Parrotbill, a couple of Hornbills, a Yellow-rumped Honeyguide, a Red-billed Leiothrix, a Fire-tailed Myzornis etc. The park had lived up to its reputation as a preferred bird observation junction! Rhododendron in bloom There was also a variety of Rhododendrons in bloom in many shades of red and orange in the sprawling park. As we were about to leave the location, the pièce de résistance of the day was the very adorable Red Panda sauntering on the treetops in a playful mood; again, unfortunately dwindling in numbers across the globe due to loss of habitat. Takin The Takin continues to befuddle taxonomists, and the famous biologist George Schaller once called it a 'bee-stung moose'. However, these animals are on the decline and need effective conservation strategies for survival. Red Panda 6

Day-6 was the most fruitful due to the sheer number of birds seen, along with fabulous views of the snow-covered mountains at Dochula Pass, located at an elevation of 10,170 feet. Our travel guru, Wangdi, had wisely chosen a hotel perched on an elevation that offered fantastic views of snowy mountains changing colours from a range of pink to orange as the sun moved from east to west. At Dochula Pass, we observed quite a few species: White-throated Laughingthrush, Scarlet Finch, Black-naped Oriole, Scarlet Minivets, Bhutan Laughingthrush, Small Niltava, Spotted Laughingthrush, Spotted Nutcracker and a whole lot of other winged wonders. the successful trip, I made a list of almost 80 birds in 7 days. This may not sound like much when compared to the 770 species that have been recorded for Bhutan – but, given the difficult terrain and conditions, and particular preferences of many of the species, I think we may not even have got these many if not for the expertise of Wangdi. Pine trees with cones Each year Bhutan's bird list grows longer because of Bhutan's varied biodiversity and increasing systematic birding that is happening in the kingdom. That night, I pondered about Bhutan, where GDP is ignored and Gross National Happiness (GNH) is measured as a quotient. To imbibe that GNHpleasure into me as a twitcher and trigger-happy lensman, I hope to take up a more extensive cross-country romance with Bhutan in the near future and also meet the revered and rare Black-necked Cranes. Rufous Sibia Blue-fronted Redstart female Since crisscrossing the mountainous terrain and negotiating the hills and dales takes up a lot of time, by the end of the seventh day, we had covered about 800km in our search for wildlife, flora and boisterous birds in Bhutan. Trip Report: The Earth Center, Anmaspally, Hyderabad, July 14, 2021 Text: Surekha Aitabathula; Photos: Dr G Samuel Sukumar The team at The Earth Center Accepting the invitation of Mr K Laxma Reddy and Mrs K Leela Reddy, who run the Earth Centre, we headed out one fine July Wednesday morning to Anmaspally Village in Kadthal Mandal, Ranga Reddy District. Located approximately 60km from Hyderabad, the Earth Centre is an institution that promotes earth leadership and sustainable development. This Centre, in turn, has been developed by Council for Green Revolution (CGR) – an environmental organisation that works for the protection of the environment and focuses especially on the restoration of damaged ecosystems. Inaugurated in April 2021, the Earth Centre aims to become a premier environmental education centre to bring about a positive change. The Centre envisions promoting it as an independent think tank and a research centre that will strive towards realization of Sustainable Development Goals as set up by the United Nations. Laughing Dove Everyone in the group also attempted to raise their learning curve about tree/plant identification. Terminalia chebula Ficus bengalensis We took a beaten track amidst the verdant surroundings of the Earth Centre and found 32 bird and 10 butterfly species. 9

Large Grey Babbler White Orange Tip There were also some interesting moths around. Indian Silverbill It was a cloudy day, and the butterflies hadn’t yet come out to dry their wings even after 09:00AM; however, when the sun peeped out a little later, we were treated to the usual suspects like Tawny Coster, Common Crow and Common Jezebel, as well as some not-so-common ones like the Hedge Blue and White Orange Tip. Eupterote sp Eupterote citrina All in all, a very pleasant weekday morning outing is what we were presented with at the Anmaspally Earth Centre. Hedge Blue 10

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Kentish Plover (Charadrius alexandrinus) Kentish Plover (Chennai, February 03, 2019) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Charadriidae Genus: Charadrius Species: C. alexandrinus Size: 15-17 cm Description & distribution: The Kentish Plover is a small and stocky wader of the family Charadriidae. It is regarded as sexually dimorphic: both male and female birds have a generally pale plumage, with white underparts, grey-brown upperparts, blackish legs and a short, dark bill, but during breeding, the males additionally display a distinct dark, broken breast band, and dark ear coverts. The white forehead extends as a distinct supercilium, and a clear white hind collar is present. In breeding plumage, the male has a broad black horizontal band on the head and a brighter rufous nape and crown (absent in the South Indian race, C. a. seebohmi). In flight, it shows a narrow white wing-bar and prominent white sides to the tail, which are diagnostic. Males have longer tarsi and longer flank feathers, which are believed to provide an advantage during incubation and brood care. The breeding ornaments of the male are more prominent early in the breeding season. Besides, they show a correlation to rainfall: the breeding ornaments become brighter later in the season in areas with higher rainfall, and lighter in areas with less rainfall. Two subspecies are recognized: the nominate race, C. alexandrinus, which breeds in Pakistan and is a winter visitor to the Indian coastal regions and the Nicobar Islands, and the South Indian race, C. a. seebohmi, also seen in Sri Lanka. The Kentish Plover has a wide distribution, with populations in Northern Africa, parts of Central Asia and Europe. It is a rare vagrant in Australia. While most populations are resident, some populations migrate to Africa in winter. Recently, in 2020, the southern race has been proposed to be split and renamed as Hanuman Plover, named thus after the chain of islands in the Palk Straits, which are said to have been created by the Hindu god, Lord Hanuman. Habitat & behaviour: The Kentish Plover breeds on the shores of saline lakes, wetlands, salt marshes, lagoons, coastal sand dunes, tundra and semi-arid desert. Males are territorial and defend their territories actively by chasing, fighting or posturing. When approached by a predator, the parents try to protect their young by running away, calling, crawling on the ground while flapping their wings, or through a broken-wing display. The chicks too try to find a spot where they can hide by crouching down and remaining motionless. When moving away from the nest for any reason, the parents tend to cover the eggs with nesting material, to keep the eggs insulated as well as to protect them from predators. During non-breeding season, the Kentish Plover is usually seen to forage individually, or in small, loose flocks of 20-30. Occasionally, though, they may merge with and form a flock of 250 or more individuals of different species. It is a visual forager, feeding by looking, running or stopping, catching its prey by pecking, probing the sand with their bills, or even by holding their mouths open to catch flies. Its diet consists primarily of small aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates, like insects and their larvae (for instance, beetles, grasshoppers or flies), mollusks, crustaceans, spiders and marine worms. Its usual call is a short, soft pit or doubled pidup, sometimes combined with short trills or a plaintive wheet. The alarm call is a kittup, which may be paired with a sharp too eet. Nesting: The Kentish Plover is a solitary or semi-colonial nester. It generally breeds between March and August – May and June in Gujarat, and April to August in South India. It can be monogamous or polygamous – breeding pair fidelity in subsequent seasons has been noted, but mate changes have 13

also been observed as frequently. Interestingly, some populations show extra-pair fertilisations, with both males and females copulating with members of the opposite sex other than their breeding mate. Hence, both members of the breeding pair may also parent multiple broods, or replace a failed brood with another during the same season. The nest is usually a shallow depression in the sand, above the tide mark on the seashore, or in a dry river bed, preferably among light vegetation, and away from human habitation. It may be lined with a variety of materials – pebbles, shells, fish bones, grass and leaves. The usual clutch consists of 3 eggs, though sometimes it may be 2 or 4. The eggs are sandy brown, sometimes greenish-tinged, and with blackish marks. Both male and female share incubation and parental duties, and give broken-wing displays to distract predators if threatened. Local name: The Kentish Plover is known as ‘Kentish chikhli’ in Marathi, ‘Kalarwala marwa’ in Punjabi, ‘Chinna kottan’, ‘Uppu kothhi’ or ‘Chinna mandai ullan’ in Tamil, and ‘Manal kozhi’ in Malayalam. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (Received on Whatsapp, March 30, 2021) *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 18 Number 10 October 2021 YADGARPALLY: A NEW BIRD HABITAT Report: Yadgarpally Village, Rangareddy Dt, Dec 2020-July 2021 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla West Yadgarpally A beautiful landscape with typical Deccan rock formations, lush green paddy fields, an expanse of blue water, and an abode for birds, best describes the sleepy village of Yadgarpally. Located to the north-east of Hyderabad, about 30km from Punjagutta in Hyderabad, Yadgarpally is the border village between Rangareddy and Nalgonda districts. In quest of exploring new areas of birds we made several short trips to the outskirts of Hyderabad city, and chanced upon Yadgarpally village that lay on the Shamirpet-Keesara road. On either side of this road were paddy fields. half a dozen Asian Openbills, a large number of Black-headed and Red-naped Ibis, and several White-browed Wagtails. At a small wetland patch among the fields, there were many flocks of birds. As we approached this patch, a couple of wary villagers stopped us to enquire about the purpose of our visit. When we told them that we had come to look for birds, they became very friendly. One of them suggested that we visit the eastern side of the village where there happened to be a big lake and a nature preserve. We thanked them for the information and went around listing the birds we spotted. This being the month of December we sighted flocks of Wood Sandpipers, some Common Sandpipers, Little Ringed Plovers, Red-necked Falcon with kill 1

There was also a scrubland on one side inhabited mostly by smaller birds like Bay-backed Shrike, Lesser Whitethroat, some Indian Silverbills, and a few ground birds like Jungle Bush Quails and Grey Francolins. The highlight of the day however was a Red-necked Falcon that was hunting Ashy Woodswallows and Asian Palm Swifts! Thoroughly satisfied with the outing, and with the prospect of visiting another birding ground soon, we returned home. On the map we tried to locate the lake referred to by the villagers and found The Great Ambience Lake near Gandi Maisamma Temple, and a nature preserve called Under The Moon Nature Preserve (or UTM), both of them in East Yadgarpally. Common Kingfisher On the clump of trees nearby were a Blue-faced Malkoha, Common Iora, Black-winged Kite, Indian Roller and many other birds listed below. The Great Ambience Lake, East Yadgarpally On the subsequent weekends we visited East Yadgarpally, which also had many paddy fields on either side of the approach road to the lake. On our very first visit we had the good fortune of adding a lifer to our list of birds. This was the Black-headed Bunting, spotted among a mixed flock of Baya Weavers, Scaly-breasted Munias and assorted Starlings. Booted Eagle Black-headed Bunting The drive from the field to the lake was a topsy-turvy stretch of one and a half kilometres. The lake view was really amazing. There were Spot-billed Ducks, Lesser Whistlingducks, a pair of Painted Storks, and many Great Cormorants, White-browed Wagtails, River Terns, Common and Pied Kingfishers. Common Kestrel 2

In the middle of January, it was a raptor show with various raptors like Oriental Honey Buzzard, Booted Eagle, Common Kestrel, Black Kite and a pair of Shikras. The Jerdon’s Bushlark was a regular sight at both East and West Yadgarpally, and it always greeted us with full-throated calls. However, for some reason, a part of the lakeside was fenced when we visited in March and also the number of people visiting the lake had increased. I hope the lake surroundings will remain intact so that the habitat is not disturbed. Photos: Dr G Samuel Sukumar Scaly-breasted Munia The name Kondagorre which translates to Chowsingha or Four-horned Antelope. Kondagorre Wilderness Park has been designated as India's first Wilderness Park by the Telangana State Forest Development Corporation. This Park is structured to focus on biodiversity conservation, sustainability, and rewilding with total inclusivity. The forest is spread across 2,635 acres wherein several thousand forest species saplings have been planted. A small portion of the total area is slated to be developed as an urban forest park with facilities such as jogging paths, nature trails, green cafes, cycling tracks and dormitories, in a phased manner. The whole park is protected by fencing. 4

One fine Saturday morning in July, around a dozen of us DB members set off to explore Kondagorre Wilderness Park at Lalgadi Malakpet, near the Outer Ring Road on Karimnagar Highway, with a thrill of anticipation. Spotting the Slate Flash (Rapala manea) in Kondagorre was the most unexpected pleasure. The Common Pierrot (Castalius rosimon) with its distinct black and white pattern was another sweet spotting. Ground Skimmer (aka Chalky Percher) female For some reason, there was very little bird activity. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Greater Crested Tern (Thalasseus bergii) Greater Crested Tern (Pazhaverkadu, Pulicat, December 12, 2020 & March 03, 2020) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Laridae Genus: Thalasseus Species: T. bergii Size: 46-49 cm 2000km to non-breeding grounds. When not breeding, the Greater Crested Tern roosts in medium to large-sized groups, usually on open shores or larger creeks but also, sometimes, on boats, raised salt mounds or sandbars, or coastal buildings. Its diet consists primarily of fish, although it does sometimes take cephalopods, crustaceans and insects; it has also been known to pick up unusual vertebrate prey like agamid lizards and turtle hatchlings. It catches the fish primarily by plunge diving or dipping from the surface, usually in marine environments, and swallows the fish in mid-air. It also regularly follows fishing boats for any bycatch that may be jettisoned by the fishermen. It is a territorial and vocal species, especially while breeding, and the territorial call is a crow-like kerrak. Other calls include a korr-korr-korr uttered by jittery birds near the nest, and a hard wep wep uttered in flight. Description & distribution: The Greater Crested Tern, also known as the Crested Tern or the Swift Tern, is a large tern from the family, Laridae. It is also closely related to the Lesser Crested and Royal Terns, though it can easily be told apart. Like most terns, The Greater Crested Tern also has a sleek, light build and long pointed wings that aid in fast flight. The Greater Crested Tern has white underparts and forehead, while the upperparts and inner wings are dusky grey. The short legs are black, the bill is yellow – one of the features that differentiates it from the other similar terns – and the tail is deeply forked. It has a glossy black crest that is visibly shaggy at the rear, and the tertials show clear white fringes. In winter, its upperparts become an almost uniform paler grey, and the crown becomes white, merging at the rear into a peppered black crest and mask. The sexes are similar, but juvenile birds are quite distinctive – the head is patchy white, like the winter adult, and the upperparts show a strong grey, white and brown pattern. The closed wings may show dark bars. Nesting: The Greater Crested Tern breeds in large, densely populated colonies on islands or coasts of the tropical or subtropical Old World countries, often colonially along with other seabirds. However, it is also known to use unusual nesting locations like the roofs of buildings or artificial nesting islands amid salt pans or sewage treatment plants. It is monogamous and maintains a pair bond for the year and sometimes over subsequent seasons. However, it does not show site fidelity, changing its nest site from one year to the next, and often by 200km. Breeding display includes head raising and bowing, and it may also indulge in courtship feeding. The typical nest is usually a shallow scrape on open ground amidst low shrub or on low-lying sandy, rocky or coral islands, or in coastal areas. It may be unlined, or may contain small stones or cuttlefish bones. The usual clutch consists of 1-2 eggs, which are cream in colour with blackish streaks. Chicks are precocial, and parental duties are shared by both parents. The Greater Crested Tern is present in tropical and warm temperate coastal parts of the Old World, right from South Africa, around the Indian Ocean to Australia and the Pacific. Five sun-species are recognized: T. b. bergii, seen on the coasts of Namibia and South Africa; T. b. enigma, seen in Zambezi, Mozambique and south to parts of South Africa; T. b. cristata of the eastern Indian Ocean, Australia and western Pacific Ocean; T. b. thalassina of the western Indian Ocean, and T. b. velox, seen in the Red Sea, Persian Gulf and northern Indian Ocean. These differ mainly in the colour of bill and upperparts, and all of them follow different breeding cycles, with their breeding period varying depending on population and location. Local name: The Greater Crested Tern is known as ‘Periya kondai aala’ in Tamil, ‘Chotili dariyayi dhomdi’ or ‘Motili dariyayi vabagali’ in Gujarati, and ‘Muhudu lihiniya’ in Malayalam. Cuckoo Strikes Again… At Yapral lake, Secunderabad, October 2021 Text & Photos: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao Jacobin Cuckoo chick On October 18, 2021, while driving to the city, I noticed three Lesser Whistling-ducks with 7-8 chicks trying to cross the Yapral-Kowkoor Road from the Cantonment wall towards the lake side. Due to heavy morning traffic, their attempts proved futile, as no one cared to even notice them patiently waiting in the bushes. I stopped a few yards ahead and tried to usher them to the other side, but they refused to take my offer and went in to the bushes and hid themselves. After waiting for a few minutes, I left them to their better judgement, hoping to see them in the lake the next day. Since then, I have been visiting the Yapral Lake hoping to see the Lesser Whistling-duck family, but without any luck. Yellow-billed Babbler (foster parent) with feed The Jacobin Cuckoo sunbathed for a while before descending along the bush to scoop up some water. Jacobin Cuckoo chick #1 On October 23, 2021, while scanning the lake for the Lesser Whistling-ducks, I noticed a flock of Yellow-billed Babblers feeding a Jacobin Cuckoo (Clamator jacobinus) chick. The Babblers were comfortable with my presence; however, the cuckoo chick was not. It quickly flew to the other bank of the lake and into the Acacia bushes. The Babbler family followed suit and continued to take care of the chick. Jacobin Cuckoo chick #1 drinking water from the lake 8

Previously, on August 31, 2018, I had recorded a Jacobin Cuckoo visiting the nest of Yellow-billed Babblers in the Purple Butterfly tree (Bauhinia purpurea) opposite my house, and spending a few seconds at the nest. I did observe the nest for a few days following this incident and it was business as usual for the Babbler family till either a Southern Coucal or a Rufous Treepie raided the nest. The Babblers no longer came to the nest after this clean up act. A few days later, during the routine pruning of trees by the Electricity Dept, I happened to peep into the nest and had found that it was empty. Coming back to the case of the two Jacobin Cuckoo chicks. A quick literature review suggests that while the Jacobin Cuckoo usually lays around 25 eggs per season in different nests, it usually lays only a single egg in one nest, although it does occasionally lay two. Hence, I present here a few possibilities: Jacobin Cuckoo chick #2 It was then that I noticed that the foster parents were busy feeding another chick in the neighbouring bush. On closer examination, and to my surprise, I noticed a second Jacobin Cuckoo chick. Thus it was clear that the same flock of Yellowbilled Babblers were tending to both the chicks. 1. 2. 3. 4. The same female Jacobin Cuckoo laid two eggs in one go; The same female Jacobin Cuckoo laid one egg each on two consecutive days; This could this be the work of two different female Jacobin Cuckoos, who may have tricked the hosts independently; or It is also a possibility that the Cuckoo chicks could actually be from two different nests of the same flock of Yellow-billed Babblers. The future may unfold this mystery for us. Till then I intend to keep watching them. And I am still hopeful of finding the Lesser Whistling-duck family in the coming days! Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 18 Number 12 November 2021 Trip Report: Nagarhole National Park / Kabini Backwaters, Oct & Nov 2021 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao Crested Serpent Eagle With the waning pandemic and the approaching Dussehra vacation, we decided to go on a tour to Nagarhole National Park or Kabini Forest – the names are used interchangeably. The trip was organized through Kabini Lodges run by Jungle Lodges and Resorts, surprisingly a quite professionally run government organization. The access to the forest is always through the jungle safari, organized as a part of the package which comes with your resort stay (no private tours are allowed). I had the privilege of going on 6 safaris. The resort and the forest are set against the Kabini backwaters. This was created when a dam was built against the river Kapila in order to irrigate Mysore and the adjoining areas in the 1970s. It took up forest space, but increased the wildlife due to available water source even during summers. One thing that struck me when compared to other national forests is that the conservation effort is taken seriously at Nagarhole; the Forest Department is well organized, and the forest is being preserved well. Though there are jungle safaris, less than 10% of the forest area is earmarked for access to these vehicles. The visitors get access to resident fauna who have made these areas their home. From what I gleaned, only about 5-7 tigers (out of 120+) and a handful of leopards call this zone their home. Nagarhole is a part of the Nilgiri Biosphere and home to more than 300+ species of birds, a few being endemic. In addition one can also spot several big cats and large mammals. Blue-throated Flycatcher 1

Indian Leopard Rufous-bellied Eagle juvenile Honestly, it is very hard to bird from a safari jeep; nevertheless, I kept my binoculars and telephoto lens ready for any opportunities, and I was not disappointed at all. The forests were teeming with raptors, woodpeckers and Malabar endemics; some were lifers too. Bengal Tiger (F) Grey Junglefowl Of course, a visit to Kabini Forest is never really complete without some big cat sightings. I was very fortunate to sight about 4 tigers, 2 leopards, and many gaur, elephants, sambar deer, spotted deer and grey langurs. Brahminy Kite Gaur (Indian Bison) 2

Trip Report: Kanakapura, Bengaluru, Oct 9, 2021 Text & Photos: Rama Sarvani The habitat around the Mavathur Kere I had been wanting to see the European Bee-eaters for quite some time. So, artist and fellow birder Hemant and I decided to search for European Bee-eaters which are known to visit certain areas around Bangalore during the winters. Bee-eaters are a group of non-passerine birds in the family Meropidae encompassing three genera and twenty-seven species. There are five species of bee-eaters found in the Deccan region, Green Bee-eater (Merops orientalis), Bluetailed Bee-eater (Merops philippinus), Chestnut-headed Beeeater (Merops leschenaulti), European Bee-eater (Merops apiaster), and Blue-bearded Bee-eater (Nyctyornis athertoni). Satellite view of the area around the lake Of these, European Bee-eaters are known to migrate to India. Few e-bird records show that they have been spotted in Jammu and Kashmir also; there has been evidence that those are a breeding population, although not much study has been done yet. They have brown and yellow upperparts with green wings and black beak, and the sexes are alike, though females tend to have greener, rather than gold feathers on the shoulders. They can be easily mistaken for the Chestnut-headed Beeeater, which is a resident species, barring a few morphological characteristics. Some records show they even have similar calls as a flock although some calls seemed different to me. This is the only long-distance migrating bee-eater species that breeds in Europe and migrates to Africa and South Asia in winters. Almost the entire global population migrates to Africa but some choose to spend their winters in the Deccan. European Bee-eater 7

There have been many sightings over the years and this year, I was lucky to see them at Kanakapura which is about 60km south of Bangalore city. The area has a lake surrounded by a lot of reeds which are home to dragonflies and damselflies, which the bee-eaters feed on. There is a hill on one end of the lake where we spotted our first European Bee-eater perched on a wire along with a couple of Ashy Woodswallows (Artamus fuscus). As we went further up the hill, we heard the calls of a flock circling above us in a swallow-like flight. We went atop the hill where we saw about 50 of them perched on a couple of wires which ran into the valley below. Purple Sunbird female We heard some calls coming from a neem tree on which a female Purple Sunbird (Cinnyris asiaticus) was dancing in response to the calls of a male, while a group of White-browed Bulbuls (Pycnonotus luteolus) called frantically and continuously. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Lesser Crested Tern (Thalasseus bengalensis) Lesser Crested Tern (L); Lesser Crested Tern showing bill colour difference and marked size contrast with Greater Crested Tern (R and behind) (Pazhaverkadu, Pulicat, March 03, 2020) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Laridae Genus: Thalasseus Species: T. bengalensis Size: 35-37 cm recognized: T. b. emigrata, which breeds in the Mediterranean and winters in west Africa; T. b. bengalensis, seen in and around the Indian Ocean, including India; and T. b. torresii, seen from Indonesia down to Australia. These differ mainly in the colour of upperparts, and sometimes show marginal differences in size. Description & distribution: The Lesser Crested Tern is a medium-sized tern from the family, Laridae. It is closely related to the Sandwich, Elegant and Chinese Crested Terns. Like most terns, the Lesser Crested Tern also has a sleek build and long pointed wings that help in fast flight. During summer – its breeding season – the Lesser Crested Tern has white underparts and grey upperwings, rump and central tail feathers; the flight feathers also darken during summer. The legs and head are black, and the long, fine bill is orange – one of the features (besides the marked size difference) that differentiates it from the other similar terns, like the Greater Crested Tern, with whom it is usually seen in mixed flocks. Its bill aids in differentiating it from the Sandwich Tern, the other similar tern with whom it shares some range overlaps – the bill of the Sandwich Tern is black with an orange tip. It has a glossy black crest that is shaggy at the rear, but shorter than the Greater Crested Tern. In winter, the flight feathers become lighter, and the black forehead, crown and forehead seen during summer become white, leaving only a black nape band. The sexes are similar, but juvenile birds show dark centres to wing coverts and secondaries, as well as the feathers of the mantle, scapulars and tertials, giving the upperparts a spotted appearance. Habitat & behaviour: The Lesser Crested Tern is a marine tern, and frequents coasts, tidal creeks and open sea. It roosts in medium to large-sized groups, usually on open shores or larger creeks, in mixed flocks, usually along with Greater Crested, Common and Caspian Terns. Like the Greater Crested Tern, its diet consists primarily of fish, though it may also pick up cephalopods, crustaceans and insects. It catches the fish primarily by direct plunge diving, usually in saline environments, and swallows the fish in midair. Its call is a loud, grating, upward-inflected kree-it, quite like the Sandwich Tern. Nesting: The Lesser Crested Tern breeds in dense colonies on coasts and islands, and is known to indulge in courtship feeding. The typical nest is usually a shallow scrape on open ground. The usual clutch consists of 1-2 (and rarely 3) eggs, generally white or off-white in colour with black or dark brown spots. The sub-species T. b. emigrata is known to delay its breeding to late summer, so as to avoid the predatory Yellow-legged Gulls, which generally finish their breeding depart from the nesting areas by that time. Local name: The Lesser Crested Tern is known as ‘Kondai aala’ in Tamil, ‘Nani dariyayi dhomdi’ in Gujarati, ‘Chhotojhunt panpayra’ in Bengali and ‘Cheriya kadalala’ in Malayalam. The Lesser Crested Tern breeds in subtropical coastal areas from the Mediterranean and the Red Sea across the Indian Ocean to the western Pacific, as well as Australia; some populations winter in South Africa while some stay back at the same location all year around.
