Editor’s note Some of our members had been to West Bengal for a nine-day birding trip from January 23rd to 31st, 2021. In this Special Issue of the Pitta, we are happy to bring you an account of the trip, along with a number of colourful photographs. We hope you will find this Special Issue interesting. EASTERN EXCURSION Report: West Bengal, January 23-31, 2021 Short-eared Owl (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Late January 2021 saw 6 of us setting out on a much-awaited 10-day trip to some hotspots of West Bengal – Gajoldoba, Latpanchar & Mahananda WLS. The group included Lawrence, Srikanth and his wife Sravani, and myself, besides two other friends, Kumar Kanchu, better known as KK, and Ashish. Thanks to the airline rescheduling the flights several times, we arrived at Bagdogra airport after a lot of confusion, and I actually ended up reaching Siliguri one day before the rest of the gang! Anyway, the excitement of the trip ensured that we weathered all these hiccups, and we started the trip on January 23, 2021, with a lot of anticipation. Day-1: January 23, 2021 As per the program chalked out by the guide, the actual trip was to start only on the morning of January 24. However, we could not bring ourselves to sit around in the hotel for half a day and just wait for the next morning! So, on reaching the hotel in Gajoldoba – our first port of call – we checked into our rooms, had a quick lunch and prevailed upon the guide to take us birding for a couple of hours at least. Osprey (Photo: Umesh Mani)

in India. However, they do generally tend to stay far away from the madding crowd – so we got to see only a few species this evening. Well, I say ‘only a few’ – but what an appetizer they were for the rest of the trip! Black-necked Grebe (Photo: Umesh Mani) We took a walk on the barrage, and on a bund nearby, which is the launching point for the boats that were to be our ride for the next two days. Our sightings that day included Great Crested and Black-necked Grebes, both wonderful species, a couple of Common Teals and some distant Tufted Ducks, besides some of the usual suspects – Northern Pintail, Northern Shoveler, Eurasian Wigeon, Little and Great Cormorant, etc etc – and good numbers of Ruddy Shelducks. We also saw a female Pied Harrier, a Eurasian Marsh Harrier and an Osprey in flight. Man climbing pylon (Photo: Umesh Mani) Right outside the hotel, we saw an Osprey and a Lesser Adjutant in flight – a great way to start. We also saw a man climbing a pylon with no safety gear whatsoever, leaving us wondering how we can be so casual about safety issues. Pied Harrier female (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Being still the rear end of winter up north, it was fairly chilly, and also got dark by around 5.30PM. So we wound up our wanderings and headed back to the hotel for some rest, repast and rejuvenation. This was, however, interrupted by a flutter of action caused by an Indian Scops Owl that decided to first come and perch very close to our balcony, and then lead us on a bit of a dance among the trees within the resort premises. Having got a few record shots, we retired to our rooms again, tired but excited about the coming adventures. Black-hooded Oriole (Photo: Umesh Mani) We walked along a canal for a bit, notching up some nice species like the Blue-throated Barbet, Black-hooded Oriole and House Sparrow, and soon reached the Teesta Barrage. It is a popular hangout point for the public on holidays, as well as a tourist attraction in the area – but it is also home to some of the most beautiful ducks and other waterbirds we get to see ***

Day-2: January 24, 2021: Gajoldoba (Teesta Barrage) reeds, some grassy stretches, some rocky patches and several small islands and sandbars. Naturally, this means that there is suitable habitat for a wide variety of species. Day-2, the first full day of the trip, saw us up and ready at the appointed time of 6.30AM, only to find that it was quite foggy and we could not see anything! Anyway, we decided to head to the barrage and wait there rather than hang around in our rooms. That, at least, enabled us to warm ourselves with a cup of hot chai while we waited for the fog to clear. White-capped Water Redstart (Photo: Umesh Mani) Spangled Drongo (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Near the tea shops, we got views of a couple of early risers – a Spangled Drongo and a Black-hooded Oriole. After about an hour of restless waiting – we were naturally chomping at the bit, knowing what treasures the lake had to offer – we were finally able to head to the embarkation point and board the boats. We had already been greeted by a White-capped Water Redstart which had actually been hopping around inside and on top of the boats that were tied up at the bank. As we started, we could see a small group of ducks a short distance away, not very clear through the remnants of fog. As we approached, we realized that they were Red-crested Pochards and Tufted Ducks! While we do get both species down south too – albeit in smaller numbers – I don’t think I have ever got such a close look at either of these. While the Tufted Ducks were slightly jittery and would fly off every time we approached, to settle a short distance away, the Red-crested Pochards were a lot more tolerant, and would only swim away slowly, maintaining a sort of constant distance between themselves and us. There was also a lone Great Crested Grebe. We took a few photographs for the record, as best as we could in the conditions, and decided to leave the photography for later, once the light was better. My initial reaction at the first sight of the boats was, well, a kind of sinking feeling! The boats were small – really small – and could just about accommodate two people along with gear; and once you sat down, there wasn’t much room to move anywhere – we were kind of wedged into place. Any significant sideways movement would lead to the boat tilting dangerously towards the water. I could foresee that we would return at the end of the day, sore and weary, and with unknown muscles called into action as we twisted this way and that, trying to capture photographs of all the birds! However, the anticipation outweighed all these pinpricks of concern, and we took off into the lake. Our group was divided into three boats. The boats were ‘silent’ boats – there was a boatman in each boat, who basically pushed the boat along using a long bamboo pole. A word about the lake itself – it is formed by the accumulation of water behind the barrage, and includes a variety of mini-habitats. There are large vistas of Sand Lark (Photo: Umesh Mani)

It was a beautiful male, and our guide told us that we were lucky to get it – apparently it is the female that is seen more easily, and they had not got the male during the past few outings. Of course, it does not allow very close approaches, so we had to be content with views and photographs from a fair distance. But we were happy at getting one of the species that, for so many years, we had only seen in the books. Once the male flew away, we settled down to wait, hoping that it would come back in a while and possibly bring the female along. While waiting, we had a breakfast that was unusual but strangely fitting in the circumstances – chapatis and chicken curry! Apparently it was the done thing here. Just as we finished, we saw a Harrier overhead that turned out to be the rare Hen Harrier! It was quite thrilling to see this bird – I think I was seeing it after some 10-12 years. Little Cormorant (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) Moving along, we saw a handful of River Lapwings on the grass, an Olive-backed Pipit and a few Pacific Golden Plovers. There was also the odd Grey-headed Swamphen and a couple of Pheasant-tailed and Bronze-winged Jacanas. Some way ahead, on the sandbars and in the waters, we saw a Sand Lark that stubbornly refused to turn towards us, a Black-necked Grebe, a Common Greenshank, a lovely specimen of Little Cormorant and a few Ruddy Shelducks. We then came upon a small flock of what would be my first lifer of the trip – the beautiful Northern Lapwing. The flock was a little distant and, assuring us that we would get them much closer later, our guide advised that we press on for our major objective for the day. Reluctantly leaving the Northern Lapwings behind, we moved on, seeing in flight en route a few Black-tailed Godwits, a Black-eared Kite and a Steppe Eagle. Then we reached the location where we were hoping to get the first of the ‘big’ species of the trip. After almost half an hour with not a bird in sight, we were on tenterhooks – had our target bird decided to give it a miss today? Suddenly one of the boatmen – who all seemed to have a pretty good knowledge of the birds of the area – called out something in Bengali and pointed at something way off in the distance. The other boatmen and the guide all came alive, and we immediately started moving ahead. And then we finally saw what we had been waiting for – the Common Merganser! Hen Harrier female (Photo: Umesh Mani) Having waited for almost an hour with no sign of the Merganser returning, we decided to move back and start looking for other species. On the way, we saw a group of four Black-eared Kites on a sandbar, one of which seemed to be eating something. We edged closer and were horrified to see that the Kite was trying to get at something from inside a packet of potato chips! It was very disturbing to see such a pristine habitat marred by human garbage – a sad commentary on how we treat our environment. Steppe Eagle (Photo: Umesh Mani) Common Merganser male (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Anyway, after a few minutes, we moved on. The guide told us that there was an island where a Short-eared Owl was often seen sitting at the edge of the water – an enticing vision. En route to that point, we heard the call of a Striated Grassbird but could not see it. Soon, we came to the location, and to our excitement, we did manage to see the Owl sitting near the water. It took off quickly, however, and moved some distance away. There were some other people in another boat who were also chasing this owl, so it kept flying around from place to place, giving us some nice views in the process. Northern Lapwing (Photo: Umesh Mani) We – the two people in my boat, that is – decided to move on to the next sandbar, and were overwhelmed to see that the flock out there comprised of Northern Lapwings – over 200 of them! What a way to get a lifer – 200 at a time – it was unbelievable. Short-eared Owl (Photo: Umesh Mani) After some time, we got back to the boats and headed towards the main lake. We could see a couple of sandbars that seemed to be loaded with waders. One of our boats stopped at the first sandbar, which had a large flock of Pacific Golden Plovers and, amidst them, a number of smaller waders – notable among them was the Dunlin. Northern Lapwing (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) The Northern Lapwings were also quite confiding, and allowed us to approach pretty close in the boats. And as they would turn, the sun, hitting them at different angles, would bring out different colours. As a result, we were able to get some really nice photos of the Lapwings. And when they took off in a cloud, it was a rainbow of flashing metallic colours flying around us – a magnificent, unforgettable sight. Dunlin (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Having photographed them to our heart’s content – well, maybe not exactly content, but reasonably satisfied! – we moved ahead, and were rewarded with a mega-bonus. The female Mergansers, which had refused to put in an appearance earlier in the morning, had turned up right here! Of course, true to their nature, they kept moving away as we approached. They also generally keep a very low profile in the water, and it was not easy photographing them in between the waves from a bobbing boat, so we had to be satisfied with decent photos from a distance; some of us were unfortunate to miss out because they had taken a bit of time to get here after the Lapwings.

Common Merganser female (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) River Lapwing (Photo: Umesh Mani) Ruddy Shelduck (Photo: Umesh Mani) Citrine Wagtail (Photo: Umesh Mani) By this time it was getting on for 3.00PM – time for the boat ride to end. So we started moving back to shore, photographing some of the numerous Ruddy Shelducks along the way. Most of the ducks here seemed to be generally quite accommodating – I don’t think I have ever got so close to them in all my 15 years of birding. We also saw a Siberian Stonechat, a beautiful River Lapwing that allowed us quite close, a Citrine Wagtail, and some more Tufted Ducks. After that, we reached the shore and disembarked, tired but quite happy that our major target for the day – the Common Merganser – had been achieved, along with some other awesome species like the Northern Lapwing. It was now time for some food – and what else could satisfy some hungry souls better than that staple of winter birding up north – piping hot Maggi! It gets dark fairly early here during winter so, having refreshed ourselves with Maggi and chai, we moved back to our rooms, winding up for the day. *** Day-3: January 25, 2021: Gajoldoba Day-3 dawned not-so-bright and not-so-early – although we were ready at 6.30AM and had reached the chai shops near the boarding point soon after, we were forced to delay our start till almost 8.00AM because the fog was impenetrable. It was so bad that we couldn’t see more than 10 feet, and we were beginning to worry that the day’s birding was going to be affected. Today was another important day, because some of the key duck species were on the target list today. So, once some sunlight started filtering through, we decided to start, reasoning that by the time we got to the right locations, it would be brighter and the fog would have cleared to some extent. We were given a morning welcome by a Spotted Owlet that was perching on a tree right next to the boats. And, as always, the Tufted Ducks and Red-crested Pochards were there to greet us. Since today was ‘duck day’, we spent a little time photographing these ducks before moving on. A ghostly boatman in the thick fog (Photo: Umesh Mani)

approaches, and I was pleasantly surprised that we got reasonably close. There were also a few Eurasian Wigeons, Tufted Ducks, and a Tricolored Shrike on a bush. Tufted Duck (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) Eurasian Wigeon (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) We then took off on a half-hour ride without any major sightings en route, and reached another part of the lake, where we got our first mega-sighting of the day – a pair of Common Goldeneyes! This is a really big species to find, since it comes in small numbers, and more importantly, is hyper-sensitive – it seems to take off even when you are a hundred metres away! – making it practically impossible to see and photograph well. We managed to get a few record shots before they took off again, and it was impossible to track them since it was still quite hazy over the water. Red-crested Pochard male (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) Common Goldeneye pair (Photo: Umesh Mani) Gadwall female (Photo: Umesh Mani) The next patch, marked by some reeds and other aquatic vegetation, yielded some Northern Pintails, Common Teals – and Gadwalls! Again, they usually don’t allow close We waited for a while, hoping they would come back to the area we had seen them in, and they did give us a couple of flybys, but did not settle down. We then decided to go ahead and look for other birds. As usual, Red-crested Pochards, Tufted Ducks and Ruddy Shelducks were plentiful, as also the odd Eurasian Wigeon, River and Red-wattled Lapwings, Asian Pied Starlings etc. A flock of Gadwalls gave us a lovely view as they flew past – it was good to see them in a flock rather than as just individuals!

This bird is a winter visitor to northern India, but is quite difficult to photograph, given that it is incredibly shy and tends to take off very early when you try to approach. No wonder we were thrilled. Gadwall flock (Photo: Umesh Mani) We reached a part of the lake that had a lot of reeds – this was apparently the area where our next target bird was often seen. Eyes peeled, we were all straining to find the bird when the guide pointed to a pair of birds in the water and excitedly whispered, “Shot maro, shot maro!” At the time, two of our boats were at the spot, and Srikanth and I shot off a flurry of photographs. On review, however, the guide said that what I had captured was a Common Teal female, and I was crestfallen at having missed such an important species. It turned out later, when I was reviewing the photographs at home, that the guide and I had probably not been able to see the bird properly in the camera LCD – it can be difficult in the sunlight – and that I had, in fact, got the bird. Lawrence, in the third boat, had also got the bird, but from the other side of the reeds, when it took off. And we did get it 2-3 times later. So what WAS it? You can understand why it was such a big deal when I tell you that it was – the Falcated Duck! As we moved out from that area, we saw more of the usual ducks – Gadwalls, Ruddy Shelducks, Eurasian Wigeons, Common Teals, and Northern Shovelers, some in eclipse plumage – before we came upon some action – an aerial dogfight between a Greater Spotted Eagle and a male Pied Harrier! I personally could not get very good photographs, what with the distance and the bobbing boat – but I was happy that I had finally seen the male Pied Harrier, which had been eluding me all these years. Greater Spotted Eagle (L) & Pied Harrier (R) (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) Falcated Duck (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Striated Grassbird (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) The reeds also yielded glimpses of the Striated Grassbird and the Golden-headed Cisticola, though Srikanth was the only one who managed to get any photographs. We got another flyby from the Goldeneyes, enabling somewhat better photographs than earlier, and a Black-necked Grebe also gave good views. Falcated Duck (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan)

We then headed back to the hotel for lunch and a short break, where I discovered that I was locked out because the room key was with Lawrence, who had been in the last boat and had not yet got back! I passed the time by photographing a Red Collared Dove and a Brown Shrike in the lawns, before we sat down to lunch, where we were visited by a Long-tailed Shrike. This site is known for its records of the Smew and the Greater Scaup, two enigmatic ducks that had been visiting this lake the past couple of years, but had not been seen this year. Obviously, these were on top of our list too. However, we were not fortunate enough to see them. There were a number of false alarms, because some Tufted Duck females do show a Scauplike white face patch (9993) – and whenever we saw any of these, we kept getting excited and then deflated! Red Collared Dove (Photo: Umesh Mani) The plan for the post-lunch session was to get a better look at the ducks, and of course to search for the Falcated Duck that we had ‘missed’ earlier. Back on the lake, we were rewarded for our persistence almost immediately – the Falcated Duck had come to ‘our’ part of the lake! We had to chase it around a bit before we could get some proper views, and some photographs for the record. Tufted Duck with Scaup-like head (Photo: Umesh Mani) Anyway, that was it for the day, more or less, barring another distant look at the Common Goldeneyes. As we turned back for the ride home, we saw a huge flock of Common Greenshanks, some Common Teals that allowed us fairly close, some Common Redshanks and some more River Lapwings. The Red-crested Pochards, as always, were cooperative. We saw some baskets that had been strung up on one of the bushes – an ingenious contraption that was apparently used to catch fish! Northern Lapwing flock (Photo: Umesh Mani) We got a fantastic fly-by from a large flock of the Northern Lapwings – it was beautiful! There were also small groups of Tufted Ducks, Eurasian Wigeons and Ruddy Shelducks, as usual, along with a couple of Gadwalls and Great Crested Grebes. Some of the Northern Pintails seemed to have longer tails than I have seen down south. Baskets used for catching fish (Photo: Umesh Mani) Northern Pintail (Photo: Umesh Mani)

When we reached the bund where the boats would be tied up, we were surprised to see that the Spotted Owlet that had seen us off in the morning was still sitting in the same tree, dozing – we wondered if it had spent the whole day sitting there! Common Redshank (Photo: Umesh Mani) Tomorrow would be another day – our last day here before we moved to our next location – but for now, we were satisfied with what we had got during a good day of birding. We drove back to the hotel, riding in the e-rickshaws that are the norm here – a good, environment-friendly measure. Spotted Owlet (Photo: Umesh Mani) *** Day-4: January 26, 2021: Gajoldoba & Latpanchar Today was the day we had to move to our next location, Latpanchar. But of course, we wanted to get in a morning session of birding at Gajoldoba before leaving – and there were still a couple of important species we had not yet got! So we got ready early as usual and were at the boating point by 7.30AM. Bronze-winged Jacana juvenile (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Great Crested Grebe (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) We got the customary sendoff by the White-capped Water Redstart, and the Red-crested Pochards, Tufted Ducks and the Great Crested Grebe gave good views. But today our focus was different, so we pushed off to another part of the lake, clocking en route the Wigeons, Common Teals, Gadwalls, a Bronze-winged Jacana, a Siberian Stonechat and a group of four Great Crested Grebes. We then saw something we had not seen from day-1 – the Common Coot. But we did not tarry there – we had more important species to find! We came across a group of Common Pochards but, though we wanted to approach closer, we decided to press on. And then we spied what we had been looking for. Interspersed between the Wigeons, Gadwalls, Coots and Tufted Ducks was a dark brown bird with a white rump, silvery bill and striking white eyes – the Ferruginous Duck! We moved closer, but the bird seemed to be a little jittery and kept flying off. But we did not give up – we kept tracking where it went to, and finally it allowed us to approach somewhat close and take a few decent photographs.

Ferruginous Duck male (Photo: Umesh Mani) Grey-headed Lapwing (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) We got back to the hotel, packed up and started for our next destination – Latpanchar. We were in a bit of a hurry because we wanted to get in an evening birding session before dark. After a quick lunch on the way, we drove on, and neared our homestay after a bone-rattling ride on a road that seemed to be more of a bunch of rocks and potholes stuck together with bits of road here and there. Ferruginous Duck female (Photo: Umesh Mani) It was now getting on for our onward journey, so we turned our boats back towards the jetty. We saw some Common Pochards from fairly close, and a couple of Grey-headed Lapwings, besides some of the commoners – White-breasted Waterhen, Grey-headed Swamphen, Indian Moorhen et al. When we got back, I got to know that Srikanth had seen a Lesser Adjutant and a Rosy Pipit. All this was forgotten in an instant, though – when our driver suddenly slammed on the brakes, quietly reversed a little, pointed to a tree down the slope on the left, and said “Hornbill”. We jumped out of our vehicles, grabbed our gear and went rushing down the steep steps between those tiny houses that you typically see in these mountainside hamlets. Reaching a vantage point, we strained our eyes but couldn’t see anything. Was the driver mistaken? But our guide pointed out a dark patch inside the foliage and said, “That’s the Hornbill… Wait, it will come out”. After a few minutes of waiting, some movement became visible, and the palpable sense of excitement became even more heightened. And then it slowly came into view – first the orange-brown of the head and neck, then the yellow bill with deep markings, then a blue eye-patch – our first look at the Rufous-necked Hornbill! Rosy Pipit (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Rufous-necked Hornbill (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan)

It was feeding on the berries in that fruiting tree and, over the next half hour or so, gave us some nice views – although the dense foliage meant that we would have to keep scampering from one point to another to keep it in view. The residents of that hamlet were quite amused at our antics. As the guide said, many times groups spend 2-3 days there and don’t get even a glimpse of the bird. So we were thrilled, and counted ourselves lucky, that we had got this Hornbill so early – even before we reached our rooms. We were to get it another 3-4 times over the next couple of days, but there is nothing so special as the first sighting of such an iconic species. I had a bad half hour then, as my camera chose that moment to stop working – and nothing I did could get it working again. I thought I would have to spend the rest of the trip without a camera – this was a disaster. Thankfully, though, KK had a spare camera that he spontaneously offered me, and very generously allowed me to use for the next few days – a gesture that I will not forget. Sultan Tit (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) As we drove on towards the homestay, we came upon some activity en route and decided to bird rather than spend good birding time driving up and down. We saw a small flock of the beautiful Sultan Tits – they stayed very high up in the canopy, sadly, and refused to come down – along with some unidentified Yuhinas and a Streaked Spiderhunter that Sravani located. In the trees on the lower slope, we saw a Small Niltava, a Bluefronted Redstart and a Chestnut-bellied Rock Thrush. Some members got the Snowy-browed Flycatcher. We also heard the calls of the White-throated Bulbul, the Pale-headed Woodpecker and the Chestnut-headed Tesia – all species that we wanted to see and photograph, but couldn’t – leaving us quite frustrated. The guide, however, assured us that we would try to get most of these birds over the next few days. At this point, I must make mention of the fact that, although a relatively less experienced birder, Sravani turned out to be an amazing spotter, and was often the first to locate birds in the thick forest – I would not be wrong in saying that every day, she alone must have added at least a handful of species to our daily lists that we may otherwise have missed. With this, we wound up for the day. We finally reached the homestay – a quaint structure with cosy wood-panelled rooms – and settled down for the night. *** Day-5: January 27, 2021: Latpanchar Today was going to be our only full day at Latpanchar, and we wanted to make the most of it. The local residents had told us that the Rufous-necked Hornbill would return to the same tree the next morning between 6.30AM and 7.00AM so, making an early start, we headed to the site and were in place by 6.30AM – and, like clockwork, the Hornbill turned up at 6.45AM! We watched it feeding on the berries of the fruiting tree for around half an hour before it decided to take off. It flew to a distant tree overlooking the valley, and settled in to rest. We waited, expecting it to return to the fruiting tree and feed some more. Fulvous-breasted Woodpecker (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati)

Bar-winged Flycatcher-shrike (Photo: Umesh Mani) Meanwhile, a few other birds were seen – Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker, Fulvous-breasted Woodpecker, Spangled Drongo, Indian White-eye, Tricolored Shrike, Barwinged Flycatcher-shrike – and a Malayan Giant Squirrel! Streaked Spiderhunter (Photo: Umesh Mani) Anyway, after around half an hour, we decided to move on. A Streaked Spiderhunter gave us excellent views, as it sipped on the nectar of a flowering plant right next to the road. We were looking for the Black-backed Forktail, which is sometimes seen in the area, when we came across a fairly cooperative Snowy-browed Flycatcher female, which allowed us to take a few photographs before it took off into the underbrush. Also seen was a Grey-throated Babbler. Malayan Giant Squirrel (Photo: Umesh Mani) After having waited nearly an hour, the Hornbill finally took off, but went further away from us. We then decided to go ahead and look for the next big species we were hoping to see – the Red-headed Trogon. After quite a bit of searching, we were able to locate a female bird. But it was inside the thick tangle of trees and a fair way down the lower slope, so it was quite difficult to get good views. To complicate things, it kept flying from one place to another and back – leading us to go running up and down the road too! Snowy-browed Flycatcher female (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) We came across the Rufous-necked Hornbill again on the same tree – it tormented us for another half hour before finally coming out into the sun and allowing us to take some decent photographs. It has blue eyelids! – something I had not realized before, though I knew about the blue facial patch – and with the pink-and-orange balloon at the throat, yellow bill with black striations, rufous head and underparts, and the glossy greenish-black upperparts, it is a veritable painter’s palette! Red-headed Trogon female (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati)

Rufous-necked Hornbill (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Orange-bellied Leafbird female (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) At the same spot we saw a Taiga Flycatcher foraging – which reminded us that it was already past 10.00AM, and we were also hungry! We headed back to the homestay for breakfast, but were interrupted on the way by views of a majestic Crested Serpent Eagle surveying the valley that seemed to be its domain. We then went to an area where some of us had seen the Snowybrowed Flycatcher the previous day. We found a patch that had some good activity – a Streaked Spiderhunter, 3-4 Rufous Sibias and a Rufous-bellied Niltava. Rufous Sibia (Photo: Umesh Mani) Crested Serpent Eagle (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) In these parts, every house seems to take pride in maintaining a flower garden, however small. At the homestay too, while we waited for breakfast, our attention was caught by some activity in the flowering bushes right in front – we found a beautiful female Orange-bellied Leafbird feeding quite unconcerned – obviously used to human presence. It took off after a few minutes, allowing us to finish our breakfast, before it came back again – and this time, we were able to watch and photograph more of its feeding activity. Rufous-bellied Niltava (Photo: Umesh Mani) A couple of Chestnut-bellied Nuthatches were also active. A little further ahead, a small flock of Scarlet Minivets entertained us for a while with their antics, before we decided to take a break for lunch.

Tree Sparrows near the homestay. While we were waiting, a small raptor flew overhead which got us all excited – it turned out to be the Oriental Hobby! A good close to the day. Yellow-browed Warbler (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Latpanchar has some fantastic species, but not a great number of species, generally speaking. So, after lunch and some rest, we headed back to try and get another look at the Red-headed Trogon. En route, we saw a Yellow-browed Warbler and a Large Niltava. It took us another half hour before we could locate the Trogon. Still no male, though – we had to be content with further difficult views of the female which, as before, stayed inside the tree cover and kept moving about. Eurasian Tree Sparrow (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) Oriental Hobby (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Large Niltava (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Later that evening, while we were hanging around after dinner, Srikanth heard the call of the Mountain Scops Owl and the Himalayan Wood Owl. We debated the idea of going nightspotting to look for the Owls, but the vehicles were not available and we had to drop the idea. By now it was close to 5.00PM, and the skies were beginning to darken, so we decided to wind up and headed back to the homestay for some much-needed tea. We saw a few Eurasian After a little souvenir-shopping, we retired early – tomorrow we were to shift base again, this time to Siliguri, and it was going to be a very early day. *** Day-6: January 28, 2021: Latpanchar & Mahananda WLS Making an early start, we started driving down from Latpanchar. Just a little while into the drive, the car ahead came to a sudden halt, and we realized they had seen something. We also got down from our vehicle, and saw what they had spotted – a Long-billed Thrush! It was foraging on the side of the road in characteristic fashion – hopping around in a small patch, flipping the leaves over and looking for prey underneath. We slowly edged forward, taking photographs all the while – and were amazed that the Thrush allowed us to approach really close – not more than 5-6 feet away! A couple of times, it hopped up and away into the bushes above, but when we waited quietly, it came back to the same patch again and continued foraging. In fact, it was so unconcerned that finally we had to make the choice to move on, because we were getting late!

Long-billed Thrush (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Himalayan Griffon (Photo: Umesh Mani) Reaching Siliguri, we quickly dropped our baggage at the hotel and took off for birding. The first bird we saw on the way was a soaring Himalayan Griffon. After watching it for a few minutes, we moved ahead and reached a point that had a huge fruiting tree next to the road. Interestingly, the track that carries the Darjeeling Toy Train passed right under the tree! Apparently the train was not running that day, which was a bit of a disappointment – we had been hoping to catch a glimpse – but the birds more than made up for it. The main target species at that point was the Great Indian Hornbill, and we got one right away. But it was deep inside the foliage and, while we waited for it to come out, we looked around for other birds – and what nice birds there were! Asian Barred Owlet (Photo: Umesh Mani) Another smaller tree nearby had a lot of Blue-throated Barbets actively foraging, and we watched them for a while. Suddenly the guide pointed out one of the Barbets, and said, “That one is not Blue-throated”. With some drama, he asked us to look at its ear patches – it was a Blue-eared Barbet! Possibly the rarest of the Barbets seen in India, it was a thrill to finally get this species. We took some photographs, although it was not easy to keep track of it amidst the clutter of the branches and in the middle of all the other similar-looking Blue-throated Barbets. Blue-throated Barbet (Photo: Umesh Mani) Blue-eared Barbet (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) As we drove down the hills, we saw an Asian Barred Owlet, a couple of Black-crested Bulbuls, and a Blue-throated Barbet. As always, a number of Blue Whistling Thrushes were also seen en route. Suddenly a cacophony of bird calls from behind us caught our attention – the Hill Mynas had arrived! The Common Hill Mynas, seen in the Himalayan foothills and the north-eastern parts of India, have the golden ear wattles joined with the wattles on the nape of the neck, unlike the Lesser Hill Mynas seen in the south. They are very entertaining birds, and we watched their antics for a while as they hopped around, feeding on the berries.

By now, a few more Hornbills had arrived in the tree. There was some comic relief when one of them plucked a berry that had a leaf attached – and was not able to get rid of it. It spent what must have been a frustrating few seconds trying to nip it off, shaking it back and forth, before finally managing to separate the fruit and toss it up in characteristic Hornbill fashion before swallowing it. Thick-billed Green Pigeon (Photo: Umesh Mani) I spotted a Green Pigeon that turned out to be a very interesting species – the Thick-billed Green Pigeon. Sravani pointed out another individual in the same tree – and this one was a different species, and an even more interesting one – the Pintailed Green Pigeon! And to top it off, a Yellow-footed Green Pigeon was also seen. Blue Whistling Thrush (Photo: Umesh Mani) A Blue Whistling Thrush walked around on the railway line, quite close to us and a Lemon-rumped Warbler hopped around in the fruiting tree above. The Barbets, Hill Mynas etc were all creating a ruckus in the tree, and one of the Hornbills flew to a bare tree, finally giving us some clear views. A Bronzed Drongo, a Grey-headed Woodpecker and some Scarlet Minivets made their appearance at another patch nearby. Pin-tailed Green Pigeon (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) As we were trying to get some photographs of these Pigeons, the Great Indian Hornbill also decided to show itself – and we were really torn, trying to decide which one to focus on, and not wanting to miss anything! Great Indian Hornbill trying to shake off a leaf (Photo: Umesh Mani) We then headed to another area called Shivakhola, where we hoped to see the Black-backed Forktail, but that did not happen. Instead, we saw a Long-tailed Shrike, a couple of beautiful Black-crested Bulbuls, a pair of Rufous Sibia, and a small flock of Necklaced Laughingthrushes, that probably included both Greater and Lesser, but was too far down in the valley to be able to identify properly. The calls of the White-throated Bulbul alerted us to their presence, and we finally got to see them for a short while. Unlike most Bulbuls, the White-throated Bulbuls are skulkers, staying inside the underbrush or in thick mid-level canopy – this makes it really difficult to see them well or photograph them. White-throated Bulbul (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan)

The same patch yielded the Snowy-browed Flycatcher – but the female again, still no male! The guide explained that in this species, the male is more shy and rarely puts in an appearance, while the female is more confiding. Just as he was explaining this, though, the male did turn up, and we got a fair look at him. By now it was beginning to get dark. We waited a little more, hoping to see the Forktail, but to no avail, so we decided to wind up for the day and head back. Snowy-browed Flycatcher male (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) *** Day-7: January 29, 2021: Mahananda WLS Today was going to be an important day – the plan was to try and complete as many of the target species as possible, so that the next day and a half could be used only to try and fill the gaps. So, after the usual early start, we stopped for a quick cup of tea at the usual tea point. We were shaken out of our inertia by a sudden burst of activity in the trees right in front – a mixed hunting party! The first bird we saw was a Yellow-vented Flowerpecker which, sadly, none of us managed to photograph. This was followed in quick succession by the Olive-backed Pipit, some Indian White-eyes, a Chestnut-bellied Nuthatch, and a Spangled Drongo. This frenetic activity whetted our appetites and, quickly finishing off our tea, we drove on. Black-crested Bulbul (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) Olive-backed Pipit (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) We came to a patch where we found a pair of the beautiful Black-crested Bulbuls sunning themselves. They gave ample opportunities to take photographs. The guide then pointed out some activity in a tree that turned out to be the Common Green Magpie. This is such a beautiful bird, and we had all been wanting to see it, so it kept us on our toes for quite some time while we waited for it to come out of the clutter. We were distracted by a Great Barbet and an Orange-bellied Leafbird, a Small Niltava showed itself for a few moments, and the Green Magpie gave tantalizing glimpses before diving back into foliage – we would have to wait a little longer! Chestnut-bellied Nuthatch (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati)

Then came the first major sighting of the day – the Whitebellied Erpornis. We had been hearing the calls, and searching desperately for the same – although a member of the Yuhina family, which are naturally gregarious, the Erpornis is a shy bird and rarely seen out of the thick bamboo aggregations that it prefers to inhabit. It gave us several brief glimpses as it dashed around inside the bamboo, making for reasonably good views but very difficult photography. Small Niltava (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) The Spiderhunter and the Black-crested Bulbuls entertained us for a bit, along with a Himalayan Bulbul, before the next burst of activity – a group of 4-5 Large Woodshrikes – arrived and grabbed our attention. One of them found a caterpillar and proceeded to batter it on the tree branch in characteristic fashion before gobbling it up. Large Woodshrike (Photo: Umesh Mani) Scarlet Minivet male (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) A Streaked Spiderhunter – which had turned out to be reasonably common during the trip – foraged nearby, as did a small flock of the lovely Scarlet Minivets, their colours literally glowing in the morning sun. We also saw a Hoarybellied Squirrel – a very interesting sighting. The Minivets were still around, and kept zipping in and out of view. The next interesting sighting soon followed – a Maroon Oriole – with an immature in tow! This was another species that I had seen earlier, but not got decent photos of, so I was naturally excited to see it. It stayed in the higher canopy for quite some time, though, and didn’t really make it any easier for us to get proper photos. Maroon Oriole adult male (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) White-bellied Erpornis (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Maroon Oriole immature (Photo: Umesh Mani) We decided to move ahead a little and try a different patch of forest. We came across an Asian Barred Owlet that allowed us to watch it for a while. A Maroon Oriole appeared out of nowhere and gave some good views – finally! – before it found a caterpillar and hopped away to enjoy it in peace. A Scarlet Minivet female had also found what appeared to be a dragonfly. Black-winged Cuckooshrike (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) We took a break for breakfast, and then returned to the area where we had earlier seen the Snowy-browed Flycatcher. As soon as we reached there, we found a female bird hopping around in the undergrowth. We waited for a while, hoping to get the male, but to no avail. An Ashy-throated Warbler was also there, creating further confusion as we searched for the male of the Flycatcher! By now it was getting quite warm, and the activity had tapered off. After a while, we got to see another species that is often seen, but generally not easy to photograph because it is usually so hyperactive - the Little Pied Flycatcher. For a change, it did not move around much, giving us adequate time to watch and photograph it. White-browed Scimitar Babbler (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) We had a welcome encounter with a White-browed Scimitar Babbler, a Spangled Drongo with a lovely twist to its tail and a Fulvous-breasted Woodpecker. A pair of Great Hornbills gave us a flypast and settled down on a tree, and a Blackwinged Cuckooshrike appeared for a few moments. Little Pied Flycatcher (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Chestnut-bellied Rock Thrush male (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Greater Racket-tailed Drongo (Photo: Umesh Mani) By now, it was late afternoon, and we decided to take a break for a cup of tea and some refreshments – a welcome break after some frenetic birding and a good bit of walking. Chestnut-bellied Rock Thrush female (Photo: Umesh Mani) After an early lunch, we decided to try another area. Some Black Bulbuls chittered in the upper canopy, distracting us with their calls and movement as they fed on some berries. A pair of Chestnut-bellied Rock Thrushes gave us some great views, as did a Golden-fronted Leafbird and a Lesser Yellownape. Another interesting sighting was a Greater Racket-tailed Drongo with a single tail streamer. Lesser Yellownape (Photo: Umesh Mani) Feeling recharged, we then headed to the same area where we had seen the Blue-eared Barbet a couple of days earlier. As soon as we reached there, we were rewarded with a sighting of a pair of Blue-bearded Bee-eaters, a little distant but at eye level. This was again unusual, since this Bee-eater tends to usually stay on top of the high canopy. Blue-bearded Bee-eater (Photo: Umesh Mani)

Also up to their usual boisterous antics, and creating quite a ruckus, was a flock of Common Hill Mynas – but they are such beautiful birds that it is impossible to be irritated by them! We enjoyed watching them for a while, before our attention was again grabbed by the arrival of the Great Indian Hornbills. We have all seen those movies where the hero tosses peanuts up in the air and they pop right into their mouths – well, they have a thing or two to learn from these Hornbills! They went about their business of gorging on the berries, repeatedly doing the characteristic slow-motion toss in the air before swallowing the berries whole. We watched them for quite some time before moving on. Himalayan Buzzard (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) In between, the same spot also yielded us a Himalayan Buzzard circling high above and a Himalayan Griffon. The Blue-throated Barbets were still around, and active – but the Blue-eared Barbet unfortunately seemed to have moved on, and had been replaced by a Lineated Barbet that stubbornly refused to turn around. Great Indian Hornbill (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) We were nearing the end of the day, so we decided to try one last patch before winding up. A Lemon-rumped Warbler flitted about in the branches, but it was difficult to get a proper view in the thick foliage. We gave up after a while and walked along. Lineated Barbet (Photo: Umesh Mani) Common Hill Myna (Photo: Umesh Mani) Banded Bay Cuckoo (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati)

– still high, but at least it was in the open. Another bird was responding to the call from somewhere close. The Cuckoo gave us plenty of time – it moved around in the same tree and kept calling for almost half an hour. I kept hoping that it would come down lower, and it finally did, enabling us to see it well. Since it was already nearing evening, the light was already fading, but I was still glad that I had managed to get some passable photos. We decided to wind up for the day and, as we started back for the hotel, I left happy that finally this jinx had ended. Then came the sighting that, for me personally, was an important one – it broke a jinx that had been following me for almost 15 years. I had seen this bird a few times, way up in the canopy; I had heard it innumerable times – but I had never once managed to get a decent photo, and I had begun to feel that maybe this was never going to happen. But I guess maybe today was the day – with our last sighting of the day – the Banded Bay Cuckoo! We first heard the call coming from somewhere nearby, then Sravani spotted the bird in the middle of a tangle of branches *** Day-8: January 30, 2021: Mahananda WLS The first bird we were targeting today was the Crimson Sunbird, so we headed off to an area where it was apparently seen regularly. En route, we saw a couple of Lesser Yellownapes and an Asian Barred Owlet. A Green Magpie gave some glimpses before disappearing into the trees in the valley, and a Common Iora – a familiar face after quite some time! – made a brief appearance, as did a Black-crested Bulbul. Another main target – the Long-tailed Broadbill – kept calling from the canopy on top of a hillock, but try as we might, we could not see it. The same was the case with the White-bellied Erpornis and, disappointingly, the Sultan Tit. Chestnut-bellied Nuthatch (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) The Crimson Sunbirds were around – we could hear them calling, and see them moving about in the trees on a small hillock – but they refused to come down. I decided to go up the hillock to try and catch the Sunbirds there, but they chose that moment to come down, enabling the others in the group to get some nice views! Suddenly we got information that a Jerdon’s Baza had been seen at a nearby location, so we got into our vehicles and rushed off there. We reached just in time to see it perched on a tree; it took off soon after and moved to another tree a little further down the valley. We did see a very cooperative Taiga Flycatcher, which gave us some very nice close-up views. Jerdon’s Baza (Photo: Umesh Mani) Taiga Flycatcher (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) A Chestnut-bellied Nuthatch came down to the road to pick up some nesting material. We then decided to return to the first spot to look for the Crimson Sunbird again. This time, we were fortunate to witness some interesting action, as the Sunbird hovered in the air and fed on the nectar of some beautiful flowers.

Crimson Sunbird (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) Some Long-tailed Minivets also put in an appearance, along with a Maroon Oriole. A Himalayan Buzzard gave some nice views, circling nearby for a few seconds before gliding off around the side of a hill. White-throated Bulbul (Photo: Umesh Mani) We had a sense that the trip was soon coming to an end, and we wanted to maximize the time left. So, after a quick break for lunch, we were back on field again in short order. We were now in Shivakhola, another area that was supposed to have good birds. The afternoon session started with an Olivebacked Pipit and another Maroon Oriole – we were quite surprised at the number of Maroon Orioles we had seen during the trip. There was a temple on a river bank that was very interesting – the legend was that it was an ancient temple of Lord Shiva, and the statue carved out of a rock certainly seemed to bear it out. Long-tailed Minivet female (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) We moved to another area to look for the White-throated Bulbul again – although we had heard its call several times, and got some distant views once earlier in the trip, we were yet to see it properly. This time we were successful, managing to get some good views for a few minutes. Long-tailed Shrike (Photo: Srikanth Bhamidipati) A Long-tailed Shrike showed itself for a bit, and a Bluebearded Bee-eater gave good views. A Great Hornbill flew past, and its massive wingspan and heavy flapping gave a hint as to why it is such an awe-inspiring bird.

Great Indian Hornbill (Photo: Umesh Mani) Yellow-browed Warbler (Photo: Umesh Mani) A Yellow-browed Warbler fed on some berries as did another flock of the delightful Common Hill Mynas. With that, we wound up the day and returned to the hotel. Tomorrow would be our last day! *** Day-9: January 31, 2021: Mahananda WLS We had only an hour or two of birding in the morning before having to leave for the airport, so we got ready bright and early and started off. We decided to make one last attempt to get some good views of the Common Green Magpie, which had eluded us all these days – and as luck would have it, that was the first species we saw! In fact, we saw the Green Magpie with a catch of some sort, which we could not identify. Grey-headed Woodpecker pair (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) Giving it company was a Lesser Yellownape, a pair of Greyheaded Woodpeckers and a small mixed flock of Greater and Lesser Necklaced Laughingthrushes. Spangled Drongo (Photo: Umesh Mani) Spangled and Greater Racket-tailed Drongos were around, as also a White-browed Scimitar Babbler skulking in the undergrowth as always. A Maroon Oriole and a Goldenfronted Leafbird gave some parting views, and a Great Indian Hornbill flew past with its characteristic heavy, noisy wingbeats. We stopped at a point where we noticed some movement in the thick underbrush, and after a lot of tracking, I got some photos of what we thought was a Chestnut-headed Tesia – but which sadly turned out to be a Common Tailorbird! Greater Necklaced Laughungthrush (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan)

Common Tailorbird (Photo: Umesh Mani) Common Green Magpie (Photo: Lawrence Mathappan) We were now running out of time, so we wound up and started moving towards the airport. We decided to stop for one last cup of tea, and lo and behold – after all the struggles of the past few days, a Common Green Magpie came and perched right in front of the tea shop, giving us possibly the best views of the trip! It was a great way to end the trip. The trip had been planned at somewhat short notice, and we did have some big misses during the trip. However, there were also plenty of big hits – iconic species that we had been waiting to see for many years, that we had finally got during this trip. It had given us a sort of trailer of the treasures that the North-east holds, and we resolved to visit again soon. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 18 Number 13 December 2021 MYSURU BIRDING SCENE Report: Mysuru, Aug-Oct 2021 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao A scene at Narsambhudhi Lake Thanks to remote working and the waning of the Covid pandemic, I chanced upon the opportunity to work from my native city of Mysuru. Birding during my trips back to Mysuru has always been incidental and I have never had a real opportunity to do some serious birding. Thanks to my extended stay during the pandemic, I had the great pleasure to observe and document almost 120 bird species during this monsoon season (Aug 15 – Oct 15, 2021). Mysuru itself boasts of a very active birding community and some extremely serious birders who have been contributing over the last few decades via Mysore Nature (https://www.Mysorenature.org/). I was particularly impressed by an ardent Mysuru birder Mr. Shivaprakash Adavanne who has, over the years, helped with building a fantastic map of Mysuru birding scene. Mysuru is known for its serene natural setup with great rivers like Cauvery, Kabini and Hemavathi converging; the meeting of the Eastern and Western Ghats thus creating great many wetland and scrub forests – ecological prefectures that support extensive avifauna. As per eBird, there have been close to 411 birds documented till date from this region. Eurasian Spoonbill, Grey Heron & Darter One area I have been visiting often and feel is actually a bigger hotspot than recorded is the Narsambhudhi Lake (near Nanjangudu, around 25km south of Mysuru City – a semiwetland with scrub forest and extensive cultivation around the periphery. I was able to observe around 104 birds in just 12 visits. The list includes the following birds: 1

Malabar Starling Coppersmith Barbet I also had the pleasure of reporting from this place a first sighting of a pair of Malabar Starlings. Also, the hard to photograph Blue-faced Malkoha gave me a generous pose for a few seconds, allowing me to click a nice little picture. Painted Stork juvenile (L) & adult (R) In addition to this, it supports a good number of water birds like Painted Storks, Asian Openbills, Eurasian Spoonbills and Spot-billed Pelicans. Also, it is home to regular winter migrants like Sykes, Booted and Blyth’s Reed Warblers. Blue-faced Malkoha Other interesting sightings Apart from this, I have had many interesting observations in and around Mysuru. One particular scene was with many (more than 100) Coppersmith Barbets and Yellow-footed Green Pigeons making merry on an early October morning on a heavily fruiting Ficus tree. Yellow-footed Green Pigeon Important note on conservation Apart from birding, the onus lies on us of being responsible birders and promoting conservation. Unfortunately, like so many other areas that we are all aware of, Narsambhudhi is no different – human growth and destruction of habitat is happening with impunity. Some serious issues that I have noted include overfishing, logging by villagers of dead wood which I believe are great nesting areas, and regular cattle and sheep grazing. I have also noticed some wire-traps, which indicates that some traditional poachers are still lurking around. I have reported this to the local district Forest and Fisheries departments; unfortunately, it seems to work for a few days and then these activities get back in full swing. I have, in just these two months, noticed subtle changes for the worse. I am working with Rotary International, Nanjangudu Club to put up notices and create awareness within the village panchayat and help in their conservation efforts. It is a drop in the ocean indeed, but I do hope it will have an impact in the long run so that the future will have an opportunity to see this great diversity of avifauna. I will provide more information at the next available opportunity if I am able to make any headway. 3

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Terek Sandpiper (Xenus cinereus) Terek Sandpiper (Pazhaverkadu, Pulicat, March 03, 2020) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Xenus Species: X. cinereus Size: 22-25 cm believed to be quite possible that the Terek Sandpiper may mate with them and produce hybrid offspring. It forages in small groups of 5-25, but usually scattered along the coast, at high and low tide, and feeds mainly on invertebrates, marine insects and larvae, beetles, flies, crustaceans, molluscs, arachnids and some seeds. It catches its mobile prey in a distinctive manner, chasing after it as the water recedes, and often running to the water to wash its prey before consuming it. It may also sometimes probe the wet ground for worms. Description & distribution: The Terek Sandpiper is a smallsized wader and the only member of the genus Xenus. Named after the Terek River near the Caspian Sea, where it was first observed, it is a monotypic species and no subspecies are recognized. It is slightly larger than the Common Sandpiper and is easily identified by its long, gently upcurved bill. As the specific name cinereus (ash grey) implies, it has grey upperparts, face and breast, the belly is whitish and the legs and feet are dirty orange-yellow. The black bill has a yellow base, and it sometimes shows a white supercilium. In flight, conspicuous white trailing edges to the wings are visible. Its flight call is a clear, fluty tjiy-tjiy or dwitt-dwitt, softer than the Common Redshank and Common Sandpiper; it also utters a trilling du-du-du-du or a softer hu-hu-hu. The alarm call is a sharp tu-li. Nesting: The Terek Sandpiper breeds between May and August in most of its breeding range, in small colonies, and is monogamous. The typical nest is usually a shallow scrape lined with grass or plant matter, on open flat ground near water and sparse vegetation. The male performs an aerial or ground display during breeding, with fluttering wings and raised tail, while loudly singing a melodious whistled klueeu or a long musical prerrr. The usual clutch consists of 2-5 eggs, generally buff or cream with black or dark brown spots and blotches. Incubation is done by the female, but parental duties are shared by both parents. The Terek Sandpiper breeds in the Arctic tundra and taiga areas from Finland east across Siberia to the Kolyma River, Kazakhstan and Ukraine, and winters south to the muddy coastal areas of eastern Africa, Arabian peninsula, Indian subcontinent, south-east Asia and Australia. There have been occasional reports from western Europe, and in recent years, from Alaska and nearby areas. Habitat & behaviour: The Terek Sandpiper is usually seen along with Ruddy Turnstones, Stints and Plovers on coastal areas, mangrove forests, lakes, estuaries, marshes, intertidal mudflats and salt pans, between 0-100m altitude. In fact, it is closely related to the Spotted and Common Sandpipers, it is Local name: The Terek Sandpiper is known as ‘Uppukothi ullan’ or ‘Kadakarai ullan’ in Tamil, ‘Terek manaloothi’ in Malayalam and ‘Tutvari’, ‘Chanchal’ or ‘Dhariyayi’ in Gujarati. *** 5

Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 19 Number 1 January 2022 Trip Report: ICRISAT, Dec 16, 2021 Shilka Chaudhari Darter (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) “The birds of hope are everywhere, listen to them sing.” ~ Terri Guillemets At the crack of dawn, on a bleak winter day, a few birding enthusiasts gathered at ICRISAT. This birding spot continues to remain a top favourite and a paradise for all bird watchers. Located in Patancheru, the campus is spread over 3000 acres. The lush green eco-system has been a holy grail for resident and migratory bird species for a long time. Gaining access to this restricted spot is difficult but thanks to Wing Commander Yella Prakash Rao uncle, we got the required authorizations. We were permitted to take our vehicles inside the campus for bird watching, which is usually not allowed. A group of ten members were present for this birding trip. Green Bee-eater (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) 1

As we started driving around the campus, we spotted a flock of 12-15 Cattle Egrets (Bubulcus ibis) feeding in the green field. Further ahead we saw Black Drongos (Dicrurus macrocercus), Green Bee-eaters (Merops orientalis) and a group of Little Cormorants (Microcarbo niger) in flight. We reached the first lake and stepped out to photograph River Terns (Sterna aurantia) busily fishing for breakfast. Meanwhile a White-throated Kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis) perched on top of an electric pole was making a meal of a small fish. We walked down an unpaved road and observed a flock of Barn Swallows (Hirundo rustica) and Asian Palm Swifts (Cypsiurus balasiensis) flying around on top of one of the trees. We also spotted Indian Pond Herons (Ardeola grayii) and Purple Herons (Ardea purpurea) on the muddy banks of the lake. River Tern (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Purple Heron (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) A few Indian Peafowl (Pavo cristatus) were perched on the rooftop of a building, and two males were foraging in the nearby fields. Indian Peafowl (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) White-throated Kingfisher (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Paddyfield Pipit (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Barn Swallow (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Prakash uncle was busy photographing Paddyfield Pipits (Anthus rufulus) flying around. We all noticed a small group of Chestnut-tailed Starlings (Sturnia malabarica) in flight. Someone spotted a bird perched in grasslands which, initially, I thought to be a House Sparrow (female). Later, Samuel uncle and Prakash uncle mentioned it was a Zitting Cisticola (Cisticola juncidis). We photographed the little bird and verified it in Grimmett's book. Voila – the senior birders were spot on! 2

Walking around and inspecting the second lake, we heard many loud quacking sounds. The lake is surrounded by tall trees and semi dry grasslands. We saw a few Indian Pond Herons basking in the sun on the banks of the lake. There were a few Black-winged Stilts (Himantopus himantopus) swimming in the lake. Zitting Cisticola (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) As it started getting warmer, we heard loud calls of Grey Francolins (Francolinus pondicerianus) from the banks of the lake but were unable to spot the birds. Loud calls of Common Hawk Cuckoo (Hierococcyx varius) did not go unobserved. Prakash uncle mentioned he could hear the calls of Blyth’s Reed Warblers (Acrocephalus dumetorum) from the shrubs close to the lake. He had also noticed a Plain Prinia (Prinia inornata) in the same area. Northern Pintail female (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Northern Pintail male (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Plain Prinia (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Spot-billed Duck (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Black-winged Stilt (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) We noticed Indian Spot-billed Duck (Anas poecilorhyncha), Northern Pintail (Anas acuta), Oriental Darter (Anhinga melanogaster), Northern Shoveler (Spatula clypeata) and Gadwall (Mareca strepera) in the third lake. We saw Common Moorhen (Gallinula chloropus), White-breasted Waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus) and a few warblers flying around. Prakash uncle got lucky – he got to photograph the Lesser Whitethroat (Sylvia curruca) and a Blyth’s Reed Warbler. 3

Lesser Whitethroat (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Black-winged Kite (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Blyth’s Reed Warbler (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) We also heard the calls of the Clamorous Reed Warbler (Acrocephalus stentoreus) and saw an Ashy Prinia (Prinia socialis). Noisy Rufous Treepies (Dendrocitta vagabunda) created quite a ruckus while flying around amidst the thick, tall trees. We got to see Yellow-billed Babblers (Turdoides affinis), Greater Coucal (Centropus sinensis), Black-winged Kite (Elanus caeruleus), Spotted Dove (Spilopelia chinensis), Barn Swallows, Scaly-breasted Munias (Lonchura punctulata) and Shikra (Accipiter badius). Several Blue-tailed Bee-eaters (Merops philippinus) were flying around. We spotted Eurasian Golden Orioles (Oriolus oriolus), Redvented Bulbuls (Pycnonotus cafer) and Asian Koels (Eudynamys scolopaceus). A Spotted Owlet (Athene brama) sat on a large banyan tree and a lone Intermediate Egret (Ardea intermedia) was busy foraging in an open field. Shikra (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Intermediate Egret (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) 4

Blue-tailed Bee-eater (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) Pied Bushchat male (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) We decided to drive down to the fourth lake. On our way we came to Patancheru Lake and observed a number of waders in and around the lake. A good sighting of a single juvenile Greater Flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) was nice. Greater Flamingo juvenile (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) The lake was populated with Common Coot (Fulica atra), Pheasant-tailed Jacana (Hydrophasianus chirurgus), Greyheaded Swamphen (Porphyrio porphyrio), Intermediate Egret, Black-winged Stilt, Lesser Whistling-duck (Dendrocygna javanica) and Red-wattled Lapwing (Vanellus indicus). Pied Bushchat female (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) As we continued our drive we observed bird species like Scaly-breasted Munia, Pied Bushchat (Saxicola caprata), Siberian Stonechat (Saxicola maurus) and Green Bee-eater. On our arrival, we noticed colonies of Great Cormorants (Phalacrocorax carbo) on the small island in the middle of the lake. We spotted Darters feeding their young. There was a colony of Black-headed Ibis (Threskiornis melanocephalus) on one of the islands. We again spotted Rufous Treepies. The local name for the Rufous Treepie is ‘taka chor’. Literally translated, this means ‘coin thief’. Scaly-breasted Munia (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) 5

saw Spot-billed Pelicans (Pelecanus philippensis), Ruddy Shelducks (Tadorna ferruginea) and Red-wattled Lapwings too. A few of the birders had spotted an Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark (Eremopterix griseus). Great Cormorant colony (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) Asian Openbill (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Black-headed Ibis colony (Photo: Shilka Chaudhari) The serene atmosphere of birds flying about, the fresh air, fresh water lakes and lush green surroundings was a welcome change from my daily routine. Spot-billed Pelican (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) A sumptuous breakfast had been arranged in the campus canteen. After a hearty brunch, Samuel uncle and I photographed some Rose-ringed Parakeets (Psittacula krameri) flying around. Indian Roller (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) We continued our journey towards the final lake. We were surprised to see the lake full of water. We came across Indian Rollers (Coracias benghalensis), White-browed Wagtails (Motacilla maderaspatensis), Asian Openbill (Anastomus oscitans) and Common Sandpipers (Actitis hypoleucos). Indian Silverbill (Photo: Dr G Samuel Sukumar) Ruddy Shelduck, Red-wattled Lapwing & Little Cormorant (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) *** Trip Report: Mahavir Harina Vanasthali National Park, Nov 14, 2021 Text: Sagarika Melkote; Photos: Dr G Samuel Sukumar Blackbuck With Covid waning across the country, we at Deccan Birders couldn’t wait to resume our monthly outdoor trips. However, the most important thing was to tread with care, which meant avoiding crowds, using masks and practicing social distancing. With all this in mind, we decided to go somewhere nearby. Day! The newbies were full of enthusiasm and raring to go, and we sincerely hoped they would not be disappointed. As it turned out, we needn’t have worried. Despite the climate, we did spot about 25 species, albeit mostly the usual suspects. The Mahavir Harina Vanasthali National Park at Vansthalipuram seemed to beckon. Spread over an area of approximately 15 kilometres, the park is home to the endangered Blackbuck, besides other mammals. It is fairly thickly wooded with some small water bodies within the park. The weather was not the usual for the month of November. Due to the heavy rains in Tamil Nadu, the sky was somewhat overcast and the sun was playing hide and seek with the clouds. Undeterred, twenty of us arrived in quick succession at the gates of the park. Though not a great day for birding weather-wise, we decided to explore the park. Considering there were about five people who were newcomers, the old timers could only hope for a reasonably good birding experience. We were also joined by two young pre-teen birders – it was nice to see them on the occasion of Children’s Black-headed Ibis A lone Blackbuck greeted us as soon as we entered the gates of the park. 9

The local person, who had been instructed to accompany us, first led us to a water body. Though it was a small one, it had a bund on one side. A lone Black-headed Ibis (Threskiornis melanocephalus) was rummaging along the bund. Just then, we spotted its cousins – a flock of Glossy Ibises (Plegadis falcinellus) flying in the sky. White-throated Kingfisher Indian Pond Heron A couple of raucous Black Drongos (Dicrurus macrocercus) were squabbling over something known only to them, and a Little Cormorant (Microcarbo niger) made an appearance. Grey (Motacilla cinerea) and White-browed (Motacilla maderaspatensis) Wagtails on the opposite bank were engaged in doing what they do best – wagging their tails. A surprise entrant was a female Black Redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros), which kept flitting in and around the bushes that lined the shores of the water bodies. Red-vented Bulbuls (Pycnonotus cafer) and Green Bee-eaters (Merops orientalis) were, of course, in full attendance as were some House Crows (Corvus splendens). The first-time birders were entranced by the whole scene. Anita Negi, one of the senior birders, kept them engaged with tips on spotting and identifying. The camaraderie was wonderful – to share and to learn – factors which make the group so cohesive. Birds of a feather flock together? Yes, spot on, I’d say! Indian Grey Hornbill Shikra Moving on, we spotted Indian Grey Hornbills (Ocyceros birostris), yet more Bee-eaters, Bulbuls, Sunbirds, a few Plum-headed Parakeets (Psittacula cyanocephala) and a couple of Spotted Doves (Spilopelia chinensis) in flight. Indian Pond Herons (Ardeola grayii) and assorted Egrets were standing in the water, their gaze intently fixed on the surface of the pond. White-throated Kingfishers (Halcyon smyrnensis) called and swooped in and out of the water, and a Shikra (Accipiter badius) perched briefly on a branch before, presumably, moving on to better things in life. Little Grebe & Common Moorhen 10

The second water body, too, did not disappoint. A Taiga Flycatcher (Ficedula albicilla) was flitting about. Little Grebes (Tachybaptus ruficollis) and Common Moorhens (Gallinula chloropus) made their entrance. A few Indian Spotbilled Ducks (Anas poecilorhyncha) were swimming there as well. More Intermediate (Ardea intermedia) and Cattle Egrets (Bubulcus ibis) were foraging in the water. The water body was unusual – it looked more like a mangrove, with tree trunks sticking out of the water. We found a lot of peafowl feathers along the paths. The call of a Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (Cyornis tickelliae) beckoned and had some of us in hot pursuit. However, much to the disappointment of those who were hoping to see it for the first time, it did not make an appearance. It seemed like the bird was in a mischievous mood that morning, for we heard its call for the second time as we proceeded up the path. It seemed to emanate from a bamboo clump, but we had no luck spotting the bird. The neighbouring trees had a bunch of warblers flitting about, but these restless birds did not sit still for even a moment, making it impossible to identify them. But we were well compensated by the sighting of a Sulphur-bellied Warbler (Phylloscopus griseolus), which obliged us by staying still long enough for Anita to identify it. Calliandra haematocephala The park definitely merits another visit. It offers diverse habitat in the form of tall trees, wooded areas, bushes and water bodies. There is also a good variety of butterflies and mammals. According to their website, the park is home to about eighty species of migratory birds. Surprisingly, most of the usual species like Babblers, Prinias, Shrikes and Robins were conspicuous by their absence that day – possibly the weather did not draw them out. In spite of this, the enthusiasm of the first-time birders was infectious and the interactions that followed were animated. Sulphur-bellied Warbler Rhesus Macaque Cassia auriculata Common Mormon 11

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus) Glossy Ibis breeding (L) and non-breeding (R) (Marakkanam, Tamil Nadu, January 15, 2022) Order: Pelecaniformes Family: Threskiornithidae Genus: Plegadis Species: P. falcinellus Size: 55-65 cm subcontinent; in North America, birds from the northern parts winter further south. In India, the species is generally considered migratory, though there is a resident population in western India, and possibly also in other parts. It is also seen in Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. Description & distribution: The Glossy Ibis is the most widespread member of Threskionithidae, the family of Ibises and Spoonbills. Its Latin name derives from the ancient Greek word plegados and the Latin falcis, both of which mean ‘sickle’ and refer to the distinctive shape of the bill. Habitat & behaviour: The Glossy Ibis is usually seen in flocks in marshes at the margins of lakes and rivers, and also in jheels, lagoons, flood plains, swamps, reservoirs, sewage areas, irrigated farmland and paddy fields, mud flats and salt pans. It forages in very shallow water, using its long curved bill to probe in mud, soil or water for its prey. Its diet is eclectic and includes fish, amphibians, lizards, small snakes, aquatic insects, molluscs and crustaceans. The breeding Glossy Ibis is mostly deep chestnut-maroon – dark enough for the bird to appear almost black from a distance or in poor light – and the wing coverts show glossy metallic green, bronze and purple tones. The long legs can vary from olive-grey to dark brown. The long bill is brownish-grey, lores are bare and delineated by a thin cobalt-blue, bluish-grey or white line. Non-breeding birds show a dark brown neck and head with white streaking. The sexes are alike. Juvenile birds are similar to adult non-breeding birds, but are dark brown with white mottling on the head, and only a faint gloss on the upperparts. In flight, it shows a graceful, sleek appearance with outstretched slender neck, and legs and feet projecting well beyond the tail. In flight, flocks tend to fly in V-formation. Its calls include a variety of croaks and grunts, and a hoarse or bleating grrr during breeding. Nesting: The Glossy Ibis breeds between April and July, in colonies along with various other herons, storks and ibises. The typical nest is a platform of twigs and vegetation, and is built on emergent vegetation, low trees or bushes, at least 1m above the water or ground. The usual clutch consists of 2-3 eggs, blue-green in colour. Incubation duties are shared by both parents. The Glossy Ibis is a very widespread species, and breeds in warm regions across Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia and New Zealand, as well as the Atlantic and Caribbean regions of the Americas. European populations winter in Africa and sometimes in parts or Central Asia and the Indian Local name: The Glossy Ibis is known as ‘Kawari’ or ‘Chhota baza’ in Hindi, ‘That kankanam’ in Telugu, ‘Chemban ibis’ in Malayalam, ‘Karuppu kottan’ or ‘Anthril paravai’ in Tamil and ‘Nani kankanasar’ in Gujarati. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 14 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 19 Number 2 February 2022 Trip Report: South Andaman Islands, Dec 17-22, 2021 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao Daurian Starling flock years, giving rise to unique and rich biodiversity and creating a hotspot for endemic flora and fauna. It has always been my dream to visit Andaman Islands, especially for birding, given its diverse avifauna. The pandemic had not helped, but the waning of the pandemic, coupled with vaccinations, really bolstered our hopes and we decided to visit at least South Andaman Islands in the month of December 2021. The best time to visit is ideally between October-February (winters) given that it is a hotspot for several migratory birds as well. South Andaman Island (Source: ebird.org) Introduction Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a group of 572 islands from 6° to 14° North latitudes and from 92° to 94° East longitudes. It has been isolated from the mainland for several million Given that it is an island, it has highly diverse habitats, including giant evergreen forests, tropical forests, mangrove forests and bamboo forests, all transitioning into each other and making it extremely suitable for a variety of fauna to thrive. One very surprising aspect is that the evergreen forests are extremely thick and rich despite it being isolated and far away from the main landmasses of South Asia. 1

Avian Endemicity The isolation of Andaman and Nicobar Islands has resulted in several birds becoming endemic, and some sub-species have deviated genetically, for example the Scarlet Minivet (Pericrocotus speciosus) – though common in mainland India, the sub-species found in Andamans has genetically diverged (P. s. andamanensis Beavan, 1867); the same applies to many resident birds over the last several million years. Red-whiskered Bulbul Endemic Birds of Andaman & Nicobar Islands There are 20 bird species that are endemic to the Andaman Islands, and another 8 that are endemic to Nicobar Islands. Given below is a list of these species; I have highlighted the ones that we were able to record (either see or hear). We did not go beyond the South Andaman Islands, or to the Narcondam Island, which lies approximately 75km east of North Andaman, so we missed out on the Narcondam Hornbill and the Nicobar endemics. Hopefully our next sojourn will take to these beautiful islands to spot these endangered birds. Scarlet Minivet male Another interesting observation is that the Red-whiskered Bulbul has proliferated significantly and diverged giving rise to Pycnonotus jocosus whistleri [1] that has a slightly browner back when compared to the original Pycnonotus jocosus. There is a belief that it was not introduced recently to the islands [3]. (Note: Although the Nicobar Imperial Pigeon is named that way, the bird in not endemic to just Nicobar Islands, but rather found across Malay Archipelago and as far as Solomons [5]).
