Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Indian Silverbill (Euodice malabarica) Indian Silverbill (Rollapadu, October 12, 2019) Order: Passeriformes Family: Estrildidae Genus: Euodice Species: E. malabarica Size: 11-11.5 cm in small groups, and feeds mainly on a wide range of grass and weed seeds, rice, as well as other crop species, taken from the ground or off the feathery ears on low shrubs and grass stalks. It may also occasionally take winged termites. Its usual call is a feeble musical chirrup, similar to most other Munias. The contact call is a tchrip or tchreep, flight call is a repeated chirrup and the song is a series of short, abrupt trilling notes. Description & distribution: The Indian Silverbill, also known as the White-throated Munia, is a small passerine seen commonly across Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka and nearby regions (except Bangladesh) in drier parts up to about 2000m elevation. It is also an introduced species in many other parts of the world. Nesting: The Indian Silverbill is a resident breeder across most of its range. It can breed practically around the year, with local variations – it generally nests in winter in southern India, and after summer in northern India. The typical nest is a large, untidy globular structure with a side opening, made of coarse grasses, lined with softer flowering grass; cotton wool taken from nearby fields may also be used. Nests are usually placed on low shrubs, though they are often seen below the platform nests of storks or vultures. It also often utilises abandoned nests of the Baya Weaver, and its own disused nests serve as family dormitories through the year for roosting. The usual clutch consists of 4-8 pure white eggs. Incubation and parental duties are shared by both parents, although other birds may be involved in rearing the young. The Indian Silverbill is easily recognized, with its thick conical silver-grey bill, plain earthy brown upperparts and white underparts with buff flanks. The tail is black with white upper tail coverts, and the wings are dark brown, contrasting with a white rump. The tail seems pointed as the length of the tail feathers is maximum at the centre and reduces outwards. The sexes are alike, though the female is duller with a plainer face and less barred flanks. Juvenile birds have buff underparts, dark mottling on rump and a shorter and more rounded tail. Local name: The The Indian Silverbill is known as ‘Charchara, ‘Charga’, Charakka’ or ‘Pidda’ in Hindi, ‘Jinuwayi’ in Telugu, ‘Vayalatta’ in Malayalam, ‘Nellu kuruvi’ in Tamil and ‘Piduri’ or ‘Sar munia’ in Bengali. Habitat & behaviour: The Indian Silverbill is gregarious and usually seen in flocks of up to 60 birds in dry open scrub country. It inhabits dry, open cultivated areas, scrub and bush areas, as well as fallow land, but avoids humid tracts. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 19 Number 4 April 2022 Trip Report: Masinagudi & Nilgiri Forest, Feb 25-27, 2022 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao A view of the Nilgiri Hills from Masinagudi The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve lies within the Nilgiri mountains, which are part of the Western Ghats in southern India. Given its unique location, mountains and water sources, it creates a unique and diverse forest, including habitats ranging from scrub all the way up to moist montane forests. This mix makes this area an important birding hotspot due to its excellent habitat. Shola forests of the Nilgiri Hills My visit was just for two days, and yet I was able to spot close to 135+ birds, indicating the great birding diversity. Given the unique forest, especially around the hills reaching around 8000+ feet, it has many endemic species along with unique migrants coming all the way from the Himalayas to winter here. In fact, these forests are so unique that they are called Sholas and represent tropical montane forests found around these valleys, with patches of grasslands that makes it distinctive and supports varied avifauna. The region has been severely impacted over the last few decades with the proliferation of tea estates, which do looks pretty, but they must have come at the cost of destruction of a good amount of the shola forests. A view of some tea estates at the Nilgiri Hills Masinagudi is a town abutting the Mudumalai National Park and is a good place to halt, to explore both the foothills and the Nilgiris mountains. The tourist influx has been significantly cut down here of late, as several resorts that had sprung up (mostly illegally, on forest land inside the Mudumalai Tiger Reserve buffer zone) have been shut down. There are a lot of homestays with fairly basic facilities, some of which could be operating illegally, too. However, there are, of course, a few resorts being run legally, though with limited capacity. 1

Day 2: Morning session – birded around the foothills and Masinagudi areas followed by a drive to the Ooty Botanical Gardens and back – with birding along the way, of course. This was followed by some more evening birding at Masinagudi foothills. Day 3: Morning session – Started birding early at 5:30AM, to record any Nightjars. Birded in and around Masinagudi scrub forest areas for local birds and raptors. Left Masinagudi by 4:30PM. Spot-bellied Eagle Owl Red-headed Vulture Black-and-Orange Flycatcher White-rumped Vulture Blue-bearded Bee-eater My itinerary Day 1: Arrived at Masinagudi from Mysuru around 5:00PM. Note that entry is not allowed after 6:00PM, so plan accordingly. I still managed about 30 minutes of birding around the homestay, which was in a forested area. Bonelli’s Eagle 2

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Common Snipe (Gallinago gallinago) Common Snipe (Chennai, April 04, 2022) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Gallinago Species: G. gallinago Size: 25-27 cm Description & distribution: The Common Snipe is a mediumsized, stocky member of the Scolopacidae family of sandpipers, curlews and snipes. It is the most common among all the snipes. The upperparts are a dark mottled brown with straw-yellow stripes running down its head, nape and back, while the underparts are white, with some brown markings on throat and flanks. The legs are short and greenish- or brownish-grey in colour. The neck is short, and the dark bill is straight, very long (5.5 to 7cm), and flexible, to enable probing in the mud for its prey. Wings are pointed. It has a dark stripe running through the eye to the sides of the head, with yellowish stripes above and below that serve to demarcate the eye-stripe. Irises are dark brown. The sexes are alike. It is very similar to Wilson’s Snipe of North America, which was until recently considered a sub-species of the Common Snipe. In India, it is also very similar to the Pintail Snipe and the Swinhoe’s Snipe – telling them apart is very difficult unless a view of the spread tail is obtained. One sub-species of the Common Snipe, G. g. faeroeensis, seen in Iceland, Faroe Islands and thereabouts, is more richly toned on its head, upperparts and breast. The nominate race is distributed almost throughout the Palearctic: it breeds in the regions east from Iceland across northern British Isles, northern Portugal, central France, northern Italy, Bulgaria and Ukraine, as well as European Russia and Siberia. In Asia, it breeds in Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Turkestan, the Middle-East, Afghanistan and east to Manchuria; it is also known to breed in north-western India (Kashmir and parts of the Himalayas). European populations winter in southern or western parts of Europe or in Africa, while Asian populations winter in tropical southern Asia, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Migration flights are usually at night. Habitat & behaviour: The Common Snipe is usually seen singly or in small wisps – the collective noun for snipes – of about 5-20, although larger groups numbering several hundred have also been observed at times. It is usually seen in fair proximity of other shorebirds, in wet grassy areas near lakes and rivers, meadows, swamps, marshes, bogs, tundra, rice fields, estuaries and, occasionally, salt pans. It forages in soft mud in small groups, starting early in the morning before it is even fully bright, and feeds mainly on invertebrates: terrestrial and aquatic insects and larvae, worms, crustaceans, molluscs, earthworms, snails and, sometimes, some plant matter. It uses its long bill, which is packed with nerve endings and highly sensitive, to probe for prey on or below the soft mud. It is a very shy bird and tends to freeze and disappear into the grass when it feels threatened. Its cryptic plumage helps it camouflage and blend well with its habitat, often making it difficult to spot from a distance. When flushed, it tends to burst from its cover with an unnerving scape scape squawk, flying away in a twisted, zigzag course before dropping back to cover suddenly. 10

Breeding birds give a repeated hard, sharp jick call when excited, a chip-per call between males and females, and a harsher chip that the male makes when landing to court a female, or the female makes as a male winnows overhead. dives with a loud drumming sound, the mystery of which was unravelled by Philip Manson-Bahr, who worked out that the drumming sound was produced by the snipe holding out two tail feathers at ninety degrees to the direction of flight. The usual clutch consists of four olive-brown or olive-green eggs with a number of dark brown blotches or spots. Incubation is done by the female, but parental duties are shared by both parents. Nesting: The Common Snipe breeds between April and June in most of its breeding range (May-June in India). It is monogamous and highly territorial, but do often show a high degree of promiscuity. The typical nest is usually a shallow depression in a dry spot, concealed in grasses or other vegetation, and lined with grass or plant matter. The male performs an elaborate aerial display during courtship, known as winnowing, flying high in circles and then making shallow Local name: The Common Snipe is known as ‘Chaha’ in Hindi, ‘Muku puredi’ in Telugu, ‘Mor ullan’, ‘Ullan kuruvi’ or ‘Korra kuthi’ in Tamil and ‘Chuntan kata’ in Malayalam. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From Facebook, March 23, 2022) *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 19 Number 5 May 2022 DECCAN BIRDERS: 33rd ANNUAL GENERAL BODY MEETING Minutes of the Meeting Date: Time: Location: May 14, 2022 6:00PM to 8:00PM Vidyaranya High School, Hyderabad  The President, JVD Moorty, started the proceedings by welcoming all members present to the AGM and thanking them for attending.  The quorum required is 20 members as per Bye Law #26. As the quorum was not there, the meeting was adjourned & reconvened after 15 minutes, as per the Bye-Laws.  Meanwhile 3 other members also arrived; the final tally of members present was 22. President’s Address  The President remarked that the last AGM was held on April 27, 2019, and the next AGM would have been due in April 2021. However, the onset of the pandemic in March 2020 threw all schedules haywire. The feasibility of an online AGM was discussed by the Executive Committee, but the modalities appeared complicated and hence it was decided to wait a while till this physical meeting could be held.  He informed the members present of the sad demise of three of our members during the pandemic, and requested that a twominute silence be observed in their memory. The three members are: o G Ashok Kumar o Thomas Rajendra Prasad o D Avinandan  He read out the minutes of the last AGM, held on April 27, 2019. After some discussion on the same, and since no amendments were suggested, Aasheesh Pittie proposed that the minutes be taken as confirmed, and the same was seconded by Humayun Taher. Secretary’s Report  The Secretary, Surekha A, shared the details of the field trips, indoor meetings and other activities for the past three years (2019-2022).  A total of 11 indoor meetings were held in 2019. There were no indoor meetings in 2020 and 2021.  Since the pandemic had put a stop to all gatherings, a series of webinars had been organised in lieu of the field trips and indoor meetings. Between April 2019 and November 2021, a total of 44 webinars were organised, involving experts in their fields (Ornithology, Zoology, etc); they delivered fascinating talks on a range of topics of interest to our members.  The highlight, and truly a session to remember, was a very lively one-on-one interactive session with Richard Grimmett, Carol and Tim Inskipp, the authors of the field guide, Birds of the Indian Subcontinent. 1

 Other activities included the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) in 2021 (on a small scale) and 2022, and the HSBC Bird Race (which saw the final session being conducted online).  The support given by the German Centre (Goethe Zentrum) to the society in organising indoor meetings at their centre was placed on record. Treasurer’s Report  In the absence of the Treasurer, Dr Krishna Nagarajan, who was unable to attend the AGM, the Vice-President, K Bharadwaj presented the accounts for the period April 2019-March 2020 and April 2020-March 2021.  Members present were given a copy of the audited Balance Sheet and Profit & Loss statements (attached below).  Income for the society included Fixed Deposit interest income, Membership fees, and Income from Sale of merchandise (Deccan Birders T-Shirts & Caps).  Expenses for the society showed a decline as the pandemic prevented many activities from being taken up.  Details of various expenses over the intervening period were shared by the Vice-President during the course of the presentation.  A couple of queries were put forth by members. Aasheesh Pittie enquired about the hosting and other charges for the website. Humayun enquired about tax-saving procedures being adopted by the Society and suggested a few measures for the same.  The present auditors for the Society are CKS Associates. It was suggested by the President that the Society continue with the same auditors for the forthcoming period. The same was proposed by Nanda Kumar and seconded by Aasheesh Pittie.  The accounts for the said two years were taken as read. This was proposed by Aasheesh Pittie and seconded by Rajashekar Tummala. Membership Update & Pitta  Umesh Mani, who maintains the member database and the e-group, gave the members present an update on the current membership of the Society, which stands at a grand total of 502 members, of which 444 are Life Members. The number of egroup members stands at 428.  Aasheesh Pittie proposed that the Pitta be made available to non-members as well. The President acknowledged the same and said that the Executive Committee would take it under advisement.  Aasheesh Pittie placed on record his appreciation for the amount of work being done by the editors of Pitta in ensuring its high quality and regular publication every month; the same sentiment was echoed by other members present. Other Matters  Shafaat Ulla proposed that Aasheesh Pittie be made President Emeritus of the Society. This suggestion was enthusiastically and vociferously received by the members. Aasheesh, however, very graciously declined to accept the offer with the remark that a doyen of ornithology had already been conferred with this status, and he felt it would not be right for him to accept it.  Humayun Taher suggested reviving the tradition of honouring conservation efforts by members and proposed the name of K Mrutyumjaya Rao as the first recipient of the honour, which was seconded by Aasheesh Pittie.  Dr Ajit Kumar suggested instituting an annual award in the name of a senior Deccan Birders member, which was seconded by Surekha A. Aasheesh Pittie, however, suggested that the award should be in the name of Deccan Birders and not a specific person, and also that it should be ad hoc (awarded whenever there was a deserving person) and not necessarily an annual conferral.  Aasheesh Pittie was very vocal about the role Deccan Birders plays in society and said that the data gathered on birds during the AWC and other activities is not just the property of the Society, but should be shared with any organisation who may request for such data from time to time. Deccan Birders, he said, is firstly and finally a birdwatching society. Dr Ajit Kumar also pointed out that there was no legal liability in sharing the data with others.  Rajashekar Tummala raised three points: o He reported that the University of Hyderabad noted the poaching of Peafowl on their campus and wanted to know how the Society could help to prevent this 2

o o He also said that there exists a toll-free number for reporting the use of Chinese manja in kite strings; he proposed that the same be publicised on the website and in the Pitta, especially during the Sankranti period He suggested that Deccan Birders should approach the Posts & Telegraphs Department for the release of a Special Cover celebrating four decades of Deccan Birders. This suggestion was enthusiastically received by the members  Srikanth Bhamidipati implored members to participate and get involved more actively in the activities of the Society, to make it more visible and spread awareness of conservation to a wider spectrum of population.  As Surekha A had announced her decision to step down from the Executive Committee and from the position of Secretary, the President placed on record his appreciation for her contribution to the activities of the Society during the difficult pandemic times. Surekha, in her response, thanked all the members present and also the Executive Committee for their cooperation in all matters official. New Executive Committee (for the period 2022-2024)  The term of the existing Executive Committee came to an end with this AGM. To oversee the election of a new Executive Committee, Humayun Taher was made the Returning Officer.  As per the Bye-Laws of the Society, the outgoing Executive Committee is expected to suggest names of people for the next term of the Executive Committee. For this purpose, outgoing Executive Committee suggested the following names to continue as Executive Committee members: o o o o o o o o JVD Moorty K Bharadwaj Dr Krishna Nagarajan Umesh Mani Srikanth Bhamidipati Sagarika Melkote Gowthama Poludasu Sudhir Moorti  In addition, two places had fallen vacant with the resignation of Vinay Kumar Akula and Surekha A. In response to an earlier call for nominations to the Executive Committee, sent out to the members of the Society, two nominations had been received – from Gokul Krishna Addanki and Sathvik Reddy.  Since there were only ten nominations received for the ten-member Executive Committee, the Returning Officer declared the above-mentioned ten persons elected.  As per the Bye-Laws of the Society, the new Executive Committee, in their first meeting, would decide amongst themselves the names of the various office-bearers. Vote of Thanks  In his summing up, the President then re-emphasised that Deccan Birders had been successful in building a degree of global visibility, especially during the series of webinars over the past two years – wherein we had been able to secure the contribution and participation of several luminaries of the ornithology world, as well as the attendance of participants from countries as far and wide as the Philippines, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, South Africa and the Americas. He exhorted the members to work for greater recognition of the Society.  He expressed his thanks to the members of the outgoing Executive Committee for their dedication and service to the Society during the term gone by, and expressed the hope and confidence that the incoming Executive Committee would strive to take the Society forward to even greater heights.  The meeting was closed with a vote of thanks to Vidyaranya High School for providing the room, amenities and personnel for the AGM, and to all the members present at the meeting. 3

Trip Report: Pulicat Lake Bird Sanctuary, March 2022 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla A view of Pulicat Lake The Pulicat Lake Bird Sanctuary is situated partly in Andhra Pradesh and partly in Tamil Nadu. The lake is fed by the river Arani in the southern tip and the Kalangi river in the North west. The lake is a rich source of aquatic life forms such as prawns and fish. Many migratory birds stop over at the lake. Be it the terns and gulls, or the waders like curlews, whimbrels and flamingoes, or the storks and pelicans, you get to see them in large numbers here. The largest of the wading birds, the Greater Flamingo, is seen visiting the sanctuary in thousands. There were only a few of them on the Tamil Nadu side of the lake when we visited in mid-March. However, a few weeks earlier we had seen thousands of flamingoes near Meezuru village on the Andhra Pradesh side of the lake – but that is a story for another day. Caspian Tern Our boatman was a very enterprising guide and took care not to miss any bird. He maneuvered the boat deftly around the lake and showed us most birds from a safe distance so as not to disturb them. He also took care to stop at the right spot so that lighting is ideal for photography. Greater Crested Tern, Lesser Crested Tern and Caspian Tern Our visit to the Tamil Nadu side of the lake was mainly to see the varieties of terns and waders that we were informed would be on view. We spent about two and a half hours boating around the lake. The Greater Crested Tern was the first to be sighted, and close on the heels of this sighting were the Lesser Crested Terns. The main differences between them are the size of the bird and the color of the beak – while the former is bigger with a yellow beak, the latter is smaller and sports an orange beak. Next was the Caspian Tern, the largest tern in the world, which is easily recognizable by its prominent orange-red bill with a black tip. We saw two of them from close range and, a little further ahead of them, were flocks of Little Terns and Whiskered Terns. Little Tern On the sand bars were Sanderlings, Greater and Lesser Sand Plovers, Terek and Curlew Sandpipers, a few Eurasian Curlews and Whimbrels, as well as a lone juvenile Pallas’s Gull. I was happy that we were able to get some very good pictures. 8

Sanderling Pacific Golden Plover Brown-headed Gull Terek Sandpiper As we moved further to the broader sandbars, we saw flocks of Brown-headed Gulls, some terns once again of different types, and a rare sighting of the Eurasian Oystercatcher, standing distinctly among them. Apparently, it is rarely sighted at that time of the year, may be having stayed longer due to the abundance of food. The Terek Sandpipers were very actively foraging. Just then, a White-bellied Sea Eagle glided past above us, and it was a great sight. Though the heat was building up after mid-day, we continued with our birding for a while, as we were thrilled to see so much bird activity. Overall it was a fantastic trip for us with four lifers. At another point of the lagoon, we had an amazing sighting of a colony of Pacific Golden Plovers, around thirty-five of them, or possibly more, well-camouflaged in the golden sands. We had never seen so many of them at one place and were able to get some good pictures and videos. In between the Golden Plovers were the Greater and Lesser Sand Plovers. Trip Report: Ramadevarabatta WLS & Cauvery WLS, Karnataka, Feb 19-22, 2022 Text & Photos: Umesh Mani Entrance to the Ramadevarabatta Wildlife Sanctuary In mid-Feb 2022, three of us – Dr Arun and Mrs Vasanthi, birder friends from Chennai, and I – decided to undertake a quick trip to Ramadevarabatta WLS and Cauvery WLS in Karnataka. Ramadevarabatta WLS is well known as one of the few breeding locations of the Long-billed (or Indian) Vulture in South India, and we were hopeful of spotting not just this, but other Vultures as well as other raptor species. The journey to Ramanagara – the station where we need to disembark for the Ramadevarabatta WLS – is a very convenient one from Chennai – a late-evening train gets us to Ramanagara early the next morning, in time to freshen up and start birding. cliff; Sasi informed us that they had continued to breed in the same area for the past several years. We had been watching them for a few minutes when my attention was caught by a brownish bird preening in the clutter of a tree nearby. On checking, I was happy to find that it was the Sirkeer Malkoha – this was a bird that I had seen so many times, but never managed to photograph properly, and this sighting kindled my hopes again! Ramanagara is a fairly nondescript, generic town like the hundred other such towns that have come up along our National Highways. However, Ramanagara has a unique claim to fame – this is where possibly the most iconic and pathbreaking Hindi movie of all time, Sholay, had been filmed. The walls outside the railway station bear witness to this, with several scenes from the movie painted all over. We reached Ramanagara as planned, excited about what sightings were in store for us. We were fortunate to have the assistance of a local birder friend, Sasi, who had made the necessary arrangements for our trip. Day-1: Feb 19, 2022, morning session: Ramadevarabatta WLS White-browed Bulbul After freshening up at Sasi’s place, we had to wait a little as our vehicle had got delayed. So we decided to start birding nearby, and quickly chalked up a few nice species – Whitecheeked Barbet, Jerdon’s Leafbird, etc. Then the vehicle arrived and we headed off to the sanctuary. As soon as we entered, we saw a pair of Indian Vultures up on a cliff. On a visit a few years ago, we had seen the Vultures on the same We tracked and followed it for a while as it hopped from tree to tree before finally disappearing over a small rocky hillock. Still no photos for me, and I wondered if this was to be another of those days. Anyway, moving on, we ticked off the Redvented and White-browed Bulbuls, Laughing Dove, Purple Sunbird etc, before settling down to watch the Vultures for some more time. We were now a little closer to the cliff, and the views were somewhat better. 10

Long-billed (aka Indian) Vulture Puff-throated Babbler with nesting material Walking ahead, we saw the females of the Purple-rumped Sunbird and Golden Oriole, and a Red-whiskered Bulbul – but still not the Bulbul that is a specialty of the Western Ghats – the Yellow-browed. A pair of Jerdon’s Leafbirds and a Greenish Warbler also made their presence felt. Blue-faced Malkoha with prey Jerdon’s Leafbird Greenish Warbler A little further, we came upon a patch of forest that was completely covered with fallen dry leaves. Hearing some rustling, we stopped to check, and found a pair of Puffthroated Babblers moving around there foraging, as well as sometimes collecting nesting material. It was nice to know that this beautiful Babbler was nesting in the area. Suddenly, there was a bit of commotion in the trees above and, looking up, we saw a Blue-faced Malkoha – and one more – and then one more! It was a veritable party, as they hopped all around, looking for caterpillars. I saw one of them catch what seemed to be an alate (termite with wings), and another grab a moth, which they proceeded to consume with great relish. Sirkeer Malkoha But they were soon upstaged by the arrival of – the Sirkeer! A pair of them hung around for a while – this time, for a change, in the open branches of a dry tree, and in good light to boot – and I finally managed to get some photos of the Sirkeer – not perfect, but decent, and my first in more than sixteen years of birding! Naturally I was happy. After a few minutes, the Sirkeer Malkohas decided that they had obliged me enough, and flew off. 11

done with us – as we were leaving, we were blessed with a view of a Shaheen Falcon that also seemed to have made its home in the same cliffs. Sasi witnessed the mating of the Long-billed Vultures, which the rest of us unfortunately missed. At a small pond near the sanctuary gates, we also saw the Common and White-throated Kingfishers. That was it for the morning. We then got back to the room after a quick lunch en route, washed up and started off for Cauvery. Day-1: Feb 19, 2022, afternoon session: Cauvery WLS Polypedates sp At a small Forest Department building nearby, we saw a frog that turned out to be a member of the Polypedates genus of Tree and Shrub frogs. The delicately coloured frog was quite beautiful. At the same place, we saw a huge mass of the Daddy Longlegs spiders (Pholcidae sp). It was quite incredible – I had never seen so many spiders together earlier! The Cauvery WLS covers an area of around 1025 hectares and is located at the junction of Mandya, Chamarajnagar and Ramanagara districts of Karnataka. It has a unique combination of riverine, dry deciduous and tropical dry thorn forests, and hence is home to a good variety of birds. We reached the Cauvery WLS around 3:00PM. Sasi had made arrangements for us to stay at an ecotourism resort near the sanctuary at Bhimeshwari, so we dropped off our bags there, had a quick cup of tea and took off for birding. It was too late to go to any of the main forest areas, as the light was expected to fade in a couple of hours, so we decided to bird near the resort, which was on the banks of the Cauvery (aka Kaveri) River. Black-hooded Oriole Daddy Longlegs spider (Pholcidae sp) Common Iora Shaheen Falcon We then started walking back, since we had to move on from Ramanagara to Cauvery WLS that afternoon, a three-hour drive away, and hoped to get in at least a couple of hours birding in the evening. However, the sanctuary was not yet The list for the afternoon session started with a handful of commoners – a pair of Black-hooded Orioles, along with a Common Kingfisher, a Common Iora, a Red-rumped Swallow, and several White-browed Wagtails. Then we came upon the first special sighting of the evening – the beautiful Chestnut-headed Bee-eater. It was quite distant, though. 12

White-browed Wagtail Grizzled Giant Squirrel Grey Junglefowl female White-bellied Drongo After watching it to our hearts’ content, we returned to our resort, where we saw a pair of Grey Junglefowl within the premises. This was to be a regular sight over the next couple of days – although we never did manage to photograph them properly. Day-2: Feb 20, 2022: Cauvery WLS Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker We took a short drive to a nearby patch of forest, where we notched up several White-bellied Drongos and a Browncapped Pygmy Woodpecker. Nearby, on the river, we saw a lovely Woolly-necked Stork. As we walked around, we got lucky and came upon a beautiful specimen of something that normally takes some finding – the Grizzled Giant Squirrel! While the area is known for this Squirrel (Ratufa macroura), it is not so easy to locate it, and we thanked our stars that we had chanced upon it like this. Although the Squirrel was feeding, it also seemed to be curious about us, especially at the beginning, and spent a few moments staring at us – giving us a good view, too, and a good opportunity to take some photos. A view of the Cauvery River from Bhimeshwari We started the day with birding at the river bank near the resort. The first bird we saw was a fairly uncommon one for us – the Stork-billed Kingfisher – along with its cousin, the Common Kingfisher. A couple of trees in the middle of the river were loaded with Great and Little Cormorants, which had presumably roosted there overnight. There was a small stream parallel to the main river, which presently was dry. As we walked on the bed, we came upon a curious structure which was like a mound made of cement, with lots of stones stuck on it. We could not figure out what its purpose might be – one of the possibly wild theories was that maybe it was meant to act as a breakwater in case of floods! Strangely, it also had an electrical cable running across its top. 13

Pied Kingfisher The structure in the dry stream bed Oriental Turtle Dove Green Imperial Pigeon As we walked along, a raucous flock of Green Imperial Pigeons arrived, and we had the opportunity to feast our eyes and take a few photographs. A Mugger slowly glided past on the river, reminding us that we should be careful about venturing too close. Woolly-necked Stork A Woolly-necked Stork flew lazily past, allowing us to admire its fluffy looks. River Terns were active on the river, and so were a group of Rhesus Macaques on the river bank. We witnessed a mock fight, with a couple of them hissing and making faces at each other. Mugger A pair of Pied Kingfishers were actively hunting – it was interesting to watch them as they made a few sorties from their perch on a bare stick in the middle of the river. Oriental Turtle Doves turned out to be quite common in the area, and we had plenty of close encounters with them. River Tern 14

Rhesus Macaque Then came the sighting I personally had been waiting for – my first lifer of the trip, the Lesser Fish Eagle. Sasi located a nest in a tree on the other side of the river but, in spite of all attempts, I could not see the nest, although we did see the pair of eagles carry twigs to the nest a few times. The action was way too far, and in the midst of a lot of clutter, to be able to take good photographs, and I was a little disappointed. Sasi informed us that the eagles do occasionally come across to this side of the river too. Another view of the Cauvery River It was only around 9:30AM, but it was already quite hot. Realising that the action was probably over for now, Sasi and I decided to walk back, and look for more birds en route. Almost immediately, I came upon a couple of Chestnutheaded Bee-eaters, closer this time, and I was able to get some decent photographs. After a half hour or so, the others decided to walk around a little, and look for other birds. I decided to stay put, however, hoping that the eagles would oblige me with a better view at some point. After nearly an hour of waiting, I was beginning to wonder if they would ever move out, when one of them decided to take pity on me, and flew over to another tree – still on the other side of the river, but a more bare and exposed tree, so at least I could see the eagle properly. And, in spite of the distance, I took quite a few photographs – after all, it was a lifer! Chestnut-headed Bee-eater Lesser Fish Eagle Like most raptors, the call of the Lesser Fish Eagle is a most unlikely-sounding one, but quite piercing nevertheless. I heard this individual calling away, possibly to convince his mate to take a break from nesting duties. However, she did not oblige and, after a fairly long but fruitless period, this eagle flew back to the nest. Stork-billed Kingfisher We also saw another Stork-billed and a Common Kingfisher. Moving along, we were informed that a Brown Hawk Owl was present in one of the trees nearby. As we approached, we saw our friends there, craning their necks to get a view. However, it was directly overhead and almost at the top of the tree, making it impossible to see properly. 15

In the evening, a couple of Forest Department staff told us about a watchtower atop a small hillock a few kilometres away, and took us there; this afforded a great view of the sweeping expanse of the Cauvery River. Common Kingfisher View of the Cauvery River from the watchtower There weren’t too many birds there, although one interesting species we saw was the Crested Treeswift – I was seeing this bird after several years, and it was very satisfying to watch them in action. Around 4-5 of them were flying around, accompanied by a couple of Red-rumped Swallows. Brown Hawk Owl Crested Treeswift After some time, the Forest Department staff asked us if we would like to walk down the hillock and along the river, back to the resort. The others took up their offer, while I decided to drive back and bird near the river. Initially there was nothing much to see, and I perched myself on the sand near the river, all the time keeping an eye out for the Mugger! A few Cormorants and River Terns later, I shifted my spot a little further, and saw the Mugger basking in the evening sun on a rock in the middle of the river. He looked like he was quite enjoying himself! Agama (Psammophilus sp) White-browed Wagtails were aplenty, including a few juveniles. We also saw a young Agama (Psammophilus sp). We then had a few hours to kill before embarking on the evening session. A quick nap before lunch seemed to be in order, although when I woke up, I was surprised to note that Arun had instead gone for a long solo walk, lugging his heavy gear, in the hot sun! Mugger basking 16

I saw a few Sand Martins flying around over the river, hawking insects in flight. There was also a Macaque with half an arm missing – I wondered at the events that led up to that. By now the sun was beginning to go down, and the others also arrived. I was relieved to hear that that I didn’t miss any special sightings! We then retired to the rooms to charge our batteries and recharge ourselves. Tomorrow was going to be an important day – Sasi told us that we would drive towards some other patches of forest that were usually quite productive. Day-3: Feb 21, 2022: Cauvery WLS We started off around 7:00AM and immediately saw a Grey Junglefowl on the side of the road. We did not stop, however, as we had a lot of ground to cover today. The first sighting in the forest was a pair of Crested Serpent Eagles. This was followed almost immediately by a pair of Darters on the river, and the customary Mugger. Green Bee-eater We were puzzled to see some cattle on an island in the river, and wondered how they had got there. A basking Green Beeeater gave good views, a Jerdon’s Bushlark scuttled among the dry grass, and a couple of Indian Silverbills also came by. Crested Serpent Eagle Jerdon’s Bushlark Suddenly we saw a Shikra inside the tangle of the scrub which turned out to be not a Shikra but a Common Hawk Cuckoo! It allowed us to watch for a few seconds before hopping deeper into the scrub. Darter Common Hawk Cuckoo Cattle on the island 17

Greater Spotted Eagle Short-toed Snake Eagle A Short-toed Snake Eagle put in an appearance, circling around a few times before moving away. A Steppe Eagle preened itself on a tree, engaging us for a while. A few Crested Treeswifts made their presence felt. Another Greater Spotted Eagle perched right at the tip of a dead tree had us puzzled for a while. We also saw a Black Eagle in the distance. Grey Langur Then came the first of the raptors – a Greater Spotted Eagle perched on the top of a small tree. It took off after a while, and we drove on. Red-rumped Swallows were aplenty. A Grey (aka Hanuman) Langur sat, arms akimbo, bang in the middle of the track. We stopped to watch it for a while, and Arun felt that it was playing watchman – keeping an eye out for predators while the rest of his group moved to safety. Happy at the slew of raptor sightings – although quite confused! – we drove on. We came to a small eco-camp run by the Jungle Lodges; they told us that an Indian Scops Owl was there, and very kindly allowed us to enter their premises to take a look. It was comfortably ensconced in a small tree hollow, and seemed to be fast asleep. As we approached, the owl cracked open one eye, took a look at us, then went back to sleep. We watched it for a while and took a few record shots. We weren’t really satisfied, as the angle was far from ideal – but an owl is an owl! Indian Scops Owl We also got some really good views of a Grizzled Giant Squirrel, which foraged for a while before settling down, seemingly to sun itself. Then we drove ahead. A Jerdon’s Bushlark was seen well by the track, and a very plain-looking Pipit had us puzzled. It was later identified as a Blyth’s Pipit. Steppe Eagle 18

Many-keeled Grass Skink We stopped at a restaurant for breakfast, and saw a beautiful Skink which was later identified as a young Keeled Indian Mabuya (Eutropis carinata), also known as the Many-keeled Grass Skink or 'Golden Skink'. View at Sangam We came to a place called Sangam which, as the name suggests, is the confluence of the Cauvery and Arkavathi rivers. There were a number of pilgrims taking a holy dip in the water, but there were also some birds on some sandbars a little way away. I stayed back on this shore, while Sasi and Arun decided to make the crossing, wading through waistdeep water with all their gear! It turned out to be well worth their effort, though, as they got excellent views of a pair of Small Pratincoles. House Sparrow adult (L) and young (R) While we were waiting, we heard a commotion outside the window, and saw a young House Sparrow demanding to be fed. Like most youngsters, this one too was perfectly peaceful while the parent was away – but at the first sight of the parent, the racket would start again! We got to watch the young one being fed at least 2-3 times before it came our turn to feed. Small Pratincole Red Hairy Caterpillar (Amsacta albistriga) We also saw another pair of House Sparrows mating – breeding season seemed to be in full swing. White-browed Wagtail pair I saw a pair of White-browed Wagtails engaged in what seemed to be a courtship ritual, as they flew around each other, darting at each other and occasionally bumping into each other in flight. I also saw another ‘one-armed bandit’ – a Macaque with a truncated arm. This was the second one I was seeing in two days, and I wondered what might be the reasons. Results of a fight or a predator attack, maybe? 19

Driving on, we came across a wooded patch where we saw the Brown-capped Pygmy and Yellow-fronted Woodpeckers and several White-bellied Drongos. One-armed Rhesus Macaque We then decided to drive on, and came across a pair of Yellowwattled Lapwings, one of which seemed to be incubating. We did not get down from the vehicle, not wanting to disturb or scare the birds – but we did get to see one of them engaging in a broken-wing display! It was amazing to watch. Grizzled Giant Squirrel peeling a Sweet Lime We came to another Jungle Lodges property, this one at Galibore. Here we saw another Grizzled Giant Squirrel, which was busily stripping the peel off a Sweet Lime – the dexterity with which it handled the fruit, turning it round and round as it removed the peel, was incredible. One of the staff told us that it was a female, and was going to take the fruit to feed its young. It was afternoon and getting on for the time we needed to start moving back towards Ramanagara for our night train back to Chennai, but we still had an hour or so, and decided to try and spend some time at a spot on the Cauvery where Smoothcoated Otters were said to be seen every now and then. Yellow-wattled Lapwing broken wing display A couple of Indian Rollers were also around, hunting actively. We saw them make repeated sallies in the air and to the ground, picking up insects. View from ‘Otter Point’ Indian Roller Cinereous Tit We stopped for a quick lunch at a roadside eatery, and saw a flock of Small Minivets hopping around in the nearby trees. 20

We did get a few glimpses of the Otters, but not enough to feel satisfied about. While we were waiting, I walked around a little, looking for birds. I managed to notch up a few more species – Common Woodshrike, Shikra, Cinereous Tit, another Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker – and another pair of Lesser Fish Eagles! This time they flew past pretty close by – as if to say goodbye. It had been a bit of a whirlwind trip, but quite productive. For me personally, besides my two lifers – the Lesser Fish Eagle and the Grizzled Giant Squirrel – there had been a bunch of other interesting sightings, and there were so many areas not yet explored. We left with the feeling that we would be back soon… fingers crossed! Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Streak-throated Swallow (Petrochelidon fluvicola) Streak-throated Swallow (Rollapadu, October 12, 2019) Order: Passeriformes Family: Hirundinidae Genus: Petrochelidon Species: P. fluvicola Size: 11-12 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Streak-throated Swallow is usually found in medium to large congregations in cultivated areas and open country near water; and near rivers, moats, canals, reservoirs and lakes, where it is usually seen hawking midges and other insects via aerial sorties, often close over water, and usually in the company of other swallows and House Swifts. In winters, they are often seen in groups of up to several hundreds, perched on telephone wires in close-packed lines and sunning themselves. Its usual call is a twittering chirp, and a sharp trr trr may be uttered in flight. Description & distribution: The Streak-throated Swallow, also known as the Indian Cliff Swallow, is a resident species of swallow across most of its range, which extends from Afghanistan and Pakistan east through Jammu & Kashmir, along the base of the Himalayas (including Nepal), all the way to the Sikkim Dooars and Bangladesh; and south across the entire Indian peninsula to about 10⁰N (Point Calimere). Besides, it is occasionally reported as a vagrant from Maldives, Sri Lanka and the Middle East. It was originally placed in the genus Hirundo. Nesting: The Streak-throated Swallow breeds almost across the year, but mainly from December to April and July to October. It is a colonial nester; the nest is an agglomeration of mud, with several 'pots' fused together, each with a short tunnel entrance. Nests are usually built under bridges over canals or gateway arches etc, usually near water, and often within urban boundaries. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 eggs, normally white but sometimes with brownish smudges. The Streak-throated Swallow, like most other swallows, is glossy steel-blue above, and has a pale brown rump, lightlystreaked mantle, dull chestnut forehead and crown. The underparts are whitish with bold brown streaking on chin, throat and upper breast. The tail is long, broad and squarish with a slight fork, much like the Dusky Crag Martin. The sexes are alike. The juvenile has a duller, browner crown and a brown-toned mantle and wings with buff fringes. Local name: The Streak-throated Swallow is known as ‘Nahar ababil’ in Hindi, ‘Nahari ababil’ in Punjabi, and ‘Bhekhad ababil’ or ‘Nanu tharodiyu’ in Gujarati. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 24 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report: Bhavnagar, Gujarat, March 11-12, 2022 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla A scene at Bor Talav Lake The city of Bhavnagar is situated on the south eastern tip of Saurashtra region of Gujarat state. A short trip to Bhavnagar came our way in the second week of March and though it was the fag end of winter, we thought we will make the trip anyway. Before leaving we went through the checklists of birds at various places in Bhavnagar and decided to visit Bor Talav Lake, Velavadar National Park and Nalsarovar Bird Sanctuary. The next step was to identify reliable guides who would show us around in the limited time that we had. 1

We came to know that a vagrant Red-breasted Goose was at Nalsarovar and were very keen to see it. We put up in a place very close to the Bor Talav Lake, also known as the Gowrishankar Lake. The man-made lake, measuring 381 hectares in area, is home to many endemic and migratory birds. It is a scenic spot with a walkway on the bund and a pier stretching into the lake. Walking on the beautiful lake bund, we scanned the waters and, lo and behold, the first birds that came in our view were none other than the Great Crested Grebes that we had been trying hard to see without any luck for nearly two years! Whiskered Tern Above us were flocks of Black-headed and Brown-headed Gulls and Whiskered Terns. At one point some people were seen feeding the gulls and terns; the birds were seen picking up this food and landing on the pier nearby. All along the bund, there were hundreds of Yellow Wagtails in their breeding colors. After a sumptuous lunch we went back to the lake to checklist the birds and to also see the sunset. There were three to four islets on the lake where the gulls settled down for roosting. Great Crested Grebe The Great Crested Grebes were spotted along with Tufted Ducks, Eurasian Wigeons, Knob-billed Ducks, Eurasian Coots and Spot-billed Ducks. There were eight of them that we could count and, the lighting being perfect, we clicked some great pictures and videos. It took us quite a while to photograph them as they would dive under the water and surface in a completely new place! Montagu’s Harrier Early next morning we drove to the Velavadar National Park, which was just an hour’s drive from Bhavnagar. Though the Montagu’s and Pallid Harriers winter here in good numbers, the guide informed us that most of them had already left for their breeding grounds. Tufted Duck He, however, was keen on showing us the Indian Wolf, Striped Hyena and the Jungle Cat, besides some wetland birds. The 34 sq km park is home to the endangered Lesser Florican and its conservation, along with the conservation of the Indian Wolf and Blackbuck, is an ongoing program at the park. Black-headed and Brown-headed Gulls Blackbuck 2

We then went on to the wetland side of the park and here we saw a huge flock of Demoiselle Cranes in all their grandeur. They landed at the waterbody in front of us, where the Greater Flamingos, Pied Avocets, Eurasian Spoonbills, Great White Pelicans and other waders were already foraging. Huge flocks of Demoiselle Cranes were also seen in flight moving to other areas in the park. The Great White Pelicans, on the other hand, were seen circling in the sky. Indian Wolf After a quick lunch we set off to Nalsarovar, which was more than 100 km away. The guide there was waiting for us and he took us around the wetland in a boat. It was a fascinating boat ride of almost 45 minutes gliding through the reeds with the atmosphere reverberating with various bird calls. The Indian Wolves at Velavadar prey on Blackbuck in the park. The guide sighted one wolf that was in the open, and told us that it was preparing to hunt. It was exciting, as it was our first sighting of a wolf in the wild. Further on, we also spotted a Jungle Cat that was so well camouflaged that we could not have seen it but for the keen eyes of the guide. Red-breasted Goose and Bar-headed Goose Jungle Cat The raptors in the grassland side of the park included two Short-toed Snake Eagles, one Montagu’s Harrier, one Pallid Harrier, one Greater Spotted Eagle and two Marsh Harriers. Finally, we arrived at the point where the Red-breasted Goose was present, and the boatman parked the boat noiselessly behind a patch of reeds. From here we could clearly see the goose. There it was, along with six Bar-headed Geese, foraging on the sandbar. It was an amazing view point and we watched the geese for a full five minutes before they flew away. The guide said that the goose had first visited Nalsarovar in January 2021, and was later also sighted at Little Rann of Kutch in November 2021. As daylight began to fade, we began to row back. On the way we saw many Garganey, Green-winged Teals, Small Pratincole, Collared Pratincole, Dunlin, Black-tailed Godwits, Northern Shovelers and Northern Pintails. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Black-winged Stilt (Himantopus himantopus) Black-winged Stilt adult (L) (Gujarat, February 8, 2019) and chick (R) (Chennai, August 22, 2021) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Recurvirostridae Genus: Himantopus Species: H. himantopus Size: 35-40 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Black-winged Stilt is usually found in scattered small to medium groups, in flooded tropical and subtropical grasslands, montane wetlands, coastal lagoons, marine, brackish and freshwater lakes, saltpans, tidal mudflats, estuaries, marshes, swamps, rivers, streams and creeks; also in irrigated or flooded agricultural lands, fish ponds and canals, up to about 4200m altitude. Usually seen walking gracefully and deliberately, its diet consists mainly of aquatic invertebrates, including fish, crustaceans, aquatic and terrestrial insects, molluscs, spiders, worms and amphibians, which it picks off the surface of the water, or by immersing its head and probing the shallow waters for prey; it may also occasionally take seeds from aquatic vegetation. Its flight is weak and involves fairly heavy flapping, with neck extended and legs trailing behind the tail, and the usual call is a squeaky, piping chek chek chek or kwik kwik kwik, uttered when alarmed and in flight. Description & distribution: A very widely distributed member of the Recurvirostridae family of Avocets and Stilts, the Black-winged Stilt is an easily identifiable, very long-legged wader with black upperparts and long thin bill, white underparts, pink legs and deep red or reddish brown irises. The head and neck are primarily white with quite a marked variation in the amount of black or dusky grey on crown and mantle, between the subspecies as well as between summer and winter. The black wings may sometimes show a greenish gloss. Females are somewhat browner on the back, contrasting with black remiges. Immature birds are usually grey rather than black, with a sandy tone to the wings, and light feather fringes showing as a whitish line when in flight. The Black-winged Stilt is distributed across most parts of the world, including Asia, Africa, Australia, Europe, North and South America. The nominate subspecies, H. h. himantopus, is seen across Africa, Madagascar, Europe, central Asia, Russia, China, Mongolia, Taiwan, Indochina, South-east Asia, Borneo and Philippines; in India, it is seen in almost all the states except possibly the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Nesting: The breeding season of the Black-winged Stilt varies widely over its range. In India, the Black-winged Stilt breeds mainly from April to August, and the nest is a depression on the ground on the fringes of a lake, or a raised platform of pebbles or small stones in shallow water or amongst grass or sedge, lined with vegetable matter, soft reeds etc. It is also known to breed in large colonies, as sometimes seen in heronries. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 eggs, drab off-white or cream, with dense black blotches. The other four subspecies are H. h. leucocephalus, seen in Sumatra, Java, New Guinea, Australia and New Zealand; H. h. knudseni of the Hawaiian islands; H. h. melanurus of South America, and H. h. mexicanus, seen in North America, parts of the Caribbean, and South America. Local name: The Black-winged Stilt is known as ‘Gaz paon’ or ‘Gaj paon’ in Hindi and Gujarati, ‘Pavalla kaal ullan’ or ‘Paduva kali’ in Tamil, ‘Pavizhakkali’ in Malayalam and ‘Kalpaksh prawalpad’ in Sanskrit. *** For Private Circulation Only 6 Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Red-necked Falcon (Falco chicquera) Red-necked Falcon (Gujarat, December 29, 2021) Order: Falconiformes Family: Falconidae Genus: Falco Species: F. chicquera Size: 31-36 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Red-necked Falcon, also called Redheaded Falcon or Red-headed Merlin, prefers open plains and scrub country around villages and cultivated areas. Its flight is strong and fast, and the pair often hunts cooperatively, usually at dawn and dusk, with one heading off the prey while the other attacks and strikes it down. Its diet consists mainly of small birds, rodents (e.g. rats, mice, squirrels), lizards and insects, though it may also occasionally take bats. Its usual call is a high-pitched ki-ki-ki-ki-ki, but it may also utter a rasping yak, yak, yak or a screaming tiririri, tiriririeee. Description & distribution: A mid-sized bird of prey, the Rednecked Falcon is known to have two separate populations, one in Africa and the other in India. The nominate, Falco chicquera chicquera, is the Indian subspecies, and has a distinctive rufous crown, nape and narrow moustachial stripe, bluish-grey wings and upperparts with fine dark barring, yellow legs, ceres and eye-ring, a clear throat, and white underparts with light, narrow blackish or brownish barring. At rest, the wingtips do not reach the tip of the tail, which is white-tipped and has narrow black bars with a broad black subterminal band. The bill is yellow with a black tip. The African subspecies, F. c. ruficollis, is sometimes considered a full species (Falco ruficollis) and is quite similar except that it has pale grey wings and upperparts, the face is white with black chinstraps passing through the eyes, and a rufous foreneck band that is not present in the Indian subspecies. The sexes are alike, with the female being a little bigger.The juvenile is similar but darker, with fine streaking on head and fine rufous fringes to upperparts and underparts. Nesting: The Red-necked Falcon breeds mainly from January to May. The nest is a well-made cup or platform of twigs lined with grass and roots, built up in a tree or on top of a building, but it also often uses old twig nests of other birds. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 eggs, pale reddish-white, thickly speckled with reddish brown. It is bold and aggressive during nesting season, and may attack and chase away even bigger birds that may wander near the tree where it is nesting. Local name: The Red-necked Falcon is known as ‘Turimti’ or ‘Turumtari’ (for the female) in Hindi and Gujarati, and ‘Chatwa’ (for the male) in Sindhi and Gujarati; ‘Jellaganta’, ‘Jelgadda’ or ‘Jale gadda’ in Telugu; and ‘Laal siri turmati’ in Punjabi. It is found mainly in the drier parts of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report: Maguri Beel, Assam, March 27-28, 2022 Text and Photos: Aditya Rao A view of Maguri Beel Maguri Beel or Maguri Bill is a vast wetland close to DibruSaikhowa National Park near Matapung village in Tinsukia district in Assam. We spent 2 morning sessions in Maguri Beel on March 27 & 28, 2022, looking for grassland and wetland birds. This was part of an 8-day long trip to the North-east that included Dehing Patkai and Mishmi Hills, about which I will write a separate report later. The area is extremely rich in avifauna and is well-known for two species: the Swamp Prinia, also known as Swamp Grass Babbler (IUCN status: Endangered) and the Swamp Francolin (IUCN status: Vulnerable). Unfortunately, we could not cross the river (rapids due to water let out from upstream) to see the Prinia which is only seen and spotted on some island grasslands. But we were lucky enough to spot the Swamp Francolin after waiting patiently for a few hours. 1

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Eurasian Collared Dove (Streptopelia decaocto) Eurasian Collared Dove (Rollapadu, October 10, 2019) Order: Columbiformes Family: Columbidae Genus: Streptopelia Species: S. decaocto Size: 32 cm Description & distribution: A medium-sized dove, the Eurasian Collared Dove is pinkish-grey or buff-grey overall, with the upperparts being slightly darker than the underparts. It has a blue-grey underwing patch which is visible in flight. The main diagnostic feature is the white-edged black halfcollar that goes around the back of the neck. The legs are short and red, bill is black and irises are deep reddish-brown (although difficult to see from a distance, as it is a narrow rim around the black pupils). There is a narrow bare ring around the eye, white in the nominate and yellow in the sub-species S. d. xanthocycla (which also has a darker grey head and darker pink underparts). Tail feathers are buff-grey above, and dark grey with white tips below. The sexes are alike. The juvenile is similar, but has an indistinct or poorly developed collar and brown irises. The specific name, decaocto, is said to come from the Greek word for ‘eighteen’, and is based on a mythological story about a servant girl who was paid only 18 coins a year, and was transformed by the gods into a dove to set her free from her sufferings. The Eurasian Collared Dove is not migratory; however it is strongly dispersive and has extended its range across many parts of the world. Its original range, in late 19 th century, was the warm temperate and subtropical regions of Asia, east from Turkey to southern China, and south through India till Sri Lanka. In the subsequent decades, it successfully colonized many parts of Europe, spreading rapidly across the Balkans, Germany, Great Britain, Norway and northern Russia, as well as southwest to the Canary Islands and northern Africa, from Morocco to Egypt, and east to central and northern China, and Japan. Besides, starting with a few pairs of escaped birds in the Bahamas in the early 1970s, it is now found across many parts of North America too. Habitat & behaviour: In its original range, the Eurasian Collared Dove would typically inhabit semi-arid regions with scattered trees, mixed thickets or orchards. They have since adapted and are now almost completely an urban species, preferring spaces like urban gardens, parks, scrub patches, agricultural fields close to human habitation etc. The Eurasian Collared Dove is diurnal, and is often seen in pairs, either on a branch or foraging on the ground. It is gregarious, and groups of up to 10,000 birds have been reported, although smaller flocks of 10-50 birds are more common, especially at prime food-rich locations, like farms with threshing equipment, where split grain may be found, or outside grain stores. At times it has also been observed to demonstrate a fondness for sunflower seeds, even visiting feeders that stock them. Besides grain, its diet includes seeds from grasses and cereals, buds, berries, fruits, shoots, insects and other invertebrates. It is generally peaceful, even feeding in mixed flocks without incident, but may occasionally turn aggressive towards other species. It is one of the few species that can drink water ‘head down’, submerging their bills and sucking up water as through a straw. Its flight is fast and direct, with clipped wingbeats. Its usual call is a harsh, screeching hah-hah, especially in flight just before landing, or a monotonous krou-koou-kou repeated many times, while the song is a cooing goo-GOO-goo. When excited they may also utter a rapid and nasal kwourrr. 7

Nesting: The Eurasian Collared Dove breeds around the year if food is abundant, though rarely in winter in areas like Europe that have severe winters. The male engages in a mating display which, like most pigeons, includes a rapid, almost vertical ascent followed by a long glide back to ground in a circle, with wings held back in an inverted V below the body, and tail fanned. Nesting is usually close to human habitation, where food resources are easily available and there are trees for nesting. Nests are almost always within 1km of inhabited buildings. The nest is made of sticks, and 3-4 broods per year are usual (though up to 6 broods per year have been recorded). The usual clutch consists of 2 white eggs. Parental duties are shared by both parents. Instead of insects, which most species feed their chicks to meet their protein needs, the Eurasian Collared Dove gives its chicks a fat- and protein-rich ‘crop milk’, a whitish fluid which comes from liquid-filled cells that slough off the lining of the crop, a portion of the esophagus. Local name: The Eurasian Collared Dove is known as ‘Dhor fakhta’, ‘Parki’, ‘Panduk’ or ‘Gugi’ in Hindi, ‘Pedda bella guwa’ in Telugu; ‘Pottanchangali’ in Malayalam, ‘Kalli pura’ or ‘Sambal pura’ in Tamil, ‘Kukil’ in Kashmiri, ‘Par ghughu’ in Bengali, ‘Ghuggi’ in Punjabi and ‘Dhol holo’ in Gujarati. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From Instagram, November 16, 2021) *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Editor’s note Our member, Mohd Adnan Uddin, has been documenting birds and other wildlife of Nizamabad District, Telangana, over the past more than two years. He had earlier submitted a report covering his observations in June and July 2020, which was featured in the Pitta September 2020 issue. In this Special Issue of the Pitta, we bring you a report covering the period from August 2020 to July 2022, along with a large number of colourful photographs. We hope you will find this Special Issue interesting. BIRDING IN BODHAN & BEYOND Report: Observations on Biodiversity of Nizamabad District, August 2020 - July 2022 Text & Photos: Mohd Adnan Uddin Scaly-breasted Munia flock at Bodhan During the COVID-19 pandemic, working from home became the norm for many organisations and businesses, and the education sector was no exception. As an educator, my work also moved to virtual mode. So I moved from Hyderabad to my hometown Bodhan in Nizamabad District, Telangana and, having the flexibility and time, started exploring the place. The initial months of birding resulted in spectacular findings of the rich biodiversity in the small town, about which I had written a detailed report in the Pitta September 2020 issue. I am writing this report as a follow-up for the period between August 2020 and July 2022. Since it is difficult to write a detailed account of two years of birding in one go, I will only share some of the key findings in this report. After spotting 108 resident species during my monsoon birding in 2020, I was eagerly waiting for the migrants to arrive. Much of my initial birding was confined to my hometown Bodhan, respecting the COVID-19 guidelines. Later as the pandemic situation eased, I slowly started travelling to nearby towns and villages. Every visit of mine resulted again in surprising findings of the rich flora and fauna in this rural hinterland. Among the resident species in Bodhan, I finally found some shrikes which I had been trying to locate for months. Brown Shrike Tussar Moth 2

I also spotted a few Common Moorhen which I could not find at Bodhan. I was also looking for storks everywhere and it felt so nice to finally see the Woolly-necked Stork near Kopperga. A lone bird was feeding in a paddy field. In October 2020, I went to Ali Sagar, a very popular picnic spot, around 18km away from Bodhan. The area has a reservoir, deer park and has a good range of forest. I have very fond childhood memories of Ali Sagar. The place is lush green and has very tall trees. I can never forget my first sighting of Indian Paradise-flycatcher at Ali Sagar during my early days of birding. Watching the flying bird in its white morph felt almost like a scene from paradise. This time, though, I saw a male bird of the rufous morph. Long-tailed Shrike A cousin had informed me about the presence of many antelopes and deer in Kopperga village, which is around 18km away from Bodhan. Monsoon had changed the landscape completely by then and it became challenging to spot the Blackbuck. With the help of a farmer, I tried to track the animal and finally we managed to find a female Blackbuck near the soyabean crop. There was a Painted Francolin calling from a thicket in the undergrowth while the blackbuck was leaping in the air. Quite an enjoyable moment that was. Indian Paradise-flycatcher male Common Moorhen Orange-breasted Green Pigeon Spotting a flock of Orange-breasted Green Pigeons really pumped me up. The shy birds were foraging quietly and slowly walking along the branches of the tall trees. Woolly-necked Stork

Given the rich habitat, Ali Sagar is home to several resident and migratory bird species. I found White-naped Woodpecker, Black-headed Cuckooshrike, Small Minivet, Grey-breasted Prinia, Rufous Treepie, Blyth's Reed Warbler, Black Redstart and Jungle Babbler among others. Yellow-footed Green Pigeon At Bodhan, I spotted a flock of Yellow-footed Green Pigeons. Their flight is very fast and direct, and their diet consists mainly of fruits and seeds. This flock remained in Bodhan for several months and I had a great time watching them regularly. It appears the birds migrate locally, as I have not found them throughout the year in the town. Blyth’s Reed Warbler Black Redstart Black-headed Cuckooshrike female Jungle Babbler Grey-breasted Prinia Indian Bullfrog

On the way to Ali Sagar from Bodhan, there is a village named Jamlam which falls under Yedapalle Mandal. There is a lake at the village which had good numbers of herons and egrets. The locals guided me to a small kunta (pond) in the village which had shallow waters and a wetland, ideal for waders and other aquatic birds. Cotton Pygmy-goose Gadwall As winter approached, the landscapes began transforming again. Several migratory birds started arriving. I spotted big flocks of Red-headed Bunting in Bodhan. These birds feed on the seeds and other plant material on the ground. Common Snipe This place was teeming with great avian populations. There were migratory species numbering in several hundreds, majority of which were Garganey, Northern Shoveler, Gadwall and Wood Sandpiper. The Common Snipe was another highlight. Resident species like Cotton Pygmy-goose and Eurasian Coot were in huge numbers too. I also spotted a lone Red-crested Pochard in the pond. Red-headed Bunting Black-headed Bunting Eurasian Coot with chick

Siberian Stonechat Chestnut-shouldered Petronia Indian Silverbill Chestnut-shouldered Petronias seem to migrate locally. In the winters, I spotted them in big numbers near the paddy fields, feeding on the grains alongside other species like Indian Silverbill, Red Avadavat and Tricoloured Munia. Common Rosefinch female There were a few Black-headed Buntings, Siberian Stonechats and Common Rosefinches as well. Several flocks of Chestnuttailed and Rosy Starlings also visited the town. They deliver a constant cacophony of chattering calls which is soothing to hear. Red Avadavat male Rosy Starling

Baya Weaver flock Red Avadavat female Black-breasted Weaver The nesting activity of the weavers peaks in the monsoon, with abundant supply of nesting material in the cultivation and palm trees around. I have spent months documenting the weavers and it always fills me with great delight to be in their company, marvelling at their architectural abilities. Tricoloured Munia Another fascinating aspect of Bodhan is the presence of different types of weavers. I have counted about a thousand Baya Weavers, scores of Streaked Weavers and a few Blackbreasted Weavers too. Yellow-wattled Lapwing In January 2021, I was birding near the lake but this time taking a different route through the fallow fields. I chanced upon a flock of Yellow-wattled Lapwings. There were about ten birds, moving hither and thither due to human presence there. Later they dispersed in groups and started foraging in the fallow fields. I was so happy to have seen them after a long time. Streaked Weaver

Red-crested Pochard One day I was pleasantly surprised to find a pair of Redcrested Pochard in the lake. The Greater Painted-snipe with its beautiful plumage is also found near the lake. Grey-headed Swamphen Bellal lake in Bodhan has been filled to the brim since a few years, because of which there has not been much scope for aquatic birds to arrive. Due to excess water hyacinth and other vegetation, there are several Grey-headed Swamphens and Bronze-winged Jacanas in the lake. There are a few Pheasanttailed Jacana too. One day our milkman informed us that ‘big birds’ have visited his village Saloora which is 8km away from Bodhan. It was December 2020. I set out to visit the village which really had many surprises for me. I first went to the river Manjeera in the village outskirts which marks the border between Telangana and Maharashtra. White Wagtail Bronze-winged Jacana Little Ringed Plover Pheasant-tailed Jacana On the river bed, I found a couple of White Wagtails and Little Ringed Plovers. Since it was winter, the river was not flowing and it was broken up into small streams with shallow waters, thus harbouring several waders. I saw Common Sandpiper, Common Redshank, Marsh Sandpiper, Little Stint, Temminck's Stint, Kentish Plover, Great Thick-knee and Eurasian Spoonbill at the river.

My joy knew no bounds when I saw a flock of Bar-headed Geese and Ruddy Shelduck flying in the sky. I really wanted to know where these birds were going. Manjeera is also host to other birds like Lesser Whitethroat, Small Pratincole, Black-winged Stilt, Asian Openbill and Painted Stork. Marsh Sandpiper & Common Redshank Lesser Whitethroat Great Thick-knee Painted Stork Temminck’s Stint Asian Openbill Kentish Plover There are at least four lakes in Saloora village. One of the lakes had a very healthy population of Lesser Whistling-duck whose whistling calls resounded all around the place. 9

Lesser Whistling-duck There were a few Knob-billed Ducks and several Eurasian Coot. One day, walking near the lake, I found around eight Woolly-necked Storks foraging far away in the agricultural fields. I was so happy to see so many of them. IUCN has downlisted their conservation status to ‘Near-threatened’ in 2019 from their earlier classification in 2014 as ‘Vulnerable’. Water Scorpion Baronet Common Teal Near Saloora is a small village named Fatehpur where there is a small lake. I found several Northern Shovelers, Knob-billed Ducks, Eurasian Coot and a pair of Common Teal. The area around the lake is a good habitat for other species like Baya and Black-breasted Weavers. Yellow Orange Tip Indian Crab After covering waterbodies in Bodhan, Jamlam, Ali Sagar, Saloora, Manjeera, and Fatehpur, I was looking to find more sites to find migratory birds in December 2020. This quest made me discover Pedda Cheruvu in Rudrur town which is about 8km away from Bodhan. What started as a routine birding outing turned out to be such a blessing that I could not have imagined. It was like a fortunate stroke of serendipity. 10

Mixed flock at Rudrur Eurasian Wigeon The lake in Rudrur offered a jaw-dropping scenery of birds. I had never seen a site like this in my lifetime. The lake was teeming with thousands of waterfowl species! There were about four thousand Lesser Whistling-ducks, three hundred Northern Pintail, two hundred Northern Shovelers, a hundred Eurasian Wigeon, Black-tailed Godwit and Blackcrowned Night Heron among several others. There were several scores of Indian Pond Heron, Cattle Egret, Wood Sandpiper, Common Pochard, Rosy and Asian Pied Starlings. It was a mesmerising sight to see thousands of diverse birds at one place. I was so ecstatic to have ‘discovered’ the place. I spent three days straight at the lake soaking in the experience. Northern Pintail Common Pochard Black-crowned Night Heron Asian Pied Starling

Geese alongside 39 Greylag Geese. A soaring Peregrine Falcon was another highlight of the day. Indian Grey Mongoose River Tern The lake is a roosting site for several species. As darkness approaches, big flocks of species like Whiskered and River Terns, Glossy Ibis and Cattle Egret start arriving at the lake for roosting. Greater Flamingo & Black-winged Stilt I visited the lake again in the summer. The lake shrunk to almost half its size and there were mostly resident bird species. Surprisingly there was a lone Spot-billed Pelican at the lake. In December 2021, I saw a pair of Greater Flamingos too. Common Picture Wing I was told by the locals that the Gram Panchayat has passed a resolution to protect the birds at the lake and that there will be a fine against anyone harming the birds. In my visits, I have not found any significant threat to the species. However, it is important to conserve the habitat to guard against any future threats. Rudrur’s Pedda Cheruvu deserves immediate legal protection. Greylag Goose In January 2022, on a routine birding trip to Rudrur, I was surprised to find a flock of Greylag Geese. There were more than 30 birds on one of the ‘islands’ of the lake. I immediately shared this finding with the Deccan Birders fraternity, who were overjoyed to hear this. The very next day Guru and Sathwik joined me at the lake. We also found eight Bar-headed Blackbuck pair

Wasp Moth Black-winged Kite There were many other high points of my hiking experiences, like watching Blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra) and the Indian Fox (Vulpes bengalensis) at Chinnayanam in Nandipet Mandal, observing the Black-winged Kite devouring a rodent, a Checkered Keelback (Fowlea piscator) hunting fishes, Indian Monitor (Varanus bengalensis) foraging in the undergrowth at Ali Sagar, thousands of fishes captured by fishermen at Ambam Cheruvu and the most recent finding of several Spot-billed Pelicans near Bodhan. The pursuit of birdwatching has always been quite rewarding. Sri Lankan Bullfrog Checkered Keelback with fish Common Tree Frog Spot-billed Pelican The major threat to biodiversity continues to be the loss of habitat, because of which species are declining. Poaching remains another concern. I have also observed a significant increase in feral dog populations which actively hunt birds, especially the ground-dwelling ones. These threats have to be addressed with earnestness. With sufficient documentation, the next step should be towards conservation of species and their habitats. I am looking forward to working on this front in the future. 13
