Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 19 Number 10 September 2022 FIELD TRIP-1: Sunday, 11th September 2022: Narsapur Reserve Forest. Meeting Point-1: Mangatrai Pearls, Punjagutta, 4.45AM; Meeting Point-2: Opp. Dindigul Air Force Station, 5.45AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Sathwik Reddy (Mobile: 9985807186), Gokul Krishna Addanki (Mobile: 9945346585) Located in Medak District, Narsapur Reserve Forest is about 50km from Hyderabad and spans over 3500 hectares. The forest has a diverse range of flora and wildlife, various natural rock formations and ponds, and is a dry deciduous forest known for several medicinal plants. The highlight is a cosy lake tucked away in the heart of the forest where we can just sit by to admire the serenity and tranquillity of the place while observing waterfowl. We will look out for Jerdon's Nightjar, Jerdon's Leafbird, Yellow-crowned Woodpecker, Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker etc, as also the winter migrants that may have started arriving by now. This will be a half-day trip. Carry water and breakfast/snacks, and rain gear if required. Strict Covid protocols will be followed, so please ensure you wear masks, carry a sanitiser and maintain social distancing. Members are requested to wear their Deccan Birders ID cards. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. Deccan Birders T-Shirts and caps will be available for sale. FIELD TRIP-2: Sunday, 25th September 2022: Details to be announced Trip Report: Zaheerabad, August 28, 2022 Neil Rahul Gala White-bellied Minivet male (Photo: Sravan Kumar R) Early on the morning of August 28, 2022, a group of Deccan Birders members set out to Zaheerabad for our monthly outing. It was a half-day trip, which would maybe offer a lot of surprises. All of us met at the first meeting point, which was BHEL, and then at the second one, which was the Taj Dhaba, where we all got down and had a chat. After a short while, once everyone had gathered, we resumed our journey. We soon reached our destination, and immediately saw a couple of Tricolored Munias, a lifer for me. There were some spots where it seemed like it had rained the previous night, and I was just hoping that the rain did not cross paths with us. I was excited to see what surprises were waiting for me. After parking the cars we started our search for the main protagonist of the trip, the White-bellied Minivet. 1

birds, I bumped into Sathwik Uncle, who told me about a fox that he saw. Later on I saw the fox for the first time in a photograph taken by Abhishek Uncle. Grey-breasted Prinia (Photo: Dr Chitra Shanker) We entered the area and started looking for the Minivet. Once we thought we heard the Minivet, but it turned out to be just the Grey-breasted Prinia mimicking its call – we saw it fly over our heads and disappear into the greens. Some time later, we started moving back to where the cars were parked. On the way back, we saw the Indian Fox for the second time, along with a few more birds. Report: Sighting of Little Egret dark morph, Hyderabad, August 29-30, 2022 Text & Photos: Dr Chitra Shanker Little Egret dark morph A dark morph of the Little Egret Egretta garzetta was observed in the rice fields of ICAR-Indian Institute of Rice Research on ICRISAT campus (17.49ºN, 74.27ºE), Hyderabad, Telangana, India, on 29 and 30 th August 2022. At first sight, it appeared like a Reef Egret, but the upper mandible was seen to be uniformly dark. The completely yellow feet and the narrow plumes on the nape suggest a Little Egret. There are some mentions of a dark morph of the Little Egret in recent literature: 1. The article by Ramit Singal on the Birdcount website (https://birdcount.in/little-reef-egrets/) mentions it to be relatively rare. Little Egret white morph 2. Putative hybrids between a Little Egret and a Western Reef Heron E. gularis, which have shadowy and sometimes blotchy plumage colours, have been reported from India. 3. A dark morph Little Egret has also been reported from Uttar Pradesh earlier (https://indianbirds.in/pdfs/IB_17_3_Chauhan_LittleEgret.pd f). 4. Wikimedia commons has an upload of a dark morph from Kannur in Kerala (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a3/Little _egret_dark_morph_5.jpg), though the colouration is not as dark as the bird observed here. 5. However, the dark morph observed at Embilikala, Sri Lanka (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Little_Egret_Grey_morph_1.jpg) looks similar to the bird observed now. Little Egret dark morph Whether the putative dark morph is a hybrid of Reef Egret and Little Egret needs to be ascertained. The present bird was a little skittish and disturbed easily, and also stayed aloof from the other Little Egrets in the field. *** 7

Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani White-eared Bulbul (Pycnonotus leucotis) White-eared Bulbul (Gujarat, September 22, 2021) Order: Passeriformes Family: Pycnonotidae Genus: Pycnonotus Species: P. leucotis Size: 20 cm Habitat & behaviour: The White-eared Bulbul is a lowland species of tropical dry forests, scrub, forest edges, agricultural areas, parks and gardens, and can also be seen quite easily in urban areas in its range. It is usually seen singly or in pairs, although occasionally it does form small flocks, twittering together as they hop around in the branches. Its diet primarily consists of fruits on trees, like berries, dates and figs, and pealike vegetables; it also consumes nectar, insects, and food on the ground. It is a fairly tame bird, accustomed to human presence, and is also known to enter houses to be fed or for kitchen scraps. Its flight is typically bulbul-like, undulating with intermittent wingbeats. Its call is a low raspy chuk, but it does not generally call very often. The song is also not consistent, comprising of a set of melodious notes which it may utter in different combinations; however, the song is described as ‘pleasant and fluid’. Description & distribution: The White-eared Bulbul is a typical bulbul, somewhat rotund in appearance, and has an overall brownish-grey body. Underparts are a lighter dull greyish white. It has a black head, chin and throat, with a large white cheek spot, due to which it is also known as the Whitecheeked Bulbul. The crest is usually a rounded black tuft, but sometimes may be longer and forward-pointing. The bill is short and black, eye rings are bare brownish or yellowish, legs are black and vent is bright yellow. The tail is relatively long, starting off as black or dark brown and ending in white tailtips. The sexes are alike. The White-eared Bulbul is a resident in most parts of its range across south-western Asia, from the western parts of India like Gujarat and Rajasthan, west through Pakistan, southern Afghanistan, coastal Iran, Kuwait, most parts of the two-river basin in Iraq, and the island of Bahrain, where it is the national bird. It is also an introduced species in the other Arabian Gulf countries like Saudi Arabia, Oman, the UAE and Qatar, and is popular as a pet in many countries in its range. Nesting: The White-eared Bulbul breeds generally between March and September, with some local variations. It is monogamous and territorial, defending its territory aggressively against other males nearby. The nest is an untidy cup made of twigs, rootlets, dry grass and plant fibres, concealed in thorny bushes or small trees, usually under 2 metres. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 pinkish-white eggs, profusely blotched with purplish-brown patches. Parental duties are shared by both parents. Two sub-species are recognized, the nominate P. l. leucotis, and P. l. Mesopotamia, slightly heavier than the nominate, and seen in north-eastern Arabia, southern Iraq and south-western Iran. Local name: The White-eared Bulbul is known as ‘Safed kaan bulbul’ in Hindi, ‘Kanara bulbul, ‘Kachchi bulbul’ or ‘Ran bulbul’ in Gujarati; ‘Bhooroo’ in Sindhi, ‘Safed gallacha bulbul’ in Marathi and ‘Shwet karna bulbul’ in Sanskrit. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Editor’s note Some of our members had been to Gujarat during September 18-25, 2021, for an eight-day birdwatching trip, mainly focusing on the Passage Migrant species. In this Special Issue of the Pitta, we bring you a report on that trip, along with a number of colourful photographs. We hope you will find this Special Issue interesting. SEEKING THE SEPTEMBER SUPERHEROES Report: Passage Migration birding, Gujarat, September 18-25, 2021 Text & Photos: Umesh Mani European Roller Passage Migrant birds are those species that stop somewhere along their migration path for a short while, before resuming their onward journey. Around 10 bird species are considered passage migrants in Gujarat. Since Gujarat is on our westernmost coast, and more or less on the regular migration path of many of these species, these birds find it a convenient place to make a pitstop, refuel and recharge, before moving on to their eventual wintering grounds. With reference to India, while every region may regard some birds as passage species, Gujarat is considered the best location to see a large number of passage species at one place. The window to see these birds is small – they typically halt in Gujarat for only a short while, ranging from a couple of weeks to maybe a month – so September is generally the best time. Therefore, a visit to Gujarat during this period had been high on my list for a long time. After the pandemic, which had put paid to travel plans for most of us, things finally fell into place in September 2021, and a group of 12 of us were able to make this trip. The group comprised six of us from Hyderabad – Lawrence, Srikanth, Nandakumar, Sagarika, Vinay and I – and six other birding friends from Chennai. Day-1: Sep 18, 2021: Nalsarovar Barring a couple of members who decided to get there early, the rest of us reached Ahmedabad early on Sep 18, 2021. We were picked up from the airport and, after a quick breakfast en route – a besan-dominated combination of dhokla, fafda, gathiya, jalebi etc – we started off for Nalsarovar by around 9:00AM, high on energy and spirits, and on anticipation of the birds we were going to see! The first bird we saw was also the first of the passage migrants – the European Roller. It created a flutter of excitement, and we were quick to jump out of our vehicles to see and photograph the bird. It was also quite cooperative, giving plenty of time as we manoeuvred into position from different angles. After about half an hour, during which we also sighted a few other species – Long-tailed Shrike, Rufous-fronted Prinia, a distant Delicate (formerly Graceful) Prinia, Barn Swallow, Eurasian Collared Dove – we decided to move on. 2

Eurasian Collared Dove Long-tailed Shrike Sarus Crane Barely a few kilometres later, the vehicles came to a screeching halt again – we had seen a pair of Sarus Cranes in a field near the road. Trooping out of the vehicles again, we spent some time taking in the visual of these beautiful birds in their preferred habitat. They were foraging, unconcerned about the people who were working the fields nearby – which says a lot about how the people here allow birds and other creatures to peacefully co-exist, thus also enabling the birds to not feel threatened when people venture nearby. House Sparrow female A suspicious Long-tailed Shrike gave us the eye, and some other commoners populated the wires above – Plain Prinia, Grey Wagtail, Green Bee-eater, House Sparrow, and a small mixed flock of Bank Mynas and Rosy Starlings, including a few juveniles. Bank Myna Rosy Starling adult & juvenile

Woolly-necked Stork By now, we were getting late for Nalsarovar, so we drove nonstop till there, met up with our guide, and drove straight to the first birding area for the day. A group of 3-4 Woolly-necked Storks welcomed us and, while we were looking at them, we had a flypast from a Eurasian Marsh Harrier and a Collared Pratincole. Whiskered Tern An immature Purple Heron was around, as was a Whiskered Tern that seemed to be exiting breeding plumage. A River Tern gave good views – a relative novelty for some of the Chennai people. Eurasian Marsh Harrier with prey Collared Pratincole Paddyfield Pipit We also got to see the Harrier pick up a prey – possibly a young bird – from the irrigated field as a few Painted Storks looked on. Other commoners like Paddyfield Pipit and Crested Lark, and one of the western region endemics, the White-eared Bulbul, also showed up. Purple Heron immature

Common Teal Crested Lark White Stork Pallid Harrier We then had a bit of a walk – around 1.5km – to reach the place where a single individual of one of our main target species was present – the White Stork. It was lovely, standing majestically atop a bund, along with a few Woolly-necked Storks, Grey Herons and Painted Storks. There was also a flock of Eurasian Spoonbills, including some in breeding plumage, assorted Egrets and a few Black-winged Stilts. A small flock of Common Teals floated on a small patch of water. A beautiful Pallid Harrier flew by, giving us an opportunity to see and photograph it, as did a Greater Spotted Eagle. Greater Spotted Eagle, Painted Stork & Grey Heron Eurasian Spoonbill It was quite hot by now, though, and we started walking back towards the vehicles. We noted that even the Marsh Harrier had taken shelter in the shade under a clump of prosopis. A White-eyed Buzzard also flew over – suddenly we had been treated to a slew of raptors!

We then decided to take a break. During lunch, a sudden shower had us worried for a while, but it soon stopped. The next few birds were all rain-drenched – White-eared Bulbul, Bay-backed Shrike, Rufous-fronted Prinia, Chestnutshouldered Petronia, Siberian Stonechat, and a Grey-necked Bunting foraging in the wet grass. Eurasian Marsh Harrier White-cheeked Bulbul in the rain White-eyed Buzzard A group of five Common Babblers sat on a dry clump, trying to dry themselves. Near a patch of water, we saw another Rufous-fronted Prinia with a catch – no confusion this time! – and some commoners – Red-vented Bulbul, Green Sandpiper, etc. Then, just as we were thinking of winding up for the day, given the rain and poor light, we saw some activity in a field that gave us our next passage species, and a lifer for many in the group – the Red-backed Shrike. It was a little far, though, and we hoped we would get better views in the coming days. As we drove to the next spot, a handful of Weavers in the reeds by the road turned out to be the beautiful Black-breasted Weavers. Red-backed Shrike Black-breasted Weaver Another European Roller turned up, perched atop a twig – it was amazing how it could balance there! – and then one more, this one looking very plain. The variation in plumage between different individuals was quite vast. Yellow-wattled Lapwing juvenile

Spotted Owlet European Nightjar Finally moving ahead, we saw a juvenile Yellow-wattled Lapwing in a field. After spending a few minutes there, we headed back towards our hotel. Nearby, we added some more birds – a pair of Spotted Owlets, Small Minivets, Shikra, Golden Oriole, and a Cuckoo in the distance that led us a merry dance before we could get a decent look at it. But it was well worth the effort, because the bird turned out to be the Eurasian (aka Common) Cuckoo! Another passage migrant, another lifer for many of us in the group – and a great way to close the birding for the day. Three of the passage species done – what a day it had been! We still had a long drive ahead of us, though, since we had to reach our next location at the Great Rann of Kutch tonight. So we got back to the hotel, quickly packed up, and left. Day-2: Sep 19, 2021: Greater Rann of Kutch (GRK) Having reached here only by 11:00PM last night, today’s start was slightly later than usual. After a morning cup of tea, we started off around 7:00AM. We were initially entertained by a pair of Red-vented Bulbuls that were perched on the vehicle mirrors, checking themselves out. We gave them a few minutes before moving out. This was possibly the most difficult of the passage species to locate, and we were excited and enthused that we had got it. We spent nearly an hour there, trying to get better views from different angles, and taking photographs, but keeping our distance to avoid disturbing the dozing bird. From time to time, it would crack open one eye, check us out, then go back to sleep. We were amazed at how the guide had managed to locate the bird at all! After a while, we decided to move to another area, where our next target bird was supposed to be seen. This was near a temple, and with ample shaded areas nearby, we decided to sit down and first finish our packed breakfast. As we ate, we kept seeing birds flitting around in the trees, and in a Eureka moment, I realized that most temple areas offer good sightings of at least a few species. Here too, as we walked in, we first encountered a European Roller and, soon after, the bird we were looking for – the Spotted Flycatcher. Initially inside the prosopis, it flew out and perched on a mound, making it easier for us to see. A few Common Babblers were also there, moving around and creating confusion as we tried to keep track of the Flycatcher. Somewhat unusually for species named ‘Common’, the Babblers actually turned out to be common all along our trip route. The first sighting was an overflying Knob-billed Duck, a reminder that the early migrants had started arriving. A Spotted Flycatcher, one of the passage species, gave a fleeting glimpse before flying off. We were consoled by the guide saying that they would be around and we would surely get a better sighting soon. We drove to a scrub forest site, parked the vehicles and walked in. About a half hour later, our guide, Bharat, found what we were looking for, and gestured to us to quickly come over. We all rushed to where he was standing, and he pointed us in the direction of a thick prosopis patch. With a lot of bending and straining, we were able to spot, deep inside the scrub, what he was showing us – a sleepy European Nightjar! Common Babbler 7

Grasshopper, and a Variable Wheatear female which gave plenty of time for photographs, were interesting sightings. Black-headed Bunting Variable Wheatear female By now it was getting hot, and we headed back to the resort for lunch and a short break before heading out again. En route, we saw a bedraggled Long-tailed Shrike and a Red-tailed Shrike on the wires. The lake nearby had some Eurasian Spoonbills nesting – we saw a nest with a couple of young birds clamoring for food. Unusually, the young ones seemed to be picking out food from inside the adult’s mouth, rather than the adult placing the food in the young one’s mouth as is normally seen! I felt this must be because the large spatulate bill of the adult may be too big to place inside the chick’s mouth. Indian Bushlark A Black-headed Bunting on a wire engaged us for a bit – it is not common towards Chennai. An Indian Bushlark perched on an old-style exhaust pipe made for an interesting picture. Eurasian Spoonbill feeding young A Dalmatian Pelican, a lifer for most members in the group, took a lazy flight around the lake and was soon joined by another. At one point, they came head-on to us, giving us an idea just how massive their wingspan is! Isabelline Wheatear Then we saw the first Wheatear of the trip – an Isabelline Wheatear. A Rufous-fronted Prinia gave good views. A European Roller, with a kill that looked like a Painted Dalmatian Pelican

After this action we got back to the Spoonbills, only to find that the young ones were still begging. It was interesting to see that the young ones had already started developing the spatulate bills that they are named for. Just as we were thinking of moving back, we saw a couple of Bee-eaters on a dry bush that turned out to be our passage species #5 – the Blue-cheeked Bee-eater. Unfortunately they were not very close by. We did find a couple of Green Beeeaters though. Oriental Garden Lizard Striolated Bunting A mossy rock face nearby yielded a Striolated Bunting looking for insects, and a Common Tailorbird. We saw the Bunting pick up some nesting material, and the Tailorbird also came up with a prey – a Boll Worm Moth (Helicoverpa armigera). Then it came closer – and we suddenly realized that it was not a Tailorbird but a Rufous-fronted Prinia – the red on the head was, well, redder – and we had been foxed by this! Just goes to show that even the most ‘familiar’ birds cannot be taken for granted on the field. House Sparrow female Suddenly we were informed that a snake had been spotted in the bushes near the outer periphery of the resort, and we rushed there to see it. It was a Saw-scaled Viper, which was slithering around in the cactus at first, then came down to the ground. It was a beautiful, healthy specimen, nearly 6ft long. Saw-scaled Viper By now, lunch was ready, so we decided to finish lunch and take a brief rest before heading out again for the evening session. Rufous-fronted Prinia with Boll Worm Moth prey The resort has several water bowls and a couple of feeders which usually attract several birds. As we waited for lunch, we saw a Variable Wheatear female hanging around near the lunch area, as also a White-eared Bulbul. An Oriental Garden Lizard and a House Sparrow were also active. We started off around 3:30PM, and drove to Vekariya Rann area, where a vagrant pair of Marbled Ducks had been seen over the past few days. Naturally, we wanted to see them too. Initially, besides a few Blue-cheeked Bee-eaters, all we saw were a Northern Shoveler – quite an early arrival, we felt – a Wood Sandpiper, a Cormorant, a couple of Common Coots, a few Terns, some Black-winged Stilts, a bunch of Little Grebes – all the usual suspects, in fact. A flock of 40-50 Black-tailed Godwits, a Spoonbill and a Blue-cheeked Bee-eater flew over, and there was a Black-headed Gull in the water.

Little Grebe Grey-necked Bunting The grass seemed to be a popular feeding ground, because we also saw a pair of Grey-necked Buntings foraging there, besides another couple sunning themselves on the prosopis. A female Black-headed Bunting found a nice perch on a bare stick, only to be knocked off the perch by a (probable) young Red-backed Shrike. A flock of Rosy Starlings flew past, and a Common Stonechat and a Variable Wheatear hung around for a while. Black-headed Gull Srikanth and the guide had been searching for the Marbled Ducks all this time. Unfortunately the water had receded a lot, and the birds in the water were really far away. Srikanth did manage to get a record shot where the Marbled Ducks could be seen, but they were so far away that we could not discern any features. It was disappointing, since this could well have been the biggest highlight of the trip. But then, this is what birding is – we don’t always get what we want or how we want it. So we reconciled to the fact that it would have to be another day, and started back for the resort. Day-3: Sep 20, 2021: Greater Rann of Kutch (GRK) The day started with a familiar face, the Black-winged Kite, by the road. We were driving to a site that has large swathes of scrub vegetation. As soon as we reached there, we saw a juvenile Red-backed Shrike. This was followed by a pair of Tawny Pipits foraging on the grass. We followed them for quite some time, as they meandered their way across the grass. Tawny Pipit Black-headed Bunting female Common Stonechat 10

We were looking for our next target species, which was known to be a shy, skulking bird with the tendency to fly away at the slightest disturbance or threat perception – the Rufous-tailed Scrub Robin. After searching for quite a while in the scrub, during which interval we faithfully followed in his footsteps, our guide suddenly stopped and said, “Udhar hai.” For a few moments we could not even see it, but then a slight movement helped us locate the bird, and our cameras went into action. Quite characteristically, it gave us just a few seconds before zipping off into the bush. A couple of Baya Weavers and an Indian Bushlark distracted us, but we soon got back to looking for the Scrub Robin. We were not satisfied with the views, though, and hoped we would get it again later. and we started off after it. It kept shifting perches as we tried to approach, but we finally managed to get a proper view – the Eurasian (aka Common) Cuckoo. A Blue-cheeked Bee-eater landed up on a wire with what seemed like a bee catch, and gulped it down in a jiffy. A Rufous-fronted Prinia diverted us for a few minutes, as did a Plain Prinia. The Grey-necked Bunting still seemed to be around. A beautiful Booted Eagle flew past and gave us a very good view, as did a Common Rosefinch female. Booted Eagle Indian Bushlark Common Rosefinch female Red-backed Shrike On the way back to the resort, a washed-out looking European Roller on a wire had me puzzled as to why the plumage was so pale. We saw another individual with the usual plumage at a water puddle, though. Black-winged Kite A Red-backed Shrike and a pair of Ashy-crowned Sparrow Larks were interesting, as was a hovering Black-winged Kite. Suddenly someone saw a Cuckoo on a bush a little way away, European Roller

The customary Common Babblers were around as always – one came up with a moth catch. The moth was later identified as a Convolvulus Hawk Moth (Agrius convolvuli). The Babbler had quite a task, defending its prey from the other Common Babblers around, and finally flew off with the prey to find a safe place to consume it. An eye-catching insect on an iron pole, which we thought was a Cicada, later turned out to be a Red-spined Tree Locust (Anacridium rubrispinum). A beautiful Indian Grey Mongoose kept us engaged for a while – the ease with which it walked around amidst the thorny branches was amazing. Red-backed Shrike immature An immature Red-backed Shrike was very cooperative, but the adult not so much! A Rufous-fronted Prinia tried to make up for it, sitting nearby and allowing some time for photographs. We also – finally! – got a Blue-cheeked Bee-eater up close and had it sit for a while, maybe due to the heat – it did seem to be panting for quite some time. Red-spined Tree Locust Blue-cheeked Bee-eater Back at the resort, we had a brief rest followed by lunch. Then, as usual, we had some time before we had to start off for evening birding. Indian Grey Mongoose Common Babbler with Convolvulus Hawk Moth prey

White-cheeked Bulbul Painted Francolin For the last short pocket of time, we drove to a patch that had good scrub. We were immediately welcomed by good views of a Rufous-tailed Scrub Robin sitting in the open on some dry branches – possibly the rain had brought it out. The same patch also gave us a pair of Painted Sandgrouse hanging around in the wet grass, Sykes’s Warbler, Grey-necked Bunting, Rufous-fronted Prinia, and an unexpected bonus, a small mixed flock of Small and White-bellied Minivets, unfortunately too far and in poor light to photograph well. Red-wattled Lapwing juvenile We got started and took off for an evening session. Suddenly it started raining, and we got a little worried as to whether any birding would be possible at all. Nevertheless, there were still some interesting sightings – a rain-drenched White-cheeked Bulbul, House Sparrow, Variable Wheatear, a pair of foraging Grey Francolins in a field, a juvenile Red-wattled Lapwing, and our first Bay-backed Shrike of the day. Sykes’s Warbler Small Minivet & White-bellied Minivet That brought the day to a close, and we headed back for dinner and a well-earned rest. Rufous-tailed Scrub Robin

Day-4: Sep 21, 2021: Greater Rann of Kutch (GRK) A Paddyfield Pipit on the grass drew our attention to a Greynecked Bunting that was perched quite near us! A Marsh Harrier flew over, and a Spotted Flycatcher perched on some dry twigs gave excellent views – it gave plenty of time as it sunned itself, and those of us who had missed it yesterday were able to see it to their full satisfaction. I don’t think I have ever seen another Flycatcher so cooperative! It was quite hot by now, and we started driving back towards the resort for a break. En route were some commoners – Laughing Dove, Red-vented Bulbul, Red-wattled Lapwing, Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark and a beautiful Common Sandpiper. Near the lake, the Red-tailed Wheatear was still around, and we got to see some interesting views as it hopped around on the rocks. Black Francolin The day started with a bang – near the lake, the first bird we heard, and then saw, was a Black Francolin on a bund. Next came an early arrival, the Red-tailed (aka Persian) Wheatear – quite a bonus, as this bird is not easy to get. A Grey Francolin also put in an appearance, as did some usual suspects – Common Babbler, European Roller, Variable Wheatear, House Sparrow, White-eared Bulbul, Chestnut-shouldered Petronia, Red-backed Shrike etc. A Lesser Whitethroat gave good views. Red-tailed Wheatear A preening Red-vented Bulbul made for some interesting photos. Lesser Whitethroat Red-vented Bulbul We now reached the resort, had lunch and a couple of hours’ break. After lunch, since we had by now already got all the main target birds – the passage species – we decided to try our luck with the Marbled Ducks one more time. We felt that although it was a long drive, the species would be well worth the effort. Spotted Flycatcher Accordingly, we drove to Vekariya Rann and started searching for the Marbled Ducks. The water had receded a fair bit, and was now standing in small pools everywhere around the grassy area, so we had to scan every bit to see if we could locate the birds. It was frustrating, because every duck would raise our hopes and, once identified as something else, would bring them crashing down once again!

We located Spot-billed Ducks, Northern Pintails, Common Teals, Little Grebe, Great Crested Grebe – but no Marbled Ducks. We were naturally quite disappointed, but then, there was nothing to be done about it. Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse Eurasian Marsh Harrier A beautiful Eurasian Marsh Harrier quartered the ground, looking for prey. It flew quite close to us, and we got some excellent views. But it was poor consolation for missing out on a major duck species. We entered Banni and immediately came upon a foraging Crested Lark. In the same area, we found a pair of Chestnutbellied Sandgrouse and a small flock of Blue-cheeked Beeeaters. They were perched on a patch of damp ground and some dry twigs, and these were easily the best views we had got of this species! Anyway, after scanning the waters repeatedly for more than an hour, we decided to wind up and get back to the resort. Tomorrow would be an important day, as it was to be our last day at GRK. Day-5: Sep 22, 2021: Greater Rann of Kutch (GRK) Starting early, we headed to Banni Grasslands to look for birds that we had not seen so far on the trip. The first sighting was a Eurasian Cuckoo, which we had seen earlier, but since it was early morning, the bird was preening and warming up, and we were able to get a good look at it. We saw a Booted Eagle inside a tree, and a fresh-looking European Roller up close. A Red-backed Shrike gave beautiful views. Blue-cheeked Bee-eater First winter Red-tailed Shrike Red-backed Shrike A first-winter Red-tailed Shrike perched on a prosopis was quickly followed by an adult. A Montagu’s Harrier took off from its perch the moment we laid eyes on it. The prosopis seemed to be a favoured perch – we also found another handsome European Roller.

Montagu’s Harrier Desert Wheatear female A small flock of Collared Pratincole engaged us for quite some time. They were hanging around near a small puddle of water, and did not seem too concerned by our presence, so we were able to watch and photograph them for quite some time. Crested Lark Collared Pratincole The Crested Lark seemed to have actually lain down and gone to sleep – it was flat on the ground, neck extended along the sand, and with eyes closed, for nearly 6-7 seconds – which was so unusual. After a few seconds it opened its eyes, shook itself, got up and had a dust bath! It indulged in at least 5-6 rounds of dust bathing, as we watched, engrossed. A few Blue-cheeked Bee-eaters were also around. We saw one with a catch of what seemed to be an ant – we watched it manoeuvre the ant into position before swallowing it whole. Red-tailed Shrike adult Driving on, we saw another Red-tailed Shrike and then an addition to the list, a Great Grey Shrike. A Marsh Harrier flew past, and a beautiful Crested Lark gave nice views. Then came a Desert Wheatear – after a long time! Eurasian Cuckoo We took a break for a field breakfast before moving ahead. The first sighting was a Eurasian Cuckoo on an electric wire – and it stayed put there for quite some time, allowing us to approach fairly close.

Common Kestrel Siberian Stonechat We got to see the Rufous-tailed Scrub Robin again – it seemed to be as curious about us as we were about it, and sat around looking at us for quite some time. Great Grey Shrike A Common Kestrel flew past in leisurely fashion, and a Rufous-tailed Lark made an appearance. A Great Grey Shrike, perched on some dry branches, was very obliging until it was displaced by a Spotted Flycatcher. A Red-rumped Swallow and Siberian Stonechat also gave very good views. Rufous-tailed Scrub Robin With that, our morning session came to an end, and we returned to the resort for lunch and a rest. In the evening, some members of the team were to go on to Jamnagar, while the rest were to return to Ahmedabad and thence to Hyderabad. As we were waiting for a cup of tea before starting to Jamnagar, our eye was caught by some action in the scrub behind the resort dining area. We realized that a pair of Spotted Flycatchers – a species we had spent considerable time looking for earlier – had actually landed up at the resort itself! We spent some time watching them as they went about trying to catch insects. Red-rumped Swallow Yellow-eyed Babbler

We were diverted by another bird moving around in the bushes. There was a lot of excitement when we realized that it was the lovely Yellow-eyed Babbler. As is its wont, though, it kept scuttling around inside the bush, and it was not easy to get a good look at it. It suddenly started drizzling, and we thought that would be the end of the bird activity. Strangely, however, the Yellow-eyed Babbler decided to come out and perch on an open branch, perhaps to enjoy the rain. The drizzle stopped soon enough, and some other birds came out to dry and preen themselves – Red-vented Bulbul, House Sparrow – and a very judgemental-looking White-eared Bulbul! However, although we were supposed to get a move on, we could not restrain ourselves from birding on the way – after all, when birds are there, how can a birder not look at them? We saw a few mostly common species – Red-wattled Lapwing, Black-winged Stilt and what turned out to be a juvenile Ruff. As it was getting dark, we settled down for the long drive and, finishing dinner on the way, reached Jamnagar and checked into the hotel late that night. Day-6: Sep 23, 2021: Balachhadi, Bedi Bundar & Lakhota Lake, Jamnagar The plan for the day was to start our birding at Balachhadi beach, then move on to the other locations. Although a smaller group now, we were all quite excited at the prospect of finding some new waterbirds. It was an overcast, somewhat drizzly day, so we crossed our fingers and got started. Heuglin’s Gull White-eared Bulbul It was getting late now, and we started off to Jamnagar, bidding goodbye to our friends who were returning to Hyderabad, and to the resort staff, who had taken such good care of us over the past few days. At the spot we parked, there were a few bedraggled-looking Laughing Doves on the wires, and some warbler activity in the trees nearby, but we could not see it properly. Moving ahead, we were greeted by a Heuglin’s Gull and a pair of Common Redshanks in flight. Three Pied Avocets flew past – there is something about their upturned bills that tends to immediately perk up your spirits! Lesser Sand Plover Ruff juvenile

It had been low tide since the past few hours, and the water had receded so much that the mudflats extended for more than 100m – meaning we had to wade through a lot of the slush to get anywhere within viewing distance of the birds. It was tiring, and the rainy weather added to the gloom, but the thought of possibly getting some new birds kept us going. A Eurasian Curlew strolled along the edge of the water, and stray individuals of several other species were also seen – Whiskered Tern, Painted Stork, Little Ringed Plover, Lesser Sand Plover, Western Reef Egret, Black-winged Stilt, Little Stint, Terek Sandpiper, Common Greenshank, Grey Heron. A Dunlin and a Curlew Sandpiper were seen in the distance. It was at a fair distance, so I did even not realise at the time – it was only when going through the photographs at the time of writing this report that I noticed that one of the Bar-tailed Godwits had leg rings on both legs! And fortunately, in one later flight photograph, the ring was clear. I have now sent the details to the BNHS banding team, and am awaiting some details regarding the bird’s migration path. It just goes to show the value that photographs add to birding – even after a year, we are in a position to find some information about the migration of this particular Godwit. Bar-tailed Godwit with leg rings Curlew Sandpiper I saw a group of around 15 Eurasian Curlews hanging around in the water. There were a single Slender-billed Gull on the far side, too far to even see properly. A Grey Heron was busily preening. Suddenly a flock of around 25 Lesser Whistling-ducks flew past, giving a trailer of bigger flocks we could expect to see. There was a little excitement as a small group of seven Greater Flamingos flew over, graceful as ever. A white morph Western Reef Egret strode around purposefully, and it was interesting watching it trying to catch small fish in the mudflats. I felt like cheering when it finally caught a fish after numerous efforts! Eurasian Curlew Western Reef Egret white morph By now, the group had got scattered around, each member watching or following whichever bird caught their fancy. I moved to another patch of mudflats closer to the shore, where there seemed to be some action. A Eurasian Curlew flew past with its characteristic whistling in-flight calls. I finally found a flock of Godwits, which included both Black-tailed and Bartailed. Grey Heron

Large group of Eurasian Oystercatchers Then came the next surprise. I saw a Eurasian Oystercatcher standing in the water, but it took off almost immediately, and landed a little way off. As I tracked its flight and landing, I was thrilled to see that there was a large group of Oystercatchers there. I managed to get 22 (!) birds in one frame - that has to be one of the highlights of the trip for me – a fabulous sight! A lovely Western Reef Egret graced the shores, and there was also a Black-tailed Godwit in breeding plumage, beautiful though a little far away. The Curlews took off and landed again almost in the same spot, giving some nice flight action. Wonder what makes them do this – possibly just to warm up, I surmised. I suddenly noticed a couple of preening birds that looked different. On checking, these turned out to be Great Knots! When they moved along a little later, I realized that there were more Knots there – a total of around 15 birds – along with some Bar-tailed Godwits. Dunlin Moving ahead, I saw a small group of about 6-7 Dunlins hanging around with some Sand Plovers and Turnstones. Interestingly, most of them were still in partial breeding plumage, with the trademark black belly. After about half an hour, the flock took off, and I started moving back towards the shore, which the other members are also heading towards. Great Knot Eurasian Curlew We came upon a beautiful Eurasian Curlew, another Dunlin – this time a non-breeding individual – and a Common Redshank. A Baya Weaver was busily building his nest on a nearby palm tree, and we stopped to watch for a while – this sight never fails to engross! Western Reef Egret

the photographs. The bird had a metal ring on one leg, and two plastic flags on the other. Caspian, Lesser Crested, Gull-billed & Little Terns Dunlin with leg ring and flags It is so exciting to see ringed birds, because it triggers us to think about which parts of the world it may have been to! In this case, later enquiry with BNHS revealed that this adult bird had been ringed in the Sachana area near Ahmedabad on January 7, 2020, and was reported once in April 2021 – so our report was the first of this migratory season. It also showed that the bird showed pretty good site fidelity – Jamnagar is only about 275km away from where it was ringed. Grey Plover A mixed flock of Terns was resting on the ground – Caspian, Lesser Crested, Gull-billed and Little Terns. There was also a lone Grey (aka Black-bellied) Plover nearby, in full breeding plumage. By now it was quite late, and we decided to break for lunch. While moving back to shore, we saw an Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark hopping around beside the track. We saw a mixed flock of what seemed to be the earlier Oystercatchers with a handful of Gulls and Terns – strangely, they were all facing exactly away from us! Black-tailed Godwit Little Stint At another small pool of water, along with a few Little and Temminck’s Stints, we saw another Dunlin – and this one was ringed! Again, I did not notice the leg ring at the time; it can be difficult while reviewing photos in the camera LCD panel in the sunlight, so I realised this only later when going through After lunch and an hour’s rest, we were ready for a short evening session. We started with a couple of Northern Shovelers in eclipse plumage, interspersed with a few Blacktailed Godwits.

Red-wattled Lapwing Spot-billed Duck Just as we were getting warmed up, though, it started raining. We did see a Red-wattled Lapwing, and a bunch of House Sparrows looking miserable in the rain. Whiskered Tern in partial breeding plumage House Sparrow flock Since we still had some time, we decided to move to another area where we hoped that there would be no rain. It was quite overcast, though – and through the gloom, we saw a few Lesser Flamingos and a few assorted waders – Little Stint, Dunlin, Ruff etc. At another spot nearby, a couple of Spot-billed Ducks and a few Common Coot were also seen, along with a Red-wattled Lapwing, a River Tern, a few Caspian Terns, a couple of Whiskered Terns still showing some of their breeding plumage – and a Knob-billed Duck! Knob-billed Duck Ruff By now, it was getting darker, so we decided to wind up for the day.

Day-7: Sep 24, 2021: Charkhala & Dhinchada, Jamnagar Charkhala, where we were to start our birding today, is a little over 100km from Jamnagar. We reached the beach by around 9:00AM and started birding. The very first sighting was a Dalmatian Pelican, lazily treading water near the edge, along with a Grey Heron and a Great Egret. A few Ruddy Turnstones in non-breeding plumage foraged in the foreground, and a Common Sandpiper ambled past. It was very overcast and gloomy, but there were still some birds around. We spotted an Osprey sitting on a lamppost, but it took off soon after. Some other commoners were seen – Little and Indian Cormorant, Greater Flamingo, Grey Heron, River and Whiskered Terns. Greater Flamingo Ruddy Turnstone in non-breeding plumage Osprey Wire-tailed Swallow A beautiful Wire-tailed Swallow in fresh plumage sat patiently on a roadside rock and allowed us to take a few photos, then flew on to an electric post. We saw a very dark-looking Western Reef Egret, and a few non-breeding Little Grebes swimming around in the rain. A beautiful Pied Kingfisher also hung around on a rock. Little Cormorant Little Grebe

Pied Kingfisher As the rain showed no signs of letting up, we then decided to try another area. En route, we saw a few River Terns in flight, and a small flock of Terns on a sandbar that were identified as Saunders’s Terns at the time – causing much excitement – but later turned out to be Whiskered Terns – so poor was the light! A Grey Heron fished on the shore. Coppersmith Barbet White-throated Kingfisher Grey Heron with catch We took a break for lunch, and a short rest, before moving to the next spot, Dhinchada. This is known as a place that usually gives good sightings, and we hoped to find some interesting species there. The first sighting was a Pied Avocet that was actively foraging in the shallow waters, walking around while swiveling its bill in trademark scything fashion. It seemed to be an immature bird. We spent almost 15 minutes watching and photographing the Avocet. White-eyed Buzzard After a break for tea, during which we also hoped that the rain would let up, we got started. A few minutes later, we saw a lovely White-eyed Buzzard preening on a post. A Coppersmith Barbet, the first of the trip, also sat nearby. A little way down the road, we saw a White-throated Kingfisher with a lizard kill. Pied Avocet

Ruff having a bath Black-winged Stilt adult & immature A small group of Painted Storks foraged a little further away. A few Ruffs were active in the water, feeding, bathing and chasing each other around, and making for some very interesting birding! There were also a few Black-winged Stilts there, including some immature birds, and a Western Reef Egret. Barn Swallow Greater Flamingo adult & immature Another marshy spot nearby rewarded us with some fairly close sightings of a mixed flock of around 30 Lesser and Greater Flamingos, including several immatures. A flock of around 25 Lesser Whistling-ducks flew over. Other birds at this spot included Whiskered Tern, Common Redshank, Red-wattled Lapwing, Black-winged Stilt, Wood Sandpiper, Common Greenshank, River Tern, Western Reef Egret, Little Stint etc. A small group of Barn Swallows, including some juveniles, were perched on a wire. A few Lesser Sand Plovers were foraging, and a Eurasian Curlew and a Black-headed Ibis strolled across. A few Black-tailed Godwits hid among knee-high grass, which I found quite unusual. Lesser Flamingo & Painted Stork Black-headed Ibis

Black-tailed Godwit Pacific Golden Plover We then moved to a nearby area that had some salt pans – and struck the jackpot almost immediately – we saw a small group of 5-6 Red-necked Phalaropes leisurely swimming around, along with a Marsh Sandpiper that insisted on sticking with them. Just as we were thinking about closing for the day, we came across a Pacific Golden Plover across the water, a Common Redshank, a few Dunlins (with a Great Knot and a Little Stint) in flight and, a bit of a misfit at the salt pans, an Indian Silverbill. And a Pied Avocet came to say good night! Day-8: Sep 25, 2021: Dhinchada, Jamnagar Today was our last day, and we had only a few hours available for a morning session, so we made an early start. We decided to go back to Dhinchada since that was the nearest location and offered the possibility of sighting some birds that we had not seen so far. Red-necked Phalarope The day’s tally started with a Paddyfield Pipit and a female Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark. We were watching a foraging Western Yellow Wagtail, probably a first-winter individual of the thunbergi subspecies, when our attention was caught by a very white-looking bird with a patchy head – it turned out to be a moulting Ruff. Then we found another individual which was also at a different stage of moulting! A Black-necked Stork flew across in the distance, too far to photograph. It was fun watching the Whiskered Terns fishing, and trying to catch the moment. After innumerable tries, I managed to get a couple of decent captures. Whiskered Tern with catch A Common Sandpiper, Lesser Sand Plover and a Great Egret were all looking for their last meal before retiring for the day. Ruff moulting

Marsh Sandpiper A Marsh Sandpiper also foraged at the edge of the water. Our guide called us to point out a small bird silently swimming around – the Great Crested Grebe. The whole scene was so serene! Black-winged Stilt A lovely Black-winged Stilt, which I feel is one of our most beautiful yet most ignored birds, sedately walked past. A small colony of Gulls on a far-away sandbar engaged us for a while as we tried to identify them – the flock included Slender-billed, Brown-headed and Black-headed Gulls. An Osprey turned up and created a flutter. Greater Flamingo Another Yellow Wagtail – this time it seemed to be an adult thunbergi – caught our attention, before we were distracted by a pair of Common Sandpipers chasing each other around. Yet another Yellow Wagtail had a curious blackish necklace-like demarcation and a faint dark wash on its chest. Several Little Grebes, also in breeding plumage, floated around along with some Common Coots. A Whiskered Tern surveyed the scene from above. A pair of the resident Spotbilled Ducks were seen, as was a flock of Greater Flamingos flying past. A dark-morph Western Reef Egret flew over us before settling down nearby. Yellow Wagtail with chest markings Then came the best part of the morning – we saw a pair of Great Crested Grebes engaging in their famous courtship ritual, bowing and bobbing around, raising their heads to the skies, and puffing out their crest and neck feathers! Western Reef Egret dark morph

We saw a couple of Curlew Sandpipers in the water. A few Little Stints, Lesser Sand Plovers, Great Egrets, Black-tailed Godwits, Painted Storks, Northern Shovelers and a few Eurasian Spoonbills (including juveniles) were also around. There were several Dunlins and Broad-billed Sandpipers in a mixed flock, along with the Sand Plovers and Little Stints. Great Crested Grebe pair courtship ritual It would have been great to capture the sequence on video, but I was too enthralled – and too scared to take my eyes off for even a moment to switch to video mode, for fear of missing any of that spectacular display. Curlew Sandpiper Broad-billed Sandpiper (extreme left), Dunlin, Lesser Sand Plover, Little Stint A few Greater Flamingos gave some photo opportunities as they walked around, foraging. A couple of immatures were also seen. Western Reef Egret & Little Cormorant A small group of Little Cormorants seemed to be schoolfishing at the edge of one of the salt pans – and some Eurasian Spoonbills and several Western Reef Egrets seemed to be opportunistically feeding alongside, leapfrogging over each other as they chased the fleeing fish! We had seen some great action today, but it was now approaching 9:00AM, and it was time to start for Ahmedabad, from where we were to catch our return flights. With heavy hearts we decided to wind up and get moving – of course, with the hope and confidence that we would surely bird there again another day! Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 19 Number 12 October 2022 BIRDS: A CLASS APART Trip Report: Narsapur, September 11, 2022 Mallika Chandrasekhar Oriental Magpie Robin with scorpion kill (Photo: Chethan Prathap Vadla) This Sunday turned out to be a beautiful surprise with an invitation to go bird-watching with a group of bird enthusiasts from Deccan Birders, Hyderabad. We congregated in the early hours at the designated place before heading to Narsapur Reserve Forest, which is around 50km from the city of Hyderabad. The weather was anything but sunny. There was a light drizzle from the previous night which continued to this Sunday morning too. But that neither deterred nor dampened the collective spirits of the bird-watching group. I felt glad to be joining them on my maiden birdwatching trip. I realized very soon that just loving birds is not enough. We have to visit and view birds in their natural habitat and be respectful of their world without disturbing or imposing upon their space. Narsapur Reserve Forest is a perfect place to experience a vast expanse of flora and thus a variety of birds as well. It took me a while to get used to the binoculars. I had to finetune both my visual focus and hand adjustment to appreciate the beauty of what a (borrowed) pair of binoculars could do. The result was a magnificent, breath-taking view of a faraway bird perched high above. The first was a Yellow-footed Green Pigeon that was perched in a stately manner on one of the cable lines above. I Googlesearched it after reaching home to find that it is the state bird of Maharashtra. It is a fairly common urban bird found in lowland forests and forest edges, as well as parks, gardens, and orchards. It is not a very vocal bird and occasionally just gives out some cooing whistles. 1

Chalky Percher (aka Ground Skimmer) female (Photo: Asif Husain Arastu) Indian Grey Hornbill (Photo: Asif Husain Arastu) Bird songs and bird sounds permeated the whole area. I remember a spellbinding moment just listening to the cadence and symphony of two distinct birds calling from high up in the trees. It was a celebration of all that is pure and pristine in nature. Such sounds cheer the heart and awaken the soul. Indian Silverbill (Photo: Chethan Prathap Vadla) Initially, we could only see around 25 bird species – with the sun refusing to show up, the birds seemed to have kept themselves out of sight. Our visit seemed not to have elicited much enthusiasm from the birds. Had the sun come out in all its glory, perhaps we would have had more birds to view and be in awe of. But since this was my first time, I was just happy to be in the midst of such fresh air, vast open spaces, and bird sounds. Fortunately, by the end of the outing, more birds turned up and we finished the day at over 60 species. A view of Narsapur Lake (Photo: Mallika Chandrasekhar) We also visited Freedom Park, another gorgeous landscape in Narsapur. There is a huge lake on one side and lush greenery on the other side. The scenery is simply spectacular. The green environs near Freedom Park (Photo: Mallika Chandrasekhar) Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher (Photo: Chethan Prathap Vadla) The light rain added an allure of romantic realism. Nature somehow evokes the best in birds, beasts, and beings. I know I am a better person after experiencing this bird-watching trip. 2

BIRDING IN MISHMI HILLS & LOWER DIBANG VALLEY Trip Report: Arunachal Pradesh, March 27-31, 2022 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao Blyth’s Tragopan, the star bird of Mishmi Hills Introduction It is well known that North-east India abutting the Himalayas forms a unique subtropical or tropical moist montane forest supporting large distribution of avifauna. We had the fortune of visiting Mishmi Hills for a unique birding adventure during the end of March 2022. Mishmi was part of our 3-hop journey that included the Dehing-Patkai National Forest in Assam, Maguri Beel grasslands and finally Mishmi Hills. This article covers the birds found exclusively in Mishmi Hills and other areas we visited at Lower Dibang Valley district of Arunachal Pradesh. Red-billed Scimitar Babbler Black-breasted Parrotbill Red-throated Thrush 4

Geography (source: Wikipedia) Geomorphically, the Mishmi Hills are divided into 2 sections – the flood plains of tributaries of Brahmaputra River and the Arunachal Himalayas consisting of snow-capped mountains, lower Himalayan ranges, and Shivalik ranges. The Hills reach heights above 5,000 m (16,000 ft) but have not been properly mapped. This hilly area is characterized by steeply sloping landform, sub-tropical evergreen forest and high rainfall. The central part of the Hills wraps around both sides of the Dibang Valley. The Mishmi Hills are part of Shan-Malaysia plate are found. The endangered red panda is seen in the northern reaches and the Hoolock Gibbon is in the lower areas. Hoolock Gibbon pair Golden Babbler Beautiful Nuthatch Yellow-throated Marten View of Mishmi Hills from Mayudia Pass Travel View of the cloud forests at Upper Mishmi Hills The Mishmi Hills experience heavy rainfall with pre-monsoon showers from March. The humidity and rainfall are about 90%. There are about 6000 plant species, 100 mammal species and about 700 bird species. There are also many butterflies and other insects. Temperate conifers, sub-alpine woody shrubs, alpine meadows, bamboos and grasslands are found in this region. Tiger, common leopard, clouded leopard, snow leopard, golden cat, jungle cat, marbled cat and the leopard cat Travel to Mishmi Hills is a breeze these days, thanks to the fantastic infrastructure – special mention is needed for the Bhupen Hazarika Bridge, this bridge connects the Tinsukia district (Dibrugarh Airport) of Assam seamlessly to Arunachal Pradesh and is over the Lohit River, a major tributary of the mighty Brahmaputra. The bridge is close to 10km long and a fantastic tourist spot and engineering marvel. The roads are also excellent with great infrastructure, given the tactical need to maintain easy access to Arunachal Pradesh and its interiors. 5

A view of Tiwarigaon, village hamlet halfway to Mishmi Hills Mishmi’s montane forests, with extremely unpredictable weather conditions White-hooded Babbler We spent about one day at Lower Mishmi Hills (near Roing city) and about 2 days on top of the hills near Mayudia Pass (highest pass). Given the montane forests, rains are completely unpredictable, we had a few sessions which was a total washout, but nevertheless got some excellent opportunities to bird for important birds of Mishmi Hills. Hodgson’s Frogmouth Mayudia Pass, highest point on road to Hunli village White-breasted Parrotbill Elephant Grass fields at Jia Grasslands, near Roing in the lower valley Long-billed Wren Babbler 6

Environment Concern, hunting & impact Given that Arunachal Pradesh is strategic due to its location at the border, there has been a rapid investment to build infrastructure to help movement of military and associated assets. Also, locals have an imbibed culture of serious bird hunting, and it is not very uncommon to see people with airguns and slings. This makes it extremely hard to bird, given that birds are inherently scared of humans, and this has had a clear effect on the bird life and distribution. Significant social impact is needed through awareness to ensure that the birds are protected, and hunting, if at all necessary, becomes sustainable. It is also extremely disappointing to see the entire stretch of the hills highly polluted with plastic everywhere: either the tourists who visit the hills, or the workers engaged in various government projects, blatantly abuse the environment, and there is no mechanism to ensure upkeep of the hills. Also, there are several hydroelectric and dam projects being envisioned for Dibang valley that will surely have serious impact on the beautiful setup we have today. Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani Dunlin (Calidris alpina) Dunlin breeding (L) and non-breeding (R) (Jamnagar, Gujarat, November 23, 2021) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Calidris Species: C. alpina Size: 16-22 cm shorter distances, to the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of North America, although birds nesting in northern Alaska generally travel to Asia in winter. Some Dunlins are also observed to winter along the Iberian south coast. Habitat & behaviour: As with most small waders, the Dunlin frequents coastal mudflats, sandy beaches, intertidal pools, sand bars, tidal creeks, river banks and flooded fields. While foraging, it makes short, fast runs over wet mud or wades in shallow water at the edges, where it makes characteristic ‘sewing machine’ actions as it seeks to locate the aquatic invertebrates like molluscs, worms and crustaceans that make up the most part of its diet. It is also known to take insects and seeds. It is gregarious and usually seen in mixed flocks along with other waders. Its flight is fast, and it tends to fly in formation with other individuals. The call is a typical sandpiper-like sharp tue-ep or wee-wee-et, and the display song is a harsh trill. Description & distribution: The Dunlin is a small wader that derives its name from ‘dun’ (meaning dull brown) with a suffix ‘-ling’ (a person or thing with the mentioned quality). First described by Carl Linnaeus in 1758 as Tringa alpina, it was later moved to genus Erolia before finally being added to the genus Calidris along with 23 other species which include sandpipers, knots, sanderlings and stints. Ten subspecies are recognized, varying mainly in the amount of rufous coloration shown during breeding. In breeding plumage, the adult Dunlin is unmistakable, showing a black belly that no other wader of its size has – this has also given it the alternate name of Blackbellied Sandpiper. In non-breeding plumage, the Dunlin has white underparts and delicately marked grey upperparts, indistinct supercilium, black markings on the flanks, and a clear white wingbar in flight. Juveniles are brownish above, with streaking on the belly, rufous fringes to mantle and scapulars, and a buff or whitish V on the back. The legs are black, and the black bill is slightly downcurved – a feature the Dunlin shares with the Curlew Sandpiper. Females have slightly longer bills than the males. The tip of the blunt bill has a mass of nerve endings that enable the Dunlin to use it as a sensitive probe to locate its invertebrate prey in wet mud and sand. Nesting: The Dunlin nests extralimitally in the circumpolar regions of Asia, Europe and North America. The nest is a shallow scrape in the ground, lined with vegetation. The usual clutch consists of 4 eggs, buff with marked brown splotches. Incubation is done by both parents, with the male handling a larger proportion of brood care, as the female is known to abandon the brood and even leave the breeding area. Although the chicks are precocial, brood care is provided in the early stages of development. Some apparent hybrids with Whiterumped Sandpiper and Purple Sandpiper have been reported from the Atlantic coasts of North America and Europe respectively. The Dunlin is a circumpolar breeder in the Arctic or sub-Arctic regions of Asia, Europe and North America. The breeding population from northern Europe and Asia are longdistance migrants, traveling all the way south to the temperate, subtropical and tropical regions of Africa, Southeast Asia and the Middle East. Birds from Alaska and Canada migrate Local name: The Dunlin is known as ‘Kalopet kichadiyo’ in Gujarati, an apparent reference to the black belly seen during breeding. It is also known as ‘Ruzani panlowwa’ in Hindi and ‘Jalaranka’ or ‘Karada tilawa’ in Marathi. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report: Meezuru, Andhra Pradesh, March 06, 2022 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla Mixed flock of shorebirds at Meezuru The village of Meezuru in Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh is situated on the North-western side of the Pulicat Lake. It is about 120km from Tirupati town and houses a major portion of the Pulicat Lagoon. On the advice of some students of IISER Tirupati who are avid birders, we travelled to this village via the Abaka-Karikadu road. It is a vast birding habitat for raptors, land birds as well as waders. We travelled nearly 10km on this road that goes to Meezuru. The village is a fairly large area on the map and includes a lagoon as well as agricultural fields with human habitation at the far end of the road. We stopped at several places along the way to observe bird activity. The first birds we saw were the Blue-tailed Beeeaters, Jerdon’s Bushlarks, Ashy-crowned Sparrow Larks, Indian Silverbills, Scaly-breasted Munias, Indian Roller, White-breasted Kingfisher, Red Collared Dove and Purplerumped Sunbirds. 1

Pied Avocet White-eyed Buzzard As we drove further, we saw several raptors including two White-eyed Buzzards, one Short-toed Snake Eagle and a Marsh Harrier. We were amazed to see that the lagoon point was jam-packed with birds. There were scattered flocks of Eurasian Spoonbills, Asian Openbills, Grey Herons, and Great, Intermediate and Little Egrets. There were also three Western Reef Egrets and around six Spot-billed Pelicans that we saw from close quarters. There may have been more, farther away. Little Egret & Western Reef Egret Spot-billed Pelican Short-toed Snake Eagle Flying above this ground spectacle were many Whiskered, Common and Gull-billed Terns. The brackish waters driven by the tides of the sea probably brought in lots of food for these birds. Greater Flamingos lining the far shore of the water The surprising sighting was a long stand of Greater Flamingos. There were hundreds of them standing in two to three rows foraging in the brackish waters alongside large flocks of Pied Avocets, Ruffs, Northern Shovelers, Little and Temminck’s Stints, and Little and Great Cormorants. Whiskered Terns in flight We spent a couple of hours here trying to spot all the birds in the lagoon. After a brief lunch we travelled further on the Karikadu road that passed through the lagoon, stopping now and then to capture pictures of some fantastic views of the lagoon. 2

we saw such murmurations were that of Rosy Starlings and Rose-ringed Parakeets at Lakhota Lake at Jamnagar, Gujarat. That was Meezuru, the wonderland of birds. Even though there were no lifers it was a rich birding experience, especially the Flamingo stand. Ruff, Marsh Sandpiper & Northern Shoveler At one point we saw hundreds of waders very close to the road. It was a mixed assortment of Common Sandpipers, Marsh Sandpipers, Little Stints and Ruffs. As we looked at the birds, adding more species to our count, a large murmuration of shore birds came into our view. It was only 3:30PM, probably two hours to sunset, and we thought it was too early for murmurations. We were just looking at it when more murmurations began to fill the sky. It was a wonderful sight to watch so many flocks of birds. Trip Report: Goa, September 10-12, 2022 Dr Jairamchander Pingle & Dr Rahul Lath Lesser Adjutant (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) Bird trip to Goa? Who goes to Goa for birding? ‘Goa is all beaches and partying’ is what most people believe. But Goa and the surrounding region is home to more than 400 bird species (resident and migratory). Some good birding spots in Goa are Bondla Wildlife Sanctuary, Bhagwan Mahaveer National Park, Salvador do Mundo wetlands, Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary (Chorao Island), Carambolim wetlands, Cotiago wetlands, Socorro plateau, Curtorim wetlands and Zuari River, to name a few. We did a 3-day trip to Goa for birding and saw many birds including a few lifers which we will highlight in this article. Although it was the monsoon season with heavy rains predicted, we were lucky to get clear periods in between the rain showers. It was a challenge to keep our equipment dry and bird in the rain. Ponchos, umbrellas and rubber boots are a must for birding in the rain! Day-1: Sept 10, 2022 We drove ourselves in a hired car and birded on our own. We covered the regions of Siolim wetland in North Goa, Socorro Plateau and the Salvador do Mundo wetland. White-cheeked Barbet (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) The highlights of the day were Brahminy Kite, White-cheeked Barbet, Vigors’s Sunbird and Black-hooded Oriole. Black-hooded Oriole (Photo: Dr Rahul Lath) Brahminy Kite (Photo: Dr Rahul Lath) 4

Vigors’s Sunbird (Aethopyga vigorsii), also known as the Sahyadari Sunbird or Western Crimson Sunbird, is a species of sunbird which is endemic to the Western Ghats of India. It has been considered as subspecies of the Crimson Sunbird. The male has a scarlet throat and breast, while the rest of its underparts are uniformly grey. Its wings are grey-brown and tail is green. In the females, the upper parts are dark olive while underparts are grey. Day-2: Sept 11, 2022 We went with our birding guide by road to Bondla Wildlife Sanctuary, which is an hour’s drive from North Goa. 50 bird species were observed by us over a 6-hour period. The lifers seen were the Vernal Hanging Parrot, Emerald Dove, Little Spiderhunter, Grey-fronted Green Pigeon, Fork-tailed Drongo Cuckoo, Bronzed Drongo and Bar-winged Flycatcher-shrike. Greater Flameback (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) We walked in the forest looking for the Blue-eared Kingfisher – it fishes in the streams in the forest covered by canopy, so that it is not disturbed by the sunlight reflecting on the water – but we were not lucky enough to see it. (Note: The Bondla Wildlife Sanctuary and surrounding forest is home to a variety of venomous snakes, and it is advisable to wear gumboots). Little Spiderhunter (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) Grey-fronted Green Pigeon (Photo: Dr Rahul Lath) Malabar Grey Hornbill (Photo: Dr Rahul Lath) The Grey-fronted Green Pigeon (Treron affinis) is found in the Western Ghats in India. It is usually seen singly or in small groups. The male has a reddish mantle while the female has a green mantle. Other highlights were a large family of twelve Malabar Grey Hornbills, a pair of Malabar Pied Hornbills, and Greater and Black-rumped Flameback woodpeckers. Vernal Hanging Parrot (Photo: Dr Rahul Lath) Black-rumped Flameback (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) 5

The Vernal Hanging Parrot (Loriculus vernalis) is a small parrot which is resident in the Indian subcontinent and some areas of South-east Asia. It is a small, predominantly green, hanging parrot. It measures 14cm in length and has a small tail. The adult male has a red rump and bill and a blue throat patch, while the female has a green patch. Malabar Pied Hornbill (Photo: Dr Rahul Lath) east Asia. Unlike typical sunbirds, males and females are similar in plumage and are found near flowering plants. Day-3: Sept 12, 2022 We took the early morning Ribandar Ferry on the Mandovi River and crossed over to the Chorao Island, which is home to the Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary. There we took a boat ride along the mangroves for about 90 minutes and saw 35 species of birds, including the Collared Kingfisher and the Stork-billed Kingfisher. Collared Kingfisher (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) The Malabar Pied Hornbill (Anthracoceros coronatus) is also known as the Lesser Pied Hornbill. At 65cm length, it has mainly black plumage with a white belly and throat patch. The bill is yellow with a large black casque. Females have white orbital skin which is lacking in the male. It is a common resident breeder in Western Ghats, Central and Eastern India and Sri Lanka. The Bar-winged Flycatcher-shrike (Hemipus picatus) is found in the tropical forests of southern Asia. It is found hunting in the mid-canopy of forests and is insectivorous. It perches upright and has a distinctive pattern of black and white. It is black-capped, with black wings that contrast with the white body. A white slash across the wing stands out in contrast. Stork-billed Kingfisher (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) Other birds seen were Rufous Woodpecker, Malabar and Chestnut-tailed Starlings, Lesser Whistling-duck, Common Sandpiper, Common Redshank, Striated Heron, Lesser Adjutant, Wire-tailed and Red-rumped Swallows, and Common Kingfisher. Bar-winged Flycatcher-shrike (Photo: Dr Rahul Lath) The Little Spiderhunter (Arachnothera longirostra) is a species of long-billed nectar-feeding bird in the family Nectariniidae, found in the moist forests of South and South-Malabar Starling (Photo: Dr Jairamchander Pingle) 6

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Painted Stork (Mycteria leucocephala) Painted Stork adult (L) (Chennai, October 30, 2022) and juvenile (R) (Bharatpur, December 13, 2019) Order: Ciconiiformes Family: Ciconiidae Genus: Mycteria Species: M. leucocephala Size: 93-100 cm also frequents irrigation canals, flooded crop fields, tanks and village jheels, river banks and tidal creeks. It is absent from deserts, very dry regions and hilly areas. It has historically been rare in Kerala, though it appears to have expanded its range into Kerala in the late 1990s and is now seen regularly there. It is usually seen feeding in groups, foraging mainly in the day. It feeds mainly on small fish, though it is occasionally known to take crustaceans, frogs, eels or snakes. While foraging, it walks slowly, disturbing the water with its feet to flush the fish, and also senses them by touch while sweeping its half-open bill side to side as it walks. Once fed, it may stand still on the shore for long durations. Being a big bird, its flight is slow and ponderous, and it is often seen to take advantage of thermals as it soars along with Asian Openbills. The call is a harsh, croaking call. Description & distribution: A large, easily identifiable wader in the stork family, the Painted Stork has a heavy orangeyellow bill with a pinkish downcurved tip, bare orange head, waxy, unfeathered yellow face, and white neck and throat. The most distinctive feature is the bright pink-tipped tertial feathers, which also extend over the back and rump when at rest. Primary and secondary feathers, and the tail, are black with a glossy greenish sheen. It has a black breast-band with white scaly markings, running into the under-wing coverts, white belly and vent, and white back and upperparts. Legs are yellowish or reddish, but can appear white due to their tendency to defecate on their legs while standing. The sexes are alike, but the males are larger. Juvenile birds have a duller bill and brownish head and neck, and no pectoral band or pink feathers, giving the entire bird a brownish appearance. Nesting: The Painted Stork nests mainly between August and January, shortly after the monsoons, with some variations based on local conditions. Painted Storks breed on large trees, either by themselves or along with other species like Asian Openbills, Black-headed Ibises, Spot-billed Pelicans, and assorted Egrets or Cormorants. The nest is a large stick platform with a shallow depression in the middle, lined with leaves and straw, built on trees standing near or in water, and include trees on islands. The usual clutch consists of 3-5 eggs, somewhat dirty white, with sparse brown streaks or spots; early breeders are known to have larger clutches. Incubation and feeding duties are done by both parents. The Painted Stork is widely distributed across the plains of Asia, south of the Himalayas and east of the Indus River system, extending east into South-east Asia, and including India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, South China, Indo-China and Sri Lanka. It is resident in most areas in its range, but can make seasonal movements. Young birds are known to disperse quite far (several hundred km) from their breeding sites. Local name: The Painted Stork is known as ‘Janghil’ or ‘Dokh’ in Hindi, ‘Yeru kala konga’ in Telugu, ‘Chenga narai’ or ‘Sanguvalai narai’ in Tamil and ‘Jhangil’, ‘Ram jhankar’ or ‘Sona jangha’ in Bengali. Trip Coordinator(s): Srikanth Bhamidipati (Mobile: 9738840070) Trip Report: Theog, Himachal Pradesh, October 04-07, 2022 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao A view at Theog After a long hiatus after 2 years of Covid, we as a family decided to go on a vacation. We had been to Shimla and Manali before and we had heard about Theog, a quaint town nestled in the Himalayas. We had the good fortune of staying in Theog, situated in Shimla Dist, for about 4 days. Being a family of nature lovers and birders, literally every trip that we take as a family has birding thrown in along with a lot of nature walks. Rock Bunting 1

October was a low season (also much before the migrants begin their sojourn south) and of course holiday times for kids due to Dussehra, so we headed off to the hills via Chandigarh. Asian Barred Owlet Lush forest at Shimla Water Catchment WLS We also drove a day to trek within the Shimla Water Catchment WLS, which is a must do activity; though birding is hard given the thick deodar forests, but more than 150+ birds have been reported here and I was able to get great pictures of one of my favorite birds – the Rufous-bellied Niltava. Coal Tit Rufous-bellied Niltava The lush forests of Shimla Water Catchment Wildlife Sanctuary are a must visit for nature and bird lovers. Whilst the birds are very hard to find due to thick canopy, the nature trail for 15+ kms is simply amazing. Walking trail at Shimla Water Catchment WLS Chestnut-bellied Rock Thrush We also enjoyed walking the trails through Shimla Water Catchment WLS, including an extremely well maintained walkway for more than 8km. 2
