Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Little Stint (Calidris minuta) Little Stint (Chennai, February 18, 2021) Little Stint (Jamnagar, September 23, 2021) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Calidris Species: C. minuta Size: 13-15 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Little Stint is gregarious and usually seen in medium to large flocks, usually along with other small waders like Dunlin, Sand Plovers, Ringed Plovers, Sandpipers etc. It frequents coastal areas, lake edges, paddyfields, lagoons, tidal creeks, estuaries, marshes, intertidal mudflats and salt pans. Little Stints are given to take the occasional flight in large numbers, and the coordinated banking and turning, alternatively flashing white (underparts) and silverybrown (upperparts) is one of the most beautiful sights to watch. While foraging, the flock spreads out, running around actively on the mud, picking up the aquatic insects, ants, crustaceans and mollusks that form the main part of their diet. They may also take mosquitoes, larval and adult flies, small beetles and plant matter. Its call is a sharp stit, a soft musical wit-wit-wit, and a low tr-rr or a weak pi-pi-pi, uttered in flight. Description & distribution: The Little Stint is a small-sized wader that breeds in the arctic regions of Europe and Asia, and is a long-distance migrant, wintering in the Mediterranean region, the Middle East, Madagascar, South Asia and Africa, with some birds straying to North America and Australia. The genus name comes from the Ancient Greek kalidris (or skalidris), which was a term used by Aristotle to describe some grey waterside birds. It has mottled dark brown, greyishbrown or dusky upperparts and whitish underparts, straight, fine blackish bill and dark legs with unwebbed toes. It is one of the two stints with dark legs seen in India (the other being Red-necked). Irises are dark, and it shows a faint whitish eyering. Rump and middle tail feathers are dark brown, while the outer tail feathers are smoky brown. When in flight, grey sides to tail and a narrow whitish wing bar may be visible. The summer (breeding) plumage is darker, with rufous fringes to upperpart feathers. A rufous-orange wash on the face, neck sides and breast is also seen, besides a white throat and wellmarked white V on the mantle. Sexes are alike. Nesting: The Little Stint breeds generally between June and July in most of its breeding range in North-eastern Europe and Siberia. The typical nest is usually a shallow cup-shaped depression on grassy marshland, lined with willow leaves or other plant matter. The usual clutch consists of 3-5 oval eggs, greenish to off-white or buffish stone coloured, spotted and blotched with reddish brown. Chicks hatch out after 20-25 days of incubation, and are precocial, able to feed themselves almost immediately. Local name: The Little Stint is known as ‘Chhota panlowwa’ in Hindi and Marathi, ‘Kosu ullan’ in Tamil and ‘Kalapag khichdiyo’ or ‘Nano khichdiyo’ in Gujarati. In winter, the eastern population of the Little Stint is seen throughout India, as well as in Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. *** We wish all our members a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year 2023 For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Report: Birds of Chennayyagunta, Tirupati, January-December 2022 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla A view of Chennayyagunta, with Tirumala Hills in the background The Seshachalam Hills in Tirupati are an exciting bird haven. We moved to the town of Tirupati a year ago and almost immediately began to look around for bird habitats near our home on the outskirts of the town. Luckily for us a small wetland, at walkable distance from our home at Green City, Chennayyagunta, was a great find. In fact, it was like backyard birdwatching for us and we would walk around this place whenever we had some time. Chennayyagunta is located in the Urban mandal of Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh. Most of this area is a marshy habitat with clayey soil. The wetland-like area, measuring about 15 acres approximately, is filled with hydrophytic plants like cattail reeds and different grasses, and is bordered by many weed plants like Lantana, Prosopis juliflora, Calotropis procera, Cassia auriculata, Prickly Pear Cactus and trees like Pongamia pinnata (Kanuga tree), Copper Pod and Neem, to name a few. Adjacent to it there is also a lake, parts of which are seen as sand bars except during the rainy season when it fills up. An important feature of the Green City colony is that it houses a recently created Miyawaki Forest, the third in Tirupati District. 1

We made a checklist of birds of Chennayyagunta covering the period from January to December 2022, and the tally was 120 species! The first birds that we saw were hundreds of Ashy-crowned Sparrowlarks in the grassland next to a small rainfed stream. These birds would fly around now and then like a black and white carpet in the air. The wetland area and the lake attract a number of Wood and Green Sandpipers, Little and Temminck’s Stints, Little Ringed and Kentish Plovers, Lesser Whistling-ducks, Spot-billed Ducks, Eurasian Coot, Little and Great Cormorants, Grey, Purple and Indian Pond Herons, and hundreds of Western Yellow Wagtails. The Striated Heron that we spotted here was a lifer for us. Cinnamon Bittern The Greater Painted-snipes were seen many times in the open in the marshy areas. In the marshes, and flying around them, we had a number of sightings of Cinnamon and Black Bitterns, as well as a lone Yellow Bittern. Striated Heron Large flock of Western Yellow Wagtail An eye-catching sight near the lake is the presence of hundreds of Western Yellow Wagtails. We had also seen them in great numbers on the lake bund of Bortalav Lake in Bhavnagar, Gujarat. Black Bittern Greater Painted-snipe female (L) and male (R) Yellow Bittern 2

The Blue-tailed Bee-eaters are numerous during winter. Among the shrikes were Bay-backed, Long-tailed and Brown Shrikes, and also the Black-headed Cuckooshrike and Common Woodshrike. The Common Woodshrikes move around in threes and fours; one day we saw five of them perched on the wire! Tricoloured Munia The marshes were also home to a large number of Tricolored and Scaly-breasted Munias, while the White-rumped Munia was sighted here only a couple of times. Baya Weavers made nests on Prosopis plants that were growing on the edge of the marsh. There were also a few Bengal Weavers, but no nests were seen. A few Streaked Weavers were also seen occasionally. Common Woodshrike Common Snipe In winter months, the marshy areas attract a large number of Common Snipes. It is a beautiful sight to watch so many of them at once. Normally it is quite difficult to photograph snipes and bitterns, as they are elusive and hardly visible in their marshy habitat. But at Chennayyagunta, we would see the bitterns perched on the cattail reeds at a very close distance, and it was therefore easy taking pictures and videos of these birds. The Blyth’s Pipit is a winter visitor here. The migratory Rosy and Chestnut-tailed Starlings were seen only for a few days in November and were probably passage migrants. Black-headed Cuckooshrike female Chestnut-tailed Starling Rosy Starling & Black Drongo 3

While the Indian Paradise-flycatcher is the only flycatcher that we could sight, the warblers included Sykes’s, Paddyfield, Blyth’s Reed and Clamorous Reed Warblers. Jacobin Cuckoo Indian Spotted Eagle The Jacobin Cuckoo is resident here and can be seen during all seasons. Common Hawk and Grey-bellied Cuckoos were sighted a couple of times. Coming to the doves, the list includes Red Collared, Eurasian Collared, Laughing and Spotted Doves. Any description of the birds in this locality would not be complete without the mention of the large flocks of Yellowwattled Lapwings that we see here. One particular day, we counted about twenty-seven of them in one flock huddled together in the grassland! The dainty Common Kingfishers, the noisy Pied Kingfishers and the White-breasted Kingfishers always have dainty morsels in their mouths. Openbill Storks, Painted Storks and large flocks of Glossy Ibis could be seen flying overhead on an almost daily basis. Bonelli’s Eagle In the month of August, the Indian Spotted Eagle (a lifer for us), Oriental Honey-buzzard and Bonelli’s Eagle were seen. Surprisingly the Black Kite is seen rarely here, indicating an absence of garbage dumps. The Blue-faced Malkoha is also common and we loved seeing the bird so much in the open. Glossy Ibis Birdwatching is an amazing experience at Chennayyagunta, because of the abundance of species, be it wagtails, sandpipers, stints, plovers, sparrowlarks and, more so, the Common Snipes which seem to be present literally in the dozens. The birding was exciting all year round and as the seasons changed, so would the birdlife vary. Almost every week, we would add a new species to the list of birds that we had seen at Chennayyagunta. Here’s to many more! The full list of birds seen is given below: Blue-faced Malkoha 4

While we connected and discussed about our whereabouts, on the spur of the moment, we planned a flying visit to my favourite hotspot where the largest flying birds in the world thrive in the National Capital Region (NCR). 6

The quick trip was to check on the health of an ecological niche called Dhanauri Wetlands, nestled inside a mosaic of crop fields. Located a mere 70km from Delhi border, in Greater Noida in Uttar Pradesh, this tiny group of villages offer a conducive habitat for the dwindling Sarus Cranes. If one is lucky, on any given hot summer evening, there can be over 150 Sarus Cranes roosting together, a splendid spectacle. But our trip was on the December 17, 2022, so we noticed just five of them as the rest would be far afield, foraging and feeding. Of course, a lot of other birds were seen, too. Eurasian Hoopoe Sarus Crane The first time I saw the splendid Sarus Crane was at the 29 sq.km Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary of Rajasthan in 1987, as two pairs walked nonchalantly with the feral cattle at Kadam-Kunj marshlands. It is not unusual to fall in love with the subject of your scrutiny, or be smitten by the distinct behaviour of a birdof-feather, or even photo-capture them in their best feathery costumes. The Sarus Crane is no exception – it is a pleasure to watch a lovey-dovey pair, standing side by side, grooming or partaking in silent gossip. They even utter guttural calls in unison that shatter the silence of the lingering landscape and also reassure themselves of their mated status. Since that first encounter, the Sarus Crane has been my muse for three decades now. Purple Heron Since ancient times Sarus Cranes in India have been known not only for their extreme fidelity, but also their dramatic dance rituals, performed before and during mating, and sometimes even after the nesting season. Sarus Cranes have been explicitly painted in the pages of ‘Akbarnama’ (Book of Akbar), and is the official chronicle of the reign of Akbar, the third Mughal Emperor of India (1556–1605). Presently there are three global populations of Sarus Crane thriving independently in western and northern India, Southeast Asia and Northern Australia. Sarus Cranes have been more or less decimated from our neighbouring countries, and now primarily survive by the scruff of the neck in India, explains an official from the International Crane Foundation (ICF) stationed in India. Sarus Crane, the State Bird of Uttar Pradesh The Sarus Crane also happens to be the state bird of Uttar Pradesh, as 70% of the population of Sarus found in India resides in the state. Interestingly the largest state of India, densely populated with about 23 crore human population, and intensely farmed, still plays a perfect host to the Sarus Cranes. The mighty, perennial Ganga River, with multiple tributaries, passes through the entire geography of UP and keeps the terrain naturally well irrigated. These waterways continuously help refresh and retain wetlands during cultivation by farmers, and this has led to the proliferation of mosaics of marshy stretches. Favourable conditions have given a geographical advantage to over 300 species of aquatic birds, particularly the dominating Sarus Cranes for feeding, breeding and brooding in Uttar Pradesh. 7

Professor BC Choudhury, the Executive Trustee of Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) and a wetland resources professional with over 45 years of experience, is the first-generation wildlife biologist of India who spearheaded the first three national level Sarus counts 21 years ago. Presently, his involvement with the community participation in conservation of the Sarus Crane and its wetland habitats in eastern Uttar Pradesh for the last seven years has paid rich dividends. He and his team have been identifying Important Sarus Wetland Sites (ISWS) in the agricultural landscape of eastern Uttar Pradesh, as the region was long ignored by giving preference to western Uttar Pradesh. Northern Shoveler male Uttar Pradesh has given the Sarus an esteemed position by declaring it as the ‘State Bird’. Information is available about the population in western Uttar Pradesh and Terai region, but such information was lacking in eastern Uttar Pradesh. This information gap necessitated implementation of a project by the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) in 2013 with support from Tata Trusts in this region. It is meant basically to encourage and involve the community in the conservation for Sarus Cranes. Red-wattled Lapwing Grey-headed Swamphen We spent two full hours at Dhanauri Wetlands, and discussed various issues regarding its protection status that need to be tackled urgently and not-so-urgently. Meanwhile, Nalini, the prolific birder, was busy preparing her checklist (attached below). Bronze-winged Jacana While driving down the Yamuna express highway, towards our destination, Choudhury explained that wetlands, the primary habitats of the Sarus Crane, are facing various forms of anthropogenic pressure like reclamation of wetlands for urbanization and agriculture expansion, and intense use of Agrochemicals. Damage of Sarus nests and stealing of eggs, pestering by feral dogs as well as electrocutions further add to the threats that the tallest flying bird of the world faces. It is pertinent to mention that BC Choudhury, formerly with the premier Wildlife Institute of India (WII), spearheaded the first three national Sarus Crane surveys two decades ago. He explains that the aim was to research the ecology of the Sarus Crane and to provide the necessary base-line data towards its habitat conservation. Country-wide information on the Sarus Crane was pertinent to involve people from all walks of life, both in the preservation of the species and also spreading awareness. The intention was to obtain data about Sarus Crane on a national level and to understand the population dynamics. Though annual counts are carried out at Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary since the 1980s, nation-wide quantitative data was unavailable. The Sarus population is largely outside the protected areas, primarily in agriculture dominated landscape dotted with wetlands. Though the rice paddies provide the Sarus a nearnatural habitat, changing cropping patterns from rice to cash crops like sugarcane have reduced their habitat. The Sarus, therefore, are now localized to areas where there is a mosaic of rice/wheat cultivation, and natural wetlands. Nilgai at Dhanauri 8

Wildlife Institute of India (WII) and associated organisations in their three-year national Sarus Crane survey in 1999-2001 found that involvement of states and dedicated volunteers was essential to arrive at a realistic Sarus status in the country. The report, however, clearly depicts that UP has had the majority of the Sarus numbers, and the bird invariably migrated within the state with some spill-over into neighbouring wetlands in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. Sarus Cranes love the countryside and evidently evolved as a bird with a clear preference for certain landscapes. With no comprehensive survey of Sarus Cranes conducted in recent years at the national level, the countrywide guesstimate of Sarus population is pegged at approximately 25000 individuals. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Wood Sandpiper (Tringa glareola) Wood Sandpiper (Chennai, March 18 & 25, 2021) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Tringa Species: T. glareola Size: 18-21 cm diagnostic. The summer (breeding) plumage is more vibrant, with heavy streaking and barring on breast and flanks respectively. Juvenile birds show warm brown upperparts with buff speckling and a lightly-streaked buff breast. Habitat & behaviour: The Wood Sandpiper is gregarious and usually seen in ones and twos, or in small flocks, not mixed with other species. It frequents inland freshwater bodies, paddyfields, lagoons, tidal creeks, marshes, intertidal mudflats and lake edges. It typically forages by running along on the mud, picking up tit-bits, or by probing into the mud. Its diet mainly consists of beetles, termites, ants, larvae, worms and mollusks; they may also take spiders, frogs, shellfish, small fish, aquatic invertebrates and plant matter like seeds. When nervous or alert, it bobs its tail up and down like the Common Sandpiper, but not habitually. It does not usually call when on the ground, but utters a shrill chiff-chiff-chiff as it takes off. Description & distribution: The Wood Sandpiper is a midsized, long-legged wader, and the smallest member of the Tringa genus of shanks and sandpipers. It breeds in the subarctic wetlands, from the Scottish Highlands east across Palearctic Europe and northern Asia, and migrates in winters to Africa, southern Asia (especially India), South-east Asia and Australia. Vagrant birds have also been reported from the Hawaiian Islands and from Palau and Mariana Islands in Micronesia. The species name glareola comes from the Latin word for ‘gravel’, and the genus name Tringa comes from the name given to the Green and Solitary Sandpipers, although it is not closely related to them; rather, it is most closely related to the Common Redshank and the Marsh Sandpiper. Nesting: The Wood Sandpiper breeds generally between May and June in most of its breeding range in Europe and northern Asia. The typical nest is usually a scantily-lined depression on a dry patch amidst marshy, grassy areas, but it may also use abandoned tree-nests of other birds. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 pale green eggs. Incubation and parenting duties are carried out by both parents. The Wood Sandpiper has a finely-streaked greyish-brown head, neck and breast. The throat and underparts are white, with some pale brownish streaking on the breast; the upperparts are sepia-brown or greyish-brown with a somewhat variable but strongly marked scaly pattern, while the lower back and rump are white. Bill is straight, fine and grey in colour. Lores are greyish-brown, and there is a white eye-ring and a clear white supercilium running from the bill to the nape. Legs are long and greyish-green or greenish-yellow. When in flight, white rump and barred brown-and-white tail are Local name: The Wood Sandpiper is known as ‘Chupka’, ‘Shobaha’ or ‘Titvari’ in Hindi, ‘Chinna ulanka’ in Telugu, ‘Kottan’ or ‘Vaya ullan’ in Tamil and ‘Kata kokku’ in Malayalam. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Report: Birds of Wild Ass Sanctuary, Kutch, Gujarat, January 9-10, 2023 Text & Photos: Dr Krishna Nagarajan A view of the flat barren lands at Wild Ass Sanctuary, Little Rann of Kutch While planning a family trip to the White Desert at Dhordo, Kutch, we decided to make a pit stop at the Wild Ass Sanctuary on our way back to Ahmedabad. The sanctuary turned out to be a birding paradise and we ended up having our best bird-watching outing as a family, post Covid. We stayed for a night at the Royal Safari Camp resort at Bajana, about 100 kilometres west of Ahmedabad. The resort provided a jeep safari trip as part of the package. Our plan was primarily to sight the Wild Asses at the Sanctuary and do whatever birding we could do along the way. A pair of binoculars, a birding camera, and a soft copy of Grimmett’s ‘Pocket Guide to the Birds of the Indian Subcontinent’ are part of our travel checklist. After checking into the resort, we went for the evening safari of the Sanctuary. The jeep driver who was assigned to us, Mahboob, turned out to be an excellent bird-watching guide. He became excited when he realised that we were into bird-watching as well. The Wild Ass Sanctuary is said to be spread around an area of 5000 sq km. We entered the sanctuary from the Bajana gate. Adjacent to the gate, you see a huge lake at the right. The water seems to be coming from the river Okaro Kharagoda, which terminates here by forming the lake. Crested Lark As soon as we entered the gate and headed towards the lake shore, we came across a flock of Crested Larks and Wheatears. Desert Wheatear Hume’s Wheatear 2

The lake was full of migratory and resident birds: Great White (or Rosy) Pelican, Greater Flamingo, Common Crane, Painted Stork, Eurasian Spoonbill and Greylag Goose. Great White Pelican Little Cormorant Common Crane Great Cormorant Greylag Goose There were also good numbers of Northern Shoveler, Blackwinged Stilt, Common Sandpiper, Little, Indian and Great Cormorants, Grey-headed Swamphen, Ruddy Shelduck, etc. Ruddy Shelduck It was interesting to see the Spoonbill fishing while walking around in the lake with its bill inside the water. It was also interesting the way the Greater Flamingos were swinging their necks left and right sieving through the water surface. 3

So on one side, you have a lake full of migratory and resident birds, and on the other the land is completely flat and barren which makes it easy to sight the birds even if they are a 1000 metres away! This makes it a really fascinating and unique bird-watching location, especially for sighting the birds of prey. Even after all these years of bird-watching, I find it difficult to properly identify the birds of prey. They are hardly seen sitting around to study them carefully. They don’t flock either. The males and females can also differ significantly and identifying them in flight is even more confusing. Re-watching the ‘Raptors’ webinar by Deccan Birders is on my list of things to do. Eurasian Spoonbill As you drive away from the lake towards the left, you immediately notice that the land is barren with hardly any vegetation. There are just a few shrubs here and there. The dry land is flat and full of cracks, apparently due to the abundance of the salt underground. We were told that during the rainy season, the whole area is flooded with water converting it into a wetland. Steppe Eagle The best and the fun part of bird-watching at the Wild Ass Sanctuary was that you can sight the birds of prey such as the Steppe Eagle, Imperial Eagle, Greater Spotted Eagle, Montagu’s Harrier, Marsh Harrier, etc, from a distance. They are usually sitting on the ground or on top of a shrub. Then you drive the jeep to a closer distance. They don’t seem to care and hardly budge from their place. You get plenty of time to study the birds and take pictures to your heart’s content! Eastern Imperial Eagle Indian Wild Ass Montagu’s Harrier As we started driving into the dry land, which is vast, we immediately ran into a herd of Indian Wild Asses. These are listed as “Near Threatened” by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). I was surprised how healthy and strong they looked. In fact, they almost looked like a strong horse but shorter in height. Amazing. 4

At the end of the safari as the sun was setting, we drove back to the lake to watch the sun set. It was made even more memorable, when we saw a solitary Black-necked Stork fishing in the lake. This was a first for us. After the sunset, we drove back to the resort, content and with the thought that the unexpected birding extravaganza made the overall trip something to remember for a long time. Lesser Flamingo Driving further into the Sanctuary, we reached the inner lake shores where we found a huge flock (more than 200) of Lesser Flamingos. CLOSE ENCOUNTERS OF THE MALAYAN KIND Text & Photos: Umesh Mani The Malayan Night Heron (Gorsachius melanolophus) has been in the news lately in Chennai, with sightings being reported from a couple of locations in quick succession. The first, was from Guindy National Park (GNP), which was not surprising given the thick forest/scrub habitat available there, and another was from the area surrounding a lake at a place called Manampathy. After the first report from GNP, 3 of us (Chitra from Hyderabad, Manjula from Bengaluru, and I) made a visit to GNP on Jan 21, 2023, to try and get a look at the bird. It is not easy to get into GNP, but Chitra somehow managed to get permission, and off we went, all excited! A roughly 4km walk later, we reached the location where it had been sighted the previous week. We were, of course, a little tired, but the anticipation of seeing the bird kept us going. But when we reached the spot, it began to sink in that this was going to be tough. The forest was really thick there – it was, of course, impossible to venture in – and we had perforce to bird from the trail only. So the bird really had to be at the edge of the patch, if we were to get a view. And then it happened. We came upon a small gap in the shrubbery, and there it was, right in front of us, not more than 4-5 feet away. The bird was as startled as we were! Manjula and Chitra managed to fire off a few record shots, but being at the rear end of the group, I could only get a glimpse of the bird’s rear as it took off and scooted from there. I had been hoping to see it properly and get a few good photographs, of course. So I was slightly deflated, but I can’t say I was too disappointed – at least we did see it, and more importantly, it was a lifer for Manjula & Chitra. Another long walk later, we were sitting around breakfast and talking about the Malayan Night Heron, and my mind went back to my first sighting at IIT. Susy, who lives inside the IIT campus and is an excellent birder, had been kind enough to enable my entry into the campus. That day too, the heron kept to the thick scrub, and the location was such that we could just about manage to get a view of the bird – the next photo will give an idea what the location was like. Anyway, we walked around for a bit, searching for this enigmatic bird that, unlike most other herons, seems to be a solitary bird as well as a shy one – which basically means that it is difficult to locate! After some time, we decided to walk ahead and explore other nearby parts of the forest – all of it was, after all, suitable habitat. My first sighting of the Malayan Night Heron, back in 2017, had been at IIT campus, which is adjoining GNP. From my observations there, and from some reading, I knew that the Malayan Night Heron often frequents the underbrush in thick scrub forest, and not far from water. So we walked to a nearby lake, to see if the heron was hanging around there. Another long walk along the lake edges not yielding any result, we decided to move further on the trail, trying to check inside any mini-trail or opening that we could find. Malayan Night Heron (Chennai, February 12, 2017) (Photo: Umesh Mani) From across a small stream adjoining the site, inside a temple premises, precariously balanced up on a wall, half-bent to avoid the overhanging branches, I somehow managed to get a few photos… it was quite a circus. Malayan Night Heron (Chennai, February 12, 2017) (Photo: Umesh Mani) Malayan Night Heron (Chennai, February 21, 2023) (Photo: Dr Chitra Shanker) 7

However, though it kept a watchful eye on us, maybe the bird took pity on us, because at least it gave us time. And after a while, when we decided to wind up and move back, the bird too changed its location and came a little closer to the road! I was able to find a small gap through which I could get a few photos, and was much satisfied at the unobstructed view, and grateful for the opportunity to see a bird that is generally quite difficult to find. I realised that I had been more than a little fortunate! Malayan Night Heron (Chennai, February 12, 2017) (Photo: Umesh Mani) *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From Instagram, February 9, 2022) *** 8

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Marsh Sandpiper (Tringa stagnatilis) Marsh Sandpiper (Chennai, February 11, 2023) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Tringa Species: T. stagnatilis Size: 22-25 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Marsh Sandpiper is usually seen singly or in small flocks, usually interspersed with other sandpipers and shanks. It favours the swampy edges of lakes, streams and creeks, as well as freshwater or brackish ponds, jheels, paddy fields, aquaculture ponds, etc, and less often in tidal mudflats and estuaries. It feeds by moving along, randomly pivoting in semi-circles, and picking its prey with its bill. Its diet consists mainly of insects and their larvae, worms, crustaceans, snails, shrimp and small frogs and fish. Its call is a melodious, repetitive tuee-u, tuee-u or a shrill piping cheweep che-weep, uttered while taking off. Description & distribution: The Marsh Sandpiper is a smallsized member of the Tringa genus of sandpipers and shanks. It breeds in the open grassy steppe and taiga grasslands from the eastern parts of Europe, across to the far eastern parts of Russia, and winters mainly in Africa, India, Nepal and Sri Lanka, with some populations going all the way to South-east Asia and Australia. Nesting: The Marsh Sandpiper breeds generally between April and June in most of its breeding range. It is monogamous and breeds in loose colonies. The typical nest is a shallow cupshaped depression built on a mound on grassy or marshy lake edges. The usual clutch consists of 2-4 pale buff eggs with heavy mottling. Incubation is carried out by both parents. The Marsh Sandpiper resembles a smaller, more elegant version of the Common Greenshank, with a long, dark, fine bill, greenish or yellowish legs, and greyish upperparts that turn a muted greyish-brown or light brown during breeding season. The upperparts also show fine mottling with delicately coloured feathers, some diffuse brown spotting on neck and breast, and irregular barring on flanks. Forehead, sides of the head, supercilium, lower back and rump are pure white in winter. Irises are black. In flight, it shows a distinctive white wedge up its back, and the legs extend well past the tail tips. Sexes are alike. Local name: The Marsh Sandpiper is known as ‘Chhota gotra’ in Hindi, ‘Biler balubatan’ in Bengali, ‘Chhanbhi chaha’ in Punjabi, ‘Gandapug tutvari’ or ‘Nani lilapag tutvari’ in Gujarati, ‘Chikhli tutvari’ in Marathi and ‘Cheeti ullan’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. HSBC Hyderabad Bird Race, February 26, 2023 This year’s edition of the Bird Race was held with great success on February 26, 2023. A total of 18 teams, comprising 70 members, participated, and a total of more than 160 unique species were sighted during the day. There was also a gathering in the evening, where team members submitted their logbooks, as well as shared their experiences and anecdotes from the day, and a great time was had by those present. The top three teams were: Team BLACKBIRDS (Abhinav Krishna, Lawrence Mathappan, Sanjeevani, Chitra Shanker) with 141 species; Team FRANCOLINS (Prakash, Ramakrishna, Abhishek Ravindra, Mahendar Alpula) with 140 species; and Team EAGLES (Naresh Vadrevu, Ramakanth, Nanditha, Kiran Kumar) with 114 species. We bring you a report by Sanjeevani from Team Blackbirds, along with a number of colourful photographs. 1

Report: HSBC Hyderabad Bird Race, February 26, 2023 Sanjeevani Illambaruthi At the Flag-off (Photo courtesy: Srikanth Bhamidipati) The HSBC India Bird Race for Hyderabad was organized by Deccan Birders on February 26, 2023. It is an exciting event for birders new and old, through all ages. This was the first physical Bird Race after the pandemic, and was much awaited by many avid birders. I could not sleep the previous night and kept checking my alarm. We got ready at 5:00AM and left home when it was still dark. All participants had to assemble before 6:00AM and register to make teams of 4-5 people with one team captain. Many people formed groups with others who were strangers, meeting for the first time with only one thing in common – love for birds. Large Cuckooshrike (Photo: Dr Chitra Shanker) After the flag off at 6:00AM, every team had till 5:00PM to bird all around the city of Hyderabad and make their entries in the booklet provided, after which the teams would assemble at the venue and wait for the judges to finish going through booklets of every team. Our team, named Blackbirds, consisted of young Abhinav, me, Chitra aunty, Lawrence Uncle and Srikanth Uncle. Our vehicle was a Thar jeep and we were seated at the back. Srikanth Uncle drove at literally breakneck speed (as fast as it was safe!) which is why we could reach many hotspots. Indian Blue Robin (Photo: Dr Chitra Shanker) Brown-breasted Flycatcher (Photo: Sanjeevani Illambaruthi) We started birding while driving and ticked off many of the common birds en route to our first destination – the Damagundam Reserve Forest. The highlights of this location were the sighting of the Indian Blue Robin, Malabar Whistling Thrush, Large Cuckooshrike, and Orange-headed Thrush, among many others. 2

Fulvous Whistling-duck (Photo: Dr Chitra Shanker) Indian Paradise-flycatcher (Photo: Dr Chitra Shanker) We did not stay for long here and moved towards Yenkathala grasslands in Vikarabad. On the way we saw the White-eyed Buzzard. Walking on the banks of the lake was a wonderful experience though we were disappointed with the lesser number of birds we saw. Clamorous Reed Warbler (Photo: Dr Chitra Shanker) During the closing event, all teams introduced themselves and talked about their experiences. It was very interesting to hear how the day went for the other teams. There were people from all ages and most teams had a mix of children and adults. The youngest member was two and a half years old, and the oldest above the age of 70! Siberian Stonechat (Photo: Sanjeevani Illambaruthi) By now it was getting really hot. We moved towards Manjeera Wildlife Sanctuary, which was our main spot for water birds. While driving we saw a huge water body on the left and, on checking the map, came to know that it is the Pedda Cheruvu. We decided to offroad and drive around the lake which turned out to be the best decision. We saw so many terns and other water birds here. But photography was not easy as we were seated at the back and the birds were far away. Our next stop was Manjeera Wildlife Sanctuary. We saw Fulvous Whistling-ducks, Cotton Pygmy-goose and Clamorous Reed Warblers calling loudly. It was past 2:00PM by then, and we stopped for lunch. After this we had to rush back due to paucity of time. We were told that there were 18 teams with 70 participants and that 160 unique species had been spotted on this single day, indicating the rich biodiversity we have around Hyderabad. We were getting apprehensive when our team was not called, but finally we were placed first with 141 species spotted, closely followed by Team Francolins with 140 and Team Eagles with 114. The Chief Guest, Mr A Sankaran, who is Officer on Special Duty with the Telangana Forest Department, also gave his thoughts on the wildlife and forest conservation in India. That brought us to the end of a long tiring day, but left us happy, satisfied and grateful to have had this experience. I loved spending my day with nature. Our Bird of the Day was the Malabar Whistling Thrush, with its majestic violet plumage and melodious calls. To me, the Bird Race was more than just about birds – I also got to socialize with a lot of kids my age, and it is something I will look forward to each year. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Long-toed Stint (Calidris subminuta) Long-toed Stint (Chennai, October 28, 2020) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Calidris Species: C. subminuta Size: 13-15 cm slightly beyond the tail, unlike other stints. Juvenile birds, like the breeding adults, show rufous fringes to upperparts and whitish mantle stripes, but have finer streaking on breast. Habitat & behaviour: The Long-toed Stint is usually seen singly or in small numbers, usually along with other small waders like stints, sand plovers, ringed plovers, sandpipers etc. It frequents a variety of wetland habitats like fields, flooded meadows, freshwater or brackish water areas, lake edges, floodplains, sewage ponds, lagoons, tidal creeks, estuaries, marshes, intertidal mudflats and salt pans. The Long-toed Stint forages by probing the wet mud with its bill, looking for prey that primarily consists of aquatic insects, amphibians, crustaceans, mollusks and other invertebrates; it also picks up seeds. Its usual calls are a quiet prrrrp, similar to the Curlew Sandpiper, uttered in flight, or a soft, rippling brrt-chrrup or chulip, and a sharp tik-tik-tik. The song is a slow kroer, usually repeated. Description & distribution: The Long-toed Stint is a smallsized wader that breeds in the northern regions of Asia, and winters in South and South-east Asia (including Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Maldives), and in New Guinea and Australia. It is also a very rare vagrant to Sweden, South Africa, Hawaii and northwestern America. Like the other 3 Stints seen in India, the Long-toed Stint belongs to the genus Calidris, which gets its name from the Ancient Greek kalidris (or skalidris), a term used by Aristotle to describe some grey waterside birds. It has white underparts, with the breast being speckled with brown. Upperparts are mottled dark brown, greyish-brown or dusky, with darker feather centres, and it has a brownish crown with a distinct supercilium. The head is small, with a short, straight, pointed blackish bill; the base of the lower mandible is yellow or pale brown. Legs are greenish or yellowish – a feature it shares only with the Temminck’s Stint in India. In non-breeding season, the upperparts become more greyish rather than brownish. Neck is slender, and the long legs are set well back on a rounded belly. The toes are long and slender – especially the middle toe. In flight, the long toes project Nesting: The Long-toed Stint breeds generally between June and July in most of its breeding range in Northern Europe and Siberia. The typical nest is usually a well-hidden, shallow depression on a mound of sedge or dried grass, in areas with sedge, moss and willows. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 (sometimes 5) cryptically coloured eggs. Local name: The Long-toed Stint is known as ‘Pachai kaal kosu ullan’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. The local host was Eco Pro Organization, an NGO working in the field of Environment & Social Sector in Chandrapur, and the venue was the Forest Academy, also known as Rangers College, managed by the Maharashtra Forest Department. The theme for this year was conservation of the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard (GIB) and the vulnerable Sarus Crane. There were presentations from senior ornithologists, researchers and conservationists working for the conservation of these 2 bird species and their habitats. Black-hooded Oriole It was a great learning experience for us, though we also felt sad about the depleting numbers of these two wonderful birds – less than 150 GIB and 15,000-20,000 Sarus Crane. So it was quite encouraging to see the conservation efforts of Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun, who have been working on captive breeding of the GIB with some significant success. We got to know and meet so many fellow delegates from all over Maharashtra who have common interest in Birds and Wildlife. We also had a wonderful Bird Walk in the Forest Academy campus, where we spotted some good bird species like Green Imperial Pigeon, Greater Flameback, Black-hooded Oriole, Spotted Owlet, Shikra, Indian Grey Hornbill, Alexandrine, Rose-ringed and Plum-headed Parakeets, Rufous Treepie etc. Green Imperial Pigeon Spotted Owlet 6

It was good to be a part of a congregation of around 200 bird lovers, talking, listening and observing only birds. This renews our interest and hope that there are more people around who care about, and are working for conservation of, our feathered friends. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Temminck’s Stint (Calidris temminckii) Temminck’s Stint (Chennai, March 21, 2021) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Calidris Species: C. temminckii Size: 13-15 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Temminck’s Stint is generally seen singly or in small groups, usually along with other small waders like Sand Plovers, Ringed Plovers, Sandpipers etc. It frequents coastal waters as well as inland freshwater habitats like irrigated fields, lakes, ponds, paddyfields, lagoons, tidal creeks, estuaries, marshes, intertidal mudflats and salt pans. When startled, it tends to take flight straight up like a snipe. It forages by mouse-like movements, picking up insects and their larvae, annelids, crustaceans and mollusks and, occasionally, plant matter, from the surface of the mud – it does not usually probe the mud with its bill. It usually calls during flight, uttering a sharp, rapid stuttering tirrr, often repeated, or a more prolonged tirrr-r-r. During displays, a rhythmic, rising and falling kilililili or sirrrrrr can be heard. Description & distribution: The Temminck’s Stint is a smallsized wader that breeds in the arctic regions of Europe and Asia, from Scandinavia east through north-western Russia and northern Siberia, and occasionally in Scotland. It is a longdistance migrant, wintering at freshwater locations in the Mediterranean, northern tropical Africa, the Middle-east, the Indian subcontinent, and Indochina and parts of South East Asia, including southern China, Taiwan, Malaysia, Borneo and sometimes Philippines. The genus name comes from the Ancient Greek kalidris (or skalidris), which was a term used by Aristotle to describe some grey waterside birds, and species name commemorates the Dutch naturalist Coenraad Jacob Temminck. Nesting: The Temminck’s Stint breeds generally between May and July in most of its breeding range. The typical nest is usually a shallow cup-shaped scrape on the ground. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 eggs, off-white or buffish stone coloured, spotted and blotched with reddish brown. Breeding involves bigamy by both male and female, with the female usually laying a second clutch of eggs; however, both (separately) incubate one clutch only. In its non-breeding plumage, it is a drab-looking bird, with mainly plain grey-brown head and upperparts, and whitish underparts with a greyish-brown breast showing heavy brown streaking. Bill is short and dark, with a pale base to the lower mandible. Legs are yellowish or olive green – it is one of the two stints with greenish legs seen in India (the other being Long-toed). Breeding birds show more rufous mantle and scapular feathers with dark centres and grey tips. The tail is long, with white outer retrices and dark central feathers. Sexes are alike. Local name: The Temminck’s Stint is known as ‘Chhota panlowwa’ in Hindi and Marathi (a name it shares with the Little Stint), ‘Manjakaal kosu ullan’ in Tamil and ‘Ujalapag khichdiyo’ in Gujarati. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report: Ladakh, August 20-28, 2022 Text & Photos: Dr G Samuel Sukumar A view of Leh High in the Himalayas, the abode of snow-capped mountains, is Ladakh, the roof of the world. It is a land that I had always dreamt of visiting during my official tenure as geologist in the Geological Survey of India. The main purpose of this visit was not only to be on the top of the world, but also, to look for evidence of the origin of the mighty Himalayas. How the Himalayas originated is a question that was answered by Dr. Alfred Wagner (1850-1950) with his theory of Continental Drift and Plate Tectonics in 1912. According to the theory, the earth is composed of giant plates called tectonic plates and, on these plates lie the continents and the oceans of the world. The continents are said to have originated 250 Mega annals (Ma) ago from a single land mass or supercontinent called Pangea, which was surrounded by a large ocean. Around 200 Ma ago, there was a sea stretch called Tethys along the latitudinal area presently occupied by the Himalayas. Around this period, the supercontinent Pangea gradually started to split into land masses, and moved in different directions about 70 Ma ago. The mountain building process began when two land masses collided with each other. And around 65 Ma it resulted in the gradual disappearance of the sea and creation of high mountain ranges. Although the major upheaval has passed, the Himalayas are still rising at the rate of 5 mm /year. That means the Himalayas are still geologically active and structurally unstable. For this reason, earthquakes are a frequent occurrence in the Himalayan region. 1

Evidence of these geological changes can be found in the fossilised remains found in the dry ocean bed of the Baltic region 250 Ma ago and also discovered in the Himalayas. Another example is the presence of saline water in Pangong Tso Lake which could have been part of the ocean at one time. Today this saltwater lake mesmerises visitors with its shades of turquoise when the sun’s rays fall on it. us from Deccan Birders – Nanda Kumar, DB Chaudhari, Shilka Chaudhari, Sheetal and Swetha Vyas, and I joined the BHNS trip. We took precautions and safeguards that are required to be taken to circumvent Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS). We reached Leh at 12.00 noon on 20 th August. We were picked up at the airport and comfortably placed in warm rooms in the hotel Caravan Centre. We assembled for lunch and briefly rested to acclimatise. The Himalayas are considered as the folded mountain ranges formed due to the collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate. Evidence of this is seen in this fold which is called the recumbent fold. Old Monastery at Leh Recumbent fold Shanti Stupa Yak In the evening we were taken to the Leh Monastery, Shanti Stupa and Leh market. Leh Monastery is a 9-level monastery built with wooden logs and mud bricks. The Shanti Stupa is a Buddhist stupa built in modern times. We also had a brief stroll in the market. The terrain is mostly a lunar landscape with cold desert conditions. A few tribal people occupy the land and mostly depend on barley cultivation. Yak is domesticated for milk, fur, hide and dung. Even human night soil is retrieved annually from the raised dry toilets. The human excreta is covered after every use with ash from yak dung which is burnt to heat their homes during winter. The houses are built with unburnt clay bricks made by labourers from Bihar and West Bengal. The roofs are made up of dried willow tree logs and branches. The labourers have tanned skin due to the sun’s radiation which is very high here. Mobile communication is very limited, and in many areas, electricity is generated from diesel generators for a limited time. Ladakh lies between Central Asia to the north, China to the north and east, and Kashmir to the southwest. It is a part of the Central Asian Plateau, a vast lunar landscape with a desert climate. The day and night temperatures differ astronomically. The Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) arranged a birding camp from 20th to 28th August 2022 at Ladakh. Six of Mountain Chiffchaff 2

Oriental Turtle Dove European Roller White Wagtail On the 21st, we went for birding along the marshes of the Indus River looking for Ibisbills. As the current was strong and muddy and the flow heavy, we could not find the bird. We did spot many other birds, though: Long-tailed Shrike, White Wagtail, Mountain Chiffchaff, Oriental Turtle Dove, Rock Pigeons, Common Hoopoe, Common Rosefinch, Fire-fronted Serins, European Roller and the Large-eared Pika, a mammal found in these areas. Large-eared Pika Here we saw Sea Buckthorn berries (popularly known as Leh Berry) – yellowish-orange in colour, and a rich source of vitamin C. It is made into jams and juices. In the winter, these are food for the birds. Sea Buckthorn After lunch we visited the Hemis National Park. The entry into the park had outcrops of sedimentary rocks, mostly ferruginous (iron-rich) conglomerates – cobble-sized, wellrounded quartzites. We spotted birds like the Black Redstart, White-winged Redstart, Horned Lark, Chukar, wagtails, etc. Common Hoopoe 3

We were lucky to see a whole family of Bharal or Blue Sheep grazing on the hill slope very close to the village and barley fields. They generally graze high above, occasionally peeping over the rocky ledges. Black Redstart pair A herd of domesticated Yak passed by – wild ones are very rarely seen. Yaks in Ladakh are a source of meat, milk, butter, leather for boots, fur for ropes, dung for fertilizer and for heating in the winter. The burnt ash is not wasted but used in the specially made high and dry toilets, to cover the night soil and is annually taken out through an opening at the base and used as organic fertilizer in their fields. Blue Sheep (Bharal) White-winged Redstart Barley Horned Lark Chukar The only crop grown is barley. The water from melting snow flows as streams all along and is used for irrigation. Open areas are used as camping sites. While returning from Hemis, we stopped by to see the Mallards, Common Hoopoes and Eurasian Magpies near a local pond. Mallard female 4

Eurasian Magpie Mountain Weasel On the 22nd, we started for Pangong Sor Lake (14,500 ft) about 155 km from Leh. We had to drink water periodically as the elevation increased and the oxygen in the atmosphere was low. We passed through Chang La Pass (17, 688 ft), the third highest motorable road in the world. En route, we saw White-winged Redstarts, Robin Accentor, Himalayan Marmots, Mountain Weasel, Pallas’s Gull and Brown-headed Gull. Pallas’s Gull In the afternoon we reached the shores of Pangong Sor Lake. It was a mesmerising sight with its waters the shades of blue and turquoise. Pangong Lake, one of the most famous lakes in Ladakh, derives its name from the Tibetan word, ‘Pangong Tso’, which means ‘high grassland lake’. Robin Accentor Pangong Lake Himalayan Marmot Pangong Lake is an endorheic lake (a basin or lake: having no outflow to an external body of water such as a river or ocean, and only losing water through evaporation or seepage into the ground), spanning eastern Ladakh and West Tibet. We stayed at Pangong Panorama which was partially tented and hutment accommodation. In the evening we went for a stroll along the banks of Pangong and it was quite cold. After a sumptuous dinner we retired to the comfort of warm beds. Electric supply is given from 6.30 in the morning to 10.30 in the evening, during which time all our batteries (mobiles and cameras) had to be charged. There is no mobile connectivity in this area. 5

On the 23rd, after an early breakfast, we moved out of Pangong for Hanle about 180 kilometres away. As we travelled along the road which followed the banks of Pangong Lake, we saw the ‘four fingers’, now guarded by our valiant Indian army, as they patrolled the mountain peaks for intrusions by the Chinese. With brief stops for birding, we reached Hanle and stayed at Gua Tibetan Gazelle Homestay, where we had homecooked dinner. A natural arch In the Hanle marshes we saw the Black-necked Crane, Eurasian Eagle Owl, Upland Buzzard, Pallas’s Cat, and House Sparrows. We could also see a lone Tibetan Wolf in the fields. Eurasian Eagle Owl House Sparrow feeding young Upland Buzzard Tibetan Wolf Pallas’s Cat Hanle Observatory 6

There is a Hanle Observatory on a hilltop. The night skies are clear here and devoid of dust and light haze, making it possible for us to see the stars and the Milky Way. On the 24th, we went birding around Hanle marshes. We spotted a solitary Black-necked Crane at the edge of a barley field. It gave us enough opportunity to photograph this bird before it flew to join a juvenile and another adult. There were several juveniles and pairs in this area. Desert Wheatear Hanle Monastery We made a brief visit to the Hanle Monastery which was preparing for the annual festival of traditional dance with masks. Most of these dances are accompanied by Surna, Daman, Piwang which are musical instruments. In the monasteries they blew the Tibetan horn. On 25th we went to the Tsokar Sor Lake. We started from Hanle and en route saw the Upland Buzzard sitting on a rock by the edge of the river, a pair of ravens on a telephone pole, Eurasian Roller, Desert Wheatear, Ruddy Shelduck, Tibetan Wild Ass or Kiang, Black-necked Crane pair with a juvenile, Hill Pigeons, Sulphur-bellied Warbler, Tibetan Snowfinches, etc. Tibetan Wild Ass (Kiang) Common Raven Sulphur-bellied Warbler Black-necked Crane adult (L) and juvenile (R) 7

Citrine Wagtail Tibetan Snowfinch We reached Tsokar and stayed at Durk Resort. In the evening we walked around the marshes till the village of Tsokar where we saw Twites. Horned Larks, Hill Pigeons, some Snowfinches, etc. In the marshes we spotted wagtails, both Grey and Citrine. In the afternoon we went to the other side of the Tso Kar Lake. This lake is composed of both saline and fresh water and is divided by a thin landmass. Salt precipitations were seen as white masses resembling snow. This was used as common salt earlier. However, with improvement in transport, salt is brought from nearby towns. Hill Pigeon Tibetan Sandgrouse The Tso Kar or Tsho Kar is a fluctuating salt lake known for its size and depth and is situated in the Rupshu Plateau and valley in the southern part of Ladakh. It is called Tso Kar, meaning ‘white lake’, because of the white salt efflorescence found on the margins due to the evaporation of highly saline water. The Tso Kar Basin is an A1 Category Important Bird Area (IBA) as per Bird Life International and a key staging site in the Central Asian Flyway. It is also recognized as India's 42nd Ramsar site. At the edge of the lake we saw Upland Buzzards sitting on the rocks. The drive was to see the Tibetan Sandgrouse and Groundpeckers. From a distance we saw a flock of Sandgrouse busily feeding. Before we reached this spot of open field, we saw adult Horned Larks, Twite and Hill Pigeons, all busily picking things from the ground. On 26th, we drove along the marshes on one side and the gradually sloping mountains on the other. We saw a pair of Red Foxes warming themselves in the rising sun. Twite Red Fox 8

or the Bearded Vulture juvenile on the ground. The guide showed us its nest. The adults were not to be seen. Blanford’s Snowfinch Mountain Vole By the roadside a lone Mountain Vole was busily eating grass. I had seen several holes in the fields and marshes made by voles, and I thought I would return without seeing one. This Mountain Vole was so busy munching that it gave me time to take a few video shots. The Voles and Pikas were busy collecting grass and other food material, enough to be stored in their holes or burrows for their hibernation during the winter, which was just a few months away. We reached Leh and were back in the Caravan Hotel. Most of us went shopping in the Leh market to purchase dry apricots, walnuts and some souvenirs. Little Owl On 27th early morning at 5.45 am, we went out to see the Little Owl. We were lucky to spot one by the roadside, sitting on a wolf trap rock edge. I got a few good, clear shots of this very shy bird before it moved to a safe distance. The next day we flew back to New Delhi. The aircraft rose high above the snow-clad Himalayas. We were happy that we drove on some of the highest motorable passes and saw many endemic birds and mammals living on the roof of the world – Ladakh. We returned to the Durk Resort, had breakfast, and after loading our luggage, we started on our return journey. We crossed the Tanglang La Pass (14,482 ft), considered the second highest motorable pass. WE LOVE OUTDOORS Report: Penjarla, Mahbubnagar District, March 18-19, 2023 Text & Photos: Dhiraj & Vijaya Kaveri The children during the trip As exams got over, the students of our Stay Active Kids Program wanted to go for an outdoor overnight camping trip. We decided to plan a short trip to a farm house in Penjarla off Bangalore Highway, which is just 40 kms from our community PBEL City. while the parents accompanied us with equal enthusiasm. Vijaya and I were ready with our birding kit. While we were worried about camping in the hot temperature, the weather in Hyderabad took a sudden turn with heavy showers, thunder and at some places hailstorms. So as to not disappoint the kids, we decided to go ahead with the plan. It was a short weekend trip from March 18 (Saturday afternoon) to March 19 (Sunday morning). The camping was organized by our friend Ramya, while the local arrangements were done by caretaker Raju and his family. Ramya's friend Venu took care of the stargazing session where we all observed Sunspots, Nebula, Venus and Morning Moon. At night we had a campfire and some games before we retired to our tents. Indian Peafowl male A view of the camp The next morning, we started with our favourite activity – the Bird Walk. The kids brought along their small binoculars, a guidebook, and sketch pens to write down the birds’ names, Yellow-wattled Lapwing 13

The farm house was surrounded by tall trees, shrubs, open plots, grasslands and farmland. In a span of 90 minutes, we identified around 23 bird species, like Indian Peafowl, Rufous Treepie, Eurasian Collared Dove, Laughing Dove, Yellowwattled Lapwing, Little Egret, Green Bee-eater, Indian Jungle Crow, Black Drongo, Indian Robin, Common Myna, Redvented Bulbul etc. Indian Robin Eurasian Collared Dove It was a short but fun learning outing for kids accompanied by parents. Bird watching is a silent, peaceful, engaging, meditative and enriching activity. It will now remain a permanent feature of all Stay Active Outdoor events. As promoters of health & environment we feel birds are an excellent gateway to observe the beauty of nature and understand the local ecology and biodiversity. Red-vented Bulbul For most of the kids it was like a discovery and treasure hunt – when they saw the same bird a second time and tried identifying it, they felt excited as if they were on a treasure hunt! Even the adults started enjoying our activity and got drawn towards it. At the end we shared the list with all and discussed birds, trees and nature. Green Bee-eater The participants at the camp Red-wattled Lapwing The full list of birds seen during the trip is given below: 14

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Stork-billed Kingfisher (Pelargopsis capensis) Stork-billed Kingfisher (Thrissur, Kerala, January 8 & 9, 2023) Order: Coraciiformes Family: Alcedinidae Genus: Pelargopsis Species: P. capensis Size: 35 cm It is a large kingfisher. The adult has an olive-brown head and pale reddish bare skin around the eyes, dark greenish-blue mantle and upperparts, blue wings and tail (and a paler blue rump, obvious in flight), while the underparts and neck are buff-orange. The very large stork-like bill and legs are scarlet or bright red, with a purplish distal end. Sexes are similar. Juvenile birds show dusky edges to the feathers of breast and hind neck. Description & distribution: The Stork-billed Kingfisher, earlier Halcyon capensis, is a tree kingfisher that is widely but sparsely distributed, and is resident across its range, which spans across the tropical parts of the Indian subcontinent and South-east Asia. Habitat & behaviour: The Stork-billed Kingfisher inhabits well-wooded habitats near lakes, rivers or coasts. It tends to perch quietly while waiting to spot prey, and can easily be missed in spite of its large size. It is quite territorial, and may even chase larger birds like eagles and other such predators. Its diet consists mainly of fish, frogs, crabs, rodents, reptiles, and young birds and eggs. The flight of the Stork-billed Kingfisher is laboured and flapping, but direct. The call is a loud and far-reaching peer-por-por repeated about every 5 seconds, as well as a cackling ke-ke-ke-ke-ke-ke contact call, repeated 6-10 times. Thirteen sub-species are recognized: the nominate P. c. capensis, seen in Nepal, India and Sri Lanka), P. c. osmastoni (Andaman Islands), P. c. intermedia (Nicobar Islands), P. c. burmanica (Myanmar, Indochina, northern parts of Malay Peninsula), P. c. malaccensis (central and southern parts of Malay Peninsula, Riau Archipelago, Lingga Islands), P. c. cyanopterix (Sumatra, Bangka Island, Belitung Island), P. c. simalurensis (Simeulue Island, off the coast of Sumatra), P. c. sodalis (Banyak, Nias, Batu and Mentawai Islands, off the coast of Sumatra), P. c. innominata (Borneo), P. c. javana (Java), P. c. floresiana (Bali to Flores in the Lesser Sunda Islands), P. c. gouldi (north Philippines) and P. c. gigantea (central and south Philippines). The sub-species mainly show some differences in plumage, but P. c. gigantea has a white head, neck and shoulders. The insular forms, P. c. nesoeca of the Nias and Batu Islands, and P. c. isoptera of Mentawai Island, have been subsumed within P. c. sodalis. Nesting: The Stork-billed Kingfisher breeds generally between January and July. Like other kingfishers, the nest is the typical horizontal tunnel excavated in the raised banks of forest streams, vegetated edges of water bodies, decaying trees, or tree termite nests. The usual clutch consists of 4-5 roundish oval, glossy white eggs. Local name: The Stork-billed Kingfisher is known as ‘Bada kilkila’ or ‘Badami kourilla’ in Hindi, ‘Gurial’ in Bengali (a name derived from the original sub-species name), ‘Kukuluppan’ or ‘Meenkotti’ in Tamil, and ‘Kandu taleya meenchulli’ or ‘Kakka ponman’ in Malayalam. Interestingly, the birds of India were first placed in sub-species P. c. gurial, but this was later merged with the nominate subspecies after it was found that the type specimen, earlier believed to have come from the Cape of Good Hope in Africa, was identified as having actually originated from Chandannagar in West Bengal. *** For Private Circulation Only 16 Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 20 Number 7 June 2023 FIELD TRIP: Sunday, 25th June 2023, 7.00AM: Zaheerabad. Meeting Points: Miyapur Metro Station, 4.30AM; BHEL Bus Stop, 4.45AM; Taj Dhaba, Muthangi, 5.00AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Srikanth Bhamidipati (Mobile: 97388-40070); Gokul Krishna A (Mobile: 99453-46585) Zaheerabad, close to Chincholi, is located near Telangana-Karnataka border. The forest hosts rich biodiversity. Apart from medicinal herbs and trees, species like Red Sanders and Sandalwood are found abundantly in the adjoining social forest, which has good dry deciduous and moist deciduous forest in the core, with Acacia and Teak plantations on the fringes. The forest area is also home to various species of birds: look out for White-bellied Minivet, Small Minivet, Fork-tailed Drongo Cuckoo, Black-headed Cuckooshrike, Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse, Tree Pipit, Rain Quail, Jungle Bush Quail, Rock Bush Quail, Barred Buttonquail, Painted Francolin, Baya Weaver etc. This will be a half-day trip, so carry adequate water and breakfast/snacks, and protective gear if required. Strict Covid protocols will be followed; please ensure you wear masks, carry a sanitiser and maintain social distancing. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. BIRDS OF COSTA RICA Trip Report: Monteverde, Costa Rica, March 13-16, 2023 Text & Photos: Dr Jairamchander Pingle Keel-billed Toucan Since a long time, I had the great desire to visit Costa Rica to see and photograph the beautiful birds of that country. My daughter had arranged to do so in April of 2020, but unfortunately due to the Covid pandemic, it was not to be. Well, this year we were able to make it – my wife Surekha, daughter Divya, granddaughter Riya and I went to Costa Rica on March 12, 2023, for 5 nights. We travelled to Monteverde, the flight being from Orlando in the US to San Jose, and on by taxi to our stay at the Hidden Canopy Resort, where the rooms were in and above the forest canopy. 1

Divya and my son Karthik had visited Costa Rica last year and, through their guide, fixed up for me with Oscar, an excellent guide. He would pick me up every morning of the 4 days I had, promptly at 6:00AM to return at 12 noon. As all the sanctuaries opened at 8:00AM, we used to first go down to the Santa Elena village, lower down, and walk around there. Slate-throated Redstart We could see quite a few birds like the Grey-headed Chachalaka, Black Guan, Brown Jay, Slate-throated Redstart, Great-tailed Grackle, Emerald Toucanet etc, and, flying over us, the Black Vultures. Grey-headed Chachalaka Great-tailed Grackle Black Guan Emerald Toucanet Brown Jay 2

where one needs to trek. The pathways are well maintained, though. White-headed Capuchin Monkey At about 7:00AM, we would have a quick bite of bagels for breakfast. Usually, during breakfast, we would see the Whiteheaded Capuchin Monkey and a few Howler Monkeys and some Variegated Squirrels, before proceeding to the sanctuaries. Resplendent Quetzal male Howler Monkey Resplendent Quetzal female We walked into a clearing and were extremely fortunate to see the Resplendent Quetzal birds, both male and female, and they gave us a good chance to photograph them. As we continued walking, we saw several of the amazing Hummingbirds – varied in their numbers, with many species to see. Variegated Squirrel The Monteverde Rain Forest is such that in the morning it was either cloudy or sunny, and by 12 noon it would start to rain sporadically. Rain ponchos are essential, though I only used it once. On the first day, March 13, 2023, we went to Curi-Cancha Reserve, which had some amazing trees and thick forest, Magenta-throated Woodstar female 3

Mexican Violetear We spotted and photographed the Magenta-throated Woodstar, which is a very small hummingbird and has a characteristic way of hovering while sucking nectar from the violet-coloured Delphineum flowers, and also the Mexican Violetear and the Green-crowned Brilliant Hummingbirds. Blue-gray Tanager We returned to the resort and, in the afternoon, I had a treat of hummingbird photography at the nectar feeding station, where the hummingbirds and several other birds such as the Hoffman’s Woodpecker, Blue-gray Tanager, Slate-throated Redstart etc would also come for it. On March 14, Oscar picked me up – this time Divya came along – and we went to the same village and then proceeded to the Monteverde Rain Forest Sanctuary. The forest was indeed amazing. Rufous Hummingbird The less common Rufous Hummingbird was a nice catch – one has to be quite quick to do so, as they are very fleeting. Azure-hooded Jay We also saw the bee hive of stingless bees, busy as ever, and Oscar showed the nest entrance through his Swarovski telescope. Hoffman’s Woodpecker Collared Trogon male 4

Collared Trogon female Yellowish Flycatcher As we walked through, we were lucky to see and photograph the Azure-hooded Jay foraging on the forest floor. We saw the Collared Trogon, male and female, and were also lucky to spot and photograph the Resplendent Quetzal again, though with some difficulty, through the foliage. Common Agouti Violet Sabrewing Clay-coloured Thrush White-nosed Coatimundi We saw the Agouti and the Coatimundi in the forest, foraging very close to us, and quite unafraid. The other birds we saw were the Summer Tanager, Yellowish Flycatcher, Violet Sabrewing hummingbird, Clay-coloured Thrush – but the highlight were two hummingbird nests, in one of which there were three tiny chicks. 5

We watched and photographed them from a distance. I was informed by Oscar that the mother feeds the chicks with a combination of insects and nectar. Oscar took some video of feeding on my iPhone through his telescope, as I kept taking still photos. On March 15, after the early morning routine, we went to Finca Ecologica San Luis. My granddaughter accompanied me to where there are hides and fruit for birds to come and eat. Here we photographed the Keel-billed Toucan, Emerald Toucanet, Crimson-collared Tanager, Scarlet-rumped Tanager, Yellow-throated Euphonia, Great Kiskadee, Baltimore Oriole, Lesson’s Motmot etc. Yellow-throated Euphonia Keel-billed Toucan Great Kiskadee Crimson-collared Tanager Scarlet-rumped Tanager Lesson’s Motmot 6

Baltimore Oriole The social nest of the Montezuma birds was interesting – it looked like a bunch of Baya Weaver nests stuck together. At a great distance, we saw the nest of Black Hawks and saw them mating too. I did photograph them but not well. We returned at noon and I went to the feeders at our resort and enjoyed photographing the hummingbirds. Long-tailed Manakin Three-wattled Bellbird Pale-billed Woodpecker On March 16, our last day there, I went to Bajo del Tigre with Divya. Oscar showed me the Manakin birds which are beautiful and competitive for female attention, and dance to get it. Needless to say, it was very difficult to photograph them, but luckily I did manage to do so. Oscar managed to show me the Three-wattled Bellbird, which I could photograph and video, with its resonating bell sound which could be heard for a kilometre. Wilson’s Warbler 7

We saw the Pale-billed Woodpecker, a rather large woodpecker, the White-eared Ground Sparrow, Wilson’s Warbler, Chestnut-capped Warbler and Black-and-white Warbler. All in all, it was a most memorable trip, and I would strongly recommend it, especially for birding. Summary Report: ASIAN WATERFOWL CENSUS, 2023 Summary data provided by: Humayun Taher As our members would be aware, the Asian Waterfowl Census (AWC) is an annual exercise that takes place generally during January every year (and sometimes a couple of weeks before and after). The main purpose of this exercise is to track changes in presence and populations of a specified list of water- and water-dependent birds. During this exercise, volunteers visit various waterbodies in their areas, and attempt to estimate and document the abundance of the said species. We present below a summary of the sightings documented during the Census this year, along with a comparison with the data from the past two years. Going forward, we plan to present a similar summary every year. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani European Roller (Coracias garrulus) European Roller (Great Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, September 23, 2022) Order: Coraciiformes Family: Coraciidae Genus: Coracias Species: C. garrulus Size: 31 cm head and rufous-brown nape in Indian Roller), (2) Blue underparts (rufous breast and blue lower belly in Indian Roller), (3) Plain blue throat and ear coverts (streaked white in Indian Roller), (4) Flight feathers (primaries and secondaries) are black (turquoise band across primaries in Indian Roller), and (5) Black corners to tail (dark blue-black terminal band to tail in Indian Roller). The juvenile European Roller has a turquoise-blue cast to ear coverts, crown and nape, contrasting with browner mantle, which makes it easy to differentiate from juvenile Indian Roller, which lacks this blue cast, and also has heavy streaking on throat and ear coverts. Description & distribution: The European Roller is the only member of the roller family that breeds in Europe. Two subspecies are recognized: C. g. garrulous, which breeds in northern Africa (from Morocco to Tunisia), southern and central Europe, and east through north-western Iran to southwestern Siberia, and C. g. semenowi, which breeds from Iraq and southern Iran east through Kashmir and southern Kazakhstan to Xinjiang in western China. The European Roller is a long-distance migrant, wintering in two distinct regions in southern Africa: (1) from Senegal east to Cameroon, and (2) from western Ethiopia east to Congo and south to South Africa. Some of these populations migrate to Africa through India – hence, in India, the European Roller is a passage migrant, being seen mainly during the passage migration season from late August through September to early October. It is easiest seen in northern Gujarat (especially areas like Nalsarovar, Little Rann of Kutch and Great Rann of Kutch) and parts of Rajasthan, although there are records from many other Indian states, including as far south as Chennai and other parts of Tamil Nadu. During migration, it travels during the day, singly and in a steady stream spread over a wide front. Habitat & behaviour: The European Roller, much like the Indian Roller, prefers open cultivated country, scrub and light deciduous forest. It tends to perch quietly on vantage points like telegraph wires while waiting to spot prey, and once it catches the prey, it tends to return to the same perch or fly leisurely to another nearby perch, where it batters the prey to death and swallows it. Its diet consists mainly of beetles and other large insects, but it also takes lizards and frogs. The flight is slow and may sometimes involve sudden changes of direction. The call is a harsh scream, usually uttered during the aerial breeding displays. Nesting: In its breeding grounds, the European Roller breeds generally between May and September. The nest is a tree hollow, and the usual clutch consists of 5-6 pure white eggs. Both male and female share parental duties. The European Roller, slightly smaller than the Indian Roller (C. benghalensis), is a stocky, brightly coloured blue and brownish bird.
