STOCKHOLM CITY BIRDING Report: Stockholm, Sweden, March 2023 Text & Photos: Dr Krishna Nagarajan Sweden, almost surrounded by icy seas Work required me to travel to Vasteras, a small town about 100km west of Stockholm in Sweden, during the week of March 6th, 2023. As shown in the map, Sweden is located in the northern part of Europe and, if you ask me, it has only two types of weather: either “Winter is here” or “Winter is coming”! 1

March happens to be the time when they have the “Winter is still here” kind of weather. The temperature is typically around 0⁰ Celsius, and as luck would have it, during my visit it was predominantly below 0⁰ Celsius. Although I have never birded in such cold weather conditions, I did survive severe winters during my younger days when I was living abroad. But I was hoping for a sunny winter day wherein I could do some birding. I checked the eBird website and was happy to note that there are quite a few birding enthusiasts in Sweden and, even in the peak of winter, sightings were listed in both Vasteras and Stockholm. On the first day in Vasteras, when I stepped out in the morning to visit the customer’s office for my meetings, it was so cold that my whole body was shivering in spite of wearing layered clothing that I purchased from our local Decathlon store. I noticed some birds while walking to the bus stop and my first thought was “how do these birds survive such cold conditions? No wonder they migrate to the south to escape the weather.” It was a beautiful sight but I was now doubtful whether I would be able to do any birding at all. You need to look both down and up to spot birds. If you don’t look down then there is a very good chance you will slip on the ice and fall down. I had my travel/health insurance but had no intention of utilizing it during my stay there! After I finished my meetings in Vasteras, I shifted base to Stockholm for the weekend and to eventually fly out from the Arlanda International Airport. The temperature in Stockholm was still -6⁰C to -2⁰C, but on Sunday the elements finally decided to take pity on me and gifted a beautiful sunny day. The sunlight made the sub-zero temperature bearable. So I decided against visiting the museums and immediately located a nearby hotspot on eBird – Kungsträdgården – City Centre Park. The park is next to the river, Nordstrom, which attracts many birds in the area. Eurasian Jackdaw I spotted many interesting birds like Eurasian Jackdaw, Eurasian Magpie, Hooded Crow, Bohemian Waxwing, Fieldfare, House Sparrow, and Common Wood Pigeon across the road. I was carrying my camera but when I tried to take some pictures, my fingers were so numb that I was unable to click the shutter. And when I finally managed to take a couple of pictures, my camera gave up, complaining that the fully charged battery could not handle the -7⁰C temperature and was exhausted. So now, besides keeping myself warm, I also needed to keep my camera warm by hiding it inside my winter jacket! Eurasian Blackbird Using the binoculars presented some other challenges. My fingers were simply unable to adjust the focus to properly view the birds. Reality kind of hit me on my face – techniques that work in our good old, laid-back, warmer Hyderabad will not work in Sweden. That was not all though. On the third day, it snowed heavily. All the greenery I could see during my first two days disappeared. It was replaced by a white carpet made of snow. Eurasian Magpie 2

Black-headed Gull with leg ring When I walked across the street to the river, I was rewarded by a large flock of birds: Mallard (male and female), Eurasian Coot, Tufted Duck and Black-Headed Gull (with leg ring). Hooded Crow I went to the city centre park by 8:00AM Sunday morning at 7⁰C, and obviously it was deserted. I spotted Eurasian Blackbird, Eurasian Magpie, Hooded Crow, House Sparrow, White-tailed Eagle, Great Tit, and our friendly neighbourhood Blue Rock Pigeons in the snow-covered park. Mute Swan adult Mallard pair Mute Swan juvenile Tufted Duck 3

Common Pochard Common Merganser Mute Swan, Common Pochard, Common Goldeneye, Common Gull, Canada Goose, Great Cormorant, Common Tern, Whooper Swan, Common Merganser (Female), Herring Gull, and Lesser Black-backed Gull were also there. Great Black-backed Gull Canada Goose I crossed the river via the bridge and did some more birding. I was able to spot the Great Black-backed Gull and the Great Cormorant. I saw several Mallards, Tufted Ducks, and Hooded Crows as well and by this time I was no longer in a position to take repeat pictures. The temperature was below 0⁰ Celsius throughout the Sunday and I wrapped up my birding by noon and headed back to the hotel. Stockholm is a beautiful, colorful city devoid of any modern high-rise buildings. Many of these buildings were more than 100 years old. If you remember the history, Sweden did not participate in the World War II – it was a neutral country. Therefore, unlike other capital cities in Europe, it was not destroyed and could retain the old charm. I was hoping to spot more birds but the snow and the weather limited the amount of birding I could do. Nevertheless, birding in such cold temperatures was fun and I am grateful for whatever birding I was able to do during my brief stay in the city. THE LIVING AIR by AASHEESH PITTIE Report: Book Launch, Hyderabad, June 16, 2023 JVD Moorty Aasheesh reading a passage from the book (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) The Living Air: The Pleasures of Birds and Birdwatching, a book by our erstwhile President and fellow-birder, author, and editor, Aasheesh Pittie was launched on the premises of Goethe-Zentrum, Hyderabad on June 16, 2023. Aasheesh Pittie is currently the editor of the ornithological journal ‘Indian Birds’. His penmanship has brought out books such as Birds in Books: Three Hundred Years of South Asian Ornithology and The Written Bird: Birds in Books 2, apart from a compilation of a searchable bibliographic database of over 35,000 works on South Asian ornithology. The book launch (Photo courtesy: JVD Moorty) Amita Desai addressing the audience (Photo: JVD Moorty) Proceedings started with Ms. Amita Desai, Director of Goethe Zentrum, introducing the author and briefly speaking about his twin passions of birding and writing. Ms. Anita Mani, publisher of the said book was also on stage to speak briefly about her organisation and also her personal impressions about The Living Air, followed by the formal book release. Aasheesh invited MS Kulkarni, Shafaat Ulla and yours truly to join him and jointly release the book, a very brief and emotional occasion for us to share the stage with Aasheesh. Aasheesh Pittie, Anita Mani & Sita Reddy (L to R) (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) The launch was followed by a discussion between the author and Sita Reddy, a writer, researcher, and curator whose recent work on nature has focused on the cultural histories of flora plants, trees, forests, gardens, landscapes, and ecosystems. Sita Reddy, in her opening remarks, said that the book wasn’t just a book on birding, but a book on nature writing, something that Mark Cocker, British author, naturalist and environmentalist, also mentions in the foreword. She remarked that the book belongs to that category of authors on nature writing such as EH Aitkin, Rachel Carson, Dr Salim Ali, M Krishnan to name just a few of them. 7

A section of the audience (Photo courtesy: JVD Moorty) There was also, of course, a lively interaction with the audience in a more-than-the-capacity filled hall. The first question was with regard to the title of the book, taken from the lines of English poet William Wordsworth’s poem ‘Lines composed few miles above Tintern Abbey, on revisiting the banks of the Wye during a tour, July 13, 1798’: “…And I have felt A presence that disturbs me with the joy Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime Of something far more deeply interfused, Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, And the round ocean and the living air, And the blue sky, and in the mind of man;…” Aasheesh explained how these words impacted him, and how mankind is focussed chiefly on terra firma and not on what’s above it, namely the air around. His interest in nature was kindled when in Class IX/X the prescribed book for literature then was titled ‘The Jungle Picture’ by Norah Burke, which painted a picture of the vast forests of India, along the foothills of the Himalayas, in 22 short stories. The other book that inspired him was Salim Ali’s The Book of Indian Birds which he described as “sublime”. A small list of books he has read and recommends for reading to everyone was also shared by him. Asked to elaborate upon the phrase ‘birding by ear’ or ‘seeing by song’, Aasheesh spoke on how one can enjoy birds by listening to them, as many birds are often heard more than seen. Even the urban chaos is not a deterrent to hearing a bird call overhead or in a bush, and knowing it is there gives a peculiar thrill to the birder knowing that (s)he has ‘recognised’ the bird amidst all that tumult. He said that interest in music brought out how silence between notes in music starkly contrasts with the notes and enhances the beauty of the musical piece. Sita Reddy asked him about the choice of illustrations by Sangeeta Kadur rather than photographs. Aasheesh remarked that it would have been a complete mismatch of his prose and the picture, as the artist here was sketching something in the same way that the author was drawing with words. Aasheesh interacting with the audience (Photo: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao) The attribution of human traits, emotions, or intentions to nonhuman entities, known as anthropomorphism, was considered important for a written piece on birds to rouse the interest of the reader. Aasheesh paid tribute to the late Mr Siraj Taher and the author’s late father by reading out to the audience an excerpt from the chapter ‘S is for Shikra’. It was heartening to note a reference made to the late Mr Pushp Kumar, top official in the Forest Department then and a mentor to some of the senior birders of today. Aasheesh spoke with great feeling and a just a trace of irritation on ‘birding tourism’ and the habits and practices of ‘intrusive birding’ prevalent today. He decried this behaviour and attitude in no uncertain terms. Questions from the audience were interesting, ranging from the common-place “where have the sparrows and the crows gone” to more interesting ones like “which of the musical interludes in birdsong is closer to the author, Hindustani classical or Western classical?” Aasheesh professed his preference for Hindustani classical, but also shared an anecdote of a duet between a Cello and a Nightingale recorded live in the 60s by the BBC. Another good query was on whether the birds have, over time, shown behavioral changes to rapid urbanisation; this was answered with examples cited from around us, and also how the bird calls have a higher decibel level to drown out the city noises than was earlier. The questioner continued with how increased usage of artificial lighting has altered the behaviour of birds, the response to this being that this is an aspect that is still being studied, though studies in migration have shown significant effects on bird behaviour and numbers. 8

A concerned young birder’s query on “how to interact closely with birds” elicited an amusing response “… don’t interact with them, just watch them.” photography by giving space to the bird; happily the trend is changing, he observed. He opined that the book could help if there were to be empathy amongst the policy makers and the administrators. A query on why new species aren’t being discovered elicited the reply that wide distribution makes them more visible to the humans all over the earth, apart from their largish size. This was followed by Aasheesh signing copies of the book, put up for sale by the publisher at the venue. The last questions of the evening were on the transition from birdwatching to bird photography to E-birding, and secondly how the book could serve to reach out to the policy makers to help in awareness and conservation. Aasheesh was of the view that photography does indeed help in birdwatching, but censured those who do not follow the ethics of bird A lively evening interspersed with reminiscences, anecdotes, readings, questions and answers drew to a close with a loud and sustained round of applause. The interview is available at the https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9b5SaPGrvPU URL: Aasheesh with members of Deccan Birders (Photo courtesy: JVD Moorty) *** Trip Report: Nehru Zoological Park, Hyderabad, May 21, 2023 Gokul Krishna Addanki The group present at the walk (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) On Sunday, May 21, 2023, we had a wonderful bird walk organized by Deccan Birders at the Nehru Zoological Park. Yellow-billed Babbler (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) The sun was still very easy on us and we proceeded to walk a little further down the road towards the Butterfly Park (which was closed as it still was not business time). We saw some egrets, sunbirds & Scaly-breasted Munias flocking around the flowers and giving some poses for the few photographers in the group; a lot of us were Binocular birdwatchers. Rose-ringed Parakeet (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) By around 7:30AM the sun started shining a little more brightly, and we were running around to fill our water bottles with some cold water. The Zoo was well prepared for such situations and had drinking water facilities every 100 meters. Both paid and free drinking water was available, which is good. Great Egret (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Oriental Magpie Robin female (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) We started our return walk and that is when we noticed a fight between two Barbets. After about 15 minutes, we were happy to see it fly and sit on the fence, where it also gave some time and posed for the photographers. Purple Sunbird (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) 10

Coppersmith Barbet (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Black-rumped Flameback (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) By 8:30AM, the Zoo had officially opened for the general public, and we saw the crowd size slowly and steadily increasing in the area. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Grey-headed Lapwing (Vanellus cinereus) Grey-headed Lapwing (Chennai, February 04, 2023) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Charadriidae Genus: Vanellus Species: V. cinereus Size: 34-37 cm rump show white, and the white tail shows a broad, black preterminal band. A striking contrast is seen between the black primaries, white secondaries and brown upperwing coverts. Habitat & behaviour: The Grey-headed Lapwing frequents tropical and subtropical flooded grasslands, wetlands, swamps, marshes, rivers and riverbeds, streams and creeks. It is also seen in cultivated fields (e.g. paddyfields), flooded agricultural lands and flooded pasturelands and meadows. Its diet consists mainly of invertebrates like insects (aquatic or otherwise), small fish, worms, shrimp and molluscs, taken from shallow, muddy waters or from inside wet mud. The call is a ‘kik’, ‘kerrit’ or ‘chee-it’, loud and sharp like most lapwings. Description & distribution: The Grey-headed Lapwing, also known as Grey-headed Plover, is possibly the only member of the lapwing family that breeds in northeast China and Japan. The bulk of the population from the mainland winters south to India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, Hong Kong, Taiwan and parts of North and South Korea, whereas the Japanese population winters at least partly in in southern Honshu Island of Japan. Vagrants have been seen in Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei and Sri Lanka. In India, it is seen mainly in the northern, central and northeastern parts of the country, but there are regular sightings of small numbers as far south as Tamil Nadu. During migration, it travels mainly during the day, in large flocks and accompanied by juvenile birds. Nesting: In its breeding grounds, the Grey-headed Lapwing breeds generally between March and August. The nest is a shallow depression on the ground, lined with stems or blades of grass. The Grey-headed Lapwing is monogamous and highly territorial, but sometimes two or more breeding pairs may form a defensive flock and, in the event of an intruder coming near, neighbouring pairs help drive it away by making alarm calls, flying in circles and launching attacks on the predator. The usual clutch consists of four pale green or brown eggs with dark speckles all over. Both male and female share incubation and parental duties. The adult Grey-headed Lapwing has a bluish-grey head, neck and upper breast, upperparts are ashy brown and underparts are white, separated from the upper breast by a broad black breast band. Bill is yellow with a black tip, irises are reddishorange (reddish-brown in juveniles) with a yellow eye-ring, and legs are yellow. Male and female birds are similar, but the male is slightly larger. Juvenile birds lack (or have a less distinct) black breast band, and the head and upperparts are pale brown rather than bluish-grey. AN EVENING WITH DR ASAD RAHMANI Report: Talk on ‘History of Natural History Writing’, Hyderabad, July 29, 2023 JVD Moorty A section of the audience with Dr Rahmani (Photo: JVD Moorty) Saturday, the 29th of July 2023, 1830 hours was to be the rendezvous with Dr Rahmani for a talk on “The History of Nature Writing” at Vidyaranya High School. A cloudy evening, weather inclined to being far from inclement; the wait to be awash in the flow of words by Dr Rahmani was palpable. 1

The gathering first irrigated its collective throat with cups of hot tea and whetted the appetite with the typical ‘Osmania’ biscuits. The meeting started with a visibly surprised Dr Rahmani cutting a heart-shaped chocolate cake in honour of his birthday the next day. Following this gastronomic teaser, came the auditory delight with a brief introduction of the speaker by Aasheesh Pittie. A stickler for punctuality, Dr Rahmani was as eager as always to get things under way. Transporting us back in time, the talk began with a depiction of Palaeolithic cave paintings found in Lascaux (Engl. /læˈskoʊ/ la-SKOH) in a complex of caves in the Dordogne region of southwestern France, which are renowned for their exceptional quality, size, sophistication and antiquity. Dating back to more than 20,000 years ago, these depict primarily large animals, once native to that region. The paintings were picture stories of the lives of early mankind. The written word followed much later. Moving forward in time brought us to the ancient Greeks and the Romans with Aristotle, the Greek philosopher, being mentioned. His work History of Animals (Historia animalium), ca. 4th century BC, is one of the major works in Biology, and was a first attempt to classify animals into groups based on their similarities and differences in their physiologies. It is a big treatise dealing with morphology (shapes), ecology, behaviour, and taxonomy. Aristotle’s observations, covering different species, are truly amazing. This book was preceded by his work titled Parts of Animals (Περὶ ζῴων μορίων - Perí zóon moríon), and followed by Movement of Animals (De motu animalium). Aristotle also wrote about his observations on bird migration. To name a few of his observations: the tongue of the chameleon, twisting of the neck by the Wryneck, differences between dolphin and fish, impact of climate (!), animal communication. The Arabs, after the fall of the Greek empire, then took centrestage with their translation of The Book of Animals titled Kitab al-Hayawan. The book depicted animals and birds with great clarity and accuracy. Dr Rahmani next cited Kalidasa, (ca. 4th–5th century CE), the famous classical Sanskrit author, often considered to be ancient India's greatest poet and playwright based his plays and poetry on the Hindu Puranas and philosophy. His description in his epic poem Meghadūta, he speaks about the Raj-Hansas (Bar-headed Goose) yearning for Manasa (Lake Mansoravar) and how they fortified themselves with tender lotus-stems for their migration and showed Zugunruhe, a migratory restlessness before they started their flight. Coming down the ages to the Mughal period, the speaker pointed out how all the premier Mughal rulers of the time from Babur to Aurangzeb were interested in natural history; Babur’s Baburnama is teeming with natural history observations. Jahangir was so enamoured by nature, that he had life forms captured in paintings by his master painter Ustad Mansur. Jahangir’s observations in his autobiography Tuzuk-eJahangiri, that covers the first 19 years of his life until 1621, read like that of a very observant biologist. On spotting a Brown Dipper in Kashmir, he was taken in by the bird’s behaviour and wanted to ascertain whether it was “waterfowl with webbed feet or had open feet like land birds.” He had them caught and recorded his inspection. With the advent of the British period in India came a plethora of natural history writings, among them Edward Hamilton Aitken (popularly known as EHA), Rudyard Kipling, EP Gee, Kenneth Anderson, Jim Corbett, et al. Dr Rahmani dealt with these names and a few others recounting very fascinating anecdotes. The popularity of nature writing is encapsulated in the fact that seven universities in the UK have courses on natural history writing – a new genre in literature has arisen. The offshoot led to the rise of some brilliant exponents on nature writing in English, viz. Gilbert White, James Fisher, Derek Radcliffe, W H Hudson, J A Baker. Dr Rahmani recommended Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, widely considered the most important environmental book of the 20th century, as a must-read. Iliad and Odyssey, the two classics of Greek and world literature, ascribed to Homer are replete with observations of birds, animals, butterflies, animal behaviour, physiology, neurological conditions, meteorological events, and even causes of weather conditions. Ancient Indian texts also mentioned animals and plants. The Rigveda cites about 20 birds: e.g. the Rigveda 2.42 and 2.43 describes the song of the Grey Francolin; the Atharvaveda observes that the Red-headed Merlin hunts in pairs. The pairing up of birds is a theme that fascinated many of the textwriters of the time, with mention being made of the Sarus Crane, Brahminy Ducks and the Common Myna, amongst others. The V-formation of the Demoiselle Cranes and the Bar-headed Goose was said to have been copied during the Kurukshetra war. Dr Rahmani addressing the gathering (Photo: Sudhir K Moorti) In India, the Journal of the Bombay Natural History Society published papers by hunters with keen observations. And this is where the world took notice of the father of birdwatching in India, Dr Salim Ali, whose classic paper on the Baya was based solely on field studies (The nesting habits of the Baya Ploceus phillipinus in JBNHS 34 (4): 947-964). 2

This, said Dr Rahmani, led to the start of behavioural studies in the field led by Julian Huxley in Britain, Salim Ali, Konrad Lorenz et al. Amongst the other nature writers named were Zafar Futehally, Humayun Abdulali, M. Krishnan, Jamal Ara (the first woman birdwatcher of India), Deepak Dalal, Arefa Tehsin, S Theodore Bhaskaran, A J T Johnsingh, Ranjit Lal, and Aasheesh Pittie, almost all of whom were personally known to Dr Rahmani. Dr Rahmani concluded the talk by highlighting the fact that nature writers can be conservationists as well, and how some of the works have brought about awareness for conservation and implementation. A member of the audience asking a question (Photo: Sudhir K Moorti) The group with Dr Rahmani (Photo courtesy: Sudhir K Moorti) A very captivating, informative and fascinating talk by a naturalist par excellence came to an end with a standing ovation to the speaker. *** BIRDING IN THE LAND OF SHER KHAN Trip Report: Pench National Park, February 27-28, 2023 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla White Kulu (Ghost Tree) The beautiful deciduous forest of Pench National Park consists of a wide variety of trees like Mahua, Teak, Palash, White Kulu or Ghost Tree, Bamboo bushes, Neem, Dhaora, Amaltas and many wild grasses reeds and creepers. The Park is located in the Seoni and Chhindwara districts of southern Madhya Pradesh, bordering Maharashtra, and is famous for the Bengal Tiger, Wild Boar, Chital, Sambhar, Nilgai, Chausingha (Fourhorned Antelope), Striped Hyena and Indian Wolf, among other wild animals. The National Park gets its name from the river Pench that flows from North to South through the park, dividing the forest into eastern and western zones. The Park’s Turia gate section constitutes a rich avian habitat and about 250 bird species are known to have been identified here. This is where we spent a couple of days bird watching in the last week of February 2023. 3

The Palash tree or Butea monosperma displays reddish orange honey-bearing flowers to which a large number of big and small birds are attracted. Turia Gate, Pench National Park When we started off on the first day, trekking through the forest that was dappled with early morning sunlight and alive with the chirping of Yellow-throated Sparrows (aka Chestnutshouldered Petronias), Purple Sunbirds, Alexandrine and Plum-headed Parakeets, the first birds we saw were a pair of Jungle Owlets, perched among a splash of reddish orange Palash flowers. The typical dawn calls of the Owlets were answered by Owlets on nearby trees and, after a brief chat, they all flew away into their hideouts, marking the beginning of another day. Alexandrine Parakeet The Black Drongos, Large-billed Crows, Alexandrine, Roseringed and Plum-headed Parakeets, Rufous Treepie, Brahminy Starlings and Common Mynas were seen pecking at these flowers, along with Brown-headed and Coppersmith Barbets. Black-hooded Oriole Jungle Owlet The Golden and Black-hooded Orioles, Jungle Babblers and assorted Bulbuls were also spotted on these flowers. It looked like the Small Minivets had imbibed the crimson colour from Palash so as to camouflage themselves. Since the trees were in full bloom and hardly any leaves on them, it was very easy to spot the birds on them. We had hired a local guide to take us through all the bird habitats in the park and he did a spectacular job of showing us a large number of birds. Flocks of Yellow-throated Sparrows were everywhere to be seen, in the bushes, on the shrubs and on the trees. A Black Redstart was seen along with a pair of Indian and Oriental Magpie Robins. There was a Long-tailed Shrike and a couple of Common Woodshrikes on the Mahua trees, and a Black-rumped Flameback was pecking at the bark. Butea monosperma (Palash Tree) 4

We moved further into the forest and into marshy area lined with reeds. On the adjacent reeds a pair of Common Kingfishers were busy making frequent dives into the water. There were Indian Silverbills, White-rumped and Scalybreasted Munias and Baya Weavers perched on nearby bushes, and the nearby pylons were inhabited by mixed flocks of Greythroated Martins, Red-rumped Swallows and Wire-tailed Swallows. Among the land birds, the fascinating sighting was that of the Painted Francolins. Though we could not get good pictures of them, their calls were heard here and there, and at one particular point we saw four of them crisscrossing two adjacent fields. have actually resulted in a decrease in the number of migratory water birds. There were however a large number of Asian Openbills, Grey and Purple Herons, Red-naped Ibis, and Citrine, White and White-browed Wagtails. On the second morning, our trek was into the forest area along an undulating stream that was mostly dried up. However, the bird activity was very high and we were thrilled to see a Large Cuckoo-shrike perched on a branch right above us. At the same time we were distracted by a rustle in the dried leaves just a few feet in front of us. It turned out to be a Puffthroated Babbler trying to hold on to a dragonfly that it had just caught. As we walked, the Greater Racket-tailed Drongos, about five in number, and two Black-hooded Orioles also moved along with us for quite some time. The list of birds became lengthier every minute and it was a fantastic birding experience. Kohka Lake The last halt before lunch was the Kohka Lake, which is located on the edge of the park. Though the lake was an ideal location for migratory birds, we could not sight any except for a few Ruddy Shelducks. We felt that possibly they had left the lake sooner than expected. Trip Report: Umamaheshwaram, March 12, 2023 Shruti Prakash The group present at the walk (Photo courtesy: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Located in the Nallamala Forest around 100km from Hyderabad, this northern gateway of Srisailam is a beautiful hill surrounded by high trees, making it a haven for birds and wildlife. After reaching the meeting point (Mehdipatnam flyover), the event was officially flagged off at 5:30AM. We had to drive through the beautiful Hyderabad-Srisailam highway to reach Umamaheshwaram. At the breakfast stop, three Indian Grey Hornbills flew over our car, giving the event a fauna flag-off. We could spot many birds on the electric wires; a few of them were the Black-winged Kite, Spotted Owlets, and 3 types of Babblers. When we stopped for the second time, we came across Ashy Woodswallow and Eurasian Collared Dove, and could hear the brain fever call of the Common Hawk Cuckoo. We reached the destination by 8:30AM and were greeted by Rhesus Macaques, Bonnet Macaques and their calmer cousin the Grey Langur. Everyone gathered at the tank area, where we spotted a pair of Loten’s Sunbirds. Indian Paradise-flycatcher (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) The other highlights at the tank area were the Indian Paradiseflycatcher, Eurasian Hoopoe, Long-tailed Shrike, Rufous Treepie and many more. Loten’s Sunbird (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) Rufous Treepie (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) 10

Spotted Dove (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) Black Drongo (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) On the way up the hill, along the stairway there was the constant companionship of our great ancestors. In between, we spotted the exotic Malabar Whistling Thrush also called the ‘Whistling Schoolboy’ for its whistle-like call. It indeed sounded like a playful whistle of joy. The other highlights while climbing was an Indian Giant Squirrel, a Crested Serpent Eagle and a White-browed Bulbul. The beautiful forest range became visible as we reached the top. The hilltop had small waterfalls (mostly dried up) giving off a sense of misty coolness to the sunny morning. I got a chance to see the beautiful endemic bird of the region, the Yellow-throated Bulbul. Crested Serpent Eagle (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) Yellow-throated Bulbul (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) White-browed Bulbul (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) Black Eagle (Photo: KVV Satyanarayana) 11

Unfortunately, I missed the sighting of Black Eagle. The majestic bird is considered the ‘King of Umamaheswaram’, and has been seen after a very long time. I sincerely hope for the ‘currents’ to come my way next time. The other highlights on the hill were the White-bellied Drongo, Verditer Flycatcher, Blue Rock Thrush, and many other birds. The trip ended with a tasty lunch, and on the way back, at the Dindi Reservoir, we saw a Common Kingfisher fishing in the waters, giving the warm feeling of “a beautiful end to the greater beginnings”. I got to know a lot about birds and met very interesting people on this field trip and will keep looking forward to further events being organized. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Eurasian Spoonbill (Platalea leucorodia) Eurasian Spoonbill Immature (Chennai, January 28, 2023) Eurasian Spoonbill Non-breeding (Chennai, February 04, 2023) Eurasian Spoonbill Breeding (Chennai, March 06, 2022) Order: Pelecaniformes Family: Threskiornithidae Genus: Platalea Species: P. leucorodia Size: 80-90 cm winter, populations may also be seen in sheltered marine habitats like estuaries, deltas, tidal creeks and coastal lagoons. The Eurasian Spoonbill is usually seen in small groups scattered along the water. It is well known for its foraging action – it sweeps its bill from side to side in a scything motion as it moves forward, trying to find prey. Its diet consists mainly of aquatic insects, mollusks, newts, crustaceans, worms, leeches, frogs, tadpoles, shrimp, and small fish up to about 1015cm long. It may also consume bits of algae or aquatic plants that are picked up along with prey. It is usually silent – so much so that even in its mixed breeding colonies, the main sounds are bill snapping and the occasional grunting and trumpeting. The flight is slow like most big water birds, with slow wingbeats and with the neck and feet extended. Flocks typically fly in V-formation or in diagonal single lines. Description & distribution: The Eurasian Spoonbill is an unmistakable bird. A large wading member of the Ibis and Spoonbill family Threskiornithidae, the Eurasian Spoonbill is easily recognized by its large, spatulate black bill with yellow tip. The rest of the bird is mostly white, except for black legs. In breeding plumage, it develops a pale yellowish brown breast patch and a prominent nuchal crest behind the head. Immature birds have a pale bill, and show black tips to primaries. The Eurasian Spoonbill is widely distributed across Africa, Asia and Europe. It is a resident breeder in most parts of its range or, if not resident, a local migrant; most northern breeding populations, however, tend to migrate south to northern parts of Africa or the warmer parts of Asia. Nesting: The Eurasian Spoonbill breeds generally between July and November, though it could be later in South India, with some variations due to monsoon conditions – they are observed to coincide their breeding with the monsoons. It is a colonial breeder, and the nest is a massive stick platform on trees in or near water, and usually built alongside other birds like herons, storks, ibises, etc in a mixed heronry. The usual clutch consists of 4 dirty white eggs, sparsely spotted and blotched with reddish brown. Three sub-species are recognized: P. l. leucorodia, seen across most of its range, P. l. balsaci, seen in some of the islands near Mauretania, and P. l. archeri, seen in the Red Sea and Somalia. Habitat & behaviour: The Eurasian Spoonbill prefers extensive, shallow wetlands with muddy clay or fine sandy beds. It is also seen in marshes, rivers, lakes, floodplains and mangrove swamps, of fresh, brackish or saline water. For nesting and breeding, locations with undisturbed islands and reeds or scattered trees/shrubs are especially preferred. In the Local name: The Eurasian Spoonbill is known as ‘Chamach baza’ in Hindi, ‘Chamcho’ in Gujarati, ‘Chamcha’ in Marathi, ‘Gante mukku konga’ in Telugu and ‘Karandi mooku naarai’ or ‘Chappai chondan’ in Tamil. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 13 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 20 Number 10 September 2023 UP THERE AMONGST THE RARA AVIS AND PAPILLONS RARE JVD Moorty Deccan Birders has lost one of the founders and the first Secretary of the erstwhile Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh, its former avatar. candour could always put everyone at ease and there wasn’t a person who did not feel a rapport with him. He loved to talk birds too, and he possessed a wry sense of humour. Prof Dr S Tej Kumar passed away on 6th September 2023. He would have been 84 on 3rd December. As a committed environmentalist and a passionate wildlife lover this passion for nature led him to being involved with the A.P. Biodiversity Board as the Butterfly specialist. It was a proud moment for us when he was invited to act as Advisor in establishing the Butterfly Park at Ramoji Rao Film City and also at Nehru Zoological Park, where his deep involvement helped in making a success of both ventures. This apart, he was also on the boards of various universities and colleges. Dr Tej Kumar has been associated with the Society for more than forty years. About fifteen years ago he turned his activities towards butterflies – in 2006, he founded and was the first President of the Butterfly Conservation Society. Insects were his first love. He worked for almost 40 years as Professor and Head of the Entomology division at Acharya N G Ranga Agricultural University. After obtaining his Masters in Agricultural Entomology, he went on to earn a doctorate in the same field and was also a Fellow of the Entomological Society of India. I first met Dr Tej Kumar on one of the field trips of the BSAP around 1982. His keen eye would catch the slightest movement of insects under and on leaves, dry or green, on branches and trunks of trees in spite of their camouflage, and there would be a quick observation on the identity of the culprit and its life style – he was a veritable fountain of unending information on these crawlies. He was a very warm, welcoming and kind person with an immensely positive outlook on life and a fundamental faith in humanity. His I vividly recall how field trips with him were something to enjoy, where his knowledge always brought wonder to the birders during an intensive day of birding and ‘insecting’. He always evoked the admiration of his fellow-birders. Till his last day on this mortal world, he felt for and loved his birds and butterflies. His personal collection of butterfly specimens was mouth-watering and jaw-dropping. May he continue to be with his beloved butterflies and the birds, and with our first President, Mr Pushp Kumar, where they can continue to revel in Nature. He leaves behind a grieving daughter and a son. May his soul find eternal peace! 1

FIELD TRIP-1: Sunday, 10th September 2023, 6.00AM: Ameenpur Lake. Meeting Point: Miyapur Metro Station, 5.30AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Sudhir K Moorti (Mobile: 96522-83335) Ameenpur is a beautiful and serene spot that is home to a wide variety of birds, making it a great destination for an outing. A man-made lake created for the purpose of providing drinking water to the city, Ameenpur also serves as a prime habitat for various bird species, including migratory ones. FIELD TRIP-2: Sunday, 24th September 2023, 7.00AM: Shamirpet Deer Park & Lake. Meeting Point: Opposite Vacs Bakery, Vikrampuri, 6.15AM. Trip Coordinator(s): JVD Moorty (Mobile: 98494-70411) The park stretches over a vast area of 54 acres with deciduous forest giving shelter to a wide array of animals. Famous as the home to the Blackbuck and the Chital deer, one can also spot monitor lizards and porcupines, among other animals. The lake is known for its serene environment surrounded by deciduous evergreen trees, climbers and grasslands. The Park is home to different species of birds, and it attracts many birds from the surrounding areas too, making it a good bird watching spot. Some of the birds seen earlier are Blacktailed Godwit, the three Cormorants, the three Bitterns, Hoopoe, Black-headed Cuckoo Shrike, Peregrine Falcon and some of the Woodpeckers, and we may spot a few early migrants too. Shamirpet Park is also home to one of the two Butterfly parks in Hyderabad, the other being Mrugavani National Park. Both trips will be half-day trips, so carry adequate water and breakfast/snacks, and protective gear if required. Strict Covid protocols will be followed; please ensure you wear masks, carry a sanitiser and maintain social distancing. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. Trip Report: Yenkathala Grasslands, Mominpet, August 06, 2023 K Sudhir Moorti A view of Yenkathala Grasslands (Photo: K Sudhir Moorti) Early Sunday morning we set off on yet another Deccan Birders trip, this time to the Yenkathala Grasslands. The grasslands, located roughly 60km from the city, have become a popular hotspot of late, and about 200 species have been observed here. It is much visited in winter since a lot of migrants like Harriers, Short-eared Owl, Peregrine Falcon etc can be found here. Quite a few of our members and keen birders gathered at the designated meeting points and we started towards a promising morning of birding, stopping at Shankarpally for a quick ‘Chai-Biskoot’ break. We reached the destination in a convoy of about ten cars. Having parked the cars, we first scouted around for the Sirkeer Malkoha, which was supposed to hang around that particular spot. Our search yielded sightings of Scaly-breasted Munias, Indian Silverbill, Ashy and Plain Prinias, a couple of Spotbilled Ducks in flight and a few other commonly found species and, finally, a brief glimpse of a Sirkeer flying away. 2

CARACAL: HIGH-JUMPING BIRD-CATCHER Praba & Sheela Sunset A plump pheasant hen pecks Silence is me Tasseled ears my asset She senses, takes flight Prime instincts propel Ten feet in the air we collide. My kittens won't go hungry tonight. With long tufts of hair in its rather large ears, the Caracal (ker-uh-kull) listens carefully as it moves in the tall grass. When it identifies a prey, which is often a hovering bird, it springs up to catch the unsuspecting creature in mid-air. This high-jumping bird-catcher has long muscular hind legs and no markings or patterns or additional colouring on its tawny sand-coloured coat. It is believed that this special ability to leap up in the air allowed people to use trained caracal for bird-hunting. About the contributors: Praba & Sheela are fascinated by all the terrestrial, marine, and avian cohabitants of our earth. They strive to bring the biodiversity of our world to children by sharing interesting tidbits about the animal kingdom with the hope of encouraging future conservationists to engage positively with their natural world. Padma Malini Soman, a freelance artist based out of Chennai. As a passionate observer and learner who finds comfort in her sketchbook, Padma loves working with pen and exploring different media. Her artwork can be seen on Instagram at @theplainpaperspage. *** 6

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Northern Lapwing (Vanellus vanellus) Northern Lapwing (Gajoldoba, West Bengal, January 24, 2021) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Charadriidae Genus: Vanellus Species: V. vanellus Size: 28-31 cm banks, wetlands and, sometimes, coastal mudflats. It forms huge flocks from late summer through winter, numbering from several hundreds to even thousands. It tends to spend the day quietly on sandbars, mudflats, arable land or other suitable locations, and feeds mostly at night when there is moonlight. Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates. It often feeds in mixed flocks along with Golden Plovers and Black-headed Gulls, both plovers occasionally getting robbed by the gulls, but receiving some measure of protection against predators in return. It flies with deep, floppy wingbeats, and the flight is slow, irregular and noisy, with its large wings making ‘lapping’ sounds. The usual contact call is a loud, shrill pee-wit. While breeding, it puts up an elaborate display, with a tumbling flight accompanied by continuous calling; these are usually wheezy pee-wit, wit-wit, or eeze-wit sounds, but they may also make squeaking or mewing sounds. Like many plovers, it also uses broken-wing display to lure potential predators away from the nest; alternatively, it may also defend the nest and young noisily while aggressively darting at the predators. Description & distribution: The Northern Lapwing, also known as the Peewit, Tewit, Green Plover or Pyewipe, is the shoetest-legged of the lapwings. It is a handsome, striking wader with a beautiful, long and wispy crest that instantly sets it apart from other similarly-built birds. It has boldly patterned plumage that looks overall black and white, but the upperparts show a beautiful green gloss in good light. Black crown, throat and face contrast with a white face and underparts. Female and young birds have shorter crests and less strongly marked heads, but otherwise the plumage is quite similar. Bill is black, legs are pink or flesh-coloured, and wingtips are broad and rounded unlike most waders. It is a monotypic species – no sub-species are recognized. The Northern Lapwing is common across temperate parts of Europe and Siberia. It is highly migratory, migrating mainly by day, with almost all populations wintering south to North Africa, northern India, Nepal, Bhutan and parts of China; the only exception is the lowland breeding population in the westernmost parts of Europe, which are resident. It is also an occasional vagrant to North America. Nesting: In its breeding grounds, the Northern Lapwing breeds generally between March and May. The nest is a shallow scrape in the ground, and the usual clutch consists of 3-4 beige eggs, heavily blotched with brown or black spots. Local name: The Northern Lapwing is known as ‘Bodal tatihri’ in Punjabi and ‘Sabaz titti’ in Bengali. Habitat & behaviour: The Northern Lapwing prefers open habitats – grassland, farmland, shrub country, marshes, river *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 20 Number 11 October 2023 Trip Report: Manjeera WLS, Hyderabad, February 12, 2023 JVD Moorty A view of Manjeera WLS (Photo: JVD Moorty) Manjeera Wildlife Sanctuary, established in June 1978, is a wildlife sanctuary and reservoir located in the Sanga Reddy district (17°57′52″N 17°57′52″N) with an area spanning 20 sq km (approximately 4,900 acres). It was originally a crocodile sanctuary, developed to protect the vulnerable Mugger crocodile; today it is home to more than 70 species of birds. The reservoir, located in the sanctuary, provides drinking water to Hyderabad and Secunderabad. It lies about 70km northwest of Hyderabad. a thick cover of trees provides nesting spots for other birds. Dry Savannah-type of vegetation is found in the sanctuary. The reservoir supports both submergent and emergent types of vegetation. Plant species like Typha, Ipomoea and Acacia cover the periphery of the waterline, while agricultural fields surround the reservoir and river. Some of the major plant species found are Ipomea, Babool, Prosopis and Vallisneria. Birds roosting at Manjeera WLS (Photo: JVD Moorty) It has nine small islands that have extensive marshy fringes, which act as nesting sites for aquatic birds. In addition thereto, Great & Little Cormorants at roost (Photo: JVD Moorty) 1

approximately 400 to 600 crocodiles in the sanctuary, helped by a crocodile breeding program that is carried out here. Manjeera has always been a popular destination for bird watchers, with the annual Asian Waterfowl Census also being carried out here in January. Among reptiles, Monitor Lizard, Mugger crocodile, turtles and cobra are present. The Indian Hare, Wild Boar, Indian Grey Mongoose and Indian Jackal have also been seen from time to time. On a closer look we also realised that the water level wasn’t very good either. On the Acacia trees and towards one small patch of reeds was a not-too-big flock of birds: Egrets, Cormorants, and Painted Storks, all of them busy making forays in and out to keep their nesthockers fed and fit. Trip Report: Corbett National Park, Uttarakhand, May 2023 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao A view of Corbett National Park Jim Corbett National Park is Indian’s oldest National Park, and is situated near Ramnagar in Uttarakhand. It was established in 1936 with over 500 sq km of forest reserves. Corbett provides a unique ecosystem, ranging from high montane regions up north to other diverse habitats like grasslands and scrub forests, it provides the perfect habitat for a large number of birds and animals, including very large mammals like elephants and bears. As the summer was ending, we were contemplating a family trip, and decided to visit Jim Corbett before the schools started. Given that we were going with the family, I booked a hotel in Ramnagar and reserved for four safaris of three hours each, over the span of three days. We could only get bookings in the Jhirna and Dhela ranges and these places are not known for regular tiger sightings. So, unfortunately, we did not spot the tiger during this trip; but we did experience rich birding all through the safaris. Our trip was all organized during the last week of May 2023. It must be noted that the park is closed during the monsoon season starting mid-June. Also, getting into Dhikala range will mean that you will have to take accommodation at the Forest Guest House, which may not have facilities good enough for families with young children. Indian Sloth Bear with cub on its back Several species of ungulates also call these areas their home – indirectly attracting the felines which make Corbett National Park famous. Given the wide range of ecosystems, being located as it is at the foothills of western Himalayas, it supports the extremely high diversity of birds too. This is especially true during winters, when several birds migrate to lower Corbett scrub forest, grasslands and human-modified landscapes. Most people go and stay inside Corbett NP and go on multiple safaris to spot the national animal – the Bengal Tiger; but little do they realize that it is the Number #1 area in terms of avian species count in the entire sub-continent. If you go to ebird.org (https://ebird.org/region/IN), you will notice the Dhikala range of Jim Corbett has close 470+ birds reported from that region alone across all seasons! Hooded Pitta One important migrant right after the summers is the Hooded Pitta – which has been split into several species in the 2023 Ebird taxonomy changes – we were able to hear, spot and photograph it at multiple locations. 8

One other Pitta that was heard all over was the Indian Pitta – given its breeding season and nesting activity, it was found literally everywhere carrying nesting materials. We spotted some other very interesting birds during the safari. For instance, the Square-tailed Drongo Cuckoo – we had a hard time spotting it; it was easier if we followed the call. Like the Fork-tailed Drongo Cuckoo which winters in the south, it has a very similar and distinct five-note call. Indian Pitta Black Francolin Egyptian Vulture Also spotted in large numbers and making significant breeding calls was the Black Francolin. We frequently spotted the male calling out from a high perch, which gave us ample opportunity to photograph these birds. Given the large expanse of forest, we were also able to spot several vultures flying in the thermals; the Egyptian Vultures were the most common and found at many locations. Bird of the Month Text and Photo: Umesh Mani River Lapwing (Vanellus duvaucelii) River Lapwing (Gajoldoba, West Bengal, January 24, 2021) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Charadriidae Genus: Vanellus Species: V. duvaucelii Size: 29-32 cm Habitat & behaviour: The River Lapwing prefers the shoals and sand banks of larger rivers and lakes, and is hardly ever seen away from these habitats. It is not very gregarious, and is usually seen in pairs or small groups. Very like the Redwattled Lapwing, the River Lapwing too feeds by running in short spurts, dipping to pick up food. It is also quite vigilant, taking off or at least moving away in response to presence of humans or other perceived threats. Its diet consists mainly of insects, worms, crustaceans, mollusks and small frogs, taken from nearby wet fields, farmland and grassland. Its flight is slow, and the call is a single-note, high-pitched did, did, did, given during display or alarm, and sounding quite similar to the Yellow-wattled Lapwing. Description & distribution: The River Lapwing, earlier known as the Spur-winged Lapwing, is a compactly-built, attractive member of the plover family. It is easily recognized by its black occipital crest, crown, face and throat, contrasting with white nape and side of the neck. It has a greyish-brown breast band and white underparts with a black belly patch. Upperparts are light brown with a black-tipped white tail and white rump. In flight, it shows striking colours, the black primaries contrasting with white underwings and upperwing secondaries and brown upperwing coverts. On the ground, its hunched posture, with head and neck drawn in, is a clear giveaway. Both sexes are similar, though the male is slightly larger. Juvenile birds show brown tips to black the black head feathers, a sandier brown back, and pale fringes to upperpart and wing covert feathers. Nesting: The River Lapwing breeds generally between March and June. The breeding display, given on the ground, is quite elaborate, and includes stooping, spinning, stretching and crest-raising. The nest is a shallow scrape amidst stones or gravel in the ground or exposed sand banks, and the usual clutch consists of 3-4 yellowish or olive eggs, heavily blotched and spotted with brown or black marks. It is a resident breeder in most parts of its range, which extends from Northern India starting from western Uttar Pradesh, south to western Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, and east across Nepal, Bhutan, the North-eastern states of India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Vietnam. It does not appear to disperse much during winter. Local name: The River Lapwing is known as ‘Zirdi’ in Hindi, ‘Chitawa’ in Telugu, ‘Aalkaatti’ in Tamil (a name it shares with most lapwings) and ‘Manjakkanni’ in Malayalam. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 18 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report: Namdapha National Park, Arunachal Pradesh, January 2023 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao A view of the early sunrise at Namdapha, en route to Halibari Overview Namdapha is one of the largest national parks in India, covering close to 2000 sq km of protected sub-montane, tropical forests of North-east India. Situated in the Changlang district of Arunachal Pradesh, it borders Myanmar to its east and Mishmi Hills to the north and west. Namdapha derives its name from ‘Nam’, meaning water, and ‘Dapha’ means origin – indicating that it is the source of Noa Dihing river which originates from the Dapha Bum glaciers. The stunning tropical forests of Namdapha Given that the national park covers an altitude range from 700 ft to almost 15000 ft, it supports a fantastic diversity in flora and fauna. A map of Namdapha Tiger Reserve put up at the guesthouse Sultan Tit A fantastic view of the Noa Dihing River, with the guesthouse in the background 6

Silver-eared Mesia Of course, it is known for its avian diversity; but more so known for its diversity of insect life, especially butterflies – the Forest Department hosts the Namdapha Butterfly Meet every year, and about 250+ species of butterflies are regularly recorded. Reaching Namdapha: Namdapha is as east as you can go in India and can be reached easily from Dibrugarh, which is approximately 150km and a 4-hour journey away. Given that it is a tiger reserve, advance booking of the lone forest guest house is mandatory; it is recommended that you plan well ahead. 7

The ideal time to visit would be between December and February, as this period brings a lot of winter migrants. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Black-necked Stork (Ephippiorhynchus asiaticus) Black-necked Stork (Jamnagar, Gujarat, February 4, 2019) Order: Ciconiiformes Family: Ciconiidae Genus: Ephippiorhynchus Species: E. asiaticus Size: 129-150 cm into the northern half of Australia, which hosts the largest population of this bird. Habitat & behaviour: The Black-necked Stork inhabits a variety of natural and artificial wetland habitats: natural freshwater bodies like lakes, ponds, swamps and marshes, flooded grasslands, oxbow lakes, wet meadows and rivers, as well as artificial habitats like flooded wheat or paddy fields, irrigation storage canals or ponds, sewage ponds and dry floodplains. They are also sometimes seen in small numbers in coastal areas like mangroves and marshes. Description & distribution: The Black-necked Stork is a large, long-necked member of the stork family. It is easily recognized: The adult bird has a glossy, iridescent bluish-black head, neck, secondaries and tail, coppery-brown crown, white back and belly, black bill with a slightly concave upper edge, and bright red legs. The sexes are similar, but the irises are differently coloured – brown for the male and yellow for the female. Juveniles below six months look fluffy and show marked brownish colour on head, neck, back, wings and tail, along with a white belly and dark legs. Iris is brownish and the bill is straight and smaller than the adult. It is not very gregarious, and is usually seen singly or in pairs, widely scattered across its feeding grounds while foraging. Although predominantly diurnal, it has been known to forage at night. It is a carnivore, and its diet includes water-birds such as Coot, Darter, Little Grebe, Northern Shoveller, Pheasanttailed Jacana, as well as a range of aquatic vertebrates including fish, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates like crabs and molluscs. In well-protected wetlands, both in Australia and India, Black-necked Storks feed almost exclusively on fish, but in agriculture-dominated Uttar Pradesh, they feed on a wider range of prey. Juveniles older than six months show a mottled appearance, especially on the head and neck, due to the iridescence being partly developed. They also show dark-brown outer primaries, white inner primaries that form a shoulder patch when wings are closed, bill as heavy as adults but still straighter, and dark to pale-pink legs. In flight, like most storks, the Black-necked Stork flies with neck outstretched; it also shows some distinctive signs, like a black bar running through its white wings, contrasting with black neck and tail. Its flight is slow and ponderous, and on hot days, it is sometimes seen soaring on thermals or resting on its hocks. They are usually quite silent, like most Storks, except at nest, where they often make bill-clattering sounds. Juveniles sometimes call using a series of warbling, high-pitched series of whistles, accompanied with open, quivering wings, especially while begging for food. It is a widespread resident breeder in India, its range extending from the west and central highlands east across the northern Gangetic plains into Assam, and into parts of peninsular India and Sri Lanka. It also breeds in central lowland Nepal. There are sporadic reports from southern and eastern Pakistan. Besides, it extends across Southeast Asia, New Guinea and Nesting: The Black-necked Stork breeds generally between August and January, with some local variations. The dance-14

like breeding display entails a pair stalking up to each other face to face, extending their wings and fluttering the wing tips rapidly and advancing their heads until they meet, then clattering their bills and walking away. The display, lasting a minute or so, may be repeated several times. The nest is large, sometimes 3-6 feet across, and consists of branches and twigs, lined with reeds, grass, water plants, sometimes with mud plaster on the edges. It is usually built on trees in secluded parts of marshes or in cultivated fields in India and central Nepal. The usual clutch consists of 1-5 (but usually 4) dull white, broad oval eggs. Nesting, incubation and parental duties are shared by both parents. Food is brought by the parents and regurgitated to feed the nestlings. Fledging success rate increases in years with higher rainfall, with the typical number of 1-3 surviving chicks going up even to 5 in good years. Local name: The Black-necked Stork is known as ‘Banaras’, ‘Loharjang’ or ‘Loha sarang’ in Hindi, ‘Pedda nalla konga’ in Telugu, ‘Periya narai’ in Tamil and ‘Lohar jangh’ or ‘Loha jangha’ in Bengali. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (Received on WhatsApp, November 28, 2021) *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. BIRD-WATCHING IN DEVBHOOMI Trip Report: Mussoorie, June 9-12, 2023 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla A trek in the foothills of Garhwal Himalayan Range in the cool summer months is one of the best ways to engage in bird watching, as the weather is conducive to the whole day activity of both birds and bird watchers. The dense vegetation consisting mainly of Oak, Beech, Pine, Teak, Sal, Rhododendron and Deodar, is home to a large number of montane and highland birds. As tourism is at its peak during summer months and getting good accommodation at Mussoorie is difficult, we halted at village Bhitarli on the Lambidhar bypass road en route to Mussoorie. The village houses a wonderful wellness resort, a getaway for all nature lovers. With an elevation of about 1600 feet and nestled in the lap of serene nature, the resort offers a good stay, a healthy menu and an oxygen enriched environment. 1

Blue-throated Barbet We reached this wellness resort at dusk and were surprised at intense bird activity. There were Blue-throated Barbets, a flock of Himalayan Bulbuls, Cinereous Tits, Black-hooded Orioles, Slaty-headed Parakeets, Yellow-throated Sparrows (aka Chestnut-shouldered Petronias) and Great Barbets. The birds were getting ready to roost and the air was filled with a multitude of calls from the tree tops. Rosy Minivet All this while there was continuous activity at the Firebush plant, Hamelia patens, a shrub with vivid fiery orange red flowers. Streaked Laughingthrush Blue Whistling Thrush From the balcony of our room, we could see almost a dozen different birds flying around. The Blue Whistling Thrush, Black Bulbuls, Jungle Mynas, Himalayan Black-lored, Cinereous and Black-throated Tits, Streaked Laughingthrush, Grey Treepie, Blue-throated and Great Barbets, Grey-hooded Warbler and Blue-capped Rock Thrush were all spotted in the first one hour. Why Write Up A Birding Trip Report JVD Moorty Birders, if I may generalize, go to extreme lengths to see new birds. Some travel for hours to see a rarity; others rise well before dawn to get some birding in before work; and still others plan their vacations, meetings and conferences around birds. One unknown researcher observed these traveling tendencies and realised how useful such birders could be to scientists needing to monitor populations of rare, hard-tostudy birds, but don’t always have the time or funding to go find them themselves. Aha! What if they could use information gathered from traveling birders to monitor unique populations all over the world? to stay, and local guides. These can be very useful as inconvenient situations can be overcome with fewer hassles. The main goal of a bird trip report, however, is to inform other birders about the species that can be seen in a specific location during a certain period of time or season. To do this, birdwatchers upload the reports to websites specifically used for that effect, e.g. eBird. Stuart Butchart, the Head of Science at BirdLife International says: “There are vast armies of birdwatchers across the world; many of them record information that can be hugely valuable for monitoring the state of the environment.” Monitoring long-term trends in population size is important for species’ conservation assessments. A word of caution here: estimates of the numbers of birds in a flock may also vary depending on the counting technique used or the skills of the birder who writes up the report. This is where a birding trip report comes in. A trip report is a document where birdwatchers share any information they consider relevant about a birding trip they just had, and which they can keep for themselves or share with other birders. There isn’t any standard model of the report, one can write it as one wishes. Nonetheless, typically these bird trip reports have some information about the location, dates and a list of birds seen. The reports can be rounded out by including a variety of things, e.g. a few photographs, information about the places visited, how to get to the locations, where to stay, and a brief weather report on the day of the outing. Equally importantly, it is an opportunity to capture the experiences and emotions of the birders themselves, which makes the report a lot more informative and engaging. But of course there are pitfalls: when compared with a systematic, scientific approach to population monitoring, birding ‘trips’ tend to focus on particular spots with abundant birds, like protected areas. Tourists and birding aficionados are likely to spend more time watching and photographing healthy populations of a particular bird, rather than noting that birds aren’t present elsewhere. In fact, birding reports almost never list a lack of sightings. There is endless variety one comes across in birding trip reports. Some are story-telling-like with detailed information on the daily routine during the trip; others are short pieces of text with concrete information. Some birders like to include details on the specific location of species observed, whereas others focus on ease of reading and the number of individuals and species seen. One other problem is that rare and endangered species are over-represented in trip reports. Today, eBird is already geared towards using birders’ data for scientific analyses, unlike birding trip reports. So, even if the method can’t be reliably used to adjust an endangered species’ status, it can be a helpful ‘alarm bell’, to indicate that a species and its conservation may need a closer look. The advantages of the method – it’s cheap, free, and can be used immediately – make it a low-risk option in a world with limited options. One often comes across detailed reports with information about the region or country, normally referring to currency, traffic, culture and costumes, common language and way of communication, best ways of transportation, suggested places So the next time you’re taking a big (or a small!) birding trip, go for it – and make sure you write up a trip report afterwards. Scientists – and, I’m certain, even the birds – would thank you! *** We wish all our members a Merry Christmas and a very Happy New Year 2024 6

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse (Pterocles exustus) Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse male (L) and female (R) (Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, November 15, 2023) Order: Pterocliformes Family: Pteroclidae Genus: Pterocles Species: P. exustus Size: 31-33 cm sandy semi-deserts, barren plains, sparse thorny scrub, and fallow fields or stubble at the edges of deserts; it does exhibit extensive local movements, and may also move long distances based on availability of food and water. In spite of living in hot, arid climates, it is heavily reliant on water and is known to travel up to 50 km in search of water, which it does usually soon after sunrise or just before sunset. It is known for soaking its belly feathers and flying back to bring water to its young ones. Outside the breeding season, or when flying for water, it is usually seen in flocks of up to 30 birds. While foraging, it shuffles along on its short legs, picking up large quantities of weed and grass seeds, sometimes supplemented by grit. It may also eat small insects or fallen berries. Its flight is fast and direct, and the call is a penetrating, far-reaching, burbling twonote kut-ro, constantly uttered in flight. Description & distribution: The Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse, also known as the Common Sandgrouse, is a large, plump, dove-like bird with a pointed tail. It is sexually dimorphic: Male birds are yellowish sandy brown with a thin breast band and solid chestnut-black belly, a yellowish wash to the face and black-fringed yellowish spots on wing-coverts, while females, also sandy brown, are streaked, spotted and barred with black all over except for a mottled neck and a plain chin. On the ground, they appear as very short-legged birds with a small head, while in flight, they seem small to medium sized, with elongated and pointed tails. Juvenile birds are similar to the females, but are duller, have less heavily barred upperparts, lack the breast band, and have shorter tails. Their extremely cryptic coloration makes them almost completely invisible when squatting still. Nesting: The Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse breeds generally between January and May. During breeding season, the male develops elongated central tail feathers and fresh plumage. Courtship involves short chases and low vocalization, and usually involves several males courting the female simultaneously; however, this lasts for only a short while, before one male forms a pair bond with the female. The nest is a shallow scrape or depression on the ground, and the usual clutch consists of 3-6 pale greyish or yellowish stone eggs, covered with blotches, spots and speckles in varying shades of brown, with lavender or grey secondary markings. The Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse is seen across most of northern and central Africa, and further east towards western and southern parts of Asia. It is also an introduced species in the islands of Hawaii. Six sub-species are recognized, of which only P. e. hindustan is seen in India. It is seen in dry areas across India, except for the Himalayas and the North East. Besides, it is also seen in Pakistan, but not in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka or Myanmar. Local name: The Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse is known as ‘Bhat teetar’ or ‘Kuhar’ in Hindi, ‘Jam polanki’ in Telugu, ‘Ka koudari’ in Tamil, ‘Deshi batavdo’ or ‘Vagadavu batavdo’ in Gujarati and ‘Pokurdee’ or ‘Pokundi’ in Marathi. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 21 Number 1 January 2024 FIELD TRIP-1: Sunday, 7th January 2024, 6.30AM: Manjeera WLS. Meeting Points: IKEA Madhapur, 5.00AM; Allwyn Crossroads Foot Overbridge, 5.15AM; BHEL Bus Stop, 5.30AM; Taj Dhaba, Muthangi, 5.45AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Sathwik Reddy (Mobile: 99858-07186) Manjeera Wildlife Sanctuary and Reservoir is a man-made reservoir that provides drinking water to Hyderabad and Secunderabad. It has nine small islands that host a variety of habitats and species. The sanctuary is home to more than 70 species of birds, including large flocks of Common Teal, Cotton Pygmy-goose, Ruddy Shelduck, Painted Stork, Eurasian Coot, Black-crowned Night Heron, and many more. Also, Manjeera Dam and the surrounding fields are good viewing points for finches, wagtails, ibises, munias and more. The area is also home to a various species of birds: look out for Watercock, Bluethroat, Small Minivet, Fork-tailed Drongo Cuckoo, Chestnutbellied Sandgrouse, Rain Quail, Jungle Bush Quail, Rock Bush Quail, Barred Buttonquail, Painted Francolin, Baya Weaver, Blackbreasted Weaver, Tricoloured Munia, Black-headed Bunting, Red-headed Bunting etc. This will be a half-day trip, so carry adequate water and breakfast/snacks, and protective gear if required. FIELD TRIP-2: Sunday, 21st January 2024, 7.00AM: Pocharam Lake. Meeting Point(s): Apollo Pharmacy, Miyapur-Bolaram Road, Near Miyapur Cross Roads, 05:20AM; opposite Dindigul Air Force Station, Hyderabad-Narsapur Road, 06:00AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Sathwik Reddy (Mobile: 99858-07186) Pocharam Lake is a part of the Pocharam Wildlife Sanctuary, a former hunting ground of the Nizam that was declared a wildlife sanctuary in the early 20th century. The sanctuary, which is a dry deciduous forest with small ponds and streams, is home to a wide variety of plant and animal species. The lake was formed by damming the Allair river, a tributary of the Manjeera river, between 1916 and 1922. The lake and its surroundings provide a unique habitat for many water birds, such as Asian Openbill, Bar-headed Goose, Ruddy Shelduck, Greater Flamingo, Greater Painted-snipe, Pin-tailed Snipe etc. Also watch out for Black-tailed Godwit, Ruff, Pacific Golden-Plover, and Black-bellied Tern. The sanctuary also has a variety of plant species, ranging from teak, bamboo and pterocarpus to exotic wildflowers that bloom in different seasons. The lake is a popular destination for birdwatchers and nature lovers, as it offers a glimpse of the rich biodiversity of the region. Both trips are also a part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC), a citizen science programme that monitors the status of waterbirds and wetlands across Asia and Australasia every January. The AWC is coordinated by Wetlands International and contributes to the conservation and management of wetlands and waterbirds at local, national, and international levels. This trip will be full-day trip, and breakfast/lunch options are minimal, so carry breakfast, lunch and enough water to keep yourselves hydrated. Also carry protective gear if required. Covid protocols will be followed; please ensure you wear masks, carry a sanitiser and maintain social distancing. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. EXPLORING THE WESTERN GHATS Trip Report: Sangli, Maharashtra, December 23-24, 2023 Text: Vijaya & Dhiraj Kaveri; Photos: Vijaya Kaveri A view of Bhigwan Bird Sanctuary, with a flock of Godwits in the foreground Our desire to extend our birding expeditions through learning and understanding different places and habitats took us to Sangli, Maharashtra, as part of 36th Maharashtra Pakshimitra Sammelan (Annual Birders Conference) on 23 rd and 24th December 2023. The event was organized by local birding research group Birdsong who are specializing in documenting and publishing sounds of birds found in Sangli District. The two-day conference had presentations from academicians, experts in the birding community and wildlife conservationists. Apart from the formal program we had an early morning birding trip to Krishna River Bank and Shantiniketan Lok Vidyapeeth School, both of which are birding hotspots. Krishna River Bank It was a foggy and breezy early morning when we reached the ghats of the Krishna River a few kilometres from the city. As we entered, we were welcomed by the pleasant sights of an Indian Grey Hornbill pair, Eurasian Hoopoe, Shikra and Asian Green Bee-eaters. Due to poor visibility we could not get clean pictures, though. Shikra Walking down towards the riverbank, we spotted a couple of Long-tailed Shrikes which gave us enough time to take pics. Long-tailed Shrike Eurasian Hoopoe Once we reached the edge of the river, we were all mesmerized by the river view and the sea of water birds foraging, soaring and basking. Everyone got busy identifying the birds and taking some good pics. 2

Ruddy Shelduck Ruff Black-winged Stilt Eurasian Marsh Harrier Shantiniketan Lok Vidyapeeth School Green Sandpiper We could spot Painted Stork, Asian Woolly-necked Stork, Pied Kingfisher, Ruddy Shelduck, Northern Pintail, Blackwinged Stilt, Little Cormorant, Indian Spot-billed Duck, Little Ringed Plover, Ruff, Common, Green and Wood Sandpipers, Eurasian Spoonbill, etc. Indian Grey Hornbill 3

to the other and just stayed perched on the branch calmly, even though the Babblers and Drongos followed it to the other tree and continued mobbing.
