This park is on a hilly area and has a beauty of its own, with the Krishna River and a dam as good picnic spots, but is less crowded than any other National Park, and also with less garbage and littering. Spotted Owlet This school was the venue of the two-day conference. It is a beautiful campus with lots of greenery. We just took a small walk around the campus and were pleasantly surprised to see Indian Grey Hornbill, Spotted Owlet, 3 varieties of Wagtails (Western Yellow, White and Grey Wagtail), Plum-headed Parakeets etc. A small temple stands guard over a sacred grove in Chandoli Western Yellow Wagtail Crimson-backed Sunbird Plum-headed Parakeet We witnessed how the Drongos and the Babblers were mobbing the Spotted Owlet. But the Owlet flew from one tree As our intention was birdwatching we focused the morning safari documenting and enjoying various bird calls like Crimson-backed Sunbird, White-cheeked Barbet, Redwhiskered Bulbul, Common Chiffchaff, Brown-cheeked Fulvetta and many more. With no wild animals to sight our birds made this safari worthwhile. 4

Blue Flycatcher, Black Drongo, Ashy Drongo and Brahminy Kite. As the dam road was already at a height we were almost at eye level with many birds, and could get some great pictures from close range. Common Woodshrike Brahminy Kite Mahabaleshwar, Wai and Panchgani White-bellied Drongo Warna Dam and Ukhli Waterfalls Red-whiskered Bulbul Ashy Drongo Not fully satisfied with the Safari we all went to the nearby Warna Dam on River Krishna, and some surrounding areas, and were happy to spot Malabar Whistling Thrush, Tickell’s Pied Bushchat female 5

Visiting the Western Ghats was one of our dreams and this trip gave us an entry to one of the biodiversity-rich hotspots of India. Being a tourist destination we chose Mahabaleshwar as our first place, not exclusively as a birding site – hence we were not that happy about our birding experience here, although we did spot Oriental Turtle Dove, Spot-breasted Fantail, Pied Bushchat, Red-whiskered Bulbul, Orange Minivet, Wire-tailed Swallow, Square-tailed Bulbul, and the very attractive Red-breasted Flycatcher. All through our journey here we could listen to the sweet birdsong of the Brown-cheeked Fulvetta but couldn't get to see this bird. Painted Stork Wire-tailed Swallow Asian Green Bee-eater Bhigwan is a paradise for water birds and for birders; the boat safari is a simply a pleasure ride. The moment you are at the backwaters of River Bhima, you are swamped with sights and sounds of birds from all over, so much so that you forget you are so close to the highway. The shore grassland invited us with a lot of small birds like Western Yellow Wagtail, Citrine Wagtail, Asian Green Bee-eater, Wire-tailed Swallow, etc. Little Egret Bhigwan Bird Sanctuary - In search of the Greater Flamingo After Mahabaleshwar we visited Pune to catch up with friends and family. Our return journey to Hyderabad was via Solapur. Bhigwan Bird Sanctuary is on the way and we were following up on news of Flamingos and other migratory birds since a long time. Woolly-necked Stork 6

Pallas’s Gull Glossy Ibis Northern Shoveler Brown-headed Gull Greater Flamingo Black-tailed Godwit Once you are on the boat and you look in any direction, it’s all birds and birds! It took us some time to identify most of the birds as half of them were lifers for us. Apart from the regular birds – like Grey Heron, Purple Heron, Glossy Ibis, Painted Stork, Black-winged Stilt, Eurasian Coot, River Tern, Asian Openbill, Little Egret, Spot-billed Duck, Northern Pintail, Little Grebe, Ruddy Shelduck – we were amazed to see many others: Bar-headed Goose, Garganey, Northern Shoveler, Black-tailed Godwit, Wood Sandpiper, Slender-billed Gull, Pallas’s Gull, Whiskered Tern, Laggar Falcon, etc. Our boat birding guide helped us with quickly identifying the birds. After almost an hour of birding in shallow waters we ventured into deep waters to reach a spot where we saw the Greater Flamingos. It was like a wish come true as all the visitors whether birders or just tourists come here to see the Flamingos, so there is some excitement and some mad rush to see these beautiful birds. We were at the same spot for almost half an hour observing these beautiful birds with very few getting into their pink plumage. It was simply meditative looking at them, but we had to leave the spot so as to make space for the other boats. We left Bhigwan with a lot of satisfaction but again we were worried with so many visitors crowding the delicate grasslands and wetlands and littering the place with plastic wrappers and plastic water bottles. There was no one from the authorities to regulate the traffic, with the boatmen engaging every visitor to make the best use of the birding season. 7

Boramani Grasslands - Sanctuary of the Great Indian Bustard A view of Boramani grasslands This vast area in Solapur District of Maharashtra is part of the Great Indian Bustard Sanctuary, with beautiful grasslands and unique landscapes giving us a feeling of being in some African wildlife park. We were lucky to have the company of two locals – Rajkumar, a Bird Rescuer from Solapur, and Balasaheb, a Ph.D. scholar who was researching on the birds of this region, especially the Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark. White-eyed Buzzard Montagu’s Harrier Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse male Eurasian Hoopoe Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse female With their help we explored the whole habitat and spotted some bird species specific to this habitat, like Ashy-crowned Sparrow-lark, Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse, White-eyed Buzzard, Short-toed Snake-Eagle, Montagu’s Harrier, Eurasian Hoopoe, Paddyfield Pipit, Rufous-tailed Lark etc. On our way back we saw 2 herds of Blackbucks grazing and dancing at a distance. This place was one of the best habitats, almost untouched by human activities. The whole area is divided between government and private land with a huge land parcel dedicated to Solapur Airport. We hope and pray this grassland will remain a paradise for all the birds who are resident in this region as well as the migratory ones. 8

pristine hill stations. We checked the Air Quality Index at a few places and realized it is not at all healthy and pleasant. We were unhappy with how much damage we are doing to the very places we lovingly visit as tourists. While the local administration is regulating the damage by its own Waste Collection system, Pollution Tax, Green Tax etc some drastic change in our consumption and exploitative behavior is needed to be a responsible tourist. Sustainable Tourism Bay-backed Shrike Solapur is well known for temple tourism with the famous annual pilgrimage to Pandharpur. But the local birders and conservationists call this place as Pakshyanche Pandhari (Pilgrimage of Birds). Plastic World While visiting all these places we couldn't ignore the huge amount of garbage, trash and plastic waste all across the tourist spots, roads, rivers and valleys. As consumers we humans show total disregard to the other beings who also occupy the same earth and try to survive amongst us. In many places, too much human activity is leading to irreparable damage to the We realised how important sustainable development and sustainable tourism is, with this trip. Rampant destruction in the name of tourism and development can lead to collapse of the place itself which will be a loss to tourism. We realised that the government is taking its measures, but ultimately it is us tourists who need to follow sustainable practices so as to maintain the sanctity of the place we are visiting. During our road trip we ensured we carried our own water bottle and never took a single packaged water bottle. We mostly ate fresh and local Maharashtrian food from small local hotels and even sometimes from roadside vendors. Whatever little trash we generated we carried in our own trash bag. We were aware and conscious of our fuel carbon footprint of nearly 2000 kms. We have decided to minimize this in our next expeditions by using public transport and car pooling as much as possible. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Black-crested Bulbul (Rubigula flaviventris) Black-crested Bulbul (Buxa Tiger Reserve, West Bengal, January 13, 2024) Order: Passeriformes Family: Pycnonotidae Genus: Rubigula Species: R. flaviventris Size: 19-22 cm Madhya Pradesh, northern Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. Eight sub-species are recognized, of which only R. f. flaviventris is seen in India. Habitat & behaviour: The Black-crested Bulbul is usually seen singly or in pairs or small groups, in bushes and lower storey of open forests, secondary scrub forest, at the edges of forests, in orchards or in shrubbery around cultivation, both near and away from human habitation. It is mainly frugivorous, but may also pick up insects occasionally. It has a very pleasant call, somewhat similar to the Red-whiskered Bulbul. The song is very sweet and musical, and goes weet-tre-trippy-weet, with no harsh notes. Description & distribution: The Black-crested Bulbul, originally described in the genus Vanga, was later moved to genus Pycnonotus. However, once this genus was found to be polyphyletic (that is, a group having members with mixed evolutionary origins, but not including their most recent common ancestor) the Black-crested Bulbul, along with four other Bulbul species, was moved to genus Rubigula. Until 2008, the Black-crested Bulbul was considered a subspecies of a complex that included the Black-capped and Flame-throated Bulbuls (both seen in India), and the Ruby-throated and Bornean Bulbuls. Nesting: The Black-crested Bulbul breeds generally between January and June. The nest is a cup of fine twigs, rootlets, grass etc, often bound with cobwebs, and usually placed fairly low in a bush or small tree. The usual clutch consists of 2-4 reddish white eggs, blotched with various shares of red. Both parents participate in nest-building, incubation and care of the young ones. The Black-crested Bulbul has olive-green upperparts, yellow underparts and a glossy black head with a prominent crest. The face and throat are also glossy black, and irises are bright yellow. The sexes are alike. Juveniles are similar but duller in colour, and have a smaller crest. Local name: The Black-crested Bulbul is known as ‘Zard bulbul’ or ‘Haldi bulbul’ in Hindi, ‘Mandiphur’ in Lepcha, ‘Pahariya kangdhara’ in Gorakhpur and ‘Hagrani dao-bulip’ in Cachari. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Curlew Sandpiper (Calidris ferruginea) Curlew Sandpiper Non-breeding plumage (L) (Jamnagar, Gujarat, January 02, 2024) Partial breeding plumage (R) (Chennai, March 10, 2022) Order: Charadriiformes Family: Scolopacidae Genus: Calidris Species: C. ferruginea Size: 18-23 cm and Australasia. It is a common winter visitor to the coastal regions of India, including Andaman & Nicobar Islands, and also Sri Lanka, and can also be seen inland when in passage during migration. Habitat & behaviour: The Curlew Sandpiper is highly gregarious and usually seen in medium- to large-sized groups on mudflats, creeks, saltpans, non-tidal swamps and marshes, bays, inlets, lagoons etc, in mixed flocks along with other waders, especially Dunlins. While foraging, it makes quick darting runs as it grabs prey by sight from the receding waters of the sea or from inside the wet mud. Its diet consists primarily of aquatic invertebrates like worms, mollusks, crustaceans, gastropods, insects and seeds, and also sometimes shrimp, crabs and small fish. The contact call is a rippling chirrip chirrip chirrip. Description & distribution: The Curlew Sandpiper is a small wader that looks somewhat similar to the Dunlin, but it is slightly larger, and the downcurved, slender-tipped bill is longer, as are the legs and neck. Bill is black, sometimes with a brown or green tinge at the base, irises are brown, legs and feet are black and rump is white. In winter (non-breeding) plumage, it has pale grey upperparts with fine, dark mottling, white underparts with the breast showing a brown wash, and a marked white supercilium (another differentiating feature from the Dunlin). In flight, it can be separated from the Dunlin by its large white rump patch; while feeding, it also feeds in slightly deeper water than the Dunlin. In breeding season, the plumage undergoes a dramatic change, with the underparts becoming more markedly patterned with rusty red, with the upperparts turning a deeper brick-red. Juvenile birds have white underparts, grey and brown upperparts with scaly feather edgings, and a peach- or buff-coloured breast. Nesting: The Curlew Sandpiper breeds generally between June and August. During breeding season, the male performs an aerial courtship display. The nest is a cup at the edge of a marsh or pool, or on dry patches of tundra. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 eggs, buff or yellowish with dark brown blotches, which are incubated by the female alone, as males leave the breeding grounds soon after egg-laying. Parental care duties are handled mainly by the female till the chicks fledge, after which, like most sandpipers, the chicks forage and feed by themselves. Reproductive success of the Curlew Sandpiper seems to be directly related to the population of lemmings in the breeding grounds – in years when the lemming population is low, predators like Arctic foxes tend to hunt and pick up Arctic-breeding waders instead. The Curlew Sandpiper breeds mainly in the Siberian Arctic region from the Yamal Peninsula to Kolyuchin Bay, Chokotka Peninisula and New Siberian Island. It is a passage migrant through Europe, north Africa, Kazakhstan, west and southcentral Siberia, Ussuriland, China, Taiwan, Japan, the Philippines, west Melanesia, Wallacea and New Guinea. In winter (i.e. non-breeding) period, it is seen throughout Africa, south of southern Mauritania and Ethiopia, along the valley of the Nile River and in Madagascar. It is also seen in Asia, from the coastal Arabian Peninsula to Pakistan and India, through Indomalaya, South-East Asia and Indochina to south China Local name: The Curlew Sandpiper is known as ‘Mooku ullan’ in Tamil and ‘Vankichanch’ or ‘Shwethpith khichdiyo’ in Gujarati. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 15 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. BIRDING AT MAHANANDA WLS & SENCHAL FOREST, WEST BENGAL Trip Report: October 5-8, 2023 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla Grey-sided Laughingthrush flock The Rufous-necked Hornbill, Jerdon’s Baza, Black Baza and other eastern Himalayan birds are some of the major attractions of Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuary (MWS). The sanctuary is at the foothills of the Himalayas in the Darjeeling district of West Bengal, and is flanked by the Teesta river in the East and the Mahananda river in the west. The forest type in the sanctuary is characterized by riverine vegetation at the foothills and mixed wet broadleaf type in the higher altitudes of Latpanchar. Due to the variations in elevation and forest type, the sanctuary is home to a large number of bird species. 1

Our guide arranged a three-day homestay at Latpanchar and from here we made tours of Senchal Forest, Bagora, Upper Sittong, Rongtong and Shivkhola. The Maroon Oriole was the first bird that we sighted here. It belongs to a clade of red and black orioles and is known to build its nest with bast-fibre and cobwebs. On the first day, we drove from Bagdogra airport to Latpanchar via Rongtong and Shivkhola forest. Though there is a shorter route to Latpanchar the guide took us through Rongtong and Shivkhola, because that is where there was maximum probability of finding the Jerdon’s Baza and the Black Baza. We passed through several tea gardens along the way and, after a brief halt at Rongtong Café for lunch, we started to watch birds en route. Rongtong, meaning ‘colours and beyond’, is an ideal place for bird watching. Here we saw Himalayan Bulbul, Spangled Drongo, Black-crested Bulbul, Scarlet Minivet, Grey-backed Shrike, Blue-throated Barbet, Chestnut-bellied Nuthatch, Olive-backed Pipits and the ubiquitous Malayan Giant Squirrel. Collared Falconet Very close to the Oriole was a pair of Collared Falconets perched at the edge of a leafless branch. True to their name, they looked like miniature Falcons, but their foraging behavior is similar to those of Flycatchers as they would make brief forays from the branch and return back. Pin-tailed Green Pigeon Malayan Giant Squirrel With no trace of the Bazas, we moved on to Shivkhola, which is about seven kilometres from Rongtong. Shivkhola is the name of the stream that houses an ancient Shiva temple on its banks. It is a picturesque location and destination for spotting many birds that are endemic to North Bengal. As we observed them, a flock of about fifteen Large Woodshrikes came along and settled around a Large Cuckooshrike. We also noticed a flock of Pin-tailed Green Pigeons on one of the trees. All this, while our guide was scanning the skies for the Bazas with no luck. Maroon Oriole Green-billed Malkoha 2

to set, we started off to Latpanchar. It is the highest point of Mahananda Sanctuary and also densely covered with pine, teak, sal and cinchona. It is home to the Rufous-necked Hornbill, Red-headed Trogon, Long-tailed Broadbill and Common Green Magpie. Common Hill Myna As we drove along, the daylight began to fade and the Hill Mynas came in small flocks and began to settle on their roosting trees. A Wedge-tailed Green Pigeon, Green-tailed Sunbirds, a Himalayan Cuckoo and several Pied Hornbills were the last on our list for the day. Long-tailed Broadbill We spent the whole of Day-2 at Latpanchar looking for the aforesaid birds. While the morning session saw us through most of the targeted birds, it was not until late afternoon that we could sight the Hornbill, and that too only one female bird. It was a beautiful bird though and the bill distinctly marked with dark ridges looked as if it was painted. Wedge-tailed Green Pigeon Rufous-necked Hornbill female Another interesting factor of Latpanchar is that it is home to a large number of butterflies of different hues and colours, suggesting a very clean environment. There were nearly 25 species of butterflies that were new to us and it was enriching to see these beautiful insects. The day was thus doubly fruitful for us. Himalayan Cuckoo The drive was a fascinating experience with no dearth of scenic viewpoints and bird watching points. As the sun began On Day-3, our plan was to watch birds of Upper Sittong, Senchal and Bagora. At Upper Sittong, there were flocks of Striated Bulbuls, assorted Laughingthrushes, Fire-tailed and Green-tailed Sunbirds, Red-billed Leiothrix, White-tailed Nuthatch, Rusty-cheeked Scimitar Babbler and Wedge-tailed Green Pigeons. 3

After a break for tea and snacks, we moved on to the Senchal general area. This is an interesting habitat with different kinds of shrubs and bushes. We found that this place was teeming with birds. Fortunately, we had extra battery packs, otherwise we would have definitely fallen short of some good pictures. Rusty-cheeked Scimitar Babbler At Senchal, we stopped at the entrance of Tiger Hill, where there were two bird feeding points. Very soon after we arrived, Grey-sided Laughingthrush, White-throated Laughingthrush and Scaly Laughingthrushes came to feed on the grain. Spotted Laughingthrush Scaly Laughingthrush White-browed Fulvetta After about an hour or so, two pairs of Hill Partridges stopped at the feed. The Hill Partridge, also known as Common Hill Partridge or Necklaced Hill Partridge, belongs to the pheasant family and the male wears an orange cap and sports distinct markings on its body. Black-throated Parrotbill Hill Partridge In an hour and a half within the open land, we saw Spotted Laughingthrush, White-browed Fulvetta, Black-throated Parrotbill, Aberrant Bush Warbler, Buff-barred Warbler, Lemon-rumped Warbler, Common Rosefinch, Grey Bushchat and Siberian Stonechat, among others. 4

The dark cloudy weather and drizzling made us wind up for the day. For the next day, our guide made a plan to drive us through Rongtong and Shivkhola before dropping us at the airport. This way we would get sufficient time to look for the Bazas once again. Aberrant Bush Warbler The Warblers were on almost every other bush and were not shy of posing for photos. The Parrotbills and Fulvettas on the other hand remained inside the bushes most of the time. As the name suggests, the Parrotbill has a robust bill, like that of a parakeet, and belongs to the family of Paradoxornithidae of passerine birds. We could not sight the Brown and Great Parrotbills despite hearing their calls now and then. Our next stop was at the Bagora Forest that is situated near Kurseong at a height of 7150 feet. It was an uphill road meandering through Pine, Oak and Fir trees with the sunrays filtering through them. The time was around four in the evening when we reached Bagora and the air was filled with roosting calls. Barred Cuckoo Dove We started off at around 7:30AM and, on the way to Shivkhola, we spotted Barred Cuckoo Dove, Grey-capped Pygmy Woodpecker, Fulvous-breasted Woodpecker, Greater Flameback, Lesser Yellownape, Rufous Sibia and Dollarbird. At this point we received information that Jerdon’s Bazas were around. On reaching the location we spotted three Jerdon’s Bazas! Chestnut-tailed Minla Rufous-capped Babbler Amidst the cacophony, we spotted Yellow-bellied Fantail, White-throated Fantail, Chestnut-tailed Minla, Rufous-capped Babbler, Black-throated Tit, Great Barbets, Grey-headed Canary Flycatcher and Common Iora. Jerdon’s Baza The Jerdon's Baza is a brown hawk with a thin white-tipped black crest, usually held erect. It inhabits foothills of Eastern Himalayas and except for the erect crest it resembles the Changeable Hawk Eagle. 5

Just as we finished observing the Jerdon’s Baza, our guide got a call from his fellow guide about the whereabouts of Black Bazas. We were excited about the news but what awaited us was beyond our expectations! At Rongtong we halted for about half an hour to try and see if we could spot some more birds. Once again it was a fruitful halt. There was the Sultan Tit, Black-winged Cuckooshrike, Asian Fairy Bluebird, Great Hornbill and Crested Serpent Eagle. Black Baza It was a spectacular sighting of 15 to 20 Black Bazas circling in the sky – presumably in preparation to migrate to their wintering grounds in the Southern part of the country. Now and then they would descend in twos and threes to indulge in active feeding before their long journey. We had tried to see them in their wintering grounds down South without much success and little did we know that we would see so many of them in Mahananda. We watched them to our hearts’ content and could also get some satisfactory pictures of them. Great Hornbill Orange-bellied Leafbird Black-winged Cuckooshrike This was a wonderful birding tour and we could see many new birds. As per our guide, two more trips in spring and winter seasons would be required to cover most of the species in this region of North Bengal. With 32 lifers in the list and wonderful sightings of the Bazas and Rufous-necked Hornbill, and many more birds to still watch, we decided to visit North Bengal once again soon. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Blue-cheeked Bee-eater (Merops persicus) Blue-cheeked Bee-eater (Great Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, September 27, 2022) Order: Coraciiformes Family: Meropidae Genus: Merops Species: M. persicus Size: 24-26 cm Africa for the winter. Two sub-species are recognized: M. p. persicus, which breeds in Asia and winters in East and southern Africa, and M. p. chrysocercus, which breeds in North Africa and winters in western Africa. Habitat & behaviour: The Blue-cheeked Bee-Eater is usually seen singly or in small groups, at neighborhood jheels, ponds, village tanks, sandy seashores, open woodland or grasslands in its wintering grounds. It seems to prefer perching on telephone wires, if available, or on bare branches at the top of bushes or scrub. Its diet consists mainly of insects like dragonflies, bees, wasps and hornets, which it catches by way of aerial sorties before gracefully circling and returning to perch, where it batters its prey to death before swallowing it. The call is a musical, somewhat interrogative tetew, repeated several times. The same call is also used as a contact call during night migration. Description & distribution: Like other Bee-eaters, the Bluecheeked Bee-Eater is also richly coloured, predominantly green but with liberally distributed flashes of other colours. It has a black eye-stripe, starting from base of bill and going through the eye to its ear coverts; it also has a yellow chin, restricted pale chestnut throat and long, pointed black bill. The white and blue-green cheek patch is conspicuous. It is very similar to the Blue-tailed Bee-eater, but can be differentiated by its bronze-green tail, whitish forehead, and turquoise-andwhite supercilium. Upperparts and underparts are green but sometimes show a turquoise wash on the belly, rump and tail coverts. The quoted size of 24-26cm does not include the two elongated central tail feathers, which can add another 7cm. The sexes are alike, but the female has shorter tail feathers. Nesting: In its breeding grounds, the Blue-cheeked Bee-Eater breeds generally between April and August. The nest is a burrow in the ground; it is a colonial breeder and several nests may be seen close together. The usual clutch consists of 4-5 white eggs. Both male and female share parental duties. The Blue-cheeked Bee-Eater breeds in northern Africa, and in the Middle East from eastern Turkey to Kazakhstan and, rarely in the western reaches of the Indian subcontinent. In the Indian subcontinent, it is seen in Pakistan south to Sindh, and northwestern India east to Kutch, Rajasthan and Delhi. In India it is generally considered a summer visitor and passage migrant, with incoming populations arriving around April-May and returning in September-October, when they migrate to tropical Local name: The Blue-cheeked Bee-Eater is known as ‘Bada patringa’ in Hindi (a name it shares with the Blue-tailed Beeeater), ‘Bada hajamda’ in Kutchi, ‘Moto patrangiyo’ in Gujarati and ‘Wado traklo’ in Sindhi. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 21 Number 4 April 2024 FIELD TRIP: Sunday, April 14, 2024, 6.15AM: Osman Sagar Lake, Hyderabad. Meeting Point(s): Taramati Baradari Resort, 05:20AM; Sri Sai Famous Tea & Udupi Hotel, 05:50AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Adnan Uddin (Mobile: 95337-01702) Osman Sagar Lake, also referred to locally as the Gandipet Lake, is a man-made lake that spans about 46 sq km. The lake is home to around 278 species of birds, including Indian Spot-billed Duck, Little Ringed Plover, Red-naped Ibis, Purple Heron, Grey Heron, Little Grebe, Indian Pied Starling, Brahminy Kite, Western Yellow Wagtail, River Tern, Blyth’s Reed Warbler, Painted Stork, Glossy Ibis, Long-tailed Shrike, Streaked Weaver, Jerdon's Bushlark, Clamorous Reed Warbler, Yellow-footed Green Pigeon and Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse among others. This will be a half-day trip, so carry adequate water and breakfast/snacks, and protective gear if required. Covid protocols will be followed; please ensure you wear masks, carry a sanitiser and maintain social distancing. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. New Deccan Birders hats and caps will be available for purchase; please carry adequate cash. Trip Report: Mokila, March 17, 2024 Dr Krishna Nagarajan Black-winged Stilt, Spot-billed Duck and Grey Heron at Mokila Lake (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Mokila as a birding destination was added to the menu recently, and I had missed the opportunity to join the group the last couple of times a trip was organized to this place. This time around, the timing was perfect as the workload at office was manageable. Our children having completed their annual exams recently, the stress levels in the house was also manageable. It was indeed a good time to get up early in the morning and sneak out quietly, not having to worry about the repercussions upon return. I decided to join the group directly at the starting point of the field trip – Gautaminagar Temple. As soon as I reached the temple, I saw a Painted Stork soaring in the sky, hinting that there must be small lakes and water bodies around. This was later confirmed by the trip coordinator Gokul. As per Google Maps, the starting point is actually in Edulanagulpalli and not in Mokila; in fact, the entire birding route including the endpoint, which is a small lake are in Edulanagulpalli. 1

Rose-ringed Parakeet (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Map of the region (Source: Google Maps) At around 06:15AM, we all assembled near the temple and started preparing our gear – binoculars, camera, notepad and pencil to prepare the checklist, etc. It was a clear beautiful morning with a lot of sunlight. Surprisingly, it was a small group of five adults and two children – I had expected more. Black Drongo against the rising sun (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) Eurasian Collared Dove (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) At the temple, we saw flocks of Rose-ringed Parakeets jetting past us in multiple bursts one after the other, as if they were doing an air show, and we were standing and watching in awe. We also sighted Spotted Dove, Laughing Dove, Black Drongo, Eurasian Collared Dove, Indian Robin, Indian Bushlark, and Green Bee-eater. Moving along, we sighted Grey Francolin, Small Minivet and Blyth’s Reed Warbler. We then decided to take a detour to the left, where we spotted a Black-headed Ibis, Long-tailed Shrike, Bay-backed Shrike and Yellow-wattled Lapwing. This was the day for taking an infinite number of pictures of the Shrikes, Yellow-wattled Lapwings and Sandgrouse – more about the Sandgrouse later! The route between the temple and the lake must have been around 1.5 km long. We started walking slowly, looking around on both sides. The ‘sunshot’ opportunity with a Black Drongo sitting on a branch with the rising sun in the background presented itself. All of us lined up one after the other and tried to get the best shot possible. Yellow-wattled Lapwing (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) 2

Birding with kids – especially aged less than 10 years – presents some interesting challenges. As parents, we would like them to get the feel for outdoors, pray that they find a bird that they connect with, maybe draw and write a few lines about it later in the day, spend quality time and take pride in our birding abilities, and hopefully pick it up as a hobby when they grow up. The reality is somewhere in between. After few minutes of trying to get a hang of things, they realize that the elders are busy spotting the birds and shouting weird bird names and claiming they sighted those birds. The kids start making up their own games instead. Everything that is flying up there is a ‘raptor’ for them. Stones and pebbles become their focus, any stray dog or cow around becomes an object of curiosity. But it is nevertheless fun birding with kids as they provide plenty of entertainment along the way. Grey and Pond Herons, Common and Wood Sandpipers, White-throated and Kingfishers, Black-winged Stilt, Common Greenshank, Small Pratincole, Asian Palm Swift, and Streakthroated Swallow. We spent a lot of time parked around the lake as there were many birds and plenty of opportunities to take pictures. We had to wait for a while for the Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse to arrive; we expected them to visit the lake, but they chose to land and settle down a bit far from the lake. The trip coordinator, Gokul, decided to give a demo on how to bird around and take pictures from a car. We all sat in the car and went hunting for the Sandgrouse. Interestingly, as we approached slowly, the Sandgrouse did not mind. They were comfortable as long as we were at a certain distance and allowed us to take plenty of pictures. Blue Rock Pigeon (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) After walking a bit, the parents decided to drive their cars towards the destination as it would be easier with the kids while returning. We spotted Red-naped Ibis, Red-wattled Lapwing, Brahminy Starlings, Sykes’s Lark, Plain Prinia, House Crow and Indian Peafowl along the route before reaching the water body at the end. I was told that the water levels have receded significantly in the last two weeks and it is likely to completely become dry in the next few weeks. Finally, we decided to walk around the water body and check if we could sight any further birds. Luckily, we did sight the Blue-faced Malkoha, Red Avadavat, White-browed Wagtail, Indian Silverbill, Common Myna and Large Grey Babblers while walking around the lake. Black-winged Stilt (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) There were a lot of birds around the water: Little Ringed Plovers, River Terns, Spot-billed Ducks, Intermediate and Cattle Egrets, Barn Swallows, Ashy-crowned Sparrow Larks, Blue-faced Malkoha (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) 3

never thought we could find so many different species of birds in this area. I made a mental note to come back again to do solo birding. It may not be long before the entire area is converted into a concrete jungle, so the sooner the better. Red Avadavat flock (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) By now, it was almost 09:00AM, and we decided to walk back to the cars and head home. While walking back we discussed about the different cameras, their advantages and disadvantages, and how it is different birding in India when compared to other countries. After the usual chatter and banter we decided to call it a day and leave for home. BIRDWATCHING AT BHUJ, GUJARAT Report: January 16-25, 2023 Text & Photos: Dr Vaithianathan Kannan Mixed flock of waders at Bhuj Bhuj, located in the Kutch region of Gujarat, India, is a haven for birdwatchers due to its diverse avian population and unique habitats. The area's varied landscapes, including wetlands, grasslands, and desert expanses, attract a wide range of bird species throughout the year. One of the most iconic birdwatching destinations in Bhuj is the Great Rann of Kutch, an expansive salt marsh known for its stunning vistas and a prime habitat for a variety of waterfowl and wading birds. During the winter months, migratory birds from as far as Siberia and Europe flock to the Rann, including species like flamingos, cranes, and pelicans. Thousands of flamingos, both Greater and Lesser, create a spectacular pink hue against the white salt flats. Common Crane Other notable species include Demoiselle Cranes, Common Cranes, pelicans, storks, and various species of ducks and geese. The wetlands provide essential feeding and resting grounds for these birds, making them a critical stopover point along their migration routes. Greater Flamingo Northern Pintail 5

The grasslands, which support a variety of resident and migratory songbirds, are alive with the calls of larks, pipits, shrikes, and wheatears, making it a paradise for birdwatchers all year round. Great White Pelican Another notable birding hotspot in Bhuj is the Banni Grasslands Reserve, a vast expanse of grassland and scrub forest. This area is home to a wide variety of bird species, including the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard, as well as harriers, eagles, and vultures – raptors such as Eastern Imperial Eagles, Short-toed Snake Eagles, Montagu's Harriers, and Eurasian Griffon Vultures can often be spotted soaring overhead. Desert Wheatear Oriental Honey-Buzzard Common Babbler In addition to these larger habitats, Bhuj is dotted with smaller wetlands, lakes, and reservoirs, each offering unique birdwatching opportunities. Chhari Dhand, Fulay, and Kutch Bustard Sanctuary are just a few examples of these smaller birding sites, each hosting a different array of species depending on the season. Black Kite 6

Black-headed Ibis Heuglin’s Gull Fulay Lake, located near Nakhatrana, is another important birding site in the Bhuj area. It supports a diverse array of resident and migratory waterbirds, including ducks, coots, grebes, and terns. The surrounding scrubland is home to species like Indian Courser, Indian Bushlark, and Greater Hoopoe Lark. The Kutch Bustard Sanctuary, as the name suggests, this sanctuary is dedicated to the conservation of the Great Indian Bustard, one of the heaviest flying birds in the world. In addition to the bustard, the sanctuary is also home to other grassland species such as Indian Courser, Desert Wheatear, and Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse. Western Reef Egret Chhari Dhand, a seasonal wetland, is a haven for waterfowl, especially during the monsoon season when it fills up with rainwater. One can expect to see a variety of waders, herons, egrets, and ibises here, along with shorebirds like sandpipers, plovers, and stilts. Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse Birdwatching in Bhuj is not only about spotting rare and exotic species but also about immersing oneself in the sights and sounds of a vibrant ecosystem and experiencing the unique culture and landscape of the region. Birding trips to Bhuj often include visits to local villages, where visitors can learn about traditional crafts, cuisine, and customs while enjoying the hospitality of the Kutchi people. Brown-headed Gull Bhuj promises an unforgettable birding experience for enthusiasts of all levels, from casual observers to seasoned ornithologists. With its diverse habitats, abundant birdlife, and rich cultural heritage, Bhuj is truly a must-visit destination for any birdwatching enthusiast. 7

My birding experience in Bhuj was absolutely breathtaking. Waking up before dawn, I often ventured out to the Great Rann of Kutch, where the soft hues of the rising sun painted the landscape. As I quietly walked along the marshes and salt flats, I was mesmerized by the sight of elegant flamingos gracefully wading through the shallow waters. The air was filled with the calls of countless migratory birds, adding to the enchantment of the moment. With each step, I discovered new species, from majestic cranes to tiny warblers flitting among the reeds. It was a truly immersive experience, connecting me to the beauty and serenity of nature in a way I'll never forget. As I continued my birding adventures in Bhuj, I found myself drawn deeper into the heart of the wetlands. With every turn, there was something new to discover - a pair of Painted Storks building their nest atop a tall tree, a group of elegant Common Cranes dancing in the distance, and the occasional glimpse of a soaring raptor scanning the marshland below. As the days drew to a close, I couldn't help but feel a profound sense of gratitude for the opportunity to witness such natural beauty up close and to be a part of this vibrant ecosystem, if only for a fleeting moment. As the sun would begin to set over the horizon, casting a warm golden glow across the landscape, I would find a peaceful spot to sit and reflect on the day's adventures. Surrounded by the tranquil beauty of the wetlands, I was struck by the sheer diversity of life that thrived in this seemingly harsh environment. Flocks of flamingos painted the sky pink as they flew overhead, while the haunting calls of distant cranes echoed across the marshes. It was a moment of pure serenity, a chance to pause and appreciate the wonders of the natural world. And as darkness fell and the stars emerged one by one, I knew that my birding experience in Bhuj would forever hold a special place in my heart, a cherished memory of some truly magical days spent in harmony with nature. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Zitting Cisticola (Cisticola juncidis) Zitting Cisticola (L) and pair (R) (Chennai, August 15, 2020) Order: Passeriformes Family: Cisticolidae Genus: Cisticola Species: C. juncidis Size: 10 cm the Golden-headed Cisticola by the absence of a golden nuchal collar. Habitat & behaviour: The Zitting Cisticola is usually seen singly or in pairs, in grasslands, meadows, agricultural areas, marshes and reeds near water. Small groups may sometimes be seen. Like most small birds, it is fast-moving and hyperactive, hopping around between the reeds or on the ground. It is insectivorous and feeds on a variety of small insects and invertebrates, especially grasshoppers; it may also take spiders, insect larvae, mantids, and even the seeds of aquatic plants. It is usually heard before it is seen, owing to its tendency to utter its characteristic single-note chik chik call in undulating flight before dropping down to the reeds (although it can also call from a perch). The song is a monosyllabic, highpitched cist, repeated in an even rhythm about once every second, and the alarm call is a short, clipped witt, repeated in series. While perched, it tends to flick or fan its tail repeatedly, which may have given rise to the earlier name of Streaked Fantail Warbler. Description & distribution: The Zitting Cisticola is a widely distributed Old World warbler that was earlier known as Streaked Fantail Warbler. Its breeding range spans from Africa (except the deserts and rainforest), southern Europe, southern Asia all the way down to Australia. Since the range is so large, there are slight variations in plumage, size and calls between various populations, and as many as 18 sub-species are recognized. Since the type specimen was from Sicily, the birds of Sicily and nearby areas like Corsica, Greece Turkey, southern France and Egypt are considered the nominate, whereas Spain and western Portugal have C. j. cisticola. Syria, Palestine, Iran and Iraq have C. j. neuroticus, northern and eastern African populations are C. j. uropygialis and C. j. perennius, and Gabon, Angola and southern Africa are C. j. terrestris. India has two sub-species, C. j. salimalii of the Western Ghats and C. j. cursitans of the plains of India and the dry areas of Sri Lanka (which shows a seasonal tail length variation not seen in C. j. salimalii). Besides, southern parts of South-east Asia have C. j. malaya, southern China has C. j. tinnabulans, and Korea and Japan have C. j. brunniceps. The other populations seen are C. j. nigrostriatus (Philippines), C. j. constans (Sulawesi), C. j. fuscicapilla (east Java), C. j. leanyeri (northern Australia), C. j. normani (northwest Queensland) and C. j. laveryi (northeast Australia). Most populations are resident, though the south Asian populations may move south to warmer areas in winter. Nesting: The Zitting Cisticola breeds any time between March and August, but generally around the monsoons. The cupshaped nest, suspended within a clump of grass, is made by binding living leaves into the fabric of grass, cobwebs and felted plant-down, with a canopy of leaves or grasses tied together overhead for camouflage. The initial nest is made by the male, who invites the female to inspect it; once approved, the female completes the nest. The usual clutch consists of 36 white eggs with deep red or brown splotches. Incubation duties are handled by the female, and more than one brood may be raised in a season. The female birds change their mates and territory frequently, while males tend to stay in the same area, and are generally polygynous. The birds in India are brown above, heavily streaked with black markings, while the underparts are whitish or sandy. The white of the throat goes halfway around the neck before blending into the darker upperparts. The tail is broad, rounded, brown and white-tipped, while the rump is rufous and vent is pale. Adult males show less streaking on the crown, and more markings on the back, than the females. It is separated from Local name: The Zitting Cisticola is known as ‘Ghas ki phutki’ or ‘Ghas ki pitpiti’ in Hindi, ‘Chhoti dharidar piddi’ in Punjabi, ‘Tinu kuruvi’ or ‘Vayalan’ in Tamil, ‘Yerdu jitta’ or ‘Yedru jitta’ in Telugu and ‘Potappottan’ in Malayalam. *** 11

Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 21 Number 5 May 2024 Trip Report: Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve, March 30-31, 2024 Report and Photos: Gurukumar KR A view of Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve Travel: We embarked on our journey to the Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve by the Dakshin Express, travelling between Hyderabad and Chandrapur. The train’s convenient schedule, with a late departure and early arrival, made our travel seamless and efficient. Tadoba Andhari Tiger Reserve: Established in 1955, the Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve is located in the state of Maharashtra, India. Covering an extensive area of approximately 625 sq km, the reserve is renowned for its lush forests, diverse wildlife, and thriving tiger population. Named after the Tadoba Lake and the Andhari River that flow through it, the reserve is a vital habitat for numerous species of flora and fauna, making it a popular destination for wildlife enthusiasts and nature lovers alike. Boating Trip: Before checking into the hotel on Day One, we enjoyed a serene boating trip in the Agarzari Zone. The lake, formed by an upstream dam, provided a picturesque backwater setting for our early morning excursion. As we glided through the calm waters, we were treated to a delightful array of bird sightings. Among the species we encountered were Rose-ringed Parakeets flitting among the trees, Common Kingfishers diving gracefully for their morning catch, Pied Kingfishers hovering above the water’s surface, and White-throated Kingfishers perched on overhanging branches. 1

shallows, while Red-naped, Glossy and Black-headed Ibises adorned the shoreline. Rose-ringed Parakeet Glossy Ibis Cotton Pygmy-goose Median Egret & Black-headed Ibis Lesser Whistling-duck The sight of majestic storks, including the Open-bill, Painted Stork and Lesser Adjutant, added to the spectacle. Herons, egrets, jacanas, and terns also made appearances, showcasing the rich avian diversity of the reserve. Red-naped Ibis We also observed the elegant Cotton Pygmy-goose, Lesser Whistling-duck and Spot-billed Ducks paddling through the Striated Heron 2

Safaris: Over the course of our two-day visit, we were fortunate to embark on three safaris, each offering a unique perspective of the reserve’s diverse wildlife. Day One – Junona Buffer Zone Noon Safari: Our adventure began with a noon safari in the Junona Buffer Zone. Departing at 10:30AM and concluding at 2:30PM, we explored this area and encountered a variety of flora and fauna under the midday sun. After driving around the reserve for hours, when it was almost time to end the safari, excitement peaked as we finally spotted a majestic Bengal Tiger near a watering hole. It was a female, gracefully crossing the water and disappearing into the tall grass on the other side. Our forest guide, most masterfully, positioned our Gypsy in a way that gave us a splendid view of the tigress lying low in the grass, cooling herself from the scorching heat. The sight of this magnificent creature in its natural habitat was truly aweinspiring and left an indelible mark on our safari experience. Other highlights of this safari included a Mottled Wood Owl perfectly camouflaged in the boughs of a tall tree, a Savanna Nightjar blending seamlessly with the leaf litter, and the vibrant calls of various bird species such as the Indian Peafowl, Common Iora, Golden Oriole, 3 types of babblers, and many others. Day Two – Moharli Core Zone Early Morning Safari: As the sun began to rise on the second day, we eagerly embarked on an early morning safari into the core Moharli zone. The morning was heavily overcast due to the rains from the previous evening, casting a mystical ambience over the forest. Despite the cloudy skies, the forest was alive with the calls of various bird species. The haunting cries of the Peacock echoed through the trees, while the melodious songs of the Ioras, Orioles, Babblers, and myriad other birds filled the air. Each call added to the symphony of nature, creating a mesmerizing atmosphere that enveloped us as we journeyed deeper into the wilderness. Amidst the tranquil surroundings, Grey Langurs swung gracefully through the trees, their agile movements a testament to their mastery of the forest canopy. Mottled Wood Owl Grey Langur Savanna Nightjar As we traversed the winding paths, we kept our eyes peeled for signs of wildlife, hoping to catch a glimpse of the elusive Sloth Bear as also more of the tigers that roam these woods. However, the rains seemed to have had an effect on the sightings, as both bear and tiger remained elusive, hidden away in the dense undergrowth. Spotted Deer Indian Peafowl 3

Sambar Despite this, our safari was not without its highlights. We were delighted to encounter herds of Indian Gaur, Spotted Deer, and Sambar, peacefully foraging in the lush vegetation. Their presence added to the sense of tranquillity and harmony that permeated the forest. Additionally, we were treated to a sighting of the elegant Greater Racket-tailed Drongo, with its glossy black plumage and distinctive long tail, adding to the enchanting atmosphere of our safari. Day Two – Zaripeth Zone Late Afternoon Safari: Our final safari of the trip took us to the Zaripeth Zone in the late afternoon. Despite the scorching heat, anticipation was high as we ventured into this buffer area known for its thriving tiger population. Our safari provided us with a diverse array of wildlife encounters. Laughing Dove We spotted an impressive Indian Bison (aka Gaur) and a large male Nilgai or Blue Bull, along with various deer species, including Spotted Deer and Sambar. The avian diversity was equally captivating, with sightings of Spotted and Laughing Doves, Black Drongos, and other birds enriching our safari experience. Bengal Tiger Indian Bison (aka Gaur) The highlight of the safari was an unforgettable tiger sighting. Initially hidden among the dense bamboo and tree shadows, it took the expertise of our forest guide to locate the resting tiger. Patiently waiting for almost an hour, we were rewarded as the tiger stirred from its slumber. The safari experience was not without its challenges, however, highlighting the need for responsible tourism practices. Not all tourists had the patience required. Some impatient individuals resorted to hooting and disrupting the tranquillity of the forest, while others opted to leave prematurely. The forest guides had to constantly remind tourists to behave respectfully towards the environment and its inhabitants. Wild Boar 4

The Zaripeth Zone late afternoon safari provided us with an exhilarating finale to our Tadoba adventure. Witnessing the tiger’s serene passage through the wilderness served as a poignant reminder of the importance of conservation efforts to protect these magnificent creatures and their habitat. However, the challenges posed by irresponsible tourist behaviour also served as a sobering reminder of the need for ongoing education and advocacy in the realm of ecotourism. Overall, the experience left us in awe of nature’s beauty and the raw power of the animal kingdom, making it a journey we will cherish forever. Reflections on Responsible Tourism: Irresponsible behaviour of tourists underscores one of the perils of ecotourism. While the allure of encountering wildlife in their natural habitat is undeniable, it is imperative that visitors are educated and mindful of their impact on the ecosystem. Responsible tourism practices, including maintaining silence and respecting wildlife habitats, are essential to minimize disturbance and ensure the well-being of the animals. Education initiatives are crucial to instil an understanding of the importance of conservation efforts and to foster a culture of respect towards nature. Indian Roller Yellow Wagtail *** Trip Report: Kistareddypet Lake, March 3, 2024 Report: Neil Rahul Gala; Photos: Mohd Adnan Uddin Flock of Garganey at Kistareddypet Lake Kistareddypet Lake, set amidst a picturesque backdrop in Telangana, is a lake area which remarkably portrays its natural and ecological features. Being people fond of outdoor activities and adventure, especially going close to nature, the group chose this picturesque place. Despite the fact that not many people are likely to have heard of the lake, it is of considerable environmental and ecological value, which makes it a preferred site for nature enthusiasts and bird fanciers such as ourselves. our excursion proved to be a captivating journey into the heart of avian diversity. The single most distinguishing facet of the lake lies in the fact that it supports many types of bird life. Kistareddypet Lake is a very good place for bird watching as both resident and migratory birds can be found around the lake. When we visited, there was lush vegetation around the lake and the water was so calm that you could see the mirror kind of reflection. The spirit of tranquillity right from the start of the exploration created a serene environment for the day, and Common Sandpiper (L) and Wood Sandpiper (R) 7

Marsh, Common and Wood Sandpipers displayed their adeptness at hunting as they tirelessly scoured the shoreline for small invertebrates. Barn Swallow From the delicate wading of sandpipers to the graceful flight of swallows, each species showcased its unique adaptations and behaviours, enriching our appreciation for the natural wonders that abound in this serene habitat. A confrontation between two Little Stints Of all the bird species seen, gracefully floating in the shallow waters, elegant Greater Flamingos stood out as a sight to behold because of their pink feathers. The Pratincoles flew low, low across the lake, their streamlined bodies soaring like swift falcons as they skimmed the waters seeking food – and when they landed, they would almost completely disappear into the hoof marks left by cattle in the wet mud. Various types of waterfowl leisurely floated on the water, while cormorants and pelicans impressively dipped towards the water to hunt fish. Kentish Plover The lake hosts a good number of Little Stints, which displayed remarkable agility while feeding on aquatic invertebrates. The lake is also a good habitat for Little Ringed and Kentish Plovers. We saw many of these charming birds moving around the banks of the lake with cautious steps and watchful eyes. Small Pratincole Black-winged Stilt mating Marsh Sandpiper Watching the Black-winged Stilts at lake made me really happy. There were over two hundred Stilts in the lake. Seeing a pair mate was a special moment. 8

Amongst them all, the Little Grebe paddled quietly, its small size and bobbing movements adding a touch of charm to the serene scene. Each bird brought its own special qualities to the lake, reminding us of the rich diversity of life thriving in this beautiful habitat. Great Egret The Great Egret stood tall and elegant, with its snowy-white feathers shining in the sunlight. Nearby, the Eurasian Spoonbill waded gracefully through the shallow waters. Its distinctive spoon-shaped bill is a unique adaptation for feeding. Garganey We were also lucky to spot some other migratory birds like Garganey, Northern Shoveler and Black-tailed Godwit. These birds travel long distances every year to find food and warmer places to live. Seeing them was really exciting. It made me think about how amazing nature is and how these birds travel so far just to survive. Eurasian Spoonbill and Little Egret The Great Cormorant impressed us with its sleek black plumage and skilled diving abilities, disappearing beneath the surface in search of prey. Black-tailed Godwit in breeding plumage The place becomes more lively and teeming with life especially during the peak migration season of the birds; one example of this was the number of Yellow, Grey and White Wagtails we saw all around. Little Grebe 9

It is not only birds that can thrive on its ecosystem: the lake suggests a home to numerous other forms of wildlife, due to an availability of water plants as well as fish in large numbers, thus enhancing the balance of the aquatic ecosystem. Vegetation, especially trees, shrubs, and reeds, augment the habitat – with birds, for instance, using the vegetation for nesting and hiding from predators. But due to the rising dominance of humans and development of urban facilities, Kistareddypet Lake has several issues. Pollution, encroachment and loss of its natural habitats pose a real threat to the species. An attempt must be made to work together and protect this natural asset. It will require partnership between the local water authorities, environmental groups and the people for proper implementation of proper measures such as better control and enforcement of fishing methods, reduction of pollution sources and increasing public awareness for the conservation causes. White Wagtail Research carried out by our group revealed that Kistareddypet Lake can serve as an important hotspot for the conservation of birds as well as other biodiverse fauna in Telangana. People living nearby have to recognize the fact that in order for Kistareddypet Lake to be preserved, people have to contribute to its conservation as well as implement sustainable policies. In this way, beauty and biological richness can be preserved for future generations as an outstanding environmental asset. Discussing and musing on these aspects, we bid farewell to the tranquil shores of Kishtareddypet Lake, carrying with us cherished memories of our encounter with its feathered inhabitants, and eagerly anticipating our next foray into the enchanting world of birdwatching. Grey Wagtail Yellow Wagtail The climate of this region is friendly to birds and many of them migrate thousands of kilometres to find a home in this area. This shows that the lake is equally important in promoting the continued well-being of bird species all over the world since it provides shelter to these birds as they take their migratory rests as well as have food for recovery and rejuvenation. The campaign is run by a group of passionate citizens called Nature Lovers of Hyderabad (NLH), and is focused on saving some 900+ banyan trees, which are almost 150 years old, from being cut by NHAI. The National Green Tribunal has stayed the NHAI project at the moment and asked NHAI to come up with an Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) before cutting the banyans. 12

The majestic banyans of Chevella – a living heritage for people of the region NLH has meticulously geo-tagged all the banyan trees along the highway. The group also wanted to document the avifauna in the area, which gave rise to this survey. The 2-day survey was conducted on April 13-14, 2024, and was a perfect citizen science project for us. The whole route was divided into 25 cells and each team got 2 to 3 cells to survey. Our team, consisting of Omar Ali Khan, Vijaya & myself, was allotted cells 15 and 16. We started surveying cell no. 15 at 6:30AM. The weather was a bit cloudy and we didn't see much bird activity except for Indian Peafowl, Red-vented Bulbul, Purple Sunbird, Asian Koel and Southern Coucal. This cell had few fruiting trees so we didn't see many birds. Red-vented Bulbul By the time we started surveying the 2nd cell, there was good sunlight and we could document some good birds. Just one banyan tree yielded the majority of the birds of the day. Indian Peafowl Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher 13

highway devoid of these majestic banyans, which give shade, shelter and food to so many birds, is not a good bargain in the long run. It is inflicting cruelty on ourselves and these innocent birds. Yellow-footed Green Pigeon This fruiting banyan was feeding Coppersmith Barbets, Redvented Bulbuls, Indian Golden Oriole, Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher, Small Minivet, Yellow-footed Green Pigeon and our favourite, the Indian Grey Hornbill. And even with the bright and mighty sun and scorching heat, under the banyan it was very cool and we didn’t feel the heat at all. We wondered that if just one banyan can do this, we can only imagine what would be the negative effect with all these banyans gone. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Blue Whistling Thrush (Myophonus caeruleus) Blue Whistling Thrush (Manila, Uttarakhand, May 10, 2024) Order: Passeriformes Family: Muscicapidae Genus: Myophonus Species: M. caeruleus Size: 33 cm glistening silvery-blue. Forehead, shoulders and fringes to wing and tail are slightly brighter blue. The median coverts have white spots at their tips. The bill is yellow and stands out in contrast to the rest of the bird. The sexes are similar. The juvenile is browner and lacks the blue spangling; its wings and tail are also a duller blue than the adult. Description & distribution: The Blue Whistling Thrush is not a true thrush; it is, rather, a member of the Muscicapidae family of Old World flycatchers. It is widely distributed, ranging across Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Laos, Macau, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Tajikistan, Thailand, Tibet, Turkmenistan, Pakistan and Vietnam. In the Himalayas, it makes altitudinal movements, descending to lower altitudes in the winter. Habitat & behaviour: The Blue Whistling Thrush is usually seen singly or in pairs, in temperate forests, subtropical or tropical moist montane forests, ravines, and wooded areas, close to streams. It is a restless bird, rarely seen sitting at one place for long. It hops onto rocks, jumps to the ground, turns over leaf litter or small stones while looking for prey, and moves around in short spurts. It spreads and droops its tail when alarmed. It is active well after dusk. Its diet consists primarily of fruits, earthworms, insects, crabs and snails, the latter typically being battered on a rock before they are eaten. It is most well-known for its musical, rambling whistling song, which is a very familiar sound in the early mornings in the hills. Its alarm call is a shrill kree. Based on clear variations in size and plumage between some of the populations, six sub-species are recognized: The nominate M. c. caeruleus, with a black bill, in central and eastern China; M. c. temminckii, with a bill that is narrower at the base, in the Himalayas and other mountains of central Asia, west China and north-eastern Myanmar; M. c. eugenei, lacking the white spots on median coverts, in central Myanmar, east Thailand, south China, and north and central Indochina; M. c. crassirostris in south-east Thailand, Cambodia, and north and central Malay Peninsula; M. c. dichrorhynchus, with smaller spangles, in south Malay Peninsula and Sumatra; and M. c. flavirostris, with the thickest bills, in Java. Nesting: The Blue Whistling Thrush breeds between April and August, and the nest is a cup of moss and roots placed in a ledge or hollow beside a stream. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 eggs, and the pair may sometimes raise a second brood. Local name: The Blue Whistling Thrush is known as ‘Pahari neeli kasturi’ in Punjab, ‘Kuljel’ or ‘Kaljit’ in Uttar Pradesh, and ‘Kasturaa’ in Himachal Pradesh and Kashmir; another beautifully evocative name used in Kashmir is ‘Hazaar dastaan’. The Blue Whistling Thrush is an easy bird to recognize. The Delectation Of Window Birding Text and Photos: Syed Murthuza Hussaini Indian Peafowl I work at Focus High School, which is conveniently situated near Salar Jung Museum’s backyard, the part which is not open to the public and where its flora is at its healthiest. There is a lot of shrubbery and a good mix of large and mid-sized trees covering a long stretch bordering the Museum, which itself is in proximity with the Musi river and its ecosystem, and only a stretch of road separates both. The front of the school looks at a dilapidated government property. The long years of neglect were to the advantage of nature and gave rise to abundant vegetation. And till very recently, our school ground had, amongst other small trees, a large banyan tree, which very sadly got uprooted a short while ago due to high gale and winds. 1

To my utter advantage, the school has large glass paned windows on all sides. It was designed to allow natural lighting. This in turn provides a very convenient all-round view of trees, which attract a host of urban birds, and this my friends, is how I indulge in the delight of window birding. It was back in 2021 that I was first introduced to the pleasure of bird watching by my dearest friend and colleague Asif Arastu, who himself is an avid bird watcher and photographer. One day I went on a birding trip to Ameenpur Lake with him. What an exhilarating experience that was, watching the little guy actively pumping its lungs with each note, what precision and what plethora of colours! In later days, other familiar sounds were traced to a Greater (now Southern) Coucal, then a Tailorbird and then the Sunbird and so on. “Listen carefully, do you hear the sound like snipping scissors? It's a Zitting Cisticola,” Asif said. Then we approached the lake and he pointed out the various water birds: Cormorants, Herons, Egrets, Ibises, Moorhens, Jacanas and so on. That day, something changed in me. From that day onwards, I suddenly became aware of the presence of birds all around me. After this, whenever I went out and looked at trees, poles, or electric wires, I could see birds; in fact I was actively seeking them. One day I was standing in our school grounds and I was hearing this rhythmic, metronome-like sound coming from the top of the banyan tree. It was a familiar sound that I was aware of but could not place it and till now never paid attention to. It was like listening to a very old friend, it's just that I acknowledged its existence today. I have been hearing this sound all my life. When we were children and running around in the courtyards, this sound was our constant companion. Getting overwhelmed, I called Asif and described to him the sound I heard and he told me that it's a Coppersmith Barbet. The name sounded exotic so I searched for the bird online. Purple-rumped Sunbird male Today my day starts with the familiar sounds of the Barbets, Tailorbirds, Sunbirds, Koels, and Babblers. The picture I saw took my breath away. Before that, for me, the birds were the usual crows, pigeons, parrots, eagles, sparrows etc. I could never comprehend that such a beautiful bird lived in our vicinity, so close, yet so far that I never saw it. From that day, I actively started watching the tree tops from my third floor office window and one fine day I saw it. Large Grey Babbler Coppersmith Barbet 2

Asian Koel female Later in the morning comes the White-throated Kingfisher, trilling sharply and making such a commotion, and perching on his favourite branch, comically looking left and right with its oversized beak. Indian Grey Hornbill I don't know for how long this joy of mine may last. Our landscapes are changing. The big banyan tree which was a host to the first Coppersmith Barbet that I saw, and hundreds of other birds, is no more. It was already destined for destruction, as the land it was standing on is marked for road widening by the Hyderabad Metro, and the only satisfaction is that it gracefully accepted its fate at the hands of nature and not the axe. But I am hopeful that my ten years old daughter Marzia is showing a keen interest in birds. Whenever she sees a bird, she comes running back to me with the description and demands an identification. Also, I still have so many trees around and I will continue to watch birds from my windows. White-throated Kingfisher Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher Later we are greeted by the melodious Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher and in the afternoon a Grey Hornbill may pay its obeisance by making shrieking calls. Spotted Dove *** 3

BIRDWATCHING AT GOA Report: October 6-8, 2023 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao Mixed flock of Greater & Lesser Sand Plovers, Gull-billed Terns, Sanderlings and Great Knots at Goa Goa is a well-known go-to tourist hub, known especially for its wonderful beaches and as a big family getaway. It is not a big secret either that Goa is bestowed with one of the most diverse environments, with beaches, estuaries, mudflats & fantastic forests of the Western Ghats hosting a great diversity of avian fauna. Goa is especially good for birding during the months of October to March, when a plethora of birds come there for wintering. Also, early April could be very good to observe some birds in their breeding plumage. very good birder but also has deep knowledge of the Goa ecology in general, making it a pleasure to travel with him. My travel was also during early October; in hindsight, if you are planning to travel to Goa for birding, it is recommended that you start mid-November or later, so that you can witness some additional migrants, especially the kingfishers and other shorebirds. Day-1 (Oct 6, 2023): Agacaim Mudflats and Mahavir National Park Since we were staying close to Panjim, we decided to start with Agacaim Mudflats. It is an estuary in North Goa formed by the Zuari River meeting the Arabian Sea, creating a fantastic ecology of both freshwater, sea and terrestrial avifauna. Given that it is a mudflat ending into a sandy beach with water everywhere, we quickly realized that it is best for gumboots, floaters or even barefoot (recommended if you are comfortable). Flock of Gull-billed Terns and Greater & Lesser Crested Terns We also realized that given the sheer distances, a spotting scope is highly recommended. Of course, you can make do with a good pair of binoculars, but 10x may not be enough to identify birds at a distance. When birding in Goa, one would need to travel between South and North Goa districts to cover both the seashore and the amazing forests. As always, my birding trip was planned post a business trip when I had a little over two days (weekend) to spare. I was guided by a well-known naturalist, Omkar, who is not only a Greater & Lesser Sand Plovers and Sanderlings 4

Sanderling As we got into the mudflats, we immediately saw a large flock of small waders running with the waves; they mainly included Lesser and Greater Sand Plovers along with Sanderlings, Dunlins, Little Ringed Plovers and a few Terek Sandpipers. Great Egret Pied Avocet As we started walking along the mudflats, we realized that this going to be a treasure trove of birds. To our very pleasant surprise, we were greeted by a lone Pied Avocet, which is rather rare in this part of India. Broad-billed Sandpiper Lesser Sand Plover, Broad-billed Sandpiper and Great Knot White-bellied Sea Eagle Further along we several White-bellied Sea Eagles hovering for a possible scrap or opportunity. Also we noticed several common Egrets, like Great and Little Egrets, busy hunting near the edge of the tide. On closer observation (through the spotting scope) of several large flocks roosting on the sandy beach, we realized that it is a complicated mixed flock and, on patient scanning, were able to spot the Broad-billed Sandpiper and Great Knot, rare sightings for the season. Of course majority of the birds were in their non-breeding plumage, making them blend into each other, making it especially difficult to isolate the rare ones. 5

Common Tern Gull-billed Tern On the beachside we also noticed several other terrestrial birds like Blue-tailed Bee-eaters in very large numbers. We also saw a few White and Grey Wagtails, indicating the arrival of winter migrants. It was interesting to also observe several herons like the Black-crowned Night Herons roosting on the trees. Birding around the shores and mudflats of Goa can be very productive. Since the monsoons had just receded, it was very humid and sultry unfortunately. Little Tern A coastal view at Goa So, around 11:00AM, and we decided to grab some brunch and head over to Bhagwan Mahavir National Park for some forest birding. Greater Crested Tern juvenile (L) and adult (M & R) We also observed several terns that included the Common, Little, Greater & Lesser Crested and Gull-billed Terns. Crimson-backed Sunbird 6

Day-2 was scheduled to be a forest birding day around two locations in South Goa – Bhagwan Mahavir National Park and Bondla WLS. Given that the monsoon had just passed (although, I was told it was not a great monsoon this time), it was a very thick green cover, making it very hard to spot birds, and the migration season had not started either. Loten’s Sunbird Unfortunately, given the temperatures, the activity was rather sedate – of course Crimson-backed, Purple and Loten’s Sunbirds were rather busy visiting any available flower, given their energy needs and metabolism. Tambdi Surla Mahadev Temple, a wonderful area with lots of bird activity Little Spiderhunter We also spotted a few Little Spiderhunters around Banana plantations, especially feeding on the inflorescence. Malabar Trogon male Day-2 (Oct 7, 2023): Bondla WLS & Bhagwan Mahavir National Park The entrance to Bondla WLS Malabar Woodshrike 7

Flame-throated Bulbul Malabar Pied Hornbill We did get great sightings of the residents, although they were far apart. Some important sightings included the Malabar Trogon, Malabar Woodshrike, Malabar Pied Hornbill, Malabar Grey Hornbill, Malabar Barbet, Malabar Parakeet, Flame-throated Bulbul and Yellow-browed Bulbul. Malabar Flameback Malabar Barbet Malabar Parakeet We also spotted several resident woodpeckers like Blackrumped Flameback, White-naped Woodpecker, Malabar Flameback (split from the Greater Flameback), Rufous Woodpecker, Speckled Piculet and the Heart-spotted Woodpecker – most of them endemic to the forests of the Western Ghats. Speckled Piculet 8

Small streams and rivers make for great birding sites in the forests of Goa Unfortunately, it is common to see road kills, we saw a Green Vine Snake slithering and struggling on the road; we lifted it up and put it back away from the road. White-naped Woodpecker Green Vine Snake Heart-spotted Woodpecker We also regularly spotted several Nilgiri Flowerpeckers around the flowering and fruiting trees. Given the time of the year we could not spot Oriental Dwarf Kingfisher, Blue-eared Kingfisher and the Black-capped Kingfisher which are otherwise found regularly in these forest streams later in winter. Day-3 (Oct 8, 2023): Agacaim Mudflats On the final day, we returned to the Mudflats to continue our search for some birds we had missed on Day-1, and we were not disappointed. Nilgiri Flowerpecker Bar-tailed Godwit 9

Black-tailed Godwit Caspian Tern The place we stayed at in South Goa amid the forest had a host of books in its library. I was super inspired and ordered some of these great hardbound books! Ruddy Turnstone On this particular day, though we started a little late due to the travel, we spotted Bar-tailed and Black-tailed Godwits, Whimbrels, Curlew Sandpipers and Ruddy Turnstones, and also spotted the Broad-billed Sandpiper and the Great Knot in the mixed flock. We continued to see extremely large flocks of Sandpipers and Terns all through the mudflats. Some of the books at the eco-resort To sum up, it was an enthralling birding experience indeed. Except for the monsoon season, it is generally very productive to bird in Goa, though I would strongly recommend later part of winter from December to February for the best experience. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani White-throated Fantail (Rhipidura albicollis) White-throated Fantail (Sattal, Uttarakhand, May 12, 2024) Order: Passeriformes Family: Rhipiduridae Genus: Rhipidura Species: R. albicollis Size: 19 cm gardens. Like most small birds, it is fast-moving and hyperactive, flicking or fanning its tail as it moves. It is insectivorous and feeds on a variety of small flying insects, sometimes through aerial sorties, but mainly by foraging along the forest floor or through lower, middle (and occasionally upper) storeys of undergrowth. It is often seen along with mixed-species foraging flocks. It utters a harsh contact call chuk chuk; the clear, whistling song is melodious, consisting of several tinkling notes repeated as the bird prances about. It uses the same song year after year with a few minor changes, with the result that the song can sound quite different after 45 years. Description & distribution: The White-throated Fantail is a small passerine that is widely distributed across tropical southern Asia, through the Indian Himalayas east through Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos and Malaysia upto Indonesia. It is mainly slate-grey on the upperparts and underparts, with a black eye mask and white throat and short white supercilium. The tail is distinctive and an easy identification feature – a shade darker than the body, fan-shaped and edged with white tips to all feathers except the central pair. Iris is brown, and bill and legs are black. The sexes are alike. Juvenile is like the adult, but with lesser white on the face and brownish edges to the dark body feathers. 9 sub-species are recognized, with considerable variation between them in terms of plumage colour. Besides these, the White-spotted Fantail (R. albogularis) was also, until recently, considered a sub-species of the White-throated Fantail. Nesting: The White-throated Fantail breeds between March and August. The neat cup-shaped nest is made of moss, fine grass, shredded leaves and fibres, plastered outside with cobwebs, and usually built in a fork or junction of twigs or branches, within 3 metres from the ground. The usual clutch consists of 3 pinkish cream eggs with a ring of small brown specks around the broad end. Incubation duties are shared by both parents. Local name: The White-throated Fantail is known as ‘Machharya’ or ‘Chakdil’ in Hindi, ‘Chitta gal nacha’ in Punjabi, ‘Tapkili nayan’ in Gujarati, ‘Nachan’ or ‘Nachra’ in Marathi, and ‘Dasari pitta’ in Telugu.
