SHADOW OF A BIRD IN FLIGHT Trip Report: Osman Sagar, April 14, 2024 Text: Arafat Ahsan; Photos: Mohd Adnan Uddin Grey Heron with fish I rose with the birds that Sunday in April while it was still dark out. Got dressed, made myself a cup of tea, grabbed my binoculars, and a hefty field guide, that somehow is always carried but seldom consulted in the field. Instead, I find myself relying on a handy pocket guide, a gift and a nudge from two old friends, both ardent birders. The pocket guide is all of six leaflets long and folds compactly like a map, thus making it quite portable and a lot easier to consult while one's out and about. Being fairly new to birding (this was only my third outing with a group, and my first with Deccan Birders), I find myself frequently immersed in the guides, trying to place what I was seeing, albeit with varying degrees of accuracy. Looking down when I should have been looking up. While ambiguity is alluring, dwelling on it is also exacting. One of the meeting points for this trip was Taramati Baradari. Adnan, who had organized this particular outing, was already there waiting, as I rolled in at the agreed time of 5:20 AM. Another regular member of the group also arrived soon after. Having made our acquaintances, we headed out towards the second and final meeting point, which was much nearer the birding site. The sky was getting lighter as we met up with two other members. We quickly fortified ourselves with some tea and drove on towards the peripheries of the Osman Sagar Lake, which was now only a ten-minute drive away. The actual site was accessible via a kilometre-long dirt road that ended in a clearing, which was to serve as our parking spot. As we got out facing East, to our left stood a temple, in whose compound the rustling leaves of a Peepal tree paid obeisance to the rising sun. Up ahead, beyond some wet and marshy fields, lay the waters of Osman Sagar. As we carefully picked our way through, walking on the bunds, we could see the waters in front of us dotted with at least two dozen Eurasian Coot. Amongst them we also spotted a few Spot-billed Ducks, Little Grebes and Black-winged stilts. As we took in the sight, a couple of River Terns, with that distinctive fork in their tail, flew over our heads, announcing our presence to one and all. Spot-billed Duck For the photographers amongst the group the light was brilliant – with the sun slowly coming up, the waters were aglow, and dawn seemed to unfold at an unhurried pace around us. The tripods came out and lenses whirred. The quiet broken only by the Terns still circling and cackling over our heads. Perhaps we were perilously close to a nest? Painted Stork 2

To the North stood a few scattered trees that, for now, had escaped the agriculturalist's axe, and flitting about in its branches we saw an Indian Robin. Turning South and slowly walking towards the south-eastern bank of the lake, we spotted a Black Drongo perched atop a power line. A few Barn Swallows put up an acrobatic aerial display for us. Further afield, in the slightly muddy grounds, we could see two Common Sandpipers, their heads bobbing as they pecked and foraged. It was then that, on slightly drier ground, we spotted what looked like a Yellow Wagtail, with an almost golden breast that glistened in the early light; or perhaps it was a Grey Wagtail, and it was only the light playing tricks on us; or maybe we saw both! Grey-headed Swamphen We could see a number of Little and Intermediate Egrets, Little Cormorants posing as they must, Grey-headed Swamphens, a Bronze-winged Jacana, Grey and Purple Herons, a solitary Black-headed Ibis, and later a Glossy Ibis. We stayed a while in that spot watching them watching us, a bit warily, and rightly so. Yellow Wagtail The Drongo was gone, in its place now a Green Bee-eater. The sun was climbing fast now, as we walked gingerly over the bunds, trying to get closer to the south-eastern waters that, in the form of a fist, had punched their way into the land. On the farther embankment, what appeared at first to be small rocks and boulders curiously strewn about, on closer inspection, turned out to be a family of Lesser Whistling-ducks. This part of the lake, not as easily accessible to human feet, exhibited a greater diversity in its congregation. Grey Heron Purple Heron Little Egret 3

The group at the outing As I drove back, with the gravel crunching under the tyres, I marvelled at what I had seen that morning and what had eluded me. Was it a Yellow Wagtail after all with the breast of gold? And that silhouette in the sky that I could not make out, with the sun in my eyes. I had seen and not seen, seen partially and occluded. And I was reminded of what one of the Persian poets had once aptly said, translated for your convenience: Indian Grey Langur By now, the sun had really started to bear down upon us, and we decided to call it a day. It was proposed that we stop for some breakfast on our way back, but two of our fellow birders very graciously invited us to share with them the home-cooked food that they had brought along. And so there, in a nicely shaded spot, we enjoyed a sumptuous fare of homemade parathas, washed down with multiple cups of tea. We reminisced about trips taken, old and new, and the ones yet to come about, and lamented at the fast changing face of this city. Fed and nourished in more ways than one, we dispersed, silently pledging to ourselves to do this again. Soon. OUR TREK FROM MIAO TO VIJAY NAGAR, ARUNACHAL PRADESH Trip Report: January 27 – February 3, 2021 Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao A view of Dibang River (Photo courtesy: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) This is a trip report of a trek that was undertaken by me and my 25-year-old son Prashant in the year 2021 between Miao and Vijay Nagar, in the Changlang district of Arunachal Pradesh bordering Myanmar. This trek is 125-158 km long, depending on the season & weather, and traversing through jungle, riverine and hilly terrains, and generally takes 5 to 8 days. This trek was primarily undertaken to unleash the spirit of adventure and to get a few days of living away from civilisation. It also gave us insights into how challenging, and yet simple, life can be away from the cities and villages. The trek route (Source: Google Earth) The Indian Government realised the strategic importance of this land mass of Arunachal Pradesh, jutting into Myanmar and secured the same by establishing a limited-use air field called an Advance Landing Ground (ALG) at Vijay Nagar, which happens to be one of the Eastern-most villages of our country. There existed a motorable road between Miao and Vijay Nagar in the seventies; however, due to the collapse of some of the bridges the road went in to a state of disuse. The problem was further accentuated by very heavy rain for most part the year aiding thick undergrowth and vegetation, leaving only a foot track for the commuters. Thus, in the absence of a motorable road this distance of 158km is covered mostly by foot. Majority of the road track is located in the Namdapha National Park which has an area of 1985 sq.km. The 35-minute helicopter ride along the Dihing River from Miao to Vijay Nagar is very enchanting with rich broccoli-like wooded canopy visible till as far as the eyes can see. The Government of Arunachal Pradesh operates a scheduled service to this ALG twice a week. Since the seats are limited, a few lucky passengers get to fly from Miao to Vijay Nagar and back. My association with Vijay Nagar dates to 1995, from my years with the Indian Air Force. The IAF and its Mi17 helicopters air-maintained Vijay Nagar ALG and the surrounding hamlets. Another prominent village in the vicinity is Gandhigram, established by the government by settling Gorkha soldiers and their families. Gandhigram is approximately 15 kilometres west of Vijay Nagar. This trek had been on my mind since several years, and I had been gathering inputs from residents and army personnel living there. My current assignment as a civil pilot with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh rekindled my desire to walk this route and helped me realise this plan. A scheduled night halt in Vijay Nagar in December 2020 helped me interact with various support elements and give the finishing touches to my trekking plan. I discussed about the trek with my family and my elder son Prashant readily accepted the challenge. I did articulate the requirements to successfully complete the trek while stressing on the perils and dangers that awaited in any adventure of this nature. Injury, disease, wild animals, mosquitoes, leeches, lack of communications and weather were some of the major obstacles that were addressed adequately. All the obstacles were objectively discussed and remedial measures were rehearsed. To ensure suitable physical fitness for the trek, we calculated that one must walk 30 km a day in the plains with ease, to be able to do the jungle route of 20 km per day to enable us to complete this trail in a reasonable time. Thus, we trained to sustain ourselves for a continuous walk of 25 km a day during the actual trek. The trekking gear was carefully chosen and accustomed to before leaving Hyderabad. Thus we were ready by end-January 2021 to commence the trek. 5

D Minus 2 (Jan 27, 2021) I flew from Hyderabad to Dibrugarh via Kolkata while Prashant who was on a trek in Himachal Pradesh with his friends reached Dibrugarh via Delhi. Post lunch we set course for Miao town (Western edge of Namdapha) in a cab gliding smoothly amongst the tea plantations of Assam. All was well till we entered Arunachal Pradesh, where we received a message that the following day’s helicopter flight to Vijay Nagar was cancelled. Board showing distances from Miao to various places (Photo: Prashant Yella) We went to the village market and bought rations and camping requirements sufficient for 6 persons for 8-10 days. The camping requirements were mainly rations, cooking utensils, tarpaulin for tenting, candles and batteries. First aid kit, sleeping bags and water purification tablets were arranged from Hyderabad. Rest of the requirements were planned to be sourced from the jungle itself. Entrance to Miao town (Photo: Prashant Yella) Our original plan was to proceed to Vijay Nagar by helicopter and trek down along the river, a gradient of about 3000 feet in 5 days. However this last minute cancellation of the scheduled flight forced us to trek upslope from Miao to Vijay Nagar which of course was the Plan B. In the Defence Services we are trained to expect the unexpected and thus Plan B, which was prepared with as much care and detail and was unveiled at once and with ease. We reached Miao shortly after sunset and settled down in the Inspection Bungalow. Over an early dinner meeting with the local staff we decided to spend the next 24 hours in the preparation for the trek. Black-hooded Oriole immature (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) D Minus 1 (Jan 28, 2021) The locals too were excited about our adventure and rendered all possible support. The day was spent identifying the porters and a guide. We identified 3 porters and one guide and carried out necessary briefing. The porters were experienced, lived in Miao and undertook regular trips to Vijay Nagar. The guide, Mr Aphu David was originally a resident of Gandhigram, and is settled in Miao. He has an ancestral house in Vijay Nagar as well, and a cardamom farm with a log hut halfway between Miao and Vijay Nagar that would serve us for the night halt on the second day of the trek. D-Day (Jan 29, 2021) We commenced our move at 07:30AM after gathering all the Team members. We hired a pickup truck that dropped us close to Deban village (15 km from Miao towards our destination) which was the farthest point where a vehicle could go. Once at the road head we repacked our luggage in to the bamboo baskets to be carried by the porters. Each porter had to carry a load of 35-40 kg of baggage. The porters generally take the river bed route to save on distance to be travelled in the jungle along the zigzagging hill slopes. 6

Another view of the bamboo bridge (Photo: Prashant Yella) Breakfast time (Photo: Prashant Yella) Resting point for the porters (Photo: Prashant Yella) Bamboo bridge crossing (Photo: Prashant Yella) A porter crossing a bamboo bridge with load (Photo: Prashant Yella) By 10:00AM we repacked and were all fresh and raring to go. This enthusiasm saw us covering a lot of distance along the river and crossing temporary bamboo bridges that were constructed by locals. These bridges further straightened our path and helped reduce the trek distance in all by 30-35 km! The local folks who built these bridges levied a fee which varied from Rs 10 to 50 per person depending on the length of the bridge and the tactical value the bridge offered in reducing the ground distance. We reached the confluence of the Dapha and Dihing rivers by about 2:00PM. This river Dapha originates from Dapha Bhum which is the highest peak in the area, and the Dihing River is the one we were trekking along and which flows down towards Miao from Vijay Nagar. We spent time admiring the landscape and the wide valleys and felt the urge to set up a night camp. This was also the place where the hornbills show up in the mornings and evenings for crossing over to the other bank of the river. However, our guide Mr Aphu David advised that we should cover some more ground so as to reduce the burden on the following day. Thus, we walked for another hour and found a small camp on the river bank set up for construction of a culvert over Burma Nallah. The incumbents welcomed us and offered their ration store for sleeping which was a small wooden log hut. Few desi chickens too gave us company for the night! We quickly lit up a fire to cook. Our dinner was ready in no time thanks to the experienced porters, and we were ready to sleep by 7:00PM. Day-2 (Jan 30, 2021) After a refreshing non-stop sleep, we were awake well before sunrise and made arrangements for breakfast and lunch. We heard a number of Hoolock Gibbons howling on either side of the river. Our porter friends were very resourceful and experts in living off the land. One of them had laid a mosquito net in the river the previous evening and was successful in catching half a dozen fish which were an add-on for breakfast. The kitchen was quickly wound up, all utensils were washed and packed in a jiffy. 7

We set off walking by around 07:30AM, earlier than expected. The river now passed through a narrow gorge and thus left no space for walking along. We were forced to climb up and walk on the road track, which was full of slush and thick mud. Some parts of the track remain wet for the entire year owing to rain and lack of sunlight. Almost all of us slipped/skidded and fell in the mud on the second day. In some cases, the shoes and socks got wet and required a change. The track was full of a thick slurry in which the feet would get stuck and it required sustained efforts to lift the foot out. Thus, our pace suffered but that did not deter us from achieving the day’s target of 26 km to reach our guide’s Large Cardamom farm. We did also see a couple of nice birds that enthused us. edge of its territory. A little after sunset we reached the camping point which was a log hut on the edge of a spur. Large cardamom farm (Photo: Prashant Yella) Below was the cardamom farm of our guide Mr Aphu David. He lives in Miao and visits the farm once in two or three months depending on the status of the crop. The hut had a fireplace in the centre and enough space around for all of us to sleep for the night. Black-chinned Yuhina (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) Yellow-bellied Fantail (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) The trek was a long and tiring one. Day 2 was surely the toughest of the 5 days and tested us both physically and mentally. Upon reaching the hut we quickly executed the duties we were assigned and prepared dinner and readied the sleeping area. One of the porters had managed a cabbage from a wayside settlement and same was boiled in salt and turmeric. We relished the same and it was voted one of the best dishes of the trip! Soon the lights went out and we called it a day. Day-3 (Jan 31, 2021) We woke up well ahead of sunrise as a matter of routine now. We performed our assigned duties and the food was ready in no time. The menu was simple. Rice, dal and some fresh chutney made from onion, green chilli and dry fish. Once the food was done, the ash-covered embers were used to boil up the stream water for drinking. Water thus boiled was cooled and filled in to empty water bottles. This was then treated with water purification tablets, one tablet per litre of water. This process was adopted for all the five days and it ensured that none of us had any stomach-related problems. Like nomads we once again packed everything in to our bamboo baskets and moved on towards Yachale Village which was around 24 km from the current roosting spot. The track this day was not as bad as the previous, and we moved at the expected pace. We met a friend of our guide en route and stopped over at a suitable place to prepare tea. The tea was served in mugs made of freshly cut bamboo. Black-backed Forktail (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) Towards the afternoon, a Black-backed Forktail led us along the track for over a kilometre and peeled off probably at the Tea stop (Photo: Prashant Yella) 8

The bright blue skies gave way to local Cumulonimbus clouds and we were pounded by moderate rain for an hour or so, but we continued to walk after deploying our rain gear. On the way we got to see a number of Great Cormorants, Crested Kingfishers and Brown Dippers. Nepal Fulvetta (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) Brown Dipper (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) Short-billed Minivet (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) Black-crested Bulbul (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) The village headman of Yachale Village warmly welcomed us to his abode as he was a friend of our guide Mr David. We were offered the kitchen hut to cook and sleep. We were offered firewood too and this gesture saved us a lot of time and effort. By now we knew exactly how to go about the kitchen activities and cook tasty meals. The host gave us company for dinner and narrated about their daily activities. Sleep was next on the agenda and it was instantaneous. Day-4 (Feb 01, 2021) Next morning we got a glimpse of the village life and we too participated in helping our host in collection of firewood from the jungle. After the usual breakfast ritual we bid farewell to the village headman and his family, and moved on towards Gandhigram which was our roosting spot for the fourth day. White-throated Bulbul (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) We also saw a few other birds – Black-crested and Whitethroated Bulbuls, Nepal Fulvetta and a Short-billed Minivet. Asian Fairy Bluebird male (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) 9

Asian Fairy Bluebird female (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) White-naped Yuhina (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) As we exited the village, we were greeted by a large flock of Asian Fairy Bluebirds and Himalayan Bulbuls perched on a tree that bore some tomato-sized sweet red fruits, locally known as Chinese Apples. There were also some other birds moving around in the vicinity. We maintained our pace and stopped for tea after a few hours of trek. Three days having passed, we decided to bathe as the river was very welcoming in the morning sunshine despite its near freezing waters. Once refreshed we resumed our walk to Gandhigram. Bar-winged Flycatcher-shrike (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) The Bell 412 helicopter deployed on the weekly shuttle service (Photo: Prashant Yella) On the way we witnessed the weekly helicopter shuttle service descending through the valley for landing at Vijay Nagar. We also met a number of porters transporting goods on mules and bicycles as we made our way towards Gandhigram. Himalayan Cutia (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) Entering Gandhigram (Photo: Prashant Yella) 10

This day’s trek was an easy one as the distance to be covered was only 15-odd km on a track that is well established due to the continuous movement of people between these two villages. Along the way, we also saw a few birds. Gandhi statue at Gandhigram (Photo: Prashant Yella) As we reached the outskirts of the village we were greeted by fierce-looking local dogs. We reached our roosting site, which was our guide’s home, well in time. Our guide Mr David wanted to treat us to a country chicken curry but could not manage one as it was already too dark. A surprise awaited us the following morning about which we had no idea. We wasted no time in preparing our dinner which was a vegetarian meal and called it a day. Common Green Magpie (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) Dinner time (Photo: Prashant Yella) Day-5 (Feb 02, 2021) After a good night’s sleep at our host-cum-guide’s residence, we woke up early as usual and started our preparations for the final day trek to Vijay Nagar. As we were making preparations for breakfast-cum-lunch, a lady appeared at our house with a consignment of rice, dal, large cardamom, some spinach and a country chicken. She was appreciative of the fact that someone from a far-off land visited their village by foot. Moreover, she probably got to hear that our guide and village resident Mr David was looking to buy a country chicken the previous evening. She insisted we accept them as gifts which we refused to do. We paid for the chicken after an extended discussion and persuasion. We savoured the chicken for breakfast and prepared to move towards Vijay Nagar, our final destination. Some local handicraft products (Photo: Prashant Yella) White-browed Shrike-babbler (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) We reached Vijay Nagar at about 3:00PM and settled down at the Government Guest House on the Eastern edge of the Air Strip. Northern Lapwing (Photo: Wg Cdr Y Prakash Rao) 11

We were welcomed by a flock of Northern Lapwings and a couple of Redstarts. We sent messages to all concerned about our arrival at our destination. Mr David treated us all to a sumptuous dinner at his home and we took a long walk back to the Guest House and went to bed after having resolved to wake up late in the morning. The lights went off at 10:00PM as the gen-sets that powered the village in the evening fell silent. Day-6 (Feb 03, 2021) We woke up, automatically, and well ahead of the sunrise, admiring the eastern glow beyond Myanmar. We decided to spend the day trekking in and around the river Dihing. However, there was another pleasant surprise awaiting us. As we went to the local PCO to make a call to the Arunachal Aviation Department to confirm our helicopter tickets for the following Saturday, we learnt that there was a special chartered flight bringing in some state officials and that we were to take the return flight to Dibrugarh in the same. Our happiness knew no bounds and we quickly made our way to the guest house and packed our belongings. While we waited for the helicopter, we distributed all the left-over rations including those that were packed and sent to Vijay Nagar as per the initial plan. The return flight (Photo courtesy: Prashant Yella) Our trip to Vijay Nagar was truly historic, as there were very few who did such an adventure in the past. This trip had tested our limits of endurance and grit especially on the second and the third days. The weather gods too had played their role with some winter showers on the fourth day. The age-old saying ‘well begun is half done’ perfectly fits this trip. Planning and preparation paid rich dividends during the entire trip. Luck too favoured us despite temporary setbacks at each stage. Birdwatching during the trek was only incidental, as the primary objective each day was to reach the designated night halt location – but we did get to see some great birds! We are truly grateful to a lot of agencies who supported us in ensuring the success of the trek. All in all, it was a once-in-alifetime and a very memorable trip. A view of Vijay Nagar valley (Photo: Prashant Yella) The chopper came as per plan and we made a giant leap from Vijay Nagar to Dibrugarh via Miao in under 90 minutes. We were just in time to catch the Hyderabad flight via Delhi and reached home the same night. Thus, we surprised everyone involved with our trip by our arrival at Hyderabad at least 3 days ahead of the schedule! Trip Report: Kistareddypet, March 7, 2024 Text: Shilka Chaudhari; Photos: Dr G Samuel Sukumar Northern Shoveler Krishna Reddy Pet, also known as Kistareddypet, is a small village situated in Ameenpur Mandal of Sangareddy district in the state of Telangana. Its land area covers about 450 acres (1.8 sq.km). The lake can be reached by taking a right turn at Beeramguda arch on NH-65; the area can also be reached from the Outer Ring Road via Exit 3. The lake in this village has caught the attention of birdwatchers recently as it happens to be a hotspot for migratory bird species. This biodiverse birding spot was a top favourite of many participants for the HSBC Bird Race 2024. 8 of us visited the lake on March 7, 2024, a few days after the official Deccan Birders outing to the same place. After a lovely breakfast, while we were en route to the lake, we spotted the Indian Roller, Black Kite and a few House Sparrows. Upon reaching the lake, we located a Grey Hornbill by its call; later it flew all the way to some nearby trees in the area. Ashy-crowned Sparrowlark Indian Peafowl Indian Grey Hornbill 14

Northern Shovelers. This remote spot is also a saviour for many waders and shorebirds. Garganey We saw a small flock of Indian Silverbills and some other birds – Indian Peafowl, Ashy-crowned Sparrowlarks, Garganey, Ruff and a solitary Purple Sunbird (female) busy collecting spider webs as nesting material. Painted Stork Black-tailed Godwit Little Ringed Plover Eurasian Spoonbill We saw some Painted Storks, Great Cormorants basking in the sun, and Little Ringed Plovers busily foraging along the lake’s edge. We also noted a flock of Glossy Ibises flying by and Barn Swallows skimming low over the lake and scooping up water. We noticed Grey and White Wagtails walking slowly along the edges of the lake. Ruff The lake was almost dry with only a small portion having some shallow water. The lake is home to several migratory bird species like Black-tailed Godwit, Eurasian Spoonbills and White Wagtail 15

River Tern Black-winged Stilt Wood and Marsh Sandpipers River Terns flying over the lake were lovely to watch. Wood Sandpipers, Spot-billed Ducks, Marsh Sandpipers and Grey Heron were also seen. Little Stint The lake is also home to Black-winged Stilts and Little Stints. We were welcomed by the Small Pratincoles on the dry mudflats and along the edges of the lake. Grey Heron Small Pratincole 16

the other hand, mistook a Shoveler for Common Shelduck, which was corrected after referring to the book by Grimmett. Samuel uncle had got some very nice shots of the wetland birds spotted on that day. We decided to call it a day due to rising heat, as it was almost afternoon. We made a note of 48 bird species on that day. Personally, I had seen Spoonbills, Pratincoles and Godwits for the first time on this trip. Temminck’s Stint Other common species which we spotted were White-throated Kingfisher, Grey Francolin (by calls), Blue Rock Pigeon, Blue Rock Thrush (female) and Cattle Egret. Though the size of this lake was small in comparison to the other lakes we had visited earlier, the presence of a diverse group of birds did not disappoint us. The village is inside the Outer Ring Road and is zoned as a Multipurpose Residential Zone by the HMDA. This would be posing a real concern as residential developments in the area would deplete groundwater and other natural resources. As the number of lakes are on decline due to human population and odd weather patterns, the natural habitat needs to be preserved in order to protect the waders and migratory bird species. Ecotourism posters and protecting the wetlands can bring a positive change in conservation. Planting trees around the lake, developing the spot for eco-tourism, and saving it from encroachments so as to protect the natural water bodies from pollution and decay is very important. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Painted Sandgrouse (Pterocles indicus) Painted Sandgrouse male (L) and female (R) (Greater Rann Of Kutch, Gujarat, April 15, 2024) Order: Pterocliformes Family: Pteroclidae Genus: Pterocles Species: P. indicus Size: 28 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Painted Sandgrouse is less gregarious than other Sandgrouse species, and is usually seen in pairs or small groups in dry country with thorny scrub or open rocky areas, open forest, rough grassland, low hills, firebraeaks in deciduous forest, and shallow rocky ravines. It is very well camouflaged when sitting, and can stay still until almost trampled upon, when it takes off with a clucking yekyek-yek-yek and a noisy flapping of wings. Its flight is fast and well-coordinated. Large numbers may congregate near favourite water holes at dusk, when it arrives in small groups, continuing till almost dark. It is also said to drink in the morning, well before sunrise. When flying to and from the water hole, it utters a distinctive chirik-chirik call which, quite often, may be the only indication of the presence and movements of the Painted Sandgrouse in the dark. It feeds on grain, seeds and shoots. Description & distribution: The Painted Sandgrouse is a small, stocky ground-dwelling bird, slightly smaller than the more familiar Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse. It is sexually dimorphic, with the males and females looking markedly different. The male has heavily barred upperparts with a clear buff shoulder patch, a strong black band cutting across a white forecrown, unbarred buff-orange neck, breast and inner wing coverts, fine black longitudinal lines on the nape, bare white patch surrounding the eye, and an orange bill. The underparts are closely barred with bold but finer lines, and it has a tricoloured (i.e. chestnut, buff and black) gorget. The female is a duller greyish brown, has heavy chocolate, black and buff barring all over, and lacks the male’s patterning on head and breast. Nesting: The Painted Sandgrouse breeds mainly between March and June, though nesting activity has often been observed at other times of the year. The nest is a scrape on rocky ground, under cover of a bush or grass clump. The usual clutch consists of 3 cream to salmon pink eggs, sparsely spotted and blotched with purplish red or reddish grey. The Painted Sandgrouse is endemic to the Indian region, being found only in north and north-west Pakistan and India. It is a resident bird in most parts of central India and the Indian peninsula, but is not seen in the North East or the southernmost parts of India. It is monotypic, and no sub-species are recognized. Local name: The Painted Sandgrouse is known as ‘Pahari bhat-teetar’ or ‘Bhat-ban’ in Hindi, ‘Gutila teetar’ in Hindi in parts of Uttar Pradesh, and ‘Palki’ or ‘Kal gojal hakki’ in Kannada. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Shaheen Falcon (Falco peregrinus peregrinator) Shaheen Falcon (Masinagudi, July 03, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Sub-species: Size: Falconiformes Falconidae Falco F. peregrinus F. p. peregrinator 25-30 cm subcontinent, including India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and south-eastern China. There have also been occasional records from the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Habitat & behaviour: The Shaheen Falcon is usually seen singly, or in pairs on cliffs and rock faces. They typically mate for life. Known for its swift and powerful flight – up to 240kmph in level flight and up to 320kmph while diving – it is an efficient hunter, usually hunting its prey in flight, striking the prey in mid-air with its powerful hind claw and taking it away to a favoured perch to be consumed. Flight is usually a few rapid wingbeats interspersed with long glides. Its diet usually consists of other birds like ducks, partridges, pigeons and parakeets, which has also enabled it to adapt well to urban surroundings. Description & distribution: The Shaheen Falcon, also known as the Black Shaheen, is a small, powerful falcon with dark slaty upperparts, black head, nape and moustachial stripes, rufous underparts with fine dark barring on belly and thighs, and a white throat and belly. The full black face mask is clearly delineated from the throat. It has distinctive rufous underwing coverts that are clearly visible in flight which, along with the rufous underparts, help separate it from the Peregrine Falcon (F. p. calidus). It has a strong dark bill with yellow around the base and nostrils, yellow feet with dark talons, and barred uppertail. The sexes are alike – although the female is larger – while the juvenile has darker brownish-black upperparts than the adult and paler underparts with heavily-barred flanks and striped breast. Birds in South India and Sri Lanka may show an almost completely black hood with no distinct moustachial stripe, and almost uniform underparts. Nesting: The Shaheen Falcon breeds mainly between March and May. The nest is a platform of twigs and grass on a ledge on a cliff face. The usual clutch consists of 2 or 3 pinkish-buff to pinkish-red eggs, variably marked with purplish or dark brick-red marks. Local name: The Shaheen Falcon is known as ‘Bhyri’ or ‘Bhyri bacha’ (for female and male respectively) in Hindi, ‘Bhyri dega’ in Telugu, and ‘Kayal pullu’ in Malayalam. A sub-species of the Peregrine Falcon, the Shaheen Falcon is resident practically all through the hilly regions of the Indian *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 18 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. The slight delay in beginning the meeting was due to the fact that the members could not reach the venue in time owing to Ganesh festivities causing traffic jams that were not anticipated on routes not taken earlier. The writer was one such victim. The meeting began at 6:00PM and was promptly adjourned for lack of quorum. As per the byelaws, there was an adjournment of 15 minutes, and the members present assembled again to constitute the quorum and start the meeting. 1

The President, JVD Moorty, began the meeting by greeting the members present. The minutes of the last AGM were then taken up and read through. A couple of points in those minutes were clarified by Srikanth Bhamidipati upon being queried by Aasheesh Pittie. The minutes were then deemed to have been accepted after they were proposed and seconded as such. Our Life Member, K Mrutyumjaya Rao, then took over and enthralled the audience with his brief Powerpoint presentation on his struggle as an environmentalist and conservationist. His zeal and passion were deeply appreciated by the audience. The Hon. Secretary, Srikanth Bhamidipati, then read out his report for the period 2022 to 2024, giving details of the field trips, outstation camps, conservation initiatives and project works taken up during the aforementioned period. An earnest appeal was made to the members requesting them to also contribute articles and trip reports to our monthly newsletter, the Pitta. The Hon. Treasurer, Dr Krishna Nagarajan, put forth his presentation on the screen and explained the numbers and figures lucidly to the members taking it all in. The current auditors were named and it was decided unanimously that they would continue to be the auditors for Deccan Birders for a further period of two years. The accounts were then duly passed, as were the names of the auditors. With this, the term of the existing committee came to an end. The returning officer, Sagarika Melkote, announced that there were no new nominations for membership in the Executive Committee and, as the existing committee of 10 members had indicated their interest and willingness to continue for a further period of two years, they were unanimously declared as reelected. BIRDING WHILE TREKKING THROUGH BINSAR WLS Trip Report: Binsar, Uttarakhand, May 18-20, 2024 Text & Photos: Dr Krishna Nagarajan Wedge-tailed Green Pigeon “Really?” was my first reaction when I was informed that the only way to reach our home-stay in the buffer zone of Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary is by trekking 4km downhill from the nearest drop-off point. It immediately presented a mental picture of living in some remote area without electricity, cell phone coverage, and urban restroom facilities. Our home-stay was located in a beautiful pristine village called Gaunap. Ours was a family trekking trip and my wife, Nikhila, was the trekking leader and planned the entire itinerary. birds in my early birding days but not in the recent past and, as they say, out-of-sight means completely out-of-mind. Second, trekking and birding simultaneously does not gel well together – ideally, you either do birding or do trekking. I was trying to do both and needed to be careful to not hegemonize a carefully planned trekking trip. I would have to rely on taking pictures as and when I sighted the birds during trekking, and study the birds offline to identify them. Third, news from the Uttarakhand region reported severe forest fires in the month of April. Forest fires are common in summer and they usually get quickly contained naturally due to the presence of several streams within the forest. This year however was different – the region had had deficit rainfall and all the streams and local rivers had completely dried up. Although our trekking route was not affected by the forest fires, I was not sure about birding – the birds might have moved to other safer regions and this may limit the number of birds that I could sight during the hike. A view of Gaunap Village The trip presented a great opportunity for birding. I checked eBird and found that around 200 species of birds have been reported in and around the Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary. As is always the case, there were multiple challenges: First, when I browsed the eBird checklists, I realized that I was totally unfamiliar with the birds in the region and did not have sufficient time to do the homework of reviewing the common resident birds in the region. I might have sighted most of these Blue Whistling Thrush 4

On the first day, as soon as we started our hike towards the home-stay from the drop-off point, we were greeted by the Blue Whistling Thrush. The yellow bill, glistening blue body, with clear white dots on a curved line on the coverts made me temporarily forget the pain in the knees when hiking downhill! Streaked Laughingthrush Niltava (both male and female), Red-billed Leiothrix, and the Oriental White-eye. Rufous-bellied Niltava female Rufous-bellied Niltava male Great Barbet Green-backed Tit By the time we completed the 4km hike to the home-stay, we had sighted the White-eared Bulbul, Streaked Laughingthrush, Red-vented Bulbul, Great Barbet, Green-backed Tit, Small Red-billed Leiothrix 5

We were pleasantly surprised upon reaching the Gaunap village. The village comprised only 9 families! It has electricity (with interruptions of course), cell phone coverage (not all the service providers though), modern restroom facilities (relief!) and a functional primary school run by a single teacher who lives in the village (even though only 4 kids currently attend the school). On the second day we trekked in and around the Gaunap village. We visited a temple on top of the hill, walked around and greeted the entire village (remember only 9 families), and covered some local hills. Our trekking guide was quite knowledgeable and helped identify the birds. Oriental Turtle Dove Besides the usual widespread residents (House Sparrow, Spotted Dove, House Crow, Common Myna, Red-wattled Lapwing, and Blue Rock Pigeons), we spotted Rufous Sibia, Himalayan Bulbul, Grey Bushchat, Little Pied Flycatcher, Slaty-headed Parakeet (unique yellowish long tail was interesting), Oriental Turtle Dove, and Wedge-tailed Green Pigeon. Grey Bushchat male Russet Sparrow male Russet Sparrow female Slaty-headed Parakeet Other birds we saw were Russet Sparrow (male and female), Black Drongo, Brown-fronted Woodpecker, Black Bulbul, Grey-winged Blackbird and a Crested Serpent Eagle soaring in the sky. 6

On the third and final day, our way out of Gaunap village was a moderate 9km hike to a small town called Dhoulchhina. Our focus was to get to the destination as soon as possible to minimize the exposure to the summer heat. Verditer Flycatcher Grey-headed Woodpecker During the hike, besides the birds spotted on the previous day, we also spotted the Grey-headed Woodpecker, Himalayan Woodpecker, Verditer Flycatcher, and Black-headed Jay. A TRIP TO THE REALM OF KINGS AND DACOITS Trip Report: Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary & National Chambal Sanctuary, February 22-24, 2024 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao A view of Bharatpur wetlands from the watchtower INTRODUCTION Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary, also known as Keoladeo Ghana National Park, is a national park located on the outskirts of Bharatpur, Rajasthan. It was declared a national park in 1982 and a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1985. Additionally, since it is a large wetland, it was designated a Ramsar site in 1981. plethora of bird species, turning it into a prime bird-watching destination. The sanctuary's name, Keoladeo, is derived from an ancient Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Shiva, situated within its premises. Over the years, it has become a haven for over 370 species of birds, including both resident and migratory species. The park was particularly famous for its significant population of Siberian cranes, which used to migrate here in winter; in the past couple of decades though, there have been no sightings of these magnificent birds, possibly due to habitat loss and hunting along migratory routes. Having said that, it is still a much preferred wintering destination for a large number of bird species. Besides birds, the sanctuary is home to various animals, including deer, boar, jackals, and turtles, making it a crucial site for biodiversity conservation in India. Map showing Bharatpur and other sites visited (Source: ebird.org & google.com) BACKGROUND Keoladeo National Park, Rajasthan The sanctuary spans over 29 sq.km and features a diverse ecosystem of wetlands, woodlands, and grasslands. It originated in the late 19th century when the Maharaja of Bharatpur created a hunting reserve by diverting water from a nearby river. This artificially created wetland attracted a Spotted Deer 9

Indian Jackal Water Rail National Chambal Sanctuary, Madhya Pradesh The National Chambal Sanctuary, also known as the Chambal Gharial Sanctuary, is a prominent wildlife sanctuary situated along the Chambal River in northern India. Spanning the states of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh, it covers an area of approximately 5,400 square kilometers. The sanctuary was established in 1979 primarily to protect the critically endangered Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus), a unique crocodilian species endemic to the Indian subcontinent, as well as other threatened aquatic species. Nilgai Gharial male The Chambal River, which originates in the Vindhya Range and flows north-northeast through Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh before merging with the Yamuna River, provides a pristine and unpolluted habitat crucial for the survival of its diverse fauna. The sanctuary's creation marked a significant conservation effort in response to the alarming decline in Gharial populations due to habitat destruction, poaching, and illegal sand mining. Dusky Eagle Owl Gharial female 10

Additionally, the riverine ecosystem hosts a rich avian population, including species like the Egyptian Vulture, Indian Skimmer, Black-bellied Tern, and Sarus Crane, making it an important bird area. Gharial juvenile Historically, the Chambal region has been steeped in folklore and legend, often associated with dacoits and bandits. Its rugged and ravine-riddled terrain made it a natural hideout for these outlaws, adding a layer of mystique to the sanctuary. Today, this same ruggedness has helped preserve its natural environment, making it one of the least polluted river ecosystems in India. The sanctuary is not only a stronghold for the Gharial but also supports a variety of other species. The critically endangered Red-crowned Roof Turtle (Batagur kachuga) and the vulnerable Smooth-coated Otter (Lutrogale perspicillata) are notable residents. Egyptian Vulture Conservation efforts within the sanctuary have included breeding programs, habitat restoration, and strict antipoaching measures. Collaborative initiatives between the government, non-governmental organizations, and local communities have been essential in sustaining these efforts. The sanctuary also promotes eco-tourism, offering activities such as river safaris and bird watching, which help raise awareness and funds for ongoing conservation projects. In recent years, the sanctuary has faced challenges such as water extraction for irrigation, illegal sand mining, and pollution from upstream industrial activities. Despite these threats, the National Chambal Sanctuary remains a vital refuge for some of India's most endangered wildlife, exemplifying the country's commitment to biodiversity preservation and the importance of protecting its natural heritage. VISITOR EXPERIENCE Red-crowned Roof Turtle (Batagur kachuga) Scenic walkways adjoining the lake Desert Fox (Vulpes vulpes pusilla) 11

Seating arrangements enable people to sit and absorb the serenity of the lake Indian Scops Owl pair often seen near the eating area I found Bharatpur to be particularly interesting due to its wellorganized facilities. The park features efficient ticketing systems, well-maintained pathways, and designated rickshaw pullers who are authorized by the park itself. These rickshaw pullers, who now use battery-operated rickshaws instead of the traditional pedal-powered ones, have extensive knowledge about the birds and can guide visitors to spots where rare birds are often found. Although the new rickshaws are less comfortable due to their lack of suspension, they are environmentally friendly. Entire park is dotted with Salvadora persica or Toothbrush Tree, aka Miswak For first-time visitors without a guide, hiring a local rickshaw puller is highly recommended. These pullers are registered and authorized, ensuring a knowledgeable and reliable tour of the sanctuary. MY TRIP This visit to Bharatpur was a short extension of my official trip to Jaipur. The journey from Jaipur to Bharatpur takes about three hours by road, with excellent roads leading up to Bharatpur. There are well-established hotels catering to the birding community where visitors can stay. I spent about two and a half days in Bharatpur. The first day was entirely dedicated to birding within the sanctuary, focusing on resident water birds. View of Chambal River from the boat On the second morning, I traveled to Chambal National Reserve on the Chambal River for a boat safari. This safari aimed to spot endangered birds such as the Indian Skimmers and Black-bellied Terns, as well as the Gharial, which are a must-see at Chambal. Hot lunch delivered to designated eating spots by the hotel Indian Skimmer 12

Black-bellied Tern Indian Jackal protecting its territory Once known for dacoity and looting, the Chambal valley is a lot more peaceful now, with these activities having been eliminated or significantly reduced. However, sand mafias are still said to operate at scale, making conservation of Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) and the Mugger Crocodile (Crocodylus palustris) very difficult. This is one of the very few sites where you can spot these fantastic reptiles in large numbers. Moustached Warbler The Chambal riverside, allegedly a scene of rampant sand mining One enthralling experience was watching a near war between a Crested Serpent Eagle and a Woolly-necked Stork. In general, I observed that whenever a raptor made a kill and came to ground to eat it, several other birds would start circling the area, waiting for an opportunity to steal the kill. I returned to Bharatpur the same afternoon and spent the rest of the day birding. Although it wasn't summer, the afternoons were quite warm. Being my last day, I had only half a day in Bharatpur before heading back to Jaipur for my connecting flight home, and I was keen to make the most of it. Black Kite & Woolly-necked Stork trying to steal kill from Crested Serpent Eagle Bluethroat On this occasion, I saw the Crested Serpent Eagle catch a very large snake (possibly a Rat Snake). Immediately a few other birds started flying around the area, but this also invited a large Woolly-necked Stork, which pecked at and eventually managed to chase away the Crested Serpent Eagle and steal the prey. 13

Snake making a last-ditch attempt to escape before being swallowed by Woolly-necked Stork White-tailed Lapwing The pond known locally as Darter pond is where one can find the most numbers of Oriental Darters. Here we can see lots of Darters hunting for fish and trying to consume them through harpooning and the characteristic tossing to align the fish correctly and get it to go down head first. Bharatpur's rich and diverse avifauna attracts numerous birders from around the world, especially from Europe and North America who spend significant amounts of time birding in the sanctuary. This visit was a memorable and enriching experience, and I would highly recommend it to anyone interested in birdwatching or wildlife conservation. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Streaked Spiderhunter (Arachnothera magna) Streaked Spiderhunter (Buxa Tiger Reserve, West Bengal, January 13, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: Passeriformes Nectariniidae Arachnothera A. magna 19 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Streaked Spiderhunter is usually seen singly or in pairs, but may move around with mixed flocks. It is a large and noisy inhabitant of tropical and subtropical moist lowland or montane forests, dense evergreen forests, and abandoned cultivation (especially those holding wild banana trees). Flight is somewhat woodpecker-like, undulating over longer distances. While it relishes the nectar of the wild banana blossom, it also takes spiders – sometimes hovering to take them even from the centre of their webs – and may also glean invertebrates from foliage. It calls frequently, giving out a loud, sharp, decisive-sounding chirirk, chiririrk, in flight or while feeding. The song is a soft, monotonous vijvitte vij. Description & distribution: The Streaked Spiderhunter is a distinctive bird in its range, coloured golden yellowish olive with a long, curved, black bill, specifically adapted for a nectar diet, and yellow-orange legs and feet. It is boldly marked with heavy streaking on its olive-yellow upperparts and white or pale yellow underparts. The tail is greenish and has a dark subterminal band and is tipped with buff spots. In juvenile birds, the feathers are slightly more filamentous than in later plumages due to lower barb densities, and juvenile remiges, primary coverts, aula, and rectrices are relatively narrow, browner, and tapered or rounded at the tips. Nesting: The Streaked Spiderhunter breeds mainly between March and July. The nest is an inverted dome of skeleton leaves tied together with cobwebs, and usually fixed on the urderside of a large leaf. The usual clutch consists of 2 or 3 brown eggs, which are darker at the broad end. Nest-building and incubation duties are shared by both parents. The Streaked Spiderhunter is resident in most parts of its range, from the eastern states of India and the eastern Himalayas practically all across Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Thailand, and Vietnam. It is not migratory, but does show vertical movements in the hills. Local name: The Streaked Spiderhunter is known as ‘Domsiriok-pho’ in Lepcha and ‘Ydong-pichang’ in Bhutia. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report: Edulabad Lake, August 25, 2024 JVD Moorty Painted Stork (Photo: Sudha Nair) Field trips are something to look forward to – a few unguaranteed surprises, the usual culprits, and the mundane species, that we often tend to look askance at. The trip to Edulabad was organised on August 25, 2024 with a slightly more ‘comfortable’ departure time of 7:00AM, as the location was within the limits of the Outer Ring Road, city limits, so to speak. Yours truly was the coordinator and had three passengers to pick up – Sharad Murdeshwar and his family. The metro that brought them to the NGRI pick-up point was über punctual! It had rained the night before, an ominous foreboding of a low turnout of both birders and birds. An overcast sky was a grey reminder of the rain-to-be. But the day, despite being cloudy – the absence of sun and a cool breeze made the morning very pleasant – offered some good sightings. 1

The drive to Edulabad was uneventful and traffic free – almost. The topography of the place had changed beyond my recognition. A black-topped road, a far cry from the peaksand-troughs track of yore, was a pleasant surprise, so much so that I could afford to look around for birds whilst driving. The lush green paddy fields spread out to as far as the eye could see. And that’s where we stopped to bird; stopped by a flock of roughly 7-8 Scaly-breasted Munias that undulated across the windscreen of the car with their typical flap-no flap wingbeats. A Jacobin Cuckoo flew in on to the electric cable above to observe us, thus providing a photo-op. We later found out that the rest of the group had also seen it. Anxious phone calls and messages alerted us to the fact that others were waiting on the bund of the lake, the rendezvous point. The bund, an earthen levee, raised basically to prevent water from running out, was a walking path in my memory. But today, it was something to drive on, paved with piperailings on either side and vegetation on its sloping embankments that harboured a few Plain and Ashy Prinias calling ceaselessly while flitting rapidly through the leaves. Asian Pied Starling (Photo: Sudha Nair) Plain Prinia (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) Baya Weaver (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) Our attention was then drawn to some roughly built nests of the Baya Weavers swaying to the tunes of the gentle breeze, when a sudden flash of yellow announced the arrival of a couple of male Bayas involved in the real estate that we were keenly watching. They had strands of building material and busied themselves with the intricate knotting and weaving under the critical eye of a female who arrived to watch their fervent activity. Ashy Prinia (Photo: Sudha Nair) It was a small group that awaited us there and we were gently chided for showing up late, our explanation for midway birding notwithstanding, to which we pleaded guilty. Pax romana having been restored, we got down to exchanging notes. They told us that they had seen a pair of Barred Buttonquails in the bushes on the embankment at the edge of the paddy fields – and we rued the fact that we had missed them! Jacobin Cuckoo (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) 2

Barred Buttonquail (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) The lake, located near Ghatkesar, Hyderabad, is also known as Edulabad water reservoir. Industrial sewage and waste from Patancheru on the western side of the city had polluted this lake, killing fish and causing illness in lakeside communities in 2002. The lake at that time had a pinkish hue due to the chemicals in the sewage industries. But today the water body appeared to have regained some of its health, given the abundance of paddy crop and the lush greenery nearby. Pied Kingfisher (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) We saw several water birds nearby: Asian Openbills, Whitethroated Kingfisher, Pied Kingfisher, Cattle Egrets accompanied by their kin Little Egrets, Black-headed Ibis, Great and Indian Cormorants. A view of the fields near the lake (Photo: Sudha Nair) Little Egret (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) White-throated Kingfisher (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) Great Cormorant (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) 3

The fields and the trees had several Indian Silverbills, Scalybreasted and Tricoloured Munias, Zitting Cisticolas and Siberian Stonechats. Ashy Woodswallows huddled together wing-to-wing on the overhead wires as if they were affixed to each other. Indian Cormorant (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) Also seen were a few Darters, a lone Brahminy kite, Grey and Purple Herons, the ubiquitous and unobtrusive Pond Herons, Red-rumped and Barn Swallows flying around tirelessly. Ashy Woodswallow (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) Shikra (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) Grey Heron (Photo: Sudha Nair) Driving down the bund brought us to a fairly large stinky dump-yard, but on the positive side we saw a water tanker that was watering the plants along the edges of the bund. Hopefully these workers were also entrusted with the task of removing the garbage, though I had my own doubts about it. Around 11:30AM the sun waging a lone battle with the clouds won, and the day turned quite warm and sultry enough to send us home. Edulabad lake with a surface area of 5 square kilometres and a surface elevation of 1,759 feet (536 meters) irrigates the paddy fields, feeds the water birds, supports fish, and provides drinking water to the village. This water body is now crying out loudly for help. Are we listening? The list of birds seen during the trip: Purple Heron (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) 4

Report: Birds Of Kashmir, Sep 2023 & June 2024 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla Yellow-breasted Greenfinch It was a journey through six districts and 10 different bird habitats of the Kashmir valley during September 2023 and June 2024 that left us in awe of the spectacular birds in this part of our country. The Tawny Owls of Chadoora, the Ibisbills of Kangan, the assortment of Finches and Grosbeaks of Sinthan Top, the Rock Buntings of Naranag, the Kashmir Flycatcher of Dachigam, the Little Bitterns of Inner Dal Lake, the Kashmir Nutcrackers of Yousmarg, the Brown-flanked Bush Warbler of Rajparian WLS are some of the fascinating avian species of the valley. Nestled in the western Himalayan temperate coniferous forests of Pine, Oak, Beech, Deodar, Cedar, Chinar, and Willow, Kashmir is home to many species of resident and migratory birds. At Chadoora it was not long before we saw the Tawny Owl hidden in the thick canopy of the Chinar trees. These are nonmigratory territorial birds that are capable of adapting to different environments. After seeing the Tawny Owls in Chadoora, we drove back to the city to our next halt at the Botanical Garden. Here we saw the Eurasian Jackdaw, lots of Russet Sparrows and many Yellow-breasted Greenfinches on the cedar trees. As the sun began to set, we began to walk back and stopped to listen to some melodious renderings of Kashmiri folk music by talented musicians who were performing in the garden. It was heartening to see a lot of school children who were visiting the garden and who formed an enthusiastic audience for the musicians. The visit in September 2023 was to Chadoora town, Sinthan Top and Yousmarg. It was a one-hour drive from Srinagar city to Chadoora town, and at many places, we stopped to look at the river Jhelum gushing through the rocky terrain in the backdrop of tall mountains. We saw the Brown Dipper and Plumbeous Redstart at many places. White-winged Grosbeak Tawny Owl 7

The next visit in June 2024 was to Yousmarg, which was an equally enchanting location. Here the Kashmir Nutcrackers were in abundance. The Rusty-tailed Flycatcher, Rufousnaped Tits and Tytler’s Warbler were the highlights here. We visited the valley again in June as we wanted to see birds such as the Ibisbill, European Bee-eater and Little Bittern which can be spotted during this time of the year in Kashmir. This time we went to Kangan, Naranag, Wangath, Rajparian Wildlife Sanctuary, the Inner Dal Lake Road and Royal Springs Golf Course premises in Srinagar. Kashmir Nutcracker The next day at Sinthan Top, we stopped at various heights of the Pir-Panjal range. We spotted White-winged Grosbeaks, Kashmir Nutcrackers, Plain Mountain Finches, a pair of Spectacled Finches, Dark-sided Flycatcher, Common Buzzard, Tree Pipit, Eurasian Wren and Blue-fronted Redstart. Ibisbill The Ibisbill was spotted at Sindh River valley at Kangan in Ganderbal district. We looked for it in other parts of the country but we were not lucky. At Kangan, we luckily spotted it, standing on the rocks amidst grassy bushes. We were thrilled to see it in all its grandeur and it stayed there for a long time and gave us plenty of good views. Blue-fronted Redstart Sinthan Top is a mesmerizing range of landscapes and the junipers spread on the slopes as dark green patches are signature plants of the region. The juniper can exist in various forms, from short shrubs to tall trees. A couple of Black Kites were flying over it and we thought that the Ibisbill’s nest may be nearby. The Ibisbill prefers a habitat of rocky rivers and streams where it is easily camouflaged. It is a dainty bird with a long down-curved red bill, black face, grey upper parts and white belly. The special feature about this bird is that it is the only member of the family Ibidorhynchidae. Having seen the Ibisbill, we proceeded to Wangath valley and Naranag to see Forktails. The valley houses an ancient Shiva temple dating from the 8th century AD. The temple is in ruins now, although it is a protected monument. On the way to Naranag we spotted Rock Buntings, Brown-fronted Woodpecker, Brown-flanked Bush Warbler and Western Crowned Warbler. Rufous-naped Tit 8

Rock Bunting The trip to Wangath was on a Saturday and the place being a great picnic spot, it was buzzling with school and college children. There were a few Grey Bushchats feeding their chicks. There was no sign of any Forktails though, and we quickly then moved to Brein Nishat to try and look for the European Bee-eaters at the foothills of the Zabarawan mountain ranges. Grey-winged Blackbird The approach area was fenced and so we had to take a detour through a steep rocky terrain. By the time we reached the spot, light began to fade. But we were lucky to spot them flying close to where we were. One of the Bee-eaters landed on the fence and we could take some very good pictures of it. We were also rewarded by panoramic views of the Dal Lake and Srinagar city. Scaly-bellied Woodpecker From here we proceeded to Dal Lake interior to see the Little Bittern. It was a three kilometre long walk on a road that was surprisingly busy with traffic. On either side were the floating vegetable gardens of cucumbers and melons and also lotus farms. Farmers on boats were seen sowing some grasses. European Bee-eater The next day we spent a couple of hours in the morning at Royal Springs Golf Course, and found that the place was a hotspot for birds. There were many birds there: Long-tailed Minivets, Grey-winged Blackbirds, Scaly-bellied Woodpecker, Ultramarine Flycatcher, Indian Cuckoo, Great Barbet, Brown-flanked Bush Warbler, Rufous-naped Tits, Himalayan and Black Bulbuls, Tickell’s Thrush and Blue Whistling Thrush. We scanned the reeds on either side of the road for the Little Bittern when out came the Clamorous Reed Warblers and Sparrows. After about an hour of walking along this road in the lake, we had a fleeting glimpse of the Little Bittern as it flew from some reeds at the side of the road and disappeared into the far-off marshes. We stopped under a tree to have our breakfast accompanied by some salted tea and waited to see if the Bittern would come back. As there were no signs of the bird, we headed back as our trip to Kashmir was coming to an end. We had on our list about 20 lifers from these two visits to Kashmir, with the Ibisbill and European Bee-eaters as the highlights. 9

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Striated Laughingthrush (Grammatoptila striata) Striated Laughingthrush (Sattal, Uttarakhand, May 14, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: Passeriformes Leiothrichidae Grammatoptila G. striata 28 cm Description & distribution: The Striated Laughingthrush is a very distinctive bird – it is a large, bulky laughingthrush, predominantly chestnut-brown with thin white streaks all over. It has a bushy crest and stout bill, blackish-brown or dark horn, with a paler lower mandible. The nominate subspecies, G. s. striata, has a chestnut crown, with and a floppy crest with long feathers. The upperparts are rufescent brown with bold white shaft streaks, while the wing fringes and tail are dull rufescent brown. The side of the head, from above the eye to chin and throat, is chestnut-chocolate with bold whitish shaft streaks, while the upper breast and side of neck are similar but paler. Mid-breast to lower underparts is buffy with long white streaks, while flanks, thighs and vent are dirty ochre. It has a brown to brick-red iris and greyish orbital skin. The legs are slate to greyish-brown. Sexes are similar. Juvenile birds are warmer above than the adult, and the streaks on underparts are narrower and fainter. Earlier placed in the genus Garrulax, it was moved as the only species in the resurrected genus Grammatoptila following the publication of a comprehensive molecular phylogenetic study in 2018. Four other subspecies are recognized: G. s. vibex, seen in the central Himalayas, western and central Nepal and south Tibet, has upperparts very slightly darker than nominate, darker underparts, and narrower shaft streaks on breast and belly. G. s. sikkimensis, seen in the central Himalayas from eastern Nepal to south-eastern Tibet, southwestern China, Sikkim and Bhutan, is darker still, with less contrast between crown and upperparts, more chestnut wing fringes and tail, and narrower shaft streaks below. G. s. brahmaputra, seen from Bhutan east to Arunachal Pradesh and western Myanmar, is duller-crowned than the earlier two subspecies, has a less streaked crown, with broad blackishbrown lateral crown-stripe, paler upperparts with more obvious paler dull rufous-brown fringing, more contrasting breast-feather pattern, and less pronounced streaking below. G. s. cranbrooki is similar to G. s. brahmaputra, but with broader blackish lateral crown-stripe and less obvious streaking on forehead and above the eye. The Striated Laughingthrush is resident in most parts of its range, in the northern temperate regions of the Indian subcontinent, including Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Tibet and Nepal. It may sometimes show altitudinal movements. Habitat & behaviour: The Striated Laughingthrush is usually seen singly or in pairs, although it may sometimes move around in mixed flocks and especially with other laughingthrushes. It is an inhabitant of tropical and subtropical moist lowland or montane forests, broad-leaf evergreen forests, secondary forests, scrub jungle, thickets, bamboo and wooded patches around villages. It is more arboreal than most laughingthrushes, foraging mainly in the middle to lower canopy, feeding in the canopy of tall trees as well as in lower branches and undergrowth. It feeds primarily on insects (including beetles), berries and 13

seeds (including bramble), aromatic wintergreens, flowers like rhododendron, and gelatinous lichen. coarse grasses, twigs, creeper stems, rootlets, dead leaves, green moss and green fern fronds, lined with coarse roots, fine black roots and dry grasses, and generally placed 1 to 6 metres above ground in the branches of larger trees or among climbing plants. The usual clutch consists of 2 or 3 pale greenish-blue eggs (although sometimes almost white), unmarked except possibly for a few dark brownish-red specks. Incubation duties are shared by both parents. The song is a repeated loud, vibrant, rolling prrrit-you, prritpri-prii’u, with several variations. When agitated, it emits a low grumbling aawh, aawh, aawh’o aawh, aawh. Calls include a soft, nervous, fairly high-pitched wer-wer-wer-werwer or wuh-wuh-wuh-wuh-wuh wu-wúh, and a gentle, rising wu-wiw. Trip Report: Yenkathala Grasslands, October 20, 2024 Gokul Krishna Addanki The October field trip to Yenkathala on October 20, 2024, organized by Deccan Birders and coordinated by me, aimed to enjoy Yenkathala’s lush greenery before the landscape changes later in the season. The group of 10 participants had arrived around 6:30AM, intending to explore the mixed forest of shrubs, grasslands, and the nearby lake. But a routine birdwatching trip turned into an extraordinary experience when my son, 10-year-old Abhinav Krishna Addanki, made a remarkable discovery during the field trip. Abhinav spotted a rare Pied Harrier, much to the delight of the group, as they explored the rich biodiversity of Yenkathala. Pied Harrier (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) 1

The area is known for its diverse bird species, including Harriers, Eagles, Black-headed Cuckooshrike, and various quails. On this day, too, more than 60 bird species were seen – it was a very productive day. Abhinav, a passionate birdwatcher for over three years, has already logged nearly 300 species on his personal list, an impressive feat for someone his age. His ability to observe, identify, and remember bird species is nothing short of remarkable. Yellow-eyed Babbler (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) Yellow-crowned Woodpecker (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) The Yenkathala region, where the trip took place, is a haven for birders. Its unique landscape supports a variety of bird species, making it a popular spot for birdwatching. In addition to the Pied Harrier, birders can expect to spot species like the Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse, Painted Francolin, and the Baya Weaver. Abhinav’s sighting of the Pied Harrier was the highlight of the trip, earning him the admiration of the group – and a promise of ice cream as a reward for his sharp eyes! White-eyed Buzzard (Photo: Abhishek Shroti) As the group prepared to leave at around 10:00AM, they were excited to spot a Common Kestrel soaring through the sky. Just as they were about to drive off, young Abhinav, keenly observing from the back seat, peered out of the car window and shouted, “Raptor!” “At first, we couldn’t tell what he had spotted, but when we saw the bird and adjusted our camera settings, the black-andwhite plumage became clear,” said one of the participants. Despite the cloudy conditions, the group soon confirmed the sighting as a Pied Harrier, a rare raptor not commonly seen in the region. Cheers erupted, and high-fives were exchanged as everyone marvelled at the young birder’s find.
