Meghalaya & Kaziranga, April 2024 Text: Shraddha Vyas; Photos: Rishik Vyas Indian Elephant with calf & Cattle Egret at Kaziranga National Park The North-eastern parts of India have always fascinated me right from childhood. When in our Social Studies class, we heard the place with highest rainfall was Cherrapunji in Meghalaya, I was very attracted towards it. I used to imagine lush green jungles with moist-moist winds or black cloudy sky with thunderstorms or heavy downpour of rain…… Wondering what all flora and fauna we would find in those regions? 3

I never thought I would be lucky enough to visit Meghalaya and Assam this summer. But the calling of the North-east was very powerful, I guess, and I couldn’t resist the urge. Along with my sister and 12-year-old nephew Rishik, I planned our trip to first reach Shillong, visit all beautiful locations of Shillong and then proceed to our main destination, Kaziranga National Park. We loved the mystic cloud-laden hills of Shillong. We literally felt we were driving into the clouds, chilled winds crossing our car, causing shivering in month of April. The thought was thrilling! Reaching Dawki from Shillong was a lengthy road trip but after reaching the river we felt it was really worth the effort. The clear water of Dawki River was mesmerizing. We could only see mountains all around us, with small and big waterfalls springing up from the mountain crevices slowly falling into the river. There were lots of trees, really dense trees all along the mountains. The clear waters, the river, the sound of our boat men rowing with the oars, and the melodious chirpings of exotic mountain birds took me into another world – a beautiful world free from urban hustle-bustle, the chaos of daily life, noise, pollution, screens and social media. I had just left everything behind, immersing, literally soaking my soul into the magical Dawki River, when my thoughts were interrupted by the melodious humming of our boatmen in Khasi language. We didn’t know the language but the songs sounded very sweet. After thoroughly enjoying the magical bliss of Dawki we returned to Shillong. On our way back, we also visited the cleanest village of India, named MAWLYNNONG. It was so beautiful, dripping with its green world charm, huge trees all around, small clean lanes and by-lanes with small cozy houses providing home-stays at reasonable prices. We also had a chance to climb onto a watchtower made of bamboo on a huge jackfruit tree; the view from top was breathtaking. As the evening moved along, we also visited the world-famous living root bridges of Meghalaya – two of them, a single bridge and also a double bridge named Sohra. Elephant Waterfalls We visited the famous Elephant Waterfalls, named after the shape of the rock from which the waterfall originated, which resembles an elephant head. We could spot the White-capped Water Redstart dancing at the rocks close to the waterfalls. We enjoyed the picturesque view of the hill tops while visiting the beautiful clear water river Dawki; we also enjoyed and learnt about the Khasi tribe. My nephew really looked a prince in the Khasi tribal royal costumes! The way the roots were connected to improve the tensile strength of the bridges was amazing. Clear water, rocks, valley full of melodious birds – couldn’t make out most of their IDs though, thanks to my eye-sight – it was an unforgettable experience. The serene silence along with birds chirping still soothes me immensely when I think of it. Next day, while heading towards Assam, we left Meghalaya, literally ‘the beautiful state of rainy clouds’, with a promise to return to its unexplored beauty once more, soon. Reaching Assam, we were super excited to enter the beautiful home of the One-horned Rhinoceros – Kaziranga National Park. Our driver mentioned that often the Rhinoceros were seen grazing outside the park too. Just as he spoke, my nephew spotted a rhino grazing calmly across the grassland amidst submerged marshy lake. The driver told us that it generally remains calm but attacks fiercely if disturbed. We also spotted a Wild Buffalo grazing on Eichhornia (Water hyacinth) in the marsh. Done with the formalities of check-in at our beautiful Resort Iora, we arranged for our elephant safari the next day early morning and also a jeep safari in the afternoon. A view of the Dawki River 4

The elephant safari was arranged at the Kohra zone. Early morning fog, bird sounds loud and clear in the misty foggy morning – the forest was so welcoming. We were escorted towards the elephant stand from where, by turns, we climbed onto the elephants. The elephant ride was smooth; swaying through the huge trees, we reached the clear grasslands. The Mahout said that the elephant safari would only take us through the periphery of the jungle, but for deeper forests we would need to take the jeep safari. Everyone was enjoying the safari ride when I suddenly spotted the beauty of North-east, a large Great Indian Hornbill, flying across the grassland and landing on a high perch of silk cotton tree or semal tree. The first sighting of Great Indian Hornbill was unforgettable. Meagre leaves on dry branches of semal tree facilitated a clear view of the bird although we missed out on taking a shot. Indian Elephants at Kaziranga National Park As we reached the watchtower, we spotted a large group of wild Elephants enjoying themselves at the river side. We were lucky to spot a small baby elephant feeding from its mother by the river side. There were huge tuskers too in the herd. There were almost 20-25 elephants in the herd, having a great time by the river. As we watched them from the watchtower, we could spot them clearly – otherwise, the elephants are easily hidden in the large elephant grass characteristically found at Kaziranga. We also spotted a large number of water birds at the river side, like White-breasted and Pied Kingfishers, Greater and Lesser Adjutants making noise in large numbers, Black-necked Stork, Painted Stork, Red-wattled Lapwing etc. After enjoying the elephant sightings, we reached our jeep and proceeded further. We were informed about a Tiger sighting by earlier jeep riders, but we missed it by few minutes. We all were silent and closely listening to the bird sounds, alarm calls if any in the forest, to locate the tiger on its prowl. But it just hid itself perfectly in the dense forest and eluded us. One-horned Rhinoceros with calf Our attention was then diverted towards a One-horned Rhinoceros calf feeding from her mother, slightly away from the Semal tree, near a river. The sight was very beautiful. Slowly, steadily enjoying the forest, our elephant ride ended. But we were still excited about the jeep safari in the afternoon. Chances of sighting a Tiger or Wild Elephant were higher in the jeep safari. In the mid-afternoon, we entered the forest reserve from the West zone. We were thrilled and expected some very good sighting in the forest. The forest was very dense, with huge trees of different varieties, of which I can markedly remember the Silk Cotton Tree. The driver informed that the forest was home to many wild animals like Barking Deer, Hog Deer, Swamp Deer, Wild Boar, Wild Elephant, Tiger and of course One-horned Rhinoceros, and that it was a hub to many migratory birds as well. We also happened to spot the Yellow-footed Green Pigeon – it was pecking at the ground, but as our jeep reached it flew away; we missed its shot!! The driver showed us the scratches recently made by a tiger on a tree bark; he also told us that jungle is host to a variety of snakes as well. As we moved further one of the earlier jeep riders showed us a Cinereous Vulture, at its nest on a large silk cotton tree. We rejoiced at the sighting of the vulture, as vultures across the globe are heading towards extinction and their conservation is crucial. As dusk approached, the forest became all the more beautiful. Lush green dense forest with lakes and rivers here and there, huge elephant grass and small wooden bridges across the lakes was mesmerizing me with its magical charm. We crossed a huge river, a tributary of the Brahmaputra, while returning towards the exit – it had some huge noisy flocks of migratory birds, which my nephew identified as Spot-billed Pelicans. 5

Besides the charm of the jungle, Kaziranga also provides interesting tourist attractions. We made a visit to the Orchid Garden, which was so beautiful and filled with fragrance from around 8000 species of Orchids. Most of the orchids across India are transported from Assam. Fragrant orchids with vibrant colors, unique shapes and sizes were breath-taking. A large flock of Spot-billed Pelicans Hooker's Pitcher Plant (Nepenthes X Hookeriana) Red-wattled Lapwing A visit to the tribal village, tribal museum, looking at their art and handicrafts and world-famous cultural events, is mandatory. The people of Assam are simple and sweet, they sing melodiously and dance beautifully, and are very well versed with different musical instruments. We listened to their sweet songs sung by world famous artists and thoroughly enjoyed watching the Butterfly Dance and of course most famous Bihu dance. We really had many golden memories to take back with us at the end of this wonderful journey. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Malabar Grey Hornbill (Ocyceros griseus) Malabar Grey Hornbill (Dandeli, Karnataka, October 30, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: Bucerotiformes Bucerotidae Ocyceros O. griseus 45-58 cm screeching calls, and is easy to trace and identify through the calls. Being a large frugivore, it is an important seed dispersal agent for many species of fruit bearing forest trees. It also feeds on small vertebrates and, in captivity, will readily take meat. Description & distribution: The Malabar Grey Hornbill is endemic to the Western Ghats and associated hills in Southern India. A large bird, it is still smaller than the rest of the Asian hornbills. It has an overall grey appearance, with the upperparts being a darker grey than the underparts, which have whitish streaks. The tail is long and blackish with a white tip, and the vent is cinnamon. The head is grey with a broad white superciliary band going down all the way to the neck, broadening behind the eye and contrasting with the darker earcoverts. The bill is big but lacks a casque that other hornbills have. The sexes are alike, except that male birds have a reddish bill with yellow tip, while female birds have a plain yellow bill with black at the base of the lower mandible and along the culmen. Wings are brownish-grey, and shows a white carpal patch and black primary flight feathers tipped with white. Juvenile birds show browner upperparts, a yellow bill and dull white or yellow irises. Nesting: The Malabar Grey Hornbill breeds mainly between January and May. It is a secondary cavity nester, being incapable of digging its own nest, and hence nests in large cavities in trees. It is monogamous, and a pair may use the same nest for several years. Like other hornbills, the female incarcerates herself within the cavity, closing the entrance with a cement made from her droppings, leaving a narrow opening through which the female disposes of excreta, and receives food from the male. The male is responsible for bringing adequate food for the female and the young; the food includes berries, insects, small rodents and reptiles. Males tap the tree to indicate to the female that they have arrived with food, then pass the food through the nest opening. Berries are regurgitated one at a time and passed to the female, while other food may be passed directly. The usual clutch consists of three or sometimes four white eggs, after laying which, the female begins a complete moult of her flight feathers. Habitat & behaviour: The Malabar Grey Hornbill is usually seen in pairs or small groups, feeding on figs and other forest fruits. It is a large and noisy inhabitant of dense forests or rubber, arecanut and coffee plantations. Flight is heavy and ponderous, with a strong flap-and-glide pattern; while on the tree also, it hops around heavily on the thicker branches of fruiting trees. It emits loud, hysterical cackling, laughing and Local name: The Malabar Grey Hornbill is known as ‘Saraattaan’ in Kadar and ‘Seriyan oongal’, meaning ‘small hornbill’, in Muthuvan respectively (Kadar and Muthuvan being Dravidian tribal languages). It is called ‘Solai kaka’ in Tamil, ‘Kaldal hakki’ in Kannada, ‘Kozhi vezhambal’ in Malayalam, ‘Gobre vayare’ in Konkani and ‘Chhota peelu’ or ‘Dhanesh’ in Marathi. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 7 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Trip Report: Manjeera Reservoir & WLS, November 17, 2024 Raabiah Arastu Clamorous Reed Warbler (Photo: Asif Husain Arastu) I wanted a short break from my daily routine and studies as it was a Sunday and I could not think of anything better than tagging along with my father, Asif Husain Arastu, for a birding trip with Deccan Birders to Manjeera Reservoir. I saw a Blue-faced Malkoha. It had a long tail and it was grey and black in colour with a pale blue eye ring and ivorycoloured bill. Some members in the group saw two! It was a small refreshment for me as nature is always healing. The weather was chilly and pleasant, the group had gathered at the backwaters of the Manjeera Dam and that was where the maximum number of birds were spotted – so many different species were seen. In the end the total number of bird species spotted by the group was more than 80 species. We stayed there for several hours as we walked around and enjoyed the tranquil beauty of nature and the bird calls in the background. It was exactly what I needed! The bird of the day for me was the Red Avadavat. It was red and covered in white spots with dark wings and tail with a red beak, and was building a nest. Adnanbhai took a great shot of the Red Avadavat with its nesting material. Blue-faced Malkoha (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) Eurasian Coot (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) Bronze-winged Jacana immature (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) 2

I also saw a Eurasian Coot and a Eurasian Moorhen in the water. A River Tern, flying around, had a full black cap, pale grey wings and a yellow beak. Brahminy Starling (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) Grey-headed Swamphen (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) I also saw a Little Grebe, which was fairly common. It was dark overall with a rusty head and neck. The Purple-rumped Sunbird was really beautiful with the sun shining on it, and was very colourful. It had a green metallic crown with a dark brown body and lemon yellow underparts. The Ashy Prinia was an energetic bird with a black bill, pale cinnamon underparts, a grey head and a brownish-grey back. Indian Pied Starling (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) Purple Heron (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) Tricoloured Munia (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) Grey Heron (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) Many other birds were also seen: Grey and Purple Herons, Glossy Ibis, Baya Weaver, Brahminy and Indian Pied Starlings, and the beautiful Tricoloured Munias. Finally my favourite, the Common Kingfisher – the little bird, of blue and orange colour and a long pointed bill, flying over the water – and also the White-throated Kingfisher, with its electric blue-black wings, red bill and patches on the throat. The blue colour of its wings were shining gorgeously in the sunlight. We had spent most of our time at the backwaters and it was fun. As it started getting late, to wrap it up the team had chai and talked about all the birds they had spotted. It was a tiring yet great day. 3

It is a thought how people go on a leisure trip or when they enjoy nature they do not notice the number of different birds surrounding them. These birding trips make you realize how beautiful and different each bird and its call is – even our morning starts with the calls of different birds, but we just never appreciate and realize how birds contribute in our daily lives and make it lively with their sweet calls. There are so many different species of birds around the world of different shades and colours… if one colour or feature is identified incorrectly then the complete bird species changes. Editor’s Note: One of the highlights of the trip was the sighting of a hepatic Grey-bellied Cuckoo. A note on the sighting follows. A note from a beginner birder Text & Photo: Dr C R Sundaresan Grey-bellied Cuckoo hepatic morph I was taking in the sky and the terrain on one side of the lake when a splash of brilliant colour on a dry branch caught my eye. The cloudless azure blue sky was a striking background enhancing the bird. I was seeing this bird for the first time, and was charmed by the exquisite colours – it was a blend of reddish brown and black. It was brilliantly lit by the rising sun with not a shadow on it. Its perch on a dry branch eliminated all clutter, and the blue of the sky gave a good contrast. Thanking my good fortune, I quickly captured it digitally. Given that the perch was in deep water, there was no scope for me to capture from different angles, but luckily there was no need, as the view was entirely satisfying. I bent to review the frames and looked up. The bird had flown away! Eventually I learnt it was a Grey-bellied Cuckoo. I read the description of the bird and found that this was the ‘hepatic’ variant. Indeed the ginger-orange tone imparted the colour of the liver to the bird. The comparison was apt. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (Received on WhatsApp, February 4, 2024) *** 5

A JOURNEY TO LEH: EXPLORING BIRDS AND STARS Trip Report: Ladakh, June 30 – July 06, 2024 Text & Photos: Vikram Penmetsa Red-fronted Serin Pre-Departure Preparations Having experienced the majestic landscapes and rich biodiversity of Leh, during our previous trip to Ladakh organised by Umesh in June 2022, I was eager to plan another trip. This time, the journey was primarily for my son Prithvi, who had just completed his Intermediate studies and developed a keen interest in astrophotography. To combine his newfound passion with our shared love for birding, we decided on a Ladakh trip. We reached out to the same person who had planned our last trip, Mr Lobzang. After finalizing our itinerary with him and booking our tickets early to get cheaper fares, we were set for our adventure. Day 2: July 1, 2024 – Exploring Leh Our birding guide, Stanzin, arrived at the hotel early in the morning. He was knowledgeable and enthusiastic, ready to share his expertise. We started our day with a gentle walk along the banks of the Indus River. The serene surroundings and the early morning light made for an excellent birding experience. I made elaborate arrangements for the cold climate at Leh, based on my past experience in 2022. We packed jackets, thermal wear and, as it was the first trip for Prithvi, I carried body warmers just to keep him warm in case he could not take the cold climate. On June 29, 2024, we set out on our journey from Hyderabad to Delhi and then to Leh early the next morning. Day 1: June 30, 2024 – Arrival at Leh We boarded our early morning flight from Delhi to Leh, departing at 04:55AM and arriving at Leh KBR Airport at 06:15AM. This KBR, though, stood for Kushok Bakula Rimpochee, a 19th century Buddhist monk! The bright, hot Saturday morning welcomed us with a temperature of 18°C. At the airport, our driver was already waiting, holding a placard with my name. We were promptly driven to our hotel, which was neat, tidy, and conveniently close to the Leh Market. The first day was dedicated to acclimatization, essential to avoid altitude sickness. So, we stayed at the hotel, taking it easy. I attended to some office work before calling it a day. Eurasian Magpie We spotted several species, including the elusive Ibisbill, the Carrion Crow, the elegant Eurasian Magpie, the vibrant Bluethroat, and the Citrine Wagtail and Mountain Chiffchaff. These initial sightings were promising and set a positive tone for the rest of our trip. 6

Bluethroat Golden Eagle After a satisfying morning of birding, we returned to the hotel for lunch. The food was a delightful mix of local Ladakhi cuisine and familiar dishes, ensuring we were well-fed and ready for the afternoon adventure. After a short rest, we set off for Hemis National Park, known for its rugged terrain and unique wildlife. The journey to the village of Rumbak within the park was an adventure in itself, with narrow winding roads and stunning mountain vistas. Tibetan Snowcock Chukar Bird activity in Hemis was minimal, likely due to the time of day, but we did spot Hill Pigeons, Chukars, Red-billed & Yellow-billed Choughs and Eurasian Magpies. The tranquil surroundings and the beauty of the landscape were rewarding in themselves. We returned to the hotel by 6:00PM, feeling content and ready to rest before our early departure the next day. Robin Accentor Day 3: July 2, 2024 – Journey to Pangong Lake We started our day early, departing at 5:45AM for Pangong Lake via the Changla Pass (17,688 ft). The journey was long and arduous, but the stunning scenery made it worthwhile. Early sightings included a magnificent Golden Eagle perched high on a rocky hillside after we passed a place called Sakti Leh, and a little further close to the Zingral Transit Check post we saw the Himalayan Snowcock, the Tibetan Snowcock blending perfectly with the rocky terrain and the Robin Accentor with its cheerful song. White-throated Dipper 7

As we drove past the Changla Pass, Stanzin and I saw a silhouette resembling a Dipper on a rock next to the stream and both of us screamed in chorus to stop the vehicle. By the time we stepped out of the car, however, the bird flew away, and we had to scan the stream for about ten minutes before it reappeared – it was the White-throated Dipper! These encounters added to the excitement and anticipation of the journey. Our next break was at the ‘Jab Tak Hai Jaan’ place – this place was named after the film. We were thrilled to spot a Bearded Vulture (Lammergeier) soaring gracefully in the sky. This sighting was one of the highlights of the day. We had lunch at the Pangong Lake and then travelled further to our homestay in Merak by 4:30PM. It was a charming and cozy place that offered a warm welcome after a long day of travel. We about an hour of rest we set out for a birding walk along the shores of Pangong Lake. The lake, with its changing shades of blue and green, was a sight to behold. We spotted several species, including the Great Crested Grebe and the Woolly Hare, which added to the charm of the evening. We stayed out till sunset, hoping to spot the elusive Tibetan Sandgrouse, but luck was not on our side. Other birds we saw today were Chukar, Red-billed Chough, Common Raven, White-winged Redstart and the Black Redstart. Tibetan Partridge We had an impressive list of bird sightings today morning in addition to the birds mentioned above: Great Crested Grebe, Hill Pigeon, Eurasian Magpie, Hume’s Lark, Eurasian Skylark, Tickell’s Leaf Warbler, Black-winged Snowfinch, Twite, Citrine Wagtail and the Common Rosefinch. Today was an important day for Prithvi as he attempted his first astrophotography session. Despite some difficulties with camera settings and light pollution, he managed to capture some beautiful shots of the Milky Way, a testament to his growing skills and passion. Day 4: July 3, 2024 – Exploring Merak and Journey to Hanle We began our day at 5:30AM, eager to explore the birdlife around Merak. The morning light was perfect for photography, and the crisp air was invigorating. We spotted Tibetan Partridges and a Woolly Hare, which made for an exciting start to the day. We also saw the Himalayan Rubythroat along the bushes on the road side, and a couple of Ruddy Shelducks flying near the shore. Little Owl Our journey to Hanle was equally rewarding. We saw a Little Owl perched on a wooden pole placed between some boulders on the middle of the road close to the Rezang La Memorial, its large eyes surveying the surroundings. We stopped at the Rezang La Memorial, a poignant site commemorating the bravery of Indian soldiers who lost their lives fighting the Chinese Army in 1962. The visit was a humbling experience, reminding us of the sacrifices made in this remote and challenging terrain. Himalayan Rubythroat Moving past the memorial we saw a pair of Black-necked Cranes in a small wetland. The sun was bright and hot. There was a stretch of road where it resembled a desert. I was stunned to feel hot air blowing through the car window during our travel through this stretch of the road. 8

Just before entering Hanle we stopped for lunch. The service was very slow – it took us almost an hour! We finally reached our homestay in Hanle at 3:00PM. The place was simple but comfortable. We wasted no time and set out for birding around Hanle. The area was teeming with birdlife. That night, despite strong winds, Prithvi managed to capture some excellent shots of the Milky Way, his skills improving with each session. Day 5: July 4, 2024 - Umling La Pass and Hanle Ecosystem We added a trip to Umling La Pass to our itinerary. Prithvi was eager to explore one of the highest motorable passes in the world. Departing at 5:30AM, we began our ascent. The journey was challenging, but the stunning views made it worthwhile. Eurasian Eagle Owl We spotted the Eurasian Eagle Owl perched majestically, an Upland Buzzard soaring high and then settling down, the Tibetan Lark singing cheerfully, and the Citrine Wagtail adding a splash of colour to the landscape. Great Rosefinch We spotted Great Rosefinches along the way, their vibrant plumage standing out against the rocky terrain. We also saw a pair of Black-necked Cranes with a chick, a heart-warming sight. The Tibetan Gazelle and the Tibetan Wild Ass were also spotted, adding to the day's excitement. Upland Buzzard The highlight of the day was undoubtedly the sighting of a Pallas's Cat with four kittens. This elusive and rare species was a thrilling find, and we felt incredibly fortunate to witness such a sight. Black-necked Crane pair with chick After traversing a few kilometres through sandy stretches and some mountainous roads, as soon as we hit the black top road we halted for our packed breakfast. While we were having our breakfast, we had an unusual guest starring at us from a distance, the Tibetan Gazelle. Pallas’s Cat At around 9:15AM we reached our destination, the Umling La Pass, at 19,024 ft – it was an exhilarating experience. The altimeter marked our ascent, and we felt a sense of accomplishment standing at such a high altitude. The views were breath-taking, with snow-capped peaks and vast expanses of rugged terrain stretching as far as the eye could see. After taking some photos we started our descent. After returning to Hanle for lunch, we continued birding in the afternoon. We spotted a Jackal in the wetland, its sleek form moving gracefully through the grass. 9

We continued our journey, passing through the villages of Nyoma and Mahe before reaching the geothermal area near Puga. The geothermal activity in this region is fascinating, with hot springs and steam vents dotting the landscape. Common Kestrel Tibetan Sandgrouse My Concern about the Hanle Ecosystem: A Fragile Paradise Hanle is a unique ecosystem characterized by its high-altitude wetlands, which support a variety of bird species and other wildlife. However, rapid urbanization poses a significant threat to this delicate environment. The influx of tourists, primarily drawn by the Umling La Pass, has led to the proliferation of homestays and infrastructure development. Roads cutting through wetlands isolate pockets of habitat, endangering the species that rely on this fragile ecosystem. If unchecked, this urbanization could irreparably damage Hanle's wetlands, leading to the loss of many unique species. We arrived at Tsokar in the late afternoon. The high-altitude lake, also known as the ‘White Lake’ due to the salt deposits on its shores, is a haven for birdwatchers. We spotted many birds here: Tibetan Sandgrouse, Blanford's Snowfinches, Barheaded Geese, Brown-headed Gulls, Great Crested Grebe, Red-eared (aka Black-necked) Grebe, Tibetan Sand Plover and Common Redshank. The wetlands in Hanle are a crucial habitat for several bird species, including the Black-necked Crane, which is listed as vulnerable. These wetlands provide nesting and feeding grounds for these birds, making them vital for their survival. The wetlands are also home to other species like the Pallas's Cat, Tibetan Gazelle, and various migratory birds. The delicate balance of this ecosystem is threatened by human activities, and urgent conservation efforts are needed to protect it. Day 6: July 5, 2024 – Journey to Tsokar We departed Hanle after breakfast, filled with memories of the incredible wildlife we had seen. Our first stop was near Loma, where Stanzin spotted a Brown Accentor, a bird we had not yet seen on this trip. Ground Tit Brown Accentor Horned Lark 10

The Ground Tit, Horned Lark, Desert Wheatear, Blackwinged Snowfinch, Black-necked Crane, Northern Pintail, Eurasian Wigeon, and Eurasian Coot were also seen. The variety of bird species in this area was astounding, and we spent the evening spotting them through the scope as the birds were deep inside the lake far away from the shore. We thanked Stanzin and our driver for their excellent guidance and patience throughout the trip. Their knowledge and expertise had made our journey enjoyable and enriching. Conclusion Our Leh trip was a remarkable blend of birding and astrophotography. Despite the challenges posed by rapid urbanization, the region's breath-taking beauty and biodiversity left us with unforgettable memories. Special thanks to Mr Lobzang for arranging such a meticulously planned and enriching experience. As the sun set, painting the sky with hues of orange and pink, we called it a day and returned to our homestay. That night, Prithvi hoped for clear skies to continue his astrophotography, but the weather was cloudy, and he had to postpone his session. Day 7: July 6, 2024 – Return to Leh We woke up to a stunning sight of the mountain peaks covered with snow. It had been drizzling in Tsokar during the night, and it was snowing on the mountain peaks, creating a beautiful contrast to the previous evening's landscape. The snow-capped mountains glistened in the morning light, adding a magical touch to our last day in the highlands. In contrast to my expectation of experiencing very cold temperatures, the temperature was pretty warm and, except for some low temperatures at night, the entire trip was pretty warm. The journey had been a perfect mix of adventure, relaxation, and learning. We had witnessed some of the most beautiful landscapes and unique wildlife that Ladakh has to offer. The memories of this trip will stay with us forever, reminding us of the beauty and fragility of nature. Departing Tsokar at 7:00AM, we made our way back to Leh. The journey took us through the Taglangla Pass (17,482 ft), one of the highest passes in the region. The steep descent from the pass was challenging, but our driver navigated it skillfully. We joined the Leh-Manali Highway and arrived in Leh by early afternoon. Prithvi's interest in astrophotography had grown, and he was eager to continue exploring this new hobby. The trip had also deepened our appreciation for birdwatching and conservation. As a family, the trip brought us closer together. We returned home with a renewed sense of wonder and a commitment to continue exploring and preserving the natural world. Back in Leh, we had some time to explore the local market and buy some souvenirs. The bustling market offered a variety of handicrafts, textiles, and local products, and we enjoyed immersing ourselves in the vibrant atmosphere. Himalayan Marmot *** 11

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Jungle Owlet (Glaucidium radiatum) Jungle Owlet (Dandeli, Karnataka, October 30, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: Strigiformes Strigidae Galucidium G. radiatum 20 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Jungle Owlet is usually seen singly or in pairs or, occasionally, small groups, and is usually found by its calls at dusk or dawn. Its preferred habitat is scrub forest, open deciduous and moist deciduous forests, and mixed teak and bamboo forests. It is largely crepuscular and nocturnal, but does not seem to be much inconvenienced by sunlight, and is often seen moving around in the daytime. Its call is a loud kaokao-kao, followed by kao-kuk, kao-kuk, kao-kuk, increasing in tempo and then fading in volume before stopping abruptly. Nestlings produce tick calls that sound like the Pale-billed Flowerpecker. The Jungle Owlet is often mobbed by Drongos, Treepies and Sunbirds while at the daytime roost, and maybe as a result, prefers to roost inside tree cavities. It is often seen on open wires or branches, basking in the sun before moving to the daytime roost. Its diet consists mainly of insects, small birds, reptiles and rodents. Its peak foraging time is one hour before sunrise or after sunset, but it has been known to capture Phylloscopus warblers during the day also. Description & distribution: The Jungle Owlet, also known as Barred Jungle Owlet, is a small owlet with a round head and fine brown barring all over. It does not have a clearly demarcated facial disk. Upperparts are dark black-brown with white barring, Wing coverts have white and rufous patches, while the primaries and secondaries are dark brown with paler chestnut barring. Underparts are whitish or pale rufous with dark barring. The chin, upper breast and centre of the abdomen show a whitish patch. It has bright yellow irises, dark bill and tarsi with black claws. The sexes are alike. It is a widespread resident, with its range extending patchily from Himachal Pradesh east to Bhutan, and south across the Indian plains, with another subspecies inhabiting the Western Ghats. It is unrecorded in Rajasthan and adjoining arid areas; it is also not seen in the North East, where it is replaced by the Asian Barred Owlet. Two subspecies are recognized – the nominate, G. radiatum, is seen in the plains of India and Sri Lanka, whereas G. r. malabaricum, seen in the Western Ghats, has a shorter tail and shows more brown on the head; it is possible that the Western Ghats subspecies may be elevated to a full species status in future. Nesting: The Jungle Owlet breeds mainly between March and May. It in natural tree hollows, usually unlined, and located between 3-5 metres from the ground. The usual clutch consists of four roundish eggs (three in G. r. malabaricum). Local name: The Jungle Owlet is known as ‘Jangli choghad’ or ‘Kala khusat’ in Hindi, ‘Chhota kalpencha’ in Bengali, ‘Van chibri’ in Gujarati, ‘Sinna andai’ in Tamil, ‘Chemban nathu’ in Malayalam, and ‘Adavi pagadigante’ in Telugu. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 12 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 22 Number 1 January 2025 FIELD TRIP-1: Sunday, 19th January 2025, 6.30AM: Edulabad Lake. Meeting Points: NGRI Metro Station, 6.30AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Gurukumar KR (Mobile: 99858-07186) Located near Ghatkesar, Edulabad Lake houses 171 bird species including many waders by the shore. The newly built pathway gives the near perfect elevation to birders for easy spotting. The gorgeous Red Avadavats and Tri-coloured Munias are the Guests of Honour that are an eye feast here. This will be a half-day trip, so carry adequate water and breakfast/snacks, and protective gear if required. Covid protocols will be followed; please ensure you wear masks, carry a sanitiser and maintain social distancing. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. New Deccan Birders hats and caps will be available for purchase; please come prepared! OUTSTATION TRIP: Saturday & Sunday, 25th & 26th January 2025: Turkum Cheruvu, Nirmal. Meeting Point(s): Apollo Pharmacy, Miyapur-Bolaram Road, Near Miyapur Cross Roads, 05:20AM; opposite Dindigul Air Force Station, HyderabadNarsapur Road, 06:00AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Sathwik Reddy (Mobile: 99858-07186) Organised by Deccan Birders in association with the Telangana Forest Department, this exhilarating birding expedition and overnight stay at Turkum Cheruvu offers an exceptional opportunity to engage in the Asian Waterfowl Census (AWC), explore the vibrant birdlife around the lakes, and immerse yourself in the area's rich natural beauty. Turkum Cheruvu is a picturesque lake in the heart of the Nirmal district, surrounded by dense forests and diverse wetlands. The area is rich in avian life, making it a prime location for birdwatching. The lake is a vital freshwater body, attracting a wide variety of waterfowl and migratory birds. The surrounding forests are home to numerous species of flora and fauna, creating a perfect blend of wetland and woodland ecosystems. Till date, over 150 bird species have been officially recorded in the region, with many more spotted by birding enthusiasts. The area has consistently yielded sightings of species such as the Asian Openbill, Black-necked Stork, and several species of waders, making it an excellent site for both novice and experienced birdwatchers. If time permits, we will also visit Kawal Tiger Reserve on 26th January 2025, providing an exciting opportunity to spot a tiger. More details will be shared on email. NATURE CAMP & BIRDING AT TURKAM CHERUVU Report: Camp at Turkam Cheruvu, Nirmal Dist, November 23-24, 2024 Text: Vijaya & Dhiraj Kaveri; Photos: Vijaya Kaveri Telangana Forest Department (TFD) and Hyderabad Tiger Conservation Society (HyTiCoS) organised a Nature Camp and Birding Event at Turkam Cheruvu and Venganna Cheruvu on November 23 and 24, 2024. These 2 lakes are considered hidden gems of Nirmal District in Telangana. The campsite area is part of Kawal Tiger Reserve (KTR) in Nirmal Division. This event was an experiment to explore the possibilities of developing the area into an eco-tourism spot. The participants of the event were representatives of the birding community, wildlife photographers, students, nature conservation NGOs and environmentalists from across Telangana. It was nice to meet people from diverse backgrounds. As birders and nature lovers, our focus was obviously birds and the natural ecosystem. Even before we reached the venue our eyes were constantly looking for birds. One thing which struck us was the numerous nests of the Baya Weavers built on electric wires on the road sides. During the welcome session it was mentioned by the organisers that it is an unusual habit or adaptation by the Baya Weavers, and is not a very good sign. 1

A view of Nirmal Division Forest (L) and Kawal Tiger Reserve (R) After the official inauguration of the event by senior forest officials, we headed for a nature safari at Kawal Tiger Reserve nearby. The forest landscape is tropical dry deciduous and is a catchment area of the Godavari River and its tributary Kaddam River. Birders instinctively know where to spot the birds, so we asked the safari driver to stop at a water body. While we were enjoying watching and clicking photos of a pair of Alexandrine Parakeets in their best mood, suddenly we realized there were 2 raptors – Crested Serpent Eagle and Changeable Hawk Eagle – on a single tree! Yellow-footed Green Pigeon We did our first bird walk next to a tiny stream, where we spotted Yellow-footed Green Pigeon, White-browed Wagtail, Grey Wagtail, Jungle Babbler, Black Drongo, Great Tit etc. After spending some time there, we continued on our safari. Crested Serpent Eagle (below) and Changeable Hawk Eagle (above) This was the highlight of our safari and we literally lost track of time taking their photos. Alexandrine Parakeet Crested Serpent Eagle 2

We also saw several other birds – Black-headed Ibis, Glossy Ibis, Little Cormorant, Common Kingfisher, Eurasian Collared Dove – and a family of Lesser Whistling-ducks, including some chicks. As it was already getting dark we headed back to our campsite for dinner, where we spent the night in our camping tents next to a bonfire. Changeable Hawk Eagle The bonfire Glossy Ibis Next morning, in the chilly weather, we started our bird walk around our campsite Turkam Cheruvu, which is surrounded by dense forest. We were split into small groups and headed in different directions. As the weather was cloudy we were initially only hearing bird calls, which we were identifying using Merlin Bird Sound ID, which was very useful. We also had with us one of our Deccan Birders members, Gokul Krishna, and his 9-year-old son Abhinav, who is an avid young birder – this made the task of bird identification easy. We spotted a lot of birds in this area, like the Common Kingfisher, Chestnut-shouldered Petronia, Rufous Treepie, Eurasian Hoopoe and Common Woodshrike. Eurasian Collared Dove Common Kingfisher Lesser Whistling-duck with chicks 3

Chestnut-shouldered Petronia Venganna Cheruvu Eurasian Hoopoe But the highlight of this bird walk was the Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker which drew everyone's attention for almost half the time. White-browed Wagtail Asian Woolly-necked Stork Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker We then returned back to the campsite for breakfast and then proceeded for our next birding spot, Venganna Cheruvu, which is another popular birding hotspot and is considered a paradise for bird-watchers. Indian Pond Heron 4

All the birders spread across the length of the lake. We spotted a lot of water birds, like Asian Woolly-necked Stork, Asian Openbill, Little Cormorant, Pied Kingfisher, White-browed Wagtail, Citrine Wagtail, Indian Pond Heron and Grey Heron. For us the highlight of this spot was the Blue-tailed Bee-eater which took a lot of our attention and time. Red-wattled Lapwing Blue-tailed Bee-eater We then returned to our campsite for a quick lunch, closing event and feedback session. Oriental Darter While we loved the place at the first instant and wish to come here as many times as possible, we are equally concerned about opening these pure and pristine forest areas for tourism. We have already seen littering of plastic and waste in the forest area. If this place is going to be developed as an eco-tourism spot, we just hope and wish that it is maintained as it is now, without disturbing the core nature of the forest and with minimal to zero waste by tourists. Sunrise at Turkam Cheruvu Medium Egret Red-wattled Lapwing, Oriental Darter, Medium Egret, Indian Spot-billed Duck, Black-winged Stilt, Ruddy Shelduck, Lesser Whistling-duck, and a few other birds like Indian Roller, Spotted Dove and Greater Coucal, were also seen. “And into the forest I go to lose my mind and find my soul.” - John Muir The list of birds seen during the camp: 5

SOME NOTES ON THE BIRDS OF THE MACHILIPATNAM AREA (Originally written March 2004. Edited and updated, December 2024) Text & Photos: Colin Conroy Introduction The area covered by this paper is situated on the coast of Krishna District, Andhra Pradesh, around the town of Machilipatnam and stretching for about 15km up the coast and 45km down the coast. The paper is mainly based on observations made by the author between January and June 2001, with additional observations made by J. Harjula (JH) during two brief visits in 1999, and by Dave Bookless (DB) in May 2000. Since the original writing of this article, some further observations were made by the author during a return visit to Machilipatnam in November 2005. The most interesting records from this visit are included in the species list that accompanies this article and, where appropriate, are referred to in the text. It by no means represents a comprehensive study of the birds of this area, as many places within the area were not visited and others were only covered cursorily. Even in these areas, however, some interesting observations were made, which are worthy of mention here. Also, for various reasons, most observations were made from roads or from tracks navigable by bicycle. Bird Habitats The area falls entirely within the "Eastern coastal plains" of Andhra Pradesh, as described by Taher and Pittie (1989). The topography here is extremely flat and much of the land lies at, or below, sea level. A large proportion of the land area is taken up by agriculture, mainly rice paddy with a smaller area given over to groundnuts and other crops. Immediately adjacent to the coast, much of the land formerly covered by either mangroves or paddy-fields, has been converted for fish and prawn aquaculture. Besides this, many former mangrove areas are now barren, mainly due to cutting for firewood, with only a small amount of salt-tolerant vegetation, and only covered by the highest tides (about once every three months). Reasonably healthy mangrove forest, with a good diversity of tree and shrub species, still exists along the creeks near the villages of Polatithippa and Gilakaladindi, at the mouth of the Gunderu Drain. However, due to cutting and grazing pressure in the past, there are few very tall trees, with most being well below the maximum height for their species. This area currently has no protection and continues to be under threat from cutting for firewood and building materials, pressure to convert it to aquaculture, and the development of a new port complex at Gilakaladindi. Besides this area, mangroves are also found going down the coast as far as the northern part of the Krishna River, near the villages of Malakayalanka and Palakayathippa. However, the mangroves here are mostly very stunted and species poor, with many large barren areas. Both these areas have been the targets, since 1998, of a project aiming at the restoration and conservation of mangrove habitat, involving the local community. This work is facilitated by the Coastal Community Development Programme (CCDP), based in Machilipatnam. [Dec 2024 Update - the work of CCDP, and all its programmes including the mangrove restoration work officially closed in December 2015. Visits since then by a former CCDP staff member (Eliah Gowri pers. comm.), plus examination of the series of satellite photos available on Google Earth) appear to indicate that most, if not all of the planted mangrove trees have survived and are growing well. The natural mangrove habitat near Polatithippa and Gilakaladindi also appears to be still flourishing.] As stated by Taher & Pittie (1989), the soil here is very sandy and this can be seen in the area which stretches north-east from Machilipatnam, where there are large tracts of short, sandy grassland, heavily grazed by cattle, with scattered palm trees and Casuarina plantations. However, notwithstanding these dry areas, the predominant theme in the whole area, and arguably the most important factor from an ornithological point of view, is water. There are many reed-fringed ponds hidden amongst the paddy-fields, and a large number of man-made channels cross the area. Many roads are lined on both sides by large beds of reedmace (Typha spp.). This is particularly true of the road going south from Machilipatnam, through the village of Chinnapuram, along which large numbers of Weavers and Munias can be found nesting, and three species of Bittern are seen regularly. Finally, the coastline itself offers habitat for birds in the form of sandy beaches and muddy creeks. Migrating and wintering waders make good use of these, as well as of the numerous ponds, drains and flooded areas. Species As you travel around this area, the most visible groups of birds, aside from the ever-present Rollers, Bulbuls and Drongos, are those associated with water, particularly the Heron family, the Kingfishers and the waders (aka shorebirds). Of the passerines, the most noticeable and numerous are also those which are found around water, such as the Weavers and Munias. Three species of Weavers and three Munias are common throughout most of the area. Of the Heron family, 11 species are regularly recorded and two more are seen occasionally. Although breeding hasn’t been proved for most of these species, from the presence of good numbers all year round it seems likely that several of them, including all three Bitterns (Cinnamon, Yellow and Black) and Purple Heron, do actually breed here. So far, with a relatively small amount of coverage, 28 species of waders [Dec 2024 Update - the observation of 2 flocks of Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) by the author in Nov 2005 increases this number to 29] have been seen and conversations with local people suggest that several more species occur here regularly. With more observation, at the right time of year, particularly on the coast, the wader list for this area could probably be increased to 33 or 35 species. 7

Four species of Kingfisher can regularly be seen in the area. White-throated Kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis) is the commonest of these, and the least tied to water. Pied Kingfisher (Ceryle rudis) is frequent around flooded areas and aquaculture ponds. Common Kingfisher (Alcedo attthis) can be found in mangroves and wet channels just back from the coats. The rarest species here is Black-capped Kingfisher (H. pileata) which appears to be tied to the larger channels in the intact mangrove areas near Polatithippa. The Crakes and Rails are also well represented, with six species recorded, plus the similar-looking but unrelated Bronze-winged Jacana (Metopidius indicus). All of these are likely to be resident, although all except White-breasted Waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus) and Bronze-winged Jacana are probably represented by fairly low numbers wherever there is suitable habitat. If one looked at the species list alone, the other groups of waterbirds, such as wildfowl, Cormorants, Ibises, and other long-legged waterbirds, would appear to be fairly well represented. However, many of these birds are not common here, and only one or two records have so far been made. It seems likely that the majority of these records are of birds on passage, while other species might be more numerous just outside the area covered by this paper, notably in the river deltas to the north and south and along the channel of the Krishna going inland towards Vijayawada. In the large areas of dry scrubby habitat and sandy grassland, the avifauna is less diverse, with three Larks, two Cuckoos, one Pipit and a smattering of birds from other groups, being recorded regularly. there are other sites along the coast where these birds occur. If so, this would constitute a significant range extension. [Dec 2024 update - publicly available records on E-bird reveal that there have been several records made of this species in Krishna District and neighbouring districts of Andhra Pradesh since 2001, all between the months of December and April, and at least some involving small groups of birds. This would seem to imply that Grey-headed Lapwing is indeed a regular winter visitor in the region.] Long-toed Stint (Calidris subminuta) A single individual of this species was watched for three hours in April 2001. Very good views were had, photographs taken (albeit poor quality) (see photos below) and a detailed description written down. Although the Helm Identification Guide, Shorebirds (Hayman et al. 1986), shows the wintering range of Long-toed Stint as covering the whole eastern side of India including some of Andhra Pradesh, it seems that there has been only one other documented record from Andhra Pradesh, at Pulicat Lake in the extreme south of the state (Grimmett et al. 1998, Taher & Pittie 1989, Bombay Natural History Society pers comm.). This species breeds in a broad band across Siberia and winters in south-east Asia, Indonesia, the Philippines and parts of Australia. It may well be fairly regular along the coastal strip of Andhra Pradesh, although lack of observers and the similarity of the bird to Temminck’s and Little Stints may have resulted in it being over-looked hitherto. So far only six species of raptors have been recorded here, and only two, Black Kite (Milvus migrans) and Indian Shikra (Accipiter badius), are at all common. Being on the coast, this area is important for migration, particularly of waders, but also of passerines such as Wagtails and Warblers. Consequently, particularly during the peak migration times, almost anything can turn up. Interesting / unusual bird records during Jan-Jun 2001 During the main study period several observations were made which were interesting or unusual for one reason or another. Grey-Headed Lapwing (Vanellus cinereus) The small wintering flock of Grey-headed Lapwings which was present from at least the 6th of February 2001 until 3rd May, when the last bird was seen, constituted the first record of this species for the state of Andhra Pradesh (Conroy 2003). According to Grimmett et al. (1998), the nearest place where Grey-headed Lapwings regularly occur is 1000km away in West Bengal, where they winter. Outside West Bengal and North-East India, they are rare elsewhere in the country and so a group of 12 on the coast of Andhra Pradesh is a very interesting record. The question that now has to be asked is “was this just a freak occurrence or is this a regular wintering site?” This can only be answered by careful searching of the area in future years. As coastal Andhra Pradesh receives relatively little coverage by birdwatchers, it is possible that Long-toed Stint (Calidris subminuta) (Machilipatnam, April 20, 2021) © Colin Conroy, 2001 8

[Dec 2024 update - the publicly available records for this species seem to show that the above prediction was accurate. There have been several records of this species in coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh since 2019, often including multiple birds, with most records being in the months between September and March] Streaked and Black-Breasted Weaver (Ploceus manyar & P. benghalensis) The distribution information in Grimmett et al. (1998) and Taher & Pittie (1989) would seem to indicate that these species do not occur at all in the whole coastal zone of Andhra Pradesh. Observations in 2001, and also previous years, show that this is incorrect. Both species were present in abundance during 2001 in suitable habitat, and nest-building of both species was observed. Moreover, a trip to Kolleru Lake, in the neighbouring West Godavari district, on the 1st of May 2001, revealed that Streaked Weaver at least, was abundant here also. Blue-tailed Bee-eater (Merops philippinus) present in summer and apparently breeding The Blue-tailed Bee-eater is generally considered to occur in winter in peninsular India, and then migrate to other regions to breed (Grimmett et al. 1998, Fry et al. 1992). However, the situation around Machilipatnam in the first six months of 2001 appears to tell a different story. There were no records at all of this species made until 25th of March, after which point they started to be seen with increasing regularity, both in the mangroves and in other areas near the coast. On the 30th of May at least 25 were seen at the same place that the Greyheaded Lapwings had frequented, and then on the 6th of June, searching of the sandy grassland just back from the coastline revealed an area of shallow pits containing at least 4 nest holes, one of which was seen with a bird going into it. At least fourteen birds were seen in this area, and there were many small pits suitable for Bee-eater nest-sites, and so it seems likely that several pairs bred here in 2001. Moreover, this area fits very closely to the description of Blue-tailed Bee-eater nesting habitat given in the Helm Identification Guide, Kingfishers, Bee-eaters and Rollers (Fry et al. 1992) - “dry loamy or sandy soils in open flat areas such as coastal dunes”. About 30 birds were seen later in the month near the village of Malakayalanka, further down the coast. Also, at least 6 were seen at the Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary, East Godavari District, on the 15th of June 2001, and so it seems as if this is another case of insufficient coverage leading to a misleading picture of a species’ occurrence. Rufous-tailed Lark (Ammomanes phoenicura) There were two records of this species, both from the banks of the Krishna estuary, one of which was of a pair behaving in a way that indicated that they might have been breeding. This is a range extension for this species which has hitherto not been thought to occur in the coastal strip on the east side of India (Grimmett et al.1998, Taher & Pittie 1989). Predictions for future additions to species list It is almost inevitable that regular, ongoing observations by competent birders will continue to add new birds to the list for this area for some time to come. However, the group which is most likely to be the source of these additions is the waders. In a relatively short period of time, with only very incomplete coverage, 28 species have been recorded here, including one which was new for the district (and only the second for the state). There is a large amount of suitable habitat for waders on passage and in winter, although much of this is difficult to access. Species which seem likely to occur, either regularly or occasionally, include Pin-tailed Snipe (Gallinago stenura), Jack Snipe (Lymnocryptes minimus), Black-tailed Godwit, Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica), Spotted Redshank (Tringa erythropus), Sanderling (Calidris alba), Dunlin (C. alpina), Broad-billed Sandpiper (C. falcinellus), Ruff (C. pugnax), Indian Thick-knee (Burhinus indicus), Great Thickknee (Esacus recurvirostris), Eurasian Oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus), Pied Avocet (Recurvirostra avosetta), Grey Plover (Pluvialis squatarola), Common Ringed Plover (Charadrius hiaticula) and Greater Sand Plover (Anarhynchus leschenaultii). Another group which may well be better represented than existing records would appear to show is the migratory Warblers. These birds are often both inconspicuous and hard to identify and so diligence and experience are needed to complete this part of the picture of the birds of Machilipatnam. Species which might be expected include Paddyfield Warbler (Acrocephalus agricola), Thick-billed Warbler (Arundinax aedon), Booted Warbler (Iduna caligata), and Greenish Warbler (Ph. trochiloides). Outlook for conservation of birds and other wildlife in Machilipatnam area The most important habitat, from a conservation point of view, in this area, is of course, mangrove forest. This habitat has been so heavily impacted in the past that there is very little left. The only area of reasonably healthy and diverse forest in the study area is the forest around Polatithippa and Gilakaladindi, and currently this is not protected in any way by the law. It continues to be exploited for firewood and building materials, and may well be affected by the new port development in Gilakaladindi, which is currently under construction. Also, in common with mangroves all over the world, it has hanging over it the ever present threat of conversion to aquaculture. Despite these threats, the outlook is rosier than it might otherwise be, as a result of the work of CCDP in the area. This project aims both to protect existing mangroves through education and by helping people find alternative sources of income, and to increase the area of mangrove forest by planting nursery grown seedlings in former mangrove areas. Most of the other bird habitats in the area are almost entirely artificial, being the result of agricultural practices. Most of the paddyfields immediately adjacent to the coast have already been lost, when they were converted to aquaculture in the 1990s. This must have had a negative impact on bird populations as it would have led to the loss of all the habitat which is found around and in between paddyfields in this area, particularly the reed-fringed pools and ditches which provide homes for birds such as Crakes and Rails, and also Weavers and Munias. 9

It would also have meant a change from a freshwater habitat to a brackish-water one. This would certainly affect invertebrates and amphibians and so presumably would have an effect on birds too. Any similar rapid change in agriculture in the future will probably have similar effects on birdlife. Conclusion The coastal area of Krishna District in Andhra Pradesh has been little visited by birdwatchers in the past, perhaps because it is a largely agricultural zone with little in the way of pristine natural habitat. It is also a little off the beaten track and away from areas normally visited by tourists. However, as this article shows, it is far from being a bird-free zone and offers opportunities to increase the body of knowledge about the distribution and behaviour of many species. Of particular interest are the waders, as is made evident by the fact that one new species, and one second record for Andhra Pradesh were recorded in a short period at the beginning of 2001. Further visits would almost certainly result in more additions to the district or state bird-lists. References 1. Conroy, C., 2003. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Malabar Pied Hornbill (Anthracoceros coronatus) Malabar Pied Hornbill adult female (L) and male (R) Malabar Pied Hornbill immature (Dandeli, Karnataka, October 30, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: Bucerotiformes Bucerotidae Anthracoceros A. coronatus 65 cm fruits or berries, although it does also eat lizards, small mammals, rodents like mice, reptiles, insects and baby birds. It is arboreal, and moves around with heavy hopping movements inside large fruiting trees. It prefers evergreen or moist deciduous forests, mostly near human habitation. As with most Hornbills, flight is heavy and ponderous, with a strong flap-and-glide pattern, with wingtips upturned. It emits a variety of nasal squeals, loud cackling and screams – Salim Ali likens the calls to “the protestations of a dak bungalow murghi, seized by the cook, and also the yelps of a smacked puppy!” Description & distribution: The Malabar Pied Hornbill, also known as the Lesser Pied Hornbill, is a monotypic species. It is a large bird, predominantly black in colour, but with a white belly, throat patch, tail sides and trailing edge to its wings. The heavy bill is waxy lemon yellow, with a prominent, mainly black casque. The casque is axe-shaped (as opposed to cylindrical in the Oriental Pied Hornbill, with which this bird may sometimes be confused) and has a pronounced tip, and a large black patch along the sharp upper ridge. In juvenile birds the casque may be missing or not very noticeable. The two sexes are similar, except that the male birds have blue-black orbital skin as against pinkish in the female birds; female birds also have a smaller casque. Outer tail feathers are all-white (as compared to white-tipped black feathers in Oriental Pied Hornbill). Nesting: The Malabar Pied Hornbill breeds mainly between March and June. It is a secondary cavity nester, being incapable of digging its own nest, and hence nests in large cavities in trees. Like other hornbills, the female locks herself within the cavity, blocking off the entrance with a mixture of mud, droppings and fruit pulp, and leaving only a narrow opening through which the female disposes of excreta, and receives food from the male. Once the chicks have grown too large, the female breaks out, then rebuilds the wall around the opening, after which both parents feed the chicks. The usual clutch consists of 2-4 white eggs with wood-brown stains. The Malabar Pied Hornbill is endemic to the Western Ghats (western Maharashtra south through Goa, western Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and Kerala), some parts of Central and Eastern India (western West Bengal, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, northern and eastern Madhya Pradesh, northern Andhra Pradesh, and north-eastern tip of Telangana), and Sri Lanka. In Local name: The Malabar Pied Hornbill is known as ‘Dhan chiri’ in Hindi, ‘Suleimani murghi’ in Deccani, ‘Irattai chondu kuruvi’ in Tamil, ‘Vezhambal’ in Malayalam, ‘Batta chupanati’ in Telugu, ‘Kanari’ in Konkani, ‘Kuchla kha’ in Odiya, ‘Bagma dhanesh’ in Bengali, and ‘Poruwa kandetta’ in Sinhala. Trip Report: Ananthagiri Hills, Vikarabad, December 01, 2024 Preethi Velagapudi White-naped Woodpecker (Photo: Aditya Rao) My journey to the lush hills of Ananthagiri began with an unexpected discovery. I was to stay in Hyderabad for two months and had searched for local birdwatching spots in the area. I expected to find little in terms of resources since none of my Indian family ever understood my love for birds, but I eventually stumbled upon the Deccan Birders Facebook page. The prospect of spotting new birds with like-minded enthusiasts thrilled me despite the fact I barely knew anything about Hyderabad or the people in it (much less the people I would have to spend my day with). My love of birds didn't start in the States but rather rural Andhra from observing the koels, babblers, and the crows - especially the crow, a creature I find so clever and captivating. Obviously, Indian birds intrigue me more -- the birds I would see back home in Dallas I could find on any day in the US, but the ones here are much more of novelties. I spent hours poring over their vibrant images, hoping for the day I'd get to spot a Blue-faced Malkoha or an Indian Paradiseflycatcher. And so, I woke up on a Sunday well before dawn to catch five members of the group at the first checkpoint. Twenty minutes later we were at the second checkpoint to combine with another group for breakfast and small talk. After a 70 km drive to Vikarabad, our group joined an even larger group of forty to ultimately make our final troupe of birders at the trailhead. 1

Here, Sathwik and the other more senior birders gathered us in a circle. They gave us advice on how to identify birds in the fore, middle, and background; how to identify their location in trees using clock positions; by their colours; and by their sizes as compared to the more common species like sparrows, pigeons, or crows. In any case, with Anita’s and other birders' help, I spotted precious birds I would have missed on my own, such as the Indian Grey Hornbill, Coppersmith Barbet (gorgeous and with such a phenomenal voice), and the Indian Paradise-flycatcher (I have been dying to see this one for ages!). I quickly introduced myself to a couple of other birders and was soon taken under the wing of a very enthusiastic senior birder, Anita, who was adept at spotting a bird by the briefest flap of its wings and identifying it with hardly any more information. Of course, the birds here are new to me and I didn’t know where to look for certain ones. Beyond that, however, the ones here still seemed harder to spot. Perhaps because of the crowds from the weekend trekkers and temple goers, or the foliage providing them a hideout. In the US, the birds seem more comfortable coming close to humans, and somehow, feel more visible. Indian Paradise-flycatcher (Photo: Aditya Rao) Orange-headed Thrush (Photo: Aditya Rao) By the end of the day, I'd spotted about 37 species. I was tired, but satisfied to have seen so much with the welcoming likeminded people of the Deccan Birders group. Jacobin Cuckoo (Photo: Ali Hyder) Indian Grey Hornbill (Photo: Aditya Rao) White-throated Kingfisher (Photo: Ali Hyder) Blue-capped Rock Thrush (Photo: Aditya Rao) 2

I also noticed differences in the people watching the birds. Perhaps due to a long history of conservation in the US, it seems more commonplace to spend time with and develop an appreciation for the natural world in the US, unlike in India. Back home, I usually birdwatch with friends or my local Audubon society, the Trinity River Audubon Center of Dallas, who host their birdwalks two to three times a month at their park in southeast Dallas. Oftentimes, it’s more casual or inexperienced birders that will join for these guided walks, while the more experienced ones will birdwatch elsewhere by other parks or lakes with their long camera lenses. Large-billed Leaf Warbler (Photo: Aditya Rao) There were some birds that felt very different from the ones I knew in the States – the Grey Hornbill, for example, has a beak so thick I couldn’t think of a similar bird from America. In contrast, the warblers here reminded me of the warblers back home, but I came to know that Old World warblers and New World warblers are not closely related at all. Perhaps they convergently evolved to fill similar ecological niches as their American cousins. It was nice though, to know that the ibises and coots are closely related to the ones back home. In contrast, this birding trip was less guided and many of the birders split apart into smaller exploratory groups. Many of the forty birdwatchers from this day seemed to have plenty more experience under their belts and yet perhaps because of the structure (well-organized trips with the ability to meander on one’s own), they’re incentivized to stay together. In addition, these trips are far from the city, often an hour or two away. Going against the grain culturally and often putting hours into a trip, I can confidently say that the birders in this group are in some ways more dedicated than the ones I’d gotten to know in the US. Indian Silverbill (Photo: Ali Hyder) Green Bee-eater (Photo: Ali Hyder) Indian Blackbird female (Photo: Aditya Rao) All in all, a good trip. My favourite bird? The Coppersmith Barbet. It made such a melodious sound that absolutely did sound like metalsmithing. So aptly named and colourful, it made me happy. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Malabar Trogon (Harpactes fasciatus) Malabar Trogon immature (Dandeli, Karnataka, October 31, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: Trogoniformes Trogonidae Harpactes H. fasciatus 31 cm Habitat & behaviour: The Malabar Trogon is usually seen singly or in widely separated pairs, in evergreen or moist deciduous forest, and mixed foothills bamboo forest. It is a fast but reluctant flier, preferring mostly to sit quietly, in a bolt upright position, for long periods of time, on tree stumps or low branches, occasionally making agile sallies through the thickets to catch insects. Its diet also includes caterpillars, beetles, cicadas and other insects, besides some leaves and berries. When foraging on bark, they have been observed to use their tails to prop themselves up, akin to woodpeckers. Its call is a series of guttural or purring notes, while the song is an unhurried series of 3-4 kyau or mew notes. The alarm call is a churrr, and a similar call is also used at roosting time. They are not migrants, but in the Nilgiris region, they migrate altitudinally, moving up to higher reaches in summer. Description & distribution: The Malabar Trogon is the smallest of the Trogons seen in India. It is a resident in its range, which extends from Peninsular India south of Gujarat, through the more humid parts of the Western and Eastern Ghats and the hills of western Tamil Nadu to Sri Lanka. Like most Trogons, the Malabar Trogon is sexually dimorphic. The male is very brightly coloured, with its crimson belly separated from the black head, neck and breast by a white border. The back is yellowish-brown, while wings are black with fine white vermiculations. The tail is long and graduated: the central tail-feathers are chestnut with a black tip, with the second and third pairs from the middle having more black than chestnut. The outer three pairs have long white tips. The female does not have the contrasting crimson and black; rather, its head and breast, only slightly darker brown, merge into the olive-brown of the back. The underside is ochre. In both sexes, the bill and orbital area are bluish black, irises are dark brown and feet are pale bluish. Nostrils are protected by tufts of filoplumes. The feet are heterodactyl, a feature unique to the Trogons, with the digits I and II facing back and digits III and IV pointing forward. Nesting: The Malabar Trogon breeds mainly between February and June. Its nest is an unlined natural hollow in a low, preferably rotting and hence soft, tree stump inside deep forest. The usual clutch consists of 2-4 roundish, glossy ivory white eggs. Incubation duties are performed by both parents, and they also continue to feed fledged juveniles for up to 6 months. Local name: The Malabar Trogon is known as ‘Kufni chiri’ in Hindi, ‘Karna’ in Marathi, ‘Kakarne hakki’ in Kannada, ‘Theekakka’ (‘fire crow’) in Malayalam, and ‘Loha wannichcha’ in Sinhala. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 7 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. MONSOON BIRDING Trip Report: Thattekad Bird Sanctuary & Munnar Sholas, Kerala, July 04-05, 2024 Text & Photos: Aditya Rao Sri Lanka Frogmouth female (L) and male (R) Bird enthusiasts in inland India often consider July and August less interesting due to the incessant rains, dull weather, and limited bird activity. However, in my opinion, this period is underrated. Many birds breed and hence are highly active during the monsoons. While the wet conditions can be challenging, the cool relief after the intense summer heat makes it worthwhile. Additionally, from a photography perspective, the soft light and lush greenery create an ideal setting to observe and capture the beauty of these wonderful birds. I was traveling for work to Kochi and I was not going to pass up an opportunity to visit the fantastic birding spot called Thattekad, just about 42km from Kochi Airport, and the Sholas of Munnar, about 60km from Thattekad. Thattekad Bird Sanctuary Thattekad Bird Sanctuary, nestled in the picturesque Western Ghats of Kerala, is a paradise for bird enthusiasts and nature lovers alike. Spanning over 25 sq km, this sanctuary is also known as the Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary, after the eminent ornithologist Dr Salim Ali, who played a crucial role in its establishment and conservation efforts. The sanctuary is renowned for its rich biodiversity, especially its avian population. 1

Apart from birds, Thattekad is also home to various other wildlife species including elephants, leopards, sloth bears, and several species of snakes and amphibians. Given the number of elephants in the Sanctuary, many areas are cordoned off regularly by the Forest Department staff. Thattekad Bird Sanctuary stands as a testament to Kerala's commitment to biodiversity conservation and eco-friendly tourism. Whether you are a seasoned birder or a casual nature enthusiast, a visit to this sanctuary promises a memorable experience amidst the sights and sounds of some of India's most captivating birdlife. A view of the thick tropical rainforests of Thattekad Its diverse habitats, including tropical evergreen and deciduous forests, grasslands, and rivers, provide a perfect haven for a wide array of bird species. Over 300 species of birds have been recorded here, making it one of the richest bird sanctuaries in India. One of the key attractions of Thattekad Bird Sanctuary is the opportunity to spot endemic and rare bird species. The Malabar Grey Hornbill, a striking bird with its grey plumage, is commonly sighted here. The vibrant Malabar Barbet adds a splash of colour with its crimson throat and green plumage. The sanctuary is also home to the elusive Sri Lanka Frogmouth, known for its camouflage and nocturnal habits, making it a sought-after sighting for bird watchers. Also sometimes seen here is the Sri Lanka Bay Owl - a mystic bird indeed. Sholas of Munnar The Shola forests of Munnar, nestled amidst the Western Ghats in Kerala (and parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka), are a unique and vital ecosystem renowned for their biodiversity and ecological significance. These montane evergreen forests are characterized by their distinctive dwarf trees, dense undergrowth, and mist-covered valleys, creating a habitat that supports a rich variety of flora and fauna, including several endemic bird species. One of the key endemic bird species found in the Shola forests of Munnar is the Nilgiri Wood Pigeon. This large, colourful pigeon with its distinctive yellow legs and red facial patches is a highlight for birdwatchers exploring the higher altitudes of the Shola forests. Another endemic species is the Nilgiri Flycatcher, a small and strikingly beautiful bird with its blue and black plumage, often seen darting between branches in search of insects. Of course, the Black-and-Orange Flycatcher is not to be missed. Black-and-Orange Flycatcher Sri Lanka Bay Owl Birders also come here for the Great Eared Nightjar, but it is extremely hard to spot this bird. Another notable resident is the Indian Pitta, with its colorful plumage of green, blue, and rusty orange. The sanctuary's riverine habitats attract numerous water birds such as the Indian Cormorant, Little Cormorant, and several species of herons and egrets. The Indian Roller, with its striking blue and cinnamon plumage, is a common sight, often seen perched on wires or trees. Walking in Eravikulam National Park, known mainly for the endemic & highly endangered Nilgiri Tahr 2

Nilgiri Pipit An information board about the Nilgiri Tahr Neela Kurinji, the blue inflorescence that blooms once every 12 years, and from which the Nilgiris gets its name White-bellied Sholakili Additionally, the Palani Laughingthrush, with its cheerful song and yellow underparts, is another endemic species that thrives in the cool, misty environment of Munnar's Shola forests. The stunted trees and open grasslands of the Sholas, misty and wet The Nilgiri Pipit, a small bird known for its distinctive piping call, is also endemic to the Shola grasslands and open patches within these forests. The White-bellied Sholakili, a shy and elusive bird found in the dense undergrowth, adds to the allure of the Shola forests for bird enthusiasts. Palani Laughingthrush 3

In conclusion, the Shola forests of Munnar stand as a wonderful example of the biodiversity and natural beauty of the Western Ghats. Through concerted conservation efforts and responsible tourism practices, these unique ecosystems can continue to thrive, providing a sanctuary for endemic bird species and preserving the ecological balance of this remarkable region. Crested Serpent Eagle Conservation efforts in the Shola forests of Munnar are crucial for protecting these endemic bird species and their habitats. The Kerala Forest Department, along with various conservation organizations and local communities, has implemented measures to preserve the biodiversity of these fragile ecosystems. This includes initiatives such as habitat restoration, controlled tourism activities, and communitybased conservation programs. Efforts are also focused on raising awareness among visitors and locals about the importance of conserving the Shola forests and the endemic species they support. Sustainable tourism practices, such as eco-friendly trekking and birdwatching tours, are promoted to minimize the impact on the delicate ecosystem while providing opportunities for people to appreciate and learn about these unique environments.
