WINGS OVER HYDERABAD: REFLECTIONS FROM THE HEART OF A HOPEFUL BIRDER Text & Photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati There are moments in life when your heart swells with something bigger than joy. For me, one such moment was standing ankle-deep in dry grass under a July sun, watching a Yellow-eyed Babbler flit across a bush like it had stock in caffeine. That’s when it hit me – this isn’t just a survey. This is a movement. A map of belonging. A hopeful hymn to Hyderabad’s skies. The Hyderabad Bird Atlas (HBA) is one of those rare citizen science projects that feels both rigorously scientific and profoundly soulful. With 180 carefully selected 1.1 sq. km. cells scattered across 11% of our city, and biannual surveys planned for three full years, it’s a methodical attempt to decode the avian soul of Hyderabad. Hyderabad Bird Atlas Season-1 closing get-together But for those of us out in the field, waking before dawn, chasing elusive lifers, and scribbling notes while sipping lukewarm chai, it is also a labour of love. And oh, what love it is. If I had a personal tattoo-worthy motto, it would be: “There is always a bird.” Why? Because no matter where you are – beneath a neem tree or beside a noisy flyover – there’s always a little winged miracle happening nearby. 2

There’s a bird because there’s a tree. There’s a bird because there’s a building. There’s a bird we missed today, and a bird we’ll chase tomorrow. This truth anchors my birding life, reminding me that discovery never ends. It only evolves. World over, birders have spoken of similar sentiments. The late Phoebe Snetsinger, the first person to record over 8,000 bird species, famously said: “Every bird is a possibility. A maybe. A promise.” Closer home, Dr Sálim Ali himself, India’s most celebrated ornithologist, often recalled that it was a Yellow-throated Sparrow that first captured his heart as a ten-year-old, a spark that lit a lifelong fire. His story isn’t unique. Many birders, me included, began their journeys in similar serendipitous ways – one flutter, one call, one curious moment that refused to fade. That’s why bringing children into this fold is not just desirable, it’s essential. Let’s face it – today’s children are more likely to identify a Naruto than a Purple Sunbird. But hand them a pair of binoculars, and something magical happens. Curiosity kicks in. Screens dim. Senses ignite. And suddenly, they’re no longer observers; they’re explorers. Young naturalists in Crocs and backpacks. Rishi with other members of the team during a survey Birdwatching trains attention. It cultivates patience, observation and listening skills that digital lifestyles tend to erode. But more than that, it builds a bond with the natural world that no textbook ever could. A child who has waited ten minutes for a Tailorbird to emerge from a bush learns more about mindfulness than any app can offer. Just imagine a generation that grows up not only knowing where the Black Kite nests, but why it matters. Imagine a Hyderabad where children debate the difference between Barbets and Bee-eaters rather than cartoons and console games. That’s the vision the Hyderabad Bird Atlas is helping to shape – a city where the guardians of tomorrow are already tuning into the wings of today. One of the most beautiful aspects of the HBA has been the coming together of diverse birding communities – veterans with field journals older than smartphones, and beginners with more questions than field marks. It’s a glorious, featherflecked mess of checklists, debates, and laughter. There's something inherently comic about ten people silently pointing at a distant speck and whispering, "Is that a Drongo or a disoriented Myna?" Or a group pausing a survey to break into impromptu song because someone saw a Pied Bushchat (yes, it happened). These aren’t just surveys. They’re social symphonies with binoculars. And in every group, there's that one friend who always spots the lifer after you’ve packed your gear. You know who you are. And yes, we still love you. Abhinav in action On our last trip, 9-year-old Abhinav, a regular birder since 3 standards, spotted some birds and asked his dad with wideeyed wonder, “Is that its name or its superpower?” That’s when I realized we don’t need to teach children how to be fascinated. We just need to give them the chance. Then there’s Rishi, another young birder who was ‘doctored’ into birdwatching at age 6 – although, truth be told, now it is he who drags his mother out before sunrise. His teachers say he’s more focused in class. His parents say he’s more grounded. And I believe him when he says, “I feel like birds know me now.” At its core, HBA isn’t just about spotting birds. It’s about protecting what we still have. The data we gather helps map biodiversity, identify urban pressure points, and most importantly, make a case for conservation in a city galloping toward vertical growth. With the right momentum, this project can inform policies, designate birding hotspots, and perhaps save species from slipping into silence. But data is sterile without stories. That’s where we come in. Each eBird entry is a stanza. Each checklist, a chorus. And together, they’re composing the greatest song Hyderabad has ever sung for its birds. These aren’t isolated stories. They're part of a quiet revolution. 3

A big thank you to every volunteer, society, and birding group who made the Hyderabad Bird Atlas possible – your dedication and love for birds have truly lifted this project. Congratulations also to all participants – from seasoned birders to first-timers, cell coordinators to data validators. Every effort, big or small, helped stitch this avian story together. Waiting to be heard. And most importantly waiting to remind us that we, too, can soar. And special thanks to our young birders and mentors – you reminded us that birding is both legacy and future. Whether you were in the field, behind the scenes, or cheering from afar – you are the wings of this movement. Together, we haven’t just counted birds – we’ve created a community. So here’s my earnest call to schools, families, and communities: Bring your children. Bring your curiosity. You don’t need to be an expert. Just be open. Be still. Be present. Let’s ensure that the next generation doesn’t inherit bird books as nostalgia, but as living, breathing companions to their everyday lives. Because in the end, there is always a bird. Painted Francolin Waiting to be seen. *** BIRDING IN SOUTH AFRICA (Part-2) Trip Report: Madikwe Game Reserve, South Africa, April 18-21, 2024 Text & Photos: Sita Susarla Arrow-marked Babbler The decision to visit the Madikwe Game Reserve was made for two reasons. First, it is a malaria-free zone and second, the weather is favourable throughout the year. This is a private reserve situated in the North-western province of South Africa near the border with Botswana and the vegetation is mainly Bosveld (from Afrikaans: bos means 'bush' and veld is ‘field’) and semi-arid Kalahari. The Madikwe game reserve is the fifth largest reserve in South Africa, and is known for its diverse mammalian population and rich bird life. The unforgettable safaris into the reserve – one in the morning and the other in the afternoon – saw us through a series of amazing adventures into the wilderness during the three-day stay. This report is a sequel to the report about the birds of Cape Town, which appeared in the Pitta of last month (June 2025), and dwells upon the spectacular birds that we sighted during the safaris, as well as those we saw during the bird walks within the premises of Tau Lodge in which we stayed. Since the lodge is located inside the reserve, all the birds are categorised as Madikwe birds. Tau has a water pool adjacent to its restaurant where all the animals would come twice daily for a sip of water, and the elephants entertain the onlookers by splashing the water around. The birds of course were in plenty, ranging from ducks to waders to land birds, having sand-baths, mud baths and splashes to clean their feathers. 4

As we approached them, their characteristic loud alarm call went ringing, ‘kweh’, or ‘go-away’. This disturbed a flock of blue-green Cape Glossy Starlings on a nearby tree and a flock of Blue Waxbills (also called Southern Cordon Bleu) foraging on the ground. The name Waxbill refers to the bright red bill of the Common Waxbill, which resembles the red sealing wax. The Waxbills are very colourful birds, especially the Violeteared Waxbill. Grey Go-away-bird Madikwe reserve has an array of colourful birds, about 300 species of them, which are found in abundance across the sprawling reserve. The first birds we saw were a couple of Grey Go-away-birds nibbling at the yellow acacia flowers. These birds feed on fruit such as wild figs and berries, flowers, buds, leaves, termites, and snails. An interesting feature is that the Grey Go-away-bird feeds voraciously on flower petals of a variety of trees thus facilitating pollination. metres, that they finally allowed us to pass. The Helmeted Guineafowls are known to consume large quantities of ticks that would otherwise spread the ‘Lyme Disease’. It was once part of the Pangea or supercontinent which split into Gondwanaland and other land masses starting from 335 million years carboniferous to about 200 million years (Triassic to Jurassic period). The Himalayas are divided into three folded mountain ranges viz. 1. Great Himalayas 2. Lesser Himalayas 3. The Shivalik Hills. 10

The Great Himalayas constitute the Himadri, Everest being part of the high ranges above 6000 metres. The Lesser Himalayas are south of the Great Himalayas, and the Shivaliks are the foothills ranging from 900m to 1100m in elevation. They are a store house of several fossil records indicating their age. Geologists have recorded and studied the various fossils found from Cambrian (trilobites – the first crawling life on Earth) to Triassic to Jurassic species. Maldevta, about 20 to 25 km from Dehradun, is on the seasonal-flowing Song River. The area has rock formations indicating the snowball effect, evidence of glaciation of unsorted crushed rock moved by a glacier, involving a period of 60 million years of glaciation. The place is visited by students of Geology from various universities – in fact we actually met students of IIT Roorkee there. The Doon valley in the Shivalik hills is an unusually long and wide valley in the lesser Himalayas located in the Indian states of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Haryana. Dehradun is the capital city of the State of Uttarakhand, and located within this valley. The town was established when Ram Rai, the son of the seventh Sikh guru Har Rai, built a gurudwara in the 17th century. Crested Kingfisher Dehra Ram gurudwara Ram Rai, who went to the durbar of Aurangzeb as an emissary, found favour of Aurangzeb who granted him a jagir, and that town was later called as Dehradun, after Dehra referring to Ram Rai’s shrine. During the British colonial rule, it was called as Dehra and later changed to Dehradun. Considered as a safe city, it has several government organisations like the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) for civil services training in public administration in Mussoorie, The Indian Military Academy (IMA), Forest Research Institute (FRI), Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, Indian Institute of Remote Sensing, Oil and Natural Gas Company (ONGC), The headquarters of the Survey General, Survey of India (SOI) etc. From 10th March 2025 to 20th March 2025, as part of Geotourism, we, a team of retired Directors of the Geological Survey of India dealing with our geo-heritage – viz. Vundavalli Ravi Kumar, Dr BM Faruque, Dr G Samuel Sukumar, PV Sesha Rao, V Hanumanth Rao, geophysicist JV Rama Rao along with Sri Ajit Kumar Addl Director General (Rtd) – visited many places around Dehradun to suggest some of these areas as socio-religious and cultural sites along with their importance as signature sites of Himalayan orogeny. We were joined by Officers of Geological Survey of India from Uttarakhand, the local Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH), Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, Oil and Natural Gas Company (ONGC), and some Retired Professors of Universities who have worked extensively in these areas. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Nilgiri Pipit (Anthus nilghiriensis) Nilgiri Pipit (Munnar, Kerala, October 1, 2017) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Passeriformes Motacillidae Anthus A. nilghiriensis 17 cm Vulnerable Habitat & behaviour: The Nilgiri Pipit is seen mostly in singles or in pairs in its preferred habitat, which is primarily the short montane grasslands, marshy areas and small streams, above 1000m in the Ponmudi Hills, and above 1500m in the Nilgiris, Palani and High Ranges. Like most pipits, they tend to forage silently, looking for their primary diet items like grass seeds and small insects, with the proportion of invertebrates increasing during breeding season. When flushed, they usually fly into a low bush or tree, behaviour possibly remnant from its being closely related to the tree pipits, from whom it diverged in the Pliocene era (5.33 to 2.56 million years ago). Description & distribution: The Nilgiri Pipit is a distinctive species of pipit that is endemic to the high altitude hills in the Nilgiris and the Anamalais in southern India. It is richer brown in colour than the rest of the pipits seen in the region, with dark lores and a buff supercilium and throat, and no malar stripe. Bill is dark, and the crown, mantle and upperparts show heavy dark streaking. Breast, sides of neck and flanks are a brighter buff. It is different from other pipits in that the fine streaking on the breast also continues along the flanks. Outer tail feathers are also buff, and there is no white anywhere in the plumage. Tail feathers are pointed, with the second outer feather showing a tapering triangle along the shaft, and the third outer feather ending in a small triangle at the tip. Nesting: The Nilgiri Pipit breeds mainly between April and July. Its nest is a cup made of grass, and built within short grass. The usual clutch consists of 2-3 grey-brown speckled eggs. Local name: The Nilgiri Pipit is known as ‘Nelvayil nettaikaali’ in Tamil and ‘Paranirangan’ or ‘Pullolian’ in Malayalam, the latter meaning ‘someone who hides in grass’. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 24 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. GASTRONOMY, REMINISCENCES AND THE BLOOMER AWARD Report: Deccan Birders Annual Dinner 2025 & Felicitation of Aasheesh Pittie Text: JVD Moorty; Photos: Wg Cdr Yella Prakash Rao The annual dinner of Deccan Birders – held, well, annually – was a special event this year. With the monsoon in an upbeat mood, it was an event that had the organisers a bit more sentient of the ill-weather prognostications and the cascading effect on the inflow of invitees. Weather notwithstanding, though, it was indeed a pleasure and delight to meet up with some cheerful faces and older bodies – or is it buddies? – of yore. With each attendee being welcomed by huge smiles, handshakes, and occasional warm hugs by Aasheesh – he knew them all – and then among each other, interspersed with Krishna flitting wristily tagging each person, the not-soclement weather was soon forgotten. Coffee, tea and biscuits were the accompanying morsels feeding ceaseless conversation. Sagarika, the emcee for the event, brought things to order, and everyone was put in their places. On the dais, under the eyes of the audience, were seated Mr A Sankaran, DCF (Retd) and currently OSD (Wildlife), Telangana Forest Department, the Guest of Honour Dr Gopi Sundar, Dr BC Chowdhury, our past President Aasheesh Pittie, our current President JVD Moorty, and our past Secretary Shafaat Ulla. The distinguished guests on the dais 1

The proceedings got under way. The Linnean Society citation goes as follows: JVD Moorty opening the proceedings The President, normally very loquacious, prioritised brevity, and after a few quick introductory remarks, went to the first highlight of the evening – felicitating Aasheesh Pittie for being awarded the HH Bloomer medal – a first for a person from Asia! For the uninitiated, this award was instituted by the Linnean Society, London, United Kingdom in 1963 from a legacy by the late Harry Howard Bloomer FLS, and is awarded to an amateur naturalist for an important contribution to the knowledge of natural history. “To the larger natural history community in India (and beyond), Mr Aasheesh Pittie is probably best known for his work as a bibliographer of South Asian birds and as foundereditor of the ornithology journal Indian Birds. Over a lifetime of amateur birding, he has been instrumental to the growth of birdwatching and ornithological studies in the erstwhile State of Andhra Pradesh, India, as a key driver of the Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh (now Deccan Birders) from the early 1980s until today. He has published five books and over 280 notes, reviews, journal articles, popular pieces in the mass media, including descriptions of behaviour, range extensions, observations of bird-plant interactions (a particular passion of his), and conservation. In 2015, he converted his huge bibliographic database (c. 38,000 references from 1713 to date) into a freely accessible online resource (Bibliography of South Asian Ornithology). Mr Aasheesh Pittie’s contributions to Indian ornithology cannot be understated.” I quote Aasheesh’s words from their home page: “I am deeply humbled on being selected for the H H Bloomer Award for 2025, and overjoyed at this recognition of the contribution of amateur ornithologists to South Asian ornithology. I accept this honour with gratitude. I thank The Linnean Society of London for nominating me.” The HH Bloomer Medal Dr BC Chowdhury – who also completed a mind-boggling fifty eventful years in the field of conservation! – along with JVD Moorty, placed a shawl around Aasheesh, and Shafaat Ulla presented a memento on behalf of the society to Aasheesh. 2

Aasheesh was gracious in his thanks and spoke of the guidance he received from Dr BC Chowdhury, Suhel Quader’s encouragement and help in going digital, and the support received from the members of the birding fraternity, and his own family in particular in his journey to where he has reached. Dr BC Choudhury and JVD Moorty honouring Aasheesh with the shawl Aasheesh displaying the memento Dr Gopi Sundar speaking on the Sarus Crane Then followed some delightful, humorous and anecdotal reminiscences by the old guard. Dr BC Chowdhury, who was then working at the Hyderabad Zoo, recalled that Aasheesh showed up on his first-ever birdwatching field trip in a bright red T-shirt! Dr Gopi Sundar then took over for his presentation titled ‘The natural history of the Sarus Crane: insights into the life of the world’s tallest flying bird.’ His talk was peppered with witty comments – the crane pundit – and the research that he has been carrying out on the social and marital life of Sarus Cranes was both a visual and an acoustic treat – he is indeed a Craneac, whispered to me as an aside! The talk was followed by an interactive Q&A session, with the questions posed by the audience handled deftly by Dr Gopi. Rajeev Mathew had a few amusing stories to narrate, among them the never-to-be forgotten experience of sighting the nocturnal and extremely rare Jerdon’s Courser, which incidentally has not been sighted again since then. Suhel Quader spoke about the single-mindedness of Aasheesh in pursuing his passion and the dedication and zeal with which he worked on his books, especially the 876-page tome ‘Birds in Books.’ He exhorted the younger minds in the audience to follow this example. With Cronos moving on rather quicker than usual, this part of the evening was brought to its inevitable conclusion. I would like to suggest that those who missed speaking at the event about their birding experiences and interactions with Aasheesh and the Deccan Birders may please share the same on the email and WhatsApp groups of Deccan Birders. Rajasekhar Tummala recalled how Aasheesh inspired him to become a philatelist. Srikanth Bhamidipati then proposed a Vote of Thanks to bring the formal event to an end, before the inescapable group photo of all the attendees huddled together – like Ashy Woodswallows on a wire! – on the stage which very bravely held its own. Dr Vikramjit and Dr Madhusudan spoke about their birding passion being fired up after becoming members of Deccan Birders with Aasheesh at the helm. The gastronomic fare that followed was enjoyed by everyone, and a word of thanks to the kitchen staff for having rustled up a delightsome meal. “Parting is such sweet sorrow” spake Shakespeare, and indeed it was – with more photographs as well as the now ubiquitous selfies being clicked, and there ended the evening as it began – with hugs, handshakes and even bigger smiles. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Dollarbird (Eurystomus orientalis) Dollarbird (Thattekad, Kerala, September 30, 2017) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Coraciiformes Coraciidae Eurystomus E. orientalis 28 cm Least Concern Sumatra; E. o. pacificus (also known as Australian Roller), found on the Lesser Sunda Islands, northern and eastern Australia; E. o. waigiouensis, found on New Guinea, western Papuan islands, D'Entrecasteaux Islands and the Louisiade Archipelago; E. o. crassirostris, found in the Bismarck Archipelago; and E. o. solomonensis, found in the Solomon Islands. Description & distribution: The Dollarbird is a member of the Roller family which gets its name from the distinctive pale blue or white coin-shaped marks on its wings. It is also known by various other common names like Eastern or Oriental Broad-billed Roller, Dark Roller and Dollar Roller. An overall dark-blue bird, the upperparts show a heavy bluish-green or deep turquoise wash that can make the bird appear almost black from a distance. Underparts and undertail coverts are a lighter blue. Head is flat and dark brown to dark grey, throat shows a bright glossy blue, bill is short and bright red or deep red, and irises are black. Underwing coverts show a pale blue or white ‘coin’ or ‘dollar’ that gives the bird its name. Immature birds are much duller than the adults, lack the bright blue throat patch, and have brown bills and feet. Habitat & behaviour: The Dollarbird is seen mostly in singles or occasionally in pairs in its preferred habitat, which is open wooded forests with hollow-bearing trees, or heavy secondary evergreen forests and nearby clearings. It is usually seen perched on power lines or on top of tall dead trees, from where it makes aerial sallies for insects, typically returning to the same perch. Its diet consists of mainly insects like beetles, grasshoppers and other flying insects, but it may also take small invertebrates at times. It is usually quiet, but sometimes utters a raucous check check. Flight is usually sedate with deep, powerful wingbeats. Nesting: In the northern hemisphere, the Dollarbird breeds mainly between March and May. Its nest is an unlined natural hollow, or an old barbet or woodpecker nest, in a large tree in a forest clearing, and is often used in subsequent years also. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 white spherical eggs. Incubation duties are performed by both parents. The Dollarbird is distributed across a wide range. Ten subspecies are recognized: E. o. cyanocollis, found from the Himalayas through China to south-eastern Siberia, Korea and Japan; E. o. orientalis, found from the southern Himalayas to Indochina, the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java, Borneo and the Philippines; E. o. laetior, found in south-western India; E. o. gigas, found on southern Andaman Islands; E. o. irisi, found in Sri Lanka; E. o. oberholseri, found on Simeulue, off north-western Local name: The Dollarbird is known as ‘Pulupporukki’ in Tamil, ‘Kattu panamkakka’ in Malayalam, and ‘Kes kavuda’ in Sinhala. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 4 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. It was an inspiring learning experience — witnessing young scholars present their research, and experts deliver insightful talks on environment and wildlife conservation. 1

One of the key takeaways for us from the conference was Prof BC Choudhury’s plenary talk and his strong message on Preventive/Proactive Conservation. We also engaged with delegates from across the country, exchanging thoughts on the conservation challenges and initiatives happening in different regions. The air was filled with the songs of Red-vented, Redwhiskered and Himalayan Bulbuls, and Oriental Magpie Robins. Some even nested in the corners and crevices of the homestay itself! Though the WII campus is known as a birding hotspot, the monsoon clouds and intermittent rain kept us from exploring much of its avian life. A walk into the woods at the resort Serenity by the river 6

Margosa Rewild Resort, where we stayed, is definitely a must visit destination for any birdwatcher with its beautiful river, greenery and peaceful ambience. We had an idea about the resort being full of natural beauty, but the view of the river by the resort especially at sunset and sunrise was completely mind blowing. The calm peaceful woods with wooden benches by the river side was just the perfect spot for any bird watcher to catch a glimpse of the waterbirds catching their prey. The beautiful time around sunset The best part of my stay at the resort was spending time watching the Manjeera river, the tranquillity of waters, the swift breeze across them, and the beautiful skies. I thoroughly enjoyed the morning walks amidst the green canopies and the sunset by the river. An added attraction for the kids was the green maze made of small hedges which was fun to run around play in between. The sun playing hide and seek A few boatmen silently fishing through small fishing nets also caught my attention, and the entire scene seemed like a beautiful painting. Located 16.5km from Margosa Rewild Resort is Manjeera Wildlife Sanctuary, situated near the Manjeera river and its reservoir. Established in 1978, it is known for its diverse ecosystem with lots of birdlife, wildlife and also crocodile breeding. The sanctuary follows the river for 36km. It protects a wide range of wildlife, around 70 species of birds, as well as submergent and emergent vegetation like ipome and Typha. One of the added attractions of the sanctuary is that it can be accessed through boat and that can be a boon for birdwatchers. Manjeera Sanctuary is famous for variety of migratory water birds like Bar-headed Goose, Ruddy Shelduck, Common Teal, Garganey, Lesser Adjutant and Common Pochard. The green maze Overall the experience was great, a nice ‘green’ break so close to the city. It must be more suitable to visit the resort in winters where we could get lucky to sight some migratory birds as well by the river. We hope to do that next time! We had been to the resort during peak summer season, around the last week of April, and so were not fortunate enough to sight many of the birds. Some of the birds sighted were only in the early morning at sunrise and water birds in the river especially around sunset. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Sri Lanka Bay Owl (Phodilus assimilis) Sri Lanka Bay Owl (Thattekad, Kerala, October 02, 2017) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Strigiformes Tytonidae Phodilus P. assimilis 22-27 cm Least Concern The Sri Lanka Bay Owl is endemic to Sri Lanka and the Western Ghats south of Goa, and mostly in Kerala. Two subspecies are recognized: The Sri Lankan race, P. a. assimilis, is the nominate, while the Indian subspecies, P. a. ripleyi, is the other subspecies. Description & distribution: The Sri Lanka Bay Owl is a member of the Tytonidae family of bay owls. It was earlier considered a subspecies of the Oriental Bay Owl P. badius, but has now been elevated to full species status some years back, based on differences in call and plumage, and due to clearly disjunct geographical distribution. The genus name Phodilus, from the Ancient Greek phōs for ‘light’ or ‘daylight’, and deilos for ‘timid’ or ‘cowardly’, refers to its tendency to mostly stay hidden in thick shrubbery during the day. Habitat & behaviour: The Sri Lanka Bay Owl is very secretive and rarely seen – it is often detected only when an injured specimen is found. Hence it is believed to be rare throughout its range. It prefers subtropical or tropical montane forests and high-altitude grasslands, wet evergreen or mixed evergreendeciduous forests, mangroves, or partially harvested forests, on level terrain or in the foothills. Not much is known about its diet, but it is believed to hunt beneath the forest canopy, where it probably hunts nocturnal rodents and invertebrates. During the day it is seen to roost on relatively open perches, 1-1.5m above the ground. It is a smallish owl with short rounded wings and tail, and short legs that are feathered till the feet. The head is distinctively shaped, with a broad forehead, V-shaped frontal shield, oblong facial shields that protrude as short ear tufts, broad dark vertical stripe running through the large all-dark eyes and a dark necklace that demarcates the head from the underbody. It has brown upperparts with heavy spotting, golden nape and scapulars, and pronounced barring on wings and tail. Pinkish white underparts have variable dark spotting on breast and flanks, reducing down the belly. Bill is yellowish, while the toes are pale greyish brown. Sexes are alike. Juvenile is presumed to be similar to adult, but is undescribed. Nesting: The Sri Lanka Bay Owl breeds mainly during winter. During this period, its song, an eerie whistling whi-whoo-eeyo, consisting of multiple whistles with many inflections, can often be heard. The call is a series of 3-4 tremulous whistles, the notes initially rising and then falling. Nesting habits are very poorly known – one nesting record from Sri Lanka showed three young of different sizes, indicating that they may have hatched asynchronously. The nest was built in a brokentopped fishtail palm. Local name: The Sri Lanka Bay Owl is known as ‘Riply moonga’ in Malayalam and ‘Bassa’ in Sinhala. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 8 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. THE BEAUTY OF BIRDS IN THE MONSOON Trip Report: Tadoba National Park, August 17-20, 2025 Text & Photos: N Shiva Kumar A view inside Tadoba National Park Most people avoid visiting National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries during the monsoon, and understandably so, as the core zones of the jungles are closed to visitors. Few, however, realise that the buffer zones remain open. Knowing this, I set my sights on Tadoba National Park in Chandrapur district, Maharashtra. The 400km drive from Hyderabad was an openroad invitation I couldn’t resist, rain or no rain. If the skies decided to drench me during a safari, so be it. I was armed with my container of cameras, and obviously there was a rain coat and umbrella to keep out that intermittent drizzle. 1

When the first monsoon clouds rolled over Tadoba, the forest seemed to exhale. The brittle, sun-baked browns of summer melted into an endless expanse of greens. Once-dry nullahs brimmed with pools of fresh rainwater, Sal and Teak leaves dripped with diamond-like droplets, and the very air pulsed with the intoxicating scent of wet earth. The transformation was so dramatic, so complete, it felt as though the land itself had been reborn and only shades of lush greens were visible. In this rebirth, it is the birds that take centre stage. The monsoon in Tadoba is not only the realm of prowling Tigers or the watchful eyes of Sambar and Chital, it is the season when feathers outshine fur, when the forest becomes an openair amphitheatre for a spectacular avian performance. By the swollen streams, Kingfishers claim their own spotlight. The Common, White-throated, and Pied varieties perch like ornaments against the grey drizzle, their plumage electrifying in its brightness. Then, in a flash of movement, they dive with surgical precision, re-emerging with a fish that glistens briefly before disappearing down a slender throat. Drongos, Bulbuls, and Ioras fill the misty mornings with a cheerful racket, their voices rising above the steady drizzle, while Barbets and Cuckoos keep up a patient, rhythmic chorus. If that was not enough, the Racket-tailed Drongo goes about strutting its long tail feathers just like the Paradise-flycatchers. Asian Openbill A massive male Tiger, up close Birds greet the rains with an infectious energy, their joy both audible and visible. For many, this is the season of courtship and breeding, so their plumage glows richer, their calls more insistent, as if they too cannot resist the romance in the air. The Indian Pitta, secretive for most of the year, suddenly appears on the damp forest floor, its emerald, sapphire, and crimson plumage gleaming like scattered jewels. With its sweet, rhythmic call, the Pitta is the herald of the rains, its colours mirroring the fresh monsoon palette of the forest. Tadoba’s quieter wetland pockets, Kolsa, Telia, and other rainfed meadows, become sanctuaries for monsoon-loving waterbirds. Painted Storks and Openbill Storks wade elegantly through the shallows, while Indian Spot-billed Ducks paddle between reeds heavy with rain. Indian Thick-knee Indian Peafowl Peacocks, those timeless emblems of grace, seem to come alive like never before. In clearings and along misty forest tracks, they unfurl their celestial fans, shimmering with iridescent blues and greens, and dance with a regal flamboyance. The patter of rain on leaves becomes the percussion to their performance, and the wild mango trees stand witness as they call out in echoing notes that carry far into the drenched canopy. Among the grasses, almost invisible until they move, stand the Indian Thick-knees, their large eyes shining with alertness. In the tangles of rain-drenched undergrowth, Paradiseflycatchers flit past, the white-tailed males streaming long ribbons of grace through the air. Red-wattled Lapwings patrol the wet ground with their chicks, fussing over them like attentive teachers. An occasional Purple Heron and Grey Heron play statue with angled neckline to catch lurking fish at their feet. 2

Black-hooded Oriole Red-wattled Lapwing juvenile Even the raptors, those masters of stillness, seem changed by the season. The Crested Serpent Eagle and the Changeable Hawk Eagle spread their wings wide to dry in brief moments of sun, perched like living sculptures against storm-grey skies. With sudden sweeps over the meadows, they remind the forest that beauty and power are often found in the same frame. My own most unforgettable sighting was of a young Fish Eagle, fresh in its independence, wheeling effortlessly above the rainsilvered landscape and testing perches along the lake’s edge, each movement a study in strength and freedom. Alas, they are endangered and their numbers are dwindling. In these months, birds become the soul of Tadoba’s wilderness. Some dazzle, like the Black-hooded Oriole, a golden flame against the greens, while others charm with their understated elegance, relying not on colour but on voice to make themselves known. Together, they turn the monsoon forest into a living, breathing orchestra, a celebration of resilience, courtship, survival, and sheer, unrestrained joy. Seeing five Tigers was of course a bonus but in the subdued light conditions under the cloudy sky photography was a big challenge with long lenses – I sighted 119 bird species but managed to click only a few of them. Grey-headed Fish Eagle juvenile An interesting signboard at Tadoba For those willing to brave Tadoba during what many call the ‘off-season’, the rewards are unmatched. Safaris in the monsoon are unhurried affairs; the forest is quieter, the mist clings low to the ground, and the grass is heavy with dew. The soundtrack is a blend of rain tapping leaves, distant peacock calls, and the liquid notes of the Orange-Headed Thrush or the sudden, insistent cry of the Brain Fever bird. As you leave Tadoba in the rains, you carry with you not just photographs but memories of a forest alive with wings, a place where every drop of rain seems to add a note to a song that has been sung for centuries. In the monsoon, Tadoba does not merely host birds. It becomes them. Trip Report: Keesara, September 07, 2025 Surekha Aitabathula A view of the Keesara quarries (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) It was one fine beautiful morning that took around fifteen of us to Keesaragutta Range, hoping for a good bird outing. Although the monsoon was overactive in the past week, the weather held to allow us to sight over 40 species! deep down that we must never approach birds right up front – we must approach in an arc, either to the left or the right, so as to not disturb them. One of the first rules of birding I learnt. Our trip coordinator, Gowthama, led us efficiently on a very wide circular pathway surrounding the rampantly quarried rocky hillocks. We covered good ground this way, finding many wonderful creatures and plants besides the birds. Rainwater had collected in between this illegally quarried stone. Several large troughs of rainwater were a pleasant sight – a saving grace. That said, it was sad to see the ugly result of stone quarrying. My first thought was how beautiful the rockies would have looked when untouched. Now they look like a desolate apology to the Grand Canyon with man-carved hillocks. Homo sapiens the plunderer never rests till he destroys nature. Ashy-crowned Sparrow Lark (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Spot-billed Ducks, Glossy Ibis, Dusky Crag Martin and Asian Palm Swift flew by making all of us crane our necks and train our binoculars to watch them fly by, displaying clearly their wing shapes to us against a not-so-blue sky. Green Bee-eater (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Our group was first greeted by Grey Francolin calls. Green Bee-eaters and Ashy-crowned Sparrow Larks were foraging boldly right ahead of us. It is a great feeling for every birder when the birds do not fly away on our approach. It feels like they trust us not to harm them. However, birders also know Crimson Rose (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) 5

Common Rose as well as Crimson Rose butterflies were flitting across, sometimes showing their wings and sometimes alighting softly on flowers. Gomphrena celosioides (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) It also goes without saying these days that Lantana camara was all pervasive here, and there were many other flowers all around. Common Sopubia (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Rains had made way for many wild flowers. One such gorgeous flower was the Common Sopubia (Parasopubia delphinifolia). It is a small pristine white flower with a sudden purple patch within that immediately arrests your attention. Sopubia is a herb known to grow around laterite hillocks, moist grasslands and swamps, and is said to have medicinal properties, useful in healing sores. Tropical Speedwell Evolvulus alsinoides (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) White-browed Wagtail meeting (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Common Wireweed (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Common Wireweed (Sida acuta) was a pretty discovery that sprouted lovely mustard flowers. Google describes this weed as an ethno-medicinal plant with traditional uses for malaria, fever, ulcers, wounds and elephantiasis. Gomphrena celosioides was another interesting weed we spotted. The flowers are a delicate whitish to pink coloured with a papery look and feel. The White-browed Wagtail is always a pleasure to watch. A dynamic bird whose tail continuously goes up and down alternately showing flashes of white and black. And a brow that looks like it was perfectly set in a beauty parlour! The Guest of Honour today was the Oriental Honey Buzzard, giving us a grandstand view right on top of the canopy. It sat still and looked proud and intense as only the raptors can. As it took flight, we were in awe of the majestic wing span that engineers the aerodynamics of a bird flight. No birder worth his salt can ever have enough of raptor take offs. 6

Common Iora and Indian Robin staged an opera with the accompaniment of Tailorbirds, Prinias and Lapwings, all for our listening pleasure. Oriental Honey-buzzard juvenile (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Ashy Prinia (Photo: Mohammed Ali Hyder) The group in action (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) Baya Weavers kept us entertained for a while, perching quite visibly to our utter delight. Whirligig Beetles (Photo: Sudipta Bhattacharya) Another exciting new-found species for me was the Whirligig Beetles. These are water beetles that swim on the surface of the water if undisturbed, and underwater when threatened. They get their name from their habit of swimming rapidly in circles when alarmed. They are ellipsoid in shape and notable for their divided eyes which enables them to see both above and below water. They shone like platinum jewels on the surface of the water. Brilliant sight this! Baya Weaver (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) After the wide parikrama of the Gutta we walked back to our transportation, very satisfied with the day's birding. Or should I say day's blessing? The city sighs into silence. Streetlights spill their amber glow, dogs curl into quiet dreams, and even the breeze forgets to move. And then slicing through stillness comes a cry: “Brain-fever! Brain-fever! Brain-fever!” The Common Hawk Cuckoo has begun his aria. To the uninitiated, it is noise, maddening and insistent. But to those of us who watch birds, it is both familiar and oddly comforting, the call of summer nights, of restless passion, of seasons turning. For a birder, this isn’t disturbance. It’s a lullaby, if a slightly mischievous one. When Daytime Birds Dream Aloud Most birds tuck into quiet roosts at dusk, but some carry their songs into the darkness. Why?    Because love cannot tell time: Males sing even at midnight if their hormones demand it. Because the moon is a spotlight: Bright nights extend the stage. Because silence is a drum: With traffic gone, every note carries farther, echoing like ripples in water. The night, for these singers, is not for rest. It is for auditions. And we, the sleepless listeners, become their unwilling judges. The Indian Idol of the Night Close your eyes, and the darkness turns into a stage. The moon is the chandelier. The neem tree is the mic stand. The whole neighbourhood is the audience. And one by one, the contestants arrive. The Hawk Cuckoo: The Drama King He belts out brain-fever! with all the force of an Idol contestant convinced that volume equals victory. We, the jury, beg for mercy but he only grows louder, as though the stars themselves are his panel of judges. The Grey-Bellied Cuckoo: The Repeater His soft, plaintive pee-pip-pip-pip drifts through the air. Sweet at first, then endless. This is the contestant who sings one line again and again, until you wonder if the record is stuck. Yet there’s tenderness in it, like a child repeating a lullaby to soothe himself. The Indian Nightjar: The Scooter Beatboxer His chuk-chuk-chuk is the percussion section half-scooter, half-snare drum. For some, it is irritation. For birders, it is the rhythm of the countryside, the background score of countless summer nights. The Asian Koel: The Filmi Crooner Ah, the koel. Romantic, filmi, forever rehearsing for a Bollywood soundtrack. In the soft hours of dawn, his ku-oo is honey. At 3:00AM, it is karaoke that forgot to end. Yet, what birder doesn’t smile at his persistence? The Peacock: The Drama Queen With a piercing may-awe! the peacock enters, feathers hidden in the dark, voice echoing like a prince denied his throne. If there is an anthem for overacting, this is it. But oh, what joy to hear such royalty in the stillness of night. 9

The Hawk Cuckoo is the hero who will not stop singing. The Barn Owl: The Horror Artist Then comes the shriek: raw, chilling, unmistakable. For villagers, it is a ghost. For birders, it is simply Tyto alba, master of shadows. You listen, half laughing, half shuddering, as if the woods are whispering secrets too long kept from the sun. The Koel is the filmi lover who thinks every night is playback practice. The Peacock is the diva, the Owl the ghost, the Owlet the gossiping cousin. The Greater Coucal: The Bassline Coop-coop-coop, slowly, steadily, like the drumbeat that keeps the orchestra in sync. No drama, no fire, just a voice that grounds the night. Together, they are not noise. They are the theatre of night. When next you are woken at 2:00AM by a Hawk Cuckoo or a Koel, don’t bury your head in the pillows. Step out. Look at the moon. Breathe. Listen as a birder does: with patience, with humour, with wonder. The Spotted Owlet: The Gossip Queen And finally, the owlets chatter Chee-wee-wee! as though exchanging gossip under the banyan tree. Their chorus is playful, busy, endlessly curious. It feels less like music, more like a bedtime story told by children who refuse to sleep. Surrender to the rhythm of the Nightjar and the pleading cry of the Cuckoo, to the screeching Peacock and the shriek of an Owl. This is your lullaby: bizarre, ear-rending, hilarious, yet pulsingly alive. These nocturnal calls aren’t just sounds; they are memories woven into India’s cultural fabric:    And when you do fall unconscious, it will not be silence that holds you, but the ghosts of voices in the dark assuring you that the world is still awake, singing still, crammed with feathered tales. Farmers once waited for the Hawk Cuckoo to announce the rains. Poets gave the Koel to lovers, the Barn Owl to ghosts, the Peacock to gods. Naturalists like Salim Ali called the Hawk Cuckoo’s cry “hysterical.” Yet to birders, it is just summer’s signature tune. At last, dawn arrives. The Koel softens. The Owlets return to their hollows. The Hawk Cuckoo, spent, bows out. The orchestra hushes, the day-birds tune up their morning ragas. Each note is history, folklore, and biology rolled into one. To listen at night is to step into the same soundscape our grandparents once knew. For the birder, it feels like leaving a late-night concert: tired, amused, filled with stories. To a non-birder, these cries are chaos. But to us, they are a lullaby: not the gentle kind that rocks you to sleep, but the playful kind that keeps you awake with stories. And you realise: this wasn’t insomnia. It was a performance. A birder’s lullaby. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From Facebook, March 15, 2024) *** We wish all our members a very happy Deepawali 2025 10

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Velvet-fronted Nuthatch (Sitta frontalis) Velvet-fronted Nuthatch (Dandeli, Karnataka, October 31, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Passeriformes Sittidae Sitta S. frontalis 10 cm Least Concern Habitat & behaviour: The Velvet-fronted Nuthatch is a resident breeder in many types of forests, from deciduous to evergreen mangrove forest, secondary forests, and even coffee plantations. It is quite a noisy bird, and easily located by its sitsit-sit call. It has very strongly curved claws which enable it to work its way down vertical trees, unlike the woodpeckers that can only climb upwards. It moves jerkily up, down and around branches or trunks of trees, as it forages actively for spiders and other insects found under the bark of trees. It is usually seen in pairs or small groups, and also found quite often in mixed hunting parties. Description & distribution: The Velvet-fronted Nuthatch is a short-tailed bird with a relatively long, heavy pointed bill and strong feet. It is purplish blue above and greyish lilac below; it has a velvety, jet black forehead and lores, lavender cheeks and a whitish shin and throat. There is a prominent black superciliary stripe running above the eyes to the nape, which is lacking in the female. Bill and legs are bright red. Juvenile birds are duller versions of the adult, but without the black forehead. Nesting: The Velvet-fronted Nuthatch breeds between February and April in South India, and between April and June in North India. The nest is usually a tree hollow lined with leaves, moss, feathers and grass, with the mouth walled up with mud plaster, leaving a small, round entrance. Old woodpecker and barbet holes are also commonly utilized. The clutch usually consists of 3-6 white eggs, heavily speckled and blotched red or purplish. Incubation is done mainly by the female, but both parents participate in feeding duties. Five subspecies are recognised. The nominate is Sitta frontalis frontalis, of the central Indian and south Indian hill forests, Western & Eastern Ghats, and Sri Lanka; this includes the Himalayan population (although Hodgson proposed the name S. f. corallina for them). Besides, there is S. f. saturatior of the Malay Peninsula, including Penang, Singapore and Sumatra; S. f. velata of Java; S. f. corallipes of Borneo and S. f. palawana of Palawan and Balabac in the western Philippines. Local name: The Velvet-fronted Nuthatch is known as ‘Tandan kili’ in Malayalam, ‘Pasai edukira kuruvi’ (a bird that takes out gum/resin) in Tamil, ‘Siri’ in Hindi, ‘Makhmali siri’ (literally, velvety bird) in Marathi, and ‘Makhmali zad-chad’ in Gujarati. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 11 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 22 Number 12 November 2025 FIELD TRIP-1: Sunday, November 02, 2025, 7.00AM: Anna Sagar Lake, Jogipet. Meeting Point(s): Mangatrai Pearls, Punjagutta, 05:45AM; Taj Dhaba, Muthangi, 06:15AM. Coordinator(s): Srikanth Bhamidipati (Mobile: 97388-40070) Nestled near the Andole Jogipet area of Sangareddy District, Anna Sagar Lake is a scenic freshwater haven and a birding hotspot boasting 200+ species throughout the year. During winter, the lake transforms into a lively avian airport: Flamingos glide in gracefully, Avocets sweep the shallows, and Godwits probe the mudflats like professional foragers. Add in a chorus of ducks, sandpipers, stilts, and the occasional surprise migrant, and you have a birder’s paradise. The lake’s wide open basin, bordered by farmlands and gentle hills, makes for great viewing and photography. FIELD TRIP-2: Sunday, November 30, 2025, 6.00AM: Yenkathala Grasslands, Mominpet. Watch out for some spectacular avian residents and visitors, including raptors like Harriers and Eagles; ground birds like Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse, Rain Quail, Jungle Bush Quail, Rock Bush Quail, Barred Buttonquail and Painted Francolin; and forest and open country species like Black-headed Cuckooshrike, Tree Pipit, and Baya Weaver. SOJOURN FOR THE SABINE – AND OTHER SPLENDID SPECTACLES Trip Report: Nalsarovar, Gujarat, June 04-06, 2025 Text & Photos: Umesh Mani Sabine’s Gull There comes a time in the life of every birder, when he decides that enough is enough, and now he HAS to go birding. In fact, of late this sort of time seems to come more and more often, but that is another matter. 1

One such episode hit me a couple of months back. We had just shifted back to our apartment, and all the incomplete tasks were driving me up the wall. Add to that the Chennai heat, some health issues in the family, and the fact that I had had to drop out of a long-awaited trip to Munsiyari – to cut a long story short, I was desperate to get out, even if it was just a couple of days. I settled down to wait, hoping that the bird would grant me a closer audience. Within a few minutes, my wish came true! Taking off from the rock and making a few lazy circles in the air, it came and landed in the water pretty close to where I was sitting and, a minute later, walked out of the water on to the shore. Fortuitously, right at this time came the reports of a Sabine’s Gull being sighted at Nalsarovar in Gujarat. This was apparently only the second time that this bird had been seen in India, the last being a record from Kerala in 2012. So obviously, it was extremely rare in India. And Nalsarovar is easy to get to, being just a 1.5 hour drive from Ahmedabad. So the call was made, tickets were booked, and off I went. Just for the record, in all my 20 years of birding, never once have I gone after – or ‘twitched’, in birder’s parlance – a single species like this. Locally, sure, but never out of town. So it was quite an uncharacteristic thing for me. Some friends, in fact, thought that I was going for some other purpose and just not telling them the truth! Anyway. Reaching Ahmedabad in the afternoon, I drove straight to Nalsarovar and met up with the guide. With vagrant bird sightings like this, it is not just the mystery of how it landed up here – there is also the uncertainty of how long it will stay! After all, it may very well decide to move somewhere else at any moment. And in this case, the Sabine’s Gull had been around for a week to ten days already. Hence, the guide was also a little jittery, and told me that we should go straight to Nalsarovar Lake and at least see the bird once – he did not even give me the time for a cup of tea! But I appreciated his keenness to ensure I did not miss the bird, so we drove directly to Nalsarovar Lake. Sabine’s Gull It walked around, unconcerned by the 8-10 people who were sitting around – or lying around! – waiting for closer photographs. After about 20 minutes, it suddenly took off, possibly startled by a stray dog that had wandered up there. But it came back soon enough, giving more photo ops. And there it was! When I reached there, around 4:00PM, it was sitting on a small rock in the water, about 20-25m away from the lake shore. After seeing it through the binoculars, and taking a few record shots, we relaxed. It was quite a thrill, to be honest, to see one of the rarest birds reported from India – only the second time, as I mentioned earlier. Whiskered Tern There were a few other birders also there, all waiting for a better view. I was informed by the guide that nearly a hundred people had visited Nalsarovar in the past few days to see this bird, and that the bird was nevertheless very cooperative, possibly used to human presence back wherever it came from. Also, that it seemed to be sticking to one small area – the rock I mentioned earlier, the waters near the rock, and a small patch of lake shore – it seemed to be shuttling between just these places. That naturally made it easier for everyone to see and photograph the bird. Marsh Sandpiper 2

Black-winged Stilt with catch Alongside them was a whole bunch of Egrets, comprising of Little, Medium and a lone Western Reef Egret with a few Black-headed Ibises. Red-wattled Lapwing While waiting, I took a look around for other birds, and saw a few: a couple of Whiskered Terns, a foraging Marsh Sandpiper, a Red-wattled Lapwing randomly flying around, a few Little Grebes in breeding finery, and a few Black-winged Stilts. Mixed flock of Medium, Little and Western Reef Egrets with Black-headed Ibis The Egrets foraged in the water, picking up some morsels, as did the Sandpiper. One of the Little Egrets strutted around, seeming particularly proud of his breeding plumage! Little Grebe in breeding plumage Non-breeding Little Grebe Little Egret in breeding plumage A flock of around 20 Glossy Ibises flew past in the distance. There was also a Blue-tailed Bee-eater in non-breeding plumage which turned out to be actually a Green Bee-eater with some marked blue wash on its underparts! 3

Green Bee-eater Grey Heron The Sabine’s Gull came back to shore, and I spent some time watching and photographing it. Although predominantly black, white and grey like most Gulls, it IS a beautiful bird. The black bill has a striking yellow tip, which really stood out against the blue of the water and the green of the grass. Western Reef Egret Sabine’s Gull with catch Suddenly, I noticed a big black-and-white bird come flying across – a Woolly-necked Stork. It was nice to see this bird, because we don’t really see them too often – but imagine my excitement when I realized that it was actually a group of 4 of them! Glossy Ibis flock A Grey Heron, a Western Reef Egret and another large group of Glossy Ibises flew past, reminding me that roosting time was approaching. We therefore, decided to wind up and move back for a badly needed cup of tea, and then on to the hotel. Day-2 We had decided to come back to the Sabine’s Gull for another look in morning light – but there was some other birding to be done first. Accordingly, we made an early start and went to a spot that had a lot of reeds. The guide had told me, “Yahan par Bittern milta hai”. Woolly-necked Stork A small group of Black-headed Ibises, including a couple of juveniles, joined the Egrets, foraging near a bunch of beached fishing boats – presumably there were enough fingerlings discarded by the fishermen for the birds to feed on at that spot. That turned out to be the understatement of the trip – in the next half hour, we saw 6 Yellow Bitterns (including one juvenile), 2 Cinnamon Bitterns and 3 Black Bitterns (including a juvenile)! 4

Other notable sightings were a Clamorous Reed Warbler with a catch, two beautiful Black-breasted Weavers, and an overflying Eurasian Spoonbill. Yellow Bittern juvenile Clamorous Reed Warbler Cinnamon Bittern Black-breasted Weaver After that, it was time to head to the lake. En route, we saw a few Jungle Babblers squabbling, and a few birds on the wires – a couple of Pied Kingfishers, an Indian Roller, a few Green Bee-eaters, and so on. Black Bittern juvenile At the lake, the Sabine’s Gull was there, nicely settled on the rock, and so were about 20 birders/photographers on the shore. Like yesterday, the Gull made a few warm-up flights and went back to the rock a few times, before finally deciding to come to this side of the shore. As the Gull foraged around and had its fill, so did the shutterbugs. River Tern Black Bittern 5

Pied Kingfisher Red-naped Ibis Besides the Sabine’s Gull, many of the birds seen yesterday were still around – Woolly-necked Stork, Little and Medium Egrets, Pied Kingfishers – and one addition to the list, a River Tern. We don’t get them very often around Chennai, so I enjoyed watching it as it wheeled around for a few seconds before moving on. The Little Egrets showed off their fishing skills, and a Pheasant-tailed Jacana in flight also made for a nice sight. Black-winged Stilt chick Pheasant-tailed Jacana I now wanted to catch some birding outside the lake area – and some breakfast! – so we started off. The grassy areas around the lake gave close-up views of some common species – Eurasian Collared Dove, Ashy-crowned Sparrowlark, Rednaped Ibis and so on. Outside, at a patch of water, we saw a Black-winged Stilt chick walking around alone. Just as we were wondering why it was alone, one parent turned up – and flew off again, chasing away a Red-wattled Lapwing that ventured too close. Over the next few minutes, we saw the Stilt parent do this repeatedly. How tough it must be to constantly stay alert to such threats! Back near the sanctuary entrance, the guide told us about another patch that had some terns. We decided to go and take a look. This involved a 1-1.5km walk in the hot sun over burning sand, and a short walk through a slushy pond. Nevertheless, the guide assured us that it would be worth it. Eurasian Collared Dove Purple Heron immature 6

River Tern with Whiskered and Little Terns Little and Indian Cormorants And was it! The first thing we saw, besides a couple of breeding Pheasant-tailed Jacanas and an immature Purple Heron, was a bare tree packed with around 50 Little & Indian Cormorants, followed immediately by a flock of around 200 Greater Flamingos. Slender-billed Gull A pair of Little Terns engaged in courtship feeding – it was interesting to watch the male bring a small fish and delicately place it into the bill of the female. Greater Flamingo We saw a Kentish Plover nest with 3 eggs inside and the parents nowhere in sight, but we moved on quickly nevertheless. Little Tern courtship feeding A Collared Pratincole flew around and gave great views until it settled down and began to preen. And we finally saw the bird we had been waiting for – the White-winged Tern. River Tern juvenile The first sandbar held 20-odd River Terns, mostly in breeding plumage; around 30 Whiskered Terns, also in breeding plumage; and assorted Glossy Ibises, Painted Storks and Egrets. 3 Slender-billed Gulls were seen floating in the water. A White-winged Tern in full breeding plumage had been sighted from here recently, but unfortunately, it seemed to have moved away somewhere in the days prior, and no one had sighted it in the past couple of days – so we had to satisfy ourselves with a non-breeding individual. But it was a beautiful specimen, with the characteristic black stripe looping around its eye. 7

Indian Common Clubtail Ictinogomphus rapax White-winged Tern A Kentish Plover in breeding plumage was also interesting to see. It had been a frenetic, action-packed period of ‘Tern-ing’, but after baking in the sun for an hour plus, we were ready to get back. Accordingly, we packed up, met the Flamingos and Cormorants again as we trudged back, and headed off to the hotel. Kentish Plover in breeding plumage Sarus Crane The evening session started only by 04:30PM, which I felt was quite late, but the guide assured me that there would be plenty of time to bird. The first bird we saw was a lone Sarus Crane, quietly foraging a few metres from the highway, and I wondered where its partner was. Right after that we saw a Woolly-necked Stork, again pretty close. Dancing Dropwing Trithemis pallidinervis Woolly-necked Stork 8

Rufous-tailed Lark As soon as we reached our target patch, we saw a pair of Rufous-tailed Larks. They kept foraging, unconcerned at our presence. After watching them for a few minutes, we moved ahead and came to a small pond which held a good number of Egrets. One, strangely, had its head stuck inside the water for so long that we started feeling maybe it was dead! After nearly a minute, however, it pulled its head out, leaving us wondering what it had been up to. Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse female with chick We circled around to get a better view of the Sandgrouse family, and were able to get some photographs. It was wonderful to see how the chick would sidle and hide under the parent when they were nearby. But even otherwise, they would freeze, squat on the grass, and basically disappear! – if not for the sharp eyes of the guide, I wonder if I would have ever been able to locate the chicks at all. Little Egret We moved ahead, and came upon a Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse family – parents with 2 chicks. The chicks looked so different! The guide informed me that many birds had just completed breeding for the season, and we were likely to see more birds with chicks. That kindled my anticipation! Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse chick Just for the record, to avoid stressing out the birds, these photos were taken without getting down from the car, and from a safe distance with an 800mm lens! There were many small groups of Ashy-crowned Sparrowlarks on the ground – we estimated at least 50 of them – and a Delicate Prinia sang with great vigour from a bush top. Common Babbler A Common Babbler inside a huge thorny bush presented a striking picture. Delicate Prinia 9

Another Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse family had 3 chicks – this time, the chicks were bigger. We even saw one of them having a dust bath! A Small Buttonquail popped out of a bush just as we were driving past it, and ambled around, did a wing stretch – all too close for me to focus! That was so frustrating – the only other time I had seen it earlier, many years back, it was for about 0.2 seconds as it flew across a path in a field! We knew the chick would be somewhere in the vicinity, so we refrained from going any closer. Scanning the ground through the binoculars for the chick proved in vain – all I could find was broken eggshells. But the guide, of course, was able to locate the chick, and pointed it out to me. So well was it camouflaged that even with his directions, it took me a while to spot it, scrunched down next to a small plant – a cute little ball of fluff. Fortunately, it was comfortable walking around, and slowly moved into focusing range, so that I was able to get some photographs. A few minutes later, I realized that there was actually a pair! Collared Pratincole chick Small Buttonquail female We were there for barely a minute, but the parent put on a display to distract us. I couldn’t make up my mind whether it was a broken-wing display or a display of aggression, since the bird had both wings extended. Also, instead of moving away, it actually took a few steps towards us. This made me feel that it was probably an aggression display. Small Buttonquail male Collared Pratincole aggression display To avoid stressing it out, we quickly moved away and around, and put some more distance between us. Parking a little further distance away, we switched off the vehicle and settled down to watch, hoping to see some parent-chick interaction. Unfortunately that did not happen – presumably the parent was still watchful – so we moved away from there. We found another individual a little distance away, and were able to take a few good photographs. A little later, we spotted another chick crouched down on an open path – it probably saw us before we saw it! Collared Pratincole adult We watched them for a while as they went about foraging in the grass. Then we decided to move to another spot where the guide had earlier seen a bird with a chick – and as soon as we got there, there it was – a Collared Pratincole! By now, the light was beginning to fade, so we decided to wind up for the day. As we left, we saw a Paddyfield Pipit carrying what initially looked like a bagworm but later turned out to be some other insect, and a Red-necked Falcon sitting on a pylon – with a kill! 10

Day-3 We started the day with an excellent view of a Black Bittern followed by a juvenile Yellow Bittern, a pair of Black-breasted Weavers and a Striated Heron beautifully silhouetted against the rising sun. Cattle Egret in breeding plumage Striated Heron A juvenile Black Bittern was seen hiding amongst the reeds, another adult Black Bittern gave great views and a pair was briefly seen. Clearly, the Bitterns were thriving at this place. The commonest of birds, a Cattle Egret, looked beautiful in its breeding plumage, complete with pink bill base. With not much time available today – I was to return to Chennai in the afternoon – we decided to go to an area where raptors were supposed to be seen quite often. We saw a juvenile Spiny-tailed Lizard peeping out of its burrow, and the guide told me that this area usually had plenty of these lizards, which is why many raptors liked to drop in here. Spiny-tailed Lizard juvenile Black Bittern juvenile We were not so lucky today, though – not a single raptor turned up. There were a few more of the Lizards though. So I kept busy looking for and trying to photograph them and, over the next couple of hours, managed to get some decent shots of the adult and juvenile Spiny-tailed Lizards. Greater Coucal A handful of Black-breasted Weavers chased each other inside a bunch of reeds. In an adjacent field I saw a group of 4-5 Greater Coucals together, a very unusual sight. Unfortunately, by the time we could stop the car and find a gap in the bushes through which to photograph them, they had all but vanished. Spiny-tailed Lizard adult 11

Finally, around 09:30AM, we decided to start moving back. On the way we saw a couple of White-eared Bulbuls perched on a bush close to the road – strangely, a bird I had not photographed at all over the first 2 days. Grey Francolin family There were a couple of interesting sidelights: A family of Grey Francolins, comprising two adults and five not-so-small chicks, ambled across. And an Indian Courser suddenly turned up and walked around for a while, giving us some excellent views, before taking off. Sarus Crane pair Back on the highway, we spied a pair of Sarus Cranes foraging. Although we were running a little late, one cannot ignore the Sarus! – so we stopped to take a few photographs. Suddenly, the male threw its head back, courtship style, and let out a loud call – and the female did the same! I am not sure how accurate this is, but I had been told that while both partners participate in the courtship dance, it is only the male that calls. So it seemed quite unusual to see the female also calling. Indian Courser Anyway, that was it for the moment. What a way to close the trip! Keeping that in mind, I made my way back to the hotel and thence to the airport for my return flight. Though it had been a whirlwind couple of days, I was quite happy that I had managed to capture some really nice memories. Text and Photos: Gokul Krishna Addanki Indian Courser Our June Deccan Birders outing, led by Srikanth B on Sunday, June 29, 2025, took us to the Yenkathala grasslands. It is a place that always holds such promise for birding, yet lately, it’s also a poignant reminder of the relentless march of development, with mining and real estate interests encroaching on this vital habitat. This grassland, as our eBird checklists collectively show, is home to a remarkable close to 140 bird species1, many of them grassland species whose very existence depends on these open spaces that are rapidly shrinking. 13

The morning began, as most birding days do, with a sense of anticipation. The weather was a mix of cloudy skies and welcome bursts of sun, with a hint of rain in the air – perfect for observation. Even before the dramatic events that unfolded, Yenkathala was already showing off. Among the other birds, we were particularly thrilled to spot multiple Indian Courser chicks, tiny bundles of camouflage, scuttling across the grass with their watchful adults nearby. We managed to get a few precious clicks of them. Then, around 9:10 AM, as we were winding down our initial foray, something caught our eye. A House Crow was acting rather strangely, hopping around with something small in its beak. Both House Crows and Jungle Crows share this habitat, but the distinct size and coloration, clearly visible even from a distance, confirmed this was a House Crow. was an Indian Nightjar. The chick itself looked barely a day or two old, no bigger than the crow's beak, and its bones appeared visibly undeveloped in the images. Indian Nightjars, as many of us know, aren't nest-builders in the traditional sense; they lay their eggs directly in small depressions on the ground, often among grass, rocks, or bushes. While we had noted a potential nesting spot nearby, confirming it as the nest is always difficult without nesting material. Observing their breeding behaviour, especially at the nest site, is exceptionally rare since they are primarily nocturnal. The crow, it seemed, wasn't yet done. After the first chick, it proceeded to pick up another one, equally tiny and vulnerable, before flying off. The entire incident, from start to finish, unfolded in about five minutes. It left us with a swirl of emotions – a deep sadness for the nightjar parents, yet also that stark realization that this is, indeed, life in the wild. No alarm calls from other birds were heard, our group's collective focus completely riveted by the drama. House Crow with prey (Indian Nightjar chick) What followed was quite a sight, and genuinely unsettling. The crow began toying with its catch, tossing it up in the air. My immediate thought was that it would tear the prey apart. But to my surprise, after a few tosses and twitches, it simply gulped the entire object whole. It was a moment of stunned silence for our group. We couldn't quite make out what the crow had consumed until, moments later, it suddenly shooed away an adult bird that flew up from the very spot. White-eyed Buzzard adult Despite the initial shock, we knew Yenkathala had more to reveal, so we continued our birding for another 30-40 minutes in the area. Our perseverance paid off – we were treated to excellent sightings of White-eyed Buzzards. We watched two flying low, keenly scanning the ground, with another one perching on nearby rocks, clearly on a morning hunt. House Crow with Indian Nightjar chick as the adult flies helplessly away Looking back at the photo I managed to capture – the one showing the crow with its meal and that adult bird taking flight in the same frame – we realized, with a sad certainty, that it White-eyed Buzzard juvenile 14

Later, we were thrilled to see a juvenile White-eyed Buzzard mirroring its elders, and were even lucky enough to witness it expertly catch and consume a dragonfly right near our vehicle. These raptors are incredibly sensitive, so we were extra cautious not to step out of the car, understanding that any sudden human presence could easily send them soaring away. Our continued observations added many more species to our trip list. The vibrant Blue-tailed Bee-eaters were striking, with three individuals perched gracefully on a dry tree2. A Whitebrowed Bulbul was seen on a mound, also quite unusual. The familiar calls of the Oriental Skylark rang through the air, with two individuals observed, a clear sign of healthy grassland. Grey-breasted Prinia This intense encounter served as a powerful reminder of the vulnerabilities faced by ground-nesting birds in habitats like Yenkathala. With increasing human encroachment, including mining and real estate development, these open/dry grasslands – critical for species like the Indian Courser, Little Ringed Plover, various larks, nightjars, and lapwings – are shrinking. Such disturbances can inadvertently expose nests and young, making them more susceptible to predation. White-browed Bulbul We noted a lone Rufous-tailed Lark, perfectly at home in this dry, open landscape. A well-camouflaged Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse offered a brief but satisfying glimpse, and a Black Drongo held its prominent perch. Several Grey-breasted Prinias were seen, and even a magnificent Indian Peafowl graced us with its presence, adding a touch of splendour to our morning. Our eBird checklist for the day captured a rich total of 43 species (+1 other taxa) during our focused observation. Documentations like this, though difficult to witness, are crucial for maintaining records of such rare behaviours, which are indeed a fundamental part of the life cycle for these birds. More importantly, this experience underscores a vital conservation message for all members: It is crucial to not drive into open grasslands for birdwatching. Many species lay their eggs directly in the grass. Hence I would urge everyone to keep vehicles strictly to defined paths and explore other areas on foot, always with keen observation of the ground to avoid disturbing potential nests or eggs. This mindful approach is essential to help protect these vulnerable species in their precious habitats such as Yenkathala. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Blue-eared Kingfisher (Alcedo meninting) Blue-eared Kingfisher (Thattekad, Kerala, October 02, 2017) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Coraciiformes Alcedinidae Alcedo A. meninting 17 cm Least Concern and Indochina; A. a. phillipsi, seen in south-western India and Sri Lanka; A. a. scintillans, seen in southern Myanmar and Thailand, and A. a. rufigastra, seen in the Andaman Islands. Habitat & behaviour: The Blue-eared Kingfisher prefers dense shaded forests with small streams which form its main hunting grounds; it is also seen around pools and creeks in subtropical or tropical moist lowland forest and mangroves, inland wetlands, permanent or seasonal rivers/streams/creeks; estuaries and plantations. It is usually seen below the altitude of 1,000m. It perches on branches overhanging the forest streams or pools, where it dives to capture its prey. Its diet mainly consists of crustaceans, dragonfly larvae, and fish; it is also known to pick insects, including grasshoppers and mantids. Its flight is fast, direct and low over the water, with the short wings whirring rapidly. Description & distribution: The Blue-eared Kingfisher is a small kingfisher that is distributed across the Indian subcontinent (Himalayan foothills, North-eastern, Eastern and South-western parts of India), Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, and in many parts of Indochina and south-east Asia. It has the typical short-tailed, large-headed kingfisher structure: dark cobalt blue upperparts, rich rufous underparts, bright orange legs, and a large bill which is all black in the adult male and two-toned (dark upper and reddish lower mandible) in the adult female. It has an orange spot in front of the eye, white ear tufts on the sides of the neck, and a prominent skyblue ‘river’ down the centre of the back. It is differentiated from the similar-looking Common Kingfisher by its blue ear patch (which is rufous in Common Kingfisher). Juvenile birds are similar but show a rufous ear patch (like the Common), but can be told apart by the mottling on throat and upper breast. The bill is also reddish with whitish tips. Several subspecies are recognized: The race A. a. meninting, seen in the Malay peninsula, Borneo, southern Philippines and some parts of Indonesia, is the nominate; the other subspecies are A. a. coltarti, seen in Nepal, north-eastern India, northern Thailand Nesting: The Blue-eared Kingfisher breeds mainly between May and June in northern India and January in south-western India. The nest is usually a one-metre long tunnel in the bank of a forest stream, and the usual clutch consists of 5-7 white, almost spherical eggs. Local name: The Blue-eared Kingfisher is known as ‘Chhota kilkila’ in Hindi, ‘Chhota machhera’ in Punjabi, a‘Ponnan kuruvi’ in Tamil, ‘Podi ponman’ in Malayalam and ‘Neela buchigadu’ in Telugu. (All these names are also applicable to the Common Kingfisher). *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 22 Number 13 December 2025 FIELD TRIP-1: Sunday, December 14, 2025, 6.30AM: Mokila. Meeting Point(s): Morine Bakery, Narsingi, 06:00AM. Coordinator(s): Sathwik Reddy (Mobile: 99858-07186) Mokila is a dry-deciduous scrub habitat which holds a rich birding. This place serves as an important habitat for various bird species due to its diverse environments. The combination of agricultural areas and water bodies not only enhances its ecological richness but also makes it a significant spot for birdwatching enthusiasts. Birdwatchers visiting Mokila are encouraged to maintain an ethological approach to observing and documenting the avifauna.
