Trip Report: Birding in Zurich, Switzerland, September 14-18, 2025 Text & Photos: Dr Krishna Nagarajan View from the hotel window in Baden, Zurich A couple of months back, a work requirement took me to Baden, a suburb of Zurich, Switzerland. Usually, I look forward to such trips as they help break the monotony and expand my world view. However, this time around, I had just recovered from Chikungunia and was still under the severe grip of the arthritis flare-up that comes as an aftermath. So my goal was to primarily focus on the business meetings and if my health was up to it, do some basic trekking/birding (besides the famous Swiss banks, Zurich is also known for its diverse trekking options). 1

Fearing backlash from my family, I decided it was best to not divulge my plan for extra-curricular activities during the trip. I stealthily packed my Nikon bridge camera and a generous supply of Crocin Pain Relief tablets. The weather in Zurich during the month of September is somewhat similar to our early winter months in Hyderabad. There is daylight all the way up to 8:30-9:00PM in the evening, giving plenty of outdoor time to explore after business hours. I checked into my hotel around 4:00PM and, when I looked outside the window, the view was surreal. It was a blend of the old and the new – there were green hills in the distance, old and new style buildings, a metro train running on a bridge, lots of trees and shrubs nearby, the Limmat river, and a lamp post! available. The Limmat River stream was flowing within a few meters from the hotel and there was a trail along the stream. I decided to explore the trail. Should I go left or right? There was no sign of any humans on either side of the track. As if to help me arrive at an answer, three Mallards flew by towards my right – so right it was! After walking for about 500 meters, I ran into a bund. I first noticed the familiar Grey Heron sitting on a sign board along the embankment. There were several Eurasian Coots and Mallards (males, females, and some juveniles) swimming in the water. Given my health condition, I thought how nice it would be if all the birds just came one by one and sat on the lamp post – I know that was a big ask but in my defense, I was barely walking and I was not familiar with the local birds. I needed to take their pictures to be able to identify and study them offline. A Common Raven came and sat on the lamp post as if to pacify me! I also managed to sight a Common Redstart and a Garden Warbler from the hotel window. Grey Heron Common Raven Red Kite Western Reef Egret The next day, after completing my business meetings, I scanned e-Bird to check what I can expect to see in and around the hotel I was staying at. Surprisingly there were no listings Eurasian Moorhen adult 2

Common Chaffinch Common Pochard A Red Kite was hovering in the sky. I crossed the bund and continued walking slowly along the trail. I noticed Common Pochard, Eurasian Moorhen, and Common Merganser along the way. A sign post showed 19km to Zurich downtown. I realized that this is a long trail and I can’t keep walking. At some point I need to turn back and head to the hotel. I noticed a Common Chaffinch further down the trail and decided to walk some more. I also spotted another bird, about the size of Common Myna, dark brownish in color with some striations on the head and neck, nestled among the red berries on a tree branch. I could not recognize immediately, but was able to take nice pictures. Later, I found out that this was the female Eurasian Blackbird. Poster showing the birds of the Limmat River After a few hundred meters, I noticed a sign board along the bank. It had pictures of birds along with their names in their local language (probably German). I was delighted – I am walking along a trail which seems to be popular for bird watching! Eurasian Blackbird female I was exhausted and decided it was time to turn back to the hotel. It was around 7:30PM, but the evening sun was still shining brightly. I decided to relax a bit on the bench overlooking the river stream. A pair of Mallards and a Little Grebe were swimming slowly along the bank and within a couple of meters from the bench where I was sitting. Yellow-legged Gull I limped along with vigour further down the trail. In the middle of the stream, I noticed a Yellow-legged Gull with a carcass of what looked like a Mallard. It was a large Gull, but could it have preyed upon the Mallard? I don’t know. Mallard male 3

Mallard female The female Mallard came out of the water and started slowly walking towards me. I was not expecting this. My brain became silent but my amygdala started processing – flight or fight? In an alien country, I am sitting alone on a bench along a trail with no other humans in sight. A skirmish with an avian is not an engagement I need in my current condition. But on the other hand, it's just a Mallard – definitely not going to bite. I sat still and our eyes were locked. I sensed grace in its eyes as it continued walking towards me. Then it occurred to me that it may be expecting me to offer some food! Eurasian Blue Tit On the way back to the hotel, I ran into a juvenile Eurasian Moorhen and the Grey Heron was still hanging around near the bund. It was probably used to people feeding food and was comfortable enough to approach me without fear. It was disappointed when I had nothing to offer and walked back to the stream. Eurasian Moorhen juvenile On my day off, I decided to explore Zurich downtown. Most downtowns usually have a lake or a river flowing through. As we have our own Hussainsagar Lake, downtown Zurich has Lake Zurich from which the Limmat River flows out and passes by Baden, where my hotel was located. Several parks and trails were located around the lake, and e-Bird showed a good count of birds that can be sighted. Great Cormorant immature I sat there for some more time and noticed some movement on the walnut tree nearby. I could not spot the bird, but decided to take a picture where I saw some movement. Later, I was elated when I noticed that the picture actually captured a Eurasian Blue Tit sandwiched between two walnut fruits! House Sparrow male 4

House Sparrow female Eurasian Blackbird male I started walking through the parks from the Southern side of the lake. I immediately saw a bunch of House Sparrows hopping around. A bit further, I ran into a flock of Blue Rock Pigeons. One of the birds in this flock stood out in its plumage and at first I thought it was a different bird. Later I realized it was a melanistic Blue Rock Pigeon – it had a dark bluish color all around. White Wagtail I then spotted the Carrion Crow, Common Wood Pigeon, European Robin, Eurasian Blackbird (male), and the White Wagtail. Melanistic Blue Rock Pigeon Herring Gull adult Common Wood Pigeon Herring Gull juvenile 5

Black-headed Gull Red-crested Pochard male I moved around and reached closer to the lake shore to find the Great and Little Cormorants, Herring and Black-headed Gulls, and a juvenile Eurasian Coot. I was surprised at how different the juvenile Coot looked and the transformation it would undergo when it becomes an adult. The juvenile had a yelloworangish beak, white plumage on the face, chest, and had dark black eyes. On reaching adulthood, it would become completely black with just a white patch on the forehead and reddish eyes. And then the feet – did you ever notice the beautiful pattern in an adult's feet? Red-crested Pochard female I walked along the shore and cleared all the tourist yachts that were lined up. In the middle of the lake, I found the Redcrested Pochard, a pair of Mute Swans, and the Great Crested Grebe. in a metal cage, these birds will fly in the open blue sky. Envious? You bet! Great Crested Grebe non-breeding There were several Eurasian Coots and Mallards as well. I picked up a cup of coffee and settled down to recharge. Within the next few weeks winter will settle in and most of these birds will start migrating to the South – maybe some of them will travel all the way to our neighbourhood. Spanning nearly 3,500 hectares, this dry deciduous forest is a mosaic of rocky outcrops and ponds – a favourite destination for birders seeking both forest and wetland species. Journey and Weather The convoy started early from Hyderabad, with participants joining at Punjagutta and Dindigul AFS points. The drive was refreshing, and as always, troops of monkeys lining the roadside signalled the beginning of the Narsapur forest stretch. The day was pleasantly cool and crisp after recent rains, lending the forest a fresh, earthy scent and adding sparkle to the morning light filtering through the canopy. Forest Trail — Medalamma Temple Side The group’s first stop was near the Medalamma Temple area, where the forest slowly came alive with the dawn chorus. A much-awaited moment for many was the sighting of the Jerdon’s Leafbird – high on the wish list of several birders visiting this region. There she was, perched beautifully and calling persistently. Cameras clicked in unison as the bright green bird posed amidst the foliage. Though the light was subdued, the Leafbird’s repeated, liquid calls became one of the most memorable sounds of the morning. 7

that natural clearing surrounded by trees turned into a perfect observation point. As the rising sun illuminated dried branches, birds emerged from their roosts – Rose-ringed and Plum-headed Parakeets, Indian White-eyes, Indian Golden Orioles, and Green Bee-eaters among them. Jerdon’s Leafbird Soon, the birding trail deepened into the forest canopy, and activity picked up. Woodpeckers provided a delightful show – both the Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker and Yellowcrowned Woodpecker were seen energetically drilling into bark in search of insects. The rhythmic tapping echoed softly through the trees. Indian Golden Oriole male After a hearty birding session, the group began walking back. As we began to retrace our steps, the morning light grew softer, and the forest seemed to wake up anew. It was then that the migrants began to make their presence felt. A flash of turquoise blue announced the arrival of the Verditer Flycatcher, its vivid plumage glistening even in the gentle shade – a sure sign that the winter migrants are arriving in the Deccan. Spotted Dove The usual forest regulars soon followed – Jungle Babbler flocks, Red-vented Bulbuls, Spotted Doves, Indian Paradiseflycatchers, and Tickell’s Blue Flycatchers darting among sunlit branches. The White-browed Bulbul, often heard but seldom seen, kept challenging birders to spot it among the dense canopy with its teasing calls. Verditer Flycatcher Plum-headed Parakeet female Recent rains had left the forest floor moist, and a large water body had formed midway, gently limiting our movement. Yet, Asian Brown Flycatcher 8

Nearby, the Asian Brown Flycatcher, more modestly attired in soft browns and greys, made quick sallies from its perch to catch insects mid-air. The contrast between these visiting flycatchers and our familiar Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher, with its rich orange breast and indigo-blue head, was striking – a reminder of the seasonal rhythm that brings new life and colour to Narsapur’s canopies each year. Common Kingfisher Overall Experience The Narsapur field trip beautifully combined the quiet charm of forest birding with the liveliness of wetland activity. While the signs of habitat change were unmistakable near the lake, the forest still offered moments of calm and wonder that every birder cherishes – the rhythmic call of the Leafbird, the steady hammering of Woodpeckers, and the sight of kingfishers and terns slicing through the air. It was a deeply satisfying outing, reminding everyone of both the rich biodiversity that surrounds Hyderabad and the responsibility to preserve it. Indian Grey Hornbill To cap the morning, an Indian Grey Hornbill made a majestic appearance, perched openly for everyone to enjoy before gliding away into the trees. Towards Narsapur Lake After the forest trail, the group moved towards the Narsapur Lake area, which lies closer to the town. Here, the contrast between nature and encroaching urbanization was stark. The once-wooded stretch along the road, with its ancient temple ruins, has now been largely cleared. Fencing and signs of an Eco-Park were visible – a reminder of changing landscapes and the delicate balance between conservation and development. Small Minivet male Despite this, the lake itself, rejuvenated by recent rains, offered a serene sight. The expanded waters gave a sense of its true scale and former glory. The group sat quietly on the banks for a while, watching birds and monkeys going about their morning routines. One of the most memorable moments here was witnessing a River Tern diving sharply to catch a fish, only to be chased mid-air by another tern trying to snatch the catch – a thrilling display of skill and survival. Along the banks, White-throated and Common Kingfishers, Little Cormorants, Little Egrets, Grey Herons, and Ashy Woodswallows completed the lake’s avian ensemble. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Heart-spotted Woodpecker (Hemicircus canente) Heart-spotted Woodpecker Pair (L) (Dandeli, October 31, 2024) & Female (R) (Thattekad, Kerala, September 30, 2017) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Piciformes Picidae Hemicircus H. canente 16 cm Least Concern particularly dense and wet areas with bamboo and teak, although it is also seen in drier forests. It is easily identified by its oversized head on a stubby body, and its tendency to frequently call while foraging also makes it easy to locate. It typically forages in pairs or small groups, flying from tree to tree in sharp, short flights, and may also join mixed hunting parties. Its main diet consists of invertebrates and other insects like ants, grubs and termites that it picks up from under the bark of thin outer branches, although it is also known to probe Cassia fistula pods for insect larvae. The calls include a twangy ki-yeww, a sharp twee-twee-twee trilling call which sometimes leads to a duet of several notes, and a series of susee calls. Description & distribution: The Heart-spotted Woodpecker is a small woodpecker that is widely distributed across large parts of Asia, including south-western and central India, the Himalayas, and east into Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. Northern birds are slightly larger in size than the ones closer to the equator. It has a slightly top-heavy appearance, with a large crest that makes the head look too large for its small body and short rounded tail. Both male and female are predominantly black, with heart-shaped black spots on their white shoulders that give the bird its name. They also have broad white scapular patches and barring on flight feathers. The forehead and crown is buff on the female, and black with small white spots on the male. It has a white throat and dark grey underparts. It is a monotypic species – no subspecies are recognized: H. c. cordatus, described by TC Jerdon from the Western Ghats, is not considered distinct. Nesting: The Heart-spotted Woodpecker breeds mainly between November and April. The nest is usually a 3-4cm hole in a dead tree, with the tunnel sloping down about 20cm before it widens into a chamber. The usual clutch consists of 2-3 unmarked white eggs. Local name: The Heart-spotted Woodpecker is known as ‘Shyamdil lakkad khod’ or ‘Tapkilo lakkadkhod’ in Gujarati, ‘Pulli maramkotti’ or ‘Chitranghan’ in Malayalam and ‘Badami thipkyancha sutarpakshi’ in Marathi. It is also sometimes referred to as the Shakespeare Bird or Sweetheart in birding circles. Habitat & behaviour: The Heart-spotted Woodpecker prefers tropical or subtropical moist lowland and foothill forests *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 11 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. The habitat of Rudrur Lake is a mosaic of open shallow water, marshy edges, and vegetated margins. Exposed mudflats and damp shorelines become important feeding grounds for small shorebirds like waders and stints. Surrounding farmlands, scrub patches, and uncultivated fields further enhance the habitat by providing additional foraging areas and safe roosting sites, particularly for ducks, geese, and passerines. Although Rudrur Lake is not formally designated as a bird sanctuary, it is locally recognised by birdwatchers as an important wintering and stopover site. The lake attracts a diverse assemblage of waterfowl and wetland birds, especially during the winter migration period, when migratory species arrive from Eurasian and Central Asian flyways. Notable species to watch for include Greylag Goose, Comb Duck, Little Stint, Eurasian Teal, Northern Pintail, Northern Shoveler, Eurasian Wigeon, and Lesser Whistling Duck, among others. The seasonal nature of the lake, coupled with its strategic location among regional wetlands, supports high avian diversity and makes Rudrur a rewarding site for winter birding in inland Telangana. WHERE SKY MEETS WINGS AND WILDERNESS Trip Report: Bhigwan, October-November 2025 Text & Photos: N Shiva Kumar Short-toed Snake Eagle pair One fine day, we rolled out at 4:00AM, long before sun-up, giving ourselves time for relaxed tea halts, roadside banter and the comforting rustle of snack packets which is part of any Indian highway journey. The road ahead lay quiet, still wrapped in pre-dawn indigo, while our spacious vehicle hummed steadily under the weight of camera gear, tripods, beanbags, binoculars and luggage packed with more excitement than clothes. We had promised ourselves four action-packed, indulgent safaris at Bhigwan, and the cosy little hotel near the highway seemed the perfect anchorage for our birding odyssey. Most travellers speak of Bhigwan as if it were a single dot on the map. But step into its geography and a far more intricate mosaic reveals itself. The region is a living tapestry where grasslands, drylands, wetlands and agricultural fields merge into a grand stage of life. Rashin, Kadbanwadi, Baramati etc – each grassland patch lies about 40 km away in a different direction, each harbouring its own specific wilderness and wildlife. Only the backwaters sit close to town, a short, breezy drive away, unfolding suddenly into a vast, shimmering expanse that seems to swallow the horizon whole. Open-boat rides ferry you straight into the kingdom of the water birds and waders. Unfortunately Bhigwan’s most iconic visitors, the flamingos were yet to arrive... But still we loved Bhigwan so much that we returned within a month. Both trips were long but effortless 7-hour drives, about 470km from Hyderabad, on well-laid national highways just 100km short of Pune in Maharashtra. The first tour was in the last week of October 2025, when winter migrants had just begun arriving, and the second in late November 2025, when the wetlands were brimming with bird life. Each time, we reached just around lunchtime, freshened up quickly, and gobbled our food. By 3:00PM we were ready with a battery of cameras, our heads tucked into cosy caps, and plenty of water to keep us hydrated for the safaris. Beckoning Backwaters By the time the clock nudged past 3:00PM, the golden hour had already begun draping Bhigwan’s backwaters in liquid sunlight. The lake, calm and composed with hardly a ripple, almost sighed in welcome. Every afternoon safari felt like stepping into a world you think you know, only to realise that nature has rearranged the script entirely – a bewildering wilderness. Having engaged one of the local guides at Bhigwan, we were ready to venture into the wilds. A multitalented young lad in his mid-twenties, and an enthusiastic naturalist, Akshay knows his birds, beasts, and the lay of the land with effortless confidence. On the day, he single-handedly eased the wooden vessel off the shore, the oar slicing through the still water in a soft, unhurried rhythm. A mild, earthy fragrance wafted from the wetlands, one of those scents you soon learn to associate with life itself. The lake stretched ahead like a giant mirror, holding clouds, colours, birds, and time suspended on its glassy surface. Soon, the migratory ducks began their symphony, beautifully juxtaposed against the calls of the resident waterbirds. Great masses of Shovelers, Gadwalls, Teals, and Pintails lifted in swirling formations, circling the lake in shimmering ribbons. The sound of hundreds of wings cutting the air is something no camera can truly capture. In their gleaming white plumages, scores of Gulls and Terns hovered over the waters, hungry and hopeful, as the lake was full of fish and life seemed generous that morning. Eurasian Spoonbill 2

like just another raptor resting, but as our boat drifted closer, its calm silhouette sharpened. In its striking black-and-white plumage and gleaming sharpshooter eyes, it suddenly opened its wings and lifted off. Only then did we realise, with a pleasant surprise, that it was clutching a massive half-eaten fish. The moment felt almost theatrical, nature displaying, with effortless finesse, the eternal dance between hunter and hunted. Black-winged Stilt Closer to the aquatic reeds and weeds, Grey and Purple Herons, long-legged Stilts, Egrets, Herons, Spoonbills and Painted Storks, delicate as brushstrokes, tiptoed along the waterline. Osprey As the sun dipped toward the horizon, the entire lake turned surreal. Thousands of Rosy Starlings gathered, stirring in elegant, synchronized waves until they merged into a single living entity. It was roosting time, and as always, they treated the sky to a prolonged, mesmerizing performance before settling, only to rise again like a fast-moving cloud. They were enacting the celebrated murmuration, an exceptional bird behaviour in some species. Their silhouettes, backlit by molten gold, etched a memory we knew would stay with us forever. It wasn’t just birdwatching, it was a timeless performance, delicate yet powerful, stirring emotions we didn’t know we carried. A moment where wilderness, rhythm, and raw beauty blended seamlessly across the open water world. Painted Stork Great Egret Meanwhile the beautiful black Cormorants, Coots and Darters sliced the shallow waters with their alert outlooks. Sometimes the Herons and Ibises broke the monotony with sudden, lazy flaps, their reflections trailing them like slow-moving shadows. The highlight of the evening was the powerful fish-eating raptor, a lone Osprey, its talons curved like heavy hooks and its beak bent like a polished sickle. From a distance it seemed Gossamer Grasslands If the backwaters of Bhigwan are poetry, then the grasslands are its prose, raw, earthy, unvarnished, and gloriously unpredictable. At Rashin and Kadbanwadi grasslands, early mornings and long evenings stretched out like sepia-toned frames. Tall, tawny grasses swayed with an ancient rhythm, hiding secrets that revealed themselves only to patient, observant eyes. Step into these rolling hills and plains and suddenly the landscape begins to breathe, alive with untold episodes from the wild. Montagu’s, Pallid, and Marsh Harriers performed low sweeping flights, barely inches above the ground, scanning for the slightest quiver of life below. Their wings sliced through the stillness like silent arrows of dusk, offering no hint of their presence. Overhead, Kestrels held their signature pose, hovering motionless in midair, every feather taut with concentration as they studied the earth for the faintest flick of prey. Thousands of Larks appeared and disappeared in a heartbeat, hopping, skittering, and scurrying with nervous bursts of energy. 3

With a Near Threatened status worldwide the elegant Indian Coursers either scampered away or froze into perfect statues. Only our long lenses, with their relentless eye-tracking precision, caught them posing for us. And then, in a fleeting phantom of movement, the Indian Fox would materialize, russet, nimble, elegant, darting between clumps of grass, its bushy tail catching the last gold of the sun like a brush dipped in bronze. At times it would stop and give out a shrill howllike growling scream for its unseen fellow friends. Fascinatingly these Indian Foxes, according to scientists, have nearly 30 different vocalization calls used for various purposes – it is a language by itself. resets the senses. Every moment stitched itself into memory, the chilled air of those 4:00AM starts, the comfort of hot tea in steel flasks, the long straight highways. The first glimpse of the lake through the vegetation, the thrill of spotting a flurry creature in hurry as a blur, the hush that fell every time a thousand wings rose together. Bhigwan gave us more than sightings. It gave us stories – momentary, delicate, powerful stories of a wild world functioning in perfect rhythm. Stories of colour, chaos, stillness and movement. Stories that made us pause and breathe a little slower or a little faster. As we drove back to Hyderabad, the mind replayed every flight of the raptors or a duck afloat or that rapid mesmerising murmuration, every fox sprint, every hiding hyena, every quiet moment on the boat when the world seemed to pause. Sunset at Bhigwan One evening, at the cusp of sunset, when the world softened into bluish half-light, we watched groups of migratory Harriers drift across the sky like a whisper, silent, smoky, effortless. Unlike many birds, they prefer to rest and roost directly on the grasslands, gathering for a night’s repose under the star-lit sky. That moment, their collective, soundless surrender to darkness, felt worth the entire journey. Rodeos Return Because Bhigwan doesn’t merely show you birds and beasts, it reawakens something within you. It offers a rare stillness, a sense of belonging to something timeless, raw, pure and unhurried… Something far larger than the frantic carousel of everyday life. It reminds you that beyond the choking cities and restless highways lie virgin grasslands, undulating horizons and gentle lakes waiting under the rising sun. And sometimes, in that quietness, a massive raptor, like the Shorttoed Snake Eagle, Spotted Eagle, or White-eyed Buzzard would be visible. A Shikra or even a lightning-swift Peregrine or Red-necked Falcon would make a lofty skydive, as if calling you back, urging you to return and witness its wild magic all over again. When the Flamingos fly in, in about a month’s time, we will certainly ride in like the rodeos. Even the wind behaved differently here, as it was crisp, cool, sharper around the edges, tinged with the faint scent of drying earth. The grasslands seemed empty at first glance, yet they offered wonder in the yonder every few minutes, miracles revealed not by movement, but by the simple act of pausing to look. A chinkara would suddenly give us a fleeting view only to vanish into the grasslands in its galloping gait known as stotting. Nostalgic Nights Back at the hotel, nights were filled with that familiar hum only birders understand. The day’s dust was brushed off the camera gear, and batteries were lined up for charging. Memory cards were swiftly examined with equal parts hope and heartbreak but all downloaded on to hard discs. Silence followed when a particularly stunning frame appeared on someone’s screen. Tea was always brewing; so was our anticipation and plans for the next morning – made and remade to satisfy our trigger-happy state of mind. Short-toed Snake Eagle By 5:00AM, the ritual began again. The world was still asleep, but we were already on the road, driving into that magical hour when the horizon first begins to glow and Bhigwan prepares to unveil yet another day of marvels. Fulfilling Finale In the end, Bhigwan became far more than a simple satisfying birding spot. There is no orientation session. No sign-up form. No moment where someone hands you binoculars and says, “Welcome, this is your life now.” Birdwatching happens quietly. Gradually. Often against your will. It usually starts with a question that seems harmless enough. “What bird is that?” This question is dangerous. Because once you ask about it, you notice that birds exist. And once you notice birds, you realise they are always there watching you rush around, stare at screens, walk past trees without looking up. Which is awkward, because they seem to be doing just fine without our attention. 10

Birdwatching begins with looking up. Which feels strange at first. Slightly risky. Like you’re about to walk onto a lamppost. They thrive where humans thrive. They adapt faster than most species. And frankly, they have survived things we haven’t even documented yet. But when you look up, the world changes. Birdwatching humbles you that way. It forces you to reassess who you’ve been dismissing. Take the Red-vented Bulbul. And then comes the moment of delight. You’ve seen it a thousand times. On balconies. In gardens. On that one plant you forgot to water. You probably never thought much of it. But once you start watching, you realise the bulbul is a professional multitasker – singing, fighting rivals, scolding cats, and somehow always appearing in photographs you didn’t mean to take. A sunbird hovering briefly like a jewel with wings, visiting flowers you didn’t even know had nectar. Suddenly, that random plant on your balcony becomes important. You water it more carefully. You protect it. Because now, it’s not just a plant – it’s a food source. Birdwatching turns ordinary spaces into ecosystems. Bulbuls are often the first birds people truly notice. Not because they are rare, but because they are unapologetically present. And that’s how birdwatching begins, not with the exotic, but with the familiar. Then there are crows. Ah yes. The birds everyone claims to hate, until they actually start watching them. And sometimes, it surprises you entirely. Like the first time you spot a Barn Owl. Silent. Pale. Watching from a beam or tree at dusk, looking like it stepped out of a myth. You won't forget that moment. Ever. And suddenly, nights feel alive in ways they never did before. Crows are brilliant. Problem-solvers. Strategists. Entire research papers have been written about their intelligence, while they casually steal food, recognise human faces, and remember grudges longer than most people. Birdwatching does that. It expands your sense of time. Of a place. Of who else is sharing the world with you? Once you start birdwatching, you stop calling them “just crows.” You start calling them suspiciously clever. You realise they hold meetings on electric poles. You suspect they know more than they’re letting on. It’s about attention. Here’s the secret: birdwatching isn’t really about birds. And then there are sparrows. In a world addicted to speed, birdwatching rewards slowness. Birds do not cooperate with urgency. They arrive late, leave early, hide behind leaves, and reappear only after you’ve given up and sat down. Or rather, the absence of sparrows. This lesson teaches patience. And humility. Mostly humility. For many people, sparrows were childhood background noise, chirping from rooftops, hopping around courtyards, completely unremarkable. Which is why their disappearance felt strange only in hindsight. It also teaches joy. The joy of recognising a bird without looking it up. The joy of hearing a call and knowing who said it. Birdwatching teaches you that the most important losses are often the quietest ones. When sparrows vanish, something fundamental has shifted. Urban design, pollution, food sources are things you never thought about and suddenly matter. The joy of being wrong, corrected gently, and learning anyway. And then something sneaky happens. Birdwatching makes the invisible visible. You start to care. Of course, no journey into noticing birds is complete without confronting a Blue Rock Pigeon. Yes, that pigeon. The one everyone complains about. The one accused of being boring, dirty, and overly confident and yet, once you actually watch pigeons, you realise they are extraordinary navigators, loyal partners, and deeply committed parents. Once you notice birds, you notice when they’re missing. A bulbul doesn’t sing where it used to. Sparrows don’t return. A tree feels quieter than it should be. This is how birdwatching quietly becomes conservation without slogans, without speeches. Birdwatchers are often the first to notice changes. Not because they are experts, but because they pay attention. 11

Of course, birdwatching has its challenges. On a balcony. Habitats are shrinking. Cities are louder. Green spaces are fenced off. Sometimes you go to your favourite spot only to find construction instead. The birds, understandably, have moved on. Of a tree. Of a park. Of a lake. They speak up when something changes—not because they are activists, but because they notice. There is also social media where birdwatching occasionally turns competitive. Rare birds attract crowds. Silence becomes optional. Someone plays the bird calls loudly on a speaker. In a distracted world, birdwatching offers something rare: grounded hope. The bird leaves. Everyone looks confused. Not loud hope. Quiet hope. Despite all this, birdwatching endures. Because it offers something radical: connection without consumption. The belief that attention matters. That noticing accumulates. That care does not require grand gestures; sometimes it just requires looking up. You don’t take anything. You don’t buy anything. You don’t fix anything. You simply observe. In a world obsessed with ownership, this feels quietly rebellious. You don’t need binoculars to begin with. You don’t need knowledge. You don’t need permission. Birds will meet you where you are – on wires, rooftops, drains, trees, and traffic signals. They are remarkably accommodating that way. This is also why birdwatching is powerful for children. Teaching kids to watch birds isn’t about names. It’s about observation. About sitting quietly. About noticing details. About learning that patience often leads to rewards. All you have to do is look up. A child who learns to watch birds learns empathy early. They learn that the world does not revolve around them—and that’s a good thing. And once you do, you may realise something unsettling and wonderful: The world never stops being interesting. We just stopped noticing. Birdwatching also erases the hierarchy. Out in the field, no one cares what you do for a living. A student and a scientist will get equally excited about the same sunbird. Knowledge is shared freely. Mistakes are laughed at. Everyone remembers their first confident misidentification. Learning to look up isn’t about escaping reality. It’s about reconnecting with it. And in such a noisy, hurried world, that might well be one of the most important skills we can relearn. And slowly, birdwatchers became guardians. *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (From Facebook, August 19, 2022) *** 12

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Bluethroat (Luscinia svecica) Bluethroat adult (L) (Bikaner, Rajasthan, November 18, 2023) & 1st winter (R) (Nalsarovar, Gujarat, January 01, 2026) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Passeriformes Muscicapidae Luscinia L. svecica 15 cm Least Concern spring and summer; after the summer moult, the fresh new feathers have pale tips which obscure the throat pattern. These tips then abrade in late winter and early spring to reveal the brighter and more colourful bases of the feathers. Habitat & behaviour: The Bluethroat is usually seen singly on damp ground, flower-strewn grass under flowering trees, reedy tank margins, and sugarcane fields. It is a sprightly, robin-like bird which nevertheless is a skulker, often moving through tangled bushes and underbrush or hopping around quietly with cocked tail and drooping wings as it forages, stopping now and then to pick up an insect. Its diet consists mainly of caterpillars, tiny beetles and other insects. Its winter call is a harsh, quiet chur-r or chuck chuck, while in the breeding season, it utters a sweet, loud song from an open perch. Description & distribution: The Bluethroat is a small passerine member of the Old World flycatcher family that occurs widely across Europe and Asia, while in North America it is restricted to northern and western parts of Alaska and the Yukon. It breeds in most parts of Europe and northern Asia, while it winters in the Iberian peninsula, northern half of Africa, and south Asia, including India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan. There are eleven sub-species, of which only one, L. s. abbotti, breeds within the Indian subcontinent limits (Gilgit, Baltistan, Ladakh and Kashmir). Nesting: In Ladakh, the Bluethroat breeds mainly during June and July. The nest is usually a deep cup of dry grass on wet ground, hidden amongst grass and scrub. The usual clutch consists of 3 or 4 olive-green to olive-brown eggs, minutely flecked all over with dull reddish spots. The adult male has a brilliant blue throat and breast, with a white or chestnut patch in the middle, while the female and young male show only a gorget of brown spots across the white breast. Upper parts are olive brown, and it has a whitish or buff supercilium and black moustachial stripes. Additionally, the female may also show a sub-moustachial stripe. In flight or when spread, a black-tipped orange-chestnut tail is prominent. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 23 Number 2 February 2026 FIELD TRIP: Sunday, February 01, 2026, 7.30AM: Rudrur Lake (Pedda Cheruvu), Nizamabad Dt. Meeting Point(s): Taj Dhaba, Muthangi, 04:00AM. Coordinator(s): Gowthama Poludasu (Mobile: 94409-10967) Rudrur is a village tank (freshwater lake) located in Rudrur Mandal of Nizamabad District, Telangana, set within a predominantly rural and agricultural landscape. The habitat of Rudrur Lake is a mosaic of open shallow water, marshy edges, and vegetated margins. Exposed mudflats and damp shorelines become important feeding grounds for small shorebirds like waders and stints. Surrounding farmlands, scrub patches, and uncultivated fields further enhance the habitat by providing additional foraging areas and safe roosting sites, particularly for ducks, geese, and passerines. Although Rudrur Lake is not formally designated as a bird sanctuary, it is locally recognised by birdwatchers as an important wintering and stopover site. The lake attracts a diverse assemblage of waterfowl and wetland birds, especially during the winter migration period, when migratory species arrive from Eurasian and Central Asian flyways. Notable species to watch for include Greylag Goose, Comb Duck, Little Stint, Eurasian Teal, Northern Pintail, Northern Shoveler, Eurasian Wigeon, and Lesser Whistling Duck, among others. The seasonal nature of the lake, coupled with its strategic location among regional wetlands, supports high avian diversity and makes Rudrur a rewarding site for winter birding in inland Telangana. This will be a half-day trip, and we plan to start our return journey to Hyderabad by around 12:00PM. Of course, those who wish to stay back and continue birding in the area are welcome to do so at their own convenience. Please note that the areas we will be visiting include farmlands and lake beds, where conditions may be muddy or slushy. We strongly advise wearing gumboots or rubber boots to handle the slush comfortably, or making suitable footwear arrangements as per your preference. Carry adequate water and breakfast/snacks, and protective gear if required. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. New Deccan Birders hats and caps will be available for purchase; please carry adequate cash. Trip Report: Rudrur, Nizamabad Dt, February 01, 2026 Riyaansh Pandiri Eurasian Spoonbill (Photo: Gurukumar KR) While the sun was still sleeping, I woke up to the harsh sound of the alarm. I checked the time and it was 2:30AM, probably the earliest I have ever woken up to go birding. By 3:30AM, we were already on the road. We reached the meeting point, Taj Dhaba, at 3:50AM. The place was packed with unruly crowds. Apparently, Hyderabad has officially resigned from sleeping, just like Delhi. 1

The other senior birders arrived at 4:00AM. After meet and greet, the group had tea, though not me, and then we started to Rudrur. My brother slept through most of the drive, and at around 7:00AM we reached Rudrur. Even before we reached, we clocked around 20 species at the crack of dawn. happy until I saw it drop down and disappear in the paddy fields. We all went to check out where it had dropped down. We walked between paddy fields on the small bunds. It was an adventure, till we saw what happened to the eagle. Alas! It was motionless. It had just enough energy to open its beak, and its eyes were going all milky looking. My group sadly said, “I think it’s gone.” The locals, curious at the crowd with cameras, came to enquire and told that the bird must have had a drink from the paddy fields where they had recently sprayed some pesticides. Apparently, this was not the first time. Birds, even ones at the top of the food chain, have fallen prey to our indiscriminate use of chemicals, or should I say inadvertent cruelty. Any loss, when repeated, may lose its shock, but never its weight. The lake unfolds Thankfully, nature knows how to restore balance too. Our spirits were lifted when we saw Asian Green Bee-eaters joyfully mud bathing, Asian Openbills and Grey Herons moving with grace, and warblers like Clamorous Reed and Sykes’s Warblers filling the air with complex calls and sounds. Long-tailed Shrike (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Indian Pond Heron (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Asian Green Bee-eater (Photo: Gurukumar KR) At Rudrur village, we met Mr Adnan, a local birder and member of DB. We had breakfast together. Here, a local person approached my dad and asked, “Which department are you from, sir?” We all laughed. This happens a lot due to his bearing, I guess. Humayun Sir said this was still better than his experience, as people often ask him which country he is from! Adaptation and loss Not all moments were easy. We saw a Black Kite nesting on a big mobile tower, and it got me thinking: should I be sad because its natural habitat, the trees, are lost, or should I be happy that it has adapted so well and is nesting in a communication tower? Guess there is no answer for that one. The saddest moment, and the most unforgettable, was when we encountered a Greater Spotted Eagle. You would have thought, why sad? You should have been happy. Yes, I was Grey Heron (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) 2

Plain Prinia (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) Soon enough, we reached the path which led to the lake. It was all mushy and squishy, the way a paddy field should be, and we all got stuck up to our knees in the mud at least twice. But my brother—he just threw his shoes off and started helping other people who got stuck, stepping into the paddy fields like he was born in them. But before the lake came an obstacle. It was a wall of thorny shrubs, and we had thorns embedded into our legs and bags. After that, we saw the beautiful lake along with a rare bird which is normally only found in North India, and one of my lifers – the Greylag Goose. Wood Sandpiper (Photo: Riyaansh Pandiri) Then we saw many other waterbirds. Common and Wood Sandpipers, greyish brown and white, caught our interest among the waders. There were also around 300 Little Stints performing an aerial show, basically a resized version of Rosy Starlings performing murmuration. Little Stint flock (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) Greylag Goose (Photo: Riyaansh Pandiri) The geese were probably the biggest birds there, and I think they would weigh 5-10 kg. Grey plumage, pinkish orange bill, and pink legs. Oh! What a sight. I was told to be stealthy, as these were a timid flock, and I tried to be extra calm. River Tern (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Purple Heron (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) All the water birds were in great numbers. There were around 250 Green-winged Teals, with their chestnut heads and green patches, which looked lovely through the binoculars; 150 Whistling-ducks; and around 50 Knob-billed Ducks, both of which are now easily identifiable for me. There were also many other ducks, and a Marsh Harrier was also seen. 3

about 600 Cormorants, mixed with a small number of Darters, just drying their wings. Then came the highlight of the day. We saw my favourite bird, the Peregrine Falcon – the fastest bird known to man. It reminded me of how I started birding and how it all basically came back full circle, since one of the first raptors I saw was the Peregrine Falcon. We waited for a few more hours, and right when we decided to leave, we saw a pair of Greater Spotted Eagles – but this time, they were not lifeless. Thank heavens! They were flying around. With that, we ended our checklists. We waded back, but took a less slushy path later. We said our goodbyes and started back. Knob-billed Duck female (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Yellow Wagtail (Photo: Riyaansh Pandiri) Greylag Goose and Northern Shoveler (Photo: Mohd Adnan Uddin) Quietly bittersweet Rudrur gave us a Sunday full of happy moments and sad thoughts together. We saw many beautiful birds, but we also saw things that made us think deeply. The drive back felt long because our minds were full of memories. Some trips end when you reach home, but this one stayed with us. This trip with Deccan Birders felt more like a family outing, and man did I love it! It’s not like the Hyderabad Bird Atlas (HBA), where we are bound by rules and time. Although HBA is knowledge-giving and fun, it’s tiring too. With DB, it’s just knowledge everywhere, emanating from all the experienced birders, and I am surrounded by this floating cloud of knowledge – snippets, anecdotes, and experiences, funny and otherwise. Wigeon (Photo: Gurukumar KR) Thank you, Sathwik Uncle, Gowthama Uncle, Guru Uncle, Humayun Sir and Adnan Sir, for all the info, and all others, including my parents and brother, for making my day wonderful. MIST, MUNIAS AND MINIVETS Trip Report: Maredumilli, October 24-27, 2025 K Sudhir Moorti A view of a forest at Maredumilli (Photo: David Johnson) Gokul, Gaurav, David, and I set off for Marredumilli – the evergreen paradise for any birder. At the last minute, we decided to take a detour through Jangareddygudem for a morning session at the Gubbala Mangamma Temple. Located deep within dense forests on the border of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, the temple surroundings offered a perfect starting point. We reached Jangareddygudem in the middle of the night after a 6-hour drive from Hyderabad and caught a couple of hours of shut-eye. The Detour: Gubbala Mangamma Temple We arrived at 6:30AM after a bumpy one and a half hour ride, only to be immediately greeted by a Crested Goshawk soaring overhead. Bypassing the temple, we followed a trail along a stream, trekking 5km deep into the forest over three and a half hours. It was a spectacular session; we sighted over 50 species, including the Orange Minivet, Chestnut-headed Bee-eater, Rufous Woodpecker, and the Blue-throated Flycatcher. The track went further but was submerged at a point, probably due to the recent rains, so we decided to head back. After a hearty lunch at a roadside shack, we pushed on to Marredumilli, arriving at 6:00PM. We checked in to our accommodation and turned in early, eager for the next day's adventure. Marredumilli A tip regarding a rare species prompted us to change our plans and head to the Gudisa Grasslands. We set off at 4:30AM, arriving by 6:30AM. The air was thick with tension and excitement; each of us silently wondered if we would actually find our target. Scaly-breasted Munia (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Orange Minivet (Photo: Gaurav Maheshwari) 7

As we ascended the hill, we spotted some movement in the grass, and stopped to find a flock of Scaly-breasted Munias. We waited, scanning the vast golden landscape. Ten minutes later, we spotted a few small birds roughly 200 yards away. We tracked them through our binoculars for several intense seconds before the realization hit: Green Avadavats! Gokul’s hunch to wait at that spot had paid off. Green Avadavat (Photo: K Sudhir Moorti) The joy was overwhelming – high-fives all around! It was a ‘lifer’ for every member of the group. After thirty minutes of patient waiting, the small flock of four or five birds moved closer to the roadside to feed on grass seeds. We approached cautiously, capturing photographs of these rare beauties in their natural habitat. including highlights like the Brown-cheeked Fulvetta, Speckled Piculet, and the Grey-headed Canary-flycatcher. Grey-headed Canary Flycatcher (Photo: K Sudhir Moorti) We also saw both Velvet-fronted and Indian Nuthatches, alongside an absolute abundance of Minivets – Scarlet, Rosy, and Orange Minivets were out in such high numbers that it was heartening to see them thriving. We also had close encounter with a Crested Serpent Eagle, sitting on a low branch. In fact there were two or more individuals calling from inside the plantation. Green Avadavat (Amandava formosa) The Green Avadavat is a stunning, small (approx. 10 cm) bird, characterized by its olive-green plumage, distinct zebrastriped flanks, and a bright red beak.   Diet: As granivores, they forage primarily on the ground for ripening seeds from native grasses like Themeda (Kangaroo Grass) and Heteropogon (Spear Grass), which dominate the high-altitude grasslands of the Eastern Ghats. Conservation Status: Endemic to India, the Green Avadavat has a historical presence in the northern Andhra Pradesh and southern Odisha border regions. While they were once common in scrub jungles, their populations have plummeted due to habitat loss and illegal trapping for the pet trade. Recent sightings in areas like Koraput and now Gudisa are vital records for the conservation of this vulnerable species. The Coffee Plantations and the Elusive Trogon After a sumptuous breakfast in a small hamlet, we made our way back to our base at the Vana Vihari Eco-tourism Camp in Marredumilli. Having birded here since 2012, I’ve always found this region fascinating – it is a unique crossroads where one can find species typically associated with both the Western Ghats and the North-east. Post-lunch, we headed toward the nearby coffee plantations, a reliable hotspot from previous trips. The activity was nothing short of frenetic. In just two hours, we recorded 40 species, Crested Serpent Eagle with Ashy Drongo (Photo: K Sudhir Moorti) The following day was dedicated to the Coffee Plantations, the Jungle Star Camp area, and the Medicinal Plants Park. Our persistence was rewarded with a 65-species day special thanks to David, our spotter-in-chief. David, who wields a pair of binoculars – unlike the rest of us, with our Cameras and long lenses – is great at spotting birds very quickly. A White-eyed Buzzard sitting on top of a dry tree was a lovely sight; we also saw some more raptors like Oriental Honeybuzzard, Shikra, Crested Goshawk, Crested Serpent Eagle and one fly-by by a magnificent Black Eagle. While the group was particularly keen on finding the Malabar Trogon, the species remained elusive until just before sunset. 8

We finally spotted a lone female; though the low light prevented us from getting photographs, it was a ‘lifer’ for David and Gaurav. David, in particular, was content just to have sighted such a magnificent bird. Another species that eluded us was the Blue-bearded Beeeater; although we sighted and heard it a couple of times, personally I had been hoping for a decent shot. Also missing in action were the Sunbirds, Scarlet and Ruby-cheeked, which we usually got on almost every trip earlier. The Final Morning: A Return to the Grasslands On October 27th, our final day here, we couldn't resist one last trip to the Gudisa Grasslands in hopes of getting better shots of the Green Avadavat. We were successful in finding the ‘Green Beauty’ again, though they remained at a similar distance as our first encounter. Our two-hour session yielded 40 species, with the Bar-winged Flycatcher-shrike being a welcome new addition to our trip list. Indian White-eye (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) The Farewell: Sokuleru Vagu We checked out of Marredumilli and began the long drive back to Hyderabad, but not before one final stop at the Sokuleru Vagu View Point. Even this quick stop was productive, hosting 45 species. Bixa orellana (Photo: K Sudhir Moorti) We came across a flowering plant that was locally known as the Lipstick Tree or Annatto Tree (Bixa ocellana). It also seemed to attract quite a few birds. Common Hill Myna (Photo: K Sudhir Moorti) Pied Bushchat (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) Vernal Hanging Parrot (Photo: Gokul Krishna Addanki) We were treated to sightings of the Common Hill Myna, Vernal Hanging Parrot, Rosy Minivets, and various Flowerpeckers, as well as both Coppersmith and Brownheaded Barbets, and a few other birds. It was the perfect conclusion to a wonderful expedition. The wonderfully green forests, rolling hills and amazing birds really awed us. Not to mention the ‘Bamboo Biryani Lunches’ and the evening Bird List discussion sessions. I loved the way this team came together, with Gokul’s patience and perseverance, Gaurav’s energy and David’s spotting skills. It really made the trip fantastic. We headed home with full memory cards and even fuller hearts. 9

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Crested Treeswift (Hemiprocne coranata) Crested Treeswift Male (L) and Female (R) (Kotagiri, Tamil Nadu, February 1, 2026) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: even in flight by its appearance – very similar to the Asian Palm Swift, but larger and with a more deeply forked tail. It is typically seen in pairs or small groups while hawking for midges or tiny winged insects. While perching, it tends to sit upright on bare branches, with its long wings crossed on either side of the spiky tail feathers. The calls include a variety of loud and harsh notes which may be uttered either while perching or in flight; the most common is a whit-uck, whit-uck, whit-uck. Apodiformes Hemiprocnidae Hemiprocne H. coronata 23 cm Least Concern Description & distribution: The Crested Treeswift is a large, slender swift that is widely distributed across all of India (except for the arid North-western region) as well as Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, and east into Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, Laos and parts of China, usually below an altitude of 1000m. Nesting: The Crested Treeswift breeds mainly between December and July, with some local variations or extensions. The nest is usually a very small, shallow and flimsy-looking saucer made of bark scraps and feathers, stuck together with saliva, and attached to the upper surface of a bare branch, usually between 4m to 15m above ground. The usual clutch consists of just one egg, pale grey, elliptical, and almost filling the nest. It is blue-grey above and paler and whitish below, with a prominent erectile crest, long pointed wings, and deeply forked tail. The chin and throat are chestnut in the male and grey in the female. Local name: The Crested Treeswift is known as ‘Tajdar ababeel’ in Hindi, ‘Chotaliyo ababeelo’ in Gujarati, ‘Sarappakshi’ in Malayalam and ‘Wehi lihiniya’ in Sinhala. Habitat & behaviour: The Crested Treeswift is a resident breeder across most of its range, and prefers open woodland or deciduous forest areas; it is also sometimes seen in open areas near trees, and in parks and gardens. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 23 Number 3 March 2026 FIELD TRIP-1: Sunday, April 5, 2026, 6.15AM: Kistareddypet Lake, Hyderabad. Meeting Point(s): SVM Grand, Miyapur, 05:20AM; BHEL Bus Stop, Lingampally, 05:45AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Gurukumar KR (Mobile: 96188-27407) Kistareddypet Lake, located near Patancheru, has recently caught the attention of birders. The lake is home to more than 110 species of birds, including large flocks of Little Stint, Black-winged Stilt, Black-tailed Godwit, Garganey, Gadwall etc. One can also spot Ruff, Spot-billed Pelican, Common Snipe, Greater Flamingo, Common Redshank, Temminck’s Stint and other shore birds. The surrounding areas also host species like Mongolian Short-toed Lark, Citrine Wagtail, Baya Weaver, Indian Golden Oriole etc. This is a great opportunity to observe and record the diversity of migratory waterbirds and shore birds in this important habitat as winter draws to a close in the state. FIELD TRIP-2: Sunday, April 26, 2026, 7.30AM: Damagundam Reserve Forest, Nizamabad Dt. Meeting Point(s): NMDC, Masab Tank, 05:00AM. Coordinator(s): Srikanth Bhamidipati (Mobile: 97388-40070) Damagundam Reserve Forest, a hotspot for avian diversity and endemism. Damagundam Reserve Forest is located in Vikarabad district of Telangana, about 70 km from Hyderabad. It is one of the two major reserve forest blocks in Vikarabad forest range, along with Ananthagiri. The forest is home to a variety of habitats, including dry deciduous, scrub, grassland, wetland and rocky outcrops. We will cover different habitats and look for the resident and migratory birds that inhabit them. Watch out for Painted Spurfowl, Small Minivet, Yellow-footed Green Pigeon, Indian Blue Robin, Taiga Flycatcher, Ultramarine Flycatcher, Booted Eagle, Bonelli's Eagle, Eurasian Kestrel, Brown Fish Owl etc.; also watch out for rare sightings like Indian Pitta, Malabar Whistling Thrush, Orange-breasted Green Pigeon, Blyth's Paradise-flycatcher and Blue-and-white Flycatcher. Both trips will be half-day trips, so carry adequate water and breakfast/snacks, and protective gear if required. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. New Deccan Birders hats and caps will be available for purchase; please carry adequate cash. THE HIDDEN WORLD OF INDIRA PARK Trip Report: Indira Park, Hyderabad, March 15, 2026 Shreyas Mishra (Class XII, Sri Chaitanya Junior College) My introduction to birding was due to my Maths lecturer Harsh Sir's interest in nature and his wish to take us for birding. He had identified a day where everyone was free from their daily routines. Sir took this opportunity to introduce us to four of the many awesome people he knew. I was also looking forward to this event as it was a new experience for me, and after this I must say that I have a new developed new appreciation for nature. It may be a cliché but it needs repeating, that nature relieves the stress and strain of routine life. In my case it was a break from the endless preparation for IITJEE. It turned out to be more than just a walk in the park. The event was scheduled on a Sunday morning, between 6:30AM and 9:30AM at Indira Park. Though I was unsure of what to expect, and mildly groggy from waking up early on a Sunday, the experience that followed made it one of the most memorable mornings I have had in a while. As I entered the park, I spent around ten minutes searching for my friend Sai Ram. Once we found each other, we quickly made our way to the main gate where the event was to begin. Luckily, the session had not yet started, and we were just in time to join the group. 1

he set new standards for us on how to stay fit. His survey of the park and general exposition was peppered with valuable life advice and witty jokes that often caught us off-guard. He left a deep impression on all of us and gave us a lot to think about. His emphasis on living a plastic-free life and live demonstration of pH value of carbonated drinks made us ponder our lifestyle choices. We are better people for having met him, if only for a few hours. A sketch made by Yadavalli Nimisha after the walk The event was guided by four experienced experts: Ajit Kumar Mahendra Sir from Deccan Birders, Sadhana Ramachander Ma’am from Nature Lovers of Hyderabad, Praveen Kumar Sir, also from Deccan Birders and Laxmi Singh Ma’am, from Hyderabad Bird Atlas. Their presence added immense value to the experience. Spot-billed Duck (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) Ajit Sir began the session by sharing the history of Indira Park, giving us a deep appreciation of the place we were exploring. He also provided three pairs of binoculars, which enabled us to observe birds up close. For many of us, it was the first time we had held professional-type binoculars. It felt like we were inducted into some elite club. Sadhana Ramachander speaking to the group (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) Sadhana Ma’am then guided us through the diverse plant life within the park. She explained the significance of various tree species and spoke passionately about her efforts to conserve Banyan trees across Telangana. Her dedication to environmental conservation was truly inspiring. Ma’am told us about Weaver bird’s nest design – how the entrance is vertical and eggs are kept isolated in a different compartment. Also, the birds keep their nests hanging from hard-to-reach spots or above water – all to keep snakes away. Seems like even the Avengers could take inspiration from Weaver birds for their headquarters! Ajit Kumar Mahendra pointing out various birds to the group (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) Ajit Sir took us around the park, pointing out the various trees and birds. His enthusiasm was infectious. For a 79-year-old, Grey Heron (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) 2

Praveen Sir introduced us to an interesting concept – how certain plants placed in lakes act as natural purifiers, helping to clean and maintain water quality. It was amazing to learn how nature has its own systems for balance and sustainability. He talked about tissue culture and plant biotechnology which helped us place our theoretical knowledge in the bigger picture. Sir even showed us an abandoned nest made by Weaver Ants. He described its engineering made from purely natural materials. What marvellous engineering it was! Nature seems to have answers to all our problems even before we have asked them. Black Kite silhouetted against the sky (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) Praveen Kumar addressing the group (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) Praveen Sir pointed out so many plants and trees along our path and described their uses – medicinal or otherwise. It was very enlightening. He even encouraged us not to restrict ourselves to Engineering. He told us that we should learn about plants, animals, farming, carpentry and anything we could get our hands on. He said that’s how their generation grew and urged us not to restrict our options. In the world of AI it seems like an excellent idea. Indian Pond Heron (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) Of course, the highlight of the event was observing the birds. We spotted several species, including Black Kites, an Indian Grey Hornbill and lively Parakeets (and not Parrots, as we learnt). Laxmi Ma’am, the bird expert, made the event even more memorable by spotting a flock of Golden Orioles flying in giant loops, weaving patterns between the sky and the pond. Towards the end of the session, we were lucky enough to see a Spotted Owlet, which was a perfect conclusion to the morning. Indian Grey Hornbill (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) Spotted Owlet (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) 3

even reminded of Harsh Sir’s reaction – at the start of the event when he saw everyone arrive, he said in apparent awe as he joined the group, "Thank you all for turning up, I didn't think you all will actually turn up! I'm so proud!" I felt proud of us too. To whoever is reading this, remember, no matter what is causing your stress, whether it is preparation for a competitive exam, or workplace drama, take some time out and go naturegazing, because who knows the solution to your problems might be in the rustling of trees or in the wingbeat of birds! A note from Praveen Kumar: I felt very happy on this trip, as the younger generation showed great enthusiasm to understand the importance of biodiversity. They should be the torch bearers of the future to safeguard our Mother Earth. Some important issues that they should work on in the future are: Indian Palm Squirrel (Photo: Harshvardhan Bukka) As we were leaving I asked Sadhana ma’am and Ajit sir what message she had for us. Ajit Sir added that we the youth are the future of our country and we should take initiative in preserving the nature and act as responsible citizens and realize the importance of environmental conservation.
