THE SPARROW AT THE WINDOW A note on the occasion of World Sparrow Day, March 20, 2026 Text & Photos: Srikanth Bhamidipati House Sparrow You remember the sound before you remember the bird. It was there when you woke up. It was there through breakfast. It came from the window ledge, the gap in the roof, the balcony railing where something had made itself entirely at home. You never thought to listen for it because it was simply there the way light is there, the way the smell of tea is there – woven into the texture of morning so completely that it required no attention at all. The House Sparrow. Chidiya. The bird so ordinary it had no need of a grander name. The one that hopped along the kitchen windowsill looking for crumbs. That bathed in the courtyard dust with such uninhibited joy it made adults smile even when they were busy. The first bird most of us ever knew – not because we went looking, but because it was already there, already part of us, already woven into the sound of home. And then, at some point quietly, without announcement, it stopped coming. This is the strange thing about losing something common. It does not happen in a moment you can point to. It happens in the space between one morning and the next, across months and years, until one day you are standing somewhere familiar, and you realise it is gone. Has been gone for a while. You simply hadn't noticed when it stopped. Ask anyone over forty when they last saw a sparrow near their home. Watch them pause. Watch the calculation happen not of days, but of years. Some will say two years. Some will say five. Some will trail off, uncertain, because they cannot remember, and that uncertainty is its own kind of answer. Something that was always there simply isn't anymore. Here is what is worth understanding about the sparrow. It was never rare. That was always the point. We tend to think of birds worth caring about as the ones that are difficult to find – the crane that arrives once a decade, the owl that requires a jungle walk and three hours of patience. These birds matter. But they live at a remove from us. They do not share our mornings. The sparrow did. It chose us long before we chose it. Long before we had cities, it found the edges of human settlement and decided that this was where it belonged – near our grain, near our rooftops, near the warm gaps in our walls. It was never tame. But it was comfortable. It had been comfortable, alongside us, for centuries. And all that time, without our knowing it, it was doing something. It was eating the insects that gathered around our food and our crops. Feeding its chicks almost entirely on insects through the nesting season – tiny creatures that most of us never notice, but that form the base of a chain that everything else depends on. The sparrow was part of an arrangement, ancient and informal, between a bird and the places where people live. We provided, without meaning to, spilled grain and insects drawn to warmth and the gaps in our buildings. The sparrow provided, without us asking: a check on what would otherwise overrun us. A presence, a sound. A sound that, it turns out, we miss more than we expected. Because the morning without it is quieter in a way that doesn't feel like peace. It feels like absence. The sparrow did not leave because it wanted to. It left because we, without meaning to, made staying impossible. And we almost didn't notice. 5

Our new buildings have no gaps. Glass and sealed facades – modern, considered, and entirely uninhabitable for a bird that nests in crevices. The old trees were replaced with ornamental plants that grow no insects and offer no shelter. The grain that used to spill from sacks now comes sealed in plastic. The courtyard where dust baths happened is a parking space. The quiet riverbank where sparrows raised their young is now a road. We did not decide to remove the sparrow from our lives. We made a hundred smaller decisions, each of which made perfect sense on its own. And the sparrow had nowhere left to go. In city after city – Mumbai, Bengaluru, Delhi, Chennai – the numbers tell the same story. Down by half. In some places, down by eighty percent. The state bird of Delhi, disappearing from Delhi. So common globally that no alarm bell rings. But gone from the specific streets, the specific windows, the specific mornings where they once were simply part of what morning meant. Sind Sparrow What most of us never knew – because why would we? – when one sparrow was already so perfectly present, is that other sparrows have been living quiet lives across this country, in the corners we never thought to look. Spanish Sparrow In the farmland edges of the north and east, where the city thins into fields, another sparrow holds on where the House Sparrow has already let go. And in winter, on the open plains of the northwest, a visitor arrives from further west – restless, passing through on its own seasonal logic, a reminder that birds live across boundaries we have drawn, but they have not. Russet Sparrow Up in the Himalayan foothills, on cool mountain paths where the air still carries forest in it, a shyer sparrow moves through wooded slopes that most of the plains have never seen. In the arid west, along the reed-threaded riverbanks of Rajasthan and Gujarat, a sparrow so particular in its requirements that it will live nowhere else – not in towns, not in gardens – depends on exactly this narrow strip of intact habitat. As rivers are diverted and wetlands drained, that strip grows narrower by the year. Eurasian Tree Sparrow And then there is one that most people have walked past without knowing it had a name. 6

grain. A native plant that grows the insects its chicks depend on. A small, deliberate decision to make a little more space in a life that has, gradually and without meaning to, stopped making space for it. These are not grand gestures. They take five minutes. And they are exactly what a sparrow requires. But there is something else the sparrow offers, if you let it. A way back in. Not everyone will become a birdwatcher. Not everyone needs to. But the sparrow – precisely because it is ordinary, precisely because it asks nothing of you except a moment of attention – is a door. Chestnut-shouldered Petronia When you put out a bowl of water on your balcony railing and a sparrow comes to it, something happens that is hard to name but easy to recognise. A small connection forms. You notice whether it comes back. You begin to listen for it in the morning. And in that listening, in that small, daily act of attending to something alive, something in you shifts. The Yellow-throated Sparrow (aka Chestnut-shouldered Petronia) lives in the dry, rocky country of peninsular India the scrublands and open forests of the Deccan, where the land is hard and the trees are sparse, and the sun falls without mercy on bare stone. It is a bird of ledges and crevices in rocky outcrops, of old stone walls and sunbaked cliffs, nesting in places that look, to a human eye, like nothing could possibly live there. It has a small patch of warm yellow at its throat – easy to miss, easy to overlook, the way everything in these dry landscapes asks you to look more carefully before you pass judgement. It does not come to gardens. It does not appear in city parks. It belongs to a version of India that most of us drive through without stopping. You start to wonder about the sparrow on the mountain path. About the one in the reed bed that nobody sees. About all the lives being lived at the edges of your own, in the narrow margins of land and sky that have not yet been taken. You start to care about a ledge, a tree, a patch of sky you never thought about before. This is what common birds do that rare birds cannot. Rare birds require us to go to them. The sparrow comes to us. It lives alongside us, in the same windows, in the same mornings. And when enough of us notice it to register its presence and its absence as something that matters, the sparrow becomes more than a bird. Six sparrows sharing one subcontinent. Each asking something different of the land. Each finding that version of the land harder to hold on to than it was before. We didn't know most of them were there. And they were disappearing before we learned their names. It becomes a measure of whether the places we have built still have room for life. And that is the idea behind World Sparrow Day. It began in 2010, started by a man from Nashik who noticed that the bird everyone assumed was everywhere had, in the places where people lived, quietly started to vanish. The World Sparrow Day is now marked in more than fifty countries. Not because the sparrow is rare. But because common things, once lost, are not easily recovered and because the sparrow's story is one that almost everyone can recognise as their own. So today, go to a window. A balcony. A garden, if you have one, or a patch of sky if you don't. It doesn't need to be anywhere special. It just needs to be where you are. Listen, if you hear it – that quick, unremarkable chirp that you have been hearing your whole life without knowing it. Stop for a moment, let it register. It is not a small thing, that sound. It means something nearby is still holding on. That a bird which has lived alongside us for centuries has found, in your corner of the city, just enough to survive. It is not a day for experts. It is a day for the rest of us. For the person who hasn't thought about sparrows in years but, reading this, feels something familiar stir. For the child who has only seen them in books, and the parent who remembers them on the windowsill. For anyone who has stood on a balcony in the early morning and listened, really listened, to what is or isn't there. And if you don't hear it, let that silence mean something too. Let it ask the question the sparrow has been asking all along, in the only language it has. Not a cry for help. Not an accusation. Just a small bird at a window, checking whether there is still space. Because the sparrow does not need a conservation expedition. It does not need a national park or a rescue centre. The sparrow never asked much. A crack in a wall. A handful of grain. A morning that has room in it for something small and alive. It is not too late to answer. It needs what it always needed: a crack in a wall where a nest can go. A bowl of water in the summer heat. A handful of *** 7

MANGROVE CALLING: IN THE GODAVARI’S EMBRACE Report: Experiences during AWC at Coringa, Kakinada, 2019-2026 Text & Photos: Gurukumar KR Indian Skimmer The Godavari is a mighty river that carves its way across the Deccan before finally unravelling into the Bay of Bengal. It doesn't merely reach the coast; it expands, shattering into a vast, intricate delta of distributaries and secret channels near Kakinada. This is the East Godavari River Estuarine Ecosystem (EGREE) – a landscape of global importance where the river’s fresh water and the sea’s salt meet to create one of India's most vital wetlands. At the heart of this union lies the Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary, home to the second-largest stretch of mangroves in India. These emerald forests are the region's natural bio-shield, a silent, sturdy defence against the fury of cyclones and the slow encroachment of the sea. Beyond protection, Coringa is a nursery for life, sustaining local fisheries and sheltering rare biodiversity like the Fishing Cat and Smooth-coated Otter. For eight years, every January has found me here, participating in the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC). Coordinated by Wetlands International and the BNHS, this census is a vital annual health check for these wetlands, monitoring the birds that use the Central Asian Flyway as a bridge between worlds. What began as a hobby and a curious engagement has now evolved into a seasonal pilgrimage – a transition from casual birdwatching to a witness of the estuary's shifting pulse. The Shores of Kumbhabhishekam The journey often begins where the human world presses hardest against the wild: the shores near the Kumbhabhishekam port. Here, the air is a thick blend of salt spray and diesel. On these mudflats, Lesser Sand Plovers engage in a restless, frantic dance – their tiny, rapid movements silhouetted against a backdrop of towering berths and the slow, mechanical arcs of dredging cranes. Lesser (aka Tibetan) Sand Plover Whimbrel Scanning the shoreline, one can usually pick out the subtle differences among the residents. The Kentish Plovers and Little Ringed Plovers dart through the silt, while the larger Whimbrels and Eurasian Curlews probe the deeper mud with their long, decurved bills. 8

beauty; it is about documenting the steady, quiet rhythm of loss. Eurasian Curlew Brahminy Kite juvenile Grey (aka Black-bellied) Plover The Fishing Villages and Jetties At the crack of dawn, the village is a world of blue-grey stillness, where the air is cool and the only movement comes from the Whiskered Terns dipping silently into the freshwater reaches of the river. During these sleepy minutes, the scavengers own the streets; House Crows, Indian Jungle Crows, and both Pied Starlings and Common Mynas move with a quiet, methodical efficiency through the still air. Occasionally, a Grey Plover stands as a solitary, silver sentinel, and on the rarest of days, the mudflats host the Great Knot, a weary traveller whose presence feels like a gift. Great Knot Fishing boats at the jetty Over nearly a decade, I have watched this threshold fundamentally change. The expansion of the port – the deepening of channels and the relentless reclamation of land – has written a visible story of decline in our annual counts. It leaves the Brahminy Kites to circle over a landscape that feels increasingly fragile and hollowed out. However, as the morning sun rises, waking the denizens of the villages, the atmosphere shifts, breaking the silence with the stuttering cough of diesel engines and the rhythmic howls of fishermen hauling in the first catch. This ‘whispered’ morning gives way to the clamour of bargaining – a sharp, percussive exchange of prices that serves as a dinner bell for the birds. Now emboldened by the awakening of human energy, the crows become a frantic, bickering cloud over the silver heaps of fish, while the mynas strut with comical bravery between the legs of traders. In the palm fronds overhead, Asian Palm Swifts slice through the first exhaust-tinged light, their bladelike flight mirrored by the rising, rhythmic call of the Asian Koel, which competes with the mechanical hum of the port. Yet, life persists in the margins. When the fishing boats arrive, the scene ignites into a chaotic beauty; Gulls and Terns dive with desperate precision, fighting to reclaim a small share of what the nets have taken from the sea. It is a sobering reminder that our work in citizen science is not just about counting 9

wakes of the first departing boats, a final, graceful bridge between the waking village streets and the wide, open estuary. House Sparrow female Amidst this awakening noise, House Sparrows, Indian Silverbills, and Scaly-breasted Munias flit in busy flocks around the thatched eaves, while the edge of the scrub begins to glow with movement. Rose-ringed Parakeets scream past in emerald streaks, and both Green and Blue-tailed Bee-eaters hawk for insects from the power lines as the village electricity hums to life. Southern Coucal The Mangrove Corridors: A Vertical World Leaving the industrial hum and the bustling fishing villages behind, we move by boat into the silent, dense corridors of the Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary. In these tidal creeks, the birdlife is organized by height and habitat, from the upper canopy to the lowest waterline. Blue-tailed Bee-eater Asian Openbill In the highest branches of the older mangrove trees, Asian Openbills congregate, their distinctive arched mandibles leaving a visible gap designed for prying open snails. They often roost alongside Cormorants and Painted Storks, whose heavy, yellow decurved bills and delicate pink feathers contrast against the deep green foliage. Common Hawk Cuckoo The relentless ‘brain-fever’ call of the Common Hawk Cuckoo rings out from the taller trees, where Brahminy Starlings and Indian White-eyes move through the foliage, energized by the growing light. Near the ground, the heavy-set Southern Coucal stalks through the damp undergrowth, while Barn Swallows dip low over the water’s surface – skimming past the churning Little Cormorant 10

Slightly lower in the canopy or probing the soft mud at the roots, the three ibises of the estuary make their appearance. The Black-headed Ibis stands out with its white plumage and naked black head, often seen in small, stoic groups. In the dappled light of the inner mangroves, the Glossy Ibis transforms from a dark silhouette into a shimmering display of iridescent greens and purples. Occasionally, on the drier landward edges of the mangroves, the Red-naped Ibis – the erstwhile Black Ibis – can be found, identifiable by its crimson crown and the white patch on its wing that flashes when it takes flight. Below them, the creek edges belong to the kingfishers. The White-throated Kingfisher perches on drier branches, identifiable by its massive red bill and chocolate-brown breast. Closer to the water, the Common Kingfisher flashes past like a turquoise arrow, while the Pied Kingfisher hovers with mechanical precision over the centre of the channel. The Black-capped Kingfisher is the standout mangroves specialist, with its velvet-black crown and deep purple mantle. The real challenge of this ‘game’, however, is the huddle of Pond Herons and Black-crowned Night Herons, particularly the juveniles tucked under the shadows – they are masters of disguise. Both possess streaked brown plumage that mirrors the dappled light of the thicket. The subtlest of cues, heavier bills and the fiery yellow orange eyes of the juvenile Night Heron, contrasts with the Pond Heron’s more muted look. The mystery only truly vanishes the moment they take flight. As they break cover, the Night Heron reveals broad, dark, powerful wings. But it is the Pond Heron that provides the greatest surprise – bursting from its brown, camouflaged huddle with a flash of brilliant, snowy-white wings that were completely hidden while it was perched. Waders of the Silt While the boats are essential, the rhythmic thrum of the diesel motor is a frustrating paradox; its mechanical heartbeat precedes us, often sending the kingfishers and the Little Herons retreating into the shadows before we can even lock focus. We usually cut the motors to drift silently into the bend but nature often has its own whistle blower. As the tide pulls back, the Common Redshank emerges; it is a self-appointed, high-pitched neurotic of the mudflats. Just as the boat settles and I raise my lens, the air is shattered by a shrill, piercing ‘Twee-hu-hu! Twee- hu-hu’ – it's the sentinel of the marsh, but in that moment, it's just the bird that blew our cover. The Kingfisher vanishes into the dark tangles of the roots, and the Redshank takes flight, mocking us with its bright orange legs and white edged wings. Black-capped Kingfisher The Hidden Herons: A Game of Shadows As the boat glides closer to the muddy banks, we enter a world where visibility is a hard-won prize. Here, we play a game of shadows with the most deceptive residents of the mangroves – the Herons. Among the tangled roots, the herons huddle in the deep shade, testing every bit of our optical gear and patience. Common Redshank The Grey Heron stands tall and ashen, a motionless statue against the mud. In contrast, the Purple Heron is slimmer and more snake-like, its rich chestnut and purple hues allowing it to vanish into the reeds with terrifying ease. Along the very edge of the waterline, the small Little Heron (Striated Heron) stays crouched and stony, appearing more like a knot of wood than a bird. You sit there in the sudden, ringing silence – sweaty, annoyed, and being shouted at by a bird – realising that in this delta, you are never as stealthy as you think. We scan the silt for the more elegant Spotted Redshank in its pale winter coat, but often our eyes are drawn to the larger, sturdier Common Greenshank. It stands out with its greenish legs and a slightly stouter bill that has a subtle upward kink. Little (aka Striated) Heron Common Greenshank 11

In the shallower, freshwater-influenced pools, we find the ‘miniature’ version of the Greenshank: the Marsh Sandpiper. Much more delicate and daintier with a pencil-thin, perfectly straight bill and exceptionally long, spindly legs that give it a graceful, high-stepping gait. Shadows That Walk The mangroves are also home to some interesting mammals walking among the shadows of the mangroves. A Golden Jackal trotting along the muddy edge, its tawny coat a stark contrast to the deep green leaves is a rare glimpse into the terrestrial life of this wetland.Every year, I scan the dense roots with a sense of longing, hoping for a glimpse of the truly elusive: the Smooth-coated Otter or the endangered Fishing Cat. To see them would have been a crowning moment, yet even their absence reminds me of the wild mysteries these mangroves still guard. The Ghost of the Creek As we transition toward the open water, we encounter the ghostly gathering consisting of the towering Great Egret standing like a towering, stately statue, its long neck kinked with a patience that feels ancient. Marsh Sandpiper Great Egret Next to it the Median Egret is the ‘middle child’ – less imposing but perfectly balanced. Then there is the Little Egret with its golden slipper foot, dramatically hunting in the shallows. Its bright yellow feet flash against the dark mud as it stirs the silt to life. Common Sandpiper Joining them are the Common Sandpipers, perpetually bobbing their tails, and the solitary Green Sandpipers, which wait until the last moment to reveal their brilliant white rumps as they dart into the dark mangrove foliage. In the more open, marshy margins, the Wood Sandpiper makes a frequent appearance. Far more social than its ‘Green’ cousin, with a heavily spangled upperparts and a prominent white supercilium that gives it a bright-eyed, alert expression. Little Egret Golden Jackal The most confusing of the lot is the Western Reef Egret, appearing as either a deep, slate-grey or a pure white twin to the others. We have to look for the heavier, decurved bill and that ‘hunch’ – a posture that makes it look like it carries the weight of the estuary on its shoulders. 12

Moving away from the creeks, we gaze back through the thinning fog like most of the early hours. As the rising sun begins to add its first touch of glare to the water, the individual forms lose their edges and blue into a shimmering ghostly white line. The spectacle here is surreal. Indian Skimmers huddle in massive, mixed assemblages with a variety of terns. When the flock is spooked, they rise as one shimmering, chaotic cloud before settling back into the silt. Sorting through this ‘whiteout’ of terns is notoriously difficult. Gull-billed Tern flock Western Reef Egret The Lords of the Vertical World As we begin to leave the narrowing creeks of the Corangi (which seems to be a local way of calling Coringa) and the towering Avicennia canopy, our vertical words start to pull back. Here at the threshold of the open water, the Brahminy Kites reign as the undisputed lord. They bridge the tangled interior we are leaving behind with the vast, open mudflats ahead. You see them everywhere: perched with a regal whiteheaded stillness on the canopies, withered driftwoods or sunbleached fishing poles that jut from the mud. Their chestnut wings are a constant flash of colour against the receding green canopies. While these generalists scavenge at the noisy jetties, here they are true predators, watching the creeks from their high balconies. Our boats, census and gear are merely the outliers here – brief, mechanical intrusions into a world they have mastered for centuries. Greater Crested Tern The Caspian Tern is easy to spot by its massive, carrot-red bill, but telling the Gull-billed Tern (with its thick, short black bill) from the Greater Crested Tern (with its lemon-yellow bill) and Lesser Crested Tern (with its slim, orange-ish bill) requires a steady hand. These contrast with the Whiskered Terns, which stay in the more inland, brackish pools. The Mudflats of Etimoga and Bhairavapalem As the narrow creeks widen, the landscape opens into the vast, shimmering mudflats of Etimoga and Bhairavapalem. Here, the success of our count depends entirely on the local boatmen. Their knowledge is ancestral; they navigate shifting subsurface channels and time the tides with a precision no GPS could mimic. Their curiosity about why these birds travel thousands of miles leads to wonderful exchanges, building a bridge between science and local life. Whiskered Tern In the netted enclosures left by the fishermen, the water becomes a frenzy. Brown-headed and Black-headed Gulls hover and dive in pursuit of fish. The Brown-headed Gull is larger, with pale eyes and broad ‘white mirrors’ on its wing tips, while the Black-headed Gull is more delicate and lacks those bold white patches. Indian Skimmers with assorted terns 13

restless movement of the mixed flocks of Little Stints often complicates the plover identification process further. Brown-headed Gull Eurasian Oystercatcher Black-headed Gull Adding a flash of bold colour to this earth-toned assembly are the Eurasian Oystercatchers, their black-and-white plumage and carrot-orange bills standing out against the muted silt. Further along the mudflats, the Terek Sandpiper stands out with its improbable profile. It moves with a distinctive, energetic ‘teetering’ motion, but its most striking feature is its long, noticeably upcurved bill. Watching a Terek hunt is a joy; they often sprint after prey with their bright orange, relatively short legs, looking slightly front-heavy but incredibly graceful. Pacific Golden Plover On the drier patches, the plovers hold court. The Pacific Golden Plovers are a masterclass in texture, their backs a spangled mosaic of gold and black, contrasting sharply with the cold, silver-grey of the Grey Plovers. Near them, huge congregations of smaller plovers create an identification challenge that defines the AWC experience. The Little Ringed Plover is usually the easiest to pick out, immediately obvious by its bright yellow eye-ring and the bold, complete black collar that circles its neck. From this complete ring, we move to the Kentish Plover, whose collar is notably ‘broken’ – appearing as two dark tabs that never meet on its chest, setting it apart with its dainty, paler, sandy-grey plumage. This daintiness is in sharp contrast to the Lesser Sand Plover, which presents a much sturdier profile with a heavier, bulbous black bill, thicker, dark legs, and a more ‘smudged’ brown breast-band. However, the high-energy flight and Terek Sandpiper Ruddy Turnstone 14

Nearby, the Ruddy Turnstones provide a rugged contrast. While the other birds probe the sand, the Turnstones are the heavy lifters. True to their name, they use their short, slightly upturned, wedge-shaped bills to flick over stones and debris. Even in their more subdued winter colours, their orange legs and the bold, harlequin pattern on their chests make them unmistakable. They possess a sturdy, hunched silhouette that feels much more grounded than the ethereal stints. the grey water like clockwork, existing for only a few hours a day. In the soft light of the morning, these exposed banks become a canvas of incredible scale and beauty. It is a temporary carnival of waders where the sheer numbers defy easy counting and identification. Hundreds of Little Stints, Plovers, Waders, and Small Pratincoles descend upon these fleeting islands in a frantic, mixed population of activity. This sense of wonder continues into the air, which remains alive with the aerial displays of these winged wanderers. Watching them bank and turn in unison is a spectacle of light and motion. A massive, living ribbon that shifts as the sunlight catches it. In one heartbeat, the entire mass – a dull, earthy brown transforms into a flash of brilliant, snowy white as they reveal their bellies to the sun. This shimmering ‘turn’ of the flock over the disappearing banks is a sight of pure awe. There is no quiet here; it is a crowded, nomadic marketplace of life that knows, just as our boatmen do, that their stage will soon vanish back into the Bay of Bengal. Black-tailed Godwit Amidst the sprawling silt of Etimoga, the Godwits offer a lesson in patience. The Black-tailed Godwit is the mainstay here, often seen in healthy numbers, its long, dead-straight bill moving with the rhythmic precision of a sewing machine as it probes the deep mud. When they take flight, their bold white wing bars and crisp black tail bands create a striking graphic contrast against the grey sky. Mixed flock of Curlew and Broad-billed Sandpipers, Dunlin, Little Stint and Lesser Sand Plover The High Seas The transition from the sheltered, tea-coloured waters of the estuary to the open Bay of Bengal is a physical threshold. To reach Hope Island, you must leave the stillness behind. The high seas are a different beast; the boat rocks relentlessly, and the air is thick with a salt spray that stings the eyes and coats the lenses. Bar-tailed Godwit On much rarer occasions, a Bar-tailed Godwit might be spotted. Unlike the common Black-tailed, this visitor is far more elusive and solitary in these waters. Its profile is subtler, with a bill that carries a gentle, feminine upcurve. It lacks the flashy wing bars of its cousin, showing instead an intricate, barred pattern on its tail – a quiet, beautiful reward for those who take the time to scan the furthest reaches of the mudflats. Pulse of the Moon: A World of Shifting Sands and Banking Birds As we leave the mudflats of Etimoga and Bhairavapalem behind, the landscape enters a state of constant flux. Between the mainland and the open sea lies a world governed entirely by the moon. Here, the falling tide reveals a hidden ephemeral world – temporary sandbars and silty islands that emerge from The heaving of the deck makes it an ordeal to keep binoculars steady; your arms ache as you try to lock on to a moving speck in the distance. The cool wind of the delta is a deceptive friend – it masks the intensity of the sun on the back of your neck, leaving behind a dark, deep tan on every inch of exposed skin, a permanent souvenir. Amidst this spray and motion, there is a distinct camaraderie that only field volunteers understand. The organizers usually hand out a modest kit – some fruit, bread, and jam – and there is something profoundly beautiful about sharing that simple meal on a heaving boat. In those moments, between the splashes of saltwater and the shared laughter, the bond over our love for birds becomes as tangible as the rocking hull beneath us. Again, the boatman’s skill is the silent anchor; he reads the swells with a calm that allows us to focus on the horizon. 15

The beach itself is alive with more than just birds. The little Red Ghost Crabs (Ocypode macrocera) are the island's comic relief. With their stalk-like eyes and vibrant red carapaces, their antics are mesmerizing. They stand like tiny, defiant sentinels until you get too close, at which point they break into a frantic, sideways dash, disappearing into their sandy burrows with a speed that seems impossible for their size. Watching them scuttle away, legs blurred in motion, adds a touch of whimsy to the serious business of the census. Osprey Often, during these high-sea crossings, an Osprey would appear – gliding low over the waves with powerful, deliberate wingbeats. I have watched it hover, pause, and then plunge feet-first into the surf to rise triumphantly with a writhing fish, a lone hunter stitching together the river and the ocean. Hope Island: Godavari’s Guardian Angel As we approach Hope Island, its significance becomes as clear as the horizon. This narrow, tadpole-shaped barrier island is a gift from the river itself, formed over the last few centuries from the massive sediment load carried by the Godavari. It acts as a natural breakwater, absorbing the fury of the Bay of Bengal’s waves and protecting the Kakinada coast from erosion and the port from silting. Without this fragile strip of sand, the calm, brackish waters of the Coringa mangroves would be swallowed by the open sea. As we approach the uninhabited barrier of Hope Island, the water shallows, and we disembark to walk the windswept shores; it feels like stepping onto the last outpost of the wild.There is a profound, primal joy in walking the shores of Hope Island barefoot, feeling the wet silt between your toes as you track a flock of sandpipers. It is a moment of pure connection to the earth. But that connection is often violently broken. The modern world intrudes even here, in the form of a jagged shard of a discarded bottle or a piece of glass hidden in the sand. The sharp, sudden pain of a cut in the foot is a visceral reminder that even this remote sanctuary is not immune to the debris of human carelessness. Amidst the comedic dash of Red Ghost Crabs, the beach is a theatre of shorebirds. Huge, restless flocks of Sand Plovers and Kentish Plovers are joined by a swirling mass of stints. Sorting through a mixed flock of Little Stints and Temminck’s Stints is a masterclass in observation: Little Stints are high-energy, with brighter, more rufous tones on their mantles and dark, sturdy legs. Temminck’s Stints appear more ‘mousy’ and elongated, with a smoother, grey-brown back and, most tellingly, yellowish-green legs that distinguish them from the black-legged Little Stints. It was in one of these frantic, mixed gatherings of Curlew Sandpipers and Dunlins that I had my most memorable encounter. Among the crowd, I spotted the Broad-billed Sandpiper. It felt like a reward for eight years of persistence. While the Curlew Sandpiper is elegant with its long, decurved bill, the Broad-billed is shorter, with a bill that kinks downward specifically at the tip. But the real giveaway was its face – that unique ‘split’ supercilium, or double eyestripe, that gives it a distinctively patterned look. I have seen it only once in nearly a decade; a reminder of the rarity and fragility of these migratory journeys. Sanderling Right at the frothy edge of the tide, the Sanderlings perform their signature ‘clockwork’ dance. Unlike the stationary Plovers, Sanderlings in their pale winter coats are in constant motion, chasing the receding waves to snatch tiny crustaceans and then racing back up the slope just heartbeats ahead of the incoming foam. The easiest way to pick them out – aside from their frantic running – is the lack of a hind toe, leaving them with a clean, three-toed footprint in the wet sand. Red Ghost Crab 16

Pallas’s Gull Olive Ridley Turtle Out in the deeper water surrounding the island, the giants of the gull world take over. We spot the Heuglin’s Gull, a formidable bird with a dark, slate-grey mantle and yellow legs. Alongside them are the Pallas’s Gulls, massive and commanding. In January, many are beginning their transition, their large, powerful orange-and-black bills standing out even as their hoods begin to darken for the breeding season. The Cost of Progress: A Landscape Under Siege, Greed and Ghost Nets But the eight-year arc of my journey has not only been one of discovery; it has been one of witnessing a deepening crisis. In recent years, the horizon has been cluttered by the machinery of aggressive offshore gas exploration. The silence of the high seas is increasingly broken by industrial noise of dredging and deep-sea seismic activity. Great and Red Knots At the Kumbhabhishekam port area, I have watched the counts dwindle as the expansion of the port – the deeper dredging, new berths, and constant reclamation—erodes the feeding grounds of the very birds we come to protect. The Knots, once more common here, have been pushed to the furthest, most secluded slivers of mud to escape the industrial clamour. Sl No Species Name Scientific Name 1 Indian Skimmer Rynchops albicollis 2 Great Knot Calidris tenuirostris 3 Black-headed Ibis 4 Painted Stork 5 Eurasian Curlew Threskiornis melanocephalus Mycteria leucocephala Numenius arquata Location / Habitat I have walked the beaches of Hope Island and found them littered not with shells, but with the tragic remains of Olive Ridley sea turtles. These ancient voyagers, coming home to nest, are met instead with the lethal combination of deep exploration and ‘ghost nets’ – discarded fishing gear that drifts like invisible snares in the water. To see a beach dotted with dead turtles is a visceral, heart-breaking reminder of how our relentless greed for energy and resources kills the very life we are trying to count. A Calling for Resilience Eight years on, these annual counts remain a calling – a blend of adventure, technical rigor, and a deep, often painful connection to the Godavari. These years have shown me beauty, yes – but also erosion, indifference, and the accelerating cost of progress. What remains clear is that these wetlands cannot wait for policies to catch up, nor can they rely on the shrinking memories of those who once knew their abundance. If this estuary is to survive, it will be because ordinary people – boatmen, volunteers, children, citizens – choose to defend it. The Godavari has carried life for millennia. Now, it needs us to carry responsibility. The next decade will decide the fate of this delta. The question is no longer whether the birds will land, it is whether we will rise fast enough to ensure they have a place to land. These wetlands do not ask for perfection from us – only attention, only care, only the willingness to stand by them as they change. As I look across the mangroves one more time, I realize that resilience is not a guarantee; it is a choice – one we must make for them, and with them. And until the day the river stops calling, I will keep coming back to listen. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Rosy Minivet (Pericrocotus roseus) Rosy Minivet Male (L) and Female (R) (Kaladungi, Uttarakhand, May 09, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Passeriformes Campephagidae Pericrocotus P. roseus 18-20 cm Least Concern Habitat & behaviour: The natural habitats of the Rosy Minivet are deciduous or evergreen forest, subtropical or tropical moist lowland and moist montane forests, lightly wooded country, and sometimes even gardens. It is arboreal and somewhat sluggish moving compared to other minivets. It is usually seen in pairs, but does form flocks outside of the breeding season. It breeds in a wide range of lowland and foothill forests, including many parts of the Himalayas, and favours hill and valley forests in the winter. Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods. Its call is a squeaky whistling whiririri, and it may also give a twittering trill in flight. Description & distribution: The Rosy Minivet is a pale, washed-out looking minivet that is widely distributed across a large part of Asia, from Afghanistan east across Pakistan, India, Nepal, Laos, Myanmar, Bhutan, China, Bangladesh, Thailand and Vietnam. In India, it is found from the western Himalayas east to Arunachal Pradesh and the hills of Nagaland and Manipur up to 1800m during summers, and moves to the peninsula during the winter. Nesting: The Rosy Minivet breeds mainly between May and June in the Himalayas. The nest is usually a deep cup of roots, twigs and grass stems covered with cobwebs and lichen, and is usually built mainly by the female, with the male assisting. It is usually located 3-10m above ground on a horizontal tree branch. The usual clutch consists of 3-4 eggs, almost white but marked with blotches of brown. The Rosy Minivet is known to hybridize with the closely-related Brown-rumped Minivet, seen in parts of China. The male has a grey head, white throat, rosy pink breast, and a striking red ‘apostrophe’ on the dark grey-brown upperwings, besides pinkish-red edges to tertials and pinkish rump. The female shows yellow in place of the male’s red and pink, but is otherwise similar. Rump is olive or olive-yellow. Legs and feet are black in both, and both have prominent dark lores. The juvenile has upperparts with yellowish scales. Only one subspecies is recognized. Local name: The Rosy Minivet is known as ‘Gulabi bulalchashm’ in Hindi and ‘Dao ribi’ in Cachar. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 20 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Meeting Point(s): SVM Grand, Miyapur, 05:20AM; BHEL Bus Stop, Lingampally, 05:45AM. The lake is home to more than 110 species of birds, including large flocks of Little Stint, Black-winged Stilt, Black-tailed Godwit, Garganey, Gadwall etc. One can also spot Ruff, Spot-billed Pelican, Common Snipe, Greater Flamingo, Common Redshank, Temminck’s Stint and other shore birds. The surrounding areas also host species like Mongolian Short-toed Lark, Citrine Wagtail, Baya Weaver, Indian Golden Oriole etc. This is a great opportunity to observe and record the diversity of migratory waterbirds and shore birds in this important habitat as winter draws to a close in the state. AN IMPROMPTU VISIT TO PALMAKOLE LAKE Trip Report: Palmakole Lake, Hyderabad, February 17, 2026 Shafaat Ulla It was ages since we had been to the Palmakole Lake, so we (Nandu, Surekha, Chaudhari & self) decided to pay a visit and put in some birding there. When we reached the village of Palmakole (about 10km past the airport on Bengaluru highway) at about 07.00AM, we could not locate the turn off point to the lake as all our known landmarks had been obliterated because of road widening. However a kindly gentleman guided us to the lake shore, which was more than hundred meters from the highway. As soon as we turned left on a kaccha track, we saw a murmuration of Rosy Starlings on a tree on the right and a lonely Hoopoe pecking the grassy ground for his breakfast. Proceeding further, after crossing a small nala, we came across some thorny bushes where Green Bee-eaters were hawking insects. Further up we came to a Y junction and as advised took the track going right, and immediately spotted a Brown Shrike on a bare tree. We finally came to a canal-like structure and had to park the car there because of slushy ground. We started walking towards the lake, avoiding the slush. On the left was a Black Drongo, doing aerobatics to catch insects, and a lone Redwattled Lapwing, sitting coolly on the ground watching and repeatedly saying ‘did you do it’. We finally made it to the shore: the lake had literally become an ocean and with hardly any bird life, except an Indian Cormorant sitting on a huge rock. Next to the canal and right below, we could spot an Indian Moorhen and a Blyth’s Reed Warbler foraging among the reeds. Our attention was now drawn towards some plantations with loud noise which turned out to be Large Grey Babblers and, below, a pair of Indian Robins trying to find food. We nevertheless scanned the lake with our binocs – at the far end there was an island-like grassy patch on which we could see a Grey Heron, a Purple Heron and some Egrets. We now turned back, a little disappointed for not seeing any bird life in the lake. While walking towards the car, we spotted a Golden Oriole and a Grey Bellied Cuckoo. We were about to board the car when a White Wagtail came and sat on the canal parapet, as if to bid us farewell. We drove back to the Y junction and took the left track. Here on a wall were a House Crow, a Large-billed Crow and a Brahminy Starling – a rather strange combination. Further up, there was a small tree on which were quite a few Baya Weavers – all looked like juveniles – and there was no nests in sight. Next to the tree was a dilapidated building on which sat a male House Sparrow preening himself. We proceeded further on this trail and while driving spotted Yellow-billed Babblers, a Cattle Egret, some Peafowl and a White-throated Kingfisher. The track soon came to an end as it was inundated with the lake water. We therefore stopped and decided to explore the surroundings on foot. 1

On the left was a huge pond, with outcrops and aquatic vegetation. Here a pair of Spot-billed Ducks had made their home. Also spotted here some Coot and a lone White-breasted Waterhen. We were about to leave when came a Marsh Harrier, majestically surveying the area. was a Long-tailed Shrike. We now climbed an embankment to have a clear view of the lake. On the far end we could discern through our binocs an Openbill and a Painted Stork as also a Black-headed Ibis and some Cormorants. By now it was time to return, so we called it a day after having compiled a list of 53 species. Now we went to the right towards the lake. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Upland Pipit (Anthus sylvanus) Upland Pipit (Kaladungi, Uttarakhand, May 09, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Passeriformes Motacillidae Anthus A. silvanus 17 cm Least Concern Habitat & behaviour: The preferred habitat of the Upland Pipit is rocky and grassy slopes on hills and mountains, abandoned terrace cultivation, and open areas with grassland at altitudes above 500m, often strewn with rocks that act as song posts. It is resident in most parts of its range, and breeds in foothills and mountains, but descends during the winter. Its diet consists mainly of small invertebrates which it picks off the ground while moving along with creeping movements in horizontal posture. If disturbed, it adopts an upright posture and makes tail flicking movements. Its flight is the typical ballooning flight exhibited by other pipits, and the call is a sparrow-like chirp, while the song, uttered either from ground or in flight, is a repeated seetyu-seetyu or tyu-see, tyu-see, or a rather pleasant but monotonous weeeee tch weeeee tch or a drawnout whistling wichee wichee wichee. Description & distribution: The Upland Pipit is one of the larger pipits, and has a wide range, from Afghanistan east across Pakistan, India, Nepal, China and Hong Kong. It is, however, uncommon and sparsely distributed throughout most of its range. It is large-billed and quite bulky looking compared to other pipits, with an upright stance and heavy blackishbrown streaks on upperparts. The paler underparts can vary from warm buff (in fresh plumage) to cold and grey (in worn plumage), and show fine dark streaking. The supercilium is whitish and quite contrasting with the strongly-streaked crown, bill is short and broad, legs are pale, and the tail feathers are narrow and pointed. It has indistinct dark moustachial and malar stripes, and the iris is brown. The upper mandible is dark, while the lower is flesh-coloured with a dark tip. It may be confused with Richard’s and Blyth’s Pipits in overlapping areas, but it is more densely streaked and with a stouter and shorter bill. Juvenile birds have prominent pale buffish feather tips and edges above, giving it a scaly appearance, while the underparts are whiter with paler streaks. Only one sub-species is recognized. Nesting: The Upland Pipit breeds mainly between March and July. The nest is usually a cup of coarse grass lined with finer grass, and built under a rock or tuft of grass for concealment and protection. The usual clutch consists of 3-5 eggs. The Common Cuckoo is known to sometimes parasitize the nest of the Upland Pipit. Local name: The Upland Pipit is known as ‘Pahari dhanchidi’ in Hindi (a term also applied to other pipits), ‘Pahari charchari’ in Punjabi, ‘Pahari tulika’ in Bengali and ‘Pahari chuiya’ in Nepali. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 3 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 23 Number 5 May 2026 FIELD TRIP: Details will be announced on email An Encomium to the Iora Sudhir K A sweet short whistle brings a smile to my face A flash of black and yellow, flitters across the foliage Hopping around at a hectic pace Finally catch a glimpse of the sweet rascal Donning a Bright yellow vest The wings are black and so is the back Filled with so much zeal and zest A couple of brush strokes of white Slashed across the wings that adds some flair Come monsoon and the gentleman adorns an elegant black cap To woo the ladies with a puffed-up flip in the air Common Iora is the name and hunting eight-legged spinners and sundry is the game My day is seldom complete Without a visit from these sunlit golden nuggets Their whistling to my ears is music so sweet This my friends is my ode to the Aegithina tiphia *** 1

SIGHTING OF THE WHITE-BELLIED HERON – A DREAM COME TRUE Bhutan, April 20, 2026 Text and Photos: Umesh Mani A view of the river We, a group of ten from Chennai, went on a birding trip to Bhutan recently. It was a great trip, and gave us a pretty huge list of ~260 bird species recorded. There were many highlights, including the Ward’s Trogon, Solitary Snipe, pheasants like Satyr Tragopan, Blood Pheasant, Hill Partridge, Himalayan Monal and Kalij Pheasant, ten raptor species, 5 owls, 8 cuckoos (including the Asian Emerald Cuckoo), 4 parrotbills, and many finches, rosefinches and bullfinches, sunbirds, tits, yuhinas, and so on. The undisputed star of the trip, however, was the White-bellied Heron. Also known as the Imperial Heron or Great White-bellied Heron, it is one of the rarest birds on Earth, with the world population estimated at less than 250 mature individuals (as per IUCN Red List), although a recent Yale Tropical Resources Institute study put the number at a much more critical number – less than 70 birds. Of which, Bhutan holds a population of around 29-30 birds. And though the Royal Society for Protection of Nature runs an intense communityled conservation program for this heron in Bhutan, it is safe to say, sadly, that it is a species on the brink of extinction. To see the White-bellied Heron had been a long-nurtured dream of mine. In 20 years of birding, I had never managed to see this bird. So, when we heard of a location where a nesting pair had been seen, just a couple of days before our Bhutan trip, I was excited at the possibility of finally seeing it. entire trip – well, almost! – to go and see this bird. And fortunately, the rest of the group was in complete agreement. So we made some changes in our itinerary, cut short our stay in Paro by one day, moved to Thimphu a day earlier, and off we went. It was a long drive – around four hours on mountain roads is no laughing matter – but we started early and made good time. Finally arriving at the location, we got our first shock when we were told that we had to climb down the hillside around 500 metres. Climbing down was fine – the real worry was climbing back up again! Anyway, in the spirit of “anything for the White-bellied Heron”, we climbed down – the distance turned out to be around 30 metres, rather than 500! – maybe it was the guide’s way of mentally preparing us. At the spot, we were given another minor heart attack when, after a quick scan of the trees, the local guide said he could not see the bird. We began to wonder if it was going to be all in vain – the proverbial slip between the cup and the lip. To give you an idea of the place – it was not like the ‘heron sitting on a bare tree’ sites where we usually see our Grey Herons and Openbills and Painted Storks nesting. This spot was on the side of a hill, and we were looking at a forest containing what seemed like a million trees, across a river, and possibly a hundred metres below our line of sight. Not easy, to put it mildly. The location was quite far, though, and not even on our itinerary. However, personally I was willing to give up the 2

One of my pet peeves is that most birders are not very good at explaining a location. I have heard, so many times, people say things like: “It is on that tree” – in the middle of a forest; “It is right in front” – well, naturally; “It is in the gap between those branches” – when you don’t even know which tree; And the worst, most aggravating, exasperating one of all – “Look where I am looking!” The location It should not be so difficult to pick a reference point – puddle, rock, yellow flowers, whatever – and go “ten o’clock from there, around 15-20 feet”. After a few minutes of desperate scanning by all of us, through a variety of binoculars and cameras, the guide called out, “There it is!” – and we all breathed again. A couple of others had found the bird by now, but several hadn’t, yet. I managed to help a few members of the group locate it. A clamour of “Where? Where?” broke out. The local guide pointed out the nest to us. Well, he tried, anyway. But it took a minute – that felt like an hour – before I could finally locate it. I heaved a heartfelt sigh – happiness, relief all rolled into one. It is a fairly unremarkable-looking bird, but its extreme rarity, I suppose, lends it an aura that is larger than life. Meanwhile, the guides had set up a spotting scope – thank God! – and found the nest, so we all took turns and saw the bird and the chick to our hearts’ content. Well, not exactly, but you know what I mean. Birder-photographers seem to have many categories of Lifers. There is: Some of us took digiscoped photos and videos with our mobile phones through the scope. Those of us who had camera gear took photos with the cameras. And some of us just watched the birds. The first time I saw it; The first time I saw it well; The first time I photographed it; The first time I got a good photo; and even The first time I got a photo with this camera and lens! A few minutes later, the chick seemed to lie down and go back to sleep. That is when the adult bird put back its wing – and I realised that the adult had been shielding the chick from the sun all this while. And we saw exactly why this bird is called White-bellied! For a birder, life is much simpler. “I saw it” is enough. Of course, each individual is different. For me, I was happy to see the White-bellied Heron well through my binocs. But I did want a photograph. Good photograph. It was a watershed moment for me, after all. So I took a quick few photographs before trying to help others locate the nest – and was over-themoon thrilled when I saw that I had managed to capture the chick also, standing tall and cuddling up to its parent! The chick goes back to sleep We saw a Mountain Hawk Eagle lazily circle around and then go and perch on one of the trees a little distance away. And were suddenly worried for the welfare of the chick – Mountain Hawk Eagles are known to predate small birds, especially chicks. However, we trusted in the ability of the parents to fight off such threats. White-bellied Heron and chick 3

White-bellied Heron. All are human-originated – I wondered if we, as a species, will allow any species to survive. We can only hope and pray that at least the captive breeding program succeeds in restoring its population to some degree of health. Not an easy road – but what else have we got? Mountain Hawk Eagle The earlier group had seen a pair of adults, and the guide told us that they seemed to be taking turns – one would go to feed while the other guarded the nest and the chick – and the cycle seemed to be around 3-4 hours. Given the distance we had to travel, it seemed difficult for us to wait for the shift change, but we did hang around for about an hour, hoping to see the other adult return. A view of the other side of the river [Editor’s Note: Generally nest photos are not allowed in most birding groups, due to the potential risks to the bird. However, in this case, an exception is being made by the Editor due to the extreme rarity of the bird, which the group was able to sight in a very remote location only with the help of a local guide, and also since an egg from the clutch had already been removed by the Department of Forests and Park Services of Bhutan for the captive breeding programme, establishing prior human intervention.] After that period, though, with no other bird in sight, we decided to get back to base. It was a bittersweet moment. We were happy to have seen the White-bellied Heron – and with a chick which, to me, is always a sign of hope for the future. However, we also knew how precarious its current position is, and wondered if we would ever get to see it again. Habitat loss, human disturbance, and the destruction of breeding sites are said to be the prime threats faced by the *** Bird Humour Umesh Mani (Received on WhatsApp, July 18, 2023) *** 4

Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Sarus Crane (Antigone antigone) Sarus Crane Male (L), Immature (C) and Female (R) (Nalsarovar, Gujarat, January 2, 2026) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Gruiformes Gruidae Antigone A. antigone 156-180 cm Vulnerable Description & distribution: The Sarus Crane is a large, nonmigratory crane found in parts of the Indian sub-continent and South-east Asia, including Pakistan, India, Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam and China. In India, the Sarus Crane is primarily found in the lowlands, including the Gangetic plains, and west to coastal Gujarat, south to Godavari river, and east to West Bengal and Assam (although it is quite rare from Bihar eastwards).They were also once present in Thailand and the Philippines, but those populations are now considered locally extinct. Besides, there is a small population present in the north-eastern parts of Australia, where it is partially migratory. While the global population is under pressure, in some areas it seems to be doing well due to increase in the areas under paddy cultivation. The Sarus Crane is mostly grey overall, with only the bare red head, collar and nape standing out. It has a greyish crown, grey ear patch, long and pointed greenish-grey bill, whitish neck, long pink legs and orange-red irises. In breeding season, the red around the head and neck becomes brighter. The sexes are alike, although the male is noticeably taller than the female. Juvenile birds show a yellowish base to the bill and a fully feathered brown-grey head. Males in the Indian population can reach up to 180 cm in height, making them the world’s tallest extant flying birds. Habitat & behaviour: The Sarus Crane is a resident breeder across most of its range, and prefers open shallow wetlands, uncultivated areas or irrigated paddy and wheat fields. Numbers seem to increase as the size of the wetlands increase. In Australia, non-breeding birds have been seen to forage in areas with intensive agriculture and smaller patches of cattlegrazing areas, where they were observed feeding on grain, nuts and insects. Unlike most cranes, the Sarus Crane is mainly non-migratory. Breeding pairs are strongly territorial, and may defend their territories with a range of calls and displays. Paired birds are known to utter calls in unison (duets), either at the edge of their territories, or on the nest where they are incubating. Very rarely, they are known to allow a third member and utter calls together (triets) – this is believed to help improve breeding success rate as the third member may also help in raising the chicks. In the non-breeding season, though, the Sarus Crane is fairly social, and may be seen in groups ranging from a few birds to as large as a couple of hundreds – the largest flock ever recorded was 430 birds from Keoladeo National Park (aka Bharatpur). The Sarus Crane is omnivorous, and its diet consists mainly of insects (especially grasshoppers), aquatic plants, fish, frogs, crustaceans, and seeds. It may also, occasionally, take larger vertebrate prey like water snakes or the eggs of birds and turtles. There are also two published records of the Sarus Crane 5

hunting and feeding on chicks of the Grey-headed Swamphen. Plant matter eaten includes tubers, corms of aquatic plants, grass shoots as well as seeds and grains from cultivated crops such as peanuts and cereal crops such as rice. Its flight is slow and ponderous, with slow rhythmical wingbeats, rarely very high up in the air. The call is a loud trumpeting, uttered from the ground as well as in flight. in the middle of a flooded field or marsh. The usual clutch consists of two eggs, pale greenish or pinkish white, sometimes spotted or blotched brown or purple. Local name: The Sarus Crane is known as ‘Saras’ or ‘Sarus’ in Hindi, Punjabi and Marathi, ‘Sarasu konga’ in Telugu, ‘Bharat sarus’ in Sanskrit, ‘Khur sang’ in Assamese, and ‘Woinu’ or ‘Woinuren’ in Manipuri. Nesting: The Sarus Crane breeds mainly between July and December. The nest is a large mass of reeds, stems and straw *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 6 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034. Newsletter of Deccan Birders (formerly Birdwatchers’ Society of Andhra Pradesh) New Series Volume 23 Number 6 June 2026 FIELD TRIP: Sunday, June 28, 2026, 6.15AM: Zaheerabad. Meeting Point(s): Metro Station, Miyapur, 04:30AM; BHEL Bus Stop, Lingampally, 04:45AM; Taj Dhaba, Muthangi, 05:00AM. Trip Coordinator(s): Sathwik Reddy (Mobile: 98858-07186) The forest region near Zaheerabad, in close proximity to the Chincholi Wildlife Sanctuary on the Telangana-Karnataka border, is a critical habitat characterized by a rich tapestry of flora and fauna. This area, primarily a dry land ecosystem, showcases a unique blend of forest types and topographical features that support a remarkable diversity of life. The core of this forest is dominated by dry and moist deciduous forests, which transition into Acacia and Teak plantations on the fringes. The forest is renowned for its significant populations of valuable tree species such as Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) and Sandalwood (Santalum album), along with a variety of medicinal herbs and trees. The undulating terrain includes rocky outcrops and scrublands, typical of the Deccan thorn scrub forest eco-region. The presence of the Chandrampalli dam and several other smaller water bodies creates a vital network of reservoirs and streams. This network sustains the region's wildlife, especially during the dry seasons, and contributes to the moist deciduous vegetation found in some core areas. The forest hosts many mammals such as the Blackbuck, Indian Wolf, Striped Hyena, and the Four-horned Antelope. The bird life is particularly noteworthy: White-bellied Minivet, Small Minivet, Black-headed Cuckooshrike, Chestnut-bellied Sandgrouse, Painted Francolin, various quail species like the Rain Quail, Jungle & Rock Bush Quails, and Barred Buttonquail – besides many other resident species. This will be a half-day trip, so carry adequate water and breakfast/snacks, and protective gear if required. Non-members are most welcome; however, they are requested to contribute Rs. 100/- per person to the Deccan Birders kitty. New Deccan Birders hats and caps will be available for purchase; please carry adequate cash. FIELD NARRATIVE FROM INDIA’S REMOTE ISLAND FRONTIER Trip Report: South Andaman & Narcondam, March 16-23, 2026 Text and Photos: Aditya Rao (unless otherwise attributed) A view of Narcondam Island, dormant volcanic island rising from the Bay of Bengal Some birding journeys are built around species. Others are shaped by landscape. A very small few are defined by access, remoteness, and the sense that you are operating at the edge of what is realistically possible. The March 2026 expedition across South Andaman, Middle Andaman, North Andaman, and onward to Narcondam fell firmly into that last category – and it had been in the works for a full year before a single bird was seen. 1

Narcondam is not a routine destination. It is a dormant volcanic island in the Bay of Bengal with no permitted landings. That combination of geological uniqueness, ecological isolation, and logistical constraint makes it one of the most compelling birding objectives in India. When the trip was announced in April 2025, I immediately committed – a full year in advance. You do not pass on an opportunity like this. DAY 1 – 18 MARCH: SIPPIGHAT & FERRARGUNJ Long-toed Stint The trip started at the Sippighat Salt Marsh, producing Javan Pond Heron, Chinese Pond Heron, Yellow Bittern, and Longtoed Stint, along with several Pin-tailed and Common Snipe. The interplay between resident wetland birds and migratory species was immediately evident. Road through Ferrargunj Forest, a tunnel of trees leading to endemic territory Common Snipe Javan Pond Heron Andaman Wood Pigeon Yellow Bittern By the afternoon, attention shifted to Ferrargunj Forest, where the standout was a flock of approximately eight Andaman Wood Pigeons – a rare and hard bird at the islands, rarely encountered in numbers. The supporting cast included Andaman Cuckoo Dove, Andaman Cuckooshrike, Long-tailed Parakeet, Andaman Green Pigeon, Andaman Drongo, Andaman Treepie, Andaman Bulbul, and Asian Fairy Bluebird. 2

Andaman Green Pigeon Andaman Cuckooshrike The following dawn session at Ferrargunj added Andaman Crake, Freckle-breasted Woodpecker, Andaman Woodpecker, Andaman Shama, Andaman Drongo and Andaman Flowerpecker. Andaman Crake (Photo: Vinay Chakravarthy) Andaman Bulbul Andaman Shama Andaman Cuckoo Dove 3

A subsequent visit to Ograbraj Wetlands yielded Grey-headed Lapwing, Eastern Marsh Harrier, Edible-nest (now Whitenest) Swiftlet, and Richard's Pipit. DAY 2 – 19 MARCH: MFV CAIMAN TO DIGLIPUR Andaman Drongo MFV Caiman at Diglipur Jetty The MFV Caiman, a sturdy twin-outboard offshore cabin boat with 500hp, departed Haddo Jetty, Port Blair, for the 100nautical-mile run north to Diglipur. The sea was rough; we could barely push beyond 20 knots and the crossing took nearly six hours. Emerald islands passed one after another through spray and chop, with occasional Black-naped Terns appearing as we crossed past Rangat and Mayabunder. Andaman Flowerpecker Black-naped Tern Eastern Marsh Harrier Saddle Peak, highest point in the Andamans, near Diglipur Richard’s Pipit We reached Aerial Bay Jetty around 5:30 PM, past sunset, to be welcomed by thousands of Plume-toed Swifts and Pacific Swallows wheeling overhead in the last light – eBird logged 1,000+ swifts at the jetty that evening. A quick snack near the jetty, then Pristine Beach Resort, and a very early night. We had been up by 3:30AM. 4

DAY 3 – 20 MARCH: NARCONDAM Sunrise over the Bay of Bengal A pair of Narcondam Hornbills in flight There are journeys, and then there are arrivals that stay with you for life. The boat left at 4:30AM into complete darkness, heading northeast for 145-150 km across open water. For much of the crossing there was only sea. Narcondam did not reveal itself immediately. It appeared gradually – a distant shape, slowly resolving against the horizon into a steep volcanic rise. Narcondam Hornbill female (L) and male (R) Narcondam’s forested coastline Narcondam Hornbills appeared almost as guardians – flying from tree to tree across the forested slopes, silhouetted against green canopy. Effortless. Unbothered. Endemic. We stopped well short of shore – landing is not permitted – and observed entirely from offshore. In that moment, it was not just birding. It was perspective. The wave-eroded rock face at the base of Narcondam Island As we drew closer, the island began to reveal itself: rugged coastal faces, dense tropical vegetation, the unmistakable profile of a place that has belonged entirely to nature for millions of years. It felt untouched in a way that is increasingly rare. Narcondam Hornbill male 5

Narcondam Hornbill female Red-billed Tropicbird The eBird checklist recorded 56 Narcondam Hornbills – noted as 'literally flying around in large flocks across the island, extremely active.' Additional species included Pied Imperial Pigeon (42 birds), Pacific Reef Heron, White-bellied Sea Eagle, and a Taiga Flycatcher heard from within the forest. We spent 3.5 hours around the island. PELAGIC BIRDS – ON THE WAY BACK FROM NARCONDAM Bottlenose Dolphin DAY 4 – 21 MARCH: RETURN VIA RANGAT Bridled Tern Cutting through the Yeratta Mangroves near Rangat Wedge-tailed Shearwater (Photo: Samanvitha Rao) The return leg delivered outstanding open-water birding: Bridled Tern, Wedge-tailed Shearwater (dark morph), Sooty Tern, Common Tern, and Red-billed Tropicbird. A large pod of Bottlenose Dolphins escorted the boat for an extended period, leaping alongside in what felt like a fitting close to the expedition's centrepiece day. Great Crested Tern 6

The return passage south was calmer – four hours versus six. A detour near Rangat in Middle Andaman delivered the target: Pale-footed Bush Warbler at Sabari village – a brief but conclusive glimpse before it vanished into the thicket, classic skulker behaviour. A Great Crested Tern was noted near Kadamtala while underway. Andaman Teal Red-throated Pipit Pacific Swallow Oriental Pratincole Red Collared Dove Chinese Pond Heron Back at Sippighat that afternoon, we got the Red-throated Pipit, Oriental Pratincole, Chinese Pond Heron in breeding plumage, Andaman Teal, and Slaty-breasted Rail. The site rewarded a second visit with species that had been absent or elusive on Day 1 – a reminder that wetland sites in the Andamans shift their cast between morning and afternoon sessions. Pin-tailed Snipe 7

DAY 5 – 22 MARCH: KALATANG & CHOULDARI The day ended at Chouldari Wetland with the Mangrove Whistler – quiet, elusive, and a perfectly characterful conclusion to five days of South Andaman birding. Mangrove Whistler Japanese Sparrowhawk (Photo: Samanvitha Rao) An additional day at Kalatang, a magnificent coastal rainforest, produced Violet Cuckoo and Chinese Sparrowhawk in the morning. The afternoon return visit yielded Ruddy Kingfisher – a bird that rewards patience with one of the most vividly coloured sightings of the entire trip. FAREWELL – 23 MARCH An Andaman Coucal called from the garden at Rainbird Resort as we packed for the flight back to Hyderabad. Ruddy Kingfisher Andaman Coucal Six days. 117 species. 35 checklists. One volcanic island in the Bay of Bengal that stays with you long after you have come home. What defines this expedition is not the checklist, impressive as it is. It is the combination of access, habitat diversity, and ecological context. Narcondam stands apart not just because of the hornbill – but because of what it represents: a largely intact system, geographically isolated and biologically distinct, observed with the respect that comes from staying offshore and watching from a distance. Trip Report: Nehru Zoological Park, Hyderabad, May 24, 2026 Syeda Batool Zaidi Spotted Owlet (Photo: Ali Hyder) Imagine this. A slow, sun-kissed Sunday morning. When the breeze slightly tugs at your clothes and dances with the trees ever so often. The birds come out to play hide & seek, and their eager, early chirping makes for a sweet, soulful melody that only nature could produce. This May 24th, what is usually a boring, movie-induced Sunday start, turned into a memorable experience. This May 24th, I was out and about with Deccan Birders, who introduced me to the art of bird-watching. As a nature lover who adores trees, I learned about their residents. Fascinating and beautiful creatures whose beauty and importance often go unnoticed. The journey started out with the Deccan Birders all gathering together, and a brief meeting was held to let the newbies know about the rules and regulations. The newbies were assigned a group leader, who would tell us know where to spot the birds and the names of the birds. White-throated Kingfisher (Photo: Ali Hyder) Abhinav guided us in the most detailed way possible. He introduced us to many birds, including the Oriental Magpie Robin, a small black-and-white bird known for its beautiful, melodious songs. Another one we saw was a Kingfisher, drinking water from a nearby pond. The sun made its blues and oranges pop out even more. Our team leader was Abhinav. He knew the name of every single bird we walked past, which was highly impressive since our leader was about 10 years old. Now that was inspiring! Common Hoopoe (Photo: Ali Hyder) The group in action (Photo: Gowthama Poludasu) 12

We also noticed many Babblers, chirping away at each other. There were many more that our group leader showed us, and trust me when I tell you, each one was a beauty in its own right. welcome, and of course, my dearest Uncle, Murthuza Hussain, for encouraging us all to take part in this quiet, peaceful, and truly interesting activity. Black Kite (Photo: Ali Hyder) Some members of the group during a break (Photo: Syed Murthuza Hussaini) Indeed, I am glad to have sacrificed my sleep for a day with the winged creatures, the sun dancing between the leaves, and the wind swaying to their songs. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Slaty-breasted Rail (Lewinia striata) Slaty-breasted Rail L. s. albiventer adult (Rollapadu, September 30, 2025) Slaty-breasted Rail L. s. obscurior adult (L) and juvenile (R) (Andaman, April 11, 2026) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Gruiformes Rallidae Lewinia L. striata 27 cm Least Concern and Nicobar Islands, which is darker overall with the grey on head and neck being markedly darker. Habitat & behaviour: The Slaty-breasted Rail is a skulker and frequents reedy swamps, marshy meadows, mangroves, irrigated paddy fields, drainage ditches, and the vegetation around village tanks. It walks slowly about with an upright stance, jerking the tail at every step, but is not easily seen as it rarely comes out in the open. It may show local movements during times of drought or floods, but otherwise tends to stay in and around its patch. It is omnivorous, and its diet consists mainly of worms, molluscs, crustaceans, aquatic and terrestrial insects (including ants) and their larvae, and spiders; it also takes seeds and shoots of marsh plants. In flight, it flies with legs trailing behind the body. It is normally silent, but may occasionally utter a sharp loud whistle or short jerky screams. Description & distribution: The Slaty-breasted Rail is a widespread resident breeder in India (including Andaman and Nicobar Islands) and Sri Lanka, besides being present in parts of China, Taiwan, Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Borneo and Indonesia. The Slaty-breasted Rail is a distinctive medium-sized, shorttailed rail, easily distinguished from other rails by the combination of chestnut head, nape and sides of neck, ashyblue foreneck and breast, narrow white bars and spots on upperparts and wings, darker white-barred underparts and flanks, dark brown upperparts, and a fairly long reddish bill. Chin and throat is white, while eyes are red and legs are olive grey. The female is duller on the upperparts and has more white on the belly. The immature is like the adult but the white barring is less distinct; the upperparts, including crown and hindneck, are indistinctly streaked and darker; the breast is more brownish, and the underparts are paler. Eight subspecies are recognized, of which two are seen in India: L. s. albiventer, seen in most of India, and L. s. obscurior, seen in the Andaman Nesting: The Slaty-breasted Rail breeds mainly between midJune and October. The nest is a pad of matted vegetation, around 25cm in size, and built on the ground or on reeds, and hidden inside marsh vegetation. The usual clutch consists of 5-7 cream coloured or darker eggs, smooth, glossy, spotted or blotched red or purple. Local name: The Slaty-breasted Rail is known as ‘Piroji pan lauva’ or ‘Patawali santhakukdi’ in Punjabi, ‘Wadi kodi’ in Telugu, ‘Kanan kozhi’ in Tamil, ‘Tuttuterippan’ in Malayalam, and ‘Kirimeti korawaka’ in Sinhalese. *** For Private Circulation Only Editors: Shanti Mani, Umesh Mani Email: bsap.pitta@gmail.com 15 For information, write to: Deccan Birders, PO Box 45, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad – 500034.
