A SUMMER SOJOURN THROUGH THE FORESTS OF CENTRAL INDIA Trip Report: Pemch, May 17-18, 2026 Text and Photos: Satyajit Tuljapurkar A view of Pench Tiger Reserve In the blistering furnace of a Central Indian summer, when the land lay parched beneath a relentless May sun and the dry deciduous forests shimmered in waves of heat, my friend Vishal and I set out on a journey to Pench Tiger Reserve through the Chorbahuli Gate on the 17th of May. ravines, alarm calls echoing through the valleys, and somewhere in the shadows, the silent majesty of the tiger. Yet no imagination can truly prepare one for the experience of entering these forests at the peak of summer, when every creature gravitates toward the shrinking water sources and the jungle itself seems alive with expectancy. The very mention of Pench evokes images of Rudyard Kipling’s timeless wilderness – rustling teak forests, hidden 1

After reaching our forest resort and settling into the quietude of the evening, we retired early, knowing that the jungle awakens long before sunrise. Day One – Morning Safari: The Tigress of the Nala At precisely 5:30AM, beneath a sky only beginning to pale with dawn, we climbed aboard our Gypsy. The coolness of the early morning air still lingered, though the promise of another scorching day was unmistakable. Our forest guide, Vikas, greeted us with the calm confidence of a man who knew every trail, alarm call, and movement within the forest. As the vehicle rolled into the reserve, Pench slowly awakened around us. Peafowl called from distant clearings, langurs stirred atop skeletal trees, and the forest floor glowed golden beneath the first rays of sunlight filtering through the teak canopy. Tigress Akira with her cubs Vikas informed us that the tigress Akira had been sighted in the area the previous day along with her two cubs. She had successfully brought down a Sambar deer, and because of the kill, the tigress and her cubs had remained close to the same stretch of forest – alternating between feeding upon the carcass and visiting a nearby nala to drink and cool themselves from the punishing heat. We reached the spot and waited. The jungle around us appeared motionless, yet every rustle seemed charged with possibility. Minutes stretched into nearly an hour. The silence was broken only by the occasional call of a Red-vented Bulbul or the metallic notes of a Greater Rackettailed Drongo. Rufous Treepie Perched quietly nearby was a Rufous Treepie, its long tail swaying gently as though keeping vigil over the tiger family. Eventually, Vikas suggested we explore another location where the tigress had recently been seen. Reluctantly, we moved away. Then suddenly, the forest erupted. A sharp bark from a deer. Excited chatter from langurs high above the canopy. The unmistakable language of the jungle announcing the presence of a predator. We turned back immediately and were rewarded with a breathtaking sight. There, partially submerged within the cool waters of the nala, lay Akira and her cubs. The tigress rested with effortless authority while the cubs played restlessly beside her, splashing through the shallow water and occasionally disappearing behind rocks and reeds. Watching this intimate family scene from a respectful distance felt less like observing wildlife and more like witnessing a secret the forest had momentarily chosen to reveal. Tigress Akira After nearly twenty minutes, the tigress rose gracefully, glanced briefly in our direction, and led her cubs across the forest track before vanishing into denser woodland where the dry bamboo and teak swallowed them whole. Yet Pench had more treasures to offer. 2

orange eyes remained fixed upon us through the rocks and sparse foliage – as though the ancient guardian of the ravine had chosen merely to tolerate our presence. Day One – Afternoon Safari: Shadows Beneath the Hillock The afternoon sun blazed mercilessly across the landscape as we ventured out once more. By then, the forest had transformed entirely. The cool vitality of dawn had given way to shimmering heat, dusty tracks, and long waves of silence interrupted only by cicadas. Black-hooded Oriole As we explored deeper into the forest, the morning became an avian symphony. Golden Orioles flashed brilliant yellow through the foliage, while Black-hooded Orioles called melodiously from the treetops. Black Drongos perched boldly on exposed branches, hawking insects mid-flight with acrobatic ease. Returning toward another section of the forest near the same nala and adjoining grasslands, we once again encountered Akira and her cubs. This time they were stretched lazily beneath the shade of a hillock, surrendered completely to an afternoon siesta. The cubs occasionally rolled over one another before collapsing back onto the cool earth beside their mother. Among the many species we encountered were White-throated Kingfishers, Spotted Doves, Greater Coucals, Green Beeeaters, Red Junglefowl, and several species of babblers moving noisily through the undergrowth. Most, however, proved maddeningly camera-shy, disappearing into the foliage the instant a lens was raised. As the safari neared its conclusion, we encountered one final marvel. Plum-headed Parakeet female Above them, perched delicately upon a branch, sat a female Plum-headed Parakeet, her muted colours blending harmoniously with the dry summer forest. Around the clearing, Oriental Magpie Robins darted energetically between bushes while an Orange-headed Thrush quietly foraged through fallen leaves in search of insects. Indian Eagle Owl Perched upon a rocky outcrop overlooking a ravine sat a majestic Indian Eagle Owl. Before we could manoeuvre into position for a photograph, the owl lifted silently into the air and glided deeper into the gorge, eventually settling upon a shadowed cliff face. Even from that distance, its piercing From there, we travelled toward a nearby lake whose receding waters had become a magnet for birdlife. The shallows teemed with activity. Baya Weavers fluttered through reed beds while Asian Koels and Common Hawk Cuckoos called endlessly from hidden perches. Cattle Egrets stood motionless at the water’s edge while kingfishers flashed electric blue above the lake. As the evening light softened and safari hours drew to a close, we made a silent pact to return to the lake at first light the following morning. 3

Day Two – Morning Safari: Sunrise over Water and Wilderness At dawn the next day, we entered the forest once more. Though tempted to revisit Akira and her cubs, we instead drove directly toward the lake. Along the muddy banks moved Red-wattled Lapwings, their sharp calls ringing across the water. Black-winged Stilts waded elegantly through the shallows on impossibly long crimson legs. Indian Pond Herons, Little Cormorants, Jungle Babblers and Cattle Egrets busied themselves along the shoreline. The decision proved magical. As the first rays of sunlight broke across the horizon, the water glowed like molten gold. Mist hovered above the lake while the surrounding trees mirrored themselves upon its still surface. The entire landscape seemed suspended in silence before gradually awakening into a chorus of life. Mugger Crocodile On the placid waters of the lake floated another silent predator – the Mugger Crocodile. Resting almost motionless near the shallows, its rugged, armour-like scales glistened under the early morning sun while only its eyes and nostrils broke the surface of the water. At first glance it appeared no more than a drifting log, perfectly blending into the stillness of the lake. Yet every now and then, the reptile would slowly glide forward with barely a ripple, reminding us of the stealth and patience that define one of India’s oldest surviving predators. Red-wattled Lapwing Indian Roller Soon Indian Rollers arrived, their iridescent blue wings catching the morning light spectacularly, while Whitethroated Kingfishers darted low across the lake in sudden flashes of turquoise and chestnut. Black-winged Stilt 4

Asiatic Wild Dog (Dhole) Oriental Honey-buzzard Watching over this entire spectacle from the branch of a dead tree sat an Oriental Honey-buzzard, motionless and contemplative, like an ancient sentinel presiding over the dawn. Not far ahead, we came upon a pack of Asiatic Wild Dogs, or Dholes, resting within a watering hole after what appeared to have been a successful hunt earlier that morning. Their rustcoloured coats glistened in the sunlight as they lounged in the muddy water, panting heavily yet remaining alert. Unlike the solitary majesty of the tiger, dholes radiated restless energy and remarkable social cohesion. Throughout our journey, Indian Peafowl accompanied us almost constantly. Their calls echoed endlessly through the valleys and teak forests, becoming the enduring soundtrack of Pench itself. Before leaving the reserve, we decided to make one final stop at the ravine where we had seen the eagle owl the previous day. We suspected the gorge served as one of its regular roosting sites. Once again, fortune smiled upon us. This time we spotted not one, but two Indian Eagle Owls concealed among the rocky cliffs. One remained almost perfectly camouflaged against the stone face, invisible until it shifted slightly in the shadows. The second sat exposed upon a ledge, its large amber eyes carefully monitoring our every movement. Changeable Hawk Eagle Further into the forest, near another watering hole, we encountered one of the safari’s most magnificent birds of prey – a Changeable Hawk Eagle. Perched regally upon a low branch overlooking the water, the raptor surveyed the forest with commanding intensity. Though listed as a species of Least Concern on the IUCN Red List and relatively common within Pench, witnessing such a powerful eagle at close quarters was unforgettable. The forest, however, still had one final surprise in store. Indian Eagle Owl 5

For several quiet minutes we remained there in silence, observing these magnificent nocturnal hunters within their rugged domain. The forest breeze moved gently through the ravine while somewhere in the distance a peafowl called once more. And then, slowly, it was time to leave. As our Gypsy rolled out through the gates of Pench, the forests receded behind us – but the sounds, scents, and memories lingered long after. Pench had offered us far more than sightings. It had revealed fleeting glimpses into the secret rhythm of the wild: the patience of predators, the vigilance of prey, the brilliance of birds, and the timeless drama of life unfolding beneath the summer sun. BIRDING THROUGH THE SEASONS AT CHANDU Report: Chandu Budhera Wetland, Haryana, Aug 2025 – May 2026 Text and Photos: Sita Susarla A view of Chandu Budhera Very close to the Sultanpur National Park in Gurugram District of Haryana, there is a wetland, whose waters are fed by the seasonal rain-fed Sahibi river. This river originates in the Aravalli hills of Rajasthan and passes through Jaipur, Alwar and Gurugram of Haryana before entering the Delhi NCR region through Dhansa border. The Chandu Budhera wetland, is a beautiful and vibrant bird habitat with a lot of reed beds, shallow water bodies and some cultivated lands. Teeming with birds of various colours and hues throughout the year, this wetland is a much sought-after birding hub for the bird watchers of Delhi-NCR. What makes it an easy ground for bird watchers is that the village road passing through the wetland allows vehicles to comfortably pass through and also allow parking at a few shaded places. Around 300 resident and migratory birds visit this wetland across different seasons. From bitterns, crakes and scores of passerines to raptors, waterfowl and waders, the wetland is a weekend destination for many Delhi NCR bird watchers. We made several visits to this wetland over a period of ten months covering the monsoon, winter and spring seasons. The first of these visits was during the monsoon of 2025 to see the Little Bittern, which was a lifer for us. It took us two weekend trips to spot it. Finally, we saw about three of them flying from one reed bed to another so frequently that we were able to see them clearly and also capture some wonderful photographs of them. Little Bittern In subsequent visits in October and November, we noticed increased numbers of waterfowl and waders. The wetland is a fertile ground for some great sightings like the Greater Whitefronted Goose, Eurasian Whimbrel, Eurasian Curlew and Common Shelduck. We spotted a flock of sixteen Common Shelducks and eight Greater White-fronted Geese here. There were also the Cinnamon and Yellow Bitterns among the reeds. A few years back, apparently, the Great Bittern was also seen here. Greater White-fronted Goose 7

Common Shelduck An amazing feature of Chandu Budhera is the presence of long stretches of shallow waters that allow a panoramic view of large flocks of water birds. There are Pied Avocets, Redcrested Pochards, Garganey, Bar-headed and Greylag Geese, Eurasian Spoonbills, Eurasian Coot, Ruddy Shelducks, Eurasian Wigeons, Northern Shovelers, Northern Pintails, Tufted Ducks, Common Pochards and Green-winged Teals. Baillon’s Crake As the winter progressed, the migratory crakes arrived. The Spotted and Baillon’s Crakes were spotted in the marshy reed beds of the wetland along with the Water Rail. It is fascinating to watch as they go hither and thither between the open patches of marsh and thick reeds playing a hide-and-seek game with the photographers. Waders also can be seen in large numbers on the shore beds – Common and Spotted Redshanks, Common, Wood and Green Sandpipers, Kentish and Little Ringed Plovers, Whitebrowed, White, Citrine and Western Yellow Wagtails, Temminck’s and Little Stints, Ruff and Black-tailed Godwit. Water Rail A large flock of Ruff River Terns and Whiskered Terns would swoop down occasionally to pick up fish and this activity is continuous. Tall and elegant Sarus Cranes are seen foraging at many places in the numerous crops alongside the wetland. Spotted Crake A few furlongs from the reed beds there are patches of grasslands that are home to flocks of Spanish and Sind Sparrows, both much sought-after. The Spanish Sparrow is robust in size compared to the House Sparrow and has a chestnut crown and deeply streaked body. It is distinctly different and can be easily spotted. Spanish Sparrow 8

breeding colours, we missed the Red-necked Phalarope and Ruddy Turnstone despite strenuous efforts. Maybe next winter! Oriental Pratincole Yellow-bellied Prinia In conclusion, it can be aptly summarised that Chandu Budhera wetland is a fertile birding ground throughout the year. An amazing place to be anytime in the year and a place that provides many thrills for birders. Tibetan Sand Plover As the land gets heated up, the wetland becomes a hotspot for reverse migration: Tibetan Sand Plovers, Ruddy Turnstones, Terek Sandpipers and sometimes Red-necked Phalaropes are also seen. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Yellow-vented Flowerpecker (Pachyglossa chrysorrhea) Yellow-vented Flowerpecker (Mahananda WLS, West Bengal, January 17, 2024) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Passeriformes Dicaeidae Pachyglossa P. chrysorrhea 10 cm Least Concern other flowerpeckers, though, where the outermost primary feathers are vestigial, in the Yellow-vented Flowerpecker they are elongated and functional. Habitat & behaviour: The Yellow-vented Flowerpecker inhabits mature broad-leaved forests, forest edges and scrubland in and around tropical or subtropical moist lowland forests and moist montane forests, and is also sometimes seen around human habitation. Its diet consists mainly of insects, small fruits and berries – it is especially partial to mistletoe berries and figs. It emits a distinctive, high-pitched dzeep that is often likened to a sharp snipping sound, similar to scissors closing. Description & distribution: The Yellow-vented Flowerpecker, a member of the Dicaeidae family of Flowerpeckers, is found across a wide range in the Indian subcontinent and South-east Asia, including India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, China, Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. It is golden olive above, with contrasting blackish primaries, and white or yellowish-white below, with strong black streaking on the underparts. Besides the distinctive orange-yellow vent, a curved black bill, indistinct whitish supercilium, blackish malar stripe, and eyes that are sometimes described as demonic red, make it easy to differentiate from other flowerpeckers. The juvenile bird has duller upperparts, greyish-white underparts with less prominent streaking and a paler yellow vent. Nesting: The Yellow-vented Flowerpecker breeds mainly between April and August in India. The nest is a small pouch made of moss, grass, spider webs and soft plant down, and suspended from tree or bush branches, usually 6-10 metres above the ground. Nest-building is done by both partners within about 4-5 days. The usual clutch consists of 2-3 white eggs, and incubation and feeding duties are handled by both parents. Local name: The Yellow-vented Flowerpecker is known as ‘Phoolchuki’ in Hindi; other names like ‘Ful chuki’ in Punjabi, and ‘Poon-chittu’ or ‘Poon-kothi’ in Tamil, are applied to all Flowerpeckers found in the respective regions. Also known as Dicaeum chrysorrheum, the Yellow-vented Flowerpecker is a typical flowerpecker in size and structure, small, fast-moving and rarely settling at one place. BIRD CENSUS AT NANDUR MADHMESHWAR BIRD SANCTUARY, MHARASHTRA Report: June 28, 2026 Shilka Chaudhari A view of Madhmeshwar Bird Sanctuary (Photo: Rohit Moghal) Nandur Madhmeshwar Bird Sanctuary, also referred to as the ‘Bharatpur of Maharashtra’, is spread across 10,000 hectares and sits along the Godavari River. Located near Nashik, this vital wetland is the state’s first designated Ramsar site, and hosts around 265 species of resident and migratory birds. 1

The Maharashtra Forest Department decided to conduct a bird census in the mentioned sanctuary on June 28, 2026. The emphasis of this census was on assessing the bird population (both resident and migratory) in this important diverse ecosystem in the state ahead of the monsoon season. It is an excellent initiative to engage bird lovers and collect data on different avian species. Purple Heron (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) Participants being briefed by Forest Department officials (Photo: Rohit Moghal) At the outset, Forest Department official Mr Hiralal Chaudhari stated that the objective of the census was to undertake a scientific study of biodiversity and accurately record the population of local and migratory bird species present. The data collected is important for wildlife conservation and ecological balance of the sanctuary. He said that the rich biodiversity also includes 536 plant species, 24 species of freshwater fish and 41 species of butterflies. A team of 43 members were divided into 4 groups to conduct and report on the bird survey. Cotton Pygmy-goose (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) Walking down the muddy trail, we spotted Cinnamon Bittern and Cotton Pygmy-goose in flight. A fair amount of nesting activity was going on with Baya Weavers. Further down the wet trail, we spotted Indian Pied Starling nests on dry tree branches. Brahminy Starlings, Laughing Doves, and an Indian Golden Oriole were seen perched on trees. The Red Avadavat was seen flying with a flock of Tricolored Munia. Baya Weaver (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) My group consisted of 4 members – BD Chaudhari, Sarvesh Shinde, Rohit Moghal and me. We started the bird count by spotting Purple Heron and Common Moorhen. Laughing Dove (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) 2

Little Cormorant & Oriental Darter (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) Tricolored Munia (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) The lake was full of water lilies and the side walk of the lake was covered with blooming purple garlic vine flowers. The wetland had Spot-billed Ducks, Whistling-ducks, Pheasanttailed Jacanas and Little Grebes. At the end of the path was a watch tower which overlooked the entire lake in its full glory. We noted a large number of Moorhens, Jacanas and Greater Cormorants, besides some Darters, Pond Herons and Pied Kingfishers. Unlike other kingfishers, the Pied Kingfishers use hovering as a major hunting technique and can swallow the prey in mid-flight. We heard some sharp, harsh chuckling sounds from the dense reedbeds, and confirmed that it was from the Clamorous Reed Warblers. Calls from Greater Coucal and Coppersmith Barbet were noted. Common waders like Black-winged Stilts (in flight) along with Little Grebe, Purple Sunbirds and Baya Weavers were recorded. Our guide Rohit remarked that there were Otters in the lake, and that the Great White Pelicans were spotted for the first time in the lake after a good 20 years. A colony of resident Painted Storks was also noted. Indian Spot-billed Duck (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) Painted Stork (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) Pheasant-tailed Jacana (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) The Little Cormorants were soaking in the sun with their wings stretched out. Painted Stork juvenile, Black-headed Ibis and Little Egret (Photo: Sarvesh Shinde) 3

Many common species like Large-billed and House Crows, House Sparrows, Common Mynas and Red-vented Bulbuls were present. Overall we noted and recorded a count of 43 bird species in the grassland and wetland habitat, and many excellent photos were clicked by group member Sarvesh Shinde. The Forest Department officials accomplished a fruitful task by engaging birdwatchers, nature lovers and general citizens by assisting them and monitoring the bird species and counts. The exercise contributes towards the needs of biodiversity conservation by documenting the bird species observed in real time. Bird of the Month Text and Photos: Umesh Mani Water Rail (Rallus aquaticus) Water Rail (Great Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, December 28, 2025) Order: Family: Genus: Species: Size: IUCN Status: Gruiformes Rallidae Rallus R. aquaticus 23-28 cm Least Concern Habitat & behaviour: The Water Rail is a skulker and frequents reedy swamps, marshy meadows, irrigated paddy fields, and the vegetation around lakes or other water bodies. Like most rails, it walks slowly with a high-stepping gait, bending to pick up insects, but is not easily seen as it rarely comes out in the open. It is omnivorous, and its diet consists mainly of invertebrates during summer and berries or plant stems during winter. It can swim when necessary, and can also fly short distances just over the reeds with a weak-looking flight, legs dangling and trailing behind the body. It is known to be highly territorial and aggressively defend its feeding grounds as well as breeding areas. Its main call, known as ‘sharming’, is a series of grunts followed by a high-pitched piglet-like squeal ending in more grunts, and is used as a territorial call, alarm as well as announcement. Partners may call alternately, the male giving lower and slower notes than his partner. The courtship song, given by both sexes, is a tyicktyick-tyick often ending with a trill from the female, while the male may sing for hours. It may also emit a sharp whistle while in flight. Description & distribution: The Water Rail, also known as European Water Rail or Western Water Rail, is a resident breeder in well-vegetated wetlands in India (particularly Kashmir and Ladakh) and other parts of Asia, besides Europe and North Africa, which are warmer; it is migratory in the colder parts of its range. Three subspecies are recognized: R. a. aquaticus, the nominate subspecies that breeds in Europe, North Africa, Turkey, western Asia to the Caspian Sea and western Kazakhstan, and in a narrow band east to central Siberia; R. a. hibernans, seen in Iceland; and R. a. korejewi, which breeds in south central Asia from southern and eastern Iran east to Eastern China, and in the Indian subcontinent in Kashmir and Ladakh. Besides, another former subspecies, R. a. indicus, has now been elevated to a separate species, the Brown-cheeked Rail. Nesting: The Water Rail breeds mainly between late March June and August. The nest is a cup of dead leaves and marsh reeds, built on the ground amid dense, wet reedbeds, and often shielded by a canopy of pulled-down vegetation. The usual clutch consists of 6-11 buff eggs, and pairs may also raise a second brood in the same season. Both parents take care of incubation and feeding, though the chicks are precocial and may leave the nest shortly after hatching. Like other rails, the Water Rail has a laterally flattened body, allowing it easier passage through the reed beds it inhabits. It has mainly brown upperparts and blue-grey underparts and sides of head, black barring on the flanks, short tail and long reddish bill and red irises, and the long toes that are characteristic of rails. The white undertail differentiates it from other reed bed rails. Immature birds are generally similar in appearance to the adults, but the blue-grey in the plumage is replaced by buff. The crown is blackish, and the chin and throat are white. Flank markings are brown and buff rather than black and white. As with all rails, the chicks are downy and black.
